# Chapter 1: The Road to Shrek

## Canon Reference: SL2 era texture as ore (Star Luo freshman season; ring-age doctrine; enrollment-morning world. Canon ch 1–4 runs parallel — Huo Yuhao walks his own road the same season. No canon scene consumed here; canon persons appear as background only.)
## Timeline: Spring, age 11 — six days on the road.

---

## Part 1: The Gold Brook

Jinxi Village had forty roofs and no gate. It had one stone anvil, one brook that turned gold at sunrise, and a family of geese that thought they ran the place.

Jin Yang stood by the plank bridge in traveling clothes. His pack held flatbread, a waterskin, a change of shirt, and a letter in an oilskin sleeve. The letter was sealed in wax, and the wax carried his teacher's seal — a mountain, pressed by a ringed hand. He had not opened it. Nobody opened a letter like that except a registrar.

His mother cried on him for as long as she needed to. He let her.

"Eat warm things," she said. "Sleep inside the blanket, not on it. Don't lend money you need." She put both hands on his face and looked up at him, which she had only started doing this year. "And when the city people act proud — let them. Proud folk are frightened of something. You come from a kitchen that fed you eleven years. Behave like it."

"Yes, Ma."

His father stood with his hat in his hands, turning it slowly between work-worn hands. He grew millet, and sharpened plough blades for anyone who brought one, and he had two pieces of advice on file for the whole world. He gave his son the first.

"Strike true, or don't strike." He put the hat back on. "The planting is in the tenth month. Write if the school lets you."

"Yes, Pa."

The old gander led the flock down the bank while they talked, thirty geese in single file, and lined them up beside the bridge like an honor guard. The gander had hissed at every strange thing in Jinxi for nine years — dogs, traders, the tax man's horse. It had never hissed at Jin Yang. From the year the boy was five, it had only followed him, slowly, like something guarding a small fire.

"Walk him to the ash tree," his mother told it, seriously.

It walked him to the ash tree, honking once every ten steps.

At the tree he looked back once. The cottage was small and the smoke from its chimney stood straight up in the still air. His mother was still watching. He bowed to her, and then — because his mother had taught him that anything that escorts you has earned a bow — he bowed to the geese as well.

Then he faced the road and did not look back again.

---

## Part 2: Five Years at the Forge

The story of his awakening, as Jinxi told it, had a lion in the walls.

He was six, standing in a line of village children in the ceremony hall of White Birch City, on a rainy morning. The awakening master — **Qiao Tong, a Soul Elder in his thirties**, a man who had awakened six thousand children and expected to forget all of them — put his palm on the boy's chest and sent the light in.

The gold shadow filled the room behind the boy.

A lion, mane like poured metal, tall enough to look over every adult's head. Qiao Tong went down on one knee before he knew he had decided to. His voice came out quieter than he meant it.

"Innate soul power. **Rank five.**"

That autumn Jin Yang walked thirty li into White Birch City with a recommendation letter. The headmaster of the city junior academy — **Chu Shan, a Soul King of the fifty-sixth rank**, a thin old man with a voice like a barn door — looked at the boy's thin arms, then at the gold shape behind them, and said four words:

"You'll train with me."

Five years. Rank five to **rank twenty-three**.

Chu Shan's whole method could be written on one hand: **foundation first**. Speed without base was a house on sand, he said, and sand was for children playing. So at eight, Jin Yang was sent to learn hammer-work at **Master Gongshu Yan's forge** — a grade-six smith with forearms like ship rope — for two coppers a day and the right to be shouted at.

Sweep for a season. Bellows for a year. Hammer when told.

"Again," was the first word Gongshu taught him. It was also the second through the fortieth.

But the boy had a body that mended bruises by morning, and — after his ninth autumn — something better. That year Chu Shan took him to the forest margins for his **first ring**: a golden lion, **five hundred years** grown, while every doctrine book in every academy said a first ring's ceiling stood near **four hundred twenty-three years**.

"He is your kind," Chu Shan said, crouched in the needle-grass two hundred paces off the den. "Same blood, same metal. Your soul will want him. The question is whether your body can hold what your soul wants. Understand me, boy — if the ring tears you open, I can kill the beast after. I cannot un-tear you. There is no second cast of this die."

The lion nearly killed him twice — once through the ribs, once through the thigh — and the ring poured into him like floodwater. His body held. Nobody could explain it cleanly and Jin Yang had long since stopped asking it to be explained: he had been born with something in him that took what the world offered and made it fit. The five hundred years of the lion came out of the sifting as his own.

The skill that settled into the ring was the lion's killing blow, remade for hands. **Golden Lion Claw.**

Two winters later the second hunt put doctrine out of business completely. An **earth-armored iron dragon — nine hundred seventy years old, shedding into its thousandth** — tracked for a season, met in a ravine of wet red clay, fought from noon to dark. When the purple ring rose off the carcass and settled onto the boy's martial soul, Chu Shan went white and stood in the rain for a long time without speaking. A second ring, at that age, should have stopped near seven hundred sixty-four years. The purple said otherwise.

The old man bowed to him in private, after.

"Other academies will measure you small so you grade neatly," he said. "Shrek won't. Go to Shrek."

The second ring's skill came out of the drake, and the boy's body re-fitted it like old steel on a new haft: **Golden Lion Body** — strength doubled, defense doubled, while it ran. And under the metal of his soul, something quiet had taken root: the drake's earth, grafted deep by the clean absorption.

Metal for the kill. Earth for the standing. Chu Shan said it like a proverb and made him say it back before every cold morning drill until it sat in him next to breathing.

That spring he stood his **grade-three smith** exam — three works, cold-forged, no soul power allowed, two examiners watching his hands the whole time like the world could be tricked through fingers. It could not. That summer he filled his first gold-scale commission: a nineteen-day set of refined blanks for a soul-tool workshop, **six gold coins** for the set. Two gold had gone home the month before to put a new roof over his mother's goose-house, on account of the old roof having learned to leak directly over the nesting boxes.

On the first day of his eleventh spring, Chu Shan put the letter into his hand.

"Your name is in this season's lists at Shrek," the old man said. "Come back a finished product, or don't come back telling me stories."

Six days later the road was in his sandals.

---

## Part 3: The Caravan and the Boar

Three days out of White Birch City he joined the tail of Old Wei's grain caravan — four canvas carts, spavined mules, six contract guards, and a guard captain of the fifteenth rank who chewed betel and told the same war story eight ways, each way kinder to the captain.

Jin Yang said nothing about being a soul master. He walked in the dust of the rear cart and ate flatbread, and the mules, who should have hated him, watched him with wet eyes and stayed calm. Dumb beasts smell a predator like grass feels weather. What the mules felt from the thin boy in the road dust was not what a lion smells like. It was what a lion smells like when it has already eaten.

On the sixth night, at moonrise, the boar came out of the brush-line.

An **iron-bristle boar — three hundred years**, rank-one soul beast, hide like studded mail, maddened by the smell of grain, and in a hurry. The captain wet his blade hand and shouted for a formation, and looked around to discover his five men had already made one — behind the wagons. Old Wei stood in the road with his lantern up, alone, like a man about to reason with a flood.

Jin Yang put his flatbread down.

"Soul ring," he said, mostly to check in with himself, and called his martial soul.

Gold light stood up in the dark.

The mane came down across his shoulders and neck, near-solid, bright. His eyes went amber. The claws came out of his knuckles like drawn wire — twenty centimeters of gold-edged light. The boy's frame broadened a handspan, and the aura of the golden lion rolled out over the caravan once, a king's question asked quietly of every living thing in hearing: *will you kneel, or will you stand still?*

The rings rose behind him. **Yellow. Purple.**

The purple one bloomed.

**Golden Lion Body.**

The amplification ran through him like rain running into a brook — strength up one hundred percent, defense up one hundred percent, his body's old honest accounting of the drake's gift. Gold sheen settled over his skin, following the lines of his arms and shoulders, and under his feet the earth rose and held like a loyal thing.

The boar hit him dead center at a full charge.

He did not move. Not a step. Three hundred years of iron bristle broke against an eleven-year-old boy as against a gatepost, and the sound of it was a bell rung wrong. The boar staggered back, squealing, tusk-white.

Behind the wagons the guards made one shared noise, the noise geese make when a shadow crosses the yard.

Jin Yang raised his right arm. Soul power answered as it always answered — measured, counted, poured.

**Golden Lion Claw.**

The claws lengthened into five blades of living gold. One rake — one — shoulder to ham, through armor that had turned a dozen years of hunters' blades. The boar came apart and was done before Old Wei's lantern stopped swinging.

A yellow-white ring lifted off the carcass, floated a moment, and faded.

Jin Yang took his own count, as Chu Shan had beaten into him. The claw: about a twentieth of his reserve. The amplification, still running: a steady sip. He closed it down. Twelve minutes at full spend, from full to dregs — he knew the number like his own pulse. *A soul master who doesn't know his costs is a soul master's funeral notice.*

Old Wei lowered the lantern.

"Immortal young master," he said — how village people talked when the world showed them a shape with no word for it.

"Jin Yang, of Jinxi village," the boy said. "Is any of that grain cooked?"

The guards laughed so hard the captain swallowed his betel, which improved everyone's evening.

At the parting they tried to pay him — Wei solemnly, the captain loudly — and he took one meal, two steamed rolls for the road, and one copper coin at the third insistence, because his mother had told him once that a man who takes nothing makes his helpers feel useless. She was right about nearly everything except geese.

"Where does a boy of the twenty-third rank walk at eleven years old?" Wei asked him at the fork, half curious, half praying.

"Shrek," Jin Yang said.

Old Wei stepped back from the purse then, and pressed his palms together, and said, as you speak to weather you have already decided to respect: "May the lion carry you, child of the gold brook."

---

## Part 4: The Gate

He saw Shrek City on the seventh morning, from the last rise of the plain.

It was enormous. The walls ran past both edges of his sight. Beyond them the academy's roofs climbed in tiers toward the city's heart, where — if half the stories were half-true — a god had once planted a golden tree. Under the gate towers the enrollment crowd was already wound down the hill: a rope of a thousand people, academy banners, clan flags, mothers fixing collars, servants holding umbrellas over young masters' heads.

Jin Yang took the letter out of his shirt. The wax was warm from six days against his skin.

*Go to Shrek.* All right, then.

He walked down the hill and found the end of the line, behind a candidate in gray silk who was explaining queue reform to nobody, and ahead of two sisters with one parasol and four baskets of food. The elder sister looked at his dusty pack and his quiet face and pressed a savory cake into his hands before he had said a single word.

"You have the look of a boy whose mother lives a long way off," she said, as if diagnosing an illness. "Eat. It's free. We're entering school to help people; we might as well start with you."

He took the cake, because his mother had also had teachings about refusing food.

And so it happened that on the same morning, on the same gray stones, in the same sunlight, a thin plain-faced boy with soft black hair bought roasted wheat cakes from a gate vendor with careful coppers — forty paces ahead of the village boy with the borrowed cake. A kind-eyed young woman pointed him to the end of the line. And twenty paces behind her, a boy with hair like a clear pink-blue dawn stood measuring the line like a wall he meant to breach personally.

Jin Yang noticed none of them. The rope moved. A clerk's bell rang. Somewhere up at the tents a child flashed three rings and the crowd hummed like disturbed geese.

"Next," the bell-man called.

The boy with the gold brook at his back stepped forward to be measured.

# Chapter 2: The Measure

## Canon Reference: SL2 canon ch 4–5 as ore (enrollment morning: measurement tents, soul-steel stele, fees; canon's two-person administrative rooming governs every freshman room — Room 105 follows the same system law as canon's Room 108; the Room-108 argument exists as far-off background only). Facts cited; trajectory OURS: the tents measure him, the building houses him, both by Shrek's ordinary arithmetic.
## Timeline: The same morning, line to dormitory.

---

## Part 1: The Slow Line

By mid-morning the enrollment line had become a small town.

Clan banners stood planted wherever a servant could find dirt. Mothers did collar repairs on sons who had stopped asking for them two hills back. Somewhere ahead, a candidate in mourning-gray silk was explaining the concept of appointments, in a carrying voice, to the back of a registrar's head. The two parasol sisters, three places behind Jin Yang, had opened their second basket and were quietly feeding everyone within reach.

And four places ahead, the young master of the Qiu clan of White Birch City was telling a half-circle of younger boys, at leisure-class volume, how his family's letter differed from certain other letters one might see in the line.

Qiu Yuan. Twelve years old. Twenty-one ranks. Dressed for a coronation.

He recognized Jin Yang at the fourth turn of the line and drifted over, hands folded, walking like a magistrate entering a village he expected to purchase.

"You," he said. "The boy from Master Chu's academy. They accepted your papers?" His eyes did a quick tour — dusty shirt, rope belt, a pack that had seen weather. "Well. Shrek measures the soul, I hear. Not the sleeve."

"Shrek measures," Jin Yang said, and finished his steamed roll.

That was the entire reply. His father had repaired a plough for the Qiu estate two springs back, and his father had opinions about men who looked at sleeves before blades. Qiu Yuan waited for more words, got none, and gave his verdict anyway, louder, for the benefit of the neighborhood.

"They measure properly here, you know. Rank crystal. Age-slate. Strike stone. No favors for hometown paper."

"Good," Jin Yang said. "I don't have any other paper."

Somewhere within the Qiu system of etiquette, that sentence landed in a folder with no label. Qiu Yuan's mouth did a small administrative motion, settled on dignity, and he retreated back to his banner.

"He trains three hours a day to talk like that," said the elder parasol sister, behind Jin Yang.

"Longer," said her sister. "You can hear the practice."

---

The tents, when the line finally bled there four by four, had three instruments.

A palm-size **rank crystal** in a brass bracket. A flat **age-slate** of bone-white stone for the wrist. And behind both, standing free in the dust like an old soldier, a waist-high **stele faced in soul-steel**, chalked over a lifetime of old scars.

A senior student with a registrar's brush called numbers. A teacher sat at a tea table under the awning, and his head came up only when the crystal said something interesting. This being the Shrek gate, his head was mostly down.

Two candidates in front of Jin Yang, the boy in gray silk produced two yellow rings with ceremony, and received Shrek's exact level of wonder.

"Approved," said the registrar, without looking up. "Fee, two gold coins."

The silk took that badly, and kept taking it badly all the way into the compound.

Then it was Qiu Yuan. Wrist to the slate: twelve years, two winters. Palm to the crystal: the stone lit, climbed, stopped.

"**Twenty-one**," the registrar said, with professional warmth.

Down the line, the Qiu banner rose two inches, like it had been trained to.

"**Jia — one hundred five.** Jin Yang, of Jinxi, White Birch City? Papers."

---

## Part 2: Twenty-Three

The letter passed two pairs of hands. The registrar broke the wax and read; the seal answered her thumbnail with five soft pulses of light — mountain-sign, one pulse per ring of the man who had pressed it. Real sender, or very expensive forgery. She nodded it along.

"Age-slate."

He laid his wrist on the bone-white stone. The slate lit up from underneath, like frost catching sun.

"*Eleven winters and a spring.*"

"Crystal."

He set his palm on it and sent a thread of soul power up his arm, as Chu Shan had taught him — measured, like pouring from a kettle you plan to set down full.

The crystal climbed. Ten. Fifteen. Nineteen — the place where prodigies usually stopped and the brush was already moving — twenty-one. Twenty-two.

**Twenty-three.**

The brush did not move. The registrar's eyes went from the crystal to the boy, and then back to it, checking it for a thumbed pan. The crystal stayed where it was.

"Twenty-three," she said, in a voice that had lost its professional warmth and found arithmetic instead. "Age eleven. Cultivation twenty-three. Star Luo provincial recommendation — verified." A short silence while procedure caught up. "Martial soul, please."

Under the awning, the tea-table teacher set his cup down.

---

Jin Yang called it as he had been taught: all of it, because Chu Shan's other lesson — the one after foundation — was that a lion you hide learns to hide.

Gold light stood up in the tent.

The mane came down across his neck and shoulders, bright and nearly solid. His eyes went amber, pupils drawn thin. His knuckles broadened and the claws came out of the nail beds, gold-edged, a straight twenty centimeters. His whole frame widened a handspan inside his shirt seams. And the aura of the golden lion went out over the measuring ground like a question asked very politely of every soul present: *kneel, or be counted?*

Half the line forgot it had been measuring anything. Two candidates flinched as their own souls twitched against their skins. The younger parasol sister stopped chewing her date, mid-chew.

Behind Qiu Yuan's face, several expressions filed reports and were overruled. The sound he made instead, he would insist for the rest of the year had been a cough.

Then the rings came up.

**Yellow.**

**Purple.**

The registrar's brush recorded the first ring by reflex, as it had recorded hundreds that morning. For the second, it simply stopped in mid-stroke. Every doctrine in the world put a second ring's ceiling near seven hundred sixty-four years. A ring with the purple color of the thousand-year tier did not orbit an eleven-year-old boy.

It was doing so.

The tea-table teacher came around the awning, mug forgotten. He was a middle-aged man with quick pale eyes, the kind of face that read three questions into one scratch of a beard. A senior student murmured "Teacher Wang."

"Golden Lion, metal type, king of the ground-cats," the teacher said, not as a question. He looked at the mane like men at rare books. "The dueling stockyards could tell me your species' temper without asking." He turned the full weight of the pale eyes onto Jin Yang. "First ring yellow — four, five hundred years by the depth of it. I'll not quarrel. But the second — a second ring cannot be purple. Yours is." A pause, perfectly pleasant. "Explain that, boy."

The tent had gone so quiet you could hear the canvas creak.

"My teacher paid my life into those hunts," Jin Yang said. "The price is mine to pay. It isn't mine to sell."

Teacher Wang looked at him for a long, still moment. Then he smiled like a man whose favorite kind of morning had just walked in.

"Good," he said. "Keep it. We've heavier doors at this school than a dossier. Shrek does not collect doctrine, young man. Shrek collects the possible." He gestured at the stele. "One strike. Your best. Solidly on the face, please. You will not hurt it — better arms than yours have tried with mo—" the claws extended the last notch "—more rings."

---

## Part 3: Two Cun

Jin Yang walked to the stele.

In his head, the ledger opened by itself, as it always did. Reserve: **one hundred hundredths**. Window available, twelve minutes at full pour; not needed, not opened. The stone asked for a strike, not a war. One claw. Full measure. Nothing else spent.

His father: *strike true or don't strike.* Gongshu: the stance sets itself, your job is to listen. Chu Shan: a strike is arithmetic before it is anything else.

He drew the right arm back and drove the morning's first **Golden Lion Claw** into the face of the soul-steel stele.

The sound was a bell going off inside a mountain — and then stone itself shrieking, five furrows of chalk-white opening in one breath. When the gold light folded back into his knuckles, five parallel gouges stood faintly smoking on the old metal face.

The registrar was on her feet. Teacher Wang was already crouched with his thumb in a furrow, pressing, and then — scholars — smelling it, like the stone was a letter in a difficult hand.

"**Two cun**," he announced, thumb to knuckle, like a man measuring a fish. "Two clear cun of soul-steel face. One strike. A Grandmaster of the twenty-third rank." He straightened up. "Registrar. Your brush is dry."

"Approved," said the registrar faintly, dipping it at last. "Freshman dossier, class assignment at dawn. Certification and dossier fee — **two gold soul coins**."

Two gold coins left the oilskin purse. Twenty-nine gold and four silver remained to him, and because he had been a smith since he was eight, some part of him did the translation automatically: *one third of a six-gold commission set; sixty-odd days at a bellows.* He put the thought down with the money and did not wince for anyone.

"Badge **Jia-105**," said the registrar, handing him a wooden tag with the number branded into it. "Rules folded inside. Key on the cord. Freshmen dormitory, second court, east flank. Second floor, the room where the light lands." And then, because she had measured four hundred souls that morning and this was the first one who had made her day strange: "Your teacher's letter said you were ready. It understated."

---

He was nearly out of the tents when the footsteps came alongside — calm, unhurried, smelling of tea.

Teacher Wang did not fall in like a guard. He fell in like a colleague, which was rarer. He said nothing for thirty paces, only watched the crowd mill around them as if choosing where to set a thought down.

"That strike," he said at last. "You did not spend the second skill. The rings sat still. The claws came out, gold came down, argument over. Most students your age would have spent everything in the purse to impress a stone. Did your teacher also train you not to spend?"

"He trained me to count first," Jin Yang said. "Spending is the easy half."

"'Count first.'" Wang repeated it with approval, like a man tasting a new rice. "Half our inner-court graduates still spoil it. Keep the habit — it will embarrass your seniors and it will make you friends worth having." They came to the edge of the tent shadow. "All year, people will ask about the purple ring, waiting for a number to carry home. You'll come to know the two kinds of askers — the ones who want to learn, and the ones who want to repeat. Feed the first kind. Starve the second. The faces differ by about this much." He measured a hair between two fingers. "Enjoy the dormitory, young master Jin. The rules are long and none of them matter except the one about tea."

He was gone back into the shade before Jin Yang could thank him.

---

## Part 4: Room 105

The freshmen's dormitory stood on the second court's east flank — old stone, wax-polished floors, sunlight in the corridors. At the foot of the second-floor stairs an old man in grey was sweeping with the patience of a monk, white beard against the broom handle, no hurry in the universe.

Jin Yang set down his pack and bowed — one worker's bow to another — his father's bow to estate stewards. "Good morning, Elder."

"Morning," said the broom, agreeably, and swept on.

Room 105's lock accepted his key without complaint. Beside the door, on fresh paper in a registrar's running hand, was the room's plaque. Two names, two columns:

**JIN YANG — QIU YUAN.**

Two beds. Shrek did not ask freshmen whom they liked; the academy sorted them by list and home district and let the boys do their own settling — the same plain system that, somewhere down another corridor, on another morning, had reportedly put two boys of identical ignorance behind a door they had then spent the morning arguing about.

Jin Yang read the second name twice and let the morning give him the face. Qiu Yuan. White Birch's certificate of nobility, looking at sleeves.

Well. A roommate from home could steal no secret that mattered, because the secrets that mattered did not live in dormitories. And on the other hand — and he would not have said this for gold — after a corridor of strangers, there was a schoolboy's comfort in a face he'd already had a conversation with.

Inside: two beds, two desks, one window divided fairly, pine scrubbed to the grain. He weighed it for three breaths and took the window bed — not because it was better, but because a smith keeps his hammer where his hand knows to find it, and the bed by the window had a bedpost that could take one. Blanket rolled out. Hammer set at the bedfoot. Chu's broken-wax letter into the desk drawer.

On the board at the end of the hall, a clerk was pasting a fresh scroll in still-drying ink: **FRESHMAN CLASS LISTS — POSTED AT DAWN.** Down the corridor, behind some other door, a boy's voice was enumerating what sounded like room rules, one through four, in a tone of great and wounded precision.

Then the boots came back up the corridor — fast ones, stopping at 105 — and the door opened on Qiu Yuan of White Birch, travel-dusted boots, key in hand, his smile clearly prepared for an empty room and now being put away.

They looked at each other across one scrubbed pine floor.

"House Jin," said Qiu Yuan, in the voice of a man reading a difficult verdict aloud.

"House Qiu." Jin Yang nodded at the second bed. "That one's yours. Window's mine — the hammer stays with me, and that's not negotiable for religious reasons. I wake at forge-hour. It's early. I'll tell you the night before, every time."

"Warning the night before."

"That's the rule. A smith's room runs on announcements." Jin Yang sat on his bed and began, at last, six days of the road coming off with the left boot. "The lists go up at dawn. Whatever class we're in, the teachers here begin with running. My advice is to eat like you mean it and sleep like you're owed it."

"Running," Qiu Yuan repeated, suspicious of the mattress already. He set his case on the second bed and opened it with the ceremony of a man unpacking an embassy. "They hardly run *clans* this soon."

"House Qiu," Jin Yang said, working the second boot, "they'll run us first."

Qiu Yuan's unpacking paused, halfway through a hairbrush. Something in the boy's face — not fear; inventory — counted his roommate's certainty and weighed it. "You say that like you've seen the teacher."

"I saw the *gate registrar* lose her profession over arithmetic, House Qiu. The teachers'll be worse." The boot came off. "Sleep well. Tomorrow we'll see whose pride was worth what."

Down the corridor the rule-giving voice had reached number seven, with no end in sight. Jin Yang put the hammer exactly where a tired boy's hand would find it in a dark room, and went to sleep before the summer dark had finished settling, which was a village skill no academy taught.

# Chapter 3: Monsters Run

## Canon Reference: SL2 canon ch 5–6 — Zhou Yi's first day (Canon Scenes). Beats: the "monsters" creed; the dorm-fight stand (Huo Yuhao stands first, Wang Dong second, nobody else — canon's); **one hundred laps in one hour**; NINE cheaters expelled by name; weighted drill (**thirty jin**, two hours, last-to-finish expelled); Wang Dong runs the most laps and goes down; Huo Yuhao is the last one moving and the class gets up behind him; twin offices — Wang Dong by strength, Huo Yuhao by resolution, "no one expelled today because of him." Facts cited; trajectory OURS: the lion discovers being ordinary, keeps an ox honest, and makes a friend out of water.
## Timeline: Second day at Shrek — dawn to night.

## Part 1: The Lists (Canon Scene — backdrop)

The freshman class lists went up before breakfast, and a hundred new students read them from the bottom up, because the bottom of the list was where the good news waited, if there was any.

"**Class 1**," said Qiu Yuan, standing at Jin Yang's elbow with his hair only half-defeated. "You're in. Two lines down from you, I'm in." He kept reading, and his voice changed. "Dai Huabin."

Half the students at the notice were already whispering it. The White Tiger Duke's second son. Even printed in the same gray clerk's ink as everyone else, some names arrive taller.

"They say his rank is the best of the year," Qiu Yuan said.

"He eats porridge like the rest of us," said Jin Yang, and went to find breakfast.

Porridge, it turned out, was also the day's first casualty. Two tables over, a broad, round-shouldered boy with a hill accent dropped his steamed bun, saved it off his knee, and then lost it to the floor anyway, and stared at it like a man watching a friend drown.

"Take this one," said Jin Yang, sliding his own bun across. "There'll be running."

"Running?" The boy took the bun in both hands. "Deng Wu. Ironhide Ox martial soul, rank nineteen. My cousin wrote me from Shrek two years ago. Four sentences. One of them was: *the teachers are made of iron.*" He ate like a man settling a debt. "What's that mean, iron?"

"You two are the pair with the numbered paper on the door," said a second hill-voice — it was still Deng Wu; he had simply changed subjects without signaling. "Whole corridor saw it. Do you actually *live* by it?"

"It has four items," said Qiu Yuan. "They are all reasonable."

"It's *laminated*, brother."

Three tables down, a plain black-haired boy ate quickly and neatly, thanked the server twice, and had one fresh bruise high on his cheekbone, still deciding what color to be. Two tables beyond him, a boy with pink-blue hair like a clear dawn was eating alone, smiling at nothing, good-looking enough that the porridge line parted around his elbow without being asked to.

"Roommate fight," Deng Wu diagnosed softly, with the eye of a boy who had been in three. "Look: plain one's cheek, sunrise one's knuckles. I'd bet bread."

"Bread's scarce," said Jin Yang. "Don't stake the harvest."

The first bell went through the hall like a cook rattling pans.

## Part 2: The Old Woman (Canon Scene)

The teacher was already waiting in the classroom when Class 1 came in.

She was an old woman — or she dressed like one — with iron hair pulled back hard and a face that had clearly never once been told a good excuse. The blackboard behind her was empty. She waited until all one hundred of them had sat, and then she put the chalk down once, precisely.

"**Zhou Yi.** Your class teacher." She spoke without hurry, and the room stopped making any other sound. "I will be brief. I do not produce soul masters. I produce **monsters**. Anyone in this room who cannot be made monstrous by the end of the season will cease, with equal brevity, to be in this room. In my experience, that number runs near half."

The ceiling did something with the silence. Beside Jin Yang, Deng Wu had gone as still as a barn before a storm.

"Prerequisite audit." She walked once along the front row, reading faces. "Who fought in the dormitories last night? Stand."

Nobody stood — for one second. Then the plain boy with the bruise stood, mid-rows.

"**Huo Yuhao.** I fought my roommate."

A second after him, the dawn-haired boy stood too — slow, unbothered, and in no way sorry.

"**Wang Dong.** Same room." A beat. "For the record, he started it."

"I did *not*—"

"Sit, both of you." On the iron face, something moved that was not a smile but had read about them. "One hundred students. Two honest ones. The rest of you were too well-behaved to fight or too smart to admit it." She turned and wrote three lines on the board, in letters like razors:

**SHREK PLAZA · ONE HUNDRED LAPS · ONE HOUR**

"Finished: you stay. Caught lying about your lap count: you are done at Shrek before lunch." The chalk went down. "Begin."

On the stairs down, Deng Wu leaned over with a face like incoming weather.

"No tally-rack. No ropes. Brother — that woman is going to count a hundred runners in her *head*. That is a curse with a salary."

"Run," said Jin Yang.

"I'm writing my mother tonight. I'm putting it in a letter. *Your son was fired by arithmetic.*"

"Run first, write after."

## Part 3: The Hundred Laps (Canon Scene)

Shrek Plaza was a square of flat, pale stone, **three hundred meters to the lap**, no shade at all, and a hundred freshmen went onto it like hounds.

By lap fifteen the hounds had sorted into weather. In front: the born-runners, led by a boy running as cold and exact as a siege engine — Dai Huabin, nobody needed to be told. And behind the whole field, starting late because some boys arrive when they feel like it, came Wang Dong at a floating pace, fifteen minutes behind, who then caught the entire class like a man coiling rope.

"He's not even angry about it," Qiu Yuan gasped around lap fifty, scandalized.

"He's not sweating in the right places," Deng Wu said, aggrieved.

Jin Yang ran in the fat middle of the field, at the pace he had picked before the first step. Three years of bellows work teaches a body a rhythm, and he kept his: strike, breathe, strike, breathe. He did not think about the hundred. He thought about the lap. On his right the cavalry boots complained. On his left the ironhide ox rolled on at a cart's patient gait, not fast at anything, not stopping at all.

By lap sixty the pretty ones were walking. By seventy the plaza had developed three populations: runners, walkers, and boys standing at the fountain practicing an innocent expression. Every lap Jin Yang passed them, the expressions had ripened. Boys were settling their faces. Boys were preparing round numbers.

At the ninety-first lap, Deng Wu stopped.

He stood with both hands on his knees, face the color of old flour, and when Jin Yang looped back to him the hill boy talked to the stone, because talking to the stone was easier.

"Brother. One favor. Run ahead. Tell the teacher the ox finished ninety-one and then *fainted*. She's counting a hundred names in her skull — one more or less—" Even saying it shamed him; that was the only thing still holding him. "I'm a hills boy same as you. Brothers do this."

"Get up."

"I'm empty. I'm legally empty."

"Then get up on the empty." Jin Yang took his wrist and pulled — not gently, like a bellows arm — and the ox came up swearing at nobody. "Nine laps left. You have an ox for a soul, Deng Wu. Oxen walk past mountains. Run like an ox, not like a sack of oxes."

"Other arm," Jin Yang said to Qiu Yuan, who had stopped a length ahead and was weighing his boots against his conscience.

"I have leather to consider—" Qiu Yuan swore in a northern dialect, took the other arm, and the three of them went down the back stretch joined at the wrists like the world's ugliest wagon team.

And that was when the front of the plaza began roaring.

Wang Dong had finished first, by a gap that was honestly impolite — and had turned around and gone *back out*. All down the finish area, heads lifted. Jin Yang looked up mid-stride and saw it: the plain boy, Huo Yuhao, still twelve laps short with six minutes to the hour, still moving on some fuel that had nothing to do with legs — and the dawn-haired boy sprinting across the plaza toward him with an expression like a boy running at a bear.

The whole field held its breath at once.

Wang Dong reached him, hauled the plain boy's arm over his own shoulders, and dragged him forward, and a hundred freshmen went off like a festival — screaming two boys home over twelve last laps like an empire rested on it.

"IF HE CAN CARRY A MAN HOME," Deng Wu bellowed, forging forward between his two haulers, "I'M NOT STOPPING FOR ANYONE—" until the three of them crossed the hundred-lap line with about ninety seconds left of the hour, joined at the wrists, streaming and human.

Deng Wu lay flat on his back on the stone, wheezing and laughing.

"Alive," he told the sky. "Ox, cavalry, weatherman. All present and alive."

"That boy goes *last* on your list of people to bet against," said Jin Yang, chest heaving, watching the two figures by the finish flag. "Remember the face."

Zhou Yi's chalk scratched. The plaza quieted by itself.

"Zhuge Yun. Cheng Cheng. Tang Dao. Lin Zeyu. Shangguan Chentian. Qiu Jianluo. Tang Ling. Yun Xiaopiao. Tailong."

Nine boys stood up, faces ready. The faces did not hold.

"You told me you finished a hundred," the old woman said. "The plaza says otherwise. There is nothing to discuss with arithmetic. You are dismissed from Shrek Academy — the dishonest do not stay." She closed the book once, a small final sound. "The rest: this plaza, second bell, weighted drill. Bring what legs you have left."

Nine boys walked out under escort. Ninety-one watched them go, quiet for the first honest time all day.

Deng Wu watched the longest. "Almost me," he said finally, from his back. "I nearly went. For nothing. For the exact change of pride."

"Pride spends fastest in the morning," said Qiu Yuan wisely. "At home we don't permit it before breakfast."

## Part 4: The Iron Vests (Canon Scene)

Lunch was ninety-one trays, where the morning had set a hundred.

Nobody said *the nine*. Everybody's eyes went to the empty seats like tongues to a missing tooth. At the far table Wang Dong sat on the tabletop itself, ruling an empty kingdom of exhausted admirers. Huo Yuhao ate at the end of the same table, neatly, and twice boys came over to ask him if being carried like rice had hurt, and twice he said no, and once he said thank you for asking.

At second bell a cart stood in the plaza, and on it were black weighted vests, each one **thirty jin — fifteen kilos of plate** — that hung off the shoulders, and the vests all smelled, without exception and without favoritism, of the hundred classes of freshmen who had sweated in them first.

"Two hours," said Zhou Yi. "Run until the bell ends the class. The last one to finish is **expelled**." She did not explain what *finish* meant. The bell would explain. "Begin."

"One question. Just one," Deng Wu said hoarsely, hand up, as if this were still the classroom. "Is there a reason the vest smells of pickled—"

"You have two hours to make peace with it."

The drill went how two iron hours go.

By mid-way the vests had flattened the difference between the proud and the plain. Wang Dong still went past the world — once, twice, faster than anyone had any right to move wearing plate — but even he had started to run out of his borrowed morning. Jin Yang ran his hammer-count and banked minutes like a careful man; at the eastern turn he passed Qiu Yuan, sitting on the stone arranging his cuffs and claiming loudly to nobody that he was *strategizing*. At an hour and forty minutes, Deng Wu's knees and the ground signed a private agreement, and the ox went down slow, like cartage unloading.

And still, at the back of the whole field, more laps behind than anyone, came Huo Yuhao — and still coming.

Last place. Lowest rank in the class. And at the hour where every other freshman in the plaza had stopped running, sat down, and given their opinions to the stone — he was the only boy still moving.

Not fast. Not well. Simply: moving. One foot. Then the next. The vest hung on his frame like a sack of plate, his face was white and perfectly empty, and he ran the last stretch of the second hour on something that was not his body. Jin Yang had seen that face once in a mirror older than this place: his own, years ago, in a ravine of red clay, in the hour after noon when the iron dragon was still standing and he was not supposed to be.

A class of ninety-one students lay in the dust of Shrek Plaza and watched the weakest boy in the room show them the floor of what they had.

"Oh, get *up*," said a girl's voice from somewhere, annoyed at herself. Three boys stood together, grumbling, and began to jog. Two more went after them. And then the whole sitting field began, one shameful pair of legs at a time, to rise and go back — not after the leader, not for the drill — just following the one boy who had refused to be the last thing standing.

Jin Yang got up and walked the four meters to Deng Wu, and took hold of his vest strap.

"Up."

"Dead. Legally and spiritually. Take word to my hills—"

"You owe me nine laps from this morning. I don't carry debts across days. And the last boy finished is *expelled*, Deng Wu — *up*."

"You are a hard man, weatherman." The ox got one leg, then both, and both of them joined the marching file.

Weatherman. That was going to stick, Jin Yang realized. Everybody had seen the boy whose temper stayed even through plate and pride. Fine. A smith answers to whatever name the forge gives him; the work is what counts.

At the bell, the plaza held ninety-one ruined freshmen, one iron-haired teacher, and a silence you could have hung a banner in.

"Wang Dong. Front."

The sunrise boy walked, ran-out and glorious anyway — most laps, twice the field's count, and five final minutes flat on his face in the dust.

"First home this morning. Most laps this afternoon. The office of class president is yours." Zhou Yi raised her voice over the murmur. "Any student who defeats him takes the office — and keeps it as long as they can hold it." Her eyes traveled the ruins of Class 1 for challengers, and found none. "Wise. Now the second office. It is not mine to award.

"Huo Yuhao. Stand."

The plain boy stood. Wobbled. Stayed up.

"The drill's law was: the last one finished is expelled. This class had stopped running and become an audience — and one boy would not stop, and because one boy would not stop, the rest of you stood up and ran beside him. There was no last finisher. So the verdict does not fall today: **no one is expelled — because of him.**" The book closed with a sound like a year ending. "You are my second class president, Huo Yuhao. Bought with legs. Unarguable. The two of you will run this room together without bleeding on it. Dismissed."

The applause began in the tired ranks and moved around the square like weather.

## Part 5: Water First

There was, afterwards, the fountain, and the water gourd going hand to hand through the ruins of Class 1.

It ended with Jin Yang. Beside the basin's lip, Huo Yuhao sat with his head down and his breath coming like a forge bellows — hard draws, but calm ones, the breath of somebody who had spent everything and was not troubled by the bill. Jin Yang held the gourd out to him.

"Last of it. New legs drink first."

Huo Yuhao drank, coughed, and gave the gourd back still half-full. "Half," he said. "For your ox friend." And then, plainly, like a boy offering a name at a market: "Huo Yuhao."

"Jin Yang."

"Wang Dong," said Wang Dong, arriving, taking the gourd, and finishing what was left. "Class president, both of us. Petitions accepted during reasonable hours."

Somebody's shoe missed his ear by an inch. He ducked without looking and gave the plaza back its smile, and the laugh went around the fountain once, tired and real, and took even the shoe-thrower with it.

"He's not so bad," Huo Yuhao said quietly, watching the other president accept the crowd. "He carried me twelve laps. Complained through ten of them."

"That's friendship," said Qiu Yuan, solemn from the ground. "Where I come from, complaining is half of it."

"What's the other half?"

"Showing up," said Jin Yang.

The plain boy looked at him a moment, then nodded once — quiet, like a fact filed where facts were kept.

---

## Part 6: The Door with a Note

Night came down the dormitory wing how it came every night after a hard day: first aching and boasting through the walls, then lower talk, then lamps going out room by room until the corridor held only moonlight and somebody's forgotten candle.

In Room 105, under the one oil lamp, Qiu Yuan was updating the clan notebook — the debt book of White Birch: *name, house, threat*. The day's page was long.

"Dai Huabin — White Tiger — underlined twice. Lend nothing." Scratch of the pen. "Wang Dong. House: unknown. Legs: best in class. Personality: *sunrise.*" Scratch. "Huo Yuhao. House: none you'd write. Rank: ordinary." He stopped, thought, and wrote, in letters twice as large as anything else on the page, with the care of a man inscribing a gate: **LEGS.** He looked at it and nodded, satisfied. "That's his file."

"You'll go far, House Qiu."

"I know. That's the tragedy." He smoothed the page over to the standing room-treaty — the numbered paper, now laminated in his mind at least: *no visitors after third bell; forge-hour announced the night before; questions of cultivation are forfeit of tea.* "Item four is still pending. You said you keep your own matters off paper. Write it in."

Jin Yang took the pen and wrote, in block letters, which was all his mother's education had equipped: **What is mine stays out of this room, off paper, unsaid. Nothing against the roommate.**

Qiu Yuan read it twice, slow, like a treaty with a stronger country. "Good," he said finally, with something in his face the morning would not have owned. "Signed."

It was after that when someone shuffled up outside, hesitated, and shuffled off again. Qiu Yuan opened the door. No one, and then, at the foot of the door: a cloth bundle. Inside, wrapped twice over: a steamed bun, a little lopsided, still warm. Under it, a note written by a hand that had to fight each character:

**"for the strap. and the arm. next time on my own. — Deng Wu"**

Qiu Yuan held the bun up to the lamplight like an examiner with a doubtful pearl. "The ox has declared an alliance," he announced. "In wheat."

"In wheat," Jin Yang agreed, and banked the lamp.

"He'll run beside us every day now. That's what oxen do. Forever."

"Good." In the dark, the voice from the window bed was almost smiling. "We'll want the ones who don't stop."

"Jin Yang."

"Mm."

"Wake me before your forge hour. It's the rule. Item two."

"Sleep, House Qiu."

"Good night, House Jin."

The wing slept around them, ninety-one doors with ninety-one names behind them, where the morning had opened with a hundred. And at the threshold of Room 105, alone in the quiet hall, the day's last account sat wrapped in cloth, still holding its warmth:

one bun, one treaty, two names on one door.

## Part 1: Ox O'clock

The knock came before the sky, three slow raps, exactly loud enough.

Qiu Yuan surfaced from sleep like a man being raised from the dead and finding it overpriced. "Whatever you are," he told the door, "you have the wrong corpse."

Deng Wu's voice came through the wood, wide awake and deeply offended by the concept of dawn itself. "You said forge-hour was announced. So I'm announced."

"That was for *me*, you ox— it's a *room* rule—"

"I memorized the rule. Item the four-… the two. Announcements." The door opened a crack against Room 105's own injunction, and one round hill-born face assessed the dark. "He said before sunrise. It's before sunrise. Everything legal."

Jin Yang was already up, which was the problem with smiths — the body left the bed when the day did, no vote taken. He moved through the dark like something that had never owned a need for lamps: boots by habit, hammer by hand.

"You don't have to come," he said. "Really, Deng Wu."

The ironhide boy took visible offense. "And let the two of you be the ones who weren't still laying down when the bell went? No. My hills taught me about oxen, weatherman. You feed one one time—" he was doing up his sandals on the corridor stone, with the grief of a man doing arithmetic against his own interests, "—you've got it forever."

"That's… cattle law," said Qiu Yuan, dragging a comb through his hair with his eyes closed, "and I'm certain it's not binding."

"Binding in the hills."

The dawn drills on the frost-cold plaza began that way, three boys in a loose line — and it kept being that way all week. The field staff marking attendance on slate jotted their names together for five straight mornings, a habit the staff started and the boys never quite ratified.

On the fourth morning, warming down by the fountain, they crossed the two boys from the run that mattered — the plain one and the sunrise one, still wearing thirty-jin vests, jogging around the plaza like the vests were part of breakfast. Huo Yuhao raised a hand when he saw them — the lifted-palm motion of people who have shared a water gourd. Wang Dong raised his eyebrows instead, which was somehow warmer.

"Presidents train before the bell," Deng Wu observed, awed and aggrieved. He drank the fountain's coldest water and regretted it immediately.

"Presidents," said Qiu Yuan, "have something to prove."

"Vice-president," said Wang Dong, passing, "of a class of *ninety-one*."

"Co-president," said Huo Yuhao, breathing evenly, not breaking stride.

"Whatever the sun says," said Wang Dong, and was gone around the turn, chasing light.

Deng Wu watched them shrink. "Twelve laps carried, and the man jokes at dawn. There's no justice, brothers. There's just running."

"There is," said Jin Yang, wiping his face, "also breakfast."

"See, that's how I know you're from good stock."

## Part 2: The Cull, Announced (Canon Scene — the season's law)

The teacher had one piece of news for Class 1 in the first theory block, and she delivered it with the chalk.

"Three months," Zhou Yi wrote on the board, three slashes of ribbon-thin chalk. Beneath it she wrote two other numbers, unneedingly, because everyone in the room already knew what they were for.

**NINE HUNDRED + . . . . . HALF**

"Three months from today, this academy holds the freshman assessment," she said, turning to read the result she already knew she'd find in ninety-one faces. "Across all classes: more than nine hundred of you. After the assessment: no more than half that. Nothing about that is new — it is Shrek's oldest arithmetic, older than some of your clans, and it has broken better houses than yours. Half the students in this room will not be students here next term." She set the chalk down, precisely, like a coffin lid on a good fit. "Now you are frightened *formally*. Good. Frightened students pay attention."

The room's fear did come up, then — something like a low tide in the stomach, audible only in the shifting of benches. Deng Wu, on Jin Yang's left, had gone very still in what was becoming a recognizable fashion.

"Team events," the old woman went on. "The assessment is done in teams of three. Teams formed by the teachers from those of you who remain *worth forming*. You have three months to make yourselves into people a good teacher doesn't have to squint at. I will know each of you long before the ropes go tight. And children — " her eyes did that sweep of hers, the ungentle one, settling on nobody and sparing no one — "I do not squint."

Nobody asked questions. They had known since the ninth-page rumor of the first morning; now the cull had a date, and somehow that made it worse than when it had only been a mood.

On the way out, Qiu Yuan's face kept the even, self-possessed cast it wore on public benches, but his voice, down a notch, told the truth: "Three of three can be named already," he said. "The Duke's son, and the two presidents."

"And the fourth through ninth names are not yet written," said Jin Yang. "So the arithmetic isn't the weather, House Qiu. It just does weather's job on the skin."

Deng Wu said nothing at all for about thirty paces, which was itself a contribution. Then: "Oxen go to the butcher in twos and threes." A pause. "That's… that's the last animal thing I say today."

"Probably wise," said Qiu Yuan.

"I have a soul of a bovine, brother — this is *also* weather," and surprisingly, in the stairwell's chill, all three of them laughed, which was itself the day's first piece of good arithmetic.

## Part 3: Two Kinds of Hammer (the soul-tools hall `[design scene, canon-era system]`)

Third morning put them in a room they had not been in — a long hall of the soul-tools division, with bright lamps and iron tables and a teacher iron-gray from the trade.

His name placard said INSTRUCTOR HE; nothing else announced him, and nothing needed to — the hall was the announcement: rows of worktables, presses, soul-lamps, and at the front, two rows of finished blanks under cloth. Freshman theory came here once a week this year, because, said the notice, *the age is one of tools, and ignorance of tools is the one ignorance Shrek does not tolerate.*

"Efficiency," said Instructor He, sweeping the first cloth off in a flat, calloused hand. "This — a spike plate blank — is our line's work once today. Grade-fine, smooth-etched, ten identical pieces." He lifted one; it caught the lamplight cold and regular, shine without character, heart without a face. "Now you tell me the old way, and price it against us."

A courtyard's hands went up. The boy he glanced at — a city-academy candidate with smith-family tattoos — gave the old way in thirty well-schooled words: ore, fold, draw, anneal, refine; a master's hands a full week on one blank; the price that fetched.

"Nineteen days for a full set," said Jin Yang, who did not raise his hand, and had anyway the only voice at his bench to say the words with the weight of experience. "Nineteen hundred-swing heats of bread-price labor, three gold for six, fair-rate per the guild route." He could feel, somewhere distant in his chest, the workshop's sweet old ember-heat darken a shade.

The instructor caught the weight with a craftsman's ear, and his eyes came down rows and found the small country boy in the cheap shirt at mid-bench, and rested there like a hawk on a chimneypot. "You count like you've paid it, student. What's your name?"

"Jin Yang. I was a smith — grade three, White Birch guild."

"Ah." In the hall's humming light, the teacher nodded once, with some iron-rich courtesy given stranger-to-stranger across decade-lines. "Then you know what I'm about to say better than most: the blanks on this table are a *menu*, not an *argument*. The machine makes four this morning — yours the guild priced a week. What the machine will never make is the thing a grade-nine lives by, because the machine can't *listen* — it doesn't know where the metal wants to bend. That hunger to listen, boy, is what we buy at the top of the tower. Come see me when you're hungry to know the presses well enough to out-argue them. Everyone: open your books."

It was a tidy thing, well meant. But it had not touched the plate, which sat in the lamp-light like a very well-dressed stranger who had moved into your childhood home.

Deng Wu leaned over, cheerful and wrong in as only hill boys could be: "Brother, your face looks like a man who saw a grave."

"It looks like a *price*, child," said Qiu Yuan product-reviewingly, on the other side.

"It looks like both," said Jin Yang, and closed his book over the table with the care of a man adjusting a load.

*Third thing I know, brother,* something in his chest said to the plate and the lamplight. *After counting and stance, the third thing: everything the world cannot hear eventually answers to hands that can.* He filed it without heat, because a forge's keeper knows what to do with an ember: bank it, carry it, and don't waste it on the cold.

That night he hammered at the dormitory window-bench until third bell, on a piece of scrap, until the piece of scrap told him the truth it had been shaped around. It wasn't about the blank, exactly. It was about who got to say what a smith was for.

Qiu Yuan let the hammering run, unreported under treaty item the whatever, and judged by that single allowance, everyone stood that little bit more treated.

## Part 4: The Teacher's File (Zhou Yi panel — canon: her first days, the husband; AU: the folder contents `[design]`)

By a window in the teachers' wing, in lamplight a little warmer than the classrooms', the most-feared woman of the freshmen schedule was doing what she did most evenings of opening week: ruining her own good mood with other people's children.

The stew had gone luke at her elbow without her noticing, which was the year's first victory of the dossiers over the crockery.

"Nine already out of one class," said Fan Yu mildly, from the other end of it, toweling clean hands — the soul-tools man home late again, decade-patient, hands ink-blued at the creases and never quite off-duty. "Is the count keeping with your ambitions, Wife, or ahead?"

"I did not ask them to lie, Fan Yu. They *arrived* lying. Cheating is a home-trained skill. I just graded it." She turned a leaf. "The Duke's has a pedigree you'd believe before you met him — cold work, top of intake. The blue-haired one will have every mother's child in this class by the ears before winter, and the plain-eyed one…" The pen stopped, it being the second file she'd stopped the pen at tonight, and the iron in her face unkinked a little, into something that the classrooms never got shown. "Lowest rank in the room. Twelfth-lap heart. He's not a monster, this one — I can't make that kind. It's born in."

"And yet you have him marked *co-president*."

"He earned the room in front of my eyes, Fan Yu — that's worth more than a rating." She turned the page, and then another, and she stopped a third time, and that pause was a different animal altogether.

The fifth file on the stack, the one her predecessor at the tents had annotated in the margin in a theory-teacher's meticulous hand — *Wang's note: strike two cun into steelface. Purple second. "Priced my life into the hunts. Won't sell the pricing."* — had nothing in it that should have stopped the reader cold. The boy's numbers were open as day, right there on the paper: eleven winters, rank twenty-three, a smith's boy from White Birch with a forehead like a plough horse's patience. No intrigue. Except that the number was wrong. Wrong like a smith's hammer lying on a parlor carpet.

"Wife. What."

She realized Fan Yu had come halfway across the room, reading her face like men with blued diagrams. She closed the file, a little later than natural, as women of very few weaknesses shut one.

"Eleven years old, ring two at the thousand-tier — impossible arithmetic. He's not bragging about it. He runs mid-pack with two friends and the lantern on his desk at night doing *workman's quizzes* in my class. All his exercises in at first bell, all scored low-ordinary, by a hand that cannot be ordinary. I watched him sit down with the fallen in the run — could've finished ahead of the prince. He's *investing* where he spends, Fan Yu. A boy of eleven, from a farm. Your presses are ready to explain away every genius except the ones who hold their fire. And what this class teacher does about such a boy—" She turned the file facedown, and the iron in her went where other people keep smiles. "—she will decide by winter. He is the kind of blade you do not draw until you know the sheath."

"And that's what it is? The genius in a file." Her husband finished drying his hands, unimpressed as only wedding physics gets you to be. "You've found three in twenty years, and two of them tired you. Leave the boy his night-lamp, Wife. Let the blade be still, for once. The year is long." He picked up the cold stew and tasted it without complaint, resolute and forgiving. "Some of these children are homes in themselves. There is time to learn the boy before we teach the boy."

"Fan Yu," said the monster of the freshmen, in the tone of a woman very much used to being right about such things, "this one is a smith that got folded somehow into a hands-and-back strongest-lion shape, and I will find out *where the heat goes*."

Down the hall, the last lamplight clicked out on the folder with the smith's mark on its corner, and in the room the ink dried over: *the workman's bracket* — three names, one written twice — and, for a certain intent, a small inked star, neither favor nor assignment, just a bead dropped in a scale-pan to weigh something later.

## Part 5: Warm Names

Word moved around the freshmen wing by the old methods: over laundry lines and in the queue for hot water, inside shouted hallway jokes and quiet canteen corners. By the end of that first week, Class 1 had its small climate — the Duke's sons upwind of everything, the presidents in joint flight near the top of the flag, and a few other cold fronts and warm pockets that every new school year accumulates like sediment.

The girls at the next-but-one laundry trough knew *of* the three. "Was it them? The ones latched together crossing on lap hundred?" "The ox, there's the honest one. Cried going over — I heard— " "—did NOT cry—" "The quiet one pushed his bun away for a stranger?" — and the quiet one's roommate from White Birch had to stand for several minutes of acute overhearing with the immobile patience of an eagle being talked about in its own nest, and by the end of it he had been gifted with the one piece of intelligence the day had been put together to yield.

He delivered it over the treaty-page that night with the paper folded twice like a warrant, unreadable in his usual way.

"We have a name, House Qiu," said Jin Yang, at the shutter.

"We have *three* names. Oh, where has your ambition been?" Qiu Yuan flipped open the notebook and wrote, with the full year's ceremony: **weatherman · cavalry · ox**. "The wing is talking about the *three*. The girls call Deng Wu the ox already, and the wing as a whole—" he lowered his voice anatomically, to a register normally reserved for genealogy — "they say we cross the line *latched*. Like mountain-goers."

"My people come from the hills, not the mountains."

"Everyone's people come from better than they presently are — and it is *cattle law* in the hills, the ox told us so himself," and that was so exactly the running room-argument of the whole first week that the lamp had to be pinched before it shook, because the settled treaty's unwritten rule-zero was: *no laughing at the signatory*.

On Saturday, the whole wing had the quiet that came to Shrek's children when the week's boot-tread was let off for half a day — the muscles praising, the tongues conferring. Deng Wu slept against their corridor wall at the second bell with the unsubmission of a man holding a fort. Huo Yuhao and Wang Dong jogged their extra laps under the still sky, how worth establishes itself in persons too young to name it yet. At the fourth bell, a rolled paper clapped down under Room 105's door, standard-issue ink —

**MONDAY, FIRST BELL: COMBAT BASICS. BRING SOUL, LEAVE PRIDE.**

— and pinned under it, in the teacher's own hand, two words: **Zhou Yi**.

"Oh," said Deng Wu, waking.

"Combat," said Qiu Yuan, stricken.

"Good," said Jin Yang, and set the hammer quietly in the corner where the lamplight liked it.

## Part 1: First Bell, First Blood-Rules

The notice had said: bring soul, leave pride. Class 1 brought both anyway — you could hear the pride scraping through the doors ahead of the students.

The drill ground this morning was not the plaza but the **combat hall** — stone floor ruled into sparring squares with white lime, padded posts at the corners, and Teacher Zhou Yi standing at midfield in her iron Monday shape.

"You have run for me," she said, no good-morning anywhere in evidence. "You have suffered for me. Today you knock each other down for me — because running teaches legs, and fighting teaches **information**. About yourselves, first. About your neighbor, faster. Rules." The chalk counted on her fingers. "One square at a time. I call the pairs. Touch-count to three: shoulder and above. Rings stay home — this is body and footwork, not cannon work. First blood of pride counts double against you." She did the thin thing that passed for her smile. "Fall down *well*, children. It's the only thing you'll definitely need all year."

The square-assigning began in chalk-scratch order. The room did what rooms do the first time combat comes on a schedule — the loud boys got louder, the quiet ones went water-smooth, and everyone looked at everyone else with a slightly revised valuation.

"The Duke's son," Qiu Yuan murmured at Jin Yang's elbow. "First square. Watch him."

Dai Huabin's square was over in about four breaths, one white-gold blur of it, the other boy deposited respectfully and wholly on the floor. *Fast,* said the smith's habit in Jin Yang's head, *and cold, and already measuring the room.* The class made a collective small sound.

"The presidents," said Deng Wu nervously.

"Wang Dong," read Zhou Yi's chalk, harsh and level, "second square. Against — " her eyes ran the class, found the second name on some private register of balance, and lifted: "— does anyone object to my choice of **Huo Yuhao**?"

From among the crowded rows, the dawn-haired boy leaned out into the lime-light with joy undisguised, cracked his knuckles once, and gave Class 1 its first real show of the term.

## Part 2: The Butterfly, Public (his soul's display: canon-true by this era; the bout itself + all banter `[design]`)

Wang Dong fought like morning comes to a hill — fast, at angles, and prettier than should be legitimate.

His martial soul came up to a roar of half the class: wings of blue-gold light opening out of his back like the sky had decided to give him a second set of shoulders. The **Radiant Butterfly Goddess**, in the open air, in front of everyone. The hall's packed rows made the noise classes make when the gossip they've been trading for a week shows up wearing wings.

"Wings," said Deng Wu, in the tone of a man having vindications. "The roommate got carried by *wings*. No justice, brothers. None anywhere."

Huo Yuhao lost — approximately nobody expected otherwise — but he lost with the particular stubbornness of a boy who had spent the morning with his palms on dirt and kept refusing, by a stubborn half-step, to be exactly where he'd been aimed — twice. Wang Dong won the third touch overhead on momentum and said, into the fallen boy's ear and loud enough for the first two rows, "Yield, sweetheart roommate," and got dust and two fingers to the ribs for the compliment, on a technical and wholly uncounted fourth point.

The class's laughter had weather in it.

"Who else," said the chalk, tasting the room. "Who volunteers?"

Wang Dong did not look at the chalk. The sunrise boy was looking across the square, at a point halfway down a row of tired freshmen, with the provocative ease of somebody selecting a dessert with the whole shop watching.

"You," said Wang Dong, cheerfully, to Jin Yang. "**Weatherman.** Two days you've watched everything like it owes you numbers. Square with me."

The room's breathing changed again — gossip shifting gears.

Zhou Yi's eyebrows reached the question for her. Jin Yang met the sunrise stare the way you meet weather — neutrally.

"Touch to three," said the teacher. "Rings home. Square."

## Part 3: The Sunrise and the Post

He was fast.

The smith in Jin Yang clocked it in the first exchange — fast like a forge-fire's first second off the bellows, no waste, no wind-up, the wings themselves folded away as ordered and *still* fast from the floor. Wang Dong hit him in the shoulder, twice feather-light, before Jin Yang's stance had entirely agreed with reality about which angle the morning was arriving from.

Two touches. One left. The hall was making a pot-ready noise.

Some people, when they are behind, hurry.

Jin Yang stopped hurrying. The earth under his soles — the drake's ancient ground-seat, worn these two years like an old boot — settled one notch further through the lime, and for the third touch Wang Dong came in in a flash-slide of gold and *stopped* like he'd hit a door frame.

On the tile: a boy, still planted. Not moved. Not even much rearranged — shoulder already forgotten about the previous two defeats, eyes possessed of calm working information.

"He's *planted*," said someone in the rows, with awe.

"The ox said he doesn't move," somebody answered.

Wang Dong rocked back on his heels, tilted his head — re-measuring, from a whisker away — and there went the little gold-winged grin that the rest of the school year was going to have opinions about. Like morning having fun.

"Three," said Zhou Yi dryly, by the chalk. "Wang Dong, the square."

The class let its breath out. A spattering of applause started somewhere — the room liked winners, and it liked anything else that kept the morning strange.

And this was the moment the boy from White Birch stepped down off the lime, dusted the tile-chalk from his knuckles, and said, in the level voice of a man repeating basic facts of weather —

"Fast, **softy pretty boy**. Nobody's moved me like that. Ever."

The hall went absolutely still, and then — louder than it had been all morning, so loud the chalks rattled — **exploded**.

Wang Dong had gone the color of his own dawn.

"—*softy*?" Someone in the girls' third row was already weeping with delight. "—he said *pretty boy* — he said it to *Wang Dong*—" Half the boys were standing; Deng Wu had both fists pressed into his own cheeks like the hull of a ship around two trying pumps. "—oh he'll die — oh this is — **softy pretty boy**—" "—bleach the floor, they're *foaming*—"

The sunrise, being glared at from the center of the square in profound, total cold by its own self, tasted the room's verdict and made the only move actually native to him: he smiled back, sharp as slivers, and matched fact for fact.

"*Softy*," he said, tasting it. "Block." And let the word leave the tips of his teeth like the last item on a receipt. "Fallen twice in a square, still lying about measurement. **Block.** An anvil that talks. You hear me, farm post — *good because immobile*?"

"Good because still standing," said Jin Yang, walking off the lime.

"Tomorrow," said Wang Dong, to his spine, with enormous cheer. "We do it until you *move*, block-boy. Three touches compares all arguments — including whether a pretty thing can flip a stone."

"Whenever you like, softy."

The word had a life of its own by third period. By lunch the whole wing said *softy* with the reverence of a password; by the fourth, less delicate rumor had exported the complete exchange, inaccurate by then in both directions.

## Part 5: The Post's Own Evening

The gossip arrived at Room 105 by its normal freight, of course — Qiu Yuan came home with the wing's report on the tip of his nature, but he was preceded through the door by Deng Wu, who was so full of quotable material he had forgotten to knock.

"—told the whole east wash-line — 'the farm post didn't *blink*, I think he yawned' — and by the girls' wing it's *softy* said three different ways — brother, they're going to start it as a *greeting*—"

"HOUSE JIN." Qiu Yuan, at the desk, the full-White-Birch voice of office. "You have been *named*. *To the whole student population.* Counter-name and *all*. The wing takes these things seriously. You're the *Block* of our corridor — it makes everything we do *news*, we're *notables*—" he caught this about a half-breath too late to unsay, and had to recalibrate. "…I mean — *children* say these things cruelly—"

"You're delighted, House Qiu."

"—*delighted* doesn't come into it, it's a political *position*, anyone useful to the — put it this way, I know what it buys in corridors: until somebody beats 'block,' we're safe from being teased. **The room's pronouncements.**" He flipped open the treaty notebook and put the day's balance in writing, all the gravity of the clan: **Block welcomed — softy pretty boy returned — courage accounts satisfied; the sunrise content remains, though, its morning's complaint.** He looked up, and there was something in his look which was not entirely unlike friendship. "So you chose a *prince* for study purposes, farm post. Why him and why words?"

Jin Yang drove the towel down over the back of his neck and thought about it, honestly, like a boy with experience sorting iron.

"Because he flies like it's free," he said finally. "Everything else I know costs." He set the hammer at the bedfoot, the day's first quiet motion that had no square underneath it. "Somebody in this room should learn what a boy who isn't weighed can do. I decided it should be me — and somebody should tell a sunrise it can be looked at plain. I decided that should be me too."

"'It costs at *his* side,'" said Deng Wu slowly, from the floor, like a boy unexpectedly touching something that agreed with his whole education. "*That's* his price."

"What is?"

"Friendship with a prince. Brothers, that's *dear*. Not due to him, mind. Even sunrise — dear, as coin goes. The Duke's second won't care what's owed, nor should he." He nodded to himself, happily lost in some provincial economy now, and then remembered his errand. "Teacher Zhou left cards. Spar files, signed by her own chalk — monday slots all month. *Second square*, you know whose—"

There were two cards indeed: **CLASS 1 · COMBAT ROTATION · SQUARE TWO** in that razor script. The paired names were written in underneath. As of this week, for the following weeks —

— *Wang Dong*, first name, in her board-razors' hand.
— *Jin Yang*, under it.

"Monthly," said Qiu Yuan, warily, formally. "He will not let go."

"No," said Jin Yang, pocketing.

"Good," said Deng Wu, wide, content. "Future running weeks, brother." And then, intoning as the freezer wind: "Watch out around the corner about you, sunrise. Ah — what — that's *superstition*, brother, in the hills you see *ominous things* if a name be too long followed — go ahead and follow."

"Now," said Qiu Yuan, "you're suddenly superstitious?"

"I'm from a thousand years of hills! I am *announcing*!" the ox said, muffled in the mattress, and the night held four boroughs of Class 1's liege-laughter, and then Shrek's lamp budget went out.

## Part 1: The Rotation Finds Its Weight

A term, it turns out, is a kind of weather: it doesn't knock, it settles in around you while you're busy under it.

Combat basics ran on schedule now. Square One cold and fast — Dai Huabin's square had stopped being a lesson and started being a processing center for falls. Square Two chalked weekly **WANG DONG / JIN YANG** in Zhou Yi's razor hand, for reasons she had not deigned to attach commentary to. "File it," was all she'd said, the first morning, when the bracket had stood before the card like three boys looking at weather. "File everything."

So they filed.

Wang Dong took Square Two that week too, three touches to none — *faster*, second time, like morning learning the room. The first two Jin Yang paid for honestly in chalk-line bruises of pride: the sunrise had adjusted his entry by half a breath, somewhere in the week, and the adjustment cost exactly what good adjustments usually cost. Nothing wasted, everything recorded — there was a freezer wind in Jin Yang's head filing footwork, as his grandfather once filed weather patterns that only mattered three years later.

The third touch mattered though.

Not because it changed the score — three to none, clean, chalked, done. The post took the third touch standing so awkwardly wrong-shaped that Wang Dong's follow-through landed on geometry that hadn't been there when he launched it, and the sunrise came up out of his own momentum with his eyebrows informally taking minutes. "That's not a stance," Wang Dong said, breathless and delighted about it. "That was a *warranty*."

"Try it again in three weeks, softy."

"Oh, *when* the warranty expires!" Wang Dong announced to no one, and walked off the lime happy.

Deng Wu learned to fall, the week's true curriculum. Teacher Zhou demonstrated it once — how a body meets lime without arguing — and then refused, by method, to demonstrate it ever again. "You'll have the ground whenever you like," she said, "for free." On Thursday the ox finally came down from **Xiaolei**'s shifted hip-throw — Xiaolei across the hall, who had threatened this on day two and kept her accounts — with all four limbs agreeable about it, sat up in the chalk, and announced to the sky, "**DEPOSIT**," which the girls' side of the room took up as a blessing.

Qiu Yuan, who fought by information, drew a second-week spar against the wing's long-limbed girl with the steel fan `[design: Fang Ruo, Class 1]` and lasted seven touches past his own expectation by the simple device of *having watched Tuesday*. The brackets' evening debriefs — instituted Wednesday, unplanned, at the usual wall — had acquired an unofficial title by Friday: *the filings*. File the butterfly's acceleration line. File how the Duke's son never feints high twice. File, and file, and file.

The weatherman had become strange and small: properly their own, by then. Strangers said it about desk-gossip on Tuesdays — *storms earlier this year; the Block's line said so Tuesday* — and Jin Yang had stopped blinking at it by then, which Deng Wu said was growth, and Qiu Yuan said was *corridor citizenship*, and both were probably correct.
