## Part 2: The Prince's File — evening practice (Dai Huabin panel — canon: his persona (proud, exacting, strongest by work); canon-adjacent venue: extra-hours training ground; AU: subject `[design]`)

The east training ground kept its light late for people who paid for it in effort.

Dai Huabin was still drilling turns when Zhu Lu came out of the shadowed colonnade with her hair down from the day and the wing's whole report carried in her bearing like laundry. She brought him news in the evenings without being asked — had since they were small, since White Tiger halls first — not because he demanded it, but because she had opinions about what the house of the Duke's second son should *notice*.

This week the wing had only one headline anyway, and both of them already knew it.

"Square Two's the talk," she said, settling on a plinth at the court's edge, lacing her fingers with tidy finality. "The whole week. You saw the card today — they're leaving those two paired, Teacher Zhou's keeping it."

"I saw the card."

"They say," Zhu Lu reported, with professionally level cheeks, "'block takes two and walks; sunrise takes three and *lauds* it,' and that the farm post said *warranty*—" she paused, because the story was also annoying her, visibly, in its seventh retelling. "It's just chatter, then, Huabin. Chatter going *-up*, though. Corridors. Girls' side. Wash-price of a boy's entire reputation, these days."

Dai Huabin finished the rotation of his turn — heel, center, the White Tiger balance he had spent nine years on — and only then answered, without heat, like a man commenting on arithmetic done well by other hands:

"Then the corridors can't read."

"Hm?"

"Watch Square Two next week, Lu. Actually watch." He set to the next repetition, unhurried, not one syllable performing. "Three to nothing twice, and he'll be there for *three-to-nothing* every week until it isn't — because every week he isn't **spending** anything. Two years somebody taught that boy to cost every motion twice, and now he comes to a spar like a *receipt*." The turn completed, clean. "Butterfly's faster. Butterfly will stay faster six months. The other one — " and here the Duke's son did smile, faint and completely without humor, "the other one is filing **us**."

Zhu Lu considered this with the seriousness it deserved; it sat fully inside her training. "He's sharp-clawed, the third-year aunties say — rings, and they say the measure-officer had teachers coming to look at a *pair* round his name—" then, with precision: "Strength to waste, White-Tiger-blood. Even so. Sharp is what sharp *does*."

"To waste," said Dai Huabin, evenly. "He's had a year of yellow and one of *nearly millennial ring* under this roof, and in ten days of drills he's spent a claw and a half, by my count. That's not waste, Lu. Something priced his strength for him before Shrek did. Find me his square-card changes and his Sundays, both." No malice anywhere in it — a prince's homework, assigned in the tone of a man ordering the weather. "'Storms earlier this year,' the wing quotes him now. Fine. The Duke's house reads weather too."

"And the softy-butterfly?"

"Wang Dong." For the first time in the exchange, edge: a cold, collegial, genuinely unmet-yet edge, aristocrat sized. "Hooyuhao's friend. President-mannered." He considered. "He can stay reigning six months. Sunrise is paid for in *mornings*. It's a currency that runs out at noon."

Zhu Lu filed both, which was her whole education, and rose to leave. At the colonnade she paused — loyalty's last errand — "The gap line, from the first day? In the plaza. He's kept it unpaid, Huabin."

"I know." White Tiger eyes catching the court lamps. "That's why he's interesting."

## Part 3: Hands, Week Two (day 13, Sunday, soul-tools hall `[canon-era system]`)

Instructor He had a way of being already at his bench when you arrived, no matter the hour — a hall truth Jin Yang had classified under *settlement*, like dew.

Week two, they moved off blanks and onto **edges**: real blade-steel, plain park-grade, learning the single line of work a soul-tool edge would be — a cutter's bevel, drawn inch by inch under a lens-small formation plate that warmed the steel just shy of arguing. Watch a machine-press form a blank in one down-stroke, first, as wolves watch courier hawks. Then take the same edge a hand-length at a time, two hours, believing in increments.

Jin Yang hammered. The work came easier than anything else in this city — easier than a three-touch loss, easier than memory post claw-days — and by the second hour the line he was chasing had stopped being He's assigned line and become *his own argument about the same steel*.

He stopped the boy gently once, by sitting on the tool rail nearby, holding his tea.

"You're pulling the bevel long again. On purpose, now, I hope?"

"Shorter dies," said Jin Yang, between strokes, on the exhale. "You showed us Thursday — press blank, snap-test at notch, it *sings* there. A drawn bevel bends before it breaks. Weight for weight, the hand one stays a tool longer. Not… a better edge. A more patient one."

"Hm. And if the School only pays for the fast one?"

The hammer stopped, resettled.

"Teacher," said Jin Yang, eyes still on the steel, in the tone of somebody asking for a true number, because he had been raised by people for whom numbers were bread — "if the blanks are made by machines and the School buys the fast one… why are hands still on the workbench at all?"

The instructor took a slow drink of the cooling tea, and set the cup down, and gave the boy the honest unspiced version, as the hall gave everything:

"Because a machine stamps a thousand edges alike before lunch, boy — and learns nothing from any one of them breaking. A hand remembers. Mines a life of breaks into forearms; *listens*, strike by strike. The age of the tool, son, is an age of people who want to hold a thousand of a thing." He retrieved his tea. "I keep the old bench because sometimes a thing needs holding *once*, and right, and by some poor fool who means it. Your salary can read it however it must." A pause; the small dry smile. "The paid word for you this week is *tolerances*."

The boy hammered until the bell, thinking — chiefly of a man named Chu Shan who had once snorted at a "fancier than the window" blade, and of what exactly was stamped and what exactly listened, and he made the bevel long again anyway, and Instructor He watched him do it and did not stop him a second time.

*Stamped,* he thought, slipping his chalk notes into his satchel at gate-light. *Or listened to.* He kept both words, in the drawer with the silver-fish sign, which was starting to fill.

## Part 4: Three (day 14, Monday — the year's first official shape)

Monday before first bell, the class board carried a new chalk in a class-board script:

> **NEW-STUDENT TERM ASSESSMENT — 10 WEEKS.**
> **TEAMS OF THREE. SELF-FORMED, SIGNED, FILED BY FRIDAY.**
> **Z.**

The plaza crowd pressed in and began transforming in place into negotiations — Class 1 had officially become a marketplace, currency: each other. Overhead, the cloud of the term's business; underneath, boys and girls trading harmonies and doubts at three voices each.

The market, predictably, found them before the board did.

The bracket had drifted to its usual wall — out of the negotiation crush, the three of them in surveyor's spacing — and it was exactly there that the offers arrived, in the order of everything else at Shrek: fastest first.

"Jin Yang." A girl from the southern rows — House Zhe, Zhe Yun `[design, Class 1]` — ponytail fierce as a flag, two friends bracketed behind her like economic policy. "Team of three. We lack a front. One of any number of boys would answer; I'm asking you because you didn't fall in ten days and I keep accounts."

The ox beside him was opening his mouth with the comprehensive wonder of a man watching lightning count.

Jin Yang answered like a man asked the price of a thing he wasn't selling: "Grateful for the asking, House Zhe. Our three's already together."

Ponytail considered this without offense — Shrek bred them brisk — marked the flank with a glance, and withdrew with her cabinet in good order. "When it isn't," she said.

"You won't last a week waiting," Qiu Yuan murmured behind his hand, delighted and appalled in practically equal shares; and Deng Wu said, still awed, "It counted *ten days*, brother. Nothing escapes these people."

Two more inquiries before the morning bell — one from the twins with the staves `[design]`, politely declined; one from a boy of the crafts rows `[design]` whose entire pamphlet was *steady*, declined with regret — and then the bracket stood alone again at the wall with nothing visibly achieved and everything, in fact, concluded.

The bracket didn't negotiate.

It stood looking at the board in its usual configuration — fence-line spacing, like three boys habitually covering three directions — and Deng Wu said, with pain and nobility both, "I'll be understanding, brothers, if you're shopping up—"

"House Deng," said Qiu Yuan, already withdrawing the treaty notebook, "*if*," in the clan-office voice that had no exits. "You may sign first, then, as the one whose name needs the clerks' correction least."

The three of them signed the form against the wall of the corridor, leaning, taking turns with Jin Yang's carpenter pencil, their three names standing four square in a line and nearly even: **JIN YANG · DENG WU · QIU YUAN**.

It took the whole bracket's combined composure not to react when, on their way in, Square Two's other signed name caught their eye — across the yard at the second form-desk — **WANG DONG · XIAO XIAO · HUO YUHAO**, inked in handwriting so confident it was already famous on sight.

Wang Dong caught Jin Yang looking, and wasn't even decent enough to smirk: just touched his fingertips incline-wise to an invisible hat brim, courtly and fake-rustic as a cat in a parlor, like spring bowing at winter.

"Neighborhood teams!" announced Deng Wu, inspired, aggrieved, immensely pleased with them all. "Named north and south of the same *dawn*."

"Oh, *look* at everybody, all matched up," Qiu Yuan said, with genuine warmth and utter irony both in the same voice somehow.

Zhou Yi watched the signatures come in from her sill above the plaza. Unreadable, right hand sheltering chalk-dust, left hand shading her eyes against morning. *Ten weeks,* she was thinking, like someone laying out a whole winter. *Ten weeks to learn what they cost.*

## Part 1: Iron (week 3)

The weighted racks appeared on a Monday, no announcement: rows of dull iron plates with straps, stacked at the drill-ground gate like an unasked question.

"Twenty laps," said Zhou Yi. "Armored. Last one past the post runs twenty more tomorrow before dawn." She looked across them all without appetite for anything they were about to feel. "Class 1 gets one soul, children. Here's where you find out you share it."

The class's young philosophy of suffering met iron, and learned it had been suffering decoratively.

Wang Dong, who would sooner have been on fire than last, went out at a pace to die on. Jin Yang ran his own weather: fifth at first, seventh, settling to a sustainable sixth-place metronome — the ox on one flank and Qiu Yuan on the other, because the bracket had signed its paper Friday and discovered, by lap eight, exactly what paper was worth against iron.

What was worth something: shoulders.

Deng Wu's plate came off at lap eleven into Jin Yang's right hand, and the bracket ran lopsided after that, ox crying quietly, Qiu Yuan counting laps aloud through his nose like prayer beads. Ahead, the sunrise boy had found the end of mornings and was still going anyway out of unbriefed pride, wings night-folded, legs writing checks.

But the whole thing — all of it, all term, as Class 1 later remembered itself becoming Class 1 — happened at the back.

Because at the back, a scrawny boy with a fish-stall body was failing arithmetic in public: steps not reaching, breath not coming, plate heavier than he was, twenty laps plainly seven laps more than he had in him. Huo Yuhao was last by half a lap and getting laster. The post was already out of air standing at it. *Who's last* is the only arithmetic Zhou Yi had set, and everyone in the class, running around their own flames, did it once a lap at the back of their heads.

Jin Yang didn't think it in the tallies. What he thought, at lap sixteen, was his grandfather's, out of the dark around a winter fire: *you never let a man go down on the road ahead of you and not go back, boy. That's the only rule that's also chain-mail.*

He dropped back. No words. Natural as evening — the Block, easing off his own weather, settling in half a stride to the boy's left rear shoulder where Zhe Yun's pamphlet would have called it *carry-duty spacing*, all the dignity of a boy choosing to be slower than he was. Twenty minutes' teaching that was just being where a falling boy's shoulder wanted company.

It cannot be said what linked to what, after that. Wang Dong, doubling back belated and horrified and somehow loftily furious, took the other shoulder without asking, as though he had trademarks on the lane. Deng Wu and Xiaolei, sooner or later. Zhu Lu, dry-eyed and sharp. Qiu Yuan, gasping. The class, lap by lap, by ones and pairs, without anyone's speech, piling back into last place until the slowest boy in school history was running inside a moving wall of mostly-strangers who had elected him their pace.

At lap twenty-one Zhou Yi watched the front of the pack come around the post all together, ragged and molten, carrying in their midst a boy who could hardly lift a foot — Huo Yuhao's face running with water he hadn't the air left to be ashamed of — and finish line etiquette had broken down entirely. There was no last.

"Tomorrow," she said, when she could be heard over the panting, with the thinnest line at the corner of her mouth that her class had yet earned, "no armor."

Nobody cheered, for lack of equipment. But Class 1 found, going home under the lamps, strewn across its corridor like the dead who had grown chatty, that it had in fact run together — and run into something, though nobody said what. The way weather meets the ground of a place, and after it rains everything is that place a little more.

## Part 2: Fish, By the Lake (week 5)

Shrek Academy's lake shore, lit with stalls on free evenings, had been going about its own business long before any of them enrolled. The bracket went down to the lake the first time as the poor and the news-hungry go anywhere — Qiu Yuan navigating, Deng Wu sniffing, Jin Yang following with his whole seven-silver week about him and no plans for most of it.

And there, where the smoke smelled like somebody who meant it, was their class's back-of-the-pack boy, barbecuing fish at a little stand with the efficient serenity of a much older soul. Two copper a skewer. *Yuhao's grilled fish*, the wing had already learned to call it, first thing It had learned about him when it found out he was doing it *for rent*.

"Brother," said Deng Wu, moved past protocols. He held up fingers like a man ordering weather. "Six."

They paid from the common purse the treaty still didn't have, because folk are descended from wolves wherever you find them, and stood by the stall's little edge of fire with their sticks and their day, and — because the shore's whole plot was older than their worries — watched everything there was to see.

They weren't the only ones watching. Down the shore a small snow-pale girl was buying skewers with the regularity of custom. They knew her by corridor-sight — Jiang Nannan of the second class. And three older outer-court boys knew who she was, too. They got in the way of her evening at the stall's edge, with the kind of senior swagger that assumes only some people are real.

What happened next was a lesson in what kinds of people are real.

A tall youth came out of the dusk and dropped *into* the swagger like Providence with a broad chest and a genuinely foul mood — Xu Sanshi, they would all know soon, of the fifth year, unfathomable to Children — and the three swaggers were re-sorted into various horizontal attitudes with the brisk efficiency of waste management. Then, because the scuffle had gone through half the stall, he reached into his sash without looking, took out two gold soul coins, and laid them on Huo Yuhao's board like weather clearing.

"For the fish," he said, neither asking pardon nor granting it. "The rest was on the collateral." He reclaimed the girl's company with the profound relief of a man re-entering a temple, and the two of them went up the shore path, snow and stone.

Two gold. More at a stroke than Jin Yang had touched in a month at White Birch market. Yuhao, behind his counter, just went on flipping fish to the next customer as though comets did this nightly — calm already the shape of a town.

Only the stall smoke had opinions, drifting up over the lake. Qiu Yuan, in the tone of a man entering data onto stone: "*Fifth year*." Deng Wu, reverently: "Two *gold*." And Jin Yang, eleven, skewer cooling in his hand, simply fixed the moment away. What he had seen was economics with shoulders — two kinds of strength hurrying past each other on one little plank. The kind of moment you get up tomorrow and forge toward. The running that goes somewhere.

## Part 3: The Works (weeks 6–10)

There came a morning — week six, hall Sundays settled to habit by then — Instructor He took his tea down the steps to the hall doors and stood looking out into the yard for a long minute, because a boy with fish-smoke hands and Class 1 sleeves was being walked in at the superintendent's elbow, and the superintendent was Teacher Zhou's own husband.

Fan Yu of the soul-guidance division had the calm of men who run furnaces and have opinions about everything human passing through them. The yard masters bowed. The works hummed on. Jin Yang, breaking wire at tolerance-station six, was a small enough sight to miss. But Huo Yuhao, coming through the big doors on the first day of the rest of his life, looked around the hall with a stranger's care. He kept looking. At the far bench he found, mildly surprised, the boy who had once dropped back beside him at sixteen laps for no reason anyone had said out loud.

Two beats. No words were available yet at that distance. Huo Yuhao nodded — the nod the whole class had learned to read since the run, the one that meant *counted*.

"Knowledge is counted here," said Instructor He, at Jin Yang's elbow, watching the quiet boy walk the works at the superintendent's elbow. The instructor didn't smile, but he had that settled-around-the-eyes look of a man watching his hall become relevant to canon's own train-track. "Now it matters what you've already been becoming here, boy. The School has begun its real division — watch it. Remember where you stood to see it."

"Yes, teacher."

"And bring your square-foot in Saturday. Your tolerances are ready for coin."

So weeks six through ten, in the ledger of hands, went like this: two mornings of real silver, earned on fitted edges the catalog buys and the press can't hear; five Saturdays without missing bell; one small lime-scorched thumbnail. Zhou Yi's classroom went from gates to grind: stance ladders, three-element drills for the teams, filing still gospel. The bracket came apart and back together daily, as all good instruments do. They found their instinct in October-fine: ox forward in patience, like weather-forecast thunder. Qiu Yuan overhead in the picture's rear-corner, his accuracy up a full letter-grade since he had started calling everything *reports*. And at the block between them, one boy dependable as a sledge on a chisel.

Sundays aside, they saw the fish-stall boy only at speed. Division boys lived in canon's own fast lane. But once in a while, at the yard wall in second bell, somebody would say — *division's littlest one teaches them metal while still chewing rice*, or *they say the superintendent took the quiet one* — and a small warmth would pass along Class 1's bench, irrationally, how houses are warmed by fires burning three rooms over.

## Part 4: The Series (week 11)

Wang Dong took Square Two the eighth time, eighth week of card: 3–0.

The ninth time, at eleven weeks, it went differently, and the whole wing was restructured by the news before twilight.

What changed was eleven weeks' worth of changes, plus one extra gear nobody had filed yet out of the boy who everyone nevertheless filed compulsively for reasons they could no more resist than the road. It happened at two-and-a-half touches, chalk-line balance. Wang Dong glided in for the finish, his octobered speed tuned to the post's now-famous compass. And the Block was gone — not from the square, but from the spot the sunrise's eyes were already deciding was his. He came back in with his shoulder instead of his stance. And touched Wang Dong on the scapula with his knuckles, as politely as knocking at a door.

Three to one. First touch, eight bouts in coming, no crowd.

The square detonated anyway. Girls sat down on the lime. Qiu Yuan, forgetting cavalry, climbed a post. Deng Wu lost the power of sentence in both of his languages. Zhou Yi's chalk, by its register's edge, *did not write the score* for a full second — and then did, even-handedly, with a small renewed interest in her whole life.

Wang Dong did the only rational sunrise thing. He stood there with a hand on the touched spot, staring at nothing, delighted. Then he pointed like a duelist, at close range. Unclean triumph in every syllable —

"**THE WARRANTY IS EXPIRING.**"

"The warranty," Jin Yang agreed, breathing from the real third hour of his life, "is expiring."

## Part 5: Ninety Days Later (week 12, assessment-eve)

The notice went up on the class board on the first morning of the third month, in the hand they had all learned to read faster than they'd learned some people's:

> **THE NEW-STUDENT ASSESSMENT. CLASS 1 SECTION B PUTS OUT AT SIX.**
> **TEAMS SIGNED. SQUARES CIRCUIT, EAST GROUNDS.**
> **NOW I KNOW EACH OF YOU.**
> **Z.**

*Now I know each of you.* Qiu Yuan, arriving first at the board, stood and accounted for winter silently at the bottom of the page — it was the phrase's fourth month in his files, promised long since on a teacher's sill above a plaza he had stood by, and kept.

The bracket stood at their wall before sixth bell like priests at the new year. They hadn't said *assessment* aloud since signing, because Shrek gives children nerves as spring gives streams flood. The purse was 24 gold 1 silver (the dividends of small silver in the works, the common purse still refused). The body of the weatherman's boy went eighteen minutes now in the cold dawn rites where it had once gone twelve; his square series with the sunrise stood at many-to-one, one; the two coins' memory from the lakeside still did arithmetic in the back of his head when things like tridents and fifth-years crossed his mind. The ox fell well now, and started up like morning rain. The treasurer had filed three hundred and eleven reports, all of them eventually read.

Deng Wu straightened, enormity fitting him these days like a doorframe.

"Brothers," he said. "I have only one superstition left."

"Have the others been paid out?"

"Burned, brother. Wages of the square." The ox took a breath, old hills around the shrine of his face. "One superstition. Before a work that bends a family's story, say where it stands when it's bent."

There was a silence the treaty would have knighted.

"Third," said Qiu Yuan, at last, irreversible with quiet. "We're third. Behind the sunrise's three and the cold ones. Nothing else, this month, guesses closer than that, on my books."

"Third it is," Jin Yang said — the smallest agreement of all; a number to walk out onto a field in the morning with in your teeth. And because he was a boy raised in the country of full baskets and plain-speaking men, under the eaves of three months of learning what school is, he said the true thing too, without lighting on it: "Whatever's bent there, when it's bent — all three names still on it."

The bell woke up the grounds. By the east gate the squares were already taking their lime from the morning, four by four, pale in the mist like rules that had decided to be weather. Huo Yuhao's team turned in at the far arch together — division hours on his sleeves; Xiao Xiao spinning a kettle of steady cheer at his elbow; Wang Dong arriving as day does over hills, looking for someone specific, and finding him with a rival's whole month in his eyes.

*Third,* the legs, fine, knew by heart, coming down the row. *Bow to the line; walk in.*

The assessment began as all prophecies do: with chalk, breath, registration paper, and the noise children make when they realize there is now nowhere further to wait.

## Part 1: What a Team Is (day 1)

"The assessment," said Zhou Yi, "is not a tournament for children who want applause. It is the School taking attendance of the future. Humor the terminology-from today, because the examiners will: **an assault-system soul master does not stand where his safety-system brother must stand. A control-system soul master does not do the assault's dying for him. You have been a class.**" The chalk made four columns on the board — assault, defense, control, sub-support — and raked them with a line like frost across a window. "From this week you are instruments. Stands are carved by the team, not the boy. Square three will pair mixed, square four will pair real, and God help the team that picks its three favorite friends and calls the mixture a formation."

The class laughed the thin laugh of people who had all picked their three favorite friends.

"Filed," Qiu Yuan breathed, two seats over, with the shiver of a man watching his whole world arch into regulation. Jin Yang, beside him, was doing different arithmetic under the lecture's noise: the bracket's three names, the four column names, the honest holes between them.

*Ox: front-stand, close, patient — defense.* *Weigh-man: seeing, angles — control, or near it.* *And the post between them…* The smith's boy looked down at his own hands. Eleven and hammer-worn. Two rings that belonged to none of the four columns in any way he could feel proud of. He thought what boys in his village thought when the harvest chart came out strange: *the chart is not the field. The field is what stands in it.*

Still. The columns were the first piece of school language that smelled, even faintly, of craft.

## Part 2: The Class Walks the Works (day 3 — canon ch 10, caught late: G-row logged)

Tuesday's third hour, the notice on the course slate read: *Class 1 — Soul-Guidance Works orientation. Attendance compulsory.*

The whole corridor went down the east slope in a chattering clot — most of them stepping into the giant furnace-hall for the first time in their lives: sixty-odd freshmen milling under the big beams, goggling up at the presses like calves in a cathedral, while masters in forge-aprons went on about their business with the unbothered speed of weather.

Instructor He and two colleagues did the walking — the founding speech, plain as bread: the age of the soul-tool, the age of the tool that thinks for you, the wars fought since the forging machines grew wings. The class drank it in a version of silence.

Jin Yang walked near the back, in the strange billow of a boy revisiting a place through sixty fresher pairs of eyes.

He watched Huo Yuhao most of all. Not spying — how you watch weather when weather matters *this* week. The fish-stall boy stopped longest at the tolerance benches, head bent over a machine-formed edge. Nobody could see what his eyes were doing there. But his quiet was the kind the bracket's own post recognized from classrooms. A boy receiving a second education through his pupils while the first one went on around him. *Division-bound,* Jin Yang thought, unjealous, filing it in the language of hammering: *different ore. Same earth.*

At the hall's far end, his own bench — tolerance-station six, his edge-scraps still pinned to the blotting-board — a master leaned over and noticed a freshman standing beside it with the proprietary patience of somebody home.

"And yours?" the master said, eyes crinkling toward Instructor He.

"Six Sundays," said Instructor He dryly, from under his tea. "The boy with the spare key."

By evening there were eleven new dark-fingered freshmen sworn to weekend visitation, and the wing's talk of the works had changed its sound, and the block of Class 1 said nothing at supper about having stood at center of anything. The ox said it for all of them without being quite sure what he meant: "Brother, the hall looks *smaller* once they've all breathed in it."

"No," said Qiu Yuan, with rare quiet accuracy. "The class got bigger."

## Part 3: The Spring (day 4, evening — the lake stall; G09 paid)

Thursday dusk: a first-autumn wind off the water, smoke-thread rising from the stall line, and the bracket at *their* boards by now — which is to say, at Huo Yuhao's fish counter at the hour the regulars thinned and the owner could finally lean on his own stack of skewers and let his shoulders come down from the day.

They were trading weather for fish, the standing economy of the shore. Deng Wu demolishing. Qiu Yuan interrogating the menu's margins. Jin Yang paying by the old rule of his purse. Then the proud young woman two stalls up — the pretty-sharp one with the river-governor skirt and the flickable temper — cursed in a most un-lake-like register, and shook out of her sleeve a thing that went *tik* and clattered to the counter in pieces.

Tang Ya of the Tang Sect scooped it up and sat glaring at the world as though the mechanism had betrayed HER.

"Third time this week, sister Tang," said Bei Bei, mildly, from the neighboring stall — big-brother calm, big-sleeve grace, and the tribal patience of somebody who has watched many springs die of over-enthusiasm. "The sleeve-box hates rebuilds in this damp. You should let it rest at the workshop."

"Let it rest," the sect-master of the Tang Sect echoed, dangerous with innocence. "The legendary hidden weapons of the glorious past, *resting*. I can see the ancestors *resting* — oh, hush, they've felt worse rooms than mine—"

And her sleeve spilled again the little dismemberers of her trade: the spring-coil, three tiny feather-pale darts. Then the whole cursed thing, mechanism and all, rattled loose onto the fish-counter between the stalls, and slid. It came to rest against Jin Yang's five fingers, which had come down over it like the lid of a toolbox, half out of reflex.

The shore hushed itself as shores do.

What the boy from White Birch Province was holding was a failure of manufacture. The spring-coil was mis-seated by less than a wheat-grain's thickness; the feather-darts had picked up grit between their folds; the firing-lever wore a burr where — *three minutes on Wei's bench, old bench files, one heat, one polish, half a thought* — where in his family's forge, this would have been finished work before the tea got cold. All of it crossed his face, unmerchantlike, entirely legible to the two people watching him hold the broken thing.

Jin Yang did what White Birch men do before saying anything about somebody else's tools: he set the pieces down, aligned, exactly where he'd found them, and said with careful, vagrant-boy respect: "The spring's seating shifted. Not the spring's fault. The seat just needs closing half a grain, and the lever wants ten seconds at a light file."

Tang Ya stared at him.

"Half a *grain*," she repeated, not mockingly… precisely. "And the lever — *ten seconds*?"

"At a fine file," said Jin Yang. "Coarse would eat it."

"Bei Bei." Tang Ya turned on her senior brother with her face absolutely blazing, speaking in the rapid whisper of people who have just received divine instruction at a fish stall. "Do you see. The marble-hall students of majestic Shrek walk past my broken box every day for *three years* — and this boy, in less time than it takes to order dinner— do you *see*— we can't— he *already* speaks hidden weapon! This isn't recruitment, this is *reclamation*—"

"Deep breaths, sect-master Tang," said Bei Bei, smiling at last with something that was not wholly mild. "I see it."

What with one thing and another — the two gold on the board from three weeks ago, the calm fish-stall boy sliding to the stall's far side, the whole shore tucking its knowledge quietly away — what with all of it, the next minutes moved like a rope's end finally finding its splice. (Sect-brothers, everyone would learn much later, run errands about one another like departments of a very small weather system.)

Tang Ya planted herself in front of Jin Yang, folded arms, and looked *up* into the face of the tallest boy of the bracket with the full momentum of the Tang Sect's several thousand years sailing visibly in her stern little body.

"Name."

"Jin Yang. White Birch Province."

"Your people. Smiths?"

"Three generations back before me. Iron, farm-gear, and winter mending. My grandfather added anvil-keeping to weather-watching," he said plainly, and then, because evasion had never been a White Birch crop: "My family grew up on the Tang Sect's legends, sirs. The old stories. The heroes before there were soul tools to name them. We were told them for winter work."

*That* stopped even Tang Ya a moment.

"The old stories," she said, more quietly. "You listened in the winters." Her chin came up like a banner lighting. "Then hear a new story, boy from White Birch. The heroes you were told about came out of a brotherhood that the soul-tools age is even now swallowing, an inch at a time — and the Tang Sect is not dead. It is *small*. There's a difference. You're looking at its head. And it wants, for the first time since your grandfather's grandfather had his hair, a smith's apprentice-mind with three generations of anvil-nerves in his hands and a weather-eye in his brain — to learn our techniques, our hidden weapons, and *everything else we are*, in exchange for a promise to be something it can be proud of, somewhere it can no longer reach."

"Yuhao," Bei Bei said, warmly, over the stall's little fire, not looking up, "you're about to have a small sect to look after."

"The little one's already troublesome," Tang Ya fired at him without heat, in the voice siblings are made of. "Sect-brother senior!" she declared to Jin Yang, with the glee of a fortune she fully meant to keep properly. "Say it back to your senior, so I can see whether you can do it without choking—"

Huo Yuhao, behind his board, set his knife down with the kind of perfect dignity reserved for these lake-side ambushes — and looked across, full-faced, at the boy who had once dropped back half a lap for him in the iron, and smiled without any staging at all: tired, small, entirely real.

"Sect-brother," Huo Yuhao said.

In the pond of clear evening quiet after the word, Jin Yang from White Birch Province — son of anvils, admitted student of monsters, the standing post of Class 1 — stood looking between the brothers and sisters this age had managed to leave: the legendary brotherhood patched and poor around a lakeside fish fire, still deciding not to die.

"Sect-brother senior," he answered, steadily, without choking. To *both* of them.

## Part 4: The Old Man Is There (day 4, night)

On the way back through the dormitory gate, the lamplight lay down the passage like a measuring tape of brass, and at the gate's foot the old doorkeeper dozed in his chair as usual, at midnight's first edge, all bones and weathered plainness, no crest anywhere on him, no weight in the world that Shrek usually bothers weighing.

Deng Wu, ahead, bumbled through the gate unthinking, lore-drunk on sect-tales. Qiu Yuan was already three corridors deep in contingency-filings about the sect economy. Jin Yang stopped.

No one at Shrek stopped for the old man. The boys of the wing had two years of afternoon practice at not-stopping. The old custodian's hour-strung face lay open to the lamp like a page that hadn't been picked up from the floor.

"Old man holds the gate," thought the boy who had been raised by people who hold gates.

He could not have entirely said why he did it, only that the village of his bones found it intolerable to go into a warm building past a man asleep in a draft, unacknowledged. He stopped and — young-loud as a door-brace being driven home — said, "Good night, old man. The gate's watched over well this year, and we don't thank it nearly loud enough."

The old gatekeeper's eyes never opened. One could almost have believed the mild face hadn't heard. Except the old man murmured — sleepily, shatteringly gentle, all age and quiet — "Gate doesn't thank back, boy. **On, go; nights are for your own candle, not for standing in mine.**"

A little draft of mild warmth seemed to pass the passage, nothing more. Jin Yang bowed an inch lower than he had intended, and went on up the steps feeling slightly scalded and inexplicably soothed.

(He would come back, of course. He would, without ever once being told why, make a whole habit out of that gate's mostly-sleeping tenant. That is the end of what this chapter can prove.)

## Part 5: Eve (day 5, before the divide)

The bracket's wall, last light: the lamp-dole done, and the school breathing around them the breath of a place existence-tested tomorrow.

"He joined it," Qiu Yuan said. It wasn't triumph; it was reverence, bankerly. "The *Tang Sect*. The one from the legends. The boy signs with the *folklore* anchored to his ancestry — I keep the boy between an ox and a ridiculous amount of weather-henceforth prognostication, and he *brings home the sect of heroes*—"

"The quiet at the stall though," Deng Wu said, slowly — the ox had said little of it all evening, generous consternation working through his mountain of loyalty. "When senior-fish-brother said the word back. Brother." He looked across at Jin Yang with the world's most guileless astonishment forming on the great porch of his face. "You feel like home now. You felt like one of us before, it is true. But something got *younger* in you today, at the shore. For the first time I seen anything get younger in you."

Jin Yang, half-silhouetted in the sundown rest, did not answer right off. He had the manual of the Xuantian Skill folded small in his inner robe-pocket, like a fresh-winter woodnote. The Mysterious Jade Hand's first six movements stood pressed into knuckle-memory from Bei Bei's two lantern-hours' showing at the fence behind the works. and at stall-adjusted mathematics, the whole exchange — the spring, the seat, the reel of smallest machines the ancestors left behind — sat very small, and very solid, against the great big machines thumping away east of the dormitories.

He picked up his slate; wiped its whole day clean; with the carpenter-pencil drew, once and only once, the same small neat figure his father chalked on the shed-beams back home at every good closing: the slant-ticked five of a ledger summed out. He pressed the chalk down through the centermost line.

"Some legends," said the weatherman's boy, "aren't for your remembering."

His eyes left the shed-beam figure and found the arc-lamps — no — the east-gate sky, which had sluiced itself properly toward dark while they spoke, as if the weather itself were filing.

"They're for closing the seam they're meant for. And tomorrow," he said, cool as the chalk the whole wall knew by heart: "the assessment counts a seam. So get up at dawn."

# Chapter 1: The First Hunger

The shell had been a wall for as long as he had been anything, and then it hurt. That was the first thing: the shell pressing in from every side at once, water-tightness giving way to a thin, cold wet seeping in, and something in him that had been waiting a very long time deciding that it was done waiting. He pushed. The push was not a thing he chose. It came up out of his back and his neck and his legs together, like a cough coming up out of a chest, and the shell split somewhere near his head with a small sharp sound.

Light came through the split. It was white and thin and it hurt too, and he did not know it was light, only that the world beyond the shell was colder and louder than the world inside it.

He worked himself free, half pushing and half falling, and then he was lying on his side on hard wet ground with the pieces of the shell under him and the wind moving over his skin. The wind was the second thing. It was cold and it did not stop, and his skin was wrong for it: soft, pale, thin, no armor to it at all. He curled up, and his own body was the only warm thing anywhere.

Something in him was already working. He had no word for it and no thought about it. Even then, in the first minutes, it was going quietly about its business as it had in the egg, taking the cold and pushing back with something that was not quite warmth and not quite skin, a slow thickening that would show only later. It never stopped. It never slept. Every hard thing that happened to him after that would be met by that slow answering.

He was hungry. That was the third thing, and it was the biggest.

The hunger did not arrive and leave like the wind. It lived in him, low and steady, older than his eyes. It was there before he had eyes to see the mountain with, and it would be there when his eyes were done. It said one word, always: eat.

So he turned his head and ate the shell. The pieces were dry and sharp and they cut the inside of his mouth, and he ate them anyway, all of them he could reach, and then he lay still and felt something of the shell stay in him, a warmth that spread out through his belly and reached, faintly, into his legs and his tail. It was the first lesson the world gave him, and it was simple. What he ate became him.

---

The mountain was not built for something as small as he was. He learned that in the first days. His scales were pale and soft and the cold went through them. His legs were thick and clumsy under a body too light for them. His tail was too long and got in the way when he turned, and his head was too heavy for his neck, so he moved as new things move: badly, and often downhill.

He fell off a rock shelf on the second day and lay at the bottom of it for a while, stunned, and then he got up and went on, because the hunger did not care about the fall. The hunger kept his time. It rose and he obeyed it and it went quiet for a while, and the quiet was the only rest he had. He drank at a seep where the water came out of the stone cold and clean, and learned to come back to it. He learned where the sun lay longest on the rocks, and lay there. He learned to keep to the low ground when the wind got up.

He learned the slope as water learns it. By going down it many times.

There was a seam of rock near the top of his hollow that held the sun all afternoon, and beetles worked in the grit of it — the smallest soul beasts of the mountain, too small to have years worth counting, slow and armored and stupid. He learned to catch them. He got his first one with a clumsy snap of his jaws and crunched it shell and all, and the hunger said eat, and after that he went back to the seam every warm afternoon and crouched in the grit with his nose down, waiting.

There was a lower slope where the stone went soft and wet and the seep ran down it in a green thread, and blue silver grass grew along the thread. It was thin grass with a silver vein in every blade, the commonest soul beast of the whole world, and it was worth nothing to anything that counts years. He ate some of it anyway when the hunger was bad and there was nothing else. It tasted like wet stone. It kept him walking.

And there was a broken pine low on the slope with a hole in its heart, and things nested there. Small things with beaks.

He learned about the beaks on the third evening, when he put his head into the hole out of the plainest hunger he had ever felt. Something in the dark stabbed him above the eye, twice, fast, and he pulled his head back and the whole side of his face was suddenly hot and wet. He sat down in the fern and licked the hurt until it stopped, and after that he walked past the pine slowly, every time, on the downhill side. That was the first rule the mountain taught him that he never once had to be taught again: the things that live in the dark can hurt you even when they are small.

---

The first true hunt was for the stone-runners. They lived in the talus where the slope went wide — low, thick, quick things the color of the rock they lived in, with small eyes and a fatness about them that the hunger could feel from across the stones. They came out when the sun did and sat up on their haunches and looked around, and they ran between the rocks along paths they had worn smooth.

He wanted one. He wanted it as he had wanted the shell.

He went at the first one straight, fast, all at once, as the hunger told him to go. He was two paces away when it saw him, and it was gone into a crack between two stones before he reached the spot, and he hit the boulder behind it shoulder-first and lay there with his ears ringing.

He tried again that evening. Same thing. Again the next morning.

The third morning he did not go at anything. He lay down in the sun on the warm side of the talus with his chin on his forelegs and watched.

He watched the runners for a whole day. He watched where they came out, and where they went back in, and which cracks were too narrow for a body his size, and which rocks they liked to sit on — the same three rocks, all morning, over and over. He watched one of them dig at the grit with its small hands and stand up and look at nothing at all for a long time.

Something in him settled while he watched. It was not that the hunger went away. It stayed exactly where it always was, low and steady, saying eat. But the running and snapping part of him went quiet and lay down behind the watching part, and the quiet felt like the right shape for the moment, though he had no words for it and never looked at it directly.

He lay on the warm rock until evening. Then he went down the talus on the downhill side, into the place where the runners' paths all came together between two boulders, and he got low in the grit there and waited.

It took a long time. The light went orange and then grey. Twice a runner came close and he felt the go-fast part of him jump in his chest, and both times he held it down and lay still, and both times the runner turned aside at the last moment and went another way.

Then one came along the path in the last of the light, hurrying, and it did not see him until it was almost on him. He came up out of the grit.

It broke left. He had watched them break left at that spot for two days. He was already moving left when it moved, and his jaws closed on it, and it was done.

The thing kicked twice and stopped. He stood over it with his whole body shaking, and the shaking was not fear. It was something else, hot and simple, and it wanted more.

He ate it down to the bones and the pelt and most of the bones. When the fullness came, the sleep came with it, and the sleep was the deepest thing he had ever felt. It came down on him like stone out of the sky. He lay in the grit beside the bones of his first kill and slept through the night and most of the next day, and while he slept the meat worked in him, thickening his legs, hardening the first of his scales from pale to grey.

He woke bigger. He did not know that yet. He only knew that the world smelled stronger than it had, and that he was hungry again.

---

The great wings came back on the fifth day, and he learned the law of the mountain. He was on the warm rock above his hollow when the shadow went over him. He looked up, and there was a winged thing crossing the valley, wide as three of him laid end to end, with a long neck and a stillness in how it held itself that he knew at once, as a small thing knows a large thing, without being told.

It was not hunting him. It was not hunting anything. It was riding the warm air above the valley as a leaf rides water, and the whole valley watched it, and nothing moved that did not have to.

Then the wings went down the far side of the valley to a stand of old trees, and something happened there that he saw only in pieces: a rush, a cracking of branches, a high thin crying that stopped. When the wings came back up, they carried something.

He sat on his rock with his whole body still and his eyes wide, and something in him stood up and reached toward the wings. That was the strangest thing of his short life. It was not fear. His fear was already there, flat and complete, the fear of a small thing under a big thing. But under the fear, one layer lower, there was a pull. The same hot simple pull that had shaken him over the stone-runner, only taller. It said: I should have that. It said it about a creature that could have carried him off without noticing.

The pull rose until his legs were trembling with it and his jaws were wet, and the wings went by overhead, close enough that the wind of them pushed him flat against the rock, and nothing happened at all. They did not see him. They were not looking.

He stayed flat on the rock until dark. That was the second rule, and it was harder than the first: what lives above the mountain is not food. Not yet. Not while the pull in him could make him stand up and shiver at the edge of a rock and be seen.

He never let the pull stand him up again. He would think about that rule for years afterward, in worse places, with better reasons.

---

The days made their habit after that. Hunger, hunt, feed, sleep, hunger. The first winter came at him slowly — a cold that went from uncomfortable to hard, and the stone-runners going fat and then scarce, and the beetles gone from the rock seam, and the grass at the seep going brown, and the wind coming down off the peaks at night with a smell like iron on it.

He was bigger than the hatchling had been. The grey had come into his scales from nose to tail now, and the muscle under them was real muscle, and he had learned to dig out a stone-runner's crack with his hands when the weather made the hunters lazy. He was still small. He knew that now, because he had the wings to measure against.

He was hungry all the time, and he did not die, and those were the two small facts of his first season in the world. Then, in the last grey days before the real cold, the wind brought him something and it was new.

It came from beyond the shoulder of the mountain, up beyond the pass, on a wind that had crossed snow to get to him. It was a thin smell, and it was not the smell of any beast or any green thing or any water. It was smoke, though he had no name for smoke. Under the smoke there was a smell like wet iron and a smell like the inside of a cave, and under both of those, faint and strange and impossible to place, the smell of something that walked on two legs.

He stood on the slope with his nose up for a long time. Nothing in him had a shape for it. Nothing in his world had ever had it. It was exactly the size of a fear and it did not feel like any fear he had met yet, because fear came with the thing that made it, and this thing was far off and did not know about him at all. That made it worse, in a way he could not have explained to anyone.

He did not go toward it. He did not go away from it either. He turned his back on the pass and went down-slope to his hollow and slept badly, and in the morning the wind had turned and the smell was gone.

He kept it anyway. He put it in the same place he kept the beaks and the wings and the crack in the talus where the runners lived. There was nothing to do with it yet. There was nothing to do with a thing that far away.

But he remembered it, and that was the whole of the danger: he was the kind of creature that remembers. When the last of the warmth went out of the ground, and the water at the seep froze at the edges at night, and the stone-runners went into their cracks for good, he climbed up the slope one evening and stood looking down the long grey country toward the smoke side of the mountain and away from it both.

The cold was coming. He did not know what winter was. He had never seen one.

He turned down into the hollow, out of the wind, and lay down with his head on his forelegs, and the hunger said eat, and there was nothing to eat, and so he slept. That was the first season of the world.
