By the grey days at the end of the winter he could come down through a stand of feeding hare-kinds and take one off the end of the line with the rest never lifting their heads. The quiet that had been a way of hunting had become a way of being.

---

And in the still hours, the deep drawing had learned to feed itself. It had begun in the storm, when the fasting had gone past the point of arguing and the pull had turned itself downward into the mountain's own ancient quiet. That had been necessity. What came after was habit. He found, on the long windless afternoons when there was nothing to do and the sun lay thin along the snow, that if he stood still enough and let the hunger stand in him without giving it anything, the drawing opened by itself and took in the mountain's faintness as a rooted thing takes water.

It was thin. It was nothing like the flood of the storm, and it would never feed him like meat. But it was always there, and it cost him nothing, and every hour of it went into the same deep well as everything else he ate.

Sleep went deepest of all. He spent the coldest days of that winter in the old hollow of the fallen giant on the high ground above his valley, a place where a great tree had come down long ago and left a bowl in the earth under a shelf of black stone. The stone there was old — older than the forest around it, old as the ravine country was old — and the drawing went deeper in that hollow than anywhere else he had ever lain. He would go down into it in the grey afternoon and come out of it in the dark, and the faintness of the mountain's old stone would have passed through him the whole time, and he would stand up at the end of it with the hunger that had no meal a little less loud than before.

He did not understand what he was doing. He did not have to. His kind had never had words and had never needed them, and the body learned what it could use as water learns the shape of a country.

---

The thaw came, and the country stood up again, and everything in it knew him. That was the strangest spring of his life. He walked down out of the high ground into the summer, and the summer made room. The low lives came out of the winter thin and hungry and quick, and everywhere he went they went flat and silent before him — the fox dens, the ground-birds, the burrowers, the whole small nation of the country — and it was not as it had been in his second spring, when they had merely feared him. They feared him deeper now, and from farther away, and the older ones among them did something he had no name for.

They gave him ground. Not the ground he was standing on; ground on either side of him, a wide respectful emptiness that walked down the valley with him like an escort.

He walked through the spring with the order standing around him, and the whole bright season with its births and its green and its young was his — his to hunt, and his alone, and no beast in the low country even argued about it. Sometimes, in the evenings, he would remember being a pale soft thing that fell off a rock shelf, and the memory was so far away it might have belonged to another country.

---

The sense of years read the ravine on the first clear spring night. He had kept away from the black ridge all winter, as he kept away from the roof of the world. But the sense of years was new in him and the shape of the country was new in it, and one evening in the first week of the summer he let it run north as he had once let his eyes run, and the ravine answered.

It came back at him as a depth past all depths. The ancient ones of his own country — the old boars, the great grey stags of the high fern, the heavy things that had lived through a hundred winters — burned in his sense like the last coals of a fire. The thing in the ravine was the sun. Its years did not stand up out of it; they went down, and down, past where the sense of years could read, until it bowed out over the edge of the depth and came back with nothing but the fact of it.

Under the depth, thin and clear and singing, the pull ran. His blood answered as it had answered on the ridge in the summer: fear first, flat and complete, and then the other thing, the thing that was not fear, standing up in him along the pull as long as the pull was there.

The feeling was a pull. That was the evening's real news — not the size of the thing in the ravine, which he had known, but what the knowing did inside him. Reading the ravine, with the sense awake, was like standing at the edge of a ledge with the wind at your back: there was a part of him that wanted to go down into the depth as the pull had wanted him to go down to the lodge lights.

He did not go. He had the wide ground habit in him now — the rule of the ridge, kept whole since the first summer — and he put the feel down as a beast puts down a heavy thing it has decided not to carry, and lay in the fern until the pull went quiet.

He would hold that shape, he decided, as he held everything. He would hold it until he grew to the size of it.

---

The men were deeper that spring, and he found their new work at the end of the summer. He had gone east over the pass trail, into the wide country beyond the ridge, hunting the heavy years that stood in his sense out in that direction. And on the third day he came down a long slope into a bowl of country he had never walked, and stopped, because the country below him had been changed by hands.

There was a line across a game trail at the bottom of the bowl — not the bright line of the pass snare; this one was of wire and wood, low and long, worked into the ground at both ends. Beneath it, in the litter of the trail, lay the old tracks of many beasts walking through a place where a beast would want to walk. The ground around the trail's mouth had been swept and re-swept. There were the prints of men, and the prints of spirit hounds, and the ash of a small camp fire, and there were the cut branches of a blind built up off the trail where a watcher could sit.

They had come deeper. The winter's snare at the pass had been the edge of their country; this new one was in the country of the heavier lives, where the years stood thick, and they had built it as a beast builds — patient, and read into the ground.

The hunger ran both ways of the trail. That was what he understood, standing on the slope above their work. He hunted the heavy years, and they hunted the heavy years, and the trail to the heavy years was one trail, and there was no law in the whole low country that could be made to say which of them it belonged to.

It was a race. He had known it since the fern country, and it had never been stated as plainly as it was that afternoon, in the signs left by men's hands on his own range. He went back west at dusk without crossing their line, and the shape sat in him the whole walk home, heavy and clear.

---

The last thing that spring taught him was a truth about his own country, and he did not like it, and it was true. He was hunting the low valley in the last month of the summer. He took a boar-kind, a good heavy one, and ate it down to the bones, and the fullness came up over him warm and complete — and the hunger that had no meal sat up in the middle of it and said, quietly: more.

The country could not feed him. Not any more. A beast could live a hundred winters on the crops of that valley and never go hungry, and he had eaten down past what it had to give in three springs. The heavy years were few and getting fewer. Every season of hunting took the biggest beasts out of his range, and the young of those beasts took ten winters to become heavy again, and he was finishing in a season what the country took a decade to grow.

He lay on the warm rock above his valley in the last of the light and let himself read it plainly, as he read the land: this country was his home, and it had made him, and it could not take him any further. North and east of him, over the black ridge, past the ground of the thing in the ravine, lay the deep forest. Its faintness came to him at the far edge of his sense on the clear nights. It was a place where the more stood thick on the ground, where the years lay as heavy as the boulders. The sense of years had been telling him so all spring. Every clear night, the deep forest stood out beyond the ravine like a banked fire bigger than all the fires of his range put together.

The pull that had brought him here from the slope had been a pull of belonging. The pull now was different. It was the pull of need, and it pointed into the deep forest the same way the sense of years pointed at heavy years, and both of them pointed north.

He held the shape without deciding anything. That was the only honest thing to do with it, and the beast in him knew it: the country that made him was watching him, and the roof of the world lay between him and what he needed, and nothing was ready yet — not the season, not his own weight, not the crossing of the ravine.

He sat on the warm rock until the last of the light was gone, with the whole low country laid out in his sense, heavy and thin, and the deep forest banked at the northern edge of it like a fire that would not go out. Then he went down to his roots-house and slept, and the shape went down with him, and waited.

---

He worked his way down the slope along the high side until the wind brought him voices. He lay above the camp with the whole picture of their work in front of him.

"A line here, and a line at the second spring," said the man with the axe. He was a broad man with his sleeves cut off and he was notching a post as he spoke. "That closes the ground. Anything in that ground comes to one of the two, and the run between them is a day. We can work both lines out of one camp."

"The ground is too big for one camp," said the younger one. He was sitting on a stone with a skin of water, watching the hound. "We had three men at the water and two came home."

"Then we build the fence," said the first. "You build the fence at the second spring and we work the ground in two halves. That is the trade. Your line is short and the fence is long, and the fence will stand past the thaw."

"Do we have the wire for a wall that long?"

"We have the wire off the old water line," said the first man. "The line at the water was pulled when the permits came, and every length of it is coiled in the store at the lodge. Wire goes round a wall as well as it goes across a trail."

"What did the water give us last season?" said the younger one.

"Four lights and the pelts, and the lodge took half of both," said the axe man.

"Half."

"Half, and the ground, and the wire, and the man who argues with the list in the ninth month."

The younger one looked up at the bowl, at the ground the men were closing inside it, and did not answer. The hound got up from the ground, walked to him, and stood with its muzzle against his leg, and his hand went down onto its head without his looking at it.

"Say it," said the man with the axe.

"The ground here has been worked before," said the younger one. "The sign on the north side was left by a hunting line, and it is nine years old, and the man who made it is not on this list. Somebody's granduncle had this ground and lost it."

"Then somebody's granduncle was careless."

"Or something up there was patient."

The axe man put the post down. He wiped his hands on his coat and waited.

"Nine years," he said. "Nine years and no line in it, and the beasts have been breeding in there the whole time. That is not patience. That is good ground going to waste. We will take four lights out of it this season and six the season after, and the sign we leave will be the sign the next man reads."

"And the north side?"

"We put a line on the north side too," said the man with the axe. "That is the whole point of the north side."

"How long will the fence take?"

"One man, a hundred paces of wire, and twelve days."

"Then we sleep in the camp."

"We sleep in the camp, and we eat out of it, and in the spring it is ours."

The boy came up from the stream with the water and set the skin down by the stones. The hound took two steps toward the north ridge and stood, and the man with the axe called it back.

"Nothing up there but trees," he said.

The boy looked at the ridge without answering, and went to build the fire. The hound lay down by the fire with its head toward the north.

"The camp goes in the book with a name on it either way," the axe man said. "That is the part that matters. A camp with our line in it is ours to work. A camp with no line in it is a fight every time we come up."

He drove the post. The sound went up the slope to where the dragon lay in the high grass, one dull knock after another, steady and slow, all the afternoon.

# Chapter 8: The Deep Country

The deciding was not a moment. It never had been, and this one was less of a moment than most.

The shape had been sitting in him since the last spring — the need pointing north, the barrier of the ravine between, the deep forest banked beyond it like a fire — and one morning at the end of the summer he simply woke up doing it. He went down to the stream bend and drank, and then he turned north instead of going to his den, and the walking was the deciding, and he did not turn around again.

He stopped once, on the high fern slope, and looked back at his own country. There it lay: the slope where the shell had split, the rock seam and the talus with the stone-runners wintering under it, the broken pine, the seep, the stream bend, his roots-house with its two ways. His range, whole and small and his, laid out in the morning sun. He looked at it as a beast looks at a thing it is putting down, and then he lifted his head and went on north toward the black ridge.

He did not know whether he would ever see it again. He did not think in those terms. But something in him made the look, and gave the country its due, and only then let him go.

---

He crossed the serpent's ground on the third day, and it took him the whole of that day to do it, and half of what he knew he did not do at all — he simply stopped being a thing that could be seen. the sense of the ground had taken him all spring. He knew the shape of the ravine country as he knew his own valley: where the black ground began, where the trees stopped growing straight, where the weight lay thinnest. The old ones have their own kind of quiet. The weight of the great thing in the ravine thinned in the deep hot hours of the day, when all the ancient lives of the country lay down in the heat and let their eyes close, and he went in the quiet, in the middle of the day, by the high rim of the ground and never through its heart.

He held the quiet from the first step. It had never been strained like this. He held it whole, over the whole of himself, as a beast holds a breath down deep, and he walked the rim of the ravine country with his body low and slow, up where the old stone lay bare and the trees came apart, watching the ravine the whole time with every sense he had.

Halfway across, it moved. There was no sound. The weight simply turned over, as a sleeper turns in the deep middle of the night, and the whole of the ravine country bowed under it, and the birds went quiet, and he became nothing.

It was not a plan. His body did it before he could have chosen to. He went down flat behind a slab of old stone with his quiet shut down to its last shadow, his breath gone to almost nothing, his blood gone quiet. His own presence was pulled in against his bones, until there was nothing on the rim of the ravine country but black rock and a hard thin animal lying still on it.

And the thing in the ravine — the great thing, the roof of the world — passed its attention over the rim of its ground. He felt it come. It was a weight and a looking at once, and the looking did not hate him and did not spare him; it had no colour to it at all. It touched the place where he lay as a hand touches a table. And the sense of years, which he could not shut off, read it completely and without flinching, as it read any living thing: depth beyond all depth, stacked years past the counting, an appetite the size of the whole low country, and under all of it the thin clear thread that ran from that blood to his own.

His blood answered. There was nothing he could do about that either; it answered before his will had a word in it, and the first crown along his skull and neck went hot, and the pull in him sang its one thin note up into the weight above.

The attention stayed on him for as long as the looking took. Then it passed, and the sleeper turned over, and the deep weight settled back down into its own ground, and the ravine country let its breath out, and he lay behind the stone for a long time after the weight was gone.

He got up at last, when the light had changed, and crossed the last rim of the ground and went down into the far country. The lesson of the rim went with him, and it stayed, and he never had to learn it again.

The greatness above was not malice and it was not mercy. It wanted nothing and it gave nothing. Its ground was paid for in the whole of the care — not because it was cruel, but because being in its country at all was a debt you paid with everything you had.

---

And then the deep forest opened, and it was a different world. He understood it in the first hour: the forest he had grown up in was the edge of this. The trees here stood farther apart and taller than any trees he had ever walked under, with bark like old stone, and under them the ground was deep and quiet and held smells he had no names for. And the lives — the lives stood thick on the ground.

His sense of years had read a country of thin bright small things and scattered heavy ones. The deep forest's sense came in like weather: great slow heavy lives everywhere, standing in the fern, in the rocks, in the streams, in the trees. He walked ten paces into that green and stopped, because the ground under his feet had more years in it than the whole of his own valley had ever held.

Then he looked farther, and his sense reeled. Beyond the thick lives, past the edge of what he could read properly, there were depths he could not read at all. They did not stand up like fires as the heavy ones did. They stood as absences — wide, patient, unlit places in the feel where his sense went out and came back with nothing, as an eye comes back from fog.

The sense bowed. He felt it happen in him, in the middle of a green he had never seen, and it was not fear. It was the thing the sense did when it met its own limit: it stopped, folded down, and left the whole truth of the matter as a shape with no measurement in it.

The ancient ones of the deep forest were beyond his sense, and the map that had been the whole world in his head had, in the space of ten paces, grown more room than he had years to fill. He was small again. That was the second thing the deep forest did to him, and he stood in the tall green and let it be so, because it was true.

---

The country read him back the same day. He came down out of the old trees into a fern break toward evening, and the fern break was full of the lesser lives of the deep forest — hare-kinds grown big as the fox-kinds of his valley, ground-birds with long legs, small quick things in the thickets. They did what the lesser lives of his own country did now: they went flat.

But not all of them. He learned the difference before dark.

Some of the deep forest's lesser folk did not go flat. They moved apart from him, unhurried, giving him a ground he had not asked for — and the giving was not fear. It was how a small nation moves aside for a name it has heard in its old stories. Their blood remembered something.

And there were others that did neither. In the last light he came up a rise and a beast stood on the path above him: not a giant, something of the heavy dozen-years sort, low and broad with old fight in its face. It looked at him as an equal looks, and did not move off the path, and for a moment neither of them did anything.

He gave the ground. Not out of fear. It was the feel that did it: the beast was standing on ground that belonged to something else, and something in the country behind it was old and heavy in a way his own blood answered to without any argument. Some of the deep forest's words were older than his.

He walked around it, and the beast watched him go, and the crown on his neck was hot and the lesson was clear: he was a dragon in the deep forest, not the dragon of the deep forest. That night he dug a new hollow under a shelf of roots above a stream — one way in, another way out, as he had been taught by a slope a long time ago — and slept in it with the deep green all around him, and nothing happened to him at all.

---

He hunted on the fifth day. He had read the country hard before he chose. That was the whole of the trick that had kept him alive: he did not hunt the greatest thing he could see, and he did not hunt the smallest; he took what was alone, heavy, old near the end, and unaware. And on the fifth evening the feel gave him one: a beast of the far edge of the deep forest, huge and slow and old, a jawed thing with a hide like bark, standing alone at a wallow in the last of the light, chewing on roots that only its kind could dig out.

It was the largest thing he had ever hunted. He worked it for two days. He learned its hours and its wallow and its trail as he had learned the stag, and on the second evening he came out of the ferns at the wallow when the old beast was in the water up to its shoulders.

And then he had the hardest fight of his life. The beast's hide was a thing his jaw could not pass. He came in low and fast and got his hold at the base of the neck, and his teeth found the hide and stuck there. The hide did not split; he had to work, tearing with his whole body. The beast came up out of the wallow with him hanging from its throat and shook him as a tree shakes in the wind. Its strength was a wall. Its head came round and its arm-thick hind limb came down and caught him across the shoulder, and the blow tore him off the hold and opened his flank like a knife, and he went into the mud.

He got up. He circled. He went in again, and this time he used the thing the deep forest had just given him — the voice.

It came up out of his chest low and heavy, and it was not the full roar of the winter; it was short and low, the weight of his blood spent on the air between them. The old beast had never heard anything like it. It faltered — half a step, no more — and the half step was the whole of the fight, because the falter turned its head and opened the line under its jaw, and he was in it.

The hold found the thin place under the jaw. He set it, and got his forelegs locked, and the beast took a long time to die. In that time it did more damage to him than any beast had ever done: the shoulder torn down to the muscle, the flank opened, the ribs on his left side cracked somewhere under the armor. But it died, and he held until it was done, because letting go is what kills a beast that is winning.

He ate it before he slept, though he could barely stand. The lesson of the deep forest had already been written that day: the years' blood smells go where smells go, and lives heavier than his own had followed the kill in the outer country. He ate fast, and he ate the deep cuts, and then he limped into the dark with the meat down in him and the smell of the kill standing behind him in the open.

---

The devouring was not like the outer meals. It was not like anything.

The years of the deep beast went down into him like roots going down into deep wells, and his body took them as dry ground takes the whole of a rainstorm. He lay in his hollow for two days and the deep sleep held him under, and while it held him the change worked through him in the dark:

What the beast had been — the strength, the thickness, the slow endurance of its long patient life — that part of it went into his body and stayed there. His frame thickened; the cracked ribs knit; the new scars laid over the great beasts.

And the deep part of it — the years, the true long fire of the thing, the part that had made it heavy in the feel and old at the wallow — went down past his flesh and into his blood. He felt it go as a beast feels a fever break: the blood drank, and the blood was more dragon for the drinking. The blue-grey of his scales went darker, deep as the underside of the old trees. The crown along his skull stood a shade higher. And far inside him the pull that ran to the ravine, and beyond the ravine, sang a little clearer than it had ever sung.

He woke on the third morning stronger than he had ever been, and the hunger that had no meal was a bonfire. It stood up in him whole that day, the bloodthirst of his kind with the deep years of a great beast underneath it, saying there, and again, and louder than it had ever said anything. He stood in his hollow with his legs braced and the red thing trying to walk him out into the summer. He held it with the whole of the life he had behind him — every winter, every mistake, every scar, every meal lost and every wall broken. The holding was the hardest thing he had done in the deep forest so far.

He held it. Then he went out and drank at the stream and did not hunt that day at all.

---

At the end of the summer he came on men's work again, and the race was where he had left it. In the low ground under the giants' trees, where the brooks came together, the men had a camp.

They had been in the deep forest eleven days. There were three of them, and a hound, and a boy, and they built their fires small and their beds off the trail. They walked the country as men walk ground they mean to keep: slow, in daylight, reading every sign twice.

"Nine kills on this brook in eleven days," said the oldest of the three. He sat with a ledger open on his knee and a stick of charcoal in his hand, and he had been writing all morning. "Four boar-kind, two deer-echo, one cat, one bear, and one thing I have no name for."

"Read it to me."

"Cat at the third crossing, four days old. Bear on the high ground, two days old." He set the charcoal down and turned the page. "And this one. Eleven paces of it, up the brook and out. No print. The ground rolled flat where it walked, in a line as straight as a road."

"Big."

"Big and walking," said the oldest man. "Something at the far edge of the deep forest walks a straight line, and a straight line is a thing beasts do not walk."

The younger man came in from the brook with his sleeves up and his arms wet to the elbow. He stood dripping over the fire.

"The water is low," he said. "Three crossings dry above the second spread, and the fourth has a wall of stone across it that one man cannot move."

"Then the line goes at the fourth," said the oldest man, "and we take the water as it comes down to it. That closes the edge of the deep forest from the brook to the ridge, and anything that walks the edge of the deep forest walks the line."

"And what walks the line?"

"Whatever the edge of the deep forest holds, by my count," said the oldest man. "Four boar-kind, two deer-echo, one cat, one bear, and the thing that walks straight."

The boy looked up from the fire, where he was turning meat on a stick. He was the youngest of the four and the quietest.

"Is it the one that took the man at the water?" he said.

"Nobody was taken at the water."

"The story says a man."

"The north is full of stories," said the younger man, "and the men in them are always careless. Turn the meat."

The hound got up from the fire, walked thirty paces down the brook, and stood with its muzzle up, and did not come back. The oldest man watched it for a while and then shut the ledger.

"Careless or not," he said, "that thing is reading us. She has been reading something for two days. We do not camp on the brook again."

"Reading it as what?" said the younger man.

"As a beast that walks in a straight line and goes where it likes," said the oldest man. "Which is a thing that will be in a book one day, or a thing that will eat one of us. Either way we do not sleep on its road."

They turned the fire, and the boy turned the meat. The deep trees stood over them in the last of the light while the country went on with its own long business around them.

---

The beast on the fern slope a day's walking east had read the camp through the ground and the air long before the words came. Then the wind carried pieces of it up the slope, and he took the pieces for what they were: sound, and work, and men.

"Line up through the break."

"Both banks. Every crossing."

"The hound's got it again."

"Let her work."

Then the noise moved off east through the low ground, and he lay in the ferns and let the deep forest carry it away. They were on the same trails, working the same heavy kinds, and they had brought their reading and their hounds and their long quiet death into the country of the great years. The deep forest was wide, wider than any hunger could finish. There were years in it that no beast and no line of men could take in a hundred seasons.

The sharing was still the race. That was the shape, kept whole and laid with the others: his list and their list, written over the same country.

He went back to his hollow at dusk and slept in the deep dark, and the deep forest let him stay. Not forever. That was clear to him without anybody saying it. It was letting him stay as a big animal lets a smaller one sleep at the edge of its ground: for now, and because he had paid, and for as long as he went on being worth the room. The earning had only begun.

# Chapter 9: The Keeping Earned

The deep forest was hunting him from the first week, and it took him a month to understand that it was the kill that had done it. He had eaten the great beast at the wallow and gone, as he always went. That had always been enough. The smell of a kill fades; the ravens clean the bones; the country forgets. But three days after the wallow, working a fern break a day's walking east of the kill, he came up out of the ferns with a full belly and caught a line of smell that did not belong.

He read it as he read everything, and it stood in him flat and cold: something had been walking his trail. Not following him — ahead of him, working his own route, where he had walked two days before, and the smell on that ground was the smell of a beast that had been reading his blood.

There is a part of a kill that clings to the eater. He had known it in his body without knowing it in his head; it was why the country had never let him lie down fat and stupid the way other beasts did. The deep part of the meat went into the blood and stayed in the blood, and the blood said where he had been.

He had been carrying the smell of that kill on the whole of his body. Every beast of the deep forest that knew how to read had the right to come for him.

---

He learned the lesson in the worst way first, and then he learned the trick of it. the beasts that came to his kills came for him two days later. He was eating at a fresh kill in the low fern when the country around him went wrong, and he came up with his muzzle red and read the summer: two of the lean ones, hunters from the far edge of the deep forest, standing in the shadows downwind and waiting for the meal to be over. They were not alone. He could smell the third one.

He ate the deep parts of the kill fast and got moving, and he made the mistake of moving along the valley floor. For the rest of that night and the whole of the next day he was a beast being worked, with the lean ones behind him and the smell of his own kill laid along his whole trail like a rope.

He only lost them at the cold stream. He went into it chest-deep and walked it upstream until the water took the smell off the last of the blood on his hide, and he came out of it on a shelf of bare rock half a day north of where he had gone in.

The cold water took the smell of him off. He sat dripping on the rock in the last of the light with his chest heaving and understood the shape of the whole thing.

The deep part of the kill belonged to the eater. The rest of the kill did not have to.

---

He spent the next month making the new craft, and the month after that proving it, and the whole of it went like this: He took his kills at the distance, always, with water or bare stone between him and the place he would sleep. He ate the deep part at the kill itself — the heart, the hot meat behind the ribs, the parts that hold the fire — and he did not carry it anywhere. He washed, always. And when he wanted a beast to go somewhere, he made a word out of what he left behind.

The decoy came together by accident and was proven on purpose. He had taken a heavy beast in the far south of his range and had eaten it down and gone, and the beasts that came to his kills had come in behind him as they always did. Three days later, standing on the high ground above the break, he read the answer still working the kill's ground while he lay full in his hollow a long walk away. The kill had spoken, and the country had gone to the kill, and he had never been closer to it than the high ground.

The rest is a tool. That was the thing. The bones and the blood and the left meat were not waste and they were not bait: they were a word he could leave in a place on purpose.

He laid his first decoy at the end of that month, at the edge of a country he did not want to hunt, and watched the beasts come to it from three directions over the following days while he hunted the other side of his range unbothered. The season had turned him from the hunted thing into the thing that writes. He did not have a name for it. He only had the shape, and he kept it.

---

The voice learned its lesson the hard way too, and it learned it in one day. He called on a hunt for the first time that summer — called the low heavy note of the blood-weight, of his own choosing, not in the storm and not in terror. The beast he was hunting was a broad shy thing of the edge of the deep forest years, old and canny, and it had read the shout of him three mornings running and gone; so on the fourth morning he stood up in the open, in front of it, and let the weight come out of him all at once.

The beast went flat. He took it in the next fifty paces, clean, and it never got up. The voice had bought the whole hunt.

Then the deep forest came for the roar. The low note had carried further than his ears could follow. Inside half a day he had drawn a hunter of the middle deep — a moving hill, some great low creature of the kind that had never once been made afraid of anything — straight to the ground where he had called. It came through the fern on his own trail, and he went up the rocks ahead of it and lay still and watched it go by below, and it went by for a long time.

He rebuilt the quiet that evening while the hill was still in his sense. That was the second half of the day's lesson: the quiet is not the quiet. Stillness is the body; the quiet is the quiet around the body, the thing that tells the country there is nothing here. He had been treating them as one thing.

By the end of that summer he could hold the quiet while he was moving — not perfectly, not always, but in the long smooth stretches of a stalk — and the deep forest tested him on it twice more and lost the feel both times. The voice went onto the list of the things he owned. So did the quiet. They were two different tools, and he never confused them again.

---

The men came up the giants' country in the middle of the summer, and the first thing they left behind was a husk. He found it on the fourth morning: a beast of the heavy years, twice his own weight, lying dead in a break with its hide opened and its meat untouched and its years gone out of it. The flat grey place where its life had been stood in his sense like a hole cut in the summer.

Under the hole, on the ground beside the body, there was a light. He had seen a light taken once before, from a root-wall above the fern country, three years ago. This was the same thing and it was not the same thing. It stood in the moss beside the husk, banked and dark and turning slowly: a ring-light, the deep colour of old wine in the last of the light, so deep that his sense did not so much see it as fall into it. It was darker than the pale gold of the first killing, much darker. It was the colour of a thousand years.

He did not touch it. He understood that it was not his, as he understood the fire of the lodges was not his. But he stood over it a long time before he went, and what he carried away from that break was not fear of the men. It was the plain arithmetic of the country, standing out in the open at last: the men of the deep forest were not hunting for meat any more than he was. They were hunting for exactly the thing he hunted, and a beast like the one lying dead in the break would have fed his own blood for a season.

The race had gotten into the deep forest. It was no longer a line of smoke on his map. It was a husk in the fern and a light standing on the moss, and it was a day's walk from his own hollow.

---

He was under his ledge when the hunt came through beneath him, and that was where he learned what the men had brought with them. He had made his resting place that summer on a shelf of stone above a green break, one of the places where he could lie in the sun and read the country both ways. In the middle of the afternoon the hounds came into the break below.

He had heard them in the distance for two days. He had never heard them this close.

They came up the break in a loose line with the men behind them, and they were working. Not running a scent hot — working it slowly, as he worked his own trails, reading the whole break for anything that had been through it. One of the men carried the curved bow of the long death with an arrow on the string. Another was older and walked behind the hounds with his eyes on the ground, and he was reading it, standing stones and all, as a beast reads water.

"Fresh mark at the fork," said the one with the bow. "Two days old at most, and the pads are as wide as my hand."

"Wider," said the old reader. He knelt at the print without touching it and laid his own hand flat beside it, and the print was bigger than his hand by the width of two fingers. "And it is not a bear. A bear walks with the front of the pad down and the heel off the ground. This one puts the whole foot down."

"Cat?"

"A cat does not walk a break in daylight with its whole foot down." The old man got up and rubbed his hands. "Something heavy walked this break two days before us, and it walked it like a man walking his own road. Out one end and in the other. Not hunting, not feeding. Going."

"Then it lives near here."

"Everything lives near here," said the old man. "That is what the deep forest is. Work the line."

"Then we are hunting a thing that lives here."

"We are hunting its ground," said the old man. "We read where it walks, and we put a line where it walks, and one morning it walks into the line. That is the trade, and it is the only trade there is. Nobody in this country has ever hunted one of the big ones face to face. The men who tried it did not come up the break a second time."

"What if the hound reads it before the line does?"

"Then I take her head, and you hold the bow on the ground in front of her, and we walk out of the break backwards, slow."

"Slow."

"Slow, and never turn. Turn and you are prey, and the deep forest does not care which of us that is."

They worked the line up the break with the hounds spread and the boy at the back with the pack. The older man read the ground behind the hounds, and the one with the bow walked with his eyes on the walls.

"What did the box take last night?" said the one with the bow.

"A thin light off a cat," said the boy from behind. "Pale. The old man says the lodge will write it down and pay half."

"The lodge writes everything down and pays half."

"The lodge pays for what it can count," said the old reader. "So we count. And a light off a beast that dies thirty paces from the line is a light that stands where it fell and goes to nobody, because the man who takes a light has to be standing at it with the box open when it rises. That is two days of walking for a light we were not there for. So we do not wound. We kill where we mean to stand."

"There was one standing at the water, three weeks back."

"There was," said the old reader. "A bull went through a line at the water and walked thirty paces and lay down, and the light stood over it for two days before anyone got back to it, and by then it was pale as ditchwater. Write that in the book too. We lost four days and half a light to a beast that would not die where it was told."

The hounds moved up the break all this time, noses down, working the ground a length at a time. And then the wind turned.

He felt it roll up the break from the low country and go through the fern, and he lay on the ledge and pulled the quiet down over himself whole. The lead hound lifted its head.

It stood in the middle of the break with its head up and its ears forward, and its whole body went still, and it looked at the ledge. He could see the whiteness of its eyes from where he lay. It looked at him — at the place where he was, at the exact short length of ledge that held him — and it whined once, low. Then the old man behind it spoke.

"What's she got?" said the one with the bow.

"The wind," said the old man. He walked up beside the hound without hurrying, and put a hand on the back of its head. "Wind off the ledge, and she'll take it for a beast every time. Down, girl. Down."

"Is there something up on the ledge?"

"Rock," said the old man, "and fern, and rock again. We walked the tracks at first light and the tracks ran south. Whatever we are after is on the south bank by now, and we are on the wrong side of the water."

He pulled the hound's muzzle down toward the ground and said the short flat thing that meant follow. The words were flat hard sounds to the beast on the ledge; he kept the shape of them and nothing else.

The hound went back to the ground. The whole line moved on down the break and out of it, and the afternoon went back to being the afternoon, and he lay on the ledge a long time with the quiet holding.

They had read their way to the bottom of his ledge. They had not found him, and they had come closer than anyone had ever come, and the reason they had not found him was one old man's hand on a hound's head. He moved his resting place the next morning, and from then on he never used the same ledge twice in a season.He moved his resting place the next morning, and from then on he never used the same ledge twice in a season.

---

The thing on the high ground came for him at the end of the summer, and it was not a beast, and it was not the men. He was working back to his hollow along the top of the long ridge, in the grey time before the last light, when the world stopped.

There was no sound and no smell and nothing to see. The whole country simply stopped, as a heart stops: the birds in the air, the insects, the small lives in the fern, all of it gone quiet at once, and every hair on him stood and his blood went cold, and something put its attention on him.

It was not a weight that pressed. It was a looking. He had felt the ravine's weight and he had felt the crush of the deep forest's unreadable depths, and this was different from both. The attention had no malice in it and no mercy and it wanted nothing at all. It looked at him as the sky looks at a stone.

He went down into the fern and pulled the quiet to its last shadow, as he had under the ravine, and he became nothing, and the attention stayed on him anyway. the quiet was not enough. the quiet had never been made for this.

And then the thing in his blood stood up on its own. The first crown along his skull and neck went hot, and the pull in him rose, and the roar of the dragon went out. It was not his call and not his choosing. It was the deep voice of what he was, spoken by the blood itself into the attention above him, as a small king's name is spoken in the ear of a greater.

The attention went around that word, and read it, and knew it. He was weighed. It was like being held on a scale, and he could not move and did not try, and somewhere in the middle of it the ancient thing above him found what it was looking for, and put the scale down.

The attention lifted. The country came back in a rush: birds, insects, wind, the whole green breathing again all around him. He lay in the fern for a while. Then he got up, and his own legs went and he sat down again heavily, and after a time he got up a second time and started for home.

He walked slower than he had ever walked anywhere, and he did not stop until his own hollow's dark was around him. The deep forest had one more thing in it, then. Not a beast, and not a nation of beasts, and not a hunger. A greatness that lived past all his sense, that read the whole of him in the time it took a bird to call, and that had weighed him and let him go.

He did not know why he had been let go. He would carry that question as he carried the barrier: without an answer, all his life.

---

The red thing nearly killed him in the last month of the summer, and the voice saved him. He had been working a heavy beast all day in the broken country south of the giants, and it was a long slow hunt. Somewhere in the last length the standing patience broke open into more than standing. The red thing came up in him whole and took the spring before he had given it, and carried him at the beast with his jaws already open.

The jaw went to the standing leg. That is what the red thing does: it goes to whatever the body is nearest to. His teeth closed on the leg — and it was the wrong leg, the bone under the hide was thick as a young tree, and his teeth were not made for bone. They skated, they tore his own mouth, and the beast turned on him.

It turned on him, and the horn of its shoulder opened his side, and he was down in the rocks with the whole of its weight coming and nothing left in him but his own life and the noise in his own head. He called.

The voice came up out of the red thing, out of the deepest part of him where the rage and the blood and the weight all lived together, and it was the hardest calling of his life. It went out low and heavy and short, straight into the beast's face at four paces.

The beast faltered. It was the length of a breath, no more — the standing leg set wrong, the great head came round — and in that breath he had his hold.

He found the neck. He held through everything the beast had left, and it was a long time, and it cost him blood he could not afford. When it was done he lay in the rocks beside the kill with his own side opened and his mouth split, and the red thing still standing in him, walking him in circles inside his own skin.

He held it. Then he ate the deep part of the kill and went to the water and lay in the cold stream until the red thing lay down.

Afterward, thinking it over in the long way of his kind, he understood what the day had cost him and what it had bought. The red thing had sprung him at the beast and nearly got him killed — the flaw had carried him, as it had been carrying his whole line into the ground since the beginning.

And the voice had saved him. The one thing he had made out of his own blood, in three seasons of learning, was the thing that had pulled him back. He carried both facts the rest of the summer, and he did not stop hunting, and he did not stop riding the red thing down.

---

At the very end of the summer, he stood on the high rocks above the giants' country and read himself. His scales were darker than the spring had made them — deep blue-black, the colour of the underside of the old trees. The crown along his skull and neck stood higher, and when the light was low it caught the light differently from the rest of him. And inside, down in the blood, the pull sang a line cleaner than any he had carried, running north to the ravine.

He was more dragon than the beast that had crossed the rim of the ravine ground in the spring. The deep forest kept him now. Not wholly — never wholly; the giants' trees still stood over him and the unreadable depths still stood in his sense as absences — but truly. He slept in it, hunted it, wrote his words in it, and the country answered him as a large house answers a tenant who pays.

He would need to pay again. He knew that without being told. He had not yet earned the middle of the deep forest, or the ground of the fallen giants, or anything at all in the far north where the absences stood. But the first keeping was his.

# Chapter 10: The Cold Country

The cold came up out of the ground, and he did not believe it. That was the first thing the deep forest's winter did to him. The outer country had taught him the seasons as a mother teaches: the sky went grey, the wind turned, then the snow came. Here the ground itself went cold first, days ahead of anything in the air, and the heavy lives of the deep breaks read it and moved. He came back to his own hunting ground on the third morning of the new cold and found the hollers and the wallows empty, the heavy beasts gone up into the high country where they wintered among the rocks.

He did not read what the country had written. He set his ambush anyway, in the wallow where the big ones came to drink, as his outer-country lessons said to do, and he lay in it for three days.

Nothing came. On the first day he told himself the beasts were shy. On the second day he was hungry. On the third day he was cold and light-headed and the ambush was clearly empty.

He went up after them. The finding was the whole of the lesson. The heavy kinds had gone up into the hot springs — hollows of the country where the water ran hot under the rock and the snow did not lie — and the hot springs were where the winter's eating was. He found them by the nose, following the smell of green water up a long gorge, and he came out at the top into a shallow bowl of steaming ground with the heavy kind standing fat and calm in it. He stood in the rim of that bowl with the steam going past his shoulders and paid the account of the three days honestly.

The deep forest's winter was a new country. It had its own rivers and its own high country and its own rules, and his old map was worth nothing in it. He wrote it down, in his blood, as he wrote everything, and went into the hot springs to hunt.

---

The men wintered in the deep forest, and that was the second thing. He smelled their fire before he saw their smoke. It came to him one grey afternoon on a wind from the far ridge, the sharp thin smell of the light that eats wood, and his whole body went still, because the fire-smell belonged to a place he had left behind: the lodges, the pass, the outer country. Men did not winter in the deep forest. That was a rule he had carried since his first winter, written into the same page as the cold coming down from the sky.

He went up on the ridge on the second morning and found them. There was a camp in the breaks across the valley, sheltered by a spur of the giants' rock, and in that camp the smelt stood up in a thin line all day. Not a camp that came and went. A winter place. There was a wall of cut brush and piled stone, and a frame of poles, and the light that eats wood burning under it in the dark, and around it the ground had been swept and trodden until it had the flat patient look of ground a man owns.

They were staying. He lay on the far ridge and read the camp as he would read a beast's den. Two men at least. Their spirit hounds. The light that eats wood, which they kept alive all the day and all the night, and which was the thing in all the world that most made him want to go down and tear and eat. And the smoke standing over the camp day after day, so that even when he was a day's walking away he could turn his head and read them.

The map changed that morning. His country had one line on it that he had never had before: a place where men lived in the winter, deep in the deep forest, on his own breaks, hunting his own heavy kinds.

The race had stopped being a season. It was a country now, and he was sharing it.

---

The cold taught his two tools what they were worth, and it did it in a week. The voice went first. He called it on a hunt in the second month of the snow — a heavy beast gone to ground in a snowbound break, and the low note to buy the falter. It worked. The beast went still and he took it.

And then, standing over the kill in the falling snow, he could not get warm again. It was not the ordinary cold. The voice had spent something more than air: it had spent heat, and the heat had gone out of him over the snow with the sound, and he stood over his own kill with his whole body shuddering, and it took him most of a day and the whole of the hot meat to put the heat back.

He put the voice away after that, like a tool that cost too much to use. Through the whole middle of the winter he called it twice — once at a hunt he could not take without it, and once at a beast that stood between him and his hollow in the dark. Twice in three months. He paid the price both times, willingly, and the discipline of it changed how he hunted: he got used to winning without it.

The quiet broke differently. Fear had never been able to break the quiet. He had carried it through the reaching of the hounds and the weight of the ravine and it had held. Hunger broke it inside a week.

The lean stretch came in the third month, when the hot springs froze at their edges and the heavy kind moved again into country he did not know. Six days of hunting that fed him once. And through those six days, he could not hold the quiet at all.

It was the hunger that spoke through him. Fear had been sharp and thin and it had made the quiet easy — fear narrowed him, and there was less of him to hide. Hungry, his whole body was loud: the pull stood open in him, the sense reached out of him whether he asked it to or not, and every living thing in the country could read the shout coming off him.

The quiet is fed on attention. He learned that as he learned everything: by working out what had gone wrong on ground where nothing could be done about it. When his whole attention was bent on the next meal, there was nothing left over to hold the quiet, and the country read him and went quiet ahead of him.

By the cold month's end he had taught himself to hold the quiet while hungry — badly, in fits, as a beast holds anything new. He could do it now by feeding the quiet a share of his own hunger: hold the shout down, and let the belly be angry about it.

He lost four kills learning that. He gained a rule for the whole of the rest of the winter, and the rule was this: the quiet is fed on attention, and attention is the only coin he has.

---

The hunger was the winter's last and hardest teacher. He had carried the red thing in two shapes since the first summer. The boil was the old rage of his kind, the rampage that came up out of fullness. The hunger was quieter than the boil and worse: it waited. It stood behind his eyes in the long grey hours and pointed at the heavy lives in the country and whispered the hunt before the hunt had begun.

In the cold, with the deep years everywhere in his sense and his belly lean and the hunger that had no meal standing in him the whole time, the hunger grew into the shape of the winter. The grey stag was the nearest loss.

It was a beast of the second water, up in the high hot springs, heavy with years — a creature nearly the size of the old stag of the fern country, standing in his sense like a banked fire. He marked it as he marked everything: its hours, its water, its ground, its habits. He watched it for a week.

And on the eighth morning, going up the long gorge to the place where he meant to take it, the hunger spent the hunt before it began. He could not say afterward where the control went. Somewhere in the climb he stopped hunting and started wanting; he hurried, he cut ground he should not have cut, he came up over the rim of the warm break with the quiet broken and the shout of himself going out ahead of him for half a morning, and the stag was gone. Not frightened — it had simply walked. He found its tracks going out the far side of the break, unhurried and steady, in the snow. It had read him coming from the other side of the morning.

He stood in the empty hot break and let the day go. He learned the shape of it that evening, lying over the water with the hunger in him and nothing to show for a day and a half of hunting. The hunger spent the hunt, or the hunger sharpened the hunt, and there was no third possibility, and the choosing between them was the whole of the riding. It was the same law as the boil, in its colder and more patient form.

He proved it nine days later on a beast of the middle years in the lower breaks. He carried the hunger through the whole stalk like a coal in his chest, and it did what coals do: it lit the feel, it steadied the stalk, it put the last length on the end of the spring when the moment came. He took that beast clean.

He ate it in the warm break with the steam going up around him, and the fact sat in him as solid as any rock on his first slope: the hunger is not the enemy. The hunger is the fuel. What rides it is the choosing.

---

In the deep middle of that winter, the country gave him the last layer of its map. It came on the cold clear nights, when the air stood still over the break and the whole sky was a lid of stars. His sense of years, sharper in the cold than it had ever been, reached farther than it had ever reached — out past the giants' country, past the far edge of the deep forest, up into the north he could not read — and on those nights the absences gave up their shapes.

They were standing lights. That was the thing his sense finally told him. The depths he could not read were not places; they were lives, fixed in their own grounds the way mountains are fixed, each one standing in the country around it like a pole in a tent, and everything in the country stood in relation to them. The ravine's weight away south was one. The unreadable north held others.

The cold country's walking had become a walking between them. He could feel the old standing lights when he moved through the high hot springs; he could feel where their grounds began and where a careful beast went around. And deeper in his blood than all of it, thin and clear and carried farther on the cold air than it had ever carried before, the pull sang north toward the ravine.

The last dividend was the quietest one and he noticed it before any of the others. The cold had less hold on him than it should have had.

His outer-country winters had gone into his bones; he had carried the cold out of the last two as a beast carries a debt. This winter the cold sat on him lightly. His blood kept its own fire now — deep meals and deep sleeps had paid for it, season after season — and the snow country that had nearly killed the hatchling was, to the beast he had become, merely the season.

He did not think that to himself in pride. He simply noticed it, as he noticed everything, and kept it.

---

And then the season turned, and the first line of the war was written in other hands. He was up in the high hot springs on the day the men took the grey stag. He never saw it happen. He came down the long gorge two days after, and the stag's ground was a husk: the great body lying opened in the snow at the second water, the meat left for the ravens, and beside the beast's head, pressed deep into the moss, the two small prints where a man had knelt to take what stood over it.

There was no light. He read the place as he read everything, and the place told him what had happened in it: the light had risen when the beast went down, which takes no time at all, and a man had knelt in the moss and drawn it away. The smell of the drawing was still there, thin and sharp, gone into the moss and the snow. The deep colour of it was on his sense like the ghost of a fire, and it was the same colour he had watched stand over the other husk in the summer.

The men had come up the gorge, taken the light he had marked, and gone down again. They had not even been near the ground when he walked it.

He had marked that stag. It had been on his list, with its hours and its water and its ground, and the men had walked into the deep forest in the winter and taken it without ever knowing he had wanted it.

He looked at the light for a long time. Then he did what he did with everything. He wrote it down.

His list, from that day, was not a list of beasts any more. It was a list of what the country had promised him and what had been taken out from under the promise: the bristle-back, the deer, the stag of the fern country, the great stag of the high fern, the deep beasts. And now the grey stag of the second water, marked, watched, and taken by other hands before he ever walked its ground.

Their list was on paper, in a winter place in the deep forest, written in a hand he would never see. His was in his blood. Both of them were written over the same beasts, in the same breaks, in the same hours of the same cold seasons.

He turned north out of the stag's ground and went up over the rocks, and behind him in the moss the two prints of a kneeling man filled slowly with snow. That was the war. Not a fight — he had not seen a man in his life close enough to fight. The war was two lists over one country, and the country would decide what each of them got.

He went back up into his own range with the cold on his back, and the place beside the stag's head stayed in his sense like a sign of a claim, and the claim was not his. The cold year turned. The deep forest kept him, the pull sang north, and somewhere down in the breaks under the giants' rock the men had a light in a box that had been on his own list. The next move in that war would be made in the thaw, and whichever list took it, the country would decide what both of them got.

---

The two men in the camp were splitting wood on the third morning, and their voices came up to the far ridge clean on the cold air. The boy worked the water and moved the hounds out of the wind.

"If we work the second water again we should work it north," said the kneeling man. He had a wedge and a mallet, and he was taking the split wood and stacking it tight against the brush wall. "That water has been hunted two winters. The heavy kinds are learning the south end."

"They learn," said the other from behind the poles. He was the older of the two, old enough that the winter in this camp had been his plan and not his luck, and he came out from under the frame with his hands wet from the water-bucket. "That is why we are still alive. The ones who do not learn the country starve in it. The beasts stay because the warm water is here. We stay because they stay."

"And the line?"

"The line goes in at the thaw. Second water, north end, both banks. And this year we do not pull it."

"Not pull it? The permit says the line comes out at the season's end."

"The permit says the lodge writes down what the line takes," said the old man. He threw the last of the water down the bank and set the bucket by the fire. "What the lodge knows is the lodge's business. Do you know what a light of the deep colour is worth in the low country? It buys a house. A house, a wife, and a winter with no line in it. A beast of that kind has been read at the second water twice in three winters, and I do not mean to stand in the thaw and watch some other man's line take it out from under me."

"You have been saying that for two winters."

"And for two winters the thing has not walked into a line," said the old man. "That water is deep and wide, and the beast that drinks at it does not come every night. Fine. This year we do not wait for the night it comes. We close the whole north end and we sit on it for the snow."

"With what? Two hounds and the two of us."

"We have the boy," said the old man. "The boy can hold a hound. And at the thaw the lodge sends two more men up if the camp is worth working, and the camp is worth working because I say it is."

"Then why not go where the big lights are?" said the kneeling man. "North, past the black ridge, where the deep forest starts."

"Because the men who went north did not come back," said the old man, "and their wire is still hanging up there in the trees."

"That is a story."

"That is a ledger," said the old man. "The lodge wrote them down as gone, and the lodge pays for wire whether we set it or not, and the wire up there was paid for and never used. I have read the page. Have you?"

The kneeling man said nothing and went back to the wood. The boy came up from the water with the bucket and stopped on the flat stone by the fire out of habit, and the old man looked at him as a man looks at a tool he has not decided about.

"What does the box hold?" said the boy.

"One light," said the old man. "A thin one. You carried it up yourself, so you know as well as I do."

"Then why is it up here and not at the lodge?"

"Because the box goes down when I go down," said the old man, "and I go down when the line is set and the list is made. That is the whole reason we live up here in the snow with the wind."

"There is nothing up here," said the boy.

"There is worse than nothing," said the old man. "Work."

He went back under the frame. The wood split and the smoke stood straight up out of the camp all day, and the dragon lay on the far ridge with the cold air going past his crown, and read every word he could not understand, and went home in the dark.

# Chapter 11: The War of the Lists

The thaw came up out of the ground. Snow on the low slopes went soft, then rotten. Water ran under it in the dark, and the moss under the water came green before the air believed in spring. He had lived three winters by then and he knew the rule of them: the ground woke first, and everything that ate and was eaten woke with it.

He came down out of the high scree on the first still morning, thin from the cold months and hungry in the honest way. He went to the high break first, because the broad-antler wintered on it, and because a beast that has wintered well is a beast that has not yet learned to be careful.

The run was empty. He knew it before he reached the standing stone. No beast-smell on the path. No new rub on the stone where the antlers had worn it pale for years. And under the rot of the thaw, the other smell.

Blood. Days old. With man-smell laid over it.

He read the ground from the outside in, slow. Boots. Two sets of them, walking. Poles dragged. The beast had gone down in the moss at the mouth of the run and had not gone far. The blood was spread wide and dark, and the flies had found it and gone, and where the head had lain there was a shallow pressed place in the new green.

Above that place the ground held a color. He had seen a light stand in the air when a beast died. He had never seen a light sink into ground and stay there a while. But it had stayed: pale gold, thin, gone down into the earth like water into sand, and what was left was the color sitting in the moss.

A hundred-year light. Not the deep light. The low fat of a winter, paid to other hands.

He had marked that beast at the turn of the year. It was the second line of his list, and he had kept it in the deep place through the snow, with the patience he had paid for in blood, and this was what the patience had bought him: the ground, the color, and the man-smell.

He stood a long time in the cold green. Then he did what he did with everything. He wrote it down.

He carried his list in his blood, not on paper. A line taken went into the deep place and stayed there, flat and hard, like a scar on the inside. Two lines now. The grey stag of the second water, taken at the turn of the year with its ring of deep purple carried off in their hands. And now the broad-antler, taken in the same country, in the same season, at the hour he had kept for it.

He walked the ground around the kill twice more and read the rest of it. No second kill. No wasted meat. They had eaten what they wanted and left the rest for the ravens. They had not hurried. And they had come to this run at the hour the beast came to it, on a path no man-shaped thing had walked all winter.

He sat down on his haunches in the new green and let that settle. They read the ground. That was the thing. They read it as he read it: patiently, in signs, and from the signs they knew where a beast would be and when. They had read the broad-antler's habit and taken him on the strip of moss where he had been eating for years. They had done it without noise and without waste, and then they had gone.

And below the smoke-line, which had stood over the winter place all winter, there was no smoke any more. The winter place had been struck at the thaw. They had taken it apart and carried it down-country, and the going had a shape he had learned to read in the cold months: they had gone to work for the season, and work does not go home.

His list had two lines taken by other hands. Their list had two lines on it that he had never seen. The two lists sat over the same country, and the country was the thing they were both spending.

He made the first decision of the summer before he left the moss. He would not wait. Their patience was longer than his patience, and their hands never tired. He would take his own line first, in the days when their line was deep and far, and the line he chose was the thick-paw of the summer run.

He knew the thick-paw by the tracks it left: the wide paw-print in the soft ground, one blunt toe dragging, the bushes broken at the height of a tall beast's chest. It was slow and heavy and bad at running, and it had fed well in the hot springs since the melt, and it fed on the same slopes a man could walk. A line that reads the ground could read the thick-paw too. It was on both lists already. It only had to be taken.

For nine days he kept to the high ground and let the hunger work. Then he found what he had been waiting for: fresh sign of the hunting line, moving down-country of the giants on the long march, two days of walking away from the summer run.

He went after the thick-paw that same evening. He found it in the last of the light, rooting in the fern at the edge of the run, and he did not go at it at once. He stilled himself and let the country settle. The hunt was a long slow thing done in short hard pieces, and he had learned the pieces in three winters of it: walk, stop, read, wait, then the one piece that is all of it.

The thick-paw went down the run at first light, as it did every morning. It was a heavy thing, all shoulder and neck, the head low and the tusks dirty from the rooting feed, and it moved with a rolling confidence that came from never having been chased by anything faster than itself.

He was faster. He let it get the length of the run ahead of him, because the run was cut with old gullies and thorn, and a beast that runs on bad ground breaks its own legs. He stayed high on the slope beside the run where the ground was clean and his own feet were sure, and he ran, and he shut everything else out.

The summer was thick and loud with spring and it did not want him moving through it at speed. Twice the fern closed over the run and he lost the shape of the beast and had to take the high line again. Once a pair of low lives — some small pale thing and its young — turned their heads as he passed above them, and he went down in the fern at once and held the quiet while the two heads turned back and forgot. The quiet cost him time. Time cost him ground. When he came up again the thick-paw had gained the run's far bend and was not running any more; it had turned.

It had turned, and it was standing in the open with its head down and its tusks up and its weight set back on its haunches, because that was what the thick-paw did. It did not run well. It fought well.

He came at it low, from the side of the run where the bank was cut and the beast could not swing the tusks without losing its feet, and the short hard piece began. The thick-paw came off the bank with a short grunting rush and caught him across the ribs with its shoulder and drove him into the fern, and the breath went out of him and the world went white for a moment. He rolled with it, not against it. That is the whole of the art: not against. He took the second rush into his own shoulder and gave it ground, and the tusks grated along the hard plates under his hide and did not find the soft place, and then his head was past the tusks and his jaw had the thick-paw behind the ear.

The hold went in. The thick-paw screamed and tore backwards, dragging him through the fern and the thorn, rolling, all its weight and fear come up at once, and he held. The jaw's work was quiet: a slow deeper set, muscle and bone, no hurry. The beast thrashed a long time and then was still.

He did not let go for a while after it was still. He had learned that too.

Then the two red things stood up over the meat. They always came at a kill, and he always felt both. The first was the boil: the bloodthirst of his kind, the old rampage that wants the meat taken whole and the body torn and the ground washed red, the thing that has killed more of his kind than any hunter. The second was quieter and worse in its way: the hunger. He had carried the hunger since the deep summer — the red pull that had made him mark beasts and spend nights over them and lose the grey stag to his own delay. The boil and the hunger met over the thick-paw's body, and he stood over the meat with his jaw still holding and put the choosing between the two of them, and the choosing said what it always said: the hunger is yours and the hunger is yours and neither of them is you.

He ate. The meal was good meat and the deep sleep did not take him, because he did not let it. When the meat was down and the body was left, he used the oldest trick of the deep forest. He took the kill and set it in the ground around the place: his own scent put down in a wide ring: a sign that says a thing. The heavy kinds of the run would find it and move off the ground he had marked. It would keep them away from this place. It would keep him safe from other beasts while the meat was on him.

He stood at the edge of the summer run in the last of the light. His sign stood in the ground behind him. His list was shorter by one line, and their list the same. And he understood, for the first time, that his own trick was a thing said out loud in a country that now had listeners who could read.

---

At the winter place, the fire was out, and the poles were down, and the two of them were packing the last of it onto a back-frame while Old Qin walked the ground at the edge of the camp. He walked it as he walked every ground, with his hands behind him and his eyes on the moss, and at the far edge he stopped and called, and the two of them left the packing and came.

"Same ground," said Gao Tie. He crouched and looked at the print in the moss without touching it. "Same shape as the deep place. Same as the water, two years back. Day old, no more. Whatever it is, it ate here, and it walked off south."

"South is the water line," said Xiao An.

"South is the water line," Gao Tie said.

"A thing that signs and does not show itself," said Xiao An. She was younger than the other two and she had learned to read the ground fast, and she read it again now, the print in the moss and the drag of the kill beside it. "It takes what we take. It takes it a day after we set it out, every time, and it leaves its own sign in the ground after. Old Qin. It is not reading us. It does not know us at all. It never comes near the fires. But it knows the country, and it knows where a beast will stand, the same way we know."

"It leaves signs," said Old Qin. "Then it is a line on the list." He took the list out of his coat and set it flat on his knee, and took out the brush and ink from the small case, and wrote, and the writing was slow and careful, because the list was the work.

"One line," he said, when he had done it. "No name. The beast only, and the ground, and the season. A thing that signs and does not show."

"The old hunters of the north border say the deep forest has its own keepers," said Gao Tie. He said it for the record and not as a belief, the way a man sets down a story he has no use for.

"Then write it under what we know, and not under what we guess," said Old Qin. "What we have is sign, and a bank. Sign goes on the list."

"And what does the list do with it?" said Xiao An.

"When it is seen, the list goes to it," said Old Qin. He looked back down the country at the low breaks, and then at the two of them, and his voice had no heat in it, because the list never needed heat. "The stag's light is in my coat. It goes down the road with the rest of them; the tables buy depth for frames that have grown to hold it, and we buy the season's bread with the price. That is the work. That is all the work. But the beast is a line on the list now, and a line does not sit on the list forever. Nothing does."

He folded the list and put it away. It had the sound of a thing being decided.

"The old bull of the hot springs," he said. "His years stand low and deep, and the deep light is worth a year of the season's bread. We keep him on the list for the season, not for an hour. We take at the water's edge, where the ground is soft and the beast is slow. And if the beast comes while we are at it —" he looked at the two of them, one after the other, "— we pull back. The list does not buy a season of the border with the whole of a hunting line."

"And the hound?" said Gao Tie, because the hound had wintered badly and had come out of the cold thinner than it went in.

"The hound goes," said Old Qin. "The hound always goes."

"Then we walk the water line first, and the breaks after," said Gao Tie. "Same as the winter."

"Same as the winter," said Old Qin. "And Xiao An walks the tracks. She reads them faster than the hound does, and the hound does not argue."

"The hound never argues," said Xiao An.

---

He learned about the old bull from a hillside, without wanting to. It was the second week of the summer when he came down off the giants' shoulder and found the hot springs full of the heavy kinds, all of them fat and slow with the new feed. And one of them was different. The bull stood alone on a rise above the water, and the old beast had gone dark with the years, and when he read it at a distance his sense did not close on anything. The years of it did not read down into the ground as the old stag-kind's had. They stood low and deep and went down out of reach, like a shaft into a mountain, and what came back up was a weight.

He sat on the hillside a long time with his sense low and small in him. The thick-paw had been meat. This was a line, and the line was the deepest one the summer had to give, and it was standing in his own reading as though it had been standing there since the melt, waiting to be seen.

He marked it that evening. He set his sign in the ground above the water where the old beast came to drink, and he went back up the shoulder, and he did not take it that day, because the deep line is a season's work and not a day's. Behind him, down the long low country, two fires stood in the country of the giants.

---

# Chapter 12: The Bull at the Water

The summer stood at its height, and the hot springs wore it thick.
