Every fern run was loud with the young of the year, and the heavy kinds were fat on the new feed, and the water in the low ground ran brown and quick. It was the best season he had known. He spent the first half of it doing nothing, and the doing of nothing was the work: the bull's run had to be read the deep forest's way: slowly, in signs, before a line was spent on it.

The bull came down to the water every day at the edge of the dark. He learned the beast's whole day. Where it slept, on a dry shelf above the ravines. Where it fed, along the low breaks where the feed was thickest. Where it drank, at the wide shallows where the bank came down smooth and the ground under the water was firm, and how long it stood at the water with its head down and its ears working. He kept to the high ground a week, and then lower, and then close, and the beast never read him once, because he was careful and because he was patient and because patience was the thing he had paid for with the stag.

He did not know, that first week, what his own word was costing him. It came to him as the important things came now, in the feel of the country. The heavy kinds of the hot springs were drifting. The old feeding lines along the low breaks were being walked out and left, and the heavy ones were up on the high ground where they had never fed before, and the run he had marked the thick-paw on stood with the sign of his kill still on it and no beast near it.

He put the two things side by side. His own sign was written in the ground in a dozen places now, and it said: this ground is watched, and I am near it and eating. The beasts of the country could not read a name, and they did not know what he was, but they could read what the ground read, and the ground read danger, and they had moved.

They had moved the bull with them. The beast's hours shifted in the last days of the summer. He came down to the water in the hot middle of the day now, when the flies were heavy and the flies had made him stupid. He drank fast and went back up to the shelf. The shallows stood empty at the edge of the dark, where he had drunk every evening for years.

It was his own word that had moved the old beast. He sat with that for a while. In the deep forest a kill taken wrong is a lesson, and he took the lesson: the cry that guards the country guards the hunter too.

Then the heat came, and the flies, and the feel of the water, and he set his trap. And while he was setting it, the smoke stood up over the forest.

---

Two fires, down-country of the giants, where no fire had stood before. He read them from the high shoulder in the last of the light. They had walked in off the long road, gone up the giants' country, and split. One line went down toward the low breaks. The other stayed on the water line. The staying line was the dangerous one, because a line that stays is a line that has read something and wants it.

It was the hound that told him the rest. The wind on the third evening came up out of the low country and he stood in the fern with the wind on his face and read them whole. Men-smell, and iron, and the light that eats wood, and under it the hound-smell, coming up the line the water made between the two countries. They were working the water line. And they were not walking blind, because he could smell the hound working the ground out ahead of them, reading the country as he read it, wanting what the ground had been near in the last day or two.

He stood in the fern a long time with the wind on his face and his jaw shut. They had marked the same country he had marked. They were working toward the same water. And on the old bull's run his own word stood in the moss in a dozen places, telling every beast with a nose that the ground was watched, and telling one hound the same thing.

He could not take a deep mark off the ground. He could only add to it.

He went up to the water that night and walked the shallows end to end, and where the old beast came down to drink he set a second word, low and careful, where the bank came down. Then he went up to the high shelf above the ravines and lay in the fern and waited.

The bull came down at the hot middle of the next day. He took it there, at the water, and the taking was the whole of what he was paid for.

The old beast came down the break at the same slow walk it used every day of the summer. It reached the shallows and put its head down. The moment its mouth touched the water he came off the high fern in a long silent rush and hit it in the ribs.

The bull did not go down. That was the first thing, and he felt it in every bone: he might as well have hit the bank. The beast came round on its back legs with the horns swinging, and the deep weight came with it, and he took the first horn along the shoulder plates and was thrown wide into the shallow water, and the water went up, and the world was a roar and a wall of brown.

He came up with the mud in his eyes and the bull was on him. It had turned faster than anything that size had a right to turn and its head was low and it drove at him, and he saw the horn coming and the horn was the whole of the world, and he met it — that was the whole of the fight in the end, the meeting. He took the horn on his jaw and turned it, and the blow went along his skull and out through his neck, and it was like catching a falling tree.

Then the jaw had the bull's head. He set it deep, as he set the thick-paw, but the bull's neck was the thickest neck he had ever closed on, and the old beast did not scream and did not run. It braced. It went down on its forelegs with its whole weight set forward and dragged him through the shallows, and it threw him off its head twice, and both times he came back onto it, because that was what had to be done and there was no art in it past that. His jaw locked higher, into the base of the skull. The bull rolled in the water. It rolled again, and its legs were in the air, and the water came up brown around them both, and it was still rolling when the rolling began to slow.

The light came up out of the old body while the body was still moving. He had read a hundred lights by then and he had never read one like this. It rose low and slow, purple, deep enough that the eye wanted to go down into it and could not, and it stood in the air above the horns for a long breath and then went down into the ground. It went down like a stone down a well. The feel of it went down past everything he could reach and came back up as a weight.

Then the bull was meat, and the meat was the deepest meal the summer had to give. He ate, and the two red things came, and this time neither of them frightened him.

He had thought the hunger would come for him at a kill like this one. The hunger had spent a year making him mark beasts and lose them while he sat watching; the hunger had cost him the grey stag. It came now, the red pull with the meat in it, and he stood in it and let it burn and did not move, because there was nowhere to move to; the bull was lying in the shallows and the meat was his. And the boil came as it always came, the old rampage of his kind, and this time the rampage and the hunger met the choosing, and the choosing held them both without a fight.

He ate until the belly was tight and then ate again, because the deep meat of a thing like that does not keep in the summer and the flies were already working the shallows. The dark came down and he was still at the water, heavy, too heavy to move far, and that was the danger. A beast that heavy can fight but cannot run.

So he lay down in the fern at the top of the bank above the shallows, and let the meat go down in him, and while it went down the change came into his blood. It came as it had after the beast from the far edge of the deep forest two summers back, only deeper: the meat and the years of the bull going down into the places of him and coming back out as the old blood, and the old blood grading itself higher, scale by scale, in the dark. He felt the plates on his back lie tighter over him and the crown of his head weigh more, and the pull of the old thing in his blood — the pull that had sung once in the deep summer — turned over once in its sleep. He slept, and did not sleep deep, and in the cold of the early morning he heard the men come.

---

They came at the water's hour, because that was their craft. He came up out of the sleep with the shapes standing in his nose: men-smell, iron, the smoke of their fires still on them, and the hound out ahead of the line, working the bank. He lay flat in the fern at the top of the bank with the dawn coming grey and the shallows below him and about thirty paces of open ground between.

He could not run. That was settled, with the bull's meat in him, and he did not waste time arguing with it. So he did the other thing. He lay in the fern and stopped being a thing that was there.

The quiet went over him like water rising. It was the deep stilling, paid for in the deep forest and rebuilt all that summer, and he had never held it over ground this wrong. The shallows brown and torn. The bull's body in the water. His sign and the blood on the bank. Thirty paces of open ground, and a hound working it.

The hound came down the bank first. It was a low grey thing with a heavy chest, and it came down the bank with its nose close to the ground and its whole body in the feel, and he knew the moment it came on his line. The hound checked. It came up the bank a few paces and stopped with its head down in the torn moss where he had lain through the night and where the bull's blood had run into the bank, and it stood there for a long moment, and then it sat down.

It sat down, and put its head up, and told the men. The men came up the bank slow and spread. The one in front was the tallest; he carried the iron in both hands and there was no fire in his face at all. The young one came beside him with the list. The hound sat in the moss between them, head up, its whole body pointed at the fern.

He held the quiet. It was costing more than it had ever cost. His blood was loud with the bull's meat and the grading, and the meat was a heat the quiet could not put out. He lay in the fern with thirty paces of open ground between himself and three men and a hound, and the hound's certainty stood in the air like smoke.

The tallest man looked at the fern for a long time. Then he took the iron in both hands and walked three paces toward it, and he stopped, and he stood, and he looked, and behind him the hound sat and did not come. And the young one said something quiet, and the tallest man answered without turning his head, and the iron came up — and then came down again, and the man turned around and walked back to the water.

He did not know what they said. He was not meant to, and it would have changed nothing if he had.

He took them out of the country as the ground carries a secret — by not being anything, for as long as it took. They stood at the water a while. They read the shallows, and the bull's body, and the bank, and the hound's sitting. Then they went back down the water line as they had come, and he lay in the fern and let the quiet down slowly. The letting-down was its own cost: the ground had to learn him again after a quiet that deep, and the learning took the day. He slept in the fern that night, one country of sleep, and woke with the cost paid and the meat settled and the plates tighter on his back.

---

At the water's edge, when the men had come back down the bank and stood in the shallows, Gao Tie put his hand on the hound's head. He left it there for a while.

"It holds it like a name," he said. "It's been on this bank since before the light. It doesn't hold an hour for a piece of grass. There is something on this bank, and whatever it is, it was here last night with the bull."

"Then it killed the bull," said Xiao An. "Bull, and sign, and the body picked over, and it was here when we came. Not the day after. Not a day behind. Here. We walked on it."

Nobody spoke for a moment. The water went past their boots, brown and quick.

"You saw the fern," said Gao Tie. "Thirty paces of open fern, and nothing in it."

"I saw it," said Xiao An. "I walked it twice."

"And the hound?"

"The hound sat," said Xiao An. "The hound does not sit for nothing."

"Beasts leave sign," said Gao Tie. "A beast that size leaves sign going in and sign going out. There was no sign going out."

"There was no sign going in," said Xiao An. "Only the beast at the water and the bull's blood on the bank. Whatever ate the bull came out of the forest, took it, and went back into the forest the same way it came."

"The ground at the fern," said Old Qin. "Did you see it? Nothing. No track, no sign, no beast standing in thirty paces of open fern with a hound pointing at it." He looked at the fern a while longer. He was not a man who was ever in a hurry. "That is past reading," he said. "That is a thing that signs, and does not show, and now it shows that it can stand in front of us and not be seen."

He took out the list, and the brush, and the ink, and he wrote. The writing was careful and slow, as always.

"What do we put down for it?" said Gao Tie. "A name? We have no name. A kind? We have no kind. We have sign, and a bank, and a smell the hound will not leave."

"We put down what we have," said Old Qin.

"Two lines on it now?" said Gao Tie.

"One line, and the sign of the seen on it," said Old Qin. "When a line has been seen, the list goes to it. We do not go hunting the hot springs again for the deep lights. We go where the country says the beast has been, and we find what leaves these signs, and then the list will have its face and its name on it, and the season will have paid for itself twice."

He folded the list and put it away. "The stag's light and the bull's if we can take it — those go down the road with the rest. The tables buy depth for frames that have grown to hold it. That is the market, and the market is the work. But the beast —" and he looked one more time at the empty fern, "the beast is a line now, and a line does not sit on a list forever."

"The bull goes down the road with the stag's," said Old Qin, "if we can take the light off it in the state it's in, and we can. The tables pay for depth, and we have a season's bread standing in that water. That is settled."

"And the other thing?" said Gao Tie.

"The other thing is a line with no face on it," said Old Qin. "We do not hunt what we cannot see. We hunt where it has been, and we read it, and one day we will read it wrong and it will be standing in front of us. When that day comes, we will find out what it is. Until then, the list."

They went back down the water line, and the hound went last. Twice it turned its head.

---

In the high fern, with the day's cost paid and the old bull's years working down in him, he read the water country in the last of the light. He read the track of their going down the water line. He read the fires come up again down-country of the giants.

He did not know what they had written. He never would.

But he had lain in the fern with three men and a hound thirty paces away and a hound pointing at him, and he had come out of it, and the plate on his heart knew the price of that. He had carried the quiet further than it had ever been carried, and it had held; and the second thing he knew was that it would not hold twice in the same way. A hound that has found you once can find you again.

He had spent a season learning that the cry that guards the country guards the hunter. Now he had spent a morning learning the other half: that a line with no face is a line that keeps its freedom, and the day it gets a face, the hunting changes.

Two lists over one country. Their list had the sign of the seen on the trail that was him, and the next hunt of theirs would not come with hands only. It would come with eyes.

---

# Chapter 13: The Keepers' Line

The bank had learned him. He came back down to the water on the fourth day, hunting the heavy beasts of the low country, and he studied the place from the high ferns before he went near it.

The mud at the crossing was churned and dry. The bull's bones lay scattered where the ravens had picked them, and the hunters' boots had gone down to the shallows and back, hard-edged now in the sun. Under all of it, standing in the ground like a stain the rain had not touched, lay four days of his own killing. He had killed the bull there, in silence, and the ground remembered it.

The small creatures had not come back. The burrows under the bank came up short of the water and turned away, and the burrowing birds had moved a little upstream. The bank used to be a place where the country went about its small business with its head down. Now everything there kept to the far edge of what it knew.

He paid for it through the end of summer. His hunting came back to him a little at a time. On the second morning he took a hare at the end of its run and nothing in the ferns lifted its head at him, and on the fourth morning he took a young boar in the low wallows and held the quiet over the whole meal. That was when he understood what he had been doing all along. Every beast he ate, every rest he left behind, wrote his name into the country in a hand anything could learn to read. He had been leaving signs on his ground since his first summer, and no one had ever read them.

Three mornings later someone did. He came down out of the high ferns to a meadow he had hunted since he was young, soft grass with a wallow on the low side and two game trails through it, and he stopped on the ridge because the meadow had been used by other hands.

A dead beast lay in the open grass, cut open down the belly. It was heavy, a full-grown one, and its meat was untouched. Its light was gone, taken by a man standing over the kill. A wire ran low across each of the two trails, set at the height of a chest. Upwind of the wallow, off the ground on a frame of poles, sat a blind of cut branches that smelled of men, and down by the spring a spirit hound lay staked on a short line with its muzzle toward the meat. In the middle of the afternoon a man came out to the hound, looked over the meadow for a while, and went back into the blind.

Nothing hunted. Everything waited.

He lay on the ridge through the grey end of the day and read what he saw. The hunters had made a kill of their own and taken its light and left the meat standing with a watch over it. It was his own trick turned around: the kill was the bait, the bait brought beasts in, and the man behind the poles wrote down whatever came.

He did not eat. He had never eaten a kill that another hunter had made and left for him, and he did not start now. A snare catches one animal and teaches a hunter nothing, so the wire was not there to catch him. He gave the meadow up that night, without hurrying, and crossed east over the ridge.

---

Three days up-country from the water, the hunters made their kill. They took an old, heavy beast at a wallow in the last of the light, with an arrow out of the dark trees and a run of two hundred paces after it.

Old Qin did the work at the head with the short knife. He opened the hide and put his hands in where a beast's light sits, and the light came up pale and slow over the body. Xiao An knelt on the moss with the box open and held it there until the light was in and the lid was shut.

"Pale," said Gao Tie. He crouched by the body and turned the empty hide back with two fingers. "A young beast would have given more."

"A young beast is not worth a watch," said Old Qin. He wiped the knife and stood up and looked at what they had made: the opened hide, the meat whole, the body lying in the open. "Leave the meat. The meat is not for us this time."

Xiao An came up from the moss with the box against her chest.
"Both trails?" she said.
"Both," said Gao Tie. "Set at the chest, anchored at the ends, low enough to hold a bull."
"Then the thing that reads this meadow will read the wire. It has read everything else we have put down."
"Then let it read," said Old Qin. "A snare catches one animal, and we have caught animals all our lives. I want the ground it walks over, the hour it comes, how it eats, and how it leaves. I want the beast that leaves signs and never shows itself to write its own print on ground I chose for it."

Gao Tie ran the last of the wire through his hands and set the anchor post true with the flat of his boot.
"Once, at the water, I had a hound pointing into thirty paces of open fern with nothing in it to see," he said. "I am done with that. The next time she points, I want to mark the ground and go and look at it after."
"Then we hold the watch," said Old Qin. "Four days here. The ground is soft at the wallow, so anything that comes will print. If nothing comes, we carry the kill a day's walk and set again and hold four days there, all the way up toward the giants' water."
"And if it comes while we hold the watch?" said Xiao An.
"Then we do not shoot."
"Not shoot."
"Not shoot," said Old Qin. He put the list down flat on his knee and took out the brush and the ink. "Nobody in this line has ever shot first and learned second. If it comes to the meat and we are behind the blind with the hound staked, the three of us sit still and count. How big it is. How it eats. Whether it stands and eats like a beast or eats and watches. How much meat it takes, and which parts, and where it leaves the rest."
"And the hound?" said Gao Tie.
"The hound stays staked," said Old Qin. "If it comes, she will smell it before we do. This time we keep hold of her collar, and nobody lets go of anything."

The younger lodge man came up from the spring with water.
"What do we put on the paper for a name?" he said. "The men at the lodge will ask."

Old Qin wrote for a while, the brush moving slowly as it always did, and the light went down over the kill-ground while he wrote.
"One line," he said at last. "Something that leaves the deep kills standing. Where it has been read: the water bank, the high breaks, the low meadow, and the fern country south of the giants' water. What we took today: one thin light, an old beast. Next: the watch here, four days, then the kill carried a day's walk north and four more days."
"And the name," said the younger man.
"The keepers' line," said Old Qin.
"Keepers?"
"The old hunters of the north border say the deep country has its own keepers," said Gao Tie.
"I do not know what keeps the deep country," said Old Qin. "I know that something in it has been feeding on our heavy beasts for two summers and has never once shown itself. So we keep looking until we find it, and the line is the keepers' line, and it has one name on it: the beast that leaves signs and never shows itself."

He shut the list and put it away, and the four of them went down to the camp under the trees, leaving the kill standing in the open with the wire across both trails. Behind them the hound got up, walked to the end of her line, and stood with her muzzle up, smelling the wind off the high ground.

---

He found the second kill four days later, in the grey before dark: another heavy beast cut open in the open grass, the meat untouched, two wires low across the two trails, the blind up on its poles, and the hound staked short by the water. He lay on the ridge through the night and watched, and this time he did not need a day to understand it. The kill had been carried a day's walk north, which meant the watch was not fixed on one meadow. The hunters were working their way up the country the same way he hunted, a step at a time, and behind every step they left bait and a hidden man with paper.

They had not come to eat him or to take his years. They had come to find out what he was.

He spent the next days making the country lie. It was his oldest trick and he had never once used it against men. He took a heavy beast far to the south, in a meadow he never meant to visit again, ate the deep parts at the kill and left the rest standing, the wet hide still on it and the bones broken open, as loud as a kill can be made. He did that twice in the south, and once more in the low country outside his range, at a wallow the men had used two summers back. Then he kept to the hard ground and the stone and the high ferns, and he hunted small and quiet while the season turned, and he learned what it was like to be a rumour instead of a sign.

The small creatures came back to him all the same. On the fifth morning of that run he came down a stone trail and a hare sat at the end of its run and did not go flat, and then did, too late, and ran. The country was forgetting him a little every day, and the forgetting was the only cure for what he had spent at the water.

---

He went north once, at the end of summer, and he used his voice at the edge of the deep forest. The edge was where the giants' trees stopped and the world changed its mind about trees. He walked there in three days over ground he knew, and on the fourth morning he came out into country where the trunks stood far apart, the light fell whole, and the ground under him had no trails at all. Nothing that made trails lived there. The great beasts did not make trails. They stood.

He felt for them as he always did and found nothing: wide, patient, unlit places where his sense went out and came back empty. Three of them stood within his reach that morning. He walked between their grounds all day, up one side of a ground and down the other, and nothing stirred and nothing was set for him and nothing hid from him.

At the last of the light he came to a bare stone rise above a long valley, and beyond the valley the country climbed into ground he could not feel at all. He stood on the stone and roared. It came short and low, because the summer's work had made it that way: one thick note instead of a long tearing bellow, and it went out over the valley like a stone dropped into deep water.

The country went quiet in answer, and it was not the silence he knew. Nothing ran, nothing hid, and no ground was given up. The country simply stopped being busy, like a room when someone walks in who can read. Whatever lived out there had heard him and taken his measure: a thing with no name and a weight that could be counted. Nothing answered. The great beasts did not stir.

He spent his voice once and once only that summer, and came down out of the deep forest knowing the price. The kills he left standing wrote his name for anything that reads with its feet, and his roar wrote it for anything that reads with its depth. He could not take either of them back.

---

The hunger woke on one of the grey days at the turn of the season, and it did not wake the way it used to. He was lying on the warm stone above the hot springs, fed and easy, with the old bull's years settled into his bones, and one grey afternoon the hunger stood up in him and looked north. In the old days it had always come up hot. It had spent hunts before they began and hurried him up a gorge with the quiet broken behind him, and he had lost a stag to it in his second winter.

This was not hot. The hunger stood in him quiet and heavy. It did not want the next meal or the next heavy beast, and it did not care how long the waiting took. It wanted the deep years. It wanted the ground under the great beasts, and it wanted it the way a mountain wants weather: without hurry and without end.

He held it as a beast holds a current, and the holding did not end. He had done it through the whole summer and through the fight at the water, and the carrying was the difference between a beast with an appetite and an appetite with a beast. But he kept what he had learned from it, and he kept it carefully: the hunger was growing up, and it had learned to wait.

---

The summer turned. The hunters had carried their kill three times up into the deep forest, and three times they had watched it for four days with a hound staked by the water and a man behind the poles, and by the end of the season their line had reached the low end of his own range. He was not going to show them his face this year. A hunt with no face on it is blind, and he had spent the whole season keeping his face off it, hunting small on hard ground and writing his signs in countries he did not sleep in. The barrier at the thousand years stood far off in the middle of it all, as far as it had ever been, and he did not feel it. He went down off the rocks at dark and crossed the hard ground toward his own range, and somewhere far down-country, past the giants' trees and the hunters' camp and the wire, a hound that had once smelled him for one hour lifted its head off its paws, smelled the wind, and found nothing.

# Chapter 14: The Wrong Face

The snow came early that year. It started under the ground, days before it started in the sky. He knew winter was close by the hot springs: more beasts came down to the warm water than in other years, the steam hung thicker over it, and the small creatures went into their holes and closed them behind. He left the high stone country and moved down to the edge of the deep forest, and made his winter den under a shelf of roots above a stream, with one way in and another way out.

The hunters moved north with the cold. They had set three camps on the high trails before the end of summer, and by the second month of winter their line had reached the edge of the deep forest where he hunted. From a ridge at dusk he studied their newest camp: a fresh kill left lying in the open, wire strung low across both trails, a blind built of poles and cut branches, and a spirit hound staked by the water with its nose toward the meat.

He did not go near it. He took his own hunting down onto the hard ground where tracks do not hold, and he ate small, and he watched the hunters work their way up the country like water finding a crack.

---

The danger came in behind his own kills. At the end of the second month he found tracks going back to a kill he had left as bait in the low country outside his range: a heavy beast he had eaten deep and left standing. Something big had come to it. The tracks were wider than his own by a hand's width. They had come up to the kill out of the south, walked once around it without hurrying, and left the meat untouched.

Beasts come to meat. That is what meat is for. Something had come to the kill, read what it was, and walked away from the food, and only one kind of creature does that: one that is hunting something bigger than a meal.

He found the tracks again a week later, and a third time, closer, on a trail he used to reach the hot springs. Something was following him. He had left kills to send the hound and the hunters away from his range, and he had taught a different hunter to follow him. The new one was heavy and lean and patient, and it had killed nothing he could find. His own trick had grown a second edge, and the second edge was pointed at him.

---

The hunters met it before he did, and he read the whole of it from the ground. He came down the long slope on the third morning after a hard night and stopped on the ridge. The camp below him was wrecked. The kill was scattered and half eaten. Both wires were down. The blind had been knocked apart and one pole leaned over with a long dark smear down the wood. The snow around the water was cut over with tracks: boots, and the wide pads he now knew, and one line of tracks that went away south without ever breaking into a run.

There was blood on the bank, and it was not the beast's. He read the ground for the better part of a day. The hunters had made their kill and set their watch and sat behind the poles as they had five times before. The beast came up the trail in the last of the night, crossed the wire without touching it, and walked to the meat as if the wire were drawn on the ground for it to read. Then the ground broke up: boots going out, the wide pads turning, something heavy dragged down the bank, and the hound's line snapped clean at the stake.

One man had gone down by the water. The others had carried him west toward their camp. He sat on the ridge a long time after that. None of it was his doing, and all of it had come out of him. He left the wrecked camp at dark and did not go back.

---

The hunters carried their dead west and made camp in a hollow of black stone, and the four of them sat at the fire with the fifth one wrapped in his coat. The older lodge man had been carried a day and a half and had not spoken since the water. A long tear ran down his leg and another across his ribs where the wide forepaw had come down, and the younger man had packed both with moss and bound them with the last of the spare line.

"He should have stayed behind the blind," said the younger lodge man.
"He did stay behind the blind," said Gao Tie. "It walked past the blind. It walked past the wire, past the meat, past all of it, and it came to the water where he was filling the skin, because that was the job I gave him."

The older lodge man spoke from the fire, and the whole camp turned to him. His eyes were open, and his voice came out low and level.
"Read it back to me," he said.
Old Qin took the list and read it: the water bank, the high trails, the low meadow, the fern country south of the giants' water, five camps, the kills left standing, the wire, the watch, four days.
"Now the new one," said the lodge man.
"A beast of the deep forest. Heavy, wide-tracked. Stood the wire and never touched it. Killed at the water and went south."
"Good," said the lodge man. "Put my name under the list, and the winter's pay to my sister's house."
"You will carry the list down yourself," said Gao Tie.
"I have read enough ground in my life to know what I am lying on," said the lodge man. He shut his eyes. "Write the beast. Leave the story."

Old Qin had the list open on his knee, and the brush lay in the ink beside him. He had not written a word.
"Write it," said the younger man. "A beast in the camp, a beast that kills. That is a line. That is the line you wanted."
"It is not the same line," said Xiao An.
She had come in from the ridge, where she had walked the tracks twice.
"It leaves signs and never shows itself," she said. "That is what is written on the keepers' line. Five camps, and not one print in the meat, and the hound never once smelled it, and the wire was never touched. This beast left prints everywhere it went. It left a man dead. It ate the meat it came for."
"Something came to the sign and killed for it," said Old Qin. "Find me the difference that matters to the list. The lodge asks one question: did we put a beast on the paper. This beast walked into a camp we set for the thing we have been hunting, killed the best hand we had on the mountain, and went south without hurrying. If I write the thing we have been hunting and leave this beast off the page, we go home with a blank line and a dead man."
"Then write two lines."
"Two lines for one beast is one line too many," said Old Qin. "What we are hunting is a beast. It reads, it kills, and it has been on our heavy beasts since the first water. Now it has a shape and a size, and a name can wait."
"Then the line goes south when the ground softens," said Gao Tie.
"At the first soft day," said Old Qin. "South on the wide tracks, with the wire off the camps and the hound on the front. If the beast on the paper is the thing we have been hunting, we will not know it until it is dead on the ground. If it is not, we come north again in the summer and we will have spent a season to learn one true thing."
"Which is?" said the younger man.
"That this country has more than one hunter in it," said Xiao An.
"It tore the hound's stake out of the ground," said Gao Tie. "That is the thing I keep coming back to. It walked past the wire, and it did not go round the blind. It went into the middle of the camp and did what it liked and it left."
"Then the paper carries the thing we can prove," said Old Qin.

He dipped the brush and wrote, and the writing went on for a while in the quiet. The wind came down the hollow over the stone and moved the coat.
"What did you put?" said the younger man.
"A beast of the deep forest," said Old Qin. "Heavy, pale-sided, wide-tracked. Stood the wire and never touched it. Killed at the water and went south. That is the beast of the keepers' line until another beast proves otherwise."
"And the other one?"
"The other one is a smell the hound will not leave, a shape on paper, and a bank at the water," said Old Qin. He shut the list. "If the two are the same creature, then we have written it. If they are not, then the one we have written will take us south, and it is a killer, and killing it is work we know how to do."
"And after the south?" said Xiao An.
"After the south, the season is spent, and we take the list down to the lodge and stand in front of the table with a beast on the paper and a light in the box." He put the brush away. "That is as close to the truth as this country lets a man stand."

Then Gao Tie got up and put more wood on, and the younger man went out to the hound. Xiao An stood where she was, with the tracks of two beasts in her head and one line on the paper.

---

He crossed the high ground above their camp two nights later, and that was when the hound smelled him for the second time. He had not meant to come near the camp: the hard ground above the hollow was the driest crossing in the west, the wind came off the black stone with no scent of men in it, and he had held the quiet since the first ridge.

Halfway across, the country below him changed. He felt it as he felt a trap. The small creatures of the hollow went still all at once, and the wind came up the slope carrying men and fire and wet wool, and under that, thin and cold, a hound's voice asking a question of the dark.

He went down into the lee of a stone and pulled the quiet down over himself to its last limit, and it cost him as it always cost him now. The hound worked up toward him, not baying and not running, walking with its nose low, stopping every so often to stand and smell the air. Once, near a stand of black pines, it gave the long thin whine that is not finding and not losing.

It had two smells in its nose. It had the wide-pad smell from the water, fresh and strong, and it had the old smell it had carried for an hour at the water in the summer. The two of them crossed on the same ground in the same night, and the hound could not make them one, and it could not leave either, and its whole body was the argument.

A man's voice came up the slope, flat and low, and called it in. The hound stood a while longer with its muzzle up and its ears working, and then it turned and went down, and the men took it into the camp, and the fire went on burning behind the stone.

He crossed the rest of the high ground at its western end, in the dark, without leaving a print worth reading. The kills he had left as bait were confusing their hound, and the confusion was protection he had never planned and could not count on twice.

---

The hunger asked its question at the turn of the cold, and a full belly could not answer it. He took a heavy beast in the second month of winter, out of the hot springs, an old slow creature of the outer forest that had come down to the warm water as they all did. The hunt took three days and the kill was clean, and he ate the deep parts first and then the rest over the next two days. He came up out of the long sleep stronger, with heavier blood, and the pull toward the ravine felt a little clearer. The hunger that had no meal sat up inside him the moment he was awake.

He tried to feed it. He took a second heavy beast and ate it down. He took a thin one. He ate the deep parts of three kills in eight days, and every meal went in and every meal was good, and the hunger never once changed its note.

It was not asking for meat. The meat lay in him warm and whole, and the hunger stood over it and asked for the same thing as always, and the thing was not meat and not sleep.

He lay on the rock above the hot springs one grey evening and reached out north, and the dark places were there, and the answer was the same: the deep years, the ground under the great beasts. The hunger had stopped being about any beast he could kill. He held it as a beast holds a current, and the holding did not end.

---

What he did with his voice at the end of that month, he did because of the tracks. He went south into the low country where he had left the bait kills and where the wide pads had gone. On the third day he found the tracks running east along a dry watercourse, and he followed them at a distance for half a day, and in the last of the light he saw the beast itself for the first time.

It stood in a killing ground of its own making, under a shelf of old rock. It was not as big as the great beasts of the deep forest. It was bigger than anything else he had ever hunted: pale along the sides, heavy in the shoulders, with a long scarred jaw and a low head. It stood over the opened body of a heavy beast and ate, and everything about it said that it had never once hurried in its life.

Its ears came forward before he had moved. The two of them looked at each other across the killing ground, and neither moved for a long moment. He felt for its age, and found it old, the years in it thick and black and deep, and strong in a way that had nothing to do with the size of its body.

Then it took one step toward him. He roared, and this time he kept it short.

The sound came up out of his chest heavy and low, one breath long and no more. It went into the air between them and one pace past the beast's jaw. It landed as a stone lands in deep water: no long roll out over the country, no snow coming off the rocks, no small creatures going flat in the valley.

The other beast stopped, one forefoot still forward and its head low, and the long jaw came open a little, and the feeling it had been making went still. For one breath the two of them stood in the same killing ground with one sound between them, and the sound was his kind's whole meaning, and it went into the other's ears four paces away and left nothing to answer.

Then the beast turned off the kill and walked south, unhurried, as it did everything, and did not look back. He stood over the dead beast and ate the deep parts and left the rest. By then his legs had gone soft under him and a dimness sat behind his eyes. The walk home took two days longer than it should have. The second day he spent lying in a stone shelter with the whole country sounding loud and near and too bright.

His voice had cost him breath and blood before. This time it cost him something more. For two days the country read too warmly, the way a bank reads after a flood goes off it, and he lay there and knew that the aiming had been the price. He came home to his den with the lesson whole. His voice was not a shout any more. It was a word, and a word said to a hunter is a word the hunter keeps. Somewhere south, in the pale beast with the scarred jaw, there now walked the sound of what he was.

---

The season turned with the hunters still in his country and a wrong beast on their paper. One camp was struck, and then another, and the hunters' tracks turned south where the wide pads had gone. He crossed above their last camp on the night before they left it: the meat in the open, the wire low on both trails, the poles and the cut branches, and the hound staked by the water with its nose to the east.

The hound lifted its head while he watched. It stood up on the end of its line and smelled the wind coming down off the rocks, and the long thin whine came up the slope to him once, and then the man at the fire called it and it lay down again.

He went on north in the dark, over the hard ground, toward his own range. The paper had a face on it now, and the face was wrong, and he had not put it there. What he had put there was a kill left in the open as bait, and the bait had brought a hunter of his own weight, and the hunter had taken the watch off his ground.

South was where the hunters were walking, with the wire and the blind and the paper and the boy on the hound, and south was where the two of them would meet. And he would be north, and free, and the freedom would have been bought with bait that had grown legs. He came down into his range at the grey end of the night, and went in under the roots, and slept.

# Chapter 15: The Hound's Third Time

He woke with water moving under the ground.

It had run in the dark below the den for three nights, and that was how he knew the winter had broken. He came out onto a slope where the snow had gone grey and soft, and the air smelled of wet stone and roots, and the stream below the den was running loud for the first time since the autumn. Out in the low country the ice was going out of the water, and it went with a sound like a herd crossing a long way off.

He walked his own range for two days and read what the winter had left. The camps on his ground were down. At the first one he found the fire ring under new water with grey ash around it, and the cut poles of the blind lying in the pine needles where they had been thrown, and a bald patch where the snow had been beaten flat. The wire was off both trails. Nothing of the men was left in his country but the smell, and the smell was going out of it day by day.

He worked the high stone for the two days after that, because the thaw had opened it. The springs came up warm out of the rock in the middle of the snow, and the small beasts of the slope had come out of their holes to sit in the steam: beetles first, then the stone-runners, then a thin fox-kind that looked at him once and did not come back. He ate beetles off the warm rock, which was not hunting but was food, and he drank where the water came out of the ground already warm, and lay in the steam with the sun on him and let the winter come out of his hide. On the second evening he took a young stone-runner up on the scree, sitting at the mouth of its hole with its cheeks full, and it was one mouthful and he ate it and went on.

On the second evening he stood on the high ridge and looked south. The low country lay under its own mist, and down near the edge of the fern there was one thin line of smoke. The men were south yet, on the ground where the wide pads ran. He watched the smoke until dark, and he did not go down while it stood. He slept that night on the ridge with the smoke smell in the wind. In the morning the wind had turned and there was nothing to smell but his own country coming awake.

---

The smoke was gone on the fourth day, and he went south into the ground he had not walked since the autumn.

He did not go for the men. He went because he had spent one whole roar on a heavy beast in the winter, and a thing like that leaves a debt in a country, and he wanted to read what the debt had become. Two days of walking brought him down the long slope and along the low water, and on the third day he found the place where the men had kept their watch.

It was a fine open bit of ground above a pool, where the low trail crossed the wide pads, and the men had worked it hard. The wire was gone from both trails, and the blind was down, and the fire ring was cold under a shawl of wet ash. But the ground told him more than that. Men had walked it for days; the same two pairs of boots went in circles he could follow; and by the water there was a patch of torn moss, worn through in a circle no body of that size makes by standing once.

He went over that patch twice. The hound of the men had stood there a long time. Her tracks were all over it, pointed and re-pointed, and a man's boots had come to her twice and led her off, and she had come back to it both times. Whatever she had found there, it did not have a print. The moss was torn, and the mud under it was old, and there was nothing in the whole patch for a nose that was not a hound's to take hold of.

He made his own circle of that ground, wide, and left it the way he had come.

He crossed his own trails once on the way north, the ones he had used all winter on the hard ground, and read them the way he read everything. Nothing had walked them but him. Whatever the men had learned in the south, they had not brought it up onto his range, and the wide pads had not come north either. He went along the trails to the top of the range and stood a while at the edge of the deep forest, where the ground rises, and looked north into the trees, and then went back down.

---

He took the low country a day at a time after that, and there was a lot to take.

The two waters were the country's whole business, and he learned them the way he had learned the high ground in his first year. The upper water ran down out of the stone country and cut a soft valley through the fern, with pools at the bends and gravel bars between them. The lower water came up out of the men's country far south and ran flat and brown between low banks, and the two of them joined at the bottom of the country and went south together. Everything that drank there drank between the two, and everything that crossed the country crossed between them, and there was no way from the deep forest down to the south country that did not pass through his ground.

It was open ground. No camp stood on it, and no fire would stand on it again before the next winter at the earliest. No other heavy beast had walked it since the autumn. The thaw was bringing the meat down to the new water, the slow heavy kind that had wintered in the fern, and the low country was the road. Everything that came up out of the men's country into the deep forest came up through it, and everything that went down out of the deep forest went down it. Whatever walked the road first saw everything else that used it.

So he took it. He walked its two waters and its fern edge over two days and put his own quiet over the ground, and on the third evening he took the first meat on it. The kill was a heavy grazer at the lower pool: an old one, alone, thin from the winter, down at the last of the light. He came down to the pool against the wind and lay in the reeds above the bank to watch her. She was one of the slow kind, old, thin from the winter, and she stood in the shallows with her head up for a long time before she drank, the way the old ones do when they have heard a thing or two in their lives. He did not move. The reeds stood still around him and the water talked at the bank, and he let all of that be the only sound in the country.

She put her head down and drank. He came up out of the reeds at the shoulder and took her at the neck in the first stride, and the water broke around the both of them, and she went down and was still. He stood in the shallows and ate the deep parts while the light went out of the sky. Two crows came down and sat in a dead pine above the pan and waited for the rest. He dragged the rest well off the trail and left it to them.

The hunger came up when he was full, as it did at the end of every meal, and asked the same question it had asked all winter. He had stopped trying to answer it with meat. He carried it, and it stayed, and it did not change.

---

On the fifth day he went further south, because he wanted the pale beast's ground read before the season turned.

He found the wide pads at the far end of the low country, at a pool below a shelf of old rock, and he read them a long time with his nose down. The big one had come down to drink in the last days of the winter and gone back up onto its own ground, unhurried, the same walk it had used all its life. Its track was wider than his own by a hand's width. The age was in the print itself, in how little the toes spread: a beast that had stopped hurrying long before he was hatched.

He stood over the prints with the sun going down and read the size and the years out of them. The beast had come down to drink and stood a while at the pool, and then gone back up onto its own ground the same unhurried way it did everything. The tracks of one animal are a road it has spent its life building, and the road in these said the same thing at every step: this is a beast that has never once run.

He did not follow them, and he did not roar. The sound he had spent on that beast in the winter walked somewhere behind those tracks, in the meat of it, and the roar had not come back to him and would not. It was not a debt. It was a thing said once between two of his kind, and it would stand as said.

---

He turned back north before the light went, and he crossed above the place where the men had last camped on the southern ground, on the high dry crossing, and that was when he saw the hound for the third time.

She was on a short line at their fire, and she was working the ground the way she worked everything, in slow arcs, nose down. Halfway across her arc she stopped. She went down into the moss with her whole head and stood there, and then she walked a few paces to her left and did it again. Then she stood still, tail low and body pointed. The man with her stood up and came to her and looked over the same patch of moss, and there was nothing there to see. He looked a long time. Then he put a hand on her collar and spoke to her and led her back toward the fire, and she went, and she looked back at the moss twice.

He knew the ground she had been standing on. He had lain in that moss for the better part of a night in the summer, with his quiet drawn over himself to its last limit, and the hound had climbed the slope toward him in the dark and lost him in it, and the men had called her down.

She had his old smell in her nose and she could not make it a thing a man could see, any more than she could make a scent into a track. And the man had come to her and stood over her patch and looked, and had found nothing, and had taken her away from it.

He crossed the rest of the high ground at its western end, in the dark, without leaving a print worth reading.

---

South was where the men walked now, with the wire and the blind and their paper, and their hound had put his smell on the ground twice in one year and could not spend it. North was the deep forest, and the great beasts' country, and the pull he had carried since the first summer, and the sound of his own voice standing somewhere in a heavy body to the south.

The low country lay between the two, and the low country was his, and he walked it now the way he walked his own range — not reading it any more, only using it.

He came down into it at the grey end of the night, to the fern and the new water and the road, and he went along it at a walk, and the small kind heard him and went quiet and let him pass, the way they did when the country was working right.

The springs were giving off their steam in the cold of the morning. The beasts of the low country were at the warm water: the slow kind, the small kind, the birds, crowded in together with their heads down, drinking. He smelled it all from the top of the slope. For a while he only breathed. The country was waking up all around him, and none of it knew he was ten strides above it.

The whole low country lay under his nose like a map. The waters. The road. The springs. The high ground at his back, and the deep forest standing north.

# Chapter 16: The One Print

The heat came up the low country in the first weeks of summer, and the water went down.

The two streams that crossed the country went thin and slow, and by the middle of the season they were chains of pools with long flats of cracked mud between them. The fern stood as high as his shoulder and hid everything that moved. The low country was his range now, and he hunted it the length of it. On the fourth evening he took a heavy grazer at the lower pool: the slow kind, old and thin from the winter, come in out of the fern alone. He lay in the reeds above the bank and let her drink. She put her head down and drank a long time, and when she lifted it he came up out of the reeds at the shoulder and took her at the neck. The water broke around the two of them, and then it was quiet, and he stood in the shallows and ate the deep parts while the light went out of the sky.

That was how the summer went. The meat came down to the water in the evenings, the water held it there, and the low country gave him a meal every few days without a fight.

The nights taught him the water's hours, and he hunted by them. The slow kind came down in the last of the light and drank long. The small quick things came at dark, in and out in a breath. The pigs came at the black of the night, and the birds at first grey, working the drying edges for what the night had left. He took his share of all of it and slept the hot middle of the day away in the shadow of the shelf, with the flies walking on him, and woke to drink when the sun was going. He ate deep and slept the hot hours away in the shade of the stone shelf, and the flies worked at him, and the country steamed. He grew heavier as the summer went on. His kills he kept off the trail, and what he could not eat he dragged away into the fern and left to the crows. Nothing else heavy had walked the low country since the spring.

The hunger came up after every meal the same as always. Over a full belly, in the heat, on bare stone, it asked its question, and the question was never meat.

---

In the middle of the summer the smoke came back up the country.

The wind turned south on a grey morning and brought it: wood smoke, and men, and the wet wool smell, thin and far. He knew the smell. He had left it in the south at the thaw, and now it was walking north again, and it was going to cross ground that was his.

He read them before he saw them. On the second evening the smell was strong enough to have a direction in it, and on the third morning he lay high on the rim of the low country and watched them come up the low trail: four men and the hound. An old man walked in front, then one with the hound on a short line, then one who walked with his eyes on the ground, and then a last one with the packs.

He could have gone down onto the trail and been away over the ridge before they came level with him. He did not. The low country was his, and the men were walking through it to somewhere else, and a beast who moves in front of men is a beast they follow. So he lay on the rim and let them pass along his own trail, and when they camped that night at the lower pool, he kept his quiet over himself and did not go down for water.

He watched them the whole night from the fern above the camp: the fire, the four shapes around it, the hound lying by the water. The youngest of them did the camp work — water and wood, twice out to the fire and back — and the one with the hound sat a little apart with his hand on the collar. Near the middle of the evening the youngest one stood up and looked out at the dark for no reason, the way men do, and looked a long time at the fern above them without seeing it, and then sat back down and put more wood on. Near the middle of the night the hound got up and worked a slow half-circle out to the edge of the firelight with her nose low. He pulled his quiet down over himself to its last limit and lay without moving. She stood at the edge of the light a while with her whole body in the feel, and then she went back to the fire and lay down, and the men had not noticed her go. When the grey came up he was still there, and he drank at a stream higher up when the sun was high, and he went that night and the next without a kill.

In the morning the four men and the hound went north off his low ground and up onto the high ground, and he stayed on his own side and let them have the bare ridges.

He read their camp ground the day after they left it, the way he read every ground they touched. They had set the fire in the lee of the bank, close to the water, and slept in a row with their feet to it. The hound had been staked downwind of them, on a line short enough that she could reach the water and no further, and she had walked circles at the end of it most of the night, or lain and got up and lain again. There was a place under the bank where one of the men had knelt with a cup and drunk, and a place where the youngest had sat a long time by himself in the fern, facing nothing. And that was all of the use they had made of his country: a fire, a row of men, a hound at the end of a string.

---

Three days after their smell had gone off the high ground, he came up and read what they had done.

The dry ground showed him less than the wet ground would have, but men write loudly when they stop. He found their walked line along the ridge, four men and the hound in it, and he found the two places where they had stood a long time: the bank of the upper stream, and the bare pan in the middle of the high ground. Two of the men had gone down on their knees at the edge of the pan and had stayed down long enough to leave the shape of their knees in the dust, and the prints of their hands where they had leaned in over the rim. The hound had lain down once in the dust by the east edge, in the shape of a dog that had been waiting a while.

He walked round the pan himself, once, as they had. The hound's tracks went all round it too, and off the north edge onto the stone and back, and down to the stream and back, the same line twice. And in the middle of the pan his own print lay where he had made it, in the setting mud of the wet season, dried hard, cracks running through it, with the marks of men's knees in the dust beside it at the edge.

He stood over it a long time.

The wet season's pan had taken his shape and kept it all summer, the way the wet country writes down everything that walks it. He had crossed that pan once, in the first soft days, on his way up to the deep forest, and stood in the middle of it a while, looking south at the low country under its mist, and then gone on. One crossing was all it had taken. The mud had run out from under his feet while he stood, and the sun had dried the whole thing into one piece, and the piece had kept him.

He read the rest of it the way he read any ground. The hound had put her nose into the middle of the pan and stood there, and then worked both ends of the line the men wanted — off the north edge onto bare stone and back, and down the grass to the stream and back — and given it up. Two of the men had knelt at the rim and read his print with their eyes for as long as men read anything. And north of the pan, four stones had been set in a row on the ground, out in the open, where a man coming up the ridge would find them.

He looked at the stones from the outside and did not go near them. He did not know what men did with stones in a row, and he did not need to. He understood the shape of the thing well enough without the why of it: men had marked this place, and men mark a place in order to come back to it.

Twice now he had used the writing trick. He had left kills standing in the open with the meat untouched so that men who read ground would read the wrong thing, and the trick had worked, and the working had taught them. The men had learned to read his signs, and the hound had learned to hold his smell, and now the mud itself had learned to keep his shape and hold it up to them, ready-made, on the bare hill all season.

So he would not write for them again.

---

He did not touch the pan. A pan torn open would be one more thing to read: a place visited twice, once by a beast and once by whatever came after it and tore the ground. So he gave them nothing.

From that morning he took the long way. He crossed the streams at the rock bars, where the water runs over stone, and he walked the high ridges where there is nothing but stone underfoot, and he left the mud flats to the grazing kind. Twice that month he passed up a kill he could have taken, rather than cross a soft pan to reach it, and went a day hungry instead.

The second time was a young grazer at a soft flat below the first spring. It came down to drink at dusk and stood in the open with its head down, and there was a pan between him and it, three strides of cracked yellow mud, and the grazer was thin and quick and the light was going. He stood a long while at the edge of the stone and turned it over. Three strides, and meat for three days, and one print going and one print coming back. He went without, and the grazer drank and went away up the far bank without ever knowing he had been there, and he went and lay in the shade with his ribs showing the summer's lean.

He paid it.

The four stones stood where the men had set them, in a line at the north edge of the pan. He walked round that ground once more before he left it, and took the long way down to his own country, on stone.

---

The summer turned over after that, and the low country stayed his.

The meat kept coming down to the water, and he kept taking it at the bank, and dragging what he could not eat off the trail; and when the flies were at their worst he lay up in the shade for a day and a night and let the country work. He grew heavier still. The pull toward the north was there the same as always, under everything, far off, and the hunger stood up over every meal, and neither of them changed.

Twice he walked to the edge of the deep forest where the ground rises, and stood under the first of the great trees with the forest going away north in front of him, dark and full of years, and listened. The deep forest was the same as it had been every season he had stood there: the great beasts' business going on somewhere inside it, far off, patient, none of it about him. He did not go in.

When the light began to come up colder in the mornings, he crossed once more to the ridge above the high ground and looked at the pan from a long way off. The four stones stood in their row. The pan lay in the sun with its one print in the middle of it, and nobody had come back for it all summer, and nobody had touched it.

The wet would come again before long and run the mud soft. Whatever walked the pan after that would write its own line there. He had already chosen where he would walk when the soft ground came.

He went down off the ridge and back to his own country. The low water was low, and the fern was turning, and the meat was still coming down to drink. He took a heavy one that week and ate deep. The nights were getting longer. He knew where the cold would come from, and where he would put his winter den, and which of the trails he would keep and which he would let go.

# Chapter 17: The Long Wet

The rain came up the country in the middle of the spring, and after the first week it did not stop for more than a day at a time.

The streams came up first and then went over their banks, and the low water spread out of them across the flats until the whole country south of the fern edge was one brown sheet with the tops of bushes standing out of it. The meat came up out of it at the start. The slow heavy kind that could not swim well pushed up onto the ridges, and he took two of them on the second and third days, easy, without a fight, standing in water to his chest to do it, and eating on the high ground with the flood running past below him in the dark. Then the water spread further, and the meat went out of the country: the slow kind went north toward the dry ridges, and what was left in the low land was water and birds.

He moved up onto the stone. His old den under the shelf of roots was under the flood, and he went back to the ravine den in the outer forest, up on high rock with the stream running past the mouth of it. He stood in the mouth of it on the first night and looked out at his own country under the water. Rain came off the lip of the den in one long line, and the flood smelled of wet earth and drowned grass. He was hungry inside a week.

The flood brought him one gift before it finished rising. A day after he moved to the rock a heavy grazer came down the current, dead and turning, drowned somewhere up in the low country and carried along like a log. He went into the water for it where the stream ran wide over a shelf, caught it in the current and worked it out onto the stone. It was old and the flood had been at it, but it was meat, and it had cost him no print at all — the water had written it, and the water would take its own writing back. He ate there on the bare rock in the rain for two days, with the dark water going past and the crows standing off in the pines.

---

He learned the rain's hours.

The wet country writes down everything. Mud, soft moss, the flats — even the hard grass went soft enough to take a print, and a print that stays is a thing men can carry away in their heads. He worked it out in the first weeks: in the heaviest rain, nothing keeps. He crossed the open ground only in the middle of a downpour, and he stood and watched his own print go. The rain filled the pad first, then the toes, and then the edges slumped. Inside the hour there was a shallow place in the mud the size of his foot, and no more shape to it than a puddle. Nothing to read.

So he took his hunting routes along the rock bars, where the streams ran over flat stone, and slept on stone, and drank where the water came off ledges rather than from the banks.

It cost him. Hungry as he was, he passed up two kills in the first month of it, both of them in soft ground, and once he stood over a stranded beast on a mud island and did not take it and went away upstream. He could not eat a meal and unmake the print he had made getting to it. So he learned where to stand and how to wait, and he ate what came to the rock, which was little. The cold water ran off him all day. His ribs came up under the hide again for the first time since his first winter, and he slept light.

The ravine den was a good place for a wet like that one. It sat high on the rock with its mouth looking down the stream, and the water ran past below the lip of it and covered the sound of anything moving in the country. He slept with his back to the stone wall and his head toward the mouth, and the stream talked all night, and the rain came and went outside like something walking around the hill. Two of the small kind lived in the rocks above the den that season: a stone-runner and a fat grey burrower. They got used to him, or as near to it as their kind ever comes. By the end of the wet they went about their business on the same shelf while he lay in the mouth of the den with one eye on the whole of it.

The hunger used the thin weeks. It came up in him after every mouthful, and on the days he ate nothing it came up anyway, and asked its question. The question was not meat. He lay in the mouth of the ravine den in the wet dark with the water going past, and the pull toward the deep forest was there the same as always, far off, under the great beasts, and the answer was the same as always: not yet, and not food.

Twice in that month he saw their smoke off to the north, on the high ground above his old low country. It hung low and grey in the rain and did not move. He knew the place it came from without going near it, and he did not go near the high ground, not once, and when the wind came off it he took his water lower down.

---

A light came over the high ground near the end of the wet, on a night when the rain let up for an hour before the next band of it came through.

He was on the rim of the high ground, hunting the dry edges above the flood, when is came up over the northern lip of the country: a light, small and white, standing up off the ground where no fire should be. He went still and read the air. No smoke belonged to it. It did not move the way a fire moves; it stood, one long thread of light in the rain-glare, up in the middle of the high ground where the ground was bare and the watching country was.

He knew what a light rising and standing meant. He had seen it done in his first years, to the quick slender beast in the fern country, and twice again at the wet breaks and the high fern, both times read from the ground after. When a beast dies with its light still in it, the light stands up out of the body and burns where it stands, and men with their iron and their boxes come and take it away. He had never watched one stand from the beginning, the whole length of it, before this night.

He lay on the rim and watched it. It stood in the rain for a while, one clean line of light in all that grey, and it did not move and it did not shorten. Then it was gone — not faded and not fallen, just gone, the way lights go when the men's work reaches them. After it went out he stayed a long while in the fern with the rain starting again on his back. He worked at the thing the way he worked at a track. Something up there had died and left its light standing. The men had been close enough to take it. There was nothing else to know about it, and he would not go and look.

He went down to his rock and slept.

---

He read the whole of it from the ground ten days after they left.

The wet was going out by then and the rock was drying in patches, and he came down off the ravine rim on the stone side and read the place from outside first. The wire was gone from both sides. The lean-to was gone, and the poles' holes in the moss were the only marks where it had been. The fire ring was scattered. There were boots all over the grass side, and drag-marks, and then, out on the rock past the edge of the pan, cut bones, picked at by crows and rained on for a week.

He walked out to the bones and read them. Heavy, slow kind, young, of the low water. One of the herd that the flood had driven up onto the high ground, just as it had driven him. It had come up through the wet country and gone into the men's wire in the dark and died there.

He read the kill the wire had made. The beast had come in from the low side and hit the wire low, and gone round the pan once, fast, dragging the stake, and the men had worked it half a night with their poles. It was all there in the ground if a body took the time: the circle, the drag, the deep pressed places where it went down and got up again, the boot marks closing in when it stopped. It had come up through the wet country and gone into the men's wire in the dark and died there. The bones were cut the way men cut what they will carry, and the hide was gone, and the skull had been left where the crows could get at it. Whatever light that body had carried had stood up over this rock, some wet night while he lay hungry in his den, and the men had taken it down the country with the rest.

Then he walked the pan, and the pan had one thing to say, and it said it in every line it had. The season lay written across it: the hound's circles round the edges, the poles' holes, the boots, and the great smeared track of an ox that had come up out of the low water and died there. He walked the whole pan twice, and in the middle of all of it there was not one print of his own.

A whole wet, soft as the country would ever be, and the page had written everybody who walked on it except him.

He stood at the north edge of the pan a while, a good way off from the four stones. He understood the trick now, whole; not the why of the stones, but the length of the thing. He had kept his body out of his own country's writing for a year and a half of seasons, and the price of it was the lean weeks in the ravine and the kills passed up and the ribs under the hide. He paid it again that morning, standing on wet stone, and did not go near the mud.

---

The wet broke in the last days of the season. The water went down off the flats, the streams came back inside their banks, and the low country came out from under the flood brown and soft and rich, with the drowned grass lying flat and the new shoots already coming through it.

He went down for the first time in two months and drank at the stream's edge where the water was still quick, and then he hunted. The first kill after the flood was an old grazer standing in the shallows where the flats were coming out: no fight and no long stalk, just the bank and the shoulder and the water closing over the two of them. The water was still high and quick everywhere, and his print in the shallows filled and went before he had finished eating. He ate deep for the first time in a season, and the hunger stood up over the full belly and asked its question, the same as ever.

The water was going down. The low country was coming back, and the meat with it, and the road between the two countries would be open again before the warm season.

He slept that night on bare rock, well back from the mud, with his country under him and the deep forest standing north in the dark, and the pull under the great beasts where it had always been.

In the morning he crossed to the ridge above the pan one last time before the season turned. The four stones stood in their row. The pan held its page, with the ox written across it and nothing else, and the crows were working at the cut bones on the rock. Then he went down to the low country, where the work was, and left the high ground to its stones.

The spring was coming up the whole country by then. The road between the two countries was open again, and the low water was clear and quick where it had been brown and slow. He went down the long slope on the second morning after the break and put his nose into the new grass at the edge of the fern. Shoots, small feet, old scent washing out of the ground. The country turned over from one year to the next, the way it had turned every year of his life.

# Chapter 18: The Dry Country

The water went down all summer and the low country came apart into pools.

By the middle of the season the two streams were chains of still water with long cracked flats between them, and everything that lived in the low country walked the same lines between the same pools. The slow heavy kind came down to drink at dusk. The birds worked the drying edges. And at the far end of each chain, where the water still ran over stone, the runs stayed quick and clear and cold.

He drank at the runs.

He had learned the still water in the first week of the dry, when he came down to the main pool one night and smelled the hound before he reached the bank. She was staked in the reeds above the water on a short line, and there was a fire behind a screen of cut branches, and boots went round the edge of the pool in the morning's mud. The men were back, and they were sitting on the water, and they did not mean to leave it while the dry lasted. He backed off and drank two miles up, at a run that came out of the rock, and lay there in the dark with his ears on the low country.

So the summer made its own rules. He hunted the upper water, where the meat came to drink at the runs. He took his kills standing in the stream over stone, ate in the water, and left the rest up on the bank for the crows. He crossed on the rock bars, gave the still pools and their long soft edges all the room they wanted, and drank where the water moved. It cost him miles and hunting hours every day, and the season was hot, and twice a month he came in with the flies at the cut places and lay up a day in the shade.

He paid it. Nothing of him lay anywhere the ground could write.

The hunger came up after every meal the same as always. Over a full belly, in the heat, on bare stone, it asked its question, and the question did not change.

---

The hound was the thing that would not settle.

He watched her from the rim of the low country, from the fern, from the far edge of the light, more than once as the season went on. She was slower than she had been; he could read the years in how she moved and how deep she slept in the day.
