But every night the man with her put her on her line above the water, and every night she worked the dark bank with her nose up, and some nights she did more than that.

Three nights he saw her stand and point at nothing.

She would be lying at the pool's edge, and then she would stand — no warning, no sound — and go to the end of her line and stand with her whole body pointed up the water, into the dark north where the run came down. She would hold it there, pointed like a thrown spear, while the fire burned behind her and the man came out of the blind and stood beside her. He would look at the same dark, and see nothing at all, and still stand. The first night he watched her hold it a quarter of an hour. The second night, longer. And after the third night the man moved his bed out of the blind and down to the pool's edge beside her, and slept there with his hand on her line, night after night.

She was reading the air for a smell that was not there — not on the nights he watched, because on those nights he was a long stone's throw away in the dark, lying still. She did it because the smell had been there before, in her lifetime, twice. She had held it in her nose at a water crossing two summers back, and she had never once lost it since, and she believed it would come again.

He read her patience the way he read a track. She was old for her kind, older than the men around her knew, and the work she was doing was the work she had done all her life, and it had never failed her before.

He lay in the fern above and watched her stand there, pointed at the empty dark, with the firelight on her ribs. The ground had stopped writing him a long time ago. The air had not.

---

The kill was up at the first of the runs, and he took it the way he took everything that summer: from the water, standing in the current.

It was a grazer of the slow kind, come down the stream to drink at sundown. He came up out of the shallows below the run and took it at the shoulder, and the two of them went down together in the deep part, and the water carried the red away downstream while he ate. He ate the deep parts there in the shallows, on the gravel, and left the body where the drag-mark showed, and went up onto the stone to sleep.

Two days later he read the men at his kill.

They had walked it in boots, four of them — one with the lodge road's dust on it, so the old man had come up from the south for this. They had stood on the bank a long time. And then they had gone down on their knees in the gravel, all of them in the same small patch, at the head of the run, in the shallows where his feet had stood while he ate.

He went over their marks slowly, and read the line of the morning for himself. The hound had come down the bank working hard, and at the water's edge she had put her nose down into the shallows where he had stood, and she had barked once. He could hear the shape of it in the ground she had left, all four feet planted and her weight forward. Then she had stood at the running water and would not step into it. She never had. He had watched her refuse a stream the summer before, and she had refused this one, with his smell in it, standing over the very stones his feet had crossed.

The men had looked at the water a long time after that. He read their boots going up the bank in little steps, and the prints of their faces where they had turned and looked north up the run, where the kill had come from and where he had gone. More than once, from the marks: a man standing and looking at fast water with a hound's word in his hand and nothing to put with it.

---

He understood the shape of the summer by then.

They had brought their wire and their hound and their paper to the water, and the ground he walked gave them nothing, because he had stopped writing. But the hound did not need his print. She read him out of the air, and out of the water, and out of a smell two summers old that she had never once let go. She had led them to his kill and stood over the shallows where his feet had stood, and the men had knelt in the gravel at the head of the run, at the one place in the whole low country where his own smell lay thick on the ground.

And they had no more use for that than they had for a fire in the rain, because it could not be carried: no track, no print, no body, and a hound standing where a beast should be and nothing there to see.

The drink was the problem now, and the drink could not be dropped. He could go a week without meat and he could not go two days without water in the heat. The men were on the main pool and the hound was on the air, and the country was going to get drier before it got wet.

So he answered it the only way the country let him. He drank at the runs, in the black of the night, standing in the current, with the taste of stone in the water and his ears on the low country behind him. He hunted the upper water, took his kills in the stream, dragged what he could not eat onto the stone and into the fern. He kept to rock, and to the dark, and to the fast water, and he made the men's water a place he did not go.

---

The dry ended, and then the thing he had been waiting for all summer happened without any warning at all.

He came down off the stone in the last week of the season to read the pool one more time, the way he read it every few days, and the work was gone.

The wire was up off both trails and gone into the packs; he found the two ends of its run and the holes where the stakes had stood. The blind was down, the poles lying in the reeds. The fire ring was scattered, and the ground around it put back to grass as well as hands can put it back. The hound was gone, and the line with her, and the men. Their trail walked south along the water and then turned down out of the low country, onto the long country, the road to their own places — and nothing about it was a patrol's walk. The packs had been heavy and the men had walked like men walking home.

He went over the whole camp twice. The ground had been used hard all summer and then left clean: no blood, no gear dropped, no dead man in the reeds. They had simply and finally finished, and gone, and taken their papers and their iron and their hound down the road with them, and nothing of the whole summer's watching stayed in the low country except the marks of it, which the grass would take in a season. And when he had read the last of it he stood on the pool's bank in the sun with the water going slowly down at his feet, and the low country empty around him, and the thing that had been in his way for three seasons was not in the country any more.

No fire came up the country that autumn. He read the low trail twice a month, and no boots walked it. The winter came down out of the north and he took his winter ground above the deep forest, and when the snow broke and the water ran and the spring came up the country, still no smoke stood anywhere in the low country. Their lodge was somewhere down-country, and the men who knew this ground were down there with it, and what they had learned of him they had carried away.

The country was his, all of it — the low trail and the springs, the road, the high ground with its pan and its four stones, the ridge above the deep forest where he sat in the evenings. And this time there was nothing in it that hunted him in return.

He crossed the high ground once that spring and stood with the pan below him and the four stones in their row at the edge of it. Grass had come up through the cracks in the pan and the old print was gone under it. A crow sat on the windward stone, and got up when it saw him, and went away down the hill.

---

He walked the whole of it in the first weeks of the spring, from the southern fern to the dry edge above the deep forest, and slept in a different place most nights, and drank where he liked.

It took him six days to walk it all, which was longer than the walk itself needed, because he went slowly at the edges. At the southern end he stood where the low trail went down out of the country, the road the men's boots had used for years, and read the last of their going in the wet mud: heavy packs, the hound's pads set among the boots, two of them walking together and two apart. The trail went down the long slope and out of sight, and the country behind it went on being the country.

The deep forest stood north where it had always stood, and the great beasts worked their country up and down inside it, and the pull under them was there the same as it had been since his first summer, far off and steady. The hunger stood up after every meal and asked its question, and there was no meal in the low country that could answer it, and he had long ago stopped expecting one to.

He was six winters in the world, or near enough, and the country that had seemed as wide as the world when he crawled out of the shell was one piece of the border of a forest that went on for a hunter's whole life in every direction. South, there were the men and their lodges and their lists. East, the mountain country. North, the deep forest, and beyond the deep forest, the country of the great beasts, and under all of it the slow pull that had been in him since the first hunger.

He stood on the dry edge at the end of that spring, with his own country behind him and nothing in it that could read him, and he looked north for a long time.

Then he went down into the low country to hunt, because that was the day's work, and the road to the north was a road for years.

# Chapter 19: The North Road

The wolves came to the kill before the moon was up.

He had taken the old grazer at the bank below the second pool, as he had taken a grazer at that bank every thaw for years: down off the rock in the last of the light, at the shoulder, in the shallows. It had gone as it always went. The meat was deep and the night was cold, and he was eating with the water running over his feet when the first voices came down off the mountain side of the country.

They were a winter pack, down from the high country because the high country had nothing in it that winter. They did not come at him. They came to the edge of the fern and stood in a line, twenty of them and then more behind them, thin as winter wolves are, and their feet went in little steps, and their voices went up and up, and not one of them would cross the line of ground his body had already drawn at the fern's edge.

He ate. The pack waited. The moon came up and found them all in the same places — the meat between them, the water talking to itself over the stone, and the wolves crying at the edge of the dark like the dark itself was hurt.

That was the wrong of it. He stood in the shallows with the blood going off downstream and heard what the night was carrying. The noise went out over the low country in every direction, the same cry, hour on hour. For years he had kept his feet off the soft ground and his prints out of the mud and his body out of any light, and the country held nothing of him. The wolves were writing him into the air with their voices, all night, for anything with ears.

He left the meat.

He took what his belly needed and left the rest standing in the shallows, and the pack had it before he was a hundred paces up the stone. The crying stopped the moment the first wolf reached the water. That was the price and the lesson in one shape: the meat gone, and the quiet bought back with it. He went up the run in the dark and did not look back.

He came back at gray morning and read the ground, because a thing is not finished until its ground is read. The kill was gone to hide and hair. Pads by the hundred ran the bank and the fern, cut up with the drag of the half-eaten body through the shallows, and over all of it the ordinary tracks of the pack's going home — single file up the mountain side, their bellies heavy on the snow between their legs. They had told the whole country where the meat was, and then they had told it where they had taken the meat, and by noon every crow in the low country knew both.

The next thaw he did not kill at the bank. He took the grazers where he found them, up-stream and down, one ground one season and another the next, and never the same bank twice in a year. A map is a thing habit makes, and anything with a nose can read one.

---

The years after the men went home were quiet years, and the country spent them taking the men's marks back.

The south trail grassed over first, then lost itself; by the fourth spring it was a deer path, and by the sixth it was nothing but a seam of darker green down the long slope. The pan on the high ground filled a little more every wet season, and two of the four stones went over in a hard winter and lay where they fell. The wire at the old camp ground rusted into red stains, and the stains fed the grass, and the grass took them. No smoke ever came up the country. Not once, in all the quiet years, did a man's shape cross any ground he could see.

The packs came down most winters, the way winter does. Each year they gave their ground sooner, and sang at a greater distance, until the last pack to find a kill of his stood on a far ridge and cried and would not come down at all. The slow kind that drank at dusk knew him without seeing him. Their ears went still when his shadow crossed the water, and their feet made their decisions before their eyes had found anything to decide about.

The meals were steady. The thaw's grazers came down to the new water every spring, the flood left its gifts on the ridges in the wet years, and the dry drove everything to the runs as it always had. He ate, and the years went into him the only way years go into a beast. Twice in the quiet years the early snows came down deep and held. He found a rock hollow out of the wind and let the long sleep take him, and woke each time to a thaw — the armor under him harder than the armor he had lain down in, his shadow on the water longer than the shadow he remembered. That was all the sign the years gave of themselves, and it was enough.

The hunger stood up after every meal, the same as always, and no meal in the low country answered it. He had stopped asking the country to. That was not the country's work.

That work was north.

---

In the sixth wet spring, the south fell quiet.

There was a roar that had come up out of the south country all his life — in the wet mostly, sometimes in the dry, a long broken sound, like a hillside letting go. He had never once answered it, and it had never once stopped coming. He heard it as he heard the river: part of the country being the country.

That spring it did not come.

He lay on the rim at dusk, in the rain, and listened for it — the first night, and the second, and the wet went on and the wind went on and the roar stayed out of both. The river's own sounds stood bigger in the dark with the roar gone out of them, as a room is bigger when a snoring sleeper leaves it. There was no track to read and no body to find and no going south to look. The pale beast's ground was its own; he had never crossed onto it; a silence was not a reason. He read what there was. The country south had gone one voice quieter, and that was all the south would say.

He did not think of it again that spring. But he kept it, the ground keeps a track that ends.

---

He walked the low country once more before he left it — the whole of it, at the edges, six slow days, the same walk he had given it the spring the men went home. The runs ran. The pools sat in their flats. The bank he had given up had healed into ordinary bank, and the grazers came down to it at dusk in their slow files, and nothing was ever killed there again.

On the seventh morning he went north.

He passed the ravine den in the afternoon and slept a night in it, on the high rock with the stream talking below the mouth — the ground he had held through the flood and the dry. The rock still smelled of him, and the den's dark fit his body like old ground. He left it in the morning with nothing carried and nothing written. A road was not a leaving.

Past the den the forest changed, and then it changed again. The outer forest was old country, walked and known, every path a decision already made. North of it the trees stood older, the dark came earlier, and the ground stopped being paths and became distances. He walked two days in country he had only ever smelled from the rims, and every smell was a question he had not asked before — new herds, new dung, new flowers going over, cat-sign on a trunk wider than his own foot. He hunted the first night out, because a road is walked on meat. The animal he took was a stranger to him — a squat brown thing of the fern shadows with a musk he had never tasted. He took it as he took everything in the dark, at the shoulder, and ate it listening to a country he did not know. The taste of it was the taste of the road itself: new, and not wrong.

On the second evening he came out on a ridge with his head up and looked at the world. The forest went on north past all seeing, a dark with no far side to it, and for the first time in his life the country he owned was the small thing on the edge of the map instead of the map. East stood the mountains with snow on their shoulders. And under the whole of the north, at the bottom of his sensing, the pull lay exactly where it had lain all his life, and he was three days nearer to it.

On the third day the birds went out of the country.

That was the first word of the deep forest. Not a sound — a silence with a floor under it. A whole hollow of country with no birds in it, no small beasts at its edges, the wind moving the high trees while nothing under them moved at all. He stopped at the edge of the birdless ground and stood a long time, and nothing came out of it, and nothing went in.

Then he went in, and the ground told him why before his eyes did. There was a path through the birdless country, and it was not a beast path. It was a road the width of a river, pressed down through the trees and beaten to bare clay, wider than any feet he knew, and the smell on it was deep water and old smoke together — and the smell was fresh.

He was a long stone's throw off it, standing still, when the weight came across the ground and settled on him like weather. His body answered before his mind did: belly low, feet set, the whole animal still. Somewhere on that river-road was a beast his blood did not press on. His blood moved small country. This was not small country.

He gave the river-road the whole of the birdless hollow and held his own line north, and the weight fell away behind him slowly, the way deep water falls away from a hull.

At dark he made his camp in a root hollow, far from the river-road, and lay with his head north. Far off, deeper in, a light stood on the ground. It did not flicker like fire. It stood, like a lit window seen across a plain, the color of deep water in a cave, and while he watched it, it did not move at all.

The pull was under everything, and the pull was north. It had been in him since the first hunger, steady and far, the same the whole of his life. That night it was nearer — by exactly the distance a body walks in three days, and by nothing else. No calling. No leap. Just the road under his feet, doing its slow work.

He slept. In the night the far light went out, or the country between them took it, and the dark came back ordinary, and he slept on.

In the morning he went north, because that was the day's work now.

# Chapter 20: The Road Itself

The ground told him before the trees did.

A weight was coming through the forest north of him, slow and enormous, each footfall a felt thing in the earth rather than a sound. He had crossed that ground at dark, meaning to hunt the small quick kinds at dawn, and now there was no time to be anywhere else. He slid under the trunk of a fallen giant, into the hollow its roots had left, and flattened himself into the cold leaf-mold with his chin in the dirt.

The giant came at gray light.

He never saw all of it. The legs went by like standing trees walking, and above them the body was a wall that took the sky away, and the smell of it rolled over the hollow first and pressed everything down — the small voices, the birds, the insects, the whole morning. It was not hunting. It walked and fed as it walked, stripping the crowns of trees the way a river takes a bank, and where its feet came down the ground gave a slow deep note that he felt in his own chest.

He lay still and let it pass. There was nothing else in him that could have answered it, and he knew that in his body before his mind said it: the holding still was not a trick this time. It was the truth of what he was on this ground.

In the low country, his shadow crossing the water had been weather. Beasts had made their decisions at the mere shape of him. Here, in the deep forest's first miles, he was a scent on the wind and not a large one. That morning under the trunk was the first full lesson of the road, and it was given in one piece: the world did not lower its voice for him here. He had walked out of the country where his blood was a law.

When the giant was long gone, he backed out of the hollow and went on north, and he walked differently from that morning on.

---

The road's first season taught him the rest of it.

He had learned the small thing's tricks once already, ground by ground, in the years the watchers worked his country. He had learned to cross on stone and to drink at running water in the black of night. He had learned to leave no print, to keep off soft ground, to sleep high or deep where nothing could come at him without noise. The lessons were the same lessons. Only the size of the world around them had changed.

So the road made its rules and he paid them. He walked the rock and the ridges where the ground could not write him. He drank in the dark at the fast water. He ate small and quick and often — the quick kinds, the sleeping kinds, whatever a small hunter could take without a fight — because a small thing cannot be choosey, and because a real meal here drew real things. He kept his kills off the trails and his hours off the pattern. Twice in that first season a weight passed his ground in the night, and both times he was rock-still and high before it came, and both times it went by without slowing.

The hunger stood up after every meal the same as it had always done, and the road did not answer it either. But the road fed him in the other way, the one that mattered to a body that was all there was of him: every mile north was new ground, read and held, and the map of his life was growing faster now than it had grown in all the quiet years.

Seasons turned. He walked.

---

The first real meal of the road, he took in a rock country where a spring came down out of a cliff and made a shallow pool in bare stone.

The kind that came to that water at dusk was nothing he had met — heavy through the shoulder, low on its legs, with a head made for pushing and one eye ruined and closed. Its years were heavy. He could read them standing in the dark of the trees, the deep slow weight of an old one of its line, and the read of it made his mouth run. He had eaten small for a season. His body wanted the deep years, and here they were, walking down to the water on four slow legs with one blind side.

He took it at the shoulder, in the shallows, in the last of the light.

It did not go as the low country's meals went. The old thing did not fall. It dropped its head and pushed, and the pool's whole skin of water broke over the two of them, and he learned in one slamming moment that a fight in shallow water is a fight in the other's weight. The bottom was smooth stone. His claws found no hold. The push took him under and along, rolled him against the pool's lip, and the world was water and pressure and his own breath going nowhere.

The jaw held. That was all he had, and it was the thing he had always had: take, and keep. He was under the old one's neck, dragged blind through its own red, and he kept the hold and worked it, and the push weakened before his breath did. It knelt down into the shallows by degrees, the way heavy things fall, and the water closed over it and went still.

He lay half in the water a long time, getting his breath back, with a tear across his ribs where the stone lip had taken him. Then he ate, deep and long, in the pool, in the dark, and the years of the old one went into him like the flood goes into dry ground. It was the road's first real payment, and it had cost real blood to get, and he slept a week in the rocks above the spring while the rib-tear knit, and he did not leave the water running red below him until the crows had come and gone and the ground had stopped telling.

---

The hunter found him the week after.

It was a kind of the long low country he had left — no, it was of this forest, quick and rangy, a hunter-kind with a head like a wedge, and his blood pressed it not at all. It read near his own weight and years, and it had found the rib-tear's blood on his trail, and it meant to collect.

That week was the worst week the road gave him. He could not fight it — not with the rib half-knit, not on its terms, on ground it knew better than him. So he lived by the tricks, and the tricks saved him four times and failed him once.

The once was the third night. He crossed a ridge in the dark and the hunter was upwind of him, which was wrong, which should not have happened — and in the open, for one breath, he did the thing he could do: went quiet, deep into himself, and stood in the low brush like a stone in a field of stones. The quiet held for most of a heartbeat. Then the strain of it, with the rib torn inside him and the hunter's whole attention sweeping past him like a lamp, broke the quiet — and the hunter's head came around, and its eyes found him standing there, found him whole, and it came.

He went down the ridge in the dark with the hunter's breath on his heels, hit the stream at the bottom going full, and let the fast water take him down through the rock country half a mile before he crawled out on stone. It did not follow him into the current. Nothing of that kind had ever followed him into fast water.

The rest of the week he paid meat. When he made a kill and the hunter found it, he walked away and let it have the blood and the body both, and took his share first and small. Twice more it happened. The third time he understood the price was not going down, and he moved his whole line west for ten days, into harder, colder country, and the hunter let him go. He had bought quiet with meat once before, in the low country, from the wolves. He had thought it a lesson of that ground. It was a lesson of every ground: when you are not the heaviest thing eating, the meat is never only yours.

The rib healed honest, as his wounds did. He went back to the north when the trail was cold, thinner than the road had made him yet, and slower about the ground, and better at it.

---

The far light he saw twice more that year, always at night, always from high open rock, standing in the north like a lit window across a plain. Once it seemed nearer. Once it was gone before the moon set. He could make nothing of it and stopped trying; it was a thing of the deep forest's own, and the deep forest kept its own things.

What the road gave him instead, at the turn of the second year, was the pass.

The ground north had been rising for days, breaking into long ridges and deep cuts, when he came out on a shoulder of rock and saw the country whole. North went through a cut in the land, a wide pass between two broken ranges, and the pass was open ground — grass and low wood, miles of it, under the sky. He could see the far side of it from where he stood. He could see, in the pass's middle distance, the thin shine of the river that ran through it and went on north.

He could also see that nothing lived in it. No birds worked its grass. No trails crossed its floor. On both ranges, right up to the pass's edges, the forest stood thick and loud with its small life, and then it stopped, as water stops at a lip.

He did not need to go in. He read it from the shoulder, and what he read was enough: there was a weight in that pass. Old, deep, and patient, sitting in the ground itself just as the river-road's weight had sat — only this one was not passing through. It lived there. The whole pass was one held thing, and the road north ran through the middle of it.

He spent four days walking the edges, because the road had taught him to check what could be checked. West, the ridges stacked up into blind rock with no water and no way through. East, the cuts dropped into wet dark country that smelled of older things than he wanted to meet. There was no going around. The road went through the pass, or it did not go.

On the fifth day he found the high seat — a shelf of rock on the south range, off the pass's ground, with the whole of it in view — and he made a camp there in the rocks, and lay in the thin grass, and watched.

He had nothing but years. The ground could be learned; every ground he had ever owned, he had learned, one watch at a time, and this ground was only bigger than the others. He watched what came to the pass's edges at dusk and turned away. The first dusk taught him the edges' habits. A herd of the slow kind came down the south range's feet and fed to within a long stone's throw of the open grass, and then, all together, with nothing showing anywhere, they turned and went back up. A bird worked the wind over the pass, slid off its air at the middle distance as if the air itself ended, and beat away south. At full dark the river's sound carried whole across the quiet ground — the pass's one voice was water, going north when nothing else would. He marked the herd's turning ground and the bird's leaving line, and the country between them and the river, and lay still, and let the ground teach. He watched the river's shine go gray, then dark. Somewhere below, in the middle distance, under the grass and the silence, the weight sat in its ground and did not move at all.

The road went through. First he would learn what the ground held.

# Chapter 21: The Watch and the Pass

The pass kept its own hours, and the watch taught them to him a few days at a time.

The holder slept in the ground and was never seen. What he had instead was the ground's own behaving: the weight under the grass moved with the sun. In the mornings it lay in the middle distance, near the river. In the afternoons it drew slowly south and west, a tide of attention with no body showing, and by dark it was back at the river again. It never hurried and it never stopped. It kept its rounds as the water keeps its runs — not going anywhere, only being where it was, all the way to the edges of itself.

The edges' laws he learned first, because they were shown to him every dusk. The herd of the slow kind came down the south range's feet and fed to the same line, always the same line, and turned back up with nothing anywhere in sight. The birds crossed high or not at all, and the one place their lines bent around was the middle of the pass, a wide nothing in the air itself. At the lips, morning and evening, the small life of the forests stood at the edge of the grass and looked in and did not go in. A pass full of food, crossed by a river, standing empty between two loud forests. Nothing in his whole life had ever shown him a country so plainly owned.

The river's hours he learned by lying still and letting them happen. The pass's one voice was the river, and the river was busiest at night. In the black hours, quick small shapes ran the south lip — a fox-kind, a kind like a low cat, once a whole file of the quick beasts — each one hugging the bend where the river came closest to the range, crossing the open grass at a dead run and never once stopping to drink. They crossed in the hour after the moon set, when the grass was blackest. He counted their crossings as he counted everything else in his life: by watching. They came, they ran, they were gone into the north trees, and the ground under the pass never so much as turned over.

He came to know one file of them apart from all the others. They crossed on the same nights, coming down a dry run-off gully on the south range. There was one in the middle of the file that ran wrong — a young one, or a hurt one, whose stride broke twice on the open grass. The file slowed around it without a sound, closed it into the middle, and they all went into the north trees together. The ground under the pass turned over for none of them. He lay in the dark and watched that happen four times. On the fourth night he understood he was watching the whole shape of the pass at once: the lip-bend's grass was a road, walked nightly by the small, and the middle's grass was a mouth, and every beast on that ground knew which was which without ever being told.

A storm came in the second week, and the pass taught him its last hour. The rain came down hard and flat, and the river rose and browned and lost its voice in the rain's own noise — and the crossings stopped. The quick kinds came down the gully to the lip, stood at the edge of the grass in the wet, and went back up. Even the file with the hurt one. He lay through that whole night in the rain and saw nothing cross, and by morning he had it: the river's noise was not the river's. It was cover. A night when the water could not be heard apart from the rain was a night the road was closed, and everything that lived around the pass knew it without a sign.

So it could be crossed. He watched the quick kinds do it and held the watching close.

What the watch could not teach him, the pass taught instead, one fogged morning, in one breath.

An old grazer of the heavy kind came down the north range in the gray before sunrise and walked out onto the grass. It was big and slow and its years were heavy in it, and it walked as though it had crossed this ground all its life. It went out past the herd-line, past the birds' bent-around nothing, and on toward the river, and it was lowering its head to drink — and it was not there.

There was no rush of wind. There was no sound at all. The river's voice went on. The fog stood where it stood. The grass where the beast had been lay pressed flat in one long swept place, as if the ground itself had closed its hand, and before the fog moved the pressed place had begun to spring back up. The whole crossing had taken less time than one beat of a hunting heart.

No crows came. That was the part that stayed with him afterward, the part he turned over on the high seat for days. Every kill he had ever made or found had been answered — crows, foxes, the beasts that come to the kills of others, the whole gray procession of the ground's economy. The pass's taking had no procession. Nothing came down to the swept place, that morning or any morning. The pass kept what it took, all of it, down to the last feather of interest, and the country around it had long since stopped pretending otherwise.

He lay on the high seat with his own heart going hard, and he did not move for a long time, and he learned the last lesson of the pass from the far side of it: the holder did not chase, and did not need to. The middle of the pass was not ground you crossed. It was ground that decided about you.

The quick kinds crossed the lip-bend. The old grazer had crossed the middle. He was not a fox-kind; he was heavy, and long, and his shadow at night was nearer the grazer's than the fox's. But he had one thing the grazer had not had. He had watched.

He spent one more moon on the high seat, and then he went.

---

He went in the hour after the moon set, in the blackest grass, at the south lip's bend.

He came down off the range where the river ran close against the slope, and he went into the water itself. The river through the pass was shallow and fast over stones, no deeper than his legs, and its noise was a wall around him — his own sounds gone into it, his own smell pushed down and apart by the moving water. He had taken his meals standing in currents since his second summer. If any ground in the world was his ground, moving water was.

He kept the south lip at his flank and the river's bend tight against the slope, and he crossed the open grass inside the water's own noise, low, at the pace of the current, a shape of wet dark among wet dark. The stars over the pass were hard and small. Nothing moved on the grass. The herd-line lay far off to his left, an invisible seam he had promised himself not to touch. The middle of the pass, the swept place, the holder's morning bed — all of it far to the north of him across the empty grass, and he did not look at it. Looking is a kind of going. He kept his eyes on the water and the near bank.

The weight noticed him anyway.

It did not rise. It did not come. The ground under the river simply changed its mind about him — the current's voice ran on exactly as it had, but the water around his body went still, still as a held breath, a skin of quiet moving with him in the middle of the river's noise. He could feel the whole attention of the pass standing under him like a floor. A pressure moved over him, slow and total, the way a hand moves over stones in a field, reading each one — along his sides, over the ridge of his neck, down the new scars the road had given him, weighing what he was.

He did not stop. Stopping was a decision, and decisions belonged to things that had a say. He walked on in the current, in the little envelope of still water, with his heart going like a bird's, and his feet found the next stone and the next.

And under the pressure, the red thing rose. It was old in him and it knew every road out, and being touched without leave — weighed, read, gone over like ground — lit it like a struck match. The boil came up his neck and into his jaw and his feet wanted to stop and turn and answer the touch with his one answer, the take-and-keep, the oldest thing he had. He walked. He let the current carry the boil the way the current carried his sound — out, apart, downstream — and the red thing spent itself against the walking, and was gone, and the pressure above him did not so much as pause. It had not even noticed the war in him. That was the worst of it, and the truest: he had fought his own blood to a finish there in the cold river, and the pass had missed the whole battle.

The pressure finished with him. The still skin of water let go of him all at once, and the river took his flanks back, cold and loud and ordinary, and behind him the ground's attention slid away north across the grass like the shadow of a cloud, unhurried, already elsewhere.

He gained the north lip's trees with the gray light coming, and stood in them a long time, wet and whole, breathing.

It had read him and let him go. Not mercy — he knew the difference by now, better than anything alive. The pack's cry was noise; the hunter's chase was hunger; this had been neither. It had weighed him as a flood weighs a straw, found him nothing to its purpose, and gone back to its sleep. For the first time since the shell, being beneath notice had saved him, and he stood in the gray trees and let that fact walk all the way through him. The deep forest did not care about him. That was its danger, and its mercy, and both of them were the same thing.

The new country's first smell came to him with the gray light: wet stone and rot-sweet and a cold moving under the trees that was not wind, and under all of it the old deep smell of the great forest, thicker here than it had ever been on his border. He hunted at midmorning and took a small quick thing of the fern shadows, a stranger-kind like the one on the road's first night, and ate it listening, and the listening was the meal's other half: a country he did not know, reading him back. The first meal of a ground had been the road's taste once already. It tasted like that again.

The pull ran under the new ground, north, unchanged. Far off, deeper in, once, for a breath, he thought he saw a light standing on the land — and then not. He did not trust his eyes after a night like that, and he did not need to. The road knew where it was going.

He shook the water off, and ate, and went north. The pass was behind him, and he had crossed it as the country allowed: not by strength, and not by luck, but by knowing what the ground was.

---

Below the frost line, a seed was doing what seeds do.

It did not know it was a seed. It did not know that there was a word for the cold ground
holding it, or that the dark it lay in was dark. It knew water — thread by thread between
the grains of soil, moving past, and drinking was good — and it knew one other thing,
which it had nothing in its short existence to compare it to: that it was *there*.

The soil was full of its kindred. Dozens of them in the space around it, sleeping the sleep
that has no waking in it, patient and mindless, waiting for the same thaw and the same
permission to become exactly what their parents had been. None of them felt the water go
by. None of them knew the dark was dark.

This one felt.

There was nobody in the soil to tell it that this was wrong, so it did not know it was
wrong. It only went on doing it — learning the water's slow paths around the grains,
learning the weight of the cold and how the weight shifted, learning the shape of the dark
it lay in. No seed that had ever lain in that ground had learned a single thing in all the
ages of the world.

Something had been done to it before the thaw. It could not have said so, having no words
and no self to say them with, but the doing was in it, part of the grain of it, working the
way a river works — without thought, without choice, by being what it is.

Then the season turned.

It came down to him as a change in the water: the threads that had crawled slow and cold
began to move faster, warmer, fuller, the whole dark world loosening at once as if the
earth had been holding its breath a long time and had decided to let it go.

The grain swelled. It split along a seam it had always had and never used, and put out the
one thing it had been built to make — a thread of white root, tender as anything alive,
turning down because down was where the water was.

He drank properly then, for the first time, and the drinking was a kind of arrival.

Above him the soil gave way and a blade came up into the light.

---

The glade was a bend in a slow stream, sheltered on three sides by the old growth of the
middle forest, open on the fourth to a stretch of meadow that ran down to the water. In
the deep summer it was the kind of place a traveller would have called pretty and walked
past: green, shaded, a heron's worth of quiet, grass to the knee and thicker by the bank.

The grass was Blue Silver. It was everywhere on the continent. It grew in city cracks and
on grave mounds and in the trampled yards of villages, and nobody anywhere looked twice at
it, because it was the commonest, weakest, most trodden plant in the world, and because it
had no soul power, and no mind, and no value to anyone except as the thing you stood on
while you looked for something that mattered.

That was the world's judgement of his kind, and it was correct.

It was also, in his case, wrong, and it would be wrong for as long as he lived, and the
whole of his long life would be spent inside the gap between those two facts.

He grew. It was all he could do and it was enough: root down, blade up, take the sun, take
the water, hold on. By midsummer he was a hand's width of green in a sea of identical
green, and nothing in the glade — not the heron, not the herd that came down to drink, not
the digging family that lived under the far bank — had any reason to distinguish him from
the ten thousand blades around him.

He had no eyes yet. He had no words. He had the ground, and the water, and the light on his
blade, and the record that was already keeping itself inside him without his knowing what a
record was.

And then, in the last heat of that first summer, three men came into the glade.

---

They came from the meadow side, walking the way people walk in a forest that can kill them:
spread out, quiet, the front man reading the ground and the other two reading the trees.

The one in front was broad and unhurried, maybe forty, with the flat practical face of a
man who had done this a thousand times and expected to do it a thousand more. Two rings
showed at his wrist when he gestured — yellow, yellow. Behind him came a younger pair, a
woman with a coil of thin rope at her hip and a boy who could not have been much past
twenty and kept touching the hilt of his knife for no reason.

"Sign's two days old," the broad man said. "He's not running. He's holding."

"Holding where?" the woman said.

"Water. Everything holds at water." He stopped, looked at the stream, and then at the far
bank where the digging family lived. "There. Soft ground. He'll have gone to ground in the
bank and he'll come out at dusk to drink."

The boy said, "How big."

"Four hundred years, the track says. Could be five." The broad man spat. "Yellow either
way. Clean yellow if we don't spoil it."

*Four hundred years.* The phrase meant nothing to the grass by the water. It had no words
at all yet, and no concept of a number, and no way to know that the men standing in it were
speaking about age the way merchants speak about coin.

It did know pressure. Three large warm bodies in its ground, and the heaviest of them
carrying something the others did not — a weight in the air around him, a density, the way
the stream felt different downstream of the deep pool. He was, without knowing it, feeling
a Soul Elder's cultivation for the first time, and the thing inside him did what it always
did with anything new: it took the measure of it, and kept it.

They spread out and waited.

They were very good at waiting. That was the first thing he learned about human beings, and
it stayed true for the next seven centuries: they were patient in exactly the way a root is
patient, only they were patient on purpose, and for something they wanted.

Dusk came down. The heron went. The light went amber in the meadow grass.

And the burrower came out of the bank to drink.

---

It was a grey-backed thing the size of a large dog, low and thick, with a spade of bone at
the nose and small clever eyes. It came out the way wild things come out — a nose first,
then a long stillness, then the body in one committed movement — and it got as far as the
water's edge.

The woman's rope took it behind the shoulders.

It did not die quickly, and the men did not pretend otherwise. The broad one went in with a
short blade and finished it in a practiced place, and the thing went down in the shallow
grass twenty feet from where he grew, and the water at the bank went briefly dark.

The grass by the stream felt the whole of it. Not as horror — it had no word for horror,
and no self to be horrified with — but as a huge disorderly fact arriving all at once in
its ground: heat going out of a body, weight settling, the long tremor of something very
alive becoming something not, and the roots under it taking all of that in whether it
wanted to or not.

Then the broad man knelt beside the body and did something the grass had never seen
anything do.

He waited.

He waited with his hand flat on the dead thing's flank, and the two others stood off and
watched the trees, and for a long moment nothing happened at all.

And then the ring came up.

It rose out of the body the way a bubble rises out of mud — slowly, and then all at once —
a hoop of pale yellow light, the width of a man's two hands, turning over itself, and the
broad man breathed out through his teeth and said something low and satisfied, and put out
his other hand and *took it*.

It went into him. That was the strangest part. The light did not scatter or fade; it went
into the man the way water goes into dry ground, and he stood there with his head back and
his eyes shut for a count of twenty, and when he opened them again the weight in the air
around him was heavier than it had been.

"Third," he said. "Four-twenty years. Better than the paperwork promised."

"Clean?" the woman said.

"Clean. Give me a minute." He wiped his hand on his leg. "Skin it. Fangs and the plate.
Leave the rest, we're not carrying meat."

The boy was already kneeling. He was quick with the knife and quieter than he had been all
day, and after a while he said, without looking up, "Do they know."

The broad man sat down on a stone to wait. "Do what."

"Before. Do they know it's coming."

"Some of them." The broad man shrugged, not unkindly. "The old ones do. That's why the old
ones are worth something. Four hundred years of knowing is what you're paying for, boy.
You think a white ring costs what a yellow costs? A white ring is ten years of a rabbit.
Anybody can have one. This—" he flexed the hand the light had gone into "—this is four
centuries of a thing being alive and careful, and now it's mine."

"That's four hundred," the woman said. "Not four centuries."

"Same thing. Sounds better."

The grass by the water kept all of it.

---

It could not have told you what it had kept, because it could not have told you anything.
But the record in it — the thing that had been keeping itself since the dark under the
frost, the reason no seed in that soil had ever learned a thing before — took the evening
apart and put it away in pieces, the way his roots took apart the soil.

*The light comes out of the dead.*

*The man took it and became heavier.*

*They counted its years and the years were worth something.*

*Yellow for four hundred.*

And under all of it, deeper than any of it, in the place where a plant keeps what it cannot
use: *things with years get taken.*

He did not know that he had years. He was one summer old. He had no ring and no rank and
no value in the world's arithmetic, and the three men had walked within twenty feet of him
without once looking down, and the only reason the grass by the water was still alive at
the end of that first summer was that it was grass.

That was the whole of his safety, and it would hold for a very long time, and when it
stopped holding it would stop all at once.

The broad man stood up and looked around the glade while the other two finished — the
habitual sweep of a professional checking a place he had just killed in — and his eyes
went across the meadow grass and the bank and the stream, and did not stop anywhere.

Then they went, back the way they had come, taking the plate and the fangs and the four
hundred years, and the glade went quiet, and the heron came back at full dark and stood in
the shallows where the water had gone dark and looked at nothing in particular.

---

Two things happened after that, in the long warm weeks before the first frost.

The first was ordinary. The body they left behind rotted into the bank, and the bank got
rich, and the grass above it grew darker and faster than the grass ten feet away, and by
autumn there was a patch of him — because it was him, the dark patch was him and the blades
in it were his — that stood four inches taller than anything else in the glade and had a
faint blue-silver sheen to it in low light that the other grass did not have.

He had not decided to do that. The thing in him had done it, the way it did everything,
taking the material that was actually there — a dead four-hundred-year body, its years
leaking back into soil that had once been his ground — and turning it into growth. He was,
in the plainest terms available, feeding on the aftermath of the only killing he had ever
witnessed, and he would go on doing versions of that for the rest of his life, and it would
never once occur to him that there was anything strange about it, because a plant does not
choose what falls into its ground.

The second thing was not ordinary.

Frost came early that year. It came down hard in the last week of the turning, a white
night that killed the meadow grass flat and put a skin of ice on the shallows, and in the
morning the whole glade was brown and silver and dead-looking, and the grass by the bank —
his grass, the dark patch, the four inches taller — was still green.

Not dramatically. Not in any way a passing animal would have noticed. But green, when
everything within sight of it was not.

He did not know he had done that either. The thing in him had taken the cold the way it
had taken the water and the light and the dead thing's years, and had measured it, and had
made a small change in the substance of his blades, and the change had cost him — three
weeks of not growing, a third of his root mass given over to something that was not
drinking — and it had held.

The first lesson of his life was not a lesson. It was a habit. *The cold hurt. Do not let
it hurt that way again.*

And the second lesson, which was the one that mattered, was older than the frost and had
been sitting in him since the evening by the water:

*things with years get taken.*

He had no years. That was his whole defence, and it was a good one, and it was going to
last him a hundred and forty years before anything in the world looked down at him twice.

---

*He did not see the second party. They came through the glade eleven days after the first,
walking fast, not hunting, going somewhere — three different men with a Spirit Hall badge
on the lead man's coat, and a rolled map-case, and the brisk irritated air of people doing
a job for somebody else. The lead man stopped at the stream to let the others catch up, and
while he waited he looked across the meadow the way the broad hunter had looked, and then
he looked again.*

*He was not looking at a plant. He was looking at a patch of green in a dead brown field,
and he was doing arithmetic about it, and the arithmetic was small and unimportant and he
did not write it down.*

*But he looked twice. In the whole of the glade's long quiet history, nothing had ever
looked twice at the grass by the water.*

*The man shrugged, said something to the others about the cold, and went on.*

*It was nothing. It was the smallest thing that happens in a forest, a man glancing at a
field on his way to somewhere more important, and it meant nothing at all, and it was the
first entry in a file that would not be opened for four hundred years.*

The world taught him by hurting him.

The herd came first. They came down out of the meadow in the dry weeks, forty-odd heavy

That was the first scar-lesson, and it would be the pattern of all of them: *this hurt. Do

He felt it from inside, which is the only way anything has ever felt it.

herbalist on the continent would have walked past it and thought nothing.

has a way of eventually noticing things that look different.

ring — ten years of a rabbit, as the broad hunter had said, the least valuable thing a

The second party came through the glade in the late summer of his fortieth year.

five of them and they moved badly — too close together, too loud, the front man hacking at
undergrowth with a blade he clearly did not know how to hold — and they had the smell of
towns on them, and one of them was complaining constantly about the mud.

"Guide lied."

"Guide said two days and took four silver to say it."

They were going somewhere and were lost, and they were the kind of men who had money and no
skill, which is the kind of men who die in Star Dou Forest, and the grass by the water had
no opinion about any of it.

They camped on his bank.

That was the whole event. They came down to the stream at dusk because water meant a place
to sleep, and they trampled forty years of his growth flat in the making of a fire ring,
and the one with the bad blade looked around for something to tie the pack-frames together

and he did not cut it well, and he hacked at it twice more when it did not come free.

The pain was not like the herd's.

The herd had cropped the tips, the way a grazer crops, taking the blade and leaving the
crown. This was the crown. This was the part of him that had been alive since the silt,
cut at the base, and lifted, and *carried away*.

He went up out of his ground in a coil.

It is not possible to describe what that was like to a thing with no nervous system and no
words, and it would be a lie to try. What can be said is that the record in him — the thing
that had been keeping itself since the frost — took the whole of it in, in pieces, the way
it took everything: the sudden absence of the ground, the wrong angle of the light, the
smoke, the hands, the sound of five men talking about a thing that was not him at all
while holding the oldest part of his body in one of them.

"Useless stuff," the man said, twisting him. "Tough, though. Won't break."

"Everything's tough out here."

"Not the grass. Grass should snap. This is like rope already." He pulled, testing it. "Feel
that. That's not normal grass."

"It's grass."

"It's *tough* grass." He shrugged and finished the knot. "Somebody's been feeding it."

They used him to lash two pack-frames and a rolled blanket, and they slept on the rest of
him, and in the morning they went on downstream, and they left the coil tied to the frame
because it had held, and it went with them out of the glade and down the water and away,
and he lost it.

He never got it back. It was forty years of himself, gone in an afternoon, and the men who
took it did not know they had taken anything, and if you had told them they would have
laughed, because it was grass.

Two things happened next.

*Cut at the base. Do not let the base be where it can be cut.*

*Four hundred years later, in a stone building in a city neither of them would ever see, a

middle-band section that made him stop and squint.*

read the ledger after him thought about it either, because it was a note about grass.*

*It stayed in the ledger for another four hundred years.*

*And then, one autumn, a man with a real reason to look went through the middle-band
section line by line, hunting for anything plant-type that had ever been described as
vigorous, and he found it, and he put his finger on it, and he sat there for a long time.*

*But that is a long way off. In the glade, in the fifth summer after the cutting, the patch
by the stream was back to full and denser than it had ever been, and the heron was standing
in the shallows, and nothing in the world knew that it existed.*


She arrived in the sixty-first summer, and she arrived the way everything in his life had
arrived — by walking into his ground and doing what she wanted there.

He felt her before he knew her: a lightness, then a weight, then a lightness again, moving
across the crown of him in short precise stops. Six points of contact. A body built for
stillness. Something that hunted by not moving, in a place where nothing else was worth the
trouble of not moving.

She was jade-green, longer than his tallest blade, with the flattened prayerful forelegs of
her kind folded under her chest and a head that turned all the way around to look at things.

She looked at him.

That was the first strange thing. Everything that had ever come into his ground had looked
*through* him — the herd, the heron, the hunters, the boy who had cut him for rope. She
looked at him the way a person looks at a chair they are considering sitting in: with
assessment, and then with satisfaction, and then she settled down on the broadest blade of
his crown and folded her legs and stayed.

She stayed for forty-three years.

---

Her mind was not like his, and it took him a decade to learn how to be around it.

She thought in movement. Not in words — she had no words, and neither did he, and for the
first ten years of their acquaintance neither of them had anything that could have been
called a thought in the way a person would mean it. She had patterns: *still, strike, still,
clean, still.* He had patterns: *water, light, hold, grow.* They sat in the same patch of
ground for a decade and did not once communicate anything at all, and it was the best thing
that had ever happened to him.

What he learned from her was that a predator could choose.

The herd had not chosen him. The flood had not chosen him. The man with the bad blade had
not chosen him; he had chosen cordage and there had been grass there. Every single thing
that had ever touched him had touched him by accident, and here at last was a creature
sitting on top of him because she had looked around the whole glade and picked this spot.

She had reasons and he could feel some of them. His crown was the densest cover in the
glade. It was warm — the dark blue blades held the evening heat longer than the meadow
grass, and she liked to be on him at dusk when the moths came. It did not move. And when
the wind came up, the whole patch leaned together and held, and she did not have to hold
herself.

She used him. That was the honest word for it. He was furniture, and cover, and warmth, and
she would have left in a day if any of those had stopped being true.

And she stayed.

In his ninety-second summer a weasel came into the glade and took the digging family's
young out of the far bank, and on the way back it passed within a foot of his crown, and
she came down off him so fast that he felt the blade she had been sitting on go springing
afterwards for an hour.

It was not a fight. It was a thing that took perhaps two seconds. But she came *off* him to
do it, which meant she had been on him, which meant she had been on him when a weasel came,
and it was the first time in his life that anything had spent itself in his vicinity on
purpose.

He kept it. He did not know what he was keeping it for. He kept it the way he kept the
flood and the cutting and the frost, in the deep place where a plant puts what it cannot
use, and it sat there, and years later it would turn out that he had been keeping the first
thing he ever loved.

---

The killing happened in his ninety-eighth year.

They came in the early autumn, two of them, and they were not lost and they were not
hunting for money, and that made them worse.

The father was thin and grey at the temples and had the careful unhurried way of a man who
had done this enough times to be bored by it. The boy was eleven or twelve and had been
dressed for the forest by somebody who had never been in it — new boots, a clean coat, a
knife at his belt with the wrapping still bright on the grip.

The boy talked the whole way in.

"Does it hurt them."

"Yes."

"When they see you."

"They don't see me, they see you." The father said it without unkindness. "You're the one
it'll come at. That's how it works. It comes at you, you hold, I do the rest. Don't drop
the knife."

"What if it comes at you."

"Then we'll both be embarrassed."

They came down to the stream and the father read the bank for a while — the same reading
the broad hunter had done forty years before, the same soft ground, the same conclusion —
and then he pointed at a hollow under the roots of a fallen tree on the far side and said
that a hundred-year badger-line beast had its bed in there, and that it would come out at
dusk, and that the boy was to stand where he was told and not move.

The grass by the water understood none of the words.

It understood the waiting.

---

The beast came out at dusk, and it was smaller than the boy.

That was the thing that stayed with him afterwards, in the deep place, longer than the ring
or the light or the sound: it was *small*. A grey blunt-nosed thing the size of a fat cat,
squinting in the last light, and it came out because it was thirsty and it had come out of
that same hollow every dusk of its hundred years and nothing had ever been standing there
before.

The boy held. That much he did right. He was shaking so hard the knife rattled against his
belt, and he held.

The father did the rest.

It was over in the time it takes to draw a breath twice, and it was not cruel, and it was
not kind, and the grass forty feet away took the whole of it into its roots because the
ground carried it and the ground was him.

Then the father knelt and put his hand on the body, and he told his son to watch, and the
ring came up.

It was small. It was white — a thin pale hoop, barely the width of two hands, and it came up
slowly and wobbled in the air the way a soap ring wobbles, and the boy made a sound that
was not a word.

"Ten years," the father said. "Maybe twelve. It's a good first. Don't be disappointed, a
white first is a proper start, half the men in this province started on white and lived to
be Soul Elders." He nodded at it. "Go on. Hand on it. Breathe."

The boy put out his hand.

It went into him the same way the yellow had gone into the broad hunter — not scattering,
not fading, going *in*, the way water goes into dry ground — and the boy sat down hard in
the grass with his mouth open and his eyes shut and stayed there for the best part of an
hour while his father sat beside him and said nothing and watched the trees.

The grass by the water watched the trees too. Not because it was being careful. Because
there was nothing else to look at, and because something had just happened in its ground
that it had no way whatsoever to respond to.

Twelve years. The thing in the hollow had been alive for a hundred and had come out for a
drink and had been worth twelve to a boy who was frightened of it.

And the men did not leave.

They camped on his bank — the same flat ground, the same fire ring, the same trampled forty
feet — and the boy was different in the morning, quieter, older, sitting up straighter, and
the father made him carry his own pack, and they stayed two nights and went.

They did not cut him for rope this time. Nobody needed rope.

---

He could not have named what he learned that autumn. He had no names for anything. But the
record in him took the evening apart and kept the pieces, and the pieces were these:

*The small one came out for water.*

*The boy was frightened and did it anyway.*

*The years came out of the body and went into the man.*

*They slept on me.*

And under all of it, in the place where the cutting and the flood already were, something
new went down and settled for good, and it did not come back up again in seven hundred
years:

*everything that comes here ends, and I do not.*

---

She was on his crown when they left.

She had been on his crown for most of the two nights, motionless through the whole of it,
and afterwards she came down and cleaned her forelegs the way she always did and settled
back onto the broadest blade and folded herself up.

She was not comforting him. She had no idea anything had happened. She was a predator on a
warm platform in a glade full of moths, and the platform was hers.

But she stayed.

That was the whole of it, and it was enough. She had six more years, and all through those
years she was there — the lightness, the weight, the lightness again — and every dusk when
the moths came she unfolded herself and did the thing she was built to do, and every night
she came back down and folded up on the same blade.

He did not know he loved her. He had no word for it and no self clear enough to have one.

But when she did not wake, one autumn not long afterwards, he waited through the whole of
the winter for her, the way roots wait, and in the thaw he felt for the first time the full
size of the silence where her weight used to be — and the ground where her warmth had
rested stayed strange to his roots for a whole season, because the pattern of one small
life was gone from the place.

That is a long way off. In the ninety-eighth year, on the bank by the stream, a hundred-year
grass with silver veins and a jade-green hunter on its crown stood in the last of the
autumn light while two men packed up their camp, and nothing in the world looked down.

*"Something took this," she said.*

*"It's torn," one of the others said.*

"It's *bound*." She put her finger along the fur above the wrist. "Look at the pattern.

still in the shape of it." She stood up. "And there's no tooth mark anywhere on the leg."*

*"Snake, then."*

*"A snake doesn't take a leg and leave the cat alive." She looked back down the ridge,
toward the valley they had come up out of, and she did not look interested. She looked
mildly annoyed, the way a competent person looks when the world hands them something that
does not fit.*

*"What do we do."*

*"Take the ring. It's still worth three thousand years with a bad leg." She sheathed her
blade. "And I'm writing it up. Not the ring — the leg."*

*"Writing up what."*

*"That something in grid nineteen binds," she said. "And that it isn't a snake, and it
isn't a cat, and it isn't a bear, and I've been working this forest for thirty years and I
can't think of a single thing it is."*

below a hundred-and-twenty-year-old note about unusually vigorous grass at a stream bend in grid
nineteen, and the clerk who copied it forward that winter did not connect the two entries,
because they were a hundred and twenty years apart and one was about vegetation and one was about a
mauled cat, and no reasonable person would connect them.*

*Somebody did, eventually. It took another two hundred years.*
