# Chapter Five — The One Who Watched

```
◆ STATUS — Chapter 5: years 190–240
KIND      : Blue Silver Grass, common line. The bank is his, and the meadow beyond it is
            leaning his way.
AGE       : ~240 at the chapter's close
CLASS     : upper thousand-year class. The deep band has started to notice the seam.
THREAT    : a Spirit Hall surveyor comes into the glade on purpose, following her own
            thirty-year-old report. She stands in him for an afternoon. She does not find
            him — because every instrument she has says grass.
```

---

The forest took forty years to change its mind about the glade.

That is not a figure of speech. The forest has a memory the way soil has a memory, and it
is kept in the same place, and it changes slowly. What changed was this: a several-thousand-
year shadow cat had come out of grid nineteen on three legs, and something had bound it,
and nothing in the forest's long experience of the middle band accounted for it.

The word went around the way word goes around in a place with no words. Not as a story —
as a pressure. The mid-forest half-light hunters began going around the stream bend instead
of through it. The hawk that had worked the meadow for two generations stopped stooping at
the bank. A pair of the deep-fringe dogs that had ranged the ridge in his grandfather's
time — or would have, if grass had grandfathers — did not come down into the low ground at
all after the spring of his hundred and seventieth year.

None of them knew why. None of them could have told you what they were avoiding.

But the ground by the water had done something, and the forest had noticed, and the forest
did what it always did with anything that had done something: it made room, and it watched.

He felt all of it and understood none of it. What he understood was that the glade had
gone quiet around him in a new way, and that the quiet was not empty, and that for the
first time in his life the world was pointing at him from a direction he could not see.

Then the woman came back.

---

She was older. That was the first thing.

Thirty years had gone by since she had stood over a mauled cat on a scree slope and written
up a leg. She was past seventy now and moved slower, and there was a fourth ring at her
wrist — purple, purple, purple, black — and the Spirit Hall issue coat had been replaced by
a better one with a different cut at the shoulder, and she walked into the glade with a
junior behind her carrying an instrument case.

She went straight to the bank.

Not to the stream. Not to the far ridge where the cat had been run. She came down off the
meadow, crossed the trampled ground where the herd came to drink, and walked into the deep
blue grass at the bend, and stood there, and looked at it.

"This is the grid," she said.

The junior was already opening the case. "Nineteen, stream bend, per your thirty-one report.
Ma'am, with respect — the report says vegetation."

"The report says a cat came out of this grid bound." She crouched and took a handful of
the blades and rubbed them between her fingers. "And the vegetation note is a hundred and
fifty years older than mine and it says the same place, and I have spent thirty years not
being
able to stop thinking about that."

"It says vigorous grass."

"It says *tough* grass, and it says blue-silver, and it says worth a look." She let the
handful go and stood up and looked at the whole bank, slowly, the way she had looked at the
cat's leg. "Nobody writes 'worth a look' about grass."

He felt her.

That is the only way to say it, and it does not say enough. Every large warm thing that had
ever come into his ground had come with pressure — the herd's blind weight, the cat's
terrified density, the hunters' casual solidity. She came with pressure and *attention*,
and the attention was aimed, and he was in the middle of where it was aimed, and it was the
first time in two hundred and forty years that anything in the world had looked at him and
meant it.

She stood in him for the whole afternoon.

---

She was thorough, and thoroughness is what nearly ended him.

She took blade samples. Not one — nine, from nine places, cut at the base and laid out on a
cloth in a row while the junior went through the instrument case. She dug a soil pit at the
bank's edge, three feet down, and sieved the silt. She walked the whole forty feet of his
ground counting something under her breath. She had the junior put a palm flat on the
crown and stand there for a quarter of an hour with his eyes shut.

"Nothing," the junior said.

"Say it properly."

"No soul power. No response at all. It's grass, ma'am. It's really just grass."

She did not answer. She was holding one of the nine blades up to the light and turning it,
and the silver veins in it caught the afternoon and ran the length of the blade like wire.

"It's tough," she said.

"Grass is tough."

"This is tougher than grass. Feel the base." She held it out. "Feel where the crown meets
the root. That's not growth, that's *structure*. Something has been laying that down for a
long time." She put the blade down on the cloth with the others. "And it's the wrong colour.
Blue Silver is blue-silver. This is deep blue with silver in the veins, and the colour is
at the base, and the base is where a plant keeps what it's made of."

The junior, who was young and honest and had read the same manuals she had, said the thing
that saved his life.

"Ma'am — plants don't cultivate."

She looked at him for a moment.

"I know that," she said.

"It's the first rule. Plants don't cultivate, they don't hold soul power, they don't have
martial value, and a plant-type soul beast is a hundred-year minimum before it's even worth
registering, and there is no such thing as a cultivated grass." He gestured at the nine
blades on the cloth. "Whatever bound that cat, it wasn't this. It's grass."

She stood there in his ground for a long time.

He felt the whole of it, and he did not know what he was feeling, and afterwards — much
afterwards, when he had words and a self and a name — he would think about that afternoon
more than any other in his long life, because it was the closest he ever came to being
found by someone who was actually looking, and the reason she did not find him was not that
he was hidden or clever or lucky.

It was that nobody in the world had ever been told to look for him.

"You're right," she said at last. "It's grass." She began gathering the samples. "But I'm
taking these, and I'm noting the grid as surveyed-and-unresolved, and if anybody out of the
Hall comes through grid nineteen in the next fifty years I want them to read the note
before they read the map."

"What should the note say."

She thought about it while she tied the cloth.

"That the grass here is wrong," she said, "and that I could not prove it."

---

They went at dusk, taking nine blades of him in a cloth and three feet of his soil in a
tin, and the glade went quiet behind them the way it had gone quiet behind everything.

He was missing nine blades. It was nothing. He had regrown a third of a bank.

What he was not missing, and would never get back, was the anonymity.

Because the note went in. And the note said *surveyed and unresolved*, and in the whole
long history of the Spirit Hall's forest registry there had never been a note like that
about vegetation, and the note sat in the middle-band section of the ledger next to a
four-hundred-year-old entry about vigorous grass and a thirty-one-year-old entry about a
bound cat, and the three of them together made a shape that no clerk copied forward without
a small pause, and the shape was not a shape anybody could name.

Yet.

---

*The deep band began testing him that winter.*

*It was not dramatic. Nothing in the deep band was ever dramatic; the deep band had been
old when the glade was silt, and it did not do drama, it did pressure. What happened was
that the boundary — the soft, unmarked, entirely notional line between the middle depth
where the hundred- and thousand-year families lived and the deep where the great things
moved — began to be leaned on.*

*A low-water hunter from the deep fringe came down to the stream in the cold weeks and
stood in the shallows for two nights looking at nothing. A digger that had no business
being that far out of the deep tried the soft ground under the fallen tree on the far bank
and found it woven shut with root it could not get through, and went away. Something very
large crossed the ridge above the glade at three different times over the following decade,
always at night, always going past, always close enough that the ground under him went cold
with the weight of it.*

*The deep band had smelled him. That was all. It had not decided anything. It was doing
what the deep band did with anything new on the seam, which was leaning on it, season after
season, to find out what it was.*

*He had no idea. He felt the pressure and he did not have a category for it, and the thing
in him did what it always did — took the measure of it, kept it — and he went on growing,
because growing was the only response his body had ever been given.*

*But the keeping had started. That was what those leanings were, in the long view: the
forest asking the seam a question, over and over, and the seam holding, and the asking
going on for a hundred and fifty years until the answer stopped being interesting because
it never changed.*

*The forest would eventually give that answer a name. It would call him the keeper.*

*He was a hundred and forty years from that, and standing in a bank of grass that nine
blades had just been taken out of, and the last light was going off the stream, and the
heron was standing in the shallows where the water had gone dark once, a long time ago, in
the ninety-eighth year of his life.*

# Chapter Six — The One Below

```
◆ STATUS — Chapter 6: years 240–300
KIND      : Blue Silver Grass, common line. The bank, the meadow, and now the first hundred
            feet of the low ground on both sides of the stream.
AGE       : ~300 at the chapter's close
CLASS     : upper thousand-year class, climbing. The consolidation well opens in this
            chapter and cracks in the doing — the first time his growth has ever cost him
            something he could not grow back in a season.
THREAT    : a ten-thousand-class serpent of the deep band comes up through the ground under
            him. Not hunting him. Hunting through him.
```

---

He had been keeping the seam for sixty years without knowing there was a seam.

That is the honest way to say it. The deep band had been leaning on the boundary since the
winter after the surveyor came, and he had been holding, and holding had not felt like a
decision — it had felt like growing, because growing was the only thing his body knew how
to do in response to anything. Pressure came down into his ground. He grew denser against
it. Pressure came again. He grew denser still. Sixty years of that, and by his two
hundred and fortieth year the whole low ground for a hundred feet on either side of the
stream was one continuous woven mass of root, and nothing that came at it from the deep
side had got through it, and he had no idea that this constituted an achievement.

He did not know there was a boundary. He did not know there was a deep. He did not know
that the pressure coming at him from one direction was different in kind from the pressure
of everything else in his life, because it was *deliberate*.

The serpent taught him.

---

It came up out of the ground under the far bank on the fourth night of the cold season.

There was no approach. That was the horror of it and he had no capacity for horror, so what
it registered as was simply that the ground he had been holding for sixty years opened
underneath him and something came through.

It came up through four feet of silt and woven root as if neither were there. It was thick
as a man's body and longer than the stream was wide, and it did not surface the way a
burrowing thing surfaces — it *arrived*, all at once, in the middle of his ground, and the
ground over it went up in a long low ridge that ran the length of the bank.

Ten thousand years. He felt the density of it the way he had felt the cat's, and the cat's
had been a bonfire on a hand and this was the sun.

It was not hunting him.

That was the second thing he learned, and it took him a while. It was moving *through*. It
had come up on the deep side of the low ground and it was travelling, under the soil, in a
line, and the line went straight through the middle of everything he was — and the reason
it was travelling was that something had pushed it out of the deep.

He felt that too, afterwards: the old pressure-signature of men with rings, four ridges
east, going the wrong way, and the whole deep band unsettled behind them the way a pond is
unsettled behind a thrown stone. Hunters. Running something. And what they were running had
gone to ground under a bank of grass in grid nineteen because a bank of grass was soft and
easy and nothing in the world thought anything of it.

They came into his ground the way the cat had come into his ground. Because he was nothing.

The serpent surfaced at the far edge of the meadow, took a breath of cold air, and went
back down.

And on its way back down it turned, because it was a ten-thousand-year thing and it had
been in the ground long enough to know what root-mass felt like, and it had felt a hundred
feet of woven, held, deliberate root under a patch of grass, and it was curious.

---

It bit him at the crown.

Not to eat. He was a plant; it had no interest in a plant. It bit him the way a man tests a
door — hard, once, with the whole weight of it behind the strike, to find out whether the
thing would give.

He did not give.

Sixty years of holding against the deep band, and a thousand years of substance, and a
hundred feet of root woven into silt that had been laid down by a flood when he was thirty
years old — it all went taut at once, the whole bank standing up off the ground like the net
it had become, and the serpent's strike came down into it and stopped.

What happened next lasted most of the night, and he survived it for one reason, and the
reason was not strength.

It was that he could be hurt and go on being.

The serpent was ten thousand years of a thing being alive and careful, and it was stronger
than he was by a margin that made the comparison obscene, and it could have pulled the
whole bank apart root by root if it had wanted to spend the season doing it. But it did not
want to spend the season. It was a predator that had been run out of its own ground by men
with rings, and it was tired, and it was testing a patch of grass, and every moment it
spent finding out that the patch of grass would not give was a moment it was not spending
somewhere more useful.

So it struck him eleven times over four hours, and each strike tore a hole in him the size
of a man, and each hole was still there when the next strike came, and by the ninth he had
lost the whole crown of the far bank and a third of his root mass had come up out of the
silt and would never go back down.

And he held. Not because he was strong. Because he was *still there*.

The serpent went back into the ground at the end of it and did not come back, and it did
not die, and it did not learn anything it would have called a lesson, and the hole it left
under the far bank stayed open for a season before the silt filled it.

He spent eleven years growing the far bank back.

---

What the night did to him, in the long run, was not a wound.

It was the well.

He had been consolidating since the solitude after the mantis — folding the record tighter,
making the root-memory fluent, turning the whole accumulated substance of himself into
something held rather than something merely accumulated. The thing in him had been doing it
for two centuries, slowly, the way it did everything, and by the night the serpent came
there was a depth to him that had no name yet and would not have one for a long time: a
place where the kept essence of two hundred and forty years sat, dense and quiet, below the
ordinary working of the plant.

The serpent cracked it.

Not opened it — cracked it, the way frost cracks a stone, by putting more pressure on one
place than the place had ever held. And what came out of the crack went into the regrowth,
and the regrowth that came back over the following eleven years was not the same growth
that had gone before it.

The new bank came in denser. The blades came in with a harder base. The root-mass laid
itself down in layers instead of in a scatter, and the layers held each other, and the
whole hundred feet of low ground became, over that decade, something that a digger could
not get through and a grazer could not crop and a serpent could not tear open in a night.

That was the well's first true depth, and it was bought with a third of his body, and the
arithmetic of it went down into him alongside everything else:

*what is held can be spent. What is spent can be held again. Neither is free.*

---

*The hunters came into the glade eleven days later, following the serpent's track, and they
did not find it.*

*There were six of them and they were not the Hall. They were private — a contracted party
out of a city two provinces over, working a commission, with the flat efficient manner of
men who were paid by the result and knew exactly what a ten-thousand-year ring was worth on
the open market.*

*They read the ground where the serpent had surfaced. They read it well. Their leader was a
thin man with two black rings at his wrist who spent a long time on his knees at the edge
of the meadow with his fingers in the torn silt.*

*"It came up here," he said.*

*"And went down where."*

*"That's the thing." He stood up and brushed his hands and looked at the far bank, at the
long low ridge where the ground had gone up and come back down, at the hole that was
already half-filled with new growth. "It came up here and it went down there, and between
them it fought something."*

*"Fought what."*

*"I don't know." He walked the length of the ridge, slowly, and then he walked it again.
"There's no blood. There's no tooth mark on anything. There's no body and there's no track
and there isn't a single thing in this grid that could have stood in front of a
ten-thousand-year serpent and lived through the night." He stopped at the crown of the far
bank and looked down at it. "Except the grass is different here."*

*The others looked at the grass.*

*"It's grass."*

*"The grass on this side of the bank is three feet tall and the base is as hard as rope and
the roots are laid in layers." He crouched and took a handful and tried to pull it, and it
did not come. He tried with both hands, braced, and it did not come. He let go and looked
at it for a while.*

*"Hall's got a note on this grid," one of the others said. "Surveyed and unresolved. Thirty
years old."*

*"Unresolved what."*

*"That's all it says."*

*The thin man stood up in the middle of a hundred feet of deep blue grass that would not
come out of the ground, in a grid the Hall had marked unresolved nearly five decades before, at
the near end of a fight between a ten-thousand-year serpent and nothing at all, and he did
the sensible commercial thing.*

*"It's gone," he said. "Track's cold and it went deep and we're not going deep after it.
Pack up."*

*"And the grass."*

*"What about the grass."*

*They packed up. They went east, after the serpent, and they did not find it either, and
the commission went unpaid and the party broke up two seasons later over money.*

*But the thin man wrote a letter first, because he was the kind of man who wrote letters,
and the letter went to a cousin who kept a shop in a city two provinces over and sold
information to whoever paid for it, and one line of it said that there was grass in grid
nineteen of the Star Dou middle band that would not come out of the ground with both hands,
and that the Hall had a note on the same grid, and that he did not know what any of it
meant but he would not have camped there.*

*Letters are not ledgers. Letters get read.*

# Chapter Seven — The One Who Keeps

```
◆ STATUS — Chapter 7: years 300–360
KIND      : Blue Silver Grass, common line. The low ground is one woven mass for a hundred
            feet either side of the stream, and the seam is holding because of it.
AGE       : ~360 at the chapter's close
CLASS     : upper thousand-year class. The well is deep and quiet and held.
THREAT    : an organised expedition, Hall-contracted, working the grid on purpose. Turned
            at the boundary — not fought off. Turned.
BOND      : the night-walker. The former keeper of the seam, come back to look at its old
            post. First two-way speech of his life.
```

---

It came down off the ridge in the sixtieth year after the serpent night, and he knew before
it arrived that it was different, because the forest went quiet in front of it.

Not the way the glade went quiet around him — that was avoidance, the wordless making-room
of small things. This was deference. Every pressure in the middle depth went still and
stayed still in a widening circle that crossed the valley and kept going, and the circle
moved toward him at the pace of something very old taking its time.

It was enormous and it was thin, and it walked on four legs with a shoulder that dropped at
every third step, and it had the long low head and the heavy forequarters of a walker that
had walked a great deal, and it was so old that the cultivation coming off it did not
register in his roots as pressure at all. It registered as *weather*.

It came down to the stream. It drank. And then it walked the length of his ground, slowly,
from the far bank to the meadow and back, and it stopped at every place where the root-mass
was thickest, and it stood there for a while, and it went on.

It was reading him.

He had been read before — the surveyor had stood in him for an afternoon with nine blades
on a cloth and an instrument case. This was not that. This was something that knew exactly
what it was looking at and was taking its time about it, the way an old craftsman looks at
a piece of work by somebody else.

It finished at the crown of the far bank, where the serpent had torn the hole, where the
new growth had come in layered and hard. It stood there for a long time.

Then it lay down at his edge, and it put its great head on the ground, and it tapped.

---

Two blows. Deliberate. Spaced.

Not a hoof shifting. Not the ground settling. Two blows put into the earth on purpose by
something that meant them, and the earth carried them the way the earth carries everything,
and they came up through his roots as *shape* rather than sound.

He did not answer. He did not know that answering was a thing one could do. He had no words
and no self and no framework in which a tap in the soil was a question rather than a tap in
the soil.

It tapped again. Two blows. The same two blows. The same spacing.

And then it waited.

That was what did it. The waiting. Because waiting in a particular way, after a particular
thing, is the oldest grammar there is, and his roots had been reading the ground for three
hundred years and knew the difference between a thing that happened and a thing that was
put there.

He answered. One pulse. The only thing he had. The root-pulse he had used to tighten the
bank against the deep band's leaning for sixty years — not a signal, not a word, just the
whole hundred feet of him going taut at once and letting go.

The great head on the ground went still.

And then it tapped three times, and he pulsed once, and it tapped two, and he pulsed once,
and it went on like that for the length of an afternoon, and by dusk there was, between an
ancient last-of-its-kind walker and a bank of grass, a vocabulary of four things:

*here. yes. more. stop.*

It was the first conversation he had ever been in. It had four words in it. It would be
another two hundred years before the vocabulary passed thirty, and the whole of it would
always be taps and pulses, and it would be the only true speech he had until he was a King,
and it would matter more than anything else in his life except one thing.

---

The old one had kept this ground.

That was what it took him a decade to understand, and he understood it the way he
understood everything — through the soil, slowly, from the inside.

It walked a round. Every night for the first three years it walked the same round: the far
bank, the low ground, the meadow's edge, the ridge path, and back — and the round was the
boundary. Not a line on a map. A *route*, worn into the ground by an age of walking, and
the ground remembered it, and the ground was him, and he could feel the old path in his own
root-mass the way a man feels an old injury when the weather turns.

Something had walked this seam for a very long time before him. And it had stopped, and the
boundary had gone unkept, and the deep band had leaned on it for sixty years while a patch
of grass held it without knowing what it was holding — and now the thing that used to hold
it had come back to look.

It tapped him the keeper's knowledge over the following decades, four words at a time, and
what it could not tap it showed him by walking.

*Where the deep comes through.* Three places. The soft ground under the fallen tree. The
old watercourse at the low end, where a digger could get purchase. The ridge path, which
was not a hole but a habit, and habits are how the deep moves.

*What the deep wants.* Not him. Never him. The deep did not care about a bank of grass any
more than the herd had cared. The deep wanted the low ground — the water, the cover, the
soft silt, the small warm things that lived in his crown. He was not the target. He was the
door.

*What a keeper does.* Not fight. He tapped this one over and over for a whole season, two
blows and a pause and one long drag, until he understood that the old one was correcting
him: *you do not drive it out. You make it go somewhere else.* A boundary is not a wall. A
wall gets tested until it breaks. A boundary is a place where the going-through is more
trouble than the going-around, and the making of that is the whole of the office.

He had already been doing it. That was the strange part. Sixty years of holding against the
lean, and he had been doing the office without knowing there was an office, and the old one
had walked four hundred miles of ridge to look at a patch of grass that had, entirely by
accident, been keeping its post.

---

The expedition came in his three hundred and fortieth year, and it was the first time
anything had come at the seam on purpose.

There were nine of them. Hall-contracted — the same flat efficient manner as the thin man's
party, but better equipped, and with a Hall assessor walking in the middle of the column
carrying an instrument case, and with the thin man himself at the back, older, thinner,
holding a rolled copy of a ledger page.

They did not come hunting. They came *surveying*, which was worse, because a hunting party
wants one thing and leaves, and a survey party wants to know.

They came down off the meadow and the assessor stopped at the edge of the low ground and
put his palm flat on the crown and stood there with his eyes shut for the length of an
hour.

Then the old one walked into the middle of them.

It did not charge. It did not roar. It came down off the ridge at its own pace, with its
dropped shoulder and its great head low, and it walked into the expedition the way a man
walks into a room he owns, and it stood between the assessor and the bank and looked at
them.

The thin man went white.

He was the only one who knew what he was looking at, and what he was looking at was the
reason the ledger page in his hand had been marked unresolved for a hundred and forty-seven
years and the
reason his cousin's shop had sold the letter to a buyer who had sold it to the Hall, and he
said one word very quietly, and the word was not a word the others knew.

"Back," he said. "Everybody back. Slowly. Now."

"What is it."

"Back."

They backed. Nine armed men with a Hall assessor and two black rings in the column went
backwards off the low ground at a walking pace without once turning around, and the old one
stood in the middle of his grass and watched them do it, and it did not follow, and when
they were up on the meadow it lay down again at the edge of the bank and put its head on
the ground.

The expedition did not come back. The grid was reclassified that winter — sealed-pending,
a designation that meant the Hall had decided the information was worth more than the
territory — and the note went into the ledger under a new heading, and the heading was not
about grass.

It was about the thing that had kept the grass.

---

*That was the mistake, and it was a reasonable one, and it would take the Hall another two
hundred years to undo it.*

*They filed him under the walker. Ancient, last of its kind, tens of thousands of years,
territorial, non-aggressive unless approached — a known quantity, a mapped quantity, the
kind of thing the registry was built to hold. The grass stayed in the vegetation column
where it had always been, three hundred years old and unresolved and uninteresting, and the
whole weight of the Hall's attention went onto the great thin thing that walked the ridge
at night, because that was the thing you could see.*

*Which meant that for the next two centuries, every party that came into grid nineteen came
to look at the keeper.*

*And none of them came to look at the keeping.*

```

KIND      : Blue Silver Grass, common line. The low ground is his and the seam holds.
```

The old one was dying, and it took him forty years to be sure of it.

That was not indifference. It was that dying, in a thing that old, looked exactly like
living — the same round walked at the same pace, the same head on the ground at the edge of
the bank, the same two blows at dusk. The only difference was the dropped shoulder. It had
walked with the dropped shoulder since the serpent night, and for the first twenty years
the drop had been a limp, and then it had been a favouring, and then it had been a leg that
did not set right at all, and by his four hundredth year the old one was walking its round
on three good legs and a fourth that it carried.

It did not slow down. It did not stop walking the boundary. It tapped him the same keeper's
knowledge at the same four words a season, and it lay down at his edge every night, and
every night it was a little less heavy on the ground.

He had no word for what he was watching. He had four words and a pulse and a vocabulary
built out of taps, and none of them were the word he needed.

So he did what he had always done, which was grow, and hold, and keep the record — and
somewhere in those forty years the record stopped being a record and became grief, though
he would not have known the difference if you had shown him both.

Then, in the winter of his four hundred and second year, something came through the
boundary from the deep side and did not get pushed back.

---

It was very small.

That was the first thing, and it stayed the most important thing: it was the smallest
creature that had ever come at his ground. Not a grazer of the middle band — those were
vole-sized and confident. This was smaller than that and thin, a grey blunt thing with a
coat that had gone patchy at the flank, and it came to the low ground in the deep of winter
and stood at the edge of the woven root-mass with its nose to it, and it did not try to
come through.

It waited.

He had spent eighty years making that boundary impossible. Three places the deep came
through, all three woven shut. The old watercourse door netted with root down to bedrock.
The soft ground under the fallen tree held in layers that a digger could not get purchase
in. He had turned a nine-man Hall expedition by simply not being worth the trouble, and the
deep band had been leaning on his seam for a century and a half and had never once got
through it.

And now something small stood on the far side of the best boundary in the middle band and
waited, and the waiting was not the waiting of a thing looking for a hole.

It was the waiting of a thing that had nowhere else to go.

He let it through.

---

He could not have told you why, and it is worth being honest about that, because the whole
of the rest of his life came out of it and it was not a decision.

He had no concept of mercy. Mercy is a word for a choice made by a being that could have
done otherwise and knew it, and he had four words and a root-pulse and no self clear enough
to hold a principle. What he had was eighty years of holding against *pressure* — deliberate
pressure, the deep band leaning on purpose — and this was not pressure. This was a small
cold thing on the wrong side of the only warm ground for four miles, and the woven mass
under it was not being tested, it was being *stood on*, and the difference came up through
his roots as clearly as the difference between a hoof and a hand.

was no gap a predator could have followed. The top layer simply went from held to
permeable for the length of a small grey body, and it came through, and the layer closed

It stayed for two hundred and twenty-eight years.

refugees.

something wrong in it. Not a beast. Not a man. A *wrongness* — a stretch of the deep
country where the ground went sour and the small things died in it and the great things
moved off it, and whatever it was it was spreading slowly west, and everything too small to
hold territory against the things fleeing it was being pushed the same direction.

Toward the seam. Toward the low ground. Toward the water.

They came one and two at a time over the next eighty years, and they came the way the first
one had come — to the edge of the woven mass, in the cold season, and they waited. Not all

century and a half, and got nothing, and went away. But some of them stood, and some of
them were small enough that the difference between pressure and standing came up through his
roots clearly, and the top layer loosened for those, and they came in.

He did not feed them. That is important and it would be a lie to say otherwise — he was a
plant, he had nothing to give them, and three of the eleven died in their first winter
because there was not enough in a hundred feet of low ground for eleven small things and a
bank of grass. What he gave them was cover, and warmth, and the fact that nothing on the
deep side could get at them and nothing on the middle side wanted them, and that turned out
to be enough for eight.

And in the long quiet the first one — the small grey grazer that had stood at his edge in
the winter of his four hundred and second year — stopped being afraid.

It began crossing back.

That was the thing that changed everything, and it happened slowly, over a decade, the way
everything in his life happened. It went out through the loosened layer at dusk and it came
back at dawn. Then it went out and stayed a night. Then two. Then it went out and came back
with another of its kind behind it, and the other one stood at the edge of the mass with its

He had not made a door. He had no idea he had made a door. What he had done was hold a
boundary so completely that the only way through it was by being let, and then let one small
thing through, and the letting had become a *route*, and a route is a different object from

The old one watched it happen. It walked its round on three legs and a carried fourth and
it tapped, and what it tapped that winter was a new thing, a shaping he had not had before,
and it took him a season to read it, and when he read it he understood that the old one was

It was telling him he had done something the office had never done in all its long age.

A keeper holds a line. That is the whole of it. The line is the office, and the office is
the line, and every keeper who had ever walked that round had walked it to keep the deep on
one side and the middle on the other, and not one of them in the whole age of the post had

The old one had kept that line for longer than the glade had been a glade. And it lay at
the edge of his crown with its head on the ground and tapped out, four words at a time, the

*a wall is a wall. A door is a door. You have made a door. Keep it as a door.*

*The Hall came back into grid nineteen in the spring of his four hundred and thirty-eighth
year, and they did not come for the grass and they did not come for the walker.*

*They were twelve men with nets and cages and a commission to take as many low-class soul
beasts out of four grids as they could carry, and their foreman was a broad cheerful man
named Pell who had worked the middle band for twenty-two years and had a system.*

*"Rot's pushed everything west," Pell said, on the first morning, standing on the meadow

weaned."*

*"We work west." He folded the map. "And we do not work grid nineteen."*

were good at it, and they worked within four hundred feet of the best-kept boundary in the
Star Dou forest on six of those nine days, and not one man in the party looked at it,

direction, eleven small refugees of the deep band's rot lay in the warm dark and did not
move, and the ground under them held, and the men with nets went past, and the door stayed
shut, and the keeper kept it without ever knowing they had been there.*

The old one stopped walking the round in the spring of his four hundred and sixty-eighth
year.

It did not announce it. There was no announcement available; there were four words and a
pulse and a vocabulary of taps, and none of them were the word for this. What happened was
that the round did not get walked at dusk, and the great thin body did not come down off
the ridge, and the head did not go onto the ground at the edge of the bank, and at some
point in the second night he understood that the not-coming was not a delay.

It was in the meadow, forty feet from the crown, lying in the grass on its side with its
head up, and it had got that far and no further.

He could not go to it.

That was the whole of the first night and it is worth stating plainly because it was the
cruellest thing that had ever happened to him and he had no capacity to experience it as
cruelty, only as the absence of any option whatsoever: the thing that had walked four
hundred miles of ridge to look at a patch of grass, that had tapped the keeper's knowledge
into him four words at a time for sixty years, that had stood in the middle of nine armed
men and watched them back out of a field — was dying forty feet away, and he was a plant.

He could not cross forty feet. He could not have crossed four. The only thing he had ever
been able to do in his entire life was grow, and hold, and keep the record.

So he grew.

---

It took him the whole night and most of the following day, and it was the fastest he had
ever grown in his life and it was not fast.

The crown reached. That was all it could do — the long deep-blue blades of the bank, the
densest growth he had, extended out across the meadow grass toward where the great body
lay, and the reaching was not a movement so much as a *leaning*, the whole mass of him
pulling in one direction the way a bank of grass leans in a wind that was not blowing.

By dawn the leading blades were within reach of it. By the middle of the morning they were
in its coat.

He could not lift anything. He could not warm anything. He could not have done a single
thing for it that a creature with legs could not have done better in a moment. What he could
do, and what he did for the whole of that day, was *be there* — a hundred feet of living
ground reaching across forty feet of meadow to touch a dying animal, and the touching was
the only gift his body had ever been given to make.

The old one's head came off the ground once, near the end, and turned toward him.

It tapped. Two blows, on the earth, with the last of it.

*Here.*

He pulsed. Every root in a hundred feet of low ground, all at once, the whole seam going
taut and letting go — the answer he had been giving for sixty years, the only word in the
vocabulary that was his.

*Here.*

And then the great body settled into the meadow grass and did not get up, and the forest
went quiet around it in the way it had gone quiet in front of it, and the quiet lasted
three days, and nothing came to the body, because the pressure that came off it did not
stop when it did and every scavenger in the middle depth knew the difference between a
dead thing and a thing that had been very much alive and might still be.

He kept the vigil over all of it, from forty feet away, touching it with the tips of his
blades.

That is what happens. It is the plainest fact in the world's arithmetic and it had been
shown to him twice before at a distance — the badger-line beast in the ninety-eighth year,
the cat's leavings, the small things that died in his crown every winter. A soul beast dies
and its years go back into the soil, and the soil gets rich, and the grass above it grows
darker and faster than the grass ten feet away.

taller than his kind off a dead four-hundred-year body and thought nothing of it, because a
plant does not choose what falls into its ground.

had been a glade. And what was going back into the meadow soil forty feet from his crown
was not the leavings of a hunt — it was the single largest quantity of accumulated
cultivation that would ever be within his reach in the whole of his long life, lying loose

there is no law anywhere in the world that says a root cannot draw on the returned years of
a thing that died in its ground, because there has never been a root in the world that
could.

principle. What he had instead was the mantis, sitting in the deep place where a plant puts

part of the substance of him:

*a keeper keeps.*

the ridge where nothing in the registry said there was anything to worry about.*

only thing that had been holding it was a bank of grass, and a bank of grass is a door and
not a wall, and a door lets things through in both directions.*

*What came through behind the rot's refugees, over the century and a half, was not many
things. But it was not nothing. And the deep band west of the ridge had been receiving, for

*Kesh put both hands flat on the table because the shaking was worse when they were in her
lap. "We were four miles west of the ridge. Good ground. Deep ground, but good — we'd read

stock and one territorial ancient in nineteen, and nineteen was behind us."*

*"And."*

*"And the forest stopped." She looked up. "Not quiet. Stopped. You know the sound a deep
forest makes? It goes all night, every night, it never stops. It stopped. In a circle. And
the circle was moving toward us and it was moving at the pace of a walking man."*

nineteen. The walker is territorial and it does not leave its round and every report on it
for a hundred and fifty years says it does not leave its round." She took her hands off the
table. "Whatever came at us was not the walker. And it was not one thing. There were four
of them and they came out of the ground."*

*The assessor wrote for a while.*

*"You lost nineteen men."*

*"Nineteen."*

*"To four deep-band fauna."*

*"To four deep-band fauna that were not supposed to be in four grids of low ground." Kesh
leaned forward. "Listen to me. Something moved them. Something moved four ten-thousand-year
things four miles west of their territory in a single night, and the registry has nothing in
that country, and I want the grid reclassified."*

*"The one that's already sealed." She sat back. "Nineteen. Reopen it. Send a real team.

*The assessor wrote that down too, and it went into the file, and the file was read by
nobody, and the report that went to the Hall that autumn blamed the rot's displacement,
which was not wrong, and blamed the party's routing, which was not wrong either, and did not
mention grid nineteen at all — because nobody in the column had gone within four miles of
it, and nobody in the Hall connected a sealed-pending grid to a massacre on the far side of
a ridge.*

*But the walker's round did not get walked that spring, and the deep band noticed, and the
leaning on the seam stopped for eleven years — which was the only mercy anything in that
country ever showed him, and it was not mercy, it was the deep band working out whether the
thing that had held the post for an age was still in it.*

*It was. It was a hundred feet of low ground and a bank of grass and eight small refugees
of a sour place in the deep country, and it held, and the leaning came back in the twelfth
year, and the seam went on being kept by something the entire world had filed under
vegetation.*

He had been alone for forty years when the found one answered him.

That is not quite right, and the correction matters. He had not been alone — there were
eight small things in his crown and the whole middle depth went quiet around him the way it
had gone quiet around the old one, and the deep band leaned on his seam every season with
the regularity of weather. But nothing had ever answered him. The vocabulary of taps had
died with the thing that invented it, and the only sound in the whole of his life that had
ever been *addressed to him* was two blows on the earth at dusk, and there was no more of
that.

So he went on pulsing. Not to anyone. The root-pulse was the only thing he had that was
not growing, and he used it the way the old one had used the round — as a habit that had
outlived its purpose, the whole hundred feet of the seam going taut and letting go once at
dusk, because that was what had been done at dusk for an age, and because a keeper keeps.

The found one heard it.

It had been hearing it for a hundred years. That was the thing he had not understood: the
small grey grazer that had stood at his edge in the winter of his four hundred and second
year had been living inside the pulse its entire adult life. It was the rhythm of its home.
It went out through the loosened layer at dusk and came back at dawn, and it came back to
the taut-and-let-go the way a bird comes back to a nest, and in the forty-first year of the
alone-keeping it did something it had never done in two centuries.

It stamped back.

---

Two blows. With its feet. On the packed ground over the old one's place.

He felt them come up through the root-mass and he did not understand them, because he had
no framework in which a small grazer's stamping was a reply rather than a small grazer's
stamping. He had watched the eight of them move across his crown for two hundred years and
every step of it had been noise.

So he pulsed. Once. The way he always did.

And it stamped twice again.

Same two. Same spacing. The same spacing the old one had used — because the old one had
lain at the edge of this bank for a hundred and sixty years with its head on the ground,
tapping two
blows at dusk, and a small grazer had been living forty feet away for sixty-six years
listening to it, and small grey things remember a rhythm.

He had no words. He had four, inherited, and none of them were his. But he had two hundred
and thirty years of ground-listening and a root-mass that could read the difference between
a hoof and a hand, and what came up through him in that moment was the same thing that had
come up through him when the tapping first stopped: the difference between a thing that
happened and a thing that was put there.

He pulsed twice.

It stamped three.

They went on like that until dawn.

---

The vocabulary took seventy years to build and it never got past eleven words.

That is worth saying plainly, because it would be easy to make this larger than it was. It
was not a language in any sense a person would recognise. It was eleven shaped patterns of
blows and pulses, passed back and forth between a bank of grass and a small grazer, over
ground, at dusk, in a glade in grid nineteen, and it was the entire content of the first
conversation he had ever had with anything that was not the old one.

*Here. Home. Safe. Danger. Gone. Cold. Many. One. Come. Stay.*

And the eleventh, which the found one invented, which took eleven years to agree on, and
which he would go on using for the rest of his life — a single blow, hard, once, that meant
none of the other ten:

*I am here, I am answering, I am one of the ones who stays.*

It was a small thing. It was the second true speech of his life and it had eleven words in
it and a grazer on one end of it.

And it taught him something the old one's sixty years of taps had not, which was that
speech is not what a keeper does with a keeper. The old one had passed the office to him —
the round, the three places, the difference between a wall and a door. It had given him a
job. The found one gave him something else, and it gave it by accident, by stamping back at
dusk because the rhythm was the rhythm of its home, and what it gave him was the discovery
that the keeping had a *who* in it.

He was not keeping a line. He was keeping eight small things, and one of them knew his name.

Not his name. He had no name; he would not have one for another hundred and sixty years, and
it would come from the far end of the wire and it would be the oldest word in a grazer's
drum. But it knew *him* — the taut-and-let-go at dusk, the loosened layer, the warm dark in
the crown — and it answered, and answering is what turns a post into a home.

---

It taught the fringe young.

That happened without him deciding it, the way everything in his life happened. The found
one ranged back across the boundary and returned, unhurt, and some of the fringe's small
and lost followed it to the line — and the ones that followed it learned the stamping,
because the stamping was how you stood at the edge of the woven mass and said *I am small
and I am cold and I am not trying to come through you*, and the ones that learned it got
let in, and the ones that did not learned it from the ones that did.

By his five hundred and sixtieth year the drum was not one grazer. It was a hundred small voices at the
edge of his ground at dusk, stamping the eleven words in the packed soil, and the ground
carried all of it up through his root-mass at once, and he answered the whole of them with
one pulse, and the low ground by the stream was the only place in the Star Dou middle band
where the deep band's refugees had a language for asking.

He had made a people. He had not meant to. He had no concept of a people. But the door had
become a route, and the route had become a habit, and the habit had become a vocabulary,
and a vocabulary shared by a hundred small things is a people whether or not anybody in it
has the word.

*The Hall assessor came into grid nineteen in the summer of his five hundred and
fifty-seventh year and stayed a whole season, and he was the first person in four centuries to look at
the grass and mean it.*

*He was not a hunter and not a surveyor. He was a records man — thin, patient, fifty, named
Orrin Vase, with no rings at all and a Hall issue coat that had never been in a fight — and
he had been sent because the sealed-pending designation on this grid was four hundred years
old and had never been justified by anything the registry could point at, and somebody two
levels up had decided to know why.*

*"Nine weeks," his superior had said, handing him the file. "Nine weeks, one mule, and if
the walker is alive you come straight back."*

*"And if it's dead."*

*"Then the designation comes off and the grid opens for hunting, and you'll have saved the
Hall a survey team." The superior tapped the file. "It's a dead walker, Vase. They die.
That's what they do."*

*He did not go looking for the walker. He went looking for the paperwork.*

*He spent nine weeks in the glade. He walked the boundary — the actual route, the old one's
round, which he found in the ground the way you find a path in a field, and which he walked
every day for nine weeks with a measuring cord and a notebook. He dug four soil pits. He
counted the small things at dusk from the meadow ridge, and he counted them again the next
dusk, and the third, and he wrote the numbers down and compared them.*

*On the twenty-second day he wrote to his superior, and the letter took six weeks to go and
six weeks to come back, and the reply was two lines:*

*"You are asking me to send a specialist team to look at grass. Explain yourself in one
sentence or come home."*

*He sat with that for three days. Then he wrote back.*

*"The boundary of grid nineteen is maintained daily, against pressure, by something that is
not the walker, and I have walked it forty-one times and it has not moved."*

*The reply came back in the autumn, and it was one line:*

*"Granted. One team. Vase, if this is grass I am putting you on latrine rotation at the
western post until you retire."*

*And on the forty-first day, while he waited, he sat down in the middle of the low ground
with his notebook open and stayed perfectly still for four hours, and at dusk he felt the
seam go taut and let go under him, and he wrote one line, and then he sat for another hour
and felt it again, and he wrote the time.*

*The team came in the spring. There were four of them and a Soul Ancestor, and they spent
eleven days in the glade, and on the twelfth day the Soul Ancestor came and stood over
Vase's notebook and read it, and he was quiet for a while.*

*"You've been out here nine weeks," he said.*

*"Nine weeks and four days."*

*"Alone. Four miles from the ridge. In a grid the Hall has had sealed for four centuries."
The Soul Ancestor looked out at the low ground. "And you found a plant."*

*"I found a boundary, sir. The plant is what's keeping it."*

*"Plants don't cultivate."*

*"No, sir."*

*"Then what is it."*

*Vase had been asking himself that for nine weeks and he had written the answer down
eleven times and crossed it out eleven times, and he said it anyway, because he was fifty
years old and he had no rings and he had walked a dead animal's round forty-one times.*

*"I don't know what it is," he said. "I know what it does. It keeps that line, every day,
and it has been keeping it since before the walker died, and if we take the seal off this
grid the low ground opens and everything in the middle band west of the ridge comes through
it within a season." He closed the notebook. "I'm not asking you to believe me about the
plant. I'm asking you to believe me about the line."*

*The Soul Ancestor stood there a long time, and then he walked the round himself, once, with
the measuring cord, and he came back at dusk, and he stood in the low ground and felt the
seam go taut and let go under his feet.*

*He did not say anything. But the seal stayed on.*

*His report went to the Hall that autumn. It was eleven pages and it was careful and it was
the first document in four hundred years that did not put the grass in the vegetation
column.*

*It said: the sealed-pending designation on grid nineteen is justified, but not for the
reason recorded. The walker in this grid is dead and has been dead for approximately one
hundred and forty years; the round it walked is still being kept, by something else. The
boundary of this grid is maintained. It is maintained continuously, it is maintained
against pressure from the deep side, and it is maintained by the vegetation.*

*It said: there is a plant-type growth at the stream bend covering approximately one hundred
feet of low ground which will not come out of the soil, which is layered rather than
rooted, and which responds to contact by tension. There is a population of low-class
deep-band fauna resident within it, estimated between eighty and one hundred and twenty
individuals, which enters and leaves by a route I have not been able to locate, and which
appears to be regulated.*

*It said: I do not believe this is a soul beast. Plants do not cultivate, and there is no
soul power detectable at this site by any instrument I carry, and I am aware of what I am
suggesting. I am suggesting it anyway, because the boundary is kept, and something is
keeping it, and I have eliminated everything else.*

*It said: recommend reclassification of the grid and specialist assessment. Recommend the
specialist be somebody who will take the vegetation seriously.*

*The report went into the registry in the autumn of his five hundred and fifty-seventh
year, and it sat there, and the specialist assessment did not come for another hundred and fifty
years, because the Hall was busy and the middle band was quiet and one records man's
eleven pages about a patch of grass did not move anybody who mattered.*

*But it was in the file. And it was the first time in four centuries that anybody had
written down, in an official document, in the registry of the largest institution on the
continent, that the grass in grid nineteen was keeping a boundary.*

*In the glade, at dusk, a hundred small things stamped eleven words into the packed soil
over an ancient keeper's grave, and the seam went taut and let go, and the assessor sat in
the middle of it with his notebook open and did not move, because he had spent nine weeks
learning what the sound meant and he did not want to interrupt.*

# Chapter Eleven — The Liar at the Door

```
◆ STATUS — Chapter 11: years 580–650
KIND      : Blue Silver Grass, common line. Keeper of the seam. The door has a language now.
AGE       : ~650 at the chapter's close
CLASS     : upper thousand-year class, ≈9,000 carried, at the edge of the next gate.
THREAT    : a mid-forest hunter learns the drum. It stamps the eleven words, it is let
            through, and it kills inside the sanctuary.
LOSS      : the found one. It passes old at the door, in the winter of his six hundred and
            eightieth year, and drums its last word against the ground first.
LAW       : the law of the door is written in this chapter. Keep even the liar. Cage only
            the act.
```

---

It came to the edge of the woven mass at dusk in the autumn of his five hundred and
ninety-second year, and it stamped.

Two blows. Three. The pattern for *small, cold, not trying to come through you* — the
asking that a hundred small things had been making at the edge of his ground for eighty
years, in the packed soil, with their feet.

It was not a small thing.

It was a mid-forest half-light hunter, lean and grey-brown, the size of the shadow cat that
had come into his crown two centuries before and a good deal less cultivated — perhaps four
hundred years, perhaps five, with the flat patient skull of an ambush line and a coat gone
thin at the ribs. It stood at the boundary and it stamped the asking, and it stamped it
*correctly*, and it waited.

He let it through.

That was not a mistake and it is important not to write it as one. The door was a door. The
whole of what the old one had tapped into him over sixty years, the one correction it had
ever made, was that a wall gets tested until it breaks and a door is a place where the
going-through costs more than the going-around — and a door that only opens for the things
you have already decided are safe is not a door, it is a wall with a preference. The
boundary of his ground had never been about the size of the thing asking. It had been about
the asking.

It asked. It was let in.

It killed two of the eight in the first night.

---

He felt both of them go, and the feeling was not new — he had felt small things die in his
crown every winter for two hundred and eighty years, of cold and age and the ordinary
arithmetic of a hundred small lives in a hundred feet of low ground. What was new was the
*shape* of the dying. Cold took a thing slowly. Age took it more slowly still. This was
fast, and it was warm, and it was inside, and it was deliberate.

The hunter did not overhunt either. That was the second thing, and it was worse than the
first. It took two and then it settled into the densest part of the crown — the blue-silver
cover, shoulder-high, the exact texture and colour of shadow at the base of a stem — and it
went still, and it stayed still for four days.

It had learned the stamping. That was the whole of it, and it was the ugliest thing that had
ever happened in his ground. Somewhere in the middle forest, over some number of years, a
four-hundred-year ambush predator had stood at the edge of a glade in grid nineteen and
watched a hundred small things get let through a boundary that nothing else in the Star Dou
middle band could cross, and it had worked out what the stamping was for, and it had
learned to do it.

It had learned his language. And it had used it as a key.

The root-mass under it went taut on the fifth night and did not let go.

---

He had never made a cage before, and the making of it was the fastest thing he had ever
done except the reaching across the meadow.

It was not a weapon and it was not a fight. It was the same craft he had used for two
centuries on the deep band's diggers — root laid in layers, layers woven against each
other, the whole hundred feet of low ground held as one continuous mass — turned inward,
and closed, and hardened, in the space around one lean grey-brown body lying in the cover.

The hunter came up out of the grass the way the cat had, in a single convulsion, and it
tore at the ground the way the serpent had, and the ground held the way the ground had held
for sixty years against the leaning, and by dawn it was in a hollow four feet down under a
woven ceiling it could not get purchase on, and it was not hurt.

That mattered. It mattered more than anything else in the chapter and it would matter more
than anything else in the next four hundred years of his life, and he did not know it
mattered, because he had four words and a drum and no self clear enough to hold a principle.

He did not hurt it.

He had it. It was in his ground, in his root-mass, four feet down, and the whole of his
thousand-year substance was wrapped around it, and there is no creature in the Star Dou
middle band that could have stopped him from closing the weave down and simply not opening
it again. The two small things it had killed were in his record. The four days it had lain
in his crown were in his record. The learned stamping — the taking of the only language he
had ever been given, the language a grazer had invented out of its own fear and taught to a
hundred refugees of a sour place in the deep country — was in his record.

He held it for eleven days.

He held it the way the ground holds: completely, patiently, without malice, and without
once tightening on it. It got water from the silt. It got air from the weave. It raged for
the first two days and went quiet on the third, and by the eighth it had stopped testing
the ceiling, and on the eleventh he opened the weave on the far side — the deep side, the
side it had come from — and it went out, and it did not come back.

He had no word for what he had done. The drum had eleven words and none of them were it.

The law went down into him anyway, in the place where the mantis was and the arithmetic and
the whole sixty years of taps, and it was the last thing the keeping ever taught him:

*keep even the liar. Cage the act, not the animal. The door stays a door.*

---

The found one died in the winter of his six hundred and thirtieth year.

It was old. That was all it was — it had come through the loosened layer in the cold season
of his four hundred and second year, a patchy thin thing with its ribs showing, and it had
lived two hundred and twenty-eight years in the warm dark of his crown, which was perhaps
four times what its kind lived in the deep fringe, and it had stopped being afraid somewhere
around its fortieth year and had not started again.

It did not die in the crown. That was the thing.

It went out through the loosened layer at dusk, the way it had gone out every dusk of its
adult life, and it did not go to the fringe. It went to the far bank, to the forty feet of
densest silver-veined growth between the crown and the place where the old one had lain,
and it lay down in the packed soil there, and it stamped.

One blow. Hard. Once.

*I am here. I am answering. I am one of the ones who stays.*

It stamped it three times, and on the fourth it did not lift its foot, and the small warm
body in the packed soil over an ancient keeper's grave went still in the deep of the
winter, and he felt the whole of it from a hundred feet away and could not go to it, which
was the second time that had happened to him and was no easier than the first.

He gave it to the ground.

Not into the well. That was not a decision either; the well had not been fed from anything
but his own growth since the meadow, and it was not going to start now. The small grey body
went back into the soil over the old one's place, and the soil took it, and the densest
silver-green patch in the glade got denser, and the two kept places lay side by side in the
ground for the rest of his life.

The drum did not stop.

That was what he had not expected, having no framework in which to expect anything. The
found one had invented the eleventh word and taught it to the fringe young, and the fringe
young had taught it to the next of the small and lost who followed the route to the line,
and when the thing that invented it died the word went on — a hundred small voices at the
edge of the woven mass at dusk, stamping *I am here, I am answering, I am one of the ones
who stays* into the packed soil, to a bank of grass that answered once, every dusk, the
whole hundred feet of the seam going taut and letting go.

The door had a hundred voices now.

And the keeper had none.

---

*The hunter came back four years later, and it did not stamp.*

*It came down off the ridge in the cold season and stood at the edge of the low ground and
looked at it for two nights, and it did not stamp the asking, and it did not test the
boundary, and on the third night it went away up the ridge path toward the deep country and
did not come into grid nineteen again.*

*But it was not the only thing that had learned the drum, and the thing that learned it next
had hands.*

*They were two, and they were fringe men — not contracted, not Hall, the kind who work the
soft edges of the middle band with snares and a cart and no commission at all, and they had
been watching the dusk stamping for two seasons from the meadow ridge.*

*"They line up," the older one said. He was called Drem. He had a snare-maker's hands and a
very good memory for a pattern. "Same place, same time, every dusk. Two, then three. Then
the ground opens."*

*"The ground doesn't open."*

*"The ground opens." Drem squatted in the dirt and drew it with a stick. "Look. Two, three.
Wait. Two, three. And then something lets them in — I've watched forty of them go in and
not one of them has ever had to dig." He looked up. "If I can stamp it, I can stand at that
edge at dusk and whatever comes out, comes out to me."*

*His brother was seventeen and had the sense Drem had lost somewhere. "Drem. That's the
sealed grid."*

*"The sealed grid is a dead walker."*

*"The sealed grid is a dead walker that a Soul Ancestor walked the round of and then left
sealed." The boy kicked the drawing out. "Pell's outfit worked nine days in here and never
went near the bend. Pell. Twenty-two years."*

*"Pell's a coward with a system."*

*"Pell's alive."*

*Drem went anyway, on the fourth night, and he stood at the edge of the woven mass in the
dark and he stamped two and three, and he waited, and the ground under his boots went from
hard to soft, and he took one step in —*

*and the ground closed.*

*Not on him. Around him. He stood in it to the knee in root that had been silt a moment
before, and it held him the way a hand holds a wrist, and it did not squeeze, and it did not
pull, and it did not hurt him at all, and he stood there in the dark in grid nineteen with
his snare over his shoulder and he understood, with the total clarity that only comes at
three in the morning, exactly what he had done.*

*They let him go at dawn. He walked out of the low ground on his own legs with both his
boots and all his fingers and his snare still over his shoulder, and his brother was on the
meadow ridge with a cart and a face like paper.*

*"What happened."*

*"Nothing happened." Drem got into the cart. "Drive."*

*"Did it — was there something in there, was it the walker, did you see—"*

*"Drive."*

*They drove. Drem did not say another word until they were two grids east, and then he said
one thing, and he said it to himself, and his brother heard it and never repeated it to
anybody.*

*"It had me," Drem said. "It had me by the leg for six hours and it never once squeezed.
And I was there to rob it." He looked back toward the ridge, and then he looked away.
"There's something in that grass that's better than I am, and I'm not going back within
four miles of it, and if anybody asks we never worked this grid."*

*Nothing in the forest knew why the hunter did not come back. It had learned something in
eleven days under a woven ceiling, in the dark, without once being hurt, and what it had
learned was not a lesson about grass — no creature in the Star Dou middle band ever learned
a lesson about grass, because grass was not the kind of thing a lesson came from.*

*What it had learned was that there was a place in the middle band where you could kill two
small things inside the best-kept boundary in the forest and come out alive, and that the
reason you came out alive was not that you had been lucky.*

*The deep band's word for that place was not a word. It was a pressure-signature, a shape in
the ground-memory that meant *go around*, and it went into the deep country's long slow
record the way everything went into it, and it stayed there, and it was still there four
hundred years later when a King of the grass line walked out of the middle band on his way
to the valley, and every ancient thing on his road already knew what he was before he
arrived.*

*In the glade, at the end of the six hundred and thirtieth year, a hundred small things
stamped the eleventh word into the packed soil over two graves, and the seam went taut and
let go, and the keeper of the boundary — alone now, in the way that matters, for the first
time since the old one stopped walking its round — answered them once, and the winter went
on.*
