# Chapter Twelve — The Ten Thousandth Year

```
◆ STATUS — Chapter 12: years 650–700
KIND      : Blue Silver Grass, common line. Keeper of the seam. From this chapter: a King.
AGE       : ~700 at the chapter's close
CLASS     : ten-thousand-year class. The gate crosses in his six hundred and sixty-fifth
            year — Stage Three of the King form. He is still rooted. That is the whole
            problem of the rest of the book.
THREAT    : the assessor's report is finally read. The grid is reclassified. A black ring
            is now possible in grid nineteen, and a black ring is worth more than a city.
```

---

The well had been filling for five hundred years, and in the winter of his six hundred
and sixty-fifth year it was full, and the gate took him.

It did not arrive. That is the thing about the gates that no one who has not crossed one
ever believes: there is no arrival. There is no light and no sound and no moment. There is
a long slow accumulation — every year of growth folded in, every scar of the flood and the
serpent and the eleven nights and the four hours, every winter of holding against the
leaning, the whole seven centuries of a thing being alive and careful — and then one season
the accumulation is of a kind that the world's arithmetic recognises, and the arithmetic
moves, and what was a thousand-year thing is a ten-thousand-year thing, and the season in
which it happened was ordinary in every respect except that one.

What changed in him was not power.

That is the part he would have got wrong if he had been asked, and he would have been asked
soon enough. Power went up, of course; the well was deep and it had always been available
to the root-mass and there was a great deal more of it now. But the gate did not change
what he could do. It changed what he *was*, and the change was in the world rather than in
him:

The forest could feel him.

Not the way it had felt the boundary, or the seam, or the hundred feet of low ground that
would not come out of the soil. Those were places. This was a *presence* — a ten-thousand-
year cultivation signature sitting in the middle band of the largest forest on the
continent, and it registered in the ground the way the deep band's great things registered,
and it registered in the same register, and from the winter of his six hundred and
sixty-fifth year every ancient thing within four hundred miles of grid nineteen knew that
there was a King at the stream bend.

They did not come to look. That was the first surprise. The great things of the deep had
been leaning on his seam for two centuries and had never once crossed it, and they did not
start now. What they did was *route around him* — the same way the mid-forest half-light
hunters had routed around the glade for two hundred years after the cat, the same way
twelve men with nets had worked within four hundred feet of the best-kept boundary in the
Star Dou middle band without once looking at it.

The forest had been making room for him since the ninety-eighth year of his life, slowly,
one pressure at a time, without ever being told to.

At ten thousand years it stopped being avoidance and became deference, and the difference
was that deference is given on purpose.

---

The other thing the gate did was put a number on him.

He had no idea about numbers. He had four words and a drum of eleven and no concept
whatsoever of the economy that his entire existence sat inside — and from that winter he
was, objectively, in the most valuable single bracket the human world had, because a
ten-thousand-year soul beast yields a black soul ring, and a black soul ring is the fourth
tier of five, and the men who take them do not take them from anything they can avoid.

The registry caught up in the spring of his six hundred and seventy-second year.

It took seven years and it took a war. Not a war in the forest — a war in the Hall's
budget, two provinces over, in which somebody who had been a junior records clerk when the
assessor's eleven pages went in was now a senior records clerk with a shortage and a
quota, and who went looking through the sealed-pending designations for anything that could
be reclassified as a resource. He found grid nineteen. He found the vegetation note, four
hundred and fifty years old. He found the walker entry, dead for a hundred and fifty. He
found the assessor's report, which he read twice, and then he went and got his superior,
and the superior read it, and the superior said the thing that had been said about him
every time anybody had looked at him in seven hundred years:

"It's grass."

"The report says the boundary is maintained by the vegetation."

"The report also says the man didn't think it was a soul beast and says he knows what he's
suggesting, and if he'd been sure we'd have sent somebody in two hundred years ago." The
superior put the eleven pages down. "Plants don't cultivate. That's the first rule."

"Then what's keeping the grid."

"A dead walker's territory and a hundred low-class animals with nowhere else to go." He
pushed the file back across the desk. "Reclassify it as low-yield fauna habitat, open the
hunting on the small stock, and leave the vegetation alone — it's not worth the assessor's
time and it's certainly not worth a team."

They opened the hunting on the small stock that summer.

---

It was the worst year of his life and he did not know it was a year, having no word for
one.

They came in parties of four and six, contracted, working the middle band's grids for
everything low-class and mobile, and they worked grid nineteen for eleven weeks because
grid nineteen had been reclassified as low-yield fauna habitat and low-yield fauna habitat
is exactly what a contracted party works when the good grids are taken. They took the
refugees. Not all of them — the door was a door and the door had a hundred voices and the
hundred voices knew the sound of men with cages better than they knew the eleventh word.
But they took thirty-one small things out of the low ground in eleven weeks, and they took
them at the edge of the woven mass, where the loosened layer was, because that was where
the small things came out at dusk to stamp.

They learned the drum.

That was the thing. It took them three weeks and it was not clever — a contracted hunter
stands still at the edge of a glade at dusk and watches what the small things do, the same
way a four-hundred-year ambush predator had stood still at the same edge eighty years
before and worked out what the stamping was for. The stamping was the asking. The asking
opened the ground. And a man who could stamp could stand at the edge of the only place in
the middle band where the deep band's refugees came out on purpose.

He felt all thirty-one go.

He could not stop it. That is the plain fact and it is the fact that made the rest of the
book: a King of the grass line, ten thousand years of cultivation, the keeper of the best
boundary in the Star Dou middle band, the thing every ancient creature within four hundred
miles routed around — could not move. The gate had made him a King and the gate had not
given him legs, because he was grass, and grass is rooted, and the whole of his kingdom was
a hundred feet of low ground that he could not take with him.

He could have killed them.

That is worth saying, because it is the first time in six hundred and seventy-two years
that the option had ever existed. The root-mass could have taken a man's ankle the way it
had taken the cat's foreleg. The weave could have closed over a body the way it had closed
over the liar. There were six of them in his ground in the ninth week and they were
standing on the packed soil over two graves with cages at their belts, and every root in a
hundred feet of low ground was his, and he did nothing.

He did nothing because the law was the law and the law had been written in the eleventh
year after the liar, in the dark, without malice, by a thing with four words and no self
clear enough to hold a principle:

*keep even the liar. Cage the act, not the animal. The door stays a door.*

The door stayed a door. Thirty-one small things went out of it in cages.

---

*They stopped coming in the twelfth week, and the reason was not him.*

*It was that the small stock ran out. Eleven weeks of a contracted party working a
low-yield fauna habitat will empty it, and by the end of the season grid nineteen had
nothing left in it worth a net, and the parties went to the next grid, and the
reclassification that had opened the hunting was quietly marked exhausted and nobody in the
Hall ever looked at it again.*

*Which is how the whole of the second half of his life was decided — by a budget shortfall
two provinces over, and a senior records clerk with a quota, and the fact that a hundred
feet of low ground in the middle band of the largest forest on the continent was worth less
to the largest institution on the continent than the cost of sending a team to look at it.*

*They never sent a team.*

*And in the glade, in the winter of his six hundred and seventy-second year, a King of the
Blue Silver line stood rooted in a hundred feet of low ground that had gone quiet again,
and the door had eighty voices left instead of a hundred, and the seam went taut and let go
at dusk the way it had for two hundred years, and the ancient things of the deep band
routed around grid nineteen on purpose now, and the whole of the human world had filed him
under exhausted habitat.*

*He had forty-odd years left at the stream bend.*

*He did not know it. He had no word for leaving, and grass does not leave, and the going —
the thing that would take him out of the middle band and across four hundred miles of
country to the valley of his line, in the last decades of his life — had not been earned
yet, and could not be earned by anything he had ever done.*

*It would be earned by the one thing he had never once done in six hundred and seventy-two
years.*

*It would be earned by wanting to go.*

# Chapter Thirteen — The One Who Goes

```
◆ STATUS — Chapter 13: years 700–735
KIND      : Blue Silver Grass, common line. A King of the grass line, in motion.
AGE       : ~735 at the chapter's close
CLASS     : ten-thousand-year class, ≈10,000 carried. Stage Three. Still rooted — always
            rooted. The going is not walking.
THREAT    : a serious party, Hall-contracted, four rings in the column, comes for the black
            ring. First time anyone has hunted him on purpose.
COST      : twenty-one years on the road. The low ground is left behind. The door is shut
            for good, and eighty small voices are still stamping at an empty edge.
```

---

The going was not a decision. It is worth being exact about that, because everything in
the second half of the book depends on what he actually was when he left the stream bend.

He did not choose to go. He could not have chosen anything; he had four words and a drum
of eleven and no self clear enough to hold a plan, and a plant does not have the equipment
for a plan. What he had, from the winter of the King gate onward, was a pull — a direction
in the ground, a shape in the root-memory that was not his and had not come from anything
in his own seven hundred years, and it pointed southwest and it did not stop pointing.

The old one had known the place.

That was how he knew it existed at all. Sixty years of taps, four words at a time, and the
keeper's knowledge had included the deep-country memory entire — the round, the three
places, the routes of the great things, the shape of four hundred miles of forest as an
animal that had walked it for an age understood it. And in that memory, at the far
southwestern edge of everything the old one had ever known, there was a valley, and the
valley had a pressure-signature in it that was not a beast's, and the signature was *the
same kind of thing as him*.

He had never once gone to look at it. He was grass. Grass does not go.

At ten thousand years the pull started, and it did not stop, and the low ground by the
stream went on being kept for another forty-nine years while the whole of him leaned
southwest in a direction he had no means of travelling.

Then the door emptied, and there was nothing left to keep.

---

They took the last of the small stock in the autumn of his seven hundred and sixth
year, and after that there was nothing in grid nineteen but a hundred feet of low ground
and a bank of deep blue grass and a herd that still came to drink and did not know the
difference.

Eighty voices had been stamping at the edge of the woven mass at dusk. By the winter there
were thirty. By the spring there were nine, and the nine stamped the eleven words into the
packed soil over two graves to a seam that went taut and let go, and the loosened layer
opened for them because the door was a door and a door does not shut, and there was nothing
left on the other side worth opening it for.

He had kept that boundary for three hundred and forty years. He had held it against the
deep band's leaning and a nine-man Hall expedition and the rot's refugees and a learned
liar, and he had made a people out of the small and lost of four grids, and the people had
been taken out of it in cages by men working a quota, and the men had not even known what
they were emptying.

The keeping had not failed. That is the honest reading and it took him a decade to arrive
at it, in the slow root-way he arrived at everything. The keeping had *finished*. A
boundary is kept for what it protects, and when what it protects is gone the boundary is
not defeated — it is done, and the only thing left in it is the keeper, standing at a door
with nothing on either side.

So, in the spring of his seven hundred and fourteenth year, the root-mass lifted.

---

It is the single hardest thing that ever happened in the serial and it is not dramatic at
all, which is exactly right.

A plant does not walk. That is the canon floor and he stood on it the whole way: he was
never, at any point in the twenty-one years of the going, unrooted. What he did was the
thing the deep band's diggers did, which he had spent two centuries learning to stop — he
went through the ground.

A hundred feet of low ground, lifted. Carried. Set down again, four hundred feet further
on, and re-rooted into silt he had never touched, and held there for a season while the
new root-mass wove itself into foreign soil, and then lifted again.

The first lifting took him a whole year.

That is not a figure of speech. It took a full season to work the root-mass free of the
stream bend — three hundred and forty years of layered growth, woven into silt laid down by
a flood when he was thirty years old, holding the ground under two kept places — and the
working-free was not a pulling, it was a *letting go*, root by root, and every root that
came up out of that soil was a root that had been laid down by the thing he had been, and
the whole of it had to be released before any of it could move.

He could not take the graves.

That is the cost of the chapter and it is the only cost that mattered. The forty feet of
densest silver-veined growth between the crown and the old one's place stayed where it was.
The packed soil over the found one stayed. The stream bend, the herd's drinking ground, the
shallows where the water had gone dark once in the ninety-eighth year of his life — all of
it stayed, because a plant cannot carry a place, and a place is where the dead are.

He left them, and he went southwest, and the going took twenty-one years.

---

The road was four hundred miles and he was hunted on it, and the hunting is the part the
world remembered, because the world only ever remembered the parts it could see.

They found him in the ninth year, in a low valley two hundred miles southwest of grid
nineteen, and they were not a contracted party. They were Hall — six men, a Soul Ancestor
leading, four rings in the column, working a commission that had come down from somewhere
high enough that nobody in it asked why a ten-thousand-year plant-type soul beast was worth
the expense.

Their leader was a Soul Ancestor named Ilen Marr, and on the second night, four hundred
feet from the root-mass, she said the thing out loud that the other five had been thinking
since the ridge.

"It's grass."

"It's the file, ma'am," the youngest said. "Eleven pages. Nine weeks on site. The man walked
the boundary forty-one times."

"The man had no rings." Marr turned the page over on her knee by the fire. "The man had no
rings, no combat assessment, no field authority, and he wrote eleven pages about a patch of
grass and then he died, and his nephew sold the file to a broker, and the broker sold it to
us, and somewhere along that chain it stopped being a record and started being a
commission." She held it up. "Plants do not cultivate. That is the first rule of the
registry and it has been the first rule for six hundred years."

"Then why are we two hundred miles out with a Soul Ancestor and a black-ring cage."

"Because," Marr said, "the walker in grid nineteen was dead for a hundred and fifty years
before anybody checked, and the grid was sealed the whole time, and when we finally opened
it there was nothing in it worth a net. Somebody has been wrong about that grid for four
centuries." She put the file down. "And I am not going to be the second."

On the third morning the forest stopped.

The reason it was worth the expense was the assessor. He had died eleven years before, an
old records man with no rings at all, and he had left his eleven pages in a personal file
rather than the registry, and the file had gone to a nephew, and the nephew had sold it,
and the buyer had done the arithmetic that no clerk in four hundred years had done: a
ten-thousand-year soul beast yields a black ring, and the registry said there was no
ten-thousand-year soul beast in grid nineteen, and the registry had said the same thing
about the walker for a century and a half.

They came for the black ring.

They did not get it, and the reason was not that he fought them, because he did not fight
them, and it was not that he killed them, because he did not kill them, and he would not
have killed them if he could have, and the whole of the remaining three hundred and seventy years of his
life would be shaped by the fact that he could have and did not.

The reason was the deep-country memory.

Four hundred miles of forest, and every ancient thing in it had been routing around grid
nineteen on purpose for sixty years, and the routing was a shape in the ground-memory that
meant *go around*, and the shape had followed him out of the middle band because the shape
was about *him* and not about the grid. The six men went into a low valley two hundred
miles from anywhere and found that the forest in it had gone quiet in a widening circle
that kept widening, and that the ground under them was wrong, and that whatever they had
come for was not alone in the way they had been told it was.

Marr stood up in the middle of the quiet and she did not sit back down.

"How far does it go."

"Ma'am —"

"How far does the quiet go. Walk it." The youngest walked it. He came back in an hour and
he was grey. "Well."

"It goes to the horizon, ma'am. In a circle. And it's still going." He sat down by the fire
without being told to. "There's nothing in it. There's no birds, there's no insects, there
isn't a single thing in four miles that makes a sound, and I stood in the middle of it and
listened and the only thing I could hear was the stream."

"Then it's a domain."

"A plant doesn't have a domain."

"No," Marr said. "It doesn't." She looked across four hundred feet of open ground at a
hundred feet of low blue-green grass standing in a low valley two hundred miles from
anywhere, and she looked at the black-ring cage on the cart, and she looked at the file on
her knee. "Pack the cage."

"Ma'am, we came four hundred miles—"

"We came four hundred miles for a black ring." She was already standing. "A black ring is a
ten-thousand-year beast. A ten-thousand-year beast does not stop a forest four miles wide
from making a sound. Whatever is in that grass, it is not what the file says it is, and I
do not have six men and I do not have the authority and I do not have the stomach." She
threw the file into the fire. "Pack the cage."

They left on the third day. Two of them did not leave at all, and what took them was not
him and not anything he did — it was the ordinary arithmetic of six men going into deep
country without a walker to route around, and the deep country being what it was.

He felt both of them go, in his ground, four hundred feet from where they had camped, and
he did nothing, and the four who walked out of that valley walked out because the ground
let them, and the letting was the same letting that had opened the loosened layer for a
small grey grazer in the winter of his four hundred and second year.

The door stayed a door. It stayed a door the whole way to the valley.

---

*They arrived at the southwestern edge of the old one's memory in the autumn of his seven
hundred and twenty-seventh year, and the memory ended there, because the old one had never gone
further, and beyond the memory there was only the pull.*

*It took eight more years.*

*The country changed coming into it. The deep band's great things thinned out and then
stopped altogether, which was not the way the deep band behaved — the deep band did not
stop, it went on being deep for a thousand miles in every direction, and the stopping was a
boundary, and the boundary was older than the old one's round, older than the glade, older
than the flood that had laid down the silt he had been born in.*

*Something had kept this country for a very long time before anything he knew had existed.*

*The soil changed under the root-mass in the last two years. It went from the ordinary
mineral poverty of the deep forest to something rich in a way that had no natural
explanation — rich the way the forty feet over the old one's grave had been rich, rich the
way soil gets when a great deal of cultivation has gone back into it over a great deal of
time, and the richness was not scattered. It was in lines. It was in a pattern.*

*He had no word for a pattern in the soil. He had eleven words and none of them were it.*

*But the pull had been pointing at this ground for seventy years, and the root-mass
came down into it in the spring of his seven hundred and thirty-fifth year and wove itself
into the richest soil he had ever touched, and held, and the holding felt different from
every other holding in eight centuries, because for the first time in his life the ground
under him was the same kind of thing he was.*

*He had three hundred and sixty years left, and he did not know it, and he was standing in a
valley in
the southwest of the largest forest on the continent with a hundred feet of low ground
around him and nine small voices still stamping eleven words into the packed soil at an
empty edge four hundred miles away.*

*And he was not the only thing in the valley.*

# Chapter Fourteen — The Ground That Remembers

```
◆ STATUS — Chapter 14: years 735–753
KIND      : Blue Silver Grass, common line. A King of the grass line, in the line's valley.
AGE       : ~765 at the chapter's close
```

The valley was nine miles long and it was full of grass, and the grass was the same kind of
thing he was.

That is not a small statement and it took him four years to be certain of it. He had spent
eight centuries as the only one of himself in the world — the only Blue Silver Grass in the
Star Dou middle band that had ever cultivated, the only plant anything had ever kept a
boundary, the single deep-blue blade in a forest of ten thousand species that had, entirely
by accident, become a person. He had no framework in which another one of himself was
possible, and when the root-mass came down into the valley soil in the spring of his
seven hundred and thirty-fifth year and the ground under him answered in his own register, the
answering was so far outside everything he had ever felt that he spent a whole season
reading it as a mistake.

It was not a mistake.

The valley floor was Blue Silver. Not a bank, not a meadow, not a hundred feet of low
ground — the whole floor, nine miles of it, wall to wall, growing in the dense layered
structure he had spent two centuries developing against the deep band's leaning, with the
same silver veins and the same hard base and the same held-and-let-go tension under contact.
And in the middle of it, in a ring, stood the nine.

They were not grass.

They were the great ones.

---

He had no word for what they were, having eleven words and none of them near enough, and
the word the world would eventually have used was Emperor — but they were not that either,
not anymore, and the difference is the whole of this chapter.

Nine of them. Rooted. Immobile. So old that the cultivation coming off them did not
register as pressure the way the old one's had not, and did not register as weather either.
It registered as *the valley*, because they had been standing in it so long that the ground
and the growing and the nine great bodies were one continuous object, and the object had
been there before the flood that laid down the silt he was born in, before the old one's
round, before the deep band had a seam to lean on.

They did not speak. That was the second thing, and it was worse than the first.

The nine were alive. They were the most alive things he had ever been near, by a margin
that made the serpent's ten thousand years feel like a candle, and they did not answer him,
and they did not turn toward him, and they did not do anything at all except stand in a
ring in the middle of a valley of their own grass and be rooted in the way that a thing
which has been rooted for an age is rooted — completely, permanently, past the point where
rootedness is a condition and becomes an identity.

They were not keeping the valley. That was the third thing, and it took him six years, and
it was the first piece of the truth.

The valley did not need keeping. The boundary that stopped the deep band's great things
dead at the valley's edge was not a kept boundary — it was a *pressure*, the accumulated
weight of nine ancient cultivations sitting in one place for so long that nothing in the
forest would come within nine miles of it. The valley kept itself. It had always kept
itself. The nine were not guards.

They were what was left.

---

The old king was dying, and it was the only one of the nine that had anything to give him.

It stood at the ring's northern point and it had been standing there for a very long time,
and it was old in a way the other eight were not — not older, *further along* — and in the
ninth year after he came down into the valley soil, in the deep of the cold season, it
reached for him through the ground.

Not the way the old one had tapped. Not the way the found one had stamped. It reached the
way a root reaches, and it came into his root-mass from below and it did not ask, and it
did not wait for an answer, and it gave him the valley's memory in the only form the line
had ever had for giving anything.

Through the ground. All at once.

---

There had been four hundred of them.

That was the first number, and it came down into him through the soil the way everything
in his life had come down into him, and he had no concept of a number and the number was
not a number to him — it was a *shape*, a ring of nine that had once been a ring of four
hundred, standing in this valley, in this grass, with the deep band stopped dead nine miles
out in every direction and no need to keep anything because there was nothing in the world
that could come at four hundred.

And the ring had thinned.

Not quickly. That was the cruelty of it and the thing he would have called cruelty if he
had had the word. The ring had thinned over an age — one here, three there, a gap at the
western point that stayed a gap for four hundred years, and the thinning had felt, from
inside the valley, like age. Great things die. Great things die slowly and at the end of
enormous lives and go back into the ground and the ground gets rich and the ring gets
smaller and that is what time does.

The ground knew otherwise.

That was the whole of the reveal and it had been under him the entire time, in the soil he
had woven himself into in the spring of his seven hundred and thirty-fifth year, in the
richness he had noticed coming into the country in the last two years of the going — the
richness that was not scattered, that was *in lines*, that was in a pattern.

He read the pattern in the eleventh year, and what the pattern said was this:

The dead had not gone back into the ground at the ends of their lives.

---

A soul beast that dies of age returns its cultivation slowly. It settles. It goes back over
seasons, the way the old one's went back over four days, the way the found one's went back
into the packed soil over a winter. The ground takes it gently and the ground gets rich in
a soft irregular bloom, and that is what four hundred feet of soil over an ancient grave
looks like from underneath.

The valley's soil was not like that.

The valley's soil was rich in *lines* — narrow, deep, vertical, running down through nine
miles of ground in a pattern that repeated, and each line was a place where a great
cultivation had gone back into the earth all at once, in a single season, in the middle of
what should have been an enormous life. Not settled. *Cut*.

He counted them by reading, over three years, root by root, and the count came up through
him the way every true thing in his life had come up through him, and the count was three
hundred and ninety-one.

Three hundred and ninety-one of the four hundred had gone back into the valley's soil in a
single season each, and not one of those seasons had been the end of a natural life.

The line had not dwindled.

The line had been *harvested*, slowly, over an age, one great body at a time, by something
that came into a valley that nothing in the forest could enter and took a member of the
ring and left, and came back, and took another — and the valley had gone on keeping itself,
because the valley did not know it was being emptied, because a pressure that stops the
deep band dead at nine miles does not register the difference between three hundred and
ninety-nine great cultivations and nine.

The nine were not what was left of a line that had aged.

They were what was left of a cull.

---

The old king gave him all of it in one season and then it went, and the going was the
quietest thing in the whole of the serial.

It did not die in the ring. That is worth saying, because it is the same thing the found one
had done, four hundred miles away, at the end of a life two hundred and twenty-eight years
long — it left its place. The great rooted body at the northern point of the ring came out
of the ground in the spring of his seven hundred and forty-sixth year, and it could not
move, and it did not try, and what it did instead was let go of the valley floor and put
the whole of itself down into the soil under the ring, and the going-back took one season,
and the soil under the northern point got rich in a soft irregular bloom.

At the end of a natural life.

It was the first one in three hundred and ninety-one.

He felt the whole of it, and he did not feed.

That is the second refusal and it was harder than the first, and the reason it was harder
is that this time he understood what he was refusing. The old one's ten thousand years had
been an accident of proximity — a dying animal forty feet from his crown, going back into
soft ground, available to a root-mass that had no reason in the world to decline it. This
was a King of his own line, at the end of an enormous life, putting itself into the soil
under a ring of its own remaining great ones, in a valley nine miles across that was made
of nothing but the returned substance of its own dead.

The whole valley was food. Nine miles of it. Three hundred and ninety-one great
cultivations, cut down in the middle of their lives and gone back into the ground, lying in
the soil under him in lines he had spent three years counting.

He did not take a single year of it.

He had four words and a drum of eleven and no self clear enough to hold a principle, and the
principle had been written for him anyway, four hundred miles away, in the eleventh year
after the liar, in the dark, by a thing that could not have explained it:

*a keeper keeps.*

A keeper does not take. And the line's dead were the line's dead, and the valley was the
valley, and what had been done to the ring had been done by taking, and he was not going to
be another thing that took.

---

*The report went into the Hall's registry in the autumn of his seven hundred and
fifty-first year, and it was four lines long, and it was the first document in nine
centuries that named the valley.*

*It was written by an assessor named Tefer Hallum, who had stood at the boundary of that
country for two days with an instrument case that would not read past it, and who had come
back to the southwestern post and dictated the whole of what he had seen to a clerk in
under a minute.*

*"Valley, southwestern grid, unentered," he said. "Vegetation continuous across the floor,
nine miles, will not come out of the soil."*

*"Cultivation reading."*

*"None. That's the thing." Hallum rubbed his face. "There's no reading. My case reads to
sixty thousand and it reads nothing, and there are nine — nine — structures at the centre of
it that are not structures, they're growth, and my hand went cold standing two hundred feet
from the boundary."*

*"Cultivation estimate."*

*"In excess of sixty thousand years each." The clerk stopped writing. "Write it down."*

*"Ma'am, if that's right—"*

*"Write it down and write the recommendation." Hallum was already putting his coat on.
"Recommend no approach. Recommend the grid be sealed."*

*"And the party. Six men went out with you."*

*"Four of them wouldn't cross." He looked at the clerk for the first time. "I wouldn't
cross. I've assessed in the deep band for nineteen years and I stood at that line for two
days and I did not cross it, and I'm not going to pretend to you that I know what's on the
other side." He took his case off the desk. "Seal it. Seal the whole grid. And put my name
on it, because in ten years somebody with a quota is going to want to open it and I want
them to have to read my name first."*

*They sealed it. The valley had been sealed by nothing at all for an age and was now sealed
by a Hall designation as well, and the designation went into the registry next to grid
nineteen's exhausted-habitat note and the walker entry and a dead records man's eleven
pages, and nobody in the Hall connected any of them, because they were four hundred miles
apart and one was about a dead walker and one was about grass and one was about a valley
nobody could enter.*

*Somebody did, eventually.*

*In the valley, at the end of the seven hundred and fifty-first year, a King of the Blue
Silver line stood rooted in the soil of his own dead with a hundred feet of low ground
around him, and eight great ones stood in a ring with a gap at the northern point, and the
ground under the gap was rich in a soft irregular bloom, and the deep band stopped nine
miles out and had always stopped, and three hundred and ninety-one lines ran down through
the soil in a pattern that said the same thing over and over.*

*He had three hundred and forty years left and he did not know it.*

*And in the spring of his seven hundred and fifty-third year, at the eastern edge of the
valley, in the blue-silver grass that grew up to his own crown's height, something moved
that was not wind.*

It came through it.

thing he was, and he had spent eighteen years rooted in it and holding it and reading its
surface, and he could no more go through it than he could go through the air. Whatever was

miles of the valley floor answering to it the way the low ground at the stream bend had

first.

She could read him. He could not read her.

Every root in his crown was a sense organ and he had spent eight centuries learning to use

She had been counting.

She had been carrying it.

That was what he understood, standing in the open ground at the edge of his crown with a
hundred feet of low ground around him and a King's cultivation in the well and four words
and a drum of eleven, and the understanding was not a word and not a thought — it was the
same thing that had come up through him when the tapping stopped, when the small grey body
went still in the packed soil, when the great one at the northern point let go of the
valley floor and put itself down into the ground at the end of a natural life.

The recognition of another thing that had been keeping something alone.

---

Her domain drew.

That was its nature and it is written down in the law of her blood rather than in anything
she chose: the Blue Silver Domain takes vitality from the grass it unfolds in, and it had
been unfolded over nine miles of the line's own growth, and the drawing was not cruel and
not deliberate and not stoppable, and everything in the valley that could give was giving.

He refused.

Not by force. He had no force that meant anything against a domain of her blood; the well
was deep and it was a thousand-year King's well and she was an Emperor's daughter standing
in the grass of her own dead. What he did was the thing he had done at the meadow four
hundred miles away, and the thing he had done under the ring three seasons ago, and the
thing he had done in the eleventh year after the liar, in the dark, without malice, without
knowing he was doing it:

he held.

The whole hundred feet of low ground, layered against itself, woven, kept — the same craft
that had stopped the deep band's diggers for two centuries and held a ten-thousand-year
serpent for four hours and closed over a learned liar without once tightening. The domain
drew and the ground did not give, and the not-giving was not resistance, it was simply what
the ground was, and after a while the drawing went around it the way the deep band's
pressure had gone around it, the way the mid-forest hunters had gone around the glade, the
way twelve men with nets had worked within four hundred feet of the best-kept boundary in
the middle band without once looking at it.

She stopped.

Not because he had beaten her. Because she had felt what the not-giving was made of, and
because she had been listening for an age, and because the whole of the last three hundred
and ninety-one lines in the valley's soil had gone down through the ground in single
seasons, in the middle of enormous lives, taken by something that came in and took and left
— and here, at the edge of her own valley, in grass that was common and blue and had no
gold in it anywhere, was a thing that had been offered the whole of it and had not taken a
single year.

She had been counting the dead for an age.

She had never once counted a keeper.

---

She named him at the end of the seven hundred and fifty-third year, and the naming took
the whole winter, and it was not a word.

That is the honest account and it is the only one the serial has ever had for him: she did
not give him a sound. She had no mouth and he had no ears and the whole of the vocabulary
between them was taps and pulses and eleven stamped patterns in packed soil, and what she
gave him was a shape in the ground — a pattern of pressure laid down through the valley
floor at the edge of his crown, in the same register as the three hundred and ninety-one
lines, only soft, only deliberate, only put there on purpose by something that meant it.

And the shape was the shape of a kept place.

Not a grave. Not a line. Not a single season's worth of a great cultivation going back into
the earth because something had come into a valley that nothing could enter and taken it
and left. A *kept* place — the forty feet of densest silver-veined growth between a crown
and an ancient keeper's body, the packed soil over a small grey grazer, the hundred feet of
low ground at a stream bend where the door had been and the seam had gone taut and let go
at dusk for four hundred years.

She laid that shape down at the edge of his crown, and she held it there, and the holding
was the naming, and the name was the oldest word in the drum and the only one of the eleven
that had never been about asking:

**Home.**

The first name the Blue Silver line ever gave a wild blade. Not a title, not a rank, not a
designation in a registry — a name, given by the youngest of an age-culled ring to a common
grass from the middle band of a forest four hundred miles away, for the crime of having
kept a boundary that did not need keeping, for a hundred small things that had been taken
out of it in cages, and for having stood in the soil of three hundred and ninety-one of her
own dead and not taken a single year of any of them.

He had no way to answer. He had four words and a drum and no self clear enough to hold a
name, and the name went down into him anyway, into the place where the mantis was and the
arithmetic and the sixty years of taps and the law that had been written in the dark by a
thing that could not have explained it, and it stayed there for the rest of his long life.

The valley went on. The eight stood in the ring with a gap at the northern point. The deep
band stopped nine miles out and had always stopped.

And four hundred miles away, in a records room with no windows, somebody finally connected
them.

Her name was Berrit Ohn and she was thirty-one and she had been given the southwestern
consolidation because nobody else wanted it — eleven grids, four centuries of
designations, and a directive to reduce the Hall's sealed-territory overhead before the
end of the fiscal year.

"It's just arithmetic," her superior had said. "Sealed grids cost us patrols. Find the ones
that are sealed for no reason and open them."

She had found nine in eleven grids. All of them sealed for no reason. All of them sealed by
a dead walker, or a report nobody had read, or a records man who had walked a boundary
forty-one times with a measuring cord.

Then she got to grid nineteen, and then she got to the southwestern valley, and she put the
two files side by side on a desk in a room with no windows and she sat there for a long
time.

"Ma'am." Her assistant was in the doorway with a lamp. "It's the fourth night."

"I know what night it is."

"You haven't eaten since—"

"The vegetation note in grid nineteen is four hundred and fifty years old." Berrit did not
look up. "It says the grass is blue-silver, it says the grass is tough, and it says *worth a
look*. Nobody writes worth a look about grass." She turned the second file around. "The
valley report says the floor is continuous vegetation, nine miles, will not come out of the
soil. And it says nine plant-type signatures at the centre in excess of sixty thousand
years each."

"Those are four hundred miles apart."

"They are." She put her finger on the third file — the eleven pages, the personal one, the
one the nephew had sold. "And this man spent nine weeks in grid nineteen and walked a dead
animal's round forty-one times and wrote that the boundary is maintained daily by the
vegetation, and he asked for a specialist team, and the specialist team came, and the seal
stayed on, and then the grid was opened for hunting anyway because of a budget shortfall,
and then it was marked exhausted." She looked up. "Do you know what's in a grid that gets
marked exhausted?"

"Hunted-out low-class stock."

"Right. And do you know what the valley floor is." Her assistant did not answer. "Neither
does anybody. But it's the same kind of thing, four hundred miles away, and it's nine miles
of it, and it has nine sixty-thousand-year signatures standing in a ring in the middle of
it." She closed the file. "That's not two grids. That's a line. And something has been
killing it."

"Ma'am — that's—"

"That's what the files say." Berrit stood up. "Four hundred and fifty years of a note that
says worth a look, a hundred and fifty years of a seal on a dead walker, a records man who
asked for a team and got a joke, a Soul Ancestor who threw a commission file into a fire
two hundred miles out, and a valley nobody can enter with nine things in it that my
instrument case cannot read." She picked up all three files. "I'm filing a consolidated
designation. Both grids. Permanent seal, highest class, and a standing request for an
Emperor-level assessment."

"They'll laugh at you."

"They laughed at Vase." She walked to the door. "And they opened his grid for hunting
anyway, and it came back exhausted in eleven weeks, and nobody ever asked why a grid with a
hundred-foot boundary that wouldn't come out of the soil went empty that fast." She stopped
in the doorway. "Something took forty-one small things out of grid nineteen in eleven weeks
and then stopped, and I want to know what it was doing before that, and I want to know what
it went on to do after."

She filed it. The consolidated designation went into the registry in the spring, and it sat
there, and the Emperor-level assessment was not funded that year, or the next, or the next
fourteen.

But the seal was permanent, and the seal was highest class, and the seal was in Berrit
Ohn's name, and in forty-seven years, when a young man from a fallen clan came
out of the Star Dou Forest with a spider on his wrist and the whole continent started
looking for the Blue Silver line, the first file anybody pulled was hers.

And at the edge of the crown, in the blue-silver grass, a common blade of the line that had
no gold in it and no blood and no history stood rooted in the ground of its own dead with a
hundred feet of low ground around it, and it was named, and it kept.

It would keep for another three hundred and forty years.

It would never once kill.

# Chapter 1: Awakening Day

## Canon Reference: canon ch 1–6 — "Awakening Day" through the awakening ceremony.
## ⚠️ Canon ch 7–22 are **SKIPPED here** and compressed into ch 2–3 (recorded, not hidden).
## Timeline: Story start, age 6, Glorybound City
## Canon anchors held: Glorybound City on the border of the ocean and the eastern coast of the Sun-Moon
## Federation · Red Mountain Academy, an elementary comprehensive academy for **two thousand** students, white
## roofs and red walls · the **Awakening Chamber** is a circular building with **seven floors**, one chamber
## per floor; the boys are taken to the **third** · the Spirit Master wears a **simple orange robe embroidered
## with the form of a soul beast** and comes from the **Spirit Pagoda** · **Bluesilver Grass** (canon spelling,
## one word) · Wulin's innate soul power **rank 3** · the golden lines on his forehead spreading to his four
## limbs, which the Spirit Master has never seen in tens of thousands of children · Tang Ziran a machine
## repairman of ordinary skill and meagre wage · the "one in a thousand" rarity of soul power.

---

Glorybound City sat on the border between the ocean and the eastern coast of the Sun-Moon Federation, which meant it smelled of salt and hot metal in equal measure, and that nobody who lived there thought either smell was worth mentioning.

On the morning of the annual Awakening Day, the streets in front of Red Mountain Academy were so packed that a dog could have crossed the square without touching the ground.

Everybody on the Douluo Continent had a martial soul. It woke on your sixth birthday, it decided what you were for, and once a year the academies opened their doors and found out. If your martial soul was a hoe, you would till fields better than other men. If it was an animal, you might carry some of what that animal could do. And if — one child in a thousand, the teachers said, though nobody had ever met the person who counted — you woke with soul power as well, then your whole family's fortune turned over like a card.

So the parents came. They came in their best clothes, which for most of them meant their only good coat, and they stood in the sun and did not say what they were thinking.

Two boys stood a little apart from the crowd, because they had arrived early and had already been told twice to stop climbing the wall.

"If I get a hoe," said Tang Wulin, "I'm going to be very good at it."

"You'd be terrible at it," said Lin Hao. "You cried when you dropped a spoon."

"That was a *good* spoon."

"It was a spoon, Wulin."

Lin Hao was six years old and already the reason two older women had stopped in the street to ask his mother whether he was something to do with the theatre. He had dark brown hair that fell across his forehead in a way his mother had given up on, and amber-brown eyes that gave the impression, fairly or not, that he had already heard the end of the joke and was being polite about it.

Beside him, Tang Wulin was a pretty boy with short black hair, taller than he should have been at six, with large clear black eyes and eyelashes that his mother's friends found unfair. He wore commoner's clothing and did not seem to notice it.

"Dad," he said, "what do you think mine will be?"

Tang Ziran was a middle-aged man of medium build and average height, everything about him average, which was a thing he had made peace with and also a thing that occasionally sat on his chest at night. He was a machine repairman who specialised in soul machines, and his skill was ordinary, and so his wage was meagre, and he knew exactly how much a family like his needed the one-in-a-thousand.

"Dad doesn't know," he said. "It's all luck."

He said it kindly. He also sighed inside, where his son could not hear it.

"What about yours, Hao?" Wulin turned, bright-eyed. "What do you want?"

"A sword."

"Everybody wants a sword."

"I'm going to *get* one," said Lin Hao, with the complete absence of doubt that only the six and the very old can manage. "Dad's got Iron Sword. Mum's got Gale Eagle. One of those has to come out, and if it comes out and it's a hoe, I'm going to have some questions."

Behind him, Lin Wei laughed — a broad-shouldered blacksmith with hands rough enough to strike a match on, and eyes that were unexpectedly soft. "Don't get ahead of yourself. Martial souls don't take requests."

"And whatever you get," said Lin Mei, his mother, a slender seamstress who moved like someone whose martial soul had been something quick, "we're proud of you."

"I'll definitely have soul power, right?" Wulin asked his father. It was the third time he had asked.

Tang Ziran put his hand on his son's head. "Whether you do or you don't, Dad will always love you."

Which was the right answer and also, both of them knew, not the one he wanted.

The crowd thinned and thickened and thinned again as families came out. Most came out sighing. Now and then one came out making a noise that turned every head on the square, and there was no need to ask, and the envious looks followed them all the way home.

The sun climbed. Wulin's enthusiasm, which had started at a run, began to walk.

"Tang Wulin!" A teacher came out of the academy with a list.

"Here!" Wulin was up and moving before his own brain had agreed to it.

Tang Ziran was pulled forward by one small hand.

"Follow me," said the teacher, and turned and went, in the flat apathetic manner of a man on his four-hundredth child of the day.

They walked in through the small path, and Wulin took it all in the way he took everything, completely. Red Mountain Academy was an elementary comprehensive academy holding two thousand students. The buildings were simple and unadorned — white roofs, red walls — and the grounds were exceptionally clean, and inside the walls it was peaceful in a way the street outside was not, as though the noise had been asked to wait.

Lin Hao walked beside him with his father behind, and was counting the windows.

He had been counting things for as long as anyone could remember, and he had never thought it was strange, because he had never met anybody who didn't. Forty-one windows on the long face. The bricks in the path were laid two-across, one-along. The teacher's left shoe had a worn heel, which meant he turned his foot out when he walked, which meant — he stopped that line of thought, because it didn't matter, and he had learned very early that most of what he noticed did not matter, and that the trick was knowing which parts did.

The teacher brought them to a circular building.

"Parents wait here," he said.

Tang Ziran crouched down. "Listen to the teacher. Good luck, son."

"I'll get a powerful one, Dad."

Lin Wei put a hand on Lin Hao's shoulder. "Whatever happens. We're proud of you."

"Dad." Lin Hao looked up at him with great seriousness. "If I come out with a hoe, I want you to know I'm going to be very good at it, and I'm going to be *furious* about it the entire time."

Lin Wei barked out a laugh and shoved him gently toward the door.

---

There was not one awakening area in the Awakening Chamber but seven — seven floors, one chamber apiece. Tang Wulin and Lin Hao were taken up to the third.

Both of them stopped in the doorway.

Every surface — floor, walls, ceiling — was carved with inscriptions in a pattern that seemed at first to be decoration and then, the longer you looked, seemed to be a sentence in a language that had simply run out of room.

In the middle of the chamber stood a middle-aged man in a simple orange robe embroidered with the form of a soul beast.

Wulin had heard about Spirit Masters his whole life, in his father's stories, where they were always the ones who arrived late and fixed everything. They were from the Spirit Pagoda. They were powerful and mysterious and held a status on the Douluo Continent that had nothing to do with what your father did for a living. He had never seen one.

"Hello," said Tang Wulin, shyly.

The Spirit Master smiled. "Come here, children. Stand in the middle."

They stood in the middle.

"Lord Spirit Master," said Wulin, who could not hold a question for long, "what kind of martial soul will we get?"

"I don't know either." The man sounded genuinely amused. "You'll see when it wakes. Though—" he looked at Wulin properly for the first time "—your eyes are so pretty it would be a shame if you didn't get something to do with them."

"Soul eyes?" Wulin lit up. "I heard the first master of the Spirit Pagoda had spirit eyes—"

"Quiet," said the Spirit Master, not unkindly. "I'm about to begin."

He raised his right arm. A gentle white light came out of his hand, and both boys stopped breathing, because that was soul power — the thing only one in a thousand had — and it was floating in the air in front of them like a held note.

The white light shivered and went up and broke open into something like fireworks, and the inscriptions began to fill from the ceiling down, running along the walls with a vitality that made them look, for a moment, less like carving and more like something that had been asleep.

The lines met beneath the boys' feet.

---

Lin Hao had felt it before.

That was the strange part, and it was the part he had never told anyone, because he had never been sure it was the sort of thing you told. There was a feeling — had been for as long as he could remember — of something in him *arranging*. Not a voice. Nothing so simple. More like the way you can feel a room is not square without measuring it. It had been working on one thing for six years, patiently, the way water works on stone, and he had never known what the thing was.

Now the light went into him, and the arranging stopped.

It stopped the way a held breath stops.

For one moment he understood, with a clarity that was almost frightening, exactly what it had been doing: it had been folding two things into one, over and over, six years of quiet folding, and now the fold was finished and there was nothing left in his hands to fold.

*Oh,* he thought. *That's what you were for.*

And then something else in him, which had been waiting its turn like a second child at a door, stepped forward and began, very quickly, to look at everything else instead.

"Ah—!"

The scream was Wulin's.

An ordinary child feels almost nothing at awakening. A very small number feel a great deal, because their bodies are not ready to carry what has come into them, and the Spirit Master was moving before the sound had finished — crossing the chamber in a single blur, arriving at Tang Wulin's side with his hand already rising to stop the ceremony.

He stopped it about halfway.

Golden lines were flickering on the boy's forehead.

They spread — down his neck, along both arms, out to his four limbs — a network of gold that pulsed once, twice, with a light that did not belong in a room, and then went out as suddenly as it had come.

The Spirit Master from the Spirit Pagoda, who had conducted this ceremony for nineteen years and had put his hands on more children than he could count, stood very still and looked at Tang Wulin's forehead as though it had insulted him personally.

In tens of thousands of children, he had never seen that.

Lin Hao saw the man's face.

He filed it — not because he decided to, but because that was simply what happened — and he noticed that he had already worked out the important part, which was that whatever had just come out of his best friend, the person whose entire job it was to know had not seen before.

Wulin was bent double, teeth gritted, and he slowly raised his right arm.

A small patch of green grass appeared in his palm. Thin. Weak. Utterly unremarkable.

Bluesilver Grass.

The Spirit Master's face went carefully neutral in the way adults do when they are about to say something unkind and would prefer not to. "Bluesilver Grass. Now put your hand on the crystal, child."

He held out a blue crystal ball. Wulin, still shaking, put his hand on it. It glowed faintly, the pale embarrassed glow of a lamp with almost nothing behind it.

"Innate soul power, rank three."

There was a murmur from the line of children waiting their turn. Everybody in Glorybound City knew what Bluesilver Grass was. It was the one they told you about so you would feel better about the hoe.

"Thank you, child," said the Spirit Master gently. "Step aside."

Wulin stepped aside with his head down.

Somewhere in the line, a boy with a fat face and a knife for a martial soul said, loudly enough to be helpful, "Trash soul. Rank three. He'll never be a Soul Master."

---

"Lin Hao."

He had known it was coming for four seconds, which was long enough to decide how he was going to walk, and he walked to the middle of the chamber at exactly his ordinary speed, because he had noticed — again, without deciding to — that the Spirit Master was watching him now, and that adults read a boy's hands before they read his face.

He put his hands where they could be seen.

The Spirit Master raised his arm. The light went up, broke, ran down the walls, and came into Lin Hao.

Wind moved.

Not a draught. Not the door. The air in the chamber turned and gathered around him in a slow visible coil, and his hair lifted, and the children in the line took half a step back without any of them agreeing to. There was a sound like a hand drawn along the edge of a glass.

Something crackled — small, bright, gone — a thread of lightning no longer than a finger, running along the inside of his forearm.

And a sword came into his right hand.

It was not a big sword. It was silver-blue and it was light and it was, unmistakably, *good* — the kind of thing a man who made swords for a living would pick up and go quiet about. Wind ran in fine lines along the flat of the blade, and along the edge there was a restlessness, as though the metal had not entirely decided to stop moving.

The Stormbringer Sword.

The Spirit Master's eyebrows went up.

"Well," he said. Then, after a moment: "Well."

"Is it a sword?" asked Lin Hao, who knew perfectly well it was a sword.

"It is a sword."

"Dad's got Iron Sword," said Lin Hao, conversationally, "and Mum's got Gale Eagle, so I've been told to expect one of those and to be grateful, and instead I appear to have been given both at once and a thunderstorm, so I'd like to register that I consider this an acceptable outcome."

Two of the children in the line laughed. The Spirit Master's mouth twitched, which was possibly against the rules.

"This is a high-grade martial soul," he said. "Wind and lightning in one manifestation. That is rare in a child of the capital, let alone here." He held out the crystal. "Hand."

Lin Hao put his hand on the ball.

It glowed — steadily, moderately, more than Wulin's and considerably less than the light the room had been hoping for.

"Rank five."

A good number. Not a number that made anybody's fortune. Combined with the sword, though, it was enough that the Spirit Master looked at him for a second longer than he had looked at anyone else that morning, and wrote something on his list that was not just a name.

"Very good, young man. You have a real future if you keep it."

"Thank you," said Lin Hao, and was already looking past him.

Wulin was standing against the wall with the grass still in his hand and his chin tucked down, and he had gone very still, in the way children go still when they have decided not to cry in front of people.

Lin Hao crossed the floor to him.

He did not hurry, and he did not slow down, and he did not look at the Spirit Master, or the stocky boy with the purchased knife, or his father, or the list that had his name on it with a mark next to it that nobody else's name had. He walked across a room that had spent the last four minutes finding out he was the best thing in it, and he stopped in front of the only person in it who had already been found out to be the worst, and he held out his hand.

"Let me see it."

"It's grass."

"I can see it's grass. Let me see *it.*"

Wulin gave it to him. Lin Hao turned the Bluesilver Grass over in his fingers the way his father turned over a bar of stock on the anvil — properly, the whole of it, taking his time about it, the way you handle a thing when you are trying to find out what it is rather than what it is worth. And the room, which had been watching the sword, slowly stopped, and started watching this instead, because there is something arresting about a six-year-old examining a worthless object with total seriousness.

"It's got threads," Lin Hao said.

"So?"

"So it can be woven." He handed it back. "Nothing else in this room can be woven. That knife can't be woven. My sword can't be woven. You've got the only one in Glorybound City that can be tied into a knot, and you're standing there like you've been handed a hoe."

"Hao."

"And I've known you since we were three," Lin Hao said, "and you have never once in your life been given anything that you did not turn into a weapon, so I am going to go and stand over there with my sword, and you are going to stand here with your grass, and it is going to be exactly the same as it was yesterday, and if anybody in this square says otherwise I would like you to tell me and I will deal with it."

And he went and stood where he had been standing, and Wulin looked down at the grass in his hand for a long moment, and put his chin up.

Tang Ziran, who had watched all of it from four metres away and had not said a word, put his hand on his son's head, and looked across at Lin Wei, and Lin Wei shrugged in the way he shrugged when a piece of work had come out better than the drawing.

---

Outside, the sun had got higher and the square had got louder, and the parents came forward to collect their children and find out what they had been given.

"A sword!" Lin Wei turned it over in his mind the way he turned over everything, appraising. "Wind *and* lightning? That's my Iron Sword and your mother's Gale Eagle in one piece. Son, that's a good day's work."

"Rank five," said Lin Mei, holding him. "That's wonderful, Hao."

Lin Hao accepted this with good grace and looked over his mother's shoulder until he found what he was looking for.

Tang Wulin was holding up a thin green sprig to his father.

"It's just Bluesilver Grass, Dad. Rank three."

Tang Ziran's face did the careful neutral thing, and Lin Hao watched him do it, and thought — with the total, unreasonable certainty of a six-year-old — *that is the worst thing I have ever seen and I am going to do something about it immediately.*

"Excuse me," he told his parents, and went.

"—isn't—" Tang Ziran was saying.

"It isn't trash," said Lin Hao, arriving.

Both of them looked at him.

"What do you mean?" said Wulin.

Lin Hao shrugged. He had noticed, on the way over, that there were four boys coming across the square in a loose group and that one of them was stocky and had the expression of a boy who had heard a rumour and was looking forward to it, and he decided to be quick.

"I mean the man in the orange robe has done this for nineteen years," he said. "Nineteen. He's probably seen forty thousand kids. And when it was your turn he crossed the room so fast he went blurry. He didn't do that for anybody else, Wulin. Not one."

Wulin blinked. "He came because it hurt."

"He came because he didn't know what was happening." Lin Hao said it flatly, the way you'd read out a number. "Gold came out of your forehead and went down your arms and he stood there like somebody had insulted his mother. Grass doesn't do that. Grass is grass."

There was a silence.

"Also," said Lin Hao, "I have a sword, and you have a weed, and I am still standing next to you, so evidently the weed does not disqualify you from anything I care about."

Wulin's mouth did something that was almost a smile and wasn't quite brave enough.

"You really think it's not trash?"

"I think rank three means you work harder than everyone else," said Lin Hao, "and I've known you since we were three, and you are the single most stubborn person in this city, so I'm not especially worried."

Tang Ziran looked at Lin Hao for a long moment. "Thank you, Hao."

"That's very kind of you," said a voice behind them.

The stocky boy had arrived, with his three behind him. He had a knife for a martial soul and his family had paid extra for it, and he knew exactly what that meant and had decided it meant something about him.

"Bluesilver Grass," he said. "Rank three. My dad says that's the bottom. My dad says they give those to kids so the ceremony doesn't look empty."

The three behind him laughed on cue.

Wulin went red and looked at his shoes.

Lin Hao did not step in front of him, which was the thing everybody expected and which he had already decided against, because standing in front of somebody tells the whole square that they need standing in front of.

Instead he stepped *beside* him, and turned to face the stocky boy, and smiled — and the smile was warm and pleasant and did not reach his eyes at all, and the stocky boy, who was six and not yet good at reading this, nonetheless felt something go wrong with the afternoon.

"You're right," said Lin Hao.

The stocky boy's face changed. "I am?"

"Completely. Bluesilver Grass is the bottom. Rank three is the bottom. You have a knife and I have a sword and you're the one who walked over here to tell a stranger about your father's opinions, so let's be honest about who's had the good morning."

"Shut up."

"No, but genuinely," said Lin Hao, still smiling, "I'm fascinated. You've got a knife. A *knife*. Did you choose that, or did your dad choose it and now you've got to explain it to people at parties for the rest of your life?"

One of the three behind him made a noise that was very nearly a laugh and then decided, on reflection, not to.

The stocky boy's face went the colour of the academy walls. "At least I don't stand next to trash."

Something in Lin Hao's face closed, like a shutter.

The sword was in his hand. He had not made a decision to draw it and he could not afterwards have described doing it. The wind came up around him and turned his hair, and along the edge of the blade that restlessness woke up and there was one thin bright line of lightning, no longer than a finger, running the length of the steel.

"Say that again," he said, quietly, "but this time think about it first."

The stocky boy looked at the sword. He looked at the wind. He looked at the small bright thing moving along the edge of the metal, and he understood, at six years old and for the first time in his life, that there were rooms he could walk out of and rooms he had better not have walked into.

"Whatever," he said. "Come on."

They went. They did not run, because running would have been an admission, but they went quickly.

Wulin was staring at him.

"You didn't have to do that."

"Yes," said Lin Hao, and let the sword go. The wind sat down. "I did. You're my friend. Nobody calls you trash in front of me and then gets to have a nice afternoon."

Tang Ziran put a hand on his shoulder and said thank you again, and Lin Hao, who could not bear being thanked for more than about four seconds, immediately brightened and said, "Right. Wulin. Race you home. Loser carries the winner's shoes."

"You don't wear shoes home, we live next door—"

Lin Hao was already running.

Wulin stood there for a moment with the grass still in his hand, and then he smiled — really smiled, for the first time since the ceremony — and went after him, and Tang Ziran called after them both about the road, and did not much mean it.

---

They ate at the Lins' that evening, both families around one table in a front room that was not big enough, because Lin Mei cooked like a woman who had been told there would be four and had decided there would be nine.

Wulin ate four bowls. His mother was not there — nobody said anything about that, because Wulin's mother had been gone a long time and the Tangs had made a decision about it years ago — and Lin Mei put food in front of him at exactly the same rate she put it in front of her own son, and did not comment on it once, which was the kindest thing that happened to Tang Wulin that year.

"Rank five and a sword," said Tang Ziran, raising his cup. "And rank three and a weed. Between the two of you, boys, you've got the whole range covered."

"Dad," said Wulin.

"I'm joking, Linlin."

Lin Hao, who had been working out for eleven minutes how to say the thing without making it a speech, put down his chopsticks.

"Wulin's is going to be better than mine," he said.

The table went quiet.

"Hao—" Lin Mei began.

"No, listen, I've thought about it." He was six, and he had the total confidence of a person who has thought about something for eleven minutes. "The man in the orange robe has seen forty thousand kids. Mine was a sword. He wrote it down and he moved on, because a sword is a sword, there's a sword in every city, you can go and buy one. But gold came out of Wulin's *head*, and that man crossed the room so fast he went blurry, and then he looked at him like he'd been personally offended."

He looked at Wulin.

"Nobody has ever seen that. Which means nobody knows what it does. Which means nobody knows what it *can't* do either." He shrugged. "I got a good hand. You got a card nobody's got a rule for. I'd rather have your card."

Wulin stared at him.

Tang Ziran set his cup down very carefully, the way men do when they are trying not to make a face.

"That's a good way of putting it," said Lin Wei at last.

"It's the right way," said Lin Hao, and went back to eating, because he had said the thing and could now be six again.

Outside, the sun went down over Glorybound City and the soul lamps came up the street one after another, and somewhere in a small room at the back of a house two doors down, a man named Mang Tian took a piece of cold metal out of a rack and looked at it for a while and put it back, and thought about a boy he had not met yet.

Neither of the boys in the front room knew anything about that.

They knew they were six, and that they had martial souls, and that tomorrow the real work started, and — which was the part that mattered — that they were going to do it in the same city, at the same academy, at the same desk if Lin Hao could arrange it, which he fully intended to.

# Chapter 2: A Thousand Strikes

## Canon Reference: canon ch 2–8 — the ordinary class, Na'er, and Mang Tian's workshop.
