The days after the awakening ceremony were the worst days of Tang Wulin's life, and he was six, so he had no way of knowing that they would also turn out to be the useful ones.

Red Mountain Academy sorted the new children the way it sorted everything: by what they had. Powerful martial souls and high soul power went up. Weak martial souls, or no soul power at all, went down. There was no ceremony to it and no cruelty in it either, which somehow made it worse — it was simply how the academy was built, the same way the roof was red and the walls were white.

Wulin, with Bluesilver Grass and innate soul power rank 3, went to the bottom.

Their teacher was a middle-aged man with the permanently bored expression of somebody who has explained the same thing four hundred times and stopped expecting anyone to hear it. He gave the class the meditation instructions. He gave Wulin the meditation instructions. He did not give Wulin anything else.

"Bluesilver Grass," he said, in the tone of a man reading a weather report. "Just sit and see if anything happens."

At lunch Wulin ate more than any other child at the table, and then more than any other child in the room. His appetite had gone strange since the awakening, as though his body had been handed a bill and was trying to pay it in advance. By the end of the first week the class had named him **Rice Bucket**, and he discovered that he did not mind, because a nickname meant they had noticed him, and being noticed for eating was better than being noticed for the grass.

What he minded was the rest of it.

"That one with the pretty eyes. Bluesilver Grass. Rank three."

"His friend got a sword. Rank five. Must be nice."

"He'll never be a Soul Master."

Wulin sat with his knuckles going white under the table and thought, with the flat grim practicality that was going to turn out to be the most important thing about him: *Dad says success is ninety-nine parts effort and one part talent. So if the talent is no good, I'll just have to be very good at the other ninety-nine.*

He finished lunch. He went back to class. He did not tell his father.

---

Lin Hao was waiting for him outside the gate, leaning against a soul lamp with his arms folded, looking like a man who had been leaning against soul lamps his whole life.

"How was it?"

"Fine."

"Wulin."

"It was bad," said Wulin.

"Right." Lin Hao pushed off the lamp and fell into step beside him. "Who was worst?"

"What?"

"Who was the worst one. I want a name. I'm not going to do anything about it, I just want to know, because I'm keeping a list and I'd like it to be accurate."

Wulin, despite everything, almost laughed. "There isn't a worst one. It's all of them."

"That's worse for the list, actually, that's a lot of writing." Lin Hao considered this. "Did the teacher say anything?"

"He said sit and see if anything happens."

"Ah." Lin Hao nodded slowly, in the manner of a man receiving confirmation of a theory he had held for some time. "That's the tell. When a teacher gives you the short version, it means he's already decided what you are and he's saving his breath. You should be flattered. He thinks you're a settled matter."

"He thinks I'm trash."

"He thinks you're *known*," said Lin Hao. "Those aren't the same and he's wrong about both, but he's more wrong about the second one, so let's start there."

They walked. The soul lamps were coming up along the street, one after another, and Glorybound City smelled of salt and hot metal the way it always did.

"I'll train with you," said Lin Hao. "Every day after school. I'll push you and you'll push me."

"You don't have to—"

"I absolutely have to, I've got a sword and rank five and no idea what either of them is for, and you're the only person I know who's stubborn enough to stand there while I work it out." He punched Wulin lightly on the shoulder. "Also you owe me. You made me watch you get sorted into the bottom class and I had to stand there and be polite about it."

---

They found Na'er on the fourth day, in the alley behind the fish market, and neither of them ever agreed afterwards about who had seen her first.

She was five and a half. She had short silver hair and eyes the colour of amethyst, and she was wearing clothes that had been somebody else's three times over, and she was standing very still in the way that small children stand still when they have learned that moving attracts attention.

There were three older boys with her, and they were not being kind, and what they were saying made Lin Hao stop walking.

He understood it, in the abstract, because Glorybound City was a port and ports have edges. There were people who bought children. There was a market. It was not a thing anybody said out loud at dinner.

"Right," said Lin Hao.

"Hao—" Wulin had hold of his sleeve.

"Wulin." Lin Hao did not look at him. "I want you to go and get a policeman. There's a tower on the square, I've counted, it's four minutes if you run. Can you do that?"

"What are you going to do?"

"I'm going to stand here and be extremely visible."

Wulin went. He went fast.

Lin Hao walked into the mouth of the alley and stopped, and put his hands in his pockets, and looked at the three boys with an expression of friendly interest.

"Hello," he said.

The largest of them turned. "Get lost, kid."

"I will," said Lin Hao, "in about four minutes, which is how long it takes to run to the Administrative Law Enforcement tower from here. I've done it. I was curious."

Something changed in the alley.

"You're bluffing."

"I'm six," said Lin Hao. "I don't have the range for a proper bluff, I've tried." He took his right hand out of his pocket. "But I would like to tell you a fact, because I think it's relevant and I don't think you know it. The government keeps records. The Spirit Pagoda keeps records too, separately, and they compare. Every child who wakes with soul power gets written down — name, martial soul, rank, address. It's how they find the good ones."

He let that sit.

"So if you take her, and anybody ever looks for her, there's a piece of paper somewhere with her name on it and a man in an orange robe who read it out loud. And if she *doesn't* have soul power, then she isn't worth what you think she is, and you'll have committed a very serious crime for nothing."

The largest boy said something rude.

Lin Hao drew the sword.

He had been practising. It came out of the air the way it had come out in the chamber — silver-blue, light, restless along the edge — and the wind in the alley turned over and picked up a fish wrapper and carried it past everybody's ankles, and there was one thin bright line of lightning running the length of the steel.

"I'm rank five," he said. "You're what, twelve? You'd win. But you'd have to explain the sword, and the wind, and the fact that a six-year-old in this city has a martial soul like this, which means the records, which means the orange robe." He smiled, pleasantly. "I'm not threatening you. I'm doing your arithmetic for you."

They left.

They did not leave because of the sword, and Lin Hao knew it, and he thought about that for a long time afterwards. They left because of the paperwork.

---

Na'er came home with them because there was nowhere else, and Lang Yue — Wulin's mother, who had been dead in the way the neighbourhood understood and alive in the way that mattered — no. Lang Yue was alive. Wulin's mother was alive and a good cook and had opinions about how thin the girl was.

They put a divider up in the boys' room.

Na'er ate like someone who had been told food might stop. She and Wulin competed. Within a fortnight the Tang household's food bill had become a subject of quiet conversation between Tang Ziran and his wife, conducted in the kitchen, at volume, on the assumption that the children could not hear.

She did not say where she had come from. She said she did not remember. She was, everyone agreed, very good at not saying things.

---

Mang Tian's workshop was at the end of a lane that smelled of scale and quench-water, and it was the only building on the lane with no sign, on the principle that anybody who needed to find it already knew.

He was a tall, dark-skinned man with a full beard and hands the width of shovels, and there was nothing remarkable about him at all, which was the first thing people got wrong — because his martial soul was a hammer.

Not a beast. Not a plant. **The Earth Hammer.** A tool soul, brown-veined, heavier than it looked.

Wulin found this out the hard way, on the second week, when a piece slipped and Mang Tian caught it — not with his hand, but with a hammer that had simply *appeared*, and then a second one, and then, rising from under his feet, four rings of light: **one white, two yellow, one purple.** A ten-year white rabbit. A hundred-year yellow pair of hammers. A thousand-year purple brown bear.

The first of them, he said later, without any particular pride, was **Tenacity**.

Fortieth rank. **A Soul Ancestor.** The man who had been shouting at them about their shoulders for a fortnight was a Soul Ancestor with four rings, and he spent his days in a workshop at the end of an unsigned lane in a town nobody important visited.

"My first ring was a white ten-year," he told them, once, when Wulin asked. "Weakest thing there is. I got the hundred-year because I saved. I got the thousand-year because I'm a blacksmith and blacksmiths make money." He shrugged, which with shoulders like his moved the whole doorway. "That's the whole secret. It isn't a secret. It's a price."

Lin Hao had gone because his father had gone. Lin Wei knew Mang Tian the way blacksmiths know each other, which was mostly by reputation and partly by argument, and he had said: *take the boy, he'll either hate it or he won't, and either way he'll be useful.*

Mang Tian looked at Lin Hao for eleven seconds, which Lin Hao counted, and then looked at Wulin, who had come along because he had come along to everything for three years.

He looked at Wulin longer.

"You," he said. "Pick it up."

It was a lump of metal on the floor, the size of a man's two fists, and it did not look heavy, and Wulin bent down and nearly fell over.

"That's your test," said Mang Tian. "Two hammers. Five kilos each. You hit that one thousand times. When you're done, we talk."

"One thousand?" said Wulin.

"You can stop whenever you like," said Mang Tian. "That's the whole test."

He set them up in the back, where the light was good, and went away, because that was the kind of teacher he was.

Lin Hao stayed. He had not been invited and he did not leave, and Mang Tian, coming back an hour later with tea, found him sitting cross-legged on the floor three metres away with a stick, drawing lines in the dust.

"What are you doing?"

"Counting."

"He can count."

"He counts wrong," said Lin Hao. "He speeds up when he's tired and then he hits flat and the sound goes dull and he doesn't notice. So I'm counting the flat ones." He looked up. "There's been forty-one."

Mang Tian, who had been a blacksmith for thirty-one years and who had a specific opinion about children, looked at the lines in the dust, and then at the boy, and then at Tang Wulin — who was red-faced and shaking and had done, by then, six hundred and four.

"Say something when it goes flat," said Mang Tian.

So Lin Hao did.

*Thump. Thump. Thud.*

"Flat."

Wulin adjusted. He did not know what he adjusted. He only knew that a voice behind him said *flat* every so often, and that when it did, something about his shoulders was wrong, and that if he fixed it the sound came back.

He finished in half an hour.

Mang Tian, who had expected him to stop at two hundred, and who had prepared a speech for two hundred, stood in the doorway with his tea going cold and did not use the speech.

---

"You understand," said Mang Tian afterwards, to both of them, because Lin Hao had not left and Mang Tian had stopped expecting him to, "that most men never learn to hear it."

"Hear what?" said Wulin.

"The metal." Mang Tian held up the lump. Under a thousand strikes it had not changed shape very much. It had changed *colour*, slightly, and it had got denser, and if you tapped it now it rang instead of thudding. "It talks. It talks the whole time. Every man in this trade thinks the work is the hitting. The work is the listening. The hitting is just how you ask the question."

He put it down.

"Three months of this. Nothing else. No components, no shapes, no pretty work. You hit metal and you listen and you get it wrong and you hit it again. After three months I'll teach you extraction. After that, simple components." He looked at Wulin. "It'll be two and a half years before you make anything I'd let a stranger touch."

"That's fine," said Wulin.

"You say that now."

"It's still fine."

Mang Tian grunted, which in his idiom was applause.

Then he looked at Lin Hao, who had been very quiet, in the way that Mang Tian was beginning to recognise as the boy *working something out*.

"And you?"

"Can I do it too?"

"You've got a sword."

"I've got a sword *and* I've got hands," said Lin Hao, "and I've been watching, and I'd like to say for the record that Wulin's problem is his shoulders and mine won't be, because I'm already doing it differently, but I'd like to find that out properly."

Mang Tian looked at him for a long moment.

"Five-kilo hammers," he said. "Same test."

---

Lin Hao took eleven hundred strikes, because he did not stop when he reached a thousand, and Mang Tian — watching from the doorway, tea going cold for the second time that day — did not tell him to stop.

The boy was not stronger than the other one. That was the interesting part. He was considerably less strong. But somewhere around strike four hundred he had stopped hitting the metal and started hitting *with* the metal, and his shoulders had never once gone flat, and he had never needed anybody to tell him.

Mang Tian had a theory about this and he kept it to himself, because he had learned that theories about children were mostly about the theorist.

What he said, later, to Lin Wei, over a cup of something stronger than tea, was: "Your boy hears it. He heard it before I taught him anything. I've had apprentices older than me who never got there."

And then, after a while: "The other one is better."

"Wulin?"

"The other one is *better*," said Mang Tian. "Your boy hears it like he was born hearing it. Tang Ziran's boy hears it like it's a language he's learning and refuses to stop practising. First one gets you to journeyman. Second one gets you somewhere I can't see from here." He drank. "This child's talent in forging far surpasses my own. I'd like to be annoyed about it. I find I'm not."

---

The Spirit Pagoda branch in Glorybound City was three layers, which meant it was the lowest rank of branch, which everybody in the city knew and nobody said.

Inside, behind glass, were the spirit souls.

The woman at the counter was polite in the flat way of somebody who has given this exact tour to every child in the city for eleven years.

"Seventy-three ten-year white spirit souls," she said. "**Seventy thousand Federation Coins** apiece."

Wulin did the arithmetic on his fingers and stopped.

"Eleven hundred-year yellow," she went on. "**One million.**" She allowed a small pause, because she was not unkind, and because the pause was the honest part. "Or the draw. **Thirty thousand.** Random. You might get something good. You might get something that isn't a spirit soul in any meaningful sense. We don't refund."

"How much does a Soul Master earn?" asked Lin Hao.

"Official stipend is **a thousand Federation Coins a month**," she said. "More at Soul Grandmaster. Not a lot more."

They walked home in silence for two blocks.

Then Wulin said, "So a white one is seventy months."

"Nearly six years," said Lin Hao.

"And a yellow one is a thousand months."

"Eighty-three years. You'd be ninety."

"I'd be dead."

"You'd be dead at the counter," said Lin Hao. "They'd find you leaning on the glass."

Wulin was quiet for a while. "Thirty thousand for the draw."

"Wulin."

"It's the only number we can reach."

"It's the only number anybody can reach," said Lin Hao, "and that's the whole point of it, that's not an accident, that's a wall with a slot in it." He kicked a stone along the gutter. "Three years of saving. Every coin. For a *chance*."

"It's still a chance."

Lin Hao looked at his friend — at the boy with the trash martial soul and rank three and an appetite that frightened his mother, who had just done arithmetic in his head and arrived at the same answer and refused to be frightened by it — and felt something shift in his chest that he did not have a word for at six and would not have for a long time.

"Yes," he said. "It is."

---

That was the shape of that year.

Wulin pounded metal and learned to listen, and ate, and meditated at night with a stubbornness that his teacher would have found alarming if his teacher had ever watched him. Lin Hao pounded metal and heard it immediately, which was less admirable and more annoying, and spent his remaining hours working out what a sword was *for* — because a sword, he had discovered, was not a thing you swung; it was a thing that had opinions, and the opinions changed depending on how you held it, and nobody had told him this and he was furious that nobody had told him this.

Na'er lived with the Tangs and did not say where she had come from.

And in the garden behind the house, on a night when the moon was up and Wulin was asleep, a small girl with silver hair sat bolt upright in bed because a ring of light had come out of her body — yellow, green, red, blue, purple, gold and silver, seven colours turning one by one — and it went in between her eyes, and she did not scream, and she did not tell anybody, and she did not sleep much for the rest of that week.

Nobody in Glorybound City knew.

The records said nothing about her at all.

---

## Part 1 — The Three Years

The first three months, Mang Tian taught them nothing at all.

He gave them metal and he gave them hammers and he went away, and when they asked what they were supposed to be making he said, with the patience of a man who has been asked this by every apprentice he has ever had, "Nothing. You're not making anything. You're hitting it."

So they hit it.

Wulin was better at it than he had any right to be, and the reason was not talent. The reason was that Wulin had decided, at six years old, in a school cafeteria, that if the one part was no good he would simply be extraordinary at the ninety-nine — and he had meant it in the flat, unglamorous, entirely literal way that he meant everything. He came in the mornings. He stayed late. He hit metal on the days Mang Tian did not ask him to, which Mang Tian noticed and did not mention, because mentioning it would have made it a thing between them, and Mang Tian did not do things between him and apprentices.

Lin Hao was worse at it, which infuriated him.

He heard the metal immediately — that had been true from the first afternoon — and hearing it turned out to be almost useless, because hearing a thing and doing a thing are separated by a distance that no amount of hearing will cross. His shoulders went flat. His left hand arrived late. His strikes rang true and then, two hundred in, went dull in a way he could hear perfectly well and could not stop, which was the specific hell of being good at noticing.

"You're listening for the right sound," Mang Tian told him, around the four-hundredth afternoon. "Stop it."

"Stop listening?"

"Stop listening for *right*. There isn't a right. There's this piece, today, at this heat, and it's not the same as yesterday's." He tapped the lump with one knuckle. "You're comparing it to a sound in your head. That's why you're late. You're always a beat behind because you're checking."

Lin Hao, who was seven and had never in his life been told that thinking was the problem, said nothing for a while.

Then he hit it, and did not check, and the sound came back.

"That," said Mang Tian.

It took him eleven days to be able to do it twice in a row.

---

After the three months came extraction — pulling the impurity out — and after that, simple components, which were ugly little brackets and pins that went into soul machines and that nobody would ever look at.

Wulin made his first acceptable simple component in the fourteenth month.

Lin Hao made his in the ninth, and Mang Tian held it up to the light for a long time and then put it in the reject box, and when Lin Hao asked why, he said, "Because you made it in nine months and you're pleased with it, and I don't want you pleased with it."

He made his second in the eleventh month and it went in the good box.

Medium components came at two and a half years, which was, Mang Tian said, fast. He did not say how fast. He had stopped volunteering comparisons some time around the point where he began needing them.

At the end of the first year he took both boys into the back room and gave them hammers.

**Thousand Refined Tungsten.** Forty kilos apiece. The handles were cut with a spiral that dug into the palm, and the heads were black, and on one face of each you could just make out a petal pattern that was not decoration — it was what the metal looked like after a thousand foldings and there was no way to put it there except to do the work.

Wulin nearly dropped his.

"These are yours," said Mang Tian. "You're blacksmiths now. That's what it means — not the skill, the hammers. You carry them, you keep them, you don't lend them." He looked at Lin Hao. "And you don't show them to anybody until you can hold them all day without your form going. Which you can't."

"How long?"

"As long as it takes."

---

There is a thing that happens to a boy who spends three years hitting metal, and neither of them could have described it at the time, and both of them would have denied it if you had suggested it.

Wulin got strong in the way that is not impressive — slowly, unevenly, in the shoulders and the forearms, so that by nine he could lift a thing another nine-year-old could not lift, and did not think anything of it, because he had been lifting it since he was seven.

Lin Hao got *accurate*. Which was different, and which he noticed, because he noticed everything. He noticed that he could put a strike exactly where he had decided to put it, and that the deciding had got faster, and that the gap between deciding and doing had got so small he could no longer find it. He noticed that when he watched somebody move he could see the moment before they moved. He noticed that he had started reading the grain of a blade the way other people read a face.

He did not have a word for any of it. He was nine. He assumed everybody's head did this and that it was simply impolite to mention.

What he did have, by nine, was a sword he understood and a trade he was good at and a best friend who ate like a famine and worked like a man serving a sentence, and he had begun — very quietly, without telling anybody, because he had noticed that people got strange when you told them — to work out how much money all of that could be turned into.

Because Wulin was saving. And Wulin had a number in his head. And Lin Hao had worked out, some time in the second year, what the number was for.

## Part 2 — Thirty-Eight

The Spirit Pagoda tested spiritual power once a term, for free, because the Spirit Pagoda was interested in children the way a fisherman is interested in the sea.

The man who ran the machine in the Glorybound branch was in his fifties and had the flattened, courteous manner of somebody who has watched forty thousand families be disappointed.

Wulin went first, because Lin Hao pushed him.

The crystal took his hand and the needle went up and stopped, and the man leaned forward slightly, which was the first unprofessional thing he had done all afternoon.

"**Thirty-eight.**"

"Is that good?" said Wulin.

The man looked at him for a moment. "At nine? It's advanced Spirit Origin. It's a long way above average." He straightened up. "Most children your age are in the teens."

Lin Hao went second and got forty-one, and the man wrote it down without comment, because forty-one after thirty-eight is not a story.

Then Wulin — who had been building up to this for eleven minutes, and who had clearly decided that the way to ask a frightening question was to ask it very fast — said, "What's yours?"

And the man, who could have said anything, and who had possibly not been asked in a decade, smiled the thin smile of a man who has made peace with something.

"**Eighty-seven.**" He let that sit. "I'm a twenty-eighth rank Soul Grandmaster. Four rings. I've cultivated for forty-one years." He tapped the machine. "Spiritual power isn't effort. You can't grind at it the way you grind at soul power. It grows with the body and it grows with the mind, and some people get more of it than other people, and that's the whole of it."

"So what is it?" said Wulin. "What's it *for*?"

The man glanced at the door, which was the gesture of a man deciding to do something slightly outside his job.

"It's the ladder," he said. "**Spirit Origin** — that's where everybody starts, that's you two. Above a hundred is **Spirit Connection**, and that's when your mind and your spirit soul can actually talk to each other. Above that is **Spirit Sea**. Then **Spirit Abyss**, then **Spirit Domain**, and then **Divine Origin**, which is a word for gods and I've never met anybody who's said it out loud without laughing."

He leaned on the counter.

"Here's the part that matters, and nobody tells children this. **Your spiritual power decides how much spirit soul your body can carry.** Spirit Origin? One. Maybe one yellow one. Spirit Connection? Two yellows, or one purple. Spirit Sea?" He shrugged. "Five yellows. Three purples. A black one if you can afford it, and you can't."

Wulin was very still.

"Because a spirit soul is what gives you rings," said the man, "and rings are what give you soul skills, and soul skills are the entire difference between a man who can fight and a man who can't. So the ladder isn't a ladder. It's a *ceiling*. And it goes up before you're born."

He straightened up, glanced at the door again, and went back to being a man doing a job.

"Thirty-eight is a good number, son. Don't let anybody tell you it isn't."

---

They walked home without talking for two blocks.

Then Wulin said, "Eighty-seven. Forty-one years."

"He said it isn't effort."

"He said it isn't *only* effort." Wulin's jaw had the particular set it got when he had hold of something. "He said it grows with the mind. Minds do things."

"They don't do much."

"They do if you make them." Wulin stopped walking. "Hao. I'm going to get to a hundred."

Lin Hao looked at his friend — nine years old, rank eleven in soul power, thirty-eight in the thing that mattered, wearing a shirt his mother had let out twice — and did the thing he had been doing privately for three years, which was to look at Wulin and to find, to his continuing astonishment, that he could not work out what the boy was going to end up being.

He could work out everybody. He could not work out Wulin.

"Right," said Lin Hao. "Well. I'd better keep up, hadn't I."

---

## Part 3 — Thirty Thousand Two Hundred

It took Wulin three years.

He did it the way he did everything, which was completely and without charm. He took in mending. He swept the workshop on the days Mang Tian did not need him, for coin. He carried things. He ate at home, always, which his mother noticed and said nothing about, and which Lin Hao noticed and said a great deal about, and which Wulin waved away because he had a number in his head and the number was more real to him than dinner.

On the morning of his ninth birthday he had **thirty thousand two hundred Federation Coins.**

He went to the Spirit Pagoda branch with Lin Hao beside him and put the money on the counter in a cloth bag, and the woman behind the glass — who had given them both the tour three years ago and who remembered, because she remembered everybody — looked at the bag and then at his face, and her expression did something complicated.

"The draw," said Wulin.

"Child—"

"The draw, please."

"**Thirty thousand,**" she said. "You understand there's no refund. You understand that the draw can produce something that is not, in any useful sense, a spirit soul."

"Yes."

"You could get a ten-year white. You could get nothing." She looked at the bag again. "Seventy-three white ones behind me at seventy thousand. Eleven yellow at a million. Those are the ones that work. The draw is—" she searched for a word that was not cruel and did not find one "—the draw is what poor people buy."

"I know," said Wulin. "That's why I can afford it."

She opened the drawer.

---

It came out of the light in the woman's hand, and it was a snake, and it was ten centimetres long.

Earthen yellow. Rhombus scales, neatly ranked, the size of a fingernail paring. It moved in a way that snakes move. It had, by every test the Spirit Pagoda applied, the shape of a spirit soul.

It had no soul-beast genes.

The woman held it up to the lamp for a long moment, and her face went into the flat professional neutral that Lin Hao had already learned to read as *bad news arriving politely*.

"It's defective," she said. "It's a Grass Snake. It's—" she turned it slightly "—it's essentially a very well-made picture of a snake."

Wulin did not move.

"Can I still fuse it?"

"You can. It'll give you a ring. It won't give you much else." She set it down gently, the way you set down something that has cost somebody everything. "Ten-year white. Weakest category there is. I'm sorry, child."

Wulin picked it up.

It curled around his finger and lay there, and it was, Lin Hao thought, the saddest thing he had ever seen — not because it was weak, but because Wulin had carried a cloth bag of coins for three years and gotten exactly what the woman had told him he would get, and because he was still holding it very carefully, the way you hold something alive.

"What do you want to do?" said Lin Hao, quietly.

"I want to fuse it," said Wulin.

---

## Part 4 — Morning to Evening

They did it in the garden behind the Tang house, because Mang Tian had said a fusion needed room and privacy and had then, characteristically, not come.

It began at dawn.

Lin Hao sat on the wall and watched, because he had been told to watch — *"if his soul power goes wrong you run and get me, you don't try to be clever"* — and he had agreed, and had then discovered over the following nine hours that watching Wulin work was the most interesting thing he had ever done.

The Grass Snake went into the Bluesilver Grass.

That was the only way Lin Hao could afterwards describe it. The small earthen-yellow thing uncoiled from Wulin's palm and went *into* the thin green sprig, and the sprig took it, and nothing happened for a while.

Then the grass began to change.

It thickened. It lengthened. The thin weak blades that had been the joke of a school cafeteria in Glorybound City ran out along the ground and up the wall and over the top of it, and as they ran they put on **scales** — fine, overlapping, the same rhombus pattern the snake had had — and along the length of each one there came a **stripe of gold**, thin as a thread, running the whole way.

It was not grass any more.

It was a **vine.**

Wulin screamed around noon. Lin Hao was off the wall and halfway across the garden before he remembered the instruction, and then he stopped, because Wulin's eyes were open and Wulin was looking at him and shaking his head very slightly, which was, in the vocabulary the two of them had built over six years, *stay there.*

So he stayed.

The golden veined pattern came last. It appeared on Wulin's forehead — the same place it had appeared at the awakening, three years earlier, the thing the Spirit Master had never seen in tens of thousands of children — and it ran down his neck and along his arms. And at the same time, separately, another pattern **rose from his tailbone**, up the small of his back, and the two met at his spine and joined.

It finished at dusk.

Wulin lay in the grass with a vine the length of a clothesline lying across his chest, and he was **rank eleven.**

He had gone from rank three to rank eleven in one day, and he looked up at Lin Hao with an expression of total, exhausted, unembarrassed joy, and said, "I'm a Soul Master."

---

## Part 5 — What Mang Tian Could Not Tear

Mang Tian came the next morning, and the first thing he did was try to pull the vine apart.

He did it casually, the way a man tests a rope. He was a **fortieth-rank Soul Ancestor with four soul rings** and thirty-one years of hands, and he put his first soul skill into it — **Tenacity**, the white ten-year rabbit, the weakest ring he owned and the one he used for exactly this — and he pulled.

The vine did not break.

He pulled harder. Tang Ziran, who had come out with tea, put the tea down.

And then Mang Tian stopped, and let go, and looked at his disciple with an expression Lin Hao had never seen on him before, which was the expression of a man revising something.

"You felt that?" he said.

"My soul power went," said Wulin. "It just — went. Like it got eaten."

"Yes." Mang Tian sat down on the step, which he did not usually do. "Sit down. Both of you. You're going to learn a word today and I want you to learn it properly."

He held up the vine.

"**Variation.** Under special circumstances a martial soul varies. It happens when you fuse with a spirit soul that's very compatible with it — or very *in*compatible. It happens when something outside stimulates it. Some people are born varied. Some vary during the awakening itself." He turned the vine in his hands. "And there are good variations and bad ones. A strong martial soul can be weakened by varying. A weak one can be made strong."

"Bluesilver Grass becomes a vine," said Lin Hao. "That's normal, isn't it. You said."

"It's *possible*. It's what's supposed to happen, and it's what happened to a man I knew — his Bluesilver Grass went to a vine thicker than this one and I tore it apart with my bare hands." He lifted it an inch. "I cannot tear yours. With a soul skill in it. That is not possible. Not unless the strength of the martial soul is tied to the soul power behind it, which means—" he let go "—which means I can't break this until you run out. And you're eleven."

There was a silence in the garden.

"Is that good?" said Wulin, in a small voice.

"That's the best thing that has ever happened to you," said Mang Tian. "It isn't *absolutely* good — it depends entirely on how well you control it, and a vine is a control-type soul, and if you tangle with a man whose soul power is higher than yours he'll struggle free and bleed you dry, so it's a war of attrition you'll lose. Use it like a whip. Don't hug people with it." He stood up. "And there may be another variation when you take your second ring. I can't tell you what it'll be. Nobody can."

He went into the workshop.

Then he came back out, because he was Mang Tian and he could not leave a thing half-said.

"You asked me once," he said to Wulin, "whether it was really true that your grass was trash. It isn't any more. You've profited from a disaster. Go and be insufferable about it somewhere else."

---

## Part 6 — Goldlight

That night, in the garden, with the moon up and his parents asleep, Wulin called the snake out.

It came — ten centimetres, earthen yellow, rhombus scales, worth thirty thousand Federation Coins and nothing at all — and lay in the hollow of his palm, and it had been with him for a day, and a spirit soul stays with its master for life and dissipates only when the master dies, which was a fact Wulin had read three times and had not, until that moment, properly understood.

"Thank you," he said to it. "You gave me hope and I turned my back on you for about a month and I'm sorry."

The snake raised its head and flicked its tongue.

"I should give you a name."

The little scale on its forehead flashed gold.

Wulin sat up straight.

"Do that again."

It did not. It could not; it had the intelligence of a very small animal and no comprehension whatsoever of what was being asked of it. But the gold was there, in the scale, where it had not been before the fusion, and Wulin looked at it for a long time.

"**Goldlight,**" he said. "Because you can turn gold, and because if your whole body ever does that, I want you to know I'll have seen it first."

The snake did not object.

So its name was Goldlight — a simple name, and a good one, and the first thing in Tang Wulin's life that had been given to him for nothing and had turned out to be worth having.

---

## Part 7 — The Hawk

Lin Hao had taken his ring six months earlier, and he had not made a fuss about it, which in retrospect everybody agreed was the most Lin Hao thing about the whole affair.

He had saved separately from Wulin — not three years, because Lin Hao had begun selling components in his second year and Mang Tian had taken a percentage and then, noticing what the percentage was doing, had quietly stopped taking it — and he had not bought the draw, because he had done the arithmetic on the draw and found it obscene.

He had bought a **Gale Hawk.**

Wind, with lightning in it. Ten years. White. Cheap, in the way that ten-year things are cheap, and exactly suited to a sword that already had wind and lightning in it, which the woman at the counter had called a coincidence and Lin Hao had not.

Fusing it had taken an afternoon. The ring had come up white around his feet and settled, and the Stormbringer Sword had got *quieter*, which he had not expected — the restlessness along the edge had stopped being a tremor and become a decision, as though the blade had been asking a question for three years and had finally been given enough information to form an opinion.

His rank went to eleven.

And something else happened, which he told nobody, because he had learned at six years old in an alley behind a fish market that information was a thing you kept until you knew what it was worth.

The hawk had looked at him.

Not at the room. Not past him. At *him* — with the flat golden attention of a bird that had been dead for ten years and was somehow still, in some sense Lin Hao could not define, in there — and it had looked at him for perhaps two seconds, and then gone.

He had thought about those two seconds every day for six months.

He had not worked out what they meant. He had, however, worked out that he intended to.

---

Three years. Two rings. One vine and one sword.

And in a small room at the back of a house two doors down, a girl with silver hair who had no martial soul at all and no record anywhere in the Sun-Moon Federation sat up in bed, once a week or so, while seven colours turned slowly around her and went in between her eyes.

Nobody knew.

The three of them were nine years old, and Glorybound City was very small, and none of them had the faintest idea what was coming.

## Part 1: The Year of the Sword and the Hammer

The year after the Spirit Pagoda was the year the two boys stopped being children who trained, and started being cultivators who lived it.

For Lin Hao, the year measured itself in dawns. Master Chen Long's courtyard, cold stone underfoot, the old sword master's breath fogging in the early dark.

"Again."

Lin Hao reset his stance, the Stormbringer Sword steady in his grip. His arms ached. They ached every morning, and every morning the ache was a little less than the day before — his body rewriting itself overnight to meet the demand, the way it always did.

"What did you change?" Chen Long asked.

"The last form. My weight was forward on the transition. I'm carrying it back now, through the hips."

Chen Long grunted. Two months ago, the answer would have been *I don't know, it just felt wrong.* Now the boy named his own flaws before the correction was given. The old man had stopped testing him for it.

"You're rank nineteen now," Chen Long said one morning, watching the wind curl along his student's blade like it belonged there. "Twenty before the snow. Do you know what that means?"

"That the climb gets steeper?"

"It means the climb *changes*." Chen Long sheathed his own practice blade. "Every rank past ten is worth three of the ones below it, and the ones past twenty are worth three of those. And there's the other matter — that hawk of yours. A hundred-year soul doesn't pour itself into one ring, boy. When you hit the wall at twenty, it will have a gift waiting on the other side." The old man's eyes crinkled. "Talent is a horse. Discipline is the road. The horse goes nowhere without the road."

"Yes, Master."

The wall came in the first week of winter, exactly where the old man promised — rank twenty, soul power piled against a ceiling it could not pass. Lin Hao sat with it the way he sat with everything: breathing, letting his Awareness take the measure of the obstacle. And on the third night, the Gale Hawk — which had grown fat on a year and a half of fed-back cultivation, seven hundred years of condensed wind riding quietly inside him — stirred, unfolded, and laid a **second ring of yellow light** around his soul like a promise keeping itself.

Rank twenty-one. Then twenty-two before the thaw. A Soul Grandmaster at ten years old, two rings from a single spirit soul, and his spiritual power pressing up past the far shore of Spirit Origin into territory the textbooks said belonged to grown men.

"You'll carry all of that to Eastsea," Chen Long said at their last lesson, "and you'll meet boys and girls whose families have been feeding them spirit resources since the cradle. Find out what the road is made of." A pause. "I expect a letter every month. If your forms get sloppy, I'll know."

Across the city, Wulin's year measured itself in heat.

Mang Tian's forge, the hammer rising and falling, the ring of steel from dawn to dusk. The Thousand Refinements — the old blacksmith's word for the work that turned iron into something worthy of a soul master's hands. Wulin's arms had changed; the thin boy from the awakening ceremony was gone, replaced by corded muscle built one hammer strike at a time. His appetite had grown to legendary proportions — the "Rice Bucket" nickname had followed him out of the ordinary class and somehow become, over the years, a term of grudging respect.

Two streets over, the Lin family's rice bin emptied at a rate that defied its single teenager. Lin Hao ate like his training burned — which was exactly the case; something inside him rebuilt itself a little more every night, and rebuilding was hungry work. Lin Mei had stopped counting meals and started counting pots. "Two blacksmiths in this house," she told the neighbors, "and one of them is a furnace with legs." Lin Hao, mouth full, would only grin. He'd noticed the hunger himself — noticed that on the weeks the family money ran thin and the bowls got shallower, his meditation crawled. Whatever his talent was, it ate first and optimized second. So he never complained about the food, and he never skipped a meal, and Mang Tian's workshop — where the boys' paths crossed most evenings — fed him with the resigned generosity of a man already feeding one bottomless pit.

His cultivation had changed too. The first seal's power hummed under everything — a furnace banked low, warming his meridians while the spiral technique carried soul power through them in slow, golden-edged turns. Rank eleven had become twelve, then thirteen, and each rank had come slower than the last, the way his father's forge work came: not by force, but by repetition.

Some nights, deep in meditation, he felt the second seal — a knot of sealed fire somewhere behind his sternum, pulling at its chains.

*Not yet,* Old Tang's voice would come, gentle as always. *A vessel that fills too fast cracks. You're building the vessel, Wulin. Every hammer strike. Every turn of the spiral. Let it be slow.*

And Na'er — Na'er had grown too. Nine going on ten, taller, her silver hair long past her shoulders now, her quiet ways settling into the Tang household like a held note finally allowed to ring. She still followed Wulin everywhere. She still said little. But she had started leaving small things on the workbench at Mang Tian's workshop — a wrapped bun, a cup of warm water — for a boy who forgot to eat until his stomach roared.

By autumn's end, the letters came.

Eastsea Academy. Intermediate division. Both of them.

## Part 2: Silver

The strangeness began in the winter, and — this was the part Lin Hao never stopped turning over, afterward — he had noticed it first. Not because he was watching. Because his body always noticed.

It was small things. Na'er standing at the end of the street after dusk, face turned toward the sea, so still that the snow gathered on her shoulders. Once, murmuring in her sleep — not words, exactly; a sound like a language made of bells, beautiful and wrong. Once, a stray dog that had snarled at every child on the street took one look at her and lay down in the slush, whining, on its belly.

Wulin noticed too, the way you notice weather. "She's dreaming about home," he said once. "Wherever it is. She'll remember someday."

He said it warmly. He had always wanted her to remember.

She remembered in the last week before departure.

Lin Hao was at his own house, packing, when the shouting started. He was across the street before his mother could say his name — and found Wulin in the middle of the Tang family's front room, turning in slow circles, as if the room might have somewhere to hide a person.

The window was open. The winter air stood in the room like floodwater. On the sill, where the latch should have been frost-bitten shut, the metal was warm.

"Na'er?" Wulin said, to the room, to the street, to the sky. "Na'er!"

They searched until past midnight — every alley, the market, the harbor wall, the shrine road, the clearing behind the Lin house where the three of them had watched a thousand sunsets. Lang Yue searched with them, calling until her voice cracked. Tang Ziran went to the authorities, and the authorities, who kept careful records of every child with soul power in the city, found no record of a silver-haired girl leaving by any gate, any road, any train.

Because there had never been any record of her at all.

Toward dawn, sitting on the curb outside the empty house while Wulin stared at nothing, Lin Hao let himself feel what he had been refusing to feel all night. His head had a habit he had never entirely made peace with: it remembered everything, and it compared everything, and it did both without being asked. And what it laid out now, quietly, in the dark, like evidence on a table, was this —

In four years, his perception had never once read Na'er as *only* a girl.

There had always been something under the smallness. A depth his senses went quiet beside, the way a room goes quiet beside a sleeping predator. He had told himself it was mystery. Everyone has one.

It was not mystery. It was the surface of something vast, held carefully still — the way the sea is still, over things.

*What are you,* he thought, *and who took you home?*

He said none of it. Not then. Not for a long time. Because Wulin was sitting beside him with his hands around a cup of tea he wasn't drinking, and grief was the only thing on the table that belonged to anyone.

"I'll find her," Wulin said, when the sky went gray. His voice wasn't loud. It had the flat, forged quality of hot metal laid on an anvil. "I don't know where she went. I don't know who she was. But I'll get strong enough to look everywhere, and I'll find her."

Lin Hao looked at his friend — at the jaw, the hands, the terrible calm — and felt the old protective knot in his chest pull tight, and then, strangely, settle. There was nothing to protect Wulin from here. This was a fire Wulin needed.

"Okay," Lin Hao said. "Then we'd better not miss the train."

## Part 3: The Soul Train

They left Glorybound City on a morning so cold the harbor steam stood in pillars.

And neither of them said the thing that was sitting on the platform between the two families, which was that one boy had a sword that made the Spirit Master's eyebrows go up, and the other had grass.

Lin Wei had looked at his son's blade on the testing floor and had not said anything for a long time, because a man who makes horseshoes does not have a word for what his son had been given. And Wulin's father had looked at a handful of grass and had said *that's all right, son, that's all right,* in the voice of a man who had already worked out what he was going to do about it.

**And Lin Hao had looked at both of them, and had chosen the worst class, and had not told anybody why.**

That is the butterfly, and it is the first one, and everything else in this story grows out of it. **In a story without him, Wulin goes to the worst class because the worst class is where a boy with grass goes, and the worst class stays the worst class, and the grade learns nothing.** In a story with him in it, the worst class has a boy in it with a sword that made a Spirit Master's eyebrows go up, and the worst class stops being the worst class within a month, and the grade learns a thing it would not otherwise have had any reason to learn.

He did not choose it for Wulin. He would have said that if anybody had asked, and it would have been a lie, and he knew it was a lie, and he chose it anyway, and he has never once explained it to anybody, and he does not intend to.

Both families came to the platform. Lin Mei cried and made Lin Hao promise, again, to write every month. Lin Wei said nothing, only gripped his son's shoulder once, hard, in the way of men who had already said everything important the night before, over a sword. Tang Ziran pressed a letter into Wulin's hand — thick, sealed, addressed in Mang Tian's blocky writing.

"Master Mang's own hand," Tang Ziran said. "His workshop in Eastsea City, and the Blacksmith's Association besides. He says: *the boy eats like a furnace, so someone had better keep him employed.*"

Wulin managed a smile that didn't reach the rest of his face. Behind his father, Lang Yue was looking at the empty space beside them — the small space, exactly Na'er-shaped, that no one had mentioned all morning and everyone had carried to the station.

The soul train drank its charged soul stones and pulled the world flat. Countryside became streaks of white and gray; Wulin's forehead found the window and stayed there. Lin Hao, across the aisle, closed his eyes and let his Awareness settle into the train — the rhythm of the rails was not noise to his body; it was information, a pulse to breathe against. He slowed his circulation to match, and his meditation deepened past anything the courtyard had given him. He filed the trick away. *Any repeated rhythm is a resource.*

He opened his eyes to find Wulin watching him.

"You're doing it again," Wulin said. "The face. Where you look asleep but you're taking everything apart."

Lin Hao opened one amber eye. "I resemble that remark." A pause. "What are you taking apart?"

Wulin looked back out at the white country. "How strong I have to be," he said, "to look everywhere."

Eastsea City arrived the way oceans do — gradually, then all at once. Flat country wrinkled into hills, hills into suburbs, suburbs into a skyline of glass and stone threaded with soul-powered transit lines. Wulin had thought Glorybound City large. Eastsea City made Glorybound City a neighborhood.

It was the **second largest seaside city in the Sun-Moon Federation**, and everything about it followed from that — the port first, a nexus for the shipping lanes and for whatever came up out of the ocean, and then three million people arranged around it.

Lin Hao had read the shape of the country on the train, in a free pamphlet he had taken because it was free. **Eighteen first-class cities, in five regions** — north, east, south, west and centre. The centre had only two, **Heaven Dou City and Shrek City**, and the pamphlet said this was fewer than the others and then spent two paragraphs explaining that it did not matter, which Lin Hao took to mean it mattered a great deal. The east had **five first-class coastal cities that made up something called the Skysea Alliance**, and Eastsea City was **second of the five**.

"Second," Wulin said, when Lin Hao told him.

"Second of five. In the east."

"That's still second."

"It's second of five *first-class* cities in a region, in a federation of eighteen," Lin Hao said. "Which is a sentence I did not know existed this morning." He put the pamphlet in his bag, because he kept things. "There's a tournament. Every three years — the Alliance one. And a bigger one every five, for the whole continent."

"Where's the big one held?"

"**Shrek City.**"

Neither of them said anything after that for a while, because they were ten, and Glorybound City had been the whole world until Tuesday, and the word *Shrek* had arrived in the middle of a free pamphlet next to an advertisement for soul-lamp repairs. And old. Older than the glass. For several hundred years the Federation had taken particular care of the ancient buildings here, so the skyline was a city of towers with a much older, plainer, unadorned city still standing intact between their feet — and the soul trains, when they came in, were nearly all dark blue, every one of them, which was the sort of detail Lin Hao noticed and would have been unable to explain.

"Look at the size of it," Wulin whispered.

Lin Hao, who was gawking the hardest, didn't even deny it.

## Part 4: Reporting In

There was a sign at the end of the platform — white letters on blue, **EASTSEA ACADEMY** — and a chair behind it, and a row of seventeen-year-olds in blue sportswear who had been given this job as a punishment and had decided to enjoy it.

The girl who stood up when she saw them had black hair and a pair of red phoenix eyes and the moderate, unhurried build of somebody who was not in a hurry and did not need to be. She had the sort of face that made people feel they had arrived somewhere.

"Little brother," she said, "are you here to report?"

"Yes," said Wulin. "I'm Tang Wulin."

She looked at him, and then looked again, in the particular way Lin Hao had already learned to recognise — the second look was the one that meant somebody had worked something out and was deciding how polite to be about it.

"I'm **Liu Yuxin**," she said. "First grader, class one of the **advanced** academy. I'm receiving new students this year, which means I'm your senior sister whether you like it or not." She held out a clipboard. "Fill this in. Then show me the recommendation letter from your elementary academy."

Wulin dug it out of his rucksack, where it had been folded three times by his mother and pressed flat again by his father.

Liu Yuxin read the form aloud as he wrote, which Lin Hao suspected she did for everyone and which nonetheless made Wulin's ears go red. "Tang Wulin. Ten years old. Graduated from Glorybound City's Red Mountain Elementary Academy." Her voice changed register on the next line, only slightly, the way a good clerk's does. "**Rank thirteen. Plant system. Martial soul: Bluesilver Grass.**"

She looked up.

"You know what that is?" said Wulin, flatly.

"Of course I know what it is." She said it briskly, without pity, which was the kindest thing anybody had done for him all week. "Our academy recognises it. Soul Masters have been developing for tens of thousands of years — the martial soul isn't nearly as important as it used to be. And to reach rank thirteen at your age with Bluesilver Grass, honestly, that isn't easy at all."

Wulin, who had braced himself, found he had braced against nothing.

Then Lin Hao stepped up and put his own form on the clipboard.

Liu Yuxin read it.

She did not say anything for a moment, which with her was more informative than anything she might have said.

"Rank twenty-two," she said. "*Soul Grandmaster.* Two rings." She turned the page to the spirit-soul assessment and her eyebrows came together. "One spirit soul. Gale Hawk, wind attribute, purchased at ten-year classification — and this gauge reads its cultivation at somewhere near **seven hundred years**." She set the clipboard down on the chair, carefully, the way you set down something you have decided not to be holding. "That gauge is not wrong, is it."

"The gauge is fine," said Lin Hao.

"You bought a ten-year hawk and it is seven hundred years old."

"I bought a ten-year hawk," said Lin Hao, "and then a great deal happened to it, and I'd rather not go into it on a platform, because there's a man in a black suit eleven metres away who has been pretending to read a timetable for four minutes."

Liu Yuxin's eyes went to the man in the black suit. Then back.

Then she laughed — a short, surprised sound — and picked up the clipboard again.

"Right," she said. "Well. You'll want to know how this works, because you're both going to be disappointed. **Classes are assigned at the opening ceremony, tomorrow, by the Director.** Not by me, not by that form, not by anything you can argue with. Martial soul quality and soul power. There are five classes and the smaller the number the better the class, and there are a hundred and eight of you this year."

"One request," said Lin Hao. "Whatever class he's in, I'm in it."

"That's not how assignment works."

"I understand. I'm making the request anyway, so that it's written down." He smiled at her, and Liu Yuxin — who was eleven months his senior, a first grader in class one of the advanced academy, and entirely capable of handling a ten-year-old — had the distinct and unfamiliar sensation of being *managed*. "You'll pass the forms up. Somebody will read them. And when they get to that line they'll wonder whether the boy who wrote it meant it."

"Did you mean it?"

"Completely."

She looked at him for a long moment. Then she stamped both forms, took two brass keys out of a box, and handed them over with the metal placard that let them through the gate.

"**Dormitory is behind the school building. Twelve floors. You're in room two-oh-five, second floor.**" She glanced at the key tag. "Four to a room, two bunk beds. You'll find out who the other two are when you get there, and my advice, as your senior sister, is to be extremely pleasant to them for the first forty-eight hours and then reassess."

"Why forty-eight hours?"

"Because that's how long it takes."

---

They found the dormitory without difficulty, because it was nearly as tall as the school building and there were eleven-year-olds going in and out of it carrying suitcases.

**Room 205, second floor.** The door was already open and there was already somebody inside.

Two bunk beds, enough for four. Two square desks. Four chairs. Two cabinets. One roof lamp. That was the whole of it.

The two bottom bunks were taken. The one on the left was occupied by a boy who was taller than Wulin by half a head and thicker than him by more than that, with short hair and eyes that bulged slightly and, at ten years old, an air of ferocity he was clearly working at. The one on the right held a thin, frail-looking boy wearing glasses and holding a book, who looked up with the mild interest of somebody who had already worked out how this was going to go.

"Hello," said Wulin. "I'm Tang Wulin. I've just arrived."

The frail one nodded. "**Yun Xiao.** The Yun from cloud. The Xiao from big and small."

The tall one rolled his eyes.

"Newcomer," he said. "Clean the room first."

Lin Hao, who had been watching this with great interest from the doorway, put his bag down and said, "Before we start — is this the bit where you tell us you're in charge, or have you already done that?"

"**Zhou Zhangxi,**" said the tall boy, and grinned, and got off the bed.

## Part 5: The Worst Class

The opening ceremony filled Eastsea Academy's great plaza — the only day of the year the intermediate and advanced divisions stood on the same stones. Wulin, tall for his age, was pushed toward the back by the sheer mass of students, which suited him; from the back he could watch all of it, the way you watch a forge you don't yet understand.

Director Long Hengxu spoke from the high platform — a broad man with a voice trained to reach the last row without soul power, welcoming the one hundred and eight new students of the intermediate first grade, congratulating them, reminding them that Eastsea Academy had produced Titled Douluo, that excellence here was expected and mediocrity was merely tolerated.

"And now," he said, "class assignment."

A rustle went through the first-graders. Beside Wulin, Lin Hao murmured, "Here we go."

"It is known within Eastsea Academy that the smaller the class number, the more prestigious the class," Long Hengxu announced. "One hundred and eight students, divided among five classes. Those called first are assigned to class one…"

Names rose and fell like tide. The front of the plaza filled with the chosen — children in fine coats, children whose martial souls had glowed on the assessment platforms, children whose families had clearly been feeding them spirit resources since the cradle, exactly as Chen Long had promised. Wulin watched his own name's absence stretch, class by class, and felt the old familiar weight settling onto his shoulders — the weight he had carried since the testing stone at six years old.

It landed. It didn't crush. Three years of hammer work had changed what he was made of.

The names rose and fell like tide — and Lin Hao's came early, where the silk names were.

"…class one: Mu Tiancheng, Wei Lili, *Lin Hao*…"

He heard it the way you hear a stone skip off water. Around him, a few first-graders turned — the reporting-in clerk's gossip had traveled, apparently; the rank-twenty-two boy with the two rings was not exactly anonymous — and he felt the whole bright front of the plaza tilt toward him expectantly, a hundred silk jackets making room.

Lin Hao did not move toward them.

"Director," he said. Not loudly. He simply said it in the direction of the high platform, the way you'd continue a conversation — and the plaza's acoustics, built for announcements, carried it everywhere. "Lin Hao. I'd like to be in class five."

The silence that followed had texture. Director Long Hengxu looked down from the platform at the small, neat boy standing still in the middle of the tide, and something in his expression suggested that Liu Yuxin's paperwork had, in fact, mentioned this. "You understand," the director said, in his carrying voice, "that class five is the last class."

"Yes, Director."

"It is the worst class in the grade."

"I've heard that too," Lin Hao said. "I'd still like to be in it. My brother's in it."

He did not point. He did not have to. At the back of the plaza, in the smallest and quietest knot on the whole stone, Tang Wulin had gone very still — and beside him, a pale-haired boy in fine clothes was staring at Lin Hao with an expression like a held breath.

Director Long Hengxu regarded him for three long seconds. "…Noted," he said at last, and there was something in his tone that might have been the ghost of amusement, or the ghost of a warning. "Class five. The *whole* of it, young man — the walking and the teaching both. Continue."

"…class five: Tang Wulin, Zhou Zhangxi, Xie Xie, Yun Xiao, *and Lin Hao*…"

Five names, at the very end. The last class. The class at the back of the plaza, twenty-odd students with listless expressions, the smallest and quietest knot on the whole stone — which was quiet for an entirely different reason now, because the whole plaza had watched the rank-twenty-two boy choose to walk to the back of it, and knots, even listless ones, remember things like that.

Wulin stepped out of the crowd toward them. Halfway there, a boy fell into step beside him — pale hair, fine clothes, a face as striking as his own but worn differently, like a blade someone kept polished for display. The boy's eyes flicked over Wulin's plain coat, his patched sleeve cuffs, and stopped, briefly, on the calluses on his hands — forge calluses, which were not the same as any other kind.

Xie Xie said nothing. But when they reached the back, he chose the spot next to Wulin, and stood there with his chin up and his shoulders squared, as if daring the plaza to have opinions.

"Class teachers," Long Hengxu called, "receive your students."

Five teachers descended from the platform. Four were middle-aged and unremarkable. The fifth, heading for class five, made the listless students sit up straighter.

He was young — twenty-seven, twenty-eight at most — and tall, a full head and more above everyone near him, over a hundred and ninety centimeters of lanky arms and thin waist, white trousers accentuating legs that went on unreasonably. His hair was swept back from a face that was simply, inconveniently *handsome*: well-set nose, thin lips, bright eyes of a smoky green that matched — matched — the strange blue of his hair. His expression was a closed door.

One of the girls in class five breathed, too quietly to mean to, "The teacher is so handsome…"

The teacher's icy gaze swept the class, and the whisper died mid-flight. He turned and walked. Class five trailed after him, to the ground floor, to the innermost corner of the building, to a classroom that took longer to reach than any other — thirty desks in a room built for thirty, which told its own story about how the class had been sized.

"Take your seats." Every word came out cold. "My name is Wu Zhangkong. For the next six years, you will be under my tutelage." He let the silence ring. "And I would emphasize one point. You may disregard whatever Director Long said at the ceremony. Even if you are a bunch of trash, I will train you to be the strongest students in your cohort. That is your aim for the next six years. Unless you choose to drop out."

It should have been an insult. Wulin, listening, heard something else entirely — the same thing the hammer hears from the anvil: *something here intends to hit back.*

"Introductions," Wu Zhangkong said. "Name. Martial soul. Soul power rank. Aspiration."

The class went around, voices small. Zhou Zhangxi, shield soul, rank nine. Yun Xiao, rank ten, aspiration mumbled. Then the pale boy beside Wulin stood, and the temperature of the room changed.

"Xie Xie. Light Dragon Dagger — tool soul, speed type. Rank twenty — one soul ring, second coming this year." He sat down as if the stunned silence were furniture he owned. Rank twenty. In the worst class. Someone whispered the obvious question — *then why is he here?* — and Xie Xie's smile answered that whatever story lay behind it, he did not intend to tell it.

"Tang Wulin."

Wulin stood. He felt the whole class turn — not at his name, but at the grass. It had the reputation it had; four years had not improved it.

"Tang Wulin. Martial soul: Bluesilver Grass. Rank thirteen. One soul ring."

The murmur was immediate and not kind. *Bluesilver Grass — here? — with a ring? — someone's counting wrong—* A boy two rows over laughed outright. "Trash spirit. What's it doing past the gate?"

The laughter did not get the chance to spread.

"There are no trash martial souls in this world." Wu Zhangkong's voice was not loud. The classroom went dead anyway. The icy green eyes moved across the class, touching each face like a blade checking an edge, resting last on the boy who had laughed. "There are only trash people. Consider your own morals before calling others trash — if you aren't trash yourself, would you have landed in class five?"

Nobody moved. The boy who had laughed turned the color of old ash.

Wulin stood very still. Something hot and unfamiliar pushed up behind his ribs — he had spent four years being defended, by a friend, by a father, by a nickname that turned into respect. This was the first time a stranger had stood between him and the word, and the stranger was the coldest man in the room.

"Your aspiration," Wu Zhangkong said to him, flatly. Not unkindly. "You paused."

Wulin's hand closed, under the desk, around nothing — around the memory of a small hand that used to fit in it. For one heartbeat the answer stood right behind his teeth: *to find someone.*

"I don't have one yet," he said.

Wu Zhangkong looked at him — a long, flat look that seemed to read the lie and file it without comment. "Then find one," he said. "Next."

"Lin Hao."

Lin Hao stood, and the class's attention swung with the obvious pleasure of an audience given better seats.

"Lin Hao. Martial soul: Stormbringer Sword — wind and lightning. Rank twenty-two. Two soul rings."

The classroom's silence was a different species now. Rank twenty had been a held breath. Rank twenty-two — a Soul Grandmaster's standing, two rings, in a first-year's body — was arithmetic none of them could complete, and none of the answers put him here.

Wu Zhangkong's expression did not change by a single degree. "Rank twenty-two. Two rings. A soul like that." The green eyes narrowed, fractionally. "Why are you in my class?"

"Because he's in it," Lin Hao said, and nodded at Wulin. "I asked at registration. The director said a straight request deserved a straight answer, and the answer was yes."

Two rows over, Xie Xie's polished composure cracked into open staring. Wu Zhangkong looked at Lin Hao for three full seconds — the first genuine interest anyone had seen on that face — and said, "Sentiment is a poor cultivation method."

"It's not a method," Lin Hao agreed cheerfully. "It's a promise."

"Sit down," Wu Zhangkong said. But the corner of the closed-door mouth had moved. It might have been nothing. It was not nothing.

## Part 6: The Roof

That night, past curfew, the two of them sat on the roof of dormitory three, above the eastern training ground. Eastsea City glowed below in avenues of amber soul-light, and the harbor wind came in cold off the water, carrying salt — almost, from far enough away, like home.

Wulin unfolded Mang Tian's letter for the fourth time, though he had memorized it on the train. The Blacksmith's Association. The workshop. The note in the old man's blocky hand: *show this to Mu Chen. He is an eight-star Saint Craftsman and the finest smith this side of Heaven Dou City. He owes me a drink, which makes you his problem now.*

"Chimneys are over there," Lin Hao said, pointing down the hill toward the harbor end of the city, where a cluster of squat roofs breathed thin fire into the night, working late. "First thing tomorrow?"

"First thing," Wulin said.

Lin Hao leaned back on his hands, letting his eyes close — and immediately, the way it always did, his awareness went to work on the night. The harbor bells. The lamp-lines humming. Wulin's breathing beside him.

And under Wulin's breathing, something else.

It had been there all year — a density in his friend's soul power, like a river running higher behind a dam. But tonight, with grief and a promise and a rank-thirteen body full of forge-built strength, the water was different. Tighter. The second seal — the knot behind the sternum that Wulin had described to him in fragments — sat in that river like a stone, and the river had risen another finger's width since spring.

*It's coming,* Lin Hao thought. *Not this month. But this year.*

He said nothing. Some stones you did not point at. You just stayed close when the water took them — the way you stayed in the worst class in the academy, because that was where your brother was.

"You know what Na'er would say?" Wulin asked suddenly, at the city. "If she could see us now. Two trash from Glorybound City, sitting on a roof in Eastsea."

Lin Hao considered it. "She'd say: *be careful.*"

Wulin's laugh was short and wet and real. "Yeah. She would." He folded the letter carefully, along its old creases, and put it back inside his coat — over the ring, against the ribs, where important things went. Below them, in the dormitory corridor, room eleven's door stood open a careful inch, the way it had stood every night at home, in case a small silver-haired girl came back from a nightmare.

Wulin had not closed it.

Lin Hao looked at the open door, and at the Blacksmith's Association chimneys breathing fire in the dark, and at his friend's face turned toward a city full of places to look.

"First thing tomorrow," he said.

"First thing," Wulin agreed.

# Chapter 5: The Blacksmith's Association

## Canon Reference: canon ch 41–44 (Ranking Test, Eight Star Saint Craftsman, Second Rank), 49-50 (Xie Xie's challenge, The First Class)
## Timeline: Age 10, first week at Eastsea Academy

## Part 1: The Letter

The Blacksmith's Association of Eastsea City did not sit near the harbor with the other money. It occupied a black stone block in the old quarter — no sign, no soul-lamps on its face, only a gate of folded iron and, from somewhere inside, a rhythm.

Wulin stood in front of that gate for a long moment, listening. Beside him, Lin Hao listened too — and heard it the way he heard everything now, in layers. Forty hammers at least, spread through the building, none of them in step with the others. But underneath the noise, every few seconds, one strike would land so clean it left no echo at all. A silent hit. His father had done that maybe six times a year.

"That's Thousand Refinement," Wulin said quietly. "The metal doesn't ring because there's nothing wasted in the blow."

"Then this building is full of people better than my father," Lin Hao said. "And your master's letter had better be good."

It was. The doorman read Mang Tian's blocky handwriting, looked at Wulin's calloused hands, and let them into a front hall that smelled of hot scale and oil. A woman with a surveyor's badge took the letter, read it twice, and told them to wait.

They did not wait long. A middle-aged man came out of an inner door with his sleeves already rolled — broad, unhurried, with the calm eyes of someone who had decided the worth of ten thousand pieces of metal and was rarely wrong. On his chest, eight stars were worked into the fabric around a golden hammer.

Eight stars. Lin Hao's breath went still without his permission. In Glorybound City, a fourth-rank blacksmith was a city celebrity. His mind did the arithmetic his father had taught him — fourth rank could purify iron a hundred times over; fifth rank, a thousand; each rank past that was not a step but a cliff — and the arithmetic arrived, trembling, at a word his father only said about legends. *Saint Craftsman.*

"You're Mang Tian's boy," Mu Chen said. It was not a question. His eyes went to Wulin's hands, then — briefly, the way a smith glances at the fire he isn't using — to Lin Hao's. "And you have a blacksmith's hands too. Glorybound?"

"My father's forge. Lin Wei."

"Lin Wei." Mu Chen tasted the name, found something in it. "He made a folding blade for a merchant captain eleven years ago. Wind-pattern welding along the spine. I remember it because it should not have worked, and it did." A pause. "The apple, then. We'll see." He turned back to Wulin. "Mang Tian says you understand Thousand Refinement. At ten years old, that claim is either a lie or a marvel, and I've grown too old to enjoy guessing. The testing room is through that door." He nodded at a side chamber where a surveyor was already unlocking it. "Heavy Silver. Purify it. If you can."

Wulin's jaw set. "How much?"

"Enough," Mu Chen said, and for the first time, something like amusement crossed his face. "The hammers are on the rack. You'll want both."
