## Part 2: Second Rank (Canon Scene)

The Blacksmith's Association did not need a sign. It was grey, it was **thirty floors** tall, and at the very top of it was the shape of a hammer, which meant that nobody in Eastsea City had ever had to read its name.

Inside, past the glass doors, was a wall ten metres high with an eight-metre golden hammer sculpture set into it.

**Yun Xiaoling** at the front desk knew exactly who they were before they reached her, because Mang Tian's letter had arrived three days ahead of them and the Association had, in the manner of institutions that enjoy being efficient, already opened a testing room.

"Grandmaster Cen is on the fifteenth floor," she said, and pressed a button, and the doors of the soul elevator closed on the largest interior either boy had ever stood in.

**Cen Yue** turned out to be nothing like what Lin Hao had assembled from the word *Grandmaster*. He was a man in his forties, not particularly tall, extremely well built, with shoulders that seemed to have been put on separately, and a black jacket resting on his deltoids rather than being worn. He was looking at a design plan when they came in.

"You're Mang Tian's disciple?" he said, without looking up.

"Yes. Hello, Grandmaster Cen. My teacher asked me to greet you in his place."

Cen Yue's eyes crinkled. "Mang Tian. That man has spent his whole life trying to reach the peak, and he takes a disciple this small." He rolled up the plan. "Come on, then. I'll take you down and we'll find out whether he's gone soft."

---

The testing room was a vaulted stone cell built to swallow sound, and on the stand along one wall were **fifteen chunks of metal, each one third of a metre squared**, in every colour and quality Lin Hao had ever seen and several he had not.

"**Pick one and purify it,**" said the surveyor, a middle-aged woman who plainly knew Cen Yue well. "I grade you on the metal you choose *and* the degree of purification. **Pass sixty and you're a rank-one blacksmith.**" She glanced at the clock. "**One hour. Calcining counts.**"

She did not say what any of the metals were. That, Lin Hao realised, was the actual first test — you had to know what you were looking at before you were allowed to decide what you could do with it.

Wulin walked the line once, slowly, and stopped in the middle.

He picked up a chunk of metal the size of a man's two fists and carried it to the anvil without making a sound, and the surveyor's eyebrows went up, because it was **Heavy Silver** and it weighed **over three hundred kilograms**, and purifying it was, in the ordinary course of things, a **second-rank** blacksmith's standard.

On the rack behind the anvil hung the Thousand Refined Tungsten Hammers.

Lin Hao knew what they were before the surveyor said it, because he had lifted the forty-kilogram practice hammer in his father's forge and nearly lost a foot. These were a matched *pair*, forty kilograms each, tungsten-folded, balanced so perfectly they hung on the rack like sleeping birds.

"Most second-rank blacksmiths work Heavy Silver with one hammer and both arms," the surveyor said, watching Wulin. "Some can't lift one. You may withdraw and take the first-rank test instead. No one will think less—"

Wulin took a hammer in each hand.

He lifted them the way another boy lifts schoolbooks. The surveyor's mouth opened, closed. Beside the door, a girl who had been waiting for the other testing room leaned forward without noticing she was doing it — **tall for thirteen, exceptionally pretty, large bright eyes, golden hair combed back into a ponytail**, dressed in close-fitting clothes that made her look nimble rather than dressed, with the particular stillness of someone who had spent nine years being told she was remarkable and had decided, some time ago, to stop agreeing.

Wulin closed his eyes for one breath. Lin Hao watched the shift the way he watched everything: the small settling of his friend's weight, the breath that went down instead of up, the whole forge-honed architecture of him locking into place. Four years of Mang Tian's Thousand Refinements, of a body built strike by strike, of a first seal's furnace banked low behind the sternum.

The first hammer fell.

There was no ring. That was the first miracle — forty kilograms of tungsten meeting the densest common metal on the continent, and the sound that came back was a *thud* like a heartbeat, every scrap of the blow's energy going into the silver and none escaping as noise. Lin Hao's hawk-eyes caught the shockwave die inside the metal instead of out. *Nothing wasted. Father's silent strike — every single time.*

And Lin Hao — because he was his father's son, because he had lifted the forty-kilogram practice hammer in the Glorybound forge and nearly lost a foot, because the hawk-eyes read metal the way they read wind — did not only watch. He *read* the work, strike by strike, the way his father had taught him to read a bar: *first strike, true but a fraction high — the bar wants to go left, Wulin's holding it right. Second — there, he found it. Third — now the grain's opening; he's asking the iron and the iron's answering.* Lin Hao's own hands, at his sides, moved without his noticing — the ghost of the strike, the ghost of the turn, his body reading Wulin's forge the way it read everything, learning the silent strike by watching his brother find it. By the thirtieth strike, when the surveyor stopped writing to simply watch, Lin Hao had stopped being an audience. He was a smith watching a smith, and his hands knew the work.

The second hammer fell a half-breath later, and the third, and the room filled with a rhythm that stopped being noise and became weather. Strike. Turn. Strike. The heavy silver's sullen gray began, slowly, to lighten. Impurities were being *persuaded* out of metal so dense that persuading it of anything was considered a second-rank blacksmith's defining trial — and Wulin was not persuading it. He was informing it.

Thirty strikes in, the surveyor stopped writing and simply watched.

Fifty strikes in, the girl in the testing robe had come two steps closer to the anvil, her posture forgotten.

At the sixty-third strike, Wulin's hammers landed together — one sound, perfectly folded — and the Heavy Silver released a **note**.

It was beautiful. A single clean tone that filled the vaulted room like a struck bell, because the metal had become, at last, pure enough to sing. Lin Hao felt the note in his hollowed bones like a wind through reeds, and somewhere behind his ribs his own soul power stirred in sympathy, and he understood with total clarity that he was watching his brother become real.

Wulin set the hammers down. Only then did his arms tremble.

The surveyor found her voice. "That note… that was the first-rank standard passed. The purify-to-song is the *second-rank* standard, and you—" she looked at Mu Chen, who had arrived in the doorway at some point without anyone hearing him, "—President, he's ten."

"I can count," Mu Chen said. He walked to the anvil and put a bare hand flat on the singing silver, the way a doctor touches a pulse. His face did not change. It was, Lin Hao thought, the face of a man doing subtraction — this child, minus everything that should have made this impossible — and not liking the remainder.

"Tang Wulin," Mu Chen said. "As of this moment you are a second-rank blacksmith of this Association — the youngest in its records, which I will verify tonight and then never enjoy hearing about again." He reached into his robe and produced a bronze badge, plain as a washer. "The Association pays second-rank smiths per completed refinement, and it will have work for you every day your academy lets you breathe. Your master trained your arms. I'll train the rest." His eyes moved, once more, to Lin Hao. "And when *your* arms are old enough for the tungsten, Lin Wei's son, the door knows your father's name."

"Purification required a medium component as well," the surveyor said, when the hour was up and the silver sat on the anvil **seven percent smaller** and grey as old weather. "**Hundred Refine a rare metal and forge a medium-sized component** — those are the two requirements for second rank. You've done the first."

Wulin, who had been expecting to sit down, picked the hammers back up instead.

He made a **semi-circular joint-protection component for a mecha knee** — the piece that wears out fastest, and therefore the piece most worth putting a soul guide array into, and therefore the piece that wanted Heavy Silver's five-to-ten-percent soul-power amplification more than any other. He had worked that out before he started, and neither Cen Yue nor the surveyor said anything at all when they realised he had.

What they said, afterwards, to each other, in the corridor, was that the boy had forged **in harmonisation** — the state where a smith builds on a resonance with the metal until the two of them fuse, and where every work carries the smith's own feelings and ideals whether he wants it to or not.

---

Outside the testing room, the girl with the golden ponytail was still standing where the note had found her.

She had passed her own second-rank test **two days earlier**, in room six, and it had been the best day of her life, and then somebody at the front desk had mentioned — casually, the way people mention weather — that a boy had taken the same test in room three.

"*How* old?"

"Ten."

She had not said anything. She had gone home and thought about it for two days, and what she had arrived at was not jealousy, exactly, because she had made a decision about jealousy a long time ago.

Her father had told her, when she was small enough to have to stand on a box to see the anvil, that forging was a rough and heavy business and **not suitable for girls**. He had said it kindly. He had said it the way you say something that is simply true.

She had started anyway, at **five**, making small hammers out of offcuts. He had thought it was a joke. It had taken **two years** of her mimicking his every movement before Mu Chen — President of the Eastsea City branch, eight-star Saint Craftsman, a man with four hundred smiths under him — had come out one morning and watched her for eleven minutes and then, without any announcement at all, begun teaching her.

She had inherited his martial soul. Her figure had gone stocky from the strength work, and he had gone quietly and expensively looking for rare herbs to fix that, and she had let him, because fighting him about it cost more time than the herbs did.

**First-rank at eleven. Second rank a month after her thirteenth birthday.**

Her father had told her she had progressed faster than anyone her age. That she was worthy of being called a **child prodigy in the world of blacksmithing.**

And she had discovered, over about a year, that she hated the word.

Not because it was untrue. Because it was a word other people used to explain her to themselves, so that they would not have to think about the nine years. *Prodigy* was a thing that happened to you. What had actually happened to her was five-year-old hands and a box to stand on and two years of being thought funny.

**Her goal was to surpass her father and become a ninth-rank Divine Craftsman.** There were **three** of those on the entire Douluo Continent.

So she stood outside room three with her arms folded and watched a ten-year-old come out looking like he had been through a furnace, and she did not feel generous.

"That's him, then," she said.

"That's him," said the surveyor.

"Does he know what he did?"

"He knows he passed."

Mu Xi made a small sound that was not quite a laugh. "Then he'll find out." She pushed off the wall. "So will I."

And she went, because there was a second-rank task board on the third floor and she had every intention of being better at it than a boy who had been doing this for four years — which was, she reflected on the way down, exactly the sort of thing her father would have called *not suitable for girls*, and which she had therefore been doing since she was five.

Lin Hao, watching her go, said to nobody in particular, "She's not annoyed that he beat her."

"No," said Wulin, wiping his face with a sleeve.

"She's annoyed that he did it in an hour."

"What's the difference?"

"The difference," said Lin Hao, "is that the first one you can't fix and the second one you can, and she's already working out how."

## Part 3: Rice, Secrets, and a Fight

The academy dining hall had three windows, and the first window — the one with the spirit-nutrient meals that cost what a commoner family spent in a week — had a line of silk jackets. Wulin, holding a tray from the third window piled into a small mountain, walked past all of it with the peace of a man who had eaten.

Lin Hao, whose own mountain rivaled his friend's, had done the arithmetic differently. "The first window's food shortens cultivation time," he said. "That's what the sign says. Spirit-nutrient density."

"I know what it says."

"Then you know that for the two of us, food isn't a meal, it's a resource." Lin Hao looked at his tray, then at the bronze badge in Wulin's fist, then at the first window. "And as of this morning, you're employed."

Wulin opened his mouth. Closed it. Opened it again.

They were negotiating the economics of appetite when a voice arrived behind them like weather.

"Tang Wulin."

Xie Xie stood in the aisle with his tray abandoned somewhere, pale hair still damp from morning training, wearing the expression of a person who had rehearsed this. "Fight me. Again. I wasn't at my best yesterday."

"We didn't fight yesterday," Wulin said, which was true — Xie Xie had *tried* to start a fight yesterday, in the dormitory corridor, and gotten exactly as far as one shove before Lin Hao had appeared in the doorway doing nothing at all, and the corridor had suddenly felt very crowded.

"You know what I mean." Xie Xie's eyes flicked — briefly, unwillingly — to Lin Hao, then snapped back to Wulin, who was the actual grievance. "Two strikes. You ended it in two strikes and then you *walked away* like I was furniture. If you don't fight me, I'll tell the whole class your secrets."

Wulin, who had no secrets he knew of, blinked. "What secrets?"

"I'll make them up!" Xie Xie said with enormous dignity. "They'll be *believable.*"

Lin Hao was having the specific internal experience of watching a fire argue with a forge. "Xie Xie," he said. "He'll fight you after we eat."

"Now," Xie Xie said.

"After," Wulin said, surprising himself — and then, because Lin Hao had set the tray down with the terrible calm of a boy whose father had taught him that a promise about food is still a promise, "…fine. Now."

The training yard behind the dining hall was dirt and old straw, and by the time they reached its center a ring of first-graders had assembled with the speed of people who smell consequences. Xie Xie shed his outer robe, and his martial soul surfaced into his grip — a short dagger of pale, liquid light, the **Light Dragon Dagger**, faster than eyes and twice as pretty. Everyone in class five had already learned to watch for it.

"Two strikes," Xie Xie said. "That's all you got. My family has trained me since I could walk. I'm rank twenty. Do you even know what my soul can—"

Wulin hit him.

Not a technique. Not a soul skill. A *punch* — thrown with the whole stacked architecture of a body forged four years on Thousand Refinement hammers and fed by a sealed furnace behind the sternum, delivered with the plain, devastating honesty of a hammer meeting work. Xie Xie's speed was real; it simply arrived second. The first blow took his guard apart. The second — a controlled one, Lin Hao saw, controlled the way his friend controlled everything that mattered — put Xie Xie flat on his back in the straw with his dagger's light scattered around him like spilled quicksilver and his eyes on the sky.

Two strikes. The yard was silent enough to hear the dining hall's first window calling numbers.

Wulin extended a hand. Xie Xie looked at it, at the sky, at the hand again — and took it, mostly to get upright, and was on his feet before the pull finished.

"Tomorrow," Xie Xie said, breathing hard, straightening his collar with both hands. "Tomorrow I'll be at my best."

"You were at your best," Wulin said, not unkindly, and went back to his rice.

From the doorway of the yard, unnoticed by everyone except a boy with hawk-eyes, Wu Zhangkong watched the whole of it without expression, and left before the crowd did.

## Part 4: The First Class (Canon Scene)

"Today officially marks the start of your classes." Wu Zhangkong stood at the front of the ground-level classroom at the innermost end of the building, and twenty-odd first-graders sat in it like offerings. "Most of your lessons will be taught by me. Stand up."

They stood. Wulin and Zhou Zhangxi, the biggest boys in the class, formed one file; Yun Xiao and Xie Xie fell in beside them; Lin Hao stood at the file's edge, and the wind in the room — there was never wind indoors, but there was around him, a thumb's width of moving air — settled as he stilled it.

"For the first lesson today, you will show me your abilities," Wu Zhangkong said. "Thereafter, you will proceed into actual combat. I will be the judge. Elimination occurs after a single loss." His pale green eyes crossed the room. "Show me your true colors."

A girl's hand went up. "Teacher Wu, I'm a Tool Soul Master. Do I need to join the combat?"

"In the battlefield," Wu Zhangkong said, ice-flat, "would your enemy spare you if you told them you were a Tool Soul Master?" He pointed at the big file. "First group. From this end."

Zhou Zhangxi turned toward Wulin immediately, and his whole massive frame said what his mouth was too proud to. He had been punched out of a dormitory window in their first week — he would not say *by whom*, and everyone knew — and the wound in his pride had been sitting in a warm place ever since. "Let's compete with our strength," he said to Wulin. "I don't believe yours is greater than mine."

Wulin looked at Lin Hao. Lin Hao gave the smallest nod — *this one's yours, and it always was* — and stepped back.

"No rules as to how you defeat your opponent," Wu Zhangkong announced to the circle. "Begin."

Zhou Zhangxi was very large and very strong and had plainly spent the week deciding how this would go. It did not go how he decided. Wulin met the charge the way an anvil meets a decision — his feet slid two inches and no further — and the exchange lasted four collisions before Zhou Zhangxi went down on one knee with Wulin's forearm across his shoulders, not crushed, simply *out-argued*, and the yard-sized classroom made a sound like a held breath escaping.

"Winner, Tang Wulin," Wu Zhangkong said, without inflection. His eyes moved one place down the file. "Lin Hao. The center."

Lin Hao walked into the circle, and twenty-odd first-graders watched the smallest thing about him arrive first: the dust. It moved away from his steps in slow little tides, as if the floor had opinions.

"Your abilities," Wu Zhangkong said.

"My martial soul is the Stormbringer Sword." Lin Hao lifted his hand, and the silver-blue blade surfaced into it with its etched wind-patterns and its restless light, and the classroom's temperature seemed to lean toward him. "My spirit soul is the Gale Hawk." The hawk came — not large, not yet; a shape of wind and pale light that left his shoulder and circled the ceiling once, and every student with working eyes followed it like a compass. "Seven hundred and twenty years of cultivation. Two soul rings." He let the numbers stand in the silence a moment, because Wu Zhangkong had said *show*, and numbers were part of the showing. "My first soul skill is called Gale Talon."

He demonstrated it on nothing — a single compressed arc of wind from his sword's edge that crossed the circle and opened a clean, shallow line in the far wall's plaster, three meters of distance folded like paper. Several students sat down without deciding to.

"And your second?" Wu Zhangkong asked. His voice had not changed. His *attention* had — Lin Hao could feel the difference the way the hawk felt thermals.

"My second soul skill is Hawk-Soul Union." Lin Hao hesitated — genuinely — for the first time. "It… takes everything I have, Teacher. It's not a demonstration. It's a decision."

For one heartbeat Wu Zhangkong looked, beneath the ice, *interested*. "Noted," he said. "Combat. Elimination. Your opponent—" his gaze found the palest face in the room, "—will be Xie Xie."

"I accept!" Xie Xie said, with the speed of a boy who had been handed the exact thing he'd been screaming for all week, and the Light Dragon Dagger surfaced into his grip like a held breath.

What followed, class five would talk about until the snow. Xie Xie was fast — genuinely, beautifully fast, light pouring along his limbs, afterimages arriving before his body did. He crossed the circle in the time a blink takes to start. And Lin Hao did not try to be faster. He simply did not *be* where the blow arrived — his bones had the hollow lightness of a bird's, his hawk-eyes had read the air's pressure change before the light moved — and his flat blade turned Xie Xie's own momentum aside the way wind turns a thrown leaf. Twice. Three times. Each redirection gentler than the last, until Xie Xie was panting in the center of the circle and Lin Hao had not yet attacked once.

"That's not fighting!" Xie Xie exploded. "Fight me!"

"You asked for a fight," Lin Hao said. "I'm waiting for one." And then — softly, so only the front row and one ice-cold teacher heard it — "…sorry. I've been waiting all week to say that to someone."

Xie Xie came at him with everything — light, speed, family training, fury — and Lin Hao met the charge with a single Gale Talon fired not at the boy but at the *floor behind* the boy, and the compressed wind's crack lifted Xie Xie's heels and stole his rhythm for exactly one stride, and in that stride the flat of the Stormbringer was resting, gentle as a rumor, against his ribs.

"Yield?" Lin Hao asked.

The classroom was silent. Xie Xie looked down at the blade, up at the amber eyes, and grinned — suddenly, wildly, like a person who has been lost for a week and just found the road.

"Tomorrow," he said, "I'm going to fight you BOTH."

"Winner, Lin Hao," Wu Zhangkong said. But as the class dissolved into noise and the hawk returned to Lin Hao's shoulder as settling air, the teacher's eyes stayed on him a half-second longer than judging required — the look of a man recalculating a syllabus.

---

## Part 5: The Roof, Again

That night, above dormitory three, Wulin counted the day's coin out twice — Association wages, real federal coins, more than his father made in a week — and put it away with the careful violence of a boy who intended every coin to become a direction to look for a silver-haired girl.

Lin Hao lay back against the tiles and watched the wind over Eastsea City. His hawk-eyes could read the air out there — the long harbor thermals, the pressure-shadow of the incoming weather — and somewhere under all of it, beside him, the familiar furnace-hum of his friend's second seal, pulling at its chains, a finger's width higher than last month.

*Soon,* he thought, not unhappily. *And I'd better keep climbing, or he'll make my promise look slow.*

Below them, in room eleven, the door stood open its careful inch.

The Blacksmith's Association badge sat on Wulin's windowsill, catching the soul-lamp light, and tomorrow there would be a fight — Xie Xie had been extremely clear — and after tomorrow, class, and after class, the Association, and hammer-work, and the long climb all of it fed.

It was, both of them thought without consulting each other, a good shape for a life to have.

## Part 1: Xie Xie's Location

Xie Xie chose the location the way a general chooses a battlefield: the old training yard behind the dining hall, the same dirt he had been flattened in twice, because — and he explained this to anyone who would listen, which was everyone — *a debt is cleanest where it was made.*

He had also, it turned out, invited an audience. Half of class five stood in a loose ring under the afternoon light with the bored excitement of people who have been told there will be violence. Zhou Zhangxi had brought food. Zhou Zhangxi always brought food.

"Rules!" Xie Xie announced, standing in the center with his Light Dragon Dagger already surfacing into his grip, pale as a held breath. "One fight each. No teachers. No yielding until someone's flat or someone's blade says so. Tang Wulin first."

"You're going to lose first," Wulin observed, setting down his tray.

"I've *analyzed* you," Xie Xie said, with enormous dignity.

That should have been the warning. Wulin walked into the circle anyway, because the alternative was letting him finish the sentence, and the last two times he'd ended Xie Xie's fights in two strikes — quick, clean, and, judging by the boy's face, deeply unsatisfying for everyone involved.

The Light Dragon Dagger arrived the way it always did: first the tightening in the air, then light where light had no business being. But this time the first strike was not at Wulin's chest. It flicked low — at his footing — and the second came high while his weight was still answering the first, and Wulin, who had spent four years being hit by hammers and had opinions about momentum, simply ate the feint and let the dagger's second pass skim his forearm, close enough to part sleeve and skin in one thin bright line.

The yard made a sound. Xie Xie's eyes went wide — *I touched him* — and that was, in retrospect, the mistake. Because the line on Wulin's arm had already stopped bleeding, the furnace behind his sternum having glanced at the wound the way a blacksmith glances at a spark, and while Xie Xie was still enjoying his achievement, Wulin stepped inside the light.

Two strikes again. It was becoming a tradition.

Xie Xie lay in the dirt contemplating the sky and the specific unfairness of the universe, and then rolled onto his elbow. "The grass," he said. "My dagger can't cut your grass. I've been practicing on trees. I cut a *boat* in half yesterday. And your grass just — folds around it and springs back."

"Bloodline things are like that," Wulin said, offering a hand. He had no idea why his grass did that. Old Tang was silent on the subject, which was its own kind of answer.

Xie Xie took the hand, got upright, dusted himself with offended precision — and turned to the other boy at the ring's edge.

"You," he said. "Now. And I have questions."

---

The second fight lasted longer, and everyone who watched it understood, in the wordless way yards understand things, that they were seeing something they would describe inaccurately for years.

Xie Xie was fast. He was also, Lin Hao could tell within four exchanges, *smarter than Tuesday* — he had stopped leading with the dagger, stopped letting his light gather where eyes could track it, was arriving from angles he had plainly drawn on paper the night before. Three of those angles would have finished most first-graders. Lin Hao simply was not standing in them.

It was not speed, and the yard kept trying to call it speed. It was that the air told Lin Hao first. Light Dragon Dagger drew its light from somewhere, and before the light moved, the air above Xie Xie's leading shoulder went *taut*, the way a drum skin goes taut a half-breath before the strike — and hawk-eyes, fed by seven hundred and thirty-five years of a soul that had spent its whole first life reading weather for prey, saw the tautness the way other people saw the blade.

So Lin Hao redirected. A wrist turned here, a flat blade there, Xie Xie's own speed doing all the work of Xie Xie's defeat, until the dagger-boy was breathing hard in the middle of the yard with his hair coming loose and his fury — and this was the part the yard would remember — completely gone.

"How," Xie Xie said. Not *fight me.* How. "How do you see my first step?"

Lin Hao considered lying. He considered the truth. He split the difference the way his father split kindling — cleanly, along the grain.

"You tell the air you're coming before you move," he said. "Everyone does. You just tell it louder than most, because your soul has to gather before it shines." He shrugged. "My eyes are from further away than your feet. That's all."

Xie Xie stared at him. The yard stared at both of them. Somewhere in the distance a dining-hall bell rang, and the spell broke into noise and arguments, and Xie Xie sheathed his light with a snap.

"First window," he announced. "All of you. My treat." He pointed at Wulin. "You too. Especially you. I'm not letting you insult my character *and* skip dinner."

---

The first window served spirit-nutrient meals to first-graders in silk jackets, and it had never in its institutional memory served four boys who ordered like a harbor crew. The woman behind the counter confirmed their money twice. Zhou Zhangxi — who had attached himself to the procession the way weather attaches itself to mountains — confirmed the arrangement by eating his own pyramid and then looking, with genuine scholarly interest, at Lin Hao's second plate.

"You're small," he said. It was not an insult. Zhou Zhangxi did not do insults; he did observations, at volume.

"Eat less, forge less," Lin Hao agreed, and Zhou Zhangxi, who had heard about the Association badge and the ten-year-old second-rank smith from four separate witnesses, nodded slowly as if a theory had been confirmed.

Xie Xie, halfway through his fourth course, slammed a hand on the table. "The class match. Friday. Wu Zhangkong's putting our whole year against each other in joint training, class against class, and class one has been *smirking* at me in the corridors all week." He looked around the table with the grave air of a man proposing something reasonable. "We're going to win all of it."

"All of it?" Wulin asked, around a mouthful.

"Every. Match." Xie Xie's dagger-light flickered over his knuckles, then settled, controlled — controlled, Lin Hao noted, in a way it had not been a week ago. Loss, it turned out, was an excellent teacher, provided the student was too stubborn to quit. "They call us the worst class. So let's be the worst class that beats them, and then let's watch their *faces.*"

Nobody at the table argued. It was, everyone privately agreed, an extremely good reason.

## Part 2: Victory Streak

Friday's joint training filled the academy's main yard — a hundred and eight first-graders, five classes, one ice-cold teacher walking the lines with his hands behind his back, and Director Long Hengxu observing from the gallery with the expression of a man expecting to be bored.

The format was simple. Class against class, matched pairs, elimination. Wu Zhangkong judged. No rules as to how you won.

Class five went last, the way the smallest wave goes last against the shore, and the shore had opinions. Class one's file was silk jackets and family tutors and a girl with a mirror-polished shield soul who had been smirking, per Xie Xie's report, all week.

The first match went to class one — a tool-soul boy from class five who lasted eleven seconds and walked off red-faced. The second went to class five: Yun Xiao, quiet Yun Xiao, whom half the grade had forgotten was in the class at all, stood in the circle against a bigger boy with a rock-boar soul and simply… declined to be where the charges landed. Not fast, not flashy — *patient*. Three charges, three empty circles, and on the fourth the rock-boar boy ran into a foot placed, very gently, exactly where his own momentum wanted to put him down. The yard went quiet, then loud. In class five's corner, Wulin nodded at Yun Xiao like one accountant nodding at another's ledger.

The third match was Zhou Zhangxi, and Zhou Zhangxi did not decline anything. He had watched Wulin for two weeks — watched how the smaller boy let force arrive and then *went with it* — and he had built, on top of his mountain of a body, the beginning of an idea. The class one boy hit him like a siege engine. Zhou Zhangxi took it on his guard, staggered — and turned the stagger into a step, the step into a shoulder, and the class one boy into a horizontal person.

"My turn," Xie Xie said, and the smirking girl from the corridor got her match, and it is the considered opinion of everyone present that she did not smirk afterward.

Then class one sent their best — a rank-21 Soul Grandmaster with a silver-horned rhino soul and family money in every stitch — and Wu Zhangkong's eyes slid, once, toward the back of class five's file, and the yard understood the assignment.

Lin Hao went, and the match lasted four seconds, and that was the part nobody in the yard had a way to describe afterward, because a rank-21 Soul Grandmaster does not lose in four seconds to a boy three ranks under him and nobody could say what had happened. The rhino soul had come forward. The Stormbringer had been where the rhino soul was going to be. That was all of it.

And the thing that changed because he was standing there — the thing that nobody in that yard would have had any reason to think about if he had not been in the file — was that **Wu Zhangkong did not send Xie Xie next.** Canon's yard would have sent Xie Xie, because Xie Xie was class five's best and the format was class against class. But Wu Zhangkong had watched four seconds of a four-second match and had made a decision about the shape of his class that he did not say out loud, and the shape was no longer the shape it had been that morning.

Xie Xie noticed. Xie Xie always noticed. He did not say anything, which was the loudest thing Xie Xie had ever done.
Tang Wulin took the circle, and the match lasted one exchange, and it was not a fight so much as a *demonstration of the difference between rank and strength.* The rhino charge was magnificent. Wulin met it the way an anvil meets a rumor, and the silver horns went up, and the class one boy went down, and Director Long Hengxu sat forward in the gallery for the first time all afternoon.

"Lin Hao," said Wu Zhangkong, "you're wasting their time. Center."

Lin Hao took the circle against the last standing class-one fighter — a composed boy, careful, with a wind-blade soul and good tutors — and gave the yard sixty seconds of something that looked, to the untrained, like a storm politely declining to touch a very good dancer. He won without drawing blood, without using a soul skill, and — because Wu Zhangkong was watching with that recalculating attention — without using anything his classmates hadn't already seen. The Union stayed folded. Some doors you don't open for an audience.

Class five won the day, four matches to one. It was not, by any arithmetic that mattered, supposed to happen. The worst class — the ground-floor class, the ground-floor-end-of-the-building class — stood in the main yard with the noise of a hundred first-graders rearranging itself around them, and Xie Xie, because Xie Xie could not help himself, bowed.

It began a streak. The next week's joint training went the same way, and the week after that went faster, and by the end of the month the phrase had entered the first grade's vocabulary: *the worst class is winning.* Older students came to watch. Director Long Hengxu came twice more, and left thoughtful. And Wu Zhangkong — who said nothing, ever, about any of it — did one thing that both furnaces in his class noticed.

He made Lin Hao and Wulin each other's permanent sparring partners.

"The rest of the class will learn more from surviving the two of you than from beating each other," he said, which was as close to praise as his face was structurally capable of. It was also, both boys understood without saying, a decision about *them*: two monsters sharpening each other, because nothing else in the yard was whetstone enough.

Their first real session ended with the training yard's fence needing repairs, Wulin grinning through a split lip, Lin Hao's feather-marks glowing faint through his shirt at the shoulders, and neither of them — this was the part that frightened and delighted them in equal measure, though neither would have used either word — anywhere near the other's ceiling.

---

## Part 3: Ten Thousand Coins

The Association gave Tang Wulin his first solo commission on a Tuesday: a lump of Heavy Silver the size of two fists, and a work order, and Mu Chen's single instruction — "Same as the test. I want the note."

He took four days of evenings. The Association paid on delivery, and the clerk counted out **ten thousand federation coins** — a sum so large the clerk watched Wulin's face as he said it, the way people watch for fainting — and Wulin carried it back to the dormitory in both arms like a sack of grain and sat on his bed holding it for a long time without saying anything.

Ten thousand coins. His father made perhaps four hundred a month at the factory. This was two years of his father's hands, in his own, at ten years old, because a hammer had taught him that metal talks if you hit it honestly.

And the clerk would not have counted that money out in a story without him.

Not because the Association is unkind. **Because the commission would not have existed.** Mu Chen had given the Heavy Silver to Wulin on a Tuesday because Mu Chen had spent a month watching a boy who listened to metal, and the reason Mu Chen had been watching was that **another boy had been standing at the east window of the Association for six weeks, reading grain in metal that nobody else was reading, and Mu Chen had started looking at everything else in the building differently because of it.**

**In a story without him, Wulin is a promising boy with grass and a hammer, and the Association gives him small work for years, and the ten thousand coins never happen.** In a story with him in it, Mu Chen has already decided that this building contains something he did not expect, and Wulin gets Heavy Silver on a Tuesday, and his father's two years of hands come home in a bag.

That is the butterfly, and Wulin never knew. He would have said the money was because he worked. He worked. **But the reason the work was there was a boy at a window who had never once been introduced to him, and who would not have said it was him if anybody had asked.**

Mu Chen's actual teaching came in fragments between commissions, and it was never about the hammer. "Where does the sound go, boy?" he asked once, watching Wulin's sixtieth-something strike sing true. "Into the air means waste. Into the metal means work. Into *you* means you'll be deaf by forty and I'll have to shout at your students instead." He watched the next strike. "Your friend with the hawk-eyes — he listens like the metal owes him money. Bring him to the forge. Not to work. To listen. A smith who can hear what I can hear is worth three who can't."

And there was Mu Xi.

She had been coming to the public forging floor for two weeks — officially to work her own commissions, though her work sat finished and cooling while her eyes sat on the boy at the far anvil. She watched the way the Tungsten hammers moved in his hands. She watched the *silence* of his strikes — the thing her father's whole school was built on, the thing she had spent nine years being told she would eventually earn, and that this commoner's son did like breathing.

She had **first rank at eleven** and second rank a month after her thirteenth birthday, and her father had called her a child prodigy of the blacksmithing world, and she had learned by about the age of twelve to stop correcting people when they said it, because correcting them took longer than letting them.

It was not pride. She had checked. Pride would have been simpler.

What it actually was, and what she had never said out loud to anybody, was this: she had started at **five**, on a box, making small hammers out of offcuts, after her father told her kindly and accurately that forging was **not suitable for girls** — and every rank she held was two years of being thought funny, paid in advance. So when the Association started saying *prodigy*, it felt like somebody taking the nine years and handing back a word.

She was not here to compete with Tang Wulin.

She was here to find out what he had that she had not been able to buy with nine years.

On the fourth day she crossed the floor while Wulin was banking his forge, and stood beside him for long enough that he noticed and wiped his hands and stood up straight, and asked — in the clipped, exact tone of a person carrying a very heavy object — one question.

"The sixty-third strike. In your test. The note." Her chin was high. Her knuckles, at her sides, were not relaxed. "My strikes ring at the fortieth, if I'm perfect. Yours rang at sixty-three, and my father says yours was *purer.* Why sixty-three?"

Wulin thought about it honestly. He was not performing modesty; he genuinely turned the question over the way he turned metal.

"I don't know," he said. "The metal wasn't ready before then. You can hear it getting ready — like bread. I just kept hitting where it told me until the telling turned into the note." He hesitated, then added, because she looked like someone who had never once been told to just *listen*: "Maybe your strikes ring at forty because forty is when your metal is ready. Mine's a different lump every time."

It was, without question, the truest answer he had.

And it was the wrong shape of answer entirely for a girl who had built herself out of *doing it correctly*, because *the metal tells you* is not a thing you can practise. It is not a thing you can start at five on a box. You either hear it or you spend your life becoming good enough that it almost doesn't matter.

*The metal tells him,* her face said, briefly, before nine years of training put the mask back on. *The metal does not tell me. The metal obeys me, or I obey my father's school.*

"Thank you," she said, precisely, and went back to her own anvil.

Her strikes that evening rang at the fortieth, exactly as always, exactly on school-perfect — and she did not go home until midnight, because there was nothing else she knew how to do, and because if the metal was not going to speak to her then she would simply have to become so good that its silence stopped being the point.

Her father had reached **eight stars**. There were **three** men on the Douluo Continent who had reached nine and could be called **Divine Craftsmen**, and she had known their names before she could read properly. She had decided at about the age of seven, in the flat unexamined way children decide things, that she was going to be the fourth, and she had never once revised the plan, and she was not going to start now because a boy from a town nobody visited had a metal that talked to him.

In his office above the floor, **Mu Chen — eight-star Saint Craftsman, President of the Eastsea City branch, the only man at that rank in the entire Association, and one of perhaps forty on the continent who could name all three of the nine-star Divine Craftsmen** — watched his daughter through the window, watched the boy bank his forge and leave with ten thousand coins in a bag over his shoulder, and said nothing at all.

Which, for him, was a kind of grief. He had spent nine years teaching her that effort was the whole of it, because effort was the only thing he had ever been able to honestly promise her.

## Part 4: The List

On the roof that night, there was a letter.

It had come to the academy's post-room in the afternoon — Glorybound City postmark, Chen Long's handwriting, which was swordsmanship in ink: every stroke committed, none wasted. Lin Hao had read it twice and was reading it a third time, which for him was an event.

*Boy. Your forms are clean but you're carrying weight in your left shoulder and compensating right. I can see it from here. Whatever you're carrying, put some of it in the sword, that's what it's for. Your father's letters say you eat him out of the forge. Good. The sword arm is fed by the kitchen arm. Monthly, as agreed. — C.L.*

Below it, in smaller, different ink — his mother had taken the pen from someone, or someone from her: *Write every month. Your father checks the post-road every morning like a fool. We are well. The forge is well. Come home for new year.*

Lin Hao folded the letter into quarters and put it against his skin, under the shirt, where things that mattered went. Beside him, Wulin was doing arithmetic on the back of a work order by soul-lamp light, and the arithmetic had a title at the top of it, in careful characters:

**FIND NA'ER.**

"Ten thousand," Wulin said. "Notices in Glorybound, Eastsea, and the two port towns between — the ones with the ferry landings. The authorities here say no records, but records are for people who *use gates.*" He wrote a number beside *notices.* "Then I start saving for tickets. Coastal runs. Every harbor town north and south." He paused, pen hovering. "Someone took her, Hao. That means somewhere. Roads end. The sea doesn't end, but it has *routes.*"

Lin Hao looked at the list for a long moment. Then he took the pen and, at the top — above Glorybound, above the port towns — wrote two words, and turned the page around.

**Glorybound harbor. The night she left. The wind was off the water.**

"She went toward the sea," he said quietly. "I was there the morning after. I stood where she'd been standing for four years and I looked the wrong way — I looked at the *roads*, because that's where people go." He tapped the words. "But the whole time she lived with you, every evening, she stood facing the harbor. Not the town. The *water.* Whatever she was remembering, it wasn't behind her. It was out there." He handed the pen back. "Start at the water. Ask the night fishermen. Ask the ones who don't talk to authorities."

Wulin stared at the page. The furnace-hum under his ribs — the second seal, patient as ever — seemed, for a moment, to lean toward the same horizon.

"Friday I deliver the next commission," he said. "That's another eight thousand. I can have the harbor covered by the end of the month."

"And I'll write the notices," Lin Hao said, "because your handwriting looks like it was forged, not written."

"*It was* forged, that's the whole point—"

The argument went on for twenty minutes, which is what arguments between brothers sound like when both of them are, underneath, agreeing completely. Above them the Eastsea sky did its slow harbor thing, and the hawk inside Lin Hao's chest turned once in its sleep, heavy with another week of fed cultivation — seven hundred and thirty-five years now, and climbing toward a number he could feel the way sailors feel weather. On his shoulders, under the shirt, the feather-fine wind-marks from the week's sparring still glowed faint, and glowed, he noticed, a little longer each time.

Becoming, not changing. Slowly. The way the sea makes a route.

Down below, in room eleven, the door stood open its careful inch, and on the windowsill the Association badge caught the lamp-light like a small bronze moon, and the worst class in Eastsea Academy slept the sleep of people who have begun, without quite noticing, to carry weight — and to carry it together.

## Part 1: The Golden Scale

It happened on a Wednesday, before dawn, the way important things happened in dormitory three — quietly, and to Wulin.

He woke because his forearm itched. Not on the skin — *under* it, a deep and particular itch, the way a hammer-echo lives in the wrist after a long day. He sat up in the dark and rubbed the spot, and his fingers met something that was not skin.

A scale.

Where his forearm should have been smooth, one scale had surfaced — small as a thumbnail, golden, set into him the way a tile is set into a floor, with no seam and no blood. In the gray light it did not shine so much as *hold* light, the way coals hold heat, and when he turned his arm, the gold moved under the surface like something alive regarding him.

Lin Hao was awake before Wulin finished his first breath of panic — he had been asleep the way hawks sleep, one part of him standing watch — and he was off his bunk and across the two steps between beds before Wulin had decided whether to shout.

"Don't," Lin Hao said, "poke it like that. You're poking it like Zhou Zhangxi pokes bread."

"Hao. There's a—" Wulin's voice came down to a whisper. "There's a scale. On me. A *gold* scale. Old Tang never said anything about scales."

Lin Hao looked. And what his hawk-eyes saw, in the dim, made the breath go still in him for a half-second: the scale was not merely gold. It was *old* — old the way the deep harbor is old, old the way the thing behind Wulin's sternum was old. Around its edges, so faint he would have missed it blinking, the air lay in a different pattern than the rest of the room, the way water lies differently over a wreck.

"It's beautiful," Lin Hao said carefully. "Show me your hand again."

Wulin held out his arm.

The scale was gone.

Not faded. Not sunk. *Gone* — smooth forearm, ordinary skin, the itch already a memory. Wulin turned his arm over and over, pinched the spot, pressed his thumbnail into it until the skin blanched. Nothing. "It was there. Hao, it was *there*—"

"I saw it." Lin Hao put his hand on his friend's wrist, stilling the digging thumbnail. "Golden. No seam. Like it grew there and then decided not to. I saw it, Wulin. You're not imagining it."

Wulin sat very still. In the chest-space where Old Tang lived, something was quiet in the specific way of a teacher who has heard the question and is choosing how much of the answer a student can carry. Finally the old voice came, and Wulin repeated it aloud, slowly, the way he repeated forging temperatures:

"*The seals are not walls. They are doors, and doors have handles. What you saw was a handle. It will show itself when there is something worth holding onto. Do not chase it. Do not fear it. And do not* — " a pause, and Wulin's face grew solemn in the dark, hearing some emphasis only he could receive, "— *do not let it be seen by strangers.*"

Lin Hao nodded in the dark, and said nothing about what his eyes had told him — that the air around the scale had lain like water over a wreck, and that wrecks, in his experience, were things that had once sailed.

Some observations were his alone to carry. That was the whole architecture of their friendship: Wulin's secrets lived in Wulin, and Lin Hao's silence was the room they lived in.

## Part 2: The Listener

On Friday evening, Lin Hao went to the Blacksmith's Association — not to the public floor, but past it, to the private forging rooms, because Mu Chen had sent word through Wulin: *the boy with the hawk-eyes. Friday. Bring nothing.*

The President's personal forge was a plain room with a plain anvil and forty years of silence in its corners. Mu Chen stood behind the anvil with a Thousand Refined hammer in one hand and no ceremony in his face.

"Your friend tells me you hear strikes," he said. "Everyone hears strikes. My fourth-rank smiths hear strikes. I want to know what you hear *between* them." He lifted a bar of common iron onto the anvil. "Ten strikes. After each, you say one word: *true*, or *waste.* That's the test."

The first strike rang. "True," Lin Hao said.

The second rang almost identically — to his ears, to any ears — but under the ring, at the very bottom of the note, a thread of the blow's force had gone sideways into the anvil instead of down into the iron. "Waste."

Mu Chen's eyebrow moved. The third strike: "True." Fourth: "True." Fifth — the note was clean as a bell, and Lin Hao opened his mouth to say *true*, and stopped. Because the hawk inside him — seven hundred and fifty years of a creature whose entire ancestral life had been listening for the wrongness under things — had already gone still and attentive, the way it went still before weather. The note was clean. Under the note, the metal's grain had *flinched.*

"Waste," Lin Hao said. "The sound's right. The iron isn't. It's… flinching. Like you're asking it something it doesn't want to answer yet."

The room was quiet for a long moment. Mu Chen set the hammer down — the first time, Wulin would say later, he had ever seen the man set a hammer down mid-test — and looked at the boy across the anvil with an expression that was not pleasure, exactly. It was recognition. The look one master gives another's work when he understands, precisely, what it cost.

"That was heat-stress in the bar," Mu Chen said. "Invisible. Inaudible to nine smiths in ten, and the tenth tells me after the work is ruined." He picked up the bar and turned it in the light. "A smith who can hear what I can hear is worth three who can't. I said that about you to the boy. I did not expect to be understating it." He pointed at a stool by the wall. "Fridays. You sit there. You listen while I work, and at the end you tell me every waste you caught. You touch no hammer in this room — your friend's hands are his own, and yours are your own, and I will not have the Association saying I collect children." A pause, and then, drier: "Your father's folding weld. The one that should not have worked. I have thought about it eleven years. Sit down."

So the Association acquired something it had never had and did not officially have: a **listener**. On the floor, the smiths learned that on Friday evenings the small Glorybound boy sat by the President's door with his eyes half-closed, and that on Monday mornings the President's corrections were sharper than any of them had ever heard, and arrived, somehow, already phrased in the language of what the metal *wanted*.

And Lin Hao learned something too — that Mu Chen's waste-strikes were never wasted twice, that mastery was mostly the discipline of *hearing yourself honestly*, and that the old man's silence, like his father's, like Chen Long's, like Wu Zhangkong's, was not emptiness. It was a room. The men who mattered in this city all kept one, and they all, one by one, were letting him sit in it.

## Part 3: The Harbor

They took the first soul train to Glorybound on Saturday morning, because the notices needed posting and Wulin had decided — with the particular finality he brought to budgets — that the search would begin where the search belonged.

Glorybound City received them the way it received everything: with salt wind and indifference. The harbor at noon was a forest of masts and a babel of gulls; the notice-boards by the ferry landing were layered three years deep with lost dogs, lost boats, and lost persons, and Wulin added one more, hammered flat with a care that made the harbormaster's boy watch, then help.

And Wulin had a system. Wulin always had a system: ferry masters first, then the night-boat crews, then the women who sold dried fish at the third landing, because they stood still longest and saw the most. It was a good system. It was the best system a boy of ten with a budget and a picture could have.

**Lin Hao did not use it.**

Because Lin Hao did not ask anybody whether they had seen a girl. He asked them what they had *noticed,* and that is a different question and it gets a different answer, and by the second landing he had stopped asking about a girl at all and had started asking about **a woman who walked without looking where she was going** — because a person who takes a child does not look where they are going, they look behind them, and everybody at a harbor remembers the one person who walked the wrong way.

Two boatmen remembered. One of them remembered a grey coat. The other remembered that the woman had paid in coin and not in notes, and had paid exactly, and had not waited for change.

**That is the butterfly, and Wulin would not have got it.** Not because Wulin is stupid — Wulin's system was better than anything Lin Hao could have planned. **It is because Lin Hao does not ask people what they saw. He asks them what they noticed, and those are two different questions, and the whole of the rest of his life runs on the difference.**

The notice was simple. NA'ER. Silver hair. Amethyst eyes. Found in this city, taken from this city, roughly four months past. She is family. **Reward: 500 federation coins for verified word of her.** No questions asked of the bringer. Contact: the Association branch, Eastsea City, ask for Tang.

Five hundred coins was more than most of the men on those docks made in two months, and by nightfall — because Wulin had learned from his father how money talks and from Lin Hao how money *listens* — the notice had been copied by a dozen hands onto a dozen other boards, up the coast road and down, and the harbor's idle architecture of old men had begun, in its slow tide-way fashion, to pay attention.

The night fishermen worked the black water beyond the breakwater, and it was to them the boys went last, with tea in a thermos and the patience Lin Hao's father used on stubborn metal. Old men and the sea keep longer hours than cities. By the second hour, three of them had remembered nothing. The fourth remembered something.

He was called Uncle Gull, which was either a name or a job description, and he mended nets by lamp while he talked, never looking up.

"The night you mean," he said, "there was no wind."

Lin Hao went still. His whole self — the hawk in his chest, the wind in his bones, the air-reading that never slept — went still with him, because he had stood on this harbor every day of his childhood, and there was *always* wind.

"No wind at all," Uncle Gull said, drawing the needle through. "Sea flat as a widow's face. Old men like me, we notice such things because such things are wrong. I said to my brother: the water's holding its breath." The needle paused. "And past the breakwater — out where the lamp doesn't reach — the water was *moving*. Not waves. Movement. Like something under it, going out, taking its own weather with it." He shrugged, resumed the net. "By morning, the wind was back. Nothing in the log. Nothing on the water. But I've fished forty years, boy, and I tell you true: whatever left your harbor that night, it didn't use a boat."

Wulin stood at the end of the pier long after the lamp had gone out.

Lin Hao gave him the whole silence — all the long black minutes of it, because he had learned that his friend carried things the way forges carry heat: slowly, and better when not quenched too fast. When Wulin finally spoke, his voice was not broken. It was *set*, the way metal sets.

"She faced the water," he said. "Every evening, four years, she faced the water, and I thought she was looking at nothing." He looked out at the flat, moving dark. "She was looking *home.* And something came and took her there, and the sea covered the road behind it." He turned to Lin Hao, and his eyes were not wet — they were the eyes of a boy making an alloy, mixing grief and love in exact proportions until the result was harder than either. "Then we'll learn the sea, Hao. Every route, every port, every current. I'll forge the money and you'll read the wind, and between us we'll take her road apart piece by piece until we find which piece she's on."

On the last train back, Lin Hao watched the harbor lights shrink behind them and thought about water that moved without wind. The hawk in his chest was very quiet, and very awake, and — this was new — it felt less like an animal remembering a hunt and more like *someone* remembering a place.

He did not examine the thought too closely. Some doors announce themselves before you knock.

## Part 4: The Sea Inside

That night, back in room twelve, Lin Hao sat in meditation the way he had not sat since Glorybound — fully, without one ear on a sleeping friend or a distant harbor.

His spiritual sea opened under him like a real one.

It had been growing into this for months, though he had never stopped to look: a wide, dark, luminous expanse — Spirit Connection depth, a hundred and twenty measures of it and widening, the surface stippled with the everyday weather of his own thoughts. And out in that sea, where in the first months there had been only a warmth — a sleeping animal-shape folded into the deep — there was now a *presence.*

The Gale Hawk sat on the far water the way hawks sit on high places: composed, alert, entirely itself. Seven hundred and fifty years of fed cultivation had thickened it beyond any hundred-year thing; its edges were less like light and more like *decision*. As Lin Hao watched, it turned its head and regarded him — and he understood, with the wordless certainty of things that happen inside one's own soul, that it had known he was watching before he looked.

*You're not just growing,* he thought at it, the way he thought at his own hands. *You're waking up.*

The hawk made no answer it could have put in words. It did something better: it *showed* him. A flash, wing-beat fast — the training yard last week, Xie Xie's light gathering a half-breath early, and the hawk's attention arriving there *first*, a finger's-width of a second ahead of even his hawk-eyes. And another: Mu Chen's fifth strike, the flinch in the iron's grain — the hawk had heard it before the sound existed. And another, and another — small things, weeks of small things, laid out like a hunter laying out the day's kills: *I have been helping. I will help more. I am becoming able to.*

Lin Hao sat with it — with *him*, the correction came unbidden, and he did not argue with it — and felt, for the first time, the shape of what was coming. Not a calculation. He had done the arithmetic weeks ago and set it aside, because arithmetic was the wrong instrument: a purchasable thousand-year soul cost a million coins his family would never hold, and even held, would come to him a *stranger* — partial compatibility, careful integration, a negotiation. While this one —

This one had been folded inside him since he was eight years old. This one had been fed by his cultivation and fed him back, had rebuilt itself around his meridians and his sword and his very bones, had grown *with* him the way a brother grows with a brother. When the rank thirty gate came, and the third ring wanted a soul to come from —

*It will be you,* Lin Hao thought. *There was never a question. You're not my equipment.* The hawk's presence on the far water stirred, and he felt the answer arrive in his chest warm as a coal: *You're family.*

The sea brightened. Somewhere in its depths a threshold turned over like a sleeper — not waking, not yet, but turning toward the waking — and Lin Hao's soul power, riding the turn the way his body rode all turns, deepened past a line he had been approaching for weeks.

Rank twenty-three came in the silence of room twelve, without sound or spectacle, the way the tide comes: because it was time, and nothing on earth stops the tide.

On his shoulders, under his shirt, the feather-fine marks glowed a little longer than they ever had — and at their edges, if anyone had been watching closely, the faintest new thing: the very tips of his dark hair, where the wind sat even indoors, had gone the color of storm-light. One strand. Two. Nobody was watching. It would not stay nobody for long.

## Part 5: The Announcement

Class five was **twenty students**, and Lin Hao had counted them all in the first week, because that was what he did, and the count was the most informative thing about the class.

**Eight of the twenty were Tool Soul Masters with no battle skills whatsoever.** Not weak battle skills. None. A hoe. A ladle. A spool. Two of them, when Wu Zhangkong paired the class in the first week, had spent the entire match pushing at each other, and he had let it run its full length without saying a word, which everybody understood was worse than a rebuke. **Three more were Battle Soul Masters whose martial souls sat about where Bluesilver Grass sat** — which, as Wulin observed with the flatness of a man reading his own file, meant that the joke of Glorybound City was, on paper, mid-table here.

Wu Zhangkong had called it the worst class in the academy in that first lesson, and said it the way you read out a temperature. Then a boy two rows over had called Wulin's grass trash, and a piece of chalk had crossed the room with a spiralling force that put it precisely into the boy's open mouth, and Wu Zhangkong had said, without raising his voice:

**"There are no trash martial souls in this world. Rather, there are only trash people. Consider your own morals first before calling others trash. If you aren't a piece of trash yourself, would you have landed in class five?"**

Nobody said it again. Not once, in five weeks.

And underneath all of it, the sentence he had opened with, which the class had not understood at the time and had begun, gradually, to understand: **"My name is Wu Zhangkong. For the next six years, you will all be under my tutelage."**

Six years. Said to the worst class in the academy, in a ground-floor room at the end of a building, as though it were a promise rather than a posting.

---

Monday's first class ended with Wu Zhangkong holding the room for ten seconds longer than anyone expected — which, with him, was the equivalent of standing on the desk.

"Two announcements," he said. "The class promotion tournament begins at term's end. Class against class, full roster, the grade's board decides the standings." His pale green eyes crossed the room and rested, with what the class had learned to recognize as his maximum warmth, on the back file. "Some of you have made the worst class's name interesting. See that it stays interesting."

A rustle went through the twenty. Xie Xie's dagger-light was out of his grip and humming over his knuckles before the sentence had landed. **Zhou Zhangxi** cracked his knuckles in slow, tectonic sequence — the Titan Ape in him never entirely sat down, and in a room where eight children had nothing to fight with, he had discovered that being the largest person present was a personality. **Yun Xiao** — quiet Yun Xiao, who had not thrown a punch in five weeks and who had nonetheless become, by general unspoken agreement, the person you asked before you did anything — allowed himself a single, small, accountant's smile, and made a note, because Yun Xiao made notes.

And **Li Chushui**, two desks up, who had short light-blue hair and big eyes and who reminded Wulin uncomfortably of somebody, went very still in the particular way she went still before she moved fast.

She had shown her martial soul in the second week, when the class did its first paired work. She had bowed first — actually bowed, to a boy named Chen Long who had a ladle — and then **half of her light-blue hair had turned white**, and **one of her blue eyes had gone green**, and a white ring had come up under her feet, and a small white cat had appeared on her shoulder and sat there looking at everybody with the flat contempt only cats and Gu Yue managed. White fur had grown over her palms and claws had come out of her fingertips, and she had crossed eleven metres of floor in the time Chen Long took to lift his ladle, and she had stopped one inch from his chest, and the cat had yawned.

Agility System. A ten-year white ring. And Wulin had watched the whole of it with his stomach doing something he had refused to examine, because the white hair and the big eyes and the small careful bow had put somebody in the room who was not in the room.

He had not said anything. He had not said anything for three weeks.

"Second," Wu Zhangkong said. "The Academy has assigned a transfer student to this class, effective this week." He let the sentence sit in the silence it deserved — because transfer students went to class one; transfer students went where the silk jackets were; transfer students did not, in the history of Eastsea Academy, come to the ground-floor-end-of-the-building class. "Mid-term. Unusual. Not my decision." A beat. "Her file is sealed."

"*Her?*" Xie Xie said, with the outrage of a boy whose class, whose *streak*, whose entire emerging mythology was about to be walked into by a stranger. "We finally get interesting and they send us a — a *file?* Who does that?"

"The people who sealed it," Wu Zhangkong said, and left, which ended the class in the way his exits always did: instantly, and with thirty conversations detonating behind him.

Zhou Zhangxi leaned back across the desk. "Twenty students. Eight of them can't fight. And they send us a *girl*."

"Zhou," said Yun Xiao, without looking up from his note. "Write that down and read it back to me in a year."

"I'll read it back to you next week."

"You'll read it back to me in a year," said Yun Xiao, "and you'll say it in front of her, and I would like very much to be standing somewhere else when you do."

Walking out with the noise, Wulin fell into step beside Lin Hao, and the two of them said the same thing at the same moment, in the same tone, without consulting each other:

"Our class doesn't get things by accident."

**Liu Yuxin** caught them at the gate, which was where she caught everybody, because she had decided some weeks ago that the interesting things in the intermediate division happened to first-graders and that if you wanted to see them you had to stand at the gate.

"Wulin." She was holding something behind her back, in the manner of a person who has rehearsed this. "Senior sister has a small favour."

She produced a **soul camera**.

"No," said Wulin.

"You haven't heard the favour."

"It involves that." He pointed at the camera. "It always involves the camera."

"Take a few pictures of Teacher Wu," Liu Yuxin said, pressing it into his hands with both of hers so that refusing would have been a physical act. "That's all. He's your class teacher. You see him every day. It's nothing."

"He's—" Wulin looked at the camera, and then at the ground-floor window at the end of the building, behind which a man with hair the colour of a winter lake was probably not doing anything at all. "Senior sister, why do you want pictures of Teacher Wu?"

Liu Yuxin's face did the thing that had made her extremely popular in the advanced division.

"You don't know?" she said. "**He's the Icily Arrogant Prince Charming.** He's the number one lady-killer in this academy — the young female teachers, the senior girls, all of us. He was teaching in the advanced division and then for some reason they sent him down here, to the *worst class,* and we all think it's an injustice." She lowered her voice, which was unnecessary and which she did anyway. "He's the most formidable teacher we have. Somebody says he's the number one expert in the academy. **I saw him once with at least six soul rings.**"

Wulin stopped.

"Six?"

"**Six.** That's a Soul Emperor." Liu Yuxin nodded, pleased with herself. "Eastsea City has a handful of those. And he's *young.* And he's teaching *your class.* And you have a camera."

Wulin looked at the camera for a long time.

Six rings. He thought about the wooden sword on the rack, and the eleven seconds it had taken to stop Xie Xie without moving his feet, and the fact that he had never once seen Wu Zhangkong release anything at all.

"I'll take them," he said.

"You will?"

"Yes." He put the camera in his bag. "But not for you."

---

Above them, unseen, unbothered, the gulls of Eastsea turned in the harbor wind — and one of them, for a single beat that no one was watching closely enough to notice, turned *with* the wind rather than against it, the way a bird does only when the wind is, in some small and private sense, its own.

# Chapter 8: The Transfer Student

## Canon Reference: canon ch 62–66 (Gu Yue's arrival on the sports field; enrollment test vs Xie Xie; six-element mastery; "Elementalist?")

## Part 1: The Girl in White

She came through the gate from the direction of the academy buildings, in the middle of the afternoon class, which was the first wrong thing about her.

The second was that she was **not wearing a uniform.**

She was dressed in **white** — plain white, travel white, the white of somebody who had come a long way and had not stopped to change — and she was the same age as every first-grader on the field, and she was not, Lin Hao noticed before he decided to notice it, particularly beautiful. She was delicate. She was pretty. She had long black hair and black eyes and an average build and bright eyes that were full of something. And she walked with a rhythm to it, a particular spacing between her steps, and her whole manner had a feeling to it that Lin Hao's hawk read as *foreign* before his brain had any word for it.

Wu Zhangkong had seen her too, because Wu Zhangkong saw everything, and he had stopped the roster.

"What class are you in?"

"I'm here to attend school," the girl said. "However, I was told the registration period has already passed."

"You're not an Eastsea Academy student?"

"I'm not a student at the moment." She said it the way you'd read out a fact about the weather. "But I would still like to be one. Is that possible, teacher?"

Any other teacher on that field would have sent her to the administration building. Lin Hao watched Wu Zhangkong decide, and could not afterwards have said what the deciding looked like.

"This is a Soul Master's academy," Wu Zhangkong said. "If you want to attend here, you must have the ability."

"I can take a test."

"Your name."

"**Gu Yue.**"

Wu Zhangkong nodded once. Then he turned around and walked back across the field to Xie Xie, who had been listening with the expression of a boy watching something excellent happen to somebody else.

"Give your metal shirt to Tang Wulin. Come here."

Xie Xie gave the shirt. Wulin put it on without being asked, which told Lin Hao more about the last five weeks than anything anybody had said.

"Your physical strength is horrible," Wu Zhangkong told Xie Xie.

"We Agility System Battle Soul Masters only need a burst of power and some nimbleness," Xie Xie said. "We don't need—"

"**How shallow.**" Wu Zhangkong said it without heat, which was the worst way to say it. "Fine. I'll give you a chance today. **Defeat her and you won't have to run this afternoon.**" He looked at the sky. "Twenty minutes' rest. Then we begin."

---

The field had gone completely quiet, which was the only register in which class five ever expressed awe.

Wu Zhangkong gave Xie Xie twenty minutes' rest, and then he let him find out.

---

She was given a uniform, a key, and the back-left desk under the bad window, behind Tang Wulin.

She sat there from the first day and never once explained why.

## Part 2: The Field

Tournament training had turned the first-grade sports field into a place with weather of its own.

Class five owned the far end — not by assignment, but by the quiet arithmetic of the last month, in which nobody else wanted the ground where the worst class did its worst. Wu Zhangkong stood at the center of it with his hands behind his back, running the roster in pairs, and today the pairs meant what everyone had been waiting for: Lin Hao and Wulin, the two furnaces, sparring properly for the first time since the fence incident.

It did not look like sparring. It looked like two different disasters negotiating.

Wulin came in the way he came at everything — directly, with the whole forged weight of him, Bluesilver Grass already uncoiling in golden-threaded ropes to own the ground underfoot. Lin Hao did not meet the charge. He *wasn't there* for it, hollow-boned and hawk-read, his body leaving the collision line a half-breath before the collision decided to happen, the Stormbringer answering from an angle the grass had not yet grown into.

The hawk inside him was working harder than he was. That had been true for weeks now — seven hundred and fifty years of sharpened instinct marking the fight *ahead* of him: there, Wulin's weight committing; there, the grass's third rope feinting left to root right. Lin Hao stopped fighting the head start and started trusting it, the way you trust a hand on your shoulder in the dark, and the match climbed into a register neither of them had reached before — until Wulin's fourth rope finally caught his ankle and his wind-blade finally skidded off Wulin's crossed forearms at the same moment, and they called it even by mutual breathlessness.

"Again," said Xie Xie, from the sideline, where he had been drilling his light-step patterns with the industry of a convert. "Again, and this time Wulin, use the low ropes first, he hates the low ropes—"

"You've been counting my ropes," Wulin said, pleased.

"I've been counting *everyone's* everything," Xie Xie said, with dignity. "It's my whole personality now."

Yun Xiao, passing with two waterskins, murmured, "It's been his whole personality for a week," and was awarded the rare Xie Xie speechless-face.

Zhou Zhangxi laughed like a rockslide. Wu Zhangkong's mouth did not move, which the class had learned to log as amusement. And from beyond the field fence, where the road curved up from the academy gate — a place no student ever stood, because there was nothing there to stand for — a girl was watching.

She had been watching for perhaps ten minutes. Small, unremarkable at fence-glance distance: dark hair pulled back, plain clothes, the particular stillness of someone waiting. Two second-graders walking past gave her a wide berth without seeming to notice they were doing it.

Lin Hao noticed. Not her — that was the strange part. He noticed that his hawk had gone *quiet*, the way it went quiet before weather, and when he followed the silence to its source, there was only a girl at a fence, watching class five train, with her hands folded and her face at rest.

*Probably nothing,* he thought, and reset his stance, and the moment passed the way such moments do.
