## Part 1: Four Photographs

Zhou Zhangxi arrived at room eleven the way weather arrives — all at once, and without knocking.

"It's not good. Xie Xie, Wulin, hurry up and come see. A group of people are at the academy gates — hundreds of them — and they're holding *pictures.*" He was bent double, hands on knees, the roster-keeper's usually careful face gone round with running. "Four pictures. One of each of you. They're calling for the academy to hand you over, and I'm afraid the teachers will come out soon, and — and one of them is *enormous.*"

Xie Xie was off his bed before the sentence finished, fury already assembled: "If it's those guys from yesterday, we'll just beat them up again. Bullying people into paying protection fees, yet those thieves dare come to the academy and cry *thief—*"

"Hold on." It was Wulin who caught him — not by argument, by the arm, the way you catch a kettle. And it was Wulin's voice, slow and heavy, that put the room's temperature back where it belonged. "Don't be so impulsive. This shouldn't be that simple. Don't forget where we are — this is Eastsea Academy, a Soul Master's academy. If they dare come *here,* knowing that, it means they're confident in their backing. We're still far too weak for whatever that backing is." A beat. "We should go find Teacher Wu first."

"I stand with Wulin," Gu Yue said, appearing in the doorway with her jacket half on and her expression entirely assembled.

And Lin Hao was already in his shoes, because while the argument had been happening his mind had been doing what it now did fastest — running the forge arithmetic of yesterday. A brother with a broken arm. A brother with a *position,* because men like Guang Long did not own lanes for fun; lanes were small change, and small change flowed *up.* "He'll be there in person," Lin Hao said. "A man who sends underlings doesn't commission four portraits. Go. All of us."

Wu Zhangkong's schedule was strict — after breakfast he meditated, and finding him was not difficult. The door opened on a teacher in a traditional white chang pao, ice-cold, one eyebrow already assembled for trouble.

"What cultivation questions do you have?"

"Teacher Wu, we've caused some trouble…" And Wulin, a little nervous and entirely courageous, retold the whole of yesterday — the lane, the jars, the neck that couldn't be cut, the gold.

Well. Most of the gold. The scales left out; the file kept. Three of them had agreed on the walk over. The fourth had agreed before they'd asked.

Wu Zhangkong listened with an indifferent expression that had gone, by degrees, very still. "It seems you guys actually have some ability," he said at last, coldly — which, class five was learning, was his register for *pride.* And then the white chang pao was moving past them down the hall, delicate and light, rustling in a wind the corridor did not have, blue hair drifting up from the shoulders, and the four students of the worst class in the grade followed their teacher toward the gate the way iron filings follow a magnet: without any sense of having decided to.

## Part 2

The marks on his forearms had stopped fading. That was new — they used to be gone by morning, and now they simply stayed, faint as a healed scratch, the shape a feather makes when it is pressed flat. He had stopped rolling his sleeves down in front of people, because there was no longer anything to hide by evening.
: The Gate

Outside the great gates of Eastsea Academy stood an impenetrable crowd of at least two hundred fierce and burly people holding all sorts of weapons — and that was the part Lin Hao's eyes went to first, past the size of it, past the noise, the way his father's eyes went to the grain before the shape of a bar.

*Soul devices.* Federation-prohibited ones, on a dozen hips and shoulders; standard-issue ones on the rest. He had seen the make-work in the Association's repair yard — trigger groups, charge cells, the cheap stamped housings of things designed to let men who would never hold a ring hold something like one. The age of soul technology had shortened the old distance between soul masters and commoners, and two hundred men with devices were the arithmetic of it, standing in a lane-mob's shape but ordered like a parade. Not a gang. A *unit.*

Above them rode a banner: **MURDER MUST BE PAID WITH LIFE! DEBTS MUST BE PAID! HAND OVER THE CULPRIT!** And in front, on a stretcher, swaddled in gauze like a jar in straw, lay Guang Long. And above the banner, held up for the academy to see, four photographs — a forge-boy, a dagger-boy, a girl with an unbothered face, and a fourth boy with a sword and a look the photographer had caught mid-turn, hawk-eyed, which was the only reason the picture frightened anyone.

At the front of it all stood the enormous one. Two meters at least, shaved head with small sideburns, bare arms corded like ship's cable — Guang Long's face rebuilt bigger and meaner, an upgraded edition of a bad book. Lin Hao did not need the hawk to read the pressure coming off the man; he could have read it in his *boots,* the way the stones lay quieter around those feet. Beside him, Xie Xie's knuckles had gone white on his dagger-hilt, and Wulin had stopped in the middle of a step — the stillness Lin Hao knew: the forge, hearing a hammer it did not recognize.

Long Hengxu was already there with a dozen teachers, and his voice went out over the gates like a dropped portcullis. "What kind of people are you, to actually dare to cause trouble in front of the academy?"

"My name is Guang Biao. The one on the stretcher is my younger brother." The voice was not loud; it did not need to be — it simply *arrived,* like thunder that had skipped the sky. "I have not come as the mecha brigade's captain, but merely as an elder brother with a seriously injured younger brother. Bring out the culprits who caused this."

And Lin Hao watched his director's face change, and filed the words that caused it: *mecha brigade.* Captain. Master regiment rank — one grade under the city's chief executive and answerable to nothing in this lane. Five hundred federation soul mecha garrisoned in Eastsea City, and every burly man behind that shaved head was a Mecha Master with combat time on his record. This was not a protection fee come back for a rematch. This was a *city* at the gate of a school.

"Chief Guang Biao," Long Hengxu said, and the harmoniousness of his tone was its own kind of steel, "there must be some misunderstanding. There are four *children* in your photographs—"

"Children? My brother had been beaten so badly." The flat of a hand gestured at the stretcher, and two hundred men shifted weight on command, and the sound of it was the sound of a wall leaning. "I have given Eastsea City enough face by waiting here. If you do not hand those people over in twenty minutes, we shall search for them ourselves."

"Captain Guang Biao, you shouldn't go overboard! This is an academy — a place for cultivating students. Which of your lot *hadn't* graduated from an academy? I will not hand over the people you seek. If you have the ability, then activate your mecha and step over my dead body. Otherwise, don't think of taking one step into Eastsea Academy."

And the students of the academy — the students who grumbled at Long Hengxu's assemblies and his curfews and his weather-report voice — felt their blood boil, and stepped up behind him. Seniors first. Then everyone. And Lin Hao found himself walking forward too, with Xie Xie at his shoulder and Wulin's heat at his back and Gu Yue's silence at his flank, four small bodies adding themselves to the academy's line the way four rivets add themselves to a hull — not because it changes the arithmetic, but because a hull is *made* of rivets.

Guang Biao took one step forward.

The ground *roared.* The whole gate of Eastsea Academy trembled like a struck gong, and the front line of students swayed and went down, and the tremor walked up through Lin Hao's boots and into his hollow bird-bones and the hawk inside him flared—

—and held. Because the man was a Soul Emperor. Six rings. The kind of thing a rank-24 boy measured the way you measure the sea: not in units. *This one isn't ours,* Lin Hao decided, in the calm under the fear, the way you decide a bar is not for today's forge. *This one's the teacher's. Ours is the gate.* He said it aloud, walking volume, without turning his head: "Whatever happens next — nobody past us. Juniors behind. Now." And class five — twenty-two students who had been given a season of reasons to trust the fourth boy's reading — *moved,* and the juniors went behind, and the line held.

"I only believe in strength," Guang Biao was saying, over the ringing stones. "Where is your sense of righteousness, sheltering the culprits who wounded my brother? Since my fist is bigger, I shall go and find those I seek. I'll see who has the ability to stop m—"

"I dislike talking about reasoning the most," said an ice-cold voice from inside the academy. "Talking with our fists is much better."

## Part 3: White Robes and Blue Sword

The spectators felt a blur, and then a person was standing in front of Eastsea Academy.

White chang pao. Coral-blue hair falling down his back. Inky-green eyes that caught the morning and did not warm it. The temperature at the gate dropped several degrees the way a room drops when a window opens onto winter, and Guang Biao — Guang Biao, whose momentum had been a tornado a sentence ago — felt that momentum break apart against something the way a wave breaks against a glacier.

"Teacher Wu. It's Teacher Wu…" The cheer started in class five's corner of the crowd and could not, afterward, be attributed to class five alone.

"Who are you?" Guang Biao's eyes narrowed, rebuilding.

Wu Zhangkong mildly said: "Those four students you are seeking are my students. If you can defeat me, you may proceed. Otherwise, get lost."

He said it the way other men said the time. And Lin Hao — watching from the line he was holding, the Stormbringer very quiet in its sheath, his whole self tuned the way it only tuned for metal and for this — understood, hearing it, that he was not listening to a threat. He was listening to a *statement.* A true sword speaks first, Teacher Wu had told him, nine weeks and a lifetime ago. This was what that meant when the sword had finished growing: the sentence *is* the strike. The rest is paperwork.

"Ha ha ha! Good — I haven't met someone who dared speak to me this way before!" Guang Biao's laugh was a furnace with the door kicked open. Yellow light poured off him — and the rings came: **yellow, yellow, purple, purple, purple, purple.** Six. A Soul Emperor's six. His body expanded a half meter, metal-gray sheen sheeting from forehead to heel, and three spirit souls rose over him — two yellow lizards, identical, and a purple python vast as a moored boat. A thousand-year soul. The crowd of students made the sound of a crowd understanding it was watching history it would get wrong in the retelling.

His momentum formed into a tornado and roared across the gate at the white robes, and everyone at Eastsea Academy felt winter descend—

—and a pale blue flash answered it, and the tornado's fury halved, and then was simply not.

Wu Zhangkong stood in the same spot he had been standing, white robes afloat, right hand raised, and in the hand was a long sword the color of a frozen lake at depth. The tip like an autumn spring; the light along it flowing like a waterfall. White clothes, blue sword, suspended in the air like an immortal — and Lin Hao's breath stopped for the *sword* before it stopped for the man, because the hawk-eyes saw what the crowd could not: the blade was not reflecting the light. The blade was *deciding* it.

Rings of light rose from beneath the hilt — small rings that wandered along the sword's body rather than standing under a man's feet, tool-soul rings — and their colors went through the gate like a sentence through a room. Yellow. Yellow. Purple. Purple.

**Black. Black.**

The air stilled. The sky itself seemed to frost at the edge of the horizon. Ten-thousand-year soul rings — *two* of them — riding a blade held by a man in his twenties, and Guang Biao's tornado-momentum turned to stone, and every soul master in the crowd forgot, together, how to make sound.

Then Wu Zhangkong lowered his head and looked at his own sword, and the last cold thing about him softened. He looked at the Skyfrost Sword the way Lin Hao — Lin Hao, who had watched his father talk to hot metal his whole childhood — recognized with a start like a hand on the heart: the way a smith looks at the first blade he ever folded. *It had been ages since he'd used it,* that look said. *Old friend.*

"Hou!" Guang Biao bellowed — cornered now, two hundred subordinates deep, unable to be seen backing down — and charged, armored body bursting with metallic light, the mountain-fist swinging up at the white robes with everything a six-ring emperor owned.

"Teacher, be careful!" Wulin's shout tore out of the line.

Wu Zhangkong did not move. He rotated his right hand — all six rings vanished from the blade at once — and gently raised the tip, and met the mountain head-on.

*Ding. Ding. Ding. Ding. Ding. Ding. Ding.*

Seven brittle notes. At the first, the tyrant-dragon charge stopped, the way a wave stops at a seawall it has misunderstood. Notes two through seven were scales — Guang Biao's armored scales — flying off his fist, his forearm, his shoulder, one after another, bright as fish in light. Seven notes, seven steps backward, and the onlookers understood, dazed, that they had witnessed one sword stroke wearing seven disguises. And under the ice-qi that had entered him like needles along the veins, Guang Biao found every spark of soul power in his body committed to defense, and his soul skills would not answer, and his martial soul — the Armored Dragon that had carried him from nothing to a city's fear — had gone *quiet,* the way animals go quiet when something older walks into the clearing.

Wu Zhangkong's deep green eyes had turned purple. He thrust.

It was the simplest movement possible. A beginner's thrust. His eyes never left his own blade, from start to finish, and the sword arrived at Guang Biao's chest and the emperor's blood began to freeze — and the purple python, faithful where its master's courage was not, reared and whipped its thousand-year tail at the swordsman's flank to save him—

—and Wu Zhangkong did not dodge. Did not look. An azure light soared along him, and the tail met the light and was *cleanly cut,* and the spirit soul's scream went through the gate like a wire through wax, and its luster dimmed, and the Skyfrost Sword was already past it—

—stopped one inch from Guang Biao's nose.

The cold radiating off that inch was a net of swords, a death-aura laid over the emperor's whole body like a shawl. His palms, raised in the last reflex of a man who had clawed up from nothing, were pierced and frozen the pale blue of the blade.

"Your—" Guang Biao's voice quavered, and it was not the cold doing it. "Your eyes. You're from *that place…*"

"I was expelled from that place," Wu Zhangkong said, indifferently. "The reason was because my temper wasn't good. As such — don't let me see you again."

The blue light vanished. The white robes turned. And the whole area stayed in a silence so complete it was as if everyone's voices had frozen along with the emperor's hands.

## Part 4: What the Gate Remembered

The roar came all at once, the way thaw comes — the entire academy, intermediate and advanced, teachers and gatekeepers, screaming one name that had started as a joke in the girls' rows two years ago and was now the only word the morning had: *Prince Charming! Prince Charming!* And class five stood in the middle of it with twenty-two flushed faces and twenty-two chests improbably high, as though the six rings had been theirs by adoption — which, in the arithmetic of children, they now were.

Up on the teachers' wall, two sisters watched, and neither was cheering.

Ye Yingrong's beautiful eyes were glazed. "Sister," she murmured, "I didn't like his icy looks initially. Although he is handsome, he's like ice. Yet it seems I've fallen for him. He's handsome enough to forget those flaws."

Beside her, the woman who had waited two years for this morning said nothing for a long moment. Ye Yingluo's eyes followed the white robes across the yard with an expression her students would never have believed belonged to her — hunger, and arithmetic, and a wound that had not closed and had just been reopened wider. "Six rings. He really has six rings — two of them *black.* I thought I had a chance at pursuing him. I see now I will never even have my revenge." Her voice dropped to something flat and settled. "From what he showed just now, he could duel and beat a seven-ring Soul Sage. There's no doubt — he is from *that place.*"

"Sister, aren't you too vindictive?"

"No one has ever rejected me. He was the first." Ye Yingluo's beautiful eyes burned with a stubbornness two years old and freshly fed. "He shall pay the price for that. And his *students* are the road to it." She turned from the yard, already composing the match in her head — the dragon, the eagle, the fusion, the grudge — and the class-one teacher's smile, had anyone been watching it, would have kept a sensible person up at night. "Let the tournament finish. I'll take my price on the platform, where he has to watch."

And here is the thing she did not know, and could not have known, and which would have changed her whole plan if she had known it: **she was counting five students, and the class had six.**

In a class without him, her road runs through Xie Xie's speed and Wulin's hands and Gu Yue's weather, and all three of those are things a woman of her rank can predict and price and beat. **She had priced the class.** She had done it that morning, on the wall, while her sister was falling in love, and the arithmetic had come out comfortable.

What she had not priced was a boy who reads a sword the way other people read a face — because that is not a thing you can price until you have seen it, and the only people in the yard who had seen it were the five students who had stopped being surprised by it, and Wu Zhangkong, who had stopped being surprised by it two years before he met any of them.

**She would find out at the tournament, in front of four hundred people, and the finding-out would cost her more than the rejection had.** That is the butterfly, and nobody in the yard — least of all her — could see it from where they were standing.

Across the yard, on the stones where his tornado had died, Guang Biao stood frozen for over ten minutes, while the chill walked slowly out of his body and his pulse remembered its job. When his hands finally unclenched, blood dripped from the frozen piercings in both palms.

*That guy is terrifying. He is definitely no nobody.*

"Captain — what about us?" one of his lieutenants muttered, hand on a soul device. "Shall we activate the mecha?"

Guang Biao's backhand sent the man staggering. "Bullshit! If you want to die, don't drag me along. Wiping away today's matter is already difficult — activate the mecha at a *school,* and do you think any of us survive the Administrative Department? Go. Go back." And he stood a moment longer over his brother's stretcher, and something in the set of his shoulders — for anyone who could read that language, which included one boy by a gate who read metal and men the same way — was not rage. It was guilt. A poor family, two gifted sons, money for one. A brother pushed past his window and into the lanes, and an elder's purse behind every jar he broke. *That was why the lanes had a Guang Long.* That was why the gate had a Guang Biao.

Lin Hao filed that too. The shelf did not complain.

A wave of ice-cold soul power swept the four of them off the yard and set them, upright and unruffled, at their own dormitory door.

"Return and continue training," said Wu Zhangkong, icy as usual, already walking away.

"Teacher — aren't you going to blame us?" Wulin called after the white robes, because it had been their fight that morning started.

Wu Zhangkong gave him a glance over one shoulder. "Did all of you do anything wrong? Why would I blame you?" And then, flatly: "You are not allowed to leave the Academy at night anymore. Rest days included." The white robes went on. And then, without turning — the voice dropping one degree, aimed now not at a class but at a single student who had spent the whole fight watching a blade instead of a battle, and who had been *seen* doing it: "Lin Hao. You watched the sword, not the fight."

"Yes, teacher."

"Then tell me what you saw."

Lin Hao considered the nine weeks of homework in his arms — the servant's sword, the crutch of the eyes, the sentence his blade was too polite to finish. "The second strike was decided before the first one landed," he said. "The seven notes weren't seven strikes. They were one strike, and six of them were the *door.* And you never looked at him once. You looked at your sword — because your sword already knew where he was." He paused, and added, because the smith in him could not leave the truest part unsaid: "You didn't defeat him, teacher. You *answered* him. He just wasn't the question your sword was asking."

The white robes stopped. For one held moment, the back of the Icily Arrogant Prince Charming stood very still in the corridor.

"Then stop making your sword wait," Wu Zhangkong said, and was gone.

In room eleven, Xie Xie gripped Wulin's arm and would not, for several minutes, be embarrassed about the trembling. "I'm not cold — I'm *excited.* Did you feel it? The moment Teacher Wu drew his sword, it was as though the surroundings changed — the world froze with its appearance! That's an expert. A *true* expert. It would be amazing if I could be that powerful one day."

"Then we should quickly get back to meditating," Wulin said, slapping the hand away. "You've been sitting at rank twenty for a year — don't you know how to work hard?"

"Weren't *you* excited?"

"Yes. What good does it do me? Teacher Wu trained slowly up to where he is. We can only train hard as well."

In room twelve, Lin Hao lay on his narrow bed with his arms full of a sword that had not been drawn all morning and had never, he understood now, mattered more. Because he had seen it — the finished shape of the thing he was becoming. Not the rings. Not the ten thousand years. The *attention:* a man who had condensed his whole spiritual sea into one edge and then trusted it absolutely, the way the sky trusts its own weather. Wu Zhangkong's sword did not read and wait. Wu Zhangkong's sword did not even read. It *spoke,* and the world arranged itself around the sentence — and somewhere between the seventh note and the frozen nose, Lin Hao had understood what his own homework actually was.

Not to make the Stormbringer faster. Not to make it sharper.

To make it *certain.*

On the far water, the hawk watched the last of the frost leave the air above the yard, and turned once on its perch — not toward the harbor tonight, but toward the dormitory wing where the white robes had gone, and then, slowly, toward the boy. As if to say: *that* is a bird worth flying after. As if to say something else, which it did not, because the question between them was still the only language they shared, and it was, tonight, very nearly a conversation.

Tomorrow was class one. At the top of the ladder, a dragon waited, and an eagle, and a fusion that had made a sound the reference books had never described — and behind them all, in a teacher's cool office at the front of the building, a woman with a two-year wound was sharpening something that had nothing to do with swords.

The worst class in the grade slept like soldiers. Two of them, in the dark, smiled.


Rank twenty-six came in the week after the lane, and it came the way everything came to him now — bought. He had been hit by a rank twenty-seven with two lizard souls and had lived, and his soul had filed the whole of it, and the filing cost a rank to store.

The hawk, eight hundred years old and heavier in him than it had been before the lane, did not comment. It never did.

## Part 1: The Weld

The idea came to Lin Hao the way forge ideas came — not as a thought, but as an itch in the hands.

He found Wulin still awake, because Wulin was always still awake, the slate on his knees glowing with class-one arithmetic: *the dragon goes spectral a quarter at a time. The eagle folds over him. The fusion made a sound. Do not let them touch.* And Lin Hao sat down on the other bed and said, "That last line's wrong."

"It's the whole plan."

"It's half a plan. 'Don't let them touch' assumes we can keep three drilled two-rings apart for a whole match on a platform the size of a dinner table." He turned the slate around with one finger and drew, over Wulin's careful lines, the thing his hands had been itching to say since the gate — since the seven notes, since the two strokes, since a teacher had told him his sword needed to learn certainty. "They have a fusion skill. We've *seen* it eat a three-ring combination. Tomorrow we fight it. And the grade's entire strategy is *don't let them touch.*" He tapped the slate. "So I say we stop guessing what a fusion is, and go find out what one *feels* like. From the inside."

Wulin stared at him. "You want to *test* for fusion compatibility. Us. Tonight."

"Martial soul fusion happens when two souls are compatible enough to speak with one voice — Xie Xie told us that himself, the night of the scales; the boy reads a battle book like other people eat candy." Lin Hao shrugged. "Tests cost nothing. Two souls released, close, soul power circulated — the books say compatible souls *resonate.* And if we feel what resonance is — the seam where two voices become one — then tomorrow, when the eagle folds over the dragon—"

"—you want to know where the weld is," Wulin said slowly, "so you can break it."

"A weld is just two pieces of metal that agreed to be one piece." Lin Hao held up his hand, thumb and forefinger a hair apart. "Father taught me to break them the same way you make them: heat, timing, and the seam. You don't pry a weld apart. You *interrupt* it — before it cools." He let the silence hold a moment, and then said the other half, the quieter half, in the voice he kept for the file Wulin was the only other keeper of: "And there's something else. My soul *adapts,* Wulin. It adapted to a ninety-year hawk until the compatibility wasn't a number anymore — it was a *person,* living in my spiritual sea, thinking with me. If it can do that with a soul spirit…" He spread his hands. "Maybe it lifts numbers that are supposed to be fixed. Maybe any of us — you and me, me and Xie Xie — maybe we're standing on compatibility we've never measured. Or maybe—"

"Or maybe?"

"Or maybe it gives results the books don't have a name for."

Wulin looked at him for a long moment — the look of a boy who had watched that particular soul do unnamed things to a scale of gold — and swung his legs off the bed. "Let's wake the dagger."

Xie Xie did not need waking; Xie Xie had been lying awake *hoping.* He arrived in four seconds flat with his dagger already out and the fusion-skill speech already assembled ("—do you know what it *means* if we have one? There is NO ONE in Eastsea City—"), and Gu Yue arrived in the doorway behind him with her robe over her arm and her expression packed for refusal.

"What," she said, "is happening."

"Testing!" Xie Xie sang. "For fusion! You and me first—"

"No."

The flatness of it stopped even Xie Xie. Gu Yue did not refuse things. Gu Yue *selected* things, and refusal was simply the sound a selection made. "I'm watching," she said, and sat on the windowsill like a cat that had chosen its evening, "but I am not releasing my soul into a — experiment." Her eyes went, for one unreadable instant, to Lin Hao, and away.

Lin Hao filed the look without examining it. Examining was for later; the shelf was for now.

They went down to the training yard because rooms had ceilings and ceilings had opinions, and the yard was empty except for the lamps and, it developed, their teacher — because Wu Zhangkong lived on their floor, and Wu Zhangkong heard everything on their floor, and the white robes were already standing under the far lamp with the expression of a man deciding between punishment and curiosity and arriving, as always, at neither.

"Fusion compatibility testing," he said, coldly, before anyone had spoken. "The night before the largest match of your lives."

"The night *before* is exactly right," Lin Hao said. "Tomorrow we fight a fusion. Tonight I'd like my sword to have met one."

Something moved behind the ice — not warmth; *interest,* which was colder. "Proceed," said Wu Zhangkong, and folded his arms under the lamp, and watched the way a man watches metal he intends to judge.

Xie Xie went first, because Xie Xie went first at everything. The Light Dragon Dagger came out singing — that thin bright note — and the Stormbringer answered it the way the Stormbringer answered everything, wind rising along the blade in a lazy silver ribbon, and the two boys stood a meter apart circulating soul power the way the books said, and for six breaths nothing happened at all.

And then the notes *met.*

It was not loud. It was the opposite of loud — a thinning, a clarification, the way a room goes quiet when two people start speaking the same language. The dagger's light leaned. The sword's lightning leaned back. Where the two leaned, the air between the blades developed a *grain,* fine as hair, running from hilt to hilt, and Xie Xie's eyes went enormous.

"I feel that," he whispered. "Wulin, I *feel* that—"

"I can see it," Wu Zhangkong said from under the lamp, and his voice had lost its tribunal tone entirely. He crossed to them in two strides and stood inside the resonance the way a smith stands close to a forge, reading. "Sword and light-attribute tool soul. Non-kin, non-elemental-match." A pause with ice in it. "You two are standing in a doorway that should not exist. Children your age, souls your age — this grain should not be possible."

"Is it a fusion?" Xie Xie breathed.

"It is a *door,*" Wu Zhangkong said. "Not the room. Your soul power couldn't open it if you both burned it to the wick — a fusion skill takes years of joint cultivation and a spiritual power you do not have." His smoky green eyes went from Xie Xie to Lin Hao and stopped, and stayed a beat too long. "Compatibility is supposed to be fixed at awakening. It is a number written in the soul." Another beat. "Some souls, apparently, edit."

The blade went back into the air before the sentence finished landing, and the wind went back to being wind, and Lin Hao stood very still with his heart doing forge-work, because the teacher had just said *edit* in the tone of a man filing something away forever.

Wulin went next.

The Bluesilver Grass rose gold-veined in the lamplight, and the Stormbringer came up beside it, and Lin Hao — who had expected the grass to lean, because wind and grass were the oldest conversation there was — felt instead the sword go *heavy* in his hand, the way a compass goes heavy over a buried keel.

The resonance did not form. Something else did.

The hawk-eyes, running as they always ran, saw the grain appear — but not between the blades. It ran *lower,* along the ground between their feet, and where it crossed under Wulin it did not thin or clarify; it *spiked,* bright and sudden, in four places up the other boy's body — wrist, shoulder, spine, sternum — like nails of light driven where no martial soul grew. The grass was silent. The *seals* were answering. And under Lin Hao's sleeve the Goldsong writhed against Wulin's wrist in a panic its owner caught and smothered with a fist, and on the far water inside Lin Hao the seven-hundred-and-sixty-year hawk went absolutely, completely still — the stillness of a bird that has seen the shape of something the sky does not have a name for.

"*Enough.*"

Wu Zhangkong's voice came down like a portcullis, and the test died, and the yard was just a yard. The teacher stood between the two of them now, facing neither, his expression the closed door it had been all year. "Testing is concluded for tonight. All of you. Dormitories." And then, to the yard at large, or to the night, or to whatever he kept his own files in: "A compatibility reading is a measure of two martial souls." A silence with frost on it. "I did not just take a measure of two martial souls."

Nobody answered that, because there was nothing to answer it with. On the walk back, in the corridor's last dark stretch, Wulin's hand found Lin Hao's shoulder and squeezed once, hard — the brother-signal, the *I saw you see it* — and neither of them said a word, because the file was full and the words didn't fit, and tomorrow there was a dragon to break.

"You and Xie Xie," Wulin said at his door, very quietly. "That was real."

"That was real," Lin Hao agreed.

"And whatever mine was—"

"Is yours," Lin Hao said. "And it answered me. That's all I'm saying, and all I'm filing." He met his brother's eyes. "The books don't have a name for it. So we'll keep it until they do."

## Part 2: The Dark Eagle Dragon

The stands on the final morning were not stands. They were a city that had taken the day off.

The grade had done its arithmetic all week — the ten seconds, the twenty-one, the sky that had been walked on, the gate that had been held — and the grade had decided, in the way grades decide, that the worst class in the building was going to climb the last rung in front of everyone. The teachers' platform had a visitor row. Long Hengxu stood at the rail like a man hosting weather. And at the near end of it, alone by a full chair's width on either side, stood Ye Yingluo — pale, immaculate, patient as a drawn blade — watching Wu Zhangkong with an expression she had not bothered to disguise since the gate.

*I'll take my price on the platform, where he has to watch.*

Class one walked out to silence, the way they always did. Wang Jinxi at the point, dark and heavy-jawed, the light leaning away from him in the morning sun like water off oil. Zhang Yangzi at his shoulder, blond, watchful, a boy built like a held breath. And Wei Xiaofeng, the third two-ring, whose martial soul none of class five had ever managed to name and whose face, this morning, had the set of a boy who had been told exactly what he was for.

Class five walked out to noise.

"Begin," said Long Hengxu.

And class one did the thing Ye Yingluo had spent a week preparing, which was not a formation and not a probe. It was an execution schedule.

Wei Xiaofeng went straight at Xie Xie — his soul unnamed, its work plain: something heavy and light-swallowing around his forearms that turned the dagger-boy's speed into a debate he kept losing on points. Zhang Yangzi rose, the Shadow Phantasm Eagle folding out of him in a spill of dark feathers that were somehow also *shadow,* and the sky over the platform became his property. And Wang Jinxi walked toward Wulin the way a decision walks toward an argument, the Bone Dragon King moving under his skin like something under dark water, two yellow rings turning slow beneath him.

"They're not feeling us out," Lin Hao said, at walking volume, the Stormbringer already in his hand, the wind already leaning. "They're spending us. Watch the eagle — he's not hunting, he's *herding.*"

Because that was the shape of it, and it took him three exchanges to be sure: Zhang Yangzi's dives were not attacks, they were walls — each one closing a lane, each one pushing class five's pieces two steps closer together, and Wulin two steps closer to Wang Jinxi, and Xie Xie two steps deeper into Wei Xiaofeng's heavy light, and Gu Yue — Gu Yue standing in her cup of a corner, her hands still, her eyes running the whole geometry—

"Now," she said. "Break their line. Any line. They need us *grouped.*"

Lin Hao broke a line. The Stormbringer took Wei Xiaofeng's next heavy strike on a Gale Talon seam and turned it *up,* into the sky, and the light-swallowing gauntlets came apart in a scatter of startled dark — and in the half-second Wei Xiaofeng spent reassembling, the herding geometry lost its corner, and Zhang Yangzi banked wide to rebuild it—

—and Wang Jinxi and Zhang Yangzi touched.

It happened the way the reference books said and the reference books did not say. The eagle folded over the dragon like a wing over a bone. The two souls *met* — and the sound came, the sound Lin Hao's hollow bones remembered from the scouting morning, less a noise than a *chord struck under the world.* The platform's ward hummed. The stands went white-faced and silent. And where two boys had stood, something long and dark and doubled stood — a dragon with an eagle's architecture, shadow running through its scales like current through water, and two rings and two rings becoming a single turning light that made the four of class five's rings look like candles at a funeral.

The Dark Eagle Dragon moved, and the world's temperature went with it.

"LIN HAO!" Wulin roared, from somewhere under the thing's first sweep.

He was already going.

## Part 3: Breaking the Weld

He had met it before, in a way — he had spent the whole night meeting it. Resonance was a grain. A fusion was a *weld:* two voices agreeing, mid-stride, to be one voice; a seam running the length of the thing where the agreement lived. The hawk-eyes found the seam the way they had found it in the yard — thinner than hair, brighter than the souls on either side of it, running from the eagle's folded wing down through the dragon's shoulder, the place where two souls had shaken hands—

—and the Stormbringer was already speaking, because that was the homework, and the homework was *certainty,* and a true sword did not wait for the world to finish its sentence.

One stroke. No feint. No second thought hedging the first. The Gale Talon laid along the full length of the blade, wind and lightning braided into the edge the way they braided into everything he carried, and the sword went *into the seam* — not into flesh, not into scale; into the handshake.

The world *rang.*

And here is the thing that would not have happened in a yard without him. Class five's plan that morning had been to survive the fusion and lose well — that was the plan Wu Zhangkong had not said and everybody had understood, because class one's trio was the top of the ladder and class five was the worst class in the grade, and arithmetic is arithmetic. **Nobody had planned to break the weld, because nobody in that yard thought in welds.** Lin Hao had spent the whole night thinking in welds, because thinking in the shape of a thing is what he does instead of being afraid of it, and the yard had no way to know that until the seam opened.

That is the whole of it. The butterfly is not that he won. It is that **a fight everybody had already scored became a fight nobody had scored,** and the reason was one boy who reads seams, and the yard did not have him in the arithmetic.

The backlash came up the blade like a struck anvil's voice — soul-fire, the two-ring agreement burning where it had been interrupted — and it bit through the wind-guard into Lin Hao's palm, searing a line from thumb to wrist, and his whole right arm went numb to the elbow with the echo of a strength that was not his and had never been his, and the Stormbringer screamed in a register swords do not have—

—and the Dark Eagle Dragon *stuttered.*

The single voice cracked down the middle. For one heartbeat — one long, shining, bought heartbeat — the fusion was two souls again, an eagle stumbling out of a dragon's outline, a boy and a boy with their hands still touching and their faces wearing the identical expression of men who have felt a conversation they were having be *interrupted in a language neither knew existed.*

"NOW!" Lin Hao's voice broke across the platform, walking volume gone, and class five — drilled by nine weeks, sharpened by three matches, agreed in advance on what each of them was for — spent itself all at once.

Xie Xie took Wei Xiaofeng, and the dagger-boy's speed, freed of the herding, became the thing the grade had been calling weather all term — three touches in the time the gauntlets took to rise, and the third two-ring was on one knee with the Light Dragon Dagger's flat against his ear, hearing his own heartbeat negotiated. Gu Yue's hands finally moved — ice under the eagle-boy's landing, the ground declining exactly three degrees, exactly where a shadow-soul's footing mattered most, and Zhang Yangzi's next step arrived somewhere his body had not agreed to go. And Wulin took Wang Jinxi.

The Bone Dragon King converted — a quarter of himself going spectral, the shoulder and the arm and the ribs turning to dark water so the hammer-fist passed through him like breath through a gate — and Wulin, who had watched him do it twice now and had filed it the way his brother filed things, did not check the swing. He *continued* it, the Bluesilver Grass already woven through the spectral quarter's re-materialization window, the golden-veined vines arriving exactly where solid bone was about to be, and Wang Jinxi reformed *into* a fistful of grass and a hammer's momentum—

—and threw his own counter, the Bone Dragon Claw raking up out of the tangle, dark energy sheeting the talons—

—and Wulin's other fist met it.

Stopped. One inch from the dragon-claw. Held there — not blocked, *held,* the way a man holds a door he has decided about — and in the space of that inch, something passed between the two of them that neither had a file for. Wang Jinxi felt his martial soul — the Bone Dragon King, the top-tier dark dragon that drank light and shrugged hammers — *hum.* Answer. Lean toward the fist the way a compass leans north. And Wulin felt it too, the answering heat surging unbidden up from under his second seal, the gold wanting to rise, the bones in his right arm beginning, faintly, to *sing*—

He closed his fist. Shut the heat down like a furnace door. And let the stopped punch stay stopped, one inch from a dragon's claw, in front of the whole plaza.

"Yield," Wulin said. Quietly. The way you say it to someone you might, in some other arithmetic, have been glad to meet.

Wang Jinxi knelt in the grass with his claw still extended and his soul still humming and his face doing something the Bone Dragon King had never once asked it to do — which was wonder. He looked at the stopped fist. He looked at his own trembling hand. And then he laughed — once, short, bewildered — and lowered the claw.

"Yield," he said. "Class one yields."

## Part 4: The Top of the Ladder

"Class five wins."

Long Hengxu's voice did not need the slate this time. He looked at the platform — at the dark dragon boy kneeling in golden grass, at the eagle boy sitting down in a puddle of his own element, at the third two-ring with a dagger's flat still whispering at his ear, at the four small figures in the middle of the largest silence Eastsea Academy had ever produced — and the director of the academy consulted nothing but the morning, and said it again, slower, as if the words needed settling:

"The tournament is concluded. Class five has defeated every class in the first grade." A pause with the ghost of something in it that forty years of assemblies had never once contained. "As of this moment, you are the first grade's *class one.*"

And the grade came apart. The sound that went up off those stands had no arithmetic in it at all — the worst class, the joke, the back of the building, *on top.* The noise rolled over the platform until even the ward hummed along. Zhou Zhangxi began a song that twenty-two throats finished for him, and somewhere in it Xie Xie was hugging people who had not consented, and Gu Yue was being looked at by four separate teachers with four separate expressions, and Wulin stood very still in the middle of it flexing a right hand that had not, he noticed, entirely stopped singing.

On the teachers' platform, Ye Yingluo did not move for a long time. Her price had been sitting on that platform in the shape of a dark-haired boy and an eagle and a fusion, and a small swordsman with a burned palm had walked into the middle of it and *interrupted* — and the two-year wound had learned, this morning, something new about itself, which was that it could wait. It had waited two years. It was, she decided, turning from the rail with her composure intact and her eyes on the white robes one last time, extremely good at waiting. The price would keep. So would she.

Wu Zhangkong watched her go, and said nothing to anyone, and gave his class — his *first* class now, though no one would ever call it that — no words at all on the walk back. Only, at the dormitory door, as four very loud boys and one very quiet one filed past him into the rest of their lives: one finger, stopping Lin Hao's shoulder for exactly as long as a sentence takes.

"The seam," he said. "You read it last night."

"I read a weld," Lin Hao said. "Last night I just learned what it feels like when two souls decide to be one piece." A beat. "The strike was the homework, teacher. You assigned it."

The ice considered him. "A sword that can interrupt a fusion skill is not a sword," Wu Zhangkong said. "It is an argument." And the faintest possible movement at the corner of the cold mouth. "Make yours better than theirs. Go eat."

And later, on the roof, with the harbor doing its nightly accounting and the whole dormitory still singing two floors down, Lin Hao lay back on the tiles with his burned palm open to the stars — the sear already closing, the AT's hungry furnace eating the wound the way it ate everything — and thought about doors.

A door that should not exist, between a sword and a dagger, standing shut and waiting for years neither of them had yet. A reading with no name in it, four nails of light where no martial soul grew, and a brother's hand on his shoulder in a dark corridor. A dragon's soul that had *leaned* toward a stopped fist. A shelf so crowded the files had begun leaning on each other.

And on the far water, the hawk — who had gone still yesterday before something the sky had no name for, and who tonight was doing something it had never done in the whole of their shared life — was, very slowly, very deliberately, preening. Not the wind. Not the dark. *Him:* the turn of an old bird's head following the boy's breathing, the way a teacher watches a student's handwriting finally, finally come out level.

The question lay under all of it, unchanged, unasked, and tonight — for the first time since it had been asked — Lin Hao did not feel the need to answer it. Because somewhere between the yard and the seam, the wind had begun arriving a half-breath *before* he called it. Not much. Not yet. Just enough that the line between asking and answering had gone, like the weld's seam, too thin to see — and a boy lay on a roof at the top of a ladder with his whole life still ahead of him, and did not, tonight, know which side of the line he was on.

He slept like a room where someone had pulled up a chair.

And the chair, tonight, was not watching him sleep.

It was watching the *door.*

## Part 1: I Have a Dragon in My Body?

The question had been walking around inside Tang Wulin for nine days before he said it out loud, and when it finally came out, in Wu Zhangkong's office, with the winter light lying across the desk like a ruled page, it came out exactly the way a ten-year-old says the largest thing he owns:

"Teacher Wu. I think — I think I have a dragon in my body."

Wu Zhangkong did not look up from the paper he was writing. "What makes you say that."

Not *don't be absurd.* Not *what nonsense.* The flat grammar of the question was its own kind of answer, and Wulin — who had rehearsed this speech for nine days and lost the whole of it in the doorway — simply held out his right arm and let the gold answer for him. It came when he called it now, which was new: a single scale rising through the skin of his wrist like a coin through water, holding the lamplight the way coals hold heat. And beside him, because a brother does not stand outside a door like this one alone, Lin Hao watched their teacher's brush stop.

"The scales started small. Months ago. One, then gone." Wulin's voice had gone into the register he kept for forge-true things. "Then the lane. My eyes went — I don't know what they went. The man's arm broke like it wanted to break. And at the tournament, when I stopped my fist next to Wang Jinxi—" he flexed the hand, the one that had not entirely stopped singing, "—something in me *answered his soul,* Teacher. His dragon leaned at me like — like it knew me. Grass doesn't do that. Goldsong doesn't do that. So. I have a dragon in my body."

The brush stayed stopped for a long moment. Then Wu Zhangkong set it down, and looked at Xie Xie — who had come because Xie Xie went where the interesting went, and was for once in his life entirely silent — and at Lin Hao, and his smoky green eyes took the inventory of the room the way they took the inventory of a sparring circle: exits, threats, and students.

"What I am about to say leaves this room in none of you," he said. "Three facts. First: I do not know what it is. I have watched you since you were a Bluesilver Grass boy with a hammer, and I have seen it now with my own eyes — and heard the rest of it from a boy who does not lie to me — and I do not know what it is. Anyone who tells you they know is selling you something." He turned the paper he had been writing face down. "Second: it is powerful. The things that break men's arms at your age are not martial souls. Martial souls wait for your cultivation. This does not wait. It grows on its own schedule, it answers to feeling before it answers to you, and one day it will be stronger than you are — that is not a fear, it is arithmetic." A beat. "Third, and the only one that matters: power is not identity. A dragon in your body does not make you a dragon. A hammer in your hand does not make you a hammer." His eyes went to Linhao's sheathed sword, and back. "You are the one who decides what the thing inside you is *for.* Every day. That is the whole of cultivation, and the whole of being a man, and adults fail at it constantly. Control it — or be controlled. There is no third option that lasts."

"And if I can't control it?" Wulin asked, quiet. "If it comes out when I'm — when I'm not me?"

"Then you will owe someone an apology, and they will owe you a broken arm, and you will both be older." Wu Zhangkong picked up his brush again, which was, class five had learned, the interview over. And then, without looking up, in the coldest voice that was somehow also the opposite of cold: "But you have a brother who hears your spiral change pitch in a dark room. And a captain's sense. And — despite everything — a habit of stopping your fist one inch short." The brush moved. "Go and train the stopping. The rest of it is not yours yet."

Out in the corridor, Xie Xie exhaled like a kettle. "That was the most terrifying speech I have ever been included in."

"He told you how to live," Lin Hao said, "and then he made it homework." He was smiling a little, but his eyes were somewhere else — on the file, the shelf, the fourth nail of light where no martial soul grew, the reading his teacher had taken and never once spoken of again. *Three facts,* he thought. *He gave you three facts and kept four.*

He did not say that out loud either. The shelf was getting very good company.

## Part 2

The marks on his forearms were still coming and going at that point, faint in the morning and darker after work, and he had taken to wearing long sleeves at the Association without anyone asking him to.
: The Letter

It came four days later, in the evening post, in a hand like roots growing downhill.

Wulin read it twice in the lamplight of room eleven, and the second time his thumb went — Lin Hao saw it — to the underside of his wrist, where the gold lived.

"Old Tang?"

"Old Tang." Wulin folded the letter with the care he folded everything. "He wants me home. Glorybound, as soon as the academy releases me." He was quiet a moment. "He doesn't say why. Old Tang never says why. He says—" and here Wulin's voice did the thing it did when it was holding both a smile and a worry, "—he says, 'the water in your cup is rising, and you are drinking from it like a man who has never seen a well. Come home. There are things a spiritual guide must see with his own eyes, and things a boy must swallow that taste worse than they are.' That's all. That's the whole letter."

*A spiritual guide.* Lin Hao let the two words sit. Old Tang — the presence that had lived in Wulin's life the way weather lives in a valley, never named in any official anything, never explained, known to the family the way the family knew gravity — was asking for the boy. And Lin Hao, who had spent a year learning which silences in his brother were empty and which were full, had no trouble at all identifying this one. This silence was full. Something was happening in Wulin — the scales, the singing hand, the answer to the dragon's soul — and whatever Old Tang was, he had felt it from Glorybound City, the way you feel a storm change the well-water before the storm arrives.

"I'll go," Wulin said, to the room, to himself, deciding. "Teacher Wu will release me; I'll ask tomorrow. It's — I don't know how long. Weeks, he says. The Association keeps my Fridays; Mu Chen will curse me and keep them." He looked at Lin Hao, and the worry and the smile both came up into his face together, which was the face Lin Hao had known since they were six. "Hao. The class — the rematch talk, the platform sessions, whatever's coming — you hold it. All of it. You're the one who reads first."

"You'll miss my readings. You'll have to think for yourself."

"I've been thinking for myself since I was nine, you *barometer,* I just let you enjoy—" The argument went on for twenty minutes, which is what arguments between brothers sound like when both of them are, underneath, saying *come back whole.*

He left on the morning boat, and Lin Hao stood on the seawall and watched the ferry shrink, and gave him the thing he had made.

It was small. That was the point. A band for the wrist — forged over three Fridays from the offcuts of his own commissions, spirit steel folded eleven times, which was four more folds than the work needed and exactly the number his hands had wanted to give it. No ornament. No gem. Just the steel, dark as a harbor at night, with one hairline seam running its circuit that caught the light like a held breath — a deliberate seam, a *told* one, the way a smith signs a blade for the one person who will read it.

"It remembers its shape," Lin Hao had said, closing it around his brother's wrist — the left one; the right one belonged to the file. "Eleven folds. If you ever forget what you're made of — and everyone forgets, that's what the furnace weeks are for — you hold this and you remember that something folded you eleven times on purpose."

Wulin had not said anything clever. Wulin had hugged him like a vise and nearly cracked a rib, which is what Wulin did instead.

On the far water, the hawk watched the boat go south with an attention Lin Hao felt in his own sternum — not the stillness it kept for the gold, not the preening it kept for him; something older, the way a bird watches weather it has crossed before. He filed that too. He was running out of shelf, and beginning, without deciding to, to suspect that this was what his life *was.*

## Part 3: The Second Ring

Wulin had been gone eleven days when Xie Xie broke.

And the reason it broke in a yard instead of in a room, where nobody would have heard it, was that Lin Hao had been crossing that yard at that hour every day for eleven days, because Xie Xie trained at that hour and Lin Hao had started crossing the yard at that hour without ever deciding to.

**In a yard without him, Xie Xie breaks alone, in a room, at night, and comes back the next morning with the second ring and a face that does not match, and nobody ever knows what it cost.** That is what happens in a story where nobody is watching. Xie Xie is a person who performs, and a person who performs does not break in front of an audience, so in a yard without him the breaking goes underground and stays there.

**In a yard with him in it, Xie Xie breaks in front of the one person in the grade who has never once needed him to perform.** And that is the whole butterfly — not that Lin Hao did anything. He did not do anything. He was crossing a yard. **But he had been crossing it at that hour for eleven days without deciding to, and Xie Xie broke where somebody could hear it, and that is the only reason anybody ever knew.**

Lin Hao heard it before Xie Xie knew it — the way he had heard rank fourteen in a dark room months ago, because the ears that read spirals do not clock out. He was crossing the yard after the Association shift when the air over the training ground went *taut,* the particular tautness of a vessel a hand's width from its limit, and he was already walking faster, because he knew whose spiral that was, and he knew — the way the smith knows the color a bar throws the quarter-second before it cracks — that the dagger-boy was on the far side of rank twenty and climbing a wall with his bare hands.

He arrived as the second ring came up out of the ground.

It is not in the books, because almost no one is standing close enough to a soul when its rank-wall breaks. The yellow ring that had been under Xie Xie's feet since enrollment — the hundred-year soul his family's money had bought, the single ring that had capped him at rank twenty for a year and made him vicious about it — stayed exactly what it was. Rings do not change their color; that is the first law of them. The color is the soul's age on the day they met, and it stays that way forever. But *under* the old ring, new light was gathering, climbing — and then it set, the way poured steel sets, and the yard had a two-ring Soul Grandmaster in it, age ten, and the air let go of its tautness all at once, and Xie Xie stood in the middle of it all with his mouth open.

And the Light Dragon Dagger in his hand — released, singing, spinning its thin bright note — grew one circle smaller and one degree more *solid,* the lines along the blade sharpening into something that stopped looking like a weapon and started looking like a *fact.*

"My soul," he said. "It's *denser.* Father bought it at a hundred years — a hundred years, do you know what that cost? — and I've been swinging it at everything that moved for a year, and it got *denser.* The ring came thick. Do souls *do* that?"

"They do when they're fed," Lin Hao said. He was grinning; he had not decided to start. "Nine weeks of special training, three tournament matches, a fusion door, and a summer of you swinging it at everything that moved. Your father bought a hundred years, Xie Xie. You *earned* whatever's past it." And that was true — and it was also, he knew, the same law that had taken a ninety-year hawk to seven hundred and sixty: souls grew in tandem with the hands that used them. His brother's friend had simply been used *magnificently.*

"Test it," Xie Xie said immediately, because Xie Xie said immediately. "Now. You. Full kit. I want to know what two rings *is.*"

And Lin Hao — who had spent eleven days holding a class, answering a rematch letter's paperwork, watching a shelf, and missing his brother like a missing tooth — drew the Stormbringer, and felt the grin go from his face into his *hands,* and thought, *yes. This. This is the part I'm for.*

They went eleven minutes, and the yard collected.

Two rings was real. That was the first thing the sword learned: the dagger-boy's soul power had thickened past its rank the way the blade had thickened past its size — every meeting of steel came back up Lin Hao's arm with more behind it than rank twenty had ever carried, and the speed — the speed had always been the weapon — now had *weight* riding under it. Xie Xie took the center line twice. He turned a Gale Talon ribbon with the flat of the dagger the way a man turns a page, and once — once, and the yard would talk about this one for a term — he stepped *inside* a Wind-Step, not chasing it, *arriving,* and laid the flat of the Light Dragon Dagger across Lin Hao's ribs with a note like a struck glass.

It did not hurt much. It counted enormously.

"First blood," Xie Xie panted, circling, two rings burning under him like twin moons. "First. Blood."

"Noted," Lin Hao said, and stopped being polite.

He ended it the way he ended things now — with the homework. Not speed against speed; the sword against the *pattern:* three exchanges spent reading where the two new rings had changed the old rhythm (they had changed where Xie Xie *breathed,* which had changed where he committed, which was the whole of it), and then one stroke laid exactly where the dagger-boy's next step was already promised — the Stormbringer's flat resting against Xie Xie's throat a half-breath before Xie Xie arrived, the way a door waits for a man who has lived in the house his whole life.

"Yield," Lin Hao said, at walking volume, and the yard made its noise, and Xie Xie yielded — grinning like a struck bell, absolutely undefeated in his own opinion, which was the only opinion he had ever consulted.

Afterward, sitting on the yard wall with their shoulders touching, watching the winter come off the harbor, Xie Xie said, "When Wulin gets back, we're going to be *monsters.* You know that, right? A two-ring dagger and a whatever-rank-you and a forge that walks. We're going to walk into that rematch and they're going to wish they'd stayed class one."

Lin Hao watched the gulls. The rematch letter had come six days ago — on cream paper, in a hand like a drawn blade, with the class-one seal pressed into it hard enough to bruise the fiber: *Class two — formerly class one — requests the honor of a second meeting. The platform. The full roster. Let the teachers watch.* And under it, in the smaller script of the petition's sponsor, one line Long Hengxu had read to Wu Zhangkong with the expression of a man watching two weather systems introduce themselves: *—with the regards of Ye Yingluo.*

"They'll be there," Lin Hao said. "They've been sharpening since we beat them."

"Good," said Xie Xie, and spun the dagger — one ring's worth of habit, two rings' worth of light — and caught it. "So have I."

## Part 4: Tang Wulin Returns

He came back on the evening boat, twenty-three days after he had left, and Lin Hao was on the seawall before the gangplank was down, because the hawk had been restless all afternoon in a way that had nothing to do with weather.

The boy who came up the gangplank was the same height. That was the first wrongness, and Lin Hao's eyes went through the rest of the inventory before they shook hands: the same face, the same terrible coat, the steel band on the left wrist worn bright at the seam from a thumb that had clearly found it often. But he stood a half-degree differently, the way a furnace stands after it has been relined — the same footprint, more *inside.* His skin had gone the particular density Lin Hao had seen once before on hot metal that looked cold. And when Wulin laughed at something the boatman said — the same laugh, same key — the air over the seawall *warmed,* faintly, locally, the way it warms over a banked forge at three in the morning.

"You're different," Lin Hao said, instead of hello, because they had never once been the kind of brothers who started with hello.

"There was a storm." Wulin's smile did not entirely reach the new steadiness in his eyes. "Where I was — Old Tang's — there was a week of it, and I was inside the week, and then I came out the other side." He looked down at his right hand, and opened it, and closed it. The gold did not come. But Lin Hao's hawk-eyes saw it — *of course* they saw it: the veins under the skin of that hand had gone a shade deeper, finer, laid in a pattern that no anatomy had ever put in a boy, and behind the sternum where the first seal's furnace lived there was now — nested inside it, curled in it, asleep in it — a *second* heat. Not a seal. Something the seals were keeping. Something the storm week had *nested deeper* — the gold that had first surfaced in a gray bedroom and torn through a beef lane now folded down past the first seal, waiting, very patiently, to be needed.

Lin Hao said nothing about any of it. He took his brother's bag instead, which was heavier than bags used to be, and asked the only question the shelf allowed: "Old Tang?"

"Saw what he needed to see." Wulin's voice went careful, the way it did at file boundaries. "Gave me what he said I'd need to swallow. Tastes worse than it was, he was right about that." A pause, and then, because he was Wulin, and because a brother is not a shelf: "Hao. If — when — it comes out again. The gold. I think I can bring it *back* now. I think I can decide." His jaw set, eleven-folds set. "And if I ever can't — you'll know before I will. That's your whole job. You hear me coming."

"That's been my whole job since we were six," Lin Hao said. "You're just now making it official."

They walked up through the town in the blue dark, and Wulin ate four meat buns on the way, and described absolutely nothing about the storm week — but he described the harbor, because the harbor was the other thing he had done with his twenty-three days. "I walked the notice-line every morning. The fish-wife at the end of the pier keeps ours up — she oils the paper; she says the girl's face deserves better weather than the rest. Two are gone; the rain took them. And one boatman swore he saw a girl like the picture on a southbound freighter two years ago." He shrugged — the shrug of a boy who has learned what hope costs and pays anyway. "It's nothing. It's always nothing. But the line's still up, and the fund's still funded, and somebody down that coast is going to remember something on a day we can't guess. That's the whole plan. It's a slow plan." *That's the whole plan,* Lin Hao thought — *for both of us* — and said nothing, because the shelf had learned that some files travel better in company than in speech. And at the dormitory gate the notice board wore its new paper like a flag:

**FIRST GRADE — INTER-CLASS CHALLENGE, SANCTIONED. CLASS ONE vs CLASS TWO — formerly class one, demoted by the ladder they lost. Full roster. Third morning. Director Long Hengxu refereeing. Faculty in attendance.**

And under it, smaller, the kind of addition a posting-master makes when a teacher has leaned over his shoulder and dictated one line and meant every degree of its cold:

**Wu Zhangkong, attending.**

Wulin looked at the board for a long time. The steam went off his fourth bun in the winter air, and something behind his sternum — the nested heat, the thing the storm week had made — turned over once in its sleep, the way a dog turns when the house it guards is touched.

"They want the platform," Wulin said quietly. "And the teachers. And a second meeting." He finished the bun. "They must have missed us."

"They missed losing," Lin Hao said. He was looking at the small script of the petition's sponsor in his mind, the hand like a drawn blade, the two-year wound that had learned to wait. His sword-arm itched, which it had not done since the fusion's seam. "Xie Xie crossed a hundred years while you were gone. Two rings. He's been feeding on spite and protein."

"Good," said Tang Wulin, and the gold under his skin did not show, and did not need to. "Then we'll be monsters. Together."

Third morning. The platform. And somewhere across the city, in a cool office, a woman with a two-year patience folded a copy of the sanction notice into her desk, and waited for the morning she had been promised.


Rank twenty-seven arrived quietly, in the third week, after the second ring. Not from the ring — the ring was the gate, not the fuel. The fuel was eight weeks of a monster for a sparring partner and a man with a pointing stick who had begun, without saying so, to aim at him differently.

The hawk was eight hundred and fifteen years old that week. He noticed it the way he noticed the weather — because it had changed, and because the change had a direction.

## Part 1: The Third Morning

The stands were full before the sun cleared the harbor, which had not happened for any match in the memory of the posting-master, and the faculty row on the reviewing platform wore an expression the students had never seen on teachers: the look of people who had read the same reports and arrived at the same arithmetic.

Long Hengxu read the sanction in his weather-report voice. *Class one versus class two — formerly class one, demoted by the ladder they lost. Full roster. Rules of the Class Promotion Tournament. Referee: the Director.* And then, because the ink on the second page had been pressed hard enough to bruise the fiber, he read the attendance line, and did not look at anyone while he did: *Faculty in attendance. Wu Zhangkong. Ye Yingluo.*

They stood at opposite ends of the reviewing platform the way two weather systems stand in one sky. Ye Yingluo in her best coat, composed as a sealed letter, two years of patience folded into her sleeves. Wu Zhangkong in white, hands behind his back, watching his students the way he watched everything: entirely, and without asking them to notice.

Class two walked out first — formerly class one, wearing the demotion the way some men wear insults: openly, and with interest — and the grade saw three weeks of a teacher's price had been spent on them. Wang Jinxi at the point, both arms whole, the right one moving heavier than the tournament, the way an arm moves when its owner has been thinking with it for three weeks. Zhang Yangzi at his shoulder, watchful, the eagle's stillness in his posture. Wei Xiaofeng third, and the stands that remembered the tournament noticed the smugness was gone from him, replaced by something drilled.

Class five — class one — walked out to a noise that was not cheering. It was the sound of a city holding a breath it had been holding for three weeks.

"They studied us," Lin Hao said quietly, at the line, his eyes walking the other formation the way they walked a weld. "All of them. Wei Xiaofeng is standing a full step behind where his arrogance used to put him. Zhang Yangzi's weight is on his back foot — he's not planning to fly first. And Wang Jinxi—" he paused, because Wang Jinxi was looking exactly where the sentence said, straight at Wulin, with an expression that was not the hate the stands were hoping for and not the wonder of the tournament platform either, but something in between that had been sleeping badly. "Wang Jinxi's been thinking about you for three weeks."

"Good," Wulin said. "So have I."

"Here's the doctrine." Lin Hao's voice dropped to the forge register, and three heads came in, because nine months of being read correctly had built the habit of listening. "They lost to the seam-break. They've had three weeks with that fact. So the seam will be the bait — something about that fold will be a lie, and I will *want* to strike it, because wanting is what I do. So: nobody trusts the fold. Not even me. Xie Xie — Wei Xiaofeng is yours, and his clones are a curtain; curtains hide doors. Gu Yue — Wulin's back, until the arithmetic says otherwise, and *you* decide when it says otherwise. Wulin — Wang Jinxi. The mountain's yours."

"And you?" Xie Xie asked.

"I'll be where the lie is," Lin Hao said, and drew.

"Begin," said Long Hengxu.

## Part 2

There was a lock of storm-gray at his left temple now, and it had a sheen to it that the rest of his hair did not have, and when he walked the hair in it moved a half-second after the rest. Xie Xie had noticed it a week ago and said nothing, which was how Lin Hao knew he had noticed.
: The Lie

Wei Xiaofeng moved first, and the stands learned what three weeks of humiliation teaches.

His first ring lit and his body went *unreal* — the Green Shadow Snake's skill unfolding like a hand of cards: phantoms pouring off him in a revolving crown, each one a perfect Wei Xiaofeng, illusory air shimmering at the edges, the real body lost among his own copies the way a fish is lost in a river of itself. He did not attack Xie Xie. He *enveloped* him — the curtain of himself rolling across the platform's west side, taking the dagger-boy's fight exactly where the geometry wanted it: far.

"Wu Zhangkong taught me," Xie Xie had said once, bragging, that if you can't analyze a trick you hit it with everything you have — and he did, the golden blade of the two-ring Light Dragon Dagger carving arcs through the phantoms, scattering them like starteled birds. But the curtain did not thin. It herded. And on the east side, under the covering noise of a hundred fake footfalls, the real fight opened.

Wulin took Wang Jinxi head-on, because that was the mountain's assignment and because neither of them knew any other way to have this conversation. The Bone Dragon Claw came down in a wash of black gas, the dark-attribute soul drinking the morning light off its own path — and Wulin's fist met it, and *the ground under Wang Jinxi gave.* He went back three steps. Four. The stands remembered this from the tournament — the impossible strength of the one-ring boy — but this time it was worse, because this time Wulin's open palm flashed *gold* as it turned the second claw, a scale-ridge rising through the knuckles and vanishing inside a heartbeat, and Long Hengxu half-rose from the reviewing platform before he caught himself.

The Bluesilver Whip answered the eagle — Zhang Yangzi's shadow-dive meeting a lash of golden-veined grass that cracked like a mast in a storm and bent his flight path a full body-length off the line — and Gu Yue stood at Wulin's back, the cup that did not spill, fire and ice alternating in her hands with an economy that made the faculty row lean forward without deciding to.

And Lin Hao watched the fold.

It came in the seventh minute. He could not have said afterward what the seam-reader saw first — the eagle banking wide, the dragon's shoulders opening, the two rings and the two rings beginning their slow rotation toward each other, the dark feather-light spilling toward the bone the way it had spilled in the tournament, the way it had spilled in the yard that night the four of them learned what a weld was—

The certainty rose in him like a struck note. *There. The seam. Now.*

The Stormbringer was already moving — the Wind-Step already firing, the Gale Talon already braiding along the edge, the whole unhedged grammar of the homework pouring into one stroke aimed at the handshake between the two souls—

—and the eagle's wings closed on *nothing.*

The dark light guttered. The fold collapsed like a tent without a pole — Zhang Yangzi's shadow snapping back to his shoulders, Wang Jinxi's rings settling, the two of them standing a full platform-width apart, untouched, *unfused,* and Lin Hao's sword arrived at the seam of a weld that had never been lit. A practiced decoy. A three-week lie, rehearsed until it could stand in front of a boy who had never been lied to successfully and *hold his eyes.*

For one half-breath, the seam-reader stood committed in empty air. It was the first time in his life his certainty had been used against him — not beaten, not outrun: *aimed.* And in that half-breath, forty feet west, the curtain of Wei Xiaofeng's phantoms parted like a door.

The Dark Eagle Dragon came through it.

The real fold had happened behind the curtain — hidden by the one place on the platform where eyes were busy — and it did not seek Wulin, or Gu Yue, or the swordsman recovering from his stroke. It crossed the west side in one long dark glide, and it arrived at Xie Xie — mid-swing, weight committed, dagger extended into a phantom — with the multiplied strength of two Soul Grandmasters' souls speaking in a single voice.

Xie Xie saw it. That was the thing the stands never forgot, and the thing Xie Xie himself never let anyone forget: he *saw* it, one step too late to dodge and exactly on time to decide, and he brought both arms up in front of his face with the Light Dragon Dagger still in his right hand, because a dagger-boy blocks with what he has.

The sound was not loud. That was the other thing nobody forgot.

He went out of the air the way the persimmon stall had gone out of the air, and landed against the west rail, and did not get up, and his arms lay at angles that the whole first grade could read, because everyone in the first grade had been taught by the same three weeks.
