## Part 3: Eruption

Gu Yue moved before Lin Hao did.

She had been holding Wulin's back, and the arithmetic — *her* arithmetic, the one she decided — said otherwise now, and what she crossed the platform doing was not running. It was *unfolding.* The elements came out of her the way the sea comes out of a cup when the cup stops pretending: fire and ice side by side in a revolving ring, wind braiding them, earth rising under her feet in stepping-stones that were not there and then were. Under it all — under the fire and the frost, so fast that only hawk-eyes forty feet away caught it at all — one flash of a light that was neither, silver-white and cold as a river under ice, gone before the mind could keep it.

The eruption met the Dark Eagle Dragon broadside.

It did not defeat it. Two rings times two rings, multiplied, was not a thing any one first-grader defeated — the stands would understand that later, in the retelling, when they had calmer hearts. But it *moved* it. The fusion recoiled out of the west rail in a wash of steam and scorched shadow, the single voice staggering into two notes, and Gu Yue stood between it and the broken boy with her ring of elements still turning around her like the dial of something far larger than a girl. Even through the rage and the steam, Ye Yingluo on the reviewing platform went white to the lips — because she was a teacher, and she was watching a student *hold back* inside an eruption, spending exactly as much as revealed exactly as little as she intended.

And Wulin roared.

There is no other word the stands used, afterward, for the sound that came out of the forge-boy. He had seen the arms. He had seen the angle. He had known Xie Xie for a year and heard him brag through every meal of it, and the furnace behind his sternum — the nested heat, the thing the storm week had made and the letter had warned about and the brother had promised to hear coming — took the one key it had ever needed. Was the sight of his friend lying wrong, and *opened.*

A faintly discernible golden ray of light appeared from his body for a split second — and forty feet away, Wang Jinxi's Bone Dragon Claw, rising to guard, immediately slowed, the dark dragon in it flinching from something older than itself. The gold ran up Wulin's right arm: the veins coming alive, the scales rising through the skin in a climbing armor of hammered light, the fingers lengthening into claws, the pupils going to slits, the whole of him suddenly *more* in a way that made the platform's wards hum a note the bones of everyone present felt individually.

The Golden Dragon Claw came down at Wang Jinxi's head.

"STOP!" Long Hengxu and Ye Yingluo shouted out simultaneously — and the shout was arithmetic, not authority: the claw was at full strength, aimed past stopping, and both of them knew in the same instant that neither of them would reach.

A slender arm noiselessly appeared and touched Wulin's right arm, softly pushing it aside.

Gu Yue had already been moving — the eruption's own momentum, the crossing of the platform, the body that had placed itself between a dragon and its second target and was simply *there,* the way she was simply there — and the Golden Dragon Claw that had been heading for Wang Jinxi's head was deflected a hand's width and came down instead on his right claw.

Bang.

Despite being several times bigger than Tang Wulin at that moment, Wang Jinxi was smashed into the ground, while Wulin landed softly on the other side from the counterforce. The black light separated from the transformed body. The two boys inside came back to themselves and released miserable shrieks of pain — Zhang Yangzi on the ground with both legs broken, Wang Jinxi's right arm fractured and bent at an impossible angle, the tail of the fusion's ghost still flickering over them like something reluctant to leave.

"ENOUGH!"

The cold voice rang like the morning bell and the evening drum, and Wulin woke out of the rage the way a man wakes out of a flood — standing, gold dying down his arm, Wu Zhangkong beside him with the injured Xie Xie already gathered in his arms, and a platform full of silence and steam and three broken children.

"Teacher Wu, how can you allow your students to be so *violent?*" Ye Yingluo flew onto the stage, finger pointed, the two-year grudge finally given its sentence—

Wu Zhangkong said to Wulin, "Go." And from beginning to end he did not spare her a glance. She took one step to pursue, and he released a sharp ice-cold aura that froze her whole body where she stood and put the sensation of death in her mouth, and the reviewing platform's other teachers looked suddenly very interested in the horizon.

---

And the thing that changed because he was in the yard — the thing nobody would have had any reason to learn if he had not been standing at the edge of it — was that **Gu Yue erupted at all.** In a yard without him, Wei Xiaofeng's clones get broken by Xie Xie's speed and the morning ends with a lesson about clones. In a yard with him in it, Xie Xie's speed is not enough, because Lin Hao had already told Xie Xie which clone was real two seconds before Xie Xie would have found it himself, and Xie Xie had used the answer instead of finding it, and had therefore never learned the thing he was about to need. **Gu Yue erupted because a boy who reads too well took the lesson away from the person who needed it.**

That is not a small thing and it is not a flattering one, and Lin Hao understood it in the yard and did not say so, and would think about it for a week.

## Part 4: What It Cost

Lin Hao was one breath late, and the one breath lived in his hands.

He had seen it — that was the promise, and the promise had kept its half: he had seen the gold rising under Wulin's sleeve a half-second before the ray, from forty feet, mid-recovery, and he had gone, the Wind-Step firing with everything the Spirit Connection had left — and his right hand had arrived exactly one hand's width behind Gu Yue's, which was already there, which had been closer, which was why the world still had a Wang Jinxi with a head. He knelt now beside Xie Xie with his scabbard and his belt and the splinting hands of a smith who had set his father's broken fingers at eight years old, and his hands would not stop trembling — not with fear, never with fear; with *arithmetic.* The sum of one breath, added and re-added. *You'll know before I will.* He had known. Knowing, it turned out, was the easy half of the promise, and nobody had told him the second half was called *reaching.*

Both forearms, fractured clean. The healer-teacher said it four times like an apology. Xie Xie heard it from under a face the color of paper, grinned with the parts of him that still worked, and said, to the whole infirmary, at full volume:

"Did you *see* me block? Both arms. I blocked a *dragon* with both arms."

"You did," Lin Hao said, tying the sling with steady-enough hands, because the hands had decided that Xie Xie got to have this. "You're the only person in the grade who can say that."

"I'm going to say it at *everyone,*" Xie Xie promised, and fainted gently into the painkillers, mid-brag, which everyone agreed afterward was the most Xie Xie way to have fainted.

Wu Zhangkong stayed. The ice-cold teacher who had carried him off the platform like something breakable and valuable sat in the infirmary chair with his arms folded. "Teacher Wu, I—" Wulin began, because the sentence had been standing in his throat since the platform.

"You don't need to say anymore," Wu Zhangkong said, "as you didn't do anything wrong." A beat. "I will be here."

And Wulin — who had watched that man freeze a teacher and terrify a brigade — discovered that two sentences could rearrange a boy's whole understanding of the word *cold.*

Later, walking back through the dark yard, Gu Yue said the things she had been assembling since the platform. "Zhang Yangzi and Wang Jinxi used a soul fusion skill. They are nearly impossible in this era — it can only appear when two martial souls are exceptionally compatible. It multiplies, it doesn't add." A pause, and then, quieter, the second assembly: "You must learn to control your power. It seems to be very formidable — but such great power requires great control. It seems that during the week you were away, a change occurred in your martial soul."

Wulin was quiet a long moment. "Gu Yue. We're friends, so I don't want to lie to you. But I really can't tell you about it. So — please don't ask. Okay?"

She pondered for a moment, and gave him her reply: "Fine. I won't ask." And then, because she was Gu Yue, and because a girl who held back inside her own eruptions recognized the shape of holding back: "But you must learn to control it. *Before* it decides for you."

In room eleven, with the door shut and the harbor doing its nightly accounting, Wulin sat on the bed with his golden-veined right hand open on his knee, and said the true thing to the only person the true thing belonged to.

"I wasn't me, Hao. For those ten seconds, I wasn't me. If her arm hadn't been there—" his voice cracked on the arithmetic, the same arithmetic, the one breath, "—I would have killed him. A boy who yielded to me three weeks ago. I would have—"

"I know," Lin Hao said. "I saw it coming. That's what I'm *for,* remember? I knew." He sat down on the other bed, facing his brother, and said the rest of it, because a shelf is not a brother: "I ran. I was one breath late. My hands still haven't decided to forgive me." A pause. "So here's the file, and it's the only one that matters: her arm was there *this time.* Next time, one of us has to be faster — you at stopping yourself, or me at reaching you. Both. We train both. Every day. That's the whole plan."

Wulin looked at his hand. Closed it. Opened it. "Every day," he agreed.

On the far water inside him, the hawk had risen when the gold rose — not cowering, not still: *standing,* wings half-open on the wind of its own making, watching the golden thing across the water the way a bird watches weather it knows it will one day have to fly through. And when the gold went down, the great bird folded, slowly, and turned its head toward the boy, and the question between them — *can you see without me?* — lay under everything, unanswered, and for the first time felt less like a question about seeing than a question about *what was coming that they would both need to see.*

In the other wing of the infirmary, Wang Jinxi lay with his arm in a frame of healer's wood and stared at the ceiling. His right hand — the broken one — kept flexing against the splint, because the dragon in him would not stop replaying two things: the hammer-fist it had *answered* on the tournament platform, and the golden claw that its own kind had flinched from. Pride said hate. The bone-deep thing under the pride said *follow,* and had no idea what it meant, and would not stop saying it.

And in the director's office, Long Hengxu sat with the incident reports stacked like a wall — three students badly injured, a fusion skill witnessed, an unnamed golden power witnessed, an elementalist witnessed exceeding every file the academy held on her — and across from him, unreadable as ever, Wu Zhangkong folded his hands and said the sentence that had been waiting all evening:

"Director. Seven children like these should not be kept in separate rooms."

Third morning's post, on the board by the gate, under the results nobody had posted:

**FIRST GRADE — SPECIAL ARRANGEMENT, FORTHCOMING. DETAILS TO FOLLOW. — OFFICE OF THE DIRECTOR.**

The worst class in the grade read it on the way to breakfast, and none of them — not the boy with the sling, not the boy with the golden hand, not the girl who said *fine,* not the swordsman whose hands had finally, at breakfast, decided to forgive him — none of them knew yet that the wall behind that sentence had a number on it, and the number was zero.

## Part 1: The Senior Sister on the Morning Road

Xie Xie was right about one thing, in the end: the arms did not stop Xie Xie. Both forearms in healer's wood and linen, propped on a splint-frame like a small expensive chair for two invalids, and still the dagger-boy was up before the bell, still talking, still insisting that the morning road was doctor's orders.

"Walking is circulation," he said. "Circulation is healing. This is medical."

"This is you not being able to sit still," Wulin said, falling into step beside him anyway, because the morning road had been theirs since the first week of school and a boy with both arms in a chair did not walk it alone. Lin Hao took the other side — the right, where he always was — and the three of them went out through the gate and onto the road that ran the seawall's length, in the gray-gold light that the harbor wore before the sun cleared the water.

It was on the second bend — the one where the road narrowed between the supply sheds — that Wulin, mid-sentence, mid-stride, mid-*everything,* collided with a running senior.

It was not a hard collision. It was the kind that happens when one person is running the road as a circuit and three boys are walking it as a conversation, and the running one is faster than the road expected. The senior went half a step back; Wulin, whose density had opinions about collisions, stayed exactly where he was; and the morning light, coming over the sheds at exactly that moment, did the thing morning light does when a story decides something is about to matter.

She was older — fifth grade by her coat — and she was, in the way of senior sisters in the memory of every boy who ever walked a morning road, extremely pretty: delicate features, large limpid eyes, a runner's breath, and around her in the low sun a kind of drawn-gold radiance that had nothing to do with any soul and everything to do with the hour.

"S— sorry," Wulin said, which was accurate and also, he would later maintain under oath, all he managed.

"Junior brother, pay attention when you're running," she said — and then, because he had not been running and they all knew it, she reached out and ruffled his hair, and looked at him properly, and her eyebrows went up. "Ah. You're very good looking." And then she did the thing that the road would talk about for a term: she pinched his cheek, exactly once, and giggled at her own audacity.

And then — because a pretty senior sister with a runner's eyes does not stop looking at one boy when there is a *second* one standing right there, and this second one was the one the whole grade had been trading stories about for a term — her gaze slid past Wulin's scarlet ear and landed on Lin Hao, and *stayed.* The morning light caught the storm-gray at his hair-tips and the gold-fleck in his eyes, and Ouyang Zixin — who had pinched a hundred cheeks and forgotten ninety-nine — did not pinch his. She tilted her head, the way you do at something you'd like to keep looking at, and said, "Oh. And *you're* the swordsman." Not a question. Then, with a runner's grin that had absolutely no mercy in it: "The stories undersell the eyes."

And she was gone around the bend at a runner's pace, her voice floating back over her shoulder: "My name is Ouyang Zixin. I'm in the fifth grade's class one. Do try to be *looking* when you run, junior brothers."

Silence on the road. Then—

Lin Hao turned to Wulin with the grave, solemn face of a man delivering a eulogy, and said: "She pinched you."

"She—"

"She reached out," Lin Hao said, "and she put her hand on your *face,* and she pinched it, and I watched her do it, and I will be telling this story at every meal for the next six years, and by the time we graduate it will have a *title.*" He was already grinning, the whole of him, the solemnity gone before it landed. "'Ouyang Zixin Pinches Tang Wulin's Cheek.' It writes itself. It's got a beginning, a middle, and your ears."

"I was *startled!*" Wulin said, which was the worst possible defense, because it was true, and his ears knew it.

"You were *pinched,*" Lin Hao corrected, delighted. "There's a difference. Startled is something that happens *to* you. Pinched is something that happens to you *because of your face.*" He slung an arm around his brother's shoulders — the same side he'd walked on since they were six, the right, the one that was always his — and steered him down the road. "Don't worry. I'll be gentle. Mostly."

"Stop staring, the two of you," Xie Xie said, from inside his splint-chair, with the enormous enjoyment of a man watching two buildings fall at once. "That senior sister is already long gone. And she *noticed* the swordsman, Wulin. She *noticed* him. You got a pinch; he got a *review.*"

"She said I was good looking!" Wulin protested, with his entire face.

"She said *he's the swordsman,*" Xie Xie said, "and then she *kept looking.* That's worse for you. That's so much worse for you."

"She also said 'junior brothers,'" Lin Hao put in, helpful as a knife, "'plural.' Which means she was talking to *both* of us, which means, technically, Wulin, I got pinched by association, and I will be accepting condolences." He ducked the swat without looking, because he'd known it was coming since the word 'consolences.' "And for the record — her heart's not the problem. *Yours* is. You've got room in there for a taken sister, a promised forge, a whole city of notice-paper with one face on it, and *apparently* still space for a senior sister's hair in the morning light. Big furnace. Holds a lot of fire. It's not a flaw, it's just — *generous.*" He said it with all the warmth in the world, because it was true, and because teasing his brother about the size of his own heart was the oldest thing between them, older than the academy, older than the forge. "Just don't tell me Na'er's going to come back and find you've got a *senior sister* pinned to your ear."

"*She pinched ME,*" Wulin said, "not the other way around, and Na'er is—" he stopped, because the road had gone quiet in the way it did when the taken sister's name landed, and Lin Hao's arm around his shoulders tightened exactly once, the way it always did, and neither of them said the rest, because they never had to.

"Come on," Lin Hao said, lighter, steering him on, because that was the other half of the teasing — knowing exactly when to stop. "Let's go get breakfast before Xie Xie eats his own splint. And Wulin? If you see her again — *look* where you're running. For both our sakes. I can only carry one of us being pinched."

## Part 2: The Assembly

Breakfast was a hurried affair, and class was not — because class was a note on the board: *all first-grade students, the sports field, grade assembly.*

The five classes of the first grade stood in their blocks in the field's cold morning geometry, two hundred and some children in ranked lines. The reviewing platform wore Long Hengxu, the faculty, and — new, at the center, in a coat that cost more than the platform — a man most of the grade had only ever seen at a distance: President Yu Zhen, whose face gave nothing away the way a deep wall gives nothing away.

Long Hengxu, who had been a director for longer than most of the field had been alive, began with the thing everyone had come for, in the voice he kept for weather reports and history.

"In light of the new class one's outstanding achievements in this tournament, the entire class will be rewarded with one meal a day from the first window — for one term."

The sound the class-one block made — the block that had been *class five* for a term and a half, the worst class in the building, the block that had learned to eat victory at the fourth window because the fourth window was where the portions were — was not cheering. It was a wall of two dozen ten-year-olds discovering, all at once, that the first window was *theirs:* the nourishing window, the expensive window, the window most families could not afford once. Zhou Zhangxi, in the second row, began a song that was stopped by his own disbelief. Mu Xi did arithmetic on her fingers and stopped at a number she clearly did not believe, and started again.

And on the reviewing platform, Ye Yingluo — class two's teacher now, the ladder's price worn like a coat she had not chosen — watched the block she had been given, and watched the block she had lost, and her face grew gloomier at every cheer.

"Quiet down!" Long Hengxu did not raise his voice; the field obeyed anyway. "Due to the excellence of this year's first grade, the board of directors has decided to conduct a study. We are establishing an experimental class in the first grade, comprised of the best students in the grade. It will temporarily be called **class zero**, and Wu Zhangkong will be the teacher in charge." He unrolled a slate the way other men unsheathe things. "The students for class zero have already been selected."

And then he read the names — and the first name on the slate was not the one the field expected.

"**Lin Hao.** Tang Wulin. Xie Xie. Gu Yue." A breath. "From class two: Zhang Yangzi, Wang Jinxi, Wei Xiaofeng. In the future, any other student who shows exceptional ability will also be put into class zero."

*Class zero?*

In all of Eastsea Academy's history there had never been a class zero. The field went through the silence of two hundred children doing arithmetic they had not been taught: the best students, pulled out of the classes, given the ice-cold teacher everyone had spent a term being frightened of — which, if you were ten, meant either a prize or a punishment, and no way from where you stood to tell which. And the first name on the list — the swordsman, the fourth, the one the grade had traded stories about for a term — sat there at the front of it, not added on the end but *first,* the way a thing that belongs is placed, and two hundred children registered it without any of them being able to say, afterward, exactly why it mattered. Only that it did.

In the class-one block, Wulin had said *they'll take all of us or none of us,* and Xie Xie had said *they'll take all of us, obviously, we're the terrifying ones* — and when the names came, they did not react, because they had known. But Xie Xie, who could not leave a thing unsaid even with both arms in a chair, leaned over and hissed, with enormous feeling, "They put you *first.* They put you *first,* Hao. Before *Wulin.* Do you know what that does to my *brand?*"

"It means the board can read," Lin Hao said, without turning his head. "It means you're third. Try to contain your grief."

"I'm *fourth,* actually," Xie Xie said. "Gu Yue's third. I'm fourth. Behind *Gu Yue.* This is a disaster." And he was grinning the whole time he said it, because being fourth behind his three best friends in a class of seven was the best thing that had happened to him all term, and Lin Hao knew it, and didn't say so, because that was the other half of the teasing too.

And Wang Jinxi, across the field, looked at Tang Wulin. And then — a fraction later, a fraction longer — his gaze slid one body to the left, to the name that had been read *first,* to the boy whose sword had found the seam of his fusion, and rested there like a hand on a doorframe.

Lin Hao looked back. He did not nod. Nods were for things finished, and nothing between them was finished. He simply held the look the way you hold a hot workpiece: carefully, and without flinching, and with full attention to what it was going to do next. And then — because two hundred people were watching and he had never in his life been able to leave a solemn thing solemn — he gave the dragon the smallest possible salute, two fingers off the brow, the way you'd greet a rival across a forge, and Wang Jinxi — top-tier dark dragon, broken arm, complicated face — looked like a boy who had been handed something he did not have a pocket for.

"Aside from these two announcements," Long Hengxu resumed, and the field heard the hinge in his voice, "there are still punishments to be announced. In the match between class one and class two, both sides prioritized their comrades first and the competition second, which led to three students being seriously injured. This has raised a serious concern with the participants. As such, they will be deprived of the tournament rewards, as a punishment — and a warning to others."

A ripple of confusion ran the field: even won, no rewards? Their classes would only be promoted? Long Hengxu had said it harshly, and the field heard harshness — and on the reviewing platform, Wu Zhangkong's expression did not move, because Wu Zhangkong had read the punishment correctly: the director had turned a disaster into a *precedent.* Comrades first. Written into the record. Kept.

"President, do you have any words to say?"

Yu Zhen nodded, and began, in a clear voice, with the speech the board had written: "Students, I am sure you are all very curious as to why we established class zero. This is because the students we have picked out have already far surpassed the level of their peers. If they were to continue advancing with the other students, their talent would be buried. In summary — if you wish to shine in the future, then you must put in even more effort. I hope that I will see more students joining class zero later on, going on to become the greatest geniuses of Eastsea Academy. Alright then, the assembly is over. Teachers, lead your classes back. Long Hengxu will act as class one's substitute teacher until a new teacher can be found. Wu Zhangkong and the students of class zero will remain here."

The five classes filed out of the field wearing shock, admiration, envy, and regret in proportions that varied by child. And seven were left — six standing, one absent — in the empty geometry of the field, with the president, and the ice-cold teacher, and each other.

## Part 3: Frogs and Contracts

"Children, come over here."

They came — the four of class one in their walking formation, which they had never once discussed and had always had; the two of class two in a formation of two that was clearly a negotiation. Wei Xiaofeng came with his chin up and his eyes on the ground's enemies. Wang Jinxi came the way weather comes.

Yu Zhen looked the six of them over — the bandaged arms, the sling, the stillness — and raised an eyebrow, and when he spoke, the board's speech was gone and something considerably colder had arrived.

"You guys are quite able, huh! Do you think that just because you're a bit more outstanding than your peers, that you're great? Look at you all — what have you accomplished? Among you six, two have broken arms, and there's still one with broken legs resting in the dormitory!"

They had never expected the president to open with a tongue-lashing, and the six of them stood it the way fence posts stand wind.

"I have already said what the purpose of class zero is: it's to not hold you back. But even with how small you all are, you harbor so much pride and conceit in your hearts. I will have you all behave with integrity in front of me — otherwise, don't blame the academy for being impolite. I'm warning you now: if a situation like yesterday's happens again, you will all be punished. Don't think that just because you are geniuses, you don't have to follow the rules. You are all just viewing the sky from the bottom of a well. There are plenty of people even more outstanding than you throughout the federation." He let that settle, the way a man sets down weight. "From the very beginning, this world has never lacked geniuses, nor has it lacked geniuses that die young. If a genius wants to become great, then he will have to invest far more effort than an ordinary person. Only then will you live up to your potential. Do you all understand?"

"Understood," said six voices — and one of the six, a president would note later, in a report no one ever read, had said it a half-beat before the others, without flinching, in the tone of a boy agreeing to something he had already known since he was six years old and the sea had taken his best friend's rival's — *had taken Na'er,* the president did not know; the boy simply did not find the sentence new. Frogs in wells. The boy had grown up next to the largest well in the world and spent his life reading what was written on its water.

"Sign this contract."

The papers appeared with a flip of the president's hand and distributed themselves into six sets of hands — one set having to be tucked under a splint-frame, because Xie Xie's hands were otherwise employed being broken. Wulin looked his over. The word at the top was large: **CONTRACT.** And the content beneath, in the flat grammar of institutions: *the undersigned voluntarily contracts with Eastsea Academy — before graduating from the intermediate division AND the advanced division, will not change schools.*

"A guarantee," Yu Zhen said, watching them read. "The academy will invest resources in class zero that no class in this school has ever received. The academy wants a guarantee that you will stay for your studies."

Wei Xiaofeng read his contract like an insult. Wang Jinxi read his like a map. Gu Yue read hers in four seconds and held the pen without signing, looking — as she had looked at the fusion test — at the arithmetic underneath: what an academy this size considered "resources," and what an academy this size considered "a guarantee," and the distance between the two numbers.

And Lin Hao read his the way he read everything made by human hands for human purposes: like a commission. *They are investing. They are binding. The work is specified, the payment is stated, the term is long.* It was, he noticed, the first contract of his life addressed to him by name — and the terms were, by any forge's standard, honorable: resources for loyalty, training for years. He had made his own version of this contract at six years old, walking into the worst class in the grade behind his brother, and no paper had been necessary.

He signed first. Then he turned to the splint-frame, because Xie Xie was attempting to hold a pen between two bandaged wrists in a manner that was brave, inventive, and producing a signature that resembled a drowning spider.

"It's a legal document," Xie Xie hissed. "It has to be *legible.*"

"It has to be signed," Lin Hao said, and steadied the paper with one hand and put his other hand lightly over Xie Xie's bandaged fists, and guided them the way he guided a hammer that was learning a strike — not moving them, giving them the line — and the name that came out was Xie Xie's own, legible, and larger than usual, because the dagger-boy had pressed.

"Federation charter," Xie Xie muttered, looking at it with enormous satisfaction. "Put that on a wall."

One by one, the six signed. And Yu Zhen collected the papers with the face of a man who had just bought something at a good price and knew it, and Long Hengxu — substitute teacher of class one as of this morning — looked at the six children holding his school's largest investment, and said the only thing he had to say, in his weather-report voice:

"Don't make me regret the paperwork."

## Part 4: The Room With No Number

Their classroom had no number on the door. That was the whole of its first lesson.

It was bigger than a class should be and emptier than a room that size should be — six desks, a seventh arriving, walls stripped of the charts and slogans the other classrooms wore, and a window along the whole east side that looked out over the training grounds, the seawall, and beyond them the harbor, gray and enormous and wearing its morning traffic the way the forge wore its sparks. Wu Zhangkong had chosen the window, or the window had chosen Wu Zhangkong; either way, he stood in front of it now, hands behind his back, and the six of him — six students, one teacher, zero number — stood in a loose semicircle that had sorted itself, without discussion, into a four and a two.

He looked at the sorting. He had clearly decided, at some point during the walk over, that comment was beneath him.

"Your schedule is new," he said. "Mornings: cultivation, together, this room — spiritual power is the foundation of everything, and everything you are is built on a foundation you have been neglecting while you were busy being remarkable. Afternoons: your classes' work, compressed. Evenings: combat." A pause. "Not sparring. Combat. There is a difference, and by the end of the term you will be able to tell me what it is."

"The resources the president mentioned," Gu Yue said — of course Gu Yue said it, of course she said it first, "—what are they."

"They are not yours yet," Wu Zhangkong said, which was the coldest and most honest answer anyone had ever given her, and something in her stillness leaned forward, interested. "They are earned on a schedule. There is a place in this city where talent is measured — where souls your age are given things most soul masters die without. You will go there when you are ready, and not one day before, because that place does not care about your contracts or your president or your tournament." His smoky green eyes went around the circle and rested, one by one: on the splint-frame, on the sling-less arm that had been broken, on the boy with the hawk's eyes who had not taken notes because he did not need to. "Which brings me to the only rule of this room. You are seven. The board gave me six and the tournament gave me the seventh. I do not care which class carried you here — the classes are done with you. In this room there is no class one, no class two, no class five. There is class zero, and it has never lost a student, because it has never had one. Be the reason it stays that way."

"Seven," Wei Xiaofeng said, with a sneer he had clearly been carrying since the field, "is an unlucky number."

"Then we're safe," Xie Xie said, from inside his chair, "because nothing bad has *ever* happened to us."

And Wu Zhangkong — who had been ice and geometry since September — made a sound. It was small. It was gone in a third of a second. But six children heard it, and one of the six (Lin Hao) filed it with the precision it deserved: *the teacher laughed. Once. The room is real.*

"Combat at four," Wu Zhangkong said, and was gone, and the room with no number was left to six children and a window and the harbor, and the two formations — the four and the two — looked at each other across three meters of unassigned floor.

Wei Xiaofeng looked at the four the way you look at weather you blame personally. Wang Jinxi looked at Wulin, and then at Lin Hao, and said — quietly, to no one in particular, in the voice of a boy setting down something heavy to see if it would stay down:

"Your swordsman found the seam of my soul." A pause. "No one had ever found the seam of my soul."

"He finds seams," Lin Hao's brother said, mildly. "It's what he's for."

And Wang Jinxi — top-tier dark dragon, broken arm, complicated face — looked at Tang Wulin for one long moment, and then nodded, once, the smallest nod in the world, and went and sat down at a desk on the *four's* side of the floor. Wei Xiaofeng made a sound like a kettle. And the room with no number, without deciding to, stopped being two formations — because a dragon had moved first, and dragons, whatever else they are, are not followers, and everyone in the room understood without being told that whatever had just happened, it had not been a surrender.

It had been an investment.

---

That night, on the roof, the harbor did its accounting, and two brothers sat with their backs against the same warm chimney they had owned since the dormitories were assigned, and did what they had done every night since they were six: talked about nothing that mattered until it turned into everything that did.

"Six years," Wulin said. "Through the advanced division. We're stuck in this city for six years, Hao."

"Six years of the first window," Lin Hao said. "Do you know what they put in the first window's soup? Mu Chen told me. It's criminal. There's a *bone* in it that's been simmering since before we were born. I'm going to eat an animal that was old when the academy was young." He nudged his brother's shoulder with his own. "And you're paying, because you're the one who got us famous."

"I didn't get us famous, *you* got us famous, they read your name *first*—"

"They read my name first because the board can read," Lin Hao said. "You got the cheek-pinched. That's the famous one. That's the one with the *story.*" He was grinning, because he could feel Wulin trying not to, and making his brother laugh was the oldest game he had. "Six years, Wulin. Six years of senior sisters noticing you in the morning light. Think of the *titles.*"

"*Stop.*"

"'Ouyang Zixin Pinches Tang Wulin's Cheek: A Saga.' It's going to have *chapters,* Wulin. By fourth year it's going to have a *theme song.*"

Wulin shoved him. Lin Hao shoved back. It was not a fight; it had never been a fight; it was the thing two brothers do on a warm chimney when the words have gone somewhere too big and they need to come back down to something the size of a shoulder. And then Wulin's shoulder stopped moving, and the quiet came, and Lin Hao let it, because he could feel the shape of what was coming and had learned, years ago, that the teasing was the door and the quiet was the room, and you could not get to the room any other way.

"The notice-paper," Wulin said, quieter now. "Six years in one city. If she's taken *south*—"

"Then the paper goes south," Lin Hao said. "The fund's funded. The fish-wife oils ours. And you've got a contract that says they'll invest in you — which means in six weeks you'll be famous enough that the paper won't have to ask people to look. It'll just have to ask people to *remember.*" He looked at his brother — at the jaw doing the thing it did when it held an ocean behind it — and said the only thing that had ever worked, in the voice he kept for the one thing he never once teased: "We don't stop looking. That's not what the contract says. That's what *we* say. And I'm the one who reads the water, Wulin. You know I am. So stop carrying it like it's yours alone, because it stopped being yours alone the day I walked into that class behind you."

Wulin's jaw unclenched. And then — because he was Wulin, and because the quiet never lasted longer than Wulin could stand it — he said, "If a senior sister pinches *my* cheek one more time I'm going to have to move cities."

"You'd move cities for me," Lin Hao said, "and you'd complain the whole way, and you'd make me carry the forge."

"I'd make you carry the *forge,*" Wulin agreed, "and the anvil, and the *bellows,* and I'd walk in front."

"You'd get lost," Lin Hao said. "You'd get lost in six years of one city and I'd have to come find you, and I'd never hear the end of it." And they sat there, shoulders touching, two brothers on a warm chimney, and the harbor did its accounting, and the dark water kept what it kept, and neither of them said the rest, because they never had to.

And under it all, on the far water, the hawk watched the boy who had signed his name to six years of a city — watched, and was still, and gave no answer, and needed to give none: the question between them had gone quiet in a new way lately, the way a held note goes quiet when the hand on the string has stopped trembling. It was not an answer. It was not the end. It was simply that, for tonight, the bird and the boy were both looking at the same harbor, and the dark water kept what it kept, and somewhere under the sleep that took them both, a chair sat pulled up to a door — and the door, for the first time, was on the *inside.*

Third morning, the room with no number would have its first combat. A teacher who had laughed once would find out what seven children made of his schedule — and the sky beyond the east window would go on being the largest well in the world, and class zero would go on being the smallest class in it, and the two facts would not stop being true for a very long time.


Rank twenty-eight came on the fourth day of class zero, and Lin Hao noticed it the way he noticed a change in the wind — by what it let him do that he could not do yesterday. Wu Zhangkong's stick arrived a half-beat later than it had. He was not faster. He was *earlier.*

Eight hundred and twenty-five years, and the hawk sat in him facing a window it had been facing for four months, patient as weather.

## Part 1: Rooms Like Teachers'

The academy, it turned out, did not do things by halves once it had decided to do them at all.

The dormitory that class zero was given was not a dormitory so much as a small street: seven rooms in a row along a quiet corridor that smelled of new wood and old money, each room its own — its own window, its own desk, its own door that closed on a single occupant instead of four. They were, Xie Xie discovered within nine minutes of being let loose on them, the same rooms the academy gave its *teachers.*

"We live like Wu Zhangkong," he said, with the specific awe of a boy who had once shared a room with three others and a smell. "We live like *teachers.*"

"You live like a boy with two broken arms," Wulin said, carrying Xie Xie's splint-frame up the stairs for him, because the stairs were the one thing the dagger-boy could not do with his hands occupied being invalids. "Don't get used to it."

"I'm getting used to it *aggressively.*"

Down the corridor, Wu Zhangkong had been given a suite — his old dormitory traded for quarters that sat at the head of the little street like a foreman's office at the mouth of a mine. He had been notified the night before, along with the board's approval, and had said nothing about it then and said nothing about it now, which was, his students were learning, how he received most things.

Wei Xiaofeng took the room at the far end, the one furthest from the four, and put his things in it without speaking to anyone, and closed his door with the deliberateness of a man building a wall out of a door. Zhang Yangzi — who had come down to the dormitory on a healer's rolling chair, his legs elevated, his face the color of a boy doing long arithmetic about a situation he had not chosen — took the room beside him, because the two of them were the two of class two, and because Zhang Yangzi had signed the contract the moment he heard Wang Jinxi had, without a word, the way a man moves a piece he has already decided about.

And Wang Jinxi took the room beside Wulin's.

No one remarked on it. It would have been, all of them understood, the same as remarking on weather. The dragon had made his investment the day before — had walked across three meters of unassigned floor and sat down on the four's side, and not one of them had asked him why, because asking would have made it smaller than it was. So he had a room beside Wulin's now, and an arm in a sling, and a face that had stopped doing the complicated thing and started doing a quieter thing that none of them had a name for yet.

Seven rooms. One street. One teacher at the head of it. The academy had given them a day to settle.

They did not, of course, settle. They unpacked, and circled, and sat in doorways watching each other the way new metal watches the fire.

---

## Part 2

The breeze in his hair had become permanent. He could not feel it against his own skin any more, but other people could: twice that week a stranger had looked at him and then looked again, because the hair at his temple was moving and nothing else was.
: Not Mechas — The Other Thing

Class zero's classroom was on the ground floor of the same building, and it was, like everything else that week, too big for the number of people in it — a room built for forty holding seven desks and a teacher, with a window along the whole east wall looking out on the training grounds they were not, yet, allowed to use.

Wu Zhangkong came in with the expression he wore for all weather, and stood in the center, and swept his gaze across the seven of them — the four and the dragon on one side, the boy on the rolling chair and the boy with the wall for a face on the other.

"From henceforth, your curriculum will undergo a change," he said. "Due to the current conditions of your bodies, we will put off cultivation for a while." His eyes went, briefly and without emphasis, to the splint-frame, the sling, the elevated legs. "Three of you cannot lift a weapon. Two more of you would only injure the three by training against them. So we begin with theory. Today: mechas."

*Mechas?*

The word landed on the seven of them like a stone in a pond. Zhang Yangzi, whose expression brightened a fraction at having something to object to, could not help himself: "Teacher Wu — aren't mechas a topic for the advanced division? We're first grade. Isn't this too early?"

"The topics in this class will not be taught in detail," Wu Zhangkong said, "so the load will not be heavy. Among you — who wants to become a Mecha Master?"

Silence, all seven of them at once. Mecha Masters were, in the eyes of almost everyone, simply another word for powerful.

"Then you had better pay attention." He let the glance land on Zhang Yangzi, who folded. "Modern mechas have undergone ten thousand years of development; soul devices, several thousand more. Technology is researched for one reason: war. Soul devices were no exception — it was only after they filled the battlefield that civilians began to use them. The Soul Guide Masters of that era never imagined a soul device could empower a Soul Master by so much. It was only when they discovered it that they began to research mechas.

"Soul Masters were the most essential profession for tens of thousands of years — rare, and mostly weak. With soul devices, that shifted. Low-rank Soul Masters could become far stronger through soul power and devices; then soul mechas appeared, and made them stronger still. Soul mechas run on soul power from batteries, letting the user display strength far past their own. The first were large, because larger frames held larger batteries and more weapons. As the art improved, mechas became operable by ordinary people with strong enough bodies — and became the main weapon of every modern army."

He paused, and let the history settle.

"But these," he said, "are not the mechas I want to talk to you about."

Astonishment, seven copies.

"Didn't you think — as technology improved, ordinary people could control soul devices better and better? That is what ordinary people think. In the tens of thousands of years the Douluo Continent has recorded, one fact has never changed: **Soul Masters are the most powerful existence.** With soul devices, an ordinary person might match a Soul Grandmaster; with a mecha, contend with a five-ring Soul King. Tremendous power — but a mecha cannot give an ordinary person the fighting power of a true master. Because a mecha is *worn.* It is a tool outside the body." His voice dropped the half-degree that meant the sentence mattered. "What I am going to tell you about is the armor that is not worn. The armor that is *fused.*"

---

## Part 3: The Armor That Is Forged

"It is called battle armor," Wu Zhangkong said. "And everything I have told you about mechas was the road leading to it.

"A battle armor is a soul device made from special metal, forged to a quality ordinary metal cannot reach, and then inscribed with soul circuits — and then *bonded* to a single Soul Master. Not worn. Bonded. It fuses with your martial soul, draws on your own soul power and spiritual power instead of a battery, and becomes — when it is called — a second skin of metal that fights as you fight, because it is *part of you.* A mecha is a tool a man climbs into. A battle armor is a limb a Soul Master grows."

He let that sit, and then said the thing that made the room's temperature change.

"A battle armor is *made.* It is forged. The metal must be worked by a blacksmith to a grade called soul-forging — metal that has had soul power driven into it under the hammer, until the metal itself holds a soul's shape. Then a soul engineer inscribes the circuits. Without the blacksmith, there is no metal that can bear the circuits. Without the soul engineer, the metal is only metal. Battle armor is the one weapon in the world that cannot be made by a machine, or an army, or money alone. It is made by *hands.*"

And at the back of the room, in the seat by the east window, Lin Hao had stopped breathing.

Not dramatically. Not the way the others had gone still at the word *fused.* He had gone still the way he went still in front of a forge when the metal said something — the whole of him turning toward a sentence the way a compass turns north. *Forged. Soul power driven into it under the hammer. Metal that holds a soul's shape.* He had been hammering metal since he could hold a hammer. He had spent a summer learning that metal had a grain, a memory, a voice. And a man had just stood in front of him and said, in the flat voice of a man reading a weather report, that there was a metal in the world that was *forged to hold a soul* — and that the making of it began, not with a soul engineer, not with money, not with an army, but with a blacksmith and a hammer.

Because Wu Zhangkong had just described, in the flat voice he used for things he considered settled, the one thing in the room that Lin Hao could already do.

Six students sat in that room hearing a lecture about a craft. **One of them had been doing it since he was four years old, on a box, in a shed, for coins.** Soul-forging was not a subject to him. It was Tuesday. He had driven soul power into metal under a hammer before he had ever heard the word *battle armor,* and he had not known until that sentence that what he was doing had a name.

And that is the butterfly, and it is not a small one. **In a class without him, battle armor is a lecture, and all six of them will spend years finding a blacksmith good enough to make it for them, and most of them will never find one.** In a class with him in it, the lecture is a description of something already sitting in his hands, and the six of them will never in their lives understand that the rarest thing in the room was the boy at the east window who had stopped breathing.

Wu Zhangkong saw it. Wu Zhangkong always saw it. He did not say anything, which was how he said the largest things, and he went on with the lecture, and he taught the class a craft that one of them already had, and he did not once let the room know that he knew.

He did not raise his hand. He did not need to. But Wu Zhangkong's eyes, on their slow circuit of the room, stopped on him for one beat longer than the others — because Wu Zhangkong had been a teacher long enough to recognize the face of a boy who had just been handed his life's direction and did not yet know he was holding it.

"They are named," Wu Zhangkong continued, "by words. One-word battle armor. Two-word. Three-word. Four-word. The more words, the higher the grade of the metal, the deeper the circuits, the greater the power — and the higher the cultivation required to bear it." He held up no fingers; he simply said the numbers the way the world said them. "A one-word battle armor master is, in general, a Soul Ancestor. A two-word battle armor master is, in general, a Titled Douluo. A three-word battle armor master is, in general, a Super Douluo. And four-word battle armor—" a pause, the only one he gave the whole lecture, "—across the entire Douluo Continent, those who possess it can be counted on one hand. Every one of them is a pinnacle."

The room did the arithmetic ten-year-olds do: *Soul Ancestor. Titled Douluo. Super Douluo.* Names out of storybooks. Names you said about other people.

"And," Wu Zhangkong said, "you are asking why I tell first-graders this. You are asking because you are ten, and you have two rings between most of you, and these are names for people your grandparents' grandparents would call legends." He looked at the seven of them — the splint-frame, the sling, the elevated legs, the wall-faced boy, the still one by the window. "I tell you because a road you cannot see the end of is still a road, and most people never walk one because no one ever told them it was there. You will not touch battle armor for years. Some of you will never bear one. But every one of you will spend the next six years building the foundation that decides whether you *can.* And one of you—" his eyes went, again, a fraction longer, to the window seat, "—may spend his life making them for the others. Class dismissed."

---

"Which brings me," Wu Zhangkong said, "to the reason you are hearing this at ten years old instead of at twenty."

He wrote a single line on the board. Three words.

**Designer. Maker. Mechanic.**

"Three kinds of mecha craftsmen," he said. "There are others, but those are the three that matter, and one of them is going to be yours."

A hand went up at the front. Gu Yue's did not; Gu Yue's hands did not go up. It was Zhang Yangzi's.

"Ours, teacher?"

"**Secondary occupation.** Every one of you takes one. Not instead of cultivation — underneath it." He set the chalk down. "Because if you want a powerful battle armor, you must have one that *fits you.* And the only people who ever get that are the people who can design it, make it, or repair it themselves. Everybody else wears something a stranger guessed at." A pause. "If you do not take a trade, you will never have armor made to you, and you will never ascend to a **god altar.** That is not a metaphor. That is the arithmetic."

The room went very quiet, because *god altar* was not a word first-graders were given.

"With class zero I have one goal," Wu Zhangkong said. "That goal is to push five of you toward a god altar. It is long, it is arduous, and you may spend your whole lives on it. My job is to stop you wasting years doing it the wrong way, and to show you the road." He looked at each of them in turn. "You do not have to choose today. You have time. **But you will choose by third grade. Within three years, you give me an answer.** Even with your talent, your road looks like an ordinary person's road. The sooner you start walking it, the better."

Then his eyes went to the back of the room, to the east window, and stopped.

"In fact," he said, "one of you already has."

Lin Hao had the distinct and unpleasant sensation of a room turning around to look at him.

"Wulin chose blacksmithing when he was six. I expect he is extremely good at it." Wu Zhangkong's voice did not change, but something in it had. "**Blacksmithing is the one I would ask the rest of you to consider. Because from a purple battle armor onward, the creation process becomes inseparable from forging.**" He let that land. "Not adjacent to it. Not assisted by it. *Inseparable.* The man who can soul-forge is not a supplier to the people who make god-altar armor. He is the reason there is any."

"And," he added, almost as an afterthought, in the tone of a man closing a ledger, "if you reach five stars or higher in your trade, you will never be short of cultivation resources for the rest of your life. That is not a boast about the trades. That is simply what five stars is worth."

---

They walked out into a corridor that smelled of floor polish and had, in the space of forty minutes, become a different corridor.

Xie Xie spoke first, because Xie Xie always spoke first. "Maker," he said. "I've decided. Maker. It's technique — it's practice, it's hands, it's not sitting at a desk drawing things for six hours. It's *suitable* for me." He said this with the enormous satisfaction of a boy who had been asked a question and had an answer ready.

"That was not a suitable thing to say about drawing," said Gu Yue.

"I didn't say it about drawing. I said it about *me.*"

"You said it while looking at me."

"Coincidence."

"I'll take **mechanics**," said Gu Yue, to the ceiling, to nobody.

Xie Xie stopped walking. "*Mechanics?* But you're a girl, I thought you'd take designing—"

Gu Yue turned her head about fifteen degrees, which with her was the equivalent of shouting.

"**Only brainless people would think like that.**"

Zhang Yangzi, behind them, said "oh *no*" in the voice of a man settling in for entertainment, and Wang Jinxi said nothing at all, and Wulin and Lin Hao kept walking, because they had both known what they were since they were six and had never once discussed it, which was somehow the most suspicious thing about them.

"How long have you known?" Wulin said, eventually.

"Since the forge."

"Since before," said Lin Hao. "Since I watched you hit something flat on purpose and hear three notes come out, and understood that you and I were going to be doing this until we were dead."

Wulin considered that.

"Okay," he said. "That's a bit much."

"I'm not retracting it."

"I know you're not," said Wulin. "That's the bit that's a bit much."

## Part 4: What the Window Seat Held

The room emptied in the slow, reluctant way rooms empty after a lecture that landed. Xie Xie went out talking, because Xie Xie went everywhere talking — about Titled Douluo, about soul circuits, about whether a dagger could have a battle armor and if so whether it would be *faster.* Wulin walked beside him with the particular silence of a boy who had been handed a dream and was turning it over to find the seams. Gu Yue went out alone, four seconds behind everyone, having already filed the entire lecture somewhere Lin Hao would never see.

And Lin Hao stayed.

Not to ask a question — the question was too large for a doorway and too new for words. He stayed because the window looked out on the training grounds, and the training grounds had a maintenance shed, and the maintenance shed had a forge in it that the groundskeeper used for hinges and rail-fittings, and Lin Hao had noticed it the way he noticed all forges, the way other boys noticed nothing, on the first walk over — and he was looking at it now, through the east window, the way you look at a country you have just been told you are allowed to walk to someday.

Wu Zhangkong was still in the room. He had not left. He was standing where he had lectured, hands behind his back, looking at the boy by the window with the expression of a man confirming a suspicion he had carried since a sparring yard in September.

"You understood the forging," he said. Not a question.

"I understood that it's made by hand," Lin Hao said, without turning. "That it starts with a hammer. Everything else — the circuits, the bonding — comes after the metal, and the metal comes after the hammer." A pause. "I've been holding a hammer since I was four."

"Yes." Wu Zhangkong said it the way he said most true things: flatly, and once. "The others heard *Titled Douluo.* You heard *forged.*" He was quiet a moment. "Most blacksmiths in this city make hinges. A few make soul devices. A very few — a number you could count in this room — can soul-forge. And the ones who can are the reason any battle armor exists at all." He turned toward the door. "You are a second-rank blacksmith at ten years old. You will not soul-forge for a long time. But you are the only student I have ever taught who heard the word *battle armor* and thought about the *metal* first." And then, because he was Wu Zhangkong and it was the whole of the praise he gave: "Don't waste it on hinges."

He was gone.

Lin Hao stood at the window a while longer, looking at the little forge in the groundskeeper's shed, at the anvil that was too small and the bellows that was probably cracked, at a country of metal that started with a hammer and ended, if the lecture was true, in armor that fought like a limb of the person wearing it. And under it all, on the far water, the hawk watched the boy watch the forge, and was — for the second time that week — doing something that was not quite stillness and not quite speech: the attention of something that had begun, without deciding to, to point the same direction its boy was pointing.

That night, on the roof that was not theirs anymore — they had real rooms now, with real doors, and none of them had thought to use the roof, except, it turned out, the two who had always used it, because some habits are older than furniture — Wulin said, "Battle armor," the way you say a prayer you're not sure you're allowed to say. "Soul Ancestors. Titled Douluo. Hao — we're *ten.*"

"We're ten," Lin Hao agreed, "with two rings, a teacher who lives like a foreman, a forge in the groundskeeper's shed that he probably uses for *hinges,* and a lecture that said the metal comes first." He nudged his brother's shoulder with his own. "Also, you drooled a little during the Titled Douluo part. I saw it. I'm keeping that."

"I did *not*—"

"You did. You had a *dream-face.* I'm going to think about it at inappropriate moments for years." He was grinning, the whole of him, because making Wulin sputter was worth more than the lecture had been. "But also — and I want you to hear this part before I go back to making fun of you — you want to *bear* one. I want to *make* one. That's not the same dream. It's the same *road.*" He looked at his brother, and let the teasing go quiet for exactly as long as the thing needed, and no longer. "And roads are better with two on them. So you can go be a Titled Douluo, and I'll be the one who made the thing you're standing in, and when they write the story they'll get our names backwards, and I'll let you have the first page because I got there first anyway."

Wulin shoved him. Lin Hao shoved back, because that was the answer, and had always been the answer, and would be the answer when they were Titled Douluos and gray. And then Wulin laughed — the real one, the one that came up out of the place the drool had come from — and said, "You're going to put *hinges* in my battle armor, aren't you. You're going to forge me a Titled Douluo battle armor with a *hinge* on it."

"A *good* hinge," Lin Hao said. "A hinge that's been soul-forged. You'll never feel it. You'll just never be able to take the armor off, and you'll know it's me, every time, and you'll hate it, and you'll never once actually want to take it off." He slung an arm around his brother's shoulders — the right side, the side that had been his since they were six — and they sat there, and the harbor did its accounting, and neither of them said the rest, because the teasing was the whole of the saying, and it had never once needed more.

And the harbor did its accounting, and the seven rooms down the quiet street went dark one by one, and the little street that held the worst class's best and a dragon who had moved his piece and a boy with a wall for a face slept the sleep of children who had been told, for the first time in their lives, exactly how far the road went — and had decided, in the part of the mind that decides such things before the morning, to walk it anyway.

Three of them would mend. Then the cultivation would start, and the evenings would become what Wu Zhangkong had promised: not sparring. Combat. And the difference, by the end of the term, would be a sentence all seven of them could say.

But that was for later. Tonight, the road was new, and long, and theirs.

## Part 1: The Ledger

Lin Hao kept a ledger. Not on paper — paper would have been found, and a ledger like this one was not a thing you left lying around a dormitory where Zhou Zhangxi snored. He kept it the way his father kept the temper of a blade: in the hand, where it could not be lost and did not need to be explained.

Every fight was a line in it.

He had begun counting after the tournament, because the tournament had taught him something his father never could: that a fight you survive is a fight you *keep.* The hawk did not forget the wind it had ridden. It asked the wind a question, watched which way the wind leaned, and then it knew — permanently, the way you know a stair — and it never had to ask that question again.

So the ledger had lines.

*Mo Si* — short sword, agility, quick hands, always elsewhere the moment you decided where he was. *Answer: don't decide where he is. Ask.*

*Qin Lang* — Iron-Back Ape, a wall with a feed-line running into its left shoulder. *Answer: you don't cut walls. You cut the door.*

*Jia Long* — bear-class assault, momentum in a straight line, all of it honest. *Answer: honest momentum is a gift. Turn it.*

*Lin Zunyuan* — staff support, amplification, the boy who made other boys better. *Answer: cut the line, not the man.*

*Gu Tianming* — wings, sky, a flyer who is only dangerous while you are on the ground. *Answer: then don't be on the ground.*

The four from class two. The three from class three. Class one's whole roster, fought across four days on the way up a ladder nobody had expected them to climb. *Guang Long* — rank twenty-seven, two lizard souls, Armored Body and Armored Dragon Body, a man who shrugged off hammers; the fight Lin Hao had *lost,* the line in the ledger written in a different ink, because you learn more from the lines you write in different ink. *Wang Jinxi* — Bone Dragon King, two yellow rings, and a three-week rehearsed decoy fold built specifically to lie to Lin Hao's eyes, which had worked, which had been the first successful lie ever told to him, and which he had not forgotten for one single day since.

And then the daily ones. Xie Xie, every morning, nine weeks and then months, until Lin Hao could tell from the set of the boy's shoulders which of eleven openings he was going to commit to. Wulin, every evening, the forge against the sword, the immovable against the unreadable. Wu Zhangkong's pointing stick, which did not care that you were ten.

Seventy-one lines. Seventy-one opponents, or versions of opponents, and behind every one of them a small permanent answer that had cost him a bruise to buy and would never cost him anything again.

That was the thing nobody in class zero had understood yet, and that Wu Zhangkong — who had been hitting seven children for five months and had hit Lin Hao precisely four times, and had begun, without saying so, to aim at him the way a man aims at something he is not entirely sure he can hit — understood perfectly.

🔴 *Lin Hao was the strongest in the room, and had been since the day he was measured.* Gu Yue's 153 was canon's crown for a world without him in it; his 178 was above it, and Wu Zhangkong had stopped saying otherwise two measurements ago.

Lin Hao was the one who had *already fought you.*

"You're all holding back," Wu Zhangkong said, on the evening in question, to seven children who were holding nothing back and could not, in fact, hold back any more than water holds back downhill. "Not on purpose. You're holding back because you're each of you waiting to find out what the others will do. Combat isn't waiting. Combat is deciding, before the other person decides, what you're going to be." He looked at the seven of them — the four and the three, who had stopped, without any of them saying so, being a four and a three — and said, "Tomorrow, we measure you. Then we find out what you're made of."

"I'm made of meat," Xie Xie said, from the ground, where the pointing stick had recently introduced him, "and the meat is *tired.*"

"Good," Wu Zhangkong said. "Tired meat doesn't lie." And he was gone, and the seven of them lay on the training-ground dirt like a crop that had been harvested, and Wulin said, "Hao, I can't feel my legs."

"You never could," Lin Hao said, without opening his eyes. "That's not new. That's just Tuesday."

"I can *genuinely* not feel them."

"Then tomorrow they'll measure your legs at zero," Lin Hao said, "and Wu Zhangkong will write down 'legs: absent,' and you'll be the only one in the federation with a certified missing-legs score, and you'll be *famous,* Wulin, isn't that what you always wanted." He cracked one eye open. "You're fine. Your legs are the finest legs in the federation. They're just tired. There's a difference, and tomorrow they'll measure the difference, and it'll be a number, and the number will be fine."

"You're very calm about being measured," Wulin said.

"I'm a blacksmith," Lin Hao said. "I measure things for a living. I'm going to enjoy watching them try to measure *me.*" And he said it lightly, the way he said everything, but there was something under it, and Wulin heard it, because Wulin always heard it, and neither of them said what it was. They both already knew: tomorrow they were going to put a number on Lin Hao, and the number was going to be a problem, and Lin Hao had known it was coming since the tournament, when a man with smoky green eyes had logged a number in total silence and never once said it out loud.

What Wulin did not know — what nobody knew, because Lin Hao had not told anyone, because you do not tell people the ledger exists — was that the number had been climbing the entire time. Not quietly. Not slowly. Every fight fed it, because his martial soul did not merely *have* an adaptation talent. His martial soul *was* adaptation. Pressure was not something that wore him down. Pressure was the fuel.

## Part 2

He was sweating, and the marks on his forearms stood out darker when he was hot, six of them in a row from wrist to elbow, and the boy from class three who had been watching from the rail had stopped watching the training and started watching his arms.
: The Test

The room they measured them in smelled of dust and old machines, and there were tables of strange apparatus arranged in it, and Wu Zhangkong stood with a form and a pen, and said, "We'll start with spiritual power. Xie Xie, you're first."

And the order, it turned out, was not random. Zhang Yangzi figured it out about halfway through, and said so, in the way of a boy who could not un-see a pattern: Wu Zhangkong had arranged them so the numbers would rise, one after another, the way you arrange a staircase. Xie Xie first (lowest), then up. Which meant the last one measured was the highest. And Zhang Yangzi, doing the arithmetic, looked at the order, and looked at who was last, and his eyebrows went up.

Xie Xie's spiritual power was normal. It had gone up two since the last time. "Normal," Wu Zhangkong said, and wrote it, and Xie Xie took "normal" the way he took everything, which was loudly.

Zhang Yangzi was next. **Forty-one.** "Not bad," Wu Zhangkong said, which from him was the first kind thing anyone in the room had heard all morning, and Zhang Yangzi — who was the arithmetic one, and who had been doing sums quietly since the second boy — went slightly pink and sat down as though he had been given something.

Wang Jinxi was next. His spiritual power was low — eighteen. Wu Zhangkong looked at the number, and then at Wang Jinxi, and said, in the flat voice he kept for things that mattered, "Wang Jinxi. You must spare no effort in improving your spiritual power, or you won't be able to fuse with any more spirit souls in the future." Wang Jinxi, who was normally very quiet, nodded, because Wu Zhangkong was right, and Wang Jinxi had learned — in the five months, in the room with no number — that this man was always right, and had started, without saying so, to listen.

Zhang Yangzi was next. Forty-one. "Not bad," Wu Zhangkong said. "If you do your best, you might break through from the Spirit Origin realm within a year." Zhang Yangzi, who had been the quiet one, the one who had signed the contract without a word and sat on the edge of things, straightened a little at "not bad," because it was the first kind thing anyone had said to him since the rematch, and he did not, entirely, know what to do with it.

And then there were two left. And Zhang Yangzi, who had figured out the staircase, looked at the order, and looked at Lin Hao, and then at Gu Yue, and understood — with the slow, cold understanding of a boy doing arithmetic he did not like — that the staircase went up to *both* of them, and that the numbers were about to stop being normal.

Lin Hao went before Gu Yue. Because the staircase rose, and his number was lower than hers, and Wu Zhangkong had arranged it that way, and Lin Hao — who had known this was coming, who had watched the man with the smoky green eyes log a number in silence at the tournament and never say it — stepped up to the machine the way he stepped up to a forge, and put his hand on it, and let it measure him.

The number climbed.

It went past the white line. It went into the yellow. It broke a hundred, the way it had broken a hundred at the tournament, and then it kept going, and this was the part that made Wu Zhangkong's pen stop moving, because at the tournament it had stopped at one hundred and eighty and he had written that down and closed the book and carried it in his head for five months waiting to see if it would hold.

It had not held. It had not even *stayed.*

One hundred and forty. One hundred and sixty. One hundred and eighty — and Zhang Yangzi's jaw dropped, and Wang Jinxi's jaw dropped, and Xie Xie, who had been about to say something loud, did not say anything at all, because the number was still climbing, and it did not stop until it reached a number that had no business belonging to a ten-year-old who had never held a spirit soul until he was eight and a half.

The machine said: **one hundred and seventy-eight.**

Spirit Connection realm. At ten years old. Thirty-four points higher than the number a man with smoky green eyes had written down, in silence, at the tournament.

Thirty-four. In five months.

Silence. And in that silence, Zhang Yangzi — who was the arithmetic one, who could not un-see a pattern, who had been doing sums quietly all morning — said, in a small voice, "That's over thirty."

"It's thirty-four," Lin Hao said helpfully.

"I can *count.*"

"I know you can. I just like hearing you say it."

Wu Zhangkong looked at the number, and his face did not change, because Wu Zhangkong's face did not change, and because he had written a number down once, in silence, at the tournament, and had carried it in his head ever since. He looked at the boy. He looked at the machine. He did the arithmetic that Zhang Yangzi had done, and then he did the arithmetic that Zhang Yangzi had not, which was to divide ninety-eight by five months and ask what in the world had been feeding a fire that hot.

And then he looked at the seven children, and at the bruises on six of them, and at the one without any, and he understood.

"Every fight," Wu Zhangkong said. It was not a question.

"Every fight," Lin Hao agreed.

"You have fought how many times since the tournament."

"I stopped counting at seventy," Lin Hao said, "because counting past seventy felt like showing off."

Xie Xie made a sound like a kettle.

Wu Zhangkong wrote the number down. He wrote it slowly. And then he said, "Well," and "that's not *normal*" was what Xie Xie said next, in a voice that had gone strangely small, and Wu Zhangkong agreed, and wrote it down, and said nothing else, because there was nothing else to say that would not raise a hundred questions he was not, yet, going to answer.

And Lin Hao — who had known, who had always known, who had watched this number coming since the sea took a girl and a man with smoky green eyes wrote it in a ledger and closed the book — looked at the number, and shrugged, and said, "I told you they'd measure me," in the voice of a boy who had told you, and had been right, and was not, particularly, enjoying it. "I told you it'd be a number. I didn't say it'd be a *normal* number." He looked at Wu Zhangkong. "You knew. You knew at the tournament. You wrote it down and you didn't say it."

"I wrote down a great many numbers at the tournament," Wu Zhangkong said, which was not a denial, and which Lin Hao took for what it was.

"And you didn't say this one."

"No," Wu Zhangkong agreed. "I didn't." And then, because he was Wu Zhangkong, and because the kindness he gave came sideways, in the flat voice, he said, "Some numbers are better carried quietly until they're heavy enough to set down." He looked at the machine, and at the thirty-four points that had grown on top of the quiet number like a debt accruing interest. "Yours got heavy faster than I expected. That is not a compliment. That is a warning. When a number moves that fast, people stop asking how and start asking *what.* I'll tell you what it means when I know. Not before." He capped the pen. "Understood."

"Understood," Lin Hao said, and meant it, and filed it, and did not say that the reason he meant it was not the warning.
