## Part 3: The Monstrous One

Gu Yue went last, because the staircase went up, and because Wu Zhangkong had arranged it that way, and because Wu Zhangkong — unlike everyone else in the room — already knew what the top step was.

**One hundred and fifty-three.**

Wait.

Zhang Yangzi blinked. Xie Xie blinked. And Zhang Yangzi, who could not un-see a pattern and who had spent the last four minutes arranging the morning into a staircase with one boy at the top of it, said, in a small voice, "That's *higher.*"

"Yes," Wu Zhangkong said.

"But Lin Hao's was one hundred and seventy-eight, and he's been—"

"Climbing," Wu Zhangkong said. "Yes." And he wrote down Gu Yue's number with exactly the same expression he had written down every other number, which was the expression of a man filling in a form, and the entire room understood, in one lurching instant, two things at once: that one hundred and fifty-three on a ten-year-old elementalist was a number that did not belong to children at all. Had not belonged to them since before any of the rest of the class had been measured; and that the boy who had spent five months climbing had climbed *to second place,* which was not the same thing as failing and was also not the thing he had been climbing for.

Gu Yue looked at Lin Hao. It was the first time she had looked directly at him all morning. Her face did not do anything that could be called an expression, and yet Xie Xie, watching from the safety of the boy's own considerable cowardice, felt the temperature in the room make a decision.

And Lin Hao — because he was Lin Hao, and because the teasing was how he said things that were too heavy to say straight — grinned at her and said, "Don't worry. You're still the mysterious one. I'm just the *loud* one."

"I have not said a word all morning," Gu Yue said.

"Exactly," Lin Hao said. "Mysterious."

Something happened to Gu Yue's face then that was not a smile and was absolutely not nothing, and it lasted less than a second, and Zhang Yangzi saw it and would think about it for a year.

Wu Zhangkong said, "Next is the endurance test," in the casual voice of a man changing the subject on purpose.

The endurance test measured the power of a single blow, because for soul masters, only attack power had meaning. Gu Yue went first. And her left fist — the left fist of a ten-year-old elementalist — registered **one hundred and fifteen kilograms,** and Zhang Yangzi nearly fell over, because she was an elementalist, she was ten, and elementalist soul masters did not hit like that, and Xie Xie, who had been measured at a number he was not, yet, going to be teased about, trembled a little, and said nothing, because he had learned.

And then it was Lin Hao's turn. He stepped up and put his fist into the machine, and the machine said **four hundred and seventy kilograms** — higher than Gu Yue's, higher than Wang Jinxi's, higher than a number that had any business coming out of a ten-year-old. Zhang Yangzi's jaw dropped a third time, and Lin Hao looked at it and said, "I've been swinging a hammer since I was four," in the voice of a boy explaining something obvious, "so either the machine's broken or I've been doing it right," and Wu Zhangkong wrote the number down. Said, "Your form is wrong," because he was Wu Zhangkong, and because the kindness came sideways, "which means the number is going to be a great deal higher when you fix it," and Lin Hao, who had been carrying a number quietly since he was six, looked at the man, and grinned, because that was the first kind thing anyone had said to him all day, and it had come, as all of Wu Zhangkong's kindness did, dressed up as an insult.

Wu Zhangkong looked at his form. The numbers were monstrous. The form was, indeed, wrong — a smith's form, built for a hammer and an anvil and a fixed target that never moved, and it had never been corrected because there had never been time and nobody had thought to.

"one hundred and seventy-eight," Wu Zhangkong said, "and four hundred and seventy, and your stance is a blacksmith's stance and you telegraph your left shoulder a full breath before you commit." He put the pen down. "Which means that everything you have is *earned* and none of it is finished." He looked at the seven of them. "Get up. All of you. We're not done."

## Part 4: Six

"Here is what we are going to do," Wu Zhangkong said, and there was something in his flat voice that Xie Xie had learned, over five months, to recognize as the sound of a man who had decided something and was going to enjoy finding out whether he was right. "Lin Hao. Center of the ground."

"Yes."

"The rest of you." Wu Zhangkong looked at the six. "One at a time. In order. Full commitment — no pulling, no yielding early, no theatrical collapse, Xie Xie, I know what you do. You fight him until you are stopped. Then the next one goes." He picked up the pointing stick. "And Lin Hao does not use his wind, and he does not use his talon."

The ground went quiet.

"Sir," Xie Xie said, "that's his *kit.*"

"I know what it is."

"You're taking away the two things that—"

"I am taking away," Wu Zhangkong said, "the two things that let him not be a swordsman." He looked at Lin Hao. "Your sword. Your body. Your eyes. That is all. If that is not enough, then I have been wrong about you for five months, and I would like to find that out now rather than in three years when something is trying to kill you."

And Lin Hao, who had been carrying a number quietly since he was six years old and the sea took a girl, and who had been carrying seventy-one lines in a ledger nobody knew existed, and who had been waiting — though he would have died before admitting it, and did nearly die, several times, in the next eleven minutes — for exactly this, drew the Stormbringer.

"You're going to be *so*—" Wulin began.

"Don't," Lin Hao said. "You're going to say something kind and encouraging and I need you to say something insulting, because I fight better when I'm annoyed."

"You have terrible hair."

"Perfect," Lin Hao said. "Thank you. Go be the first one to lose."

---

**Wang Jinxi** went first, because Wu Zhangkong put him first, and Wu Zhangkong put him first because Wang Jinxi was the one who had built a decoy fold to lie to Lin Hao's eyes, and Wu Zhangkong wanted to know whether the boy who had been lied to had learned anything from it.

Wang Jinxi's Bone Dragon King rose around him in yellow light and his claw came in on the line that had broken three of class one's best.

Lin Hao did not dodge it. He *met* it — Stormbringer flat, angled forty degrees, taking the impact on the blade the way an anvil takes a hammer, and the shock went down his arms and into his feet and into the dirt, and he did not move, because four hundred and seventy kilograms is what a body looks like when it has swung a hammer since it was four years old. And then the sword spoke. Not a cut. A *question* — laid along the inside of Wang Jinxi's wrist, exactly where the claw's own momentum had committed the arm to a direction it could no longer leave.

Wang Jinxi's claw was still going. Wang Jinxi was not. He went down on one knee with the Stormbringer's edge resting against the tendons of his own wrist, and he stayed there, and he said, "You read that."

"I read it five months ago," Lin Hao said. "You told me how it worked when you built it. You were very thorough. I appreciated it."

Wang Jinxi, who was not a boy who smiled, smiled. It was a small, terrible, delighted smile, and he got up and walked off the ground, and Wu Zhangkong made a mark on his form.

---

**Zhang Yangzi** went second. Shadow Phantasm Eagle — speed, angles, the boy who could be somewhere else. He had learned a great deal in five months. He came in low and fast and feinted the left, and Lin Hao's sword was already at the place the feint was going to end, because Lin Hao had sparred with this exact feint eleven times in the last three weeks and had answered it correctly nine.

One exchange. Zhang Yangzi's blade was on the ground and Zhang Yangzi was holding his wrist and looking at his own hand with the expression of a boy who has just been introduced to a stranger who knew his name.

"You knew," Zhang Yangzi said.

"I know," Lin Hao said. "I've been keeping notes."

"On *me?*"

"On everyone. You're seventh. You're a very good seventh, Zhang Yangzi, your feint is genuinely excellent, it's just that I've seen it, and once I've seen something I don't have to see it again." He offered a hand up. "That's not an insult. That's the most expensive thing I own."

Zhang Yangzi took the hand. He had been, all morning, a boy who had been told "not bad" for the first time since the rematch. Now he was a boy who had been told he was worth keeping notes on, and he did not know — nobody in class zero knew yet — that this was the highest thing Lin Hao had to give.

---

**Wei Xiaofeng** went third, and Wei Xiaofeng went third loudly.

Green Shadow Snake. Green Shadow Clones. Rank twenty-two and a grudge, and Wei Xiaofeng had spent five months being the seventh in a class of seven and had not, one single time, been told "not bad." He came in with two clones flanking and the real one behind, which was a genuinely good tactic, which was the tactic that had beaten Lin Hao in the test spar, which was precisely why Lin Hao had spent three weeks learning it.

The Stormbringer took the left clone apart. The right clone went for the ribs. Lin Hao turned into it — not away, *into* it — because the thing about clones is that they are all committed to the same intent, and intent has a direction, and if you walk toward the intent instead of the blade, the blade has to come find you, and by then the sword is already where the intent lives.

Wei Xiaofeng went down. Both clones went with him, because clones are not people and do not survive their owner's surprise.

"That was the *same thing* I did last month," Wei Xiaofeng said, from the dirt, in a voice of pure outrage.

"Yes."

"You *stole* it."

"I *learned* it," Lin Hao said, and offered the hand, and Wei Xiaofeng did not take it, and Lin Hao left it there anyway for a full three seconds before withdrawing it, because Wei Xiaofeng would take it eventually, and because leaving it there was the kind of thing that made that eventually arrive sooner. "You're the only one in this class who's taught me something twice. You should be proud. Nobody else has managed it."

Wei Xiaofeng's face did something complicated. He got up without help. He did not, however, say anything else for the rest of the afternoon, which Xie Xie would later describe as the single most frightening event of the entire day.

---

**Xie Xie** went fourth, and Xie Xie lasted longest, and Xie Xie knew it was coming, and Xie Xie was still furious about it.

Two rings. Light Dragon Dagger. Nine weeks of mornings and then months more, and Xie Xie had, over that time, become the one person alive who could genuinely hurt Lin Hao in a spar — which is why Lin Hao had asked for him every single morning, and why Xie Xie, who was many things but not stupid, had eventually understood what he was being used for and had decided, characteristically, to enjoy it.

Eleven exchanges. Xie Xie landed two — one on the shoulder, one across the forearm, and the second one opened skin, and Lin Hao hissed, and Xie Xie's whole face lit up like a lantern.

"*I got you.*"

"You got me."

"I got you *twice.*"

"You did."

"And you still won."

"I still won," Lin Hao agreed, and the Stormbringer was at Xie Xie's throat, and Xie Xie was grinning the grin of a boy who had drawn blood off a monster, and Lin Hao was grinning back, because the shoulder was going to bruise and the bruise was worth more than the win, and this was the whole arrangement between them and had been since the first morning.

"That's your sixty-ninth," Xie Xie said, touching his own throat where the edge had been. "I'm in the ledger at sixty-nine."

"You're in the ledger at *one,*" Lin Hao said. "You're the first line in it. You get top billing. Be honored."

"Top billing for *losing?*"

"Top billing for teaching me the most." Lin Hao sheathed nothing, because the next one was already walking, but he let the sword drop to a rest. "Nobody's taught me more than you. Nobody's close."

And Xie Xie — who had spent five months being the loud one, the fast one, the one who talked through everything because talking was how he kept from feeling it — did not say anything at all for a moment. Then he said, "Right. Well. Good. Excellent. I'm going to go bleed somewhere dignified," and walked off the ground holding his arm up like a banner.

---

**Wulin** went fifth.

The Stormbringer and the hammer met, and the training ground — which had been quiet for four fights — made a noise, because this was the fight everyone had wanted to see since the day the roster was read and the two names came out first and second.

It was not a long fight. It was, however, the only one that made Wu Zhangkong step forward.

Wulin's body was not, entirely, the same stuff as the other six. He took the Stormbringer flat across the forearm and the forearm did not bruise and Wulin did not slow, and Lin Hao — who had fought this exact brother every evening for months, who knew the hammer's lines the way he knew his own — found himself in the one exchange in the ledger that had no answer in it, because Wulin did not adapt. Wulin *endured.* You could learn the angle and the angle would still break your arm.

So Lin Hao did the only thing that worked, which was to stop trying to win the exchange and win the *position* instead — one step, blade down, edge at the base of Wulin's hammer wrist where the grip lived, and Wulin's hammer stopped, because the hammer could survive anything except not being held.

"You cheated," Wulin said, delighted.

"I *adapted.*"

"You cheated *adaptively.*"

"That's the whole thing," Lin Hao said. "That's literally the entire thing. It's in the name."

Wulin let go of the hammer's head with one hand and put that hand on Lin Hao's shoulder, and left it there, and the training ground — the six, the man with the pointing stick — watched the two of them for a beat longer than was strictly about combat, and then Wu Zhangkong said, "Gu Yue," in the flat voice, and the beat ended.

---

**Gu Yue** went sixth.

She did not release a ring. She did not raise a hand. She walked to the center of the ground the way she did everything, which was as though the ground had agreed to be walked on, and she stopped one meter from the Stormbringer's point, and she looked at Lin Hao, and Lin Hao — who had seventy-one lines in a ledger, who had a sword that spoke first, who had four hundred and seventy kilograms and one hundred and seventy-eight points and five months of pressure behind him — understood, with total clarity, that he had no line for this one.

Because Gu Yue had never fought him. Not once. She had fought beside him, and near him, and she had poured a cup of water under four gripping toes, and she had looked at him exactly once that morning. But she had never, in five months, given him a single thing to write down.

"You can't," Gu Yue said, quietly.

"Can't what."

"You can't win this one. Not because I'm stronger. Because you have nothing." Her eyes were the color of a filed report. "You fight with everything you've already seen. I haven't shown you anything. So there is no fight. There's only you, and a person you don't have."

Lin Hao stood there for a long moment with the Stormbringer at the ready and the whole of his ledger — seventy-one lines, five months, every bruise he had ever been handed — completely, entirely useless.

And then he laughed. He laughed so hard he had to lower the sword, and Xie Xie, from the dirt, said, "Is he *broken?*"

"No," Lin Hao said, wiping his eyes. "No, I'm — she's right. She's completely right and it's the *best* thing anyone's ever said to me." He looked at Gu Yue with an expression that Zhang Yangzi, watching, would spend a year thinking about. "Everyone else in this class, I've got them. I've got their whole self written down. You've given me *nothing.* Do you know how long it's been since I had to fight somebody I couldn't read? Since the tournament? Since *Wang Jinxi's decoy?* You're the only mystery I've got left and you've been keeping it for five months and I didn't even *notice,* because I was so busy having the answer to everybody else."

Gu Yue looked at him.

"So don't fight me," Lin Hao said. "That's the answer. I'd lose. I'll lose every time until you show me something, and you're not going to, because you're *Gu Yue.* So instead I'm going to say the thing nobody's said to you all morning." He put the Stormbringer away. "Thank you. Genuinely. You're the only one who could have told me that, and you told me before I found out the expensive way."

Gu Yue did not fight him. Wu Zhangkong made a mark on his form that was, by his standards, a long one.

And the six were down — five of them beaten, one of them undefeated by declining to begin — and Lin Hao stood in the center of the training ground with two rings and a sword and no wind and no talon and a bruise forming on his shoulder where Xie Xie had opened him, and Wu Zhangkong looked at the form, and at the six, and at the boy, and said the thing that the whole of class zero would repeat, in one version or another, for the rest of their lives.

"Four times," Wu Zhangkong said.

"Sir?"

"I have hit you with this stick four times in five months." He turned it in his hand. "I hit Xie Xie more times before breakfast today. I have not hit you four times because you are fast. I have not hit you four times because you are strong. I have not hit you four times because after the first time, you had me — and I have six rings, and two of them are ten thousand years old, and I have fought people whose names you will hear before you die." He put the stick down. "You are the strongest in this class, and I want to be careful about the second half of this: Gu Yue's numbers are not the ones I would trade for yours. But there is not one person in this room who could beat you twice, and there is not one person in this room whom you would lose to a second time." A pause. "That is a different thing. It is, in my experience, the more dangerous thing. And it is the reason I am going to stop holding back on you, starting tomorrow, which I want you to understand is not a kindness."

"I understand," Lin Hao said.

"You don't," Wu Zhangkong said. "You will." And he was gone, and the six of them lay on the training-ground dirt like a crop that had been harvested — again — and Xie Xie said, "I have *never* been so tired and so proud at the same time, and I got beaten by a boy with a *stick*," and Wulin said, "Hao."

"Yes."

"You beat all of us."

"I beat five of you," Lin Hao said. "Gu Yue beat me and she didn't even touch me, which is the worst kind of losing, and I'm going to think about it for a year." He lay back on the dirt beside his brother and looked at the sky, which was doing the thing the Eastsea sky did in the late afternoon, which was to turn the color of cooling steel. "Wulin. Nobody's ever just *declined* to fight me before."

"She's strange."

"She's *magnificent,*" Lin Hao said. "There's a difference. You'd know the difference if you paid attention to anyone other than hammers."

"I pay attention to you."

"You pay attention to my *hair.*"

"That's attention," Wulin said, and the two of them lay in the dirt and argued about it for the length of a cooling forge, and neither of them said the other thing, which was that the boy who had kept a ledger of seventy-one fights had, today, been handed his first blank page in five months. That he had laughed about it, and then filed it, and then lain in the dirt next to his brother and felt, for reasons he would not have been able to explain to anyone, considerably lighter than one hundred and seventy-eight points.

## Part 5: What the Numbers Meant

That night, on the roof that was not theirs anymore, the two brothers sat with their backs against the warm chimney, and Wulin said, "one hundred and seventy-eight," the way you say a number you've been carrying.

"one hundred and seventy-eight," Lin Hao agreed. "Gu Yue's a hundred and fifty-three. I'm thirty-five behind her. I've had all day with it and I've stopped minding."

"She's stronger than you," Wulin said. It was not a challenge. It was Wulin being Wulin, which was to say the true thing straight, without the dressing that Lin Hao put on everything.

"She is," Lin Hao agreed, without a flicker of anything that needed managing. "She's stronger, she's faster than she has any right to be, she hits like a siege engine, and she has never once given me a single thing to write down. She'd win. Today, tomorrow, next year, she'd win." He nudged his brother's shoulder. "And I'd beat everybody else in the building twice, and lose to her every time, and I have made my *peace* with that, Wulin, which is more than I can say for you and your feelings about the boy from the beef shop."

"I have made my peace with the beef shop."

"You've made a *grudge* with the beef shop."

"That's a kind of peace."

Lin Hao laughed. And then, because the laughing was the door and the room was behind it, he said, "Do you know what Wu Zhangkong told me, after the numbers? Not the warning. Before it. He said 'some numbers are better carried quietly until they're heavy enough to set down' — at the tournament, he said that, and today he said mine got heavy faster than he expected." He looked at his brother. "It means he's carrying it too. I've been carrying it alone since I was six, since the sea took Na'er, since the day I decided I'd be strong enough that it wouldn't happen again — and today a man with smoky green eyes told me he's been carrying it too, quietly, and he'll tell me what it means when he knows. And I don't know why that's the thing that got me, Wulin. It should be the number. It's not the number. It's that I'm not carrying it alone."

Wulin's shoulder was against his, warm, and the harbor did its accounting, and neither of them said the rest, because the teasing was the whole of the saying, and the quiet was the room you got to through the teasing, and you could not get to the room any other way.

"Also," Lin Hao said, after a while, "she said I fight with everything I've already seen. And she's right. That's the whole talent. Every fight I've ever had is still in there — Mo Si's short sword, Qin Lang's feed-line, that bear's honest momentum, your brother's hammer, seventy-one lines of it. That's why the number moved. It's not that I'm working harder than everyone. It's that everyone else *forgets* their fights and I don't. Every bruise I've ever taken is still working for me." He turned his hand over, palm up, in the harbor light — the smith's hand, the sword hand, the one that had taken Xie Xie's dagger across the forearm that afternoon and would carry the line for a week. "Thirty-four points in five months. Do you know what that means?"

"That you're a monster."

"It means *the fighting is the cultivation,* Wulin. Everyone in that class sits and breathes and waits for the numbers to move. I get hit. Wu Zhangkong told me to expect him to stop holding back, and I said I understood, and I meant it, and I meant it because I understood the *other* half of it too." He closed his hand. "Every time he hits me properly, I get better. Faster than anyone in that building gets better. So the more dangerous it gets, the faster I move — and that's not a warning, that's a *schedule.*"

Wulin was quiet for a moment. "That's terrifying."

"That's Tuesday," Lin Hao said.

And under it all, on the far water, the hawk watched the boy who had been measured, and had been given a number, and had beaten six of them with a sword and a body and nothing else, and had been told — by the only person in the class who had nothing to teach him, and by the only person who had ever hit him — what he was. And the hawk, which had been asking a question for a very long time, did not ask it that night, because the boy was, for the first time since the sea took a girl, not entirely alone with it. And the question stayed quiet. And the dark water kept what it kept. And the number — one hundred and seventy-eight, and climbing, and heavy enough now to set down, though not yet set down — sat on the shelf with the rest of them, and the ledger next to it had seventy-one lines in it, and one blank page, and the blank page had a name on it that nobody had said out loud.


Rank twenty-nine arrived during the gauntlet, somewhere between the fourth opponent and the fifth, and he did not mention it, because he was busy. That was the whole mechanism, and he understood it better than anyone in the building: he did not cultivate his way up. He was *fought* his way up.

Somewhere between the fourth opponent and the fifth the hawk stirred, eight hundred and forty years of condensed wind turning over in him like a sleeper changing position.

## Part 1: What Not Holding Back Sounds Like

The first thing Lin Hao learned about Wu Zhangkong not holding back was that it had a sound.

Holding back had a sound too, and Lin Hao had known it for five months without knowing he knew it — the particular whistle of a white wax pointing stick moving at the speed a man uses when he intends to teach rather than to hurt. It was quick. It was precise. It was, he understood now in retrospect, *merciful,* and he had never once mistaken it for slow, but he had also never understood that there was another gear, because there is no way to hear the difference between a man's second speed and a man's first until the man shifts.

The shift happened on a Tuesday, in the fourth minute of the evening session, and it sounded like a sail catching.

The stick arrived at Lin Hao's left ribs. He had read it — he had read it completely, the angle, the intent, the half-beat where Wu Zhangkong's shoulder committed — and he had moved, and the move was correct, and the stick was there anyway, because the stick had been moving faster than the read.

Lin Hao went down. Not far. He went down onto one knee in the training-ground dirt with his left arm locked against his side and his breath somewhere above him, and the six of them stopped, because in five months Wu Zhangkong had hit Lin Hao four times, and the four times had looked, from the outside, like accidents.

This did not look like an accident.

"Again," Wu Zhangkong said.

"You broke my rib," Lin Hao said, from the ground, in the voice of a boy conducting an inventory.

"I bruised it. Get up."

"I'm conducting an inventory. There's a process." But he was up, because the process was, in fact, already finished, and because the part of him that conducted inventories had been quietly handed over to the part of him that wanted the next one. He rolled the shoulder. He put his feet in the smith's stance that Wu Zhangkong had called wrong in front of the whole class, and then — because he had spent the eleven days since thinking about nothing else — he moved his back foot four centimetres and turned his hip eleven degrees, and the stance stopped being a smith's stance and became, for the first time, a swordsman's.

Wu Zhangkong looked at his feet for a moment.

"Better," he said, which was the second kind thing he had said to Lin Hao all week, and which came, as always, without any of the dressing. Then the stick came again.

## Part 2

"You know they talk about you," Xie Xie said, somewhere in the middle of the second hour, lying on his back with his arms behind his head. "Not the fighting. The *face.* There are three girls in class two who have a *system* for walking past the yard. A system, Lin Hao. With a schedule."

"That's ridiculous."

"It's extremely well organised and I have watched it happen four times."
: Six

He was hit six times that evening.

This is the number that mattered, and the six of them counted it out loud, because the six of them had spent five months believing that four was a ceiling — Xie Xie kept the count on his fingers, and by the fourth hit had stopped teasing, and by the sixth had gone quiet in a way that Lin Hao found considerably more alarming than the hits.

"Six," Xie Xie said, afterwards, sitting on the ground with his arms around his knees. "In one *evening.*"

"Yes."

"In five months he hit you *four times.*"

"Yes."

"And you're *happy?*" Xie Xie looked at him with genuine distress. "Hao. Look at me. He hit you six times and your face is doing the thing."

"My face is doing the thing because I learned six things," Lin Hao said. He was lying on his back in the dirt, which was the position he did his best thinking in, and he held up his own hand and counted on it, because he was his father's son and he did not trust memory for numbers. "One. He commits with the shoulder but he *aims* with the wrist, so if I read the shoulder I'm reading a half-beat old. Two. The stick is slower than the arm on the way out and faster on the way back, which means the second hit of any pair is the one to dodge, and I've been dodging the first. Three. He breathes in before a real one. Not a big breath. A small one. I've been hearing it for months and filing it under *weather.*" He put a finger down. "Four. He does not like my left side because my left side is honest, and he's been going there all month hoping I'd fix it, and I didn't fix it, I *rotated* it, and that's the difference between a stance and a stance. Five—"

"You're doing this out loud."

"I'm *filing,* Xie Xie, there's a difference, and you're interrupting. Five. When he wants to teach me something he hits me somewhere it won't matter, and when he wants to find something out he hits me somewhere it will. Six were somewhere it will. Which means he isn't teaching me tonight." Lin Hao sat up. "He's *measuring* me."

The training ground had gone quiet, and Lin Hao became aware — the way he became aware of most things, slightly after the fact — that all six of them were looking at him, and that Wang Jinxi was looking at him the hardest, and that Wu Zhangkong had stopped at the edge of the ground on his way out and had not, in fact, left.

"What did you get?" Wu Zhangkong said.

Lin Hao looked at him. "That I can read you at about forty percent."

The six made various noises.

"Forty," Wu Zhangkong repeated.

"I get the shape of it. I don't get the timing. You're six rings and two of them are ten thousand years old and I'm ten, so forty percent is not a complaint, it's a *measurement,* and I want it said that I'm not complaining." Lin Hao got to his feet, and winced, and did not let the wince become anything. "How much were you holding back before tonight?"

"All of it," Wu Zhangkong said, and left, and the seven of them stood in the dirt and understood that they had just been told, in the flat voice, that the man who had been hitting them for five months had never once hit them.

## Part 3: The Answering Stroke

On the fifth day, Wu Zhangkong brought a second stick.

Not for hitting. He brought it because he had decided to teach, and because Wu Zhangkong taught the way he did everything else, which was by arriving with the equipment already in his hand and not explaining it until you had failed without it.

"You fight with a sword," he said.

"Yes."

"You fight with a sword the way a man who has only ever met swords fights with a sword. Which is well. It is not the same thing." He put the second stick into his left hand and held the pointing stick in his right, and stood there with his arms at his sides, and Lin Hao understood that he was being shown a posture rather than a technique, and that the posture was the lesson. "There are five things a person can be doing with a blade. Holding it. Aiming it. Moving it. Committing it. And knowing which of those they are doing. You are very good at the first four. You are the best at the first four that I have ever seen in a child, and I want to be precise about that, because I want you to hear the second half."

"The second half."

"The fifth one is not a skill. It is a *decision,* and it has to be made before the other four, or the other four are just noise." He raised the second stick an inch. "Tonight: the Answering Stroke. You will not learn it tonight. You will learn what it costs."

And then he attacked, and the lesson turned out to be that the Answering Stroke — the counter-form, the stroke that arrives at the place your opponent's own commitment has already promised — is not a movement you make with your arm. It is a movement you make with your *patience.* You have to be willing to be almost hit. You have to stand inside the arriving blade for the whole of its travel and let it come, because the answer only exists at the end of the commitment, and a boy who flinches a half-beat early gets the shape of the answer without the substance of it.

Lin Hao was hit eleven times learning it.

He was hit eleven times because eleven times he moved early, and Wu Zhangkong said nothing at all about it, only hit him again, and on the twelfth exchange Lin Hao stood still inside a stick that was coming at his collarbone and felt — for a duration of time so short that he could not afterwards say whether it had been real — the entire architecture of the attack. Not the angle. The *promise.* The place Wu Zhangkong had already agreed to arrive at.

And the Stormbringer went there before the stick did, and rested, and Wu Zhangkong stopped.

The training ground had gone quiet again, and the six of them were pretending very hard not to be watching, and Wu Zhangkong looked at the sword resting a hand's width from his own wrist and said, "What did that feel like."

"Like you'd already told me," Lin Hao said. "You told me where you were going. Not on purpose. You just — you can't commit to a strike without saying where it's going, and I've been hearing it for months and I thought it was a *sound,* and it isn't a sound, it's a decision, and the decision happens before the movement, and if I wait for the decision instead of the movement I don't have to be fast at all."

Wu Zhangkong was quiet for a long moment.

"That is the Answering Stroke," he said. "You have the shape of it. You will have the substance of it in a year, and you will have it in a year rather than ten because you are the first student I have had who heard the decision before he was shown it." He put the second stick down. "Your homework is not to practise it. Your homework is to notice that everything I have taught you so far has been *reading,* and to ask yourself why a swordsman's whole curriculum is reading." He turned to go, and stopped. "And Lin Hao."

"Sir."

"The stance you fixed. Keep it. I'm not going to correct your feet again, and if they go wrong I'm going to let them go wrong until you lose a fight to them, because a thing a teacher fixes belongs to the teacher." He left, and Xie Xie said, from the ground, "That's the meanest thing I've ever heard anybody say as a compliment," and Lin Hao stood in the middle of the training ground with his sword still in his hand and his feet four centimetres from where they had been for a year, and felt — very distinctly, the way you feel a joint come into line — something in him *set.*

Rank thirty came in the fourth week, and it did not feel like the others. The others had arrived — a settling, a joint coming into line. This one arrived and then *stopped,* the way a lift stops at the top floor, and Lin Hao sat up in the dark at four in the morning with the specific and entirely new sensation of having run out of staircase.

Twenty-one to thirty was the second-ring band. He was at the top of it. And the thing above him was not a rank he could earn, because the RANK RULE did not care how hard he had been hit: you cannot pass a bottleneck without a ring, and a third ring needed a soul that had crossed a thousand years, and the hawk was at seven hundred and seventy and had never once been in a hurry about anything.

Eleven hits, a stance, and one stroke had taken him the length of the band. There was nothing left to be corrected into.

"So that's the shape of it," he said aloud, to a dormitory, because thinking out loud was how he finished an argument. "I can be taught. I can be fought. I can be *wrong* at somebody until I'm right. But I can't be hurried, and neither can the bird."

The hawk, eight hundred and forty-five years of condensed wind riding quietly inside him, did not comment. It never did. But Lin Hao had spent four years learning which silences were empty, and this one was not empty — it was the silence of something that had its own schedule, and had known all along that the boy would arrive at the top of the stairs and have to sit down.

## Part 4: Seventy-Eight

The ledger grew by seven lines in three weeks.

Six of them were Wu Zhangkong, and they were the strangest six lines in it, because every other line in the ledger was a line about a *person* — Mo Si's knife, Qin Lang's feed-line, the bear's honest momentum — and these six were lines about a *speed.* He had never had to learn a speed before. Everyone else in his life had moved at a speed he could arrive at, and Wu Zhangkong moved at a speed he could only *predict,* and prediction was a different skill, and it turned out that he had one, and that it was good, and that it had been sitting there unused the way a tool sits unused in a drawer until a job arrives that needs it.

The seventh line was Xie Xie.

Not a new answer — he had eleven of those already, and Xie Xie had not invented a twelfth in three weeks, because Xie Xie was, for all his speed, a boy with a fixed vocabulary of violence. The seventh line was different. It was the line where Lin Hao finally wrote down *why* he and Xie Xie had never once, in months of mornings, actually hurt each other badly — and the answer, when he wrote it out, was so obvious that he sat on the bunk above Zhou Zhangxi's snoring for a full minute feeling like an idiot.

They were moving at the same tempo. Not the same speed — Xie Xie was faster, and had always been faster, and would go to his grave being faster. The same *tempo.* They arrived at decisions in the same beat, which meant that every time Xie Xie committed, Lin Hao was already committing to the answer, and every time Lin Hao committed, Xie Xie was already somewhere else, and the two of them had been doing this so long that it looked like skill and was actually *rhythm,* and rhythm was the thing you could not fake and could not teach and could not buy.

He wrote it down. And then, because he was Lin Hao and because a thing written down was a thing that could be used, he thought about what rhythm was *for.*

Wu Zhangkong had said, in the mecha lecture, that two soul masters could fuse — could speak with one voice — if their souls were compatible enough. Lin Hao had been ten years old for four months and had heard that sentence the way everyone heard it, as a fact about the world, like weather. Now he lay in the dark above Zhou Zhangxi and turned it over, and looked at the seventh line, and understood that he was holding a fact about the world in one hand and a fact about himself in the other, and that the two facts had the same shape.

He did not say anything about it. Not to Xie Xie, not to Wulin, not to anyone, and this was unusual for him, because Lin Hao said everything — Lin Hao's entire method of being alive was to say the thing, loudly, first, before the thing could say him. But this one he kept, and he kept it for a reason he could not have articulated, which was that saying it out loud would make it a *plan,* and it wasn't a plan. It was a door. And doors were not plans. You did not schedule a door. You arrived at it, one day, when you were heavy enough to open it, and until then you left it alone and did your work.

Eleven days later, Wu Zhangkong paired him with Xie Xie for the evening session, and did not say why, and Lin Hao — who had spent eleven days not saying anything — fought his oldest friend for twenty-two minutes across a training ground that had gone completely silent, and understood that the man with the smoky green eyes had arrived at the same door from the other side, and had looked at it, and had decided, without saying so, to leave it exactly where Lin Hao had left it.

Neither of them mentioned it. That was the whole of the conversation, and it was the most respectful thing anyone had ever done for him.

## Part 5: one hundred and eighty-four

The growth was not a surprise, and it was not gradual, and it was not the sort of thing that happened to people who sat in meditation and breathed.

It happened on the ninth day, at four in the morning, in the dark, and it woke him up.

He had taken the stick on the left ribs nine times in three weeks and the bruise had gone through its colours, and his soul power had been working on the problem the way his soul power worked on everything — quietly, in the background, the way the smith's fire works on a bar you've already put down. What had changed on the ninth day was that the *reading* caught up with the *body.* For eight days he had been able to see Wu Zhangkong's wrist and unable to move in time. On the ninth day he moved in time. Not all the way. Not reliably. But the gap closed, and something in him — the thing that had been fed a hundred-year soul at eight and a half, the thing that had eaten nine years of pressure and asked for more — took the closing of that gap and *converted* it.

one hundred and eighty-four became one hundred and eighty-four overnight.

Six points. From one closed gap. He lay in the dark and did the arithmetic, because he was his father's son, and the arithmetic said that the gap he had closed against Wu Zhangkong was worth more than the entire tournament had been, and the reason was not that Wu Zhangkong was stronger than a tournament. The reason was that Wu Zhangkong was *harder,* and hardness was the fuel, and he had spent three weeks being fed the hardest thing in Eastsea City and had not noticed he was eating.

"Hao," Wulin said, from the bunk below, in the voice of a boy who had not been asleep either. "Your soul power is making a noise."

"My soul power doesn't make a noise."

"It's making a noise. It's doing the thing it does when you've been sitting in the sun." A pause. "Did you grow again?"

"Eight."

"In your *sleep?*"

"In my sleep."

Wulin was quiet for a moment. "That's not fair."

"It's not," Lin Hao agreed cheerfully, and rolled over, and went back to sleep, because the arithmetic was finished and the numbers were put away and there was training in four hours and a man with a stick who had, apparently, never once hit him.


Rank thirty arrived in the fourth week, and the moment it did, everything stopped. Not the training. The *rank.* Twenty-one to thirty was the second-ring band and he was standing at the top of it, and the wall in front of him was not a wall he could climb — it was a wall that needed a third ring, and a third ring needed a hawk that had crossed a thousand years, and the hawk was at seven hundred and seventy and had never once, in four years, been in a hurry.

"You're at the top," Wulin said that night, in the tone of a boy who had been keeping count for four months and had not said so.

"I'm at the top of the stairs," Lin Hao agreed. "There's a door at the top. The door is locked and the key is a bird."

"That's the weirdest thing you've ever said."

"It's the truest thing I've ever said. Everything from here on costs something I can't forge and can't fight for. I have to *wait* for it, Wulin, and I have never once been good at that, and I've got a feeling I'm about to find out what I'm made of.

## Part 1: What Wei Xiaofeng Was Doing at Six in the Morning

Lin Hao found him because he could not sleep, and he could not sleep because Wu Zhangkong had hit him eleven times the previous evening and his ribs had opinions, and the dormitory at six in the morning smelled of cold stone and Zhou Zhangxi's snoring, so he went outside to do the breathing that his father had taught him for exactly this situation.

Wei Xiaofeng was on the training ground. Alone. Doing his clone work.

Not sparring. Not training. *Drilling* — the same feint-and-split he had used in the gauntlet, the one Lin Hao had learned in three weeks and turned back on him in eleven seconds, over and over, from the top, with the mechanical patience of a boy who had been given an answer and had decided, correctly, that the answer was not good enough.

Lin Hao stood in the doorway for a full minute watching, because it was the most interesting thing he had seen all week, and because he understood immediately what he was looking at: Wei Xiaofeng was not practicing the move. He was practicing the *variant.* Every fourth repetition he changed something — the angle of the split, the depth of the feint, the beat between them — and then he went back to the original and started again.

"You're building a second one," Lin Hao said.

Wei Xiaofeng did not jump. That was the first thing. Wei Xiaofeng, who was loud about everything, did not jump, which meant he had known Lin Hao was there for some time and had chosen, deliberately, to keep working.

"Go away," Wei Xiaofeng said, without heat.

"You're building a second variant so the next time I answer the first one, there's a different one behind it." Lin Hao walked out onto the ground. "That's correct. That's the correct response. I want you to know that I recognize it as correct, because I'm the one who made it necessary, and I'm not unsympathetic."

"You beat me in eleven seconds."

"I did."

"In front of *everyone.*"

"I did," Lin Hao agreed, "and I've thought about that, actually. I've thought about it a lot, because I liked beating you and I didn't like *how* I beat you, and those are two different things, and I'd like to explain the difference if you'll let me, and if you won't let me I'll explain it anyway, because it's six in the morning and I have ribs and no self-control."

Wei Xiaofeng looked at him. It was a long look, and it was the first look he had given Lin Hao since the gauntlet that was not made of outrage.

"You learned my technique in three weeks," he said. "How."

"I have a thing," Lin Hao said. "It's not a secret, it's just not interesting to talk about, because the interesting part isn't the learning, it's the *keeping.* I keep them. Every fight I've ever had is still in me, working. Seventy-eight of them, this morning. Mo Si's short sword, Qin Lang's feed-line, a bear's honest momentum, your clone work, my brother's hammer, Wu Zhangkong's wrist." He sat down on the training-ground wall, which hurt, and did it anyway. "And here's the part I want you to hear, Wei Xiaofeng, and I want you to hear it while you're still angry, because it'll sound better while you're angry. You are the only person in class zero who has ever taught me the same thing *twice.* Everyone else gave me one answer. You gave me a variant, and a variant is worth four answers, because a variant means the technique is alive, and a live technique grows, and everything else I have is a dead one that I know perfectly."

Wei Xiaofeng was quiet for a long moment.

"So don't stop," Lin Hao said. "Build the second one. Build the third. Make me keep coming back, because every time I come back I have to *re-learn* you, and re-learning is the only kind of learning that costs me anything." He got up off the wall. "Also it's six in the morning and you have no shirt on and it's eleven degrees and I'm going back inside, and if you tell anyone about this conversation I'll deny it and then I'll beat you again in nine seconds, which is a full two seconds faster, and you'll never hear the end of it."

"I'm going to tell everyone," Wei Xiaofeng said.

"You're going to tell *Xie Xie,*" Lin Hao said, "because Xie Xie is the only one who'll enjoy it, and you like him, and you've never admitted that either." And he went inside, and the ribs complained, and behind him on the cold training ground Wei Xiaofeng put his shirt back on very slowly, and then went back to work, and built the second variant before breakfast.

## Part 2

He caught his reflection in a window and looked away, and then looked back, because he had stopped recognising himself at speed. Storm-gray at the temple, gold-flecked eyes, faint feather-marks on both forearms. He had been ten years old a long time and none of this had been in the plan, and there had never been a plan.
: The Accident

The platform sessions were announced on the fourth day, in the flat voice, at the end of the evening session, and the announcement was four sentences long and changed the shape of everything.

"The Eastsea Spirit Pagoda has granted class zero access to the elementary Spirit Ascension Platform," Wu Zhangkong said. "You enter in two weeks. Inside, you will fight soul beasts, and the soul beasts will not be adjusted for your age, and nothing in there will care what your name is. You will be alone — the platform separates you on entry. You will find each other or you will not." A pause. "Some of you will press the exit within a minute. I would prefer you didn't tell each other which."

"Can we die?" Zhang Yangzi asked, because Zhang Yangzi asked the questions.

"You cannot die," Wu Zhangkong said, which was true, and which was not the whole truth, and which Lin Hao noticed, and filed.

And then, on the eighth day, the accident happened, and the accident is the reason that anyone in class zero learned what Gu Yue actually was.

It was a falling beam. Class zero trained in the old hall at the north edge of the grounds, and the old hall had a roof that the academy had been promising to fix since before any of them were born, and the beam that came down was not dramatic — it was not a collapsing building, it was one beam, maybe forty kilograms, coming off a rotten bracket at four meters, directly above the place where Xie Xie had been standing a half-second before and was no longer, because Xie Xie had moved.

The problem was that Xie Xie had moved *into* Zhang Yangzi.

It was the sort of thing that happens in a room full of people who are all moving fast, and it would have been nothing — a shove, a stumble, an elbow — except that Zhang Yangzi had been mid-feint with his weight committed forward and his wings half-out. The shove put him down hard on his left wrist at the exact angle that wrists do not like, and the sound the wrist made was a sound that all seven of them heard, and then the beam landed, and the beam was not the emergency.

Lin Hao was already moving. He had been moving before the beam fell, which was a thing he would think about later — that his body had gone toward the *sound* and not the *danger,* because the sound was the sound of a person being hurt and his six years of deciding to be strong enough had wired him to it faster than to anything else. He got to Zhang Yangzi in two strides. He got his hands under the wrist. He had three seconds of actual competence, because he had set his father's dislocated thumb twice and he knew what a wrist looked like when it was broken and this wrist was broken.

And then Gu Yue was there, and Gu Yue did a thing.

She did not run. Lin Hao saw it happen from ninety centimetres away and he saw all of it, and he would keep all of it for the rest of his life: the air around her went *green,* a green so pale it was almost a thought. Then there was a flash of silver that was not light exactly, it was more like the place where she had been *stopped being a place,* and she was crouching beside Zhang Yangzi's wrist with her hand already on it, and the distance she had crossed was eleven meters, and she had not crossed it.

"Hold him still," Gu Yue said.

"You—," Lin Hao said.

"*Hold him still.*"

He held him still.

What she did to the wrist was not healing — Lin Hao knew what healing looked like, his mother had a neighbour who was a healer, and this was not that. This was *cold,* a cold that came out of her palm and went into the swelling and *argued* with it, and the swelling lost. Zhang Yangzi's face went white and then less white. The bone did not go back, because she was not that, but the pain left, and the pain leaving was the whole of the mercy available, and she gave all of it.

"Splint," she said. "Three weeks. Don't let him use the wings."

"Right," Lin Hao said. And then, because he was Lin Hao, because he had been handed the single most interesting thing that had happened to him since the sea took a girl, and because the only thing he knew how to do with an interesting thing was to say it out loud: "You teleported."

"No."

"You *teleported.* Eleven meters. I was watching you and you didn't move, you just — there was a green thing, and a silver thing, and then you were here."

"I moved quickly," Gu Yue said, and stood up, and wiped her hand on her trouser leg, and looked at him with an expression that was not a warning and was absolutely not nothing.

"That's the *worst* lie I have ever heard," Lin Hao said, delighted. "Xie Xie is fast. Xie Xie is the fastest thing in this building, and Xie Xie *moves,* you can see him move, he's a blur and a blur is still a *thing that travels.* You didn't travel. You were there and then you were here and the middle part didn't happen, and I know what the middle part is, Gu Yue, the middle part is *space,* and you did something to it."

The hall was silent. All six of them were watching, and Wu Zhangkong had appeared in the doorway at some point and was leaning against the frame with his arms folded and the ghost of something on his face that Lin Hao would have bet money on.

Gu Yue looked at him for a long moment.

"You have seventy-eight of them," she said.

Lin Hao stopped. "What?"

"Seventy-eight. You told Wei Xiaofeng." Her eyes were the colour of a filed report. "You keep them. Everyone you've ever fought. That's what you told him at six in the morning on the training ground, and I know because I was there before you were, and I left before you saw me, and I have not decided yet whether I meant to." A beat. "You have seventy-eight. And you have one page with nothing on it, and the page is me, and you have been carrying that for three weeks, and you have been *cheerful* about it, which is the part I do not understand."

Lin Hao, for the first time in the four months that anyone in class zero had known him, did not immediately have something to say.

"So here is the thing," Gu Yue said. "I can tell you what that was, and then you would have seventy-nine, and the page would not be blank, and you would stop being the only person in this building who has to *work* to see me." She tilted her head a fraction. "And I have decided that I do not want that. Not because I don't trust you. I trust you more than anyone here, and I want you to understand that I am aware of how strange that is to say out loud."

"Say it again."

"No."

"Gu Yue. *Say it again.*"

"I said I don't want you to have it," she said, "not that I don't want you to have *me,* and those are different, and you are smart enough to know the difference, and you are also going to spend a week pretending you're not." And she walked out of the hall, and the six of them stood there, and Zhang Yangzi — whose wrist was splinted, whose pain was gone, who had been carried out of his own catastrophe by a girl he had never once spoken to — said, in a small voice, "What just happened?"

"I have no idea," Xie Xie said, awed. "That was the best thing I've ever seen and I have seen this one *walk up a wall.*"

## Part 3: Seventy-Nine

He wrote the line anyway.

Not the technique — he did not have the technique, and he understood now that he was not going to get it, and he had made his peace with that faster than he had expected, because there was something in *I trust you more than anyone here* that outweighed the arithmetic, and he had not known that about himself.

The line was this: **Gu Yue — does not cross distance. Rearranges it. Green first, then silver. She chose to show me and chose not to explain, which means the showing was not an accident and the silence was not a refusal. She was on the training ground at six in the morning before I was. She has been watching me the way I watch everyone.**

And underneath it, in the different ink — the ink he had used once before, for Guang Long, for the fight he had lost — he wrote: **she is not the blank page. I was the blank page. She has had me written down for months and I never once noticed, and I notice everything.**

That was the seventy-ninth line, and it was the first line in the ledger that was not about how to win.

The growth came two days later, and it came the way it always came now, which was sideways and overnight and slightly rude. one hundred and ninety-one became one hundred and ninety-one — seven points, the largest single movement since the tournament — and he lay in the dark doing the arithmetic and understood, with a mild shock, that the fifteen points had not come from a fight at all. They had come from *being wrong.* From discovering, at ten years old, that he had misread a person for four months, and that the misreading had been comfortable, and that he had preferred the comfortable misreading to the work of checking it.

His soul had eaten the correction. That was the whole mechanism, and it was more honest than he wanted it to be: the talent did not reward him for winning. It rewarded him for *updating.*

"Hao," Wulin said, from below, in the voice of a boy who had stopped being surprised. "You're doing the noise again."

"Fifteen."

"In your sleep."

"In my sleep."

"You did that last time too." Wulin rolled over. "I've decided it's fine. I've decided you're a furnace and I live next to you and I get warm, and I've stopped asking why."

"That's the most romantic thing anyone's ever said to me."

"I'm going to hit you."

"You're going to *try,*" Lin Hao said, and the harbour did its accounting, and the ribs complained, and somewhere in the dark a hawk that had been watching a girl for four months turned its head, and did not ask its question, and did not need to.

## Part 4: Two Weeks

The last thing that happened before the platform was that Wang Jinxi asked to be paired with him.

Not demanded. Wang Jinxi did not demand anything anymore. He asked, in the flat manner of a boy who had learned from Wu Zhangkong that the flat manner was how you said things that mattered, at the end of the evening session, when the other five had gone in.

"Two weeks," Wang Jinxi said. "In the platform."

"Yes."

"I want to fight you before we go in."

Lin Hao looked at him. "You lost in the gauntlet in one exchange."

"I know what happened." Wang Jinxi's jaw did something. "I know *exactly* what happened. You used my own fold against me and you told me I'd taught you how, and I've thought about it every day, and the part I can't get past is not that I lost. It's that you were *right.* I did teach you. I was thorough. I showed you the whole thing because I wanted to be certain you understood what I was doing, and being certain was more important to me than winning." He looked at the ground. "That's a thing I do. I've done it my whole life. My father says it's rigour and I've started to think it's fear."

"That's a big thing to say out loud."

"You said something big out loud to Wei Xiaofeng at six in the morning," Wang Jinxi said, "and he built a second variant before breakfast, and he has told absolutely no one, which is how I know you didn't humiliate him, you *recruited* him. So. Fight me. Not to win. I want to find out what I'm made of when the person across from me already has me written down. Because that's what the platform is going to be, isn't it. Something in there is going to have me written down."

Lin Hao considered this. And then he drew the Stormbringer, because the answer was yes, and because the answer had been yes since the second sentence, and because there was a version of himself that he was slowly becoming — a version that answered requests like this one before the request was finished — and he was beginning to like that version.

They fought for nineteen minutes.

It was the longest fight of Lin Hao's life that was not with Wu Zhangkong, and it was long because Wang Jinxi did the thing he had never done, which was to stop being thorough. He fought ugly. He fought incomplete. He threw attacks he had not finished building and abandoned positions he had spent weeks perfecting, and Lin Hao — who had him written down, all of him, the whole careful architecture — found that the written-down version was useless against a boy who had decided to stop making sense.

Wang Jinxi did not win. He could not; the gap was what it was, and both of them knew it. But he landed four times, which was three more than the gauntlet, and on the nineteenth minute he got Lin Hao's sword outside his guard and put his palm flat against Lin Hao's chest, and held it there.

"There," Wang Jinxi said, breathing hard. "That's the thing I can't do. That's *reaching.* You're never where the ledger says."

"Neither are you," Lin Hao said, "anymore."

"No," Wang Jinxi agreed. He took his hand away. "Thank you." He started toward the dormitory, and then stopped, without turning around. "In the platform. If I find you."

"Yes."

"I'm going to want to be the one who finds you," Wang Jinxi said. "Not the other way around. So if you come looking for me, I'm going to be annoyed."

"Noted," Lin Hao said, and grinned at the back of the boy's head, and stood alone on the training ground with his ribs and his ledger and seventy-nine lines in it, and thought that in two weeks he was going to walk into a forest that did not know his name, and that this was the first time in four months he had no idea what was going to happen to him, and that he could not, entirely, wait.

## Part 5: The Steel

He made the sword on a Saturday, in the side forge, because there was a thing he had been carrying for eleven days and a forge was the only place he knew to put it down.

Mu Chen was there. Mu Chen was always there on a Saturday, and Mu Chen had asked, four months ago, to strike his edge himself, which was the highest thing a smith of the Eastsea Branch ever said to a boy, and which Lin Hao had allowed exactly once and then never mentioned again, because mentioning it would have made it a thing instead of a fact.

"Second rank," Mu Chen said, without looking up from his own work. It was not a question. It was the way the older man said everything, which was as though the words had already been agreed.

"Second rank," Lin Hao agreed.

"You passed at nine."

"I passed at nine."

"I passed at nineteen." Mu Chen turned the bar in his tongs, and looked at the colour, and did not take it out. "The Branch has four hundred years of records and there are eleven names under twenty in it. Wulin's is one now, and yours is one, and there are people in this building who have been fourth rank for thirty years and who will not look at either of you." He put the bar back in. "So whatever it is you're making, make it properly, because it's going to be looked at whether you like it or not."

Lin Hao made it properly.

He had a bar of spirit steel that his father had given him at eight and that he had been saving without being able to say why, and he had spent eleven days knowing why. The bar went into the fire and the hawk-eyes did the thing they did — not finding the flaws, which any competent smith could do by sound, but finding the *grain* first, the thousand-year weather of compression and direction inside the metal, the places where it wanted to move and the places where it would fight — and he struck only where it had already said yes.

one hundred and ninety-one strikes. A journeyman needs three hundred. A journeyman who cannot read needs five hundred and gets a worse bar.

**Thousand Refinements.** He had the number in his head the way other people have a tune: not a claim, a count. He had reached it at the Association a month ago and had not told anyone, because there had not been a reason, and because the reason had arrived eleven days ago in the shape of a stick and a stance and a stroke.

Because here was the thing nobody had told him, and which he had worked out alone at four in the morning above Zhou Zhangxi's snoring: **Thousand Refinements was a swordsmanship technique.** Not a metaphor. The refinement was the same act as the Answering Stroke — you did not impose a shape on the material, you waited for the material to commit and then you arrived at the place it had already promised. Wu Zhangkong's homework had been *ask yourself why a swordsman's whole curriculum is reading,* and the answer was standing in his hands in a side forge on a Saturday, because it had been standing in his hands since he was six years old and had never once been in a sword.

He had been a swordsman at the anvil for four years. He just hadn't had a name for it.

The blade came out of the oil at the colour of the harbour before rain, and Mu Chen looked at it for a long time, and then did the thing that Lin Hao would remember longer than the gauntlet, longer than the number, longer than almost anything: he picked it up, and turned it, and put it down again carefully, the way you put down something that belongs to someone else's future.

"That's not a second-rank blade," Mu Chen said.

"It's a second-rank smith's blade."

"No," Mu Chen said. "It's not." And he went back to his own work, and did not say anything else for an hour, and Lin Hao wrapped the sword in oilcloth and carried it back to the academy under his coat, and did not show it to anyone, not even Wulin, because there was going to be a forest in two weeks and he wanted the first thing it ever cut to matter.

Nine days later the growth came again, and it came the same way it always came — not from sitting, from being *corrected* — and by then he had stopped being surprised by it, and had started, instead, to notice the pattern, which was that his soul did not grow when he won. It grew when he found out he had been wrong.

The rank did not move. The rank could not move; there was a hawk in him at eight hundred and fifty-two years and a door at the top of the stairs that would not open for a bird, and he had made his peace with that in the fourth week. What moved instead was everything the rank could not hold — the spiritual power, the ledger, the reading, the sword. He was, he understood, filling up a vessel that had stopped getting bigger, and the pressure was starting to look for somewhere to go.

## Part 1: The White Spire

The Eastsea Spirit Pagoda was the only building in the city that did not have to try.

Everything else in Eastsea City was in some kind of argument — the harbour with the tide, the market with the morning, the academy with its own roof. The Pagoda simply stood there, nine storeys of pale stone going up out of the centre of the city like something that had arrived fully formed and had been waiting, patiently, for the buildings around it to make up their minds. Lin Hao counted the storeys twice and got nine both times, which he noted, because he had been told as a small child that the Pagoda had seven, and because the difference between seven and nine was the sort of thing his father would have wanted him to notice.

"You've counted it," Xie Xie said.

"Twice."

"It's nine. My family's been coming here for six generations and it's always been nine and nobody knows why everyone says seven." Xie Xie was vibrating. He had been vibrating since breakfast. "Hao. Hao. I've wanted this since I was *four.* My father took my brother when my brother was eleven and my brother came out and said there was a mouse the size of a house and I did not sleep for a week. A *week.* I ate dinner at my brother's bedside."

"That's a very specific memory."

"It's the best memory I have."

Wu Zhangkong had brought them and had said nothing at all on the walk, which the seven of them had interpreted, variously, as ominous, as typical, and — in Gu Yue's case, Lin Hao thought — as a courtesy. At the door he stopped.

"Inside, you will be measured before you enter," he said. "The measurement is not for you. It is for the platform, which uses it to decide what to put in front of you." He looked at the seven of them, and his eyes stopped, for a fraction of a second, on Lin Hao. "Some of you will not like what it decides."

"Is that a warning?" Lin Hao asked.

"It's an observation," Wu Zhangkong said, and went inside.

## Part 2: Intake

The intake room was on the third floor and smelled of cold metal and something faintly sweet, like hot dust, and there was a woman behind a counter with a form and a machine, and the form was long, and the machine was not.

"Names," the woman said, and took them, and wrote them, and then said, "Hands on the plate, one at a time, and hold still, and don't be alarmed by the number, the number is only a number."

Xie Xie went first, because Xie Xie went first at everything. The plate took his hand and the dial above the counter climbed and settled, and the woman wrote, and Xie Xie craned to see it, and the woman turned the form away, and Xie Xie said, "That's *rude,*" and the woman said, "It's policy," and Xie Xie said, "Whose policy," and the woman said, "The Spirit Pagoda's," and Xie Xie said, "That's the rudest policy I've ever heard," and Lin Hao put a hand on his shoulder, because the queue was not moving.

Wang Jinxi went. Zhang Yangzi went, with his splinted wrist held carefully away from the plate, and winced at something only he could see. Wei Xiaofeng went, and scowled at the dial, and did not comment, which was so unlike him that Xie Xie whispered "Is he *ill?*" and Wei Xiaofeng said "I'm *fine,*" in a voice that had two variants in it now.

The form had a line for occupation, which the seven of them had filled in at the counter, and the woman read them back the way you read a list you expect to be boring.

"Students. All seven." She glanced up. "Any trades?"

"Second-rank smith," Lin Hao said.

The woman's pen stopped. "Second rank."

"Second rank," Lin Hao agreed. "Thousand Refinements."

Now the pen stopped properly. She looked at him — at the age on the form, at the face, and then back at the age, doing the same subtraction she was about to do twice more that morning — and she said, "The Association's records say the youngest second-rank in the Eastsea Branch is a boy named Tang Wulin."

"He's standing behind me."

The woman looked behind him, at Wulin, and then at the two of them, and wrote something in the margin that was not on the form.

Wulin went next. The dial climbed, and stopped, and the woman looked at it, and then looked at Wulin, and then looked at the dial again.

"Is something wrong?" Wulin asked, politely.

"No," the woman said, slowly, and wrote something, and then wrote something else underneath it, and Lin Hao — who was standing second in the queue and had a view of the form at an angle the woman had probably not accounted for — saw that she had written the number, and then drawn a small line through it, and written a different number, and then drawn a line through that too.

Gu Yue went. The dial climbed. It did not stop where the others had stopped. The woman's pen did not move, and then it moved once, and she did not look up.

Then it was Lin Hao's turn, and he put his hand on the plate.

The dial climbed.

It passed Xie Xie's place. It passed Wang Jinxi's. It passed Zhang Yangzi's and Wei Xiaofeng's and it went by Wulin's crossed-out number and it did not stop at Gu Yue's, and Lin Hao watched it go with the detached interest of a blacksmith watching a gauge that had been asked to do something it was not built for, and the needle kept going, and the woman stood up.

She actually stood up. She was a woman of perhaps forty who had, Lin Hao thought, probably been doing this for twenty years, and she stood up out of her chair and leaned over the counter to look at the dial from a different angle, the way his father stood up and leaned over a bar of steel when the bar of steel said something his father did not believe.

"That's not right," she said.

"It's usually not," Lin Hao agreed.

"Are you —" she looked at the form, at the name, at the age, and then at him, and something in her face changed, and Lin Hao watched it change and understood that she had read the age and had then done a subtraction, and had not liked the answer. "You're ten."

"I'm ten."

"Hold still." She adjusted something on the machine — a dial, a setting, something in the side of it — and the needle dropped, and settled, and climbed again, and stopped in almost exactly the same place, and she sat down very slowly.

**one hundred and ninety-one.**

The room had gone quiet, and Lin Hao became aware that all six of them were looking at him, and that the queue behind him had ceased to be a queue, and that a man in Spirit Pagoda grey had come to the door of the intake room and was standing in it looking at the dial over the woman's shoulder.

"Is the machine broken?" Xie Xie asked, in the voice of a boy offering help.

"No," said the man in the doorway. He was older, thin, with the particular stillness of someone who worked with expensive equipment. He came in and looked at Lin Hao for a long moment. "Spirit Connection realm."

"Yes."

"At ten."

"Yes."

"one hundred and ninety-one."

"That's what it says," Lin Hao said. "I'd check the machine again if I were you, but I've been told the machine's fine, and I've been told that twice now, so I've made my peace with it."

The man did not smile. He read off the form, in the flat tone of a man putting a thing on a record whether or not he believed it: "Rank thirty. Two yellow rings. Spiritual power one hundred and ninety-one. Spirit Connection realm. Age ten." He paused on the last two items the way a person pauses on a sum that does not come out. "Second-rank smith, Thousand Refinements."

"Yes," Lin Hao said.

The man looked at the woman. "Elementary platform," he said. "Standard entry tier."

"He'll clear the elementary in a session," the woman said. "Sir, the tiering is set by the number, and the number says—"

"The tiering," the man said, "is set by the number." And then he looked at Lin Hao again, and there was something in the look that Lin Hao recognized, because he had seen it once before, on a man with smoky green eyes, five months ago, in a room full of numbers. It was the look of a person doing arithmetic that had an official answer and a real answer, and who had decided, for now, to write down the official one.

"What's your name, son."

"Lin Hao."

The man wrote it on a small card, and put the card in his pocket, and did not write it on the form.

"Right," he said. "Elementary platform. Standard tier. All seven of you." And he left, and the woman sat down, and the queue resumed, and Xie Xie said, under his breath, "He *pocketed* you," and Lin Hao said, "Yes," and Xie Xie said, "Is that bad," and Lin Hao said, "It's a number," which was not an answer, and which Xie Xie accepted, because Xie Xie accepted everything.
