## Part 3: The Profound Look

The room with the boxes was on the seventh floor, and it was not what any of them had expected, and Lin Hao was the only one who said so.

"It's a hospital," he said.

"It's not a *hospital,*" Xie Xie said.

"There are seven beds, Xie Xie, there are electrodes, there is a man in white over by the wall holding a tray, and there is a smell that I have smelled exactly once in my life, in a room where my mother's neighbour's husband stopped breathing for eleven seconds. It's a hospital. It's a hospital with better lighting."

The boxes were metal, and they were waist-high, and each of them had a lid that opened on a hinge, and inside each one there was a padded surface and a headrest and a set of electrodes on articulated arms that waited, politely, above the pillow like insects standing still. There were screens along the far wall — a bank of them, seven, each one dark — and a chair, and in the chair sat the man in Spirit Pagoda grey, and behind him, with his arms folded, stood Wu Zhangkong, and beside Wu Zhangkong stood Long Hengxu, who had come out of the tournament the way weather comes out of a season, and who looked at the seven of them and nodded once.

"Here is what happens," said the staff member — a different one, younger, with a clipboard and the cheerful efficiency of a person explaining something they had explained four thousand times. "You lie down. We attach the electrodes. The lid closes. You will feel a sensation like falling, and then you will be inside. The platform separates you on entry — you will not be together, and you will not know where the others are. Inside, you fight. What you fight is decided by the platform, based on the measurement you were given at intake." He smiled. "There is a button inside, on your left wrist, that you press to come out. Press it if you need to. Nobody thinks less of you. Well. Almost nobody."

"Almost nobody," Xie Xie repeated, horrified.

"Almost nobody," the staff member agreed, cheerfully.

"What happens if we don't press it," Wang Jinxi asked.

"You come out when you're out," the staff member said. "Or when we bring you out."

"And if we get hurt," Zhang Yangzi said. He was holding his splinted wrist against his chest. He had been very quiet since the intake room.

The staff member's smile did exactly nothing at all — it stayed precisely where it was, at precisely the size it was — and Lin Hao, watching, understood that this was the question the man had been waiting for, and that the answer had been written down somewhere by somebody with a great deal of experience, and that it was not the whole answer.

"The platform is virtual," the staff member said. "But it contains a degree of reality. What you feel inside, you feel. Pain included. That's the point — you don't learn anything from a fight you can't feel. The button gets you out before it goes too far, and that's what the button is for." He looked at the seven of them, one at a time, and his eyes took a fraction longer on Zhang Yangzi, and then — and this was the part Lin Hao thought about for weeks — a fraction longer on **him.**

It was not a warning. It was not friendly, either. It was a *profound* look, the look of a man who knew something and had decided that knowing it was his job and not theirs, and Lin Hao met it, and held it, and did the thing he had done with the man in the doorway, which was to file it, and to note that he had now been given two looks in one morning by two different employees of the Spirit Pagoda, and that both looks had arrived immediately after the number.

"Hao," Wulin murmured, beside him. "That man is looking at you like you're a fire in a house he likes."

"I know."

"Is that bad."

"It's a number," Lin Hao said, for the second time that morning, and then, because the teasing was the whole of the saying and the room behind it was real: "Wulin. If anything in there is going to be a problem, it's going to be a problem *for me,* and I want you to understand that I'm not worried, and I want you to understand that the reason I'm not worried is not that I'm brave. It's that I've been the number since I was six years old, and I have never once been able to put it down, so I've made my peace with carrying it, and if the platform wants to give me something heavy, it's going to have to work for it."

Wulin was quiet for a moment.

"I'm going to find you," he said.

"You're going to be in a forest."

"I'm going to find you *in the forest.*"

"Everyone's going to be in a forest, Wulin, that's the entire premise, and Wang Jinxi has already told me he wants to be the one who finds me, and I've promised him I'll be annoyed if I find him first, and there is a limited supply of me and there is a queue."

"I'm at the front of the queue," Wulin said.

"You're at the front of the queue," Lin Hao agreed.

## Part 4: The Lid

They went in one at a time.

Xie Xie went first, because Xie Xie had asked, and because the staff member had said "whoever's brave," and because Xie Xie had said "finally, a *fair* test," and had climbed into the box with the enthusiasm of a boy getting into a boat, and had said, over the rim, "If I don't come out, tell my father I died in a forest with a *mouse,*" and the lid had closed.

Zhang Yangzi went second. He did not say anything. He lay down very carefully, protecting the wrist, and the electrodes came down onto his temples, and just before the lid closed he looked at Gu Yue — a quick, awkward, entirely unpractised look, the look of a boy who had been carried out of his own catastrophe three weeks ago and had not yet worked out how to say thank you — and Gu Yue inclined her head perhaps two millimetres, and the lid closed.

Wei Xiaofeng. Wang Jinxi, who lay down as though he had done it a hundred times, and who said, flatly, to no one, "Nineteen minutes," and closed his own eyes before the lid did.

Gu Yue went fifth. She lay down the way she did everything, which was as though the box had agreed to be lain in. She did not look at anyone. Just before the electrodes came down she said, quietly, to the room, "Don't wait for me," and Lin Hao — who was sixth in the queue, who had seventy-nine lines in a ledger and one of them hers — said, "I wasn't going to," and she said, "Yes, you were," and the lid closed.

Then Lin Hao.

He went with two swords, which the staff member looked at and did not comment on. One was the Stormbringer, which was not a sword at all so much as a fact about him. The other was the blade from the side forge, one hundred and ninety-one strikes, wrapped until that morning in oilcloth, and he had put it on his back instead of his hip because Wu Zhangkong's homework had been sitting in his head for three weeks and had finally, on the walk over, produced an answer.

*Ask yourself why a swordsman's whole curriculum is reading.*

Because the sword is the only weapon that has to be pointed. A hammer lands anywhere. A shield goes where you put it. A sword has an edge, and an edge is a *choice* — you have decided which side of the world you are going to open — and a choice requires knowing. Every form Wu Zhangkong had given him, every stance, the Grain Cut, the Question, the Answering Stroke, all of it was a way of *arriving at knowledge in time to use it.* The sword was not the weapon. The sword was the argument.

He had written it down that morning on the back of his hand, in case he forgot, and he had not forgotten.

The padded surface was warmer than he expected. The electrodes were cold, and they settled against his temples with a small precise pressure, like fingers. Above him, the inside of the lid was bare grey metal, and there was a strap for the left wrist with a button under it — red, plastic, ordinary, the least impressive object he had ever been given.

The staff member leaned over him.

"You're the two-forty-one," he said.

"I am."

"You understand what the measurement does."

"It decides what I get."

"It decides what you get," the staff member agreed, "and the platform has a great deal to choose from." He straightened up. And then, because he was, apparently, the third employee of the Spirit Pagoda to do it in one morning, he gave Lin Hao the look — the profound one, the one that knew something — and he said, very quietly, so that it did not go on any record: "The button is on your *left.* Not your right. First-timers reach with the right."

And the lid closed.

Lin Hao lay in the dark with a red button under his left hand and seventy-nine lines in his head and the smell of cold metal and hot dust, and felt the falling begin — a long, gentle, entirely unmistakable drop, the way the ground goes away under a swing at the top of its arc — and he did the thing he had done every time in his life that the ground had gone away.

He did not brace. He did not grab. He let go of the ledge, because he had learned at six years old, on a harbour wall with the sea underneath it, that the only thing you can actually do with a fall is *decide where you're going to land.*

The dark went green.

## Part 1: Zhang Yangzi's Bad Luck

He landed on his feet, which surprised him, and then he was sick, which surprised him less.

The forest was enormous. That was the first thing, and it stayed the first thing for some time, because Zhang Yangzi had grown up in a city and had seen trees the way you see furniture, and this was not trees. This was a *world* that had been left running. Insects argued in the undergrowth. Something with a good voice sang three layers up. The air was so full of life that it had a taste, and the taste was wrong for him — he was a dark-attribute soul in a green cathedral, and every breath felt like walking into a room where everyone had stopped talking.

And then he noticed the other thing.

His soul power was moving faster. Not a lot. A little — a warmth at the base of his spine that kept arriving half a beat before he called for it, the way a dog comes when it hears the bowl. The forest was feeding him. The forest that was wrong for him was feeding him, and Zhang Yangzi stood there in the green light and felt, for the first time in four months, that something in the world had been arranged in his favour.

He released his martial soul. Black wings came out of his back and unfolded, and the Shadow Phantasm Eagle settled onto his shoulder, and he put his hands into claws and went up the tallest tree in the area in eleven seconds, because that was the clever thing to do, and he had decided, on the way in, that he was going to be clever this time.

Ten metres up, the view opened, and Zhang Yangzi stopped breathing for a moment.

Green. Green to the horizon in every direction, an ocean of it, treetops rolling like swell under a clear sky. There was no edge. There was no city, no wall, no sea, no smoke. There was just the world with the people taken out of it, and it went on forever, and it was the most beautiful thing he had ever seen, and he understood, standing in it, exactly why Wu Zhangkong had looked at them the way he had.

He would find Wang Jinxi. That was the plan. Their fusion was incomplete — the Shadow Eagle Dragon had never once fully formed, and it was the reason the tournament had gone the way it had gone, and if they could complete it here, where nothing was watching and nobody was keeping score—

A bird came over the treetops.

It was big. Five metres of wingspan, green as new leaves, soaring on nothing at all, and it turned its head — it *turned its head* — and looked directly at the tallest tree in the area, and Zhang Yangzi felt something in his chest that he had been carrying since the tournament, something hot and old and entirely unexamined, stand up and take the wheel.

He had **conceded** three bouts at the tournament — a boy with a hammer, a girl with a cup of water, a swordsman who had read his feint before he finished it — and **not one of them had ever touched him.** He had stepped out of all three, because he had been coordinating, because he had been a team player, because he had spent the entire tournament being careful about what he showed. **Nobody had beaten him. He had simply declined to win, three times, in front of four hundred people, and nobody in the stands had been able to tell the difference — which was the part that had bothered him afterwards, not the losing.**

Not here.

Two soul rings came up under his feet. The Dark Devil Eagle rose off his shoulder and folded into him, and his wings went wide, and his **second soul skill — Eagle Soars the Sky** — took more than half of everything he had in a single breath, and his speed tripled, and he went off the branch like a black arrow straight at the bird.

The bird shrieked. It flapped once, hard, and three green wind blades came off its wings and met him in the air.

He smashed them. That was the good part, and it lasted about a second — black against green, the blades bursting — and then he understood, in the middle of his own triumph, that he had stopped moving.

Eagle Soars the Sky gave him speed. It did not give him *flight.* His wings could glide and they could catch, and they could not hold a boy of ten in the air on their own, and he had traded all his momentum for the pleasure of breaking something, and now he was falling, and the tree canopy was below him, and the canopy was the clever place to be, the bird could not follow him into the trees, he had worked this out, he was *clever*—

The treetops opened.

Not one bird. Not two. Green figures came up out of the leaves in every direction at once, and the sky above him filled with wings, and the cries came from all sides and answered each other, and more came, arriving from further off, joining, and Zhang Yangzi hung in the air at the top of his skill with nothing left in him and watched a hundred birds decide about him at the same time.

He pressed the button on his left wrist.

---

The box slid out and the light came in and Long Hengxu said, "Get up," without a single trace of happiness in it.

Zhang Yangzi sat up. He was in the room with the screens. He had been inside for four minutes and eleven seconds, and he was the first one out, and the screens showed six dots still moving and one that had stopped being a dot, and his face went hot all the way to his ears and he crawled out of the box on his hands and knees.

Wu Zhangkong said nothing at all. He pointed at the chair beside him.

Zhang Yangzi sat down. He was still dizzy — the platform left you that way, he understood, the body catching up with the mind — but everything was perfectly clear, and he looked up at the screens out of simple embarrassment, wanting somewhere to put his eyes.

And then he found the flock.

They were still there. A hundred green birds wheeling over the tallest tree in that sector, crying, searching, and more arriving while he watched, and Zhang Yangzi looked at the place where he had been hanging in the air and did a sum he did not want to do, and got an answer he did not want.

If it had been real, he would have been dead. Not hurt. Not taught a lesson. Dead — and there would not have been enough left of him for ten of him to make a difference.

He looked at Wu Zhangkong, waiting for it. Waiting for the flat voice to say the thing that was obviously true and that he had already said to himself.

Wu Zhangkong looked at the screen, and did not say anything at all.

And Zhang Yangzi understood — slowly, and then all at once — that the man was not going to say it, and was not going to say it *on purpose,* because a thing you are told you forget, and a thing you watch happen to yourself from the inside of your own skin you keep forever, and this was the entire method, and it had been the entire method the whole time.

*True combat experience was best gained when experienced for themselves.*

Zhang Yangzi sat in the chair with his splinted wrist on his knee and his face still burning, and felt something in him — the hot old thing, the thing that had been carrying him since the tournament — go quiet. Not gone. Quiet. And underneath the quiet, to his complete surprise, he found that he was *excited.*

Next time, he thought. Next time I go up the tree and I do not attack the bird. Next time I find Wang Jinxi first. Next time I last an hour.

## Part 2: Xie Xie

Xie Xie had been in the forest for nine minutes and had not made a sound.

He moved from one tree's shadow to the next and did not use the open ground, because he had known since he was four years old that this forest was full of things that would kill him, and because his brother had come home at eleven and talked about a mouse the size of a house for a week, and because Xie Xie had listened to every word of it and had gone to bed every night for seven days with his dagger under the pillow.

He also knew the other thing, and the other thing was why he had asked to go in first.

Everything you killed in here fed the spirit soul you had in the real world.

His spirit soul was a metal soul the Spirit Pagoda had manufactured specially — a hundred-year soul his family had paid a thousand-year price for, because it was the only one of its kind available, and because the money had bought something nobody outside his family knew about. When it fused with his dagger, it had *mutated.* Not much. Not the way Wulin's Goldsong had mutated, which everyone had seen and nobody had explained. A small mutation, a quiet one, and what it did was this: it let him take two spirit souls and make them one, if he had the spiritual power to hold both.

He had two daggers. He had always had two daggers. The Light one was the one everyone had seen, at the tournament, on the display, in every ring he had ever shown, and the Shadow one had never once left his sleeve in front of another person, because his father had sat him down when he was six and explained that a thing nobody knows about is the only thing that is truly yours.

The problem was the bottleneck. Two martial souls meant two rings at every wall, and his spiritual power was — Xie Xie had heard the number, and Xie Xie had made his peace with the number, and Xie Xie had then spent four months being loud about everything else so that nobody would look at the number again. But the platform was a way *around* the number. If the metal soul reached the purple thousand-year level, it would give him a ring by itself. At the black ten-thousand-year level, another.

So Xie Xie moved through the green dark without a sound, and looked for something to kill, and was happier than he had been in his entire life.

The feeling that arrived next was not a sound.

He dived. He did not decide to dive. Some part of him that his father had paid a great deal of money to train simply put him on the ground, and several dozen lights went through the air where his head had been and punched into the tree behind him, and Xie Xie rolled and came up running.

He looked back, and his blood went cold.

Eyes. Dozens of pairs of them, scarlet, opening in the bark of the trees all around him, at every height, patient as fruit.

*Scarlet Demon Tree.* Plant-type. He knew it — plant soul beasts came in groups, they did not chase, they waited, and the ground he was standing on was inside six of them at once.

He did not fight. He rolled sideways and ran, and the trees fired the instant he moved, and the lights stitched the air behind his heels, and Xie Xie went out of that grove at a speed he had never once produced in front of Wu Zhangkong and did not stop until the scarlet eyes were behind him and his lungs were on fire.

"That," he said aloud, to nobody, because talking was how he stayed himself, "was *extremely* close."

Then something yellow came at his face.

He stopped and slashed — a Light Dragon Blade, clean and full-strength, the strike he had practised eleven thousand times — and the yellow thing *twisted* in the air and his blade cut nothing, and the ground burst open two metres in front of him and a mouse came out of it.

It was taller than he was. Two metres of grey fur and muscle, standing on its hind legs, with a tail like a whip that had already flicked once and nearly taken his head off, and a mouth full of teeth that Xie Xie knew, from a book, could chew through uncommon metal.

**A hundred-year Longtail Mouse.**

And Xie Xie, standing in the dappled green light with his heart going like a hammer, felt exactly one emotion, and it was not fear.

"Oh," he said. "*Oh, you're perfect.*"

He kicked off the trunk and went up. The mouse's tail came for his chest like a thrown javelin and he put a Light Dragon Blade in front of it — and a ray of light flashed at the tip of the tail and his blade **split in half** and swept past harmlessly, and the mouse leapt after him with a speed that had no business belonging to something that shape.

Then the mouse shrieked.

A bloody line burst open along its flank and it went down sideways, splattering, and Xie Xie did not waste a single instant of the gift — he came off the trunk spinning, dagger-first, and dropped onto it with everything he had.

## Part 3: The Screen Room

"There were four," the staff member said. "Now there are three."

Wu Zhangkong did not answer. He was looking at the screens, and there were three dots on them, and one of the three dots was moving in a way he had not expected.

The Wang Jinxi dot had stopped.

Not slowed. Stopped — and then it went off the board entirely, without the graceful fade of a pressed button, and the light above box four went from blue to red, and the staff member was already moving.

"Prepare for emergency treatment."

The box slid out and Wang Jinxi was shaking. The electrodes came off him and it did not help; the shaking was underneath the skin, and his face was the colour of the paper on the clipboard, and a dozen people in white arrived at a run and one of them put a needle into his neck without asking anything first.

"Is it that Man-Faced Demon Spider again," somebody said, in the tone of a man who was tired.

"Yes! That thing is so violent. It didn't even give this child a chance to press the button. Ah, this child's luck is truly terrible."

Zhang Yangzi had come to his feet at some point without noticing. He was standing at the edge of the room with his splinted wrist against his chest, and he watched the people in white work on Wang Jinxi for ten full minutes, and then he said, in a voice that did not sound like his, "Teacher Wu. Director Long. Is Jinxi okay? Isn't the spirit ascension platform a virtual place? How did he end up like this…"

His words trailed off. He was looking at Wang Jinxi's face.

The staff member — the young one, the one who had explained the boxes and smiled while doing it — turned around, and the smile was gone, and what was left was a person whose job included this.

"I told you," he said. "The platform is virtual. But it contains a degree of reality. Everything you sense inside there, you sense as if you were feeling it in reality. So if you are harmed inside, you feel all of the pain." He said it evenly, the way you read a manual. "If you had been sliced into a corpse by the wind blades of those big green birds, you would have felt the exact same sensations as a corpse. Exceedingly real. And they attack the mind.

"Simply: if someone watches their own wrist being slit, they feel the blood going. They hear it dripping. And when the wound closes, and the bleeding stops — they still sense the dripping. So the brain decides it is already dead. And after that thought appears in the brain, the person truly begins to die."

The room was very quiet.

"The platform has this problem, especially for first-timers like you. Fortunately, the effects gradually decrease as your spiritual power increases. By the time you can ignore them, you won't be able to enter the elementary platform anymore — you'll have to enter the intermediate one." He shrugged. "And the sensations in the intermediate platform are even more different. Hehe. The intermediate platform…"

Zhang Yangzi sat down, because his legs had made a decision without him.

*This could actually kill us.*

Wu Zhangkong said nothing. He had walked over to the screens, and he was looking at box six, and at the dot on board six, which had not stopped, and had not slowed, and had not — the staff would mention this later, twice — pressed its button once.

## Part 4: Gu Yue

She had been walking for twenty minutes and had almost forgotten what she was.

The forest was doing something to her. Not the circulation — she had felt that, the little warmth at the base of the spine, and filed it — but the *green.* The clean air. The light coming down through the leaves in the particular broken way that light comes down through leaves, and she had walked under light like this before, and the before was not a memory, because memories belonged to a life, and this was older than that.

*So beautiful,* she thought. *I really like this feeling.*

She killed three soul beasts in the first ten minutes, and they were weak, and each time one went down a faint light came off her body and went somewhere she could not follow, and each time it happened her eyes got a little wider, because she had not been told about that part, and she and Tang Wulin had known less about this place than anyone.

She was still thinking about the light when the bush rustled.

It came out on two legs and it was over three metres tall and covered in light brown fur, with claws the length of her forearm and yellow eyes that caught the green light and gave it back wrong. It roared — a sound that came up through the ground and into her teeth — and charged.

---

In the screen room, the staff member half-rose.

"Thousand year," he said. "A thousand-year soul beast appeared. Do you want to warn her?"

"Just watch for now," Wu Zhangkong said. His eyes did not leave the screen.

It was a Crystal Bear — a mutation off the same species as the Fear Claw Bear, and weaker for it, but it had kept one thing and the one thing was enough: every strike it landed left a little of the opponent *crystallised.* A fraction. Then another fraction. The fractions stacked, and the crystallised parts did not bend, and eventually a body that could not bend shattered under the next blow. You beat it with strong soul power and fast hands. You survived it by removing the crystal before the next hit arrived.

It had no ranged attacks at all. That was its weakness.

Wu Zhangkong knew all of this, and he knew the other thing too, which was the only thing he had ever really believed about training, and which he had believed since before he had been asked to leave the place he did not talk about:

**The greater the pressure, the greater the growth of a Soul Master.**

He wanted to see what his only female student would do with a thousand years standing in front of her.

---

Gu Yue was not flustered at all.

A single yellow soul ring rose from beneath her feet and her aura strengthened, and she said, quietly, "Elemental Tide."

Her body went light. A green glow flashed out of her, and then there was a flash of silver, and she was not where she had been.

The Crystal Bear's charge went through empty air. It could not stop. It ran headfirst into a large tree and the tree lost the argument.

Gu Yue was already running, with her back to it, and she did not look behind her, and she waved her hands as she went — and a tornado came up out of the undergrowth and went into the canopy and tore a hundred leaves loose and filled the air between them with green confetti.

It was not an attack. Its defences were far too stout for wind, and she knew that before she cast it. The wind was for the *eyes.*

Behind the leaves, she flashed silver again, changed direction, and bolted.

"Beautiful," Long Hengxu said. "Her response was clever, fast as well."

Wu Zhangkong nodded, once. He was pleased, and the reason he was pleased was not the teleport — the teleport was a tool, and tools were common. It was the *decision.* She had looked at a thousand years of bear, measured it against herself, and chosen to run, and she had done it in an instant, and running was the easy part. Any coward could run. The hard part was knowing, in the first half-second, that running was the correct answer and not a failure — and then doing it, cleanly, without a single wasted movement, while a thing that could shatter her was four metres away.

He turned to the board with the three dots on it, and stopped.

The Gu Yue dot was moving fast. And it was moving in a straight line. And the line it was moving along was—

"Yi," Wu Zhangkong said, very lightly.

## Part 5: Xie Xie, Again

Two booms came through the forest, close, and getting closer.

Xie Xie had been skinning the Longtail Mouse — spiritually, not literally, the light doing what the light did — and the booms put him on his feet instantly. Somebody was making that much noise in a soul beast forest, and whoever it was either very confident or very stupid, and in this forest those were the same thing wearing different hats.

He went up a tree with lightning speed and put his back against the trunk and made himself small and made himself *quiet,* and stayed there, because staying still was the better option. The mouse had cost him. He had less than half of what he had walked in with.

The thicket exploded.

A shape came out of it running — on two legs, over four metres tall, its whole body plated in metallic scales that threw the green light back in hard flat flashes, and one horn growing straight out of its skull.

It was a **Horned Dragon.** It was extremely ferocious. And it was coming directly at Xie Xie's tree.

## Part 6: What the Forest Teaches

Lin Hao landed in a crouch, and the first thing he did was take his hand off the button.

That was not a decision he made. It was a decision his body had already made, because the staff member had leaned over the box and said *first-timers reach with the right,* and because Lin Hao had spent six years of his life converting information into behaviour at a speed that had never once failed him, and his left hand was already resting on the strap while his right hand was empty and free.

The forest came up around him. Green, enormous, loud with insects, and — he noticed it the way he noticed everything, as a fact to be used rather than a thing to be felt — his soul power was circulating faster than it had any right to.

*So that's what it does,* he thought. *It feeds you. That's the trap. It makes you feel good so you'll stay.*

He went up a tree, because he had watched Zhang Yangzi go up a tree in his own head for four minutes while they waited, and because a vantage point was worth more than a plan. Eleven metres up, the forest went to the horizon, and Lin Hao looked at it, and thought about the harbour, and thought that the sea had been the first forest.

Then he heard the pack.

Not saw. Heard — three separate sets of footfalls, out of phase, closing from three directions, and the fourth thing he heard was the absence of a fourth set, which was the most informative sound he had heard all day.

They came into the clearing together, which was the first thing that told him he was in trouble, because wolves did not come into clearings together.

Four of them. Grey, low, ribbed, with the particular lean look of things that ate regularly and not often. They fanned out without being told. They did not charge. Three of them stopped at the treeline and one — the biggest, with a scar running from its left eye down into its shoulder — walked into the open and stood there, and looked at him.

"Right," Lin Hao said. He drew the Stormbringer. "You're the clever one."

The scarred one did not move. And Lin Hao, who had seventy-nine lines in his head and who had never in his life met an opponent he could not read in four seconds, understood with total clarity that he was not being read.

He was being *studied.*

---

He killed the first one in six seconds, and it cost him nothing.

Gale Talon along the steel, the wind-ribbon laid down the length of the blade, and the wolf on his left came in low and fast and met an edge that had been given teeth, and it did not get up. That was the baseline. That was the fight he was supposed to have, and it lasted six seconds, and the other three did not react at all, and the scarred one did not look at the dead one.

It looked at the *blade.*

The second one came in from the right, and Lin Hao laid the Gale Talon again — same angle, same timing, because the timing had worked — and the wolf on the right **stopped.** Not dodged. Stopped, mid-commit, four feet short of the arc, and backed out of it, and waited.

Lin Hao stood in the clearing with the sword in his hand and felt, for the first time in four months, the specific cold sensation of a page in his ledger turning over and being blank on the other side.

*They saw that,* he thought. *Not the one that died. The others. They watched me do it and they learned it.*

The third one came in while he was thinking, which was a lesson of its own, and he took it on the blade and turned it and it went down — and as it went down the fourth came from behind, silent, and its teeth closed on the outside of his left thigh, and the pain was—

The pain was **enormous.** It was not like the stick. It was not like the bruised ribs or the split skin or the training ground. It went into him and *stayed,* and something in the back of his skull said, very calmly, in a voice that sounded like the young man at the Spirit Pagoda, *you feel the blood going, you hear it dripping, and when it closes you will still hear it dripping,* and his left hand moved toward the strap.

It got as far as the strap. And then it stopped.

Because one hundred and ninety-one.

The pain was there. It was completely, entirely there, and it was not *working* — it was not doing the thing it was supposed to do, which was to become a fact about his death. It stayed a fact about his leg. He could feel the teeth and he could feel the blood and he could hear the dripping, and underneath all of it, steady as a gauge, his spiritual power was holding the whole screaming structure at arm's length, the way his father held a hot bar with a pair of tongs: it was very hot, and it was not going to be allowed to touch him.

*That's what the number is for,* Lin Hao thought, and the thought was almost funny, and he used the almost-funny to get his feet back — and then he did the thing.

He reached behind himself, without looking, and put the Stormbringer's edge through the wolf on his thigh, and it let go, and he turned, and the four of them were three, and the scarred one was watching him do it.

Watching *how.*

His left hand went to his back and came up with the other one — the blade from the side forge, one hundred and ninety-one strikes, still smelling faintly of oilcloth. It was a small thing and it was not a soul device and it had no name, and it was the only weapon he owned that had **no history in this clearing at all.** The Stormbringer the wolves had already read. This one they had not.

So he held the Stormbringer low and the new blade high, and the scarred wolf looked at the second sword and did the thing wolves do, which was to recalculate — and recalculation, Lin Hao understood, takes time, and time was the only thing in the forest that he had more of than they did.

---

What happened next was the longest four minutes of Lin Hao's life, and he would think about them more than the tournament, more than the gauntlet, more than anything that had happened to him since the sea took a girl.

Xie Xie was already there. He had been there the whole time; he had simply been waiting for the left arm to commit, because Xie Xie had been fighting Lin Hao for nine weeks and had learned, among many other things, exactly what it sounded like when Lin Hao made a door.

The Light Dragon Dagger went into the armpit that the raised arm had opened, and the dragon roared, and the ground shook, and the roar went on for a long time.

It did not die. That was the third lesson. It turned, and it took the dagger out of itself by moving, and it looked at the two of them with the flat patience of something that had decided to go to the ends of the earth, and Lin Hao understood that they had hurt it and had not, in any way that mattered, *ended* it.

"Lin Hao," Xie Xie said, backing up. "I have a suggestion."

"I'm not going to like it."

"We run."

"That's a *terrible* suggestion."

"It's the only suggestion I have!"

And then the grass came out of the undergrowth, wrapped around Xie Xie's waist, and yanked him four metres to the left, and the dragon hit the tree he had been standing in front of, and a boy with a hammer in each hand came out of the treeline with golden scales climbing his right arm.

"You two are the loudest people in this forest," Tang Wulin said.

## Part 3: What Only He Could Do

Wulin killed it. That was never in question, and Lin Hao knew it before the first hammer landed — knew it the way he knew a bar was going to break, from the sound it made going in.

But the killing took four exchanges, and it took four exchanges because three of them were wasted, and they were wasted for a reason that had nothing to do with strength.

Wulin swung where the dragon had been. Xie Xie struck where the dragon was going. And the dragon was in neither place, because the two of them were fighting it *separately* — each one answering the dragon on his own clock, and the dragon, which was not clever but was extremely fast, simply stepped into the gap between the two clocks.

Lin Hao watched it happen twice and shouted the third.

"Wulin — don't follow it, *meet* it! It launches off the left leg, so it's already committed when it leaves the ground — go where it's landing, not where it is!"

And Wulin, who did not ask questions in a fight and had never once needed to, went where it was landing.

"Xie Xie — stop stabbing the flank, it's armoured there, you're feeding it *information* and getting nothing back! Every time you touch the side it turns into you — so touch the side and then be somewhere it can't turn *to!* Go behind the tail, it can't see the tail!"

And Xie Xie, who complained about everything and obeyed instantly, went behind the tail.

And the dragon, which had spent four exchanges stepping into the gap between two clocks, found that the gap had closed, and that there was a third clock underneath the other two setting the time, and that a boy with two swords was standing in the exact place it needed to be in order to escape.

It went through him. That is the honest account: it went *through* him, and the Stormbringer took it on the flat and the new blade took it on the edge, and four hundred and seventy kilograms of smith's body held for exactly as long as it needed to hold, which was not long, and then Wulin's claw came down out of the air where the dragon's own launch had put it.

The forest went quiet.

Lin Hao lay on his back in the shredded undergrowth with both arms numb and the taste of dirt in his mouth, and stared up at the green, and did an inventory, because that was the process.

"You're bleeding," Wulin said, crouching over him.

"I've noticed."

"In the mouth."

"Yes, Wulin, in the mouth, that's where mouths bleed." He let his brother pull him up. "How long?"

"Four minutes, maybe." Wulin looked at him with the expression he wore when he had understood something and was deciding whether saying it would be annoying. "You told us what to do."

"I told you what you were already doing wrong."

"You told *me* what to do." Wulin turned the hammer over in his hand. "Nobody tells me what to do in a fight. Gu Yue does, but Gu Yue's different, she just says 'go there' and she's right. You said *why.* You said it launches off the left leg." He looked at the dragon. "I've killed three things today and I don't know why any of them died. You walked in and knew why this one was going to."

"That's not a compliment, that's a *hobby.*"

"It's not a hobby, it's the whole thing," Xie Xie said, from the tree, where he had gone to have his dignity in private. "Hao. Listen to me. I have been fighting you for nine weeks. I know what you are. You're the strongest — I've known that nine weeks and I'm still not used to saying it. You're not the fastest, I'm faster. You're not even the best with the sword anymore, Wulin hit something today that you couldn't have hit." He dropped down out of the tree. "You're the only one who can stand in the middle of a fight and see *all of it.* And you just did it with three people you have never fought beside, in a forest, with a lizard the size of a house, and it took you four minutes."

Lin Hao opened his mouth to make a joke, because that was the door and the room was behind it, and then he did not, because there was something under the joke that had arrived while he was lying in the dirt with his arms numb.

*Four minutes,* he thought. *Four minutes to make three strangers into a team. And Wu Zhangkong spent nine evenings pairing us and got nowhere.*

## Part 4: The Girl Who Ran the Wrong Way

The silver flash arrived before the sound did.

One moment there was nobody; the next there was Gu Yue, four metres away, with green light still guttering out under her feet and her face the colour of paper.

"It's not exactly a dragon," she said. "Now hurry up and help me."

"What—" Wulin began.

And the forest came down behind her.

It was a bear, and calling it a bear was like calling the harbour a puddle. Three metres at the shoulder and going through the thicket the way a ship goes through water — every small tree it touched went pale, then crystallised, then came apart into powder that hung in the air behind it like a wake.

"That," Xie Xie said, in a very small voice, "is the biggest thing I have ever seen and I have seen this one walk up a *wall.*"

"I can't hold it," Gu Yue said. She was breathing like someone who had been running for a long time. "I've moved eleven times. I have maybe two left."

"Then don't," Lin Hao said.

"It's a thousand years."

"I can see the number, Gu Yue, it's on the—" He stopped. Because he had been looking at the bear and not at the bear, and the bear had a colour on it.

Along its right foreleg, from the wrist to the elbow, the fur was not fur. It was dark gold, and it was hard, and it caught the green light and gave it back flat. And under that, on the shoulder, a smaller patch — older, he understood, older than this fight.

"Xie Xie," Lin Hao said, quietly, because the quiet carried further. "The crystal. On the arm. Where does it come from."

Xie Xie's head came round. His whole face changed — the child who had read about every soul beast in this forest before he was ten arrived, and the boy who had been running from a lizard left.

"It crystallises what it hits," he said. "A fraction each time. It stacks." He swallowed. "It stacks. If you fight it for a long time you get slower and slower and then you can't bend and then the next hit—" He stopped. "*Shatters.*"

"How long."

"What?"

"If it hits a person, how long until they can't move. Give me a number, Xie Xie, I don't need the mechanism, I need the *number.*"

Xie Xie closed his eyes for one second, doing arithmetic he had learned at seven. "Six hits to a limb. Maybe seven. Four if it's the same place."

Lin Hao looked at the bear. He looked at the arm that already had two patches on it, which meant the arm had been hit before, by something, and had never been cleaned, which meant **the bear came into this fight used.**

"Then it's not a fight," he said. "It's a clock. And we've been standing here for ninety seconds of it."

---

## Part 5: The Clock

"You two distract it and I'll look for a chance to give it a fatal blow," Wulin shouted from the air, where the grass had already put him.

"Neck!" Xie Xie shouted back, because he had been asked a question once and had decided to be the person who answers it. "Skin's like copper, bones like iron, but the neck — all the nerves are in the neck!"

"And don't let it touch you!" Lin Hao shouted, and then, because shouting advice at people who were already fighting was exactly the mistake he had just spent four minutes correcting, he did the other thing instead.

He counted.

Out loud. Into the fight. Standing in the middle of it with two swords and a bleeding mouth and nothing at all to do with his hands except keep the thing's attention, he called the clock the way his father called the heat of a forge — not as information, as *time.*

"Gu Yue, that was one! Don't take the second on the same side! Wulin, it's got two on the right arm and one on the shoulder, the right arm is nearly done, hit the *left*! Xie Xie, you're at one, you've got five, stop being brave, five is not a lot of bear!"

And the fight changed. Not because he hit anything. He hit almost nothing; the bear was too fast for the Grain Cut and too hard for everything else, and the Stormbringer rang off it like a hammer off an anvil with no bar under it.

The fight changed because four people stopped spending themselves and started spending the *bear.*

Gu Yue, who had been teleporting out of instinct, began teleporting out of arithmetic — leaving the left side when the left side had two on it, arriving on the side that had none. Xie Xie stopped stabbing the flank that would not open and began cutting at the wrist that already had three. Wulin stopped meeting the charge and started meeting the *arm,* because a limb that could not bend could not catch a boy who was already somewhere else.

And the bear, which was one of the strongest thousand-year soul beasts in the elementary platform, which had bulldozed a hundred metres of forest to get here, began — slowly, and then not slowly — to lose the use of its right side.

It tore a small tree out of the ground and threw it at Wulin, which was clever, and which Xie Xie ducked, and which Lin Hao did not, because he was watching the shoulder and not the tree, and the tree hit him across the back and put him into the undergrowth for the second time that afternoon.

He came up spitting.

"Four," he said, to nobody, and got his feet, and went back in, because the clock was still running and he was the only one holding it.

## Part 6: The Neck

It ended the way fights like that end — not with a blow, with an arrival.

The bear's right arm went. That was the whole of it: it came round on the three of them and the right arm simply did not arrive, because the crystal had finished its work somewhere between the third hit and the fourth, and a limb that cannot bend is not a limb. And the shoulder followed it, and the bear's whole right side became a thing it was carrying rather than a thing it was using, and its head came down and to the left to compensate.

Which put the neck exactly where a boy in the air had already decided it was going to be.

Wulin came down out of the sky with the golden scales to the wrist and the whole of the dragon's blood behind the strike, and the Crystal Bear — one of the strongest thousand-year soul beasts in the elementary platform, older than any of them by nine hundred and ninety years — went down in the shredded remains of its own path.

Xie Xie sat down hard.

Gu Yue put her hands on her knees and stayed there for a long time.

Lin Hao looked at the bear, and then at his own right arm, where a patch of skin on the forearm had gone pale and flat and cold in a shape about the size of a thumbprint, and he pressed it, and it did not bend.

"One," he said.

"Hao," Wulin said, and his voice had changed.

"One," Lin Hao repeated, and he held the arm out so his brother could see it, and he made himself say the next part in the voice he used for a fact rather than the voice he used for a joke, because Wulin needed the fact and would have taken the joke and been frightened alone afterwards. "It got me once. Four in the same place or six anywhere. I'm at one. That's not a wound, it's a *count,* and the count is fine, and I'd like everyone to stop looking at me like I'm dying."

"You're *bleeding.*"

"I'm bleeding from my *mouth,* Wulin, I bit it, it's the least interesting blood on me." He rolled the sleeve down. "Look. Gu Yue. Two teleports left, you said. Don't spend them walking. Save them for the walk out, because I have a leg with a bite in it, Xie Xie has nothing left in his legs, Wulin has spent a dragon, and the three of us are going to need a girl who can be somewhere else."

Gu Yue looked up at him.

"You counted me," she said.

"I counted everybody. That's the thing I do."

"No." She straightened up, and her face was still the colour of paper, and her voice was not. "You counted *me.* You counted my teleports, and you did not ask me how many I had, and you did not spend them, and you told the others not to spend them." She looked at him for a long moment with an expression he could not read at all, which was, he had learned, the most interesting expression she had. "Nobody has ever counted me before. They spend me."

"That's because they don't know what you cost," Lin Hao said. "I know what everything costs. It's a professional deformity, I'm a smith, I know what a bar is worth before it goes in the fire."

"And what am I worth."

"You're the only one who can be somewhere else," he said. "That makes you the most expensive thing in this forest, and I'd like to stop pretending otherwise, so — yes. I counted you. Get used to it."

Behind them, in the screen room that none of them could see, Long Hengxu was on his feet, and Wu Zhangkong had not moved at all, and had not moved for some time, and was looking at the board where a single dot had stopped counting itself as one.


The hawk — eight hundred and seventy years, and it had been fed well this session — did not comment. It never did.

---


He wrote the number down that night, because Wu Zhangkong had made him start keeping a record and the record was the only thing he had that was entirely his.

**one hundred and ninety-six.**

It had been one hundred and ninety-six. Five points, from a girl who ran the wrong way and a clock that had not been a clock, and he could not have told anybody which part of the afternoon had done it.

"Do you understand why that is a problem?"

"Because I'm ten."

"Because you're *measurable,*" Long Hengxu said. "A ten-year-old who clears the elementary platform in one session is a curiosity. A ten-year-old who clears it in one session and stays in for another hour and comes out with a count on his arm and a plan in his head is a *file.* The Spirit Pagoda keeps files. There is a man in this building who has one of yours in his pocket, and he did not put it in the ledger where it belongs, and I have not decided yet whether that is irregular or whether it is the first sensible thing anyone has done about you." He capped the pen. "Go home. All of you. Eat something. Nobody meditates tonight."

---

## Part 3: What the Man in the Doorway Was Waiting For

Wu Zhangkong was in the corridor.

Not walking. Not waiting in the way people wait, which is standing with an errand in their face. He was standing with his arms folded and his back against the wall and the particular stillness of a man who had arrived before everyone else and intended to leave after.

"Lin Hao," he said.

"Yes."

"Walk with me."

They walked. Wu Zhangkong did not say anything for the length of the corridor, and then the length of the courtyard, and then the length of the path that went down toward the groundskeeper's shed, and Lin Hao — who had spent four months learning which of this man's silences were empty — walked beside him and said nothing either, because this one was full.

At the shed Wu Zhangkong stopped, and drew the Skyfrost Sword.

Lin Hao had seen it four times. Four times it had been in a hand and moving, and both times that mattered it had ended a fight in two strokes. He had never once seen it drawn slowly, and he understood, watching it come out of the scabbard an inch at a time, that he was being shown the weapon rather than the work.

"What do you see," Wu Zhangkong said.

"A sword."

"Look again."

Lin Hao looked again. He looked the way he looked at steel, because it was the only way he had, and what he saw was: a blade about a metre long, straight, single-edged for the last third, with a spine thick enough to take a hammer and an edge ground to a geometry so fine that the light did not so much reflect off it as *decide* about it. And under that, because he could not help it, the grain — the folded weather inside the bar, ten thousand layers of a smith's decisions, and the decisions were *conservative.* Whoever had made this sword had not tried anything. They had done the correct thing, over and over, for a very long time.

"Somebody made that over years," Lin Hao said. "And they never once showed off."

Wu Zhangkong put it away.

"That," he said, "is the most accurate thing anyone has ever said about my sword, and I have owned it for thirty-one years." He sat down on the shed step, which was not a thing he did, and Lin Hao sat down beside him, which was not a thing he had been invited to do. "I have been your teacher for four months. In four months I have taught you a stance, a stroke, and one sentence about reading. Do you know why it's been so little?"

"Because you're mean."

"Because I have been *finding out.*" Wu Zhangkong looked at the shed roof. "A teacher who teaches too early teaches his own sword. Every master does it, I did it, my master did it to me — you meet a child with a gift and you cannot help it, you pour yourself in, and thirty years later the child is a very good copy of you and neither of you can work out where the road went wrong." He turned his head. "So I taught you almost nothing. I hit you instead, and I watched what you did with the hitting, and I waited to see whether you would start making things I had not given you."

"And?"

"You made three strokes against a wolf pack that I did not give you, that you did not have previously, and that you could not have made from anything I taught you. You made them in the moment, under pressure, against an opponent that was reading you." Wu Zhangkong said it flatly, the way he said everything, and it landed anyway. "That was ninety-four minutes ago and I have not stopped thinking about it since."

---

## Part 4: The Part He Could Not Teach

"Here is what a swordsman is," Wu Zhangkong said. "Not what a good fighter is. Not what a strong one is. Those are different trades and the world confuses them constantly.

"A swordsman is a person whose sword can say something. Not *do* something — do is easy, I can teach a dog to do. Say. A sword that speaks has a meaning behind the stroke, and the meaning is the swordsman's own, and it is the reason the stroke works on things it should not work on." He picked up a splinter of wood from the ground and turned it in his fingers. "There are five rooms. Foundation is the body. Technique is the vocabulary. Threshold is when the sword stops being a tool — you passed that in the gauntlet, and I marked it, and I said nothing, because saying it would have made it yours instead of true. The fourth room is Sword Intent, and you were standing in the doorway of it today with two swords and a bleeding mouth, and you did not know it."

"I was counting."

"You were *meaning* something," Wu Zhangkong said. "You left a sword in a wound and walked away from it. Do you understand what that is? That is not a technique. No form I have ever seen contains it. You spent a weapon — a weapon, the most expensive thing you own — as a *sentence,* because the sentence was worth more than the sword. That is the fourth room. That is Sword Intent, and you walked into it backwards while doing arithmetic."

Lin Hao was quiet for a moment.

"And the fifth room."

"The fifth room is Sword Innate." Wu Zhangkong put the splinter down. "In the fifth room there is no sword. I don't mean you don't hold one. I mean the sword stops being the reason. You could take a stick, a chopstick, a finger, and it would still be *sword,* because the sword is not the object anymore, it's the — " he stopped, and Lin Hao watched him stop, watched the man who had six rings and two ten-thousand-year souls and a sword that thirty-one years of correctness had made go looking for a word and not finding one. "I can't tell you," Wu Zhangkong said. "That's the whole of it. I can't tell you, because I'm not there."

"You're not."

"I have been in the fourth room for twenty-six years." He said it without any self-pity at all, which made it worse. "I am a very good swordsman. I have beaten people I should not have beaten. And I have never once been able to put the sword down, and I have thought about it every day for twenty-six years, and I have concluded that the reason is that my sword is *mine* — it is the Skyfrost Sword, it came with a name and a school and four hundred years of other people's decisions in it, and I have spent my whole life being extremely good at somebody else's sentence." He looked at Lin Hao. "You don't have that problem. You never had a school. You have a hammer, a hawk, a bad stance I fixed, and four months of me being careful. Whatever your sword is going to say, it isn't going to be a quotation."

"So what do I do."

"That's the part I can't teach," Wu Zhangkong said, "so I'm going to give it to you as homework instead, which is the only thing a teacher can do with the part he can't teach." He stood up, and brushed the shed step off behind him out of long habit, and looked down at the boy on it.

"Make a style."

"...What?"

"A style. Yours. Named, and built, and written down, with forms in it that I have not seen and that you cannot do yet. Everybody's sword comes out of somewhere, and yours came out of a smithy, so it had better look like one." He started up the path. "I want the name by the end of the month. I want the first form by the end of the term. And I want you to understand that I am not being encouraging, I am being *selfish,* because I am fifty-four years old and I have been in the fourth room for twenty-six of them, and I would like to see the fifth before I die, and you are the only chance of it I am going to get."

"That's the most honest thing you've ever said to me."

"Don't get used to it," Wu Zhangkong said, and went up the path, and did not look back, and Lin Hao sat on the shed step for a long time afterwards with his arms aching and his cheek stinging and a thumbprint of cold crystal on his forearm, thinking about rooms.

---

## Part 5: Reading the Grain

He started that night, on the roof, with a stick.

Not the Stormbringer. That was the first decision and it took him an hour, and the reason was Wu Zhangkong's, though it took him the hour to understand it: if he built the style with the Stormbringer he would build it out of the Stormbringer, and the Stormbringer was a martial soul, and a martial soul came with a shape already in it, and he would end up exactly where Wu Zhangkong had ended up, which was extremely good at somebody else's sentence.

So: a stick. Roof tile warm under him, harbour wind doing its long argument, and a stick he had picked up off the training ground that was slightly too light and slightly too long and entirely ordinary.

The name arrived before the forms did, which surprised him, because he had assumed names came last.

**Reading the Grain.**

Not a school. Not a lineage. A *method* — and the method was one sentence, and the sentence was his father's, and his father had never once known he was teaching swordsmanship: **you do not cut metal where you want it to open, you cut it where it is already willing.**

He said it out loud to the harbour, and heard how it sounded, and thought: *that's either the truest thing I've ever said or I'm ten years old on a roof with a stick, and it's probably both.*

The first form took the rest of the night.

He built it out of the ledger, because the ledger was the only thing he had that was entirely his — seventy-one lines, and then eighty-three, each one a fight, each one an answer, and the answers had shapes. He laid the shapes out on the roof tile in his head the way he would lay out a bar, and he looked for the place they were all *willing,* and he found it, and it was very simple, and it was so simple that he laughed, and Wulin called up from the bunk below to ask whether he was all right, and he said yes.

The first form was this: **you do not strike first.**

Not a defence. Not a wait. The form *began* with the opponent's commitment, because a commitment was the only place in a fight where anything was already willing, and every technique he had ever made that had worked had worked because he had arrived at a place somebody else had already agreed to be. The Grain Cut. The Question. The Answering Stroke. The Unwritten Stroke. Four forms, four fights, and all four of them had begun with somebody else.

So the first form of Reading the Grain was a form you could not do alone. You needed a person. You needed their decision. And the strike itself was the smallest part of it — the last three centimetres of a thing that had started a full second earlier, on the other side of the roof, in somebody else's mind.

He named it **Open Hand**, because his father opened the bar before he ever struck it, and because it looked, from the outside, exactly like nothing at all: a boy on a roof with a stick, not moving, waiting for a partner who was not there.

At four in the morning he got up and did it against the harbour wind, and the wind did not commit, and the form did not work, and he stood there with the stick in his hand and understood the second thing about his own style, which was going to take him years.

*It only works on something that decides.*

Which meant it would work on every person he ever fought.

And it would never, ever work on a wolf.

"Right," Lin Hao said, to the dark water, and he was grinning, and he did not stop grinning for the rest of the night. "So that's what I'm for, is it. Not the beasts. The *people.*"

The hawk, eight hundred and seventy-four years of condensed wind riding quietly inside him, did not comment. But it turned its head, and Lin Hao felt it turn, and for the first time in four years he had the distinct and entirely unsupported impression that it was pleased.

## Part 1: The Letter

Xie Xie came to the forge at half past ten at night, which was not a thing he did.

He came because the side forge had a light on, and because he had walked past the dormitory twice already without going in, and because a boy who has been carrying a folded piece of paper in his pocket for six hours eventually goes to the one person he does not have to perform for.

Lin Hao was at the anvil. Not working — the fire was banked and the bar was cold — but standing at the anvil the way other people stand at a window, with his hands flat on it, thinking.

"You're doing the thing," Xie Xie said.

"What thing."

"The standing-at-it-without-hitting-it thing. My father does that. It means you've got a problem and you'd rather look at metal than at the problem."

"That's not what it means."

"That's *exactly* what it means." Xie Xie sat down on the coal sack, which was the only seat, and which he had claimed by right of arrival. "I've got a letter."

"From your father."

"How did you—"

"Because you've got your father's folding on it. He folds things four times, you fold things twice and badly, and there's a square in your pocket with four creases in it that you have taken out and put back at least nine times since you got here." Lin Hao turned round. "Sit properly. You're going to read it to me or you're going to make me guess, and if you make me guess I'll get it right and you'll be annoyed for a week."

Xie Xie sat properly.

"He wants me to sit the Association's mecha-engineering entrance in the spring," he said. "He's got me a place at the prep course. It's in Glorybound. It's four months." He looked at the letter, which he had not unfolded. "He says it's what I've wanted since I was six."

"Is it."

"Yes."

"Say it again."

"*Yes,*" Xie Xie said, louder, and then — because he was Xie Xie, and because the loud one is the one who is not sure — "obviously it is. It's the only thing I've ever wanted. Mecha Master. I've said it every day of my life. I said it on a bench when I was nine in front of half the class and Yun Xiao told me to shut up until I could beat Gu Yue, and I've carried that around for a year, and it's *mine.*"

"I didn't ask whether it was yours."

Xie Xie's mouth opened, and then closed.

"You asked whether it *is,*" he said.

"I asked whether it is. Present tense. Today."

---

## Part 2: What a Friend Does

Lin Hao pulled the second coal sack over and sat down on it, which took some effort, because the sacks were low and he had a bruise on his hip from a Horned Dragon and a crystal mark on his forearm that had gone the colour of a healing thumbprint.

"I'm going to tell you something," he said, "and I want you to understand that I know exactly how it's going to land, and I'm telling you anyway, and that's the whole point of me."

"Here we go."

"Six weeks ago you told me I'd been fighting the wrong half of you for nine weeks." Lin Hao held the look. "You were right. I had been. And the reason you were the only person who could tell me is that you'd spent nine weeks getting hit by the wrong half, and you were *bored* of it, and bored is honest. Gu Yue could have told me and didn't, because Gu Yue doesn't. Wulin couldn't have, because Wulin loves me and love is a terrible instrument for this, it's like trying to measure a seam with your thumb." He shrugged. "You told me. It cost you nothing and it changed me, and I've thought about it every day since, and I want to say the next part properly because it's the only thing I actually understand about people."

He put his hands flat on his knees, the way his father did when a bar had come out wrong and the explaining was going to take a minute.

"Every relationship has to be built on friendship, because friendship is the one you *make.* You don't get given it. Nobody hands you a friend the way they hand you a brother or a mother or a girl who looks at you a certain way — you build it, out of mornings, out of nine weeks of getting hit, out of choosing to come back the tenth week. And because you built it, it's the only one where both people know what it's made of.

"A friend is the best support there is. He's on your side. But a true friend is also your enemy, and that's not a contradiction, that's the *structure* — he supports you and he opposes you at the same time, and the balance between those two is the whole thing. He stands with you when you're wrong. He really does. If you go and do something stupid tomorrow I'll be standing next to you in it, and I'll help you carry whatever it costs, because that's the support half. And then I'll tell you it was stupid. Not instead. *And.*"

"That sounds exhausting."

"It's the only one that isn't. That's the joke." Lin Hao grinned, briefly. "Everything else — love, blood — the moment it gets hard it turns into choosing a side. And when you choose a side you stop seeing the person. You see the good and the bad goes invisible, and other people can see it and you can't, and they stop telling you because you've made it expensive to tell you. So it grows. And eventually the whole thing is held together by nobody saying anything." He tapped his own temple. "There's a name for it. People call it love sickness, like it's a weather. It's not a weather. It's a *blindness,* and it's the expensive kind, because it costs you the person you're blind about."

Xie Xie was quiet.

"And it's simple," Lin Hao said. "That's the part nobody can stand. It's genuinely simple — you support them and you tell them the truth, and you do both, and that's the whole of it. And people make it complicated on purpose. They make it complicated because they *want* something, and wanting makes you run, and when you're running you start arguing with yourself instead of with them, and then you're trying to prove you're right to *yourself,* in your own head, where nobody can check. That's not a relationship. That's a man alone in a room with a mirror, and he's been in there so long he thinks the mirror is talking back."

He stopped, and heard himself, and winced.

"That came out better than I'd planned and I want it said that I'm ten."

---

## Part 3: The Objection

Xie Xie unfolded the letter. He did not read it. He looked at the paper the way you look at a thing you have already read eleven times.

"So," he said. "Tell me."

"Tell you what."

"You just gave a speech about how a friend tells you. So tell me. Is it my dream or is it my father's."

Lin Hao opened his mouth and shut it.

"I'll tell you what I know," he said. "Your father spent a thousand years' worth of money on a hundred-year soul for you. I know that because you told me in the forest, when you thought you were going to die, which is when people say the true things. He has spent your entire life on you, and he is not a bad man, and he wants the mecha engineering because he has decided — correctly, probably, from where he's standing — that a noble family's second son with average spiritual power needs a trade that doesn't depend on the soul. That's not a father crushing a son. That's a frightened man building a wall."

"And?"

"And I don't know whether it's your dream, Xie Xie. I genuinely don't. Here's what I do know: you have said 'Mecha Master' every day of your life, and I have never once heard you talk about *building* one. Not once. You talk about *being* one. You talk about the coat, and the bench, and Yun Xiao shutting up, and the symbol of a true noble. You never talk about the circuits. You never ask Mu Chen about tolerances. You've been in a forge eleven times and you've never once picked up a caliper." He let that sit. "Whereas when you talk about the dagger — the *dagger,* not the dream — you talk for an hour and you don't notice."

Xie Xie did not say anything for a long time. The banked fire ticked.

"That's not fair," he said, at last. "That's not a fair thing to say to me."

"No."

"You don't know what it's like. You've got a *sword.* Yours came out of your hand when you were six years old, and your father is a smith, and your whole life has been one long permission. My father spent the family's money on a dagger and then spent eleven years being disappointed that it wasn't enough, and every single morning I wake up owing somebody." His voice had gone flat, which was worse than loud. "You get to have a dream because nobody had to pay for yours."

"That's true," Lin Hao said.

Xie Xie looked up.

"That's completely true and I'm not going to argue with it, because it's the sort of thing that's true whether I like it or not, and I've made a policy of not arguing with those." He turned the coal sack so he was facing his friend properly. "I got a sword. My father got a son who liked the same thing he liked. That's luck, and I'd be lying if I dressed it up as virtue. But here's the part I want you to hear, because I think it's the only useful thing I've ever had to say to anybody: **the owing is the problem, not the dream.** If you go to Glorybound because you want to build mechas, your father's money is a gift and you'll never think about it again. If you go because you owe him, you'll be in that prep course for four months and you'll be excellent at it, and you'll be miserable every day, and you'll be so busy being grateful that you won't notice you've stopped wanting anything at all. And then you'll be twenty, and you'll be a very good mecha engineer, and you'll meet somebody who asks you what you actually like, and you won't have an answer. That's the expensive version of the blindness. It's not romantic. It's just slow."

## Part 4: What Xie Xie Did With It

"So what do I do," Xie Xie said.

"I don't know."

"You never say that."

"I say it when it's true." Lin Hao got up and went to the rack, and came back with two things — a length of cold-rolled stock about the size of his forearm, and a scriber. He put them on the coal sack between them. "Here's what you do. You don't decide tonight, and you don't decide by asking yourself, because you've been asking yourself for six hours and you've come up with nothing, and that's because asking yourself is the mirror thing, and you're alone in the room with it."

"Then what."

"You find out what the work is like. Not the title. The *work.*" Lin Hao sat back down. "You come here on Saturdays. Not to watch me — I'm sick of you watching me. You learn the bench. Calipers, files, layout, the boring part, the part where nothing happens for three hours and then something is true. Six Saturdays. And separately, you get your father's prep-course syllabus and you read it, actually read it, the circuits and the tolerances and the boring parts, and you notice whether you're bored. And at the end of six weeks you'll know. Not because you decided. Because you'll have *evidence,* and evidence is the only thing that gets a man out of a room with a mirror."

Xie Xie looked at the scriber.

"And if I'm bored."

"Then you're bored, and you tell your father, and it's going to be the worst month of your life, and I'll be standing next to you in it — that's the support half — and I'll also tell you that you were right to do it, which is the other half, and you will find the combination extremely annoying."

"And if I'm not bored."

"Then it was always yours and your father was right, and you'll never have to think about it again, and I'll be wrong, and you'll bring that up constantly for years."

Xie Xie picked up the scriber. He turned it over once, and then he did something with it — a small, absent, entirely unconscious thing — scribing a line along the stock and then a second line parallel to it, checking the gap with his thumbnail, and then correcting the second line by a hair.

Lin Hao watched him do it and said nothing at all.

"What," Xie Xie said.

"Nothing."

"You're doing a face."

"I'm not doing a face."

"You're *absolutely* doing a face." Xie Xie put the scriber down. "What."

"Your second line was out by about the width of a hair and you found it with your thumb and fixed it without looking." Lin Hao's voice was carefully neutral, which was the voice he used when something interesting had happened. "Most grown men in this building can't do that. Mu Chen can. My father can. I can, but I had to be taught, and I had a *hawk,* and I've been complaining about the unfairness of it for four years." He picked the scriber back up and set it down in Xie Xie's hand. "Six Saturdays. Start now."

## Part 5: What the Style Is Called

Xie Xie stayed until two in the morning, which was the record, and most of it was not about the letter.

Most of it was Xie Xie at the bench with a file, being terrible at it, and complaining continuously, and getting marginally better, and at some point around midnight he said, without looking up, "So what's the name."

"What name."

"Your style. Wu Zhangkong wants it by the end of the month and you've got two weeks and you've told absolutely nobody, and I know you've got one because you've been standing at that anvil like a man at a funeral for a week." Xie Xie blew the filings off the stock. "Tell me."

"Reading the Grain."

Xie Xie's file stopped.

"That's *blacksmithing.*"

"Yes."

"Your sword style is called a blacksmithing thing."

"My sword style *is* a blacksmithing thing. That's the entire discovery, that's what I've been standing here about. Wu Zhangkong told me to make something that wasn't a quotation, and everything I have that isn't a quotation came out of that forge, so — Reading the Grain. You don't cut metal where you want it to open. You cut it where it's already willing." He shrugged. "And it turns out people have grain too."

"That's the most boring name I have ever heard."

"Good."

"It's *terrible.* 'Reading the Grain.' Nobody's going to fear that. Nobody's going to hear 'Reading the Grain' and think 'I should probably yield.' They're going to think you do *fences.*"

"I don't need them to fear the name," Lin Hao said. "I need them to not see it coming, and 'Reading the Grain' is a name nobody looks at twice, which is a feature. Besides — the first form is called Open Hand, and it's a form where I don't move at all, and it beats people who are much better than me, so the whole thing has a consistent reputation problem that I've made my peace with."

Xie Xie went back to filing.

"I'm going to call it the Smithy School," he said. "In front of Wu Zhangkong. In the formal setting. When there are people there."

"You will not."

"I absolutely will. I'll say 'and Lin Hao will now demonstrate a technique from the renowned Smithy School,' and I'll do the voice, and you'll have to stand there and take it, because that's the *support* half, and I'll be telling the truth about where it came from, which is the other half, and you will find the combination extremely annoying."

Lin Hao opened his mouth, and shut it, and then laughed, because it was exactly right — it was his own argument handed back at him with the sharp end first, and he had no defence at all that did not destroy it.

"That's the best thing you've ever done to me," he said.

"I've been learning from the best," Xie Xie said, and did not look up, and filed, and was, for the first time in six hours, not holding a folded piece of paper.

## Part 6: Two Weeks

He walked Xie Xie back at two, and the harbour did its accounting, and neither of them said the other thing, which was that the letter was still folded in Xie Xie's pocket and still not answered, and that six Saturdays was not an answer either, and that both of them knew it.

At the dormitory door Xie Xie stopped.

"Hao."

"Yes."

"If I go to Glorybound." Four months. Two hundred and forty days of mornings that would not happen. "You'd still tell me."

"That's not how distance works."

"Answer the question."

Lin Hao looked at him — at the boy who had been the first line in the ledger, who had drawn blood off him in a training ground and grinned about it, who had spent nine weeks being bored in exactly the right way — and understood that the question was not about Glorybound at all, and never had been.

"Yes," he said. "If you go, and you become exactly what he wants, and you're miserable, and you're excellent at it, and you never once complain because complaining would be ungrateful — I'll write to you and I'll say it, and it'll cost me the friendship to say it, and I'll pay that, because the alternative is watching you disappear by degrees and calling it support." A beat. "And if it costs the friendship, then it wasn't the thing I said it was, and I'd rather find that out than keep it."

Xie Xie was quiet for a moment.

"That's worse than a nice answer," he said.

"It's the only answer I've got."

"Yeah." He went in. Then he came back out, because he was Xie Xie. "Smithy School."

"I will end you."

"*Smithy School.*" And the door closed, and Lin Hao stood in the corridor with his bruised hip and his thumbprint of a scar and a two-week deadline and a friend who was going to spend six Saturdays finding out whether he wanted his own life, and he thought — not for the first time, and not for the last — that he would rather have this than the number.

Then he went to bed, because he was ten, and the anvil would still be there in the morning, and the grain would still be in the steel, waiting to be read.


The hawk was eight hundred and seventy-eight years old and had no opinion about the forge, or about anything, because it was a soul and not a person.
