## Part 1: The Triangle

They had it. That was the thing Lin Hao would remember afterwards, and the thing nobody who watched it ever quite believed.

Three children who had been alive for ten years had a thousand-year Crystal Bear in a triangle, and the bear did not know which of them to kill.

It stomped in the centre of its own shredded clearing and turned, and every time it turned one of them moved, and the moving was not panic — it was *agreed.* Wulin was calling it out loud, because he had stopped being able to hold it in his head: belly, eyes, rear. Xie Xie had come out of the shadows entirely, both daggers in his hands, the light one catching the green and the dark one not being there at all, and he put two blades into the bear's belly and the bear decided about him.

It came at him in strides that ate ground.

And Gu Yue filled its eyes with fire.

Not the one great fireball she had used on the Horned Dragon. Dozens, and small, and everywhere at once, and the bear threw a paw up and ducked its head, and ducking its head was the whole of what Wulin had needed, because he had spent the last nine seconds climbing a tree with a strand of grass and the entire rest of his soul power.

Lin Hao watched him come down.

He watched the right hammer stay back and the left come up in front of the chest, and he watched the gold run to the wrist, and he understood — with the flat, arithmetic-free certainty of a boy who has stood at an anvil long enough to know what a committed strike sounds like — that there was nothing behind it. Wulin had emptied himself into one blow, and if the blow did not land, there would be no second one, and there would not be time to be sorry.

A green wind blade went past with a whistle that hurt the teeth.

Gu Yue had made it to hide the sound. Lin Hao would think about that for a week: that she had spent something she did not have on a *noise,* because the noise was worth more than the damage.

Then the hammer came down on the neck, and the neck made a sound like a door being broken.

## Part 2

He could see the tracks now. Not clearly, and not always, but when he was tired and his eyes went soft there were faint lines in the air where soul power had moved, the way a boat leaves a wake. He had never mentioned it, because there had been nobody to mention it to who would not have asked him to prove it.
: What Came Out of the Bear

The bear fell.

It fell head-first, which is how big things fall, and Xie Xie made a noise that was not a word, and for about two seconds the clearing was the happiest place in the forest.

Then the light came out of it.

Yellow, and one metre across, and it did not spread and it did not fade — it simply *chose,* and what it chose was Wulin, and Lin Hao was forty metres away and running and knowing perfectly well that he was going to be too late, because the light was faster than any of them and had already made up its mind.

"No—"

That was Gu Yue. She had nothing left. Lin Hao had watched her spend it — the teleports, the tornado of leaves, the fireballs, the wind blade that was only a noise — and she had nothing left, and she flashed silver anyway and got there anyway, and put her arms under a boy who had become a statue and weighed as much as a statue, and the two Heavy Silver hammers were still in his hands.

They went down together.

Lin Hao heard the thud from forty metres and it did not sound like a person landing.

The crystal is frail. That was the whole horror of it and he understood it while he was still running: crystal does not bend, so crystal breaks, and a boy made of crystal falling onto forest floor becomes a great many pieces of boy, and this was a training platform, and a training platform was supposed to be safe, and the part of his mind that kept files had already found the entry — *residual effects. Possible permanent injury.* — and had underlined it.

Gu Yue was underneath him.

She had her arms locked and her face turned sideways and her eyes shut, and her face had gone the colour of old paper, and she was holding a thousand kilograms of frozen boy off the ground with her shoulders and her spine and nothing else.

## Part 3: The Harsher Path

Xie Xie got Wulin off her.

That was the first thing he did and it was the right first thing, and Lin Hao saw him do it and thought, *good,* because he had been afraid — genuinely afraid, for the first time in the forest — that Xie Xie would do the dramatic thing instead of the correct thing. He did not. He lifted, he dragged, he rolled the crystal boy onto his own side, and then he pulled Gu Yue out from under, and then he looked at her face and made a decision in the space of one breath.

He slapped the button on the back of her hand.

She went into light and was gone.

"You—" Lin Hao began, arriving.

"She was dying," Xie Xie said, without turning around. "Say it if you want, say it fast, I don't have long."

Lin Hao did not say it. He said the other thing. "Wulin's button."

"Can't reach it." Xie Xie's voice was flat and much too steady. "He's *crystal,* Hao. I'd have to break him to get to his wrist. I checked. I checked three times." He was breathing hard and he was not looking at anything in particular. "So. That's the arithmetic of it. One of them gets out and one of them doesn't, and I'm the one who gets to stand here and be useless next to the one who doesn't."

The thicket started to rustle.

Lin Hao heard it and Xie Xie heard it, and neither of them said anything for a moment, because saying it would have made it real, and then it was real anyway.

They came out of the green one at a time, which was worse than all at once. Dark fur along the spine. Amber eyes with nothing behind them. Ten of them, maybe twelve, and half of them peeled off toward the Horned Dragon's corpse with the professional indifference of things that had eaten their whole lives off other people's fights, and the other half did not.

The other half came toward the boy made of glass and the boy with two daggers.

**Green Wolves.** Ten-year soul beasts. Scavengers. Lin Hao's mind offered the entry without being asked — *pack, violent, will reach a hundred years on carrion if you let them* — and he pushed it aside, because the entry was not useful and the next ninety seconds were.

Xie Xie knelt.

He knelt down beside Wulin in the shredded grass and put the two daggers up and started breathing on purpose, in and out, slow, the way a person does when they have decided something and are getting their body to agree.

"Xie Xie," Lin Hao said.

"Don't."

"You've got nothing left. You spent it on the belly."

"I know what I've got." Xie Xie's jaw was set and his eyes were bright and wet at the same time, which was an expression Lin Hao had never once seen on him. "My father told me a true man can hold up heaven and earth. And men are loyal, and they face it, and they don't leave their comrades. Even for the price of the life." He laughed, once, sharply. "I'm ten. I've never done anything like this. I'm a newborn calf, he'd say, I'm not even a *calf,* I'm the idea of a calf. But I'm not going anywhere."

Lin Hao looked at him.

And the thing is — and this is the part he thought about for a year afterwards — he had arrived *after.* He had been forty metres away and running for a long time, and he had watched the button get slapped and the girl go into light, and he had stood there while Xie Xie knelt down and made his decision, and he had not said a single word to stop it.

He could have. He was faster. He could have shouted from the treeline, *run, you idiot, he's crystal and you're empty,* and Xie Xie would have listened, because Xie Xie always listened, and it would have been correct.

He had not shouted.

Because some things are a person's to decide, and a friend who takes that away from you has taken something more expensive than your life.

So Lin Hao drew the Stormbringer with his right hand and the forge blade with his left, and stepped past Xie Xie, and put himself between the kneeling boy and the amber eyes, and said, over his shoulder, "For the record. I think you're wrong."

"I know you think I'm wrong."

"You've got no soul power, no plan, and you're kneeling next to a statue."

"I know."

"And you're staying."

"I'm staying," Xie Xie said.

"Right," Lin Hao said. "Good. Then I'm staying too, and one of us should probably mention that this is the worst idea we've ever had, and I want it said that I said so out loud, in front of a witness, before it happened."

## Part 4: What the Sword Did

The first wolf came in on his left, and he killed it, and the second came in on his right, and he killed it, and the third did something he had not seen a wolf do.

It stopped.

Six feet out, in the open, with its head low, and it *stopped,* and the two behind it fanned wider instead of following, and Lin Hao — who had fought a pack that learned, in this same forest, ninety minutes ago — understood instantly and coldly that these were not the clever kind. These were simply the kind that had eaten well and were not in a hurry.

Which made them worse. A pack that learns can be lied to. A pack that is patient cannot.

"Xie Xie," he said. "How long until he thaws."

"I don't *know.*"

"Guess."

"Five minutes. Maybe ten. Maybe he doesn't and I'm talking to a lamp."

"Then we need five minutes," Lin Hao said, and the fourth wolf came, and he did a thing.

He did not decide to do it. That was the strange part, and the part he could not afterwards put in any order. The wolf came at his sword-side, and the forge blade was in his left hand and the left hand was *busy,* and the correct move — the move in the ledger, the move with a name — required the right hand to change grip, and there was not time to change grip, and so his right hand did not.

The Stormbringer went out one-handed and low and *backwards,* across his own body, from the wrong shoulder, at an angle that no form he had ever learned contained, and it went into the wolf's throat on the way past, and the wolf went down behind him rather than in front of him.

He had not aimed it. He had not chosen it. He had, for approximately one third of a second, not been doing the thing at all.

"WHAT—" Xie Xie said, from the ground.

"Shut up," Lin Hao said, and the fifth wolf came.

He got five minutes. That is the honest account of it: five minutes, twelve wolves, one statue, one empty boy, and a sword that at some point stopped being held and started being *used,* and by the end he was not counting them any more because counting required a part of him that was busy, and the part that was busy was not thinking, and the not-thinking was, he discovered, extremely good at this.

The last wolf left. They always leave. Carrion eaters do not pay for meat.

Lin Hao stood in the clearing with both arms hanging uselessly at his sides and blood on him that was perhaps a third his own, and behind him there was a sound like a window being unmade, and Wulin came out of the crystal the way a man comes out of deep water — all at once, and gasping, and furious.

"—TOLD YOU TO RETREAT!" Wulin shouted, at nobody, at the sky, still holding both hammers.

"We did not retreat," Xie Xie said, from the ground, where he had lain down at some point without mentioning it.

"I can see that," Wulin said.

## Part 5: Comrades

Wu Zhangkong was in the forest.

That was not supposed to be possible, and Lin Hao said so, and Wu Zhangkong said, "It isn't," and did not elaborate, and the two of them understood each other perfectly.

He looked at the crystal-broken ground, and the twelve wolves, and the girl-shaped absence where Gu Yue had gone into light, and he looked at Wulin, who was sitting down hard and holding his right wrist, and at Xie Xie, who could not currently be moved, and at Lin Hao, who was standing because sitting down would have involved a decision about his legs.

"Whose idea was the triangle," Wu Zhangkong said.

"Mine," Wulin said. "It was — I don't know. I could see where they needed to be."

"And the neck."

"It was the only place."

"And you bet everything you had on one strike." Wu Zhangkong's voice did not change, which was how you knew. "With two people depending on you being able to fight afterwards."

Wulin looked at the ground. "It worked."

"It worked," Wu Zhangkong agreed. "And if her fireball had been a half-second late you would have been a statue in front of a bear with its neck half-broken and two children with nothing left. Do you understand that I am not angry about the strike. I am angry that you did not *count* it first." He turned away, because that was how he ended things. "Both of you are foolish. Both of you are also the reason I have not slept properly in four months. Get your comrade."

Lin Hao and Wulin carried Xie Xie between them, which was undignified and necessary, and Xie Xie complained the entire way, which was how they knew he would live.

They pressed the button at the edge of the sector, all three of them at once, and the forest went away.

---

Xie Xie was on a bench with his feet up and a blanket he had not asked for.

A man in white came along first with a plate, because that was the procedure and the procedure did not care what anyone had just been through. Lin Hao put his hand on it without looking, and the dial went round and settled, and the man wrote the number on his board and moved on to Wulin without comment.

**two hundred and five.**

Lin Hao looked at it. He had been at two hundred and eight when he went in, and he had not sat down once since, and he had not cultivated, and he had not meditated, and there had not been a single moment in the last hour that felt like growth.

"Seven," he said, to nobody.

"That's all?" Xie Xie said.

"That's all."

"You fought twelve wolves and carried two people and I think you killed something with your *face* at one point, and you got *seven.*"

"It's a good seven," Lin Hao said. "It happened while I wasn't looking."

Wu Zhangkong was waiting in the corridor outside the box room, and he did not let them go.

"You did a thing in that clearing," he said, to Lin Hao.

"I did several things."

"You did one." Wu Zhangkong put his hands behind his back. "A backhand. One-handed. Off the wrong shoulder, through your own centre, at an angle that is not in any school I have ever heard of, and you did it because the correct grip was a third of a second away and you did not have a third of a second." He looked at Lin Hao for a long moment. "Do you know what you did."

"No," Lin Hao said. "I've been meaning to mention that. I don't know what I did, I can't do it again — I tried, in the corridor, I looked like a man swatting a bee — and I'd like to know whether I should be worried."

"You should not be able to do it again." Wu Zhangkong said it the way he said everything, flatly, and it landed anyway. "That is the point of it. A form is a sentence you have said before. What you did was not a form. You were past the forms, because you had no time for them, and the sword said the only thing left to say." He turned to go, and stopped. "Your homework was the name of a style and the first form of a style. You gave me both. And then you went into a forest and did the thing the style is *for,* without knowing you were doing it."

"When do I get it back," Lin Hao said. "The stroke. When do I get it back."

"When you stop trying to," Wu Zhangkong said, and left, and Lin Hao stood in the corridor with his arms shaking and a bandaged thigh and a great deal to think about.

Xie Xie was on a bench with his feet up and a blanket he had not asked for.

"Hao."

"Yes."

"You came back."

"I was there the whole time."

"No." Xie Xie looked at him. "After. You carried Wulin out. I watched you. And then you *came back in,* for me, and you didn't have to, and I want you to know that I noticed, because I was on the ground pretending to be unconscious and I noticed." He pulled the blanket up. "You could have gone out. You'd already done the useful part."

"I know."

"So why."

Lin Hao sat down on the bench. His legs had, at last, made their decision, and it was that they were finished.

"Because I've thought about this," he said. "I gave a whole speech about it, actually, I gave it to you, in the forge, and you were extremely rude about it. A friend supports you and tells you the truth, and does both, and those aren't in order — they're at the same time. So: I told you it was the worst idea we'd ever had. That was the truth part. And then I stood in front of the wolves." He leaned his head back against the wall. "The supporting part doesn't come with a condition where you have to be right. That's the whole thing. That's the *entire* thing. If I only stood in front of the wolves when you had a good plan, I'd be a colleague."

Xie Xie was quiet for a while.

"Smithy School," he said, at last.

"I will end you."

"*Smithy School.*" He was grinning, and his eyes were wet, and the corridor was cold, and down at the end of it a man in Spirit Pagoda grey was watching the three of them from a doorway and writing something on a card he did not put in the ledger.


Eight hundred and eighty-five years of condensed wind turned over in him, and for the first time he thought he could smell rain in it that was not there.

## Part 1: Out

They came out of the boxes into a room full of people who had been watching, which is the worst way to arrive anywhere.

Wulin was out first and shouting Xie Xie's name before his eyes had adjusted to the light. Zhang Yangzi was standing where he had been put. Wang Jinxi was twitching in a way nobody was going to mention. Gu Yue was sitting on the floor with her back against the wall and her face the colour of the wall, and she had not asked for help and had not been offered any, which suited everybody.

Lin Hao came out fourth and stood up, and the room looked at him, and he looked back, because he had decided a long time ago that looking away was the same as apologising.

Xie Xie said, "I, I'm fine. Just a bit sore."

He was not fine. His jacket was dark all the way down one side and his left leg would not take his weight, and he said it in the voice of a boy who had been asked a question in class and had not done the reading.

Wulin's legs went. He sat down hard on the tile and stayed there, and the exhaustion arrived all at once the way it does when the fear has finished, and somebody put a blanket on him that he did not thank anybody for.

Long Hengxu looked, for the first time in the four months Lin Hao had known him, like a man who had mislaid a number.

Wu Zhangkong looked exactly as he always looked.

## Part 2

The marks had taken on a faint blue at the edges since the crossing. He noticed it in the morning light, turning his forearm over, the way you notice a bruise changing colour — the same shape, a different weather in it.
: The Assessment

The staff member spoke for a while, and Lin Hao listened, because he had learned that a man praising you is a man telling you what he has decided you are, and that is useful information.

"Geniuses," he said. "They truly are geniuses worth nurturing. Are you sure these children are only ten?"

He went through them one at a time. He went through Wulin's hand — the transformed right hand, the strength several times higher than normal, the hundred-year beast killed in a strike and the thousand-year one crushed. He went through Gu Yue — the elements at the right moments, and the fact that she had held up **five hundred kilograms of crystallised boy** with her arms and her spine, and that she had done it without pausing to work out whether the pain would be real.

"That decision," he said, "is the one I would write down. People do not have time in those moments to consider whether a thing is real or virtual. She decided anyway, and she decided instantly, and she would have decided the same way if it were real. That is not a cultivation achievement. That is a *person.*"

And then he got to Xie Xie, and his voice changed, and Lin Hao understood that this was the part the man had actually been building toward.

"He knew he was no match," the staff member said. "He had no soul power. He had a leg that would not carry him. And he stayed, and he went round and round that crystallised boy like a dog round a fire, and he did not press his button, and he was sent out only when his comrade was free." He looked at the four of them. "They are ten years old. With a friendship like that, how could their coordination not be this deep?"

Nobody said anything, because there was nothing to add.

And then the man turned to Lin Hao, and Lin Hao felt the assessment arrive the way he felt a strike arriving — a fraction before it landed.

"And you," the staff member said, "were not supposed to be there."

"No."

"You were in for ninety-four minutes. The elementary session is forty. You fought a pack that a full squad of adults would have withdrawn from, you carried two people out of a forest, and your spiritual power when you came out was higher than when you went in." He said it without heat, the way you read a ledger. "Do you know what the Spirit Pagoda does with information like that?"

"Files it," Lin Hao said.

"We file it," the staff member agreed. He looked at Lin Hao for a moment longer than the sentence required. "Somebody already has."

## Part 3: What the Rain Was

It happened at about three in the morning, in the dormitory, and it woke him up the way the growth did — not with a sound, with an *arrival.*

Except this time there was a sound.

It was very small and very high, like a wet finger on the rim of a glass, and it was coming from inside his chest, and it went on for perhaps four seconds and then stopped, and in the four seconds the hair on both of Lin Hao's arms stood up and every loose piece of metal in the room — a nail on the sill, a buckle, Wulin's spare hammer head on the floor — ticked once against the wood.

Then it was quiet, and his heart was going, and he understood with total clarity that the hawk had done something.

**Nine hundred and six years.** The hawk had crossed something in the night, and it had not asked him first.

He had not counted it. He had not been counting anything. He had come in out of a forest at half past ten and eaten a bowl of rice and slept, and somewhere in the sleeping the hawk had crossed a line it had been approaching for four years, and the crossing had made a noise.

Lin Hao sat up and held out his hand.

Nothing happened, which was correct, because nothing was supposed to happen — the hawk was not a dog and did not come when called, and it had never once in four years done anything because he wanted it to. But the air above his palm was *different.* It had a texture. It was the particular wrongness that hangs over a forge floor on a dry day before you touch the bellows, and it was there, and it was not wind.

He had smelled rain in the hawk for a chapter and a half. This was the rain arriving.

**Wind and lightning.** He had known the words since he was six, because the sword had them and the sword's name had them, and he had never once questioned where the lightning was supposed to come from, because a six-year-old does not audit his own martial soul. Stormbringer. Wind and lightning. And all this time the wind had been the hawk's and the lightning had been the sword's, and the two of them had been fed by each other, and the hawk had simply been taking its time.

Now it had caught up.

He drew the Stormbringer in the dark, because he was not going to wait until morning, and the blade came out and the crackle on it — the faint crackle that had been faint for four years, that he had stopped noticing the way you stop noticing a clock — was not faint.

It ran the length of the edge in a thin blue line, and it made a sound like a small piece of paper being torn very slowly, and the hair on his arms was still up, and Lin Hao sat on the side of his bunk with his own sword in his hand and grinned at it like an idiot, because there was nobody to see.

"Right," he said, to a soul that could not hear him. "So that's what you were saving up for."

The hawk did not answer. It had never answered. But it turned over in him — slow, heavy, unhurried, the way something turns over when it has been travelling a long time and has arrived, and has no intention of explaining itself.

## Part 4: What It Was Not

Wu Zhangkong was in the yard at five, which meant he had not slept either.

Lin Hao showed him the sword without being asked, because that was the only honest way to start the conversation, and because the thin blue line along the edge was not something you could keep in a pocket.

Wu Zhangkong looked at it for a long time.

"How old," he said.

"Nine hundred and six. As of about three this morning. It made a noise."

"A noise."

"Like a wet finger on a glass. And all the metal in the room ticked." Lin Hao let the sword down. "It's the lightning. It's always been in the sword — the sword's had wind and lightning since the day I woke it up, and the hawk's only ever had wind, and I never thought about that, not once, because when you're six you don't check. The hawk's been eating the sword's essence for four years and it's finally grown the half it was missing."

Wu Zhangkong was quiet for a while.

"Do you know what that means," he said, at last.

"That my sword's going to hurt more."

"That your soul is going to catch up to your sword," Wu Zhangkong said, "and then pass it, and then you are going to find out what a soul with two attributes and a nine-hundred-year age can bestow." He put his hands behind his back. "Which is not a ring. Not yet."

"I know it's not a ring."

"Say it."

Lin Hao looked at him. "It's not a ring. A thousand years gets the ring. I'm ninety-four short and I'm at the top of the second band and the wall is still the wall, and nothing that happened last night changed any of that." He paused. "Is that what you wanted."

"That is what I wanted." Wu Zhangkong said it flatly, and then, because he was Wu Zhangkong, and because the kindness came sideways and always had: "A boy who gets a new attribute at ten and immediately starts shopping for a third ring is a boy who is going to die at fourteen. You did not shop. That is worth more than the lightning."

"And the lightning."

"The lightning is very good," Wu Zhangkong said. "Go and find out what it does. And Lin Hao."

"Sir."

"When it does the thing you have not worked out yet — and it will, because souls do not acquire attributes for decoration — do not tell anyone in this academy." He started toward the gate, and stopped. "There is a man in this city with your name on a card, and he did not put it in the ledger where cards go. You are not a curiosity yet. I would prefer you stayed that way until you are too large to be one."

## Part 5: What the Lightning Did

He found out at the Association, on a Saturday, in the side forge, with Mu Chen two rooms away and the door shut.

The first thing was the obvious thing: the Gale Talon, laid along the steel the way he had laid it a hundred times, came out with a sound he had never heard from it — not the wind's hiss but something sharper, a crack at the beginning and a crack at the end, like a whip breaking twice.

The second thing was that it cut deeper. Not much. An inch where it had been three quarters. He measured it, because he was his father's son, and he wrote the measurement down, and then he sat back on his heels and thought about *why,* because an inch was not an inch.

Wind pushes. That was the whole of the Gale Talon — a ribbon of moving pressure laid along an edge so the edge arrived faster than the arm could send it.

Lightning does not push. Lightning *goes.* It takes the shortest path between two things and it does not ask whether there is anything in the way, and the shortest path between a sword and a target is not the path the wind takes, because the wind has to travel and the lightning only has to arrive.

So the Talon was not one thing any more. It was two things happening at once: the wind shoving the edge forward, and something else getting there first.

The third thing happened by accident, at about noon, and it was the one he thought about for a year.

He was tired. He had been at it for six hours and his arms were gone and he was on the last bar of the day, and he laid the Talon along the steel out of pure habit without particularly meaning to, and the crack came out of the blade and jumped — **jumped** — a hand's width of empty air, and put itself into the bar, and the bar rang like a struck bell and split along the grain he had already read.

He had not touched it.

Lin Hao stood in the side forge with a smoking bar and a sword and no arms, and understood that the lightning was not an upgrade to the wind. It was a different *idea* about distance. The wind had to be laid along the edge. The lightning only had to be *let go.*

"Right," he said, to nobody, because Mu Chen was two rooms away and would have had questions. "So that's the second thing you do."

He sat down on the floor with his back against the anvil and his sword across his knees, and he did not cultivate, and he did not count anything, and he did not do arithmetic, because there was nothing to do arithmetic on. The rank was thirty and the rank would be thirty for a long time, and the hawk was nine hundred and six and climbing toward a thousand, and the sword had two voices in it now instead of one, and the second voice had only just started talking.

The wall was still the wall.

But for the first time in four months, Lin Hao could hear something on the other side of it.

## Part 1: The Walk Back

The warmth started in Wulin's spine about halfway down the hill.

Lin Hao noticed it before Wulin did, because he had spent four years noticing things slightly before the people they were happening to, and because the sign was not on Wulin's face. It was in his walk. Wulin had a way of going down a slope that involved his shoulders arriving a half-beat before the rest of him, and the shoulders had stopped arriving.

"Wulin."

"Mm."

"You're swaying."

"I'm not—" and then he was, badly, and Gu Yue caught him, which was the second time in two days she had put her arms under him and held up something heavier than she looked able to.

"Wulin, what's going on?"

"I don't know," Wulin said, in the voice of a boy whose mouth was already elsewhere. "I just feel really sleepy."

And then he went, completely and without dignity, into her arms.

Wu Zhangkong was in front of him before the second breath, with two fingers on his wrist, and his face did the thing it did when something had arrived that he had not scheduled. Long Hengxu came up behind and looked, and his gaze went sharp and attentive in a way Lin Hao had only seen once before, at an assembly, when a number had been read out that nobody had expected.

"He's fine," Wu Zhangkong said, and hefted Wulin onto his back like a sack of coal. "It's just that his spirit soul is evolving."

"Ah?" said four people at once.

## Part 2

The lock of storm-gray at his temple was long enough now that it fell across his cheekbone when he looked down, and he had started pushing it back without thinking, forty times a day, the way other boys pushed back ordinary hair.
: One-Tenth

They walked, and Wu Zhangkong explained, and Lin Hao listened the way he listened to everything — with the part of his mind that kept ledgers running whether he wanted it to or not.

"His spirit soul is naturally weak," Wu Zhangkong said, "so it's easier for it to evolve."

He went through it slowly, because Xie Xie had already told them the shape of it on the way in and had called it a possibility, and because a possibility that had happened to somebody standing next to you stopped being a possibility.

"For every soul beast you kill in the spirit ascension platform, you obtain one-tenth of its cultivation energy. That energy is spread evenly among your soul rings." He said *evenly* the way a man says a word he wants you to keep. "Kill a ten-year beast, your spirit soul gains a year. A hundred and ten years becomes a hundred and eleven. It accumulates, and when it reaches a thousand, it evolves. Wulin's spirit soul is ten years old. He took at least twenty years from the hundred-year beast and a hundred from the thousand-year one, and he has *one ring,* so all of it went into that one ring. Ten years became a hundred."

He shifted Wulin on his back.

"The rest of you will need to kill eighteen or nineteen thousand-year soul beasts."

Nobody said anything for a while, because that was a number you had to sit down inside.

"Because we've got two rings," Xie Xie said, at last.

"Because you have two rings. The energy splits. Each ring takes five percent." Wu Zhangkong did not soften it, which was why they all believed him. "And finding that many thousand-year beasts in the elementary platform is not a matter of effort. So. There are benefits to having one ring."

Gu Yue was looking straight ahead.

Lin Hao was looking at the road, and doing a sum, and wishing — for the first time in his life — that the part of his head that did sums would shut up.

## Part 3: The Arithmetic He Could Not Stop

The Horned Dragon was a hundred years. He had killed it. Two rings. Five percent each.

**Five years.**

The Crystal Bear was a thousand, and he had hit it eleven times with everything he had and never once landed the killing blow, so by Wu Zhangkong's rule he would have taken whatever share the platform gave to a participant who did not finish — and even at the full ten percent, split two ways, that was **fifty years.**

Call it fifty-five. Be generous. Call it sixty.

The hawk had gone into the platform at eight hundred and sixty-two years and come out at eight hundred and eighty-five.

**Twenty-three.**

Lin Hao walked down the hill behind a man carrying an unconscious boy and did the arithmetic three separate times, because the first two answers had been wrong in the direction he wanted, and he did not trust himself to want the right one.

Twenty-three years from the platform, where the rule said he should have taken five, or at an absolute stretch sixty if he claimed a share of a kill that was not his.

Which meant the platform had not done it.

Which meant the thing that had taken the hawk from seven hundred years to nine hundred and six in four months was not the Spirit Ascension Platform, and was not the cultivation energy of slain soul beasts, and was not any of the mechanisms Wu Zhangkong had just spent five minutes explaining to four children as though they were the whole of how the world worked.

It was the other thing. The thing he had never been able to name to anyone's satisfaction, including his own. The thing his father called *the boy's way of it* and the Association called *an unusual affinity* and Wu Zhangkong had never once asked about directly, in four months, which was starting to look less like an oversight and more like a decision.

His soul ate the world. That was the honest version. Not one-tenth of what it killed — **all of what it experienced**, continuously, whether he was fighting or forging or lying in a dormitory with his eyes shut, and it had been doing it since before he was born, and it was roughly a hundred times faster than the rule that applied to everybody else.

Lin Hao stopped walking.

Not dramatically. He just stopped, on a public road, in the late afternoon, because a thought had arrived that deserved to be stood still for.

Wu Zhangkong had told him, at five in the morning, two days ago, not to become a curiosity. *You are not a curiosity yet. I would prefer you stayed that way until you are too large to be one.*

And then, this afternoon, in front of four students and a director, Wu Zhangkong had explained exactly how much cultivation energy a soul should take from a slain beast.

Lin Hao put the two sentences next to each other and looked at them.

*He knows,* Lin Hao thought. *He's known the whole time. He explained the rule to everybody in order to find out whether I would do the sum.*

And then, because the next part followed whether he wanted it to or not: *And I did the sum. And I stopped walking. And he is standing thirty metres ahead of me with his back turned, and he has not turned around, and he is waiting to see whether I catch up.*

Lin Hao caught up.

## Part 4: What Wu Zhangkong Did Not Ask

They walked the last part of the way with Wulin's breathing on Wu Zhangkong's neck and the others ahead, and neither of them said anything for four streets.

Then Wu Zhangkong said, "You stopped."

"Yes."

"Why."

Lin Hao looked at the back of the man's head, and made a decision, and it was the same decision he had made in the forge with Xie Xie, which was that the truth was cheaper than the alternative and would still be cheap in ten years.

"Because I did the arithmetic," he said. "The Horned Dragon was a hundred years and I killed it and I have two rings, so I should have taken five years from it. The hawk took twenty-three in one session, and it had already taken a hundred and sixty-two in the four months before that, and I never killed anything in those four months except a bar of spirit steel and a couple of wolves in a training ground." He kept his voice level, because level was the only way to say it. "So either your rule is wrong, or I'm wrong, or the thing that's growing my soul isn't the thing you just told everybody about."

Wu Zhangkong walked on.

"Which do you think it is," he said, at last.

"The third."

"I agree."

They walked further.

"Are you going to ask me what it is."

"No," Wu Zhangkong said. And then, because he was Wu Zhangkong, and because he could not let a thing sit without putting a fence around it: "I am not going to ask you, and I am going to tell you why, and you will listen. A boy of ten who can explain his own anomaly is a boy who has been *told* his anomaly, by somebody with a reason to tell him. You have not been told. You have noticed. Noticing is survivable. Being told is not, because then there is a second person who knows, and second people talk, and there is a man in this city with a card in his pocket who is not stupid." He shifted Wulin again. "So I am not going to ask. And you are not going to find out on purpose. And when it starts doing things you cannot account for, you will come to me, and I will decide then whether we are dealing with a gift or a debt."

"And if it's a debt."

"Then we pay it," Wu Zhangkong said, "and you will not enjoy the manner of the paying, and you will survive it, and that is the most anybody can promise anybody."

## Part 5: The Warm Pond

Wu Zhangkong stayed in the dormitory with Wulin, which he would not have done for anyone else, and Lin Hao knew this because Xie Xie told him, and Xie Xie knew it because Xie Xie had asked a second-year, and the second-year had laughed.

He stayed because Wulin's martial soul was mutated, and because a spirit soul evolving in a body like that was not a thing you left alone.

Wulin soaked in it.

That was the only word for it and he would use it himself afterwards, with some embarrassment: it felt like a warm pond. The warmth came up out of his spine and went into his bones and stayed there, and his body was beaten and his spirit was spent and the tiredness simply dissolved off him the way mud comes off in hot water. He did not want to open his eyes. He had never, in ten years of being told he had a trash martial soul, felt anything so entirely without cost.

The golden halo around him went blue.

Bluesilver Grass came out of his palms — not the thin weak stuff, but strands, and then more strands, until they surrounded him — and Wu Zhangkong took one and twirled it around his finger and looked at it for a long time.

There were channels in it.

Fine, faint, gold, running the length of the grass like veins, and the veins threw light, and the light was the same gold-blue that was on the boy, and under that light the natural lines in the grass grew more distinct, as though something were being *imprinted* rather than grown.

*Just as I thought,* Wu Zhangkong thought. *His bloodline is mutating the martial soul again. And this one is beneficial.*

He sat with it for a while longer, and did not write anything down, because he had decided some weeks ago — without telling anybody, including the director — that there were certain observations about Tang Wulin that were going to live in his head and nowhere else.

## Part 6: The Ledger Gets a Line It Shouldn't Have

Lin Hao went back to his own room and sat on the bunk with a piece of paper, because he had told himself for two years that he did not keep a ledger on paper, and because tonight was the night that stopped being true.

He wrote three lines.

*The hawk: 906 years. Wind and lightning. Grew 206 years in four months without a single qualifying kill.*

*The rule: one-tenth of a slain beast, split across rings. Eighteen or nineteen thousand-year beasts to evolve. I have two rings. Wulin has one. Wulin evolved today. I will not, by that rule, for a very long time.*

And then the third line, which he wrote slowly, and which he looked at for a long time before he folded the paper and put it inside the lining of his sword bag where nobody would think to look.

*Whatever is growing my soul does not care about the rule. Wu Zhangkong knows and has chosen not to ask. There is a man with a card. So: be too large to be a curiosity, and be that before the card is read.*

He blew out the lamp.

In the dark, the hawk turned over in him — nine hundred and twelve years of condensed wind and, since three nights ago, something else that had no name yet and did not answer to being called — and Lin Hao lay on his back and thought about one ring, and two rings, and the fact that he had been handed the worse arrangement twice now, once by the world and once by his own talent, and that the second time it had come with an interest rate.

"Wulin gets the pond," he said, to the ceiling, "and I get the arithmetic."

The hawk did not answer. It never did.

But the air above his palm had that texture again — the forge floor before the bellows — and it stayed there all night, and in the morning the nail on the windowsill was standing on its end.

## Part 1: The Man in the Chair

Wu Zhangkong had been sitting in the chair since before midnight, legs crossed, and he had not slept, and he did not mention it.

Lin Hao found out later, from Xie Xie, who found out from the second-year, who found out from the dormitory mother, who had brought tea at two in the morning and been waved away.

What Wu Zhangkong had been doing all night was watching a boy sleep and thinking about grass.

He had never believed Bluesilver Grass was weak. That was the thing nobody in the city understood, because everybody in the city had looked at a ten-year-old with a weed for a martial soul and done the arithmetic that the arithmetic invited. But the strongest of the first generation of Shrek Seven Monsters had started with Bluesilver Grass. The strongest Soul Master in history had started with Bluesilver Grass, and had taken it one step at a time all the way to godhood, and in twenty thousand years nobody except the Spirit Pagoda's founder had got there at all.

So a weak martial soul was not a thing Wu Zhangkong believed in. He believed in weak *holders.*

He had also noticed, weeks ago, that Wulin's martial soul had become an extension of the boy's body and that Wulin fought with it like a man using a very good rope. He had not said anything. He had not said anything because Wulin's perception was the single most frightening thing about him, and a boy like that finds his own flaws, and a flaw you are told about is a flaw you never learn to look for.

*If it's like this,* he thought, watching the gold fade out of the grass, *then the growth of his martial soul is something to look forward to.*

The radiance dimmed. Little Goldlight opened its mouth very wide, as if to yawn, lowered its head, and went back inside.

Wulin slept like the dead.

## Part 2

The marks on his forearms glowed faintly when the lightning moved through the steel, and he had learned to keep his sleeves down in front of the other candidates. Not because he was hiding anything. Because a man who is examining nine bars of steel does not want to also be looking at a boy's arms.
: Yellow

He woke up feeling better than he had in four months, which was suspicious, and then he noticed that the swelling was gone.

Since the day the first seal broke he had felt swollen. Not visibly. In the way a boot feels when the foot inside it has grown — everything slightly too tight, everything slightly complained about. Lin Hao had never mentioned it because he had assumed it was what having a dragon in your blood felt like and that everybody's blood felt like that.

It was gone.

And his soul power was higher. Not much. Not rank fifteen. But higher than a month of sitting would have made it, and he knew exactly how much a month of sitting made it, because he had done a great deal of sitting.

"You're up?"

Wulin nearly went back through the wall.

Wu Zhangkong was in the chair by the window, legs crossed, and had the specific look of a man who had been in the same position for nine hours.

"Teacher, you—"

"Wash up and go eat breakfast," Wu Zhangkong said. "Your spirit soul has evolved, so we can go and test what the soul skill gained." And he stood, and put a hand on Wulin's shoulder on the way past, and left.

Wulin stood in the middle of the room and did not move for a while.

*Evolved.*

His spirit soul had been the sore spot. Not the martial soul — everybody laughed at the grass and he had stopped caring about that a long time ago. The *soul.* Ten years. He had watched Xie Xie's family buy a hundred years of dagger, and Gu Yue carry something nobody would name, and Lin Hao walk in with **two yellow rings at nine and a half**, and every single time something in his chest had done a small, humiliating thing, because he was competitive in a way he had never been able to hide and ten years was ten years.

He had not dared dream of it. When Xie Xie told him it was possible in the platform he had not taken it seriously, because it was not a thing that happened to him.

Wulin raised his hand.

The grass came, and the halo rose under his feet — and it was not white.

**It was yellow.** A gentle, warm, unmistakable yellow, the colour of a hundred years, the colour everybody else had, the colour he had looked at in other people's hands for four months.

Little Goldlight came out onto his shoulder. Wulin held out his palm and it went onto it, and he looked at it for a long time.

It had been a defective spirit soul. Three years of his mother's money and his own, and it had come out wrong, and there had been a week — he had never told anyone about the week — when he had sat on the floor of this room and thought about not being here any more.

"Right," Wulin said, to a small golden thing on his hand, in a voice that was not steady. "Right. Okay. You're not trash."

And then he laughed, because he had no idea what else to do, and he got dressed very fast, and he went to find the training field.

## Part 3: Bind

The Bind came out and took the room.

That was the only way to describe it and Wulin would describe it that way for years: he said one word and the room stopped being a room and became a thing he was holding. Strands went from his palms into the bedpost, the window frame, the chair Wu Zhangkong had slept in, the door, the loose board by the sill — and everything was thicker than it had been, and tougher, and it cost him *less,* which was the part that made him sit down.

And then something gold appeared in his mind that had never been there before.

"Goldlight, what's—"

Goldlight jumped.

It went off his palm and into the grass, and several of the strands **changed** — went golden, and grew a fine layer of scales along their length, and stopped being grass in any sense the word had meant an hour ago.

Wulin took hold of one and pulled.

It was tougher than the others. Stronger than the others. And it did not feel like a thing he was holding. It felt like a limb he had been born with and had only just been told the name of — not as strong as his right arm, where the scales were, but only just short of his left.

*Spirit soul and martial soul,* he thought. *Fused.*

And then he ran out of the room shouting, because he was ten.

## Part 4: The Measurement

Wu Zhangkong made them all stand in a line at the training field, which was the worst possible arrangement for Xie Xie, who had a bandaged leg and a grudge, and then he took them one at a time through the platform's aftermath the way a man checks a bridge after a flood.

"You," he said, to Xie Xie, "fought twelve wolves with no soul power and a leg that would not carry you. That was not brave. Brave is a word people use afterwards. What you did was *stay,* and staying is a decision you make again every four seconds, and you made it ninety times." He wrote something. "Your soul skill is still rubbish. Go and make it not rubbish."

"Gu Yue."

She looked up.

"You held five hundred kilograms with your spine." Wu Zhangkong did not raise his voice, and did not lower it either. "You did it without pausing to work out whether it would hurt, which is the only version of that decision worth anything. And then you sat on a floor for an hour and did not tell anyone your back was in pieces." He wrote something else. "Next time, tell someone. That is an order, not advice."

The machine was the Association's, brought over for the morning, and it had a ceiling of **five thousand kilograms**, which the man who ran it mentioned once, to nobody in particular, the way a man mentions the depth of a river.

It went around the class, and the numbers came out in the order the class had already learned to expect.

**Zhang Yangzi: sixty-one left, sixty-nine right.** He was a two-ring Soul Grandmaster and he took it badly, because he had always assumed his special attribute made up for the rest of him.

**Gu Yue: a hundred and fifteen left, a hundred and forty-three right.** Xie Xie made a noise he immediately tried to disguise as a cough. She was an elementalist. She was nine hundred grams of wrist and a ponytail. **A hundred and forty-three.**

**Xie Xie: a hundred and fifty-three left, a hundred and sixty-four right** — which relaxed him enormously, right up until the machine got to Wang Jinxi.

**Wang Jinxi: four hundred and twenty-three left, four hundred and sixty-eight right.** The slim boy looked at his own hands as though they had been swapped for someone else's while he wasn't paying attention. The total was near a thousand kilograms, which the man from the Association wrote down and then underlined, because it was comparable to a pure Power System Soul Master and Wang Jinxi had been carrying two broken arms a fortnight ago.

Then he came down the line to Lin Hao, and stopped, and looked at him the way he had been looking at him since the corridor, and said, "Machine."

"I don't—"

"You put your fist into a machine in this academy four months ago and it said four hundred and seventy, and you have fought a Horned Dragon, twelve wolves and a thousand-year bear since, and I would like to know whether the number moved or whether you have been wasting my time." Wu Zhangkong folded his arms. "Both are useful answers. Go."

Lin Hao went.

He had never thought about the endurance machine as a thing that could tell him something. It was a number other people got. It was the sort of fact that belonged in a file, and he did not have files about himself except the one in the lining of his sword bag, and that one was about a hawk.

He put his fist in.

The machine thought about it, the way the machine always thought about it, and then it said a number, and the man from the Association's Eastsea branch who ran the machine that morning said the number out loud twice, because the first time he had assumed he had misread it.

**Six hundred and twelve kilograms.**

Xie Xie made a sound.

"That's a hundred and forty-two more," Lin Hao said, mostly to himself, and then, because the arithmetic was not the interesting part and he had stopped finding the arithmetic interesting somewhere in the middle of the last chapter of his own life, "which is about a third more, in four months, and I didn't do anything different. I just kept getting hit."

"You also hit things," Wu Zhangkong said.

"That too."

"Write it down."

"I don't keep—"

"Then start," Wu Zhangkong said. "A boy who is growing the way you are growing and is not keeping a record of it is a boy who will not notice when it stops. And it will stop. It always stops. And you will want to know exactly which day."

Lin Hao looked at him for a second, and then went and got a piece of paper.

## Part 5: What the Wall Looks Like

He wrote three lines, because the paper was small and because three was what there was.

**Fist: 2,612 kg. Was 470 in the spring. Four months, no change in method.**

**Spiritual power: not re-measured. The last number was two hundred and eight and that was four days ago and nothing has happened since except watching.**

And then the third one, which took him longer, and which he wrote twice because the first time he had written it wrong.

He had been thinking about Wulin's ring all morning. Not the yellow — everybody would be looking at the yellow. He had been thinking about the *white,* and about the fact that until yesterday Wulin's ring had been white, and about what white meant.

**White is ten to ninety-nine years. Yellow is a hundred to nine hundred and ninety-nine.**

Wulin's soul crossed a hundred years and his ring turned yellow. Not because the ring was magic. Because the ring is a *picture* of the soul, and when the soul changes the picture changes.

Lin Hao sat down on the bench with the paper on his knee and worked it through the way he worked through a bar he could not read.

His hawk had crossed a hundred years **during the absorption**, in the moment of fusion, which is why he had walked out of the Pagoda at eight and a half with yellow rings instead of white ones and everybody had assumed — including him, including *him* — that it was because his father had bought a good soul.

It was not. It was because the hawk had already been over a hundred years old by the time the ring formed.

And the hawk was nine hundred and eighteen years old now.

**Eighty-two years.**

Lin Hao looked at the number for a long time.

He had been thinking about the wall for four months as a door that would not open. That was wrong, and he understood it now with the specific clarity of a boy who has been measuring metal since he was four. It was not a door. **It was a colour.** When the hawk crossed a thousand years, his two yellow rings would turn purple — both of them, the same way Wulin's white had turned yellow — and a third ring would be bestowed on top of them, and a third ring meant the third band, and the third band meant rank thirty-one, and rank thirty-one meant the wall was not a wall any more.

He would not have to break through anything. He would have to **wait for a bird,** and then stand there while his own hands changed colour.

"That's the most boring apocalypse I've ever heard of," he said, to the training field.

"What is," said Xie Xie, arriving with a cup of something and a limp.

"Nothing. Tell me about your leg."

"My leg is *fine.*"

"Xie Xie."

"My leg is going to be fine in a week and I have already decided not to think about it, which is my process, and I notice you have a piece of paper." Xie Xie sat down heavily. "Wu Zhangkong made you start keeping a record, didn't he."

"He did."

"Good. About time. I've been keeping one since I was seven and it's mostly a list of people who've beaten me and what they did, and it's extremely useful, and I'd like you to know that you are on it eleven times and I am going to enjoy writing twelve."

"You're not beating me tomorrow."

"No," Xie Xie agreed, cheerfully. "But I'm going to write down exactly how I lose, and one day that list is going to add up to something, and you'll see."

Lin Hao looked at him, and then at his own three lines, and thought that Xie Xie had been doing this since he was seven and had never once mentioned it, and that the list of people who had beaten him was probably the most honest document in the city.

"Can I see it," he said.

"No."

"Why not."

"Because it's *mine,*" Xie Xie said, and drank his something, and limped off to go and make his soul skill not rubbish.

## Part 1: The Debrief

"Tell me about your experiences in the spirit ascension platform yesterday."

Wu Zhangkong stood at the lectern and said it without enthusiasm, to five students, two of whom — Wang Jinxi and Zhang Yangzi — had dark puffy eyes and had clearly not slept. Zhang Yangzi's was depression. Wang Jinxi's was nightmares: he could not get the chill of the Man-Faced Demon Spider out of him, the one that had reached, he said afterwards, to the depth of his soul. Xie Xie's complexion was no better; he had dreamed of wolves, one after another, and had fallen out of bed at some point in the night.

Gu Yue was exactly as usual. Tang Wulin was the only one in good spirits, because his spirit soul had evolved and he had not yet been told otherwise.

"We'll go in order of elimination," Wu Zhangkong said. "Zhang Yangzi. You first."

Nobody wanted to go first, so he had named one.

"My performance was horrible," Zhang Yangzi said, standing up. "Teacher Wu, I was wrong."

"I don't need you to be wrong." Wu Zhangkong waved it away. "It's your own life. What I need is for you to be *accurate.* Sit down and be accurate next time."

He went around the room. Each of them gave an account, and each account was, Wu Zhangkong let them discover, mostly about themselves. Then he reached the end of the list, and he did not move on.

"Tang Wulin."

Wulin stood up.

"If you had been able to kill the thousand-year Crystal Bear without being crystallised," Wu Zhangkong said, "then Xie Xie would not have had to throw himself into it, and Gu Yue would not have had to burn herself out holding the far side, and the four of you would have walked out of that wolf pack without a scratch." He let that sit. "Their sacrifices were because of you."

Wulin's face did the thing it did — not crumbling, exactly. Settling. He had been proud of the result all the way home.

"Yes, teacher."

"Don't agree with me yet, you haven't heard the rest." Wu Zhangkong's voice did not rise; it never rose. "In a real fight that is not a bad afternoon. That is a dead team. You were crystallised from the ankle up and you were still standing there deciding what to do about it, and by the time you decided, two people had already spent themselves buying you the time." He tapped the lectern once. "You need to strengthen your knowledge and understanding of soul beasts. Don't think that because soul beasts are rare now, studying them is useless. **Over ninety percent of the soul skills we Soul Masters possess belonged to a soul beast at some point.** Understanding soul beasts is understanding your competitors. It is also the only thing that will keep you alive on that platform."

Then he turned, and Lin Hao understood — one full second before it happened, which was not comfort — that the turn had been for him.

"And you."

Lin Hao stood up.

"You were there," Wu Zhangkong said. "You were the fourth. You are the one in that forest who reads a situation, so I am going to ask you a question and I want the accurate answer, not the loyal one." He folded his hands. "Whose fault was it?"

The room went very still. Xie Xie, who had been about to say something, decided against it.

Wulin opened his mouth.

"He'll answer," Wu Zhangkong said, "or you'll answer for him, and then it's your answer and not his."

Lin Hao thought about it. He thought about it honestly, which took longer than he would have liked, because the honest answer was not the one that made him feel like a good friend.

"Mine," he said.

Gu Yue's head came up.

"I read the bear," Lin Hao said. "I read it early — before the first strike, I knew it was doing something with the cold, I knew the cold was *staying* on people rather than hurting them, which is a different thing, and I said 'it's building' and I did not say 'get out.' I had the information and I gave them a description instead of an order. Wulin got crystallised because I told him something interesting instead of telling him something useful." He stopped. "That's the accurate answer. It isn't the whole of it — he still walked into it — but it's the part that was mine."

There was a silence of the kind Lin Hao had learned to file.

"Sit down," Wu Zhangkong said.

Lin Hao sat down.

"Two things," Wu Zhangkong said, to the room, in the flat voice he used when he was giving something away. "Wulin: you are not the only reason anyone got hurt, and I am not going to let you carry a whole team's blood because it's simpler than carrying your third of it. Lin Hao: you have just discovered that being right early is worth nothing if you say it in a shape nobody can act on. A reading is not a warning. **A warning is a sentence that tells somebody what to do.**" He picked up his book. "Longer you survive on that platform, greater the benefit. You all have a long way to go. Morning lesson today is the soul beasts you met yesterday. Every trait, every level. Bring something written."

## Part 2: Show Me

"Do it again," Wu Zhangkong said.

"I've told you—"

"I know what you've told me. Do it anyway."

So Lin Hao did it anyway, in the empty training ground at six in the morning, with the dew still on the boards and a straw dummy standing where a wolf had been eleven days ago. He drew. He settled. He waited for the thing that had happened in the forest — the one-handed backhand off the wrong shoulder at an angle no form contained, the stroke that had come out of him when the correct grip was a third of a second away and he had not had a third of a second.

He produced a backhand.

It was a fine backhand. It was in a form. It had a name, in the sense that a movement you have done before has a name. The straw dummy lost a corner, which was roughly what a good backhand should do to a straw dummy, and Wu Zhangkong watched the whole of it without moving, and then said, "That was not it."

"No."

"What was different."

"I was doing it."

Wu Zhangkong was quiet for a moment.

"Say that again."

"I was *doing* it," Lin Hao said, and he was annoyed, because he had said it out loud in order to hear it and hearing it had not helped. "In the forest I wasn't doing anything. I was too busy. There were twelve of them and Xie Xie was on the ground and I had a leg that was going and I did not at any point decide to swing my sword, and it swung. And now I've decided, and it won't."

"How many times have you tried."

"Since the forest? Forty-one."

"And."

"And I've got forty-one backhands and a sore shoulder." Lin Hao put the sword down, because holding it while saying this felt like lying. "I've tried it tired. I've tried it angry. I've tried it at four in the morning and after eating and before eating and once when Wulin was shouting at me, which I thought was the most promising condition. Nothing. It's not a technique. I've been treating it like a technique I forgot, and it isn't, and I don't know what it is."

Wu Zhangkong looked at the straw dummy for a while.

"Sit down," he said.

---

Wulin was in the yard when he came out, sitting on the low wall with a whetstone and a hammer head, which meant he had chosen the yard rather than the shed, and Lin Hao had learned by then that Wulin chose places the way other people chose sentences.

"You did the thing again," Wulin said, not looking up from the stone.

"I don't know what the thing is."

"I know." Wulin turned the hammer head over. "That's what I mean. You've done it three times and you still don't know what it is, and you're going to go and ask him, and he's going to give you half an answer, and you're going to spend a week on it." He looked up. "Come and eat afterwards. I'm not asking you to talk about it. I'm asking you to eat."

"Both."

"What?"

"Both. I'll eat and I'll talk, because I've been doing the not-talking thing for a fortnight and it turns out I'm bad at it." Lin Hao sat down on the wall beside him. "It reaches. That's all I know. It goes at things I can't get to."

Wulin was quiet for a while, running the stone along the edge.

"That's not frightening," he said, at last.

"It's extremely frightening."

"No." Wulin tested the edge with his thumb. "It's just the first thing you've ever had that you can't read. You've read everything else your whole life — me, the steel, the wind, every person who ever stood in front of you. This is the first thing that doesn't let you." He put the stone down. "That's not a monster. That's just the first thing you've met that's as stubborn as you are."

## Part 3: The Place He Did Not Name

They sat on the bench by the weapon rack, which was not a thing Wu Zhangkong did, and Lin Hao noticed it and did not say so, because noticing things and saying them had gotten him into enough trouble.

"I had a sword once," Wu Zhangkong said, "that I could not put down."

Lin Hao waited.

"I was nineteen and I was the best swordsman in a city full of people who had been training since they could walk, and I was told — by people who were correct, at the time, about everything — that I would be the best of my generation." He turned his hands over on his knees. They were enormous hands and completely still. "And I was. For about six years. And then I was not, because a boy came through who was seventeen and had been taught by somebody better than anybody I had ever met, and he beat me in eleven seconds, and I did something about it that I am not going to describe to a ten-year-old."

"Was that why—"

"That was one of the reasons." Wu Zhangkong said it flatly, the way he said everything, and it landed anyway. "There is a place I came from. I am not going to tell you where it is, and I want to be clear that this is not a test and not a lesson and not me being difficult. I am not going to tell you because I was thrown out of it, and because the version of the story I would tell you is the version where I was wronged, and I have had thirty years to notice that I keep reaching for that version, and I do not trust myself to tell it accurately."

Lin Hao thought about that for a while.

"That's the most honest thing anybody's ever said to me," he said, "and it's the second time this month, and both times it was you."

"I have had a great deal of practice at being honest about the wrong things." Wu Zhangkong stood up. "The reason I am telling you any of it is that you have a sword in your hand that you cannot put down either, and you are ten, and you are going the same direction I went, and the direction is not a mistake — it is where people like us go — but there is a turn in it, and I would like you to arrive at the turn with somebody standing next to you."

## Part 4: The Wrong Question

They went back to the dummy.

"You have been asking the wrong question for forty-one attempts," Wu Zhangkong said. "You have been asking how to do it. The stroke is not a thing you do."

"Then what is it."

"It is what is left when doing runs out." Wu Zhangkong picked up the pointing stick, and did not use it. "Watch my arm." He held it out, relaxed. "I can move this. I can decide to move it and move it, and you can see the decision in the shoulder a half-beat before the hand goes, and every swordsman alive can read that, because deciding is a *movement* and movements are visible. That is what a form is. A form is a decision you made earlier and stored."

"And the stroke has no decision in it."

"The stroke has no decision in it, which is why it cannot be read, which is why it worked on twelve animals that had spent a minute learning everything else you did." Wu Zhangkong lowered the stick. "So. You cannot summon it, because summoning is deciding, and the moment you decide it is not the stroke any more. Forty-one attempts. You were never going to get there that way. You were standing in a room trying to leave through the wall you came in through."

Lin Hao sat with it.

"That's not a solution," he said, at last. "That's a diagnosis. You've told me why I can't. You haven't told me how."

"No," Wu Zhangkong agreed. "Because there isn't a how. There is a *condition.*" He put the stick back in the rack. "You produced it once, under a specific set of circumstances: no time, no plan, no option, and somebody behind you. You have spent eleven days trying to reproduce it in a training ground with a straw dummy and a scheduled hour, which is the opposite of every one of those conditions, and you are surprised."

"So I need to be nearly killed."

"You need to not be in charge." Wu Zhangkong said it the way he said the weather. "Which is the hardest thing in the world for a person like you, and I want to be precise about which person I mean. Not a swordsman. A *reader.* You have spent four years being the person in the room who knows what is going to happen, and the stroke only comes when you do not. So the work is not sword work. The work is learning to be the one who does not know, on purpose, while staying alive."

"That's not a technique."

"I never said it was." Wu Zhangkong turned to go, and stopped. "Your homework was a style and a first form, and you gave me both. Here is the second one. **Find me a stroke you cannot name, and teach it to Xie Xie.**"

"...What?"

"Teach it to him. If you can put it in words, it is a technique, and you will be able to do it whenever you like. If you cannot put it in words, you will find that out in front of a witness, which is where you need to find it out." He left, and the dew was going off the boards, and Lin Hao stood in an empty training ground with a straw dummy that had lost a corner.

## Part 5: Teaching

Xie Xie came at seven, because Xie Xie came at seven, and listened to the whole explanation with his mouth open, and then said, "So you have to teach me a thing you can't do."

"Yes."

"That's the stupidest assignment I've ever heard and I've been taught by Ye Yingluo." He cracked his knuckles. "Right. Show me."

Lin Hao showed him the backhand.

"That's a backhand."

"That's the backhand."

"Do the other one."

"I can't."

"Do the other one *slowly.*"

Lin Hao did the other one slowly, and it was a backhand, and Xie Xie watched it four times and then said something that turned out to be the most useful thing anybody said to him all week.

"You keep looking at the dummy."

"What?"

"When you do the real one — in the forest, you said you weren't doing anything — were you looking at the wolf?"

Lin Hao opened his mouth, and closed it.

"No," he said. "I was looking at Xie Xie."

Xie Xie blinked. "Me?"

"You were on the ground. I was between you and the rest of them. I wasn't watching the wolf at all, I was watching whether you were going to get up, and the wolf was — it was somewhere near me, and I knew roughly where, and I did the thing." He stopped. "I've been trying to reproduce it facing a target for forty-one attempts. There was no target. There was never a target. There was a person behind me and a shape in front of me and I wasn't *looking* at the shape."

"That," Xie Xie said, "is either the most profound thing you've ever said or you hit a wolf by accident."

"Both, probably."

"Right. Well." Xie Xie stood up and walked round to the other side of the dummy, and sat down on the boards with his back against it, and looked up. "Then don't look at it. Look at me."

---

It took until the fourth day, and it did not work, and then it half-worked, and the half that worked was not a stroke.

What worked was this: Lin Hao stood with his back to the dummy and his eyes on Xie Xie, and talked to him — about nothing, about the list, about whether Mu Chen would take an apprentice who was rude — and let the sword hang, and did not decide anything at all. And somewhere in the middle of a sentence about the price of spirit steel, his arm moved, and the dummy lost its head, and neither of them had seen it happen.

Xie Xie made a noise.

"That was it," he said. "That was absolutely it. Do it again."

"I can't."

"I *know* you can't, that's the whole thing, but—" Xie Xie got up and looked at the headless dummy, and then at Lin Hao, with an expression that was not often on his face. "You weren't doing it. You were talking about steel. And your arm did it."

"Yes."

"So the sword knows something you don't."

Lin Hao looked at the sword.

"No," he said, slowly, because he was working it out as he said it and it was important not to say the wrong thing to a boy who would remember it. "The sword doesn't know anything. The sword is a bar. *I* know something I don't know — I've known how to do it for four years, the same way I know how to walk, and the knowing is under the part of me that decides things, and every time I go looking for it I send the deciding part, and the deciding part can't see it, the same way you can't see your own eye without a mirror." He put the sword away. "So I can't teach it to you. That's the answer to the homework. I can't teach it, because there's nothing to teach, because it isn't knowledge, it's the thing that happens when knowledge stops being consulted."

"You're going to tell Wu Zhangkong that."

"I'm going to tell Wu Zhangkong that."

"He's going to say he knew."

"He's absolutely going to say he knew," Lin Hao agreed, "and he's going to be wrong, because he thought it was about not being in charge, and it's about not being in charge *of the right thing* — you can stop deciding and still be looking at the target, and I did that for four days. The condition isn't no control. It's no *audience.*" He looked at Xie Xie. "You were the only person who could have got me there, and you got me there by sitting on the floor and being boring. I want that noted."

"I'm not boring."

"You're the least boring person in this city and you were boring on purpose for four days, which is the greatest thing anyone's ever done for me, and I want you to know I noticed, and I'm never going to say it again."

## Part 6: The City He Did Not Name

Wu Zhangkong listened to the whole of it with his arms folded, in the yard, at the end of the week.

"You cannot teach it," Lin Hao said. "Because there's nothing to teach. It isn't knowledge. It's what happens when knowledge stops being consulted, and the condition isn't lack of control, it's lack of an *audience* — I spent four days not deciding things and staring at a target, and nothing happened, and then Xie Xie sat on the floor and talked to me about steel and my arm took a straw dummy's head off in the middle of a sentence about spirit-steel prices."

Wu Zhangkong was quiet for a while.

"You're going to say you knew," Lin Hao said.

"I was going to." Wu Zhangkong unfolded his arms. "I won't, because I didn't. I told you it was about not being in charge. That was a swordsman's answer and it was about half right, and the half I was missing is that a swordsman is always performing, even alone, because a sword is a thing you hold in front of you." He looked at the sword at Lin Hao's hip. "A reader has a worse version of the problem. You do not perform with the sword. You perform with the *eyes.* You have been watched your entire life — by your father, by an association, by a director, by a man with a card in his pocket — and you learned very young that being watched was the same as being safe, so you cannot stop being watched even by yourself."

"That's—"

"It's not a criticism. It's the reason you're good." Wu Zhangkong said it flatly. "The eyes are why you can do everything else. And they are also the thing that will not let you do this one thing. That's not a flaw to fix. That's a trade you've already made, and it was a good trade, and you will pay for it in exactly one place, for the rest of your life."

Lin Hao thought about that for most of the walk back.

At the gate Wu Zhangkong stopped, and said the thing he had plainly been carrying since the bench.

"When you can do the stroke on purpose — and you will, in ten years or twenty, because you are the sort of person who eventually does — you will be better than I ever was. Better than the boy who beat me in eleven seconds. Better than most of the people who threw me out." He did not look at him. "There is a city I was thrown out of. I am not going to name it, and I have told you why. But I am going to tell you one thing about it, because you will hear the name eventually and I would rather you heard it from me with this attached."

"Yes."

"They are not wrong about most things," Wu Zhangkong said. "That's the part nobody tells you about places like that. They are not a cabal of villains. They are correct, and rigorous, and they produce the best fighters on the continent, and they are *ruthless about the correct thing* — and the day they are ruthless about you, you will understand every reason they gave and hate them anyway." He went through the gate. "And if you ever get the chance to go there, you should take it, and you should not let them make you into me."
