## Part 1: The Letter From the Association

Wu Zhangkong had left him with a stroke he could not name and no instruction at all about what to do next, which was, Lin Hao had begun to understand, the instruction.

It came to the academy, which was unusual, and it was addressed to Lin Hao, which was more unusual, and Xie Xie intercepted it, which was the most unusual thing about it and the reason he knew the contents before Lin Hao did.

"It's from the Association," Xie Xie said, at breakfast, holding it at arm's length like something that might be warm.

"Open it."

"I *opened* it. That's what I'm telling you. I opened it and I read it and then I closed it again and I have been having feelings about it for eleven minutes." He put it on the table. "They want you to sit the third-rank examination. On Saturday. And there's a sentence at the bottom I've read six times and I still don't like."

Lin Hao read it.

The body of the letter was ordinary — the Eastsea Branch invited him to sit the examination for the third rank, Grandmaster, on the coming Saturday, and would provide material, forge and tooling. The sentence at the bottom was not ordinary.

*The Branch has been advised that your recent work has attracted attention beyond the Branch, and the examination will be observed by a visitor from the head office. This is a formality.*

"That's not a formality," Lin Hao said.

"That's what I've been *feeling,*" Xie Xie said. "For eleven minutes."

"It says 'a formality' the way a man says 'it's nothing' while he's holding his arm." Lin Hao put the letter down. "Somebody at the head office has read something about me, and they're not going to tell me what, and they've put a man in a room on Saturday to find out."

"So don't go."

"I'm going."

"Why?"

"Because I want the third rank," Lin Hao said, simply. "And because if I don't go, the man from the head office still finds out whatever he's finding out, and I'd rather be in the room holding a hammer when he does."

---

## Part 2

He kept his sleeves down in the examination room, not because the marks were a secret but because nine candidates and a man from the head office did not need one more thing to look at while he worked.
: What Mu Chen Said

Mu Chen was in the side forge, and had been expecting him, and had two bars of spirit steel on the anvil and a cup of tea that had gone cold, which meant he had been standing there a while.

"You got the letter."

"I got the letter."

"Sit down." Mu Chen did not sit down. "I'm going to tell you what the third-rank examination is, because you have never asked and I have been waiting four months for you to ask, and I've decided you're not going to."

"I wasn't going to."

"You weren't going to." Mu Chen picked up one of the bars and turned it in his hands the way Lin Hao turned things in his hands, and Lin Hao noticed that, and Mu Chen noticed him noticing, and neither of them said anything. "Second rank is: can you do it. Third rank is: can you do it *when it goes wrong.* Every smith alive can refine a bar that behaves. The examination gives you one that doesn't."

"Deliberately?"

"Deliberately. They hand you material with a fault in it and they don't tell you where, and you have four hours, and what they are actually examining is the moment you find out. Some men find it in ten minutes and some find it at three hours and fifty and some never find it and hit it, and the ones who hit it are the ones we send home." He put the bar down. "You will find it immediately. That's not the test."

"Then what's the test."

"The test," Mu Chen said, "is what you do in the four hours *after* you've found it, when you already know the answer and you still have to do the work. Because a man who knows where the fault is and rushes it makes a worse bar than a man who doesn't know and goes carefully. I have failed eleven third-rank candidates and nine of them failed because they were *clever.*"

Lin Hao thought about that for a while, and recognised it, because it was the same shape as everything else that had happened to him this month.

"So it's the audience thing again," he said.

"I have no idea what that means."

"Neither do I, properly. But I've been told it twice this week by two different men and I'm starting to think it's the only thing anybody's actually trying to teach me." Lin Hao picked up the second bar. "Can I practise on this."

"You can practise on both." Mu Chen finally sat down. "And Lin Hao. There's a man coming from the head office, and I've known you since you were nine and could barely lift a hammer, and I want you to hear this from me rather than work it out on Saturday. **You are better than me.** You have been for about a year. I asked to strike your edge in front of the whole Branch because I wanted them to see it before I had to admit it, and I have never once said it out loud, so I'm saying it now, and I'd like you to not make a face."

Lin Hao made a face.

"I told you."

"You *told* me and I still made it."

---

## Part 3: Saturday

The examination room had three forges, nine candidates and one observer, and the observer sat at the back with a board on his knee and did not speak to anybody, and was perhaps forty, and had the specific stillness of a man who had watched a great many people fail at things.

They gave Lin Hao a bar.

He knew where the fault was in about four seconds, because he always knew, and it was a sulphur pocket sitting deep on the far side of the centre, and the interesting thing — the thing he would think about afterwards — was that he felt a small, ugly, entirely recognisable impulse to *show* that he knew. To find it fast. To be seen finding it fast. There was a man at the back with a board, and part of him wanted the board to have something to write.

He put that part down, the way he had been putting it down all month, and started at the wrong end of the bar on purpose.

Four hours is a long time when you already know the answer.

He worked the near third properly. He worked the middle third properly, and slowly, and it cost him nothing except time, and the time was the entire point. And somewhere around the second hour he understood what Mu Chen had been trying to say, which was not that clever men rush, exactly, but that **knowing removes the reason to be careful, and care is the only thing that makes the work good.** He had spent four years being the person who knows. He had never once had to consider that knowing might be a *liability* rather than an advantage, and here it was, in a room with three forges, in the form of an impulse to be seen.

At three hours he reached the pocket.

He opened it the way he had opened a hundred of them — along the grain, following the seam, letting the metal decide — and the sulphur came out clean and the bar closed over itself without a mark, and he had ninety minutes left, and he used every one of them on the finish, because the finish was the part nobody examined and the part he actually cared about.

And then, at about three hours and forty, the lightning came.

---

## Part 4: What the Lightning Did

It was not a decision. That was the thing he noticed first and the thing he was still turning over a week later.

He was on the last pass, drawing the edge down, and the hawk — nine hundred and thirty-four years old and entirely unconsulted — did something, and the thin blue line that had been running along his sword since the crossing ran along the *hammer* instead, and went into the bar, and the edge did not so much sharpen as **arrive.**

He had not laid a Gale Talon. He had not done anything at all. He had been hammering, and the lightning had been there because the lightning lived in him now, and the steel had taken it the way steel takes heat.

The edge came out wrong.

Not bad. *Wrong* — in a way he had never seen and could not immediately name. It was too keen. The geometry was the geometry he had drawn and the finish was the finish he had planned, and the edge would hold an edge the way a rumour holds, and there was a faint blue in it that caught the forge light and gave it back a half-second late.

Lin Hao stood there with a hammer in his hand and a bar on the anvil and understood, with total clarity, that he had just done something in front of nine witnesses and a man from the head office that he could not explain, and could not repeat, and had not intended.

*Well,* he thought. *That's the month I've been having.*

He did not hide it. That was the decision he did make, and he made it in about a second, and he made it because hiding a bar was not possible and because he had decided in a corridor eleven days ago that the truth was cheaper than the alternative and would still be cheap in ten years.

So he put the bar on the examination table with the other eight, and it sat there among bars that were merely good, and it was very slightly blue, and the man at the back stopped writing.

---

## Part 5: The Third Rank

They called them in one at a time in the evening, which was theatre, and Lin Hao knew it was theatre, and he went in last because he had gone in first at everything else for four years and somebody had decided to change it.

"Third rank," the examiner said, before he had sat down. "Grandmaster. Your bar was the only one of the nine that the panel could not agree about, and I want to be precise about what that means. Six of us said it was the best bar in the room. Two said it was defective and should be remade. One said it was the best bar he had seen in thirty years and that he wanted to know how, and I was that one." He closed a folder. "So: how."

"I don't know," Lin Hao said.

"That's not an answer I can put in a file."

"It's the only answer I've got." Lin Hao looked at the table, because looking at the man felt like performing, and he had been given a great deal of advice about performing this month. "I was drawing the edge and something came out of my hands and went into the steel, and the edge came out keener than I drew it, and I've been trying for eleven days to do it again on a sword and I can't, and the only thing I can tell you is that it happens when I'm not doing it on purpose."

The examiner looked at him for a long moment.

"That," he said, "is either the most honest answer I've had in this room or the least useful, and I've decided it's both." He wrote something. "You're third rank. The Branch will register it this week and it'll go to the head office with the rest, and I want you to understand that I argued for you on the bar and not on the answer, because the answer would get you thrown out of some rooms." He stood up. "And for what it's worth — I've been examining for nineteen years and I've never passed a bar I couldn't explain. You're the first. I'd like to think that means something good."

---

Wulin came with him, which Lin Hao had not asked for and had wanted.

He sat on the bench outside the examination room for four hours with his back against the wall and his eyes closed, and did not come in, and did not say anything through the door, and when Lin Hao came out with a third-rank certificate in his hand and a great deal to think about, Wulin opened one eye and said, "Well?"

"Third rank."

"I know. I could hear the hammers." Wulin stood up and stretched. "You went quiet at the end. About forty minutes of going quiet. That's the part I was waiting for."

"I did something I can't explain."

"I know." Wulin started walking, and Lin Hao fell into step beside him, which was the arrangement and had been since they were six. "You always do. And then you explain it three weeks later and it turns out to be obvious and I never would have got there. It's extremely annoying and I've made my peace with it." He glanced sideways. "Your hair's standing up."

"It does that."

"I know it does that." Wulin said it easily, the way he said everything, and Lin Hao understood that this was the whole of what the last fortnight had been missing — not a conversation about the lightning, not a speech about the file, just somebody walking next to him who had known what his hair did since it started doing it.

Gu Yue was at the gate when they got back, sitting on the stone with her knees drawn up, which she never did, and she did not get up when they arrived.

"Third rank," Wulin said.

"I heard the hammers too," Gu Yue said. "I came to see whether he'd come out looking like he'd won something." She looked at Lin Hao for a moment. "You don't. You look like somebody who's been given a bill."

"That's exactly what it felt like."

"Good." She got up. "Then you'll pay it, and you'll stop looking at yourself from the outside, which is what you've been doing for a fortnight, and which I have found extremely tiring to watch."

## Part 6: The Man From the Head Office

He was waiting in the corridor, which was rude, and Lin Hao noticed that it was rude, and then noticed that he had noticed, and put that down too.

"Lin Hao."

"Yes."

"I'm not going to talk to you about the bar." The man from the head office had a voice like a closed drawer. "I watched four hours of a ten-year-old doing third-rank work and I have put down what I saw and it will go in a file, and the file will be read by people whose job is to read files, and that is the whole of it, and I want you to understand that nothing is going to happen to you on Saturday's account."

"Then why are you in the corridor."

"Because of the other file." He said it without any inflection at all. "There is a file about you that has nothing to do with the Association. It came to us as a courtesy copy, which is not a thing that happens, and I have read it twice, and I have come down here on a Saturday to watch a child hit metal because I wanted to see whether the file was describing a person or a rumour." He looked at Lin Hao for the first time with anything like interest. "It's describing a person."

"What does it say."

"It says a great many things, and I'm not going to repeat any of them, and I'm going to tell you why, and it's the same reason your teacher won't name the city he came from." He buttoned his coat. "Because the moment you know exactly what people believe about you, you start managing it, and the moment you start managing it you stop being the thing they were interested in. So: there's a file, it's accurate, it's not going to hurt you, and I'd rather you didn't know the contents." He went past, and stopped. "One thing. Not from the file. From me, having watched you for four hours."

"Yes."

"You spent ninety minutes on a finish nobody was going to examine." The drawer of a voice opened a fraction. "In nineteen years I have never seen a candidate do that. Everybody else in that room was making a bar to pass an examination. You were making a bar. That's the part I'd keep, if I were you, because it's the only part of you that isn't in anybody's file."

He went out into the street, and Lin Hao stood in the corridor of the Eastsea Branch with a third-rank certificate in his hand that he had not been given yet and a great deal to think about, and thought: *that's three men in a month telling me the same thing in three different ways.*

Wu Zhangkong: you perform with your eyes.

Mu Chen: nine of eleven candidates failed because they were clever.

And now a man with a voice like a drawer: you were making a bar.

"Right," Lin Hao said, to the corridor. "I've got it. Stop being watched. Including by me."

## Part 1: What the Mirror Said

He noticed it on the Tuesday morning, washing his face, the way you notice a thing you have stopped seeing.

The lock at his left temple had gone **storm-gray.** Not gray the way hair goes gray. Gray the way the underside of a cloud is gray, with a sheen to it, and when he dried his face the towel came away faintly damp even though his hair was dry, because there was a breeze in it. There had been a breeze in it for weeks. He had simply stopped feeling it against his own skin.

He turned his forearm over.

The marks were there, as they had been since the winter — faint, the colour of a healed scratch, running from the wrist to the elbow in the pattern a feather makes when it is pressed flat. Permanent now. He had forgotten that they used to fade.

And when he put his hand on the iron basin, the iron tasted of rain.

Lin Hao stood in front of a cracked mirror in a dormitory and understood two things at once. The first was that he had changed a great deal in four years and had not once looked. The second, which was worse, was that **everybody else had stopped looking too.** They had watched him turn into this, one degree at a time, the way you watch a tide come in — and now he was a boy with storm-gray hair and feather-marks on his arms and a breeze in his head, and nobody said anything about it any more, because it had simply become what he looked like.

"Well," he said, to the mirror. "That's not nothing."

The mirror did not argue.

## Part 2: Wulin

Wulin was on the dormitory steps with two bowls of congee, and had been sitting there long enough that his had gone cold, which was how Lin Hao knew he had been waiting rather than eating.

"You've been out," Wulin said.

"I've been in the forge."

"You've been in the forge for four hours and you came out and walked past me." Wulin held out the second bowl. "I said good morning."

Lin Hao took the bowl. He sat down. He did not immediately say anything, because there was a version of this conversation where he apologised and a version where he made a joke, and he had been doing the second one for about three weeks without noticing.

"I'm sorry," he said. "I walked past you."

"I know." Wulin was looking at the courtyard and not at him, which was how he did the serious things. "It's not one time. It's been a while. And I'm not saying it to make you feel bad, I'm saying it because you're my brother and I have noticed that I have stopped being in your day, and I don't know whether that's me or you or the forge."

"It's me."

"I thought it might be." Wulin finally looked at him. "So tell me something."

"Something."

"Something true. You've been carrying something since the examination and you've been carrying it alone, and I can tell because you've started being pleasant to people, and you are never pleasant when you're worried." He stirred his cold congee. "So. Something true."

Lin Hao looked at his brother.

There had been a night, four months ago, when Wulin had told him everything — the gold, the scales, the thing under the skin that neither of them had a word for, all of it, sitting on a floor at two in the morning with his arm bare and his voice flat. He had given all of it away, and Lin Hao had taken it, and neither of them had mentioned it since, and Lin Hao understood now that he had been treating that night as a favour Wulin did once instead of a thing that was supposed to keep happening.

"There's a file about me," Lin Hao said. "Not from the Association. Somebody sent the Association a copy as a courtesy, which the man from the head office told me is not a thing that happens, and he read it twice, and he came down on a Saturday to watch me hit metal because he wanted to know whether it was describing a person or a rumour." He ate a mouthful of congee. "He said it was describing a person."

Wulin was quiet for a while.

"Is it accurate."

"Yes."

"Then what's the problem."

"The problem is that I don't know what's in it." Lin Hao put the bowl down. "He wouldn't tell me. He said the moment I know exactly what people believe about me I'll start managing it, and the moment I start managing it I'll stop being the thing they were interested in, and he was right, and I have thought about nothing else for two days."

Wulin nodded slowly.

"You want to know what I think," he said.

"Yes."

"I think you're doing the thing you always do, which is treating yourself as information." Wulin said it without any heat at all, which made it land. "There's a file. Fine. There's going to be a file about you for the rest of your life, because you're you, and there's going to be a file about me for the rest of mine, because of what's under my skin, and neither of us is going to be allowed to be a person who just walks down a street. So you can spend your life wondering what's in it, or you can decide that you know what's in it, because you're the one who's in it."

"That's a very Wulin thing to say."

"I've been paying attention to you for four years," Wulin said. "It's the only thing I'm better at than you."

## Part 3: What It Is Not

Wu Zhangkong was in the yard, doing nothing, which was the only way he ever did nothing: standing very still, with his hands behind his back, looking at a wall.

"It did it again," Lin Hao said.

Wu Zhangkong did not turn around. "Where."

"The forge. Alone. On a piece of scrap." Lin Hao put his hands in his pockets, because he had noticed that he was opening and closing them. "Tuesday. No wolves. No examination. No audience of any kind, which I thought was going to be relevant, and turns out not to be. It just happened, and I've had two days to work out why, and I can't, and you told me to come and find you when I couldn't."

Now he turned around. And his eyes went to the temple, the way everybody's eyes did and then didn't.

"Say it properly," Wu Zhangkong said.

"I cannot account for it."

"How many times."

"Three. The forest. The examination. Tuesday." Lin Hao took his hands out of his pockets. "And I want to be precise, because you've been precise with me and I'd like to return the favour. I did not ask for it. I have never once decided to use it. The first time I thought it was the pressure and the second time I thought it was the audience and the third time there was no pressure and no audience and it happened anyway, so both of my explanations are wrong and I have run out of explanations, and I have been carrying a thing inside me for four months that does things when it wants to, and I would like to know whether I should be frightened."

Wu Zhangkong looked at him for a long time.

"No," he said. "But first sit down, and I want you to look at your arm while I talk, because you have stopped looking at yourself and I have noticed."

---

## Part 4: Neither

"It is not the soul," Wu Zhangkong said, once they were sitting. "I want to start there, because it's where everybody starts and it's wrong, and if you leave here believing your spirit soul is doing this you will spend the next ten years trying to negotiate with a bird."

"It's not the hawk."

"The hawk is nine hundred and thirty-odd years old and it is, whatever else it is, an *animal.* It does not plan. It does not wait. It does not decide to help you on a Tuesday." He said it flatly, the way he said the weather. "Animals do not have intentions, and what you are describing has the shape of an intention, which is why you are frightened, and which is why you are wrong."

"Then what has the shape of an intention and isn't one."

"You do." Wu Zhangkong looked at him. "Not the part of you that decides. The other part. The part that has been running your eyes for four years without consulting you about it — the part that reads a man's shoulder a half-beat before his hand moves and does not tell you it's doing it, because telling you would take longer than the half-beat." He let that sit. "You have been calling it a talent. It isn't a talent. A talent is something you have. This is something that *runs,* and it has been running since before you were born, and the lightning is simply the newest thing it has learned to operate."

Lin Hao thought about that for a while.

"That's worse," he said, at last.

"Why."

"Because if it's the hawk I could feed it or starve it or make it a deal with. If it's *me* — the part of me underneath the part that decides — then I can't put it down, and I can't negotiate with it, and I can't even find out what it wants, because it doesn't want anything, it's just *doing,* and I'm going to spend my whole life being the person it happens to."

"Yes," Wu Zhangkong said. "That is exactly right, and it is the correct thing to be frightened of, and you are the first person I've met who got there in four months instead of forty years." He stood up. "Now. Gift or debt. I said I'd decide, and I've decided."

"It's neither," Wu Zhangkong said.

"You said you'd decide between them."

"I said I'd decide whether we were dealing with one or the other, and I've found out we're not." He began to walk, which meant the next part was the part he had thought about longest. "A gift is something given to you by someone, which implies a giver, and there isn't one — nobody handed you this, it grew, the way a hand grows. A debt is something you owe for something you took, and you didn't take anything, you were *made.* So there's no giver and no creditor, and the reason I wanted to know which it was is that both of them have a way of being paid, and I wanted to tell you what to do."

"And now."

"Now I have to tell you something less useful, which is that there's nothing to do." Wu Zhangkong stopped. "It isn't a gift you can be grateful for and it isn't a debt you can settle, and the reason that's less useful is that human beings are extremely good at carrying gifts and extremely good at carrying debts and completely useless at carrying *weather.* You can't pay it off. You can't give it back. You can only learn what it does and stand where it's useful."

"That's a very unsatisfying answer."

"It's the true one, and I've noticed you prefer those even when they cost you." Wu Zhangkong turned to face him. "So here is the part that is actually useful, and it's the only thing I'm going to tell you to do. You've been treating it like a thing that happens *to* you. Stop. It isn't weather in that sense — it's *yours,* the way your eyes are yours, and you don't say your eyes happened to you. So the work isn't controlling it. The work is finding out what it's been trying to do, and getting out of the way."

Lin Hao opened his mouth, and stopped, because something had arrived while Wu Zhangkong was talking, and it had arrived from underneath, which was, he noticed, exactly where the answer had come from every single time this month.

"It's been reaching," he said.

"What?"

"The three times. I've been trying to work out what they have in common and I've been looking at the conditions — pressure, audience, no audience — and they don't have anything in common, so I was looking in the wrong place." He was talking faster than he meant to. "The forest: I couldn't see the wolf, I was looking at Xie Xie, and my arm did something at a thing I wasn't looking at. The examination: I was making an edge and the lightning went into the *hammer* and out the other side, into the steel, and it made the edge keener than I drew it. And Tuesday: a bead, on scrap, on the far side of the piece, where I was *about* to go." He looked up. "It isn't protecting me. It's never once been about protecting me. It's **reaching** — it goes at the thing I can't get to yet. The wolf I couldn't see. The edge I couldn't draw keen enough. The far side of a bar."

Wu Zhangkong was quiet for a moment.

"That," he said, "is a considerably better answer than the one I was going to give you, and I'd like it understood that I gave you the question." He looked at the marks on Lin Hao's forearm, and said, after a pause, "And for what it's worth — you have nine hundred and forty-odd years in each of two rings, and your body has been taking what that gives for four years, and you have never once in your life gone all out against anything that could measure it. You are not stuck at thirty. You are *coiled.* The rank is a number on a certificate. Everything under it is still climbing, and it has been climbing this whole time, and you have not been looking."

## Part 5: Reaching

He tried it that night, and it did not work, and then — because he had learned something this month about trying — he stopped trying in the way he had been trying.

He went down to the harbour wall at about ten, where there was nobody, and he put a nail on a post thirty feet away, and he stood with the Stormbringer in his hand and he did not decide to do anything at all. He looked at the nail. Not at the sword. Not at his arm. At the nail, which was thirty feet away and could not be cut from where he stood by anything he knew how to do.

Nothing happened.

He stood there for perhaps a quarter of an hour, and the harbour did what the harbour does, and at some point he stopped standing *at* the nail and simply wanted — not decided, wanted, the way you want a thing you have already given up on getting — to be able to reach it.

The blue went out of the sword.

He did not see it go. That was the part he would keep turning over for years: there was no line, no flash, no sound, no arc. There was the sword in his hand and there was the nail on the post, and then the nail was in two pieces on the ground, and the sword was a sword again, and the whole of it had taken no time at all and had used no method he could describe.

And on his forearms, in the dark, the feather-marks went faintly **bright** — the same blue, for the same instant — and went out again.

Lin Hao stood on the harbour wall for a long moment.

Then he walked over and picked up both halves of the nail, and looked at the cut, and the cut was **clean** — cleaner than anything he had ever made with a Gale Talon, cleaner than the examination bar, clean the way a thing is clean when it was never touched at all.

"Right," he said, to the water.

And then he laughed, because he had been frightened for four months, and frightened properly, in the way he had not been frightened by wolves or bears or a man with a card in his pocket, and the thing he had been frightened of had been *his own arm reaching for things,* and it turned out that what it wanted was not to hurt anybody. It wanted to *get there.* It had been trying to get places for four months and he had spent the whole time asking whether it was going to kill him.

## Part 6: Told

He told Xie Xie the next morning within about ninety seconds, because that was the arrangement between them and it had never once needed discussing.

They were in the yard with the rest of them, which was the other thing he had stopped doing, and Xie Xie was leaning on a post with his arms folded and one boot up on the bottom rail, and Wang Jinxi was standing very still six feet away the way he stood everywhere now, and Zhang Yangzi was sitting on the wall with his wrist still wrapped, and Wei Xiaofeng was pretending not to be listening from the far side of the yard with an efficiency that fooled nobody.

"It goes at things," Lin Hao said. "That's all it does. It doesn't protect me, it *reaches.* Thirty feet. A nail. Cut clean and I didn't do it."

"You didn't do it," Xie Xie repeated.

"I didn't do it."

"And you're telling me this in front of everyone."

"I'm telling you this in front of everyone because I've spent three weeks telling nobody anything and it turned me into a person I don't like." Lin Hao shrugged. "So. Everyone. It reaches. I can't summon it. It happens when I want something I can't get and stop deciding to get it."

There was a pause.

"That's the stupidest thing I've ever heard," Xie Xie said, with enormous satisfaction, "and it explains *everything* about you, and I have been saying for four years that you are not a normal person and everybody kept telling me I was being dramatic."

"You have been saying that."

"I have been *saying* it." Xie Xie pushed off the post. "Right. So. It reaches. Can it reach a person."

"I don't know."

"Have you tried."

"No."

"Good," said Xie Xie. "Don't."

From six feet away, Wang Jinxi spoke, which he had not done in a while, and his voice had the flat quality it had acquired since the platform.

"It reaches because you cannot," he said.

Everybody looked at him.

"You cannot reach," Wang Jinxi said. "You can read anything in a room in half a second and you can see a strike before the man decides to throw it and you cannot cross thirty feet of empty air, and it does it for you." He turned his right hand over, slowly, and the fingers did not quite straighten, and he did not seem to notice, and everybody else noticed. "I know what it is to have something do things for you that you did not ask for. Mine does it when I am asleep. It is not a gift and it is not a debt and it is not yours either. It is just the thing that is happening to you, and the sooner you stop asking it what it is, the sooner it will start being useful."

Lin Hao looked at him for a long moment.

"That's the second best answer I've had this week," he said.

"Who gave you the first."

"My brother." Lin Hao said it easily, and was surprised by how true it felt to say it out loud. "He told me to stop treating myself as information."

Wang Jinxi considered that.

"He's right," he said. "He's usually right. It's extremely annoying."

On the wall, Zhang Yangzi said, without looking up from his wrapped wrist, "For what it's worth, I'd like to be told things too. I have been sitting on this wall for three weeks and nobody has told me anything and I have been extremely curious about all of you."

"I've been telling you things," Wei Xiaofeng said, from the far side of the yard.

"You've been talking *at* me."

"That's telling."

"That's the opposite of telling," said Zhang Yangzi, and Gu Yue — who had come out into the yard at some point and was standing in the doorway with her arms folded, and whom nobody had seen arrive — said, without moving, "He's right. You talk at people. It's your worst quality."

Wei Xiaofeng opened his mouth. Closed it. Opened it.

"I'm going to go and be offended somewhere else," he said, and did not go anywhere, and stayed for another hour.

## Part 7: The One Who Did Not Arrive

Gu Yue stayed after the others went in.

She did not sit down, because she did not sit down, and she looked at the lock of storm-gray hair at his temple for long enough that he became aware of it, which was a new experience for him, because he had spent the morning deciding that nobody looked at it any more.

"That's new," she said.

"It's not."

"No," Gu Yue agreed. "It isn't. That's the interesting part. I've watched it happen for two years and I never once said so, and I don't know why I'm saying so now." She was still looking at it. "It's the colour of the sky before it decides."

"That's the nicest thing anyone's ever said about my hair."

"It wasn't nice. It was accurate." She unfolded her arms. "I was injured in the forest. I was carried out by somebody else's decision, and I woke up in a room, and nobody told me what had happened, and you were standing at the end of the corridor for about ten minutes and then you left, and you have not said one word to me about it in nine days."

Lin Hao opened his mouth.

"Don't," Gu Yue said. "I'm not angry. I want you to understand that. I'm telling you because I have spent nine days working out whether you left because there was nothing to say or because you were frightened, and I couldn't decide, and not being able to decide is the only thing I don't like."

"I was frightened," Lin Hao said.

"I thought it might be that."

"I was frightened because you put your arms under a thousand kilograms and you didn't stop to work out whether it would hurt, and I stood at the end of a corridor and I could not think of a single thing to say that wasn't either a lie or a speech, and I have never in my life been able to say a small true thing to you."

Gu Yue looked at him.

"Say a small true thing," she said.

"You're the only page in my ledger with nothing on it."

"I know."

"And I've known for weeks that that isn't because there's nothing there. It's because you're the only person I've met who reads me faster than I read them, and I have spent four years being the person who reads first, and I don't know how to be the other one." He stopped. "That's small and true and I'd like to stop now."

"All right," Gu Yue said. And then, after a moment, "It's the colour of the sky before it decides," she said again, about the hair, and went inside, and Lin Hao stood in the yard for a while and thought that he had said one small true thing and had not died, which was a genuinely surprising result.

## Part 8: What He Did Not Say

There was one thing he did not say to Wu Zhangkong, and he thought about it on the walk back, and he thought about it again for a week, and he never did say it.

The hawk had a question. It had had one for four years — not in words, because it was not a thing that used words, but in the particular way it went quiet sometimes and turned its head and waited, the way an animal waits at a door it has learned to open. He had never been able to work out what it was asking, and he had stopped asking himself, because there had been a great deal going on.

But on the harbour wall, when the blue went out of the sword and the nail came apart at thirty feet, he had felt — for perhaps a second, and he would never be able to prove it, and he was not going to claim it to anybody — that the waiting had stopped.

Not that the question had been answered. That the *waiting* had stopped, the way it stops when somebody finally gets up and goes and looks.

*Is that what you were asking,* he thought, standing on the wall with two halves of a nail in his pocket. *Not whether I can see. Whether I can **reach.***

He did not say it out loud. He had learned this month that the true things were worth saying and that the *almost* true things were worth keeping, and this was an almost true thing, and it was his, and he was going to carry it until he could prove it or drop it.

The hawk, nine hundred and forty-two years old, did not comment.

But it was not waiting.

## Part 1: What the Plate Could Not Do

Mu Chen said it on the Saturday, at the end of the shift, while he was banking the far forge, which was how he said things he had been holding.

"The machine you used in the examination," he said. "Do you know what it is."

"An endurance plate."

"It's a *child's* endurance plate." Mu Chen put the rake down. "The Association fits every branch school with them, and they are built to read a hundred and twenty kilograms comfortably and two hundred and fifty at the top of the scale, because that is the range a child is supposed to be in and there is no reason to build an instrument for numbers that do not occur." He looked at Lin Hao. "The Association's machine put **six hundred and twelve** on you last month. This plate would not have shown you that. It would have shown the end of its own travel and called that your number."

"That's what the examination said."

"The examination said two hundred and fifty, because two hundred and fifty is where it stops." Mu Chen said it without emphasis, which was how he said the important things. "The plate was at the end of its travel. You were not."

Lin Hao stood there with his coat half on and understood, with a small cold feeling that was not fear exactly, that he had known this for a while and had not looked at it.

"How do you know."

"Because the plate came back with a bent arm." Mu Chen picked up the rake again. "They sent a man out on the Tuesday to look at it, and he wrote in his report that the plate had been over-driven, and the Branch has had six of those plates for eleven years and has never once had to send for a man." He banked the last of the coals. "There is a press in the sub-level. It is not a child's instrument. It is what we use to test forged work for the Association's own records, and it has a dial with marks on it up to a number I am not going to say out loud, and I would like you to come down there with me on Wednesday when the building is empty."

"Why."

"Because I have been a third-rank smith for nineteen years and I have never once been curious about a boy before," Mu Chen said. "And because if you are what the plate says you are not, then somebody ought to know, and it should be somebody who will not write it down."

---

## Part 2: Wednesday

Wulin came, because Lin Hao asked him, and because asking him had stopped being difficult about a week ago.

The sub-level was cold and smelled of oil and hot scale, and the press stood in the middle of it under a single lamp like something that had been left there by people in a hurry. It was not beautiful. It was a column of black iron with a screw the width of a barrel and a plate at the bottom the size of a table, and the dial was brass and as wide as a shield, and it had marks on it, and the marks stopped at a number that Mu Chen did not say out loud and Lin Hao did not read, because he had decided before he came down the stairs that he was not going to know it in advance.

"Put your fist on the plate," Mu Chen said. "Not a strike. A *push.* Slowly. I want the whole of it and not the fastest part."

"What if it doesn't stop."

"It will stop." Mu Chen was already at the dial. "Everything stops."

Lin Hao put his fist on the plate.

The iron was cold enough to bite. He could feel the marks on his forearms — the faint feather-patterns that ran from wrist to elbow — go slightly more present against the metal, the way they always did against metal, and the hair on his arm lift, and somewhere above him the lamp buzzed, and he thought about the fact that he had never in his life pushed at anything as hard as he could push, because there had never been a reason to, and every person he had ever fought had been somebody he was trying not to hurt.

So he did not push hard.

He pushed *all of it,* which was a different thing, and he had never done that either.

---

## Part 3: The Marks

The needle went up.

It went up smoothly, which was the strange part, because Lin Hao had expected a jump and there was none — the needle simply climbed the way a tide climbs, without deciding, and it passed the mark that the child's plate had at its top and did not slow, and Mu Chen said nothing, and Wulin, who had been leaning against the column with his arms folded, unfolded them.

It passed the second mark.

"Mu Chen," Wulin said.

"I can see it."

"I know you can see it, I'm saying it because I'd like somebody else to say it too."

It passed the third mark. And Lin Hao, who was watching the dial over his own arm, noticed two things at once: that his shoulder had begun to shake, which had never happened to him in his life, and that the needle was still climbing, and that these two facts were both true at the same time.

And then the needle went past the last mark on the dial.

Not to the end of the dial. **Past the last mark, into the brass with nothing printed on it.**

Mu Chen took his hand off the release and stood very still for a moment, and then he walked around the press and put his own hand on Lin Hao's shoulder and said, "Stop," in a voice that was not loud, and Lin Hao stopped, and the needle came down, and the sub-level was quiet except for the lamp.

"What was it," Wulin said.

"I don't know," Mu Chen said.

"You were reading the dial."

"I was reading a needle that was in a place with no number on it." Mu Chen looked at the brass. "The marks stop at a figure I am not going to say, and it went past it, and the difference between those two things is the only answer I can give you." He turned to Lin Hao. "Take your hand off."

Lin Hao took his hand off. His arm was shaking so badly he had to put it against his leg to steady it, and he stood there in the cold and understood that the shaking was not the effort. The effort had been nothing. The shaking was the four years of never having done it.

---

Gu Yue was in the yard when they came back up, sitting on the low wall with her arms folded, which was where she sat when she had been waiting a while and did not intend to admit it.

"You went down there," she said.

"Yes."

"Without telling anyone."

"I told Wulin."

"That isn't anyone, that's Wulin." She unfolded her arms. "The needle went past the marks. Mu Chen's journeyman has been talking about it all week and he does not know what he saw, and there are now three people in this building with a version of a story about you and none of them have asked you, because you have made it extremely clear that you would rather not." She stood up. "So I am asking. What are you."

"I don't know."

"That's not an answer."

"It's the only one I have." Lin Hao put his hands in his pockets. "And I'd rather give you that than make one up, because you'd know, and then you'd have to decide whether I was lying or stupid, and I'd rather you didn't have to decide either."

Gu Yue looked at him for a moment.

"That's the second honest thing you've said to me," she said, "and I'd like it noted that I've been keeping count."

"Am I at two."

"You're at two." She went past him toward the dormitory, and stopped. "Three," she said, without turning around. "That was the third."

## Part 4: What Mu Chen Did Not Write Down

They sat on the cold floor with their backs against the press, because nobody suggested going upstairs, and Mu Chen produced a flask from inside his coat in a way that suggested it had been there for a while.

"I'm not going to write it down," he said.

"There's nothing to write."

"There's the fact." Mu Chen drank, and offered the flask to Wulin, who took it, and did not offer it to Lin Hao, which was correct. "And I've been thinking about that fact for eleven days, since the examination, and I want to tell you what I've decided, and I want you to argue with it if you can." He looked at the brass dial. "The Association believes that a body is what its rank says it is. That's not stupidity, it's bookkeeping — a rank-30 has two rings, a rank-30 has a known range, and everything in the world is filed by rank because rank is the only thing we can count. And the reason your plate bent is that you are two rings' worth of *age* in a rank-30 body, and there is no column in any ledger for that."

"How old are my rings."

Mu Chen looked at him.

"You don't know," Lin Hao said.

"I know that a hundred-year soul spirit bestows two rings," Mu Chen said carefully, "and I know that spirit souls age, and I know that the Association does not measure a member's spirit soul age because there has never been a reason to, and I have watched you for four years and I have never once seen you do anything that a hundred years would explain." He put the flask away. "I don't know how old they are. I know they are not a hundred. And I have decided not to find out, and I want to be clear that this is a decision and not an oversight, because I would rather be the man who didn't look than the man who looked and then had to decide who to tell."

Wulin said, "Why not tell Wu Zhangkong."

"Because he already knows," Mu Chen said. "He's known since before the tournament, and he has told nobody, and I have watched a man keep a secret for four years and I have decided that whatever he is protecting is not the boy's number." He stood up and brushed the scale off his coat. "It's the boy."

---

## Part 5: The Walk Back

They walked back through the yard at about ten, and neither of them said anything for two streets, and then Wulin said the thing he had plainly been holding since the sub-level.

"It's more than mine."

"Yes."

"I'm not upset." Wulin said it honestly, in the way he said things when he had already worked out how he felt about them. "I want to say that properly, because you've been waiting all night for me to be. I've had the Golden Dragon King in my blood since before I was born, and everybody who has ever looked at me has seen a weed, and I have spent ten years being told what I am by people who could not see. And you have had everybody look at you and see exactly what's there." He put his hands in his pockets. "So I don't mind. I'd rather have been seen wrong and be catching up, than be seen right and be where everybody already put me."

"That's a better way to feel about it than I would have managed."

"I've had more practice at it." Wulin glanced at him. "Your arm's still shaking."

"I've noticed."

"Is that bad."

"No." Lin Hao looked at his own hand, and at the faint feather-marks on it, which had gone slightly bright during the press and had not entirely gone back. "It's the first time I've found out what I am and it turned out to be more than I thought, and it turns out that's frightening in exactly the same way as finding out it's less. I'd have bet you either way it would feel like relief."

"Does it."

"No." He laughed once. "It feels like somebody handed me a bar I don't know how to forge yet."

Wulin was quiet for a bit.

"You'll work it out," he said. "You always do. You'll put it on the anvil and you'll hit it until it tells you what it is, and then you'll tell me, and I'll say something unhelpful, and that'll be that."

"That's exactly what will happen."

"Good." Wulin turned in at the dormitory door. "Wednesday again?"

"Wednesday."

"And Lin Hao." Wulin stopped with his hand on the door. "Next time bring Xie Xie. He'll be unbearable about not having been there, and I'd rather he be unbearable at the time than for a fortnight afterwards."

---

## Part 6: What Was Not Said

Lin Hao stood in the yard for a while after the door closed.

The marks on his forearms were still faintly bright. He put his sleeve down over them out of habit, and then stopped, and left it up, because there was nobody in the yard and because he had spent four years deciding what to hide and he was beginning to suspect that the deciding was costing him more than the hiding.

He thought about the dial. Not the number — there was no number — but the brass past the last mark, where there was nothing printed, and the fact that a needle had been there, and that the only three people who knew it had all separately decided not to say so.

Mu Chen had decided not to look.
Wu Zhangkong had known for four years and told nobody.
Wulin had watched the needle pass his own strength and said *I'm not upset.*

Three men, one week, three different kinds of not saying it.

*So that's what I am,* Lin Hao thought. *I'm the thing that makes honest men keep secrets.*

He stood with that for a while, and then he went inside, because it was late, and because there was a bar of spirit steel on his bench that he had not finished, and because whatever he was, he was still a smith, and the bar did not care.

The hawk, nine hundred and forty-two years old, did not comment.

But when he lay down, the hair at his temple was still moving, and it went on moving for a long time after he stopped noticing it.

## Part 1: Six Saturdays

Xie Xie came on the first Saturday at seven in the morning, which was earlier than Lin Hao, and said, "I'm not here to talk," and then talked for forty minutes.

He came on the second Saturday with his sleeves already rolled up, which was the first time he had ever arrived anywhere prepared, and he asked which anvil was his as though he had been allotted one, and Lin Hao gave him the far one by the window because the light was better and did not say why for a week.

On the third Saturday he stopped talking about the letter entirely.

On the fourth he cut his thumb and swore in a way that made Mu Chen look up from the far forge, and Mu Chen said, "Good," and went back to work, and Xie Xie said, "He said *good,*" and Lin Hao said, "That means you did it properly. He only says good when you do it properly."

On the fifth Saturday he made a hinge.

It was not a good hinge. It was a hinge. It had two leaves and a pin and it opened and it closed and it did not wobble, and Xie Xie held it in his hand for about a minute without saying anything, and then he said, "I made this," in the voice of a person who has understood something they will not be able to un-understand.

"You made this."

"I *made* it." He turned it over. "My father has bought me everything I have ever had. Everything. The dagger, the boots, the bed, the school, the — everything. And I have never once made a thing." He put the hinge in his pocket, where the letter used to be. "That's a horrible thing to find out at ten."

"You found out at ten. That's the good version."

## Part 2: What the Bench Said

On the sixth Saturday, Mu Chen put a bar on the far anvil and said, "Refine it," and went away.

Xie Xie worked for three hours.

Lin Hao worked beside him and did not look over once, which was the hardest thing he had done all week, because the whole of him wanted to see whether the boy was doing it right, and he had decided a week ago — after a conversation with Wu Zhangkong that had lasted four sentences — that looking was the same as helping, and that helping was the thing that would ruin it.

At noon Xie Xie put the hammer down and sat on the floor with his back against the anvil, which was where Lin Hao sat, and said, "I don't want to build mechas."

Lin Hao did not say anything.

"I want to be clear about it, because I've been saying 'Mecha Master' since I was six and everybody has heard me say it about nine thousand times, and I need to hear myself say the other thing." Xie Xie looked at his hands. They were blistered in two places and there was a burn on his wrist that he had not mentioned. "I don't want to *build* them. I want to *fly* one. I want to be in it. I've never wanted to make a thing in my life until this week, and the only thing I've made is a hinge, and I like the hinge, but I don't want to make hinges." He stopped. "I want to fight in a machine I didn't build, and I want whoever built it to be very good, and I want to be very good at flying it, and those are two different people and I've been pretending for four years that they're the same person because it's one word."

"That's not nothing," Lin Hao said.

"It's nothing. 'Mecha Master' is a word that means both and I've been using it to not decide."

"That's not nothing either." Lin Hao sat down beside him. "Here's what's not nothing. You found out in six Saturdays, on a bench, with a hinge, and your father has spent a fortune and you are ten years old and you have just found out something that most people in this city find out at forty with a wife and a debt. You did it in six weeks and it cost you a thumb."

"It cost me a thumb and a hinge."

"Right. Best money you've ever spent."

## Part 3: The Letter

Xie Xie wrote it on the Sunday, at Lin Hao's kitchen table, with Lin Hao's mother's good pen, and it took him four attempts.

The first three were to his father.

The fourth was to the prep course at Glorybound, and it was one paragraph long, and it said that he was withdrawing his place, and that he was grateful, and that he had decided to remain at Eastsea, and that he would like to be considered instead for the pilot track when he was old enough, and that he understood if that was not possible.

"Short," Lin Hao said.

"Short is the only way I can do it without lying." Xie Xie folded it. "If I write it long I start explaining, and if I start explaining I start apologising, and if I apologise he'll think I'm frightened, and I'm not frightened, I'm just wrong, and those are different."

"He's going to be angry."

"He's going to be *hurt,*" Xie Xie said, "which is worse, and I've worked that out, and I've decided I'd rather he be hurt once than be lied to for six years." He put the letter in his coat. "Can you come."

"Yes."

"I didn't ask you to come."

"I know. I'm coming anyway." Lin Hao stood up. "You told me at two in the morning three weeks ago that the letter was still folded and six Saturdays wasn't an answer, and you were right, and this is the answer, and I've decided that I'm going to be in the room when you give it, because you're my brother and that's what that means, and I'd like you to know that I've made this decision without consulting you and I'm not taking it back."

Xie Xie looked at him for a second.

"You're extremely annoying," he said.

"Yes."

"Fine."

## Part 4: The House on Fenmere Street

Xie Xie's father was a thin man with a very good coat and a room full of things that had been bought, and he listened to the whole of it standing up, which Lin Hao understood was the part that was going to matter.

He did not interrupt once.

When Xie Xie finished, he said, "You made a hinge."

"Yes."

"Mu Chen wrote to me." He said it the way you say something you have been holding. "He does not write to me. He has never written to me. He wrote to me on Thursday and he told me that his journeyman said your hinge had an honest pin, and I have been sitting with that sentence for two days because I did not know what it meant, and I have worked out that it means you made something that was not bought." He sat down, finally. "I bought your dagger for a thousand years' worth of money when it was worth a hundred, and I have never once been able to explain to anybody why, and I have worked that out too. I bought it because I could not make you anything, and I have never in my life been able to make my son anything."

The room was quiet.

"So go and be a pilot," he said. "I don't understand it and I don't like it and I am going to be extremely difficult about the fees, and I would like you to know that I am proud of the hinge and I would like you to not tell anybody I said that."

Xie Xie said, "I've already told Lin Hao."

"Then he knows more than your mother."

## Part 5: What Wu Zhangkong Did With It

He was told on the Monday, in the yard, by Xie Xie, who told it badly and at length, and Wu Zhangkong listened to all of it with his hands behind his back.

"Pilot track," he said, when it was finished.

"Yes."

"You have two rings, a dagger that cost your family a fortune, and a body that is faster than anything else in this building, and you want to sit in a machine."

"I want to fly."

"I know what you want." Wu Zhangkong looked at him for a while. "You should know that a mecha pilot is worth less than a battle soul master of the same rank, and that everybody in this city knows it, and that you are choosing the smaller thing on purpose."

"I know."

"And you still want it."

"Yes." Xie Xie put his hands in his pockets. "Because I'm good at it and I'm not good at the other thing, and I've spent four years saying a word that meant both so I wouldn't have to find out."

Wu Zhangkong was quiet for a moment.

"Then you have done the hardest thing anyone in this academy has done this year," he said, "and you have done it at ten, and it has cost you a fortune and a thumb, and I am going to write to the pilot track myself because they will not take you seriously otherwise, and I want it understood that I am doing this because you were honest and not because you were right." He turned to go. "And Xie Xie."

"Sir."

"The hinge." Wu Zhangkong did not look back. "Bring it to me. I want to see it."

Gu Yue was at the gate when he went out, which she did not often do, and she said, "You've been at the forge six Saturdays."

"Yes."

"I know. I've been counting." She was looking at the street and not at him, which was how she did the serious things. "I have been counting a great many things lately. Your Saturdays. The days since the forest. The number of times you have looked at me when you thought I wasn't looking, which is nine, and I have decided to let you have those without comment." She turned her head a fraction. "You spoke to it."

Lin Hao went still.

"You said 'hello' to something in Fenmere Street on Tuesday," Gu Yue said. "I was on the other side of the wall. I didn't know what you were doing and I have thought about it for four days, and I have decided you were speaking to the hawk, and I would like you to know that I think that is either the strangest or the most sensible thing anyone in this academy has done, and I have not decided which."

"It's not a wall," Lin Hao said.

"No," Gu Yue agreed. "I don't think it is." And then, after a moment, in the voice she used when she had decided to give something away, "I have something in me that does not speak either, and I have never once said hello to it, and I have been thinking about that for four days as well."

She went inside. Lin Hao stood at the gate for a while and understood that he had just been given the third thing, and that she had counted it, and that she had given it to him anyway.

## Part 6: What the Hawk Was Doing

Lin Hao walked home alone, which he did not often do, and the hair at his temple was moving, and it had been moving for a week, and it had started moving before the wind did.

Nine hundred and fifty years.

He knew the number the way he knew his own hands, and he knew what was at a thousand, and he had known it since Mu Chen told him what a spirit soul was when he was eight and a half, and he had never once in his life been able to do anything about it. It was not a wall he could hit. It was not a seam he could find. It was a bird, and the bird had its own weather, and the only thing he had ever been able to do was feed it, and he had been feeding it for four years with everything he had.

Fifty years.

He stood on Fenmere Street with his hands in his pockets and thought about it, and understood something he had not understood before, which was that he had been treating it like a bottleneck, and a bottleneck is a thing you break, and this was not a bottleneck.

It was a *somebody.*

"You're not a wall," he said, out loud, to a bird that could not hear him and probably could. "You're a person who's taking their time. And I've been rude about it. I've been *waiting* at you for four years like you're a door."

The hair at his temple moved.

The wind had not started yet.

Lin Hao stood on Fenmere Street for a while with his hands in his pockets and the street going on around him, and thought that he had spent four years trying to get through something, and that the thing had been listening the whole time, and that he had never once in his life asked it anything, because he had been too busy wanting.

"Right," he said. "So. Hello."

Nothing happened.

But he walked home with the feeling that something had turned over, the way it turned over before it did something, and that this time it had turned over because he had spoken to it, and not because he had wanted something from it, and that those were different, and that the difference was probably the whole of what he had been missing since he was six years old.

## Part 7: Three Hundred

Wu Zhangkong told them on the Monday, in the flat voice he used for things that were going to change their lives.

"Twice a year, the spirit ascension platform rebels."

Xie Xie, who had been leaning back, sat up.

"It began as a fault," Wu Zhangkong said. "The energies the platform is built from were unstable, and twice a year they came loose. That was fixed. What was not removed was the *effect* — during a rebellion the soul beasts grow excited and become more visible, and the danger goes up. So they kept it. They made it a feature." He looked around the room. "**The Eighteen Pillars of Heaven limit entry to three hundred people per rebellion.** The academy spent an enormous amount of money to get five of those places. For you."

"Five," said Zhang Yangzi.

"You may enter as a team of up to seven, so five is no problem." Wu Zhangkong set down the paper he had not been reading from. "There is one more rule, and it is the one that will kill you if you forget it. **If you are ejected within the hundred seconds it takes to absorb a soul beast's spiritual energy, the remaining energy goes to the nearest Soul Master.**"

Nobody said anything.

"You will not be alone in there," Wu Zhangkong said. "Three-ring Soul Masters pay a great deal to enter a rebellion, because it is the fastest route to upgrading a spirit soul. They will be hunting. Some of them will be hunting each other." He capped the pen he had not been using. "The beasts are the lesser problem. They do not lie about what they want."

Afterwards, walking out, Xie Xie said, "So we can steal theirs too."

"You can," Wu Zhangkong said, from behind him, without turning around. "If you're confident. Try it and find out what a three-ring Soul Master is."

Lin Hao stopped in the doorway.

He had been on the platform eleven times. He had a ledger of it — ninety-eight lines, every one of them about what a beast would do. He had never once written a line about what a *person* would do, because until thirty seconds ago there had not been any people in there.

"Teacher."

Wu Zhangkong stopped.

"The hundred seconds," Lin Hao said. "Does the platform tell you when they start?"

"No."

"Then the only way to know is to be the one who killed it." Lin Hao said it slowly, because he was working it out as he said it. "Which means the safe position is to never be near somebody else's kill. Which means the team has to hunt in a shape where nobody is ever within a hundred seconds of a stranger." He looked up. "That's a formation. Not a tactic. A formation."

Wu Zhangkong regarded him for a moment.

"You have three days," he said. "Bring me one."

And he went, and left the five of them standing in a corridor with three hundred places in it and three days to work out how to come home.

## Part 8: Room Two-Oh-Five

He went back on the Sunday, because he had worked out that he had not been in room 205 in eleven weeks, and that this was a fact nobody had said out loud.

The corridor was the same. The door was the same. There were four bunks in it and two square desks and two cabinets and one roof lamp, and it was exactly as small as he remembered, which was the part that got him, because he had not thought about the size of it once since the day the academy had given the six of them rooms like teachers and he had carried his things down the stairs without looking back.

**Zhou Zhangxi** was on the lower left bunk. **Yun Xiao** was at the desk with his book, in the same place, at the same angle, under the same bad window.

"You're tall," Zhou Zhangxi said, without sitting up.

"I'm the same height."

"You're tall *in here.*" He rolled onto his side. "That's the thing nobody tells you. You lot got the big rooms and the food and the platform, and the actual cost is that this room got small, and now when you stand in it you can't pretend it was ever big."

Lin Hao sat down on the floor, because there was nowhere else, and because he had sat on that floor for a year.

"How's the roster going?" he said.

"We won three," Yun Xiao said, without looking up. "Lost two. I have the numbers if you want the numbers."

"I want the numbers."

"You never wanted the numbers before."

"I want them now."

Yun Xiao turned a page and read them out — four numbers and a ratio, in the flat voice he used for things he had already decided were true — and Lin Hao wrote them in the back of his ledger, in the column he kept for things that were not about himself, which was shorter than the other column and ought not to have been.

Zhou Zhangxi watched him write.

"You're still doing that," he said.

"Doing what."

"The paper." He propped himself on an elbow. "Wu Zhangkong made you start it, and you're still doing it, and I want you to know that I've told four people you're insane and none of them agreed with me, which I find insulting on your behalf."

"Thank you."

"I'm not being kind." Zhou Zhangxi lay back down. "I'm being accurate. Yun Xiao's been accurate at me for a year about you and he's never been wrong yet, so I've stopped arguing."

There was a silence, and it was not an uncomfortable one, which surprised Lin Hao, because he had rehearsed this visit nine times on the walk over and in none of the nine had it gone quietly.

"We've got three days before the rebellion," he said. "Five places. Up to seven in a team."

"I know."

"I can't take you."

"I know," Zhou Zhangxi said. "Three rings can go in. I've got one." He said it flatly, the way he said most things now. "That's not your fault and it isn't the academy's either, it's just where the arithmetic landed."

"Yun Xiao's got one too."

"And Yun Xiao's got a book," Zhou Zhangxi said, "and he'll have the numbers on all three hundred of you by the second day, which is worth more than either of our fists and we all know it." He looked at the ceiling. "So go. Bring back something we can use. That's the whole arrangement, and it always was — you go and get hit, and we're the ones who tell you what it meant."

Lin Hao looked at Yun Xiao, who had not looked up once, and who said, to the page:

"Noted."

He stayed another hour. He did not know why, and neither of them asked him to, and when he left the room was exactly as small as it had been when he arrived, and he went down the stairs of the twelve-floor dormitory slowly, which was not like him, and which he did not examine.

## Part 9: The Distance

He found Wu Zhangkong where Wu Zhangkong was always found at that hour, in the empty training ground with the wooden sword back on its rack and the wards humming at the edge of hearing.

"Teacher. The rebellion is three days. What comes after it?"

Wu Zhangkong did not answer at once, which with him meant the answer was a real one.

"After it comes the third year," he said. "And after that the exam."

"What exam?"

"**Shrek Academy.**" Wu Zhangkong looked at the rack, not at him. "They hold it **once every three years.** There is no second attempt, and there is no next year. If you are thirteen when it comes and you are not ready, you will be sixteen when it comes again, and by then you will be somebody else's generation."

Lin Hao did the arithmetic, because that was what the arithmetic was for. Three years. He was ten.

"They only take monsters," Wu Zhangkong said.

"I've heard that."

"You've heard the motto. You haven't heard the number." He turned, at last. "Class zero exists because Eastsea Academy cannot get its best students into Shrek Academy, and has not been able to for some years. That is what this class is *for.* The rest of it — the food, the rooms, the platform, the three hundred places, me — is all in service of four children standing in front of a gate in three years' time."

There was a silence with a great deal of weight in it.

"Why are you telling me this now?" Lin Hao asked.

"Because you asked what comes after," Wu Zhangkong said. "And because you are the one who is going to ask the difficult questions on the way, so you may as well start with the largest one."

He was quiet for a moment, and then he said something he had not said before, in the flat voice he kept for the things that mattered.

"There is a reason this class exists in *this* city, and it is not the food."

Lin Hao waited.

"Eastsea City's Spirit Pagoda has noticed the four of you." Wu Zhangkong looked at the rack. "They noticed Wulin first. Then they noticed the girl. Then they noticed you, because you are the one whose numbers do not behave. There is a man who carries a card with your name on it and who has not written your name on a form, and you already know that, so I will not insult you by pretending it is news."

Lin Hao did not say anything, because it was not news.

"When a spirit soul crosses a thousand years," Wu Zhangkong said, "it is not a private event. The Pagoda can see it. They have ways of seeing it that I am not going to explain to you tonight." He turned. "So the plan is not to hide. Hiding four children like these does not work and I have not tried. The plan is to be somewhere with **more** of you. Heaven Dou City has great clans and no clan that dominates, and a thousand geniuses, and in a room like that a talent shines for a moment and then it is somebody else's turn."

"That's not hiding," Lin Hao said slowly. "That's a crowd."

"That's a crowd," Wu Zhangkong agreed. "And you have fifty years, give or take, before you need one." He picked up the wooden sword and put it back, exactly where it had been. "Three days. Bring me a formation."

Lin Hao walked home through a city he had learned the shape of from a free pamphlet on a train — **eighteen first-class cities, five regions, a centre that held only Heaven Dou and Shrek**, an east with five coastal cities in an alliance and his own ranked second among them, a tournament every three years and a larger one every five, held in the city whose name had arrived in his life next to an advertisement for soul-lamp repairs.

He was ten years old, and he was thirty-seventh in a ledger of his own making, and in three years he was going to have to be a monster in front of a gate.

He thought about the hawk, which was fifty years from doing something it had not yet done.

He thought about a sword that had not yet decided what it wanted to say.

He thought that three years was not very long, and then — because he was Lin Hao, and because the teasing was how he said the things that were too heavy to say straight — he thought that it was probably about the right amount of time for somebody who had already learned to read the grain.

He went home. He started the formation that night.

## Part 1: Three Days

He had thirty-one lines in the ledger about what a soul beast would do.

He had none about what a person would do, because until three days ago there had not been any people in there, and he had built the ledger the way he built everything — from what he had actually seen, and not one line further.

So he started a new column, and he titled it, in the small careful hand he used for things he was not yet sure of, **WHAT THEY WANT.**

It was harder than the other column. A Horned Dragon wanted the same thing on Tuesday that it wanted on Friday. A thirteen-year-old with three rings and an unfinished spirit soul wanted something on Monday that he would not have recognised in himself by Thursday, and Lin Hao had no instrument for that except the one he had been carrying around since he was six, which was that he noticed things and could not switch it off.

He went to the dormitory and got Yun Xiao.

"You've got the numbers on the last four rebellions," he said.

"I have the numbers on the last **six.**"

"You've got six."

"Four of them are incomplete. Two are complete." Yun Xiao closed the book, which was how he said *I am now listening.* "What do you want?"

"Survival rate by team size."

Yun Xiao looked at him for a moment. "That's a strange thing to want."

"Is it."

"Everyone wants the kill rate. Or the energy taken per entrant. Nobody has ever asked me about survival by team size." He opened the book again, and turned pages, and stopped. "Larger teams survive longer."

"Obviously."

"Not obviously." Yun Xiao turned the book around. "Look. Teams of two survive **eleven minutes** on average. Teams of five survive **thirty-eight**. Teams of seven survive **fifty-one.** But teams of seven also **lose more of their members** — because in a team of seven, six people will let one person be the bait, and in a team of two there isn't anybody to be."

"And the exam needs an hour," Lin Hao said.

"The exam needs an hour."

"So the average team of seven **fails.**"

"Most of them," Yun Xiao said. "Yes."

Lin Hao looked at the numbers for a long time.

"That's the whole thing, isn't it," he said.

"That's the whole thing."

## Part 2: What He Brought

Wu Zhangkong said "show me" on the third morning, in the training ground, with the wooden sword still on its rack.

Lin Hao did not show him a diagram. He had tried a diagram on the first night and hated it, because a diagram of five people is five dots and five dots do not do anything.

Instead he made them walk it.

"Four shapes," he said. "**Wulin is the middle.** Always. Not because he's the strongest of the four of you — he is, but that's not why, and I want to be careful about that sentence because I am the fifth shape and I am not counting myself in it. It's because his grass owns ground, and ground is the only thing in there that stays put."

Wulin, who had been appointed captain for reasons he still did not entirely believe, nodded.

"**Gu Yue is the weather.** She doesn't hold a position, she holds a *condition* — she makes the air bad on one side so nobody comes from that side. That's not a wall, it's a slope. People slide off slopes without noticing they're sliding."

Gu Yue said nothing, which was agreement.

"**Xie Xie is the answer.** He doesn't go anywhere until something happens, and then he's already there. His job is to not be predictable, which is the one thing he's genuinely better at than anyone in this city."

"I'll take that," Xie Xie said, "and I'll take the second half as a compliment and ignore the first."

"**Zhang Yangzi and Wang Jinxi are the door.**" Lin Hao looked at them. "Not a wall. A *door.* You two open and you two close, and the difference between those is the whole fight."

Wang Jinxi, who did not speak much, said, "Our fusion isn't ready."

"I know. So don't use it."

Both of them looked at him.

"Your fusion is rudimentary — Wu Zhangkong's word, not mine, and he's right. So you don't use it as a weapon, you use it as a *shape.* Eagle goes high, dragon goes low, and there's a gap between you that nobody can come through without one of you seeing them. That doesn't need the fusion to work. That just needs you to both know where the other one is." He paused. "Which is the part the fusion was supposed to do for you, and which you can simply do yourselves."

Zhang Yangzi opened his mouth, and closed it, and then said, to nobody in particular, "That's insulting and it's also right."

"And me," Lin Hao said.

"You," Wu Zhangkong said, from where he had been standing without moving for eleven minutes, "have not said."

"I'm the one who goes and gets hit."

"That is not a shape."

"It is," Lin Hao said. "It's the shape that tells the other four where the people are. Somebody has to be the one who finds out, and it should be the one who can find out and come back." He shrugged. "I read things. I'm fast. And I've got a sword that has opinions."

Wu Zhangkong looked at him for a long moment.

"You have built," he said, "a formation whose centre is a boy with a plant, whose weather is a girl nobody has a file on, whose answer is a boy with two daggers and one secret, whose door is two boys who cannot yet do the thing they are supposed to do — and whose scout is you."

"Yes."

"And the reason."

"Because those are the five people we have."

There was a silence of the kind that Lin Hao had learned to file, in the column marked *things that were not answers.*

"Walk it again," Wu Zhangkong said.
