## Part 3: The Room With The Window

They went in on the fourth morning, and they were not naive, and they released their martial souls the moment the light finished changing.

The **storm-gray lock at his temple** had grown again — long enough now to fall across his cheekbone, and he had stopped pushing it back, because pushing it back was something you did about a thing you were hiding, and he had stopped hiding it about four months ago. The **hair tips** of it had been **hawk-gold** at the ends since the spring, and Xie Xie had stopped making jokes about it, which was how Lin Hao knew it had become a fact rather than a curiosity.

Lin Hao had been in the platform eleven times and it still did the thing to him — the wrongness of a forest that had not been a forest a second ago, the smell of a place that had never had weather. This time the trees were thicker and the light came down in a colour he could not name, and everything in it was, he understood immediately, **angry.**

The rebellion. The beasts were excited. More visible. Closer.

He could feel the hawk go still in him, which was not calm. Nine hundred and fifty years of something deciding.

*Right,* he thought. *Me too.*

Two hundred metres in, Wulin's grass went out ahead of them and parted the undergrowth into a path, and they walked it in the shape Lin Hao had drawn, and for nineteen minutes nothing happened.

The twentieth minute was a boar.

The thirty-first was something with too many legs that Wang Jinxi's eagle saw from forty metres up and closed the door on.

The forty-second minute was a person.

Lin Hao knew it before the others did, because the forest had gone quiet in one specific direction, and forests do not go quiet for boars.

"**Stop,**" he said, quietly, and the shape closed around Wulin without anybody discussing it.

A boy came out of the trees about sixty metres off. Thirteen, maybe. Three rings — Lin Hao counted them the way he counted everything, and filed them, and did not like the third one, which was purple.

The boy was not looking at them. He was looking at a **thousand-year** something forty metres the other way, which had its back to both of them, and which was bleeding.

And Lin Hao understood, in the flat clear way he understood things when there was no time to be frightened, exactly what was about to happen.

The boy was going to kill it. And it was going to take a hundred seconds to take the energy. And the hundred seconds were going to start, and there were going to be two teams within a hundred seconds of each other, and the rule said the energy went to whoever was nearest.

"He's going to finish it," Xie Xie said, very quietly.

"Yes."

"And then we're nearest."

"Yes."

"So we kill him."

"No," Lin Hao said.

Xie Xie looked at him.

"**No?**"

"Watch."

---

The boy killed it.

He was good. It took him eleven seconds and it was not a clean eleven seconds, and the thing went down, and the light came up out of it the way Lin Hao had seen it come up out of things eleven times before.

And the hundred seconds started.

Lin Hao had been counting. He had started counting the moment the light appeared, because he could not help it, and because he had worked out on the second night, sitting on a floor with a book he had borrowed from a boy who made notes, that the hundred seconds were the only clock in the forest that everybody was reading.

At four seconds he said, "Gu Yue. Sixty metres, west. Make it bad."

At six seconds the air on the west side of the clearing went **wrong** — not cold, not hot, simply *unwelcome*, the way a room becomes unwelcome when somebody in it decides something.

At nine seconds the boy, who had been crouched over his kill with his eyes shut and his hands in the light, opened his eyes, because the west side of his world had stopped being a place he wanted to be.

At eleven seconds he looked east.

And he saw five children in a shape he did not recognise, standing very still, with a boy in the middle holding a plant and a boy at the front holding a sword and not doing anything at all with it.

At fourteen seconds he made a decision.

It was the wrong one, but Lin Hao had known it was going to be the wrong one, because he had spent three days in a dormitory learning what thirteen-year-olds with three rings want, and what they want is to not be interrupted, and the fastest way to not be interrupted is to remove the interruption.

He came at them.

"**Door,**" Lin Hao said.

Zhang Yangzi went up. Wang Jinxi went low. And the gap between them — the gap that had needed no fusion skill at all, only two boys who knew where each other was — closed on a thirteen-year-old with a purple third ring like a hand closing on a wrist.

He did not get through. He did not even get close. He got held, for four seconds, in a doorway made of an eagle and a dragon, and in those four seconds Gu Yue made the ground under him into something that was not ground, and Xie Xie put a dagger against a place that would have been a tendon, and did not cut it.

At ninety-one seconds Lin Hao said, "**Go.**"

They went. All five of them, out of the clearing at a run, in the shape, with Wulin's grass pulling shut behind them like a curtain.

At one hundred and four seconds, somewhere behind them, a thousand years of cultivation energy finished having nowhere to go.

---

## Part 4: What The Man In The Window Wrote

In the Spirit Pagoda's monitoring room, a staff member turned to Wu Zhangkong with the expression of a man who has been paid to be impressed and has found that he means it.

"These kids are pretty good," he said. "Teacher Wu really is very good at teaching."

Wu Zhangkong gave a humble nod, because that was the correct response and he had learned the correct responses a long time ago. "Let's see how they do first."

He did not say what he was thinking.

He was thinking about a motto that was twenty thousand years old, which had been in his head all morning and which he had not invited: *monsters, not ordinary people.* It was the kind of sentence that got carved into things, and it had been carved into him, and he had spent a long time finding out what it actually cost.

*Talent isn't the whole of it,* he thought, watching the five of them run. *Anybody can have talent. Talent is the part that happens to you.*

He watched the boy at the front of the shape — the one with the sword, the one whose numbers did not behave, the one whose name he had watched a colleague put on a card instead of a form — and he watched him do a thing that no amount of talent explained.

The boy had counted.

He had counted a hundred seconds that nobody else in the forest was counting, and he had spent four of them holding still while a thirteen-year-old with a purple ring came at him, because he was waiting for the shape to be right rather than for himself to be safe.

*Perseverance,* Wu Zhangkong thought. *And something else. Something I don't have a word for.*

He looked at the other four and made his private ranking, the way he made it every time, because it was a habit and because he did not entirely trust habits: the girl, first, and by so much that it was almost a different category — there was *no record of her martial soul in the Pagoda's history or the Academy's*, and he had looked, and looking had told him nothing at all. Xie Xie second, the twins a gift whether nature had made them or a laboratory had. The other two decent, compatible, unfinished. And Wulin, whom he had made captain, not for strength, though he was the strongest of them, but because he was *brave enough to shoulder it.*

And then Lin Hao, who did not fit in the ranking, because the ranking was a list of what people had and Lin Hao was a list of what people *did.*

*If I had to choose one of them to take the exam,* Wu Zhangkong thought, *Wulin is the right answer. He is the one who will still be standing in ten years.*

And then, uninvited, because the morning had been a strange one:

*And the other one is the one who will have made sure of it.*

---

## Part 5: Fifty-One

They came out at **seventy-one minutes**, all five of them, and the man at the door checked a board and nodded, because seventy-one was past the hour and the hour was the whole of what the exam asked for.

Yun Xiao was waiting outside with the book open, because he did not say things without the book.

"Seventy-one," he said. "The average for a team of **seven** is fifty-one."

"We were a team of five," Xie Xie said.

"I know what you were."

"So we beat the seven-minute average by twenty."

"By twenty," Yun Xiao said. "With two fewer people." He closed the book, which was how he said *I have finished being impressed and am now merely recording it.* "Most teams of seven don't make the hour at all."

Wulin sat down on the steps outside the Spirit Pagoda with his grass still unspooling slowly back into him and his face the colour of old paper, and he said, "Nobody died."

"Nobody died," Lin Hao agreed.

"In a rebellion."

"In a rebellion."

Wulin looked at his hands for a while. Then he said, "The thirteen-year-old."

"Is fine. Gu Yue made the ground soft, not sharp, and Xie Xie didn't cut."

"He'll come back."

"Probably."

"With friends."

"Probably."

Wulin was quiet for a moment. "You counted the hundred seconds."

"I count everything."

"I know." Wulin looked up at him. "You counted them and you stood still for four of them."

"Four was how long the door needed."

"You didn't know that."

"No," Lin Hao said. "I didn't."

There was a silence between them that had a great deal in it and that neither of them was going to say anything about, because they were ten years old and they had a language for this, and the language was that you did not.

Then Wulin said, "You're going to be unbearable about this."

"I'm already unbearable."

"Yes," Wulin said. "But more."

"More," Lin Hao agreed.

---

He did not tell them about the last thing.

He did not tell them that at ninety-one seconds, when he had said *go,* the hawk in him had done something he had not asked for — had leaned, the way a person leans toward a door they have heard open — and that the leaning had gone toward the energy coming up out of the dead thing, and not away from it.

He did not tell them, because he did not know what it meant, and because he had learned from Wu Zhangkong, of all people, that a reading is not a warning.

He wrote it in the ledger, in the new column, under **WHAT THEY WANT.**

It was the first line he had written in that column that was not about a person.

He looked at it for a long time, and then he closed the book, because fifty years was still fifty years, and he had a formation to walk again in the morning.

## Part 1: The Hour

"All we need to do in this first hour is survive," Wulin said.

He said it calmly, the way he said most things now, and Lin Hao noticed — because Lin Hao noticed — that he said it without looking at anybody, which was the tell. Wulin looked at people when he was asking. He looked at the trees when he had already decided.

"Captain," Zhang Yangzi said, "should we take the initiative?"

"No."

"There's a hundred-year something forty metres east."

"I know."

Lin Hao knew too. He had known for about ninety seconds, because the hawk had gone still in a particular direction, and he had learned to treat that stillness the way other people treated a shout.

He did not say it, though, because Wulin had already said it, and because there was a thing he had been working out since the dormitory floor three days ago, which was that a formation only works if the shape decides and not if six people do.

So he stayed in his place, at the front, with the sword down, and he let the hour be boring.

It was boring for eleven minutes.

---

## Part 2: What Came Down

The first thing Lin Hao knew was that Little Black went up.

Zhang Yangzi's eagle had been circling at about forty metres — not hunting, just watching, the way Lin Hao had asked it to, because the eagle could see a thing nine seconds before the rest of them could and nine seconds was the entire margin the formation ran on.

Then Zhang Yangzi's face changed.

He did not shout. He went pale in a single movement, the way a lamp goes out, and his body swayed, and he said — very quietly, as though he were apologising — "**Not good. Little Black…**"

They all looked up at the same time, because his voice had done something to them, and they saw the **yellow-green net** coming down out of the trees, and they saw the eagle in it.

It was not a fight. There was nothing to see of a fight. There were a great many limbs in one place, and the eagle was among them, and then the eagle was not.

Lin Hao had seen a spirit soul die exactly once before, in a book, described by a man in an orange robe who had used the word *recoil* and then moved on to the next subject.

He understood the word now.

Zhang Yangzi made a sound. It was not a scream. It was smaller than a scream and much worse, and it came out of a boy who had been, eleven minutes earlier, complaining about a hundred-year something forty metres east.

And his rings went dim. One of the three simply stopped being bright, and Lin Hao watched it happen and understood, with the flat horrible clarity he had come to hate, that **a third of him had just gone.**

"**RETREAT!**" Wulin shouted, and the grass went up.

Gu Yue was already moving. Her spiritual power went out in a gale that Lin Hao felt in his teeth, a wall of moving air forty metres wide, and it was — he understood this instantly, and he understood it the way you understand weather — it was *enough.* It was enough for anything that had ever been in the ledger.

The net came through it.

It did not slow. It did not sway. The wind simply was not a thing that applied.

And Wulin's Bluesilver Grass — the grass that had held a thirteen-year-old with a purple ring, the grass that had owned ground in eleven separate platform runs — touched the net and **began to smoke.**

It smoked the way meat smokes. It curled. The strands that had been golden-threaded and tough as wire went black at the point of contact and the blackness ran up them faster than Lin Hao could count.

"*It's not a net,*" he said, and heard himself say it, and did not remember deciding to.

Eight legs came down out of the trees like eight spears.

---

## Part 3: The Shape Held

What Lin Hao did next was not brave, and he would have argued with anyone who said it was.

The **marks on his forearm** had come up while he was running, the way they did now whenever the hawk went still — fine **storm-light** lines under the skin, **gold-flecked**, running the length of the bone from wrist to elbow, and they were **glowing** faintly in the shade under the trees. He had learned not to look at them in front of people. He looked now, because the only person who could see them was Gu Yue, and Gu Yue was not going to say anything.

He had three seconds, and in three seconds he did not have time to be frightened, or heroic, or clever, and so he did the thing he had actually practised, which was to say one word to the right person.

"**Door — closed, not open!**"

Zhang Yangzi could not have heard him. Zhang Yangzi was on his knees with his hands in the leaf litter and a third of his cultivation gone out of him like heat out of a room.

But **Wang Jinxi** heard him, and Wang Jinxi had spent three days being told that the door was two boys and not a fusion skill, and Wang Jinxi went low and took Zhang Yangzi by the collar of his uniform with one hand and dragged him backwards eleven metres without ever standing up.

The spear-leg came down where Zhang Yangzi had been.

It went into the ground to the joint.

"**Gu Yue — not the net, the *ground!***"

She understood him before he finished, which was the thing about Gu Yue that nobody in the class had ever said out loud: she was not fast because she was quick, she was fast because she had already decided. The ground under the spider's two front legs went soft, and then went hard, and the legs that had been about to come out of the earth found that the earth had changed its mind about them.

It bought four seconds. It did not buy more, because the spider was a hundred years old and had been doing this since before any of them were born, and it simply pulled harder.

"**Xie Xie,**" Wulin said, and his voice had gone into the register Lin Hao had only heard twice before, "**if I'm unable to break free, you're the acting captain.**"

"Wulin—"

"**Say it.**"

"I'd be the acting captain," Xie Xie said. He did not make a joke. Lin Hao filed that, because Xie Xie not making a joke was itself a fact about the world.

Wulin went in.

---

## Part 4: What It Cost

Lin Hao would remember the next ninety seconds for the rest of his life, and he would never be able to describe them properly, because they happened in a shape that language does not have.

Wulin's grass went into the spider and the spider's blood went onto the grass, and the grass **smoked**, and Wulin kept going anyway, and at some point — Lin Hao could not afterwards say when — **Goldlight came out of him** and went into the grass, and the grass stopped smoking.

It stopped smoking because it was no longer only grass. The strands went gold and scaled and thick, and they held, and the cost of holding was written on Wulin's face in a way Lin Hao had never seen written on anybody.

He was spending himself. Not soul power. *Himself.*

And then Wulin recalled Goldlight — pulled the snake back out of the grass with an effort Lin Hao could see in his shoulders — because he needed the soul power for his hand, and his hand was going to be the part that ended it.

The Golden Dragon Claw came up.

It was three inches of mirror-smooth claw under a hand that had stopped being a ten-year-old's hand, and it went into the Man-Faced Demon Spider, and the spider's yellow-green blood went everywhere.

Lin Hao was four metres away and it did not touch him, because Gu Yue had put a wall of moving air between them at some point in the last ninety seconds and had not told anybody, and because Wulin's own arm had gone gold and scaled and the blood ran off it instead of into it.

The spider came apart.

Not dramatically. It came apart the way a thing comes apart when the part holding it together stops being there.

---

## Part 5: No Room For Luck

Wang Jinxi hugged Wulin.

He did it with both arms and no dignity at all, and he was still holding Zhang Yangzi's collar with one hand, so all three of them went over sideways into the leaf litter, and Wang Jinxi did not let go.

"That was an incredible victory," Zhang Yangzi said, from the ground, in the voice of a boy who had been somewhere none of them had been and had come back with less than he left with.

It echoed what everybody was thinking, and nobody said anything, because there was a body eight metres away and a boy in the middle of them who was not going to be the same for a while.

Lin Hao sat down with his back against a tree, because his legs had decided the fight was over before his head had, and he did the thing he always did, which was to go through it in order and find the seam.

**The net came down on Little Black because Little Black was in the sky.**

That was the whole of it. The eagle was the one part of the formation that went *up*, and the spider had put a net in the trees, and the net had been waiting for the one thing that flew.

He had asked the eagle to circle.

He had asked it, by name, three days ago, in a dormitory, and he had thought it was the cleverest part of the shape, because nine seconds was the entire margin the formation ran on — and the cleverest part of the shape had been the part with a net in it.

"Wulin," he said.

Wulin was sitting with his head between his knees and his scaled hand going slowly back to being a hand. "Mn."

"Little Black died because I put it in the sky."

"No."

"I put it in the sky."

"You put it in the sky," Wulin agreed, tiredly, "and it saw the net, and it told us, and we're all alive. That's what it was *for.*"

"That's not—"

"That is exactly what it was for." Wulin lifted his head. His face was the colour of old paper and his eyes were entirely steady. "Lin Hao. You built the shape. The shape had a hole in it. The hole cost him a third of himself and it cost the rest of us nothing, because the hole was in the part that sees. If the hole had been anywhere else we'd be dead." He looked at Zhang Yangzi, who had stopped pretending not to listen. "Ask him whether he'd rather have had the nine seconds."

Linhao looked at Zhang Yangzi.

Zhang Yangzi looked back at him for a long time.

"I'd rather have had the nine seconds," he said.

---

## Part 6: What Lin Hao Wrote

They passed. They had been in for seventy-one minutes when they came out, and the hour had been the whole of what the exam asked for, and the man at the door checked a board and nodded.

Nobody celebrated. Wang Jinxi was holding Zhang Yangzi up on the steps outside, and Zhang Yangzi was letting him, which was the most surprising thing that had happened all day.

Lin Hao sat down on the lowest step and opened the ledger.

He went to the column marked *WHAT THEY WANT*, and he found that his hand did not want to write in it, and he wrote anyway, because that was the whole discipline and the discipline was the only thing he had.

*A net waits for the thing that flies. I asked the eagle to fly. Nine seconds is not worth a third of anybody.*

Then he stopped, and looked at it, and crossed out the last line.

Not because it was wrong. Because it was incomplete, and an incomplete line in the ledger was worse than no line at all.

He wrote it again.

*A net waits for the thing that flies. I asked the eagle to fly. Nine seconds bought five lives and cost one boy a third of himself, and he says he would do it again, and I believe him, and I am not going to ask him to.*

He closed the book.

The hawk turned over in him — *nine hundred and sixty-four years* of something that had, forty minutes ago, gone very still in a particular direction and been right — and Lin Hao sat on a step outside the Spirit Pagoda with the sun going down over a city that was second of five in an alliance he had learned about from a free pamphlet, and thought about a boy who had said *I'd rather have had the nine seconds,* and about the fact that he had just learned something that had cost somebody else a third of his cultivation to teach him.

That was the part he did not like.

He liked the learning. He had liked it since he was four years old and his father had let him hold a bar that was too hot. He had never once, in his life, minded the price of knowing something.

He minded this.

"You're doing the face," Wulin said, sitting down next to him.

"What face."

"The one where you've learned something and you're deciding whether to be pleased."

Lin Hao considered lying, and did not, because they had an arrangement.

"I'm not pleased."

"Good," Wulin said. He leaned back on his hands and looked at the sky, where there was nothing, because the eagle was not up there any more. "That's the first time you haven't been."

## Part 2: What A Thousand Years Sounds Like

Now it was becoming an animal, and the becoming was not gentle, and it was not cruel either, and Lin Hao understood with a clarity that surprised him that this was simply what nine hundred and sixty-four years looked like when it finished adding itself up.

He went down onto one knee in the leaf litter, because his legs made a decision without him.

"**Gu Yue,**" Wulin said.

She was already there. She put one hand flat between his shoulder blades — not to steady him, Lin Hao understood later; to *read* him — and her face went through something he had never seen on it.

"Oh," she said.

"*Oh?*" Xie Xie said. "What's *oh?* Nobody says oh, you don't even have a face for—"

"**His soul is crossing a thousand years.**"

The clearing went quiet in a way that had nothing to do with the forest.

Wang Jinxi said, "Is that— is that good?"

"It's—" Gu Yue took her hand away. "It's **visible.**"

---

## Part 3: Purple

The rings came up.

Lin Hao had seen his own rings eleven times and they had been yellow both times he had bothered to look, because yellow was what a hundred-to-nine-hundred-ninety-nine-year soul made, and he had never had a reason to think about the colour the way other people thought about the weather.

They went purple.

Not one at a time. Both, together, the way two lamps go when the same hand turns them — and the purple was not a shade, it was a *depth*, and looking at it was like looking down something, and Lin Hao knelt in the leaf litter with his own light going on around him and understood for the first time in his life that a soul ring was not a mark on a person.

It was a **window.**

And through it, something that had been folded up very small for two years began to unfold.

The hawk came.

It did not come out. It was never going to come out; he understood that with total certainty, the way you understand a fact about your own body. It came **up** — through him, into his arms, into the hand that was holding a sword that had spent two years having opinions — and the Stormbringer went from being a good blade to being something that made the air in a ten-metre circle stop moving.

Wind. Not a gust. **Wind**, the way the forest had it before anybody was in it.

And lightning, which had been reaching for four months, stopped reaching and simply **was**, running the length of the steel in a line so steady it looked drawn.

The **storm-gray lock** at his temple went **hawk-gold** to the root.

Not the tips. The whole of it, all at once, the colour running down it the way ink runs down a thread, and Lin Hao felt it happen — a small warm distinct thing at the side of his skull, like a hand laid flat.

And the **marks on his forearms stood up** out of his skin. They had been fine lines under it for two years, **storm-light** and **gold-flecked**, the kind of thing you saw only when he was loaded or angry or in the dark. Now they were **on** him — raised, feather-fine, following the bone, glowing with a steady light that had no flicker in it at all.

His **hair** had a **sheen to it** that had not been there in the morning, and there was a **breeze in it** that was not coming from anywhere.

He could **see the tracks.**

That was the part he understood last and would think about longest. The spirit energy hanging in the clearing — the four hundred years Gu Yue had counted, the hundred or two still in the air — he could *see* it. Not as light. As **tracks**, the way you see a path through grass after somebody has walked on it; and he could see where it was thick and where it was thin and where it had been disturbed. He understood without being told that this was what Gu Yue had been doing with her eyes closed for two years.

Lin Hao looked at his own hand.

"That's new," he said.

"Your hair," Gu Yue said. She was looking at him with an expression he had finally learned to read, which was that she was working something out and had not finished. "It went all the way down. Yours only ever did the tips."

"It feels like a hand on the side of my head."

"That isn't a metaphor," Gu Yue said. "That's your soul being large enough to have edges."

Then he did the thing he had done four hundred times, because his hand did it before he decided to, and the reason he would remember this for the rest of his life is that **he did not do it any differently and it came out wrong.**

He laid a Gale Talon along the Stormbringer and let it go at a deadfall across the clearing.

He had laid four hundred of those. He knew what it cost — a particular small draw at the base of the ribs, like a mouthful of cold air — and he knew what it did: the wind shoved the edge forward and the lightning got there first, and the wood opened along the grain he had already read, and the whole thing took about as much attention as walking.

The deadfall did not open.

The deadfall **came apart**, thirty metres of it, quietly and all at once, and the sound arrived afterwards the way the sound of a large tree arrives afterwards, and the leaf litter on the far side of the clearing was still moving when the noise stopped.

Lin Hao stood there with his sword in his hand.

"That was not a Gale Talon," he said.

"I know," Gu Yue said.

"I didn't do anything different. I did the same thing." He turned the sword over, slowly, looking at it as though it were somebody else's. "I did exactly the same thing and it was **more.**"

"Your rings changed."

"Yes."

"So did the things they gave you." She said it the way she said everything, which was as though she were reading it off something. "A soul ring isn't a container. It's a **permission.** You were permitted a hundred years of wind and now you are permitted a thousand, and the wind did not get bigger, the *permission* did. Your skill didn't improve. It got **older.**"

Lin Hao looked at the deadfall.

"And the cost."

"What about it."

"It cost more." He said it carefully, because he had been counting without meaning to, the way he counted everything. "About three times. I did not decide to spend three times. It just took it."

Two kilometres away, in a room that smelled of hot metal and cold tea, the staff member had both hands flat on the plate.

"That was a soul skill," he said.

"I saw."

"That was a **thousand-year** soul skill." He said the words the way a man says them when he has read about a thing and never expected to be in the room. "Teacher Wu, I have been in this building eleven years and I have seen four of those. Three of them belonged to people over sixty." He looked up. "One of them belonged to **you.**"

Wu Zhangkong did not answer that.

He was looking at the boy in the leaf litter, who was standing very still in the middle of three purple rings and doing the thing Wu Zhangkong had begun to recognise over four months, which was counting.

"He's working out what it costs," Wu Zhangkong said.

"Sir?"

"Everybody else would be looking at the tree."

---

There was one more thing, and he did not tell anybody about it for a while.

The **Union** had changed too. He could feel it the way you feel a room you have not walked into — folded at the back of him where it had always been folded, exactly where it had always been, and **larger.** Not louder. Not straining. Larger in the way the clearing was larger now that he could see the tracks in it: the same amount of thing, permitted to take up more space.

He did not open it.

He had decided a long time ago that the Union was a decision and not a demonstration, and he was not going to change that in a forest with a woman watching and a plate in the sky two kilometres up, and so he closed his hand around it the way you close a hand around a rail, and he wrote down instead what he had noticed:

*That it got bigger without being asked. That it did not ask to be used. That the cost of it will not be the cost I planned for, and that I planned for a cost, and that the plan is now wrong.*

---

## Part 4: The Third

The third ring came eleven seconds after the second went purple, and it was the part nobody was ready for, including him.

It came up out of him like something surfacing, and it was **purple**, and it was **empty**, and Lin Hao looked at it and understood immediately what it was, because he had read the rule in a book at the age of eight and had not believed it applied to anybody he knew.

**A thousand-year spirit soul bestows up to three rings.**

He had been carrying two because two was what a hundred-year soul made. He had been at rank thirty for eleven chapters because rank thirty was where two rings stopped, and he had called that a wall, and then he had let Wu Zhangkong talk him into calling it a coil, and both of them had been right and neither of them had been enough.

The coil opened.

He felt the rank go. It was not dramatic. It was the sensation of a door that had been stuck for four months simply not being stuck any more, and the number behind it being **thirty-one**, and thirty-one being a bracket he had not been in since he was eight years old.

**Soul Elder.**

Wulin sat down in the leaf litter next to him, quite deliberately, the way you sit down next to somebody so that they are not alone.

"Say something," Wulin said.

"I'm thirty-one."

"Say something else."

Lin Hao looked at the sword, which was still doing the thing to the air, and at the three rings, which were purple and two of them were full and one of them was not, and at Gu Yue, who was watching him with an expression he had never seen on her and could not read at all.

"I've been wrong about the wall," he said.

"We've both been wrong about the wall."

"Yes," Lin Hao said. "But I'm the one who kept a ledger about it."

---

## Part 5: Who Was Watching

Two kilometres away and four hundred metres up, in a monitoring room that smelled of hot metal and cold tea, a staff member put down his cup.

He did not say anything for about six seconds. Then he said:

"Teacher Wu."

Wu Zhangkong had been standing at the back with his arms folded, in the posture he had held for the whole of the rebellion, which was the posture of a man who had decided in advance exactly how much he was going to react.

He unfolded his arms.

On the plate, in the middle of a forest that did not exist, a boy was kneeling in the leaf litter inside three purple rings and a column of wind that was bending the trees.

"That's a thousand years," the staff member said. "That's a *thousand-year* spirit soul. On a ten-year-old with a ten-year hawk." He turned around, and his face had the expression of a man who has just realised that his job is going to involve paperwork. "That's going to register."

"Yes."

"That registers at the **branch.** That registers at the **headquarters.** That's the kind of thing that gets a name put on a card."

Wu Zhangkong looked at the plate for a long moment.

"His name is already on a card," he said.

---

Lin Hao did not know any of that, and if he had known it, it would not have changed what he did next, which was to stand up in a forest that did not exist with three rings around his feet and a sword that had stopped being a tool, and to say to the five people who were the only five people in the world who had seen it:

"Nobody says anything about this."

Xie Xie opened his mouth.

"I mean it."

"You don't have to—"

"**Xie Xie.**" Lin Hao looked at him. "There is a man who has had my name on a card since the spring. He did not write it on the form. I have spent four months deciding what that meant, and I have just found out, and the answer is that it meant he was waiting for this." He let the sword down, and the wind in the circle went with it, slowly, like a person sitting down. "So. Nobody says anything."

Gu Yue, who had not spoken since the clearing, said:

"They already know."

Lin Hao looked at her.

"The platform **records**," Gu Yue said. "It has always recorded. You didn't do this in a forest, you did it in a machine that somebody is looking at." She said it without any particular expression, which with her was the closest thing to kindness. "So don't waste the next four months being quiet. It won't work. **Be somewhere with more people in it instead.**"

Lin Hao stood in the leaf litter with three purple rings going slowly dim around his boots, and thought about a pamphlet he had taken off a train because it was free, and a city that was second of five in an alliance, and a centre region that held only two cities, and a boy with a sword who had been told, four months ago, that in three years he was going to have to be a monster in front of a gate.

"Right," he said.

"Right," Wulin said.

And the webs cracked, and the air still hung thick with four hundred years of something that would make them the most interesting thing in the forest to anybody who could smell it, and they got up and walked out of the clearing in the shape that Lin Hao had built, because the shape still worked, and because the shape was the only thing he had that he had made himself.

## Part 1: The Man With The Ice Staff

They found him at the bottom of a slope, backed against a rock, with four of them coming at him from the trees.

He was about fourteen. He had an ice staff, and a purple ring, and the specific posture of a boy who has worked out that he is going to lose and has decided to lose expensively.

Lin Hao had stopped the shape at the top of the slope, because that was what the shape did now — it stopped when he stopped, and nobody had discussed that either.

"**Do we?**" Xie Xie said.

"He's got four on him."

"So?"

"So there are four."

Wulin was already looking at the ground, which was how he worked out whether something was possible. "The lions aren't here."

"The lions are always here."

"The lions aren't *here.*" Wulin looked up. "Gu Yue. Can you make it cold on that slope?"

Gu Yue had been quiet for eleven minutes, which with her meant she was counting something. She said, "I can make it cold on that slope."

"Then do that, and I'll take the left two."

Nobody said *and Lin Hao will take the right two,* because it had stopped being a thing anybody said.

---

The boy with the ice staff never did work out what Gu Yue's martial soul was.

Lin Hao watched him try, from forty metres, while the two on his own side found out what a sword that had stopped being a tool could do.

A green tornado went up on the slope — not fast, not sudden, the way weather arrives — and **icicles** went into it, dozens of them, spinning in the middle of it like something in a bowl. The boy put up a wall of ice. The tornado did not care. The wall came apart in the direction it had come from.

His ring went **purple.**

His second soul skill came up and then **receded**, because whatever he had been about to do was not the biggest thing he had, and he understood in about one second that he needed the biggest thing he had.

**Fury of Ice.**

Two metres of spear came out of the top of his staff, and there were faint patterns running in the shaft of it that Lin Hao's eyes followed the way his eyes followed the grain of a bar, and he understood — with a lurch, because he had never felt anything like it — that **none of them could have stood in front of that.**

Not dodged. Not blocked. Not *survived.*

"A thousand-year soul skill," Wang Jinxi said, very quietly.

They had never seen one. They had been told about them the way you are told about weather on other continents. And Lin Hao stood at the top of a slope in a forest that did not exist and watched a fourteen-year-old throw one, and thought: **that is what a thousand years does.**

He looked down at his own three rings.

Two of them were purple. One of them was empty.

---

## Part 2: What Little Black Came Back As

Zhang Yangzi sat down against the rock afterwards with his eyes shut, and after about four minutes a small dark shape came up out of him and sat on his knee.

**Little Black.**

It was not right. It was the right shape and the right size and it had the right way of turning its head, but it was **thin** — not thin the way a bird is thin, thin the way a drawing is thin — and it did not look at anything except the direction Zhang Yangzi turned his face.

"It can come out," Zhang Yangzi said, without opening his eyes. "It can't fight. It can see, and it can give me what it sees, and that's all it can do. Full restoration is several more days."

Several more days. In a place where you could not spend several more days.

"That's fine," Wulin said.

"It's not fine, it's a third of my—"

"**Zhang Yangzi.**" Wulin sat down next to him, which was the second time in two days he had done that to somebody. "It can see. That's the part we needed. That was always the part we needed."

And Lin Hao, sitting four metres away with three purple rings going slowly dim around his boots, understood something that he had not understood in the dormitory three days ago when he had asked an eagle to go up into the sky.

He had built the shape around the nine seconds. The nine seconds had cost a boy a third of himself. And the nine seconds were still there — thinner, weaker, unable to do anything except look — and they were **still the most useful thing in the formation.**

He had got it wrong and he had got it right, and both were true, and he was not going to pretend otherwise.

He wrote it down later. He did not cross it out this time.

---

## Part 3: The Lions

They came at the thirty-ninth minute.

Lin Hao heard them before the hawk did, which was new, and he did not have time to think about what that meant. A roar behind them, and then numerous red figures in the trees, moving in the way that a *pride* moves — not together, but in the same direction, which is worse.

**Blazing Demon Lions.**

"Soul beasts absorb spirit energy too," Gu Yue said. She said it the way she said everything, flat, and it took Lin Hao two seconds to understand that she was not explaining and was instead **apologising**, because the four hundred years hanging off the six of them was the reason the lions had come.

They had killed a hundred-year spider and taken four hundred years out of the air, and now every beast within a kilometre could smell them.

"**Run,**" Wulin said.

They ran.

Lin Hao had run from things eleven times in the platform and it had always been the same arithmetic — how far, how fast, how long until the shape came apart. This time the arithmetic had a new term in it, and he found it while he was running, the way he found everything, which was too late to be useful and exactly on time.

**He had three rings.**

Two full and one empty. Thirty-one ranks. **Thirty-one ranks put him in a realm the other five were not in** — Wu Zhangkong had said it once, flatly, the way he said everything, that *the wall every ten ranks is not a bigger step, it is a different kind of thing*, and that the difference between rank twenty-one and rank thirty-one is not ten of anything. And the thing he understood, running third in a line of six children with a pride of the strongest beast race on the continent behind them, was that **he was the only one in the line who could have stood and fought.**

Not won. He was not stupid, and he had just watched a fourteen-year-old throw a two-metre spear that none of them could have survived, and he knew perfectly well what a pride of Blazing Demon Lions was.

But he could have **stood.** And the other five could not have.

*Perhaps if they all possessed three soul rings,* he thought, and did not finish the sentence, because the sentence ended in a place he was not going to look at while he was running.

---

## Part 4: What He Did Anyway

The shape came apart at the fifty-second minute, because shapes do.

Wang Jinxi went down over a root and did not get up fast enough, and the pride came around the left side of them in the way that prides do, and there was a lion between Wang Jinxi and the rest of them, and it was not a large one, and it was going to be on him in about two seconds.

Lin Hao stopped.

He did not decide to. He would think about that for a long time afterwards and never be entirely honest with himself about it, but the truth was that he did not decide — the shape had a hole in it, the hole was in the back, and he was the only one who could fill it.

He turned around and put the Stormbringer in front of him.

The wind went up.

Not the wind he had been making for two years, which had been a tool, which had been *weather he could point.* This was the wind from the crossing, and it came up out of the ground in a circle nine metres across, and it took the leaf litter and the small branches and the loose bark off the forest floor and put them in the air, and the lion that had been about to be on Wang Jinxi in two seconds ran into it and did not come out the other side.

Lin Hao stood in the middle of it with three rings around his feet — **two purple, one empty** — and the **marks on his forearms raised and glowing**, and the **hawk-gold lock** at his temple the colour of the sword, and he held the circle for eleven seconds, which was as long as he could hold it, and in those eleven seconds Wang Jinxi got up and the shape closed and the six of them got out.

He let the wind down.

His legs went. He caught himself on the sword, which was not a thing you were supposed to be able to do, and Xie Xie came back for him, because Xie Xie had stopped being the kind of person who ran first somewhere around the spider.

"You've got three rings," Xie Xie said, hauling him up.

"Yes."

"You've had three rings for forty minutes and you didn't **say.**"

"I said."

"You said it to *yourself.*" Xie Xie got his arm over his shoulder and started walking. "That's not saying. That's the most Lin Hao thing you have ever done and you have done a great many of them."

## Part 5: What Gu Yue Saw

They made the ejection at sixty-eight minutes, all six of them, and the light took them.

Outside, on the steps, in the ordinary grey afternoon of a city that was second of five in an alliance, Gu Yue sat down next to Lin Hao without being asked, which she had never done.

"You held it for eleven seconds," she said.

"Ten."

"Eleven. I was counting." She looked straight ahead, at nothing. "Your soul is not doing what a thousand-year soul does."

"I know."

"A thousand-year soul gives you more. It doesn't give you **weather.**" She turned her head a few degrees, which with her was the equivalent of turning around. "The boy with the ice staff threw a thousand-year soul skill and it was a spear. A *spear.* Two metres, patterns in the shaft, extremely good. That is what a thousand years is *supposed* to look like."

"And mine is wind."

"Yours is wind." Gu Yue considered it. "And you can see the tracks now, and your hair went gold to the root, and your marks came out of your skin, and I think—" she stopped, and Lin Hao understood that she was doing the thing she did not like doing, which was saying something she had not finished working out.

"I think you didn't cross a thousand years," she said. "I think something crossed a thousand years **and it was already more than that.**"

There was a silence.

"The hawk was nine hundred and sixty-four," Lin Hao said.

"Yes."

"And the spider gave me two hundred."

"Yes."

"So it was one thousand one hundred and sixty-four."

"Yes," Gu Yue said. "And I would like to know where the other part came from, because a hawk does not become weather, and yours did."

Linhao looked at his hands. The **marks on his forearms** were still raised, faintly, and they had not gone back under since the clearing, and he had stopped expecting them to.

"I don't know," he said.

"That's the first time you've said that to me," Gu Yue said, "and I believe you."

---

He did not tell her about the leaning.

He had not told anybody about the leaning — not the ninety-one seconds in the first hour, and not the thirty-ninth minute when the lions came and the hawk had turned toward the energy coming off them rather than away.

He wrote it in the ledger that night, in the column marked **WHAT THEY WANT**, and he did not cross it out, and he did not finish the line either, because he had learned two things in one day and the second one was that an unfinished line was sometimes the honest one.

**The hawk wants something. It is not the crossing. The crossing was forty minutes ago and it is still**

He stopped there.

Outside, the sun went down over Eastsea City, and a boy with **hawk-gold hair** and three rings sat at a window with a book on his knee, and forty-three metres away in a monitoring room that smelled of hot metal, a file was being written that would be read by somebody in a city in the centre region that held only two cities.

He did not know that either.

He was getting quite good at not knowing things.

## Part 1: What Came Out Of The Trees

Gu Yue had not come back up the slope with the rest of them, and nobody had asked her to, and Lin Hao noticed that he had wanted her to see the thing at the bottom of it and had not examined why.

Lin Hao recognised it.

That was the part he would keep going back to for years — not that it came, but that he looked at it and knew what it was, the way you know a tool by its handle, because he had read about it at the age of nine in a library book with a cracked spine and a coloured plate on page forty-one.

**Duskgold Dreadclaw Bear.**

Dark-gold fur. Over three metres at the shoulder. Shoulders like a wall that had decided to walk. And from each paw, **four golden claws a metre long**, which caught the light under the trees in a way that made them look, from a distance, like somebody had laid four swords down in the leaf litter.

*Reputed to be the strongest soul beast in the world.*

*When mature, it would not need to fear any predator. Not even true dragons.*

He had read that sentence at nine years old and thought it was the kind of sentence books put in to make you turn the page.

It was thirty metres away and it was looking at him.

Not at the six of them. **At him.**

And Lin Hao understood why in about one second, because he had three rings and the other five had one or two, and whatever the bear could smell hanging off them, it could smell most of it on him.

"**Ejection,**" he said. "Everyone. Now."

"It hasn't moved," Wang Jinxi said.

"It doesn't have to."

---

## Part 2: What Xie Xie Did

Xie Xie did not hit the ejection.

Lin Hao would think about that for a very long time and would never arrive at a version of it that he was comfortable with, because Xie Xie had looked at the bear, and then at Lin Hao, and then at the trees to the left, and Lin Hao had known — in the flat clear way he knew things when there was no time — exactly what the calculation was.

The bear wanted him. The bear was going to come for him. And if something else moved fast enough in a different direction, the bear might turn.

Xie Xie went left.

He was very fast. He had always been very fast, and he was faster now than he had been in the spring, and he crossed forty metres of forest in the time it took Lin Hao to say his name.

The bear turned.

It did not turn quickly. That was the worst part of it — it turned the way a hillside turns, without hurry, because it had never in its life needed to hurry, and when it was facing Xie Xie it went through him.

Lin Hao did not see it. He saw the beginning and he saw the end, and the middle was something he did not have, and would never have, and would spend the rest of his life not having.

Xie Xie's energy came up out of the trees in two halves, because that was what the platform did, and one half went toward Wulin and the other half went somewhere else, and the half that went toward Wulin went into him and did not come back out.

---

## Part 3: What The Wind Did

Lin Hao made the circle.

Nine metres. He had made it eleven seconds before, and he had made it with the bear thirty metres away and looking at somebody else, and he made it now with the bear four metres away and looking at him.

The wind went up.

The bear walked into it.

It did not stop. It did not slow. The leaf litter and the loose bark and the small branches that Lin Hao had put into the air went around it and over it and past it, and the bear came through the circle the way a man comes through a curtain, and Lin Hao stood in the middle of his own weather with a sword in his hand and understood, with a clarity that he would have given a great deal not to have, that **the wind was not a wall and had never been a wall.**

It had been a wall eleven seconds ago. It had been a wall against a lion.

This was not a lion.

He did not die, and afterwards he could not entirely explain why, because the bear's claw went past his shoulder and took the sleeve of his uniform and the skin under it, and something in his chest went very quiet — and the hawk, which had been leaning toward things for two days, went still in a way he had never felt it go still before.

Not still like calm.

Still like **deciding.**

And then the light took him, because Gu Yue had come around from behind the bear with her hands already moving and had put her hand on his arm, and she hit the ejection for him.

---

## Part 4: The Box

He came up out of the metal box feeling fine.

That was the strange part, and the staff thought it was strange too, and said so, in front of him, the way adults say things in front of children.

"He's awake and has feeling." A man with a clipboard prodded him with a thing that looked like a popsicle. "This is odd. He recovered this quickly?"

"Are you conscious?" another one said. "Do you feel cold?"

"Yes," Lin Hao said, because that was the answer and because he was aware, in a distant way, that he was sitting in a metal box with his sleeve gone and his shoulder bleeding and he felt **fine**, and that this was not what was supposed to happen.

**Wu Zhangkong's face** appeared above the box.

He did not say anything for a moment. He looked at the shoulder, and then at the face, and then at the three purple rings that had not gone away, because they had stopped going away two days ago and Lin Hao had not yet decided how he felt about that.

"You recognised it," Wu Zhangkong said. It was not a question.

"I read about it when I was nine."

"And you did not hit the ejection."

"Xie Xie didn't hit the ejection."

Wu Zhangkong was quiet for a moment. "No," he said. "He didn't."

**Gu Yue** was standing beside the box. She had been standing beside it, Lin Hao understood, for the whole of the time he had been in it, and she let out one breath when he sat up, and then her face went back to being her face.

"Where's the other box," Lin Hao said.

---

## Part 5: The Backlash

Xie Xie was in the next box, and the next box was full of people.

He came up out of it about four minutes after Lin Hao, and he was not fine, and everybody in the room could see that he was not fine, and nobody said anything about it, because there was not a thing to say.

He had been killed. Not ejected, not beaten, not knocked out — **killed**, in a way that the platform had rendered faithfully and completely, because that was what the platform did, and he had come back through it in about ninety seconds and he was sitting on the edge of a metal box with his hands between his knees.

"It's not real," Wang Jinxi said. He said it quickly, the way you say a thing you have been told.

"I know it's not real," Xie Xie said.

"It's the backlash. It passes."

"I *know* it's not real." Xie Xie looked up. His face was the colour of the metal. "That's the thing. I know it's not real, and I still felt it, and the part I keep thinking about isn't the dying." He stopped. "It's that I was **wrong.** I thought it would turn. I did the arithmetic and I thought it would turn and it didn't turn, and it went through me, and the arithmetic was mine."

Nobody said anything.

Lin Hao sat down on the floor next to the box, because his legs had opinions and because it was the closest place.

"The arithmetic was mine," he said. "I'm the one who reads things. You ran left because you'd watched me read things for three days and you trusted that I'd seen something."

"You hadn't."

"I hadn't."

"So it's mine."

"It's **ours,**" Xie Xie said, and his voice did something on the word, and he cleared his throat and did not do it again. "That's the whole point of the stupid shape, isn't it. It's ours."

---

## Part 6: What Wu Zhangkong Said Afterwards

He said it in the corridor, with the six of them on the benches and the sun going down through the high windows, and he said it in the flat voice he used for the things that mattered.

"You all scored highly," he said. "Which is attributable to each of you doing exactly what was necessary." He let that sit. "At the very least, you are now a **functional team.**"

They could not work out whether to be pleased or ashamed, and Wu Zhangkong watched them not working it out, and did not help.

"Tang Wulin. Your control has improved past what I expected. Gu Yue." He looked at her. "You took the decision to eject him. That was the only correct decision available and you made it in under a second." A pause. "Xie Xie."

Xie Xie looked up.

"You ran left."

"Yes."

"It was wrong."

"Yes."

"It was wrong," Wu Zhangkong said, "and it was also the second-fastest thing anybody in that forest did all day, and I want you to understand that both of those are true and that the second one does not excuse the first." He folded his arms. "And Lin Hao."

Lin Hao looked at him.

"You made a circle and a bear walked through it."

"Yes."

"Before the rest of it." Wu Zhangkong put the stick under his arm, which he did when he was going to say a number. "Rank thirty-one. Three rings, all purple, all of them compatible with you in a way I have not seen in any other person I have ever stood in front of. A spirit soul at eleven hundred and seventy-one years that has given you a skill a perfectly bonded soul gives **once.** A sword that has an opinion. And the marks." He looked at Lin Hao's forearms for a beat longer than was polite. "Rank is a measurement of how much soul power you are holding. It is not a measurement of **what you are.** Do you understand the difference."

"I think so."

"Then say it."

"Two people can hold the same amount and be different things."

"Say the other half."

Lin Hao said it, because Wu Zhangkong had the stick under his arm and because he had been counting without meaning to, the way he counted everything. "A normal three-ring Soul Elder is fourteen to eighteen years old and has two yellow rings and one purple and has never had a skill that cost him anything he hadn't planned for." He stopped. "I'm ten. And when I use everything at once I am not fighting at rank thirty-one."

"No," Wu Zhangkong said. "You are not. If you spent it all today you would be fighting at the top of what a man without a black ring can do, and there are Soul **Kings** in this continent's armies who would lose to you and would not understand why afterwards." He took the stick out from under his arm. "That is not a compliment. That is a description of a problem, and the problem is that you are the only person in this room who does not yet know how to be that, and I have four months."

Then he said the rest of it, without heat, which was the only way he said anything.

"You have three rings, and there is a full realm between you and every other child in this room, and you found out today that **being a realm above them is not the same thing as being strong.** You are not going to be able to protect them by being larger than them. You are going to have to be **smarter than the thing that comes for them.** You had one day of that and you did not manage it."

"No."

"Good," Wu Zhangkong said. "Now you know what the next four months are for."

He was about to leave, and then he stopped, because Lin Hao had said something.

"Teacher."

"Mn."

"The Spirit Pagoda." Lin Hao said it carefully. "The man with the card. He saw the crossing."

Wu Zhangkong was quiet for a moment.

"You're still young," he said, "and there are things you needn't know yet. Remember my words and you'll be fine." He looked at the high windows. "**The Spirit Pagoda does not think the way you do.** They have so much power that even the Federation is afraid of them. And they span across to the other continents."

There was a silence with a great deal in it.

"The other continents," Lin Hao said.

"You'll know what they're like when you visit them," Wu Zhangkong said. "Not now."

And he went, and left six children on a bench in a corridor with the sun going down, and one of them had three rings and a shoulder that had stopped bleeding, and another had come back through a thing that was not real and was still sitting with his hands between his knees, and none of them said anything for a while.

Then Wulin said, "Functional team."

"Functional team," Xie Xie agreed.

"That's the nicest thing he's ever said to us."

"It's the nicest thing he's *capable* of," Gu Yue said, from the end of the bench, without turning her head.

And Lin Hao, who had been quiet, laughed — one short surprised sound, because it was the first time he had laughed in two days and he had not been planning to.

---

He wrote it in the ledger that night.

*The wind is not a wall. I made it into a wall and a bear walked through it. Being the largest of the six is not the same as being useful.*

Then he looked at it, and he added the line he had not wanted to write.

**Xie Xie ran left because he trusted me to have seen something. That is the cost of being the one who reads. It is not a cost I can stop paying, only a cost I can try to earn.**

He closed the book.

The **hawk-gold lock** at his temple caught the lamplight, and the **marks on his forearms** were still raised, faint, following the bone, and they had not gone back under since the crossing and he had stopped expecting them to.

The hawk turned over in him — **one thousand one hundred and seventy-one** — and did not lean toward anything, because there was nothing to lean toward.

Lin Hao lay on his back in a room that was too small, in a city that was second of five, and thought about a bear that would not need to fear a dragon, and about four months, and about the fact that he had one day of being smarter than the thing that comes and he had not managed it.

*Right,* he thought.

And went to sleep.

## Part 1: Downstairs

Wu Zhangkong took them downstairs.

Not metaphorically. Down — out of the class-zero corridor with its wards and its quiet, down two flights, into the part of the academy that smelled of sweat and floor polish and had a **soul barrier** around every field because ordinary students put stray soul skills into walls.

**Three floors. Four fields to a floor. Thirty to fifty metres across.** Full of children from every grade.

"Are we being demoted," Zhang Yangzi said, to Wang Jinxi, in the voice he used when he was not actually asking.

Wang Jinxi gave him a look.

"You really do talk a lot of nonsense."

They had been fighting in the platform for three months. Bears. Lions. A spider that had smoked Wulin's grass. And they had been good at it — good enough that Wu Zhangkong had stood in a corridor with the sun going down and called them a functional team, which was the nearest thing to a medal that any of them was going to get from him.

And now they were standing on an ordinary floor among ordinary children, and Lin Hao understood before anybody said it.

"You want us to fight each other," he said.

Wu Zhangkong looked at him. "The platform teaches you to survive a thing that wants to kill you," he said. "It does not teach you to work with a person who does not want to be worked with."

---

## Part 2: What The Body Decided

They tried the fusion four times.

The first time, Wang Jinxi's **Bone Dragon King** came up and Zhang Yangzi's **Shadow Phantasm Eagle** came up, and the two of them went toward each other the way they had gone toward each other for three months — and Wang Jinxi's body **pushed.**

Not a stumble. A rejection. Lin Hao watched it happen from twelve metres and saw the exact moment it went wrong, which was not a moment in the technique at all. It was a moment in Wang Jinxi's *shoulders*, and it happened before either of them had done anything.

Zhang Yangzi landed on his backside.

"**Wang Jinxi.**" He was up and shouting in one movement. "*What is the meaning of this?!* Why won't you fuse with me?!"

"I didn't do anything!"

"You *did* something—"

"**Calm down.**" Wu Zhangkong said it once, and Zhang Yangzi calmed down, because that was what that voice did. "This isn't something Wang Jinxi can control."

He looked at Wang Jinxi for a while. Wang Jinxi was standing very still with his hands at his sides and his face doing something that Lin Hao recognised, because he had seen it on his own face in a mirror about a year ago, which was the face of a boy working something out that he was not going to like.

"Jinxi's martial soul has probably **mutated,**" Wu Zhangkong said. "So your two martial souls aren't compatible enough to use the soul fusion skill any more."

There was a silence.

"Mutated," Zhang Yangzi said. "When."

"I don't know when. Probably some time in the last month." Wu Zhangkong's voice did not soften, which was the only kindness he had. "It isn't a fault. It isn't a mistake. Souls do it."

Wang Jinxi looked at Wulin.

It was a short look and a strange one, and Lin Hao caught it, and Wulin caught it, and neither of them said anything, because they had both understood at the same moment that the look was not about them.

---

## Part 3: The Two Days

Wang Jinxi did not come to the dormitory that night, or the next.

He was not angry. That was the part Zhang Yangzi could not sit with — he kept waiting for the anger, because anger was a thing you could argue with, and it did not come.

On the second evening Lin Hao found him on the steps behind the training building, which was not a place anybody went, and sat down two steps below him, because that seemed like the right height.

"You're not coming back," Lin Hao said.

"No."

"Is it the fusion."

"It's not the fusion." Wang Jinxi looked out at nothing. "The fusion is how I found out. It isn't the reason."

Lin Hao waited, because he had learned that Wang Jinxi needed the waiting.

"Do you know what I found in the two days?" Wang Jinxi said. "I couldn't sleep. I couldn't meditate properly. My heart was—" he stopped, and chose a plainer word, because that was the kind of person he was. "It was loud. And I worked out that the reason it was loud was that I'd been cultivating next to Wulin for three months and I'd stopped being able to tell which parts of me were mine."

"That's not—"

"It is." Wang Jinxi turned his head a few degrees. "Bloodlines affect each other. Martial souls affect each other. The stronger the soul power, the stronger the bloodline. I'm a rank **higher** than Wulin right now, and I'm already being pulled. So what happens when he comes past me?" He said it without any bitterness at all, which was worse. "And you've got three rings. You came past me four days ago and you didn't even notice you were doing it."

Lin Hao opened his mouth.

"Don't," Wang Jinxi said. "That's the thing. You didn't notice. That's not your fault — you weren't doing it at me, you were just being larger than me, and that's the problem." He looked back out at nothing. "I'd become somebody's. I'd become Wulin's, or yours, and I wouldn't even feel it happen, and one day I'd be standing in a room doing something because the person next to me wanted it and I wouldn't be able to tell you why."

---

## Part 4: The Hardest Part

"I've thought about it for two days," Wang Jinxi said. "It's a hard decision. It hurts. I don't have another choice."

"You could stay and just—"

"No." Wang Jinxi said it gently, which was somehow the firmest anybody had ever said no to Lin Hao. "That's the thing you don't understand yet, and you will. You can't *half* stand next to somebody. Either you're next to them or you're not."

Lin Hao sat on the step with his **hawk-gold lock** falling across his cheekbone and the **marks on his forearms** faint and raised under his sleeves, and he thought about a formation he had built three days ago in a dormitory, with a door in it that was two boys, and he understood that the door was gone and that no amount of cleverness was going to put it back.

"What do I tell them," he said.

"You tell them the truth."

"They'll take it badly."

"Zhang Yangzi will take it badly," Wang Jinxi said. "Wulin will take it well, and that will be worse."

---

## Part 5: What Zhang Yangzi Did

He came around the corner of the training building at a run, and Lin Hao had exactly one second to decide whether to say something, and decided not to, and got up and went the other way.

He was twelve metres off when Zhang Yangzi reached the steps.

He did not shout. That was the surprising part, and Lin Hao heard it because he was listening, and he was listening because he had not entirely left, and he knew that and was not entirely honest with himself about it.

"**Jinxi.**"

And then Zhang Yangzi put his arms around him, on the steps behind a training building, in the ordinary afternoon, in front of whoever was walking past, and held on.

Lin Hao did not hear what was said after that. He went back inside, because there are things you do not take from people even when you could.

---

## Part 5-B: What They Did

He told them in the dormitory, at the hour when all of them happened to be in it, which he had arranged without arranging it, and he said the true thing in four sentences the way Wang Jinxi had told him to, and then he stopped talking, because he had learned that the silence after a thing like that was the part that did the work.

Wulin took it well.

That was the whole of it, and it was worse than Lin Hao had been expecting, exactly as promised. Wulin nodded once, and said *"he's right, isn't he,"* — not a question, the way Wulin said most things — and then he got up and took his own bowl off the shelf and put rice in it and sat back down, and his hands did not shake, and his face did not do anything at all, and Lin Hao watched a boy who has been putting money in a tin for four hundred Fridays absorb the second departure of his life without a single visible seam.

And Lin Hao understood, watching it, that this was not composure. This was a person who had decided a long time ago that the people he loved were going to leave and that the correct response was to not make it harder for them.

**Wulin has never once asked anybody to stay. Not Na'er. Not Wang Jinxi. Not me. And that I have been calling that steadiness for two years, and that it is not steadiness, and that I do not know what it is, and that I am going to find out before I let it happen a third time.**

Xie Xie took it the way Xie Xie took everything, which was loudly and at length and with a joke in it that he abandoned halfway through. *"Well. Good. Fine. That's— the fusion was never— he was always going to—"* and then he stopped, and said *"I'm going to go and clean my daggers,"* at nine in the morning, and went, and nobody said anything about it, and he came back forty minutes later and was completely fine, and was not.

Gu Yue said one thing.

"He is not the first person to leave a room because you were standing in it," she said. "And you are going to spend a long time deciding whether that is a compliment. I would like to save you the time. It is neither. It is a fact about weather."

And Zhang Yangzi — who had come in from the steps eleven minutes earlier with his eyes red and his voice entirely normal, who had been told nothing and had worked out all of it, who was staying in a class that had just lost the only person he had ever fused with — sat down at the end of the bench and said, "Is anybody going to say the thing."

"What thing."

"That there's five of us now, and that the five of us are going to a tournament in eight weeks, and that he would want us to be decent at it." Zhang Yangzi put his hands flat on the table, one on top of the other, the way he did when he was holding something still. "That's the thing. I'm going to say it, since nobody else has the sense to, and because he is my friend and not yours, and I would like somebody to notice that I am the one who gets to say it."

## Part 6: What The Formation Became

Wu Zhangkong stood in the middle of the field with his arms folded and looked at the five of them.

"You're a door short," he said.

"Yes."

"So stop being a formation." He said it the way he said everything, flat, and it took Lin Hao three seconds to understand that it was not a criticism. "A formation is a shape you put people in. You built one and it worked and it broke, and the reason it broke is that people aren't shapes." He unfolded his arms. "So don't build another one. **Learn what each of them will do when it goes wrong.** That's the thing that survives. That's the only thing that survives."

Lin Hao stood in an ordinary field among ordinary children with three purple rings going slowly dim around his boots, and he thought about a ledger with a column in it marked **WHAT THEY WANT**, and he understood that he had been keeping the wrong column.

He had been keeping what they wanted.

What he needed was what they would **do.**

He went and got the book.

---

He wrote it that night, and he did not cross anything out, because nothing in it was wrong.

**The door is gone. Wang Jinxi left because standing next to us was costing him himself, and he was right, and I did not see it coming, and I am the one who reads things.**

**So the column is wrong. What people want is not the useful part. What people DO when it goes wrong is the useful part.**

*Wulin stays. He always stays. He is the only one I have never had to predict.*

**Xie Xie goes left. He went left at the bear and he will go left again, and the arithmetic will be his and it will sometimes be wrong, and he will go left anyway.**

**Gu Yue makes the decision nobody else can make in under a second and does not explain it and does not need to.**

**Zhang Yangzi will be angry for about nine days and then he will be fine and he will never say that he wasn't.**

*And Wang Jinxi is not in the column any more, because he is not in the room, and that is the first line I have ever written in that book that I would rather not have.*

He closed it.

The hawk turned over in him — **one thousand one hundred and seventy-one** — and did not lean toward anything, and Lin Hao lay on his back in a room that was too small and thought about a boy on a step who had said *you can't half stand next to somebody,* and about the fact that he had three rings and could not think of a single thing they were for that anybody else needed.
