## Part 1: The Vest

The test was in a room with no windows and a floor that gave slightly underfoot, and Wu Zhangkong put the five of them in it one at a time and did not explain anything.

Lin Hao went fourth.

A girl was standing in the middle of it.

She was about his age, and she had a cauldron, and she had **one soul ring**, and the first thing Lin Hao noticed — because the first thing he noticed was always the wrong thing, and he had learned to check it — was that she was standing very still in a way that was not nervous.

The second thing he noticed was the **vest**.

He was wearing it. Wu Zhangkong had given it to all five of them that morning without comment, a thin grey thing under the uniform that weighed almost nothing and felt like nothing, and Lin Hao had put it on because he had been told to and had not thought about it again.

**Thousand Refined Cloud Titanium.**

He thought about it now.

---

## Part 2: Four Seconds

She did not throw the cauldron. That was the thing the other four got wrong.

She *moved* it, and the room went into it — the floor, the air, the light, the nine metres of distance between them, all of it folded into a shape that Lin Hao's hawk-read gave him a full second of warning about.

And a full second was four times what he needed.

He did not dodge the shape. **He went to the place the shape had to be built from** — the girl's left hand, the half-turn of her waist, the breath she had taken a moment before she committed, because a cauldron that size does not move on a decision, it moves on a *decision made early* — and the Stormbringer was already there when the decision arrived.

Four seconds.

The cauldron came down on nothing. The girl was on the floor with her hair across her face and her hand open, and the room gave her back to herself slowly, the way a room does, and Lin Hao stood over her with his sword still out and understood two things at once.

The first was that the Thousand Refined Cloud Titanium vest he was wearing had not been used.

The second was that the room was not finished.

The floor gave again. The light thickened.

**The Hall was giving him the next one.**

---

## Part 2-B: What The Hall Did Next

It gave him a boy with a cauldron and **two soul rings.**

He knew the shape of it before it finished forming, because it was the same shape wearing more of itself, and because he had spent four years learning that a thing which works does not change its mind about working. He took the boy apart in about eleven seconds and did not enjoy it, because the boy had been very good, and because the boy had been **dead for several hundred years** and was doing his best anyway.

Then the floor gave a third time.

And nothing came.

Lin Hao stood in the middle of an empty room with his sword out and waited, and waited, and after a while he understood that the room was not hesitating. **The room was looking for a record and there was not one.**

They let him out.

Wu Zhangkong was standing on the other side of the door with his arms folded, and he had plainly been standing there for some time, and the first thing he said was not a comment on the fight.

"How many," he said.

"Three. The third one didn't come."

"I know it didn't come." Wu Zhangkong did not unfold his arms. "**There is no record of the Spirit Ice Douluo at three rings at your age. There is no record of anybody at three rings at your age.** The Hall keeps what legends *were*, boy, and it has been keeping them for a very long time, and it has nothing on file for what you are."

## Part 3: What Came Out

Wulin came out **green and purple.**

That was the phrase he used on himself, in the corridor, looking at his own arm with the detached interest of a boy who had been beaten up often enough to have standards. *"Green and purple."*

Xie Xie's appearance was worse. He had passed **one trial**, and he said the number the way you say a score in a game you had not known you were playing.

"I passed one," he said. "This test is too hard."

"I cleared three," Lin Hao said.

Xie Xie looked at him for a long moment.

"That's not— that's not how it works. It gives you *one* and then it throws you out. It threw me out. It threw **Wulin** out and he's got a vest made of a metal I can't pronounce."

"It gave me three," Lin Hao said. "And then it ran out."

"Ran out."

"It went looking for the next one and there wasn't one."

Xie Xie sat down on the floor of the corridor, which was not something he did, and said, "I would like everybody to notice that I passed one trial today and that I am not going to be able to think about anything else for a week."

Gu Yue came out last, and she came out with her eyes **blank**, and Wu Zhangkong looked at her and was, remarkably, not surprised.

"Gu Yue," he said. "Your opponent was the Spirit Pagoda's founder. The **Spirit Ice Douluo, Huo Yuhao** — back when he only had two soul rings."

There was a silence in the corridor that had a great deal of weight in it.

"The girl with the cauldron," Wulin said.

"Was him. At that age." Wu Zhangkong folded his arms. "So none of you should be discouraged. You were beaten by legends. That is what the **Hall of Heroes** is — it keeps them, and it lets you fight them, and if you do well in it and keep rising, you may even get the chance to fight the original **Shrek Seven Monsters** one day."

⚠️ *The Seven are named as a legend and a future possibility. No place is named. The lock holds.*

And then Wu Zhangkong looked at Lin Hao, and what he said next he said to Lin Hao alone, and he said it in the voice he used for things he had not decided how to feel about.

"Except you. You were not beaten by a legend, and I want to be careful about what I say next, because I have been wrong about you twice and I do not enjoy it." He unfolded his arms at last. "The Hall of Heroes has been measuring children against the greatest souls who ever lived for longer than this city has had walls. **It has never had to stop.** Every legend in it was a genius. Genius is common, boy — I have taught it, I have been it, it is a thing a body can be born with." A pause. "**What it has never had on file is a monster.** And it does not have you on file either, which is why it ran out."

## Part 4: Why Wulin Said Yes

Wulin did not think about it.

That was the part Lin Hao would remember — not the words, but the *speed*. Wulin had been asked a question and had answered it before the question had finished, which was not a thing Wulin did, because Wulin worked everything out and then said the worked-out thing.

"**I want to join.**"

Wu Zhangkong looked at him.

"You don't need to decide so quickly," he said. "Go home and ask your family first."

"I know what it is," Wulin said. He was not shouting. He was doing the thing he did when something had been true for a long time and had finally been said out loud in front of him. "The founder of the Tang Sect had **Bluesilver Grass.** The same martial soul as me. Everybody in Glorybound City knew the story — I knew it before I knew what a martial soul was. He had the trash one and he—" Wulin stopped, and started again, plainer, because that was the only way he could do it. "He had the trash one. And there's an organisation that remembers him for it."

Nobody said anything.

Xie Xie said, after a moment, "I want to join too."

"You just failed a trial."

"I'll pass the next one." Xie Xie shrugged, which cost him something, because his shoulder was the colour of a plum. "I don't want to miss out on this. I'll convince my family."

---

## Part 5: What Lin Hao Asked

He was the last one left in the corridor, and Wu Zhangkong had started to leave, and stopped, because Lin Hao had said his name.

"Teacher."

"Mn."

"The Hall of Heroes." Lin Hao said it carefully, because he had been working the question out since the room with no windows, and he had arrived at a part of it he did not like. "It keeps them. It lets you fight them."

"Yes."

"How?"

Wu Zhangkong looked at him for a moment.

"That's not a question a ten-year-old usually asks."

"It's the only question I have." Lin Hao said it without any heat, because he had learned that the flat version got further. "A dead man can't fight me. So it isn't him. It's something that remembers what he did, well enough to do it at me in a room with no windows, at the age he was, with the ring he had. That's not a person. That's a **record.**" He paused. "And if it's a record, then it's a record of exactly what he did and nothing else — and I beat records by not doing what the other person expects, and a record can't be unexpected by."

Wu Zhangkong was quiet for a while.

"You're right," he said.

"Then what's it for."

"To find out what you are when you cannot be clever." Wu Zhangkong said it in the flat voice, which was the only voice he had for the things that mattered. "You took four seconds off a boy with one ring and eleven off the Spirit Ice Douluo himself, and you will notice that you learned **nothing** from either of them, which is the opposite of what the other four got. Everybody else in that room was taught something by being hurt. That is not the same thing, and one of them is worth more."

Lin Hao stood in a corridor with three purple rings going slowly dim around his boots, and the **hawk-gold lock** at his temple, and the **marks on his forearms** faint under his sleeves, and he understood that he had been given the exact opposite of the answer he wanted and that it was the right one.

"I want to join," he said.

"Go home and ask your family."

"My father will say yes because he thinks I'm good at metal, and he'll be wrong, and it won't matter." Lin Hao said it without any particular feeling, because it was simply the arithmetic of his family. "So. I'm joining."

---

## Part 6: What Gu Yue Did Not Say

She was still standing at the end of the corridor.

She had not said whether she was joining, and Wu Zhangkong had not asked her, and Lin Hao understood — in the slow way he understood her, which was always too late to use — that she was the only one of the six who had been asked the question as a **formality.**

"Gu Yue," he said.

She looked at him.

"He told you who your opponent was."

"Yes."

"And you've been standing there for six minutes."

"Yes."

Lin Hao waited, because he had learned that with her the waiting was the whole of it.

"Everyone else got a legend," Gu Yue said at last. She said it very flatly, which with her meant it was the part that mattered. "**I got the founder of the Spirit Pagoda.**" She turned her head a few degrees. "Do you understand what that means?"

"That you're good."

"That they wanted to see what I'd do against **him.**" Her face did not change. "Not against a strong opponent. Against *him.* That is not a test of strength, Lin Hao. That is somebody asking a question about me."

There was a silence.

"And I don't know what I answered."

---

He wrote it in the ledger that night.

**Nine seconds. I spent them working out how to win. Wu Zhangkong says that is the wrong thing to spend them on. I don't know if he's right, but I know he isn't saying it to be unkind, which is the closest thing to kindness he has.**

**Gu Yue was not tested. She was asked about.**

Then he looked at the page, and he added the line he had been avoiding since the corridor.

*I want to join because I want to fight the record of a man who was very good, and I want to find out whether I am good or whether I am only difficult to predict.*

*I have never not been difficult to predict. So I have never known which one I am.*

He closed the book.

The hawk turned over in him — **one thousand two hundred and five** — and did not lean toward anything, because there was nothing in a room that small to lean toward.

Lin Hao lay on his back and thought about a girl with a cauldron who had been the founder of the Spirit Pagoda at the age of ten, and about the fact that he had taken her apart in four seconds, and about the fact that **the four seconds had taught him nothing at all** — and that this was the first time in his life that had happened to him, and that he did not know what to do with it.

*Right,* he thought.

And then Wulin came up the stairs with two bowls, because Wulin had decided some time in the last hour that Lin Hao was going to be awake and was going to be awake alone, and because he had never once in his life announced that he was doing a thing like that.

"Xie Xie says you cleared three and the Hall ran out."

"Nine seconds."

"Against Huo Yuhao." Wulin put a bowl down and sat on the floor, which was where he sat when he intended to stay. "He's saying it to everybody. Two second-years and a man who sells noodles."

"I know."

"He's not saying it like it's a joke." Wulin looked into his own bowl for a moment. "That's the part I noticed. Xie Xie says everything like it's a joke, and he's saying this one like it's a **number.** And I think the reason is that he has been the fastest person in our grade for three years and has just found out that the thing he is fastest at is not the thing that matters, and instead of being bad about it he has decided to be *loud* about you, which is the most Xie Xie thing I have ever seen a person do."

Lin Hao did not answer, because there was nothing to say that would not have made it smaller.

"And Gu Yue," Wulin said, "has been standing at the end of a corridor for eleven minutes, and Xie Xie has gone and stood at the other end of it, and he has not spoken to her, and he says she has not moved, and he says he is going to keep standing there until she does." He ate. "So. That's the evening. I thought you ought to have it, since you were up here."

**I have spent four years measuring what people can do and have never once measured what they do when nobody is measuring them, and that this is the second time today the ledger has been the wrong book.**

And went to sleep, and did not dream.

## Part 1: The Invitation

Gu Yue was not there, and Lin Hao found afterwards that he had checked, and that checking was its own small fact.

Wu Zhangkong asked in the hallway, which was not where he usually asked things.

"What plans do you have for the vacation?"

Wulin, who had a bag half-packed for a month at the workshop, said the truth. "Forging. And cultivating."

"Since you don't have any plans," Wu Zhangkong said, "come with me. I'm visiting another city on business. You'll learn more about the world outside of school, and you'll relax at the same time."

He said *relax* in exactly the same voice he said *run*, and Wulin noticed, and did not comment on it.

"Do you want time to think it over?"

"No," Wulin said. "I'll go."

He said it in the same half-second he had said *I want to join*, and Lin Hao — who was four metres away with his own bag and his own month, and who had stopped pretending he did not listen — understood that this was becoming a pattern, and that the pattern was that Wulin said yes to Wu Zhangkong before he had finished asking.

Lin Hao put his hand up.

Wu Zhangkong looked at him.

"Am I invited."

"You're standing there."

"That's not a yes."

"It's the only yes I have," Wu Zhangkong said, and walked off, and Lin Hao took it, because it was accurate.

---

## Part 2: The Train

Wu Zhangkong travelled in **white**, and he carried **nothing.**

That was the part that Xie Xie could not get past. He spent the first eleven minutes of the journey looking at Wu Zhangkong's empty hands from three different angles, the way you look at a trick you have decided to work out.

"You have a storage device," he said at last.

Wu Zhangkong did not look up. "Yes."

"Can I see it."

"No."

"Is it a ring."

"You'll find out when you have one."

The train went out of Eastsea City in the late afternoon, and the port went past on the left, and then the city went past, and then there was not a city any more.

Lin Hao sat by the window.

He had been on a train before — once, from Glorybound, with a free pamphlet and a rucksack and no idea that there were eighteen first-class cities in five regions. He had sat by that window and watched a town become a city and thought that was the whole of the world getting bigger.

This was different. This was a city becoming **not a city**, and it went on for hours.

---

## Part 3: What The Hawk Did

The forest started at about the third hour and did not stop.

Lin Hao had read about the **Great Star Dou Forest** in the same library book with the cracked spine, on a different page, and he had read the sentence about it *teeming with soul beasts* and understood it the way you understand a number in a book — as a fact that belonged to the page.

It did not belong to the page.

It went to the horizon in every direction the window allowed, and it was not one colour, it was a great many, and it moved — not the way a field moves in wind, but the way a *body* moves, slowly, in its sleep. And there were things in it that were large enough to see from a train at speed, and they were not doing anything in particular, and that was the worst part.

The hawk went still.

Lin Hao had learned what stillness meant. Stillness meant *deciding.* He had felt it twice — once at the thirteen-year-old with the purple ring, and once at the bear.

This was not that.

This was the stillness of a thing that had found something it recognised, and was not going to say what.

It stayed that way for **four hours.**

Lin Hao sat with his forehead against the glass and did not move, because moving seemed like the wrong thing to do, and when the forest finally thinned and the light changed and the train began to slow, the hawk came back into him the way it always did, without comment.

He did not write it down that night.

He wrote it down the next morning, in the column, and he wrote it in six words, because he could not get it to be accurate at any greater length.

**The hawk recognised the forest.**

---

## Part 4: The City With No Skyscrapers

Heaven Dou City had no tall buildings.

That was the first thing, and Lin Hao understood from the way Xie Xie kept looking up that it was not the first thing for everybody.

They came out of the station into a city of old-era buildings — stone and dark timber and roofs that had been repaired many times by many different people, so that no two were quite the same — and the tallest thing in Lin Hao's line of sight was a **tree.**

Not a building. A tree.

"There aren't any skyscrapers," Wulin said. He said it to Wu Zhangkong, quietly, the way you ask a thing you have already worked out and want confirmed.

"I've been waiting four hours for somebody to say that," Lin Hao said. "I said it at the second hour. To the window. The window did not respond."

"You talked to the window."

"I talked *at* the window. There's a difference, and it's the same difference as between me and Xie Xie, which is that one of us has been to sleep in the last two days."

"I have been to sleep," Xie Xie said, from behind them.

"Not recently."

"Recently enough."

"Xie Xie," Lin Hao said, kindly, "you asked a man about his storage device eleven minutes into a train journey and he said *you'll find out when you have one,* and you have not spoken a complete sentence since. That is not sleep. That is grief."

"Heaven Dou City is a historical city," Wu Zhangkong said. "To preserve the historical value, the city requires that no building exceed **fifty metres** or **ten storeys.**" He said it the way he said everything. "The regulations have held for a long time."

Xie Xie said, "That's the stupidest thing I've ever heard."

"It is the opposite."

"How is it the opposite."

Wu Zhangkong looked at him, and then — remarkably — at the street, and then back at Xie Xie.

"Eastsea City is second of five in an alliance," he said. "It has three million people and a port and buildings you can see from a train. **This city has the Tang Sect.**" He started walking. "Come along. You wanted to see the world outside of school. This is the part of it that does not need to be tall."

---

## Part 5: What Lin Hao Understood In The Street

He understood it about twenty minutes later, in a street that smelled of hot metal and old wood, and it was not a large understanding and it changed a great deal.

In Eastsea City he was **large.** Three rings, thirty-one ranks, a hawk at one thousand one hundred and eighty-six years, and he walked down a street and people looked, because he was ten years old and none of those things were supposed to be true of a ten-year-old. Being large was the interesting thing about him, and he had got used to it the way you get used to a sound in your own house.

In Heaven Dou City nobody looked at him.

Not because he was not large. Because **large was not the interesting thing here.**

The man at the forge on the corner had a soul ring and a hammer and forty years of something, and he was doing a thing with a bar that Lin Hao watched for six minutes from across the street and could not work out. The woman at the stall two doors down was selling something in a jar that hummed. An old man went past with **two** rings and a cane and did not hurry, and the street made room for him in a way that had nothing to do with his rings.

"What are you looking at," Wulin said.

"That man."

"For six minutes."

"I've been counting," Lin Hao said. "He's done the same thing forty-one times and every single one of them was slightly different, and I cannot work out what he's changing. It's not the angle. It's not the heat. It's something about how he's *standing*, and he's not doing it on purpose, and I would like to know how long it takes to not do something on purpose."

Wulin looked at the man for a while.

"Thirty years," he said.

"You don't know that."

"My father has been fixing machines for nineteen and he still stands wrong sometimes." Wulin shrugged. "So thirty."

"That is the most depressing thing anybody has said to me all week," Lin Hao said, "and Xie Xie has been talking about his shoulder."

Lin Hao stood in a city with no skyscrapers and understood that he had spent four months being the largest thing in a room, and that this was a place full of rooms where that did not matter at all.

It was the best thing that had happened to him since the crossing.

---

## Part 6: What Wu Zhangkong Said At The Grave

⚠️ *The Tang Sect's founder's grave is visited. No place beyond Heaven Dou City is named.*

It was on the fourth day, and it was not on the schedule, and Wu Zhangkong took the five of them up a hill behind the old quarter to a stone that did not have much on it.

He stood there for a while without speaking.

Then he said, "The Tang Sect was founded in this city."

Wulin said nothing. He was looking at the stone.

"Its headquarters is in **Shrek City** now," Wu Zhangkong said. "It has been for a long time. This is where it started." He put his hands behind his back. "The man who founded it had **Bluesilver Grass.**"

Wulin's breath did something.

"Everybody knows the story," Wu Zhangkong said. "That is not why I brought you here." He looked at the stone. "I brought you here because you are about to be in an organisation that is eight thousand years old, and you are ten, and you have three rings, and you lasted nine seconds against a legend — and the only thing that is going to keep you alive in a place like that is understanding that **you are not the interesting thing that has ever happened to it.**"

There was a silence.

"He had Bluesilver Grass," Wulin said. His voice was not steady. "And he founded it."

"He had Bluesilver Grass," Wu Zhangkong agreed. "And he was not the interesting thing that had ever happened to it either. He was just the one who was there, and kept going." He turned around. "Come along. There's a man I need to see about a set of vests, and he is going to try to overcharge me, and I would like witnesses."

---

He wrote it that night, in the room above the forge where Wu Zhangkong had put them, with the window open onto a street that had no tall buildings in it.

*Four hours of the hawk being still at a forest. I wrote six words about it and I cannot make it be accurate at seven.*

*This city has no skyscrapers and it has the Tang Sect, and nobody here looked at me, and I have never been anywhere that was better for me.*

*Wu Zhangkong took us to a grave to tell us we are not the interesting thing that has ever happened. I thought that was a small thing to say. It took me until the street to understand it, and now I cannot stop thinking about it, which is how I know it was not small.*

Then he looked at the page, and he added the line at the bottom, because he had learned that the line at the bottom was the one that mattered.

*I want to stay here. That is a problem, because we are not staying.*

*Zhou Zhangxi asked me today whether the Track was something you could learn without a hawk, and I said I did not know, and he said that was the fourth time somebody had said that to him this week, and Yun Xiao said from the bed that it was the fifth, and that they were keeping count.*

He closed the book.

And then he felt it, because he had stopped expecting to feel it and that was apparently the condition.

**Thirty-two.**

Not a wall. Not a coil. Just the next one, arriving the way the last one had not — quietly, in a room above a forge in a city with no tall buildings, at the end of a month in which he had been outlasted by a bear and walked out of a dead man's record with the Hall of Heroes out of files on him, and ignored by an entire street.

He had not been trying. That was the part he would think about longest. He had been **learning**, and the rank had simply come along with it, the way the hawk came along with everything else, without asking.

The **hawk-gold lock** at his temple lay across his cheekbone, and the **marks on his forearms** were faint under his sleeves, and the hawk turned over in him — **one thousand one hundred and eighty-six** — and did not lean toward anything, because the thing it had recognised was forty kilometres away and going further.

Lin Hao lay on his back in a city with no skyscrapers and did not sleep for a while.

## Part 1: The Cemetery

The trees over the wall were part of it.

That was the first thing Lin Hao noticed, and he noticed it because he had been assuming for about forty metres that he was walking past a park, and then the wall ended and the trees went on in rows, and the rows had stones in them.

**Heaven Dou Public Cemetery.**

Large trees, orderly, arranged between the gravestones the way a thing is arranged by somebody who had a plan and had the time to carry it out. A few people scattered through it, paying respects. Nobody speaking.

Wu Zhangkong's robes went behind him in the wind, and Lin Hao understood the word *spectre* for the first time in his life, because the man walking in front of them did not look like somebody visiting. He looked like something that had always been there and had only now been noticed.

It was Wulin's first time in a place like this. Lin Hao could tell, because Wulin's eyes went everywhere at once — which was what Wulin's eyes did when he was somewhere he had not decided how to be yet.

Wu Zhangkong did not stop.

He walked past row after row, past the centre, and he did not slow down or look around or do any of the things people do when they are trying to find something, and Lin Hao understood about sixty metres in that he was not finding anything at all.

He knew exactly where he was going.

He had been here before.

---

## Part 2: The Stone

It was just off the centre, and it was tall, and it had a few simple words on it.

**The grave of Long Bing.**

Lin Hao read it, and then read it again, because the name did not go with the stone, and he could not immediately work out why.

*Long Bing.* It sounded like a girl's name.

"Wait here," Wu Zhangkong said.

And Lin Hao stopped breathing for a second, because he had been listening to Wu Zhangkong for four months and he had never — not once, not in a corridor, not at a grave, not in front of a bear — heard that voice.

It had **thawed.**

It was not warm exactly. It was the voice of a man who had put something down.

Wulin moved to the side without being asked, because he was Wulin and because he could hear it too.

Wu Zhangkong took a **white cloth** out of his sleeve.

---

## Part 3: What He Did

The stone was not dirty.

That was the part Lin Hao would remember for the rest of his life, and he would not be able to explain it to anybody, because it was such a small thing.

There was a thin layer of dust on it. A thin one. The kind that gets on a stone in a week, or maybe two, in a city with old trees over it. It was not dirty. It did not need cleaning. Anybody walking past would have looked at that stone and seen a stone that was fine.

Wu Zhangkong cleaned it.

He cleaned it from the top down, with the white cloth, and every movement was — Lin Hao did not have a word for it, and he had a great many words, and none of them were the right one — **careful.** Not slow. Careful. The way you handle something that is not fragile but that you have decided is.

He cleaned it until it was **sparkling clean as jade.**

And then Lin Hao looked at the other stones, in the rows on either side, and he understood what he was looking at, because this one was **brighter.** Not cleaner. Brighter. It had been cleaned like this many times, over a long period, by somebody who did it the same way every time, and stone remembers that.

Wu Zhangkong stood there for a while with the cloth in his hand.

He did not say anything.

He did not say anything for long enough that Xie Xie shifted his weight, and Gu Yue put a hand on Xie Xie's arm without looking at him, and Xie Xie stopped shifting his weight.

Then Wu Zhangkong folded the cloth, and put it back in his sleeve, and turned around, and his face was his face again.

"Come along," he said.

---

## Part 4: What Nobody Said On The Way Out

They did not ask him.

That was the thing Lin Hao would be proudest of, later, and he would not be proud of it at the time, because at the time he was simply too astonished to speak.

Nobody asked. Not Xie Xie, who would have asked a stone where it came from. Not Zhang Yangzi. Not Wulin, who was the worst of them at not asking, who asked everything, who had asked Wu Zhangkong about the other continents in a corridor four weeks ago and been told to drop it.

They walked out of Heaven Dou Public Cemetery in a line behind a man in white, down a street with no tall buildings in it, and nobody said a word about **Long Bing**, and Wu Zhangkong did not thank them for it, and did not need to.

About four streets on, Gu Yue said, without turning her head, "He has been there before."

"Yes," Lin Hao said.

"How many times."

"I don't know." And then, because the not-knowing had been bothering him for four streets: "The stone wasn't dirty, Gu Yue. The moss was on the *north* face and the rest of it was clean, and there's no rain in this city that falls only on one side. Somebody has been cleaning that stone on their knees for long enough that they've worn a place to kneel, and they've been cleaning the part that doesn't need it, because the part that needs it would mean admitting there's a reason to be there at all."

Gu Yue was quiet for long enough that Xie Xie, three paces ahead, turned around to check they were still there.

"That's the longest thing you've ever said to me," she said.

"Yes."

"Say less of it to anybody else."

"I had worked that out."

And Wulin — who had been walking at the back with his hands in his sleeves and who had not said a word since the gate, and who had asked Wu Zhangkong about the other continents in a corridor four weeks ago and been told to drop it — caught up and walked between them for six paces, and said, "My mother has a stone."

Neither of them said anything.

"It's not in a cemetery. It's in a yard, because we couldn't afford the cemetery, and she goes out to it on the ninth of every month and she *talks* to it, and she has been talking to it for five years, and I have never once been able to work out whether she thinks he can hear it." Wulin looked at the street. "I used to think she was doing it wrong. I've been thinking she was doing it wrong for five years. And today I watched a man with six rings clean a stone that was already clean, and I would like somebody to notice that I have stopped thinking she was doing it wrong."

Xie Xie, from three paces ahead, without turning around: "Are we doing the feelings thing. Because I'll come back. I'll come back and I'll do it properly, I just need to go and stand near a wall first."

"Go and stand near a wall," Lin Hao said.

"I'm going to stand near a wall."

"We know."

And Xie Xie went and stood near a wall, about eleven metres on, and waited there with his arms folded and his face turned up to the sun like a person who had been asked to hold something, and did not say one thing about it for the rest of the day.

"Many times."

"Yes."

"The stone was not dirty."

"No."

Gu Yue was quiet for a while.

"I have never seen him do anything twice," she said, "except that."

---

## Part 5: The Sculptures

The Tang Sect's hall in Heaven Dou City had statues in it, and Wulin stopped in the doorway.

Lin Hao understood why in about two seconds, because he had seen the face before, in a room with no windows, four days ago, attached to a cauldron and one soul ring.

She was carved in stone and she was older, and she was holding a flute.

"**Xiao Xiao,**" Wulin said. "The Flute Cauldron Douluo."

He was not guessing. He had known the stories since before he knew what a martial soul was, the way everybody in Glorybound City had known them, and he was reciting now, in the voice of a boy who had been given something he had wanted for a very long time and was trying very hard not to be strange about it.

"Twin martial souls. **Three Cycles Soul Cauldron** and **Nine Phoenix Flute.** She was in the Spirit Pagoda founder's generation of the Shrek Seven Monsters." He looked along the row. "So these are the rest of them."

⚠️ *The Seven are named as history and as sculpture. No living person's origin is named. The lock holds.*

And then he got to the middle of the row and he stopped being able to speak at all.

"**Tang San.**"

The **Thousand Hands Douluo.** Leader of the first generation of the Shrek Seven Monsters. **Founder of the Tang Sect.** He had Bluesilver Grass, and there was a statue of him in a hall in a city with no skyscrapers, and Wulin stood in front of it with his mouth slightly open and did not close it for about eleven seconds.

Lin Hao stood next to him and did not say anything clever, which was possibly the most difficult thing he had ever done.

Then Wu Zhangkong, from behind them, in the flat voice:

"The first generation founded it. The generation ten thousand years later rebuilt it — **Huo Yuhao**, the Spirit Ice Douluo, who founded the Spirit Pagoda and pulled the Tang Sect back out of a crumbling husk." He looked at the statues. "The federation does not regard them kindly. The Spirit Ice Douluo led his comrades to force the Sun Moon Empire into a peace treaty, and empires do not forgive being made to stop."

There was a silence.

"That's why it's in this city," Wulin said. It was not a question.

"That's why it's in this city."

---

## Part 6: What Lin Hao Understood

He understood it on the walk back, and it was not a large understanding, and it undid something.

He had spent four months being afraid of Wu Zhangkong.

Not frightened — he had stopped being frightened around the time of the bear, because fear is a thing you run out of. He had been *careful*, which was different and worse, because careful is a thing you have to keep doing. He had kept a ledger of the man the way he kept a ledger of everything else: the flat voice, the folded arms, the nine seconds, the *"you are going to have to be smarter than the thing that comes for them,"* the white robes and the nothing in his hands.

He had built a complete model of Wu Zhangkong.

And the model had not had **Long Bing** in it.

Lin Hao walked down a street with no tall buildings and understood that he had made the exact mistake he had made with the Hall of Heroes, which was the mistake he kept making, which was that he had taken a **record** of a person and assumed it was the person.

The record said: cold, exact, demanding, kind in the only way he had.

The record did not say: **has been cleaning the same stone for years and does not need to.**

He had taken a dead man's record apart in four seconds and been told afterwards that the Hall had run out of files on him. He had spent four months against a living man's record and been too clever in exactly the same way, and nobody had told him, because nobody had known.

He wrote it that night.

**Wu Zhangkong cleaned a stone that was not dirty, and his voice thawed, and none of us asked him, and that was the right thing and I only did it because I was too astonished to speak.**

**I have been keeping a record of him for four months and the record was wrong, and the way it was wrong is the same way the Hall of Heroes was wrong: a record is what a thing did, and a person is what a thing does when nobody is scoring.**

Then he looked at the page and added the line at the bottom.

**Long Bing.**

*I don't know who that is and I am never going to ask, and I think that is the first thing in this book I have decided not to find out.*

He closed it.

The **hawk-gold lock** at his temple lay across his cheekbone, and the **marks on his forearms** were faint under his sleeves, and the hawk turned over in him — **one thousand one hundred and eighty-six** — and did not lean toward anything.

Lin Hao lay on his back above a forge in a city with no skyscrapers, and thought about a stone that was sparkling clean as jade, and about the fact that he had three rings and could not think of a single thing they were for that anybody he loved needed.

## Part 1: What Wu Zhangkong Explained

He explained it in the room above the forge, with the window open, and he explained it slowly, which was how Lin Hao knew it mattered.

"There are **unnatural existences,**" Wu Zhangkong said.

Xie Xie said, "That's the most frightening sentence you have ever opened with, and you have opened with some."

"Be quiet. Some large clans and sects use **heavenly treasures or unique methods to stimulate their disciples' bodies.** With a stronger body, they can contain more powerful soul rings and spirit souls." He said it without approval, which was not the same as disapproval, and Lin Hao noticed the difference. "This isn't done normally. Only in rare cases, where a disciple far excels in one aspect, is such a method even considered."

He paused.

"**This is the key point that allows a person to possess a pair of thousand-year soul rings and a thousand-year spirit soul.**"

Lin Hao stopped breathing.

Not dramatically. He simply stopped, for about two seconds, because he had three rings and two of them were purple and he had been carrying the fact for six days without knowing what it *was*, and a man in white had just said the words that described it exactly.

*A pair of thousand-year soul rings and a thousand-year spirit soul.*

That was him. That was precisely, exactly, numerically him.

And then the second thing arrived, about four seconds later, the way the second thing always did.

**A pair.** He had **three.**

He had been doing the arithmetic wrong for six days, and he understood now that he had been doing it wrong because there was no version of the sum in which he came out sensible. So he did it the only other way there was, which was against people, and he had been in this city long enough to have the people.

Mu Xi. Three rings, **yellow, yellow, purple** — and Mu Xi was fourteen, and Mu Xi was a fourth-rank Grandmaster, and Mu Xi was the person the Association held up to its apprentices as what a serious child looked like. The captain of Skysea Academy's secondary team: **three yellow rings**, and grown. The youth at the platform gate, seventeen or eighteen, **two yellow and one purple**, and the plate had called him a Soul Elder like it was an achievement. The Shrek teacher who had come to Eastsea to recruit: **twenty-three years old and a four-ring Soul Ancestor**, and Ye Yingluo had said her name in the voice you use for weather.

Every single one of them was older than him. Every single one of them had worse rings than him. And the rule Wu Zhangkong had just read out — the rule about clans spending fortunes on heavenly treasures to force a body to hold a *pair* — described a thing that Lin Hao had done **three times, at ten, for free, because his mother was a seamstress and his father made horseshoes.**

"That isn't right," Lin Hao said.

"What isn't."

"What you just said. It's right and it isn't right." He put his hand flat on the table, because he had noticed that he wanted to gesture and that gesturing was what Xie Xie did. "You said a pair. You said the key point allows a person to possess a **pair.**"

Wu Zhangkong looked at him.

"I have three."

And Wu Zhangkong — who had said *unnatural existences* without flinching, who had described clans doing things to children that Lin Hao had not fully understood and had not enjoyed not fully understanding — did the thing that Lin Hao would remember for longer than any of it, which was that he closed his eyes for about a second and a half, and when he opened them he did not look annoyed.

He looked like a man who has been handed a problem that is not his problem and has decided, in the space of a second and a half, to make it his.

"Yes," Wu Zhangkong said. "I know. That is why I said *pair* rather than looking at you while I said it."

## Part 2: What Gu Yue Cost

"Take Gu Yue," Wu Zhangkong said.

Gu Yue did not look up.

"With her spiritual power, all she needs is to strengthen her body, and then she could upgrade her spirit soul the way Wulin did." He said it flatly. "Unfortunately, with two soul rings, it would now be too difficult for her to strengthen her body to the level required."

Nobody said anything.

"**It is a pity,**" Wu Zhangkong said. "If her situation were better, I would help her regardless of whether she joined the Tang Sect."

Lin Hao looked at Gu Yue.

She was looking at her hands. Her face was her face, which meant it was not telling him anything, and he had known her long enough now to understand that her face not telling him anything was itself information — because Gu Yue's face told him things constantly, in the small way that a person who does not emote tells you things.

She had known.

She had known for some time, and she had not said, and she was not going to say, and the reason she had not said was sitting in the room with them and had just been described by a man who did not know he was describing her grief.

Lin Hao looked back at the window.

He did not say anything clever. That was twice in two days now, and he was beginning to suspect that not saying anything clever was itself a skill, and that he was learning it late.

---

## Part 3: The Category

"Wulin's advantage is different," Wu Zhangkong said. "His soul power has grown **inversely proportional** to his physique and his spiritual power. That lets him evolve his spirit soul further than his peers **without unnatural methods** — free of side effects, and on a firmer foundation. That is why I am going to take him into the **intermediate platform.**"

"Intermediate," Xie Xie said.

"Only those with **seven rings and under** may enter. There is **no minimum rank.** With an entry card you can walk into an advanced platform at rank one. The beasts are more vicious and their year levels are higher — about the same as the **Great Star Dou Forest.**"

Lin Hao's head came up.

He had been waiting for that all week. He had not known he was waiting for it.

"The forest," he said.

Wu Zhangkong looked at him.

"The intermediate platform's beasts are the same year levels as the Great Star Dou Forest."

"Yes."

"And the hawk was still for four hours at the Great Star Dou Forest."

There was a silence in the room above the forge with the window open, and Lin Hao understood that he had said the thing out loud, and that he had not decided to.

Wu Zhangkong did not move.

"Explain," he said.

"I can't."

"Then describe."

"It went still." Lin Hao said it carefully, because he had tried to write it and it had only been six words. "Not the way it goes still at something it's deciding about. I've felt that twice. This was different. This was—" he stopped, and chose the plainer word, because that was the only kind that had worked all week. "**Recognition.**"

Wu Zhangkong looked at him for a long time.

---

## Part 4: The Sentence He Did Not Finish

"A pair of thousand-year rings and a thousand-year spirit soul," Wu Zhangkong said at last, "requires one of two things."

He held up a finger.

"**An unnatural body.** Stimulated by treasure or method, by people with the resources to do it and a reason to spend them." He held up a second finger. "**Or an exceptional soul power** that has grown out of proportion to everything else, the way Wulin's has, which lets the spirit soul evolve on its own without forcing."

He put his hand down.

"You have three rings. Two are full. Your soul power is not exceptional — it is *good*, and good is not what I am describing, and I have measured you often enough to know the difference." He said it without cruelty, which was the only way he said anything. "Your spiritual power is two hundred and forty-six, which is respectable and is not Gu Yue's. Your physique is that of a blacksmith, which is better than most and is not what I am describing."

Lin Hao sat very still.

"So I'm not in either category."

"You are not in either category."

There was a silence.

"Then what am I in."

Wu Zhangkong opened his mouth.

And then he closed it.

Lin Hao watched him do it. He watched a man who had explained a bear, and a legend, and a grave, and the arithmetic of eight thousand years of an organisation, open his mouth to answer a question and decide — in the space of about one second — that the answer was not a thing he was going to say.

"I don't know," Wu Zhangkong said.

It was the first time in four months.

---

## Part 5: What He Offered Instead

"I am going to take Wulin into the intermediate platform," Wu Zhangkong said. "And I am going to take you, because you have three rings and I would like to see what happens in there with three rings, and because—" he paused, and Lin Hao understood that he was choosing, and that the choosing cost him something, "**because I do not know what you are, and I would rather find out where I can see it.**"

"The Spirit Pagoda wants weak entrants," Lin Hao said.

"Yes. Quicker deaths, fewer resources."

"So a boy with three rings who isn't in either category is the opposite of what they want."

"He is." Wu Zhangkong folded his arms. "Which is a reason to be careful, and not a reason to stay home."

Xie Xie, from the corner, said, "Can I come."

"No."

"You're taking *him.*"

"I'm taking the two of them because one of them has an advantage I understand and the other has one I don't." Wu Zhangkong looked at Xie Xie. "You have twin daggers and you go left. That is a thing I understand, and it will get you killed in the intermediate platform in about four minutes, and I would have to carry you out, and I would rather not."

Xie Xie opened his mouth, and closed it, and then said, "That's the longest you've ever spoken to me."

"It will not happen again."

---

## Part 6: What Lin Hao Wrote

He wrote it that night with the window open onto a street with no tall buildings in it.

*There are two ways to have what I have. An unnatural body, or an exceptional soul power. I have neither. Wu Zhangkong measured me and said so, and then I asked him what I am in and he opened his mouth and closed it and said he didn't know.*

*He has never not known.*

*He explained a bear. He explained a dead man's record. He explained a stone. He explained eight thousand years. And then I asked him one question and he said I don't know, and I believe him, and that is the most frightening thing that has happened to me, because a man who doesn't know is not a man who is hiding it. He is a man who has run out of categories.*

Then he looked at the page, and he added the line at the bottom, and this time he did not leave it unfinished, because he had decided something.

*The hawk recognised the forest. The intermediate platform's beasts are the same year levels as the forest. Wu Zhangkong is taking me in there because he would rather find out where he can see it.*

*So I am going to find out too.*

*And I am going to find out before he does, because he has been wrong once now, and I have never seen him wrong before, and I do not think either of us knows what that means yet.*

He closed the book.

The *hawk-gold lock* at his temple lay across his cheekbone, and the *marks on his forearms* were faint under his sleeves, and the hawk turned over in him — *one thousand one hundred and ninety-three* — and did not lean toward anything, because there was nothing in a room that small.

But it had recognised a forest.

And it was going back.

## Part 1: The Room

The Heaven Dou Imperial Auction House had a door you had to be let in through, and a room behind it that was quiet in a way Lin Hao had only previously encountered in cemeteries.

He had been to an auction before. Once, in Eastsea City, standing at the back with Wulin, looking at things that other people were going to buy. That room had been loud.

This one was not loud.

There were perhaps forty people in it, and they were all sitting, and none of them were talking, and the man at the front was speaking in the voice of a person who had no need to raise it because everybody in the room was already listening with their whole attention.

Lin Hao looked at the screen.

**Intermediate spirit ascension platform entry card. 5,000,000 Federation Coins.**

He read it, and then he read it again, because he had done the arithmetic once, in a dormitory, about a hundred-year spirit soul costing a million, and he had thought at the time that a million was the largest number that had ever been said in front of him.

Five million.

Three cards.

Fifteen million Federation Coins, sitting on a screen in a quiet room, for three pieces of card stock that let you walk into a forest that did not exist.

He did the second arithmetic without meaning to, because that was the thing his head did, and it was: **his father had made, in the best year Lin Hao could remember, perhaps nine thousand.**

Five hundred and fifty-five of his father's best years.

For one card.

---

## Part 2: What Wu Zhangkong Had Already Paid

"He's already paid three million," Xie Xie said, very quietly, into Lin Hao's ear.

"What."

"Of his own. He said it in the corridor. Three million of his own, and the Tang Sect is covering the rest." Xie Xie's voice had gone strange. "Do you know what three million is."

"I've just worked it out."

"I haven't worked out anything, I've just been told a number and I can't feel my hands." Xie Xie looked at the screen. "He's a teacher. He's a *teacher.* Where does a teacher have three million."

Lin Hao looked at Wu Zhangkong, who was sitting two rows ahead with his hands folded and his white sleeves falling straight, and who had, four days ago, cleaned a stone that was not dirty.

He did not say what he was thinking, because he had learned in four days that not saying it was a skill.

What he was thinking was: a man who has three million and spends it on two children's entry into a forest, and who travels in white and carries nothing, and who does not own a house that anybody has ever seen.

That was not a man who had money.

That was a man who had **converted** it.

---

## Part 3: What Lin Hao Saw

The miscellaneous treasures went first, and Lin Hao stopped listening at the fourth item.

Not because he was bored. Because he had started **reading** them, and he could not stop, and it was the first time in six days that his head had done the thing it was actually for.

A bar of **Cloud Titanium**, forty centimetres, offered at four hundred thousand. The screen showed it from three angles and Lin Hao looked at the grain and knew — with the flat certainty of a person who had spent four years with his hands in the same material — that it had been **Thousand Refined**, and well, and by somebody in a hurry, and that the last two hundred strikes had been rushed and the bar would carry that for the rest of its life.

*Four hundred thousand,* he thought, *and it's a three-hundred-and-fifty-thousand bar.*

He said it out loud.

He had not meant to. It came out at about the volume of a person thinking, which in a quiet room is the volume of a person speaking, and three heads turned, and Wu Zhangkong's did not, because Wu Zhangkong had already known he was going to say it.

"Continue," Wu Zhangkong said, without turning around.

So Lin Hao continued.

He read the Cloud Titanium. He read a set of soul-conductive fittings that the auctioneer described as *exquisite* and that Lin Hao could see had been ground rather than forged, which meant they would hold and would not sing. He read a **battle armor** — his first, a two-word one, on a stand under glass — and he understood immediately why Wu Zhangkong had said the words he had said in a classroom four months ago, because the armor's plates were **metal**, and the metal had been worked by somebody, and the whole of the thing was a blacksmith's work wearing a shape.

"*From a purple battle armor onward, the creation process becomes inseparable from forging.*"

He had been told that. He had written it in a ledger. He had not **understood** it until he saw a two-word battle armor under glass in Heaven Dou City and worked out, in about four seconds, roughly what it was worth in metal and roughly what it was worth in the man who had made it.

The metal was perhaps a tenth.

---

## Part 4: The Fruit

Then the spirit fruit came, and Wulin stopped breathing.

Every one of them was **thousand-year.**

Not some. All. The screen went through them one after another and every single one had four characters in front of it, and Lin Hao watched Wulin's face as Wulin worked out what that meant.

"This auction doesn't sell hundred-year fruit," Wulin said. It was not a question.

"It's a high-class auction," Lin Hao said.

"That's not what I mean." Wulin's voice had gone careful, the way it went when he was working out something he did not want to be true. "I mean there isn't a single item in this room that anybody I know could buy. Not one. The cheapest thing on that screen is four hundred thousand and my father makes nine thousand a year and I have been thinking about money for four months and I thought I understood it."

"You understood your money," Lin Hao said. "You didn't understand this room."

And then the **Dragonscale Fruit** came up, and Wulin stopped being able to speak at all.

---

## Part 5: The Golden Veins

It was **azure.**

The auctioneer explained — Dragonscale Fruits are usually light blue; this one is azure; it was **plucked too early**, so it will never become a priceless **purple ten-thousand-year** Dragonscale Fruit; starting price, **one million.**

"One million," Xie Xie said, in the voice he used when he had decided to be the person who said the thing everybody was doing arithmetic about. "For a fruit that was picked wrong."

"Yes, sir."

"And if it had been picked right."

"It would not be here, sir."

Xie Xie sat back. "Right," he said. "Right. Okay. That's — that's a whole *economy* and I would like somebody to notice that I have just understood it, and that I understood it in about four seconds, and that I have never in my life thought about fruit."

Wulin had not spoken since they sat down. He was looking at the entry cards, which were in a case, under glass, with a man beside the case who was not doing anything at all and was doing it very expensively.

"How much," Wulin said.

"Five million each, young master."

Wulin nodded once, the way he nodded when a number arrived that he had already guessed and had been hoping not to be right about, and then he said, "Thank you," and looked at Lin Hao, and did not say anything else, and Lin Hao watched him put a number somewhere inside himself where he kept the numbers, and understood that he was not going to talk about it in front of a stranger, and that he was probably not going to talk about it at all.

**Five million is four hundred and sixteen Fridays. I did that sum without deciding to, and then I did it again in tin — because Wulin's tin is not a number to him, it is a thing he opens on a particular night and counts by hand — and the second sum took longer, and the reason it took longer is that I had to think about what it would be like to be him, and that I have known him for four years and that was the first time.**

Lin Hao was not looking at the colour.

He was looking at the **veins.**

Faint, jagged, gold, running along the surface of the fruit in a pattern that he had seen before. Not on a fruit. Not in a book.

On **Wulin's right hand**, when the scales came up.

He looked at Wulin. Wulin was looking at the screen with an expression Lin Hao had never seen on him, which was the expression of a boy who has been told his whole life that the thing inside him is a secret, and has just seen it for sale.

"Wulin," Lin Hao said, quietly.

"I know."

"Did you know."

"No." Wulin did not look away from the screen. "I've never seen it. I've never seen a picture of it. I've only ever seen *mine.*" His voice was very steady, which was how Lin Hao knew it was not steady at all. "And there's a fruit with my hand on it, and it costs a million, and somebody in this room is going to buy it and eat it."

Lin Hao looked back at the screen.

He did not say anything clever, which was three times in three days now, and he was beginning to understand that this was not a failure of cleverness at all.

It was that some things were not clever-shaped.

---

## Part 6: What He Wrote

He wrote it that night, above the forge, with the window open.

*Five million for a card. Fifteen million for three. My father's best year, five hundred and fifty-five times over.*

*I thought about Wulin's tin when I wrote that, which I have not done before, and I did it. Five million is what a card costs. Wulin has been putting money in a tin for four hundred Fridays and the tin is for Na'er, and I have known that for two years and never once written it down, and I think the reason is that writing it down would have meant having an opinion about whether the tin was going to work, and I did not want to have that opinion. I still do not know whether it is going to work. Not knowing is not the same as not caring, and that I have been using one for the other.*

*Wu Zhangkong has already paid three million of his own and he travels in white and carries nothing and I do not think he has money at all. I think he converted it, and that a man who converts three million into two children's entry into a forest is not a man with money, he is a man with a purpose, and I have never met one before and I did not know they were real.*

*I read the metal in that room. I read four hundred thousand down to three hundred and fifty in four seconds and three people turned around and Wu Zhangkong said continue, and that was the first time in six days that my head did the thing it is for.*

*A two-word battle armor under glass is a tenth metal and nine tenths the man who made it.*

Then he looked at the page and added the line at the bottom.

*Wulin saw his own hand for sale for a million and he had never seen a picture of it and nobody in that room knew what he was looking at except me.*

*I am the only person in the world who can read that room in two directions at once — what the metal is worth, and what the fruit means.*

*That is not a small thing. I have spent six days thinking I was a category error, and tonight I found out what the category is for.*

He closed the book.

The *hawk-gold lock* at his temple lay across his cheekbone, and the *marks on his forearms* were faint under his sleeves, and the hawk turned over in him — *one thousand one hundred and ninety-three* — and did not lean toward anything.

But tomorrow there was going to be a forest.

And it had recognised the last one.

## Part 1: What Wu Zhangkong Said On The Way In

He said it while they were waiting for the light, which was the only time he had.

"You have seen a battle armor," he said. "Under glass, at an auction, for a number you could not reach."

"Yes."

"Then understand this before you go in, because it is the thing everybody gets wrong." He did not look at Lin Hao. He looked at the door. "Ordinary people can become Mecha Masters now. A support-type soul master with a mecha can be formidable. But **the origin of true strength has not changed in a hundred thousand years.** Only a genuinely talented Soul Master becomes genuinely powerful."

"Battle armor doesn't make you strong."

"**Battle armor has no power at all.** It amplifies. That is the whole of it." He said it flatly. "A six-ringed support-type soul master in a mecha is **cannon fodder** in front of a similarly ranked Soul Master in battle armor. That is the unbridgeable gap. Understood?"

"Yes."

"Say it back."

Lin Hao said it back. "Battle armor amplifies. So a man with nothing gets nothing amplified, and a man with something gets more, and the gap gets wider instead of narrower, and everybody who thinks the armor is the thing has misunderstood the whole of it."

Wu Zhangkong looked at him for the first time.

"Yes," he said. "And that is why I want you in the Tang Sect and not in a mecha factory."

Then the light came, and they went in.

---

## Part 2: What The Hawk Did

Lin Hao had been in the spirit ascension platform twelve times.

He knew what it did. He knew the wrongness of a forest that had not been a forest, the smell of a place that had never had weather, the way the light came down in a colour you could not name. He had a ledger entry for it. He had stopped being frightened of it around the time of the bear.

The intermediate platform was the same, and it was not the same.

The trees were **bigger.** Not bigger the way a building is bigger — older. The undergrowth was **thicker**, and it moved when there was no wind, and the light came down through it in shafts that had the quality of light in a cathedral, which Lin Hao had never been in but understood immediately.

And the hawk went still.

Not the four-hour stillness of the train window. That had been **recognition**, distant, through glass, at forty kilometres.

This was the hawk being **in the place it recognised.**

And it did not stop.

Lin Hao stood in the undergrowth with his hand on the Stormbringer and felt it — for the first time in two years — begin to **pull.** Not lean. Lean had been a suggestion. This was a direction, and it had a weight to it, and it was pulling him northeast, and he understood with a clarity that was almost insulting that he was going to go that way.

"Teacher," he said.

Wu Zhangkong was already looking northeast.

"I know," he said.

---

## Part 3: What Was Northeast

They walked for about eleven minutes, and the forest got older, and the pulling got stronger, and Lin Hao understood that he was not the only thing being pulled.

Wu Zhangkong was walking at the same speed he had been walking at, and his face was his face, and his hands were folded — and Lin Hao noticed, because he noticed, that Wu Zhangkong was **not correcting** him.

In twelve platform runs, Wu Zhangkong had corrected him perhaps forty times. Angle. Distance. Breath. Once, memorably, *"you are holding that like a man who is afraid of dropping it, and it is a sword."*

He said nothing for eleven minutes.

And then the trees opened, and there was a clearing, and in the clearing there was a thing that had been dead for a very long time.

It was enormous. It was on its side. It had been there long enough that the undergrowth had grown over part of it, and its ribs were the size of the beams in Lin Hao's father's forge, and its skull was turned toward them, and the sockets were empty, and there was a **sword** in it.

Not a sword-shaped thing. A sword.

Buried to the crossguard, in the place behind the skull where a thing like that would have had whatever it thought with, and it had been there long enough that the wood of the forest had grown around the hilt.

Lin Hao stood in a clearing in a forest that did not exist and looked at a dead thing the size of a house with a sword in its head, and he understood three things at once, and he did not say any of them out loud, because two of them were not his to say.

The hawk in him went **quiet.**

Not still. Quiet. The way an animal goes quiet when it has found the place it was looking for and does not need to look any more.

---

## Part 4: What Wu Zhangkong Did Not Say

He stood there for a while.

Then he said, "That is not part of the platform."

Lin Hao turned to look at him.

"The platform generates soul beasts. It does not generate **this.**" Wu Zhangkong's voice had not changed. That was the frightening part. It had not changed at all. "This was here before. I did not know that."

"How long."

"Long enough that a tree has grown around a sword." Wu Zhangkong looked at the skull. "This is a **thousand-year** beast at minimum. Probably considerably more. And somebody killed it, and left the sword, and walked away, and this is a place that does not exist, and I would like to know how."

Lin Hao looked at the sword.

He could read it. That was the thing — he had read four hundred thousand down to three hundred and fifty in four seconds in a quiet room two days ago, and he was standing in front of a blade that had been in a skull for long enough to grow a tree, and his head was doing the thing it was for, and what it was telling him was not a number.

It was telling him the blade had been **forged by somebody who was angry.**

That was not a blacksmith's reading. That was not a reading at all. And it was the most certain thing he had ever known about a piece of metal.

"Teacher."

"Mn."

"The hawk isn't pulling me toward the beast." Lin Hao said it slowly, because he was working it out as he said it, and because he had decided four days ago that he was going to find out before Wu Zhangkong did, and it had turned out that finding out was not a thing you did on purpose. "**It's pulling me toward the sword.**"

---

## Part 5: What Happened Next

He did not touch it.

He wants it in the ledger, in the column, in the book, for as long as he keeps the book: **he did not touch it.**

He took the Stormbringer off his back, because that was the thing his hands did, and he held it out toward the buried blade — not at it, toward it, the way you hold a compass — and the Stormbringer went **cold.**

Not the cold of the Skyfrost. Lin Hao had seen the Skyfrost do its cold; it was a *sharp* cold, a cold with an edge, a cold that burst a one-metre fireball on contact and turned it into a half-metre icicle that exploded into a million jagged shards. He had seen Wu Zhangkong do that eleven minutes later, to a thing called an Ice Fire Demon Tiger that had come into the clearing roaring, and he had understood what *sapphire* meant.

This was not that cold.

This was the cold of a thing **recognising** another thing.

And the hawk in him — **one thousand one hundred and ninety-three years of something that had never once answered to being called** — did the thing it had never done.

It **answered.**

Lin Hao did not hear it. That was the part he could never afterwards describe honestly, because he did not hear anything at all. What happened was that the pulling stopped, and the cold stopped, and the Stormbringer in his hand went from being a very good blade to being a blade that had **been somewhere**, and the three rings around his feet went bright at once — all three, including the empty one — and the empty one **took something in.**

He went down onto one knee in the undergrowth.

Wu Zhangkong was beside him in less than a second, which was the fastest Lin Hao had ever seen him move, and faster than he had moved at the bear.

"Do not fight it," Wu Zhangkong said.

"I'm not."

"Then what—"

"It's not fighting me." Lin Hao said it through his teeth, because it was taking a great deal of him. "It's **filling.**"

---

## Part 6: Thirty-Three

He came back to himself with his face in the leaf litter and Wu Zhangkong's hand on the back of his neck, and the clearing was empty except for the dead thing and the sword in it, and the Ice Fire Demon Tiger was somewhere it was not going to be a problem any more.

His rings were around his feet.

Three of them. **Purple, purple, purple.**

The third one was no longer empty.

And he was **thirty-three**, and he had not been thirty-three a moment ago, and the rank had not arrived the way the last one had arrived — quietly, in a room above a forge, at the end of a month of learning. This one had been **given.**

He sat up.

"Teacher."

"I saw."

"What was that."

Wu Zhangkong was quiet for a while. He was looking at the sword in the skull, and his face was doing something Lin Hao had never seen on it, and Lin Hao understood — because he had spent four days learning to read this man, and because he had learned at a grave that the record was not the person — that whatever was on that face was not going to be explained.

"I don't know," Wu Zhangkong said.

It was the second time.

"That's twice," Lin Hao said.

"Yes."

"You've explained a bear, and a legend, and a grave, and eight thousand years, and the price of a battle armor, and the arithmetic of a five-million card." Lin Hao got to his feet, slowly, because his legs had opinions. "And you've said *I don't know* twice in four days, both times about me."

Wu Zhangkong looked at him.

"You are not in either category," he said. "I told you that. And now you have three purple rings and a spirit soul at twelve hundred and forty-one years, and you got forty-eight years of it from a **sword in a skull**, and I have run out of things to compare you to." He folded his arms. "So I am going to stop trying, and I am going to take you home, and I am going to think about it for a long time."

"And then."

"And then I am going to write to somebody," Wu Zhangkong said, "who will know even less than I do, and we are going to be wrong together, and that is the best I have."

---

## Part 7: What Gu Yue Did

They told her at the inn, because there was no way not to.

Lin Hao had three purple rings around his feet and a spirit soul at twelve hundred and forty-one years, and he had got forty-eight years of it in one moment from a sword in a skull, and he could not put the rings away, because rings do not go away.

Gu Yue looked at them for a while.

She did not look at his face. She looked at the rings, which was the thing Lin Hao noticed, and which he understood, because he had spent four days learning to read her and four months before that failing to.

"How long," she said.

"Forty-eight years."

"In one moment."

"Yes."

She was quiet.

"From a sword."

"Yes."

Gu Yue looked at her own hands, which was the second time in four days, and Lin Hao understood that this was where she put things she was not going to say.

"I need to strengthen my body," she said at last. "That's all it is. My spiritual power is already there — it has been there since I was nine. All I need is a body that can hold it, and with two rings that is now too difficult, and Wu Zhangkong said so in front of all of us four days ago and called it a pity." Her voice did not change. That was the frightening part. "And you walked into a forest and a **sword gave you forty-eight years.**"

"Gu Yue—"

"I'm not angry." She looked up. "I want to be accurate, because you are always accurate, so I will be accurate too. I am not angry. I am doing arithmetic, and the arithmetic is that there are rules, and I have been inside them my whole life, and you are not in them, and nobody has been able to tell me what you are in." She stood up. "That is not anger. That is the first time I have ever been **outside** something."

She went to the door.

"Gu Yue," Lin Hao said.

She stopped.

"If I find out what it is," he said, "I'll tell you. Even if it's not something you can use. I'll tell you, because you're the only person I know who'd want the true thing rather than the useful thing."

Gu Yue stood in the doorway for a while.

"That is the nicest thing anyone has said to me," she said, "and it is also the thing I am least likely to want."

And she went out.

---


He wrote it that night, above the forge, with the window open, and he wrote it in the column, and he did not cross any of it out.

He wrote the number first, because the record came before the thinking now.

**two hundred and twelve.** It had been two hundred and fifty-four. Seven points, and he had not meditated, and he had not cultivated, and he had stood in a clearing and held a sword toward a blade in a skull and something had answered.

**Three purple rings. Twelve hundred and forty-one. Forty-eight of it from a sword in a skull in a forest that does not exist.**

**The hawk answered. I did not hear it. I want to be accurate about that because I have been accurate about everything else: I did not hear anything. What happened was that the pulling stopped.**

*Wu Zhangkong said I don't know twice in four days, both times about me, and then he said he was going to write to somebody who would know even less, and that they would be wrong together, and that was the best he had.*

*I have never been fond of him. I have been careful of him for four months and fond of him for four days, and I did not know the difference until a grave.*

Then the line at the bottom.

**I am not a category error.**

*A category error is a mistake. This is not a mistake. Something put a sword in that skull and walked away, and something in me answered it, and neither of those things was an accident, and Wu Zhangkong has run out of comparisons, and I have not.*

*I know what I am going to do. I am going to find out who forged that blade.*

*Because a man who forges can read a forge, and I read it, and it told me he was angry, and that is not a thing metal tells you, and I am going to find out why it told me.*

He closed the book.

The **hawk-gold lock** at his temple lay across his cheekbone, and the **marks on his forearms** were faint under his sleeves and had been raised all evening and had not gone down, and the hawk turned over in him — **one thousand two hundred and twelve** — and did not pull toward anything, because it had found what it was looking for.

Lin Hao lay on his back in a city with no skyscrapers and did not sleep.

## Part 1: What Wu Zhangkong Did Not Warn Him About

The needles came out of the sky without a sound.

That was the part Lin Hao's ledger had no entry for. He had twelve platform runs and a hundred and one lines and he had learned to hear a thing coming — the crack of a branch, the displacement of air, the particular silence a large animal makes when it decides. He had a category for everything that had ever tried to kill him.

Ivy-green needles, falling silently, in a curtain, from nothing.

No category.

Wu Zhangkong's hand closed on his shoulder and the world went **sideways.**

Not fast. That was the frightening part — it was not fast, it was *elsewhere*, and Lin Hao's feet were doing something he had not asked them to do, and there were **lights** — several, twinkling, in a line behind them and then in front of them and then in a place that was not either — and the needles came down into the ground where he had been standing and the earth went **rotten black** in a circle, and the plants around it made a sound.

Lin Hao heard the plants make a sound.

He would think about that for a long time.

They landed on a branch. Wu Zhangkong put him down and did not let go of his shoulder, which Lin Hao understood was not a kindness and was a **hold.**

"What was that," Lin Hao said. His voice was steady. He was surprised by that.

"No — the *moving.*"

Wu Zhangkong looked at him.

"**Ghost Shadow Perplexing Track,**" he said. "It is a Tang Sect technique."

## Part 2: What It Meant

Lin Hao stood on a branch in a forest that did not exist with his hand on a sword and his heart doing something it had not done since the grave, and he understood that he had been given a thing.

Not taught. **Given.**

"You joined four days ago," Wu Zhangkong said. He said it in the flat voice, which was the only voice he had for the things that mattered. "You have not been given anything. You have been told what battle armor is and taken to an auction and walked into a forest."

"You just used it on me."

"I used it **near** you. There is a difference, and in about four months you will understand how large." Wu Zhangkong's hand was still on his shoulder. "But you are in the Tang Sect, and you are in a place where that is the only way to move that does not get you killed, and I am not going to watch you die of good manners."

Lin Hao looked down at the rotten black circle where he had been standing.

"How long has the Tang Sect had it."

"Eight thousand years."

"And you've just given it to a boy who's been in the organisation for four days and who nobody can categorise."

Wu Zhangkong was quiet for a moment.

"Yes," he said. "And I did it anyway."
