## Part 3: What Lin Hao Did That Wu Zhangkong Did Not Expect

They went on.

Wu Zhangkong's stated purpose was arithmetic: *bring the spirit soul up to two thousand years, just under the current limit, because we should not waste the trip.* Lin Hao understood the arithmetic and did the arithmetic and understood that the hawk was at one thousand two hundred and eighty-eight and that two thousand was a long way, and that the man beside him intended to walk him there.

And then the forest went **afraid.**

Lin Hao had felt the hawk go still. He had felt it pull. He had not, in twelve platform runs, felt a *forest* do anything at all, and he understood immediately that this was not the hawk.

It was the trees.

"Wu Zhangkong," he said.

"I feel it."

"Something's frightened them."

"Everything is frightened of something."

"No." Lin Hao said it carefully, because he was working it out, and because he had learned that the flat version got further. "Not frightened *of* something. Frightened. The way a room is frightened. There's a direction to it."

Wu Zhangkong looked at him.

And Lin Hao understood — because he had spent four days learning to read this man, and four months before that failing to — that Wu Zhangkong was deciding whether to trust a ten-year-old's instinct in a forest that did not exist, and that the deciding was costing him something, and that he had already decided at the grave and was only now catching up with himself.

"Point," Wu Zhangkong said.

---

## Part 4: What Was There

Lin Hao did not meld his consciousness into anything.

He wants it noted. Wulin could do that — Wulin had a plant for a soul and could ask a field a question and get an answer, and Lin Hao had watched him do it and been furiously jealous for about eleven seconds. Lin Hao had a hawk and a sword and a blacksmith's eye, and what he did was **read.**

He read the way the undergrowth leaned.

Not the wind. There was no wind. The undergrowth leaned the way grass leans away from a door that has just opened, and it leaned **northeast**, and the leaning had a *depth* to it, and Lin Hao had spent four years reading the grain of metal and understood grain the way other people understood weather.

"Northeast," he said. "About forty metres. And it's big."

Wu Zhangkong cut.

The **Skyfrost Slash** went through the black fog and left a line of frost-covered plants behind it, and the fog came apart, and the howl came, and the thing that came out of it was not in any record Lin Hao had ever read.

**Two metres tall. Black. A head of blazing gold hair.** A shimmering **purple** aura around it, and bright **topaz** eyes, and on its face — and this was the part Lin Hao would write down, and would write down accurately, because he had learned that accuracy was the only thing he had —

**incredulity.**

It looked at them the way a person looks at something that should not be in its house.

"That's a ten-thousand-year soul beast," Wu Zhangkong said. He said it the way he said everything. "I don't recognise it either."

---

## Part 5: What He Was Given

Lin Hao did not fight it.

He wants that noted too, because he had spent six days believing that he was the largest thing in a room, and he had stood on a branch and looked at a two-metre black ape with gold hair and understood, in about one second, that he was not the largest thing in a forest and had never been the largest thing in anything except a classroom.

Wu Zhangkong fought it.

And Lin Hao watched, because that was what there was to do, and because he was a blacksmith and a blacksmith watches how a thing is made — and what he watched was a man who had **compressed his soul power so thoroughly that there was no fluctuation to sense**, which was a thing Wu Zhangkong had explained in a corridor four months ago as theory and was now doing forty metres away to something that had been alive for ten thousand years.

The Skyfrost went **sapphire.**

Lin Hao had seen it burst a one-metre fireball. That had been a demonstration. This was not a demonstration.

It lasted eleven seconds.

And when it was over, the ape was somewhere it was not going to be a problem, and the forest was still afraid, and Wu Zhangkong folded his arms and said, "That is the second thing today I don't recognise."

"That's a lot of not recognising."

"Yes."

"You said you were going to write to somebody."

"I am."

"Have you written yet."

Wu Zhangkong looked at him.

"No," he said. "Because I have been standing in a forest for two hours and every time I think I have something to write down, something else happens that makes the last thing irrelevant." He started walking. "Come along. We are not finished, and your spirit soul is at one thousand two hundred and eighty-eight and I said two thousand."

---

## Part 6: What Lin Hao Wrote

He wrote it that night, above the forge, with the window open, and he wrote the number first because the record came before the thinking now.

*two hundred and eighteen.* It had been two hundred and fifty-eight. Six points, and he had not meditated.

*One thousand two hundred and eighty-eight.* Forty-seven of it from an ape that was not in any record.

Then the rest.

*Wu Zhangkong used the Ghost Shadow Perplexing Track on me. He said it is a Tang Sect technique and that they have had it for eight thousand years and that I have been in the organisation for four days and that he did it anyway and he would like me to notice that.*

*I noticed.*

*I have spent six days being a category error and four days being something nobody can name, and tonight a man who has said I don't know twice put his hand on my shoulder and moved me out of the way of something that was going to kill me, using a thing his organisation has kept secret for eight thousand years, and he did not explain it and he did not apologise and he did not ask me anything.*

*That is not a teacher. That is a person who has decided.*

Then the line at the bottom.

*I read the undergrowth and found a ten-thousand-year beast and Wu Zhangkong trusted me and cut where I pointed, and afterwards he said nothing about it at all, which is how I know it mattered.*

*I am not the largest thing in a forest. I have never been the largest thing in anything except a classroom.*

*I am going to learn the Track.*

*Zhou Zhangxi came to the training field tonight and stood at the edge for twenty minutes and did not say anything, and Yun Xiao came with him and wrote something down, and neither of them asked me anything, and not-asking has become the thing they do, and that I have not earned the asking.*

He closed the book.

And then he went downstairs, because there was a light on in the room along the hall and he had been in a forest for six hours and had not thought about anybody in it except a man in white and a thing with gold hair.

Xie Xie was awake. He was sitting on the end of his bed with his daggers across his knees and he was *cleaning them*, which he did when he was working something out, and he did not look up.

"Six hours," he said.

"Yes."

"He took you and not me."

"Yes."

"I'm not going to say I'm fine about it." Xie Xie ran the cloth along the flat of the blade. "I said that in the corridor four days ago and you told me that was the longest he'd ever spoken to me, and I've thought about it, and I've decided I'd rather say the true thing, which is that I sat in this room for six hours and worked out fourteen ways I would have handled the needles."

"How many of them worked."

Xie Xie stopped cleaning.

"None of them," he said. "But I'd have looked better dying."

"That's the most honest thing you've said to me."

"I'm exhausted." Xie Xie put the dagger down. "Go to bed. And tomorrow you're going to teach me whatever that moving thing was, because he gave it to you and not to me, and the only thing I can do about that is learn it off you, and I have made my peace with that, and it took six hours."

Lin Hao stood in the doorway.

"I don't know it yet," he said. "He used it *near* me. He said in four months I'd understand how large that difference is."

"Then in four months," Xie Xie said, "you're teaching me."

"Yes."

"Good." Xie Xie picked the dagger back up. "Go to bed. You've got forest on you."



The *hawk-gold lock* at his temple lay across his cheekbone, and the *marks on his forearms* were raised and had not gone down in two days, and the hawk turned over in him — *one thousand two hundred and eighty-eight* — and did not pull toward anything, because it had found what it was looking for and was, apparently, willing to wait.

He slept.

In front was where you stood when there was a direction the danger was coming from, and you had decided that it was going to arrive at you first, and you had decided that this was acceptable.

## Part 1: The Sixth

Class zero had five students and one teacher, and it had had five students and one teacher for most of a semester, and then on the first morning of the new term there were six students, and the sixth was a girl Lin Hao had never seen.

She was standing in the doorway with a bag over one shoulder and the expression of a person who had rehearsed an entrance and was finding that the room was not shaped like the entrance.

**Xu Xiaoyan.**

She had a **Starwheel Ice Staff**, and she had two rings, and she had transferred in from somewhere with better resources, and she looked at the five of them in the room that smelled of floor polish and floor polish only, and Lin Hao watched her do the arithmetic on the room and understood from the way her face went that the arithmetic had not come out the way she wanted.

"Teacher Wu," she said. "I'd like to test my spiritual power again. At night."

Wu Zhangkong turned to look at her.

"Does the night affect your spiritual power?"

"Yes."

It was, Lin Hao understood, the first time anybody in that room had volunteered a secret to Wu Zhangkong.

"Alright," he said. And then: "Combat test. In pairs."

---

## Part 2: What Gu Yue Said

"Tang Wulin with Xu Xiaoyan," Wu Zhangkong said. "Xie Xie with Gu Yue."

Xie Xie went silent, in the particular way Xie Xie went silent when he was working out whether he had been insulted.

Gu Yue frowned.

"Teacher Wu, that's not fair."

Everybody looked at her, because Gu Yue did not say things like that. Gu Yue said accurate things. *Fair* was not a word she used.

"We have two rings," she said. "They only have one. You should pair a one-ring with a two-ring. I'll go with Wulin, and Xie Xie can pair with Xu Xiaoyan's Starwheel Ice Staff, because Xie Xie's soul power is the highest **of the four of you** — and I did not say of the five of us, and nobody in this room has said that out loud before."

Xie Xie made a sound.

"Just how much do you loathe me," he said.

"I'm being accurate."

"You're being *murderous.*"

Lin Hao put his hand up.

He had not decided to. That was becoming a pattern, and he had begun to suspect that it was not indecision at all but the thing his body did when his head had already finished.

"There's a problem with the arithmetic," he said.

Wu Zhangkong looked at him.

"Explain."

"Gu Yue's right that the rings are uneven," Lin Hao said. "She's wrong about who has how many." He held up three fingers, because it was easier than saying it, and because he had learned that in a room like this the visual version landed faster. "I have three."

There was a silence.

Xu Xiaoyan's face did something.

"That's not—" she started.

"It's all of them purple," Lin Hao said. "And the spirit soul is at one thousand three hundred and forty-four years, and Wu Zhangkong has said *I don't know* twice about how that happened, and I'm telling you this now rather than in four minutes when you find out in a fight, because I would rather you knew."

Xu Xiaoyan looked at Wu Zhangkong.

Wu Zhangkong did not say anything, which was the confirmation.

---

## Part 3: What Wu Zhangkong Did

"Then the pairing changes," Wu Zhangkong said.

"That's not what I asked for," Gu Yue said.

"I know what you asked for." Wu Zhangkong folded his arms. "You asked for fairness. There isn't any available, because there is no one in this room who can be paired with Lin Hao and have it be fair, and I have spent four months discovering that, and I would like the six of you to discover it in one morning rather than four months." He looked at Xu Xiaoyan. "You will pair with Tang Wulin, because you are new and he is the only one of them who will not take the pairing as an insult. Xie Xie with Gu Yue. And Lin Hao—"

He stopped.

And Lin Hao watched him stop, and understood that this was the third time in four days that Wu Zhangkong had arrived at a place where the answer was not available, and that the arriving was beginning to be a habit.

"—will take all three of you," Wu Zhangkong said, "one at a time."

"That's not a test," Xie Xie said.

"It's the only test I have."

---

## Part 4: What Happened

Xie Xie went first, because Xie Xie always went first, and because he had spent six hours the week before working out fourteen ways to handle something and had decided that the only cure for that was to be in front of it.

He lasted nineteen exchanges.

That was, Lin Hao understood afterwards, the longest anybody had lasted against him in four months, and the reason was not that Xie Xie had got better, though he had. It was that Xie Xie had spent six hours **thinking about him**, which was the thing nobody else did, because everybody else adapted in the moment and Xie Xie had adapted in advance.

"You've been planning," Lin Hao said, afterwards, from the floor, because he had gone down and had not got up yet.

"Six hours."

"It worked for nineteen exchanges."

"It worked for nineteen exchanges and then you did the thing with the wrist that I planned for and then you did a *different* thing with the wrist." Xie Xie sat down beside him. "I have a new complaint, which is that you are not consistent, and inconsistency is the only thing I cannot plan around."

"I'm consistent."

"You're consistent about being inconsistent."

Gu Yue went second, and Gu Yue was the only one who did not lose.

He wants it noted, and he wants the noting to be exact, because the exact version is the one that frightens him. She did not beat him. She could not — she is rank twenty-one and he is rank thirty-three, and there is a realm between those two numbers, and Wu Zhangkong had explained to the class once, flatly, the way he explained everything, that **the wall every ten ranks is not a bigger step, it is a different kind of thing**, and that a Soul Grandmaster who beats a Soul Elder has done something that does not happen. So she did not beat him. She did not touch him and he did not touch her and it lasted four minutes, which was **nine times longer than anybody else in that room had lasted**, and at the end of it he was on his knees with his soul power scraped to the floor and she was standing, and the reason was the only reason she has ever had.

She is the one he cannot read.

*"That is the fourth time,"* she said.

*"You haven't beaten me."*

*"No,"* she said. *"I've outlasted you. Four times. You can read everybody in this room, and you cannot read me, and every one of those four times you spent more than you had because you were still trying."* And then the thing she actually came to say: *"no, you're reading. I told you those are not the same thing."*

Wu Zhangkong, from the doorway: *"That is not a win for her and it is not a loss for him. It is the only honest result available between those two, and I want both of you to notice that I am calling it honest."*

Xu Xiaoyan went third.

She lasted eleven seconds, and she did not say anything afterwards for a while, and then she said, "I thought one month was plenty of time to prove myself," and Wu Zhangkong said, "so did I, about a different thing," and she looked at him and did not understand, and Lin Hao understood, and did not say.

---

## Part 5: What Long Hengxu Did

He came to the room at the end of the morning, which was not a thing he did.

Lin Hao had met Long Hengxu four times and had spoken to him once, and the speaking had been about a class assignment, and the Director had the manner of a man who ran a very large institution and had learnt that most problems could be solved by assigning somebody to a room.

He looked at the six of them.

He looked at Lin Hao for rather longer than he looked at anybody else.

"I have spoken to the President," Long Hengxu said. "The board has been questioning the resources we put into this class since two of you left." He said it to all of them and looked at Wang Jinxi's empty desk while he said it, and nobody mentioned it. "So we are going to display your strength. There is a tournament, and you are going to go, and you are going to be decent, and you are going to garner some prestige for this academy."

"And if we're not decent," Xie Xie said.

"Then the board will stop funding you, and you will all go back to the classes you came from, and I will be right and the President will be annoyed, and neither of those outcomes will affect any of you as much as you think." Long Hengxu folded his hands. "You are young. Be decent."

And he left.

And Gu Yue said, to nobody in particular, "He is not telling us the whole thing."

"He's telling us the part that's ours," Wu Zhangkong said, from the doorway, where he had been standing for the whole of it. "The part that is his is that he has bet his own standing on six children, and he would like us to know that, and he is not going to say it, because he is a Director and Directors do not bet."

---

## Part 6: What Lin Hao Wrote

He wrote it that night, above the forge, and he wrote the number first out of habit, and there was no number, because nothing had been measured, and he noticed that he had written a dash where the number went, and that the dash bothered him, and that this was worth writing down.

*No number this week. I wrote a dash and the dash bothered me and I would like to know why, because I have never cared about the number before, I have only cared about the record, and those are not the same thing either.*

*Gu Yue told me I read and I do not know the difference, and today she was right twice — once about the rings and once about me.*

*Xu Xiaoyan thought one month was plenty of time to prove herself and Wu Zhangkong said so did I about a different thing, and I understood him and she did not, and I did not tell her, because I have decided that noticing the things I don't say is as important as noticing the things I do.*

Then the line at the bottom.

*Long Hengxu has bet his standing on six children and is not going to say it.*

*Wu Zhangkong has bet something too, and he has said it twice, in a corridor and in a forest, and both times in the form of the words I don't know.*

*I am the sixth. I have three rings and a hawk at one thousand three hundred and forty-four and a track I have learned badly and a sword that has stopped being a tool, and there is a tournament, and I am the thing the arithmetic was not written for.*

*I am going to be decent. And then I am going to be more than decent, because I have seen what standing in front of costs, and there are six of us now, and I would like to be one that somebody can stand beside.*

He closed the book.

The *hawk-gold lock* at his temple lay across his cheekbone, and the *marks on his forearms* were raised and had been raised for a week, and the hawk turned over in him — *one thousand three hundred and forty-four* — and did not pull toward anything.

It was waiting.

And for the first time, so was he, and he had begun to suspect that the waiting was the same waiting, and that this was worth noticing too.

## Part 1: What Xie Xie Had Built

Wu Zhangkong had said *"it's the only test I have"* and had then not come, which was, Lin Hao decided, also part of the test.

They practised in the training field behind the dormitory, because the training field was free and because nobody in class zero had ever been given a place to practise that was not free.

Xie Xie went up.

Lin Hao had fought Xie Xie eleven times and had a ledger of every exchange, and he knew the Light Dragon Storm the way he knew the grain of a bar — the shape of it, the timing, the particular way it committed. He had an answer for it. He had had an answer for it since the fourth time.

The Light Dragon Storm came, and he answered it.

And then the **Shadow Dragon Storm** came at the same time.

Lin Hao went down.

Not badly. He went down the way you go down when something you have an answer for arrives with a second thing attached to it, and the answer you have is for one thing. He was on his back in the training field with the sky above him and Xie Xie standing over him looking both pleased and slightly sick, because the Twin Dragon Storm cost what it cost.

"**Twin Dragon Storm,**" Xie Xie said. "Light and Shadow merged. I built it last month."

"I noticed."

"You noticed after."

"Yes."

"That's the point." Xie Xie sat down beside him, which he did when he had done something he wanted acknowledged. "Who wouldn't feel pressured to improve in that room? You've got three rings and a realm on every one of us and Gu Yue outlasted you and Xu Xiaoyan lasted eleven seconds and I have been the fourth-best thing in that room for a month, and I decided I would rather build something than be fourth."

Lin Hao looked at the sky.

"How long did it take."

"Three weeks. And I threw up twice."

"That's the most impressive thing anybody in this academy has done."

"I know," Xie Xie said. "I've been waiting for somebody to say it."

## Part 2: What Mu Chen Wanted

The soul communicator rang that evening, and Lin Hao looked at it for a moment before answering, because he did not own one and had borrowed Xie Xie's, and because the person calling was not a person who called.

"**Lin Hao.** Come and see me when you're free. I have something to talk to you about."

**Mu Chen.**

His voice was lower than usual. That was the part Lin Hao noticed, because he noticed, and because Mu Chen's voice was the voice of a man who had been calm in front of him for eight months and had never once been anything else.

"Yes, Teacher. I'll come now."

"Mn. I'll be waiting."

Lin Hao put the communicator down and stood in the room for about four seconds, because he had worked out that a man does not call you at that hour in that voice to tell you something good, and because he had learned from Wu Zhangkong that the space between knowing and saying was where most of the things that mattered lived.

Then he went.

## Part 3: What He Was Offered

Mu Chen's forge was on the fourth floor of the Skysea Alliance's smithy, and it was quieter than the floors below it, and the quiet was the kind that cost money.

"You're forging second-grade," Mu Chen said. He did not look up. He was looking at a bar on his anvil. "At third rank."

"Yes."

"How long have you been making second-grade."

"About three weeks."

"And before that."

"Fourth-grade. For eight months."

Mu Chen put the bar down.

"Do you know what the gap is between those."

"Yes. I don't know the mechanism."

"There isn't one." Mu Chen looked at him for the first time. "That's what I want to talk to you about. There isn't a mechanism. You watched something and your hands changed, and I have been a fourth-rank Grandmaster for eleven years and I cannot tell you what you did, and I have decided that not knowing is not a reason to stop."

He turned the bar around on the anvil.

"**Fourth rank,**" he said. "**Grandmaster.** I'm putting you up for it."

Lin Hao did not say anything for a moment.

"I'm not ready."

"No."

"You just said—"

"I said I'm putting you up for it." Mu Chen said it in the calm voice, which was somehow worse than the low one. "Not that you're ready. Those are different, and you're the only student I've ever had who would notice the difference, so I'm not going to pretend I didn't mean both." He picked the bar back up. "The test is in four days. It has two parts. You know the first — refine to a standard. The second is new to you."

"What is it."

"**The Halo.**"

---

## Part 4: What The Halo Was

"A Thousand Refined metal is metal that has been given life," Mu Chen said. "You know this. You did it at nine, which I was not present for and which I have opinions about."

"Yes."

"The fourth rank asks a different question. Not *can you give the metal life* — that's the third rank, and you can, and it stopped being interesting the day you did it at nine." Mu Chen put the bar down again. "The fourth rank asks whether the metal can hold a **shape** while it's alive. Whether the life you put in it will keep a form you gave it, without you holding it there."

"And the Halo."

"The Halo is what it looks like when it does." Mu Chen said it the way he said everything. "A ring of light around the work. Not bright. Not impressive. It's the metal saying it has decided to be what you asked it to be, and it's going to keep being that, and it does not need you any more."

Lin Hao thought about it.

"That's the same thing as the sword," he said.

Mu Chen looked at him.

"Explain."

"Wu Zhangkong told me a sword that has something to say is not a tool," Lin Hao said. "He said the difference between a blade and a sword is that a sword has an opinion. And I've been making blades for four years and one of them stopped being a blade about six weeks ago, and I did not make it stop." He stopped. "The Halo is the metal having an opinion. That's the same thing. It's the same thing in a different material."

Mu Chen was quiet for a while.

"That is either the smartest thing a student has ever said to me in that chair," he said, "or the smartest way of being wrong, and I have been sitting here for about a minute trying to work out which."

"Which is it."

"I don't know." Mu Chen picked up the bar. "Go and find out in four days."

---

## Part 5: What Happened In Four Days

The metal was **Thousand Refined Blue Coppertite**, and it was the worst bar Lin Hao had ever been given, and he understood immediately that that was the point.

Coppertite was forgiving. It took a shape and kept it and did not argue, which was why third-rank work was made of it, and why a bar of it that had been **deliberately badly refined** was the hardest thing you could put in front of somebody who was good, because every flaw in it was a place where it would rather be something else.

Lin Hao stood in front of it for about eleven seconds.

Then he started.

He did not know what he was doing for the first two hundred strikes. That was the part he would remember. He had made second-grade for three weeks and he had a method, and the method did not work, because the bar had flaws in it that his method went around rather than through, and going around was the thing that had been working and was now the thing that was failing.

At about strike two hundred and forty he stopped going around.

He does not have a good account of the next hour. He has the ledger, and the ledger says he struck nine hundred and eleven times, and that he broke two hammer faces, and that at some point he stopped hearing the room, and that the last thing he consciously decided was to stop asking the metal what it wanted and start **telling it**, which was not a thing he had ever done, and which he had been told four months ago by a man in white was the difference between a blade and a sword.

The Halo came at the end.

It was not bright. Mu Chen had said it would not be. It was a ring of light around the work, the colour of the metal, and it was the metal saying it had decided, and Lin Hao stood in front of it with two broken hammer faces and his hands shaking and understood that he had not made it decide.

He had **asked**, and it had said yes, and the asking was the part he could not describe.

Mu Chen looked at it for a long time.

"Fourth rank," he said. "Grandmaster."

"How long did that take you."

"Eleven years." Mu Chen said it without any particular feeling. "And I want you to notice that I am telling you that, and that I am not upset, and that I have been sitting with not being upset for about eleven years, and that you are the second person who has made me do it."

"Who's the first."

Mu Chen looked at him.

"Your teacher's teacher," he said. "And I am not going to say more than that, because I have decided that the things I don't say are as important as the things I do, and I notice you have started doing that too."

## Part 6: What Lin Hao Wrote

He wrote it that night, above the forge, and he wrote the number first out of habit.

*two hundred and twenty-six.* Still. Not re-measured, because nothing had measured it, and the not-knowing had stopped being a thing he minded — which he noticed, because a month ago it would have bothered him, and the not-bothering was its own small fact.

Then the rest of it.

He wrote it that night, above the forge, and he wrote the number first out of habit, and there was no number again, and he wrote a dash, and the dash did not bother him this time, and he noticed that too.

*Fourth rank. Grandmaster. Eleven years for Mu Chen and four years for me, and he told me that and was not upset, and he said I am the second person who has made him not upset and he would not say who the first was, and I did not ask.*

*The Halo is the metal having an opinion. I said that in the chair and Mu Chen said it was either the smartest thing a student had said to him or the smartest way of being wrong, and in four days I found out it was the first, and I cannot explain why, and I no longer need to.*

*I stopped asking the metal what it wanted and started telling it. That is not a thing I had ever done. Wu Zhangkong told me four months ago that a sword has an opinion, and I thought he was talking about swords.*

Then the line at the bottom.

*Xie Xie built the Twin Dragon Storm in three weeks and threw up twice, and Gu Yue outlasted me for four minutes without beating me, and she has beaten me five times in her life and every one of them came before the third ring, and I still have not worked out how both things are true — and Xu Xiaoyan lasted eleven seconds, and I got a fourth rank in four days, and there is a tournament, and Long Hengxu has bet his standing on six children.*

*We are not ready. Wu Zhangkong said there is no one who can be paired with me and have it be fair, and Mu Chen said I am not ready and put me up for it anyway, and both of those men have said the true thing to me in the same week in the same form, and I have begun to understand that this is what it sounds like when adults decide to stop protecting you.*

*I am going to be decent at the tournament. And then I am going to be more than decent, because I am a fourth-rank Grandmaster with three purple rings and a sword that has an opinion, and I would like to be worth standing beside.*

He closed the book.

The *hawk-gold lock* at his temple lay across his cheekbone, and the *marks on his forearms* were raised and had been raised for eleven days and had become a thing other people had stopped mentioning, and the hawk turned over in him — *one thousand three hundred and forty-four* — and did not pull toward anything.

Lin Hao lay on his back in a city with no skyscrapers, and thought about a ring of light the colour of the metal, and about a man who had been not upset for eleven years.

He slept.

## Part 1: What The Starwheel Did

Xu Xiaoyan used it on Xie Xie, because Xie Xie had asked, and because Xie Xie had asked in the particular way that meant he had already decided and was informing them.

The starwheel came up over her head.

It was not large. It was a ring of light with marks in it that Lin Hao's eyes followed and could not read, and it turned, and the turning had a *sound* that was not a sound, and Xie Xie's soul power went out.

Not reduced. **Out.**

Lin Hao counted, because that was what his head did.

**One. Two. Three. Four. Five.**

And then it came back, and Xie Xie was standing in the training field with his mouth open, and the Twin Dragon Storm — the thing he had built in three weeks and thrown up twice for — had not been available to him for five seconds, and in five seconds a great many things could be done to a person who could not use their soul.

"How long," Xu Xiaoyan said. She was sitting down. She had not been sitting down before.

"Five seconds."

"That's the most I've ever got." She smiled, bitterly, the way people smile when they have been given something that costs. "And I can't move while it's up. If I move, the seal unravels."

---

## Part 2: What Lin Hao Worked Out

He worked it out that evening, in the room, with the six of them around a table that was too small, and he worked it out aloud, because he had learned that the saying was the same act as the thinking.

"It's not a weapon," he said.

Xu Xiaoyan looked at him.

"Explain."

"You said it's best used in coordination with a team," Lin Hao said. "And you said you can't move while it's up, and that if you move it unravels. And I've been thinking about that, because I've been thinking about it for three hours, and the thing I keep coming back to is that you've described something that is **entirely useless on its own.**"

"That's what I said."

"You said it's a restriction." Lin Hao said it carefully, because he had learned that the flat version got further. "I don't think it's a restriction. I think it's a **shape.** You can't move because you're not supposed to be the one doing anything. You're the one who makes five seconds happen, and somebody else has to be there to use them."

There was a silence at the table.

"That's the smartest thing anyone has said about me," Xu Xiaoyan said, "and my own clan's records didn't say it."

"Your clan's records say it'll gain more abilities as your cultivation rises."

"They say it's almost like a second set of soul rings. As if I had twin martial souls." Xu Xiaoyan looked at her hands. "And that during the day I'm weak, and can only use the ice staff."

"So the tournament schedule matters."

"It's at night," Xu Xiaoyan said. "The Skysea Alliance runs the finals at night. I didn't know why until about four seconds ago."

## Part 3: What Wu Zhangkong Said

He had been standing in the doorway.

Lin Hao had not known. That was worth noticing, because Lin Hao noticed, and because in four months Wu Zhangkong had never once arrived without Lin Hao knowing, and the not-knowing was its own small fact.

"Continue," Wu Zhangkong said.

So Lin Hao continued.

"Six of us," he said. "Xu Xiaoyan makes five seconds. Xie Xie has the Twin Dragon Storm, which costs him everything and takes three weeks to build and two vomits. Wulin has a thousand-year Bind that does not stop. Gu Yue has six elements and cannot be paired with anybody fairly. I have three rings and a Track I have learned badly and a sword that has an opinion." He stopped. "And the shape is that Xu Xiaoyan opens five seconds and the rest of us have to be somewhere useful when they happen."

Wu Zhangkong was quiet for a moment.

"That is the first time," he said, "any of you has described this team as a shape rather than a list."

"Is it right."

"It's the first version that could be wrong in an interesting way." Wu Zhangkong unfolded his arms. "Which is the only kind of wrong I have any use for."

## Part 4: What The Track Cost

He had been learning the Ghost Shadow Perplexing Track for nine days.

The hawk gave him nothing, which was what it did, and he had stopped asking it for things somewhere around the fourth month, and he would like to notice that **the question is still open** and that he is the one who stopped rather than the one who was answered.

He had learned it **badly** for six of them, and he wants that noted, because he had written *learned badly* in the ledger as though it were a stage, and it had not been a stage, it had been failing. The Track was not a movement. It was a decision about where you were going to be, made before you moved, and Lin Hao had spent four years being good at deciding where a blade was going to go and had assumed the skill transferred.

It did not transfer.

A blade is a thing you hold. The Track is a thing you do with the part of you that is not holding anything.

On the seventh day he stopped trying to move and started trying to **decide**, and the Track happened, and it was not impressive, and it put him four metres to the left of where he had been, and he vomited, which he had not expected, and which Xie Xie found extremely funny from the floor where he had also been.

"How long," Xie Xie said.

"Nine days."

"I took three weeks on the Storm."

"Yes."

"We're a very slow team."

"We're a team that builds things," Lin Hao said. "That's different from being slow, and I've decided I'd rather be the second one."

What he did not say, that night, in the ledger, was the part that had actually cost him.

**The thing that made the Track take nine days was the thing that made everything else take four hours.**

He wrote it three times before he wrote it correctly, because the first two versions were complaints and he had learned to recognise the shape of a complaint in his own handwriting. The correct version was this: for four years every problem he had ever been handed had been solved by reading it, and reading is a thing you do *to* an opponent, and the Track has no opponent in it. The Track is a decision you make about a piece of ground nobody is standing on. There is nothing to read. And so the single most useful thing about him — the thing Mu Chen had gone quiet about, the thing Wu Zhangkong had stopped holding back for, the thing that had let him answer six men in a row without Wind-Step or Gale Talon — had spent nine days getting in his own way.

He had been trying to read the floor.

*This is the first time a gift has cost me anything, and that I have been carrying a great many gifts for a great many months, and that I had begun to assume they only ever subtracted from the other person. That was not a belief I knew I had. I found it the way you find a stair in the dark, with the outside of the leg.*

Wulin had watched the whole nine days, which was the part Lin Hao had not written down yet.

He had not said anything useful. He had not been asked to. He had sat on the same low wall every evening with a piece of dried fish and had watched a person he has known since he was six fail at something for nine consecutive days, and on the fourth day he had said *"do you want me to go,"* and Lin Hao had said no, and he had stayed; and on the seventh day, when the Track happened for the first time and Lin Hao came off it on his hands and knees, Wulin had been the one who was already standing up, and he had not come over, because he had worked out before Lin Hao did that the thing Lin Hao needed was not a hand.

**That is the oldest thing I know about him and I had stopped noticing it. He knows what I need before I do and he does not do it unless I ask, and he has been doing that for four years, and it took me failing nine days in a row to see it again.**

And then the second thing, which was smaller and worse.

On the ninth day, when the Track finally happened and he stood four metres to the left of where he had been with his hands on his knees, Xu Xiaoyan had looked at him for a long moment and said *"oh,"* in the voice of a person revising something, and had then gone and sat down with her staff across her knees and had not said anything else for an hour.

He knew what she had been doing. He had watched her do the arithmetic on the dormitory floor the morning she arrived, and he had watched it come out wrong.

**She came here at rank seventeen with two yellow rings and a month to prove herself. And there is a girl in her class with three purple rings who has been a Soul Elder since before she arrived, who took nine days to learn a movement she learned in four, who is going to be at the tournament, and who is not her fault.** I have been the person in the room that other people have to be measured against for most of this year, and that I have never once thought about what that is like from where she is sitting, and that the reason I have not thought about it is not that I am cruel. It is that nobody told me I was the weather.

He wrote that down and then he wrote one more line under it, and the line was:

*Wu Zhangkong knew. That is what "there is no one in this room who can be paired with Lin Hao and have it be fair" MEANT, and I took it as a compliment for eleven days, and it was a warning about what I do to a room.*

---

## Part 5: What He Wrote

He wrote it that night, above the forge, and he wrote the number first.

*two hundred and thirty-three.* It had been two hundred and seventy. Seven points, and the Track had cost him nine days and one vomit, and I cannot tell you which of those did it.

*Thirty-four.*

That arrived on the ninth day, in the training field, four metres to the left of where he had been, with his stomach emptying and the Track finally doing the thing it was supposed to do. It arrived the way the last one had, which was to say without asking, and he had stopped being surprised by that, and the not-being-surprised was its own small fact.

*One thousand three hundred and fifty-one.*

Then the rest.

*The Track is not a movement. It is a decision about where you are going to be, made before you move. I have spent four years deciding where a blade is going to go and assumed it was the same skill, and it is not, because a blade is a thing you hold and the Track is a thing you do with the part of you that is not holding anything.*

*Xu Xiaoyan is not the weakest of us. She is the one the whole thing depends on, and her own clan's records did not say that, and I said it in four hours, and I said it out loud rather than keeping it, because I have decided that the saying is the same act as the thinking.*

Then the line at the bottom.

*Eleven days to the tournament. Six of us. A shape rather than a list.*

*Long Hengxu has bet his standing and will not say it. Wu Zhangkong has bet something and has said it twice in the form of the words I don't know. Mu Chen has not been upset for eleven years and put me up for a rank I was not ready for.*

*I am a fourth-rank Grandmaster with three purple rings and a Track I learned in nine days and a sword that has an opinion, and there are five seconds in this team that belong to the girl who lasted eleven seconds against me, and I would like to be somewhere useful when they happen.*

He closed the book.

The *hawk-gold lock* at his temple lay across his cheekbone, and the *marks on his forearms* were raised and had been raised for nineteen days and had become a thing nobody mentioned, and the hawk turned over in him — *one thousand three hundred and fifty-one* — and did not pull toward anything.

It was waiting.

And so was he, and the waiting had started to feel like the same waiting, and he had decided that this was worth noticing too, and that noticing it was not the same as understanding it, and that he had stopped needing those to be the same thing.

## Part 1: The Hand

Wulin put his hand out first.

That was the thing Lin Hao would remember later, and not the tournament — that Wulin put his hand out first, in Eastsea Square, in front of a crowd, without deciding, the way he did most of the things that mattered.

Gu Yue put her hand on top of his.

Then she reached sideways and took Xu Xiaoyan's hand and put it on hers, which was a thing nobody expected, and Xu Xiaoyan looked at her own hand as though somebody else had placed it there.

Xie Xie was last.

He glared at Gu Yue. "Just how much do you loathe me."

Gu Yue thought about it.

"About as much as one would loathe a housefly."

"*You—*"

Lin Hao put his hand on top, because he was the sixth, and because he had learned that the sixth hand is the one that decides whether it is a gesture or a shape.

"Six," he said. "That's a shape."

Long Hengxu, who had been standing behind them in the manner of a man who had bet his standing and was not going to say so, made a sound that was almost a laugh, and caught it, and did not make it.

---

## Part 2: What Skysea City Was

It was bigger than Heaven Dou, and it was not quieter.

Lin Hao had been to a city with no skyscrapers and understood something there, and he had assumed the understanding would transfer, and it did not, because Skysea City was a city that had decided to be large and had been large a long time and had no interest in being anything else.

The smithy was four blocks from the sea.

That was the first thing Lin Hao noticed, and it was the thing that mattered, because a smithy four blocks from the sea meant the metal came in by water, and the metal that comes in by water is the metal worth working, and he understood from the smell of the street that this was the best smithy he would stand in for a very long time.

He stood in front of it about eleven seconds.

"You're doing the face," Wulin said.

"I'm reading the building."

"You're doing the face."

---

## Part 3: The Boy Who Was Hungry

He was sitting on the seawall eating dried fish, and he was round, and he was younger than any of them, and he was wearing a uniform Lin Hao did not recognise.

That was the first thing.

The second thing was that the uniform was better.

Not richer. Lin Hao had seen rich uniforms and could read them the way he read a bar. This one was not rich. It was made well, and the making was the kind that costs more than the material, and Lin Hao stood on a seawall in Skysea City and understood in about four seconds that he was looking at something from a place that had been doing it longer than his city had existed.

"Hi," said the boy. He had dried fish in both hands. "You're from Eastsea?"

"Yes."

"Do you know what seafood is good here?" The boy said it with total sincerity. "It's my first time seeing the sea. I'm going swimming later."

"There's briny sea urchin," Wulin said, because Wulin could not help it. "Sea cucumber. Bluefin's good. The eels taste like honey. Goldhair crab beats king crab by a distance — the meat's more tender. If you want lobster, our eastsea lobster's the best, though it's pricey. Skysea lobster's firmer but—"

"You really know your food," the boy said, delighted.

"My name's Tang Wulin."

"Xu Lizhi." The boy offered a hand that was sticky. "Everyone calls me Little Glutton. You can too."

"That's the same as my friend," Wulin said, and pointed at Lin Hao, who had once eaten forty-one steamed buns in a dining hall and had never been allowed to forget it.

"That's a good nickname," Xu Lizhi said. "What school are you from?"

"Eastsea Academy."

"Oh." Xu Lizhi said it the way you say a thing you have not decided about. "I'm from Shrek."

---

## Part 4: What Lin Hao Noticed

He noticed three things, and he wrote all three down that night, and the writing was the thinking.

The first was that Xu Lizhi was not impressed.

Not rude. Not dismissive. Xu Lizhi was delighted about the sea and the food and the fact that Wulin knew about eels, and he had looked at six children from Eastsea Academy with three purple rings among them and a fourth-rank Grandmaster and a Twin Dragon Storm, and he had been pleasant, in the specific way a person is pleasant when they have no reason to be anything else.

That was the first thing. Being the largest thing in a room had been a local condition.

The second was the uniform.

The third was that Xu Lizhi had a storage ring, and that he had taken dried fish out of it twice, and that a storage ring was a thing Lin Hao had read about and never seen, and that the boy used it the way other people used a pocket.

"Where did you get the ring," Lin Hao said.

Xu Lizhi looked at his hand.

"Shrek gave it to me."

"They just give them out."

"I don't think they just give them out." Xu Lizhi considered the dried fish. "I think they give them to people who are going to need one. I didn't know I was going to need one. But I've needed it, twice, for fish, so maybe they know something."

---

## Part 5: What The Track Did

The tournament's first round was that evening, and it was not a difficult round. Lin Hao had been building toward it eleven days, and the round was not difficult, and the not-difficult was its own small fact.

Two opponents. Both one ring. Both from a city that was not Skysea.

Xu Xiaoyan's starwheel went up at the start, because it was night, and Xie Xie's soul power went out for five seconds, and the five seconds happened, and Lin Hao used the Track.

He had learned the Track in nine days, six of them failing, and had used it on a training field perhaps forty times, and this was the first time he had used it in front of anybody who was not in his class, and what he discovered was that the Track did not care.

The Track was a decision about where he was going to be, made before he moved, and the decision did not become harder because people were watching.

He was four metres left of where he had been, and the first opponent was on the ground, and the second opponent was looking at the place Lin Hao had been with the expression of a person who had been told a thing and had not believed it.

It took nineteen seconds.

Gu Yue put her hand on his arm afterwards, which she had never done.

"That's new," she said.

"It's nine days old."

"It's the first time I've seen it."

"Yes."

"I've now seen you do four things I can't do," Gu Yue said, "and I've beaten you five times, and I haven't worked out how both of those are true."

"I've been working on that too."

"Have you worked it out."

"No."

"Good," Gu Yue said. "Neither have I."

---

## Part 6: What Lin Hao Wrote

He wrote it that night, in a room in Skysea City that smelled of the sea, and he wrote the number first out of habit, and there was no number, and he wrote a dash, and the dash did not bother him, and the not-bothering had become a habit too, and that was worth writing down.

*Three things about the boy on the seawall.*

*One: he wasn't impressed. Not rude, not dismissive — pleasant, the way a person is pleasant when they've no reason to be anything else. I've been the largest thing in a room four months and I've discovered that was a local condition. I'm not upset about it, and the reason I'm not is that I've seen what standing in front of costs, and a boy who's pleasant about a storage ring has never had to stand in front of anything.*

*Two: the uniform. It isn't rich. It's made well, and the making costs more than the material, and I read that in four seconds, and I'm a fourth-rank Grandmaster, and I read a uniform the way I read a bar, and it's the same skill, and I've never once thought about what it'd be like to make something that good.*

*Three: the ring. Shrek gave it to him because they thought he'd need one. He didn't know he'd need one. He's needed it twice, for fish.*

And then the line at the bottom, which he wrote last.

*They give things to people who are going to need them.*

*Wu Zhangkong gave me the Track before I could use it. Mu Chen put me up for a rank I wasn't ready for. Both gave me a thing before I could hold it, and I said at the time that this was what it sounds like when adults stop protecting you, and I was wrong, and I'm correcting it in the book.*

*That isn't what it sounds like when adults stop protecting you. That's what it sounds like when somebody can see what you're going to need.*

*Zhang Yangzi asked me in the corridor whether the Track was a Shrek thing and I said I didn't know and he said everybody says that. I almost answered the second half of it to Wang Jinxi, who isn't here any more and hasn't been since he packed, and I still turn my head toward the place he used to stand, and three weeks hasn't fixed it, and this is the thing I chose not to say.*

*Wei Xiaofeng isn't in class zero and hasn't spoken to any of us since the tournament, and I haven't thought about him in twenty-six days.*

*I'm going to find out who forged the blade. And I've started to suspect the reason I'm the one who can read it is that somebody gave me something before I could hold it, and that this is the same thing, and that I'd like to know who's been doing it.*

He closed the book.

The lock at his temple lay gold across his cheekbone, and the marks on his forearms were raised and had been raised for twenty-six days and had become a thing nobody in this city had mentioned, and the hawk turned over in him — *one thousand three hundred and fifty-one* — and did not pull toward anything.

But the sea was four blocks away, and the smithy was four blocks away, and Lin Hao lay on his back in a city that smelled of salt and hot metal, and thought about a boy who was pleasant about a storage ring, and about the fact that he had been the largest thing in a room for four months, and about the fact that he was not upset.

He slept.

## Part 1: What The Shape Did

The first match was against a team from a city Lin Hao had never heard of, and it lasted two minutes and eleven seconds, and he counted, because that was what his head did.

The shape worked.

He had spent eleven days building it and expected the building to feel like something, and it did not feel like anything. It felt like a thing that had been decided and was now happening.

Xu Xiaoyan's starwheel went up at the start, because it was night, and five seconds happened, and in five seconds Gu Yue put earth under two of them and Xie Xie put the Twin Dragon Storm into the third, and Lin Hao used the Track to be four metres left of where the fourth one was going to be, and Wulin's Bind took the fifth and the sixth, and it was over.

Two minutes and eleven seconds.

Xu Xiaoyan sat down afterwards, because that was what the starwheel cost, and she was smiling, and she said, "That's the first time it's worked the way it's supposed to," and Lin Hao said, "That's the first time we've been somewhere useful when it happened," and she looked at him a moment and said, "That's the nicest thing anybody's said to me today," and he said, "I've said it twice," and she said, "I know."

---

## Part 2: What Shrek Was Doing

They were standing at the back.

Lin Hao had noticed them in the first match, because he noticed things, and because they were the only people in the stands not doing what the rest of the stands were doing.

Everybody else was watching the winners.

Shrek was watching the shape.

He could not see their faces from the stage. He could see that they were not moving, and that they stood in a formation rather than a group, and that the two at the back were a round boy and a girl, and that the round boy was eating something, and that none of them had reacted to the two minutes and eleven seconds in any way at all.

He used the Track in the second match, and he was four metres left of where he had been, and when he looked up afterwards the two at the back had not moved, and the round boy had stopped eating.

That was the thing he wrote down.

---

## Part 3: What Gu Yue Saw

She came and stood next to him between matches, which she had done twice now, and he had started to understand that this was what she did instead of saying something.

"They're not watching us," she said.

"I know."

"They're watching the shape."

"Yes."

"I've been watching them watch us," Gu Yue said, "for two matches, and I've worked something out, and I want you to tell me if it's wrong, because you read things and I don't, and I'd rather be told than work it out."

Lin Hao looked at the stands.

"They're not watching who wins," he said. "They're watching who does what without being asked. Xu Xiaoyan sat down and nobody told her to. Xie Xie used the Storm and it cost him everything and he did it anyway. You put earth down before anyone said earth. I went left before anyone said left." He stopped. "They're watching the five of us do things nobody asked for, and counting how many of us do it."

Gu Yue was quiet a while.

"Since Wang Jinxi went," she said, "you've been counting the room before you count the opponent."

"Have I."

"Three weeks. You used to look at the person across from you first. Now you look at where everybody's standing, then at them, and the looking-at-everybody's getting faster and the looking-at-them's getting shorter." She said it the way she said everything, as though reading it off something only she had been given. "I'm not telling you it's wrong."

"No. You'd say it if you thought it."

"I would." She considered the floor a moment, which for Gu Yue was a long speech. "You're going to be very difficult to fight. Not because you're strong. There are four rings in this city that outweigh you and two of them belong to one person. You're going to be difficult because by the time anyone's decided what you are, you've already finished, and the deciding took longer than the fight."

Lin Hao did not answer immediately, because it was the first time anybody had said the true version of it out loud, and because Wu Zhangkong's version had been about *him* — about what he was carrying, about the Kings in the armies, about the problem of being that at ten — while Gu Yue's version had been about *them*. About what it was like to be across from it.

"Is that what it's like," he said, "from where you are."

"I haven't fought you."

"I know."

"So I don't know what it's like from where I am." She picked up her cup and did not drink from it. "I know what it's like from where they are. I've watched four of them. Xie Xie plans for six hours and loses in eleven seconds and then goes and plans for six more, and I've never in my life seen a person do that so cheerfully. Xu Xiaoyan's stopped saying she'll prove herself. Wu Zhangkong's stopped saying *you are not the strongest in this class* — which he'd already stopped believing, and he said it to you twice, and the second time quieter than the first."

"That's not—"

"That's an observation," Gu Yue said. "You can have it. I'm not going to tell you what I think it means, because you'll work it out in about nine seconds and I'd rather you had the nine seconds."

"That's a recruitment," she said then, because she had finished with the other thing.

"Yes."

"They're not here for the tournament."

"No."

"And you knew."

"I knew about four seconds ago," Lin Hao said. "Which is the usual amount of time I know things by. I've stopped being impressed by it."

Gu Yue turned her head a few degrees.

"That's the third time you've said that."

"I know."

"Say it less."

"Yes."

## Part 4: What The Girl At The Back Did

Her name was Ye Xinglan, and Lin Hao learned it the way he learned most things, which was by being told by a round boy with dried fish who had decided the five of them were interesting.

Xu Lizhi came down to the edge of the stage between matches, because Xu Lizhi did not appear to have a sense of the things one did not do.

"You're the one who goes left," he said.

"Yes."

"That's a Shrek thing."

Lin Hao looked at him.

"The Track?"

"We call it something else." Xu Lizhi considered the dried fish. "But it's the same thing. It's a decision about where you're going to be, made before you move. How long did it take you?"

"Nine days. Six of them failing."

"That's fast." Xu Lizhi said it without any particular feeling. "Ye Xinglan took four months. She's standing at the back and she's been watching you go left two matches and she hasn't said anything, and that's how I know she's decided something."

"Decided what."

"I don't know." Xu Lizhi ate the dried fish. "She decides things and then tells me about them later, usually while I'm eating, and I've learned the telling happens when she's already done it."

## Part 5: What Lin Hao Wrote

That night, in the room that smelled of the sea, he took the book down and wrote the number first, because the number never asked anything of him.

*Two hundred and thirty-three.* It had been two hundred and seventy-eight. Eight points, somewhere between two matches and one conversation with a round boy holding dried fish. He could not say which had done it. He had used the Track four times in public and it had not cared that people were watching, and the not-caring was the part he had not expected, because he had assumed performing was different from practising, and it was not.

*One thousand three hundred and fifty-eight.*

*The shape worked. Two minutes and eleven seconds. Xu Xiaoyan said that's the first time it worked the way it's supposed to, and I said that's the first time we've been somewhere useful when it happened, and she said that's the nicest thing anybody's said to her today. I said the same thing twice and the second time wasn't planned.*

*Shrek isn't watching the winners. They're counting how many of us do things nobody asked for.*

*Gu Yue said the true thing today, and it wasn't about me. She said by the time anyone's decided what I am, I've already finished, and the deciding took longer than the fight. I wrote that down twice. The reason is that the first time I made it into a thing about being fast, and it isn't a thing about being fast. It's a thing about what it's like to stand across from me. Wu Zhangkong told me what I'm carrying. Gu Yue told me what I cost. Those aren't the same sentence, and I've been answering the first one for four months.*

*Xie Xie has planned six hours twice this week and lost in eleven seconds twice this week and gone and planned six more, and I've watched him do it and never once asked him why, because I assumed the answer was that he's Xie Xie. I think that was lazy. I think the answer is that he's decided the eleven seconds are his and the six hours are his and nobody gets an opinion about either, and that this is the strongest thing anyone in this class does, and it doesn't look like anything.*

*Gu Yue said that's a recruitment and I agreed, and I agreed quickly, because I've known four months that Wu Zhangkong is taking us somewhere and didn't know where, and now I know he isn't the only one taking us somewhere.*

And then the line at the bottom, which he wrote last.

*Xu Lizhi said the Track is a Shrek thing, and that Ye Xinglan took four months, and that she tells him things after she's already done them.*

*I learned the Track in nine days from a man who said I don't know twice.*

*Wu Zhangkong gave me a Shrek thing and did not say it was a Shrek thing, and he has said I don't know twice about what I am, and I have started to suspect the two I don't knows are not about me at all — they are about where he came from, and that is not a thing I have named, not even here. This is the closest I have come to asking. I did not ask.*

He closed the book.

The lock at his temple lay gold across his cheekbone, and the marks on his forearms were raised and had been raised for twenty-eight days, and the hawk turned over in him — *one thousand three hundred and fifty-eight* — and did not pull toward anything.

But the sea was four blocks away, and there was a girl at the back of the stands who had been watching him go left for two matches and had not said anything, and Lin Hao lay on his back in a city that smelled of salt and hot metal and thought about the fact that he had not asked, and about the fact that not asking had become a thing he did on purpose, and about the fact that he would like to know when he had started doing that.

He slept.

## Part 1: What The Competition Asked

The metal was blue coppertite, and Lin Hao understood the problem in about four seconds, because he had understood it once before, in Mu Chen's forge, on a bar that had been deliberately badly refined.

Coppertite was not hard. That was the trap. It *changed* — it moved under the hammer in a way that was not the way it had moved a strike earlier, and every strike you made was a strike against a thing that had already decided to be somewhere else.

A hundred strikes would finish a Hundred Refinement if you had the Stacked Hammer effect.

Lin Hao did not have the Stacked Hammer effect.

He had something else, and he had had it about six weeks, and he had never had to use it in front of anybody, and he stood in front of a bar of blue coppertite in a competition hall in Skysea City and understood he was about to find out what it was called.

He started.

---

## Part 2: What He Did

He did not tell the metal what to do.

That was the thing he had learned in Mu Chen's forge, on the ninth day, with two broken hammer faces, and it had felt like a betrayal of everything he had been taught, because four years of blacksmithing had been four years of *asking* — reading the grain, finding where it was willing, going where it wanted to go.

Coppertite did not want to go anywhere. It wanted to be somewhere else than where it was, constantly, and asking it was useless, because by the time it answered it had moved.

So he told it.

He could not afterwards give a good account of the mechanism, and that troubled him, because he was accurate about everything else and was not going to pretend about this. What he did was stop asking and start *deciding*, and the deciding was not loud, and it was not forceful, and it was the same act that made the Track work, and the same act that had made a blade into a sword, and he had never once connected those three things until he was standing in front of a bar of coppertite in a competition hall.

Eighty-one strikes.

He wrote it in the ledger, because that was the habit, and then noticed he had written it in the ledger, and that the ledger had stopped being a list of the people he had fought and quietly become a list of the things he had counted, and that he could not say when that had happened. One hundred and four lines. Not one of them a person he had not beaten, except the one written in different ink, which was still the most useful line in it.

He set the hammer down.

Wulin was in the fourth row.

Lin Hao had not known that, and understood afterwards that he had not known because he had not looked, which was the thing he would think about for the rest of the day. Wulin sat with his hands on his knees and his body angled slightly forward, the way he sat when he was watching somebody work and had decided in advance not to be a distraction, and he had brought nothing to eat, and Xie Xie was two seats down and had plainly been told to be quiet and was managing it the way Xie Xie managed things, which was loudly.

They had come to watch him hit metal. Neither had said they were coming.

Lin Hao had forged in front of Wulin for four years and had never once noticed him arrive.

The supervising staff member came over, and stumbled over his own feet, which was a thing that happened to that man, and looked at the bar.

"You're finished?"

"Yes."

"Are you sure you've hundred-refined it? If you haven't succeeded, you'll be eliminated."

"I'm certain."

## Part 3: What The Old Man Said

The white-haired old man on the stage said, "Bring that child's product over here."

And then, after a moment, in a voice that carried, because he had been on a stage a long time and had learned which sentences needed carrying:

"If he isn't spouting nonsense, then he's really a terrifying genius."

Lin Hao stood where he was and did not move, and understood that the sentence had not been about the bar.

The bar was eighty-one strikes. Eighty-one strikes was a number that meant something to perhaps nine people in the room, and the old man was one of them, and the old man had not said *eighty-one strikes*. He had said *terrifying*.

Because the old man had been watching the strikes, not the bar.

Lin Hao understood that in about two seconds, and the understanding was the most uncomfortable thing he had experienced in Skysea City, and he had stood in front of a Shrek student with a storage ring and been the largest thing in a room for four months, and none of that had been as uncomfortable as an old man on a stage saying *terrifying* about the way he hit metal.

"Fourth rank," the old man said. "Grandmaster. How old."

"Ten."

There was a silence in the hall that had a great deal in it.

"And the Halo," the old man said. It was not a question. "You produced a Halo. At ten."

"Yes."

"How long have you been a fourth rank."

"Eighteen days."

The old man was quiet a while.

"I've been a fourth rank thirty-one years," he said. "I'm telling you that in front of everybody, and I've decided I'm not upset, and I've been sitting with not being upset about four minutes, which is a personal record."

## Part 4: What Gu Yue Did Not Do

She did not participate.

That was the strategy, and it was Wu Zhangkong's, and Lin Hao understood it before it was explained, because he had been watching the other teams and noticed that the ones who won were not always the strongest, and that the ones who won were the ones who had somebody left at the end.

Gu Yue sat in the stands with her hands in her lap and watched, and Lin Hao sat next to her, because he had started to understand that this was what she did instead of saying something.

"They're conserving me," she said.

"Yes."

"I don't like it."

"I know."

"Tell me whether it's wrong," Gu Yue said. "I'd rather be told than work it out. This is the second time I've asked you."

"It's not wrong," Lin Hao said. "It's the only strategy that works. You're the strongest of us, and the strongest is the one you keep, and I've watched four teams lose because they used their strongest in the second round." He stopped. "You asked, so I'm telling you rather than letting you work it out."

Gu Yue turned her head a few degrees.

"That's the fourth time you've said the saying thing."

"I know."

"I said say it less."

And then Lin Hao asked her for something, which he had never done.

He had told her things. He had answered her. He had sat next to her and been quiet at her, and once, at the bottom of a slope, wanted her to see something without examining why. But he had never once, in the nine months since she walked into class five in the wrong uniform, asked Gu Yue for anything, and he noticed he was about to, and that noticing it was not stopping him, and that this was new.

"I want you to teach me something."

Gu Yue did not turn her head. Her hands stayed in her lap.

"What."

"My sword has two voices," he said. "Wind and lightning. They've both been in it since the forest, and I can use either one, and I can use them one after the other, and I've been doing that three weeks and getting away with it because nobody in this city has been close enough to tell me it's wrong."

"It's wrong."

"I know it's wrong. I don't know *how* it's wrong, which is the part I can't get past, because I can hear that they're two things and I can't hear what one thing would sound like." He turned the Stormbringer a quarter turn in his hand, which was what he did when he was thinking with it. "You have six elements. You've put fire and earth in the same five seconds twice this week. You're the only person I've ever met who made two things into one thing on purpose."

"That isn't the same as what you're asking."

"I know."

"Elemental fusion is a soul skill. Yours is a *sword*." She said it flatly, the way she said the difficult ones. "I can't teach you a sword."

"I'm not asking you to teach me a sword." And then, because he had decided some time in the last four seconds to say the whole of it rather than the safe half: "I'm asking what it feels like from the inside when two things that aren't each other agree to be one thing. You're the only person I know who's been there. I can get the rest from the metal."

Gu Yue was quiet long enough that the crowd two rows down started something and let it die.

"You've never asked me for anything," she said.

"No."

"Why now."

"Because I have three rings and a sword with two voices and a tournament in four days, and because I've watched you make the ground into something that wasn't ground under a man stronger than you, and because—" he stopped, and restarted, because he had heard himself. "Because you're the only person I know who can tell me I'm wrong without being pleased about it."

Gu Yue turned her head then. Only a few degrees, which with her was the equivalent of anybody else standing up.

"Tomorrow," she said. "Before the light. Bring the sword and don't bring the hawk."

"The hawk isn't a thing I bring."

"I know what it is." She looked back at the field. "That's why I said it."

## Part 4-B: Before The Light

They met on the training field behind the dormitory at the hour when the sky was the colour of the inside of a shell, and Gu Yue stood with her hands at her sides and raised nothing at all, and said, "Show me the two."

Lin Hao laid a Gale Talon along the Stormbringer. Wind shoved; the lightning arrived. The bar at forty metres opened along a grain he had already read.

"That's a wind and then a lightning," Gu Yue said.

"Yes."

"Again. Slower. Tell me where each one is."

He did it slower. And slower. And on the fourth time, going so slowly it was barely a stroke at all, he heard it — and the hearing was so simple he nearly laughed, because it was the same thing he had been doing with metal for four years and had never once thought to do with a sword.

The wind was pushing. The lightning was going. They were not two things taking turns. They were two things with different ideas about distance, and the wind had been arriving *behind* the lightning every single time, because the lightning did not wait to be pushed.

"I've been laying the wind along the edge," he said. "And the lightning doesn't need the edge."

"No."

"So the wind isn't carrying it."

"The wind is *in the way*," Gu Yue said. "You've been making the lightning go through something. Take the something out."

He took the something out.

It was not loud. That was the part neither of them had expected, and Lin Hao wrote it down twice that morning for that reason. The stroke left the Stormbringer and there was no shove in it and no crack, and the air in a line forty metres long simply ceased to be one thing and became two, and the bar at the end of it did not open along the grain.

The bar was gone from the waist up, and the top half was still falling when the sound arrived.

Lin Hao stood there with his arm up and his sword in it and his mouth slightly open, and the marks on his forearms were standing up out of his skin and glowing, and he had not decided to do any of it.

"Again," Gu Yue said, from eleven metres away, where she had arrived without him noticing.

"I don't know what I did."

"Yes. That's why I said again." Her hands were still at her sides and her face was her face, and he had known her long enough to know that her face not telling him anything was itself information. "You've spent four years finding the seam in things, Lin Hao. You've never once looked for the seam in *yourself*."

He looked at her.

"That's what you were going to say at the tournament," he said. "When you told me I'd be difficult to fight. You already knew."

"I knew you had two things and one idea." Gu Yue looked at the bar, then back at him. "I didn't know it would do *that*." And then, very flatly, in the voice she used for the things that cost her something: "Nobody's ever done that in front of me before. I want you to know I'm not pleased about it."

"I know."

"And that I noticed you knew."

Wu Zhangkong was standing at the gate. Neither of them had heard him arrive, and Lin Hao understood from the way he was standing — weight on the back foot, arms not folded, the stick held low — that he had been there for the last part and had decided not to interrupt it.

"That isn't a soul skill," Wu Zhangkong said.

"No."

"Say why not."

Lin Hao thought about it, because Wu Zhangkong only asked questions he already had the answer to, and because getting it right was the whole of the exercise. "A soul skill comes out of a ring. That didn't come out of a ring. It came out of me deciding to stop putting the wind in the lightning's way." He turned the Stormbringer over in his hand. "Anybody with a sword could do it. Nobody with a sword has thought of it, because everybody lays the wind along the edge, because that's what laying wind along an edge is *for*."

"So it's a *technique*." Wu Zhangkong said the word the way he said the important ones, which was without any weight at all. "Which means it's yours, and it means it'll grow when you grow rather than when the hawk does, and it means she taught you a thing I couldn't have taught you." He looked at Gu Yue a moment. "I have four rings of frost and I couldn't have told him that."

"You'd have told him something," Gu Yue said.

"Yes. The wrong something." And Wu Zhangkong turned to go, and stopped, and said — without turning back, which was the only way he said the ones that cost him — "He's never asked anybody for anything. Not once, since I've had him. You should know you're the first."

"I know," Gu Yue said.

"You don't," Wu Zhangkong said. "You know that he asked. You don't know what it means that he asked *you*." And he went, down the path, in the shell-coloured light, and left the two of them standing on a training field with a bar missing its top half.

Gu Yue looked at the bar.

"He's wrong about most things," she said.

"Yes."

"That wasn't one of them."

"No."

## Part 5: What Xu Xiaoyan Did

She won the daytime match.

That was the part nobody had expected, because the starwheel was a night thing and everybody had built the shape around the night, and Xu Xiaoyan had spent four days being the person who made five seconds happen and could not move afterward, and in the daytime she had an ice staff and, by her own account, was weak.

She won in forty seconds.

Not with the staff. With awareness — she put two of them in the wrong place in the first six seconds and the third in the wrong place in the next four, and then she used the staff once, on the one who was already in the wrong place, and it was over.

Xie Xie had called her a two-faced little schemer, and Lin Hao had written that down, and he understood now it had not been an insult.

"That's the first time I've won in the daytime," Xu Xiaoyan said, sitting down, because sitting down was what she did. "I want somebody to notice, because I've been the person who makes five seconds happen for four days and nobody's said anything about the other twenty-three hours and fifty-nine minutes and twenty seconds."

"I notice," Lin Hao said.

"That's the third time you've said that to me."

"I know."

"Say it to somebody else."

"No," Lin Hao said. "I've decided noticing the things nobody says is the whole thing, and you're the one nobody says them to, and I'm not going to stop."

## Part 6: What Lin Hao Wrote

That night, in the room that smelled of the sea, he took the book down and wrote the number first, because the number never asked anything of him.

*Two hundred and forty-one.* It had been two hundred and thirty-three. Eight points, somewhere between eighty-one strikes and one daytime match he had watched from the stands. He could not say which had done it. The not-being-able-to-say had become a habit, and he had noticed that too.

*One thousand three hundred and sixty-six.*

*Eighty-one strikes. The old man didn't say eighty-one strikes. He said terrifying, and he was watching the strikes and not the bar, and I've been good at a thing four years and never once been called terrifying about it. The uncomfortable part wasn't being called terrifying. It was being seen.*

*I've been the largest thing in a room four months and a Shrek student was pleasant about a storage ring, and I discovered that was a local condition, and I wasn't upset, and I told myself the not-being-upset was because I'd seen what standing in front of costs.*

"Yes."

"I know."

"Good."

Lin Wei made horseshoes.
