He had a forge in Glorybound City with a sign two different people had repainted, and he made horseshoes, and he made them well, and he had made them for nineteen years, and he had a son with three purple rings who had hit a bar of coppertite eighty-one times in front of a full hall.

That was the folder.

Lin Hao had thought about this off and on for four months, and he had arrived at a position, and the position was that he did not mind. His father made horseshoes. His father had put a hammer in his hand at six and explained nothing, and had said *don't get ahead of yourself, martial souls are unpredictable*, and had been right, and had never once said anything about being proud.

That was the folder.

And Lin Hao stood in a smithy in Skysea City and understood that the thin folder was the most useful thing that could have happened to him, because a thin folder meant there was nothing to take, and nothing to take meant there was nothing to offer him, and nothing to offer him meant that whatever happened next would happen because of what he did and not because of what he was.

---

## Part 3: What Elder Duan Said

He came to the smithy himself, on the ninth day, which was not a thing a man with a thin folder usually did.

He was old. He had white hair and a smile that had been used a great many times, and he stood in the doorway where Mu Xi had stood, and he did not stand there for eleven seconds.

"Lin Hao," he said.

"Yes."

"You hit a bar of blue coppertite eighty-one times."

"Yes."

"I've been a fifth rank twenty-two years," Elder Duan said. "I'm not upset. I've been sitting with not being upset about six minutes, which is longer than the last man managed." He turned a bar on the anvil and did not look at him. "I want you to know I'm telling you that on purpose."

"That's three people now," Lin Hao said.

"A personal record for each of us." Elder Duan smiled the used smile. "I've looked into you. Your father makes horseshoes."

"Yes."

"In Glorybound City."

"Yes."

"That's a thin folder."

"Yes."

"I want to offer you a place in the Skysea Association," Elder Duan said. "Resources. A forge of your own. A teacher at fifth rank. Everything Eastsea has given you and a good deal more. I'm offering it rather than waiting for you to ask, because I've decided you work things out fast, and I'd rather say it first."

Lin Hao set the hammer down.

"No," he said.

Elder Duan's smile did not change, which was how Lin Hao knew it had been a used smile.

"You haven't heard what I'm offering."

"I know what you're offering," Lin Hao said. "You're offering me a thing before I can hold it. I've been offered three things before I could hold them in three weeks, and there's a pattern, and the pattern is that the people offering me things are the ones who've already decided what I am." He stopped. "You investigated me two days and came back with a thin folder, and you're offering me a fifth-rank teacher, and you haven't once asked me what I'm trying to do."

Elder Duan was quiet a moment.

"What are you trying to do."

"I don't know," Lin Hao said. "That's the fourth time I've said it, and it's the true answer. You're the first person who's asked. You asked after I said no. I'd like to have been asked before."

## Part 4: What Ye Xinglan Did

Her sword was called the Stargod Sword, and it came up with two yellow rings, and there were sparks of light along the yellow blade like stars in a night sky, and it was the most beautiful thing Lin Hao had seen in Skysea City, and he understood in about two seconds that it was going to be the hardest thing he had fought.

She saw his rings.

He watched her see them, because he noticed things, and because he had learned that watching a person recalculate was the most informative thing you could watch.

Three purple rings.

Her face did something, and then it did not do anything, because she was a Shrek student and her confidence was not a thing a set of rings could move, and she had decided that before the match and the decision did not change.

"That's a thousand-year configuration," she said.

"Yes."

"To support a thousand-year ring your body and spirit both have to be powerful." She said it the way you say a thing you have worked out and are not impressed by. "There's no other explanation. You're more talented than I gave you credit for."

"Thank you."

"That wasn't a compliment."

"I know," Lin Hao said. "I took it as one anyway."

---

## Part 5: What The Track Did

She was fast.

Not Xie Xie fast. Xie Xie was fast the way a thing is fast when it has decided where it is going. Ye Xinglan was fast the way a thing is fast when it has decided where it is going *and can change its mind*, and the Stargod Sword had a reach Lin Hao had not accounted for, and the Track put him four metres left of where she had been, and she was not there any more.

He used the Track four times.

She was not there four times.

Then he stopped using it, because Wu Zhangkong had taught him that a thing you use four times is a thing your opponent has now seen four times, and the fifth time she would be where he was going to be. The Track was a decision about where he was going to be, made before he moved, and the deciding was the part that mattered, and he had been using it as a movement, and it was not a movement.

The fifth time, he did not decide where to go.

He decided where *she* was going to be.

He could not afterwards give a good account of it, and that troubled him, because he was accurate about everything else. What happened was that he stopped deciding about himself and started deciding about her, and the Track happened anyway, and he was four metres left of where she was going to be rather than where she had been, and the Stargod Sword went into the place he had been, and the sword that had been the most beautiful thing in Skysea City was in the wrong place.

He won in thirty-one seconds.

Ye Xinglan stood in the ring with her sword down and her confidence entirely intact, which was the most impressive thing he had seen in Skysea City, and she said, "That's not a Track," and Lin Hao said, "No," and she said, "What is it," and he said, "I don't know," and she said, "That's the fourth time you've said that," and he said, "I know."

## Part 6: What Wulin Said

He found Wulin on the seawall again, because the seawall was where Wulin went, and because Lin Hao had started to understand that going to find somebody was itself a thing worth doing and he had not done it enough.

"They investigated you," Wulin said.

"They investigated me."

"I know. Mu Xi told me." Wulin was eating dried fish. "She's decided she's the person who tells people things now. She resented you four days and now she tells me things, and I haven't worked out how both of those are true."

"Neither have I."

"That's the fourth time somebody's said that to me this week." Wulin ate the dried fish. "I noticed that, too."

Lin Hao sat down.

"Thirty-five," he said.

"What."

"I'm thirty-five. It happened twenty minutes ago, in the ring, after the fifth time I used the Track and it wasn't a movement. I haven't told anybody." He stopped. "I'm telling you first. I didn't plan to."

Wulin was quiet a moment.

"That's the nicest thing anybody's said to me all week," he said. "You taught me that saying a thing is the same act as thinking it, and I've stopped noticing when I do it, and the not-noticing is the part that scares me a little, and I'm telling you that too."

Lin Hao looked at him.

"I'm glad you're here," he said.

"That's the eighth time."

"I know."

## Part 6-B: The Form

The Association had a form.

It was not a large form. It was one page, because the Eastsea Branch had used the same one for forty years, and it asked for a name and an age and a martial soul, and then — under a ruled heading that said **SYSTEM** — it offered six small empty squares in a row, each with a word printed underneath in the flat grey type the Federation used for things it did not expect anybody to read.

**Assault. Agility. Power. Control. Defense. Auxiliary.**

And under the sixth square there was a blank line, because forty years ago somebody had thought to leave one, and nobody had ever used it, and nobody had ever thought to take it away.

Lin Hao sat at the desk with a pen in his hand for a long time.

The clerk had been pleasant about it. The clerk had said *"most people know before they sit down,"* and had gone to fetch a stamp. And Lin Hao had looked at the six squares and done the thing he did, which was go through them one at a time, honestly.

**Assault.** Yes. He had ended a fight in nine seconds on a stage in front of four thousand people.
**Agility.** Yes. The Track.
**Power.** His fist was past the machine.
**Control.** He had held a man's blade with wind for four seconds and the man had not been able to move it.
**Defense.** He had stood in the path of twelve wolves and walked out.
**Auxiliary.** He had spent nine weeks teaching six people to be better at themselves.

Six squares. And he understood, sitting there, that the form was not asking which of these he was *good at*. It was asking which of these he was *for*. Which one he belonged to. Which one would go on the rest of the paperwork and decide who he was put in a team with, and be the thing a stranger said about him in one breath at a bar in a city he had never been to.

Xie Xie was **Agility**. You could say it in a word and it was true and it was *his*.
Gu Yue was—

And he stopped, because that was the thing that undid the whole of it.

**Gu Yue was an Elementalist.** That was what everybody said, and had said since the second week, and what was on her form, and what the roster said, and what Long Hengxu had written in his notes about the tournament. And **Elementalist was not one of the six.** It was not on the form. There was no square for it. Somebody had looked at a girl with six elements and no System and written a word in the blank line, and the word had gone into the roster, and from that day forward every adult in that academy had described her with a category **that did not exist.**

Nobody had argued about it. Nobody had checked. Nobody had ever once said *there is no such thing as an Elementalist* — because there was now, because it was on a form, and because forms are how a thing becomes real.

Lin Hao looked at the blank line under the sixth square.

And he thought: *well.*

He wrote in it.

He wrote it in the same hand he wrote everything in, small and even and slightly slanted, and he did not think very hard about the word, because the word was obvious, and because he was ten years old and tired and had a tournament in four days and had already spent four minutes on a piece of paper most people filled in standing up.

**Comprehensive.**

Then he handed it back.

The clerk read the name. Read the age, and looked up for a moment, and read the age again. Read the martial soul. And then came to the SYSTEM line, and read the word in the blank, and did not do anything at all.

"Right," the clerk said, and stamped it.

That was the whole of it.

Nobody checked. Nobody had ever checked anybody's. Gu Yue had written **Elementalist** and it had been true ever since, and Xie Xie had written **Agility** without reading the squares because he already knew, and somewhere in this building there was a forty-year-old form with a word on it that no book contained, and the word was still in use.

Lin Hao walked out of the Eastsea Branch of the Blacksmith's Association at about half past four on a Tuesday, having invented a category of soul master in the space of eleven seconds, and did not know he had done it, and would not know for a very long time, and nobody would tell him — because you cannot congratulate a person on founding something when the founding was a word on a form that nobody read.

---

## Part 7: What Lin Hao Wrote

That night, in the room that smelled of the sea, he took the book down and wrote the number first, because the number never asked anything of him.

*Two hundred and fifty-six.* It had been two hundred and forty-nine. Eight points, somewhere between saying no to a fifth-rank teacher and using the Track five times and stopping using it as a movement. He could not say which had done it. He had written that three times now, and the writing-it-three-times was the only honest part.

*One thousand three hundred and eighty-two.*

*There's a blank line under the six squares on the Association's form and I wrote a word in it and the man stamped it and that was the whole of it.*

*Gu Yue is an Elementalist. I've known that a year. I've said it myself. It's on her form and on the roster and in Long Hengxu's notes, and there's no square for it and there never was, and somebody wrote a word in a blank line and the word became true, and not one adult in that building has ever questioned it.* So I wrote a word in a blank line. *Comprehensive.* It seemed the honest thing. It took eleven seconds. The clerk said *right.* I've thought about it twice since.

*I'm not sorry. I'm also lonely, and the reason isn't that I have no category, because I've just been given one. It's that Xie Xie has a word and everybody knows what it means, and Gu Yue has a word and everybody knows what it means, and I have a word I made up four hours ago and nobody knows what it means, including me.*

*This is the first time I've ever made something that wasn't a stroke.*

*My father makes horseshoes. That's the folder. I've thought about it four months and the position I've arrived at is that I don't mind.*

*Elder Duan investigated me two days and came back with a thin folder and offered me a fifth-rank teacher, and he'd already decided what I am, and I said no, and he asked what I'm trying to do after I said no, and I'd like to have been asked before.*

*The Track is not a movement. I used it four times as a movement and she wasn't there four times, and the fifth time I stopped deciding where to go and started deciding where she was going to be, and it happened anyway, and I don't have an account of it.*

And then the line at the bottom, which he wrote last because it was the one he had been circling all week.

*I have said I don't know five times now. Wu Zhangkong has said it twice about me. Three men have told me they're not upset. A man with a thin folder offered me a thing before I could hold it and I said no.*

*Every person who's offered me a thing has already decided what I am. Every person who's asked me a question has asked after I said no. I've started to suspect the thing I am isn't a thing anybody can decide. This is the closest I've come to being frightened, and I'm not frightened, and I'd like to know why I'm not.*

He closed the book.

The lock at his temple lay gold across his cheekbone, and the marks on his forearms were raised and had been raised for thirty-four days, and the hawk turned over in him — *one thousand three hundred and eighty-two* — and did not pull toward anything.

Lin Hao lay on his back in a city that smelled of salt and hot metal, and thought about a father who made horseshoes, and about a thin folder, and about the fact that the thin folder was the most useful thing that had happened to him, and about the fact that he was not frightened.

He slept.

## Part 1: What The Last Day Was

The last day of the tournament was not difficult.

Lin Hao had been building toward it for thirteen days, and the last day was not difficult, and the not-difficult had become a pattern, and the pattern was the part he did not know what to do with.

Class zero won.

The shape worked. Xu Xiaoyan's starwheel made five seconds happen, and Gu Yue put earth and fire into the five seconds, and Xie Xie put the Twin Dragon Storm into the part after, and Wulin's Bind held the rest. Lin Hao used the Track twice and did not need it a third time, because the third time he used the stroke Gu Yue had given him at four in the morning nine days ago.

He had never used it in front of anybody. He had practised it eleven times in a field behind a dormitory and taken the tops off two bars and a post, and each time it came out of the Stormbringer quieter than the one before, and he had begun to suspect that the quiet was not the technique getting worse but the technique getting *finished*.

It left the sword with no sound in it at all. Forty metres of air stopped being one thing and became two, and the man at the end of it went down with his shield in two pieces and no idea what had come through it, and the stands — who had come to watch a harbour-city team be decent — went quiet in the particular way a crowd goes quiet when it has been shown something it has no word for.

Gu Yue, eleven metres off, said nothing. Her hands were at her sides and her chin was up a fraction. Xie Xie, flat on his back in the part after with his daggers on his chest and his lungs somewhere else, turned his head.

"She taught you that?"

"Yes."

"In nine days."

"Before the light."

"I have known her since the spring," Xie Xie said, to the sky, "and she has never taught me *anything*, and I have asked, and I want it noted that I have asked *repeatedly*."

Four minutes and six seconds.

Then it was over, and there was a ceremony, and a cup, and Lin Hao stood on a stage in Skysea City holding the cup and did not know what to do with it.

## Part 2: What The Invitation Was

It came the next day, in a room, from a man Lin Hao had not met, and the folder was not thin.

That was the first thing he noticed. The folder was not thin.

"You have three purple rings at ten years old," the man said. "You're a fourth-rank Grandmaster. You have a movement that isn't a movement, and a man with a thin folder offered you a fifth-rank teacher and you turned him down. I've read the report about that. I'm not going to offer you a teacher."

Lin Hao waited.

"Shrek Academy," the man said. "All five of you. Not one. Not two. Five."

Nobody spoke.

"I'm offering it rather than waiting for you to ask," the man said, "because I've decided you work things out fast, and I'd rather say it first."

"That's the third person who's said that to me," Lin Hao said.

"I know. I read the report."

## Part 3: What He Had To Say

He found them on the seawall, because the seawall was where they went, and because he had started to understand that going to find people was itself a thing worth doing.

Wulin was eating dried fish. Xie Xie was up on the wall with his legs in the air. Gu Yue sat with her hands in her lap. Xu Xiaoyan was sitting down, because that was what she did. Xu Lizhi was eating a pig trotter and had not been invited and had come anyway.

"They've offered all five of us Shrek," Lin Hao said.

Nobody said anything for a while.

"That's the whole thing," Xie Xie said at last, upside down. "That's the thing everybody wants."

"Yes."

"And you said it like it was a problem."

"I said it like it was a thing," Lin Hao said. "I didn't say it was a problem."

Gu Yue turned her head a few degrees.

"You're going to say no," she said.

"I don't know."

"That's the sixth time."

"I know."

"You're going to say no," Gu Yue said, "and I'm saying it rather than letting you work it out, because I'd rather be the one who says it first. I learned that from you. I didn't know I was learning it."

## Part 4: What He Said

He thought about it for eleven seconds, which was a long time for him, and then said the thing he had not planned.

"I don't know what I am," he said. "I've said it six times and it's the true answer. Three men have told me they're not upset about it. A man with a thin folder offered me a teacher and I said no. A man with a thick folder has offered all five of us the thing everybody wants. I've been handed four things before I could hold them in four weeks, and every person who's handed me one had already decided what I was."

He stopped.

"Shrek would decide what I am too. They're better at it than anybody — they've been doing it eight thousand years. And I'm not saying no because I don't want it. I want it. I've wanted it since I was six and my father put a hammer in my hand and didn't explain a thing."

He looked at the sea.

"I'm saying I don't know yet. Not-knowing-yet isn't the same as no, and I haven't been able to tell the difference for four weeks, and I'd like to be able to."

Xu Lizhi, from the end of the wall, with the pig trotter, said, "That's the most annoying thing anybody's ever said."

"I know."

"I'm going to go anyway."

"I know."

"I'll tell them you said not-yet."

"I'd like that."

## Part 5: What Wulin Said

He stayed after the others had gone, because Wulin stayed, and because Lin Hao had started to understand that Wulin staying was itself a thing.

"I'm going," Wulin said.

"I know."

"I'm telling you rather than letting you work it out."

"I noticed."

"I'm going because my father makes machine repairs and my mother cooks and I've wanted it since I was six, and because you taught me that saying a thing is the same act as thinking it, so I thought it and I'm saying it." Wulin ate the dried fish.

He did not say the other reason. He never said the other reason, and Lin Hao had known what it was for two years, because you cannot watch a boy put every coin he earns into a tin for four hundred Fridays and not work out what the tin is for. Na'er. Shrek was in the centre, and Shrek had eyes in eleven cities, and Eastsea was a harbour at the edge of the map where a girl could be taken and nobody would think to look twice.

"I'm also going," Wulin said, "because it's further inland than this."

"I know," Lin Hao said.

"That isn't—"

"I know." Lin Hao let it sit for a second, because he had learned that the silence after a thing like that was the part that did the work. "You don't have to say it for me to have it. I've never once asked, and not asking has cost me nothing, and I've started to think not asking is the only decent thing I've done in this city."

Wulin was quiet.

"You're coming," he said.

"I don't know."

"You're coming," Wulin said. "You've said *I don't know* six times and *no* once and *not-yet* once, and I've known you since we were three, and I'm telling you you're coming. I'm telling you rather than asking, because I've decided the telling is the same act as the thinking, and I didn't know I was going to say that until I said it."

Lin Hao looked at the sea.

"That's the first time you've told me something I didn't know," he said.

"I know," Wulin said. "That's the tenth time."

And then Wulin said the thing he said about once a year and never on purpose.

"Do you remember the wall behind your father's yard."

"Yes."

"I came off it when we were four and you caught me, and you were nowhere near strong enough to catch me, and we both went down, and you broke your wrist." Wulin was looking at the harbour rather than at him, which was how he said the large ones. "And you told your mother I'd come off it too, so she wouldn't be cross with me, and you were four years old, and I have never in my life worked out where you got *that* from."

"I got it from you," Lin Hao said. "You'd have done it."

"I'd have done it," Wulin agreed at once, because it was true and because he had never once in seven years pretended otherwise about anything. "But I'd have cried about it afterwards."

"You'd have cried about it *before*."

"Both," Wulin said. "Honestly. Both."

Xie Xie, upside down on the wall, said, "I want it noted that I've been in this class two years and I've learned more about the two of you in the last forty seconds than in the whole rest of it, and I've decided I don't want to know anything further, and I'm going to stay upside down for a while."

Gu Yue said nothing. But she had been watching Lin Hao's hands, and she noticed that they went very still at the word *wall*, and she put it in the place where she kept the things she was not going to use — which was a small place, and which had never before held anything she had to think about putting there.

Because Lin Hao had broken his wrist at four and lied about it inside the hour to protect a boy he had known one year, and had never mentioned it since, and had gone on to become what he was, and she understood — with a clarity she did not enjoy — that everything she had ever measured about him she had measured from the outside, and the inside of it had been finished before she was born.

Wulin was quiet a moment.

"You're coming," he said.

"I don't know."

"You're coming."

## Part 6: What Lin Hao Wrote

That night, in the room that smelled of the sea, he took the book down and wrote the number first, because the number never asked anything of him.

*Two hundred and sixty-four.* It had been two hundred and ninety-four. Nine points had gone somewhere between four minutes and six seconds and one conversation on a seawall with a boy eating dried fish who told him something he did not know. He could not say which had done it. He had written that four times now, and the writing-it-four-times was the only honest part.

*One thousand three hundred and ninety-one.*

*Thirty-six. It came on the last day, in four minutes and six seconds. I told Wulin first. I didn't plan to. Not planning it has become the most common thing about me.*

*Shrek has offered all five of us. I said not-yet. Not-yet isn't no. Wulin told me I'm coming — the first time anybody's told me something I didn't know — and it came from Wulin and not from a man with a folder.*

And then the line at the bottom, which he wrote last because it was the one he had been circling all week.

*I have been handed four things before I could hold them. A sword with an opinion. A Track that isn't a movement. A fourth rank in eighteen days. And Shrek.*

*Three men have told me they're not upset. A man with a thin folder asked me a question after I said no. A man with a thick folder read the report about that and didn't offer me a teacher.*

*And Wulin told me I'm coming. He's the only person who's ever told me something I didn't know, and he learned it from me, and didn't know he was learning it, and I didn't know I was teaching it. It's the thing I've done that I'm most proud of, and I didn't do it on purpose.*

*Zhou Zhangxi and Yun Xiao aren't going. They were never in class zero. Zhou Zhangxi said on the seawall that he isn't upset, and Yun Xiao said from behind him that he is, and that Zhou Zhangxi is lying, and they're both telling me the truth in different ways and I haven't worked out which to believe.*

*Zhang Yangzi and Wang Jinxi aren't going. They transferred out — packed after the exam and went to another academy, the way Wei Xiaofeng went back to his class before them. Wang Jinxi said nothing when he packed. Zhang Yangzi said eleven things and I wrote down nine. Wei Xiaofeng hasn't spoken to any of us since the tournament and I haven't thought about him in twenty-six days.*

He closed the book.

The lock at his temple lay gold across his cheekbone, and the marks on his forearms were raised and had been raised for thirty-six days, and the hawk turned over in him — *one thousand three hundred and ninety-one* — and did not pull toward anything.

Lin Hao lay on his back in a city that smelled of salt and hot metal, and thought about a father who made horseshoes, and about a thin folder and a thick folder, and about the fact that he had said not-yet, and about the fact that Wulin had told him he was coming, and about the fact that he was not frightened.

He slept.

## Part 1: What He Said

He said yes on the fourth day.

Not on the first. He had said *not yet* on the first day and he had meant it, and the not-yet had been true for three days, and on the fourth it stopped being true, and he wanted that kept straight — the not-yet had been a real thing, not a stall with the serial filed off.

He said it to the man with the thick folder, in the room where they had put him. The man wrote it down.

"I'm not surprised," the man said.

"I am," said Lin Hao.

The man looked up. "That's the first interesting thing you've said."

"I've said six interesting things in four weeks. Nobody wrote any of them down."

"That's because they weren't answers."

"No," Lin Hao agreed. "They weren't."

---

## Part 2: What Shen Yi Said

She had come to Skysea City for the tournament and stayed three days, and she watched, and in a corridor where Lin Hao was not standing she said something to Wu Zhangkong that he did not hear.

He heard it anyway, later, from Mu Xi, because Mu Xi had become the person who told him things.

"His first ring is purple and his physique is excellent," Shen Yi had said. "Did you raise him to be like this?"

"No."

"If he has three rings by the time he's fifteen, his body will likely transform again." She had said it the way you say a thing you have worked out and are not pleased by. "You have an eye for disciples."

"I have an eye for one disciple," Wu Zhangkong had said. "And I did not have an eye for this."

Mu Xi told him all of this on the seawall, eating dried fish, because Xu Lizhi had given her dried fish and she had accepted it, and because she had resented him for four days and then started telling him things, and neither of those had been planned.

"Why does that matter," Lin Hao said.

"Because she's saying your body's going to change," Mu Xi said. "And she's saying Wu Zhangkong didn't do it. And she's saying she's got an eye for disciples and he's got an eye for one disciple, and neither of them had an eye for *this*, which means whatever you are isn't a thing anybody raised." She pulled a flake off the dried fish. "I've been a fourth rank five months and I've never once been a thing nobody raised."

---

## Part 3: What Wu Zhangkong Said

He said it in the smithy, because the smithy was where Lin Hao knew what he was doing, and because Wu Zhangkong had begun to understand that a thing said in the smithy landed differently from the same thing said anywhere else.

"Guide rather than oppose," he said.

"I don't follow."

"It's what I'm going to do." Wu Zhangkong turned a bar a quarter-turn on the anvil and did not look at him. "For eight months I've been correcting you, and correcting is opposing, and I've decided I've been doing the wrong thing. I'm telling you rather than letting you work it out, because you work things out fast and I'd rather say it first."

Lin Hao set the hammer down.

"You've been guiding me."

"No. I've been opposing you. I told you your blade was a servant's blade. I told you the Track was the only test I had. I said *I don't know* twice about what you are, and saying *I don't know* is opposing too — it leaves you nothing to hold." He straightened. "I'm going to stop. I'm going to guide, and I don't know how to do that yet either, and we'll work it out, and that's the first time I've said *I don't know* about something I'm going to do instead of something you are."

Lin Hao looked at him.

"That's the seventh person who's said I don't know."

"I know."

"You've said it three times yourself."

"Yes."

"I noticed."

"I know you did," Wu Zhangkong said. "That's why I said it in here."

## Part 4: What Wulin Said

They left on the ninth day.

Wulin said it on the seawall, because the seawall was where they said things, and because Lin Hao had started to understand that places carried weight and he had not used to notice which ones.

"I've been thinking about what you said," Wulin said. "About not-yet not being no."

"Yeah."

"I've decided not-yet is a thing you say when you're waiting for a reason," Wulin said, "and the reason comes after. You waited four weeks. The reason came on the fourth day and you said yes. And I want you to know I noticed you waited instead of just saying no, because that's the thing about you I understand that nobody else does."

Lin Hao looked at him.

"That's the second thing you've told me I didn't know."

"I know."

"How'd you get there."

"Because I've known you since we were three," Wulin said, "and you taught me that saying a thing is the same act as thinking it, so I thought it and then I said it, and I didn't know I was going to say it until it was out. That's twice now. I've stopped being surprised, and the not-being-surprised is the part that scares me a little, and I'm telling you that too."

Lin Hao sat down on the seawall.

"I'm glad you're coming," he said.

"That's the eleventh time."

"I know."

## Part 5: What Lin Hao Wrote

That night, in the room that smelled of the sea, he took the book down and wrote the number first, because the number never asked anything of him.

*Two hundred and eighty-one.* It had been two hundred and ninety-eight. Eight points had gone somewhere between four days of not-yet and one day of yes, and he could not say which of them had done it, and he had stopped needing to.

He looked at that sentence. He had written some version of it five times now — *I cannot say which, and it no longer matters that I can't* — and each time it had come out a little longer, and the getting-longer was the only honest part of it.

*One thousand three hundred and ninety-nine.*

*Eight years.* Eight years to the next threshold. He had written that number four times, and writing a number four times was a way of not looking at it, and this was the first time he had caught himself doing it.

Because the crossing he had been afraid of was behind him now. It had happened. One thousand one hundred and sixty-four — both rings gone purple, a third ring arrived — and he had been carrying three thousand-year rings for so long that he had started writing the number the way a man taps a pocket to check for a purse he has not actually lost. The thousand-year line was not ahead of him. He was standing on it.

Then the rest of it.

*Shen Yi says my body will change again if I have three rings by fifteen. I have three at ten. Wu Zhangkong says he didn't have an eye for this. Mu Xi says she's never once been a thing nobody raised.*

*Wu Zhangkong says he's been opposing me and is going to start guiding, and doesn't know how to do that either.*

And then the line at the bottom, which he wrote last because it was the one he had been circling all week.

*I said yes on the fourth day. The reason came after the offer. This is how most of the things that have mattered to me have happened — I have never once said yes to a thing for the reason it was offered — and that has stopped troubling me.*

He closed the book.

Then he opened it again, because there were three things in it he had not written down in a long while, and noticing that you have stopped writing something is the same skill as noticing that you have stopped looking at something, and it was the only skill he was sure he had.

*One hundred and seven. That's the ledger. I haven't written the number in a long time — longer than I've gone without any other — and it isn't that I stopped counting. It's that the number stopped being the interesting part. It used to be the whole of it. Seventy-one lines and every one an answer I could use. Now the interesting thing is that there's one person in this city I can't use the answers on, and I've stopped minding, and I don't know when I stopped.*

*The hawk hasn't asked me anything since the forest and the question is still open. I've written that before. I'm writing it again because it's the oldest open thing I have, and because every time I write it I notice I've been waiting to be asked instead of asking, and that's a thing I do, and it isn't a virtue.*

*Wulin didn't say Na'er's name today. He hasn't said it in front of me in a long time and I haven't asked, because I know where the money goes and I know what the Fridays are for, and because there's a way of asking that's a kindness and a way that's a knife, and I haven't been sure which one I'd be holding. I've been sure about a great many things this year. This isn't one of them. Not being sure hasn't stopped me doing anything, which is either growing up or being a coward, and I can't tell which yet.*

The lock at his temple lay gold across his cheekbone, and the marks on his forearms were raised and had been raised for thirty-eight days, and the hawk turned over in him — *one thousand three hundred and ninety-nine* — and did not pull toward anything.

Eight years.

Lin Hao lay on his back in a city that smelled of salt and hot metal and thought about eight years, and about the thing he had been counting toward that had already come and gone while he wasn't looking, and about the fact that he was frightened. He did not write the frightened part down. He had written *it no longer matters that I don't know* so many times it had stopped being true, and he was not going to add to the pile.

He did not sleep well.

## Part 1: The Man From Sealand

He came on the Tuesday, at half past nine, and he was polite.

That was the first thing Lin Hao noticed, and it was the thing that decided the morning for him, because he had spent four years in his father's smithy watching men who had already made up their minds pretend to be about to make up their minds, and politeness was how you could tell. A man who wanted something asked you questions. A man who had decided told you things.

The man from Sealand told them things.

He had a folder. It was thin. Lin Hao had learned in the last fortnight that a thin folder was worse than a thick one, because a thick folder meant somebody had done the work and a thin folder meant somebody had done the deciding.

"There is an irregularity," the man said.

They were standing in the yard behind the association's annex, where the tournament's leftover crates had been stacked into a wall and not yet taken away. Wu Zhangkong stood with his hands in his sleeves. He had been standing like that for eight months while Lin Hao learned where to put his feet, and Lin Hao had written down eleven things about it, and every one of the eleven meant *wait*.

"The boy's classification," the man said. "Comprehensive. It is not one of the six."

"It's on the form."

"It's on the form," the man agreed, "and it has been on file for eleven days, and in eleven days nobody at the Association has been able to tell me what it means. I have asked four people. One of them was a seventh rank." He paused. "The seventh rank laughed."

Wu Zhangkong did not move. "He wrote a word in a blank line. The blank line has been there for forty years. A girl wrote Elementalist in it before him and nobody has questioned that either."

"Elementalist is a martial soul."

"Comprehensive is a System."

"It is not one of the six."

"No," said Wu Zhangkong. "It is the seventh."

The man wrote something down. Lin Hao watched the pen and understood that the pen was not writing a definition, because the man did not have one, and that the man was writing *the teacher said so* because that was all he had, and that this was apparently how a thing became real, and that it had nothing at all to do with whether the thing was true.

Then the man folded his hands.

"The Alliance would like the file transferred," he said. "For clarity. A boy with three purple rings at ten is not an Eastsea matter. Sealand has the facilities to—"

"Sky."

The man stopped talking.

Wu Zhangkong had said it at the volume he used for a correction, the one that meant *your back foot again*, and the hawk went still in Lin Hao's chest in the particular way it went still before weather.

"Ice."

## Part 2: What Came Out Of Him

The sword went first.

Lin Hao had read that man's sword for eight months. He had never once seen it leave his hand. What happened was not the sword leaving his hand. The Skyfrost Sword went *into* him — into the middle of his chest, the way a bar goes into a fire, with no resistance at all, and Lin Hao understood halfway through the second that the sword had never been a thing the man carried.

It had been a thing the man kept outside himself so that he could stand in a classroom.

Then the light came.

Ten points of it. Forehead, shoulders, chest, elbows, wrists, hands, hips, knees, feet. Silver thread ran between them in a pattern Lin Hao read the way he read a grain, because it was the only thing he knew how to do, and the pattern was load-bearing. The thread was not on the armor. The thread was the armor holding itself up.

A crystal the colour of a winter sky came out of his forehead. A white band circled it. Five points rose into something like a crown, and two metal bands came down past his ears to cradle his cheeks, and the rest of it built itself from the neck down in about the time it takes to say the word *cold*.

Six soul rings went in.

A sword came out. A metre and a half, white hilt, snowflake at the tip, edge the blue of ice under a river. It was the same sword. It was not the same sword.

Above them, Shen Yi said, "Those fools. Now they're just provoking him. Don't they know that the calmer a person is, the more terrifying their wrath?"

And then, lower, in a voice with something in it that Lin Hao had no line for: "Now this is the real him. Sky Ice Wu Zhangkong, is back."

The man from Sealand had gone the colour of old paper. At the far end of the yard two white mechas lowered their cannons, and nobody had told them to, and Lin Hao filed that, because a machine does not lower a cannon. A man inside a machine decides something very fast.

Xie Xie went under it.

He went while it was still forming, which was either the bravest or the stupidest thing Lin Hao had ever seen him do, and Xie Xie had done a great many of both. He stood two metres beneath the faulds with his head back and one hand up, as though he could catch a piece if any came off.

"It's metal," Xie Xie said.

"Get out from under that."

"It's metal and it isn't *on* him, it's *of* him, and there isn't a seam." Xie Xie had gone quiet, which was how you knew it had landed. "Lin Hao. There isn't a seam. My father paid eleven thousand coins for a chest plate with four seams and a join under the arm that leaks when it rains. That thing up there got made out of one idea." He lowered his hand. "Every piece is thousand refined and there isn't a piece of it that isn't. Do you know how much metal that is."

"I know how much metal that is."

"You could make it."

Lin Hao didn't answer, and Xie Xie turned his head, and the grin arrived — delighted, insufferable, and entirely uninterested in whether the thing it had just announced was possible.

"I'm going to be a mecha master," Xie Xie said, "and you're going to make the metal, and I've decided that just now, standing under him, and I'm telling you out loud so you can't pretend you didn't hear it."

"I heard it."

"That's the second thing you've heard this week."

"I've heard a great many things this week."

"Not out loud," said Xie Xie. "I said out loud."

Wulin had not spoken at all.

Lin Hao looked at him, because Wulin not speaking was the loudest thing in the yard. Wulin was standing with his mouth slightly open and his hands up at chest height, holding nothing, and Lin Hao understood that Wulin had wanted to see a battle armor since he was six years old and had said so perhaps four hundred times, and that the wanting was happening, and that it had arrived too fast for him to say anything about it.

Gu Yue was two metres to Lin Hao's left.

She was looking up. Her hands hung at her sides with the fingers slightly open, which was how they sat when she was holding an element and had not decided which one.

## Part 3: Twenty Ranks

The man from Sealand said something about the Alliance's position.

Wu Zhangkong said one sentence. "You have tried to take my disciple. If he is diminished by it in any way that does not show, you will pay for the part that does not show."

That was the whole of it. The man left with his thin folder, and Lin Hao watched him go and thought the folder looked thinner than it had, and could not think how a folder could get thinner.

Shen Yi landed. The yard got quieter. She said things to Wu Zhangkong in a low voice, and Mu Chen came up the path out of breath with Duan Xuan behind him, and Duan Xuan said "a two-word battle armor master" three times to nobody in particular.

Mu Chen said nothing. He looked at Lin Hao for a long time.

Lin Hao went and stood beside him, because Mu Chen was the only person in the yard who would have a number for it.

"Tell me the ranking."

"You want the ranking."

"I want all of it."

"Four levels," Mu Chen said. "One word each. One word — every piece thousand refined, five rings minimum. Two words — spirit refined, six. Three — soul refined, seven. Four — divine refined, nine." He stopped. "Your teacher has six rings and two words. Do you know what that means."

"That he's stronger than six rings."

"A battle armor master stands twenty soul ranks above any soul master of the same soul power." Mu Chen said it the way he said everything, flat, as though reading a price. "A five-ring man in one-word armor fights like a seven-ring man. Your teacher, in that, fights like a man with eight."

Lin Hao did the arithmetic, because the arithmetic was the only thing that had ever helped him.

Six rings was sixty-one to seventy. Twenty above that was eighty-one to ninety.

"Soul Douluo," he said.

"Yes."

"He's been teaching me with six rings for eight months."

"Yes."

Lin Hao opened his mouth and then closed it, because the sentence he had been about to say — *he has never once used it* — was wrong, and the correct version was considerably worse.

He has never once needed to.

"Mu Chen."

"Hm."

"Why is there a crown. The other pieces don't have a crown."

Mu Chen was quiet for a while. "That's not a crown. That's the second word."

"And the second word is Ice."

"Sky came from the sword." Mu Chen looked at the white figure in the air above them. "Custom is you take the armor's name and put it on your own, so they called him Ice Wu Zhangkong when he was a one-word master, and Sky Ice after."

He stopped. The stop went on longer than the sentence needed, and Lin Hao recognised the shape of it, because he had heard exactly that stop in exactly that place four months ago, in front of a grave with a name on it.

"Ask somebody else about the Ice," Mu Chen said.

"I'm not going to ask anybody about the Ice."

Mu Chen turned his head and looked at him properly for the first time that morning.

"No," he said. "I suppose you're not."

## Part 4: Two Lines

He went back to the smithy, because the smithy was where he knew what he was doing, and he took the book down off the nail.

The book had one hundred and seven lines in it.

Eleven of them were about Wu Zhangkong's sword. They were there because the sword was readable — the Frost Scars had a signature, the entry angle had three variants, the wrist gave a tell at the top of the second beat — and he had used every one of them, and in eight months he had gone from being hit in nine seconds to being hit in four, and the eleven lines were the reason.

He put the pen at the end of the eleventh and wrote:

*Twelve. The sword goes into him. It does not come out of him.*

He looked at that for a while.

*I have been reading a sword that was kept outside so that he could stand in a room and teach. The eleven lines are lines about the keeping-outside. There is no line for the rest of it, and the reason is not that I have not looked hard enough.*

He turned the page, which he had never done, because he had never needed to.

*A battle armor is twenty ranks. He is six rings and two words, which is Soul Douluo, which is further than anybody I have met, and he has been correcting my back foot since the autumn.*

*I am three rings and I fight like a Soul King. That is fifteen ranks. He is twenty. We are the same shape and he is forty years further along it.*

He set the pen down on the bench and sat there with his hands on his knees.

It was not a frightening thought, which surprised him. He had expected frightening. What it actually was, sitting in a cold smithy with the smell of scale still in the rafters, was the specific relief of a man who has been told he is the only one of something and then finds out he is not.

He had spent four years being the only person he knew whose numbers did not match. Every measurement came back wrong in the same direction. Every dial went past. Every clerk stood up and leaned over a counter. He had stopped mentioning it, because there was nothing to mention it to.

And forty years up the road there was a man in a white armor with a dead woman's name stitched into it, standing twenty ranks above his own paper, teaching children where to put their feet.

Lin Hao laughed once, out loud, in an empty room, and then felt embarrassed, and then wrote it down anyway.

*He did not tell me the ceiling existed. He stood in it.*

*Yesterday in this room he said he had been opposing me and was going to start guiding me and did not know how. I think that was the how.*

## Part 5: The Seawall

She was on the seawall at the end of the day.

He sat down beside her, because he had begun to understand that this was what she did instead of saying things, and that it might also be what he did.

They didn't speak for a while. The water went on doing what the water did. Out past the third buoy a gull turned with the wind instead of against it, and he watched it do it and thought that he had watched a gull do that once before, a long time ago, in a city that smelled of hot metal, and had thought at the time it was the most efficient thing he had ever seen.

Then he said it.

He had not planned to. He found out afterwards that he had not known he was going to until the first part of it was already out, which was the third time that had happened to him in a month, and it had not stopped being frightening.

"You know I don't have a goal," he said. "Not a fixed one. Not a big one."

Gu Yue did not turn her head.

"When I awakened, my father and mother wanted me to be great. They did more than a lot for it. My mother sat up nine nights with a seam she could have sold and didn't sell. My father put a bar of Spirit Steel in my hands when I was four and didn't take it back when I dropped it eleven times." He picked at a flake of paint on the stone. "So I started on this path. Not because I wanted to be great. Because they wanted it. And I love them, and that was enough of a reason then and it's enough now."

The water went on.

"I became a blacksmith because of Wulin and my father. I started because of them." He turned his hands over and looked at them, and found he had not decided to. "It isn't that I don't enjoy it. I do. That's why I'm here. I want that part clear, because I've noticed that when people hear the first half they decide the second half for you. I enjoy it. I enjoy this. I live my life as a journey and on the journey I do the things I like doing."

"I enjoy this academy because of Wulin. And I've had better options. Three of them. I haven't told him about any of them, because sometimes he already feels like he owes me, and if I told him he'd carry it, and he carries enough. So I don't tell him. I don't tell anybody."

He turned his head.

"But I wanted to tell you."

Gu Yue was very still.

"Or I—"

He stopped.

He could not afterwards say what had been coming. He had been in the middle of a sentence and the middle of the sentence ran out, and he sat there for about two seconds with his mouth open like Wulin in the yard, and those were the longest two seconds he had ever had, and the reason he stood up was not that he had decided to.

"Nothing," he said. "I just — bye."

And then he was gone, because the Track was already under his feet and had been before he chose it, and he crossed the seawall and the lane and the whole eleven metres to the corner without travelling, and the middle part did not happen, and he understood as he went that he had learned it from her.

## Part 6: What She Did

Gu Yue sat on the seawall.

She did not move for a long time. The light went from the colour of metal to the colour of water to the colour of nothing, and the gull went out past the third buoy and came back, and the place beside her stayed warm longer than it should have.

In the last hour she had been given the whole of it.

That there was no destination. That the road had been built one piece at a time out of other people's wanting — a mother's unsold seam, a father's steel, a boy named Wulin — and that the boy beside her had walked every step of it and enjoyed every step of it and chosen none of it.

That he had had three better options and had not said so, to keep a friend from a debt he had never owed.

And *but I wanted to tell you*, which she had not been given an answer to. And *or I*, which was not a sentence.

Gu Yue looked at her own hands, because that was where she put the things she was not going to say.

In the ten months she had known him she had given him nothing. Not one element, not one ring released where he could read it, not one technique — and he had been cheerful about the blank page the entire time, which was the part she had never managed to make sense of, until the morning before dawn four months ago when she had finally taught him something and watched him take the top half off a bar at forty metres.

He had never once asked her for a reason.

She thought about the sentence he had not finished. She knew what came after *or*. She knew it the way she knew the density of a stone or the temperature of a flame, without working at it, and she had known it before he got to the word.

She did not say it.

She sat in a city that smelled of salt and hot metal, with the rest of her life in front of her and the warm place beside her going cold, and she did not say it, and she noticed — clearly, the way she noticed everything, which was the trouble with her — that not saying it was the first thing she had ever done for him that cost her anything.

Out past the third buoy, the gull turned with the wind.

## Part 7: What He Wrote

He wrote the numbers first, because the numbers did not ask anything of him.

*Two hundred and eighty-nine. One thousand four hundred and six. Thirty-six.*

Then he turned back to the page with Wu Zhangkong on it and read the two lines again, and under them he wrote a third.

*I have now learned the same lesson twice. A record of what a thing did is not a record of what a thing is. I learned it in a hall full of statues and I learned it again today in a yard, and learning the same lesson twice is not the same as learning it.*

Then he started the next line, and put the pen down, and picked it up again.

*One hundred and nine.*

*Gu Yue. I told her the whole of it and she did not say anything.*

He looked at that for a long time.

Every line in the book was about how to win. He had written one hundred and eight of them and he had never once had to think about what they were for, because the answer had always been sitting there at the top of the page like a stamp. This one was not about how to win. He did not know what it was about. He was not going to pretend.

He wrote:

*Or I—*

And stopped, and left it.

He had never left a line unfinished in that book. He thought about it with the pen hovering, and decided that a thing which stopped should be written down as a thing that stopped, and that if he finished the sentence in here the sentence would become a thing he had said, and he had not said it, and he would rather have the gap in the only honest book he owned.

Eight points today, and there had not been a fight. He had been saying for four months that the fighting was the cultivation. He had said it often enough that it stopped being something he noticed and became something he believed, and today he got eight points from standing in a yard watching a man put on his own name, and the rule was either wrong or it was not the whole of it, and he could not yet tell which.

He closed the book.

The hawk turned over in him and did not pull toward anything, and the lock at his temple lay across his cheekbone, and the marks on his forearms had been raised for forty days.

Eight years to the next ring. He wrote the number a fifth time and noticed that he had written it a fifth time and did not write anything about that.

Lin Hao lay on his back in a room that smelled of the sea and thought about a sword going into a man instead of out of him, and about twenty ranks, and about a girl on a seawall who had not said anything, and about the two seconds after *or*. He did not sleep well. He had not slept well in three nights, and the not-sleeping had a different shape each time, and he could not yet tell what the shapes meant.

## Part 1: What Was Swept

The Alliance did not apologise.

Lin Hao had waited for it the way you wait for a second thunderclap, and it did not come, and by the fourth day he understood that it was not going to. Things had been said in rooms with good carpets. The carpets had won. Somewhere in a building he would never enter there was a drawer with a thin folder in it, and the drawer was closed, and that was the whole of the apology.

The Sky Ice had been the loudest thing in Skysea City for exactly one day. By the third day it was a rumour with a picture, and by the sixth nobody was printing the picture. A hall official came to take the tournament crates away and asked them, kindly, not to stand in the lane.

Lin Hao watched the crates go and thought that news behaved like weather. It arrived, it impressed somebody, and it moved on without leaving furniture. The armor had been astounding, and astounding without follow-up sizzles away — a small episode, closed. And the five of them, the fortnight itself, went the way such displays go when the door closes behind them: a blossom from a night-blooming cactus, open in the dark, the petals withering away before dawn, and the people who missed it never quite believing the ones who saw it.

"Nobody has come to look at the crates for two days," Xu Xiaoyan said, on the last morning. "I do mornings now. I count who stops."

"And?"

"Two." She held up two fingers. "Both of them wanted the toilet."

Xie Xie had spent the last two days in the mecha bay, which was not a place students were allowed and which he had therefore entered three times, once by the roof.

"There are eleven moving parts in a white mecha's shoulder," he announced, on the walk to the carrier. "I counted from the roof. Teacher. What does a mecha master actually train?"

"Design," Wu Zhangkong said. "Machining. And a licence the army issues and can take back."

"Good," said Xie Xie. "I've decided to be difficult about all three."

Gu Yue walked with her hands in her lap, which was how she walked when she was carrying something that had no weight, and looked at the city doing its ordinary business, and did not say anything, and Lin Hao had stopped needing her to.

Wulin carried Xu Xiaoyan's bag, and Xie Xie's bag, and a crate of Gu Yue's books that nobody had asked him to carry, and he did all of it at a jog, ahead of everybody, turning back every few steps to make sure nobody had been left behind, and it occurred to Lin Hao — with the small dull shock of a thing that had always been true — that Wulin had been doing this since he was six. Carrying. Turning back. Jogging.

Wu Zhangkong saw it too.

He stood at the carrier door with his arms in his sleeves and watched the boy make his third trip for other people's luggage, and he thought: he is up before the roosters every day of his life. He has never once complained about it. He is the hardest-working child I have ever taught and the least thanked for it, and they have just finished a fortnight in which a city tried to buy him and a government tried to file him, and he is ten.

*They are still children,* Wu Zhangkong thought. *I have been demanding. Perhaps some adjustments are in order.*

He did not say it out loud. He got in the carrier, and waited for all five of them to be seated, and then he said only, "Home."

## Part 2: The President's Back Room

Mu Chen had come to Skysea three days after the tournament, looked at all of them once, confirmed that nothing was broken, and gone home. Lin Hao had known then that there would be a summons. What he had not expected was that it would include Wu Zhangkong, or that the two adults would already be mid-conversation when he came in, with tea, and a place set for him, as though he were expected to be part of whatever this was.

Which, it turned out, he was.

"I have come to discuss his future," Wu Zhangkong said.

"Which one?" Mu Chen said. "There are two of them in this city now."

"Both. But mostly this one."

On the table between the teapot and the scale-weight tin there was a piece of metal. It was the size of a man's palm, or a little smaller, and it was the colour of a river in winter, and Lin Hao looked at it for two seconds and forgot the conversation entirely.

"Weigh it," Mu Chen said.

The counter scale was on the bench by the window. Lin Hao set the piece in the pan and moved the rider.

"Three hundred and eighty grams."

"Now tell me what's wrong with it."

He picked it up. It was a scale — an armor scale, a single overlapping plate of the kind that had built itself down Wu Zhangkong's forearm in a yard in Skysea City — and it was **spirit refined**, which he knew without being told the way he knew good bread, and it had failed, and that was the strangest part, because failed metal shouts and this piece was quiet.

He turned it in the light. The grain — there was grain in it, the way there is grain in wood, except closed, running in loops that came back on themselves — the grain turned on itself, near the lower edge. Once. A hairline. A place where, in some refining he could count backwards to, the metal had decided to be two opinions instead of one.

"There," he said. "The grain folds. Twelfth refining, or near it. It closed wrong and everything after closed around the closing."

He put it down. Mu Chen looked at Wu Zhangkong.

"Eighteen men have held that piece," Mu Chen said. "In eleven years. Two of them found the fold. Both were fifth rank."

The room was quiet. The tea steamed.

"Say the rest," Wu Zhangkong said.

"Fifth rank is Master Craftsman," Mu Chen said, to Lin Hao now. "The examination is spirit refinement, and spirit refinement is the metal you are looking at and the metal that boy talked about under my armor in Skysea City. Not the hammering you know. The next thing after it. One-word battle armor is every piece thousand refined — every piece, no exceptions, a suit of it and not a horseshoe of it. Two-word is spirit refined." He turned his cup a quarter turn. "A boy in this city decided out loud, under my window, that you are going to make that metal. I have decided to find out if he was joking."

"He wasn't," Lin Hao said.

"No. He didn't strike me as a boy who jokes." Mu Chen drank. "There's a sentence I said to Duan Xuan in the spring," Mu Chen said, "about the other boy in your class. It is true of this one as well, so I am going to say it again, properly, because the first time I said it lazily." He turned his cup a quarter turn. "Duan Xuan asked me whether a boy with a soul master's talent should be spending himself on a forge at all. I told him: the foundation of a battle armor master stems from being a first-rank blacksmith. That is the whole steering of it. Convince a boy of that, and you can point him at the greatest occupation on the continent without him arriving there empty-handed."

He looked at Lin Hao.

"You have been a first-rank blacksmith since you were six. Not because you knew what you were building. Because you were small and couldn't see over the bench and kept hitting anyway." He glanced at Wu Zhangkong. "They tell me you have decided to guide rather than oppose. This is the epitome of it."

"Then I'll add my part," Wu Zhangkong said. "I am not going to tell you to take the fifth-rank examination. I am going to tell you it exists, and that the president will tell you when you are ready, and that he is harder to fool than I am."

"I put him up for the tournament when he wasn't ready," Mu Chen said, "and I'm told it went well. I don't trust it. You'll take the examination when the metal tells me you will, and not one week sooner."

Lin Hao looked at the scale on the table. Three hundred and eighty grams. The fold in the twelfth refining that two fifth ranks had missed and he had found in under a minute, because finding it was the one thing he had done in this room, the whole of his life, that needed no explaining.

"Can I borrow it," he said.

"No," Mu Chen said. Then: "Yes. One week. If you can tell me something about it in a week that I don't know, bring it back. If you can't — bring it back anyway."

On the way out, through the yard, Zhang Yangzi was on the loading dock with a manifest, because Zhang Yangzi was always on the loading dock with a manifest now, and the Association ran better for it and had not said so.

"You're back," he said.

"We're back."

"Nobody died."

"Nobody died."

"Good." He ticked something. "The east crates were wet. Tell your teacher the seal on the third one was mine."

## Part 3: The Bench

They had the members' forge in the evenings, and they had had it for a year, and this was the last evening before the term restarted, and Lin Hao wanted to hit something until it made sense.

Wulin wanted the same thing. It was one of the forty or so things they had never had to explain to each other.

They lit the lamp and put the irons in, and for a while there was nothing in the room but the two of them and two pieces of ordinary stock and the oldest rhythm either of them knew: Mang Tian's lane, the scale and quench-water, the year they were six. Wulin worked left-handed to make it fair. Lin Hao worked the way he always worked, which was too fast, and on the ninth strike his shoulder dropped and the sound went dull.

"Flat," Wulin said.

Lin Hao stopped. He turned around slowly.

"You sound like him."

"I am him," Wulin said. "Nine years of practice." He nodded at the anvil. "Again."

Lin Hao did it again, and did not go flat, and the sound came back, and something in his chest sat down that had been standing up for a fortnight.

They finished the bars and packed them and sat on the bench with the lamp down low, and Wulin said it, the way he said the real things, which was at the floor.

"I've wanted to wear one since I was six," he said. "Battle armor. Since before I knew what a soul ring cost. And on Tuesday I saw one, and it wasn't what I thought."

"What was it?"

"Metal." Wulin looked at his hands. "It was a man, but the *of-him* part was metal, and the metal was made by somebody, and every piece of it was made by somebody, and I stood under it and the only thought I had — the whole time, while Xie Xie was shouting and you were doing arithmetic — was *who made this and what did they know.*" He rubbed a thumb over an old scar. "I've wanted to wear one since I was six. I think now I want to make them. Xie Xie said it out loud so it's law, but I've been thinking it since the yard and I didn't want to say it in case saying it made it smaller."

"It won't," Lin Hao said. "I said a word on a form and it became a System. Saying things makes them bigger. That's the whole of my year."

Wulin laughed — the short one, the real one. Then he was quiet again.

"I had two commissions while you were at the tournament," he said. "Both went in the tin on Friday. And the one from the month before — I was behind on that one. It went in too."

"The whole of them?"

"The whole of both." Wulin shrugged, embarrassed by nothing, which was the most Wulin thing about him. "It's the most money I've ever moved at once. Eleven years of white ones, if you do it that way, and I don't do it that way, because she isn't a spirit soul, she's Na'er, and tins don't buy her back anyway. They find her. Somebody knows which door she went through and money opens doors in this Federation, I've checked, it's what it's *for*—"

He stopped himself. He turned his hands over.

"Sorry," he said. "Friday makes me loud."

"I know," Lin Hao said. "I do the Fridays with you. You just never noticed it's the same bench."

Wulin looked at him, and something crossed his face that had no name in either of their vocabularies, and he dealt with it the way he dealt with everything, which was by being practical at it.

"If I come out of Shrek with armor with four seams and a join under the arm that leaks when it rains—"

"You won't."

"I know," Wulin said. "But if I do — I'm going to be very good at it, and I'm going to be furious about it the entire time, and I wanted to say that now, while it's just us, in writing if possible."

"Now you've said it," Lin Hao said. "It's law."

They banked the forge and went out into a street that smelled of salt and scale, and that was the good smell, the Glorybound smell, the one that meant home had been rebuilt in a bigger city, and neither of them said anything else and neither of them needed to.

## Part 4: What Gu Yue Said

She was outside the Association when he came down the steps with the scale wrapped in cloth in his bag, and it was evening, and the lamps were coming up, and Lin Hao noted — without any surprise at all, which was itself a new thing — that she had known when he would be finished and had not told him she was coming.

They walked. That was the arrangement now, or the not-arrangement. They walked, and the walking was the conversation, and at some point one of them would talk.

"You held it for four hours," Gu Yue said, "and you didn't hit it."

It was not a question, so he did not treat it as one. "It was finished."

"Mm." Two steps. "You like things for what they do. Every day I have known you, a thing has been worth what it did. Tonight you carried a piece of metal around a city because of what it *is.*" She looked at the middle distance. "I've been waiting nine months for you to like a thing for what it is. I thought it would be a person. It was a cracked scale with a fold in it."

"It was very good metal."

"Yes," she said. "It was."

The harbour went on being the harbour. Out past the breakwater a gull turned with the wind, and she watched it do that, and he watched her watch it, and the not-talking was easy now, which frightened him more than the other kind would have.

"Line one hundred and nine," Gu Yue said.

"I know."

"Is it staying unfinished?"

"Until finishing it is true."

She nodded, once, and he understood that she had not asked in order to be answered. She had asked so that he would know she had read it, and that the reading had been kept, and that whatever the sentence had been going to be was still sitting somewhere between them with its coat on, and that she was not in any hurry about it, and — this was the part he could not have put into the book even if he had tried — neither was he.

Then she stopped walking, and gave him the truth, the way she always eventually did, flat as a scale reading.

"Wu Zhangkong is going to be gentler with you," she said. "He decided on the platform home. You didn't see it because you were watching Wulin carry bags. He's going to ease the schedule and start asking you how you are, and you are going to hate it."

"I know."

"You don't," Gu Yue said. "You've never been gentled. There's no line in that book for it. You'll want to be efficient about it, the way you're efficient about everything, and it won't work, because the entire point of it is the part you can't spend." She resumed walking. "That's all. I've been carrying that since Tuesday and it was heavy."

"Gu Yue."

She paused, half a step ahead, and did not turn around, and waited.

"The metal," he said. "When I make it — the real grade, the spirit refined. You'll be the first person who already knew I would."

She stood there for a second with her back to him and the lamps coming on along the breakwater.

"I know," she said. "I've known since the yard."

And she went, and he let her go, and did not add it to anything.

## Part 5: What Lin Hao Wrote

He wrote the number first. It never asked anything of him, and tonight he had needed that, and he had noticed himself needing it, and he wrote that down too, later, when it had stopped being true.

*Two hundred and ninety-five.*

*One thousand four hundred and twelve.*

Then he unwrapped the scale and set it on the bench under the lamp, and looked at the fold in it for a while, at the place where a refining he could count to had closed on its own opinion, and everything after had closed around the closing.

*One hundred and ten. Three hundred and eighty grams, spirit refined, failed. The fold is in the twelfth refining and I found it in under a minute, and two men past fifth rank have held this piece and missed it, and I am not telling that line to anybody except this book, because it is not a boast. It is a measurement. It is the only measurement I have ever taken of the distance between where I am standing and a road I have just been shown the whole length of.*

*Fifth rank. Master Craftsman. Spirit refinement. The foundation is the rank I started at, and I started at it when I was six and could not see over the bench, and I did not know the bench was the bottom of this particular ladder, and it was, and I have been on it the entire time.*

*Mu Chen will tell me when. Not one week sooner. That is the correct man to have guarding a door.*

He turned the page, and line one hundred and nine was on the other side of the turn, unfinished, and he let it stay there. The gap did not close. It did not widen either. It sat in the book the way it sat in him, with its coat on, and he found — and this was the thing he had not known in the morning — that a person could carry an unfinished sentence and still sleep.

He closed the book.

The hawk turned over in him, one thousand four hundred and twelve years of it, and did not pull toward anything. In the morning there would be school, and adjustments, and a teacher who was going to learn to be gentle with five children who had just spent a fortnight being treated as assets, and there would be, on his bench, a piece of failed armor that the president of the Eastsea Blacksmith's Association had trusted to nobody in eleven years and had now trusted to a boy for a week.

Three years to Shrek. He wrote nothing about the size of that, because the size of it was not a number yet. It was a road, and he had just been shown the whole length of it, and he was ten years old, and he had never in his life been so pleased to be at the bottom of something.

He slept.

## Part 1: Terms

The adjustment arrived on Monday, at six in the morning, in the yard, and none of them knew what to do with it.

They had lined up the way they always lined up. Wu Zhangkong had looked at them for a moment, and then he had asked them how they were.

Five answers. Wulin said, "Good, teacher," and kept jogging on the spot, because nobody had told him to stop and being told things was how his whole life worked. Xie Xie said, "Is this a test?" Xu Xiaoyan said, "Fine," and then heard herself, and said, "Am I allowed to be fine?" Gu Yue said, "Yes," which was a whole sentence when she wanted it to be.

Lin Hao had been warned. That was the problem. Gu Yue had told him on the breakwater, and so when the question came he had prepared an answer the way he prepared everything, which was efficiently, and the answer came out as, "Well, thank you," and the word *well* lay down in the yard and did nothing, and he stood there hating it, exactly as predicted.

Wu Zhangkong nodded once and took the morning as usual, and then ended it twenty minutes early.

The five of them stood in the loose circle they broke in, and nobody broke it. Twenty minutes is not a long time. It was longer than anything they had been given in a year.

"We can do another set," Xie Xie said.

"I know," Wu Zhangkong said.

"Then—"

"Go home, Xie Xie."

They went home slowly, the way people leave a table before the meal is finished. Xie Xie looked back twice. Xu Xiaoyan walked as though the pavement might be assessed. Wulin jogged, because it was in him to jog, and then stopped jogging, visibly embarrassed about nothing.

That evening the scale sat on his bench at home, wrapped in its cloth, and Lin Hao set his terms the way Mu Chen had set his.

Mu Chen had said: one week, and tell me something I don't know. So Lin Hao wrote the question first. He had never written a question in the book before. Numbers went first because numbers never asked anything of him, and a question was the opposite of a number, and it sat on the page looking wrong, the way a left shoe looks wrong on a right foot.

*Why is it quiet.*

Under it, in smaller writing, the way he wrote the things he did not want to find out he had known:

*Failed metal shouts. This piece doesn't. Find out which of those two facts is lying.*

---

## Part 2: The Ear

He worked at it the way he worked at everything, which was on a schedule, with instruments, in the evenings.

He hung the scale from a thread off the lamp bracket and tapped it with the handle end of a file, and made a grid on paper, and filled the grid in. Every point on the surface, tapped, noted, tapped twice. A thousand-refined piece rings true when it is good. He knew that the way he knew bread. Under the same bracket he hung one of his own finished bars and got the note he expected, and the note held, and the paper got a column it could trust.

Then the failures. He had kept his failures since he was six. They were in a crate under the bench, wrapped in paper, dated in his own hand, because even at six he had known the failures were the ones worth naming. He took the top six out and hung each of them in turn.

All six shouted.

A bad fold in a bad refining makes a sound like a cracked plate, and the sound goes everywhere, and the piece cannot hide it. That was the oldest thing he knew about metal: you cannot lie to a thread and a hammer. He hung the scale again and tapped it down every square of the grid, and the paper filled up with a word he wrote only once and then, after the fourth row, wrote as a dash because it was faster.

Nothing. Nothing. Nothing.

The fold had not taken the voice out of one place. It had taken the voice out of the piece. A flaw is local; it shouts, and the shouting is how you find it. This was not local. Whatever had gone wrong at the twelfth refining had gone wrong everywhere at once, which meant the twelfth refining had not been work done to part of the metal. It had been something done to all of it, and the all of it was still holding whatever it had been given.

Mu Xi stopped at the bench on Wednesday, on her way past with a crate of her own, and watched him tap for a while.

"You're going to sit with that all week," she said.

"He gave me a week. It would be rude to use only some of it."

She set the crate down on the end of the bench. "What is it?"

"An armor scale. Spirit refined. It failed, and it's quiet, and quiet isn't what failing does."

"Who refined it?"

"Nobody says."

"Then it isn't only metal you're listening to." She picked the crate back up. "It's whoever stopped."

She went on, and he wrote *total* in the margin beside the grid and underlined it, and then sat looking at the word, because it had a second edge and she had just handed it to him.

Broken metal shouts, because breaking is an opinion and opinions carry. This piece did not shout, and did not ring, and did not do anything at all.

*It isn't silent because it's dead,* he wrote. *Dead metal is just quiet metal. This is silent like a breath being held.*
