## Part 3: Gentled

On Thursday, theory hour, Wu Zhangkong did something none of them had a defence prepared for, because it looked like nothing. He asked them what they wanted next.

One at a time. In the register he used for attendance.

Xu Xiaoyan went first, because she sat nearest the door. "A match that starts in the morning," she said. "One. I want to walk into one in daylight with nobody arranging it for me."

He wrote it down. That was all. She had expected weight to arrive with the writing, and it did not, and she sat back as though the bench had moved.

Xie Xie said, "Machines." And then, because it was Xie Xie: "Design, machining, and the licence the army can take back. I want to be difficult about all three somewhere with a roof."

Written down, unweighed.

Wulin looked at the floor. "Make," he said. "I stood under it once, in the yard in Skysea. I want to make what it was made of."

Written down. Wulin exhaled like a man setting down a crate he had carried for a month.

"Gu Yue."

"Ask me where instead."

"Where."

"Shrek," she said, and nobody in the room could tell whether she had deflected or answered, and she looked at nobody while they failed to tell.

"Lin Hao."

"Fifth rank," he said.

And Wu Zhangkong wrote it the way a man writes a dentist appointment. No pause of the pen, no look over the page, nothing held back and nothing given. It was the kindest thing Lin Hao had ever watched him do with a pen, and it landed in Lin Hao's chest at an angle he had no shelf for, and he understood, from inside it, everything Gu Yue had said on the breakwater. He tried to be efficient about the feeling. He filed it under *adjustments* and the folder would not close, and he carried it around open for the rest of the day.

The twenty minutes kept coming back at them, too. Every morning the session ended early, and every morning somebody tried to return the time, until Friday, when Xie Xie said, "Sir, if this keeps happening I'm going to have to report the minutes as income," and Wu Zhangkong said, "Report them to your parents. It's their hour," and that was the end of the returning, because none of them had an answer for where the hour had actually come from.

Lin Hao took his share of the given time to the bench, because he took everything to the bench. He aimed the twenty minutes at the scale the way he had aimed every evening at it.

Nothing came of them. He logged the nothing. It was the first entry in the book that measured zero, and he looked at it for a long time before he let it stand.

## Part 4: The Warm Hour

Friday evening the members' forge was Wulin's. He had a commission in, a hinge run for a boat chandler, forty of them, and the tin was heavier than it had been in the autumn, and it was not heavy enough, and it was not going to be heavy enough, and he put another week in anyway, because that was the whole method of him.

So Lin Hao was not working. That was the whole of it, and it needs saying plainly because it had never once been true before: he sat on the stool by the door with the scale in his two hands, and he was not measuring anything.

They talked about the year they were six. Mang Tian's lane.

"He made us forge the day the quench-water froze," Wulin said, to the hinges.

"He said cold metal forgives nothing."

"He said we'd thank him."

"Have you?"

"Every winter." Forty.

Wulin said the hinge count under his breath the way other people say prayers, and Lin Hao held the failed scale in both hands, and his hands were warm from doing nothing, and the lamp was low, and the forge ticked.

It did not ring. Rings are struck. This came up through his palms the way a bowl comes up under a wet fingertip, one low note, somewhere near the bottom of a man's speaking voice, and it held for a second, perhaps two, and then it was gone, and the metal was as quiet as it had been for eleven years.

Lin Hao did not move. He did that on purpose, afterwards, he was proud of that: he did not move, and he did not reach for the file, and he did not say anything until the not-sound had finished being in his hands.

"Wulin."

"Hm." Forty-one.

"It spoke."

Wulin set the hinge down. He came over and looked at the scale, which lay in Lin Hao's palms looking exactly like a piece of metal, and then at Lin Hao's face, and he had known him for seven years and did not ask.

"Can it be answered?" Wulin said finally.

"Not by me. Not yet."

For one second, somewhere in that minute, Lin Hao had thought of feeding it. A thread of soul power, the smallest one he had, the way you touch a sleeper's shoulder. Spirit refinement was exactly that — the asking of metal with what a man is — and the piece was sitting there with a question sealed inside it, and he had an answer in him that wanted out.

He closed his hands around it instead, and did not.

The examination was the gated thing. The gate had a man on it, and the man had said not one week sooner, and terms are terms, and a boy who keeps a ledger knows what a kept term is worth.

That night he wrote the entry, and the entry was the strangest one in the book.

*Nine fifty-one. One second, perhaps two. Cause: nothing. I was doing nothing. Wulin was counting hinges.*

Every hour he had aimed at the piece had bought silence at full price. The one hour he had spent beside it, without meaning to, had bought the only sound it had made in eleven years.

Gu Yue had said it to him on the breakwater, flat as a scale reading. He had understood it on a bench, with warm hands, on a Friday.

The point of it was the part you couldn't spend.

---

## Part 5: What He Told Mu Chen

Saturday, nine in the morning, the back room, tea already in. Mu Chen had the counter scale out, which meant he expected the piece back weighed, and Lin Hao had weighed it at home, so they weighed it together and said the number at the same time, and it was three hundred and eighty grams, and the week had cost the metal nothing but one second of its silence.

"Tell me," Mu Chen said.

Lin Hao told him in the order he had found it, because the order was part of it.

"The fold isn't local. I hung it and tapped a grid over every square inch of it. A flaw shouts where it is; this piece is quiet everywhere, which means the twelfth refining didn't damage a spot, it stilled the whole. Whatever went in at refining twelve is still in there. It never came back out." He put the grid paper on the table. "Second. The fold is two circles crossing. Spirit refining runs in rounds; the smith asked the second question before the first was finished being answered, and the metal kept both questions, and closed on them. It isn't failed." He heard his own voice do it, drop half a register, the way it did for measurements. "It's unanswered."

Mu Chen had stopped turning his cup.

"Third," Lin Hao said. "Yesterday at nine fifty-one in the evening, in both my hands, it gave one note. One. Not struck — it came up through my palms, low, one second, perhaps two, and then quiet again. Eleven years of quiet and I got one second of it, and I got it doing nothing. Every evening I worked at it with instruments, it gave me nothing. I wrote the nothing down." He put the book on the table, open to the strangest entry.

The room held still. Somewhere in the Association a power hammer went, four floors down, slow, like a heart with a job to do.

"Show me," Mu Chen said.

"I can't. It isn't a strike. It's an hour."

Mu Chen looked at him for a moment. Then he picked the scale up off the pan and held it in both hands, and Lin Hao stood there and watched the president of the Eastsea Blacksmith's Association stand in his own back room holding a failed piece of armor with his eyes half shut, and the tea went from hot to warm in front of them, and no note came, and Mu Chen set the piece down as carefully as a sleeping thing.

"Why do you keep it?" Lin Hao asked.

Mu Chen turned his cup a quarter turn.

"Because it's quiet," he said.

He did not explain, and Lin Hao did not push, because there were locked drawers in that man the way there were locked drawers in governments, and it was not a week for picking them.

"The metal hasn't told me you're ready," Mu Chen said. "That stands. But it has talked to you, and in eleven years it has never talked to me, and I am not so old that I'll stand here and pretend that's nothing." He drank the warm tea anyway, without a face. "The fifth-rank bench runs Sunday mornings. Nine o'clock. There is a place on the floor where an apprentice stands. You will stand there. You will carry what I tell you to carry and you will touch nothing."

"For how long?"

"Until the metal tells me."

Lin Hao looked at the scale, three hundred and eighty grams of held breath, going back into its cloth, and asked the last thing at the door, because it was the only thing left.

"What do I watch for?"

"Watch what the metal is asked," Mu Chen said. "Any man can watch what a hammer does."

---

That night, in the room that smelled of the sea, he wrote the number first, because it never asked anything of him, and because after a week of questions he had needed that, and he noticed himself needing it, and wrote that down too.

*Three hundred and one.*

*One thousand four hundred and eighteen.*

The hawk turned over in him, one thousand four hundred and eighteen years of it, and did not pull toward anything.

No line for the ledger. Nothing had been adapted this week. Line one hundred and ten stayed the last line, and line one hundred and nine stayed on the far side of the page turn, unfinished, with its coat on, in no hurry, and he was in no hurry about it either, and that was Friday's other discovery, though it belonged to a different bench.

He wrote the week instead, at the bottom, in the small hand.

*One week. One second. A standing place on Sunday mornings at a bench I am not allowed to touch, and it is the best trade I have ever made.*

He closed the book. His hands still held the shape of the note, the way hands keep a weight after the weight is set down. In the morning it would be Sunday, and nine o'clock, and a place on the floor.

He slept with his hands open.

## Part 1: What Zhang Yangzi Did

The Sunday boat did not know it was Sunday, so neither did Zhang Yangzi.

He was at the loading dock at twenty to seven with the manifest board and a pencil sharpened with a knife, which was the only kind of pencil worth having. The east crates came off wet again.

"Wet again," said the freight man, who liked to be first with bad news.

"The sea does that," Zhang Yangzi said.

"The sea didn't pack them."

"No," Zhang Yangzi said, and wrote *seams* on the board, and that was the whole argument, and both of them knew it.

Little Black was asleep in the office cot, upside down, taking up the whole of it. Little Black had never once helped with a crate and Zhang Yangzi had stopped expecting it, the way you stop expecting weather to help.

The letter came with the freight, which was how the good things came now.

It was from Wang Jinxi, three pages, the big awkward handwriting that had never fitted the lines.

*The forge here is twice ours. Nobody times me. I got the arm right on the second try and the master said "acceptable," and I have learned that acceptable means he framed it in his head before I finished. Rank twenty-five, still. There is a boy in my new class who talks like Xie Xie and I do not trust him and I miss Xie Xie. Tell him the roof trick does not work here. Their roof is slate.*

Zhang Yangzi read it twice, standing between the crates with the pencil behind his ear, and then he sat down on the least wet pallet and wrote back on the back of a misprinted manifest, because paper was paper.

*East crates wet again. Your tarp man never looked at his seams either; some men are the same everywhere, that's not the city, that's the man. The seal trick you showed me holds. The dock runs. Tell your acceptable master that the boy who talks like Xie Xie is exactly what he sounds like, and tell Xie Xie himself, twice.*

He hesitated over the next part, and then wrote it anyway, because Wang Jinxi had never once needed a thing softened.

*Class zero trains mornings. I hear them from the fence some days. The little one counts sets out loud now. I don't miss being in there. I want you to know that and I want it to be true, and it is, so that's settled. Your friend, ZYZ.*

He folded it into the freight pouch going north, and hefted the next crate, and that was Zhang Yangzi's whole Sunday, and if you had asked him whether a thing had gone wrong with his life anywhere along it, he would have had to put the crate down to think. He would not have put the crate down.

## Part 2: What Xie Xie Did

There were three ways into the mecha bay and Xie Xie had used all of them, and on the fourth Sunday the bay master was waiting on the roof side with a torque wrench in her hand and no expression on her face at all.

"Roof again," she said.

"Slate," Xie Xie said. "I know a boy who says it doesn't work on slate."

"Then you know a boy who's been on a roof he shouldn't— come down the stairs like a person."

He came down the stairs like a person. She stood there looking at him, at the whole problem of him. Then she did the thing that nobody in authority had ever done to Xie Xie, which was to be practical at him.

"If you're going to be in my bay, be in it where I can see you. Hold the lamp."

He held the lamp. For two hours he held it over an open shoulder actuator while two journeymen swapped a cracked torque plate. He counted, because he could not not count. At the end, with the panel going back on and the journeymen no longer noticing him, he said it.

"There are eleven moving parts in that shoulder. Eight of them carry. What are the other three for?"

The bay master took the lamp out of his hand and looked at him over it.

"Failing," she said. "Everything fails. The three are so that when the eight are being brave about it, the machine still turns left. You skip the three because nobody ever sees them work, and then one day the army takes the licence back and it's in the paper." She set the lamp on the bench. "Who told you about licences?"

"Nobody. I asked a teacher what a mecha master trains and he said design, machining, and a licence the army issues and can take back. I've decided to be difficult about all three."

She snorted, which in a bay master is a laugh.

"Saturday," she said. "Six in the morning. Bring nothing. If you bring a tool I haven't given you, you go out the door side, not the roof side."

He walked home beside himself with it. He did not tell anybody at supper, because it was Saturday's to tell. He told the ceiling of the dormitory about it very thoroughly instead. The ceiling — he was fair about this, later, when he told the story — had held up a roof over the whole thing. Slate or otherwise.

## Part 3: What Xu Xiaoyan Did

The match was on Tuesday at nine in the morning, and it was against Wei Xiaofeng, and Wu Zhangkong had timed it for daylight on purpose, and she knew all three of those things were about her.

Wei Xiaofeng did not say anything before it, which was correct of him. He had left class zero first, on his own feet, for his own reasons, and he had never once needed the leaving explained, and he came onto the yard at nine with his hands loose and his rank twenty-six hanging off him quietly.

The starwheel was a night thing. Everybody in the yard knew it was a night thing, and Wu Zhangkong had booked the yard for nine in the morning anyway, and Xu Xiaoyan had looked at the posting board for a long moment on Monday and then copied the time onto her wrist in her small neat hand and gone to bed early.

In the dark she was a thorn-hedge with a wheel in it. In daylight she was a girl, with a staff, and a plan. The gap between the two was the assignment; she had understood that from the posting board.

She lasted three minutes and twelve seconds. She lost at the end of them, properly — put down twice, up twice, down the third. It was the best match she had ever fought, and she knew it while it was happening, which almost nobody gets to have.

Wei Xiaofeng pulled her up out of the dirt. He looked at her the way you look at work that surprised you, and then he gave her one thing, the way he did everything, on his own feet, for his own reasons.

"You kept looking at the light," he said. "The big window. You looked at it four times in the second minute. Stop looking for the light. It isn't coming to help you."

"All right," she said. "What do I look at?"

"Him." Wei Xiaofeng nodded across the yard at Wu Zhangkong and his stopwatch. "The man who booked the dark on you. He's the one telling you what you are by what he schedules."

He walked off before she could answer, which was also correct of him.

Wu Zhangkong called the time across the yard — three twelve — and wrote it down unweighed, the way he wrote everything down now, and Xu Xiaoyan stood in the ordinary daylight with dirt down one side of her and thought: *the forty seconds was a show. The three minutes is a fact. Facts are what you build with.* And then she went and washed, and was on time for theory.

## Part 4: What Gu Yue Did

The booking sheet at the Spirit Ascension Platform hall grew a dawn column this term, because the afternoons had filled up. They had filled up because in the spring a class of ten-year-olds from Eastsea Academy won a tournament in Skysea City. Everyone wanted to know whether the hall that trained them had water in it too.

The desk attendant noticed the dawn column's only regular on the third week. A small girl, hair straight as a plumb line, who booked the five-forty slot and paid in exact change and was on the platform alone, and signed the indemnity in a hand that looked printed.

"You can't have a spotter at that hour," the attendant told her, the first time, because there were rules. "Nobody's on the floor before six."

"I don't need a spotter," the girl said. "I need the clock to be the only one watching."

"What if you fall?"

"I won't be doing anything I can fall off of. I'll be doing arithmetic."

There was nothing in the rules against arithmetic."

There was nothing in the rules against a clock.

So that was Gu Yue's hour. The platform at dawn, the simulation grass grey with no sun on it yet, and six elements going off in a row like a signature she did not leave. A scorch. A frost. A wind-fret. A stain of something the cleaning crew logged as "mineral." And three and four beside them, small and exact and getting less small.

Nobody saw it. That was the entire design of it.

She had asked for Shrek in front of everyone, with a word. She had asked for the dawn with a booking. Of the two requests, the dawn was the honest one, and she knew it, and it changed nothing about the other.

Once — only once — Lin Hao was on the hall steps at six when she came off. His Sundays started at nine and his sleep had never once lasted past five-thirty. They did not stop. She came down one side of the steps' width and he went up the other. Neither of them said anything. Both of them knew the other had clocked it. It sat there between them, unspent, like everything else that mattered.

Wu Zhangkong checked the dawn column every Friday. He never signed it. He never spoke of it. The gentleness, this term, had a whole wing with no door on it, and he simply did not walk through. She had asked for the clock to be the only one watching; he could read a booking sheet. He left it alone, and considered it the hardest technique he had ever learned.

## Part 5: What Wulin Did

On Sunday the members' forge was Wulin's until noon, and the commission on the bench was a decorative gate for a chandler's wife in Skysea, forty kilograms of scrollwork, the kind of work he was bad at respecting and did anyway, because the tin did not care what he respected and neither did the city where a little girl had gone missing off a curb.

He counted strikes. That was the Sunday change, though nobody had ordered it: he used to count money on Sundays, in his head, over and over, down to the white notes. Now he counted strikes, because the strikes were the part of the arithmetic he could actually do anything about.

The letter had come on Friday. He had read it standing at the letterbox, and once more at the bench, and then folded it into the tin itself, which was where the serious papers lived.

*Dear young master Tang — I do not know if I should write, but you said in the office, if anybody ever. A girl has been at the fish market pier three Sundays now, small, by the net sheds. My wife says she is the second daughter of the Huang family that took the stall in spring. I am sorry to send a wrong one. You looked at that office like it was the last one in the world. — F. Gao, chandlery, rectifying street.*

Wrong one. Second daughter of the Huangs, at the net sheds, three Sundays, and none of them her.

He had written back the same night, and the reply had cost him one Friday's loudness to write, it was two lines, it was true, and he had posted it before he could improve it. Improving it would have been lying about the size of it:

*Thank you. Wrong is not nothing — wrong is the street checked. If you ever hear of another, I am still at this address, and I will still be for years.*

"Forty more," he told the forge at nine, which was thirty curls, and the forge, which had heard worse arithmetic from better men, said nothing.

The gate took him till eleven. Scrollwork, forty kilograms of it. He did every curl as if it were a hinge, because that was the only standard he had. The tin sat under the bench, heavier than autumn by one wrong girl and one right letter. At noon he banked the forge, and washed, and ate. He did not once say the name out loud. That was the whole of his discipline. It held. He held.

## Part 6: What Wu Zhangkong Wrote

On Saturday night, at the desk in the rooms he kept above the practice yard, Wu Zhangkong wrote a letter he had been not-writing for a month.

*Teacher,*

*I was too demanding of them. I saw it in Skysea, on a platform, watching a government not apologise and a boy carry other people's luggage like it was load-bearing. I am correcting it. I want to record that correction is harder than anything I have asked of my own body. With a sword, you are told the shape of the mistake on the day you make it. With this, you are told nothing. You only find out years on, from what the children became, and by then the instruction is over.*

*I have five of them. One has chosen machines, and I will write his Saturday letters for as long as that lasts. One runs freight better than the men I have seen run freight, and is kind without knowing it, which is the only way. One asked me for the dark. I have given it to her. I do not know yet what it is for, and I have decided that not knowing is the job. One is made entirely of carrying. And one —*

He stopped there, and sat with the pen up, for four minutes, in the room with one lamp.

*— and one has said a word on a form that I have not said to you here. When you meet him, you will understand the omission. He is already the best of them at the thing you taught me last, which I did not learn in a season.*

*I remain your student, in this as in the other thing.*

*— Wu Zhangkong*

It went out with the Monday post. The reply came on Thursday, two lines on a card, in a hand like a fencing diagram:

*Opposition I could teach you in a season. Guidance takes years, which is why nobody stays for it. You have stayed. — S.*

He put the card in the drawer with the others. The deep one. The one nobody emptied. He sat a while with his hands flat on the desk. Then he blew the lamp out, like a man putting a weight back on a scale.

## Part 7: What Lin Hao Stood

At nine on Sunday he stood on the mark Mu Chen had showed him, one pace behind the fifth-rank bench and half a pace left of the scale, hands behind his back, and watched what the metal was asked.

That was the whole of the instruction, and it was more instruction than he had ever had, because a bench where five men worked in silence asked its questions out loud. By the second Sunday he knew what the room's listening sounded like. When a pass was going to take, every man in the room went quieter a half-second before the hammer. As if the metal could be offended by talk. And when it took, the piece *rang* — one held note — and five faces did nothing at all about it. That nothing was the loudest thing on the bench.

He carried twice. The master scale moved for a consignment stock, and Mu Chen said, "Weights," and Lin Hao brought the tin, and set the weights by the pan, and went to hand the last one to the smith who had asked for it, and Mu Chen said, without turning:

"Set it down. You never hand a weight."

"Why not?" Lin Hao asked.

"Weigh your hands some Saturday," Mu Chen said, "and find out."

Lin Hao set the rest of the weights down. He thought about it for the rest of the morning. He got it on the walk home, and stopped walking for a second because of it.

Your hands are warm. A handed weight carries your hands' warm into the pan with it, and the scale reads the boy instead of the metal, and nobody down here lies to a scale, not even by accident, not even kindly.

*Set it down. Don't hand it.* It was the same sentence Mu Chen had said about the examination, and the same one Wu Zhangkong had said about the twenty minutes, and the same one the book had been saying to him all year about a sentence with its coat on. Everybody he had ever believed was telling him the same thing in different trades: the true reading has no hands on it.

That night he wrote the numbers first.

*Three hundred and seven.*

*One thousand four hundred and twenty-four.*

The ledger stayed shut. Nothing adapted, nothing defeated, nobody measured but himself and one consignment of stock that had no opinion of him.

At the bottom, in the small hand, the whole week:

*Sunday. Everybody was somewhere. It turns out a person can be somewhere too, and that is the entire entry.*

He closed the book and put out the lamp, and slept with his hands cool.

## Part 1: The Question That Came Sideways

Gu Yue asked Wulin a question at lunch on Thursday, and Wulin, who did not know it was load-bearing, delivered it to the forge that evening with the rest of his freight.

"She asked how many Sundays you've stood."

The hammer did not stop, because ten years of Mang Tian do not come off a boy in an afternoon. But the count in Lin Hao's head, the silent one under the striking one, dropped a figure.

"What did you tell her?"

"Two." Wulin turned a hinge bar with the tongs. "Then she said 'all right,' and she took my bun. She does that now. She took Xie Xie's on Tuesday and Xie Xie still hasn't said anything about it, which I find frightening in a way I have decided not to examine."

"Mm."

"She didn't ask anything else. She ate the bun and did the reading for theory and went out early." He set the bar back in the fire. "I thought you'd want it for the book. Somebody counting your Sundays."

"Whose book," Lin Hao said, mostly to the anvil.

"Yours. You count everything. I just work here."

They finished the run in the oldest rhythm either of them knew. But something had come into the room with the freight and stayed, and Lin Hao knew its name, and had known its name for longer than he was going to admit in company, and it sat on the end of the bench all evening like a fourth piece of stock, unsaleable, unreturnable, his.

Nine months of walks. A staircase crossed at six in the morning, one width apart, unspent. *She asked how many Sundays.* Not whether he was well. Not what he carried. How many. The one question that could not be asked of him without proving she had been counting.

He banked the forge badly, which had not happened in four years, and Wulin watched him do it and said nothing, which is what Wulin does with other people's loads, and Lin Hao stood in the cooling dark of the shop and understood that the sentence he had been carrying with its coat on had acquired a weight, and that weight was going to keep arriving, on freight, at intervals, until he put it down somewhere.

There was one person in the world it could be put down in front of, and he was sweeping the floor six feet away.

---

## Part 2: What Lin Hao Said

"Wulin. I want to tell you something."

Wulin stopped sweeping. He did not say "all right," and he did not lean on the broom, and he did not do any of the things a person does while waiting for a thing to arrive. He stood there the way the forge stood there: banked, hot somewhere in the middle, ready.

Lin Hao's sentences had never once jammed. At six he explained grain to a grown man. At eight he had talked a room of smiths into an ordering. At ten he had said a word onto a form and it had become a System. The machinery had never once, in his whole life, failed to deliver a sentence to its end.

"I think…" he said. "Well. I think I like Gu Yue. It's become hard for me to ignore."

The machinery had never once delivered one in that order either. *Well.* He heard himself say it and stood by it, because it was true, and true things came out in whatever shape they came out in, and this one came out crooked, with its sleeves wrong.

Wulin set the broom against the wall. Then he said the thing he had apparently been carrying in reserve, ready-made, for some time.

"I know."

"You know."

"You've never beaten her," Wulin said, "and you keep a book of everyone you've beaten. She's not in the book. There's no page for her. You walk her home on days when nothing has happened, which is most days, and you do it in the direction the wind comes from so she gets the sheltered side, and you think nobody clocks the wind. And when she talks you go quiet in a way you don't go for machines." He paused, honestly auditing it. "And you really like machines. So."

The lamp did its small work in the middle of the table. Somewhere under the floor the banked forge ticked, cooling, the way metal does when it is done deciding things.

"Does she know?"

"She reads everything," Wulin said. "If she doesn't know, it's because she's decided not to. Those are the two options and they might be the same option."

"Are you going to tell her?"

"No," Lin Hao said. Then, because the crooked order of the evening was apparently the house style now: "Not yet."

"When?"

"When it's one clean sentence."

"You say clean sentences all day."

"Not about her."

Wulin took that in with his whole body, the way he took everything in, through the shoulders. Then he did the thing only Wulin could have done, which was reach sideways into their shared seven years and come back with the exact tool, not knowing it was a tool, because to him it was just a Thursday.

"You told me about the scale," he said. "The note came when you stopped working."

"That was metal."

"You were holding it."

"Wulin—"

"I'm not good at this part," Wulin said, to the floor, which was where the real ones went. "So I'll do it the carrying way. You don't have to say it to her soon. You don't have to say it any way at all for a while. Just don't do the thing you do, where a thing that can't be measured yet gets measured anyway so it can be filed." He looked up. "Carry it. I carry things all the time. It doesn't feel like anything while it's happening. And then one day you look around and somebody's been carried the whole way. That's the whole trick. There isn't a hammer involved."

Lin Hao sat with that. The word *well* was still lying somewhere in the middle of the room where it had fallen, and he decided, in the end, to leave it there, because it had come out true.

"Say something," Wulin said, "so I know how bad that was."

"It was terrible."

"I know. I heard it happen." Wulin took up the broom again. "Do the Fridays with me this week. You'll feel normal by Monday."

They put the tools away in the order Mang Tian had beaten into them at six, which was its own kind of sentence, and that one was finished, and they went out into the salt air, and the wind came off the sea in the usual direction, and Lin Hao walked on the wrong side of it the whole way home, for the practice.

## Part 3: What Wulin Did With It

Wulin kept the secret perfectly and terribly.

Perfectly: he told nobody, and nothing in what he said at supper could have been read by anybody for anything.

Terribly: he volunteered for the drying-up. He did the drying-up at the dormitory the way he did everything, thoroughly and at a jog, and Xu Xiaoyan watched him do the inside of a bowl twice and said, "You're doing the drying-up."

"I'm doing the drying-up."

"Nobody does the drying-up."

"It's my turn."

"It has never once been anybody's turn." Xu Xiaoyan looked at him a long moment, the way she looked at posting boards, and then, because some things are not hers yet, she let it go — but she wrote it down somewhere behind her eyes, in the ledger she was starting to keep, the one with the match times in it.

Gu Yue was at the common-room table with the theory reading and the last bun, which was Xie Xie's, which Xie Xie had surrendered without a word and without eye contact, in the manner of a man paying a tax he had come to regard as weather.

"You're smiling," Gu Yue said.

"I'm not."

"You are. It's the forge one." She turned a page. "Is he all right?"

Wulin considered the shape of that for one full second — *she asks me the way I asked him, sideways, in freight* — and understood at the same moment that understanding it was not his to spend.

"He's working on something," Wulin said.

"He's always working on something."

"This one's going well."

Gu Yue looked at the page for a while without any of it going in, and then went back to the beginning of it and read it again properly, and ate the bun to the end, and none of it showed, which was the entire design of her, and later, when the dormitory was dark, she lay awake for exactly one minute longer than usual, which even the ceiling did not know about, and slept.

---

## Part 4: What Gu Yue Did Between the Third and the Fourth

At five-forty the platform was grey with no sun on it yet, and the clock was the only one watching, and that was how she had booked it, and that was what it was for.

First element. Second. Third, exact, and less small than last month.

Between the third and the fourth there was a gap. There had always been a gap; everyone has one, a place in the sequence where the intention has to be re-loaded. Hers was the length of a hall staircase, and it had been getting longer for about nine months, and she had noticed it getting longer, because she noticed everything, and she had tried, for a while, to make it shorter, the way you try to make a sentence shorter, by cutting, and cutting had not worked, because the gap was not too long. It was simply no longer empty.

She did not name what was in it. Naming was a spend, and she had never once spent early. She had a whole alphabet of things she did not say yet — had had it since the yard, since the fence, since the day the smallest boy in the intake looked at a class of martial souls and said the plain thing nobody else would say — and the alphabet was not a burden. It was a purse. You did not open a purse in the street.

The fourth element went off, exact.

The attendant, stamping her out at six, said the slot was open all winter if she wanted it, dawn didn't fill till spring. "Same slot," Gu Yue said, and paid in exact change, and went out into the actual daylight, which was not her concern, and down the steps whose width she had once shared at one remove with a boy going up, and she thought about none of it all the way to school, in the way of a person thinking about nothing on purpose, expertly, at scale.

---

## Part 5: What Lin Hao Wrote

He wrote the numbers first. That was the law of the book and the law of him, and nothing about Thursday had repealed it.

*Three hundred and thirteen.*

*One thousand four hundred and thirty.*

Then he sat with the page open at the blank after line one hundred and ten, and did not write the thing, and examined, as a smith examines a seam, why he was not writing it.

It was not fear. He had a diagnosis for fear and this did not match the symptoms. It was this: the sentence had two ends. One end was the fact of it, and that end he had put down at last, in the worst possible order, in a forge, to the right person, with the word *well* lying on the floor. The other end had a recipient, and until it could be carried to that recipient whole — one clean sentence, no arithmetic riding on it, nothing in the other hand — the book had no business holding a half. A half in the book would calcify. It would become the record. He had watched the ledger do it to a hundred and ten lines: what is written becomes what was.

*Line one hundred and nine stays unfinished,* he wrote, which was not a new line but a ruling on an old one, and therefore allowed. *Not because it is unsayable. Because the second half is a delivery, and deliveries have an address, and the address is not this book.*

He looked at that for a while. It was the cleanest sentence he had managed in two days and it had taken a forge, a broom, and the word *well* to get it.

Wulin was right about the carrying. Wulin was right about the scale. Both of those things were the same thing, and the thing was the whole year of him in one trade lesson: some pieces only speak in the warm hour, and you cannot buy the warm hour with aim, and he had a week of aim's receipts in the book to prove it.

He turned the page. Line one hundred and nine sat on the far side of the turn, unfinished, with its coat on.

One of its buttons, now, was undone.

He closed the book and put out the lamp, and slept without doing anything to the sentence at all, which was, it turned out, a full night's work.

## Part 1: The Gate Opens

It took the metal a year and four months to say yes, and it said it on a Tuesday, which Lin Hao considered typical of metal.

He had been carrying his own spirit-refined piece since spring — a chisel-length bar of closed grain, the twelfth refining asked and answered clean. On a Tuesday morning in the second winter Mu Chen turned it in the light for a long time, set it down, and said, "Saturday."

"Saturday what?"

"The examination is on Saturday. You will take it on Saturday, because the metal told me you will, and I am done being careful about it."

He passed. There is not much more to say about the passing, and Mu Chen said less than that. He took the fifth-rank stamp down from the shelf where it had sat for eleven years waiting to matter, and pressed the book. "Master Craftsman," he said. Then he ruined the ceremony in the way only he could, by being practical: "The examination was the door. The craft is the room. You are standing in the doorway of the room."

"Where do I stand in the room?"

"Nowhere, yet. Fifth rank is the licence to be bad at spirit refinement for years. That is what a licence is for."

Five years old when he started at the bench. Ten when the road was named. Eleven, almost twelve, when the stamp came down. Second-youngest Master Craftsman in the Branch's recorded ledgers. He wrote *second-youngest* in the book himself, because the record was somebody else's, and records were things you respected at exactly arm's length.

Wulin found out at supper and stood up and could not be gotten to sit down for a while.

## Part 2: What the Others Did With Their Winters

The Tang Sect took Xie Xie first.

He went in the ordinary way, the year he turned eleven — outer sect, associate, a screen and a mission list. The mecha bay's Saturdays had a ceiling and he had hit it. And the Tang Sect, he discovered, *made parts*. Not machines. Parts. The class-four catalogue had a mission that paid two hundred points for a month of filings and dimensional checks on actuator stock. Xie Xie — who had held a lamp over an open shoulder for two hours at ten and never recovered — took that mission, and every mission like it.

"Design, machining, and the licence," he said, in the spring of the first winter, at the yard. "The Sect has all three under one roof. It's disgraceful. I'm never leaving."

Xu Xiaoyan came in a year after them. Middle test, passed, inducted. Then, because her Starwheel Ice Staff was what it was, she went up the associate classes faster than any of them — class five, class four, **class three**. The Sect's clerks learned to stop being surprised by the small girl who read payout tables the way other children read dessert menus. By the third winter she was cultivating more than she was missioning. Rank **29**, peak, and holding, and the holding was on purpose: rank 30 was a door, and doors got chosen, not bumped.

Wulin ran two ledgers.

Everyone knew about the first one — the Association's, the commissions, the money, the tin. The second one lived on a Tang Sect screen and paid in points. Missions came back as metal went out; that was the whole arrangement of his life, and had been since Mang Tian's lane. In the third winter the screen's electronic voice said, over the counter, in front of everybody:

*"Three pieces of first-grade thousand-refined metal: six hundred points. Available contribution points: eight thousand four hundred and sixty-three."*

And Wulin, thirteen years old, stood at the screen and spent it nearly all. **Thousand-year Land Dragon Tendon — 3,900.** Legendary spirit medicine, refines the body, no side effects. **Thousand-year Sea Dragon Marrow — 4,500.** The same, and the qi and blood besides. He had the **Dragonscale Fruit** already — bought in Heaven Dou City three years before, on the trip with Wu Zhangkong, wrapped and kept. With the tendon and the marrow beside it, he was one item short of the set.

One item: the **Azure-veined Vine**. Under sixteen, the missions that paid enough were forbidden him. The Sect did not let its fledglings die for points — it was practically the Sect's whole personality. So the vine could wait for an auction, and the auction could wait for him.

"What's the set for?" Xie Xie asked, on the way out.

"You'll see."

"It's the seal, isn't it. The second one."

"You'll see," Wulin said, and jogged, because it was in him to jog, and the electronic voice chose that moment to clear its throat, in the manner of electronic voices, and say:

*"Tang Wulin, congratulations. You have surpassed fifteen thousand total contribution points and will now be promoted to class five."*

Class five. Before his third ring. He stood very still in front of the screen with the receipt in his hand. Xie Xie watched him do it, and had the decency — learned at the bay, at eleven — to say nothing at all.

Gu Yue did not join the Tang Sect.

This had surprised exactly nobody who had ever shared a classroom with her, and it had surprised everybody anyway. The Sect took the others; she took the **Spirit Pagoda** — a membership, a floor pass, a silence. There was a version of these three years — the one where the tournament had gone the other way, where he had been carried off that platform hurt — in which there was a reason with a wound in it: a life force spent to mend him, and a gap that opened afterward and never fully closed. **Not this one. In this one there was no wound to spend.** Class zero had won its tournament with everyone standing, and so her road into the Pagoda was not a retreat from anyone — it was the dawn slots, kept, hour after hour at five-forty, until the morning she crossed five hundred points of spiritual power and the Spirit Sea opened under her like a floor giving way to a bigger floor.

A year later she passed seven hundred, and the machine that said it had to be reset by an attendant who had never reset one before.

She told nobody the number. The others knew it anyway; these things travel, in a class of five. The custom of the class became that nobody said it. Which is the closest thing to a crown that Eastsea Academy had.

## Part 3: What the Winters Taught Him

The rank was the slow line, because the rank was gated at the rings. Everything else moved, and most of it moved through the Saturdays and the yard.

Wu Zhangkong came to the yard on the first Saturday of the first winter with nothing in his hands, which was how he carried the important things, and said, "Sit. The Sect's method. You've earned the quiet version of it."

The Mysterious Heaven Method was the Tang Sect's own way of turning breath into territory. The first lesson was four hours long and contained eleven words, which was the Sect's idea of a generous introduction. It added nothing. It removed the waste — the leak every cultivator carries in the spine, the sigh at the top of the breath, the half of every cycle that goes to noise. The same gains for less noise, and then gains on the gains, and by the second winter his cultivation had a floor under it that had not been there before — stone where there had been boards. He could feel the difference at the bench within a month: the same hammer, the same metal, and more of him arriving in the strike.

The Purple Demon Eyes came next, and they came because he was a reader.

Dawn work, at the sea horizon, in the cold half of the year, when the light comes up out of the water like something being unbolted. The discipline was simple and cruel: face the first light and do not flinch, do not blink past the burn, come back the next morning, and do it again, for years. His eyes watered for most of the first winter. Then they stopped watering. Then — the second winter — the light stopped being light and started being information.

Wulin reached the second stage at thirteen, and the whole class knew it; it was a Tang Sect thing, honored, and Wulin had earned it at the pace the Sect expects of anyone. Lin Hao reached the second stage in the second winter and the third before the fourth ring, and told nobody, and the class knew it anyway.

What they changed was the reading. When he read now, a violet light stood in the gold of his eyes — you had to be told to look for it once, and after that nobody had to be told again. He had read grain like a smith. Now he read it like weather. The seam showed sooner, showed deeper, and showed in more things — metal first, then matches, then people: where a man's weight had already decided to go before the man announced it, where a bout carried a flaw the width of a hair. Wu Zhangkong watched him watch a bout for four minutes and said, to nobody, "That's the last time that's fair."

Xu Xiaoyan asked the hawk question in the second winter, because she was the one who kept the numbers.

"It's older again," she said. The hawk was on the fence rail, mantle deep, doing its impression of architecture. "It was nine hundred and something when we were ten. What is it now?"

"Older than that."

"Rings don't do that," she said. "You take a ring at a thousand years and it is a thousand years forever. It's fixed. It's a record."

"Records don't moult," Xie Xie said, from the fence, where he had been not-pretending not to listen. "That thing has moulted twice since spring."

Wu Zhangkong had come to the fence. He looked at the hawk for a while, the way he looked at anything that kept succeeding.

"Nobody has written the book on him," he said at last. "When someone does, it will be a short book, and most of it will be measurements." He turned back to the yard. "Keep your numbers, Xu Xiaoyan. They are the only part of this that anyone will believe later."

The hawk turned its head and considered Xu Xiaoyan with one eye that had a great deal in it.

"Write it down anyway," she told herself, and did.

So the hawk aged with him, and it showed the way weather shows. The grey-brown bird they had known at nine was gone into a hawk of deep storm-slate, the feathers carrying the lightning the sword had fed them since the hawk's nine-hundredth year, so that in some lights its wings held weather in them. Each winter it sat heavier on the rail. Each winter its pressure arrived earlier: the yard dogs stopped coming near the fence in the first winter; the journeymen stopped offering to spar under its flight line in the second; by the third, when it crossed the yard, bouts paused the way conversations pause for thunder. And the marks on his forearms deepened in step with it, the raised lines edging a shade further each winter — one ladder, climbed from two sides. Gu Yue watched the hawk the way she watched everything that kept growing: without comment, without blinking, and as if filing something.

The hammer art came from the Sect too, and it came for the smith, not the swordsman: the Disorder Splitting Wind Hammer, the inner sect's rhythm, forging and fighting in the same motion, a thing no book could teach because the book would lie about when to breathe. He learned it as the Sect teaches it, with a hammer and an audience of one, on Saturday mornings, until the rhythm stopped being a thing he kept and became a thing he was. It rearranged his benchwork inside a season — the same strikes he had made for six years, all of them suddenly in time with one another, and with him — and spirit refinement bent toward him after that, the way wood bends toward the year's light.

The first time the rhythm crossed over — the bench's cadence arriving whole inside a bout, strike and step and strike with no seam between the two skills — Wu Zhangkong said nothing at all. The next Saturday the yardwork was hammer forms for both of them, master and student, two hammers, one rhythm, and the frost never settled on that grass.

His own style grew its sixth stroke in the third winter, and it was born at the bench, on an afternoon he would keep for the rest of his life, out of the quiet scale's old lesson.

It was the nothing hour — the forge banked, the light going, the shop full of the tick of cooling metal — and he was not working, only standing. A bead of quench-water ran down the hammer's cheek and hung at the corner of the peen and would not fall. He watched it gather and not fall. Everything in the shop was loud: the tick, the sea, his own blood. The bead hung in the middle of all of it, being still.

He did not strike it. He understood, in a way that arrived finished, that every stroke he owned was a question — five kinds of asking, five winds before the blow — and that there was room in the style for a stroke that was not a question. A stroke that waited until the opponent had already answered. Answered what? Anything. A feint, a habit, a fear, a question nobody had asked. Everyone answers something. The stroke lived in the instant after the answering, and nowhere else.

The bead fell. He moved the hammer through the place where it had been, slow, and the air did not move at all.

Still Water. A stroke with no wind before it. He wrote it into the book without explanation, because he had none, and Mu Chen read the page and said, "That one isn't a sword's. Keep it anyway."

And the body was the headline, because the body had always been the truth of him. Adaptation goes to the body the way rain goes to ground. Seven years of hammer and anvil. The hawk's vitality, banked into his blood a year at a time. The Sect's method refining all of it. The Association measured him every midwinter — the same machines, the same clerk, the same small room with its one mirror, which nobody was supposed to use for anything and everybody used for everything.

He was ten the first time, then eleven, then twelve, then thirteen: fist 2,612 at ten; 2,940 at eleven; 3,215 at twelve; 3,436 at thirteen — under the dragon claw's famous number, and climbing, and the clerk initialed each line the way clerks initial weather. But it was the mirror that kept the true ledger. Each winter the boy in it was less boy. At eleven his shoulders had gone first, the smith's build arriving years before his voice had decided anything. At twelve the last of the round went out of his face and the jaw came in, and the hawk-gold at his temple — the color of the sword — had deepened past fashion and into fact. At thirteen he stood at the glass and saw what strangers had been seeing for months: a youth the eye read as two years older than the register, tall for his age and heavier through the chest and arm than tall accounts for, with a stillness that was not slowness, marks on his forearms like weather systems, and eyes that noticed you noticing them.

"Height," the clerk said, the third winter, reading off the rod. "Up again. You'll want to tell your tailor. Or your teacher."

"He cuts the practice swords down himself," Lin Hao said. "He's done it twice."

The clerk looked at him — sixteen in the face, thirteen in the book — and wrote thirteen, and underlined it, as though the underline would help.

The class noticed the way families notice, which is late, and then all at once. Wulin's version was to lay his own arm alongside Lin Hao's at the bench one day, consider the difference in the forearms with the gravity of a man reading scales, and deliver his verdict: "This is offensive. You know that? This is offensive to smiths." Xie Xie's version was worse, because it was public. He presented Lin Hao to the yard, side-on, with the sweep of a man showing prize livestock: "One of those. He's going to be one of those whose face is a personality. I said it first — remember I said it first." And Mu Xi, at the members' forge, said nothing at all. She moved the second apron up the peg row two holes one Friday, without comment — that wall keeps every smith's apron at the shoulder of whoever it serves, a row of heights pretending to be storage, and his had climbed past where it hung — and being Mu Xi, she adjusted the equipment and told no one what the adjustment measured.

The lines no machine weighed moved too. The walks kept their day, all three winters, unspent, one button. Fridays kept theirs. Mu Chen's bench got a sixth chair that nobody called anything. Four letters went north and four came south. And the cards from Shen Yi came quarterly, two lines each, until Wu Zhangkong's correspondence became, without anyone naming it, the longest conversation of his life.

## Part 4: The Wall at Forty

Lin Hao's winters were Sundays, and the Sundays were a room with five men in it, and by the third winter he was the sixth.

Not a boy who stood and carried. A smith. Fifth-rank work has a bench and the bench had a place, and the place was his, and Mu Chen never said so out loud, which was how it was said. He learned spirit refinement the way the room taught it: by watching what the metal was asked, for two winters, before he was allowed to ask it anything himself. The asking, when it came, was smaller than he had spent three years imagining. A thread of what a man is, laid along grain that is already willing, and then the ordinary hammer, and then the note.

The note. His first one — his own, out of his own bar — rang for four seconds and set itself in his hands like a bird landing, and five men who had worked in silence for years said nothing about it in voices he could hear for a week.

The rest of the lines moved the way lines move when a person is ten, then eleven, then twelve, then thirteen, and everything he does is cultivation he keeps. The rank climbed — **37, 38, 39**, each one entered with its cause named — and the ledger thickened. Fifty-four lines in three winters. Most of them were Saturdays' work, floor bouts with journeymen who wanted to know whether the Master Craftsman was anything at the anvil besides a stamp. Two were Tang Sect mission escorts, a winter apart. One, entered in different ink, was a boy from the intermediate academy who had read about the tournament and did not believe it, and believed it. Line **164**.

And then, in the spring of the thirteenth year, the rank stopped, and it stopped the way a corridor stops: at a wall, with a door in it.

**Rank 40.** The ceiling of three purple rings. Beyond the door was a fourth ring, and the law of what he was left nothing to negotiate with: *ten thousand years, and not one year under.* A ten-thousand-year soul ring was black. Black rings belonged to soul masters of fifty and sixty. And the law of him — the monster law, the one Wu Zhangkong had said out loud in a Hall of Heroes with the displays running — did not care what belonged to whom.

He stood at the bench with the book open and did not write for a while.

*Rank forty,* he wrote, finally. *The door is a ring, the ring is black, and what waits behind it has been waiting since I was nine. Next time I write in this book I will be on the other side of a month that changes everything, or I will be able to say why not. Those are the terms. They have always been the terms.*

He showed the page to no one. He did show the wall to Wu Zhangkong, at the yard, on a Thursday, by saying, "Forty."

Wu Zhangkong looked at him for a long moment, and there was something in the look that Lin Hao had never had directed at him before, and it took him most of the afternoon to name it. Not pride. Not the assessment. **Appetite.** His teacher wanted to see what came through that door the way a man wants to see a coast.

"Say it," Lin Hao said.

"I was going to wait until you were fourteen," Wu Zhangkong said. "So was the calendar. Neither of us is going to get the chance."

## Part 5: The President's Office

The conversation that decided everything happened without Lin Hao in the room, which was fitting, because most of the important ones had.

Eastsea Academy's president was a patient man named Yu Zhen, and for three years his school had drunk the attendance that Wu Zhangkong's name poured into it — a battle armor master, teaching, at an intermediate academy; the Skysea Alliance had never quite gotten over it — and for three years Yu Zhen had asked for nothing, and now Wu Zhangkong had come to his office and asked for something first, and Yu Zhen's brow was creased before the door shut.

"Teacher Wu, are you sure about this?"

"From the academy's perspective, raising outstanding students who achieve great things is the highest priority," Wu Zhangkong said. "We have been nourishing class zero for three and a half years. Don't you want them to contribute? Being admitted to that academy is a better achievement than anything else. The academy can announce it. Many will be drawn here."

"Isn't it too early?"

"Shrek Academy only holds its entrance exams once every three years. They're already thirteen. If they don't go now, they'll miss their only chance."

Yu Zhen frowned, and played the card he had been holding for three years face down, the way patient men do. "But didn't you come from Shrek Academy, Teacher Wu? In my opinion, you should be more than enough to teach them."

The room went still in the specific way that room did.

"I can, to a degree," Wu Zhangkong said. "Only that much. They need a proper foundation laid down for the future. What I can give them ends."

"The future? Teacher Wu — how high can they reach?"

And Wu Zhangkong, without any doubt in his voice at all:

"Battle armor master."

Yu Zhen stood up. Sweat arrived on him in the honest way it arrives on a man doing arithmetic about giants. He breathed in, and breathed out, and made the only request of Wu Zhangkong he had ever made:

"Then I ask one thing. When they are — that — have them come back and give a talk. To our students. One talk."

"They'll give it," Wu Zhangkong said. "I'll promise it in their stead."

He did not answer the other question, the one from three years back, the one Yu Zhen had never actually asked out loud because he knew the answer would be engraved somewhere he couldn't read it. *Will you return?*

The answer was in the corridor he walked on the way out. It had been engraved for years. If his students made it in, the odds of his return were minute — and he had never once, in three winters, tried to raise them.

## Part 1: The Last Exam

The exam was survival, and the reward was announced in the yard with the whole class lined up.

"Your reward will either be a duel with me," Wu Zhangkong said, "or a spar against the other three. Your choice."

"Teacher Wu, don't be so heartless," Xie Xie said.

The rebellion platform took them at noon. It had taken them at noon for three years, and it held no pressure for them at all any more, so they went deep, because that was what the exam was actually for and Wu Zhangkong had stopped pretending it was about anything else. The lions found them first — a pride, a king at the thousand-year mark — and Xie Xie said the thing he always said now, the house prayer of class zero: "I still remember that time they slaughtered us. It's our turn now." It was their turn. That took an evening.

Deeper, the forest went dark at noon. The canopy shut. Gu Yue's wind birds came back to her hand blind.

"Every level of the spirit ascension platform is connected," she said, low. "This is Pagoda information, so hear it once. A powerful soul beast guards the barrier between levels. Only after defeating it can we cross over. Very few people ever have."

"And the platform isn't a true illusory world," she went on. "It's a mix of illusions and reality. Remember that. It matters later."

Lin Hao, at the back, said nothing. He had been at the back for a week, because the wall in him had come down to the last door and everything on the far side of the last door was listening, and the class had learned to let him be where he was.

## Part 2: The Bear

The guardian of the elementary level came at them out of the dark-gold light, and it was a Duskgold Dreadclaw Bear, and in the ordinary way of things no one with less than five rings should have been able to kill it.

The class zero of three years did not fight in the ordinary way of things.

It began with a nick. The bear's claw met Tang Wulin's claw and came away with a flaw the width of a hair, and the forest rang with its outrage — and the flaw had not been luck. Lin Hao had gone still at the start, the way he went still, and read the bear's golden light the way he read grain, and the light had a seam, because everything has a seam, because everything fails; the three parts exist so the eight can be brave about it, and he had said so once on a roof, at ten, about a machine.

"There," he had said, and pointed, and Wulin had put the whole fight after that through the place Lin Hao's finger had been.

Even so, the bear nearly took him. It ignored everyone — icicles, fire, three Xie Xies — and charged Wulin like a small mountain with a grievance, and in the half-second when the dark-gold light had Wulin's soul power too frenzied to answer, Xie Xie was there instead, and the bear's claw went through him, and he came apart protecting his captain with his last breath and his eyes saying the only thing they ever said at moments like that: *avenge me.*

Wulin avenged him. Gu Yue's four elements came down as one column of light — blue, red, yellow, green, four fused into one — and Wulin went up it, and the final strike opened the bear's neck to the bone.

The soul bone appeared where it fell, real, dark-gold, humming.

"Since a soul bone appeared," Gu Yue said quietly, "that means the beast we just killed was a spirit ascension platform guardian. Each level has one. The Pagoda builds them stronger than anything else on the level, and it costs — energy, and something real to build around. The true reward for killing it is the soul bone. You can't bring it outside the platform. You fuse with it here, or not at all."

"Wulin," she said. "It's a right-claw bone. External. It will complement the thing you already carry. Nobody else here can hold it — the rest of us would be devoured."

Wulin fused with it there, in the dark of the heart-forest, while Xie Xie's borrowed body reassembled itself nearby and complained. The change was invisible for an hour. Then his claw tipped itself in dark-gold, once, and five streaks of it cut the air a metre past his hand — and a third of his soul power went with them.

"Expensive," Wulin said, flexing.

"Everything worth having is," said Gu Yue.

## Part 3: The Barrier

They could have left. The exam was won, the bear was dead, the reward was fused. The exit was an hour south.

They went north, to the barrier, because class zero had never once in its life taken the south exit, and because Xie Xie said "it's our turn" about things older than lions, and because of the five of them, one had been standing at a wall for a week with his ear against it.

The barrier between the elementary level and the intermediate did not look like a door. It looked like a wall of winter — frost on the air itself, a seam of cold running floor to canopy, and cold water moving under the frost, uphill, in a current that had no riverbed.

The guardian came through it without hurry.

It was long as a lane and narrow as a blade, a dragon jiao of the deep-water kind, ice and water in it together, ten thousand years of patience wearing a body. The frost of the barrier was its hem. It looked at the five of them the way winter looks at a lit window.

"Lin Hao," Wu Zhangkong said — for the teacher was there; the platform allowed the attending master, and he had come, because he had known since the yard what his student was carrying — "terms."

"It's mine," Lin Hao said. "The class holds the edges. Nobody crosses the hem."

The fight lasted eleven minutes and cost him everything he had.

Not the Union — that door stays shut; it is the one thing it is for later. He spent the hawk to embers, and the hawk gave until giving was all it was, two and a half thousand years of storm poured out as talons, as wind, as the flat crack of pressure that had ended a hundred and sixty-four lines. Once, near the end, the Talon met the hem of the barrier's cold and came back from it black-edged — storm carrying winter in its teeth, the adaptation doing what adaptation does, mid-fight, without asking anyone. He spent the Track until it was not movement but habit. He used all five strokes, and the Unwritten Stroke twice, and the third time the jiao's tail took him across the clearing and broke his left arm against a tree, and he got up with the arm hanging and read the seam, because everything fails, and the dragon's seam was where the ice believed the water.

The four held the edges. Gu Yue's elements pulled the frost off him twice. Xiaoyan's ice wheel turned the tail once. Xie Xie bled in three places and stayed. Wulin caught him once, out of the air, and put him back inside the hem.

The sword went in at the seam, to the hilt, through ice that had never in ten thousand years been argued with.

The jiao did not scream. It unwound — all of it, the whole length of the lane of it — into water, and the water stood still, and in the still water there was a core.

It was not a soul bone. It was a spirit soul — a true one, ten-thousand-year, the real thing the Pagoda had built its intermediate guardian around, ice and water braided into a single coiled point of light, hanging in the empty air where the barrier's cold had been.

"It can't leave," Gu Yue said. Her voice had gone very flat, which was her awe. "Platform law. Whatever the guardian was built around, fuses here or is lost. That's the rule. It's the same rule as the bone."

"I know the rule," Lin Hao said. "I've been standing at the door of this rule since I was nine."

He looked at the class. Wulin, holding his own closed side. Xie Xie, bleeding and grinning. Xiaoyan, small and steady. Gu Yue, whom no element had ever surprised, surprised.

"You're the second person who already knew I would," he said — to her, only to her — and put his hand into the light.

## Part 4: The Month

The month belongs to the others. That is the law of what he is: the absorption takes him wholly, and the world does not pause its clock, and canon — the world's own record — goes on without him. The month still had weather in it, and mornings, and errands. The stations were lived, not listed:

Xu Xiaoyan crossed rank 30 on the ninth day, at dawn, alone in the yard, in frost, with her staff planted and her breath going up in the flat columns that mean a soul is moving house. She stood a long while at her own wall with her own door in it, and then she went in to breakfast and ate everything and began reading — everything the Pagoda library would lend a class-three associate on second spirit souls, which proved to be eleven pages and a footnote. So she wrote to the library, and the library wrote back, and by the twentieth day there were parcels. On the tenth day she was rank 30 and two rings and a question, and she carried the question like a lamp.

The Azure-veined Vine came up at auction on the twelfth day, in a room that smelled of other people's coats. The tin — four years deep, both boys' commissions — was finally deep enough, and Wulin sat very still through two lots he did not want while the number climbed, and put his paddle up once, and once was the whole story. He bought it, wrapped it in the cloth he had carried ready for a month, and set it beside the tendon, the marrow, and the fruit. Four items. One set. Complete, and waiting, because a seal breaks on purpose and fourteen was coming and not yet.

Xie Xie filed his apprentice papers at the Association on the fifteenth: first-rank mecha craftsman, candidate. The clerk read the sponsor line twice, because sponsors are usually asked first. The bay master had signed it without being asked, and when Xie Xie went to thank her she said, "Bring nothing," which was the highest thing she knew how to say.

Gu Yue kept the 5:40 slots. All thirty-one mornings. She did not say his name at the platform and did not need to; the elements went off in their row, exact — water, ice, fire, wind, in the order that is hardest — and the gap between the third element and the fourth held whatever it held, and she booked the next morning, and the next. On the seventeenth morning the attendant on duty left the row to her entirely and went to stand at the far end of the hall, which at that facility counted as a ceremony.

Zhang Yangzi ran the dock. A letter crossed the city line north: *the little one made rank 30. The other little one is asleep for a month and nobody will say at what. The sea is the sea. — ZYZ.*

And the hawk did not perch anywhere that month. That was the strange one, for anyone who knew where to look: the rail outside the yard stood empty, and the bird that had owned it was nowhere in the city — because it was in the room, in him, in the deep water where he was. A spirit is part of the whole man; where he goes, it goes; what feeds him, feeds it. What that meant, the city found out on the thirty-first day.

Wu Zhangkong taught the four, and on every one of the thirty-one days he stood for the last hour of the afternoon outside the room where Lin Hao's body slept and its soul was elsewhere, doing what the yard could not see, which was nothing at all, on purpose, an hour of nothing, stationed. On the thirtieth day Shen Yi's card arrived, two lines: *You said the calendar would decide. It has. Bring me the story. — S.*

And Mu Chen came twice, looked at the sleeping boy the way he looked at metal, and said nothing either time, and left the door ajar, because drafts matter to things that are changing.

## Part 5: Day Thirty-One

He woke at dawn and the room was fogged — every surface beaded, the window white — and he was lying in frost that was not cold to him, and the first breath he took came out of him as a slow drift of white that fell, instead of rising.

The class was in the doorway. They had felt it in the yard, all of them, the way you feel a door open somewhere in a house in winter.

Lin Hao stood, and the room stood with him — the frost sliding off the walls in a sheet, the air going still and clear and deep, the hem of something vast settling into the floorboards and stopping politely at the threshold. That was the domain, and it would never fully close again; it would only ever be folded.

The sword came to his hand, and it was not the sword he had carried at ten, or at thirteen, or for one minute at the barrier. The storm was still in it — the wind and the lightning, the whole loud first act of his life — but under the storm now there was deep water, and under the water there was ice, and the ice went down a very long way. The blade had gone blue-black at the core the way winter rivers do, and it rang, when he turned it, with a note that was low and new.

"Frost Abyss," he said, and did not know he was going to, and knew immediately that it was right. The name had been waiting in the metal the way a seam waits.

The pressure came next, uninvited: the fourth ring's skill pouring one breath of itself into the room, and the class — rank 30 and 33 and 28 and 31, veterans of a hundred platform hours — all stepped back, all at once, without deciding to. Domineer. He pulled it back in like a hand closing, and apologised with his eyes, and they unfroze.

Then Wulin did the thing that mattered. He looked at his best friend's face and did not know him for one full second — because the boy on the bed was older, sixteenish, jaw cut, eyes gone still and deep — and then he did know him, and his face did several things in a row and finished on the verge of tears he was too old for and did not care.

"You grew," Wulin said, ruined.

"Some," Lin Hao said. His own voice had a new floor in it.

Gu Yue had not stepped back with the others. She had stepped forward, inside the hem, into the domain, the only one — the cold slid around her like a river around a stone it had known all its life — and she looked at the almost-sixteen face with its new stillness and said, flat as a scale reading, in front of everyone:

"You're late. Thirty-one days, not thirty."

And that was her whole speech, and it was in different ink, and it went into him deeper than the ring had.

Xie Xie looked at him for a long moment and then addressed the ceiling. "He comes out of a month asleep looking like his own older brother. I hope everyone is taking this as seriously as I am."

Xu Xiaoyan said nothing at all. She wrote a number in the new notebook, boxed it, and showed the page to no one, and the number had nothing to do with rank.

The window was still fogged from the waking, and it made a mirror of itself, and the mirror showed him the month's other work. The third winter's boy had gone into the water, and a young man had come up out of it: height he had not earned by waiting, weight through the chest and arm that he had, the marks on his forearms gone blue-black at the edges the way winter rivers go, the hawk-gold at his temples carrying a colder thread now, like light through ice. He looked, as the clerk used to say, sixteen in the face. It had stopped being a saying. It was a measurement.

They went to the Association that same morning, because affection, in class zero, was measured in kilograms.

The punch machine's ceiling was five thousand. It had been the ceiling for forty years, and the number everybody knew was three thousand nine hundred and ninety-eight — a dragon claw's, set at nine. Lin Hao put his bare fist on the plate, unhurried, and the needle went up through his old floor like a rumour, through the dragon claw's number without pausing for it, and stopped. Not at anything in him. At the machine's end of numbers.

The attendant wrote 5,000+ in the log and looked at the boy the way the Hall of Heroes had once looked at him, which is to say: it ran out.

The arm told the rest. The jiao had broken it on the eleventh minute; the month had set it in the first week; and the last week had done what no splint does — finished the deep work, the mending going the whole way to new, the deep water seeing to its own, as deep water does. Cold could not find him either. He had stood in his own frost and felt it as furniture.

The hawk came out at the yard, when they walked him out into the morning, and the yard learned what the month had done to the other half of him. It landed on his arm heavier than it had ever been, and its feathers had changed: the deep storm-slate gone dark at the edges, every feather tipped in the blue-black of winter rivers, so that folded it looked like weather and spread it looked like the inside of the cold. It had spent the month where he had spent it, fed on what he was fed; the adaptation does not distinguish between the man and what is joined to him. The bird that had gone into the water was not the bird that came out. One ladder, climbed from two sides — and the class, who had heard the teacher say it at the fence a year before, stood in the yard and watched the second side arrive.

The Unwritten Stroke had changed register as well. What had worked because it did not exist now also did not exist in the cold, and he did not know yet what that meant, so it went into the book as a question. The book was getting more questions in it. He considered that healthy, at thirteen, and did not examine it further.

And the clerk, having written 5,000+, pulled a requisition form on her own initiative: the Association would be commissioning a machine with a higher ceiling, and she wanted her name on the order.

The book, that night: rank 45. Spiritual power 2,705. Hawk 3,055 — a month of embers, regrown in deep water, and it came out of the water dressed for it. Line 165, in different ink: *the guardian of the intermediate level, ten thousand years, ice and water, defeated at the seam. My arm has mended. The sword has a new name and so do I, a little.* And line one hundred and nine, on the far side of the page turn, unfinished, coat on, one button undone, unspent — some things do not change when everything else does.

Wu Zhangkong came at the end, and looked, for a long time, at what his student had become, and there was appetite in it still, and something quieter under the appetite that he did not say.

"The reward stands," he said. "A duel with me. When you can hold a sword."

"Sir," Lin Hao said. "Next month."

"Next month," Wu Zhangkong agreed, and left, and did not smile where anyone could use it against him.

He was thirteen. The wall was behind him. The road had turned to ice and kept going.
