## Part 1: The Longer Reach

The month after the emergence was the strangest of his life, because for the first nine days of it the new body outran its own arithmetic.

Everything he knew about his own body had been measured to a smaller man. His strokes were cut to a shorter reach. His steps were tuned to a lighter weight. The bench itself was wrong, and Mu Chen, who had watched him reach past the old pegs twice in a week, raised it two holes on a Tuesday without a word, the way an apron peg had once been moved up the row without a word, and said only, at supper: "The tool follows the hand. The hand changed."

The city itself did not know what to file him under. A butcher's wife called him *young man* and gave him the adult portion. The clerk at the Association, checking the register against the face for the third winter running, underlined *thirteen* harder, as though the pen could win.

The yard unlearned him too. Xie Xie, who had lost to him for four years, won the first three mornings outright — speed against a body that did not know its own dimensions yet — and was insufferable about it in three languages of eyebrow. Then the new reach arrived in his friend's shoulders, and Xie Xie won nothing after that, and stopped mentioning the three mornings, mostly.

Xu Xiaoyan brought the notebook to recalibration and made him do everything twice. Reach, twice. Step, twice. The Talon, three times, because the black edge had changed its weight as well as its color. One page of the notebook was only him now, times and distances in the small neat hand, and she guarded that page the way other people guard letters.

The Talon was the month's honest fright. He called it the old way, out of habit, on the second morning — the same word, the same want — and what arrived was not the skill he had called. The Gale Talon he had measured for two years had come back from every ring heavier; this one fell out of the black edge like weather closing a road. Xiaoyan's notebook caught it — forty paces of scarred frost where the old skill had ever marked nine — and made him do it twice more, because numbers that move that far are not mistakes. They are announcements. He sat with the arithmetic that night and found the reason where he should have looked first: nothing between the rings and the body argues. A perfect pairing wastes nothing — the skill comes through whole, the way a quench takes the entire bar and not the skin. What the ring was now, the skill was.

The cost had come through whole as well. The old Talon spent a breath and returned it; the new one took the breath and part of the next one, and he wrote the times in the book like prices. Nothing he owned was free anymore. Even the Union had filed its report without being opened: the hawk against his arm in the evenings was a season deeper, and the bond priced its own arithmetic — the trump card had grown with everything else, and the day it was spent it would bill its new size. He wrote that down like the others and did not open the door to check. Some prices you take on trust; the reserved ones especially.

Wulin sparred him the honest way, claw against sword, no quarter for old friendship, and came away shaking his head. "You're re-learning to be taller than me," he said. "I hate it. I'm thrilled. I hate it."

"The body is new," Gu Yue said, when her turn came, and she refused from the first minute to adapt to the new him — the elements arrived at the old timings, on the old lines, and punished every stroke that apologized for its own reach. "The readings are not new. Again." She rebuilt him in five mornings. She did this for no stated reason and stated none, in accordance with the customs of the class.

The sword was its own lesson, and the lesson was that nothing had been lost and everything had grown. The Frost Abyss balanced nothing like the Stormbringer had; the storm wanted the point, the deep water wanted the edge, and for a week every draw came out twice as large as it had been asked — the lightning coming down heavier than it had ever come, riding the storm and the water together, arriving in places he had not sent it. That was the month's real work: not searching for anything gone, but learning to hold what had arrived. Four elements now — wind, lightning, water, ice — and under the four, the fifth thing, which was not an element at all but the body they all lived in: the iron. The sword's own metal. The storm had never once been carried by air; it had been carried by iron, fused in, and the iron had been evolving since the day it fused — that was what his martial soul was. A fusion that grows. It took each new element the way iron takes a quench, and it had been doing so since he was small, which was why the blade had never once been the same sword for a whole year together. Seven years at the bench meant he knew metal as well as he knew weather, and the blade in his hands was metal he knew, all the way down. The morning the draw came out all one motion — wind, lightning, water, ice, and the iron under them, one animal — the hawk on his arm crooned once, and he wrote a line in the book that was not a ledger line: *the sword and I are introducing ourselves.*

The hawk rode his arm in the evenings while the winter-tipped feathers settled, its pressure a full season deeper than the bird the class had known in the spring, and the yard learned the new pressure the way it learned all its weather: by adjusting, and saying nothing.

Wu Zhangkong watched three Saturdays of it and issued exactly one correction for the month. "You are apologizing to the reach," he said. "Stop. The reach is not borrowed. It was paid for. Spend it."

By the fourth Saturday he was himself again at the new size, and then better than himself, and then it was the morning of the duel, and he was standing at the fence opposite his teacher with everything recalibrated and nothing left to practice — which is the condition Wu Zhangkong had been waiting for.

## Part 2: Terms

The whole class was at the fence, and Mu Chen was there with tea, which meant the Association had closed for the morning, which had happened four times in eleven years.

Xu Xiaoyan had brought the notebook. It was new since the winter — match times, opponents, conditions, light — and she opened it to a fresh page and wrote the date and *Yard, 7 a.m., overcast* in her small neat hand, because a measurement you did not write down had not happened. Mu Chen had the tea in the tall cup with the chip on the rim, the one he had carried to finals and funerals, and he held it with both hands, which was how he watched things he could not referee. Wulin's hands were flat on the top wire. He had not spoken since breakfast. The hawk in Lin Hao turned over once, felt the yard, and went still, which it only did before weather.

"Terms?" Lin Hao said.

"None." Wu Zhangkong set his sword down on the bench, which was the terms. "Come at me as though I am the barrier."

The yard was theirs. The morning was cold already, ordinary cold, sea cold. Lin Hao unfolded the domain.

It went out of him like a sheet lifted off a table. Frost ran the fence at ankle height and climbed. The puddles went white. The class's breath arrived all at once, four clouds at the wire, and Xie Xie said, quietly, in the manner of a man updating his files, "It got bigger."

## Part 3: The Boy

Wu Zhangkong walked in.

Unarmored, in shirt sleeves, hands loose — and the winter slid off him the way the sea slides off a cliff, the cold arriving at him and going around. He came to the middle of the yard and stopped, and even Lin Hao, who had built the cold, could not have said whether it was the domain failing at the man or the man declining it.

Under the grass, if you were the kind of listener who had once stood in the barrier's seam, something vast turned over in its sleep and settled again. Ten thousand years is not a colour. It is a weight, and the yard carried it that morning the way it carried the fog off the sea.

The violet light stood in the gold of Lin Hao's eyes, and the reading began — the man's weight, the man's timing, the seam every living thing carries because everything fails. The reading was the oldest thing he owned — older than the sword, older than the bench: the talent that had been taking the world apart and keeping what worked since before he had words for it. It did not feel like a gift. It felt like hunger — patient, total — and he had never once told it to stop. Wu Zhangkong stood in the cold and let himself be read, which was the lesson and the mercy at once: a master laying his own blade on the bench. *Learn what you can. It will not be enough. Come anyway.*

Lin Hao came anyway.

The wind went first, because the storm was the sword's first voice and had never once left it. The frost sheared off the ground in standing waves, a yard of air with edges in it, and Wu Zhangkong walked through the weather like a man commuting through rain he had decided not to notice.

The lightning came second, called down the flat of the blade — the sword's old second voice, three days finding its new road — a white line across the yard at the man's heart. He was not there. He had been not-there since before the draw finished, and the bolt grounded through the frost and left a scar on the grass shaped like a river, and something in the set of the man's shoulders filed the lightning away as a fact he would be hearing from again.

The Talon went third, black-edged, storm carrying winter, and Wu Zhangkong turned his shoulder and let it pass — but he turned it a half-beat late, and his eyes changed at the black of it. He had not seen that yet. Nobody had.

The fourth exchange came out of the bench. Strike and step and strike, the Disorder's own cadence, forging and fighting the same motion with no seam between the two skills — and the man's feet moved twice to one attack, and the fence understood that it had just watched a hammer art and a sword art shake hands.

And then Lin Hao went inside.

The reach was new and it was paid for, and he spent all of it at once, past the reading distance, past the courteous distance, into the country where duels are decided by kilograms — and put his bare fist at his teacher's ribs. The sound it made against the man's forearm was a door closing in a quiet house. Wu Zhangkong gave half a step.

Half a step. The fence made no noise at all, because Xu Xiaoyan was writing, and in that class nobody moved while the numbers were moving.

The five strokes went at the man in order after that, question upon question, and he answered them all with his arms and his patience, and the yard settled into the rhythm of something being taught at speed. Reading, then. The Track made the ground a rumour. The Unwritten Stroke went out — and it did not exist in the cold either, which Lin Hao had known for a month and had told no one, and the stroke arrived from nowhere in a medium of nowhere, and Wu Zhangkong moved out of its road by a hand's width, and something in the yard understood that this was now the most dangerous thing in it.

And then, because the man was still standing there, patient as a Monday, Lin Hao used the sixth stroke.

Still Water had never been drawn in front of anyone. It had no wind before it. The other five asked questions; Still Water waited until the opponent had answered one nobody asked — and Wu Zhangkong, mid-step, weight already committed to the road the Unwritten had threatened, had answered a question that was not the one coming.

The tip opened his sleeve along the outside of the forearm. A line of red, thin as a trial cut. The yard stopped.

The class did not breathe. Mu Chen put his tea down on the fence post with a click that everyone heard.

"Good," Wu Zhangkong said. He looked at the red line, and then at his student, with the whole of his face. "Now the man."

## Part 4: The Man

The Sky Ice came out of him the way winter comes out of a valley — not fast, just total. It built down his arm in plates of pale metal, over the shoulder, the collar, the mask; the two-word armor of a battle armor master. The smith in Lin Hao read it even as it closed — plate by plate, seam by seam, the maker's grain in the joining — because everything made by men has a seam, and he had spent seven years learning where metal lies. It changed nothing and it was true anyway. The yard's temperature did not drop so much as change sides. The domain met its elder and knelt. Frost that was his stopped being frost that was Lin Hao's, all the way to the fence, and the class stepped back from cold that had a different owner.

Lin Hao answered with the only thing he owned that spoke that language: the fourth ring's skill, one breath of Domineer put up against the tide. It was honest arithmetic. A candle at a coast of winter. The breath bought him his footing and nothing else in the world, and he was grateful for the footing.

Nine seconds.

The first exchange took the sword out of Lin Hao's hand. Not struck — *confiscated*, the gauntlet closing on the blade mid-line, and the Frost Abyss Sword, top-level, ten-thousand-year-ringed, was lifted from his grip like a borrowed thing. And the blade rang as it went — its own note, unasked, four full seconds of it against the armor's pale metal, metal answering metal. The whole yard heard the sword introduce itself to the gauntlet. The confiscation held. The note finished anyway.

The second exchange took the ground: a pressure he had no bracket for, Soul Douluo's weight through battle armor, and his knees learned the floor of the yard.

The third never landed. The gauntlet stopped at his collarbone, cold as a dock in January, and held there, precise, unhurried, a full second, so that everyone watching understood it had stopped and not missed.

"Yield."

"Yield," Lin Hao said, from the floor, into the frost.

The armor went back into the man like a tide going out. Wu Zhangkong reached down and pulled him up, and the yard was just a yard again, and the class made a noise at the fence that had been stored since the red line.

"Fifty years early, that ring," Wu Zhangkong said, as an aside, the way other men mention weather. "Mind it never learns your breathing for you." Then the arithmetic, so that the number would do the feeling for him: Xiaoyan's pencil never stopped: the whole fight was in the notebook before the frost left the grass, times and turns, and beside the last line she wrote a question mark and boxed it, because sixty-one did not look like losing until you unpacked it.

"Sixty-one seconds," Wu Zhangkong said. "Nine of them mine. In a year, ninety and thirteen. That arithmetic is your curriculum now. Nobody in this city has ever put a blade on me. You did it in sixty-one seconds, and you are thirteen, and I have never once in my life been prouder of anything, and I will deny this sentence under oath."

Lin Hao, arm hanging, cold gone, said the true thing, because the fight had loosened it: "You could have taken me in thirty."

"I could have taken you in nine," Wu Zhangkong said. "The other fifty-two were your education, and they were the point. Go wash. We leave for Shrek City in three weeks."

Mu Chen recovered his tea from the fence post, and the yard got the arithmetic from the other authority in it. "Do you understand what you watched?" he said, to nobody, to everybody. "Three purple rings. Every skill on that sword is a thousand-year skill — the class of thing a grown master carries one of, if he is lucky. He carries three, they answer in a storm together, and he is thirteen." He drank, with the click of a man closing a ledger. "The Association prices metals. Even I do not have a bracket for that."

At the fence, Xie Xie had his arms on the wire, and he said the thing he had been holding since the platform, canon to the syllable, his own at last: "Wulin. When we're there — you can just forge my battle armor for me instead."

Wulin looked at him. Looked at his own hands. "All right," he said, and that word, in that mouth, on that subject, was a signature.

## Part 5: What Wulin Did

While the city was still deciding what it thought about the duel, Wulin had farewells of his own to pay, and he paid them the way he did everything: thoroughly, and slightly too honestly.

The first was to Mu Chen, on the last Thursday, in the workshop with the door shut.

"Wulin. I wish you success on your trip to Shrek Academy. However, you cannot neglect your blacksmithing practice. You must forge daily." The old man said it the way he said everything that mattered, which was flatly, and then he said the thing that mattered more, which arrived out of season like snow: "In these past three years, you have made startling progress even by my standards. I'm certain that once you gain your third ring, Spirit Refinement will naturally follow."

That was not a small sentence, and both of them knew it. Wulin's first-grade thousand refining had been beyond dispute for two years — guaranteed, where most smiths attempt Spirit Refinement at a thirty percent rate, and Mu Chen himself had stood at fifty when he had first tried. The rare metals that only Master Craftsman rank could buy had been arriving on Wulin's bench for three years anyway, provided by a teacher who was hard-pressed to find the slightest fault in him and had stopped pretending to look for one.

"If you pass the Shrek exam, give me a call, and I'll make arrangements for your blacksmithing studies."

"Yes, Teacher."

Mu Chen rubbed his head, which he had done exactly never in front of witnesses before. "Be safe. Even if you don't pass the entrance exam, you can just come back, and I'll think of some way to get you into a good academy."

"Thank you, Teacher." And then the boy hugged him with teary eyes, because he was thirteen and he was Wulin, and some things are only embarrassing from the outside.

"Foolish child. What are you crying for? With today's soul technology, can't you just visit whenever you want?" A pause, and the voice went dry. "Alright. Go say goodbye to your senior disciple sister now. She's been depressed ever since she found out you were leaving."

She had been worse than depressed. She had not come to the Association in days. She rejected every call, and the girls' dormitory had a front door he did not have the nerve for.

So he did not use any door. He used the wall. Bluesilver Grass up three floors in the dark, to the washroom window that was seldom occupied, where Ouyang Zixin was waiting for him and trying not to laugh.

"Oh, you! You're getting better and better at this! Don't go philandering too much when you grow up."

"Big sis Zixin, don't tease me like this." He was blushing to the roots of his hair. "How is my senior disciple sister?"

"She's been tiger-faced the last few days. She's so glum!" Zixin got his collar straight, and put her coat over his shoulders against the corridor, and her fragrance made him redder than the climbing had. They were the same height now; that was new since spring. Xie Xie had said it once, years ago, in another yard — inside every man's heart was a pretty senior sister — and Wulin had jogged with this one every morning for three years, and had never once thought about the sentence until the last month, when it would not stop being true.

Class zero had never once, in four years, been furniture in its own city. Half of Eastsea could name the yard it trained in; after the duel, every one of them could name the minute count. Zixin had jogged beside the captain of it for three years at an hour whose only witnesses were gulls, and had heard the legend first from Xu Xiaoyu — Xiaoyan's own brother, who had watched it start — and had told nobody, which was its own kind of keeping. The mornings had been full for years without any of them knowing it: the girl at the 5:40 platform, the boy and his senior sister on the sea road, the third one on his walk with a book in his coat. The city held all of it and called it quiet.

"Big sis Zixin, are you still going to jog every day?"

"I will. I'll have no choice but to jog all alone."

He resolved himself, the way he did everything: thoroughly.

"Big sis Zixin, I like you."

A pause. "You foolish boy, big sis likes you too!"

He did not explain himself. He knew that his like and hers were different words wearing the same coat, and try as he might, he did not know how to say so. And she — girls mature earlier than boys; there was no way she did not understand the meaning — could only pretend ignorance, for the friendship's sake, the way one puts a coat over something. *If only I was four or five years younger, then maybe I would have snatched you up. I wish you the best on your path.* She thought it all the way to Mu Xi's door, where she jabbed her finger at it and whispered, "Go in. She's inside. Don't tell her I was the one who brought you here! I'm going to leave now."

"Mn. Thank you, big sis Zixin."

She left without saying goodbye, and pretended, on the stairs, that the glistening on her cheeks was a figment of a dream.

## Part 6: What Mu Xi Did

She had heard, of course. Eastsea was not big enough to contain the news that someone had cut Wu Zhangkong, and she was eighteen, and she had spent four years being precisely as old as she was.

He had come to say goodbye on the eve. Zixin had smuggled him in — he never learned that she was seen leaving in tears of her own — and he stood in her room and said *senior disciple sister* in a soft tone, and she fed him ice. "What are you doing here? Aren't you going to Shrek Academy? Shouldn't you be preparing? How did you even sneak into the girls' dormitory?" And last, the nail in the fence: "Just go. It would be bad if you're discovered. I don't want to see you either."

He took it. Then he said his piece anyway, because he was Wulin: he would never forget his blacksmith roots. If he did not pass, he would come back. If he did pass, he would not slack on smithing, and he would visit her and Teacher whenever he could. He bowed, and went out, and closed the door gently, and stood in the empty hallway being relieved and comprehending nothing. *Senior disciple sister's gaze is so heavy!*

The cold gaze thawed the moment his presence left the room, and turned into tears, and there was a reason, and the class never fully learned it. Three years ago, at the Skysea Alliance Tournament, a boy of ten had led her along his forging rhythm — and something in her had come unshackled: protected, blessed, free. Her talent had blossomed after that; fourth rank now, first-grade thousand refining, five years of progress done in three; the number-one blacksmithing genius of Eastsea City, the papers said, a title the Association's clerks had lately taken to qualifying with *of her intake*, on account of a certain other student of her father's. She had gone to Mu Chen in tears, once, to beg him to make Tang Wulin stay. Her father had answered her: "Tang Wulin doesn't belong in this small pond. His future is among the sea of stars."

Mu Xi wept through the night before he left, and would have denied it at swordpoint, and in the morning she knew the reason the way canon knows its own: she could not let him go, and he was going, and her road and his were parallel now — so close, never crossing, the geometry of it already drawn.

What she did instead of all that was walk into the members' forge on the last Friday and put a piece of stock on the bench.

"One run," she said. "Together. The old way. You take the strikes, I take the quench."

They did the whole run in the oldest rhythm, four years deep, the way they had done it at nine and eleven and every winter between, and neither of them went flat, and the bar came out singing.

The shop knew them. That was the thing about a members' forge: the racks remembered, the anvil remembered, the light through the high windows fell on the same scarred bench it had fallen on when he was nine and could barely start the strike. Four years of Fridays were in the walls. She worked the quench and he worked the hammer, and for one run, the last one, nobody in Eastsea was growing up or leaving; the metal was just hot, and the work was just work, and that was the whole of it.

She wrapped her half in cloth and put it in his bag herself, so he would find it on the train and not be able to give it back.

"For the bench in Shrek City," she said. "So it isn't all strangers." She looked at the forge, not at him, because looking at the forge was how she managed. "You were the best thing in my workshop years, Lin Hao. That's a scale reading. It doesn't need a reply."

She was eighteen. He was thirteen, and looked sixteen, and none of the arithmetic was anyone's fault.

"Write to the Association," he said. "Not to me. The Association. I answer those faster."

"Get out of my forge," said Mu Xi, and both of them heard the other sentence under it, and neither of them said it, and that was their whole farewell, and it was enough.

## Part 7: The Card, and the Train

The last Friday happened twice in the same building.

In the members' forge, Mu Xi ran the bar and wrapped her half and put it in his bag herself. In the workshop behind it, at the hour when the benches were cold, Lin Hao sat one last time in the sixth chair, which nobody had ever called anything, and Mu Chen let him sit in it for a while, which was the entire ceremony.

"Eleven years," Mu Chen said at last. "The metal told me you would be ready, and the metal was right. That is the whole speech." He turned back to his bench, and then, without turning again: "Shrek City has forges. Their metal does not know you. Introduce yourself."

The bar of fifth-rank stock was in Lin Hao's bag by the door before he left. Neither of them mentioned it. It was found on the train, beside Mu Xi's cloth — two wraps of metal in one bag, a father and a daughter, a family whose whole love language was stock.

That night Wu Zhangkong wrote the story he owed, two lines, in the hand like a fencing diagram:

*He put a blade on me. Sixty-one seconds. The calendar was right to hurry. — W.*

The reply came fast, as though the man had been sitting by the door: *Then he is ready for what the exam actually tests, which is not winning. Bring him. — S.*

And so it was decided the way the big things in class zero were always decided: by Wu Zhangkong stating them in the flat voice that had finished arguments for four years. The Shrek Academy entrance examination, once every three years, was in three weeks. They would take the Tuesday train. All five.

The tin went into Wulin's bag, four years deep. The bar went into Lin Hao's, wrapped in Mu Xi's cloth. Zhang Yangzi came to the platform with a manifest he had no reason to hold, and did not say anything, and shook every hand twice, his own included. Wei Xiaofeng said, "Eastsea will keep," which was his way, and was true, and was the kindest thing he knew. Zhang Yangzi held the manifest to the end and never handed it to anyone — it had never been for the dock. It was for the platform: a reason to be standing there at nine in the morning that was not the word goodbye. When the train breathed, he nodded once at the carriage as a whole, the way a man salutes weather, and that was his speech.

Gu Yue stood at the carriage door with the sea behind her doing its ordinary business, and did not look back at the city, and looked once, levelly, at Lin Hao, who looked sixteen and was thirteen and had lost in sixty-one seconds that morning and could not stop being pleased about it.

"Shrek," she said.

"Shrek," he said.

They took second class, the ordinary seats, the way the teacher had always taken the ordinary seats: the two girls on one side of the aisle, Wulin and Xie Xie and Wu Zhangkong across from them. The conductor, walking the carriage, looked from Lin Hao's youth fare to Lin Hao's face and back, and stamped it anyway, with the particular shrug of a man deciding the paperwork was the school's problem. Xie Xie watched the whole exchange with the joy of a man being proved right about something he had said first, and said nothing, loudly. After that he and Xu Xiaoyan chirped at intervals about nothing, which was how they managed. Gu Yue looked out the window quietly. Once, between stations, the sea appeared in her pane for a full minute, gray and busy, and she watched it the way you watch a parent from a moving train, and then the cuttings took it, and she closed her eyes and did not sleep. Somewhere past the third junction, Xie Xie nudged him. "Wulin, what's on your mind? What are you daydreaming about?"

Wulin snapped out of it and smiled. "It's nothing. I'm just going to miss Eastsea City."

Xie Xie's jaw dropped. "You — aren't you arrogant!"

"How so?"

Xie Xie looked like a man who had swallowed a lemon. "Didn't you just imply that we'll definitely pass? If that's not what you meant, then why would you miss Eastsea City?"

"You're overthinking it," Wulin said, and looked back at the window, where the truth was plainer than he was. Buried in the deepest, softest crook of his heart, he did feel that way — because there were tons of things waiting for him in Shrek City, and the first of them was old work.

Before departure he had met with Mang Tian once. Mang Tian had been convinced his parents had left for a major city, and Shrek City was the biggest on the continent. The message received after their retreat had named its price plainly: he would have the qualifications to search for them once he made fifth-rank blacksmith. Three years since Glorybound City. Not one call. No news is good news, until it isn't — if his parents were fine, there was no reason on earth not to call; at the very least, they could have reached Mang Tian. He had visited the empty house twice — the second time, a little more than a year ago — and found it a husk: no personal items, four bare walls, the smell of a place tossed aside. Except that the second visit had found the double-layered wall in his parents' room, and inside it a badge with a symbol he could not read and had never managed to stop reading. The sole clue. It rode in his storage ring now, beside the tin that was four years deep — two threads, a sister on one, a father and a mother on the other, both bound for the biggest city on the continent.

According to Wu Zhangkong's scheduling, they would arrive one week early — a week for the seal-brew and the search's first streets, and then the examination that did not test winning.

He took a deep breath, and exhaled, and took another. A journey is traveled step by step, and rice is eaten by the spoonful. Across the aisle his teacher sat back with his eyes shut, asleep in nine seconds flat, the way a man sleeps who has already done the arithmetic and likes it.

The train pulled out at nine. Eastsea went on being Eastsea behind them — the forge, the dock, the yard with its frost-burned grass, the fence four people had held on to while a boy touched the untouchable — and ahead of them was the continent, and the biggest city on it, and an examination that did not test winning.

Line one hundred and nine stayed unfinished, coat on, one button undone, riding in his bag like everything else that mattered.

## Part 1: The Announcement

The train slowed when it neared the end, and a voice came down the carriage that had been rehearsed until it was smooth as track.

*"Dear guests and travellers, we have arrived at the greatest city on the Douluo Continent, Shrek City. Shrek City's roots extend tens of thousands of years and is a cultural hub. The legendary Shrek Academy was founded here, as well as the Spirit Pagoda headquarters. As the number one city in the Federation, Shrek City boasts immense economic and political influence. Everyone, please take a look out the left window. The tower in the distance is the headquarters of the Spirit Pagoda."*

Five students and one teacher turned as one body to the left.

The tower was not there, and then it was — eight sides of silver splendor, the upper-middle portion visible and the peak simply not, tapering into cloud like a suggestion the sky had accepted. It was the tallest building on the continent. Everyone knew this; the Federation had rules forbidding any taller, the way cities have rules about standing on furniture. Xie Xie's face did several things against the glass. Xu Xiaoyan wrote one word in the notebook and underlined it, and the word was *tower*, and the underline meant she intended to measure something about it later.

Gu Yue looked at the tower the way she had once looked at a roster blank with no square for her. One breath. Then she was Gu Yue again, and the tower was a building.

Inside the city the train ran another hour just to land. The station, when it finally had them, was five times the size of Heaven Dou's and Eastsea's together — a dome like weather held still, sculptures standing along the halls as if the city had been in the middle of saying something and decided to leave it in stone. Wulin had never seen a larger room in his life. He walked with his neck at an angle, and did not fix it.

"Teacher Wu," Xie Xie said, vibrating, "where are we going first? Straight to Shrek Academy?"

Wu Zhangkong stood in the middle of the greatest station on the continent with his bag over one shoulder, and though he wore his usual mask of iciness, his eyes were doing something else — something with conflicted weather in it, there and gone, off the tower and back.

"Let's find an inn first," he said.

## Part 2: Where Luxury Did Not Exist

The word *luxury* did not exist in the dictionary of the inn that Wu Zhangkong chose. It was near the station, antique, stone and wood gone mottled with decades of sea-less weather; inside it was neat and plain, and each room had one bed, two bedside cabinets, a wardrobe, a desk, a chair, a window with a view of the trains, and a washroom only two people could fit into at one time, and that was all.

There were five of them, and the inn only had two-person rooms, so the arithmetic came out to four rooms and an apology nobody made. Wu Zhangkong took one. The girls took one. The boys took two, which meant one of the boys was a guest in his own, and Lin Hao, who had slept in a workshop's back room more than once in his life, took the floor roll without comment and heard Xie Xie claim the victory of the second bed in tones of a man who had won a tournament.

"So comfortable." Xie Xie pounced flat on the mattress the moment they entered, limbs spread, soul departing his body. "The train was so cramped I couldn't even stretch my legs. I never want to be seated again. Bury me standing."

"Wulin," Lin Hao said, "why is your bag already in the wardrobe?"

"Because we live here now," Wulin said, from the window, where he was taking in the new environment street by street with the particular hunger of a boy whose list of things to find in this city had names on it.

Xie Xie, face-down, delivered the speech he had been saving since the platform: "Wulin. Why do you think Teacher Wu is so stingy with the rooms? He should have a good salary from the academy, and he's a battle armor master! You should have seen how awesome it was! He's got to be rich since he made his battle armor!"

"Teacher Wu just doesn't care about such mundane things." Wulin laughed. "Now you. You should be a bit more modest. We're not here to have fun."

"Fine, fine. I'm going to nap first then." And Xie Xie's breathing steadied within a minute, honestly, completely, the way nothing else in his life was ever honest or complete.

Wulin took a bath, put on clean clothes, and went and pressed the doorbell of his teacher's room. The door opened on Wu Zhangkong in shirtsleeves; he let him in silently.

"Teacher Wu. Can we go now?"

"Don't be anxious." A glance at the sky, which was going orange over the greatest city on the continent. "Auctions are held in the evening. We have time. You need to be patient."

"Okay." Wulin breathed in, and steadied, and did not quite settle. His nerves were jittery in a way he could name now: this was Shrek. His martial soul was Bluesilver Grass, trashy by reputation; his two rings were thousand-year, and merely his; the claw was power without stamina. There were things he could not tell even this teacher — had never been able to, and both of them had learned to live politely around the shape of the unsaid — and one of those things was certain in him the way a floor is certain. He said the part he could say.

"Teacher Wu. The set from Eastsea. It's complete. It's been complete since the twelfth day of that month."

"I know," Wu Zhangkong said. "Let me ask you again anyway. Are you sure your strength will increase once you use all four items? If you are not absolutely certain, I recommend you not act hastily. The slightest mistake could affect your future."

"I'm certain." No hesitation at all. "And it won't be hasty. It breaks at fourteen. That was decided in Eastsea, on purpose. Fourteen is coming — I'm counting it in days now."

"I won't say anything else then," Wu Zhangkong said, and looked out the window at the trains for a while, at the city that knew him and did not know it.

## Part 3: Forty Minutes

They ate dinner at the inn, all six at a table built for four. The place was small, but it was an inn in Shrek City, and the food was unexpectedly good — good enough that Xie Xie forgave the mattress in advance. Wulin's mind was plainly elsewhere; he ate half as much as usual, and it was still more than everyone else at the table combined, and the innkeeper, watching plates go, revised something about her rates.

"Rest and meditate," Wu Zhangkong told Xie Xie, Gu Yue, and Xu Xiaoyan. "If you go out, stay within the area, and always carry your soul communicators on you."

"Teacher Wu, where are you and Captain going then?" Xu Xiaoyan asked. She had grown accustomed to calling Wulin *Captain* — she rarely called him anything else now — and she asked it looking between the three of them, because Lin Hao was already standing, and the question had grown a second person in it without anyone announcing the change.

"There are some matters to take care of. We'll be back later."

He had never once, in four years, explained his plans to anyone, and the city got the same courtesy. Outside, he hailed a taxi — a soul taxi, comfortable, dear — and Wulin stared, because he had watched this man walk across whole cities rather than spend on a cab. The reason arrived at the window as scenery: Shrek City was simply too gigantic. The taxi was faster than any bus, and it still took forty minutes.

Forty minutes, and their teacher did not look up directions once. He did not hesitate at a single turn. He said nothing, and the two boys said nothing, and both of them filed it in the same quiet place — the place where the things about Teacher Wu that did not add up lived, unadded. Lin Hao watched the streets the way he watched grain, and the streets had a repetitive toughness to them, old alloy under new plate, and he caught himself missing the sea smell of home and did not say that either.

The pointed building they stopped at had staff at the door, and the staff had a speech.

"Excuse me, may I ask if you two— three, are participating in the auction? Could you please take out your invitation letter?"

Wu Zhangkong retrieved something from his pocket and flashed it. The staffer's spine reorganized itself. "So it was our Esteemed Guests that have arrived. Please come this way."

## Part 4: The Yaluo

Past the door, Wulin understood what true luxury was. A hall of white wood ran ahead of them, golden patterns swirling across it like elegant flowers; the floor was a scarlet rug with gold embroidery running down its whole length; crystal lamps lined the walls, throwing light that flattered everything it touched, including the three of them. An unseen pressure settled on Wulin's shoulders as he walked it, and he glanced sideways at his teacher — and got the calm face, no different from the yard, and felt absurd, and kept the absurd feeling, because it was warmer than the pressure.

They were brought to an opulent room. Drinks arrived without being ordered. Then a middle-aged woman came in, bowing slightly.

"Honored guests, welcome. I am Ruo Ling, an auctioneer for the Yaluo Auction. May I ask if there is anything I can do for you?"

"Bring me your catalog," Wu Zhangkong said.

She smiled, crouched beside him, and with a flash of her golden bracelet a small soul screen stood up out of her palm. Her eyes did the rounds as she worked — the stern one, worth a fortune by the look of him; the big one, sixteen in the face and built like a smith's door; the younger one, all elbows and intentions — and she filed all three under *unusual*, and turned the wattage up, because a woman in her line valued looks and status both and was seldom handed three of anything at once.

"Spirit items," Wu Zhangkong said.

"Yes." Tap, tap. "Do you have a specific item in mind? I can help you search."

"Thousand-year Azure-veined Vine."

The listings changed: high-grade, mid-grade, low-grade, each with its starting price and its estimate in neat columns. Ruo Ling glanced up — "When will it be put on auction?" was the next question in the script, and she was already answering it in her head — and Wulin looked at the columns for a long, quiet moment, the way a man looks at a bridge he no longer has to cross.

"No," he said, politely. "Thank you. The set is complete. It's been complete since Eastsea."

Ruo Ling's smile held its exact shape while her interest recalculated. "Then perhaps something in refined metals? The evening sale often carries lots a smith would travel for." This was aimed with soft precision at the third one, the one with the forearms, and Lin Hao felt the floor of the continent shift under him slightly, because a stranger in the biggest city on it had read his hands in under a minute.

"If I want to buy a metal lot immediately rather than wait," Wu Zhangkong said, "how would I do so?"

"According to our rules, we're not allowed to sell items directly." A hesitation, words bitten back and organized. "But I can make an exception for someone as honorable as you. An instant purchase costs twenty percent more than the estimated price. We can offer an accurate quote once you've considered it."

Wu Zhangkong did not look at the screen. He looked at his students, both of them, the way he looked at a yard before terms.

"It's your money," he said, to each of them, separately, in the same breath. "Your decisions. I'll say nothing."

"Then we wait for the evening sale," Wulin said. "Three days is nothing. I have a birthday in the middle of it."

"Tickets," Wu Zhangkong said to Ruo Ling. "Three."

## Part 5: Three Days

The inn held them the way a cupped hand holds water.

Wulin and Xie Xie cultivated — the spear got sharpened late, and both of them knew it, and Xie Xie did it anyway, because his friend's diligence rubbed off on him in exactly one direction and always had. Gu Yue found the dawn. It took her two mornings to locate a platform that would rent to a girl with no local file and a foreign card; on the third morning the attendant simply left the row to her, and Shrek City learned what Eastsea's attendants had known for years, which was that 5:40 belonged to somebody. Xu Xiaoyan walked the station with the notebook for one day and the streets behind it for two, building the city's map in the small neat hand, block by block, as if the exam would be given on the geography. It would not be. She did not care. A measurement you did not write down had not happened, and this applied, in her cosmology, to cities.

Lin Hao spent the three days the way he had spent every market-day of his life: reading metal. Shrek City had forges the way other cities had drains — everywhere, under everything, the smell of hot iron riding the streets in shifts. Their metal does not know you, Mu Chen had said. Introduce yourself. He walked the forge districts with his hands behind his back and his reading on, and the city's metal was good — tougher stock than Eastsea kept, deeper seams, older grain — and on the second day, in a smelter's yard, he put his hand flat on a cooling ingot and told the smelter the temperature it had been poured at, and the number was right, and the man looked at him for a long moment and then looked at the forge, as if the forge had been talking about him behind his back.

On the second night, Wulin's fourteenth birthday was close enough that Xie Xie began organizing it. There would be cake. There would be cake *from the good place near the station*, whatever it cost, and he would pay, and there would be no discussion. The whole table watched Wulin laugh, and the whole table was counting too, for their own reasons — because fourteen was a door, and behind the door was a thing their friend had been carrying since they had known him, and after it opened he would be something more than the boy who ate half as much as usual.

The tower light came on at dusk and went off at midnight, punctual as Wu Zhangkong.

## Part 6: Item Eleven

The Yaluo at night was the hall from three days ago with the wattage doubled. They were led to the VIP floor immediately — where there were only two kinds of people, those with money and those with strength, and their teacher had never needed to be the first kind. The seats were deep. The auction beat Eastsea's the way the station beat Eastsea's: every lot a rarity, the room humming it before the gavel ever moved.

Wulin sat with the number plate in his lap, and the plate stayed in his lap.

"The eleventh item to be auctioned is a high-grade thousand-year Azure-veined Vine. The starting price is three million. The minimum bid increase is one hundred thousand. Let the bidding begin."

A smelter's yard of a room went quiet, and then it did not. Three million. Three million one hundred thousand. A vine that strengthened the constitution without side effects, a necessity for the great clans' nurseries — the demand for it was old and bottomless, and the price said so: three and a half, three-eight, then over five in a single stride, a man near the front on the verge of tears at five-four, still climbing at five-seven. Beside Wulin, Wu Zhangkong watched the storm with his arms folded, and Wulin watched it too, plate in his lap, his set complete since Eastsea, a wrapped birthday two days from spending itself, and the storm had nothing to do with him, and he felt the size of that nothing all the way down. Six-two. Six-eight. Seven million three hundred thousand — going once, twice, three times, sold — and a stranger somewhere in the dark went limp with relief and ruin at the same time, half a fortune for a leaf.

"Popular items usually exceed the estimated sales price," Wu Zhangkong said to him, quietly, without looking. "The estimate is where the house breaks even. Do you understand now?"

"I understand," Wulin said. "I'm glad it isn't my money."

"It was, once. In Eastsea." A pause, dry as the yard. "You put the paddle up once. It was correct."

Lin Hao's lot came eleventh-from-last, and it came as words on a screen: a sealed estate lot, sight-unseen, *mixed refined stock, Heavy Silver and Sky Dragon Iron, sold by weight*. The room's interest died on the word *mixed* — no certainty, no glamour; the bids crawled. He had spent three days reading this city's metal, and he could hear the lot's weight in the two porters' footsteps and read its grain in the shape of the crate's shadow, and when the crawling stopped he raised the plate once, a single clean bid nobody wanted enough to answer, and it was his. A third of his traveling money. A bench's worth of *introduce yourself.*

On the taxi back, the black box on his knees, Wulin looked at it and then at his friend.

"Worth it?"

"The crate says mixed," Lin Hao said, with the serenity of a man who had already read through the wood. "It isn't."

The tower light went out at midnight, punctual as their teacher, and in a plain room where luxury did not exist, a boy counted the last days before his door, and the greatest city on the continent settled noisily around him, and did not know yet what it was about to host.

## Part 1: The Crate, and the Style's Second Half

The rental bench in the forge district cost one federal coin an hour and smelled like every honest morning of his life.

He opened the crate with the estate lot in it in front of the yard's owner, because sight-unseen lots are opened in front of witnesses. Heavy Silver, forty-one kilograms. Sky Dragon Iron, twenty-six. Two separated strata, wrapped apart, the way you wrap things when you know what they are — which meant the estate had known, and the auction had not, and the room had bid on the word *mixed* anyway. The owner looked at the strata, and then at the boy who had paid a third of his traveling money for them, and offered, on the spot, to buy the Iron back at triple. Lin Hao said no, and the man looked at him a second time, longer, the way people in this city were starting to.

Then the bench was his, and the morning was for the sword.

The six strokes had come out of the emergence twice as large as asked, and a month of yardwork had brought them back to their sizes — but not to their old shapes. That was the discovery of the Shrek mornings, and it was still arriving: each of the five question-strokes was growing a second register. The storm asked at the surface; the deep water could ask the same question underneath, colder, slower, from a different angle, so that the question arrived twice and the second one could not be dodged by answering the first. Still Water had been the style's first answer-stroke. It had not been an ending. It had been a preview. The style was growing its second half, stroke by stroke, and by the third morning the first stroke — the oldest, the one he had written in the book at ten — could ask twice.

He worked them at the air, at the pell, at a bar of the new Sky Dragon Iron propped in the vise, and the iron rang differently under the water-register than under the storm-register, and he listened to the difference the whole morning, because the sword's body was iron, his oldest acquaintance, and it was telling him which register the metal believed.

Sword Intent itself had changed register too. It used to be pressure. Now it had temperature. He could put cold into a look and a look into the cold, and the yard owner's dog, testing him at the fence line, sat down at the second look and decided permanently.

## Part 2: The Second Spirit

The dragon grew. That was the morning's other work, and it was work now, counted.

The jiao was a month old in him and ten thousand years old in itself, and both of those things were true at once, the way a marriage is young even when both people are grown. It had come out of the barrier at full weight and then done what every living thing does in a new country: it had begun to settle, and then, past settling, to grow. Not as the hawk had grown — the hawk had five years of mornings in him, and their joining was so finished it did not deserve the word *joining* anymore; it deserved *weather*. The dragon was younger than that. The dragon was developing.

He measured it the way Xiaoyan had taught him to measure everything, which was honestly.

The deep-water joining — the step inward where he stopped carrying the spirit and started being carried by it — had held forty seconds on the ship of the first week. That morning it held ninety. The difference was not small and not comfortable: at ninety seconds the cold had opinions about his breathing, and at ninety seconds something in him that was also something in it tried, gently, to speak with his mouth, and he stepped out and stood in the ordinary warm morning shaking slightly, with the whole yard's frost already gone, and did it again. The second attempt held seventy. He wrote both numbers down. A measurement you did not write down had not happened.

The domain's hem was a hand wider than the month before. Domineer's breath, which had been one breath at the emergence, had become two — he tested it over the pell and the pell, three years honest service, split to the grain. The body deepened with all of it, because there were not two things here to begin with: the spirit grew, the body grew, one existence — the regeneration quicker by the week (he took a forge nick opening the crate's second stratum and watched it close, eighty seconds, timed, which would have been half a morning in Eastsea), the Mysterious Heaven breath one count deeper, the cold sense reading the room's drafts like a page.

The hawk sat the fence through all of it, winter-tipped, unbothered, senior. Toward the end of the morning it flew one slow circle, low, over the bench — over the Iron, over the sword, over the whole arrangement of him — the way a foreman walks a floor that is going well.

It lit on the fence afterward with one claw, and the claw gathered a rime of frost along the rail — a hand-span of it, going nowhere, not melting in the morning sun. It had not done that before the deep water. He watched the frost edge outward a fraction, stop, hold. The bird looked at the frost the way he looked at metal that had told him something new: without surprise, with the arithmetic beginning. *Storm carrying winter in its teeth.* It had come back from the barrier's hem that way in the fight; the month had only been making the introduction permanent. Nothing said so — the hawk did not say things — but his own arm under the sleeve, where the feather-marks climbed, prickled with a cold that was not the cold of the air, and the rime on the rail was the same cold, offered for the record.

He did not write the jiao an age the way he wrote the hawk one. The hawk's years were a ladder you could count rung by rung — a thousand-year soul rose like a river, fed by every crossing. A ten-thousand-year soul was a different kind of thing. The black ring on his hand WAS its age, the way a rank was a rank: a threshold, not a total. Between crossings the number did not tick upward forty years like a shopkeeper's tally; it deepened, the way a sea deepens. What grew rung-by-rung was the bond itself — the joining, forty seconds to ninety and climbing — and that was the young thing, the bookkeeping worth doing. The jiao's own next crossing was a hundred-thousand-year threshold, a door none of the people he had ever met would live to see opened; he wrote it down honestly, as a ceiling and a promise, not as a sum.

That night, in the joining, at the ninety-second mark where the cold began to have opinions, he went looking for where the thing lived — and found the place. Behind his breathing, under the place where the deep water had moved in when the ring turned black: a sea. Vast, dark, perfectly still; its surface smoked glass. Above the sea a permanent storm-sky hung, the hawk's own country — clouds moving in the wrong direction, lightning fishing once, far up, never striking down into the water that was not its territory; and the water itself was the jiao's, an abyss that did not need light to see by, with something coiled at the bottom of it, turning over once in its sleep the way a continent turns. His spiritual sea. He had read the phrase in the Sect's manuals and carried it over his own head for years without ever seeing it whole. Weather over the abyss. Every square length of it his.

Wulin came down the inn stairs while he was closing the book, saw the rime on the rail, and stopped with his hand on the newel. Then he nodded, the way you nod at weather through a window, and said: "Your winter follows you around indoors now." A pause. "That's normal, right? For you. That's — normal."

"It is now," Lin Hao said. "It wasn't yesterday. I'm told that's also how it's going."

There was a third thing he did not do, and its name was the perfect joining, and it stayed in its sheath. It had a door of its own, and the door was not today's. But it was also true, and he wrote this down too, in the book, in the plain way: *everything spent to the limit, both spirits included, the Emperor number is not the ceiling. There is a higher arithmetic. It is reserved.*

## Part 3: The Effect

He walked back through the city at noon with Wulin, and the city continued its campaign to be noticed noticing him.

The tea stall girl at the corner under the inn had started giving him the tall cup instead of the short one, unprompted, and would not take the difference. The tailor's apprentice two doors down — sent out to hand-deliver a repaired seam — had measured him with her eyes twice on the first day and now simply turned faintly pink at the counters, with the tape, professionally, every time. At the smelter's yard, the afternoon crowd had doubled; the smelter himself had taken to calling him *young master metalsense* in front of visitors, half mock and half salesmanship, and let him read two pours for customers, and both numbers had been right, and the yard's reputation was becoming his by association and vice versa. Two girls from a passing academy group walked into a lamp post between glances. The lamp post was fine. Wulin watched the second one happen, turned to his best friend with the slow dawning joy of a man collecting evidence, and said nothing, which between the two of them was the loudest available thing.

"She didn't see it," Lin Hao said. "The post."

"They never do," Wulin said, wheezing. "Xie Xie said it first, you know. A face that is a personality. He wants royalties. He's asking around about how royalties work."

"It's just a face."

"It's just a face," Wulin agreed, "that a woman at an auction house read your profession off in under a minute, and a smelter calls *master*, and a lamp post has met personally. Just one of those." He clapped his shoulder, and they bought the cake — the good place near the station, the order Xie Xie had placed with the authority of a small parliament — and carried it back flat between them like a relic, and the whole way, at crosswalks, in queues, at the bakery door, people moved around the two of them a half-beat sooner than the crowd's own rhythm, the way water moves around a stone it has an opinion about, and neither boy said any more about it, because there was nothing to do about being liked by a city except be back at the inn by six, as instructed.

## Part 4: The Sentence

The birthday committee took everyone out of the inn at dusk — Xie Xie, Xiaoyan with the map, Wulin under protest, on a mission for candles of a specific number — and for one hour the corridor upstairs was empty of everyone except the two people it was about to be empty of.

He knocked. She said, "It's open."

Gu Yue's room was the girls' room, one bed, two cabinets, a desk, a window with the station in it, and she was at the desk with the dusk behind her doing nothing in particular, which he suspected was cultivation, and suspected equally was waiting, and did not ask which. He came in, closed the door, and did not sit on the offered chair. He sat on the floor across from her, cross-legged, the way they had sat at ten, and looked at her silently for some time.

The looking was the new thing. Since the second spirit, his eyes had been a different instrument — the deep water read everything now, drafts and grain and people — and what it read when it read her had a shape to it, something old and layered and utterly quiet, sitting inside the girl at the desk the way the jiao sat inside him. He had been carrying that reading for a month. He had told no one, including her.

"Well," he said. "Many things changed after my second soul spirit. Honestly. You look more beautiful." She went very still, and he kept going, level, the way you cross a bridge you have decided on. "It isn't that you changed. I changed. I think you know why." A breath. "A person has a right to privacy. I'm not asking. I wanted to say something to you, and then I'll have said it."

For a moment he thought the room had gotten colder, and then understood that it hadn't, and that this was worse and better than cold: she was attending with everything she had, all of her, the way she stood inside a hem of frost without a mark on her.

He rose, went close to her, and looked into her eyes.

"I love you." He said it plainly, no wind before it, the sixth stroke of sentences. "The sentence isn't complete — that time, I didn't finish it. What I didn't say then was that I liked you. Now it's more. I'm telling you because I'm certain. I don't expect the same, and I'm not forcing anything. I wanted to say it because I wanted to tell you." One corner of his mouth moved, not quite a smile. "I know the others all know it. It's been too obvious the whole time, maybe. If you don't have anything — you don't need to say anything. We go as always. I won't say it again." And the last of it, the truth under the truth, given to her the way you hand over a weight with both hands: "If I tell you the truth — I'm not expecting a Yes."

The room held still. Somewhere below, the station announced a train to a city none of them had seen. The dusk moved one shade toward dark.

And Gu Yue said nothing.

She looked at him — a long, level look, the whole of her attending behind it, something in it he had no register for — and no word came. The elements in the room did not move. Nothing arrived in place of an answer, the way nothing ever arrived with her when she had decided a thing was not yet for saying.

He had set the terms himself, kindly, before he ever crossed the room: if you don't have anything, you don't need to say anything. We go as always.

So this was the answer, and it was the exact shape of the one he had promised to accept — nothing said, nothing done, no thing changed hands — as before, like before. He held the look as long as she lent it, and then he nodded, once, small, the way a man closes a ledger he has finished writing in, and said, "As always," and went out, and closed the door gently, the way someone had once closed a door in a girls' dormitory in another city, and stood in the empty corridor being quiet and finished and not sorry. The sentence was done; that was the whole of what the day had been for. Whether she kept it or put it down was hers, and he had told her so, and a promise made in advance is still a promise.

## Part 5: Line One Hundred and Nine

That night, in the room where Xie Xie slept like the honest and the fed, he opened the book.

Line one hundred and nine had sat at the bottom of its page for two years, unfinished, coat on, one button undone — a sentence begun at eleven in a yard and never completed, guarded like a door that was also a wound. He had rules about the book, and the rules had held a long time.

He wrote the sentence out, complete, all of it, the whole thing he had said and the whole thing he had carried: *I love her. Told her. Not expecting a Yes. She said nothing. That is the nothing we agreed on. Everything is as before.* And the date.

Then, because the book was honest or it was nothing, he added one more line below it, the first line of whatever came next: *I didn't tell her to get anything. I told her because I wanted to tell her. The page turns.*

He closed the book. Downstairs the committee argued about candles. Tomorrow his best friend turned fourteen, and behind that door was a thing that would change him, and behind every other door in the greatest city on the continent was an examination that did not test winning.

He slept with his hands open, and the room, if anyone had measured it, was one degree colder than the corridor, and the cold was the polite kind, the kind that was learning his breathing, night by night, exactly as fast as he was learning its.

## Part 1: Fourteen

The cake arrived at breakfast under Xie Xie's personal escort, and it had fourteen candles in it, because Xiaoyan had checked the number twice and Xie Xie had checked it once more with the bakery under formal witness.

They lit them in the inn's back room with the shutters open to the station noise, and for a minute the room was all small fire and everybody's face made of gold. Wulin looked at the candles the way he looked at loaded bars — like a thing with weight — and shut his eyes, and thought whatever fourteen-year-olds think whose doors open the same night, and blew.

Fourteen candles went out together. Everyone cheered. Xie Xie had prepared a speech and was not permitted to give it.

"Make a wish," Xiaoyan instructed, notebook closed, which for her was festivity.

"I did."

"Can't tell it?"

"Can't tell it."

Gu Yue said, "Happy birthday, Captain," which was ordinary, and warm, and exactly what she would have said yesterday, and exactly what she would have said tomorrow. Lin Hao watched the smoke of the candles go out the window in a line, and ate his piece, and said the ordinary things, and his face did its work all morning. It was a good face. It had been getting him out of rooms for years.

The day was given to idleness by unanimous sentence, and to small errands, and to staying out of the way of a boy who was about to spend three years of savings in one bath. At some point in the afternoon Wulin got quiet in the way they all knew, and went to walk the station alone, and nobody followed, because this too was a custom of the class.

## Part 2: The Candle

Here is what nobody at the party saw, because it was not showable.

He had not been expecting a Yes. That was true when he said it and it was still true at breakfast and it would be true forever — he had gone up those stairs with the sentence finished in his hand and no bill attached to it. But somewhere in him, in a room he had not known he kept, there had been a candle burning. He had never once looked at it directly. You do not look at hope directly; it goes out when you look at it, his grandmother had said that about something else, or maybe it had been about exactly this. And last night the room had gone dark so quietly he had heard nothing — no wind, no door — and only this morning, at a birthday table with fourteen small fires going out on command, had he understood the room was dark.

That was all. That was the whole injury: not a No, which he had braced for and could have carried like freight. A nothing, which weighed nothing and could not be put down.

He did not show it. He was, the class had agreed years ago without meeting about it, the steadiest of them — the boy who read seams, who did not flinch at light, who had lost a duel in sixty-one seconds and could not stop being pleased about it. Steady was a garment he had cut to his own measurements. Under it, this. He was thirteen and something like this had never once happened to him, and he owned no tools for it, and he knew it, and he said nothing.

He would not ask. That was not a decision; it was architecture. Asking was the one thing his whole self was not built for — you did not ask metal to be ready, or weather to be fair, or a scale to be kind; you read, you waited, you kept the terms. And it was not hate. It was never going to be hate. She had done nothing — nothing was the entire point — and he had told her she needn't, and a promise made in advance is still a promise. Both things were true at once and neither canceled the other: he accepted it completely, and it hurt, and the hurt was his to carry, quietly, the way the book carried lines.

So he carried it. In the afternoon, while the others idled, he walked to the rental bench and paid his coin and worked two hours on the Sky Dragon Iron with no plan at all, strikes for the sake of strikes, because metal was the one thing in the world that had never once required him to be fine. The hawk sat the rail and watched him do it, and near the end flew down and leaned its whole weight against his neck, once, firmly, the way it had done exactly never before. The cold in the room curled once around his ankles, like something checking on him, and settled.

The page had turned. Nothing was written on the next page yet. He was thirteen, and he turned it anyway.

## Part 3: Old Tang

At dusk, Wulin knocked on his teacher's door with the black box under his arm.

"Teacher Wu. Tonight."

Wu Zhangkong looked at him for a moment. "How long do you estimate it will take?"

Wulin had no answer and his face admitted it.

"If you don't even know, why bid at all—" his teacher began, and then stopped, because in this version of the conversation there had been no bidding; the vine had been bought in Eastsea with quiet money a month ago, and the only thing left to spend tonight was the boy. "Then it's the birthday. It was always the birthday." A pause. "You're sure your strength will increase?"

"I'm certain. It will definitely be a success."

"You can make your breakthrough in my room," Wu Zhangkong said. "I'll guard you." And, in the taxi that took them back from the last errand with the box on Wulin's knees, the conversation the class would have paid to hear:

Wulin, on money: three years of orders, four spirit items, the Ghost Shadow Perplexing Track unaffordable, the Soft Bone Eight Stage Drop a dream for a richer decade. Wulin, on the hammer art: *"Did you know the Disorder came from the Clear Sky Clan? Teacher told me last year. Tang San's clan — the founder's own. The clan's gone now. The hammer is all that's left of them."* And then, quieter, because it had just landed on him in a moving taxi: *"That's what he gave you, that first winter. A dead clan's whole inheritance. He just handed it over."*

Lin Hao, at the inn door, hearing this the way you hear a bearing in a machine you thought you knew: "He didn't say it like that."

"He never says anything like that."

Inside, in the room where luxury did not exist, Wulin sat on the bed, closed his eyes, and called down a voice that had been silent since it saved his life.

The golden light came, and the white space with it, and the old man in it looked him over with regret and approval in the same squint. *"Mn. Long time no see, you little rascal. You've done well improving your body all this time. It shouldn't be a problem for you to break the second seal. Have you prepared the four spirit items?"*

"I have them." His voice was thick, and not only about the money.

*"Then you're ready to start. The method is different from last time. You will ingest the Dragonscale Fruit directly. Crush the other three items into juice, dilute the juice with hot water, and bathe in it — soak and meditate. You need to do this simultaneously. Don't eat the fruit until the bath is ready. Understood?"*

"Understood."

Back in the room, he opened his eyes and found his teacher already raising the kettle, and explained the method, and Wu Zhangkong stared at him with a face like a blank mask and said, "You're absorbing it by soaking?" A quirk of the brow. "Is there an issue?"

"No problem. But it's not very efficient."

"That's fine. I'll trouble you to help, then." And Wu Zhangkong stood, sleeves pushed, and let exactly one sentence of his whole life slip out through his teeth as he reached for the vine:

"That's such a waste of money!"

## Part 4: The Brew

The Azure-veined Vine was forearm-long and azure like its name, crystal-sparkling, liquid moving visibly in the stalk, sweet-breathing into the room. Wu Zhangkong pointed a finger and a gentle stream of soul power lifted it over the bathwater; a pinch of invisible force wrung it in half, and its juices ran down into the tub until the water and the rising steam both went azure. When the husk was spent, his finger moved — and blades of Mysterious Heaven soul power, finger-swords, no martial soul anywhere in the room, stabbed the husk a countless number of times and exploded it into powder so fine that not one particle missed the water.

Wulin's eyes shimmered. He had seen his teacher fight. He had never seen him *filet*.

The Land Dragon Tendon was two tan meters of the least remarkable-looking thing in the world. "It should be five meters; it shrank in processing. You would normally boil it three days and three nights to soften it. For a broth, there is only one method." His teacher stepped his left foot out, bent into a half-squat, still as furniture — left hand Controlling Crane, right hand Capturing Dragon, palms facing, a wind standing up between them. The tendon rose and spun. Faster. A whirring. His upper body did not move at all while the tendon's revolutions howled and the tan went red and the pressure and the friction and the Sect's two hands tenderized fifteen minutes of a dragon into a scarlet dumpling, and then the red liquid started, drop by drop, each drop a puff of steam, until the whole of it was in the water and the water was dark green and the room's smell was a war between the vine's freshness and something fishy that was winning. The Sea Dragon Marrow took a moment — squeezed simple, the steam going pink, the tub now terrifying by any aesthetic ever devised.

"Go in."

Wulin bit the Dragonscale Fruit — blue-skinned, jewel-bright, sour enough to nearly kill him — felt the heat of it land in his stomach, and got into dark green water so hot he made a sound he would deny in court. *Clear your mind and calm your breathing.* The fruit's warmth made it worse, not better; his body went scarlet in a breath, a boiled shrimp, twitching, and Wu Zhangkong's hand rose with his martial soul already gathering to cool the tub—

—and stopped in the air.

On his student's forehead, faint as watermark, a golden mark had appeared. Three golden lines. Even with his eyesight he could barely make them out; and he could not identify them; and he filed the whole of it — the mark, the water, the recipe with no source — under a heading he had been keeping for this boy for four years, which had never once had a label, and stood his guard.

## Part 5: The Sentries

The class was sent to bed at nine, and one of them did not go.

Wu Zhangkong was where canon had always put him and where he had said he would be: inside, on the stool beside the bath, guarding, his senses doing the watching. And in the corridor outside the door, at his own distance, uninvited and unexplained, his student stood the hour of nothing alone — the month of Eastsea afternoons resumed, one sentry short, by request of nobody.

The corridor was dark after the station's last announcement. The tower light had gone out at midnight, punctual. Somewhere behind the door, his best friend was being boiled alive inside his own becoming, and there was nothing to do about that either, and he knew it, and stood.

Once, deep in the small hours, the door opened — his teacher, with the empty kettle, on his way to the boiler down the hall. He saw the boy against the wall. He did not order him to bed.

"You are carrying something," he said instead. Not a question. The voice of a man reading a seam.

"Sir."

"Carry it level."

"Yes, sir." And Wu Zhangkong went past him to the boiler and came back with the kettle full and went in again, and did not close the door all the way, and that was the whole exchange of permission, and the most the two of them would ever say about it.

The hawk came off his shoulder in the small hours and leaned its weight against his neck again, and the cold came and sat by his ankles like a dog, and Lin Hao stood the hour in the dark and let the room in him be dark, because that was what it was, and it was not hate, it was never going to be hate — it was just the first time, and first times are load-bearing, like first notes. He had told the truth last night, all of it. He had not told her to get anything.

But there had been a candle, he could admit that now, to a dark corridor — and the corridor was the proof it was out.

As before. Like before. He stood the hour anyway. Standing the hour was also as before.

Behind the door, at every hour anybody checked, the water was still moving.
