## Part 1: Kettle Duty

The door stayed open a hand's width, and through the gap, gold.

It came off him in pulses. That was the first thing Lin Hao learned on kettle duty, somewhere on the third trip to the boiler: not a light that shone but a light that *beat*, slow as something with a heartbeat, and by the second hour he was counting it without having decided to, because the corridor was long and the count filled it. Eleven seconds. Twelve. Eleven. Eleven. He hauled the water his teacher would have hauled, fed the class their hours, and kept the number so it would exist somewhere outside the door. The standing was never the work. The work was that nobody behind that door should want for heat.

Inside, on the stool, his teacher watched, and did nothing on purpose. What his senses gave him, they gave in full: the mark had spread in moments from the forehead down — a network now — and the boy inside it breathing calmer as it grew, as if the pain had been a door and the gold was the room on the other side. On the right arm the scales had come out more brilliant and more jagged than the scales anyone knew, shining from inside, stopping just shy of the claw. When the water began to bubble — boiling him, no other word for it — the pattern stood up brighter and a rumbling came off it, and with every breath streams of golden air left through his nose and mouth, each breath taking something and leaving something better.

*His blood essence is so powerful!* It was inconceivable, blood coursing like that. And the teacher on the stool nodded once, the smallest motion in the world, certain now of the only thing that mattered: the boy could bear it.

The pulses at the gap ran eleven seconds all night, and Lin Hao built the days around them the way a smith builds a week around a quench. He took the kettle from Wu Zhangkong without asking and the trips became shared — the teacher's unhurried step and the student's fast one, an economy neither of them discussed. He cooked, because somebody had to, and learned that Xie Xie could be kept from the washroom door by being given a knife and onions, which held for two days before it didn't. He timed the pulses between tasks, never instead of them, and logged the water like weather: first a voice, rolling and knocking; then slow; then, on the third evening, clear — clear water, gold risen off it in a low mist over the sleeping face.

Still unfinished. Three days in, the refinement had not closed, and nobody woke him, because the one law everybody in that corridor knew by heart was the law of the deep: a meditation like that was a door closing itself, and a hand that reached in to help would reach into backlash.

Gu Yue came at the same hour both evenings, stayed exactly as long as looking took, and went. As before. The room did not make it anything else.

And the exam came on toward them like weather too.

## Part 2: Two Names

The visitor arrived on the third day, at an hour arranged by message, and stood in the doorway of Wu Zhangkong's ordinary room and frowned at it.

"Zhangkong, why are you staying in a place like this? Why not pick a place closer to the academy?"

"It's enough as long as I can rest here. What difference does it make if I stay somewhere else? Besides, I don't like how noisy it is near the academy."

She came in anyway, inspecting the room the way people inspect a thing they have already decided about — and then the four of them: Gu Yue, Xu Xiaoyan, Xie Xie, and Lin Hao coming through the door with the kettle, because the room had organized itself around whoever was willing to carry things.

Shen Yi was not what the word *visitor* had prepared anybody for. White-haired, sharp-eyed, younger than her carriage. And she did not look at them the way strangers look at strangers. She looked at them the way a woman looks at correspondence she is finally checking against the originals — and her eyes did the circuit the way everybody's did, but they didn't finish at the captain's empty chair. They finished at the kettle-boy, and stayed there one beat past polite.

Because she had been writing to their teacher for three winters, and the letters had carried two names.

The girl she had wanted since the day she read the first one — the elements that came flat, one after another, like scale-readings; the shortest letter and the longest to write. Not a secret; one whole reply card had been a joke about transfer papers.

And the other one. The one the letters had never managed to explain, only to report, quarter after quarter, the way a station reports weather. A boy who chose the worst class in the school on purpose. A smith the Branch ranked Master Craftsman at twelve. A footwork a Shrek student had watched at a tournament's edge and called *a Shrek thing* — which meant the academy had held a file with that name in it since before her second reply card. She had stopped asking about him in the second winter, because the answers had stopped explaining and started describing, and a teacher who only describes a boy like that is not holding him up to the light. The boy, she had decided, she would see for herself.

So she collected the debt before business sat down. Lin Hao set the kettle down, and she held out her hand, palm up — and he understood, and put a card into it. Her own, from the winter, two lines. *You said the calendar would decide. It has. Bring me the story.*

"He's in the water," he said. "Three days now. He'll come out heavier than he went in. That's the story so far."

She read her own handwriting once more, the way people do, and put the card away, and looked at him the way a file acquires a second page. "Then I'll stay for the rest of it." A beat. "Show me your hands."

He held them out — palms up, the calluses honest, the little burn-scar constellation of a boy who had been at an anvil more years than he had been at a desk. She read them like a transcript. Whatever she concluded stayed concluded; the file went back in its drawer.

Then business came in and sat down.

## Part 3: The Clock, Not the Count

"The exams are tomorrow." She took the chair. "Are your students ready?"

Wu Zhangkong's forehead wrinkled, and stayed wrinkled. "I asked you to come because I have a favor to request of you. The others are ready, but I have one student who has entered deep meditation and still hasn't awakened. So, is there a way to delay the exam?"

The room went still in a new way. Shen Yi's brows drew together, and she was silent long enough that the corridor's clock could be heard doing its work.

"I'm afraid it's impossible. You know how strict the academy's rules are. Besides, we have so many applicants of which only one hundred will pass, and there are many rounds of examination. We can't change the exam time just for your students. It wouldn't do to make them all wait for one person's sake. It's a tough situation." A breath. "Which student are you talking about?"

"The captain, Tang Wulin."

Her heart skipped — letter-fed, this, a name three winters long — and then the rest of it landed. Deep meditation, three days in. Everyone in the room knew the law of it: disturb the door, and the door takes the hand.

"Zhangkong, you know how hard it'd be. Virtually impossible. Don't you know how inflexible teachers are?" She said it helplessly, palms open, a woman describing a wall she could not move.

And here the conversation did what ours could only do it, because Shen Yi had been carrying two names for three years, and she had not come to this room to leave empty-handed on either of them.

"Understand what's not the problem," she said. "The count isn't. The Alliance scraped together four passes, and four is a stupid number for your class — I've read the letters, I know it's five. But the academy counted five the day I showed your last card to the admissions hall. If the five of them walk in and pass, five seats will be found. Shrek has bent for less and stood firm for more; this is not the wall." She looked at the door of the washroom, and her voice went flat and sorry. "The clock is the wall. The exam is tomorrow, the halls are already drawn, a thousand children are already traveling. Nobody in that city out there moves the sun for one sleeper. Not for the girl I want, and not for the file I came to read."

Wu Zhangkong nodded, once. "Alright then. I'll have my other students take the exam first."

Xie Xie was up before the sentence finished. "Teacher Wu, that's out of the question! Wulin has been looking forward to taking this exam for years, and this is our only chance! He would regret missing it for the rest of his life."

"Teacher Wu, how can we accept Captain not participating?" Xiaoyan, right behind him, the two of them a chord.

"Then the answer's the answer," Shen Yi said, and sighed, and it was a real sigh, a teacher's sigh. "There's no point in thinking about it any further. Nothing can be done. Unless he wakes up before the exam starts, he'll have to miss it. I'm sorry I can't help you."

And that was where the silence came from which Gu Yue stood up out of.

She had been silent the entire time. She walked to stand before the two teachers, and she did not raise her voice, because she never had: "Hello, Teacher Shen. May I ask if it's possible to take the exam as a substitute? Is there a way for me to renounce my exam qualifications so Wulin can take the exam? He's stronger than I am, so he could surely pass the exam if I'm able to."

Shen Yi was taken aback — the girl she regarded so highly, saying this, and she did not know whether to laugh or cry. "Little girl, you're overthinking it. Just what kind of place do you think Shrek Academy is? If normal academies don't allow for substitutions, why would Shrek? It's true that you're strong and have a high chance of being admitted, perhaps even into the inner court, but you shouldn't be so naive."

Gu Yue shook her head. "If Wulin can't go, I won't go either. If he can't join Shrek, I also refuse to join."

Her voice was steady. Shen Yi looked at the girl and saw, visibly, a kind of person she claimed to know: the kind that decides, and does not falter. *Like teacher, like student,* she did not say, and the room heard it anyway.

Lin Hao stood, because the arithmetic would not sit down. "Four passes," he said. "Five of us."

"I know the number," Wu Zhangkong said, without turning from the door. It was not dismissal. It was a man telling a boy the count had been made before the door opened, by somebody with more of it to spend.

Then she turned — and this was ours, too — to the kettle-boy at the wall of the room, because a teacher who has just been offered one entire future does not stop at one.

"And you? The file says you're the one who chose them. Would you refuse it too — the exam, the academy, all of it?"

Lin Hao considered the exact size of the question, which was smaller than she meant it to be. "Ask the cards," he said. "They've had my answer three winters. It's short."

Shen Yi laughed — one syllable, the first anyone in that room had heard from her — and did not write anything down, and everybody understood she had just written something down.

The clock in the corridor did its work. Seconds like years. Then Wu Zhangkong raised a hand and put it on Gu Yue's shoulder, and when he spoke there was no room left in the sentence for debate.

"Take your mind off of this issue. Just go back and rest. I will handle it."

Gu Yue stared at him — the shock of meeting her own resolve in somebody else's voice — and something in her settled, like water finding level.

"Thank you, Teacher."

She left first. Xie Xie stood, bristling with a sentence, and the teacher's hand came up — one motion, no hurry — and the sentence went back down, and the students went out.

On the landing, Xie Xie stopped. "What did you want to say just now?" Xiaoyan asked him quietly.

A moment of silence. Then: "Tell me, Xiaoyan, our friends or Shrek Academy, which do you consider more important?"

Xu Xiaoyan laughed — one syllable, no doubt anywhere in it. "You don't need to ask me that. As far as I'm concerned, Captain is the most important. My chances of passing were low anyway."

"Comrades truly think alike!" Xie Xie's arm went around her shoulder, lighter than it had been a minute ago. "If Wulin can't take the exam, then I won't either!"

Then he turned it, because he was Xie Xie, on the last one out. "Lin Hao. You too. Friends or academy?"

"You're asking the wrong one," he said. "I chose a class, not an academy. Five years ago, on purpose, and the class had five of us in it by the end. The pattern holds." A beat. "Four passes and five of us isn't a shape. But she said the count isn't the problem. The clock is. So the clock's what he went to handle."

"He did say that," Xie Xie admitted, and the landing held all three of them for a second, and then let them go.

## Part 4: A Small Price

Lin Hao was two steps down when the door that never quite closed gave him the rest of it.

"Let's go then." Wu Zhangkong's voice, and something under it Lin Hao had never heard there — breathing, rapid, a man's breathing, the kind you hear through a wall when the wall is doing you the courtesy of not being a wall.

"Where are we going?" Shen Yi.

"Back to the academy."

A silence with a tremble in it, on her side of the door. "You're going back to the academy? You—"

"The children all understand, so how could I not? If I can trade my dignity for their future, that's a small price to pay. I will go back with you and apologize."

Then footsteps, and the door's shadow moved, and Lin Hao went down the stairs ahead of them and was in the corridor by the time the two teachers came out, and nobody said anything about who had heard what, because the whole design of a door that never quite closes is that hearing it is not a trespass.

He had one duty left and he did it on the way past. The bath door, the hand's width, the gold: clear water, a low mist over the sleeping face, the pulses — he timed three, because the count existed to be kept — running fourteen now. Slower. Deeper. Still in it.

In the room that smelled of steam and wood, he took the book down and wrote the line the day had left him.

*Four passes. Five of us. The clock is what he went to handle.*

He put the book away, and the hawk shifted on his shoulder, winter-tipped and heavier than the bird it had been a year ago, and from somewhere below, two sets of footsteps went out the inn's front door into the first dark of exam eve — a woman going home, and a man walking back into his own past to buy them a morning.

The count did not resolve. That was the last fact of the day, and he carried it upstairs the way he had been taught to carry everything since he was ten years old and the lesson had no name yet.

Level.

## Part 1: The Wrong Year

The city had changed character overnight, the way cities do when a date arrives. Every inn was filled to the brim — examinees, teachers, the heads of families — and the streets had gone from crowded to a thing with a current. Merchants had come out for it the way merchants come out for weather: old exam questions, rules, spirit items, soul devices, printed and reprinted and sold again.

Xie Xie bought one of everything.

Lin Hao read the pamphlet twice — the second read in the violet that stood in the gold of his eyes when he read, the cheap print going steadier and closer in it, a lamp he carried and never trimmed — and started laughing on the second page, which frightened everyone, because he so rarely did it audibly.

"They're selling the wrong year." He turned the pamphlet so the class could see the seam his eyes had found, where two printings had been stitched to look like one. "Rules from this year, questions from three years ago, one page from a different academy entirely. Somebody in this city is rich." He handed it back to Xie Xie with great ceremony. "We want our money back."

"You bought it," Xie Xie said.

"I did. That's the sad part." — but he kept the true half, the rules, and did the arithmetic where he stood, because the day would demand it. *Sent by a major city:* check. *Under fifteen:* five times over. *Rank twenty-five at the very least:* thirty-three, thirty-one, thirty, twenty-eight, forty-five. The arithmetic had never once been the problem; the problem had a clock and a bathtub in it. And under the three printed rules, the pamphlet's author had hazarded a fourth, older than printing — that the real requirement had been decreed twenty thousand years ago, and it was not a number at all. Shrek did not accept ordinary people. The pamphlet said *monsters*, in the hushed typeface of a word the author half-expected to be sued over.

The morning had already taken the two teachers — the white head and the white robe, side by side, a woman going home and a man going to a door he had knocked on in his sleep for thirteen years — and by afternoon a call had come through, one call, brief as all its sender's sentences: he was handling business; they were to keep to their rooms; under no account was the meditation to be disturbed.

The class looked at the order, and at the yard behind the inn, and did what a class does with an order that has no teacher attached to it.

"What we have," Xie Xie said, quietly, in the yard, at midnight, "is a shape. Nobody's testing us on a shape. But a harder exam is still an exam, and the shape is still ours, and I'm not walking into anything tomorrow without having touched it tonight."

So they walked it. Slow, low, silent, five figures in a yard built for drying laundry: the stack positions, the release, the five-second window Xiaoyan made and the two who could use it. And it was wrong, the way a chair is wrong with one leg turned, and everybody knew which leg.

"Zhang Yangzi's slot," Xiaoyan said, at the end of the first walk-through, and nobody had to say anything back. The shape had been built on six hands, in a square in Eastsea, and its sixth hand was on a dock four thousand li away, and the letter telling him about the exam would not even arrive for days yet. They re-spaced it — Gu Yue taking the sixth's station, Lin Hao taking Gu Yue's — and walked it again, and again, and on the fourth time it held, different, a new thing.

"A shape with five hands is a different shape," Lin Hao said. "It held. Stop trying to make it the old one."

"That," said Xie Xie, "is either very wise or very lazy."

"It's late. It's both."

Xiaoyan said nothing through all of it, because the night was hers and she could feel that plainly: the starwheel was a night thing, and the exam would be held in daylight, and her whole craft would be at half its sky. She did not say it. She just walked the shape better than she had ever walked it, and the ones who knew her knew what that meant.

Between sessions, Lin Hao worked. He had no forge, so he worked the way a smith works without one: the estate lot's stock out across the floor, the file, the whetstone, the little scale, five kits gone through strap and edge and hinge — because whatever a harder exam was, it would be walked into, and walking in was a thing that could be prepared. And once, in the cold of the last watch, the joining's cold came and sat by his ankles like the dog it had become, ninety-five seconds' worth of another existence keeping its own count, and he let it, and the whetstone kept moving.

The pulses had slowed again. He timed them between tasks, never instead of them — dusk's three ran fourteen, fifteen, fourteen, taken with the whetstone in his other hand — and the last before supper ran long enough that he counted his own heartbeat against it to be sure the watch was honest.

Line 166 still said what it said. *The clock is what he went to handle.* The night was about to find out for itself.

## Part 2: The Western Gate

He did not go to the academy. That morning belonged to two people, and this is what it held, by the city and the record and the two who walked it.

The western gate of Shrek Academy stood where the world's largest city had decided to become a school. A sign board hung from the gates with two words carved into it — *Shrek Academy* — and the man in white robes stopped dead at the sight of it, the way a man stops at a wall he has walked into before. Shen Yi came to stand beside him.

"Go inside. Teacher has missed you all these years. You're both just too stubborn to make up. I was really happy when you agreed to come back, you know!"

He lowered his head without a word and walked toward the gate, his pace brisk and faster than before — almost, a person watching might think, as if he were afraid of getting cold feet.

Two youths in dark-green uniforms guarded the gate. They saluted the moment they saw her. "Senior sister."

"This is my friend," Shen Yi said. "Please grant him entry."

She took out a hexagonal metal plate and handed it over. One of the youths examined it, nodded, and stepped aside — and Shrek's Inner City let in the man who had left it.

"I originally prepared this entry token for that female disciple of yours," Shen Yi said quietly, as they passed under the arch. "I didn't think I'd end up using it for you." She had half-carried the hope for three winters — and three winters of reply cards, too, one of which had counted five names for an admissions hall that had never needed convincing — and had still not expected this.

Inside, the city changed skins. A wide street paved in black brick, stores ancient and mostly of wood, all open, almost none occupied — as if the two of them had been transported ten thousand years into the past. She walked at his side and remembered the years she had shadowed him on this same street, the junior sister, always three steps behind, always saying the same things. That time was long past. The sunny youth who always wore a brilliant smile had become a man as cold as heavenly frost, in white robes, carrying a blue sword. When his beloved passed away, his smile froze. Since then, years of isolation in a small coastal city, refusing to return. Sometimes it seemed his spirit had already faded, and he only kept living because of a promise to the dead.

He was thirty-two years old, and a seven-ringed Soul Sage, and within reach of three-word battle armor, and she was certain he would arrive at it, because his will had never once bent. And when she had finally met his disciples — five of them, the girl she had wanted and the boy the file could not explain and three more the letters had made her love secondhand — she had rejoiced: something important had come back into his life. Along with his beloved, four more people had made their way into his heart. He had returned for the sake of his disciples.

Then he halted, sudden as a slammed door, and she walked into his back.

"Why did you stop so suddenly!?" she protested, rubbing her nose.

His cold eyes thawed, a very little, at the junior sister who had said the same exact thing for ten years running. "Where is Teacher?"

He said it absently, his hand already moving — tousling her hair the way he had done when she was small and he was the sunniest senior brother the inner city had. And the tears came out of Shen Yi's large evergreen eyes all at once, and she threw herself into his arms in the middle of the ancient street.

"Senior brother!" — choked, half a sob, entirely thirteen-years-younger.

The street was not too proud to stare. Her white hair was the most recognizable head in the academy.

"Isn't that the White-haired Witch, senior sister Shen Yi? What is going on with her?"

"She never smiles and all the juniors are afraid of her. What's *she* doing?"

"Who is that man? He's so handsome!"

"Whoa. He seems sort of familiar. Who is he?"

He patted her back once. "Let's go."

She raised her head, sheepish, eyes still brimming. "You're still my senior brother, right?"

He made himself smile, and the smile was bitter, and it was the first one she had seen in years. "That isn't up to me. Let's go." And he took her arm and drew her down the street toward the city's core, striding, a man late for his own reckoning.

"Teacher is in the inner court," she said softly, wiping her eyes.

*Inner court.* He began to shake. He took one deep breath, released her hand, and sprinted, air chilling in his wake.

## Part 3: Two Words on a Sign

The inner court announced itself as a tall mossy-green wall converging on a lavish archway with a sign at its top. Two words: *Inner Court.*

There were no guards. There had never needed to be. The words were the wall. This was the legendary inner court of Shrek Academy, continent-famous, yearned for by more soul masters than could be counted, feared by the Federation itself — and the sign was enough, two words on a board, to stop anything that should be stopped.

They stopped Wu Zhangkong completely.

"Senior brother," Shen Yi said, catching up, breathless.

"Don't call me that. I'm no longer qualified to be your senior brother. If Teacher hears you, you'll be punished."

And he dropped to his knees.

It had no ceremony in it. That was the terrible part, for anyone who had seen the man conduct a class or filet a fish or stand a month of afternoons doing nothing on purpose — the arrogance and the sternness folded down like jade pillars and mountains of gold crashing to the ground, and the white-robed swordsman knelt on the black brick before two words on a sign.

"Wait here, senior brother," Shen Yi said, her heart trembling and her voice not showing it. "I'll go get Teacher." And she drew a breath and went through the arch like wind.

The turbulence settled out of him as he knelt. A cool breeze swept by, carrying the green scent the academy grows on purpose.

*Finally, I'm back. After thirteen years — today, I have returned.*

*Thirteen years ago, I was so impulsive and proud. Now I'm able to understand — but can I get back what was lost?*

*I'm sorry, Bing'er. I'm sorry, Teacher. It was all my fault.*

*Bing'er, just wait for me. I will preserve your name with my battle armor. We will be together forever.*

*As long as you desire it, I will not hesitate to sacrifice everything for you.*

Time ticked by, slowly and quickly at once. When Shen Yi came back out she was pale, and her footsteps hesitated, and she made herself close the distance and stand in front of the kneeling man.

"T-Teacher doesn't want to see you."

"Mn. Thank you." His tranquility did not move. He knelt as he had knelt.

Hesitation crossed her face, and lost, and she said it. "Teacher said, *'just let him kneel there.'*"

His head came up. He was trembling — not at the refusal. Fury would have been survivable; fury meant the account was still open. It was the disregard that closed accounts. As long as his teacher was angry with him, he still had a chance.

"Thank you, Shen Yi." He bit his lips, and knelt on, and his back was straighter than before.

"Just keep kneeling for now, senior brother," she said softly. "You know what Teacher is like. He spouts harsh words, but his heart is soft. When I told him you had returned, I saw a trace of joy on his face for a split second — he couldn't hide it at all. He still cares deeply for you. After another round of persuasion, I'm sure he'll forgive you."

Wu Zhangkong shook his head, gently. "I don't deserve Teacher's forgiveness. But for the sake of my disciples, I implore you."

"Mn." And she turned and went back inside, to persuade.

## Part 4: The Last Hour

At the inn, the sun was going to rise soon, and Teacher Wu had not come back.

"The sun is going to rise soon. Why hasn't Teacher Wu come back yet?" Xie Xie paced the room in circles, his figure wearing a track into the boards, and nobody answered, because the answer was the pacing.

At some point in the night, the door to the washroom had been opened just a crack, for just a peek. The facts of the peek entered the record as follows. Tang Wulin was soaking in the bathtub, naked as the day he joined the class, gold-misted, magnificent, unconscious. Gu Yue's face and Xu Xiaoyan's faces had turned crimson in the steam. Gu Yue had immediately clapped her hands over *Xu Xiaoyan's* eyes, leaving her own wide open to take in the sight — an allocation of resources so efficient that even the record admires it. Xie Xie, one generation's hope of the high road, had peeled them both away from the doorway, depriving the two of them of the eye-candy that was Tang Wulin. Lin Hao passed the doorway once, with the kettle, at the exact moment the crack went crimson-and-silent: steam, the edge of the tub, and duties sorted years ago. He kept the kettle moving.

"If Wulin can't take the exam, then I won't either!" still stood, resolved and proclaimed. But resolution, Xie Xie had discovered in the small hours, was a coat with a lining. Taking the exam would still have been the best outcome. Thirteen now; sixteen in three more years — too old, ruled out, finished. The only shot any of them would ever have, leaking away through an hourglass nobody could turn.

"Let's just wait," Xu Xiaoyan said meekly, from her chair. "Xie Xie, can you stop walking in circles? We've already made our choice. If we don't end up taking the exam, we'll just treat this trip as a holiday and nothing more. In any case, we're on vacation right now. Once Captain wakes up, we can go sightseeing at Shrek Academy. At the very least, we can have him treat us to dinner. I bet his cheeks will be sore considering how stingy he is."

She giggled at the thought. It was a good thought. It was even a true one — Xie Xie's face did a strange thing, because he knew the ledger of that stinginess better than anyone: aside from the bare necessities, Tang Wulin paid for nothing, ever; every coin went into the savings like water into sand, and he rarely ate out because the price of filling that particular stomach was simply too steep.

"I keep thinking about the shape," Xiaoyan said, into the grey. "Five hands held. It's not the old one, but it held."

"It held," Lin Hao agreed. "That's the version we walk in with. Whatever they test, they test five of us at once or they're not testing us."

Xie Xie stopped pacing and looked at him, and then at the window, and the sky went from black to iron to the first grey, and his impatience went with it — not up, but out; it left him, and what settled was quieter and worse. He had done the traveling arithmetic. The inn was far from the academy, and the exam would start in one hour, and if Tang Wulin stood up that very moment, bright and new and finished, they still would not make it in time. Time waited for no one.

If they missed it, they missed it. They would carry some regrets, all of them, for a long time. All of them had also decided this already, on a landing, in front of one another — comrades over Shrek Academy — and a decision did not become less true for costing what it cost.

Into which silence Gu Yue's eyes opened.

"I'll stop mocking you in the future," she said, to Xie Xie, with the finality of a court.

"Huh?" said Xie Xie, at a complete loss, and the night let that stand.

Lin Hao took the book down in the grey light, in the room that smelled of steam and paper, and wrote the line the night had left him.

*The exam is in one hour. The water is still gold. He is still handling it.*

Dawn crossed the city at its usual rate, no faster for anyone. It found, in the inner court of the world's most feared academy, a white-robed man still kneeling before two words on a sign, back straight, thirteen years long. And it found, in a far inn, a bathtub still holding its gold, five children on a vacation with a shape nobody else had, and one hour.

## Part 1: Three of Everything

The morning after the worst night ran on breakfast, the way mornings do.

"I'll stop mocking you in the future" had needed explaining, and the explaining had gone the way of all Gu Yue's explanations, which was that Xie Xie ended up worse off and no wiser.

"What do you mean?" he eyed her, with suspicion.

"I guess you can be considered a male."

"Are you saying you treated me like I was a girl before?"

"You can take it however you want."

Xu Xiaoyan latched on to his arm, beaming. "So we're actually a group of sisters! I wouldn't have known if big sis Gu Yue didn't tell me."

"You girls are always bullying me!" He wrested his arm free, lips pinched, a man making a strategic withdrawal from a war he had lost years ago. "I bet you don't have what it takes to mess with Wulin. Oh, whatever. I'm hungry now. You two guard him while I get some breakfast. Do you want me to bring anything back?"

Gu Yue nodded. "I want meat, steamed buns, juice, and yogurt. Oh right, some vegetables too."

Xu Xiaoyan counted on her fingers. "I want some bread, jam, yogurt, and a fried egg. Actually, make that two. Yeah, I'm still growing after all."

"And the captain's," Lin Hao said, before Xie Xie reached the door. "Three of everything. He came off the first seal hungry once; this one ran three days. The number's a number. Bring it."

Xie Xie looked at him, then at the washroom door, then did the arithmetic himself and went pale. "Three of *everything*," he repeated, solemn, a man accepting a logistics assignment, and was gone before Xiaoyan could erupt — "Yeah, growing as round as a fried egg!" rattling down the stairwell after him, timed to miss her.

The pulses had run sixteen seconds all night. Sixteen meant *today*, and the room was arranged for it — and the knock came before Xie Xie did.

"He's back so quickly?" Xu Xiaoyan mumbled, going to the door — and opened it on the white-haired lady from yesterday.

"Oh, it's you. Auntie, where's Teacher Wu?"

"Your teacher is fine. He's just taking care of some matters for you all at the academy right now. Has your captain awakened yet?"

"Not yet."

A sigh escaped Shen Yi's lips. "Then all we can do is wait. When he's conscious, I'll bring you all over."

"But it's already too late!" Xiaoyan said, confused — and Shen Yi smiled faintly and tousled her hair, exactly the way a white-robed man had tousled hers in an ancient street the day before, a gesture handed down like a coin.

"Don't worry about it. Your teacher has already settled things. Your tests might be a bit harder, but you still have one last chance. We'll depart once your captain is awake."

"Really? That's awesome! Teacher Wu is the best!" — and Xiaoyan bounced, and the bounce was honest, and under it the room reorganized itself around a fact nobody had dared to plan for: both. They had given up the exam for their captain, and the exam was coming anyway, harder.

Gu Yue stared at Shen Yi in surprise, and a heavy mountain came off her face, and Lin Hao looked away from the lifting, because some weights were private coming off, too.

## Part 2: The Hall

In the washroom, the water had gone lukewarm, and the gold had thickened, and inside the sleeping boy a door he had been three days in opening finally stood open.

"Have I succeeded?"

The mystical hall was as it always was, and the old man in it was not. Old Tang stood near him in a flash of light, clearer than before — more human, somehow, as if something spent had been refunded.

"That's right, you've succeeded," he said, chock-full of satisfaction. "How do you feel?"

"Good. It wasn't as painful as the first time."

"That's because you're more prepared this time. Both your body and soul power have made remarkable progress in the last three years, especially since your soul power is compressed by your new cultivation method. It has refined your meridians and increased the load that they can bear. You also found high-quality spirit items this time. All of these factors eased the process."

The second had been easier than the first — boiled alive, and then accustomed, and then nothing but a vast filling. Then the shattering, jaws closing — and through it, this time, no brink of bursting at all. A hollow image of a pain he had already survived once.

"Old Tang, what changed with my body this time? I remember back then you said there would be a nice surprise for me!"

"That's right, there's a surprise. But you need to go experience it for yourself. I suggest you don't worry about it for now and instead focus on breaking the third seal in the near future."

"The third seal." Tang Wulin laughed, doing the arithmetic out loud. "Isn't the deadline when I'm twenty? I still have six years — five plus fifteen is twenty years old!"

Old Tang arched a brow at him. "Who said the deadline is twenty years old for the third seal? No, that's not how it's calculated. Your next seal needs to be broken by the time you turn sixteen. In other words, you have three years left. The countdown for the next seal starts immediately after you've broken the previous one."

"Are you telling me the time between seals is going to continue shrinking?"

"That's right. It shortens each time. Your preparation time will shorten by three months each time. After the ninth seal, you will only have one year to prepare for each. You'll be under a lot of pressure from now on."

Eighteen seals. Windows shrinking, seal over seal, down to a single year — and a tribulation for the unready, the old man said, and left the sentence exactly as unfinished as it needed to be. The list came, and Tang Wulin checked the prefixes of the spirit items that rose in his mind against it, and was relieved past all decency to find them thousand-year things. If they had been ten-thousand-year items, he would have just given up right then and there.

"You can go now. Continue working hard."

The world melted.

## Part 3: Seventeen Seconds

Cold.

His eyes shot open on cooled bathwater and daylight, and the first thing his body reported was not power, not gold — it was hunger, visceral, clawing, from the pits of a stomach that had been three days on fire. *How many days has it been?*

He climbed out, dried, dressed, in a hurry to stave it off — and opened the washroom door and nearly jumped out of his skin. Instead of Teacher Wu, the room held five people, one of them an unfamiliar white-haired woman.

"You're finally awake!" Xie Xie leapt at him.

"So I woke up in time?" His hopes rose on the sight of them — there should still be time, otherwise his teammates wouldn't be here, otherwise —

"What do you mean 'in time'?" Xie Xie grumbled. "We're already late."

*"Huh?"* — so shocked he forgot the hunger.

"Let's go." Shen Yi stood, giving him a meaningful look, and walked out; and Xiaoyan beamed at him, and Gu Yue got up with an apathetic face whose eyes were doing more than the face, concern standing in them openly, and Wulin turned to Xie Xie. "Who is that?"

"She's a friend of Teacher Wu's from Shrek. We're already three hours late; Teacher Wu is helping us out at the academy right now, so we need to hurry over, otherwise we might miss our chance."

Three hours. Tang Wulin slumped, and his head went down, and the dominoes fell in front of him one by one, all in a row, all with his fingerprints on them. His stinginess. The cheap room, far from the academy. The meditation he had let run. His teammates, holding the line at a landing and then at a doorway for him. A once-in-a-lifetime opportunity, leaking out of the hourglass. And all this, just for the sake of saving money.

"I'm sorry. This is all my fault."

Xie Xie chuckled — actually chuckled. "What's the point in talking about it now? When you protected us at the forefront all those times, have we ever said thanks? How's your body? How did your deep meditation go?"

"I don't know either, but I feel great." And he did — strength surging under the hunger, the body a third stronger than the immense thing it had already been, soul power up around twenty-seven or twenty-eight, and something else waiting in him, untested, the surprise an old man had promised. No time to test it. No time even to eat. He asked Xie Xie if there was anything to eat; Xie Xie shook his head; and a bag appeared at his elbow, held out in silence.

Steamed buns, and meat. He knew by the weight before he looked up, and he knew by the hand, and he did not thank her, because there are bonds — life-and-death, forge-and-fire, hand-stack — where thanks is a unit too small to transact in. Three buns and a portion of meat — and then the rest of the bag, because somebody had ordered three of everything, and the somebody was not sorry.

He finished it at a speed that would have made the continent's competitive eaters file a grievance.

And it was there, with the captain upright and fed and the shame hanging off him like a wet coat, that Lin Hao said the thing he had been carrying since a room two days ago, where a teacher with a file had asked him what the academy was worth and he had told her to ask the cards.

"I don't care about Shrek Academy."

The room went quiet. Even Xie Xie.

"Shrek Academy only helps me achieve things I should anyway — a few years earlier. That's all it is to me. A shortcut." He said it flat, the way he said numbers. "So don't think we just lost everything. We're good enough. We were good enough in a yard in Eastsea with nobody's permission, and we're good enough now — we walked a five-hand shape at midnight and it held." A breath. "Academies change their rules."

He tipped his head toward the stairs, and the street, and the sleek dark-green car standing in it — an academy's car, an academy's teacher, sent across a city to wait on five children who had missed the exam by three hours.

"And the academy came himself."

Nobody answered that, because there wasn't an answer that improved it. Wulin looked at him for a second, and something in the slump came back upright, and Xie Xie muttered "he's not wrong" in the tone of a man conceding a point to a ledger. Shen Yi, at the door, said nothing at all — but she had asked the question first, two days ago, and she had just been given the longer answer, and she filed it where she filed things.

The count, for the record, had ended at seventeen seconds — the last interval Lin Hao ever timed through that gap, unfinished, mid-number, taken with his hands full, because he was stacking the third portion's wrappings when the washroom lock clicked and the captain came out under his own steam.

## Part 4: Five Papers

The car was everything a soul car should be, and Shen Yi drove it the way Wu Zhangkong taught class: fast but smooth, reactions precise, no unnecessary movement, full speed displayed like a fact being stated.

"Get in." Xie Xie tried the back and was promptly dragged into the middle of it by Gu Yue, who took the front seat beside Lin Hao herself — Xiaoyan at one window laughing into her hand, Wulin at the other, Xie Xie between them, aggrieved. *Too controlling,* he cursed silently. *Hogging the front seat all to herself.* Nobody in the car was deceived by anybody's face.

A juice box appeared against Lin Hao's arm at the second traffic bridge. He looked at it, then at her — she was already watching the road as if the hand were not hers — and drank it, and happiness flashed through Gu Yue's eyes before she closed them to rest; her shoulder settled against his arm, cool against warm, and the back seat had the manners not to report it.

Then the woman driving the academy's car used an hour of enclosed road the way teachers do.

"The letters never said how the fourth ring went black," Shen Yi said, eyes on the traffic, voice level. "A ten-thousand-year ring at your age. The hall will want to know. I'm asking first."

"It was offered," Lin Hao said. "The metal was real. I didn't take it lightly and I didn't take it alone."

"And the footwork they keep writing to each other about."

"Is footwork."

She let three blocks go by. "Show me the sword after the exam."

"That," he said, "is the first thing anyone from Shrek has asked for that I actually want to give."

Shen Yi's eyes ticked once to her mirror — the boy in the front seat read as sixteen until he opened his mouth, and she had stopped correcting her own count of him two days ago — and went back to the road.

The city ran past the windows and did not end. The tin rode where it had always ridden, and he caught himself doing the thing three years had built into him — reading crowds for a height, a braid, a way of standing — and put it away, and it did not stay put for long. It never did, in new cities. This one was just the biggest thing it had ever not found her in.

Within the hour, the walls. They towered beyond vision, plain and undecorated, without even a signboard — an enormous dragon coiled around the academy, sleeping with its eyes open. Outside the front gate, a sea of people, the continent's cream pressing at the continent's standard. Shen Yi did not even slow down: off to the side, seven or eight turns, a small gate that opened at a button she pressed without lifting her wrist and closed behind them, and the outside world closed with it. Peace. Tranquility. An era long gone, kept.

"Are we in Shrek Academy now?" Xie Xie asked.

"This is Shrek Academy's inner city, built for the sake of the academy, so this is the core of the city as well as where students study. Only those recognized by the academy are permitted to enter Shrek Inner City." The car did not slow one bit as she explained. And then, evenly, driving fast through a world ten thousand years deep, she gave them the price:

"Because you were late, your exam will be harder than normal. You'll be tested on the same things, but will have less time to finish and might not even have a chance to rest throughout the entire process. Furthermore, if you do pass, you'll only be working students."

"Working students? What's that?" Tang Wulin asked.

"It means you'll have to pay for the costs to attend Shrek by yourself."

"Huh?" Dread gripped Tang Wulin at the mere mention of spending money — full-body, ancestral, immediate. And then the guilt did its own arithmetic: "The quotas were four," he said, mostly to his knees. "There are five of us. That's my fault too —"

"No." Shen Yi's voice did not raise and did not soften. "The quota arithmetic died when your teacher walked through that gate on his knees. Five of you are sitting in this car; the halls have five papers. Harder papers, drawn last night, for names the examiners were already holding. *That* is what the apology bought. Understand it before you carry it."

Nobody said anything to that either. It was one thing to give up an academy for each other; it was another, quieter thing to learn what had been paid for the papers in your hands.

"You're not paying the school money," she went on. "You're working for the school to pay for your tuition. Do you think Shrek Academy is short on money? Normal students all attend for free."

*Work.*

It landed on Tang Wulin like a door opening — he had never once backed down from hardship in his life; his mood lifted the moment the word arrived. It landed on Lin Hao differently, in a different part of the car, and stayed there, glowing quietly: a smith ranked Master Craftsman at twelve did not hear *work for the school* and feel dread; he heard a forge somebody else paid the charcoal for, in a city ten thousand years deep in metal. Whatever the school was short of, he was long in it. He looked out the window and did not say any of it — yet.

Xie Xie's face had gone sour, and the sourness tumbled straight out of his mouth:

"What work?"

Nobody answered. The inner city flowed past, ancient, green, and somewhere in its core a white-robed man was waiting who had knelt for thirteen of those years to buy this ride, and five children were being driven toward five harder papers, and the last thing Lin Hao wrote that day, at a stop that lasted eleven seconds, was the line the morning had left him.

*He woke. We're good enough. The academy came himself.*

## Part 1: The Pilgrimage

"Ask me again if you pass," Shen Yi said, when someone asked the question the car had been carrying. "It's still early for you to know." And the car slowed to a snail's pace before a plaza that ate the horizon.

Ashen-gray stone, slabs larger than the road-rock of the inner city; a semicircle of ancient buildings a kilometer across by eye; at the center a hundred-meter pond and a fountain and a sculpture that stopped Tang Wulin's heart mid-beat — the only man who could stand beside Tang San in any telling, the Spirit Pagoda's founder, the master of the Sea God's Pavilion, the Spirit Ice Douluo, Huo Yuhao, carved life-like with his spirit souls gathered around him like guardians. The sole being of his era to ascend to godhood. The same sculpture stood at the Tang Sect; Wulin's eyes sparkled and his chest worked.

"This is Spirit Ice Plaza," Shen Yi said, and gave them the ten-thousand-year history in four sentences, and led them toward the ring of buildings — past carvings that resolved as they came close: figures, scores of figures, every one a person.

"Inner court disciples," she said. "Every student admitted to the inner court has a sculpture made in his likeness. Commemoration — and evidence of Shrek's history."

Lin Hao walked the last fifty meters with his head tipping back, doing the thing he did to buildings. The walls had a scale to them the way a good anvil has a weight: settled, load-bearing, certain of what they were holding. Twenty thousand years of murals and stone, quenched and re-quenched, each generation's hand over the last one's — the deep past not preserved but *maintained*, which is a different thing, and a smith knew the difference. His father's shop had held four generations of hammer-marks on one stump. This hall held ten thousand years of them, and somebody paid for the charcoal forever. *Whatever the school was short of, he was long in it.* The thought had a street address now.

House Shrek swallowed them. Ten-meter ceilings under six floors; murals climbing the dome; grandeur that never once got tacky. The pilgrimage feeling the pamphlets could only advertise. All five of them felt their spines try to kowtow.

And it broke Tang Wulin's heart, in the way that shame and fire are the same burn. His fists balled, knuckles white. *I almost made my teammates miss this.* We — we all have to get in here. Every soul master in the world would have said the same; he was just the one in the room with the fingerprints on the dominoes.

Two corridors later, a round hall, twenty meters of domed ceiling with one painting on it.

A black dragon. Wings spread, golden eyes burning out of an ebony face — and violet light exploding from its body, so vivid the paint argument lost in court. Every scale countable at twenty meters. Not one missing.

The room pressed down like a mountain with opinions.

## Part 2: The Drop of Blood

Gu Yue trembled once, then got herself back — nearly his match, whatever that cost her. Xiaoyan went the other way: pale, shaking, on the lip of something her knees had opinions about. Xie Xie's knees voted first and Wulin caught him, and the fear drained out of the boy the instant he touched his captain's aura.

Lin Hao stood in it and *read.*

The pressure came in waves, each heavier than the last, and it was real pressure, the kind the deep water had taught him the temperature of — and the violet light was the tell. His own stood up in the gold of his eyes without being asked, the reading-lamp answer to a reading-light, and under the two violets the mural stopped being a picture and became a fact. A drop of blood in the paint. He didn't know how he knew; the knowing arrived the way metal's opinions arrive, up the arms, and his arms had seven years of anvil in them. Somebody had painted this with a Title Douluo's hand and bled a monster into it.

And the monster's blood recognized things.

The fourth ring — the black one, the ten-thousand-year cold that slept in a lane-long dragon jiao — *turned over.* Not woken: turned over, the way a heavy sleeper turns toward a sound in the house. The cold rose off it and met the hall's pressure, and the pressure was the GREATER mountain, and the ring went deep under it — which was water's nature, and the ring was a river thing. A tributary does not shame the river.

The sword was another matter.

The sword had never once in his life been underneath anything, and it was not underneath this. The King's pressure came down and broke around his spirit the way a current breaks around a keel — met, parted, passed on — and the Intent stood in him the way it had stood at ten years old in front of grown men: temperature, edge, and no vocabulary in it for kneeling. The blood in the paint was a king's. Kings are not obeyed by swords. The hawk tightened its grip on his shoulder to the edge of pain, winter-tipped feathers flat, his arms goosefleshed wrist to elbow over the marks — and he stood in the Gold-eyed Black Dragon King's own hall with his spine unhandled, reading the painting.

Then he stopped reading, because beside him Xiaoyan was going under, and Wulin was already moving — snorted once, golden light flaring deep in his eyes, and *scales*, more scales than Lin Hao had ever seen on him, out of the right arm and past the shoulder and down the collarbone and the torso's right side and up the neck, pulsing with more power than ever before — and his blood essence stretched out past his own skin and wrapped all of them, the whole class, like a coat.

The hall's pressure came down. The coat held it off. And Xiaoyan breathed.

The waves broke and broke. Wulin stood inside his own legend, unbothered, arrogant as spring. Shen Yi was nowhere in the room.

## Part 3: Nine

"Huh."

She came around a stone pillar with an elderly man behind her — dark-green robe, the very definition of surprise on his face, approval already nodding at Wulin.

"Not bad. He has the potential of a little monster. It has been many years since I've last seen someone capable of withstanding the Gold-eyed Black Dragon King's pressure."

So the painting had a name, and the name had a history — the strongest soul beast in the Great Star Dou Forest; a drop of blood won in a legendary battle between that dragon and Shrek's most powerful; the mural painted by a Title Douluo who specialized in painting. The hall tested spiritual power. The longer you lasted, the higher you scored. Nobody told them any of it. Examinees never got told; that was the trial.

Shen Yi was astonished twice, and the second time was about Wulin: she had labelled Gu Yue the promising one — and here was a second. And in the long history of the Black Dragon Hall, no one had ever met the mural's might with an aura of their own. Examinees endured. This boy answered.

"Elder Li, this trial's score...?"

"Give that boy full marks." A glance at Tang Wulin. Then the old eyes went around the room doing arithmetic, and stopped, and came back. "As for the rest... luck is an aspect of strength. Eight points."

They bowed without being told — and Elder Li, passing, stopped in front of Lin Hao. The look held for two full seconds, and then a third and a fourth, and it was not approval anymore. It was a man taking his own instrument out of its case and finding the scale too short.

"The hall scores endurance," he said to Shen Yi, without taking his eyes off the boy. "How long a child stands under the King's blood. This one's spirit never went under it. It answered standing." A pause with dry amusement in it. "The scale has no number for that. Call it ten. The first spirit-answer this hall has ever scored — and the first blood-answer, in the same morning." He kept walking.

"Thank you, Elder Li." Shen Yi's eyes lit, and lit, and lit.

The elder smiled humbly at the wall. "I'm just giving face to that old fellow, Zhuo Shi. It doesn't change the fact that you were all late!" And he made to leave, and turned back once more to give Tang Wulin an approving nod, and went, incomprehensibly, and the name he'd dropped — *Zhuo Shi* — sat in the air a second after him like a coin put down on a table. Shen Yi's face did something small and private and was still again. Nobody asked. Yet.

"Each trial scores ten," Shen Yi said, brisk again, herding. "Six to pass. Points totalled at the trials' end, deducted for failures, added for full scores. Your luck was good for the first section." A beat, and she did not soften it, because she was Shrek: "It's still counted against you that you were late."

Follow me.

## Part 4: The Wager

It was there — in the corridor between the hall of the dragon and whatever came next, with the marks still on the class's knees and the elder's *"late"* still on the walls — that Lin Hao stopped walking, turned around, and put the thing he had been carrying since a car ride's terms on the table in front of the academy.

"Then say the rest of it to my face," he said. "The papers are harder. There's no rest. And if we pass, we pay." His voice did not rise; it was the voice he read numbers in. "I don't take this."

Xie Xie made a sound like a kettle deciding against boiling. Shen Yi stopped mid-stride. Even Gu Yue's head turned.

"If your Shrek Academy likes monsters so much — and you have them, you keep them in the walls — then put out any student from your outer court." He let that stand exactly one heartbeat. "If even a single student defeats me, let's go how you want. All of it — the papers, the penalties, the paying. No complaint, ever." A breath. "But if I win, then you change your rules for my team."

The corridor was stone, and old, and it took a full three seconds to decide what to do with the silence.

"You know what you're asking," Shen Yi said at last, quietly — not a rebuke; a teacher checking her file against the original one more time. "The terms were bought."

"I know what they cost." Flat. Level. Carried level. "That's why I'm not spending them."

And because the academy was the academy — because the hall behind them was painted in the blood of a dragon that Shrek's strongest had gone out and *fought*, and the academy's whole soul was that sentence — the answer came not from Shen Yi but from behind them, where an old man in a dark-green robe had come back down the corridor and been standing for some of it, unhurried, interested, the way elders are interested.

"Zhuo Shi would have liked that," Elder Li said, to no one, and then to him: "Boy. Do you know what the outer court's first seat is?"

"No, sir."

"Good," said Elder Li. "Then it knows nothing about you either." He came forward, and the corridor got smaller and older and more amused. "Terms. The hall accepts the shape of your wager — *any* student of the outer court, of the hall's choosing. If the hall's student defeats you, the terms stand unaltered, and you will hear no complaint from any of the five of you, ever, and you will say *thank you* for the papers." A finger came up. "If you win — the lateness dies, the penalties die, the working-student mark dies. Your team enters as students enter. Rules changed, for your team."

The second finger.

"But the wager rides behind the trials. All five of you pass every trial first. One failure anywhere — yours, the little sister's, anyone's — and the wager is void and the terms stand. Shrek does not change its rules for a team that cannot finish an examination."

He looked at the five of them once each, ending at Lin Hao, and the amusement went all the way down to something older in it.

"And when the trials are done — if they are done — the hall puts out whom the hall puts out. You said *any.* The word is mine now."

"It was always going to be," Lin Hao said.

Elder Li looked at him for a moment, and then he laughed — a short, dry bark, an elder's laugh, rusty at the hinges — and walked away down the corridor, and did not say where he was going, and it did not matter, because the shape of the afternoon had just changed for everyone in it.

Shen Yi looked at her five examinees with an expression that in a lesser woman would have been called delight.

"Follow me," she said. "Second trial."

Behind them, Wulin's hand closed once, open once — the guilt and the fire again — and Xie Xie whispered, with the reverence of a man watching a firework go off in his own hand: "He's going to kill us. Teacher Wu is going to kill us. *After* the elder does."

"He'll understand," Xiaoyan whispered back.

"He'll *understand*," Xie Xie agreed, in a tone that meant the opposite, and meant it joyfully.

Gu Yue said nothing at all. She looked at the corridor where the elder had gone, then at Lin Hao, and filed it, and was already walking.

## Part 5: The Night That Wasn't

The second hall was another dome. "Wait here," Shen Yi said, and left them with no explanation, because that, too, was the trial.

They had learned the lesson of the last hall in the last hall. Wulin glanced; Xie Xie and Xiaoyan sat, cross-legged, meditating off what the dragon had cost them; Gu Yue shook her head once — fine — and stood in the middle of the floor with her eyes closed.

Lin Hao stood where the room's sightlines crossed, and did the thing he did: read the space. The dome had a painting of a night sky, and the floor had silver in the stone, and the silver was in *channels*, which meant the floor was a work, and works had purposes.

The hall went dark at noon.

Night, whole and instant, the painted dome waking into a boundless star-field too real to be art. Silver lights rose out of the floor channels and wove themselves into that sky, and then faded, and the five of them were floating in it — a world with no floor left that any eye could find.

And beside him, in the dark that was not dark, Xu Xiaoyan stood up out of her exhaustion like a lamp being lit.

He almost missed it. He didn't: three years of watching the yard had a vocabulary for it. The girl's craft lived at night — the starwheel, the astrological attribute, five seconds of the world reordered — and the exam was a day exam, and the day had been the problem nobody said; and now the second trial of Shrek Academy had reached down and turned the *hall itself into her element*, and nobody in this academy did anything by accident.

"Xiaoyan," he said, quietly. "It's yours."

"I know," she said, and the smile in it could be heard with the back teeth. "They *made* me a night."

Whatever came next, it would come into a night she owned.

"Hold hands!" Wulin ordered — Xie Xie's hand, Gu Yue's hand, down the circle — and two purple rings rose and Bluesilver Grass burst out and wrapped all five of them in a living barrier, because when you did not know the enemy, safety first, plan second.

The world changed.

The star-field tore, and light came back, and they stood in a wide somewhere — and the roar arrived before the room did, tyrannical, and the pressure with it, and the thing that came out of the glare was ten meters long and five tall, two horns out of its skull, one longer than the other, skin like armor around scarlet eyes.

"It's an Earth Demon Rhinoceros," Xie Xie said, solemn, hunting through three years of platform work for the entry. "At least three-thousand-years. We've never met one — it's not a forest beast. It's a lord of the savanna."

"Its attribute is earth," Gu Yue judged.

Wulin didn't speak. His hands moved — signals, stations, the shape — and the shape had five hands now, and it had held at midnight in a laundry yard, and it had never once been tested, and the wager rode on all five of them now, and the rhino put its head down.

## Part 1: The Shape, Tested

The rhinoceros put its head down, and the shape got its first test in the only school that would have known the difference.

Before the charge, three seconds of stations: Wulin front; Xie Xie flanking wide; the girls backline in the star-field's silver; Lin Hao at the right edge, where the ground told things. He had read the beast the way he read metal, and the read took one breath, and he spent it out loud, flat, the way numbers go out.

"The horn is a feint. It's a strong-beast feint, but the foot is the weapon — everything it has lands through the ground. The stomp is the fight. Xiaoyan, the ground is yours; it always was tonight. Xie Xie, the head stings best. Captain—" the ghost of a smile, one beat, gone— "hit it somewhere that offends it."

Then Tang Wulin shot forward like a rocket, Bluesilver Impaling Array bursting out of him into the charge's path, and the Earth Demon Rhinoceros ran straight into the array, its huge body barely restrained for a moment — and in that moment Wulin closed and, drawing all his strength into his fist, punched it right in the face.

The rhino lowered its horns to answer the fist.

Bang.

It was like being hit by a train. Tang Wulin flew back like a cannonball, his whole arm numb — and the rhinoceros recoiled. Both of them, off their marks. Nobody was hurt on either side, and by the arithmetic of soul beasts that was a triumph: in brute strength this thing ranked in the top three of its entire level; the Dreadclaw Bear they had never met ranked merely in the top ten. It was feared for exactly this. And a thirteen-year-old had just made it take a step back with his fist.

Wulin was proud of it in the air, even flying. He flung a strand of Bluesilver Grass as he went and lassoed the beast's neck, and the trial-space glittered around them all like the beast arenas of old — courage and riches, great rewards, a place built to seduce.

The rhino's defense was better than the bear's; its attack, worse. The problem was never surviving it. The problem was getting through.

## Part 2: The Edge Taken Off

Wulin pulled on the grass and went flying back into the fight like a released spring. Xie Xie took his moment at the flank — second ring lit, **Light Dragon Storm** — agility's explosive edge aimed with three years of instinct at the head, the softest thing on the mountain. It could not breach the hide. It stung. That was the whole assignment, and he graded himself complete.

The rhinoceros grunted, raised its right foot, and stomped.

**War Stomp.** Yellow light detonated outward from the descending foot in a ring, and the ring did not care who it caught — paralysis lived inside it, twenty-five meters of it, Wulin already clear in mid-flight and hauling Xie Xie up by their shared strand so the numbness only caught him half —

— and the ring ran to the end of itself twenty meters short of the girls.

Canon's own margin, and here is what the margin was made of: the sword.

Lin Hao had been moving before the foot came down — the read had said *the foot*, the read is why the girls stood where they stood — and as the yellow wall rolled out across the star-field floor he drew the Frost Abyss one-handed and laid the Still Water line flat in its path, edge on, and CUT the top off the wave. Not the wave. Never the whole thing — the trial was the team's and the danger was the team's to answer, and a boy who deleted his class's examinations would be doing nobody any favors. He took the edge off it. The paralysis ring crossed the girls' line with its teeth pulled, a shove of warm wind where a seizure should have been, and Gu Yue's hands were already moving through the counter and Xiaoyan's staff was already rising, unafraid, because their floor was theirs.

One stroke. In and gone. Xie Xie, ringing with numbness in Wulin's grip overhead, got one look at it and understood exactly what he had seen, and would describe it later as *unfair, in the best way.*

## Part 3: The Gold

Wulin landed on the rhinoceros's head.

Golden scales ripped across his skin and his arm became the supreme golden dragon claw, and earth's stalwart defense — the whole problem of the beast — was about to stop being one, because if the claw got through the hide, the crushing effect did the rest. A matter of time.

Then the unexpected thing happened, and the night changed color.

The instant the claw finished forming, his body blazed with heat — fire searing up the blood — and his two purple soul rings vanished.

In their place: **a golden soul ring.**

Xu Xiaoyan and Gu Yue went dumbstruck, skills forgotten. Xie Xie gaped mid-air. The golden ring shone resplendent and showered him in splendid gold, and the scales and the claw stopped being dull — brighter than diamond, a treasure-smith's dream of finish — and blood essence gathered around him in a visible aura while his body swelled with power that was not soul power at all.

At the right edge of the shape, a smith watched the gold come up in his captain like a pour completing, and knew the temper on sight. *Same gold as the water.* Three days of mist over a bathtub, and now the same temperature standing up inside a boy — the break hadn't added something; it had *finished* something. He filed it where he filed metal.

The rhino threw its head and hurled Wulin off. Too busy being born new to attack, he got the scaled arm up in front of the horn — and this time the arm did not go numb, did not weaken, did not care.

"Be careful!" Gu Yue — yellow light surging at him, earth spikes riding it. He braced on landing, and the spikes struck, and the golden light merged with his skin, and he was thrown into the air entirely unharmed, groaning only at the tumble's dead weight.

*That golden light strengthened my body?*

*Is this the surprise Old Tang spoke of?*

No time. He spun mid-air, caught the lasso-strand wrapped around the beast's head, and dove down like a hawk — and his reinforcements arrived at last. Xie Xie, still airborne, split — three light clones, and behind them three shadows hidden from sight: **Twin Dragon Clones**, both third skills at once, six of them, every angle. Two went straight for the eyes, because skin is negotiable and eyes are not, and the rhinoceros shut its thick eyelids like portcullises and took the barrage as six ringing headaches.

And then the ground it trusted betrayed it, because the ground had been hers all along.

**Starlight Shackles** burst up beneath the beast and bound it — an instant only, chains of starlight, but an instant was the whole currency of this class — and the rhinoceros's center of gravity went with it, and three thousand years of savanna lordship tipped, and toppled.

Stars littered the illusion sky. The Starwheel Ice Staff accepted the night as fact — that was the secret of it, the reason the hall had gone dark at noon — and the absolute control those false stars bought her turned a binding into a fall.

The captain came down like a hawk on a falling mountain, gold burning.

## Part 4: Win

At the door of the trial hall, unnoticed by design, a man in white robes had been standing since the stomp.

Wu Zhangkong did not enter. A teacher does not touch an examination; he had drilled that into four generations and he was not going to make an exception for the one exam his own arrogance had nearly cost them. Shen Yi stood at his shoulder, and had said, quietly, the four words she had brought him from the corridor: *your student made terms.*

He had watched the punch. He had watched the stroke that took the teeth off the War Stomp — one draw, one line, holstered before the yellow light finished dying — and his face had done nothing at all, which on him was applause. He had watched the gold come up out of his captain's body and replace two purple rings with a color he had never seen on a soul master in his life, and only then, at the door, did he look down at the boy stationed at the right edge, and the look lasted four seconds, and the boy looked back and did not flinch, because he had done the arithmetic before he spoke in that corridor.

The exchange happened between the shackles and the fall, low, between the only two people in Shrek City who talked this way.

"You wagered."

"Yes, sir."

"Terms."

"Any student of the outer court, of the hall's choosing, against me. If I lose, the terms stand and we thank you for the papers. If I win, the lateness dies, the penalties die, the working mark dies. All five pass every trial first, or it's void."

"You wagered my apology."

"No, sir." Flat. Carried level. "You paid it. I wasn't spending it twice."

Four more seconds of the look. Somewhere in them, something that was not disapproval finished becoming something else — the thing his class would have called, if they had dared, the file coming shut.

"Win," Wu Zhangkong said.

One word. It was not permission; it was not a blessing. It was a standard, set where the boy could reach it and nothing below, and it came with exactly one addition, delivered in the voice of a man assigning a smith his quench:

"The five of you pass everything. That was already the assignment. The duel is what happens if you fail."

Then the rhinoceros finished falling, and the door's two watchers were moving — Shen Yi forward to proctor, the white robe stepping back out of the light — and the golden ring burned down out of the false stars like a struck match, and the shape that had held at midnight in a laundry yard held now in the oldest school on the continent, with three seconds left on its first test.
