## Part 1: The Nape

If Xu Xiaoyan's shackles could restrain an expert of Wu Zhangkong's level — and they could — then the Earth Demon Rhinoceros had never had a chance of arguing with them.

Gu Yue, counter ready, did not launch it. She recalled her soul power and her rings, and stood down: the opening was better spent.

And the opening was spent. Wulin came down on the fallen beast's head, and the resplendent golden dragon claw descended on the rhinoceros's nape — the neck, weaker than the skull he wasn't sure he could pierce — and the moment the claw touched hide, every drop of the golden light clinging to his body converged into it, bathing it in one magnificent glow. The crushing effect activated on contact. The outer armor of the skin shattered like slag off a pour, the claw went into the breach, and a moment later the Earth Demon Rhinoceros collapsed with a rumble that ran through the whole arena floor — spine severed, and its control over its body, and its life.

It's really strong. He stared at his sparkling claw, which lacked even the tiniest bloodstain, and felt a flurry of emotions his vocabulary didn't cover.

He had reaped the second seal's benefits in full. The mysterious golden ring appeared when the claw appeared — and where Bluesilver Grass drank soul power, this ring drank **physical strength and blood essence**. The claw no longer cost him soul power at all; he could feel the blood going to it, and if he ever spent all his blood essence, the bill would arrive as — hunger. Just hunger, enormous and immediate. He could now hold the claw far longer, and it was stronger, and the scales amplified everything further and now covered the ENTIRE right side of his body, strengthening every part they lay on. He could not have slaughtered this rhinoceros so easily without any of it.

And in the back of his mind, where knowledge he had never been taught lived, the name of it surfaced the way a temper color surfaces in steel.

*Golden Dragon Body.*

An all-around amplifier — strength, speed, attack, defense — with strength amplified most of all. Today had been the demonstration: a thirteen-year-old, toe to toe with a top-three beast of its level, not backing down.

None of which, he knew, looking at the small fierce girl with the staff, happened without Starlight Shackles buying him the instant. One attack, one kill, because for one split second three thousand years of rhinoceros could not move.

## Part 2: The Score

The arena faded mid-thought, and they were standing in the dark hall, hands joined in a circle, exactly as before — as if the whole fight had been an illusion they had held hands inside. It had not been the spirit ascension platform; that was technology, and this was something else, some craft they couldn't fathom, and they were awestruck in the residue of it, five pairs of hands slowly letting go.

Shen Yi reappeared, and her expression was stranger than ever — and it was carrying two strangenesses, though only the class knew the second one. She had watched a golden soul ring replace a boy's purples. And the proctors' record showed one other thing her file had no shelf for: a single sword-line, one-handed, laid across the girls' line at the stomp — defensive, precise, taking the edge off a three-thousand-year area attack like a man trimming flashing off a casting. She had read the letters for three winters. The letters had never mentioned that the boy could do THAT.

The beast arena was the second trial. Survive one minute to pass; harm the beasts for bonus; the strength and number of beasts scaled to the number of examinees. She had deliberately not told them the minimum — and she had never imagined this. Even for HER, a three-thousand-year rhinoceros would have been annoying to kill without her battle armor. These children had slaughtered it. And the golden ring — no matter how she looked at it, the boy had to have twin martial souls. But surely Wu Zhangkong would have mentioned such a thing to her.

"The results for the second trial, the beast arena: Tang Wulin, ten points. Xie Xie, ten points. Gu Yue, eight points. Xu Xiaoyan, ten points. Lin Hao, ten points."

"Wow, how did we score so high?" Xie Xie asked, honestly surprised.

"You scored highly because you killed the Earth Demon Rhinoceros together," Shen Yi said. "The criteria for passing didn't involve killing it — so even Gu Yue, who didn't attack it, scored well. We shall now continue. Follow me."

And follow they did, while her heart welled with expectation behind her proctor's face. *These kids really match Shrek's motto. Little monsters.* High combat ability, good teamwork — and calm. Not one of the five had panicked. Gu Yue had been the calmest of all, and the rest had had excitement in their eyes — Xie Xie had named the beast out loud, so all of them had known exactly how formidable it was, and knowing it, none had cowered. You could see they had faced worse. *Senior brother, it seems you've made sure to give them a lot of combat experience!*

Wulin, meanwhile, was frowning over the ledger of costs. The scores were good; the tank was not. Soul power well spent across all five — Xiaoyan worst: ONE-THIRD of hers, gone, for a split second of absolute restraint. If he had been any slower finishing the beast, it would have cost her more. He checked Gu Yue with a look; she nodded, fine, which meant fine. And the gates of his own new strength had a tollbooth of blood essence with HUNGRY painted over it in letters he could already read. The class had learned at breakfast what three days of refining cost a captain. The bill got bigger.

After the last two trials, all of them understood what kind of exam this was. Many more unknown trials waited. This was just the beginning — and no rest came with the beginning.

## Part 3: The Gates

Shen Yi pulled a sliding door open and brought them out into the space between the stone buildings, and the third trial was already standing there like a sentence that had been waiting for them all day.

Gates, in rows, one after another — at least a hundred of them, the number in each row varying, a corridor of doorways with nothing doors in them. Each gate carried a guillotine blade: two meters wide, a meter tall, half a meter THICK — a slab of falling metal against which a full-grown cow would not be a delay.

"The third trial tests your ability to adapt." Shen Yi's voice was the same one that gave them scores; the words were the same ones that could take points back. "Once I tell you to get ready, you will have one minute to prepare. Once I shout for you to begin, you will have to pass through all of the gates. If you finish within thirty seconds, you get six points. For every three seconds you finish early, you get an additional point. For every three seconds you're late, you will lose one point. Two things you need to know. First — the closer you are to each gate, the faster its guillotine will fall. These are real guillotines. If one strikes you, you will die. Second — you can get a negative score for this trial. If you can't pass this trial, then forget about taking the later ones."

She finished speaking, gestured to the side, and the clank of metal rang across the yard as a hundred blades began to rise.

The front-most gate's guillotine fell — a booming CLANG, sparks erupting as it thudded into its recess, a sound built to put terror in the heart and doing its job on five hearts at once. Then the blade rose, and fell again. Rise. Fall. Rise. Fall. The yard filled with the smell of struck iron.

## Part 4: The Minute

"Get ready."

One minute. Five people spent it five ways.

Wulin rolled his right shoulder, feeling the scales' new whole-side country, and did his arithmetic out loud, quietly, to the class: "Thirty seconds is six points. It's a bonus trial. The rhino was the trial; this is the purse." Gold and hunger, both in his eyes.

Xie Xie was already up on the balls of his feet, grinning at the corridor of falling iron with an expression his mother would have called asking for it.

Gu Yue stood still, eyes half-closed, doing whatever she did that made stillness itself look armed.

Xiaoyan breathed the star-count breath, tired to a third of her tank, conserving with the discipline of a girl who knew exactly what one more skill would cost her — and knowing it, set it aside: the gates asked for feet, not stars.

And Lin Hao walked to the line and listened to the yard the way he had listened to shops his whole life.

Because here was the thing the trial-makers could not know about the sixth examinee, and Shen Yi's three winters of letters had never quite said: **a guillotine gate is a trip-hammer that ate a doorway.** He had grown up in a forge with a power hammer's voice through the wall — the stroke, the rise, the stroke — and a smith's child learns its cadence the way a sailor's child learns weather, in the body, before words. Rise-fall, rise-fall, and the rule of it was the shop's first rule, the one the guillotines had just confessed in their own falling: *the closer your hand, the faster the stroke.* The hammer knows your hand. Every apprentice learns where the line is by watching the man who never takes his hand back too late.

He counted blade-falls down the rows — each row's number different, each gate's timing its own, the whole yard a hundred hammers in an orchestra nobody was conducting — and found the seam in it inside forty seconds, the way the yard's rhythm opened and closed, and where a body could live between the strokes.

"I grew up next to one of these," he said, to his class, in the flat voice he gave numbers, and there was — visible, brief, real — a grin in it somewhere. "Ours was smaller. The rules are the same rules. Rows breathe in threes; the gaps run with the fall, not against it; and the blade only knows where your hand IS, so be somewhere it was. That's the whole grammar."

He gave them the grammar the way he had given them the stomp-read: free, flat, and spendable.

"Ten seconds," Shen Yi said.

The hawk shifted on his shoulder — winter-tipped, unbothered, a bird that had ridden a forge's rafters through its whole first life — and settled its grip like a passenger taking a familiar corner.

"Begin."

## Part 1: One Minute, Spent Right

The first blade fell, and the rest followed it one after another, a metal clamor filling the yard like a shop at full shift.

"Get ready. The one-minute countdown begins now."

The gears of Tang Wulin's mind turned, and turned fast, and came out with the spine of it: "We need to cross through the guillotine gates within thirty seconds. The shortest path has six gates... Gu Yue, test the power of the blades."

A cool head was the whole trial, and the class had one each and a spare.

Xie Xie was already coiled to sprint. Xiaoyan stared at the gates, pale. And Gu Yue, calm as a closed book, held out her hand, palm to the sky — blue light condensed into a two-meter icicle and shot through the bottom of the nearest guillotine.

Clang!

The blade turned most of it to fine powder and split the thickest part in two.

"The descent of one blade produces about three thousand kilograms of force," Gu Yue announced — an analysis only her spiritual connection with the elements could price.

"Can you do it?" Tang Wulin asked.

"I can protect one person."

"How about you, Xie Xie?"

Leaping from the ground: "I'm fine."

And then Gu Yue said, "How about I protect Xu Xiaoyan — and Lin Hao carries me on his back. It shouldn't be a problem with his physical strength. Xie Xie can then follow right behind us. That should work."

Wulin considered it — his own plan had been the more logical one, and hers spent the seams on carrying, which nobody could account for; he eyed her suspiciously anyway, brother to the boy being volunteered. A slight blush appeared on Gu Yue's face and was put away again just as fast.

"Ten... nine... eight..."

No time to change anything. She mounted Lin Hao's back; a wave of her hand wrapped green light around Wulin, Xie Xie, and Xiaoyan; and in the last of the countdown the class's sixth voice spent its two seconds, flat, where only the class could hear it.

"I'm the margin," Lin Hao said. "Nothing goes wrong, you never see me. Rows in threes."

"Three... two... one... begin!"

## Part 2: The Catch

Gu Yue chanted, hands raised, clinging to Lin Hao's back with her legs. Yellow light — a stone pillar shot up under the first gate and took the blade with a clang that cracked it web-wide.

"Quickly!"

And Xiaoyan's fear lost the argument it had been having with four years of trust. She clenched her jaw, leaned, and DASHED — through the first gate to join Xie Xie, who had flashed through it like a rumor.

Lin Hao ran the seams with Gu Yue on his back; Wulin held the line beside him — and directly under the guillotine, the stone pillar collapsed.

The gigantic blade plunged down at the two of them.

Gu Yue shut her eyes and wrapped her arms around Lin Hao's neck as if she had no intention of leaving it — her heart racing, probably because of the tense situation. Lin Hao noted it the way he noted everything, at speed and without comment: the rows breathed in threes, and so did he.

And Wulin was already moving — a step, a lunge, his shoulder under the falling iron his brother and his friend stood beneath.

*Isn't this just three thousand kilograms of force? And weakened by the pillar at that.*

His blood roared. The golden dragon claw appeared on his raised right arm, thrust above him, struck the enormous blade —

— and held it aloft.

On the sidelines, Shen Yi was dumbstruck. Countless students had faced this trial; every one had approached it differently; this was the first in its history to brazenly GRAB the blade. Over a thousand kilograms of iron, three thousand of falling force — she nearly shut her eyes against the blood she was sure was coming.

Clang!

Tang Wulin caught it easily, squatting a little under the load. "Up!" — and his arm filled with strength and threw the blade high, and Lin Hao stepped through the gate with Gu Yue on his back, and the captain cleared his own beside them.

"Boss, are you even human!?" Xie Xie, staring in horror.

"Gu Yue, you don't need to do anything else. I can do this by myself."

He could, and did, and it was that simple: the second gate's blade dropped and was caught and thrown up; the third, the fourth, the fifth — Xiaoyan and Xie Xie passing under each held ceiling before him — the golden dragon claw treating the academy's dreaded guillotines like toys. He walked between the gates at a stride, catching half-ton slabs of falling iron the way a farmer lifts gates for his family.

## Part 3: The Margin

Nothing went wrong. That was the whole point of the margin: it was not supposed to be seen.

Lin Hao ran the rows beside the team's route, in the seams of the falling grammar — threes, with the fall, never against it — arriving at each gate a breath before the class reached it, positioned for the failure that never came: a pillar crumbling early, a blade loosed out of time, a foot snagging on the recess lip. For six gates he was the second answer to six questions the first answer had already solved, and the trial never learned his name.

Once — only once, at the fifth gate, under the iron Wulin held sky-high while Xiaoyan and Xie Xie slipped through — he put his palm flat against the held blade for half a second. Not helping. READING. Up the arm, the way metal's opinions arrive: the release, the track, the counterweight, the spring. Six gates' worth of falling iron, priced in half a second each, on the way through.

At the far end, six gates done, the class reformed around their captain — and the margin delivered its maintenance report, because a margin that stays silent about what it has read is just scenery.

"Your sixth gate drags," Lin Hao said, to Shen Yi, in the voice he used for numbers. "Half a beat, every third fall. The spring's tired — metal's tired, it rings flat. It'll start hanging soon, and a hanging blade is a lying blade; the next examinee will read the rhythm and the rhythm will change on them." A beat. "I can show your smiths, if they'd rather see than believe."

Shen Yi looked at him. The file — three winters thick, one morning richer by a sword-line and a golden ring — acquired its third page before noon.

"...I'll pass it to the hall," she said, in the voice of a woman adding a line item to a budget she had thought was closed.

## Part 4: Fourteen

"Fourteen seconds!" Shen Yi called, and the number rang across the yard like the blades had.

Wulin swung his arm, flexed his shoulder, and let the claw go. And under the flex, quietly, the morning's other bill came due: six catches, sustained, held, thrown — the gold had been drinking blood essence the whole time, and his stomach announced the invoice to the entire yard, long and eloquent.

Xie Xie's grin arrived before anyone's dignity could organize. "Captain. You can bench a guillotine. You cannot bench breakfast."

"I ate," Wulin said, with dignity, "three of everything."

"That was BEFORE you became heavy machinery."

The arithmetic of the trial had already happened in the scoring: thirty seconds for six points, and every three seconds early one more — and fourteen seconds early by sixteen, which the cap trimmed to a full ten apiece. Five for five, three trials deep, and the wager — the duel that only happened if they failed — riding quietly behind the numbers, alive.

Shen Yi watched them bicker toward the next door and let her proctor's face do her interior for her: *this kid is looking more and more like a monster.* The trial was built to test adaptation, reaction, courage — most examinees went through one at a time, because nobody plans cooperation in a minute; most examinees under fifteen looked at the guillotines and could not move; the first trial killed the many (spiritual power too weak), the second passed the most (a simple battle), and the third weeded half of the brave remainder on courage alone. For class zero it had been the easiest morning of their lives. Tang Wulin had single-handedly dealt with everything, propping up the heavens while the others crossed under his arms — and the sixth one, the part her file kept underlining, had spent the same fourteen seconds running a seam through the falling iron so that nothing could go wrong, and then told the academy which of its springs was lying.

"Follow me," she said. "There are more trials."

"Of course there are," said Xie Xie, to nobody, with love.

## Part 1: Ten

"You all scored ten points," Shen Yi said, and strained visibly to say it tranquilly, and led the way out of the yard while the number was still landing.

Behind her face she was doing sums she had not expected to do. Consecutive trials, no rest, children — she had worried. Instead they had scored well twice and then dominated the hardest test of the three, and the record book would have to invent a column for it. *That Tang Wulin really deserves to be class zero's captain,* she thought, and filed the rest under the heading she had opened three pages ago, the one that kept growing.

Wulin, for his part, was doing the rationing arithmetic and was pleased with it. Apart from him — blood essence and soul power, spent like a man paying for five — the others had come through the gates almost whole. That had been the whole plan: he took the front of the trials now, and the strongest of them stayed wrapped for the ones to come.

"You can get down now," Lin Hao said.

The arms around his neck did not move.

He waited a beat, at speed, the way he noted everything. "Did you get injured back there?"

Gu Yue shook her head against his back — he felt it more than saw it — and then, under her breath, in the voice she used for prices: "Just carry me a bit longer. I'm a bit scared."

Xie Xie and Xu Xiaoyan pulled faces at each other. *Scared.* Of the four of them, Gu Yue was the one the word had never once applied to; strangers got the cold eyes, teammates got the arithmetic, and fear had never gotten anything at all, because there had never been anything to get. And yet since the exams began she had been — warmer was not the word. Closer to a word. The juice box. The front seat. The ride, chosen out loud, in front of the hall. *Just what is going on here?* the two of them asked each other with their eyebrows, and got no answer, because there was no answer that did not cost somebody something.

Wulin, who was the only one of them with the whole of it, studied the ceiling with enormous attention. He had been trusted with a thread when they were eleven, in a forge-smell dark, with two words and no ceremony, and he had carried it since the way he carried everything of his brother's: level, both hands, forever. So he looked at the ceiling, and kept his face brother-shaped, and said nothing at all.

Gu Yue's heart was going like a smith's hammer on a deadline. Lin Hao's was not. His face did not do crimson; steady was a garment he had cut to his own measurements, and he had hemmed it twice this month. Her hair came loose and tickled his cheek, and he noted that too, and put it precisely nowhere, and carried her a bit longer, because she had asked for a bit longer, and the asking was the thing — the first spend she had made of the treaty in nine days, deniable as ever, small as ever, and real.

He set her down at the stairs without comment. The treaty held. The purse stayed shut. Both of them kept its customs, and walked up the stairs with the others, and if the class noticed the extra half-second, the class had the manners not to price it.

## Part 2: The Gold Lines

The second floor was white, and the white was written on.

"Those are... soul device blueprints?" Xu Xiaoyan said, tilting her head at the walls. She had chosen mecha designer for her second profession, and knew the grammar of these lines the way the others knew grass — circuit and channel, arrays like sentence-structure, the whole corridor a page of somebody's handwriting in gold.

Wulin squinted at them and got approximately nothing; the diagrams swam and folded and refused him, and he was honest enough about his own spiritual power to stop squinting.

Lin Hao read the walls once, top to bottom, the way he had read the sixth gate's spring. Blueprints were promises about metal — a curve was a pour, a channel was a quench, a tolerance was a smith's opinion of himself — and the walls of this academy were a library of other men's promises, fifty years deep. He walked the corridor a half-step behind the others and read four diagrams and the margins of two, and the reading cost nothing and paid eight points by the time they reached the door, and he did not mention it, because it had not been a trial. It had been a wall.

## Part 3: One Specialty

The room they entered was large and spare. "Wait here," Shen Yi said, pointing to chairs. "I'm going to go get this trial's administrators. This trial will test your personal strength. Only one of your specialties will be examined, so consider carefully what you will present. Your greatest specialty is directly related to your strength." And she was gone, about-faced, efficient.

"Our specialty?" Xie Xie said, at a loss.

Gu Yue sat down cross-legged first and closed her eyes, which was her version of *figure it out yourselves.*

"It's simple," Wulin said, taking the seat beside her. "Your specialty is your greatest strength as a soul master. Xie Xie — you're agility. Show them the limit of your speed; embody what *agility-type* means. You're not a normal one — twin martial souls — so show them both together. Speed and the twins. Same for everyone: show them what you're best at."

Xu Xiaoyan's brow folded. "Captain. What do I do? My full potential only comes up at night."

"Then you make do with words," Wulin said, wry. "You already used it in the second trial — the proof exists, three examiners watched it happen. Explain it thoroughly and honestly. As long as you're speaking the truth, I don't think they'll demand you raise the moon at noon."

"...I got it," she said, easier.

"Then rest while there's resting to be had," Wulin said, and closed his eyes mid-sentence, meditating the moment the words were out — because blood essence ran on soul power, and there was no food in this building, and his stomach had already filed its opinion of the morning's six catches with the entire examination hall. His only option was to recover by breath what he could not recover by breakfast. The class had begun keeping a private count of the captain's meals the way other families track weather.

And the sixth sat with his back to the wall and said nothing, which was his answer to a question he was still holding: *one specialty, the one that is directly related to your strength.* He had two lives and the hall owned three pages on him already, and the wrong one of his lives, shown here, would spend the other.

## Part 4: Elder Cai

Not five minutes later, Shen Yi came back with three people.

Two were middle-aged men with the stillness of examiners. The third was an elderly lady, walking stick in hand, gait unsteady, and the room rearranged its gravity around her: the two men seated themselves on either side of her only after she had sat, and Shen Yi stood, which said everything about who outranked whom in this building.

Lin Hao's eyes went to the stick, once, the way they went to everything. The ferrule was iron, worn to a shine at one facet — a right-handed lady, decades of the same lean — and above the ferrule a repair-ring had been forged onto the shaft, old work, neat, by somebody who had liked her: a smith's promise, keeping a stick honest. He put it away. It was not a trial either. It was a wall.

The old lady looked over the four meditating children who had not noticed the door, and a smile tugged at the corner of her mouth. "These kids sure know how to make the most of their time," she said, hoarse. "Alright then, Little Yiyi — tell them we're beginning."

*Yiyi,* the sixth did not say aloud.

"Yes, Elder Cai," Shen Yi said, with no discontent at all, deference like a worn coat, and crossed to the examinees. "The administrators are here. Which of you goes first?"

Wulin opened his eyes and did the order-arithmetic — first up leaves the deepest mark; first must go with a bang — and counted his people, and there were five of them, and one of the five was a question the whole class had been carrying since the stairs.

"Xie Xie," Wulin said. "You're first." And he leaned over and whispered a few words into Xie Xie's ear that were about the twins, and about joy, and Xie Xie nodded, stood, and walked to the middle of the room.

The class's eyes flicked — all four, one flick, a unit — to the sixth, who was deciding, in the silence he was good at, which of his lives to show a table of strangers. Whatever he answered, he would answer last. The margin goes last. It was becoming the custom of them.

## Part 5: Xie Xie, Three Times

"Hello, teachers," Xie Xie said, and bowed deeply.

The old lady chuckled. "Go on, kid. You only get once — show me what you're best at."

"Yes." Three soul rings rose beneath him — two yellow, one purple — and the purple one lit.

He blurred. One Xie Xie became three, side by side, identical to the last eyelash, and the three bowed again — politely, in unison, which was somehow the most alarming thing yet — and then went transparent and broke in three directions at once, steps like rumors, each figure trailing a Light Dragon Dagger into the air.

The daggers began to hiss. Faster, then blurred, then the whole center of the room was a small private hurricane with three ghosts in it, cutting at an opponent who existed only in Xie Xie's excellent opinion, and the wind of it reached the chairs.

The two middle-aged examiners sat forward at the same time. Soul power went out from them like a hand laid flat over the arena — reading, confirming — and what it confirmed made them look at each other.

The clones were not light. They were not tricks. They had weight, and breath, and mass — three of him, tangible, all real.

Elder Cai's stick settled against her palm, and the smile at the corner of her mouth stopped tugging and simply stayed.

## Part 1: The Verdict

Clone skills were not, in themselves, anything Shrek hadn't seen — agility-types produced them like weather. Three clones was impressive and no more. Six would have been a different story, especially with half of them invisible.

Thirty seconds, and the three became one sweating Xie Xie, who bowed three times. "I'm finished with my performance."

The old lady looked at him with interest. "Kid, your twin martial souls are similar to one another, correct?"

"...Yes, that's right." Not surprised — this was Shrek Academy, after all.

"Not bad, but you still lack control. You've only scratched the surface of the Tang Sect's Ghost Shadow Perplexing Track. Don't rush your progress and don't bite off more than you can chew — refine the Track before you give all of your clones the same abilities. And your spiritual power is too weak at the moment. Complete control of three clones at once is impossible for you. Strengthen it first. If you can reach the Spirit Sea realm within three years, your future will be boundless."

Xie Xie had been rather proud of himself, as a general rule and specifically now. He could not refute one word of it. Every nail, squarely hit. He bowed again, head nearly below his knees, admiration welling up from the bottom of his heart. "Thank you for your guidance. I will do my best to improve myself."

"Mn." The old lady nodded. "Next."

He came back to the chairs with his shoulders around his ears and his face bitter, and the next one up was Xiaoyan, coached like the rest of them.

"What's wrong with you? Are you depressed?" Wulin asked softly.

"That's right! I thought I was pretty amazing, and I don't think I did too well."

"It's the opposite," Wulin said, calm as a Tuesday. "I bet you scored quite highly. That grandmother is clearly the central figure of the three. If she thought you were rotten wood, would she have given you so much advice? Besides — we're students. We came to Shrek to *learn.* What would be the point of coming if we already knew everything?"

Xie Xie opened his mouth. Closed it. The arithmetic reorganized itself in his face. *I'm not horrible. She was telling me how to get better.* Wulin patted his leg. "Let's watch."

## Part 2: Words

Xiaoyan stood in the center and bowed. "You may start," the old lady said.

"My sincerest apologies to the three examiners." Xiaoyan took a breath, and put her coach's plan through its steps. "I am unable to show you my specialty, because it is still daytime. My martial soul is different at night. From a certain perspective, I can be considered a *monster* of a soul master. That is why I have come to Shrek."

Moving examiners with words alone is not an easy task. Wulin knew that — which is exactly why the instruction had been to lead with the uniqueness. *Monster* was Shrek's motto; the word was a key cut for this lock specifically.

"Oh?" It was the examiner on the old lady's left. "Then how are you different at night?"

Xiaoyan summoned the ice staff — two yellow rings rising. "During the day, my martial soul is just the Ice Staff, which excels at controlling the battlefield and long-ranged attacks. At night, I gain the power of starlight, and my martial soul transforms into the Starwheel Ice Staff, changing my soul skills."

The spark in the old lady's eyes was instant. "I know of the Starwheel Ice Staff. It came from the Xu family long ago — though not many of them had it. Your surname is Xu?"

"That's right!" Xiaoyan blinked. "You know about my family?"

The old lady smiled calmly. "There are very few things in the world of soul masters that Shrek doesn't know about. You can go back now."

"But I'm not done explaining—"

"Since I know your origins, why wouldn't I know about the absolute control of your starlight soul skills? Go on back to your friends."

"...Oh." She bowed again and went, and Wulin was standing to meet her. "You did great. Relax." And the tension went out of her the way air leaves a tire that has been given permission.

## Part 3: My Speciality Is Power

Wulin walked past her to the center of the room.

The old lady inspected him curiously. "You seem quite confident!"

"Huh?" It caught him off guard — and then he understood, and bowed. "Greetings to the three examiners."

She smiled strangely. "They seem to trust you. Show me what you can do. Show me *why they have so much faith in you.*"

"Yes." No explanations. He understood now that the three of them had likely heard every word he had whispered into Xie Xie's and Xiaoyan's ears — truly formidable, worthy of Shrek. There was nothing to do about it but be worth the whispering.

"My speciality," he said, "is power."

Golden light flashed in his eyes, and his blood essence erupted outward. In a world of his own he could hear his blood moving in his veins like a river in flood; his right arm swelled, golden scales sheathing it — and then a golden soul ring rose into the air above him.

"Ah!" Shock wiped the smile off the old lady's face; her eyes went wide at the resplendent thing. Beside her, the two examiners gaped with her.

Every color a soul ring could be had been settled for ten thousand years. White, ten years. Yellow, hundred. Purple, thousand. Black, ten-thousand. Red, hundred-thousand. Those five, and no others — except that across the whole history of the Douluo Continent, rings of *special* colors had appeared, and their appearance signified immense power.

In the history of Shrek Academy, a golden soul ring had appeared exactly once.

Tang San — of the original Shrek Seven Monsters, founder of the Tang Sect — had killed a million-year soul beast and taken a golden ring from it. Million-year rings had appeared only twice in the continent's history: the second had belonged to the legend the plaza was named for, the founder of the Spirit Pagoda itself — Spirit Ice Douluo, Huo Yuhao. His had been white, disguisable as a ten-year ring — fused, the analysts of later generations said, with the million-year Skydream Iceworm that had slept its way to the million-year level, where Tang San's had been taken directly from the beast, and that was the supposed reason for the difference in color. The Spirit Ice Douluo's ring had become very powerful indeed.

It had still not been on par with Tang San's gold.

The hall stood in that history, with a thirteen-year-old at the center of it and gold turning over his head, and the silence had weight, and the old lady's stick had stopped tapping altogether.

## Part 4: The Word

At the chairs, the class did the only thing available to people watching their brother make history on four hours' sleep and no breakfast: they held on to each other's shoulders and said nothing that would distract him.

Which left the whispering to Xie Xie, who turned to the last of them with his eyebrows already complaining. "What are you going to show? The sword? The iron? They've got three pages on you and this lot reads pages for sport—"

"One thing," Lin Hao said, quietly, which in that hall was a different kind of silence. "Directly related to my strength."

"That's not an *answer,* that's the *rules—*"

"Comprehensive."

The word sat there. Xiaoyan looked at Xie Xie. Xie Xie looked at Gu Yue.

"There's no such System," Xiaoyan said, gently, the way one breaks bad news to the brilliant.

"There is," said Wulin — flat, immediate, brother-certain, not looking up from the gold.

And Gu Yue, who of all the people in the world had the best reason to know what it was when somebody wrote a word in a blank line that had no square — *Elementalist* was on a form somewhere, and had been true ever since — looked at Lin Hao with her cold clear eyes and said, flat as a ruled line: "You wrote it in a blank line."

"Eleven seconds," he said. "The clerk said *right.*"

Up front, the golden ring turned, and the old lady's hoarse voice came down the room without her looking away from it. "Enough, children. Next."

Which meant Gu Yue. She rose, and put a hand on Lin Hao's shoulder for exactly as long as it took to be real and no longer, and went up to make her own kind of noise.

And the hall that hears everything had heard the word.

## Part 1: The Name

Special-colored rings were so rare that all of history had produced two names to hang them on — Tang San's gold, Huo Yuhao's white and, by every account, an orange-gold besides, wrung somehow from a vicious spirit soul after the man had begun *creating* spirit souls. Legends, both. So even one golden ring, on a thirteen-year-old, held the room.

The old lady recovered, and her brows went down. "Your soul ring is quite unique. It doesn't seem to be made of soul power. I sense blood essence fluctuations coming from it — but your soul power is completely serene. Just what is going on?"

"Honestly, I don't know either," Wulin said, calm as a report. "I only know that my blood essence is very powerful. I think this ability came from my bloodline — but since it granted me a soul skill, it seems to be a type of soul ring."

The golden ring lit as he spoke, and the roar of a dragon came out of his body; muscle swelled; gold sheathed him.

"Th-this is..." The old lady sputtered. "*Golden Dragon Body?* You have the Golden Dragon **bloodline?**"

Wulin stood very still in the middle of his own light.

*The name of the soul skill appeared in my own mind. So how does this old lady know it? Has someone been in a situation like mine in the past?* The thought ran one lap. *No. That's not possible. She said Golden Dragon. What's sealed inside me is the Golden Dragon **King.** They should be two different things.*

While his mind worked, the old lady appeared in front of him. One flash. No footsteps.

"Punch me."

"...Punch you?"

He knew what a Shrek examiner had to be. He also had eyes. She looked like a woman with one foot in the grave and the other on a walking stick, and his strength had passed five hundred kilograms long ago — with the Golden Dragon Body lit, he made it five thousand.

"Don't worry about me," she said, impatient. "My old bones are quite tough. If you actually kill me, you can just enter the Sea God's Pavilion directly."

Wulin took a breath. "Please be careful, then."

## Part 2: Three Punches

**Bang.**

Something touched his arm — he never saw what — and the punch was swatted aside like a housefly.

"Have you not eaten yet?" she barked. "Use some strength!"

The sidelines had seen it. These were people who had watched him bench a guillotine forty-eight hours ago, and their awareness of his strength made the swat worse, not better. *She simply—*

Wulin drew the breath of it — belly inflating, a sharp whistle in the air, arms swelling past their own swell, scales blazing — and threw the second punch with a grunt like a falling beam. This one boomed ahead of itself and left a golden afterimage hanging where the fist had been.

**Bang.**

It stopped in her palm. She had not moved an inch, and his whole force went into her hand and *dissipated*, like hitting a wall of rubber. Xie Xie, watching, recognized the feeling from the inside and said nothing out of pure fellowship.

"Is that all?" Dry. "You're only this strong?"

The disappointment in her eyes went into Wulin like a fishhook, straight into the thing that was proud on behalf of the whole class. "I'm even stronger than this." The hand changed — golden tendrils — the claw, rumbles rolling off it, the air itself leaning.

Light moved in the old lady's eyes. "Come."

The third punch held nothing back. His blood howled; every drop of blood essence he had converged on the right arm; the roar of it was a regal dragon's; there was no sonic boom because the air got out of the way first.

And this time the old lady punched back.

Light warped around her, and the class saw **nine resplendent rings** rise — nine, in a room where three had been impressive — and then the fists met.

**BOOM.**

Wulin went back like artillery and into the wall, twenty meters, and stuck there.

The old lady returned to her seat. "Next."

The wall let him go in a tumble of debris. *"Captain!" "Wulin!"* — the class arrived as one body, and his brother's hand was the first one in, because it always was, and Gu Yue and Xiaoyan got his other side, and the question *"Are you sure you're okay?"* came from all of them at once in different words.

"I'm fine." A cough, debris in his hair. *This wall is really thick!* And it had been like punching a giant balloon — a simply overwhelming elastic force, everywhere and soft and total — and his body was more than tough enough to be embedded in masonry and walk, but the three punches had emptied the blood essence out of him, and now the hunger was back with interest. *A good meal right now and the blood would come back faster. Too bad there's no food in this building.* The class had stopped being surprised that the fate of the examinations ran on breakfast.

What the students did not see, being busy, was the faces of Shen Yi and the two examiners: jaws dropped, and not at Wulin.

## Part 3: What the Sixth Heard

Lin Hao had watched the old lady move exactly twice — the flash to the center, and the punch.

He had been reading things since before he had words for it, and it worked on seams: everything made, everything alive, everything that moves carries the place where it fails, and he had found them in masters and beasts and a two-word battle armor teacher who had let himself be read like a blade laid on a bench.

Her motion had carried nothing. No seam, no tell, no place where it failed — nothing to read, the way a perfectly balanced scale has no lean. It was the first time in his life the reading had come back empty, and he noted the failure the way he noted all numbers, honestly, and put it beside the nine rings in the same column: *a person the alphabet does not cover yet.*

Then he looked at the wall his brother had become part of, because that he *could* read: good masonry, four hands deep, lime-silver mortar, and it had held a nine-ring elastic counter through a thirteen-year-old cannonball. He filed the mix ratio with the sixth gate's spring, in the report he was not writing, and felt marginally better about the state of the world.

Beside him, Wulin got his breath back and did the arithmetic out loud, quiet, for the class only. "Her strength is unfathomable. I don't think even Teacher Wu could compare."

Nobody argued. The class had exactly one data point on Teacher Wu's ceiling, and it was the boy currently pricing the wall.

## Part 4: The Nod

"Next" had a name, and the name stood up.

Gu Yue walked to the center of the room, expression grim, and did not bow. None of the bows before her had been hers to give. She nodded, once. "I'm beginning now."

Shen Yi frowned — genuinely. In all the years of this room, no examinee had ever dared act that haughty in front of a Shrek examiner. The old lady narrowed her eyes and leaned back in her chair.

"Go on, then."

Three soul rings rose beneath Gu Yue — two yellow, one purple — and her hands turned over and made the shape of a bowl. Yellow light gathered in them: steady, gentle. Earth.

*Elemental control,* the three examiners concluded at once. *She's showing the strength of her spiritual power.* A sensible choice, cleanly begun.

Then the choice left the boundaries of sense.

She took the ball of yellow light into her left hand, and began to sculpt it with her right. Each soft touch of a finger raised a petal — one, then another, then another — until she held a yellow flower with nine petals, turning slowly at her fingertips, otherworldly, the kind of thing that gets museums built around it by accident.

At the table, the examiner on the right nodded, approving. Elemental-type martial souls were rare; her wealth of spiritual power and her steadfast control were impressive.

*However, this still fell within the boundaries of what was considered normal.*

The old lady's eyes had not left the flower. At the chairs, four people who had watched her stop a war-hammer trial with one word kept their faces still, and waited for the boundaries to find out what they were dealing with.

## Part 1: The Flower Grows

Gu Yue reached out and grabbed the air, and opened her hand on specks of blue.

They multiplied, merged, and a sphere of water-light stood on her palm — and then petals, azure, fashioned the way the earth's had been, floating up to circle above the yellow: eight over nine, the two layers overlapping as they turned together. Her three soul rings lit in turn, each aiding its own part of the work.

*Dual element control.* The two middle-aged examiners nodded approval — and then she grabbed the air again, and green winked into being, and the nodding stopped. Wind. Dual-element soul masters existed, even at Shrek; three was *unprecedented* — more was not better, the rings each touched one element, the body strained, and theory said, flatly, that so many was impossible. The whirlpool condensed; the green became seven petals above the water.

The fourth time she clutched the air, the examiner on the right shot out of his seat, and Shen Yi's eyes went wide — she had watched this girl work multiple elements at once before, and never to this degree. Embers gathered; a fireball stood in her palm; sweat rolled down her temples and her eyes did not lose their calm by so much as a hair.

The old lady leaned forward, and the mask of indifference cracked.

Four elements. Earth, wind, water, fire — the four fundamentals, the ones the world itself is made of; to hold all four was to hold a piece of the power of creation. Shrek's own records held one three-element soul master, and he had made Soul Sage before the balancing crushed him. The legends said that if the four ever came into harmony, their joined power could be harnessed. And here, in an examination room, the four turned over one another in a thirteen-year-old's hands — the first in the entirety of the continent's history.

Not much of any element — that was not the point. The point was the mind, split four ways, tending the equilibriums: earth to water, water to wind, wind to fire, each relationship a strain, the burden rising exponentially with each addition. She held it. The fire congealed into six blazing petals, blossoming above the rest, and the quad-colored flower turned slowly at her fingertips.

The class gaped with the examiners. The three people in the room most familiar with Gu Yue discovered, together, that they had not been familiar with her at all — and the tactical part of every mind present did the same arithmetic at the same time: *control like this, and a four-element fusion attack becomes possible in battle.* The examiners had already gone further: only the Spirit Sea realm could do this at all.

Then she grabbed the air a fifth time, and the old lady stood up.

The sunlight beaming through the windows came apart into golden specks and ran to Gu Yue's hand — light, the fifth — and she did not force it into petals. She spun it around the four-colored flower, a halo for a thing that should not exist, and the room understood with one voice that the show had been building to a sentence.

## Part 2: I Present This to You

"I present this to you!"

Her head came up; her gaze went at the old lady like a laser; and the flower vanished from her palm in a flash of silver light and reappeared in front of the examiner's table.

"Careful!" Shen Yi cried — no longer controlled, the four elements in the flower were already sliding toward chaos, a bomb that could go off at any moment, and Gu Yue knew it, and had done it anyway.

She had done it on purpose. The class knew the purpose without a meeting: this was the woman who had put their captain into a wall twenty minutes ago, and of all the class's many ways of saying *that was our brother you hit*, Gu Yue's was a four-element explosive delivered with a bow's politeness. The sixth, at the chairs, filed it with perfect composure as the most honest bill presented all day, and revised, slightly, his private estimate of how the purse spent when it did spend.

The old lady's surprise dissolved into a smile. Her arm waved, sleeves billowing — and behind her a crescent moon stood up into the air of the room, shining down on the flower, and **nine soul rings rose around her.**

This time the class could make out their levels. Four purple. Four black. And one **red** — the red of a hundred-thousand-year soul ring, a color none of them had ever seen on a living person, and the power rolling off her pressed the room flat.

The moonlight took the flower, and the flower froze, caught like a thing in a trance — and then, ever so slowly, melted. The elements went home. Ashes to ashes, dust to dust.

*Nine rings,* every one of class zero thought, in pandemonium, at the same time. *She's a Title Douluo. A nine-ringed Title Douluo — with a hundred-thousand-year soul ring—*

Even Gu Yue had a lifeless look in her eyes. The flower had taken her five minutes and better than sixty percent of her power to build; the old lady had annihilated it in an instant, smiling, without using her full strength — and Wulin, still pale in his chair, quietly finalized the morning's arithmetic: *so that's where the wall came from.* The sixth, who had failed to read her twice, counted the rings instead — four purple, four black, one red — and wrote the red one down in the ledger of things the alphabet does not cover, in ink.

Then the frost arrived, small as a correction in a margin, along the windowsill under his hand.

He did not call it. That was the thing he noted first. The domain stayed folded — it had stayed folded since the wager, the one restraint the room's arithmetic made easy — but the water in his breath knew where it was, and under the hundred-thousand-year ring's pressure it answered anyway: the sill's wood went white a hand-span either side of his knuckles, and a single camellia in a vase three seats down got an edge of ice on its lower petal, winter in a hall that did not have winter in it. Far below his breathing the coiled thing at the bottom of the dark water turned over once, slow as a cat in sleep and wide as a weather system — a ten-thousand-year threshold crossed in him once already and carrying its weight like a bank carries a vault; not a sum, a country. That was the thing in him the Title Douluo's pressure had least idea what to do with: pressure rolled over the surface of that sea like thunder over a lake, and down where the coil lived, nothing moved except the coil, which chose to. He breathed once, deliberately — the storm-sky above the sea answering with a single far lightning-flash — and the frost stopped at the hand-span and went no further. Restraint was a thing the margins went last at. But the alphabet did not cover what had just happened to that camellia either, so he wrote that down too, on the same page, in the same ink.

Nobody mentioned it. Wulin, two seats over, shifted his weight like a man arranging himself to be farther from the petal and closer to the door at the same time — the logistics of a captain who had already decided the room would leave in the order it arrived if anything in it went wrong. Xie Xie, on his other side, leaned the breadth of a glance over and said without moving his mouth: *That was yours.* Not a question. The frost on the camellia caught the light.

## Part 3: Good, Good, Good

"Good, good, good!" A grin had taken over the old lady's whole face, and she turned to Shen Yi. "Zhuo Shi did quite well to have me extend the exam period for these kids. This girl doesn't need to take the following trials. Let's have her directly enter the inner court. Even I can't help myself at the thought of a six-element soul master — this has to be a first in the entire history of the continent!"

The name landed on the class like a coin dropped in a quiet room. *Zhuo Shi.* Elder Li had said it once, taking their wager — *Zhuo Shi would have liked that* — and here it was again, out of Shrek's own mountain, attached to the reason any of this day had happened at all. The class did not look at each other. The class looked at each other.

And the rest of the sentence caught up: *doesn't need to take the following trials. Directly enter the inner court.* The thing they had crossed a continent and knelt at a gate for — the terms, the work, the years of arithmetic — and Gu Yue had just been lifted over the whole of it, sideways, by a woman who could not help herself. The four of them did the silent arithmetic of what this meant for a team of five with a wager riding on *passing everything*, and got four different answers, and none of them said a word, because the old lady was already walking over to Gu Yue, looking her up and down.

"Girl," she asked, with a smile, "do you want to become my disciple?"

The room held its breath. The flower's dust was still settling. Somewhere in the building a bell rang once, for nothing.

And at the long table, Shen Yi — whose file on class zero was becoming a book — felt the morning shift under her, because the old lady had stopped one examinee short of the roster. There were five chairs. Four had shown. And the fifth examinee, the one with the three pages and the sword-line and the spring report, the one whose word had gone around the hall this morning — *Comprehensive* — was still sitting at the side with his hands folded, last in the custom of them, waiting for a turn that had just been swallowed whole by a discipleship.

The hall that hears everything turned, very slightly, toward the fifth chair.

## Part 1: I Don't Want To

"Girl, do you want to become my disciple?"

Gu Yue was taken aback — and then shook her head. "I don't want to."

"You don't want to?" For the first time all day, the old lady was dumbstruck. "Why?"

"No reason. I just don't want to."

"Gu Yue!" Shen Yi crossed to her at once. "Don't speak like that. Do you have any idea who this is? Elder Cai is an elder of Shrek Academy's most guarded **Sea God's Pavilion**. Her title is Silver Moon. She is the **Silver Moon Douluo**, and she stands at the summit of this continent! You are lucky to have the chance to become her disciple!"

None of them had known the name. All of them understood the weight of the way Shen Yi said it. Six years ago the Silver Moon Douluo had gone through the continent like weather that owed nobody an explanation — a heaven-shaking eccentric, yielding to no one, doing exactly as she pleased, her rampages turning the soul master world upside down until Shrek had sent people to bring her home. Then nothing. Six years of nothing, ending in this room, holding a flower's ashes.

Gu Yue met Shen Yi's eyes, gnawed her lip, and shook her head again. "She hit Wulin. So I don't want to be her disciple."

Neither Elder Cai nor Shen Yi had expected *that* to be the problem. The examiners' table sat in a moment of pure incomprehension — the petulance was real, and its fuel was a boy-shaped dent in a wall.

"Nonsense!" Elder Cai was disgruntled. "That kid's claw is special! If I hadn't used some strength to send him flying, his claw would have gripped my old bones and *injured* me. I didn't even harm him."

The two middle-aged examiners stared. There was an apology hidden in there — an actual apology, to a thirteen-year-old, from the Silver Moon Douluo. Neither of them would ever speak of it.

"Gu Yue, I'm fine! Really! Think about this carefully!" — Wulin, the words tumbling out clumsily, because he understood exactly what was being thrown away.

She turned back to Elder Cai, and her eyes were earnest. "Wherever they are, I will also be. We won't be separated. If they enter the inner court, then I'll enter too."

"Why are you such a handful?" The sleeve flicked. "Fine. Have it your way. I don't care anymore." And the Silver Moon Douluo stormed out of her own trial.

## Part 2: The Zeros

Wulin tugged Gu Yue's arm the moment the door shut. "Why did you do that? She's a nine-ringed Title Douluo! Her *weakest* soul ring is thousand-year! She has a hundred-thousand-year red soul ring! Do you know how rare that is on this continent?"

Gu Yue met his gaze, honest to the bottom. "She hit you. So I'm not happy."

That put a lid on it. Xie Xie exhaled. "You know, I always thought I was prideful. Now I know what true arrogance is. Gu Yue, you're so *awesome.*" And Xiaoyan, laughing despite everything: "Big sis Gu Yue is so honest. Really."

Shen Yi came back ashen, and pointed a trembling finger. "You! Who do you think you are? Do you know how many people *dream* of the chance you just threw away?" Gu Yue lowered her head and said nothing — she had given her one explanation, to Wulin, and nothing else was coming out of those lips.

"I'm sorry." Wulin, anxious, formal. "It was our fault. Gu Yue is tired; she's not thinking properly. Teacher Shen Yi — can we still continue with the exam?"

"Your exam should finish here." A sigh. "But you can continue. I've notified Teacher already. Hopefully he can placate Elder Cai's rage. Let's go."

In the corridor, Xie Xie — confidence intact — asked the question. "Teacher Shen, how many points did we get for the fourth trial?"

"Zero points." Shen Yi glared. "You all got zero points."

"*Zero?*" Xie Xie nearly detonated. "Even if we weren't amazing, shouldn't we get *some*? Or are you telling me Shrek Academy can't be impartial? Is this because we offended—"

"In Shrek Academy, the **Sea God's Pavilion** makes the rules," Shen Yi said, sweeping them with a deep gaze. "If Elder Cai says zero, then it is zero. No one can dispute it — not even another elder. And now that you've scored it, you can't enter the inner court even if you're absolutely amazing in every trial that's left." Her eyes moved to Gu Yue. "Do you understand the consequences of impulsiveness now?"

Gu Yue did not retort. She followed Wulin in silence.

## Part 3: The Sixth's Ledger

Lin Hao had stood through all of it with his hands folded, watching, and inside the quiet he was good at, the ledger did what it always did: it priced things.

*Item.* The academy's summit had just been standing in front of them — the Silver Moon, the Sea God's Pavilion, nine rings with a red one at the top. And in the same room, unremarked by anyone with a rank, sat a boy whose starting four — three perfect purple and one black, at thirteen — would have been the crown of the academy's own showcase, any decade they chose. Beside him sat a girl who had just held five elements in one hand in front of examiners who called three *unprecedented.* His own level read forty-five. That alone, at his age, was absurd; under it sat a foundation nobody here had begun to measure — and the hall's answer to the whole arithmetic of them was a zero, administered twice, by temper.

*Ignored,* the ledger said, without heat. That was the finding. Not *unseen* — three pages of his file said seen. *Ignored.*

*Item.* He had not come for Shrek. He was here because four people had crossed a continent and knelt at a gate, and because one of them had just refused an empire for the sake of a boy in a wall. Take the five of them out of the arithmetic and there was no reason on this earth for him to be standing in this building at all — and the building had done nothing, to this point, to give him one.

*Item, and the sum:* the gate that priced them by quotas. A wall of other men's promises, read and left. A spring priced honestly and filed. A showcase scored zero for a bruise to an old woman's pride. His impression of Shrek Academy, to this point, itemized, totaled, and signed: **negative.**

He put the ledger away. It was not a bitter document; it was a bill, and bills got paid or they got corrected, and either way you kept the numbers. He was thirteen, and he had time, and the next room had tables in it.

*Wulin's* ledger was running too, and it read nothing like his brother's. *Will this affect our exam? Is there anything good waiting for us now that we've offended her?* — the captain's dread, doing arithmetic on five futures at once.

## Part 4: The Fifth Room

The chamber they entered was the same size as the last, and completely different: tables everywhere, and on the tables, mountains of things — the honest clutter of a hundred crafts.

"The fifth trial tests your talent," Shen Yi said. "Well — more like your second profession."

Wulin's eyes went around the room once and lit. Among the many tables, one of them was for **blacksmithing**, and the sight of it went through him like breakfast — and then the elation died, because the examiner's chair behind the table was occupied by a familiar figure in familiar disgrace.

Elder Cai looked at Wulin. She sneered.

"Elder Cai, you—" Shen Yi was out of words.

The Silver Moon Douluo snorted. "For the fifth trial, you all score zero points."

Rage came up in Gu Yue's eyes so fast Wulin got an arm in front of her without looking, and his look at Xie Xie stopped the explosion at the fuse. *This was Shrek Academy. Her home ground.* Behind his face the captain was doing the only arithmetic that mattered now: the team, the futures, the fury swallowed for all five of them.

"Don't say I didn't give Zhuo Shi any face," Elder Cai said, to the room, to nobody. "If they do well in the following trials, they will still be able to enter the inner court despite scoring zero twice. If not — they can go back to where they came from."

*Zero again.* The fifth trial and scored before touching a tool. Shen Yi's face twisted, and she stood still a long moment, because she knew the numbers nobody had told them: **ten trials, ten points each, one hundred possible. Sixty for the outer court. Eighty-five for the inner.** Two zeros meant twenty points gone forever — meant *exceptional*, in every trial that remained, or nothing. In a normal year, one or two examinees in the whole cycle reached the inner court at all.

She did not criticize Gu Yue. There was no point in that now.

And at the back of the five, the sixth looked at the blacksmithing table — the one craft in that room he had carried since he could reach an anvil, the fifth rank of it earned at almost twelve, second-youngest in a Branch's records — and the ledger opened one line, in the margin, where hope lived when it lived at all:

*Zero, twice. Eight trials left. Perfect, or home.*

They would have to be perfect. And one of them, at least, had never been anything else on that side of a forge.

## Part 1: The Bill

The Silver Moon Douluo had given them her second zero and her terms — *do well anyway, and the inner court despite it; if not, go back to where you came from* — and turned for the door, sleeve already flicking.

And the sixth spoke. First words of the day in her direction, in the voice he used for numbers, which the hall had now heard twice: once for a spring, once for a word.

"Well — I can't take it now."

Elder Cai stopped with her hand above the door.

"Your academy has shown nothing worthy enough." No heat in it at all; that was the terrible part. It was a reading, delivered the way he delivered iron. "The gate priced us by quota. The trials ran clean until the scoring got personal. And the arithmetic standing in front of you has been ignored since the wall." A pause exactly long enough. "So — I am not joking. Clearly."

The room did not breathe. Wulin's stomach dropped through the floor with the sure arithmetic of a boy watching his brother bill the continent's summit; Shen Yi stopped existing; Xie Xie forgot his own grievance the way you forget a splinter when the house catches fire. Gu Yue's head came up, and something in her face agreed with every word and would be admitting nothing.

The Silver Moon Douluo looked at him for three full seconds — the flint look, the one that had nine rings behind it and a red one on top.

"Zero was cheap, then," she said, and the door slammed behind her hard enough to move every paper in the room.

What nobody present saw, because the door was shut, was the smile forming on her lips out in the corridor.

*"Hehe. I bet that old fart Zhuo Shi is fuming right about now. Serves him right. Those brats are pretty good — tempering them a bit more should be fine."* She snorted at the thought of the girl. *"Since you dare to reject me, there will be a time when you come back begging."* Hands crossed behind her back, her steps were light as air as she departed.

The bill had been served to a woman already smiling. The ledger did not know that. Ledgers never do.

## Part 2: The Sixth Trial

Aggrieved, indignant, and down twenty points, class zero arrived at the site of the sixth trial — which was a room full of giant silver trays, and on the trays, mountains of **steamed buns.**

The sign explained everything and nothing. Fifteen buns: passing. Every additional five: one more point. Thirty minutes. **No soul power** — your own stomach or your honor.

They stood stupefied before the majesty of it. Then, as one, Xiaoyan's and Xie Xie's eyes slid to Tang Wulin.

Something flickered under the captain's calm mask — the flicker of a man seeing providence — and he turned to Shen Yi with a straight face. "Teacher Shen. Can we help each other eat for this trial?"

Shen Yi, still depressed, replied grumpily: "If you can eat enough to score full points, then you can help the others."

The trial made a strange kind of sense, for a monstrous academy. It tested willpower — eat past the body's limits, no shortcuts, medical staff on standby for the examinees who discovered that this innocent little trial was a devil in disguise, dragging people through the depths of hell and making them wish for the sweet release of death.

Today, an irregularity had appeared.

"Thank you, Teacher Shen," Tang Wulin said, sincere as a prayer. In his mind, this trial had been made for him — the morning's meager portion, the blood essence spent across four trials, the hunger that had been filing complaints since the guillotines. A mountain of buns was the most beautiful scene he had ever witnessed. He took two in each hand and began.

Xie Xie put his hands behind his head and leaned back, leisurely waiting. Xiaoyan sat down cross-legged to meditate. Gu Yue was the only one who picked up a bun, to accompany him.

"What are those two doing?" Shen Yi frowned. "Why aren't they starting?"

"Teacher Shen," Xie Xie said, smiling. "Just wait and see."

## Part 3: The Rice Tub

Eight buns vanished before she had finished the sentence.

"Eat slower—" Shen Yi began, maternal. "It doesn't matter how fast, as long as you eat enough; if you eat too quickly your digestion will—"

Tang Wulin snatched four more and put away two of them before the sentence found its end.

"Teacher Shen," Xie Xie said, smirking now, "you don't need to worry about our captain. His greatest strength isn't his combat ability — it's his stomach. He ate our dining hall into poverty. What are a few steamed buns to him?"

Shen Yi then witnessed what it truly meant to be called a rice bucket. No — a rice *tub.*

The captain calculated as he ate: fifteen buns was six points, twenty was seven, and thirty-five of the fifty on a tray was the full ten. At the eight-minute mark he had inhaled his own thirty-five, and sauntered to Xiaoyan's tray as if the record had been a warm-up: thirty-five more in seven minutes. Then Xie Xie's. By twenty-two minutes the total stood at a hundred and five, his belly had not bulged by a hair, and Shen Yi's expression had completed its journey — surprise, shock, dumbfoundedness, stupification — while the supervising examiner, who in all his long years at this trial had never seen such a glutton, quietly stopped pretending to supervise and simply watched.

No soul power. She was certain of it. That was the part that kept her staring.

At the twenty-eight minute mark, the captain finished Gu Yue's thirty-five for her and kept going, disappointed that the tray was running out of runway. "Time is up!" the stupefied examiner just barely remembered to call. Forty-eight of fifty. Two lonely buns survived.

"Teacher Shen." Tang Wulin patted his belly, wistful. "We got full marks, right?"

Shen Yi nodded and turned to leave, because her legs wanted to be anywhere else while her mind ran the phrase *was he always such a monster — is his stomach a bottomless pit* in circles.

"Teacher Shen, can I take the leftover steamed buns with me? I didn't eat breakfast this morning..."

She stumbled. She waved: do as you wish. And the boy swept every surviving bun into bags and into his storage ring, and followed her out wearing the most contented smile of the examination season, his blood essence nearly replenished on starch and joy.

At his own tray, the sixth worked through thirty-five buns — the full ten — unhurried, the last one half-cooled at twenty-nine of the thirty minutes: perfect, and not a minute wasted being perfect. The margin ate like the margin: everything the arithmetic required, on time, and not one bite past it.

## Part 4: The Report

In a luxurious room, Elder Cai listened to the middle-aged examiner's report with her face contorting into a strange expression.

"All four got full points for the sixth trial?"

"Yes, full marks. They even took the leftovers with them. It seems the majority was eaten by Tang Wulin."

She sat with that a moment. Somewhere behind the flint, a ledger of her own was adding a column to a bill a thirteen-year-old had served her an hour before — the polite one, with the three pages and the sword-line and the word she did not have.

*Nothing worthy enough,* he had said. *So I am not joking. Clearly.*

"Tempering," she said to the empty room, in the tone of a woman confirming a forecast. "A bit more should be fine."

The run, meanwhile, had turned simple again, which was the only way the class liked it: thirty points banked through three trials, twenty burned by temper, forty won back on starch. **Four trials left. The outer court asking sixty. The inner court asking eighty-five — reachable now through exactly one door, and the door had a name, and the name had already smiled on them twice without their knowing.**

## Part 1: The Old Lady's Ledger

## Part 2: The Seventh Room

The first trial had tested spiritual power; the second, combat; the third, adaptability and courage. The fourth, fifth, and sixth had taken talent, profession, and willpower. The seventh was a marathon of endurance, and it would push bodies to the limit.

The surprise of the room was that it was not empty. Other examinees were still present — hours into the examination, still grinding for the six points of a finished series, faces the color of the effort. It was the first time class zero had seen the field they were actually playing on: a room full of strangers, all paying the same price at different exchange rates.

The tests were read out. Running ten kilometers. Squatting fifty kilograms, one thousand times. One thousand chin-ups. Finish all three and six points were yours; finish inside an hour and it was ten; every ten minutes over cost a point, down to the floor of six. The same tests for every type of soul master — power-types held the advantage, which was not Shrek's problem, because the first trial had favored everybody *but* power-types. Fairness was not the design; breadth was. And this trial, at least, put no ban on soul power.

Wulin's glance at Gu Yue and Xiaoyan was brief and entirely anxious. Then the questions, in order: how many trials? — *ten.* Points to pass? — *sixty.* What do the remaining trials test? — *"I can't."* And the parts? — *two points each.*

He ran the numbers where he stood — eighty reachable, twenty of leeway, three trials unknown — and turned to the girls with the plan already load-bearing. "You two only need to run the ten kilometers. Xie Xie, we'll complete all three. Let's get started." Neither girl asked to see his arithmetic. He was stingy; stingy people are excellent at numbers; they trusted the arithmetic the way you trust a miser with a ledger.

They ran on soul treadmills. Wulin's pace was, mysteriously, fast — Shen Yi stood at the rail of his belt with wide eyes, an agility-type's trial being eaten by a power-type — and she asked the question under it: *"Why do you only want them to score two points? Aren't you worried they won't score enough later?"*

"Their bodies aren't that strong. Chin-ups and squats are basically impossible for them — if I pushed, they'd waste time *and* stamina we need for the final three trials. Conserve now, do our best there. We scored well where we scored. We still have a chance this way."

Shen Yi smiled despite the day she was having. "Excellent. What a thorough analysis."

Wulin and Xie Xie took ten minutes for the run. Wulin then did one thousand fifty-kilogram squats the way other men breathe, the Golden Dragon King's bloodline turning mathematics into a rumor — not even ten minutes — and went to the bar; all three of his tests were done before thirty minutes had passed. Xie Xie, sturdy under the agility, lagged and did not suffer: forty-five minutes, full marks anyway. The girls ran their ten kilometers in about twenty and sat out the rest, conserving, and soul power put the color back in them between sentences.

## Part 3: The Metronome

An examinee from some inland academy, four hours into his own six points, watched the fifth stranger finish his run.

The boy had stepped onto the belt out of turn, unhurried, and had run the ten kilometers the way a clock runs — not fast the way the gold-flashed one was fast, just *exactly*, the same length stride at the same point of every minute, breathing on a schedule, as if the treadmill were a bench and the bench owed him a rate. Then the squats: one thousand, unbroken, at a pace that never once consulted fatigue. Then the bar. The whole hour's work in well under half of it — and the boy stepped down looking exactly as he had stepped up, gathered the hour's ten points like a man accepting correct change, and went to stand with the others without one gram of display about any of it.

The inland examinee hated him a little, in the way you hate things that are quietly beyond you, and then went back to his own squats, and thought about the boy's pace for the rest of the day, and improved, later, enormously. Shrek's trials worked on everybody in the room. That has always been the design.

What the inland examinee could not see was the reading underneath. The sixth had spent the run the way he had spent the gates — on the seams. The talent — the oldest thing he owned, the one that had been taking the world apart and keeping what worked since before he had words for it — had turned inward for the hour and read its own instrument: this muscle's margin, that tendon's debt, where the lactic arithmetic turned, what the breath actually cost. He paced the hour to the minute not from discipline alone but from *knowledge*, the body read like any other metal — and when the reading said the ten points were banked at the lowest price, he stopped. Everything the arithmetic required, on time, and not one repetition past it.

## Part 4: The Form

They rested the fifteen minutes that cost nothing, and then Wulin asked for the numbers, and Shen Yi looked at the form she was holding.

"After the seventh trial — Tang Wulin, you have fifty points." Her eyes moved over the sheet and then back at him, because excluding the twenty that temper had burned, the boy had a full score: maximum points, every trial that had actually been scored. "Gu Yue, thirty-eight points. Xie Xie, forty-eight points. Xu Xiaoyan, forty points."

And one more line, in a hand the form had needed a second column for. "Lin Hao — fifty points."

The room did the arithmetic at different speeds. Fifty — with the two zeros standing in the middle of it like the temper they had been — was ten short of the line, with three trials and thirty points still on the table. And the fifth examinee had never yet lost a point he could see, so everybody in the room could finish that sum: the passing line was not a question of whether, only of which trial. He received the number the way he received correct change, and the class looked at him and then away, because there was nothing to say that the arithmetic had not said.

The others' situations were soberer. Wulin and Xie Xie were safe for the outer court and could not reach the inner by any arithmetic left on the table — *impossible to enter directly*, the numbers said, plain as a wall — so the minimum was the mission now. Xiaoyan's standing was not much better than precarious. And Gu Yue was in the tightest box of the five: eight points of leeway across three trials. She could lose, at most, two or three points per trial — she could not lose more than three points in any one of them, or she was eliminated.

Nobody said any of this aloud. Wulin's face did the captain's version — the plan already forming behind it — and Gu Yue looked at the wall with her jaw set at the angle the class had learned meant *the purse has seen the problem*.

Twilight was covering the horizon when Shen Yi gave them the eighth.

## Part 5: Ten Doors

"The eighth trial is a comprehensive battle. You will fight a current student of Shrek Academy. The available opponents are random, so your luck will be a factor. Last ten minutes against your opponent to pass. Defeat them, and you receive full points. Between — marks of six to ten, on performance."

A battle. Wulin let out a breath he had been holding since the buns — whatever else happened, Gu Yue would not drown here — and Xiaoyan's odds were left to the lottery.

"Together or one at a time?" he asked, heart thumping.

"You'll take turns."

"Then can we decide the order?"

"There will be ten opponents for you all to choose from," Shen Yi said. "So it isn't just your strength being tested — it's your judgement. There are strong and weak hidden among the ten. Some may naturally restrain you; some you may restrain. A large portion of your performance will be determined by your choice of opponent."

The room they entered for it was circular and much larger than any before — prepared while they had run, which meant the ten had been waiting all afternoon, listening to a wall, getting ready for children.

At the chairs, the class's eyes did the flick. Battle trials had an order, and the order was a decision, and the decision was judgement, and the judgement was about to be five people arguing sweetly in whispers over ten closed doors — three of which hid restraint, and one of which, if the hall that hears everything had any humor at all, was already smiling.

The margin goes last. The margin always goes last. But somebody had to go first, and somebody had to *choose*, and the choosing was the trial.

# Chapter 87: The Thing He Was Waiting For

## Canon Reference: canon ch 267 "The Snow Leopard of Ten" + ch 268 "Battle of Patience, Biding Time" (FOLDED — one fight, one chapter; the author's seed sits at the center) + ch 266 "To Battle" (the choosing — fetched AFTER, when the canon index exposed the numbering slip; it was never in the first fetch) + ch 269's opening facts.
