OURS: the choosing (AU — Lin Hao inserts himself into canon's draft); the order reversed by appetite; **the fifth's turn — no martial soul, no rings, the Tang Sect's answer to Shrek.** (Numbering corrected 09-01: this chapter first cited 266+267 for the fold — truly 267+268.)

---

## Part 1: The Line of Ten

They were already waiting, as promised — ten current students of Shrek Academy in a line along the circular wall, numbered, still as fence posts, each one doing the small work of not looking at class zero and doing it badly. The strongest hid in the middle of the rank and file: a slender boy holding the number two like it was an insult. The tenth was a girl with snow-pale eyes and a stillness that matched Wulin's own.

Judgement, Shen Yi had said. The choice is most of the score.

Wulin walked the line once, unhurried, the way he shopped for vegetables, and stopped at the girl. "Number ten."

The slender boy's eyebrow moved a millimeter, and Wulin came back down the line and murmured to Xie Xie, "Take number two."

"*Number two?*"

"Trust me."

Which left the order, and the class turned inward to draft it in whispers.

"Girls last," Gu Yue said immediately. "We watch everything first."
"Captain first," Xiaoyan said. "He scouts, we choose after. That's just sense."

And then they found the fifth chair already empty, because its owner was already standing, smiling.

It was a smile none of them had ever seen on him. Not the margin's flat arithmetic, not the smith's closed face. Something lighter. Something with its sleeves rolled up.

"You're supposed to go *last*," Xie Xie hissed. "It's practically your catchphrase—"

"The margin goes last when it's arithmetic." The fifth rolled one shoulder, once, like a man settling a coat he liked. "This isn't arithmetic."

"Six trials of points," Gu Yue said, studying him the way she studied prices.

"Six trials of points," he agreed. "And finally a shape I know."

Six trials of points, and finally a shape he knew. He had been waiting for this one since the gates — through spiritual power and talent and buns and all the quiet rooms where nothing could be answered properly, there had been this door at the end of the day, and behind it: somebody from the academy on the bill.

The order went Wulin, the fifth, Xie Xie, the girls. Shen Yi looked at the submitted list, looked at the fifth examinee, and wrote it down without comment, which for a person with her day was a kind of screaming.

## Part 2: The Captain's Thirty Minutes

The tenth trial of the tenth — no. The snow began almost immediately, and it did not stop.

What the room watched for twenty-five minutes was a boy being slowly, patiently buried: the girl's blizzard eating his Bluesilver Grass down to a dim spinning net, frost climbing the strands, icicles rising like teeth. She was good — conservative when her kills failed, a cheetah stalking, whittling, waiting for the one strike. At ten minutes the six-point mark passed; at twenty-five she had nine points banked and her prey rigid with cold, one white hand reaching his shoulder.

Shen Yi had already written the ending in her head — *not that talented after all, ignoring the golden ring, merely Bluesilver Grass* — and was being puzzled by the rest of class zero, who watched their captain's impending defeat without a single eyelid moving.

"How is he still *breathing*?" Xiaoyan whispered.

"He isn't," Gu Yue said. "He's shopping."

The moment the hand touched his shoulder, Wulin smiled. *It's about time.*

Rings and grass vanished; a tyrannical blood-essence aura blew the blizzard sideways. He had not eaten all those steamed buns for nothing. Purple eyes; the world's slow spin; a golden hand closing gently on a carotid; the girl went limp and he caught her before the floor did, because he was like that. The snow dispersed on a room gone silent.

Xie Xie smacked his forehead. "Captain is really getting sneakier and sneakier! Thirty entire minutes to lure her into a trap — that girl never realized Captain excels at brute force, not control!"

"Tang Wulin… ten points." Shen Yi's eyes were wide. *Fifty, plus ten,* said the arithmetic. Sixty. Passed.

"Was he waiting for this the entire time?" Xie Xie muttered — and heard, again, by the teacher whose file on this class grew a page a day. *He's thirteen,* she thought. *How is he this patient?* She did not know about the six years of hammering temper, the grindstone behind the patience. There was a great deal she did not know, and the next match was going to make it worse.

## Part 3: The Fifth's Turn

"Next."

He passed Xie Xie going down, and the class watched the fifth examinee walk into the arena the way you watch a kettle you have been warned about. He stopped in front of the line of ten with his hands behind his back, reading them — unhurried, the way he read metal, along the grain. Number two was the strongest; that had been true since the room opened, and number two was promised. Of the rest, the read said *proudest*, and pride was the grain that split cleanest.

"Number one," Lin Hao said.

Number one was a long-limbed boy with a spear type — he released it the moment the word fell: three rings rising, two yellow, one purple, a shaft of deep-ice blue settling into his hands like it had grown there. A real weapon, real rings, a current student of Shrek Academy who had won his place at this academy the honest way and had never once in his life needed a second exchange against a soulless opponent.

Across the arena, the fifth examinee stood with nothing. No light. No rings. His hands were loose at his sides, and he was still smiling, faintly, the way you smile at weather you have decided to enjoy.

"Begin," said Shen Yi, and her pen stopped.

Number one was fast and his lines were clean — three thrusts off the back foot, each one a question a spear had asked for a thousand years. The fifth put his Question inside the third thrust: an empty hand offered where an answer had to go. The body answered, the way bodies do, before the boy could forbid it — and the answer had a grain to it, the way everything answered has. The Answering Stroke arrived along that grain, unhurried, and stopped a finger's width from the wrist that owned the spear, having decided not to exist.

"Again," Lin Hao said, kindly.

Along the wall, the ten had stopped pretending not to lean. "*No soul light,*" one of them said. "*His control — is that a ten-thousand-year soul skill?*" And another, lower: "There's no fluctuation at all. That's not a soul skill. That's—" and there the sentence died, because there was nothing in the room to call it.

"Spear's honest," Lin Hao called across the sand, pleasantly. "You lean on it like family. Elbow in, it'd be perfect."

Number one was done being careful — and past being mocked. "Shrek does not lose," he said, "to a boy who won't even release his soul."

"It's rude to release everything on the first date," the fifth said. "Show me."

The purple ring flared; the spear's ice-blue became an aurora down its length, the thousand-year skill, the one that had put him on this line — a thrust that arrived in three places in one motion, honest, committed, brave.

Still Water. The fifth did not move until movement was meaningless — and then he was inside the aurora rather than under it, where the grain of the whole beautiful sequence ran to one point — and a hand that had gripped hammers since it was small closed on the shaft. It did not grip hard. It gripped *exactly*, and turned, and number one's own honesty did the rest: the strongest student of the line sat down on Shrek's floor with a sound like the trial gavel.

The spear stayed upright beside him. The fifth had set it so, of course. He waited, politely, while the boy got his breath and his pride into the same room.

"You're faster than your friends think," Lin Hao told him. "Show me the one you're hiding."

What came then was the best thing the line of ten did all day — the hidden technique, everything on it, pride and all, aimed with a spear-soul's full intention at a boy with no light on him anywhere. The Question went out to meet it, deeper this time, and was answered, and the Answering Stroke crossed the answer's grain and stopped — one inch from the throat, in front of the entire academy that could hear it not land.

The Unwritten stroke. The mercy that humiliates.

"Twice," Lin Hao said, quietly, so that only number one heard it. "That's twice Shrek's best line has shown me nothing I couldn't read standing still. Go be angry about it — properly — and be better than this when it matters."

Number one looked at the not-wound for one second. Then he raised his hand. "…I concede."

"Lin Hao. Ten points." Shen Yi wrote it down. Her pen had not moved in four exchanges; the form would show it later, a blank where the notes should be, and she would file that blank with everything else in a file that now had its own weight class.

The fifth helped his opponent up, returned the spear handle-first — the politest insult the academy had taken all day — and bowed to the ten of them, exactly as deeply as the trial deserved. "Thank you," he said, and meant it. "That was the first thing today worth waiting for."

The line of ten said nothing at all. It is a particular silence, being Shrek's pride in a room where somebody's bill is being read out line by line — *your academy has shown nothing worthy enough* — and the ledger's collector standing in the middle of it, unhurt, unlit, unbored, handing the spear back.

## Part 4: Not You

When he came back to the chairs, number two had stepped forward half a pace out of the line — the strongest of them, appetite in the set of his shoulders, the question halfway up his throat.

Lin Hao smiled at him and shook his head, and pointed at Xie Xie.

"Not you. You're his."

The twilight was gone; the round room held its lamp-light like a bowl. Xie Xie stood, rolled his shoulders until they cracked, and walked toward the slender boy with the pleasant expression of a man about to be told something interesting about himself.

"Apparently I'm ambitious," he told number two, conversationally. "My captain says so. Let's find out."

"Should we warn them?" Xiaoyan asked, watching the two of them settle into their stances.

"Which side?" Gu Yue said.

Neither released a soul. Both waited for the opening, ten meters apart, while the girl with snow-pale eyes watched from the floor where she sat wrapped in a shock blanket, thinking about purple eyes, and Wulin sat cross-legged with the Mysterious Heaven Method turning, recovering for the teammates who had nearly lost this chance for his sake.

"Begin!"

## Part 1: The Mountain That Waited

They came together at speed, and neither released a soul — two boys reading each other on the approach, rings rising only when the gap had shrunk to ten meters. Identical configurations, two yellow and one purple, and then the difference arrived all at once.

Xie Xie took the Light Dragon Dagger. Student number two *swelled.*

The slender frame inflated like a bellows, clothes bursting to shreds, the famous absurdly-elastic undergarments surviving what the academy's tailoring could not; brown hair swept up four meters of body and two arms like bridge cables, and the room's air took on the rumor of a landslide. *A giant gorilla,* Xie Xie thought, awed in the professional way. *Maybe even the—* and then the ground came at him.

What followed was Xie Xie's whole grammar, spent honestly. The ground-smash met a golden blade of light that cut lines into the arena's walls; the counter-leap came down with the might of a mountain and met *three* Xie Xies, each kicking off the other two, scattering in three directions — a trick that made the line of ten go quiet, because this boy had chosen the strongest of them and was not dead yet. Three punches answered, one per clone, air hissing; the clones kicked off nothing itself and escaped by the margin of a haircut.

By the time both sides returned to the ground, the theory was written: the attacker spends more than the defender, ranks near equal, the agility-type banking on the Mysterious Heaven Method to outlast. And the mountain simply stood in the arena's center, patient as furniture, because he could not strike three directions at once and knew something worth knowing: sustaining three clones of a thousand-year skill was bleeding his opponent white. *He'll come,* number two thought, correctly. *Soon.*

He came. The clones were faster now, and Xie Xie with them, and the second ring lit — **Light Dragon Storm**, the three copies converging into one spiraling lance of light that he had every right to believe would injure anything it touched.

Number two did not dodge. His burly arms moved in a motion that was — to almost nobody in the room — legible.

## Part 2: The Green Light

**Controlling Crane, Capturing Dragon.**

An aura expanded outward like a slammed door, and the storm broke around it; the hands pressed flat, the second ring flared, and the air *rumbled* — thunder in a closed room — and all six clones, light and shadow, were flung backward to crash into one boy again mid-air. Number two stomped and rose like artillery, first ring lit, and punched the air itself.

The shockwave crossed the arena at a speed that ended conversations. Xie Xie's mind was chaos and his reserves were ash; he could not have dodged a falling leaf.

A green light flashed over and dragged him out of the wave's path and down to the ground, gentle as a mother cat. Number two halted mid-advance, bowed to Shen Yi, and walked back to the line.

Five minutes, start to finish. Suppressed the whole way; without the teacher's hand, gravely injured. This was the strength of a Shrek Academy student — in the face of it, twin martial souls and type matchups meant nothing at all.

In the chairs, Tang Wulin — roused out of his recovery by thunder — sat with a brand-new problem: *What if I had picked him? Could I have lasted? Could I have won?* He had no answer. He could not fathom the bottom of it.

## Part 3: Three Points and a Lecture

"Xie Xie — three points," Shen Yi said, and did not enjoy saying it. "Points will be deducted at the term's end for a failed trial. You chose him yourself."

Xie Xie came back with his shoulders down and his chin already returning to its natural altitude. Not disgraceful — he had shown everything he had, and it had simply not been enough of anything.

"Why didn't you just keep running?" Wulin demanded, solemn. "You *knew* how strong he is."

"My clones eat soul power, and without them his ranged game kills me anywhere in this box." Xie Xie's laugh was bitter and honest. "A bigger arena, maybe. This one — no."

"You! *Reflect!*" And the captain opened the ledger on him in front of the hall: his opponent had been that strong *because* of a thousand-year skill — his consumption couldn't be lower; twin souls and the Mysterious Heaven Method meant attrition was the one war Xie Xie could never afford to lose; three clones in three directions; control the distance; make the mountain walk. "Do you have anything to say for yourself?"

Xie Xie slapped his thigh. "You're right! I forgot he was bleeding as fast as I was — I've been fighting too many soul *beasts* lately. I treated him like a soul beast!"

This was announced at full volume to the entire arena. Number two, halfway back into his jacket, went rigid, turned, and scowled. Xie Xie met the scowl chin-first, haughty as a proclamation: *next time.*

Wulin chuckled, tired. The lecture had been for morale, and it had worked — the boy had been in ruins one minute and was scheduling rematches the next.

## Part 4: The Question Under the Floor

The fifth examinee had watched all five minutes the way a jeweler watches someone else's shop.

The mountain's patience had been genuine — the strongest of ten, and the most disciplined, holding a ring-skill in reserve for the exact moment the clones could no longer sustain. But that was not what had opened Lin Hao's eyes for the first time all evening.

*Controlling Crane, Capturing Dragon.* The winters' first coordination — the art you learned before your hands were worth coordinating, inner-sect, taught person to person down a lineage that was supposed to end at walls. He had watched a boy of Shrek shape it with academy-polished wrists, textbook timing, no lineage in it anywhere.

When number two had re-dressed and re-joined the line, the fifth came down the floor to him — unhurried, polite, hands loose — and said, at a volume for two people:

"Controlling Crane, Capturing Dragon. Who taught you?"

Everything about number two stopped for one full second. His eyes came up and went over the smaller boy with new attention — the soulless boy, the four exchanges, the concession they would be hearing about for a year. "Where," he said finally, "does a brat with no soul light learn that name?"

"Inside," Lin Hao said.

The answer plainly satisfied nobody, and both of them knew the shape of the moment: two holders of the same question, each declining to pay the answer. Number two's jaw set. The fifth nodded once — *thank you for the confirmation* — and walked back to the chairs, and along the wall the ten exchanged the look of people recalculating an entire evening. In her seat, Shen Yi's pen moved. Her file now had a section that was just questions, and the section was the fastest-growing one.

Xie Xie dropped into the chair beside the fifth, arms over the back of it, watching the line of ten with new professional interest. "Four exchanges."

"You counted?"

"The whole academy counted." He said it without resentment, which was its own kind of progress. Then, quieter, honestly: "He wasn't even angry. That's the part I keep replaying."

"Mountains don't get angry," the fifth said. "They just decide when."

Gu Yue was already standing.

## Part 5: The Forgettable One

"Number one has fought," Shen Yi said, neutral, and the room's attention flicked to the line. Canon law and house law agreed: selections were final, and taken was taken. "Choose from those remaining."

Gu Yue walked the line once, slower than Wulin had, reading it her way — and the purse's read was not the captain's read, nor the smith's. She stopped at a boy about whom nothing could be said at all: middle height, middle face, middle stillness, the one even the scoreboard's eye had slid past all evening. Fourth in the line. The forgettable one.

"Number four," Gu Yue said.

Xiaoyan made a small sound. Xie Xie, arms crossed, muttered, "She picked the *blank* one?"

"He's not blank," Wulin said quietly, watching the boy detach from the wall and walk out with the calm of furniture being moved. "None of them are blank. That's the whole academy." Lamplight stood in the round room's bowls now; true night was assembling outside, and one trial after this one, and a staff that wanted stars. The arithmetic of the evening was tightening exactly as designed.

For Gu Yue the arithmetic was simpler and worse. Thirty-eight points, two trials after this one, and a margin that could not absorb a stumble: scoring badly here would essentially mean not passing. The whole examination narrowed to the plainest sentence in it — *winning was her only option.*

"Begin!"

Soul rings rose beneath both of them — and the hall's breath went with them.

Three rings. **All three purple.**

Not the slender mountain's two-yellow-one-purple; not anything the evening had calibrated against. Three thousand-year rings stood over the forgettable boy like a sentence in a language nobody had spoken all day, and Gu Yue — whose reserves were the deepest secret in the room — let her hands rise into her working position, her expression unchanged, as the first spell left her fingers and the ranged war began.

## Part 1: The Instant War

The forgettable boy fought like a dream someone else was having.

His first ring lit; his hand shot into the air, and a sphere of illusory light spun itself out of nothing by his palm — strands of blue, green, and white dancing around his fingers — and when he chanted, a protrusion clawed out of it, dropped, and landed as an enormous hound wreathed in flame, the fire brightening and roughening until the shape said *lion*. Smaller than any lion-type soul beast. Domineering anyway. In the chairs, Wulin did the taxonomy out loud under his breath. "A lion mastiff? Is that a soul skill *or* a spirit soul?" He sat forward. "He's summoning it — that's his spirit soul as the whole army. Nothing's too bizarre for this place."

"His soul has a *dog* in it," Xie Xie said, with feeling.

"Materialize!" Rays of light ran down the boy's finger into the beast, and its edges firmed. "Little Lion, go!"

The mastiff went — a flash of lightning with killing intent nearly solid.

Gu Yue's three rings had been revolving to a controlled beat of her hands. Then the rhythm changed, and all three rings lit at once, trembling together — which skill she was using was anyone's guess, and the correct guess would have been *several*. Azure light; a half-meter sphere of ice in her palm; and she began, unhurried, to slap it. *Slap. Slap.* The sphere shuddered and held.

The mastiff closed, fur streaming like the tail of a meteor, maw yawning a golden-red fireball — and Gu Yue, the picture of boredom, to whom all of this was a chore, threw one ice ball at it, turned her back on the war, and strolled toward Wulin.

The room's collective mind left its body. Fire met ice; the sphere burst into a cloud of homing icicles; and the cloud *changed its mind* in the air — frigid blue to deep green between heartbeats, a third of them vanishing in a flash of silver and reappearing an inch from the summoner's nose, a dome of sharpness closing on the spot. "Not good!" he said, with a prize understatement, having spent everything on his lion's offense and nothing on his own person.

Green wind took the mastiff in the flank; its coat of flame guttered; its body went transparent, then anecdotal. Shen Yi moved faster than the eye could apologize and arrived between the icicles and the boy before the dome could close — otherwise, the evening's second pincushion.

"The match is over," she said, quietly, to the boy whose war had ended inside someone else's sentence.

"Gu Yue — ten points," Shen Yi said. Total forty-eight, two trials left, hope restored.

"She turned her *back* on him," Xie Xie said, to nobody, still processing it.

"She was finished," said the fifth, without looking up. "The back was just the punctuation."

"It's night," Gu Yue said, returning to the chairs, which was her whole after-action report. The stall had done its work; the last fighter of the five wanted her stars.

In the chairs, the fifth examinee was quiet. Among the elements that had obeyed her — ice, wind, that trick of light — there had been the silver one, the flicker that moved things without crossing the space between. He filed it without a word, in the drawer where he kept the things about Gu Yue that were not his to name. The drawer was getting full.

## Part 2: The Weakest

Xiaoyan stood, and her knees made it clear they had not been consulted.

Before she went, Wulin caught her sleeve and whispered. Her head came up in astonishment. "Really? Like *that?*"

"Just try it out." A raised brow, the gentle smile. "It's time for you to go."

"Okay," she said, in the voice of someone agreeing to a practical joke in which she was both the teller and the punchline.

She was, by her own honest ledger, the weakest of the five. Team battles she could assist; alone was another country. So she had done what the captain's cultivation plan had built her for — leaned all the way into her own grammar: where a heavier spear was built to *penetrate*, hers was built to *freeze*; she had stopped apologizing for that a season ago. And she had one more asset the plan had never needed to mention: three years of side-by-side combat had taught her exactly how calm she could be while looking exactly how she liked.

Her opponent was the muscular young man, student number six — the one Xie Xie had nearly picked, the sturdy one. "Begin," said Shen Yi, promptly.

Two yellow rings rose around Xu Xiaoyan, and under them she seemed frail past the point of charity. She *stumbled* catching the thing that congealed in her hands — and the arena's collective heart tilted, because the thing was a jet-black hammer, and she leaned on her staff under its weight like a kitten under a luggage cart.

*Is that a soul device?* went the hall, in unison, silently. *The trial forbids them.*

Shen Yi looked — hard — and held her tongue, because the hammer had no more soul fluctuation in it than a rock did. Whatever it was, it was not a device. It was, in fact, a thousand-refined tungsten hammer wearing duct tape, and what Xiaoyan did next transcended strange on its way to bizarre: her first ring lit, a massive ice wheel spun up before her — and she taped the hammer to the wheel, levitated the whole swaying contraption, and aimed it at a Shrek Academy student.

It flew at him like an inebriated snail. It looked, at every moment, like it was about to be retired by gravity.

"She's going to throw a *hammer* at him," Xie Xie said. "A hammer. On a wheel."

"Please wait a moment!" Xiaoyan called sweetly, to her opponent, about the snail. The line of ten watched with furrowed brows and pinched noses — astonishing things had been seen in this academy before, never once something so uncanny.

"Is she actually—" one of them began.

"Don't blink," said his neighbor, grimly. "I blinked at the fourth one and missed a sixty scored with no soul in it." Her second ring lit; a spear of ice congealed in front of her; and the fifth examinee, in the chairs, put his hand over his mouth and kept it there.

## Part 3: Nice Acting

Number six finally moved, not knowing whether to laugh or cry. *Is this girl a comedian?* — but the guillotine trial walked over his grave, and he did not underestimate her. His tool martial soul appeared: a crystal ball flickering with opaque light, three rings hovering above it.

"Crystal, crystal, *deviate!*"

White filled his eyes; the crystal shone; and Xiaoyan's own ice spear turned traitor in mid-flight, bending away toward her own pathetic wheel. Clever — her spear against her contraption; the girl dismantled by the girl. Her heart thumped once, hard. *If he has his way, I lose.* So she chose that exact moment to reveal her cards.

Purple light shone in her eyes.

His grip on the spear — on *her* spear — stuttered, because her Purple Demon Eyes was every ounce the equal of the captain's, and the stun ran through a spiritual foundation that had been strong before it was ever tested. She waved her staff like a conductor reclaiming the orchestra, and the spear swung back around toward number six, while every eye in the room followed it — and no one at all watched the ice wheel, which had begun, quietly, to speed up.

She raised her staff high. An air of divinity enveloped her, entirely real, and she said the words as though she had been saving them all day:

"The stars in the heavens that shine forever tranquil, grant me strength — *Starwheel!*"

Starlight descended in lines onto the Ice Staff, and it became the thing it only became at night: the **Starwheel Ice Staff**, and the girl underneath it stopped pretending to be clumsy in the same heartbeat — the stumble-act dropped, her every movement suddenly smooth as a cat's. A golden starwheel kindled beneath student number six's feet.

And here was the whole architecture of the trick, the part even the hall's sharp eyes would assemble only afterward: the transformation *cut her connection* to the wheel and the spear both. The spear arrived at number six's face on the last of her guidance — his second ring lit, and his Crystal Ball spiralled light through it, *Decomposition* reducing the ice to warm mist — and with the same breath he raised his eyes to the ceiling and found the actual problem, unguided now, falling toward his skull under nothing but tungsten and gravity.

"What — is that —" he managed, and tried the easy sidestep. The starwheel beneath him brightened, and chains of starlight shot out of the ground and bound him where he stood — the absolute control of astrological-attributed skills, his body a statute, his third ring too slow to matter, sweat jumping off his brow — head tilted up, watching a black hammer spin down at his face.

It stopped an inch above his head.

"I yield!" said student number six, at speed, to nobody in particular, bound and dry-mouthed and entirely alive.

The room exhaled a population's worth of air, and then Xie Xie's whoop arrived late and loud from the chairs.

"Everyone breathe," Wulin said, laughing, sweeping the five of them with one look. "Two more of these and we're students." Shen Yi crossed the floor, took the hammer out of the air, and weighed it curiously — one hand — then stood in front of Xu Xiaoyan with an odd smile escaping around her professionalism.

"A thousand-refined tungsten hammer," she said. Her eyes went down the chairs, to the captain. "Yours?"

"Xiaoyan's," Wulin said, "as of this evening."

"Girl," Shen Yi said, turning back, the odd smile winning, "*nice acting!*"

Xu Xiaoyan smiled sweetly. "Thank you for your praise."

The hammer, the hall now understood, had never been heavy for a two-ringed soul master; any ranged-type could have carried it at a stroll. The stumble had been the entire opening act — curiosity bait, misdirection, the purchase price of one unnoticed minute for a wheel to accelerate. One mistake, any mistake, and she lost; she had bet the trial on everyone's assumptions about a small girl, and the metal thing with no soul in it — the only object in the arena the rules could not touch — was the deciding factor. It had come out of one of the captain's heavy silver bracelet rings, slipped to her in the whisper, and the plan had needed no further instruction: she had known best how to use being *her*. Shrek's students had combat experience in outrageous quantities. What they did not have, a single one of them, was any practice at being charmed.

# Chapter 90: The Highest Level

## Canon Reference: canon ch 273 "Survive" (full, on disk — `canon_extract/chapters/canon_273.txt`). The ninth trial's rules · the elders' scene (Zhuo Shi in person — a held item pays) · "the highest level" · the ancient forest · the two-hour calm. ## Part 1: The Unbelievable

*Tang Wulin is a real freak,* Shen Yi thought, on the walk down. *Full marks in six trials. I can't make heads or tails of him. Plain old Bluesilver Grass, but that golden soul ring — definitely unrelated to his martial soul. Talents not great, strength formidable. Not potential alone — potential married to temperament. Gu Yue is far ahead of the class in talent and potential, but in strength and temperament, Wulin shines brightest, and fully deserves the captain's seat.* A breath. *Senior brother, your insight is so great.*

The room she led them to was unlike any so far: dim, bare, metal-walled, a single large screen hanging in it. The class's stomachs recognized it before their heads did — *this seems similar to the spirit ascension platform.*

"Your goal for the ninth trial is to survive," Shen Yi said. "I believe you've all been in the spirit ascension platform before. Well, this is similar to that. In a sense, all the soul beasts in it are real. If you kill one and are at a bottleneck, then you'll be able to gain a soul ring. Alright. Prepare to enter." She pressed a button, and metal capsules slid out of the wall — five of them, which was the shape of the class these days.

"Teacher Shen, will we be taking this trial together?" Wulin asked.

"Yes. No matter the number of participants, they will all take the trial together. This trial tests your coordination in addition to your ability to survive. You all came together, so you have an advantage here. Good luck."

"Thank you, Teacher Shen."

Around him, his team was already glowing with it. Xie Xie's trial-eight anxieties — three points, a pending deduction — blew off him like dust: they had spent *years* in the platform; anything like it was a walk in the park, so long as nobody lunged head-first at something high-level. GY's eyes and XXY's came to rest on their captain, brimming with confidence. Together, they were unbeatable.

The fifth examinee said nothing, which was usual, and looked at the capsule the way he looked at any tool — checking the seams.

## Part 2: The Elders

The capsules sealed and slid back into the walls, and the room breathed again — and then two people entered it whom the examinees would not have believed.

One was the cranky old lady they knew entirely too well. The Silver Moon Douluo walked in like the room's lighting was a personal insult.

The other was an old man: nose high, deep-blue sunken eyes, standing tall, gray hair down to his shoulders around an unyielding air — a presence that stifled the room by arriving in it.

"Teacher," Shen Yi said, respectfully, and became furniture with excellent posture.

The old man nodded. "How have these kids done so far?"

Shen Yi had prepared several answers on the walk down. All of them fled. She used the true one. "They're unbelievable."

The Silver Moon Douluo laughed. "That's right! They're really unbelievable! I didn't let them take the fifth trial, but there's actually someone who managed to score full points so far! That Tang Wulin is marvelous — his blood essence is strong, almost a bit like yours, Zhuo Shi." She waved a hand at the screen. "Let me be frank. I don't care about the other four. I've already set my eyes on that Gu Yue."

*The other four* — a count that had grown by one since any canon of this exam was written, and Zhuo Shi's sunken eyes said he had done the arithmetic.

"And the fifth one," he said. Not a question. The page Cai had been reading all day finally came up, in the worst company: between the two of them, with Shen Yi listening.

"Mm." The Silver Moon Douluo's expression did something complicated and private. "The one your students keep failing to inconvenience. Sixty points without one gram of soul light, and a question your number two still won't repeat above a whisper." She looked at the screen, at the small figures already forming up in an ancient forest. "Ask them. I've been reading that page since the buns, old man, and it keeps getting longer. I want to see the next line before I say anything aloud."

Zhuo Shi said nothing at all — which in a man like that was a decision — and let the matter fall into the same pocket where, his look suggested, he kept several others. Then he shot her a different look, the Grandteacher one. "What do you mean, *set your eyes on her*? Don't forget that they're all my granddisciples. They don't have anything to do with you."

"What?" Her brows arched. "Are you trying to go back on your word?"

"I'm not going back on my word! I'm stating a fact. Eye them as much as you want — that doesn't mean I'll hand them over. They have to be willing too. You'll need to ask Gu Yue if she *wants* to be your disciple. If she rejects you, there's no use forcing it."

"That's nonsense! I *like* how stubborn she is." She stomped, furious, delighted. "What would separate kids from walking corpses if they didn't have strong wills? Her temperament is precisely what attracts me!"

Shen Yi watched the two of them the way one watches weather over open water.

"We can talk about this after they finish this trial," Zhuo Shi said. "If they can't pass it, it doesn't matter how high they scored on the others." And to the Silver Moon's credit, the vexation reined itself in; she held this trial in high regard too.

"Teacher," Shen Yi ventured, softly, "what test level are they taking?"

Zhuo Shi contemplated the screen a moment.

"The highest level."

Shen Yi's thoughts had to be steadied like a struck bell. *The highest level? Even adults find that level hard! That's—*

"Hurry up now," Zhuo Shi urged.

"Yes."

## Part 3: The Ancient Forest

Space warped; a flash; and class zero stood together in a world that arrived around them — a lush forest, greener than green, and *older* than anything the platform had ever shown them. They fell into the usual formation by instinct: Wulin center, the grass already alive under his feet and probing outward; GY and XX on the flanks; Xiaoyan deep. The fifth took the outer seam, the unassigned edge, the place where the formation met the unknown — which had quietly become his address over three years.

"So the ninth trial tests our ability to *survive*," Xie Xie said, rejoicing. "Fantastic. Isn't this the easiest possible trial for us?"

Wulin raised a hand, and the class went quiet.

"This place is different from what we're used to. At least from the elementary one. I've been in the intermediate level once, with Teacher Wu — the plants here and there are similar." He let that sit. "Don't forget this is still part of the Shrek entrance exam. Teacher Shen said we have to survive. She never said for how long. And if this is like the intermediate platform, we'll run into a lot of thousand-year soul beasts." A beat. "Maybe even some at the ten-thousand-year level."

Three of his teammates drew a careful breath. The fifth did not, having already priced the forest.

Xiaoyan's voice came out small and hopeful. "Captain — if I can break through to rank 30, can't I get a soul ring here? If there's a ten-thousand-year soul beast—"

"Don't even think about it." Wulin's frown was the load-bearing kind. "With your current abilities, absorbing a ten-thousand-year ring is impossible — let alone *killing* one. This would be your third ring. Normally, soul masters don't take a ten-thousand-year ring until rank 50. Your body isn't that strong to begin with. Don't think so wishfully, or you'll encounter a problem. Like the time I evolved my spirit soul to the thousand-year level."

Xiaoyan stuck out her tongue. "Got it!"

"Let's go. Vantage point first. Once we have a good line of sight, we rest and recover what the other trials spent."

## Part 4: The Evacuated Quiet

They moved carefully. Gu Yue scouted, wind birds lifting off her fingers and threading the thicket; Wulin watched their immediate surroundings; the fifth walked the seam and read the ground the way he read everything — along the grain.

The wind birds found nothing. Not beasts, not tracks, not birdsong — a forest as blank as a held breath. Wulin did not believe it for a second; this was part of Shrek's exam.

"I don't like this quiet," Xiaoyan said, at the fifth minute, the way someone names a weather they have decided to do something about. "It's the loud kind."

"The kind that's being waited *in,*" Gu Yue said. She said it flat. Her elements stayed gathered at the edge of her hands, petals not yet wind.

He let the cold out a breath's width, under his skin and half a pace beyond it — not the domain, never the domain in a forest the academy had filled with things to read; just the deep water that the coiled thing at the bottom of his spiritual sea sent up to the surface when he asked for it — a threshold crossed and held, a country not a tally — seeping out the way a man's own warmth seeps out through his coat. The frost went a half-step in every direction along the pine needles before he stopped it — small, deliberate, his own weather laid down like a road. "Walk inside that," he said. "It knows me. Whatever else is in these trees, that patch is ours."

They did, one at a time — Gu Yue first, because she had measured the offer's arithmetic and found it solvent; Xiaoyan and Xie Xie after her. Wulin came last and stood the closest, as he always did now, shoulder to shoulder where the frost met the normal forest air, and did not say thank you because they had both stopped saying it at twelve and never started again. He did reach across and close his fist over Lin Hao's shoulder for one held second, the way you'd close your hand on a rail you'd tested once in a gale. "Your winter still follows you indoors," he said.

"Outdoors now, apparently."

"Good. Keep it on the outside."

Under the frost-patch the ground was solid and gave no footfall; beyond it the forest stayed blank, and listened. Xie Xie, crouched at the edge of the cold with his clones standing watch, let out a breath he'd been holding. "This is cheating," he said, without heat. "This is cheating and I am completely in favor."

"Noted," Lin Hao said. "Where you are standing, the notes say, and don't comment on the temperature. The temperature is mine."

A while on, they found their hill, wide-viewed, and the captain dug the steamed buns out of his storage device and dealt them around like cards. The fifth ate exactly his portion — the body's price, computed and paid — and took his turn resting with his back to the others and his attention on the treeline.

Two hours. Fully recovered. All tranquil, without the slightest hint of trouble.

"Captain, something's strange," Xie Xie said at last, low, nervous. "It's been two hours already and we still haven't met a single soul beast. Do you have any idea what's going on?"

Wulin didn't answer at once. But it was the fifth who spoke, from the edge of the group, quietly, without turning around.

"It's not empty," Lin Hao said. "It's evacuated."

The class looked at him. The oldest thing he owned had spent the last two hours reading the quiet, and the quiet had a grain like everything else: no fear-signals, no territorial calls, no scavengers working the margins — not a forest without beasts but a forest *cleared by something*, every living thing gone from it the way crowds go from streets when the weather turns.

"An empty forest is a forest something bigger owns," he said. "We're not early. We're late. Everything here moved out ahead of something that's still coming."

The wind moved the ancient canopy, agreeably, like a thing with nothing to confess; and on the screen in a dim metal room, two old monsters and one teacher leaned in.

## Part 1: The Long Afternoon

The same doubt had been sitting in all of them. Points for surviving — but two hours without a peep. You could *forage* in a forest. How was this a trial?

"Should we go exploring?" Xie Xie asked.

Wulin read the sky before answering. "Not yet. It's early afternoon. We'll wait for nightfall — it'll be safer if Xiaoyan can use her Starwheel Ice Staff."

Impatience was enemy number one, and the captain did not feed enemies. Safe here meant whole later: everyone at their best condition before the forest was spent. So they waited out the sun, and the sun took its time.

The fifth spent the afternoon the way he spent every waiting period — on maintenance. Frost Abyss lay across his knees for an hour, the cloth off, the steel getting its oil; and the steel, under his hands, was *strange* today. Restless. The sword had been poured in a forge that mattered, and it had opinions about pressure the way bells have opinions about thunder — a fine continuous trembling in the metal that was not his hands. He sheathed it when the light went amber, and the trembling did not entirely stop.

*You feel it too,* he thought. *Noted.*

His brother watched him do all of this from the other side of the camp, the way Wulin always watched him do everything — completely, and without questions — and at some point had simply moved his rest-place six meters closer, so that when the forest finally spoke, the first hand in reach would be where it always was.

## Part 2: The Howl

The sun went down beyond the horizon, and in the twilight Wulin climbed a tree to look. The world ran green and endless to every edge — trees as far as the eye could see, the way the Great Star Dou Forest must have looked before maps.

The howl arrived without escort.

It did not echo so much as *flip the forest upside down* — every leaf between here and the horizon shivering once, in order, like a page being turned. Wulin's body broke out in goosebumps and his mind went white at the edges, and it was only his blood essence flaring up in his defense that dispersed the terror at all.

He climbed down madly, one question hammering: *if a single howl can do that, what is the thing that made it?* The strongest soul beast he had ever encountered was the Three-eyed Demon Ape whose spirit energy he carried — and he would never forget his teacher fighting the ten-thousand-year one. That had been the ceiling of his nightmares for two years.

This howl had walked through that ceiling without slowing down.

At the bottom, his companions wore matching horror. "W-what was that sound?" Xie Xie was pale, aghast, whispering. "That scared me to death." Even Gu Yue was restrained in the specific way that meant she was doing it on purpose.

"I don't know either," Wulin said, grim. "But it doesn't seem too far from here."

A second roar thundered before the sentence finished — sharper, a blade of a sound, and it *penetrated* their bodies and, impossibly, **dispelled the fear**, scouring it out like frost under hot water. The class looked at each other with clean, cold nerves and no idea whatsoever what to do with them.

*Two voices,* the fifth thought, from the seam. *One installs the fear. One removes it.* Only two things at the very top of a forest argue like that.

"Let's go take a look," Gu Yue said.

Wulin nodded — the logic was already load-bearing in him: a trial would not be as simple as it looked; and if they didn't look at *it*, it might come looking at *them*. Initiative was the only discount available. "Let's go."

## Part 3: The Crawling

Wind birds went ahead; Wulin led, opening the path, dragging his blood essence aura over their scent like a blanket — since they were not strong enough to be invisible, they would at least be confusing. Twenty minutes in, Gu Yue's face twitched.

"There's a valley up ahead on the left. It's over there." A beat. "My wind birds were dispersed by a gust of wind."

Nobody said what that meant about the gust. The silence said it for them.

"Everyone, be careful." Wulin's voice had gone quiet the way it did. "Follow closely behind me."

Golden scales rippled from his arm to his shoulder; the golden ring lit beneath him; the blood essence banked their nerves like a hearth. The closer they came to the valley, the more the air pressed — a weight with direction, waves of power rolling out of the valley's throat, and the five of them circulating soul power just to keep their spines straight under it.

"We're crawling from here onward." Wulin dropped to his belly, and the pressure instantly lessened — a fact they filed without discussion.

"Crawling," Xie Xie whispered, flat as a lizard. "At Shrek. On our bellies."

"It counts as a trial," Xiaoyan breathed. "It's in the brochure."

Five examinees inched to the rim of the valley and looked over it, and five breaths went in and did not soon come out. Five examinees inched to the rim of the valley and looked over it, and five breaths went in and did not soon come out.

Below, booms rolled like weather. **Two lights, each more than thirty meters across, struck each other countless times** — the earth jumping, the air whipped to froth, boulders the size of bedrooms riding the shockwaves into the walls.

Purple light rose in Wulin's eyes, and the lights resolved into shapes.

The first was dark-gold, immense, and *intimately* familiar — the ruler of the forest, the **Duskgold Dreadclaw Bear** — except the ones they had met before would have come up to this one's *ankle*. This was a colossus over ten meters tall, dark-gold light pouring down arms like bridge pylons, each slash tearing gouges into the valley walls with the casualness of a man parting curtains. The taxonomy climbed the spine uninvited: a hundred-year one had made a pride of Blazing Demon Lions beg; a thousand-year one was the absolute tyrant of any forest; a ten-thousand-year one could tear apart *ordinary hundred-thousand-year* soul beasts.

This one was beyond the taxonomy. And it was the *defender* look of the two — the cornered, furious party — because the thing it was fighting was not losing.

The second beast stood inside a ball of blinding gold: a body translucent as crystal, a lion's general plan with **flaming draconic claws** and a longer snout, fine golden scales showing through the fur like mail under a cape. And on its forehead, a vertical slit, and in the slit — **a third eye**, glaring out a bewitching red glow over the whole valley.

Wulin described it in a whisper, because knowledge is the class's currency. All eyes went to Xie Xie, who knew the most.

"From what you've said—" His brows knotted; his mouth went dry. "I think I might know. Give me a moment to think."

"Take your time," the fifth murmured, which for once was not irony.

## Part 4: The Read at the Rim

While Xie Xie thought, the fifth lay flat at the rim and let the oldest thing he owned do its work.

The valley's pressure had a grain like everything else, and the grain said *boundary*. Two apex territories had collided here — that was the evacuated forest's answer, delivered in full: not one owner but two, and everything with legs had left days ago. His body was reading the two roars even now, cataloguing them the way it catalogued forge-heat — *that one shakes the animal; that one unmakes the shaking* — and pricing, quietly, the difference between surviving a forest and surviving *between* these two.

Against his spine, Frost Abyss had gone still in the way that steel goes still — the total attention of a drawn thing not yet drawn. Whatever was in that valley, the sword had finished its arithmetic about it before he had, and its answer was a silence he chose to respect. The Intent stayed sheathed. Some pressures you did not answer with edges; you answered by being exactly where you were, flat, patient, uninteresting.

His brother's shoulder was touching his. That was all — no one watching would have called it anything — but it was the same grammar as the hand that had pulled him out of the wall at Eastsea, first in, because it always was, and the fifth let it carry its share of the weight.

Below them, the bear roared, and the crystal lion's third eye burned redder, and two kings threw themselves together again with a sound like the closing of a very large book.

"Some trial," Xie Xie breathed, barely audible, still thinking. "The highest level. Even adults find *this* hard."

"We're not fighting them," Wulin said quietly — captain's voice, arithmetic under it. "We're surviving near them. There's a difference, and our points are in the difference."

"And the exam has a way through," Gu Yue said. "It always has one."

At the rim, flat as five commas in the valley's great sentence, class zero held its ground in six-centimeter increments and waited for Xie Xie's memory to finish loading.

# Chapter 92: Seen and Spared

## Canon Reference: canon ch 275 "Auspicious Emperor" (full, on disk) continuing ch 274's rim (both cited). The legend, the departure, the descent, the cave, the gems. OURS under Law oo: Lin Hao as a person in the room — the rim-read that reframes the whole trial; the descent planned around him; consequences corrected aloud.

---

## Part 1: The Read at the Rim

"Either of them could erase us with one swipe," Gu Yue said. "So why does the exam *want* us watching them? Being here has to be worth points somehow."

"Then we watch," Wulin said. "They're spending each other. If they both end up one breath from finished, that gap is ours to walk into — maybe." He knew exactly what his team was and wasn't. Charging either of those two was a way to stop existing. And this place had removed the one comfort the ascension platform always offered: there was no leaving early here except by dying.

Below them the two lights dimmed, and for the first time the shapes stood clear: the bear's dark-gold shell cracked and guttering, its huge head low; the crystal lion hardly marked, bright as a struck bell, the third eye burning a clean red.

"It's afraid," Xiaoyan whispered. "The *bear's* afraid."

"It's not watching the bear," Lin Hao said.

"It's staring at the bear," Xie Xie hissed. "Obviously—"

"The bear. The valley. The rim." Lin Hao hadn't moved; his voice stayed down where the wind wouldn't find it. "All at once. That eye took our measure before Gu Yue's birds ever left her hands. We've been seen." A beat. "And passed over."

The class went quiet in a new way. Being hidden and being *spared* were different weights, and everyone felt the difference arrive at once.

"So it *chose* not to," Xiaoyan breathed. "We're alive on purpose."

"For now," said Gu Yue, and sent new birds north.

## Part 2: The Legend

"I've got it!" Xie Xie's whisper cracked with the effort of staying a whisper. "The golden one — it's the auspicious beast! From the legends!"

Three faces turned. Lin Hao's stayed on the valley, but tipped, listening.

"You know the Spirit Ice Douluo's story. Once, the saying goes, the Great Star Dou Forest kept an emperor of luck — while it lived, every beast under the canopy cultivated faster, like the whole forest was fed. When it died, the luck inverted. Misfortune, decline — and in the end, the tide that broke against Shrek City." Xie Xie's finger stabbed toward the gold. "That's no lion, that's the *Auspicious Emperor*. A Three-eyed Golden Lion. The Spirit Ice Douluo himself took it — its ring, its bone. The skull, Wulin. The number-one spiritual bone ever ranked."

"How smart is it," Lin Hao asked, "for 'smarter than humans'?"

"Talks-in-legends smart. Schemes smart."

"And nobody wrote down that it *talks*?"

"My family collects biographies," Xie Xie said, with the smugness of a boy standing in front of a library nobody else could visit. "There are versions normal people never touch. In one of them—" he dropped his voice further, delighted, "—the lion took a human shape. Fell in love with him. The Spirit Ice Douluo. And when death came for the man, the lion stepped in front of it — became his ring to save him. Which is why the forest after him went hungry and angry and marched on Shrek."

Xiaoyan's eyes had gone star-shaped. "It's *cool*. I want it. Can I want it? As my spirit soul—"

"Keep dreaming," Xie Xie said.

"Get in line anyway," Lin Hao told her. "It saw you first."

But Gu Yue wasn't laughing. "It traded every beast's future for one person," she said slowly. "Why? It knew what the forest was without it. It did the arithmetic and *still* chose him."

"Love doesn't do arithmetic," Xie Xie said, with the authority of a boy who had read about it.

Gu Yue's eyes did something involuntary then — a flick to Wulin, gone as fast as it came — and Lin Hao, who caught it because he caught everything at that angle, looked back at the valley and said, mostly to himself:

"Most expensive gift I've ever heard of."

Gu Yue glanced at him this time — a full second of it, filing the answer and its author somewhere — and said nothing.

## Part 3: The Correction

The earth answered for them. A rumble rolled up through the stone under their ribs, the wind stood up, and the two lights collided one last furious time and then *moved* — grinding away down the valley, north, the sound of them shrinking like a storm changing counties.

"Gone?" Xie Xie asked, tiny.

"Gone," Gu Yue confirmed, birds aloft. "Two lights. Moving fast. Arguing the whole way."

The class let a population's worth of air out through its nose.

"That's why the forest was empty," Xiaoyan said. "Them."

"Mm. This valley is somebody's ground," Wulin said. "The other came to take it."

"And if it's the *lion's* ground—" Xie Xie was already vibrating, "—then luck lives here. Treasures, Captain. They said we can carry out whatever we find."

"They also said this is an illusory world," Xie Xie barreled on. "Worst case, we die here and just… wake up. No real consequences. If we *don't* look, we'll regret it the rest of our lives."

"The rings are real," Lin Hao said.

Everyone looked at him.

"The rules said it — the beasts here are real, in a sense; kill one at a bottleneck and the ring comes home with you. Anything real enough to hand you a ring," he said, "is real enough to collect one. There's no version of this with no consequences. There's just the ones we haven't met."

"He's fun at festivals," Xie Xie told the group.

"He's right, though," Wulin said, and the captain arrived at the decision in the same breath, fire lighting behind his eyes. "We're going. But we go *together*, quiet, and nobody touches anything shiny until we're standing on real grass again. That's the price of the trip."

Groans, from exactly one person.

"It's up to you, Captain," Xiaoyan said, already smiling.

Gu Yue nodded once.

## Part 4: Down

The valley wall was steep and stupid with loose stone. Wulin's Bluesilver Grass made ropes of itself, and the plan came out of the captain already cut to the shape of five people, not four.

"Lin Hao anchors at the lip — heaviest grip, and the wall's his to watch. Xiaoyan, his line. Gu Yue with Xie Xie on mine. Nobody free-climbs past anybody."

Lin Hao went over first, found his ledge, and then did the thing none of them had thought to do and all of them now watched him do: he took each grass-line in turn where it met the stone, read the knot, and re-tied two of them.

"Smith's knots," he said, when Wulin's eyebrow went up. "If one loosens, it's my name on it."

They came down slow and steady through the battle's leavings, and the leavings were the lesson. The valley floor lay stripped bare, and its walls carried wounds in rows — gouges deep as a man, runs of stone sheared off like rind. Lin Hao put two fingers into one as they passed and stopped.

"The lip's glassy," he said. "It melted, a little, then froze. That wasn't cutting. That's weather with an edge." He wiped his fingers on his trouser leg, quietly pleased in the professional way, and added the whole experience to whatever ledger he kept about the difference between ten-thousand-year power and everything else.

The mist stood thick at the far end. And out of it, when they drew level — a mouth of dark in the rock, five meters of height swallowing itself in shadow.

Xie Xie ran the last stretch before anyone could rule on it, sketched a bow at the entrance, and then his face changed. He inhaled at the threshold twice, like a sommelier with a death wish.

"Captain. We fought a Dreadclaw — you all remember the *smell*." He pointed into the dark. "That's not it. This is clean. Faintly animal. The biographies describe it." His gulp was audible. "It's the *lion's*."

"Then we don't stand in its doorway deciding," Wulin said. "In. Fast and quiet — they could come back."

## Part 5: The Floor

The dark inside was total, a different country; then the ceiling climbed away and the space widened, and around a bend the light found them first.

Gems. The floor was *littered* with them — loose stones catching somebody's light and returning it in pieces, red and gold and green washing over the walls with every step, so that the five of them walked into a slow kaleidoscope.

"Oh," Xiaoyan said, the politically safest available word.

"Treasures," Xie Xie whispered, hands physically clasping each other behind his back in tribute to the captain's law.

Gu Yue crouched, lifted one, let it roll in her palm — careful, pricing nothing aloud.

Wulin turned a slow circle, grass already spread across the floor behind them like a tripwire crop. "Eyes working. Hands empty. That's the rule until grass."

Lin Hao knelt last, picked nothing up, and read the floor the way he read everything — the spread of it, the sizes, the way the pieces had settled all one way, like something had been bedded here and had risen.

"Eyes up," he said, rising out of the crouch. "A floor this generous has an owner."

Somewhere north, muffled by a mountain's worth of stone, the two lights were still arguing.

## Canon Reference: canon ch 276 "Three-eyed Golden Lion" (full, on disk) continuing the gem floor (canon 275's tail, cited). ## Part 1: The Floor's Price

"Do you think we can take the gems?" Xie Xie asked — gazing at the mountain of jewels the way other children gazed at candy.

"Don't be so greedy." Wulin didn't even look at them. "You see me trying anything? If anyone could walk in and take those, why would Shrek leave them sitting here for a pack of examinees? Common sense."

"He's right," Lin Hao said, and meant the whole floor of it. His eye had done the arithmetic once, quietly, on the way in: a cave of loose stones worth a district of Eastsea, unguarded, in an academy's trial — which made them not treasure but *furniture*, and probably bait. His family had priced an education once; he knew exactly what an institution looked like when it could afford to leave a fortune on the floor. It looked like this. "Anything unguarded here is part of the test. Walk on the coins, don't pocket them."

"Treasurer," Xie Xie muttered, mourning.

The gems were, in the end, just pretty stones to all of them — Wulin included. What held the class was a different question entirely: what a beast like that would want in a home.

They found out two bends later.

## Part 2: The Thing in the Nest

The cave opened, a growl rolled, and something wrapped in gold light came out of the dark at Wulin's face.

No thinking got done — the body did the century of work on its own. Golden light burst from him in answer; the right arm thickened; the hand became a claw; three meters of dark-gold edge left it in a fan. In the face of death he held back nothing.

Metal struck metal with a ring that hurt the teeth. The golden shape thudded down close enough to touch; Wulin gave seven or eight steps of ground and found his footing with blood essence boiling off his shoulders — and his team, who had been ordered to run, closed into their formation instead and put a shield of water over his retreat.

They didn't run. He'd told them to run and nobody had even *considered* it, and in the middle of a fight for his life, the fact of that landed in him like a warm meal.

Then the light around the shape thinned, and the class got its first honest look.

A lion. The same impossible lion from the valley — crystal-bright, gold-scaled, the slit of a third eye closed on its forehead — and *small*. Shoulder height of a large dog. If the one in the valley was a mountain, this was the mountain's child.

"A *juvenile*?" Xie Xie's whisper cracked upward. "Could we be any luckier?"

## Part 3: The Case for the Ring

"Lucky," Wulin said, flat with suspicion.

"Lucky!" Xie Xie insisted, and made the case at speed: the third eye was the whole identity of the beast — it opened only past some growth threshold, and past it came power and a luck that blessed its whole pack; this one hadn't opened theirs, which meant young, which meant, at a guess, ten-year rank. Hundred at the outside. "And Xiaoyan—" he turned, blazing with it, "—a hundred-year ring from THIS bloodline would beat a ten-thousand-year ring off anything common. It might even drop a BONE. Golden Lion bones rank number one. There is no better third ring on the continent. There might be no better third ring in *history*."

Gu Yue leaned to Wulin's ear. "Is this a good idea?"

He watched the small lion pace, the closed eye, the claw-marks his own strike had left in scales that had rung like an anvil — marks that said *close enough to even*. "I think we can do it," he said. "Before its parent comes home."

Nobody needed to ask who the ring was for. The class had a shape, and the shape had a hole in it with Xiaoyan's name.

"Then hear the price," Lin Hao said to her, and waited until her eyes came up. "It's yours if you can take it — the last hit has to be yours, or the ring won't know you. Nobody's spending it for you. We'll open the door; you walk through it."

Xiaoyan's hands tightened on her staff. "…Okay," she said, in the small voice she used when a thing was too big to hold, and then, louder, because she was also the girl with the hammer: "Okay."

"Come on, then." Wulin stepped forward and beckoned to it, welcoming the problem. "Let's fight."

## Part 4: The Dim Room

On the screen in the metal room, five small figures fought something small and bright, and two old monsters leaned in like men at a chess problem played for money.

"Blood essence on the grass," Zhuo Shi said. "Second seal?"

"Ask them," the Silver Moon Douluo said, which had stopped being an answer and become a policy. Then, grudging, professional: "Look at the fifth one. Not fighting. *Herding.* He's placed where the little one's flashes go to die, and he hasn't lit a single ring doing it. The children fight; he farms the edges. Zhou — I have seen Sect Masters take worse care of a formation."

Zhuo Shi said nothing. On the screen, in the corner of the cave his granddisciple could not see, the fifth examinee turned his head — as if, Cai thought with an unholy delight, he could feel the two of them watching.

"He can't see us," Zhuo Shi said.

"I know," she said, and did not take her eyes off him.

## Part 5: The Blitz

The fight taught itself in pieces. Wulin's claw met the juvenile head-on and traded it boom for boom — his second-seal blood ran into the grass itself now, the gold creeping up the strands like dawn, changing what the grass *was* at some speed the grass itself did not yet understand. Bind bought a heartbeat; the lion's answer was a bolt of light like horizontal lightning, and his answer to that was to stand flat and swing through it, because a boy whose arm had just learned it was cheaper to feed than it used to be could afford the trade.

Gu Yue's stone teeth came up out of the floor and closed on the lion like a grammar book snapping shut; gold light blew them open from inside. And then the air *tilted* — the dizziness wave, the beast's third weapon — rolling over Wulin and Gu Yue like a floor pitching in cross-seas.

It washed over Lin Hao too, and broke. An Emperor’s spirit, meet a hundred-year cub's protest: he received it the way a wall receives weather, and simply moved — one step lateral, planting himself where the wave's debris fell, between the stagger and the two girls.

"Eyes front!" he called, sharp, ordinary. "It's loud, not strong! Xiaoyan — cast, don't look!"

She cast. And when the lion came out of its broken prison low and wicked for Wulin's middle, three Xie Xies came down on it like weather — the clones and the storm together, a knife-on-glass barrage that held a hundred-year legend up in the air by sheer insistence.

"NOW — blitz!" Wulin's second ring lit; the Impaling Array roared up around the suspended lion, a hedge of spears closing—

—and the beast *glowed*, that bizarre gold gushing off it, and the spears wilted at the touch of the light, slowing, barely failing, the whole trap dying an inch from its skin—

—and under it, quietly, a wheel of stars turned.

The Starwheel Shackles took the golden beast's legs mid-thrash, and it went stiff as a statue — one breath, two — and in the space of the first one, silver light *folded* the cave. No crossing. No distance crossed at all: Gu Yue was simply there, in front of the lion, and she had brought Wulin with her, delivered like a hammer to the anvil-face of the world.

Lin Hao, herding the edges, saw the silver close over them both and knew it instantly for what it was — the thing from the drawer, the flicker that moved without crossing the space between, spent now to save, in service of a girl's third ring — and he thought, with something that was not quite awe and not quite envy: *so that's what it's for.*

The claw came down.

# Chapter 94: What the Sword Was For

## Canon Reference: canon ch 277 "Decisions" AS ORE — facts cited (the rebound and the luck · ten-year rank · the refusal chain · the hardening freeze), trajectory OURS. The deliberation scene was DEAD on arrival (D03: our protocol pre-set the kill); the refusal itself re-derived through OUR causes (ch92's seen-and-spared; XXY's own door thread) — honest convergence, cited. **canon = ore; facts cited; trajectory ours.**
