## Part 1: The Rebound

The claw came down.

Wulin rode it in from the height of the silver delivery, full weight, blood essence behind it, aiming to spike the golden beast's skull into its own gem floor — and the blow that should have ended the fight *refused*.

The dragon claw bounced. Clean off. The crash still knocked the cub senseless — it hit the floor with a boom that rattled jewels down the mound — but the crushing weight, the thing his claw did to everything it had ever struck, simply did not happen. His arm went numb to the shoulder, and Wulin stared at his own hand as if it had been overruled.

"It's the luck," Gu Yue said quietly. "Its own legend. The Auspicious Emperor's blood won't let the crushing take it."

"Mind the head, Captain," Xie Xie added, already at his shoulder. "Break the skull and we may lose the bone. Everything we want is *in* the head."

Everything we want. Wulin looked down. The cub lay where it had fallen, out cold, breathing in small hitches. The scales of its crown were smashed to bits from the rebound — golden blood, bright as the floor, trickling from the cracks. Its third eye stayed shut. It looked, in the gem light, like something asleep in a treasure pile: a child in its own bed, in its own house, with the front door broken in behind it.

## Part 2: The Choice She Already Made

"Xiaoyan." Wulin stepped back from it. "It's yours. Like we said."

She came forward with her hammer and the whole cave went with her. This was the shape they had built on the way in — *we'll open the door; you walk through it* — and the door stood wide: the beast unconscious, the defenses broken, the class in a ring around it with their weapons pointed at the floor. There was nothing in her way. That was the thing. In her way there was nothing at all — no rank to cross first, no rival claim, no living defense. Just the walk.

She raised the hammer.

The cub's third eye stayed closed. Not a challenge in it. Not even fear. Asleep.

Xu Xiaoyan stood there one breath longer, and then she set the hammer down against the gem floor with a small clack, the way you set down a cup you've decided not to drink from.

"No," she said.

Nobody moved.

"It's a child." Her voice was small and did not shake. "It hid in its house and we broke the door in. Everything else in this forest came at us — this one was just *home*. And if its mother comes back and finds it dead with our marks on it—" She stopped, and started again, plainer. "We know how to spare things now. We did it for the bear. The ring would have been the best thing I'm ever given, and I would have carried it fine. But I'd have carried *this* too, and I don't want this."

"The bone's worth a province," Xie Xie said — not arguing — saying it out loud so the size of what she was declining would be witnessed. Then he looked at the sleeping cub, and at the golden blood, and put his hands in his pockets. "I don't want it either. Ladies first, and the ladies keep declining."

"I don't want luck," Gu Yue said. "I want strength. Luck is a thing that happens to you. I'd rather be a thing that happens."

Wulin had been quiet a long moment. He had no bear's bone in his own hands to point to — the bear was alive and north of them and knew them by smell; that account was still open. "We're the visitors," he said finally. "That's the whole of it. We're the visitors, and it's the house." And then, because he was the captain and the worries were his: "Also — my arm went numb off a *lucky* bounce. This trial isn't anywhere near as simple as it's pretending to be. Nothing this far in is priced this cheap." He nodded at the cub. "Leave it sleeping. Wulin's rule: take nothing, not even the story."

Something shifted in the cave then, too quiet to name. Xie Xie looked at the little beast a long time. In this forest, until tonight, the killing had been the game the way tag is a game — and here, suddenly, was a girl setting down the best prize of their lives beside a sleeping child, and it fit her hand better than the hammer had. He didn't have a question for it yet. He had the shape of a question, and it would be his for years: *if we are the ones who come in, what does that make everything after?*

## Part 3: What Came Home

The cub had cried out once — when the scales broke. Small. The kind of sound a house makes when a child in it is hurt.

The forest heard it.

The air of the cave thickened like deep water, and at the far bend, where the dark had been merely dark, a gold light arrived — not torch-bright; *arrival*-bright, the light of something coming that had stopped pretending to approach and was simply *closing the distance*. Two golden eyes, high up, higher than a bear's. Above and between them, a third lid slid open, and the light of it was red.

"Out," Wulin snapped. "Now, all of you, the way we came—"

And space *hardened*.

It went down the tunnel like frost up a window, only backwards — the world's own grain tightening — and it caught them mid-stride, four of five, locked like insects in amber: Wulin half-turned, Gu Yue's silver guttering around her fingers, Xie Xie's clones winking out unborn, Xiaoyan's starwheel dying at her wrists. The red eye's pressure lay on them like a column of water. It was not attacking. It was *holding*, the way you hold a door shut with your hand while you look at what's inside.

It reached the fifth.

And broke.

Not loudly. The hardening came to Lin Hao and found the thing it could not freeze — spirit that outranked the beast's whole legend, a soul like deep water that had never once in its life stopped moving — and the space around him simply stayed his. He took one step, unhurried, and planted himself between the red eye and the four statues of his class.

"Go when it lets you," he said, calm as a man giving directions in the street. "Follow the gems out, then the stars. Don't wait, don't watch." He drew the breath of someone about to lift a full crate, and let half of it go. "I'll close the door."

## Part 4: The Fifth Hand Closes the Door

He had lit nothing all exam. Nine trials of edges, of herding, of being the placed stone the flashes died on — the whole academy had watched a fifth examinee farm the margins, and the margins had been the plan, because a sword shown is a price, and Lin Hao does not spend without a reason.

The reason was standing frozen behind him — four statues of his class, and the fifth the only thing still moving.

The statues had a last ten seconds of being people first. Xiaoyan found his sleeve, found it was already rimed with a film of frost like window-glass in winter, and did not let go of it anyway — her hand the one part of her the fear-lock still let move, and she used it on that. Gu Yue's glance went to the red eye and came back to him, and the arithmetic she did with it she kept to herself, which was its own kind of promise; if he were wrong about the next thirty seconds she had four elements loaded and no order to wait for. Xie Xie, who had three clones out and nowhere to spend them, laughed once, shaky, short — the laugh of a boy whose own funeral music had just turned into someone else's.

And Wulin, the space-hardening on him like a coat someone else wore, did the only thing the rules still permitted: he stood to. He couldn't reach the fight, so he reached the geometry of it — shifting his weight one half-step nearer to the girls, the captain's body arranging itself between the class and whatever came through the wall, even when the wall was Lin Hao. His eyes said the rest, because the freeze owned the rest of him: *Go on. We are here. You are not the only one in this forest.* Two of them, shoulder to shoulder, since they were three years old and the water had been just as cold.

Lin Hao held out his right hand, and *summoned his sword.*

The Frost Abyss Sword came out of him the way winter comes out of a clear night sky — no warning, total arrival. Black iron, cold past color, a blade with a library in it: four elements asleep down its length, and the iron not a fifth element but the *house they lived in*. The cave went quiet the way his family's shop went quiet on the last cold morning of a year. Even the red pressure paused to look at it.

Then, for the first time since the fourth ring had given it to him — folded at the bear, carried folded through eight trials, through ten doors and a gem floor and a blitz — he *opened his domain.*

The Frost Abyss Domain unfolded, and the cave became the other hall, the one he had been carrying all along: a place where everything is heard. The cub's hitching breath stood in the air like a written line. The hardening of space groaned at the domain's hem and settled, two immensities agreeing to share a corridor. Sound stopped being noise in there. Sound became *record*.

He released his Sword Intent.

The books on his shelf at home had used two names for it, and he had finally understood, on a roof in another city, that they were the same name: *sword intent*, and the older, better words, *sword consciousness*. The intent that knows the cut before the cut. It left him now, unhooded, and the mountain of gold light at the tunnel's end felt a boy of thirteen look at the whole of its advance and *file* it — distance, grain, temper, seam — the way a smith reads a billet before the first hammer ever falls.

And he fused his spiritual power into the stroke. All of it that the stroke could hold: twenty-nine hundred points of deep water forced down the iron's length until the blade sang one flat note, and the four elements woke in their house — lightning, wind, water, ice — braided in the iron the way they had lived there since the day the ring turned black.

One attack. He did not swing at the king. Kings of that size are not killed; they are *answered*.

He wrote one stroke across the tunnel mouth.

Water laid the seam, finding the stone's own grain so the wall would be true. Ice rose out of it a foot thick, then two, gem-bright, the whole height and breadth of the passage. Wind keyed it into the rock like a wedge driven home. And lightning went across the face of it — not thrown, *inscribed*, a white line of script on a black-iron door, which in every language beasts have ever read says the same thing: *this was made by something that was not afraid of you.*

It cost him a hundred points of spirit, spent in a breath — a month of deep water poured out through one seam — and one stroke's worth of Sword Intent, and the domain refolded itself the moment the work was done, tidy as a closed ledger. The gold light arrived at the wall at full charge.

The boom knocked the gems off the mound. The four frozen kids shuddered in their amber. The ice held.

Through its gem-bright face, close now, horribly clear: two golden eyes and one demonic red, lighting the wall from the other side like a lantern held up to a window. The red eye did not blink. Neither did the wall.

---

On the screen in the metal room, Elder Cai was standing. Nobody had seen her stand up.

"Four in one stroke," she said. "Write it down."

Zhuo Shi did not answer at first. He was watching the domain fold away — watching eight trials of a folded domain, of a boy carrying a closed fist through a showcase of a school, and spending it, in the end, on a *door*. "Second seal," he said, to his own question from the night the grass turned gold. "That's your answer. It was never the ring. The boy's been paying for the door the whole exam."

"And the little one refused a treasure a province would go to war over," Cai said. Her page had a new line on it, and under the new line, room. She looked at the five small figures running north under the stars, one of them trailing the flat cold of a spent stroke like a scent, and at the wall of ice with the unblinking red behind it, and she was done watching. The ninth trial had asked its question and five children had answered it in a language the academy had not heard in a generation.

"End it," she said.

## Part 5: North, Under Stars

They ran the valley under more stars than the sky usually admits to, and the freeze wore off the four of them in pieces — Xie Xie's hands first, then Gu Yue's silver, then their legs, until they were only running, and nobody said the name of what was behind them, and everybody checked anyway: the tunnel mouth, far back, a white seam in the hillside.

Gem-bright. Holding.

The red light in it had not blinked once.

Lin Hao ran last, at the tail of the five, where the cold was. Xiaoyan ran light. The hammer was on her back, and nothing was on her hands — not the ring that would have beaten ten-thousand-year rings, not the bone a province would go to war for. Those had stayed where they belonged, on the brow of a sleeping child in a broken house, and she found, testing the weight of herself as she ran, that she had never once been lighter.

Behind them the ice held. In a metal room under the academy, two old monsters were already moving. Somewhere under the stars, a mother was standing at a sealed door, reading a line of white script.

The night had three keepers now, and none of them were done.

## Part 1: The Answer

The door answered first.

The red eye had not blinked, and it did not roar. The maw simply opened at the end of the tunnel, and the dark turned orange — a torrent of flame down the passage, wide as the walls, hungry as a season. It crossed the space where the class had been frozen an hour ago and struck the wall of ice full on.

The ice didn't melt. It *rang.*

The lightning script flared white down its face, drinking the heat into itself, and the whole seam shed steam and light and held — one stroke's worth of Sword Intent standing off a legend's first breath. The wall groaned, wept, lost an inch, and held.

"Move!" Wulin had the four of them by voice and hand both, north along the gems, and the tunnel's last bend swallowed the light of the burning door behind them—

—and the world went white at the edges.

Not fire. Cleaner than fire. The valley's stars smeared like wet ink, the forest's dark folding at the corners the way a page lifts, and the last thing the five of them saw was each other, running, lit from everywhere at once.

Somewhere under the academy, an old woman took her hand off a switch.

## Part 2: The Room, and the Screen

Light through darkness. The hiss of seals. Five metal capsules slid out of the wall in a row, and five children sat up in them at the same time, breathing hard, in the same metal room where the exam had begun.

The big screen was live.

The cave. The tunnel. The wall of ice, streaming now, half-melted from a fire that had kept its promise even if the door had kept its — and beneath the wall, crouched in the gems, the adult. The great golden head bent low over the cub, and golden light rose around them both like water finding its level. On the screen, plainly, gently: the wounds closing. The smashed crown-scales knitting. The small body stirring, and the third eyelid — the whole exam had turned on that eyelid — flickering open, ordinary, unremarkable, a child waking up cranky in a treasure pile.

The mother pulled the cub into her chest and wrapped herself around it, and the light settled over them both like a blanket drawn up by hand.

Nobody in the metal room said anything for a while. The weight the five had been carrying out of that valley — the frozen four, the door, the bill of it — set itself down somewhere and did not come back.

"No regrets," Wulin said at last, grinning, wet-eyed, not fighting any of it. "I want that said. All of it. I'd do every part again."

"A man doesn't second-guess," Xie Xie said, which from him was a whole speech.

"I made my choice before the hammer was down." Xiaoyan was looking at the screen. "And she's happy. Look at her. That was the whole prize."

"It was the easiest choice I've ever made," Gu Yue said. "I never wanted it. I want what's mine, and that wasn't mine." 

They looked at the fifth.

Lin Hao looked back at them, at the four of them pooled out of their capsules, at the mother on the screen, and shrugged with one shoulder, the way he did at the forge when the quench came out right and there was nothing left to add. "I closed a door," he said. "I'd close it again."

Wulin put his right hand out, palm down. Gu Yue's came down on top of it. Xie Xie's on hers, Xiaoyan's on his — and Lin Hao put his hand on top of all of them, last, the closing stroke.

Five hands. It was the shape of the whole three years, and everybody knew it, and nobody had to say so.

## Part 3: The Clapping

Steady applause, from the dark of the room's far end. Shen Yi stepped into the light, and behind her, unhurried, came Elder Cai and the old man from the screen room, and Shen Yi's eyes were bright in a way proctors' eyes are not supposed to be.

"I have overseen this exam for many years," she said. "I still remember taking it. And I will remember watching you take it. You drew the hardest level of the ninth trial we possess. It tested your patience, your ability to survive — and, most importantly, your character. Which brings me to an apology: I lied to you. The fusion I promised in that world was never possible. Your character was the true test from the first step."

The five tests, laid out plain: the patience to find the valley — worth nothing in points, worth everything in time. The eyes to know a Three-eyed Golden Lion and a Duskgold Dreadclaw Bear for what they were. The courage to enter the cave — *that* one the gate itself; fail it and the whole trial scored zero. The cub: lose, and take nothing. And then the last test, the one whole teams have drowned in — the spoils.

"I have watched teams fall apart at that decision," Shen Yi said. "Turning their backs on their companions over a bone. I have watched children become wicked in that cave in under a minute." She paused. "The Auspicious Emperor has appeared once in twenty thousand years. Two of them, in one forest, for one class? They were never real. They were the best imitations this academy could build. Had you killed the cub and divided it calmly, you would have scored six points and I would have passed you and forgotten you by dinner. You chose not to kill. You'll understand if we didn't forget that."

"They were just data," Xie Xie said slowly, working it out loud, looking at the screen where the mother lay curled around her child. "The whole forest. The bear. Her." A pause. "It doesn't feel like just data."

"It isn't, quite," said Elder Cai. "The world is built, but what happens in it happens. Ask your fifth."

Every head turned.

"The stroke you put on that door," Cai said to Lin Hao, and her voice was all business again, an examiner reading off a page that had gotten longer all exam. "Four elements in a single attack, fused spiritual power behind it, Sword Intent holding the seam — I could name the techniques in it, and one day I will make a student of you and do exactly that. It cost you. One hundred points of true cultivation, spent in one breath, on a wall against a thing that was never real. The power does not come back because the beast wasn't real. It was spent true, so it stays spent." She let that sit. "I have watched Soul Emperors spend less on less. Do you understand what I'm telling you?"

"That the door didn't know it was a door," Lin Hao said.

Somewhere behind her, Zhuo Shi made a sound that in a less dignified man would have been a laugh.

"I'm telling you," Cai said, "that when the world showed you a false thing, you answered with a true one. That is the entire academy in a sentence, and we will be arguing for a week about whether you passed the trial or the trial passed you. Six points was the price for calm butchery. You'll get the ten." Her page turned. "The gems, by the way, before anyone asks again —"

"The gems were the floor," Lin Hao said. "The floor belonged to the house."

This time Zhuo Shi did laugh.

## Part 4: The Ledger Read Aloud

"The ninth trial is what we call the overruling trial," Shen Yi said. "Fail it, and you are rejected whatever your points — eighty, ninety, it avails you nothing. We do not put monsters in armor. But you should hear the rest of the law while you stand here: Shrek has never advocated the slaughter of soul beasts. The Great Star Dou Forest has declined with every generation of our strength, and greed did most of the declining. If you become students of this academy, you will not hunt in the Great Star Dou Forest. Not once. Not ever. That is the price of the armor we will teach you to build."

Wulin looked at the screen — the mother, the cub, the light like a drawn blanket — and something in him settled into place with an audible click, or the click was Xie Xie's question finally finding its first answer: *if we are the ones who come in.* They had just spent nine trials being the ones who came in, and the academy had built the world entire to watch how they came.

"The scores," Shen Yi said, and the room stilled. "Trial nine, full value. Tang Wulin: seventy points. Xu Xiaoyan: sixty. Gu Yue: fifty-eight."

Fifty-eight.

Gu Yue did not move. Xie Xie's head snapped toward the number as if it had been thrown at her.

"And Lin Hao: seventy." Shen Yi's eyes moved to him, and there was the faintest weight on the name, an old woman setting a full cup down carefully. "Xie Xie: sixty-one."

"The deduction stands," Xie Xie said, not a question.

"The deduction stands," Shen Yi agreed, gently enough. "Sixty-one is a fine score. The minimum to pass this exam is sixty. Three of you have already passed it outright. Gu Yue is two points short — and there is exactly one trial left."

"I don't want luck," Gu Yue said, to the room, evenly, her chin level. "I want the two points earned. Which trial?"

## Part 5: The Roof

"Follow me," was all Shen Yi said.

She led them down the hall and up a flight of stairs none of them had known was there, and out onto the roof, where the night was the real night, stars admitting to nothing.

Three people stood waiting for them.

In the center, an elderly grey-haired man with stillness in him like deep water — a stillness two of the five had met before, in a cave, in a wall. On his left, Elder Cai, who had followed them up after all, or had never not been there. On his right, the elder who had administered the first trial, back at the very beginning, in another life.

The class of five stopped in a row, and the expressions on four and a half of their faces turned carefully sour.

*Her,* said every face, in perfect unison, without a sound. *What does she have to do with the last trial?*

Elder Cai looked back at them with the eyes of a woman about to enjoy her job.

## Part 1: The Tenth

Shen Yi walked to the three elders and bowed, and stood aside.

"The tenth trial," she said, "is also known as the Three Hall Review. These three elders will evaluate your performance across the trials and give each of you a comprehensive score, added to your total."

Three Hall Review. The words went down the row of five like cold water down a collar — because the middlemost of the three, grey-haired and still as a closed door, was bad enough; but on his left stood Elder Cai, the Silver Moon Douluo, the examiner who had failed them twice and enjoyed it once.

Wulin glanced at Gu Yue. Her brows were drawn. But her eyes, as always, held that stubborn light.

*She's only short two points,* he thought. *This trial—*

"Tang Wulin," said the grey-haired elder, voice deep as a well. "Step up."

## Part 2: The Reads

Wulin bowed and stood at attention, and the old man studied him the way Lin Hao had seen men study metal — not unkindly, entirely without mercy.

"Full marks for seven trials, zero for two," the elder said. "Brave. Wise. A capable leader — we have been watching you the entire time. Your performance has been remarkable. Simply outstanding." A pause. "However, we will hold your score until later. We want you to take a makeup trial."

A makeup. Wulin thanked him, confusion and all, and stepped back. Seventy points; he was safe whatever happened.

"Xie Xie."

Xie Xie stepped up like a man approaching his own verdict.

"Your talent is slightly higher than average. Your situational awareness is poor." Xie Xie's face began its preparations for doom. "However, you have the courage to charge head-first in the face of danger. On the whole, satisfactory. Six points."

Sixty-seven. Xie Xie thanked the elder with the dignity of a man whose scaffold has just turned into a floor, and came back trying not to look relieved. He had feared a negative number most of all; some of his trials had been, in his own private accounting, embarrassing.

"Xu Xiaoyan."

She went up small and came back tall. "Your talent is average," the elder said, "but you have absolute control over the astrological attributes of your variant martial soul. You work well with your team, you have a clever mind, and you are never discouraged by your own weaknesses. Your potential is quite impressive. Seven points."

Sixty-seven, and a shy smile, and for a moment the roof was almost warm.

"Lin Hao."

The fifth examinee walked to the mark and bowed — correctly, the way you bow to a customer who has already paid.

The grey-haired elder looked at him for a long moment. Beside the elder, Elder Cai's page — a real page, paper, worn soft at one corner — turned.

"Seventy points," the elder said. "Full marks for seven trials, zero for two, and the two zeros are their own story. We have watched you herd your class through fire, farm the edges of every fight you were too strong to be seen winning, and close a door on a legend with one stroke — Sword Intent holding the seam, four elements in a single line, and not one ring lit above what the work needed. There are teachers in this academy who could not have kept that discipline. There are none who could have kept it at thirteen." The page at Cai's side turned again, unhurried. "Like your captain, your score is held. You will both take the makeup trial. What we want to see," and here the old man's voice went dry as a forge, "is what you do when the work is your own."

*Both.* Wulin and Lin Hao, seventy and seventy, the tie held closed like a coin in a fist.

"Gu Yue."

Gu Yue went up and bowed, chin level, and the grey-haired elder said nothing at all. He looked to his left.

Elder Cai did not stand. She didn't need to.

"Gu Yue," she said, "you're arrogant and insolent. You are gifted — I'll grant the gift, it's cheap to grant. But you lack all situational awareness, and your actions have damaged your own team. You are impulsive. You are unreasonable. I do not think you are suitable for Shrek Academy." A beat, exactly long enough. "One point. Your total is fifty-nine."

## Part 3: The Number

Fifty-nine.

The number sat on the roof like a stone on a scale. Gu Yue raised her head and glared at Elder Cai, biting her lip, trembling — and standing. Proud. Not asking.

"Tang Wulin, Xie Xie, Xu Xiaoyan," the grey-haired elder said. "You are accepted into the academy. Tang Wulin, you will take the fifth trial again in a moment. Gu Yue — you have fifty-nine points. You can go now."

The stone dropped the rest of the way.

Everyone had always said it: if only one of them made it into Shrek Academy, it would be Gu Yue. Every teacher, every classmate, every odds-maker in their year — Gu Yue, the six elements, the once-a-generation mind. And she was the one standing at fifty-nine with her chin up and the door closing.

An arm went around her shoulders. Wulin pulled her in, trembling as she was trembling, and looked straight at the three elders, and his voice came out in a way none of them — not the class, not the teachers, not once in three years — had ever heard it.

"I don't accept this."

Zhuo Shi — though the class did not yet know his name — sat back inside his own stillness, genuinely taken aback. He would not have been surprised to hear it from Gu Yue. From the captain, the steady one, the boy with seventy points and a safe bed at the finest academy on the continent — from *him*, the words had a different weight.

"Why do you not accept it?"

"Respected elders." Wulin's voice shook, and held. "May I ask if Shrek Academy is fair?"

A cold smile moved on Elder Cai's lips. "Nothing is fair in this world. If you want fair, you need strength. Justice is fought for — it is not freely and willingly given. Of course, that is on the condition that you are powerful enough to make everyone sit down and hear it."

Wulin stood still. Then he nodded to her, and bowed — a small, precise bow, the bow you give a teacher of the hard kind.

"Thank you for the advice. I've learned from it. Then I have nothing more to say." He straightened. "Elders — I renounce my Shrek Academy admittance. One day, I will come back. One day, when I'm strong enough, I'll come back and enforce the justice myself."

He turned to Xie Xie and Xu Xiaoyan, stern as a captain on a deck. "You two don't follow me. This is Gu Yue's business and mine. Stay, and cultivate properly."

Xie Xie looked at him. Then he stuck his hands in his pockets and strolled over, unhurried, grinning like a knife.

"Since my talent's only average, the academy clearly won't miss me." He put a hand on his captain's shoulder. "And Captain — you made a nobody with a mouth into part of a shape that beat everything this school could throw at it. You want to know when I decided? You put the class ahead of your own score in every single trial, and I've been keeping count since the first week. I'll follow you for the rest of my life. We'll come back when we're strong enough to *demand* justice."

"I never wanted to be a soul master anyway," Xu Xiaoyan added, arriving at Wulin's other side as if remarking on the weather. "My old man forced me. And the pressure here is far too high. Let's go home."

"You guys—" Wulin's voice failed him entirely.

He turned to Shen Yi instead, and bowed low. "Teacher Shen. I'm sorry. It seems we aren't qualified to be Shrek's students after all. It was my dream — the dream broke. May I ask where Teacher Wu is? We should tell him we're leaving."

Emotions warred openly across Shen Yi's face.

## Part 4: The Fifth's Answer

Four of five stood in a row against the roof's door, and every eye on that roof swung to the fifth.

Lin Hao had not moved. He stood where the review had left him, at the mark, hands loose, the way he stood at the forge between heats — and when he spoke, it was not to his class, and it was not heat at all.

"Elder Cai." He addressed the page itself. "One point. That's the gap. Name the price of the point — I'll pay it."

The roof went very quiet.

"Points aren't coins, blacksmith," Elder Cai said.

"Everything is coins," Lin Hao said. "You priced our character at ten. You priced a calm butchery at six. You priced her at one — that's not a grade, that's an insult with a number on it, and I've been insulted by professionals." He did not raise his voice; the roof's acoustics did the work, and the flat forge-carry reached every elder on it. "So either the number is honest and she's unfit — and every trial we just survived says otherwise — or the number is a test, and the price of the point exists somewhere. I'm asking for the counter. Name it."

For one unguarded moment, the page in Cai's hand was still.

"The makeup trial," the grey-haired elder said at last, and there was something in the deep voice that might, in a different man, have been delight, "is for Tang Wulin and Lin Hao. Not for Gu Yue. There is no counter to name, examinee. The trial is the trial."

"Then I'll take the makeup," Lin Hao said. He looked at Wulin — at his captain, arm still around Gu Yue, dream broken and set down like a full crate. "You go enforce justice your way. I'll stay and make them count honestly in front of everyone — that's mine. Between the two of us, she gets both."

Wulin looked back at him. Three years looked back. Whatever he might have said, he didn't; he nodded, once, the way you accept a tool you know will hold.

## Part 5: Grandteacher

"Good," the grey-haired elder said gloomily, into the silence. "You're all really stubborn. That stubbornness must have been taught to you. Very good. Nicely done. Now leave. Get out, all of you."

The class — mid-departure, half-bowed, one foot each into their different futures — froze.

Shen Yi darted a meaningful look at the five. "This elder," she said, quietly, quickly, "is senior brother Wu's teacher. Which makes him your *grandteacher*. Hurry up and pay your respects."

*Grandteacher.* Teacher Wu's teacher. The stillness at the center of the roof reassembled itself in every head at once: no wonder the old man sounded like a colder version of their teacher's silences.

Wulin tugged Gu Yue's sleeve and bowed. "I pay my respects to Grandteacher." Xie Xie and Xiaoyan followed. Gu Yue, nudged, bowed last of all.

Zhuo Shi's expression lightened a few shades, and not one degree warmer. "Do you all think you're something amazing? Renouncing everything for the sake of your companions, huh? You *fools*. Why did you even come here? To show off your stubbornness? Your pride? You know how to fight, but do you know how to beg? Did Wu Zhangkong teach you this stubbornness? It really is like teacher, like student — a whole bundle of stubborn fools—"

Shen Yi's mouth-corner twitched. *Aren't you the one who taught senior brother? Do your words not apply to yourself, Grandteacher?*

"Grandteacher," Xu Xiaoyan said, in her smallest, most disarming voice, "may I ask you a question?"

"Hm?" Zhuo Shi's eyes shifted to her.

Her eyes welled, reddened, brimmed. "Grandteacher — is this grandma more amazing than you?"

The question hit the old man like a dropped anvil. He side-eyed Elder Cai. "…We're about equal."

The tears spilled over, and Xu Xiaoyan, throat stiff with feeling, fired the second barrel: "It's said that once a teacher, forever a father. We've treated Teacher Wu like a father — and Teacher Wu surely treats you like one — so you're our grandfather. You're a *Title Douluo*, and a battle armor master! How can you watch your grandchildren be bullied? We would have passed with points to spare if not for this grandma. Unless—" the pause of a born closer, "—you're afraid of her?"

"Me? Afraid of *her*?" The words were out before the old man's dignity could catch them.

"You're not afraid of her," Xiaoyan said, sweetly, wetly, "and yet you don't care that your granddaughter is being driven out?"

Zhuo Shi stood dumbstruck — he, the famed stubborn ox of Shrek's inner court, he who cowed seniors with a look, out-flanked by a thirteen-year-old with tears on her cheeks and her class's whole fortune in her slingshot.

"That's right — the girl has a point!" he burst out, wheels visibly leaving the ground. "A granddaughter driven off this roof under my own watch, and I'm to stand here like a lamp? *CAI YUE'ER!* What is this? What are you playing at, bullying my granddaughter where I can see it?!"

## Part 1: The Haggle

"Stop bullshitting," Elder Cai said. "You're an old hermit without a wife. Where did you get a granddaughter?"

"The girl is right, that's where." Zhuo Shi was still riding the wheels XXY's tears had lifted off the ground. "I don't care what you say. Today I want all of these children in Shrek Academy. The final score is decided by the three of us *together*, if you recall. You say Gu Yue deserves one point. I say she's earned at least four — and four puts her in the outer court with room to spare."

"We agreed on this earlier. What are you trying to pull now? No. I refuse."

Wulin, head lowered, was having his own quiet crisis: *the grandteacher changed sides awfully fast.* The old man had gone from *get out, all of you* to *four points* in the time it took a girl to wipe her face.

"Then what will it take for you to accept?" Zhuo Shi demanded.

And Elder Cai looked at him the way winter looks at a late flower. "Have you forgotten *why* we're having Tang Wulin take a makeup trial at all?"

There was a pause — the pause of a man finding a stair in the dark. Then Zhuo Shi swerved to Wulin so fast his grey hair moved. "The makeup trial! Of course! Shrek's rules, boy — a student who scores full marks on *every* trial is owed one request. Anything within the academy's power. You're already perfect on the seven scored trials. One more full score, and you can stand there and spend your request on an extra point for that girl."

"But the fourth trial—" Wulin said. "I walked out of the fourth trial."

"Fine." Cai's voice could have iced a pond. "I'll give you ten for the fourth. Score perfect on the makeup, and the tenth goes to full marks as well. Full marks everywhere. One request."

Wulin didn't understand the shape of it yet, but he understood the hand being held out. Behind his back, where the elders couldn't see, a finger rose and made one slow, level warning motion in Gu Yue's direction. *Calm. Whatever it costs you, calm.*

She saw it. She stayed silent — not because she was told to. Because she was no fool: she wanted in, wanted it more than she had ever wanted a point of anything; and because if she were driven out, these four idiots would follow her, and their futures would follow them off the cliff. So she stood still, and bit down on the one point, and waited.

"What is your second profession?" Zhuo Shi asked. "Are you confident?"

"I'm certain I'll ace this test," Tang Wulin said.

Elder Cai snorted. "Don't be so confident, brat. Do you even know what a full score requires now?"

"Please advise me, Elder Cai."

"It is impossible to score full marks," she said, "without reaching the fifth rank of your second profession."

Zhuo Shi's eyes popped. Shen Yi's popped. The looks they traded were almost comical — *when did the fifth trial start demanding fifth-rank professionals? Most outer court GRADUATES don't carry that. That's an inner court requirement. He's an examinee. He's thirteen.*

Wulin stood very still.

Fifth rank. For a blacksmith, fifth rank meant Spirit Refinement — the great divider, the line between the grandmasters and the master craftsmen, the chickens and the phoenixes, the earth and the heavens. Thousand-refined metals went into one-word battle armor; but two-word armor and beyond — *real* armor, the kind that rewrote a soul master's ceiling — drank only spirit-refined metal. A thousand refinements opened everything a metal had. Spirit refinement *changed what it was*: soul power pressed into the metal until the metal carried spirit, until at the moment of completion the smith did not decorate the metal but woke it. Mu Chen had said it exactly once, in the shop, with the dust settling: *to spirit refine is to create life.*

He was at the peak of the fourth rank. He'd been there a while — the techniques were his, Mu Chen had seen to that; what he lacked was the raw soul power, and no amount of wanting corrected an arithmetic. Spirit refinement was supposed to demand four rings. Mu Chen had told him his innate divine strength might let him cross on three — *might.*

He looked at Gu Yue. Sparks of worry must have shown; what came back was a gentleness like nothing else the trial had produced. It settled him the way a coal settles a forge.

"I'll do it," he said. "Blacksmith!"

"And the other one," Elder Cai said, without turning her head. "You didn't imagine I'd forgotten you."

The fifth examinee stepped forward, unhurried, the way a man steps up to a counter he already knows the price at.

"Same terms," Cai said. "Full marks everywhere, one request. Yours is also held on the makeup. And before you enjoy the symmetry, blacksmith — a certification is paper. You hold a fifth-rank stamp issued by people who have never watched you work under a debt of a hundred spent points and a night with no sleep in it. Tonight, the paper gets tested. Both of you, same bar."

"Finally," Lin Hao said. "Someone here grades properly."

Zhuo Shi made the not-quite-laugh sound again.

## Part 2: The Design, Whispered

"Follow me," said the grey-haired elder.

The three of them — Zhuo Shi, Elder Cai, and Elder Li, the old man from the first trial — led the class down and into a long room at the academy's root, where staff were already rolling out a forging table and wheeling up a shelf of rare metals that made Xie Xie's eyebrows attempt to leave his face. The companions gathered behind the line painted on the floor. Two stations had been set out. Whatever else the night was, it was not improvised.

While Wulin stood at the table with his eyes shut — and stood, and stood, a full quarter of an hour, and no one hurried him — the two old monsters put their heads together at the room's edge.

"What is the matter with you?" Zhuo Shi whispered. "Why are you acting crazy? Are you calm yet?"

"Aren't you the one who taught Zhangkong to be stubborn?" Cai whispered back. "So what does that make you?"

"Fifth *rank*," Zhuo Shi pressed. "The rule was a third-rank second profession for full marks. A thirteen-year-old fifth-rank professional — when have you ever heard of such a person? Name one."

"You used a flimsy pretense yourself to set this whole stage," Cai said, and there was a chill in it that was almost warmth. "Why not one step further? Afterward you need only produce some explanations — and these children are far more mature than their age. They need to be *challenged*, Zhou. The more pressure they carry young, the stronger they grow. That Tang Wulin is the most resilient of the lot. He showed a golden soul ring in the fourth trial. He fought with a bear's strength in the ninth. What, exactly, can't he accomplish — if nobody forces him to prove it?"

She turned her page, softly, in the room where sound was record.

"And the other one," she added, so low it was almost to herself, "has the Blacksmith Association's inquiry on my desk, three pages long, because a fifth-rank stamp at his age is either the find of the generation or a clerical error, and Mu Chen's letter says *find* and I intend to know which by morning. Pressure, Zhou. It is the only teacher that never lies."

## Part 3: The Table

Wulin opened his eyes. There was a purple light in their depths that hadn't been there at the start of the quarter hour — the color of a decision that has finished deciding.

He went to the shelf and came back with the ingot his hands already knew: heavy silver. The first metal he had ever thousand-refined, in a shop in Eastsea with his teacher's arms aching in memory beside him. Some choices are arguments, and some are homecomings. He set it on the table, pressed the stud, and let the furnace take it — the bloom of heat rolling up the room like a remembered season.

At the second station, Lin Hao had already unrolled his tool-wrap. From it, wrapped in oilcloth, he took a bar of his own — not from the academy's shelf. Grey-silver, dense as an argument, a private weight.

"The Yaluo lot," he said, to nobody and everybody, answering the looks. "Bought at auction by the kilo, read through the crate." He set it in his calipers and turned it once, reading the grain the way other people read a face. "It's been waiting for a forge. It found one."

The two of them stood at their tables in the same firelight, and the room slowly understood it was looking at one profession at two altitudes. The captain was attempting the leap — fourth rank's peak to fifth rank's country, on three rings, under a night's debt, for a girl's one point. The fifth was doing something almost harder to watch: proving a rank he already held, with nothing to gain that he wanted, in front of three people qualified to see every flaw a master's hand hides. The leap and the testimony. The same hammers would tell both truths.

Lin Hao checked his own pulse the way he'd been taught — not the heart's beat; the deeper one. The joining, when he'd measured it that morning in the still dark, had held its seconds, patient as an apprenticeship. The body at a hundred points down was a body that had learned to work tired. Every smith's boy learns that early or learns it never: the forge does not care what your night was.

He looked across at his captain, and gave him the only gift the profession has.

"Rows breathe in threes," Lin Hao said. "Be somewhere it was."

Wulin's hammers came out of his soul in a flash — the heavy silver pair, worn to the shapes of his own grip. He shut his eyes again and walked the vein-patterns with his fingertips until his blood forgot where it ended. Lin Hao's hammer was already moving.

The first strikes rang, and the second strikes answered, and somewhere in the swing of it the two rhythms found each other and locked, the way they had in a yard in Eastsea once — the metronome and the storm around it, hammer and hammer, anvil and answer.

The elders watched two boys breathe life into metal, and did not breathe much themselves.

And at the door, unnoticed by everyone who mattered noticing, a man the color of winter had arrived and stood without one word — Wu Zhangkong, who had been sent for the moment the roof went loud, watching his students hammer, his face as still as the day he'd told them the price of things. His eyes went from the leap to the testimony, from his captain to his fifth, and stayed there, at the second table, where a boy was reading grain by firelight with a hundred-point debt on his shoulders and no ring lit at all.

The metal glowed. The night was long. Nobody left.

## Part 1: The Tempest

Whatever else he was tonight, he was not a soul master. The boy at the first table had put the captain away somewhere with the trial armor and the seventy points, and what stood there in his place was a blacksmith of the fourth rank, three years consolidated, opening his work the way the profession had opened its works since before the Federation had a name: three light taps, crisp as a clock starting.

Then the storm.

Power gathered at his feet and climbed his spine like something hoisted; his whole body twisted into the swing, and both hammers came down together with a boom that rattled the room's glass and everyone's teeth in it. Zhuo Shi's eyes flew wide — his body had *resonated* with the strike, veteran of a hundred wars resonating with a thirteen-year-old's hammer, and he'd had to shed the feeling on purpose. The rebound came up through Wulin's arms and he rode it into the next strike, harder, and the next, and the booms and the smaller fragmented rumbles underneath them began to fuse into one fantastical rhythm — wild, deafening, and delicate as a waltz if you had the ears to hear the floor of it.

Through all of it, at the second station, Lin Hao worked — no booms, no rattled glass; the Yaluo bar ticking under taps placed like a man writing in a ledger while a thunderstorm read over his shoulder. The room's eyes went where the noise was. The room's best eyes did not.

"Stacked hammers," Elder Cai said quietly. "The rare effect. And he can *fully control* it. That's third rank at minimum — Zhou, the Blacksmith Association has been hiding a thirteen-year-old like this."

"Judging by how he carries himself, he had a good teacher." Zhuo Shi was leaning forward now, grey hair catching the furnace light. "I heard the Association's greatest genius is a girl named Mu Xi — fourth rank before twenty. I should pay the Association a visit. Find this kid a master of his own. Maybe he can reach even her level."

"At his table," Elder Cai said, without looking away from the second station, "sits the reason the Association's three pages keep asking questions, Zhou. The master you want to visit is already in the room's address book. The letter on my desk says the boy in Eastsea found two."

"Two," Zhuo Shi repeated. "The Association's greatest genius — fourth rank before twenty. And you're telling me—"

"I'm telling you her record is already dead, Zhou. It died in an auction yard in Eastsea, and it dies again at that table tonight — a full rank beyond hers, seven years younger. Watch both tables. However this night ends, some of our records end with it."

Hundred-refined in ten strikes. The metal came down under the tempest, shrinking, its vein lines standing out like weather. The booms climbed to rings, the rings to one long note — and on the forty-eighth strike the room went white with a pillar of silver light, and everyone in it heard, unmistakably, the heavy silver *cheer* — light flying up like a small roaring dragon.

"He thousand refined it with *spirit*," Elder Li said, breaking his long silence, shocked out of the elder's gravity. "First-grade. A fourth-rank need only second-grade — this is the *peak* of fourth." He shook his head slowly, solemnly. "I say this as a man who has watched the profession for sixty years: this child is the greatest blacksmithing genius in the history of the world. Thirteen. It is unheard of. He is a monster that surpasses monsters."

Behind the painted line, Xie Xie whispered to Xiaoyan: "We *know* him. How do we know him?"

"And the other one?" Zhuo Shi asked the room — dazed, because the verdict was still ringing and the room held one table too many.

"Ask the page," Elder Cai said, and did not turn it. Her eyes had stopped pretending to watch the first table at all.

## Part 2: The Bridge

Purple light stood in Wulin's eyes, and the forging changed species.

He stepped to the metal's side and began, of all things, to *circle* it — tapping it lightly as he went, each knock carrying a spark of white, soul power riding the hammers down into the bar like a slow transfusion. And then the room saw what the fourth rank could not do, and did:

The Bluesilver Grass came out of him and wrapped the scorching metal, strand over strand, and began, visibly, to die. The grass shriveled. The grass burned. He never once looked away, and his face never once wavered, and he kept circling, tapping, patient as a man walking a child into cold water.

"You two have made a mess," Elder Li said — and there was no longer any admiration in his voice. There was fear. "Spirit gets you first-grade thousand refined. That is not spirit refinement. Spirit refinement is *life*, and life goes in through only one door — the martial soul, as a bridge, carrying the smith's own life force into the metal. Soul power, life, metal, harmonized. The rule is four rings before you even *attempt* it, and grown masters fail it and bleed for the failing. He has three. If he fails now, the backlash may be a thing he never recovers from — and then, Zhou, then you and she will learn what FENG WUYU'S wrath looks like, and I will hold both your coats."

Zhuo Shi had gone grey around the mouth. "Can we stop him?"

"He connected his life force to the metal the moment the grass touched it." Elder Li's voice was final as a closing door. "Interrupt him now and the shock could take him — could *kill* him. There is nothing left that anyone in this room can do. Pray."

"This is your fault," Zhuo Shi hissed.

"Why didn't *you* stop me?" But for once Elder Cai's retort came out at half volume, because she was watching a boy burn his own soul's grass against a bar of silver, and even her page had stopped turning.

At the door, the man the color of winter did not move at all.

## Part 3: The Testimony

And in the roar of all of it, almost nobody had marked that the second hammer had never stopped — that through the whole roar, Lin Hao had kept working.

Lin Hao worked the way deep water moves. No booms; the Yaluo bar glowed under taps that did not ring so much as *arrive* — each one placed the way his strokes had been placed on a certain cave wall, the intent arriving before the hammer did. Sword consciousness rode his hands tonight, not as a weapon but as a grammar: *the intent that knows the cut before the cut* translated whole into the one art that had owned him since a back room in Glorybound — he was not striking the metal, he was *reading it aloud*, and the metal, hearing itself said correctly for the first time, began to listen.

The elders' eyes came to him one by one, the way heads turn at a second conversation in a quiet room. Where the captain bridged life in with blood and fire and dying grass, the fifth was doing something the profession had no rank-shape for: he fanned the spark the thousand refinements had left — fanned it with *order*. Lightning first, a whisper of it, keying the grain. Wind, finding the seams. Water, laying the temper true. Ice, last, closing what the others opened. The four, in the iron that was their house, one after another, each element a sentence in a language the bar had been born knowing and never once heard spoken.

The frost on his own handle he did not do anything about. It built along the iron the way it built along every rail he sat near these days, a hand-span of winter in a forging hall where the heat stood against the face like a wall — his own body keeping its own temperature under the smith's leather, the deep water under the skin reading the hall's heat the way it read the mountain's cold: as a suggestion, not a fact. He had stopped trying to name the whole package of himself years before it was worth naming. There was the body the anvil had forged for seven years — grain-reading shoulders, a smith's wrists, the calluses. There was the hawk's share in it, storm-light reflexes and the eyes that found the seam before the eyes arrived. There was the jiao's share now, deep water and regeneration and the cold treated as furniture. Under all of it, moving through all of it, the adaptation — not a line in the ledger but the thing the ledger was written on. A body like the martial soul: an iron sword made of five things and called by none of them. A smith across the room who had stripped down to his vest was watching him work with growing disbelief; the boy at the second table had not even opened his collar.

At the first table Wulin was bridged in to the bar with blood and fire and the grass, blind to everything in the room; but when the roar dropped to its breathing for a second his eyes came over, found the frost on his brother's handle, and stayed there the half-count it takes to recognize the same weather you had grown up under, wearing its new clothes. A nod — small, the kind you give weather through a window — and back to the work. *Your winter indoors,* the nod said, the way it had said it in the inn and the frost-patch in the forest and a dozen places between. Lin Hao tapped the bar twice more and the cold went deeper, along the grain, exactly where it belonged.

Elder Li crossed the floor mid-prayer and stood at the second table, and after a long time the old man said, softly, to no one:

"He isn't *giving* it life. He's teaching it that it was alive all along."

The grass at the first table burned down to ash-wrapped silver, and Wulin, swaying, exhaustion in every line of him, kept tapping, kept circling, his heart the hammer, his soul the guide, his mind going down into the metal one ten-thousandth at a time — *their minds becoming one in ten thousand refinements of life.* That was Spirit Refinement. The boy was paying its whole price in a single night, on three rings, for one point.

The bar at the second table cooled from white to gold to a grey that held the light like a held breath. It did not cheer. It did something quieter and, in Elder Li's sixty years, rarer: when Lin Hao laid two fingers on it at the last, the metal turned toward the touch — slightly, certainly — as a sleeping thing turns toward a familiar hand.

The old man looked at the bar. Then at Lin Hao. Then at the bar again, as if one of them owed him an explanation.

"Fifth," he said.

One word. The same word, the room's older hands would later swear, that the forge-yard itself had somehow pronounced.

Elder Cai let out a breath she had been holding since the grass caught fire, and reached over and closed her page — not finished; *banked* — and looked at Zhuo Shi with an expression that said, clear as daylight: *the letter said find. The letter was right.*

For a moment nobody in authority spoke, and the room's arithmetic said it for them — the stack the academy had been assembling all exam without once pronouncing aloud.

Rank forty-five at thirteen: the youngest the academy's ten-thousand-year records held, and not by a little. Spiritual power that registered — *registered*, the way a river registers a gauge — at Soul Emperor tier: a height masters spend lifetimes failing to reach, and on him a baseline, not a summit. Elder Li, who had lived long enough to have watched the age of legends, said the name quietly, once, the way a man handles an old blade: "Not since Huo Yuhao has spiritual power like that worn a body this young." And even that reading was only where the instruments ended — not where the boy ended. Three years, nine trials, a legend's charge in a cave: nothing had ever forced him past what he was willing to show. He had never used full power. He had never needed to. The ceiling was not a number. It was a question nobody had earned the answer to.

A fourth soul ring the color of deep night — ten-thousand-year stock, an age top powerhouses count themselves lucky to wear once — set on a boy with three rings around it. A sword style with strokes in it no teacher ever wrote: self-made, at thirteen, the intent that knows the cut before the cut. A fifth-rank blacksmith, proven to the profession's own elder in one word. And the whole absurd stack carried on ONE martial soul — one — a variant hawk the Awakening halls had once filed under ordinary and would be filing corrections about for a generation.

"We spent this exam grading our scales," Zhuo Shi said at last, quietly. "And one of our examinees was never on any of them."

At the door, the man the color of winter watched the world finish catching up to his student, and his face did not move at all — which, from Wu Zhangkong, was a standing ovation.

Wulin's forty-ninth tap fell.

The whole room — elders, classmates, the winter man at the door, the fifth with his cooled and listening bar — leaned toward the silver, waiting for the metal to speak.

## Part 1: The Bridge of Blood

The room understood the moment his hand closed on the ingot, and the room was wrong about what it understood.

Both hammers went into his left hand. His right — bare, unarmored, a boy's hand — took hold of the heavy silver directly, and the metal answered the way a fire answers flesh: white smoke rolled, the sizzles filled the room like frying rain, and every smith's nightmare played out in front of three elders who could do nothing at all.

Except the hand did not melt.

Gold scaled up the arm like a verdict — he had called the grass home and the golden ring forward in the same breath — and the scales walked across his shoulder, his torso, until the boy stood in a shell of himself, clothes burst away, hammering with his left while his right held on to a temperature that should have taken the hand off and kept hammering.

And what poured across that grip, into the silver, was not soul power anymore. Soul power had run its well dry ten minutes in. What fed the metal now came up red.

"Blood essence," Elder Li said, and for once the profession's encyclopedist sounded old. "He's bridging with blood essence. Dismayed doesn't cover it, Zhou. If that bridge breaks now—"

"Let him."

The voice came from the second table — the fifth examinee, still working, not looking up, his own taps never faltering. Lin Hao said it the way he said everything that mattered, quietly and at forge-pitch, which in that room carried like a bell.

"Blood feeds iron truer than soul does. Soul persuades the metal. Blood *obliges* it. He's not failing the refinement, Elders — he's found the older door. Let him through."

Zhuo Shi looked at Cai. Cai looked at the page in her hand, and then at the boy hanging onto a miracle by one scaled hand, and did not stop it either.

## Part 2: The Hammers Drink

What no ledger in the room could hold was what happened next, though one boy in it could have told them the shape of it in advance, because it was his own grammar happening in front of him at another man's table.

The silver began to go *into* the hammers.

Every strike, a portion of the melting metal stayed behind on the hammer-faces — soaked in, gold trailing up the handles like dawn climbing a well. The cloud-patterns on the twin hammers writhed, sharpened, and became something with teeth: a dragon, baring them, plain as a signature. The hammers had been blood-sacrificed years ago; fed their master's blood essence now, at the moment of a spirit refinement, they did what blood-fed iron does — the only thing it knows.

They grew. Toward him.

Lin Hao watched his own law perform at another man's table, and packed nothing on his face about it, and thought: *the iron is the house, and blood is the door, and he has just walked in by the oldest entrance there is. Mu Chen taught him the syllabus. The blood taught him the mother tongue.* The Yaluo bar slept in its wrap, cooled, listening, proven. His night's work was done; he stood now the way smiths have always stood at another smith's miracle — hat in hand, in whatever name the profession keeps its awe.

The silver drank faster than soul power had ever fed it. That was the arithmetic nobody wanted to say aloud: blood runs out too, and a boy has less of it than a master. Wulin's circling slowed. His strikes stayed true. The ounce of silver left on the table glowed like a caught breath.

He trembled. He coughed — red, onto the metal, and did not stop. The hammer rose one more time, higher than his head, and came down like weather.

Thunder. A pillar of gold one and a half meters tall — and through the light, unmistakable, *a dragon's roar*, as if something in the metal had taken the shape the hammers wore and decided to announce it. The light didn't shine; it *declared* — an aura of life, standing in the room like a new person.

It was born.

The heavy silver was spirit refined. And the hammers, dull gold now, the dragon plain on their faces, did the last thing hammers have ever done for a smith who made them family: they melted into his hands — not into any storage, into *him* — the way the old books said and almost nobody present had ever seen. Spirit-refined metal goes home to the one who fed it, drip by drip, blood by blood. It becomes the body.

*That*, the room realized in the same cold wave, *is how battle armor masters wear their armor like skin.*

## Part 3: Straight as a Steel Rod

He fell straight as a steel rod.

Xie Xie caught him — of course Xie Xie caught him; three years of positioning finally paid its dividend — and the captain lay in his arms snow-white, breath thin, soul and blood both spent to the last readable drop, asleep the way the drowned sleep, and smiling, faintly, at whatever it is smiths see.

"He succeeded," Zhuo Shi said. The words came out with the lid off. "He actually — Zhou Shi's boy spirit-refined at thirteen. Do you understand what is standing in this room? A fifth-rank *master* blacksmith at thirteen. There is one Divine Craftsman on this continent and Shrek's best armor is three words because of it, and *that*—" his hand moved at Wulin, at the gold that had been hammers, "—that is what one looks like at the beginning. Even Shrek scrambles for this. Any academy on Douluo scrambles for this."

He took Wulin out of Xie Xie's arms himself, gently, a grandfather collecting something breakable, and the scarlet came up around him — a red aura, corporeal, jade-bright, heavy as a season, and under it the class felt for the first time what a Title Douluo actually is when he stops being scenery.

The red light poured into Wulin, and Wulin's body — golden lines threading him like makeshift veins, dimmer than the forge had left them — drank it. Not received. *Drank.* Sucked the scarlet in, brighter and brighter, the treatment going somewhere no treatment had been invited.

"Woah," said Zhuo Shi, and did not stop.

"His body isn't receiving the treatment," Lin Hao said quietly, to the room, over the light. "It's auditing it. The line decides what stays. It always has — it's why the joining counts seconds instead of spending them. Elders, you are not healing him. You are *paying tribute*." He said it without fear and without awe, the way a man reads a gauge, because someone in that room had to say the true thing in a plain voice, and the smith who audits dragons was standing right there.

Elder Cai, for once, did not score the answer.

She walked instead to Gu Yue — fists balled, breath held, tunnel-eyed on the boy in the red light — and stood beside her, almost gently. "Don't think you're done with tests now that you've passed," she said. "Battle armor masters by twenty, or forget the inner court. That is the next sentence of your life, girl. Write it." And she left, boots even on the stone, and the word *passed* lay on the floor behind her like a dropped key.

Elder Li looked over the three standing students for a long moment — and his gaze stopped on Xu Xiaoyan for a hairbreadth of a second, and something in the old man smiled without moving his mouth — and he went out with his arms folded behind him, satisfied with the world for once.

## Part 4: What the Teacher Said

The scarlet light poured. The golden lines drank. The night went long, and nobody left, and somewhere in it Xie Xie sat down on the floor where the miracle had happened and stared at the place the ounce of silver had been until Xiaoyan sat down next to him, and Gu Yue stood where Cai had left her, holding the dropped key.

Then the man the color of winter came off the doorframe at last.

Wu Zhangkong crossed to the second table first — his path had been decided for three chapters of silence — and looked down at the rolled tool-wrap, the packed bar, the boy who audits dragons. Everyone expected frost. What came was quieter and heavier than frost.

"You gave him the law when it mattered," his teacher said. "'Rows breathe in threes.' He was somewhere it was, because you told him where it was." A pause the length of a winter. "Talent is a debt, Lin Hao. Tonight, both of you paid interest." And then — the gesture nobody in Class Zero ever forgot, though only four people were awake to see it — Wu Zhangkong picked up his student's tool-wrap, and rolled it properly, and set it on the boy's shoulder like a wing being folded.

"Tomorrow the continent starts learning your names," he said. "Tonight you eat, and you sleep. That is also the profession."

At the first table, the red light poured. The dragon drank. The city around them slept under stars that admitted to nothing, and in a metal room at the academy's root, a boy who was now part hammer dreamed of nothing at all, and smiled — and somewhere north of everything, in a forest made of the academy's memory, a mother's heartbeat kept time for a cub that would never know how close it had come to being a ring.

The night kept all of it. Morning would be loud.

## Part 1: What the Dragon Drank

Even the leaving was drunk.

Zhuo Shi drew his scarlet light back out of the boy the way a man draws a hand out of water — and the water objected. The golden pattern over Wulin's skin gave a dragon's roar, thin and unmistakable, and sucked the light back in, refusing the exit. Zhuo Shi cut the connection clean and stood there a moment, a Title Douluo who had just been mugged by his own kindness.

Only Shen Yi understood what she was seeing, and it cost her thethe color of her face for the second time that night. *He's devouring Teacher's soul power. Not receiving — devouring. This boy's martial soul restrains Teacher's… and Teacher's is the Scarlet Jade Dragon. A true dragon's bloodline. A supreme soul, restrained by grass.*

A finger-flick of red; a groan; Wulin surfaced into the warm grey of a blood-debt paid, cosy for the first time in a day and a half, soul power brimming, pallor rivaling snow. He sat up. "Grandteacher."

"You five," Zhuo Shi said, and even the correction had stopped surprising anyone, "follow me."

Gu Yue got to Wulin first, steadying him, scolding him softly — *permanent injuries, you might have* — and got the meek smile that was his only defense and always had been. Behind them, Lin Hao repacked a tool-wrap his teacher had rolled, and fell into line, and said nothing at all about the ache in his own deep water, which was the ordinary ache of a night's honest craft and none of anybody's business.

## Part 2: The Kneeling Man

They found the campus holding one more person than it had at midnight.

He knelt on the path ahead with his back straight as a rule, long blue hair over his shoulders, white robe dewed, the blue sword laid across his knees — the man the color of winter, kneeling in the open where anyone could see him do it. Wu Zhangkong had left the forge before his students woke, and had chosen the longest path across the academy, and had knelt where his teacher would pass, and had waited.

"Teacher Wu!" Wulin's yelp broke the morning.

WZK raised his head. His eyes went past his students — past all five, one by one, a half-second each, an inventory with love hidden in its method — and landed on the mountain walking behind them. And the ice thawed so visibly that Xie Xie would tell people about it for years: the cold face of the coldest teacher on the continent, at war with itself, losing.

He bowed before any of them reached him. Forehead to the stones.

The class came up around him and knelt after — Wulin first, then Xie Xie, then Xiaoyan — and Gu Yue sat beside Wulin instead, back straight, which was its own kind of bow and the only kind she made.

Zhuo Shi stopped. The fierceness went out of his walk; the stiffness stayed. "Stand up."

"Thank you, Teacher."

"I'm not your teacher." Flat as a plank. "I don't have a disciple as troublesome as you."

The five held their breath somewhere behind their teeth.

"These granddisciples, though," Zhuo Shi said. "I'll recognize them."

Wu Zhangkong kowtowed a second time, deeper, and everyone understood without a word being spent: not forgiveness — never asked for, never given — but the door, left open. From this man, that was everything.

"Teacher," WZK said as the old man turned. "I was wrong."

The mountain walked on — faster, if anything — and Wulin took his teacher's arm, and the teacher let him, and that was the second everything of the morning.

## Part 3: The Island

The inner court was grass and quiet and sculptures: the Seven Monsters of the first generation, and before them three founders — Flander, the first president; the Grandmaster Yu Xiaogang; Liu Erlong. The Golden Iron Triangle. Even Xie Xie went quiet at the foot of people whose names his grandmother used to threaten him with, and bowed till his back learned something.

Past the trees, an azure lake lay open to the night, crystal under the moon, mist standing on the water like a congregation. Zhuo Shi's red light wrapped all eight of them, and the world folded — and they stood on a small island in the lake's heart.

"Sea God's Island," Wulin breathed, and meant it as a question, and it wasn't one.

The inner court's inner court. The place the rumors were polite about. Even inner disciples didn't get brought here — and a wooden house stood up the two small hills, warm-lit, simple as a truth.

"Shen Yi. Tomorrow, the registration. Tang Wulin receives full marks; calculate the others as usual." Zhuo Shi settled into the worn chair that was clearly his, and the wood knew him. "From this moment you are working students of the outer court."

"Then before it's official," Wulin said, stepping forward, because some things must be spent aloud or they were never really held: "Elders. My request. I claim it now, in front of everyone: the point. Give it to Gu Yue. That's what I want full marks to buy."

The room went still the way rooms do when a held breath finds its owner.

"Granted," Zhuo Shi said. "Sixty. She stands with you. Working students, all five — late to the exam, Elders Cai's own ruling; six years to make one-word battle armor masters of yourselves, five rings each by twenty, or the inner court never opens. That is the sentence; you already heard the judge." His eyes moved. "And the other full marks. The fifth. Your request?"

Every head turned. The lake ticked softly at the windows.

He had asked first. Hours ago — one roof, one night, the same witnesses — the price of that point had been his opening offer, before any makeup path existed: *name it, I'll pay it.* The examiner had refused the currency. Then Wulin had found a coin the academy would take — a miracle, spent on her entry, the way Wulin did everything: for the shape, all five through one door, a captain's grammar, and everyone in this room knew it, her included. And a man does not bid against a gift his captain has already given. That law was older in Lin Hao than the sword: the hand goes in first for other people; it does not go in twice through the same door, and it does not take a door out of the hands of the one already walking through it.

"Held," Lin Hao said. "Still. I'll know what it's for when I know what it's for." A beat, and then, because the night had earned plain speech: "It's narrowed, if that helps the paperwork. It used to be anything. Now it's something specific, and I don't have the word yet. When I have the word, you'll hear the request."

Zhuo Shi looked at Cai's empty chair, where the answer would have been scored, and then at the boy. "Held," he agreed. "With interest."

Gu Yue looked at Lin Hao then — one heartbeat, no longer — a look doing arithmetic it declined to show its work for. He met it evenly, and did not help her with it, and that, between the two of them, was the whole conversation.

Then the last of the family business: Wu Zhangkong on his knees a third time — *I won't run anymore. Even part-time work. Let me take care of you. A man can't live for himself alone; I made a mistake; I have a remainder of a life to pay it with* — and the mountain, dumbstruck by a stubbornness he had personally installed, muttering at last: "Fine. You can stay. Someone has to make the tea and keep the house."

The class thanked the grandteacher in a ragged chorus. Shen Yi took them out to the guest rooms, and the island kept its lights on a long time, and upstairs an old man let his favorite enemy help him up the stairs, and neither of them called it what it was.

## Part 4: The Lake at Night

Lin Hao could not sleep. Deep water does not, after a storm; it settles, and listens.

He walked the island's rim with his hands empty, and at the boathouse he stopped, because his hands had picked up a boat oar without asking him, and the oar was — wrong. Not wrong as a tool. Wrong as a *sentence*: it wanted to sweep, and his intent, forty weeks of sword-consciousness drilled into the marrow, wanted to cut, and the two disagreements woke something that had been sleeping since the forge.

He set the oar down. He took up a branch off the ground instead, a dead stick, no edge, no point, no memory of any war.

He stood with it the way he stood with the sword.

And the branch — sang.

Not broke, not whistled: *sang*, the way the Yaluo bar had turned toward his fingers, the way the silver had cheered under Wulin's forty-eighth strike. The six strokes lived in it, all six, transposed whole — Still Water ran down the stick as if wood had been waiting its whole life to be told it was allowed. Lin Hao stood very still, the way a man stands when a floor he has walked for years turns out to be a door.

*The intent was never the sword's,* he thought, and the thought had the weight of law. *The sword was only where I first met it. It lives in the purpose, not the steel — the intent that knows what the weapon is for before the weapon moves. And the purpose wears everything. Edge, point, weight, lever, stone, hand. Every weapon is one idea wearing different bodies.*

He picked up the oar. It swept — perfectly, without rehearsal, the stroke arriving before the oar did. He set it down and made a fist, and his own knuckles explained themselves to him, blunt instruments they had been all along. A stone off the ground sat in his palm like a short, patient siege. The branch again: a spear; then, held differently, a fence; then a pen, ridiculous and exact.

Somewhere in him the talent — the thing the system window had named in a word nobody could read, the thing that met anything and became it, the adaptation that had never once been loyal to a single shape — turned over in its sleep and fit the new fact like a key fits a lock. Of course. *It was never going to stop at one weapon.* A talent that adapts to everything finds, eventually, the intent that lives in everything wielded.

Sword consciousness had been the school. This was the graduation.

He did not shout, or flare, or spend a single point of anything — Lin Hao never had. The lake did not ripple. He simply stood there a while at the rim of the water with a dead branch in his hand, being — quietly, irreversibly — the youngest weapon-master the way he was already everything else: without precedent, and without anyone to tell him so.

"Again," said a voice from the trees, in the tone of a man who has been watching a long time.

Wu Zhangkong stepped out of the dark with his blue sword loose in his hand, and his face was doing something it had not done in Class Zero's entire history. He had felt it from the house — a swordsman knows — and had come down, and had watched a boy make a boat oar tell the truth.

"Show me," his teacher said, and drew.
