## Part 1: The Lesson

The blue sword came out of the night like a season.

Wu Zhangkong did not warn, and did not hurry, and the first stroke was slow enough to be a question — Skyfrost's cold laying a flat line across the moonlight, courteous as a master opening a study.

Lin Hao answered with the branch.

Still Water ran down the dead wood the way it had run down cold iron for two years — the block laid flat, the line taken away, the branch meeting the birth of the cut rather than its arrival. Bark shifted. Nothing broke. The two weapons touched and parted, and the lake went on ticking at the shore as if nothing had been said.

"Again," said the teacher, and meant the opposite of what the word usually meant: *further.*

The second stroke came faster, still a question. The branch was a spear this time — not because Lin Hao moved it like one, but because the purpose arrived before the wood did, and wood that has been told it is a spear becomes difficult to argue with. The third stroke, falling like a verdict, met a fence. The fourth, a shield that had been a stick ten breaths earlier. The transposition wasn't technique. It was grammar — the same grammar that had read the Yaluo bar aloud — and every body the idea wore, it wore completely, for exactly as long as it was needed, and not one breath longer.

Wu Zhangkong stepped back. His sword did not lower.

"Left side," he said, and struck the left side, and the branch swept — a boat oar's stroke, wide and level, born from the boathouse disagreement itself — and turned the blue line aside.

Silence. Then the teacher did something no student of his had ever seen: he laughed — one syllable, winter thawing for exactly that long.

"Twenty years," he said, "I have taught the sword as a thing. 'The sword is this. The sword is not that.'" The blue blade turned in the moonlight, edge and flat and edge. "And you come down to my lake with a stick, and the stick is more of a sword than half the blades I have owned." His eyes were bright and cold and, for once, young. "Say the law. I want to hear it in your voice, so I can steal it for my other students."

"The intent was never the sword's," Lin Hao said. "The sword is where I met it. It lives in the purpose — and the purpose wears everything. Every weapon is one idea in different bodies. Tonight the idea learned to change clothes."

"It learned more than that." Wu Zhangkong sheathed — a decision, not an ending. "It learned that from the outside. You left the sword behind tonight, Lin Hao. Don't. The idea wears every body — including the first one. The sword taught you the grammar; keep the first body fluent, or the grammar goes stale in every body at once." A pause, the length of a held blade. "That is the last correction I am qualified to give you. From tonight, we do not train, you and I. We confer."

*We confer.* From the coldest teacher on the continent, it was a knighthood.

They walked back up the island in the kind of silence that two swords make when they have agreed to be honest with each other forever, and the branch stayed in Lin Hao's hand the whole way, because it was rude, somehow, to put down a teacher's diploma.

## Part 2: The Girls' Veranda

On the veranda of the wooden house, Shen Yi was finishing the night's other lesson.

"—and conscious of your behavior inside the academy, Gu Yue. Before the seniors of this school — the ones who have lived through world-shaking events — we are nothing. Pay your respects, or your stay will be a short one, and your companions' with it. Do you understand me?"

Gu Yue nodded, silently, which from her was fluency.

Wulin pulled her hand. "Teacher Shen is right. You were too impulsive today — Elder Cai was testing my strength in the fourth trial; I wasn't even hurt. Teacher Shen — will you take us to her later? To apologize."

Shen Yi stared at him. *Thirteen,* her face said, and gave up on the sentence.

"I know you acted for my sake," Wulin went on, honest as a hammer. "But we're a team, Gu Yue. What you do lands on all of us — the way my deep meditation made five of us working students." He looked her directly in the eyes. "And Elder Cai wants you as her *disciple*. She watched you all exam. It's not easy to become a one-word battle armor master by twenty — a teacher like that isn't luck, it's a door. Doors like that don't knock twice."

Gu Yue's brows drew in, her cheeks puffed — and then, under the honest weight of him, her head bowed. "I'm sorry. I was impulsive today. I want to go apologize." He gathered her into a hug — the captain's kind, the kind that means *the shape held*, and she allowed it, crimson, and did not push it away; and over his shoulder her eyes crossed the dark toward the lake path, one heartbeat, no longer, where a branch and a blue sword were still talking, and her face did arithmetic it declined to show anyone.

Xie Xie sauntered over with his arms wide open. "That's the way!"

Her leg shot out. "Go away."

"You're *so* biased. How come the Captain gets—"

"Because he's handsome," Gu Yue said, matter-of-fact, and the veranda detonated.

"WAY handsomer than you," Xiaoyan confirmed, digging deeper with the serenity of a surveyor.

Shen Yi watched them — her own admission age bouncing in front of her — and something in her unbent for the night. "Sleep early. Registration tomorrow, and working students must be alert. Being a working student," and here her voice went quiet and odd, "is not an easy thing."

## Part 3: The Boys' Room

The boys' room held two beds and one question.

Wulin asked it into the dark, half asleep, the way the important things get asked: "Why didn't you spend yours? The request. Full marks buys anything. You could've had — anything."

Lin Hao was quiet long enough that the question began to apologize for itself. Then:

"I asked first. On the roof — you were there. Name the price of the point, I'll pay it. They refused the coin; the coin was the problem, not the will." A breath in the dark. "Then you found a coin they'd take, and you spent it on her entry — the way you do everything, for the shape, all five through one door. A man doesn't bid against his captain's gift, Wulin. He doesn't take a door out of the hands of the one already walking through it."

Silence. The shape of the answer moving in the other boy's mind — and Wulin, who was wiser about people than anyone credited, let the half of it that was about Gu Yue pass unremarked, because the Receiver Law was class law by now, and captains enforce the laws they're given.

"When you find the word," Wulin said at last, "the word the request is waiting for. Tell me first."

"After the elders," Lin Hao said. "Before the continent."

"That'll do," said the captain, and was asleep inside a minute.

## Part 4: The Dream

Wulin was the last to meditate, and the first to dream in iron.

Golden light rose off his palm, and the hammers answered out of his blood — arriving in his hands the way a limb arrives, no distance crossed. The dragon on the metal was no pattern tonight; it *roamed*, slow and gold, along the flanks of the hammers, alive because he was, the blood connection complete. He sat inside the night's arithmetic like a man sitting inside a warm house: mechas could never have this — first-grade thousand-refined was a mecha's ceiling; armor was different, armor was a circuit carved into the martial soul itself, the soul given its own armor and sublimated by it.

And the other arithmetic, the one that did not warm: the circuit had a history. Humanity's strength had soared on armor's back — and the beasts had gone over the brink under it. The Spirit Pagoda had been founded to make the peace, and then, for the sake of artificial spirit souls, had slaughtered its way through a world with the Federation's blessing; under the relentless pursuit of science, the soul beast world had crumbled; give the research a few thousand years and even ten-thousand-year spirit souls would come from a workshop. *Xie Xie's question, arriving at three in the morning with its answer:* it was never the beasts. It was the door, and who built it, and what came through it wearing armor.

Saint Blacksmiths stood level with three-word masters because without them there'd be no three-word armor. Divine was a word even Mu Chen couldn't explain — a door with no visible house around it. Wulin looked at his own goal, and at the blood ring, and did the boy-arithmetic that would one day terrify committees: armor had no strict soul-power requirement — he had proven the principle already at the anvil. Piece by piece, then. Starting with the simplest part. Not one word.

Two.

He fell asleep mid-calculation, the hammers humming themselves back into his blood like a ship's engine below decks, and the dream came and fitted him for a shape he couldn't yet see — armor with two words waiting on it, unhurried, the way everything real in his life had arrived: late, heavy, and his.

The island slept around its five. In her room Gu Yue dreamed of nothing she'd ever tell; in his WZK lay awake listening to the lake and hearing, faintly, two weapons still confer; and on the desk of a banked page across the water, Elder Cai's verdict waited for morning like a held breath — while at the house's heart, an old man who had forgiven nothing and accepted everything drank his student's tea, and found it good.

Down on the water's edge the hawk had come out of wherever it waited when the day was about people, and sat the boat-rail the way it sat every rail lately, and the frost went a hand-span outward from its claws along the wood and held, not melting, not spreading — weather the way weather is supposed to behave, only colder, only settled. The bird under the moon was not entirely the bird that had gone into the deep water on day thirty-one: the storm-cry was still the storm-cry, but there was a second note under it now if you were him and listening, low and long, the sound a lake makes when it sets, and the gold in the feathers carried a colder thread than gold was ever supposed to carry. It flew like weather and it landed like winter; ten thousand years of dragon in him, two hundred and seventy of them counted in the book, had taught even the weather to freeze on purpose. He stood at the window a moment with his hand flat to the frame — the glass white-edged under his palm the same way the rail was white-edged under the claws — and let his attention sink the way it had learned to sink, down past the breathing, into the country behind it: the dark water at rest, the storm-sky above it moving in the wrong direction, and in between them the quiet that was not stillness but a hundred slow agreements at once — the smith-forged shoulders carrying the deep water's patience, the storm-light reflexes reading the glass's temperature before the eyes did, the iron in the sword and the iron in the man the same element. Tomorrow morning the academy's instruments would try to read all that and would get, he suspected, five answers for the price of one, and none of them would be a name for the whole. That was correct. Some things did not reduce to a label; they reduced to a file that grew one page an arc, and that was the right instrument for them.

The night was long enough. Morning was already coming, and morning was loud.

## Part 1: The Verdict and the Door

Morning came to Sea God's Island the way morning comes to old money: without hurrying, and certain the room would wait.

Shen Yi walked them up the wooden path before the sun had finished clearing the lake. Five students in yesterday's clothes, four of them nervous in the ordinary way and one of them nervous in the way a ledger is nervous before an audit — quietly, and with all the columns in order.

Elder Cai received them in a room that had too few chairs for the number of people who usually wanted to sit in it. She did not stand when they entered. She had a page in front of her, and a brush, and she was writing as the door opened, the way a woman writes who has decided that the next minute of her life belongs to the sentence under her hand.

Wulin went first, because Wulin always went first, and he bowed the full bow.

"Elder Cai. We came to apologize. Yesterday — Gu Yue acted for my sake. You were testing my strength, and I wasn't hurt at all, and she should not have raised her hand to an elder of the Pavilion. She knows it. We wanted to say it before the day had its breakfast."

Gu Yue bowed beside him — lower, and held longer. "I was impulsive. I'm sorry."

Elder Cai set down the brush. She looked at the girl for a long moment, the way a jeweler looks at a stone that has refused the first setting.

"You know what I offered you," she said. It was not a question.

Gu Yue straightened. The room was very still; outside, the lake made its small, rich noise, water against wood that had heard six decades of apologies and six decades of verdicts.

"I do," said Gu Yue. "And I know what it's worth. Doors like that don't knock twice — Teacher Shen said so, and she's right." She folded her hands, and the next words came slower, each one placed like a foot on a wet stone. "I came in with a class, Elder. Five of us crossed the exam floor together. I'm not strong enough yet to be the only person through a door — not strong enough in the way that matters. Let me be a working student first. Let me walk the road they walk. If the door is still open when I've walked it… then I'll know I was the one who knocked, and not the one who was pulled through."

Xie Xie, behind her, made a small sound that he converted into a cough with moderate success.

Elder Cai's face did not change. But she picked the brush back up, and Lin Hao, watching from the second row the way he watched everything — from the margin, where the readings were truest — saw the old woman's hand move once across the page, slowly, the way you write something you intend to keep.

"Do you mistake me for a fool, child?" said Elder Cai, without heat. "I have tested two generations of monsters. A girl says *I am not strong enough to leave my people* — that is not weakness speaking. That is a decision wearing humility's clothes." She set the brush down again. "The door stays open. Decisions made to walk beside your people are not defects in a disciple. They are the better kind of backbone. Remember that you decided it — when the road gets cold and you wonder whether you were foolish, remember that you chose the long road on purpose."

Gu Yue bowed again. This one did not come back up quickly.

"Now." Elder Cai's eyes moved — past Wulin, past the girl, and stopped on the margin of the room where Lin Hao stood, having taken the smallest, most unclaimable position available, the position his father called *where the wall can see you and the customer can't.* "The other one. Step here. I didn't send for an apology from you. I sent for a verdict, and verdicts are delivered to faces, not files."

He stepped forward.

"Your exam," she said, "has no honest column. The eighth trial was scored for a floor of four. You were the fifth set of feet on that floor. The scoring structure of Shrek Academy is older than most of the people in it, and it is not going to be rebuilt in a week to hold one boy. So your official transcript will say what everyone's says: passed, placed, working student. Ordinary words. The Academy distrusts records that need a new column — a record no column can hold is a record everyone wants to touch, and touched records stop being true."

She turned the page toward her, away from him, and wrote on it while he watched. He could not read the line. He could read the hand that wrote it: unhurried, certain, and the first stroke went down in the place on the page reserved for the thing that had bothered her most.

"The cold you leave on chairs," she said, still writing. "That went first. I thought you'd like to know what an elder notices." The brush stopped. "You leave this island a working student. No door opens for you this morning. Do you know why?"

He thought about it the way he thought about metal — not for the answer that sounded best, but for the one with no cracks.

"Because a door opened for me would be in the record," he said. "And a marked boy is a watched boy. The Academy learns more from a boy it isn't watching."

Something moved at the corner of Elder Cai's mouth, and was put down.

"Also," she said, "the Pavilion does not forget a debt. You hold a request you have not named — full marks across a trial floor buy one thing in this Academy, and you left it on the table like a man leaving a coin he intends to come back for. Good. When you know its weight, the Pavilion will hear it. A request spent by a boy is a firework. A request spent by a man is an easement." She slid the page into a drawer, closed it, and folded her hands. "There are books being kept about you in this Academy, boy. I keep one. You keep one. Keep yours honest. I will keep mine."

Outside, a boat bell rang once across the water, gentle as a deadline.

"Breakfast," said Elder Cai, and that was the verdict.

## Part 2: The Black Buns

Xie Xie had spent the walk to the table spending money he did not have.

"This island," he said, helping himself to a seat and, by the looks of it, to the entire concept of the island, "is extraordinary. The energy in the air — I slept and I might as well have cultivated all night. Wulin, you should ask Grandteacher if we can live here. Permanently. I'll take the boathouse."

"Keep dreaming," said Wulin, who had missed his morning's Purple Demon Eyes for the first time in weeks and was taking it out on the air. "Shrek's rules are very strict. And I'm about to starve to death — I had one meal yesterday and it was trial buns."

Zhuo Shi was already at the wooden table, and beside him sat Wu Zhangkong, who had not gone to the verdict and did not look like a man who regretted it. The old elder pointed Wulin to the seat beside him, and then pointed at a bamboo basket.

"Zhangkong told me you have a large stomach," said Zhuo Shi. "Let's see what's left of this basket when you're done."

Inside were twenty black objects, fist-sized, odorless, the color of iron left in a forge overnight. Steamed buns, in the same way that a sword is a strip of metal with opinions.

Lin Hao took one last, and he did not bite first. He read it the way he read everything new — with the pads of his fingers, the way he read a bar for grain. Tender. Dense. Faint, faint trace of something fishy and far away, like a word shouted across too much water. The surface gave under his thumb the way cold-worked iron gives, reluctantly and with a memory of pressure.

Wulin had already taken four, two per hand, a habit of a boy whose appetite made politeness a luxury. He bit. He chewed. He was halfway through being unimpressed — *not delicious, fishy, strange texture* — and then he swallowed, and his whole body changed key.

Warmth went down his throat and his blood went to meet it like a river meeting the sea. Lin Hao watched the captain's shoulders settle, watched the hollow-eyed exhaustion of yesterday walk out of him the way a bad guest leaves when the food arrives.

Wulin ate. Four. Eight. Twelve. Zhuo Shi's eyes, narrowed to begin with, widened by degrees the way a shutter opens on something it did not expect to see — the boy's blood and aura strengthening with every bun, pulse by pulse, a change that had nothing at all to do with soul power.

Lin Hao bit into his own.

The bun was cold at the center. Not the cold of a kitchen — the cold of *depth.* The fish it was made from had lived three kilometers under water, in the black country where light is a rumor and pressure is the only weather; and the body it had grown in that country had known, the whole of its life, what three kilometers of water weigh. When Lin Hao swallowed, that knowledge went down with it.

And below him — inside him — the dark water moved.

His attention sank the way a stone sinks, past the morning and the table and the sound of Wulin eating: the still, vast sea of his own inner country, smoked-glass surface without a ripple, the permanent storm-sky overhead with its clouds going the wrong way and its lightning fishing far up, fishing, never striking. At the bottom, in the sightless dark where the jiao lay coiled — the coil turned over. Once. The way a continent turns in its sleep and does not wake. No crossing, no gate, no threshold breached; a maturing, a turning, the deep-water part of him filing away what the fish's body had known — *this is the weight of three kilometers; this is how pressure behaves; remember it against the day you need depth.* Between sea and sky, the adaptation moved through both, taking the reading, redrawing some small line of the map he would not see until the next time he looked. Overhead, the storm clouds went the wrong way, patient as weather.

He came back to the table. His bun was half-eaten. He set the other half down, and did not reach for a second.

Across the table, Wu Zhangkong's eyes were on him. Beside him, Zhuo Shi had stopped watching Wulin.

The old elder said nothing for a moment. Then, to the teacher, not the student: "The lake boy. He had one."

"One is his way of counting," said Wu Zhangkong.

"No," said Zhuo Shi. "He didn't count the buns." The old man's eyes came back to Lin Hao, and in them was the particular respect of a deep-water practitioner who has just watched a puddle recognize the ocean. "He counted the depth. Tell me, boy — what did it say to you, the fish?"

Lin Hao considered the half bun. "It didn't say anything, Elder. It was a fish. But it knew what three kilometers of water weighs, and now so does the part of me that's interested in that sort of fact." He paused. "One is a reading, Elder. Sixteen would be a claim. I'm not entitled to sixteen of anything here."

Zhuo Shi looked at him for another long moment, and then looked at Wulin, who was at that very moment patting his stomach after the sixteenth bun, beaming.

"Grandteacher," said Wulin, shining-eyed, "may I eat these every day?"

Zhuo Shi's face did a thing Lin Hao had never seen an elder's face do, and filed under *useful.*

"You can have the rest," said the old man, and stood, and left.

Wulin turned, puzzled, to Wu Zhangkong. "Teacher. Did I say something rude?"

It was Shen Yi — who had come in at the tail of the meal with the boat hour in her face — who answered, smiling the warm smile of a woman watching a family tradition happen to someone else.

"Those are Teacher Zhuo's monthly rations. He allows himself one a day." She nodded at the basket. "They're made from a deep-sea fish — lives three kilometers underwater, and it isn't a soul beast, so you can imagine the strength it takes to live at that depth at all. Only elders of the Sea God's Pavilion are granted the privilege. You just ate more than half of your grandteacher's month. And then asked for more, every day. The only way that happens is if every elder on the island yields his share to you."

"Eh…" Wulin scratched his head, abashed. "Then I'll leave the rest for him."

"He told you to take them, so take them," said Shen Yi. "An old man like that doesn't grieve a basket of buns. He grieves or he doesn't, and he's already decided." She smiled. "When you have a free day next week, Wu Zhangkong will bring you over to visit. He's fond of you. You're similar."

On the boat, the lake open before them in the daytime sun — a sapphire set into the earth, light breaking across it in handfuls — Wulin sat with the wrapped basket on his knees like a dowry, and finally said the thing he'd been holding.

"That warmth," he said quietly, to Lin Hao, the only other person at the rail who'd understand. "Down the throat and into the blood. It went straight to the seals. I could feel it — whatever those fish are, they feed the thing the seals are holding back."

"A fish that lived three kilometers down," said Lin Hao, watching the water. "That's not food for a body, Wulin. That's pressure. A body that grows up under that weight carries it like a deposit. You didn't eat sixteen meals. You made sixteen deposits."

"Deposits into what?"

Lin Hao thought about the dark sea he carried, and the continent that had turned in its sleep, and said the true thing in the boy's own currency:

"Into the bank you can't spend from yet."

Wulin looked at his basket, and at his chest, where fourteen seals waited on their own horizon, and nodded slowly, the way a captain nods when the navigator says the harbor exists but is not today's.

## Part 3: The Honest Instrument

The outer-court administration building was grandeur with a clerk's face on it.

A scholarly administrator in his fifties, with the careful boredom of a man who processes miracles before lunch, enrolled them each in turn and issued each of them a dark-green school uniform, folded with the precise indifference of paper goods. He turned to the last page of his intake memo and frowned.

"Working students from the Sea God examinee pool," he said. "Four names." He looked up at five children. He looked down. He turned the page over, as though the fifth name might be a printing error on the back. It was not. "Five of you."

"Five," said Shen Yi, pleasantly.

The administrator looked at her. She smiled and shook her head the particular smile that meant *I could explain this and I have chosen, for your peace and mine, not to.* He had, to give him credit, survived two decades of Shrek paperwork; he wrote the fifth line into the ledger in the same ink, in the same hand, and made the small annotation men of his profession make when a fact refuses a category.

"Don't bring shame to the working students," he said, handing over the last uniform, to no one and therefore to all of them.

Lin Hao turned the phrase over once, the way he turned over any metal before he struck it. Shen Yi was already herding them onward, and when he sent her the questioning look, she only smiled again, and shook her head.

*Medical hall first,* the hall clerk said. *All intake students. The working-student line is the last line; take it.*

The medical hall smelled of dried herbs and old, careful doubt. Its examiner was a woman of perhaps sixty with ink on her cuff and a face that had settled, over a long career, into the expression of a scale that intends to tell the truth regardless of who is standing on it. Her plate read **Su Wen**, and she had the tiredness particular to people who have measured two generations of monsters and would very much like one ordinary afternoon.

The ordinary students had gone through in the morning. She was plainly hoping for four unremarkable working children and an early close.

She got Wulin first, as it happened, and for three minutes she thought she had her anomaly for the year. Her diagnostic stones ran warm against his chest; the blood-essence reading came back like a small furnace reported in a residential district; she wrote it down with the faintest lift of one eyebrow, filed it under *remarkable but classifiable*, and waved the captain through with the private gratitude of a woman who has used only one page.

The next boy sat down on the examination stool.

She started with the wrists, because she always started with the wrists — the hands told the truth first. The conditioning array lit under his palms and she read the density off the stone the way she'd read it ten thousand times, and then she read it again, because the stone was reporting the forearms of a master smith — the callus architecture of years at a forge, bone set under repeated load the way riverbed stones are set — attached to a child who could not have seen fourteen summers.

She made a note. She did not yet know she would be making notes for the rest of the afternoon.

Reflexes next: the standard release test, a falling bead, the array catching the catch-time in thousandths. The bead dropped. The boy caught it — or rather, the boy's hand was where the bead was going to be, having been there, it appeared, before the bead had fully committed to falling. The array returned a figure in the band the stone only used for instrument faults. Su Wen looked at it. She reset the test. She ran it again with her own hand on the mechanism. The same figure came back, polite and implacable, and somewhere above the boy's head, for no reason the hall accounted for, the air moved as though high up and far away a weather system had turned.

She made another note, slower.

Cold tolerance: the standard tolerance crystal, pale blue, meant to be held while it drew a fixed chill and measured what the body did with it. He took it. It frosted over from *his* side — the rime climbing inward from his palm the way frost climbs a window from the outside, only this was inside and the boy was the outside. Su Wen stared at it. She reached for a probe-prick to test the circulation response, pricked the side of his finger, and turned to write the result; when she turned back, the prick had closed. She was looking at the fingertip when it finished closing, like a curtain drawn shut by a servant who has done it a thousand times.

She set the crystal down very gently.

The diagnostic stone came last — the general soul-force read, the one instrument that always had an opinion. She placed it against his chest.

It behaved the way a blade behaves when a blade master holds it.

Su Wen had felt that once before, twenty years ago, running the intake on a young man who later became a three-word battle armor master: the stone did not read the body, the body *read the stone back* — the held, waiting quality of a thing in the presence of an intent that could pick it up, wear it, or put it through the wall, all with equal courtesy. Intent, at intake. Weapon intent, riding the child's nerves like a second heartbeat.

And underneath all of it — underneath the smith's wrists and the storm-reflexes and the frost that went the wrong direction and the intent that looked out through his eyes like a second tenant — underneath, the array kept re-calibrating. Every reading settled slightly different from the reading before it, not error but *learning*: the body taking the test while the test took the body, a background field that made the other four signatures able to live on one frame at all.

Five signatures. None of them wrong. None of them belonging to the same boy.

"Step onto the soul array," she said, and her voice had the careful flatness of a woman removing a cherished instrument from its case.

The soul-soul array was the medical hall's deep instrument: a standing mirror set in bronze, ringed with tone-stones, built to read the spirit souls of new intakes for the Academy's records. He stood within the ring. The stones woke, climbed their scale — and hit the end of it and kept climbing, the needle pressed flat against the stop the way a man's shoulder presses a door that was built to stop him.

Su Wen read the result.

She reached out, turned the instrument's tone-stones down to silence, and let them wake again. She gestured him off the platform, checked the calibration with the two-tone strike she trusted more than certificates, and had him step back on. The array woke, climbed, and pinned itself against the far stop with the same patient, impossible report.

A second soul, on a four-ring intake student, reading past the ten-thousand-year gate. A threshold the instrument could not price — not a number too large, but a *gate* standing where no gate had standing room. The array's scale went to ten thousand the way a road goes to a cliff; this child's reading was the air past the cliff.

Then she looked at the mirror.

For one frame — one frame only — the bronze mirror did not show the boy. It showed dark water under a storm sky: a still, black sea reaching to every edge of the glass, clouds above it moving in the wrong direction, and far, far down, a shape at the bottom that was not landscape and was not beast, turning over with the patience of geology.

She looked again. The mirror showed a boy standing in a bronze ring, breathing fog, waiting politely for his results.

Su Wen closed her eyes for approximately one second, which is the amount of time a professional allows herself for the universe to apologize. It did not.

She opened a drawer she did not open often — the drawer at the bottom, the one her predecessor had labeled *Unclassifiable* and mostly used, in his day, for paperwork she strongly suspected he had simply hated filing. She took out a fresh folder. On the tab she wrote nothing, because nothing in the Academy's taxonomy was true on the tab yet. Inside, in the careful handwriting of a woman who had long since accepted that *impossible* is a filing category like any other, she wrote:

*Intake, working-student line. Five distinct body-signatures on one frame — smith-grade conditioning; storm-class reflex (instrument band, twice confirmed); deep-water cold signature with ambient-direction reversal; regeneration, observed closing; weapon intent present at intake. Background field: readings adapt under repeated test. No academy bracket applies.*

And below that, her hand steadier than her opinion:

*Second-soul array: result beyond instrument scale; ten-thousand-tier threshold confirmed twice on recalibration. Classification withheld pending instrument that does not exist. Annual review. — S.W.*

At the very bottom, small enough that she nearly didn't write it: *Mirror unclear.*

"Right," she said. "You're healthy. Annoyingly so. You can go."

The boy paused at the edge of the ring. "Is there… anything the Academy will need from me?"

"Come back in a year," said Su Wen. "And do try not to become more interesting before then."

"I'll try," he said.

"No," she said, already writing, "you won't."

He left. She sat for a while with the pen in her hand, and then she opened the folder again and added, beneath *Mirror unclear*, three more words, because honesty was her profession and she had never once let a profession down:

*Recheck annually.*

## Part 4: The Warm Wall

The job assignment came at the administration window, carried by a steward who clearly considered dusk a personal appointment: the five working students' first labor — Spirit Ice Plaza, the great flagstoned court before the main hall. Sweep, dispose, mop. Before dusk *on the morrow*. Not a single speck of dust, on pain of points.

"Tomorrow, then," said Xie Xie, when the steward had gone. "Plenty of dark between now and then. What do we do with the dark?"

The answer waited at the end of a key ring.

A porter with the cheerful fatalism of a man delivering orphans to a doorstep led them west across the darkening plaza and into the trees, to the quarter where the Academy housed its working students. The building showed itself by degrees: a long, single-story barracks, run-down and tucked into the forest as if the Academy hoped the trees would do the apologizing, some twenty rooms along its flank, and the far rooms with planks nailed where windows had given up entirely.

"Mostly empty this early in the year," the porter said, walking them past. "You lot are the end block." He stopped at a low gate in the flank wall, and handed over the ring of keys. "Best wall in the outer court. Nobody ever bids on the room — forge noise all night. You'll sleep through it; you're the working students." He squinted at them. "Five? The paper said four."

"The paper," said Shen Yi, who had walked them down, "is having a week."

Lin Hao stepped through the gate.

It was a courtyard the Academy had stopped trying to want — but it was a courtyard, which the barracks flank was not. A pavilion furnace-flue ran along its north side, and the stone wall there held the day's heat and would hold the winter's too, warm the year round. Beyond the wall came the breathing sound of the forge itself — bellows, the low talk of fire — and riding the sound to its source with his eyes, he found the scrap gate, low and unimportant, with a hand-painted sign nailed to it in soot-colored paint: **SCRAP IS NOT FREE. NEITHER IS READING IT.** A soot-armed figure moved behind the furnace door and did not look up.

"Jobs related to a secondary profession pay the best," Shen Yi said from behind him, following his gaze the way she followed everything — correctly. "The administration assigns basics, but a student with a trade bids for the trade work. Tuition here is 'very expensive,' I'm afraid." She said it with the odd, weighty gentleness she'd used on the island. "The price is real. That is not a cruelty — it's the one way the Academy has of saying the thing is worth real money."

But it was the tree that stopped him.

The old courtyard pine — the kind Shrek had been growing since before the current outer court was a proposal — had a branch. On the branch, in the last clean light of a September evening, spread a hand-span of white rime. Frost. At the close of a warm day. Under it stood a wiry old man with a broom and a little notebook bound in string, hands on his hips, addressing the branch.

"September," he told it. "It's September. I've got forty years of you in here, tree, and you've never frosted in September. This branch. This one branch." He prodded it gently with the broom. The rime did not melt. It sat there, white and patient, glittering against the sunset.

Lin Hao stopped. The groundskeeper looked up, and his eyes — the eyes of a man who had spent forty years believing the trees told him things and being, by and large, right — moved from the branch to the boy.

The boy looked at the branch. The branch glittered. The boy gave the groundskeeper the smallest, most noncommittal nod in the outer court, the nod of one professional to another across a difference of departments.

The groundskeeper squinted at him for a long moment. Then he opened his little book and wrote in it, and said to the tree, not the boy: "September."

He did not sound angry. He sounded like a man whose mail had finally arrived.

"Rooms aren't opened after dark this term — new rule, after the rat business," the porter said, locking the gate back and handing over the key. "Admin's got visitor beds for the new lot tonight. Bring your things in with the light; the place'll look worse before it looks better."

Which was how, while the others went ahead with the porter, Lin Hao came to borrow the groundskeeper's spare broom and spend the last gold of the evening sweeping out *their own* courtyard — the flags under the pine, the threshold of the warm wall, the little court that was theirs as of tomorrow and not one breath sooner. He swept the way his father swept a forge floor at close of day: with the grain, and the margin held.

Mid-stroke, something rose in his wrist that was not the broom.

The intent — woken at the lake, promoted by the coldest man on the continent from student to colleague — moved through his arms and looked out of his hands at the broom handle, and for one breath the broom was *nothing*, no body at all, empty air and a held purpose, and the Unwritten Stroke, the stroke that had worked all along because it did not exist, the stroke that needed no blade to live in, rose to deliver itself into empty hands in a courtyard full of sunset—

—and he stopped it.

Not here. Not yet. A thing that good spends its first coin on ground it chooses, with the correct witnesses, and a borrowed broom in an empty courtyard on moving-in eve was neither. He let the breath go. The broom was a broom again. But the master's last correction came with the breath and would not be dismissed: *you left the sword behind tonight. Keep the first body fluent.* Two days. He had not taken a single sword form since the branch on the lake, because there had been no sword to take one with — and that, he understood now, standing in a courtyard with a broom in his hands, was exactly the laziness the correction had been built to kill.

So when the light went gold and the courtyard flags were clean, he took the broom through Still Water, the first form, slowly — the block laid flat, the line taken away, the stroke meeting the birth of a thing rather than its arrival — and the broom wore it completely, for as long as it was needed, and not one breath longer. The sword's grammar, kept fluent in the body it had started in. Over the warm wall, on a branch nobody could explain, a hand-span of frost outlasted the sunset. Under the tree, a groundskeeper who believed the trees watched a boy do a slow sword-dance with a broom in an empty court, and he wrote that down too, and he did not show it to anyone, because nobody believed the tree book and that had always been the finest part of owning it.

That night, in the visitor beds the admin kept for the new lot, Lin Hao opened his own ledger at the last page and wrote the day in his honest hand: one request still unspent and now acknowledged by the Pavilion; one elder's page being kept he could not read; one file in a drawer with nothing written on its tab; one fish's depth, filed; one salt line moved, on the map only he could read; one courtyard with a warm wall and a frost branch and a gate sign that read like a price list, waiting for morning; one stroke, waited for.

Three books in Shrek Academy were being kept about the same boy now — his own, and Elder Cai's, and the honest instrument's in the bottom drawer — and none of the three knew the others' contents, and that, Lin Hao thought, settling the ledger into the bag beside the folded dark-green uniforms, was a great deal of arithmetic for one first day, and exactly the amount a working student could afford.

Outside, in the dark of the trees, the September branch held its frost through the first night, and the forge breathed slow against the warm wall, and morning — morning was going to show them the room.

## Part 1: The Slum

The second morning showed them the room, and the room explained the rent.

They came back with the key in full daylight — the visitor beds of admin had held them for one night, which was precisely long enough for the porter's "best wall in the outer court" to sound like a promise. The gate opened on the courtyard they had swept at dusk: warm flue wall, old pine, a hand-span of frost still on the branch in spite of a clear September sunrise, and Lao Zhou somewhere behind his tree pretending not to be their first neighbor. But the *room* — the room behind the warm wall, the single key the sheet had issued to all five of them — was the thing that stopped them in the threshold.

Thirty square meters. Two metal bunk frames and nothing else: no mattresses, no basin, a single string hanging from the lightless bulb like a question nobody had answered. Dust lay on everything in the settled way dust lies when it has been somewhere for years. Two of the windows were broken outright, and the wind off the trees came through the gaps with the comfortable familiarity of a thing that had been visiting for a long time.

"This…" Xie Xie stood in the doorway with his bag over his shoulder. "Isn't this just a bit cruel? Are we certain this is Shrek Academy and not the slum that lives next door to it? At Eastsea we had — we had *mattresses.* We had the concept of a mattress."

"Quit complaining," Wulin said, stepping past him, because Wulin had already begun the inventory. "If you have spare time, spend it tidying."

"Captain, how are all of us supposed to live in a single room?" Xu Xiaoyan said, with the mild worry of a surveyor noting a boundary dispute. "Men and women in one room — there aren't even walls to be improper across."

"How old do you think you all are," Xie Xie said, "nobody here has even—"

"Hmph," said Xiaoyan, and turned to Gu Yue for the support one woman is supposed to lend another in the matter of curtains.

Gu Yue was watching Wulin decide where the curtains would go.

Xiaoyan closed her mouth with the serene finality of a surveyor confirming a border nobody was disputing. *Noted,* said the set of her shoulders. *I am surrounded by forces of nature, and at the trial for this curtain, not one of you will be called as a witness.*

From the bunk frame where he was conspicuously not spirit-refining the table leg, Lin Hao watched it without watching it — the particular arithmetic of being in a room with Gu Yue, two years learned now: she was the constant, Wulin was the direction she pointed, and he was the carpenter's mark on the floor. Precise. Useful. Never the thing the compass loved. It hurt the way a ledger column hurts when the total is correct and merely not the total you had hoped for — exactly as much as it ought to, and quiet.

Wulin stood in the middle of the room with his captain's face on — the face he wore when a thing was broken and standing in front of him, which was his favorite kind of thing. "Since we've been assigned the room, all we can do is make the most of it. Cloth for the broken windows first, curtains down the middle after — boys one half, girls the other. We'll improve as we go." He looked at the warm north wall, and at the courtyard pine beyond the gate, and did the arithmetic aloud. "Listen. This is the condemned end of a barracks full of empty rooms. Down the flank it's cold, dark, and honest poverty. Ours breathes."

The wall breathed, sure enough — under the birds and the distant plaza bells, the low sigh of the forge flue on the other side of the stone, holding the heat of a hundred mornings.

"I'm starting to think," Xie Xie said slowly, "that being the mistake on the paperwork has an up side."

"Five on the key sheet," said Lin Hao, who had been turning the key over in his hand the way he turned a bar before the first strike. "The register had four names. The steward who roomed us had a wing he couldn't fill and a flue that made it *worse* for anyone normal — nobody wants to sleep against a furnace that breathes all night. He gave the unfillable room to the unfillable students. It wasn't kindness. It was filing."

"I'm choosing to hear it as kindness," Wulin said. "Xiaoyan, measure the window gaps. Gu Yue, wind for the dust — carefully, the room is the one thing we own. Xie Xie, your selves are on plank and mattress duty, all three of them, and if night-Xie objects I'll explain it to him at dawn personally." He hesitated, and his eye fell on the single desk-like table the room possessed, one leg of which was already looking at him thoughtfully. "Also. Nobody spirit-refines the furniture. I see you both looking at that leg. The leg is a civilian."

"That's fair," said Xie Xie. "That is, in fact, completely fair."

The room came clean fast — soul masters make short work of dust, when the dust has no points riding on it — but cloth they did not have, nor hot water, nor anything to eat the dust with except their sleeves. The dining hall and the bathhouse were both across the enormous plaza; the only tap the slum quarter owned was a single cold faucet behind the barracks, shared by every working student who lived in the trees.

So they went for water. The faucet, when they reached it, had company.

## Part 2: The Faucet
## Part 2: The Faucet

A boy stood at the spigot with a towel over one shoulder and a bucket under the stream.

He was frail. That was the first word for him — narrow shoulders, wrists like a girl's, the kind of frame the medic's stones would have insulted with their very politeness. He watched the water rise in his bucket with the absent patience of a person doing a thing he had done ten thousand times.

Xie Xie gulped. It was a sound Lin Hao had never heard him make.

"That's number two," Xie Xie breathed, without taking his eyes off the boy. "The exam. The second examinee. He — all right, I need everyone to understand that the following is said by a man who was *there*: he hit me once. I have been hit by a lot of people, including, yesterday, a syllabus of senior students in my imagination. He hit me the way weather hits you. I woke up with my three selves agreeing on something for the first time, and the thing they agreed on was *that man.*"

The boy's bucket filled. He turned the spigot with an economical wrist, bent, and lifted it.

Lin Hao watched the lift the way he watched everything — from the margin, where the readings were truest. And the reading was wrong, and the wrongness was the whole point. The bucket came up full, maybe thirty kilograms of sloshing water, and the boy's shoulders did not change. Not "didn't strain" — *did not change.* The load went somewhere that was not on display. The frail frame was clothing, worn over something the faucet didn't deserve to see. The boy balanced the bucket the way Wulin balanced anything, the way a balance scale balances — with the certainty of a mechanism that had never once in its life considered tipping.

Wulin walked over, bucket in hand, and put on the radiant smile.

"Hi," he said. "We meet again. I'm Tang Wulin."

The boy gave him an apathetic look, acknowledged him with the smallest nod, and — because his bucket was full — picked it up, nodded once more, and carried it off toward the windowless middle rooms without spending a single word.

Five sets of eyes followed him until the trees took him. (The count was five now; the margin watched too.)

"That guy's a working student," Xie Xie said, awed. "He's *that* and he's a *working student.* I had him filed as inner court. I had him filed as *faculty.*"

"Remember what the administrator told us," Wulin said slowly. "'Don't bring shame to the working students.'" He stood there with his empty bucket, and they could see him doing the arithmetic — the face he made when the price of a thing turned out to be lower than its value. "A boy like that, three rings, power enough to fold Xie Xie's argument in one motion — and he sleeps in the slum and draws his own water. That's not punishment. Nobody punishes a boy like that into a bucket line."

"It's a selection," Lin Hao said.

They looked at him.

"The building's a filter," he said, keeping his voice down, the way you kept a reading down when the metal was still hot. "Normal students pay twenty percent and get beds. Working students pay the whole fee in hours and get — *this.* Every comfort removed. Every minute bought. Now ask what kind of student *chooses* that, or what kind of student the Academy is willing to let do it." He nodded at the trees where the frail boy had gone. "The strongest three-ring power type we've measured. The boy the faucets are for. The administrator didn't say 'don't bring shame to the working students' as a warning about *us.* He said it the way you'd say it about a guild. The working students have a *name* in this place, and the name means something, and I don't think we're supposed to find out what by asking."

Gu Yue, who had been watching the trees with her head tilted the way a cat watches a closed door, said: "Then we find out by being ones." She turned back toward the plaza, and a faint, dangerous smile came onto her face, the smile she wore right before spending a spirit skill on housework. "Also. That plaza took us until dusk with brooms. The steward will find something else for us to clean by tomorrow. And nobody has yet told me we're not allowed to use our martial souls."

Wulin's eyes lit up. He grinned.

"All right," he said.

## Part 3: Vortex

She went out onto the plaza edge the way a smith walks to a known anvil: without ceremony, but with everyone in earshot quietly stopping what they were doing.

Her three rings rose — two purple and the yellow that the five of them no longer needed explained to each other. The first ring lit. Elemental Tide: green light gathering in her cupped palms, specks of wind-light, and then blue answering it, water drawn out of the morning air itself, two equal lights beginning to turn around each other in the smallest possible spiral.

The second ring. Elemental Control. The spiral took feed — the morning mist, the damp off the flags, the air above the plaza giving up its water the way ore gives its metal when the temperature is honest — and grew. A meter tall. Two meters. A standing whirlpool of fused wind and water, and Gu Yue standing inside the calm at its center, eyes narrow, moving a tenth as fast as she moved in a fight, because this wasn't combat, this was *craft*, and craft, as Lin Hao had been telling every bar of metal he owned since he was seven, is what power looks like when it refuses to hurry.

The third ring lit. Elemental Fusion.

The green and the blue stopped being two colors. The vortex became one thing — a ribbon of moving sky that went down the plaza in a sweeping pass, dust and water and ten years of working-student grime going up into it the way filings go to a magnet, leaving wet, gleaming flagstone behind it in a broad, absurd stripe.

"Do the slum end," Wulin called, laughing. "The whole barracks! We live there!"

She turned the vortex on the barracks — and that was when Lin Hao stopped watching the technique and started watching the courtyard.

The fused ribbon swept the flank of the condemned end block. It took dust. It took the leaf-fall. It took the rot-damp off the plank windows in a single glittering pass. It reached the old pine.

It went around the frost the way a river goes around a stone.

The hand-span of white on the September branch sat through a fused wind-and-water element storm without changing by a single crystal. The vortex moved on — Gu Yue was too controlled to force anything, and the element went where it was permitted — and left the rime exactly as it had been: white, patient, glittering at noon.

Lao Zhou was standing under the tree with his broom and his string-bound notebook, and he had stopped breathing.

Gu Yue lowered her hands. The vortex unwound itself into the air, two meters of impossible sky going back to being ordinary weather. The plaza and the barracks gleamed behind her. The works steward, coming to measure how five brooms were progressing against the largest plaza in the outer court, arrived at the far end of the wet stripe and stopped with his clipboard held at the angle of a man re-reading his own opinion.

Gu Yue was not looking at the steward.

She was looking at the branch. For exactly one heartbeat, her eyes moved from the rime to Lin Hao — the flat, measuring look she had given the spring that fed him once, back in the exam, the look that filed a thing without asking about it — and then the look was gone and she was smiling at Wulin's praise like a girl who had simply cleaned a plaza very well.

Lin Hao gave nothing back. Neither did the branch.

Under him, very far inside, in the dark water at the bottom of the country he carried, the vein of iron that ran through the sea rang once, very softly — because two hundred meters away the forge pavilion had just breathed in, and iron knows iron, even iron that is a soul and iron that is a fence.

"She didn't melt it," said Lao Zhou, to his tree, in a voice of discovery. "Winds from a three-ringed element fusion, and she didn't melt it." He opened the string book and wrote in it for a long time.

## Part 4: The Failure Wall

The scrap gate was open when he got there.

He had followed the breathing sound. The pavilion's furnace door stood wide to the afternoon, a smith working inside with his back to the gate, soot to the elbows, and the hand-painted sign over the lintel reading its soot-colored rule to anyone tall enough to read it: **SCRAP IS NOT FREE. NEITHER IS READING IT.**

"Reading's a skill," Lin Hao said, stopping at the threshold. "I've got the second one. I'm here about the first."

The smith did not turn. He was watching a pour — a small one, a workshop pour, the kind nobody famous ever watches — and he said, without looking away: "Then read me this."

So Lin Hao came off the threshold and stood where the heat first becomes a thing you have to *decide* about, and he read the pour the way his father's hands had taught him, the way Mu Chen's room had confirmed: the color of the stream as it left the lip, the speed of the skin forming on the flow, the note the mold made when the metal first touched in. He did not say anything until the stream ended and the smith tilted the crucible back.

"Sixty degrees too cold for the section it's going into," he said. "The flow will set before the mold fills. It's not your fire — it's the scrap you're running. That ingot's been poured before, twice I'd guess, and it carries the memory of it. Reforged metal cools honest but cools *fast.*"

The smith set the crucible down. He turned.

He was forty and nothing — no title on his chest, no rank-band on his sleeve, just a man who ran the pavilion's scrap and furnaces for a wage and the deep private satisfaction of being correct. He had the face of a hinge: useful, plain, built to swing the same direction for thirty years.

"Two things in that answer," he said. "The first is right. The pour's dead — I knew it before I started; I was testing the *scrap* to see what it would tell me about the batch. The second is why you're standing at my gate instead of in a classroom." He wiped his hands on his apron. "Most children who can read a pour were taught to read *good* metal. You read the trash like it owed you money. Where'd a working student learn to do that?"

"I'm a fifth-rank smith," Lin Hao said. "With no calling card in this city."

The hinge of a face didn't change. But the man's eyes went to the gate and back, the way a buyer's eyes go to a bar he hadn't expected in the lot.

"Fifth rank." He said it flatly. "At thirteen."

"The Association knows. The paperwork hasn't caught up to Shrek."

"The paperwork never catches up to anything." The smith considered him for a moment, then jerked his head at the corner of the pavilion — the scrap corner, where the off-cuts and failed pieces lived in sorted piles, and along the back wall of which ran a long, dark rack of things that were not sorted at all. Lin Hao looked at the rack. Every piece on it was a failure. Miscast fittings, cracked bars, joints that had folded, pieces whose shapes he couldn't even name because they had stopped being shapes. None of it was salvage stock. All of it was *kept.*

"The failure wall," the smith said, following his eyes. "Every smith on the pavilion hangs his firsts there. First pour. First fold. First piece he believed in and shouldn't have. The scrap pile is metal. The wall is *lessons.*" He paused. "I'm Tie Jin. I don't take apprentices — I'm not anybody's master, and I'm not on anyone's staff. I run what gets burned and what gets kept. A working student with trade-hours can buy scrap time: hours of work for hours at the pile. The reading's free, like the sign says — but free reading means I get to test you whenever I feel like it."

Lin Hao looked at the failure wall, and at the scrap pile, and past the pile, at the good metal locked up for the academy's proper students.

"Hours for hours," he said. "And for firsts?"

Tie Jin looked at him. "What're you making, fifth-rank-with-no-card?"

"Armor," Lin Hao said. "Two words. Eventually. Starting with the part it is impossible to get wrong."

A sound came out of Tie Jin that might have been a laugh, if a hinge laughed. "Nothing's impossible to get wrong," he said. "That's the wall. But the simplest piece is a wrist guard, and a wrist guard is the right place to learn that. Deal's this: you work my hours, you get the scrap and the fire. You hang your failures with the rest of us, and you do not, *ever*, melt one back down because it embarrassed you. The wall keeps them. The wall keeps all of them."

That evening, at the smallest fire in the pavilion, Lin Hao made his first piece of the two-word dream out of a piece of scrap heavy silver that no one had claimed — a wrist guard, the simplest form there is, a cuff with a seam.

He read the metal. He heated it honest. He struck it the way his father struck everything — with the margin held in reserve. And at the fourth strike, the seam folded. Not catastrophically. Quietly. A small, sickening curl, the way a lip curls when a bar is telling you the temperature was a lie.

The piece cooled on the anvil, wrong and done and unmistakable.

Wulin found him there an hour later, walking in from the barracks end with a half-mended curtain rail over his shoulder and the look of a captain checking on his whole roster one last time before sleep. He saw the failed cuff on the anvil. He did not say anything about it being a good try. He set the curtain rail down and picked the cuff up, turned it over in his big, furnace-calloused hands, and read it the way only one other smith in the city could.

"You knew at the third strike," Wulin said.

"Second," said Lin Hao. "I took two more to be sure."

"Good." Wulin put the cuff back down. "The ones you don't take the extra strikes on are the ones that teach you nothing. May I?" He held up his own hands, and his eyes went to the good-metal rack and then, correctly, to the scrap pile. "I've got a two-word dream of the same length and the same first word. If you're buying hours here, captain's order: buy two sets. I'll pay for mine with whatever the pavilion needs heaviest."

Tie Jin, who had been listening from the furnace door in the dark, said without showing himself: "You're the sixteen-bun boy. I heard about you from the island. You can have hours too. Bring the other small smith's reading and I'll test the both of you at once." He came out into the firelight long enough to nod at the cuff. "Hang it."

So Lin Hao took his first failed piece to the failure wall, and Tie Jin gave him an iron hook, and he hung it among the strangers' catastrophes — the cracked fittings, the folded joints, the shapes that had stopped being shapes — and put no name on it, because the wall did not ask for names, only that the piece stay.

On the way back through the gate he stopped under the sign, and read it again, and said, to Wulin, the last thing he planned to say about the matter for a while:

"The metal of the armor starts tonight. Both of us. Not one word. Two."

"Two," Wulin agreed.

Behind them, in the pavilion's small fire, a cuff-shaped gap of nothing was worth more than any piece of armor either of them had ever finished — because finished armor tells you what you can do, and the wall tells you what you're allowed to learn.

Somewhere over the condemned end block, Lao Zhou's tree branch caught the last of the light, and held it, the way it held everything: the frost, the secret, and the first night of two smiths buying their own fire one failed wrist guard at a time.

## Part 1: The Third

The vortex grew to five meters before Gu Yue let it land.

"Go," she said gently, and the whirlpool of fused wind and water went out onto Spirit Ice Plaza like a housewife's rag the size of weather.

The plaza hadn't even been dirty — dust, a night's leaf-fall, nothing disgraceful — which made the result more absurd, not less. Dust rose in a frenzy, whirled once around the hurricane, and was sucked inside; the flagstone came out from under it as though scrubbed by a brush that had also forgiven the stone. Lin Hao, standing the margin with two buckets he no longer had a reason to hold, watched it the way he watched a master pour: the woman moved at a tenth of combat speed, and the plaza surrendered a third at a time.

At the third she stopped, drained the whirlpool — black now, and heavy — down the plaza drains, and walked off to sit cross-legged where the stone was cleanest. Nobody suggested she do more.

"I'd be embarrassed," said Xie Xie, grinning the mischievous grin, "if I let Gu Yue do all of it."

"Then you can treat us to dinner tonight," Wulin said.

"Sure," said Xie Xie, "as long as *you're* not coming. The two girls eat like people. If we add you, I'd be concerned the restaurant even has stock. I swear your stomach is an endless hole."

"You're so insincere."

"Fine! I'll treat everyone. But you finish those black buns before we go out."

The rest of the morning and the early afternoon went to the room, and Lin Hao, with the pavilion's afternoon fire unclaimed, went to buy his first hours from Tie Jin — which was why he was not present for the furnishing, and why he heard about it afterward from Xie Xie in the tone of a man who had been used as a tool.

"It turns out," Xie Xie reported, in the courtyard, while Wulin was still at the wood yard, "that daggers are for cutting plank. Three souls, seven knives, and my captain used me as a saw. The beds are decent. The cloth divider Gu Yue hung herself — wind, obviously, she didn't even get on a stool."

The room had shaped up, and kept down. Beds where bunks had been; the broken panes closed; the curtain down the middle, boys to the warm wall, girls to the window. But nothing fine — Wulin had walked the slum flank first and counted the doors. Three or four rooms in the whole barracks showed recent life, and those were as plain on the outside as their own. Working students did not feather their nests here. It was tradition, and Wulin understood traditions the way he understood armor: you did not test the weakest plate first.

Only two things had been issued at registration besides the dark-green uniforms, and Lin Hao turned the second over in his hand while the others rested: the Shrek identification card. Metal, not wood, with soul circuits visible in it like veins under skin — needed to pass any gate on the grounds. A fine piece of work. He read it the way he read everything made, and what he read was this: a card that knew where you went was a card that could be asked where you had been. Every gate that accepted it was a pen, and the book it wrote in was not the cardholder's.

He put it in his pocket with the rest of his ledgers, and went to the pavilion to buy his first hours with work: pouring for Tie Jin while the scrap-master watched his wrists instead of the metal, and starting the second wrist guard out of another unclaimed off-cut, which folded at the sixth strike instead of the fourth. Failure moving later. On the failure wall, Tie Jin watched him hang the second cuff beside the first, and said only: 'It's learning to wait. So are you.'

The job paid at the administration window on the way back: one hundred contribution points, each, printed onto the metal cards in a small grey notation.

One hundred points. Lin Hao, standing at the window, watched the number and did the pricing the steward clearly expected nobody to do. Meals in the outer-court hall were paid in points. Five working students, three squares, and a captain whose bloodline ran a restaurant tab the fish themselves feared. One hundred points fed the five of them for a day. A day.

The points were not pay. The points were a leash with a dial on it, and the dial read: *work, or don't eat.*

## Part 2: Two Envelopes

There were two letters waiting on the boys' bunk when he got back to the room.

The first was coarse paper and a stamped seal, and it said what Tie Jin's wire had already told the city it would say: the Shrek branch of the Blacksmiths' Association summoned the fifth-rank Master Craftsman Lin Hao to bring his hands and his proof — rank registration on the continent's terms, no card needed, the card being the thing the Association existed to issue. The smiths' long wire, laid down before he had ever seen Shrek, had followed him across the map the way money follows a pour: slowly, and without asking permission.

The second was grey-edged paper, and it smelled, faintly and impossibly, like the inside of a filing cabinet.

He had seen that paper before. Eastsea. Three employees in one morning giving him the same look over the same counter, and a man in grey pocketing his name card like a man pockets a coin he means to spend.

He opened it. Wulin came in while he was reading the enclosure — came in quietly, because Wulin walked quietly when Lin Hao was doing arithmetic, the way you don't startle a man at a forge.

"What is it?"

Lin Hao handed him the letter. Wulin read the offer, and his captain's face got slowly more dangerous, the face he wore when a thing in front of him was broken and standing in his way.

Full sponsorship. Tuition dissolved like smoke in a banker's palm. Research placement in a Pagoda foundry. Spirit-soul access from the vaults that *made* spirit souls — ten-thousand-tier workshop stock, the kind men's grandmasters mortgaged estates to bid on. A stipend the point-dial would never have reached. Signed, with the precise courtesy of people who have never once needed to raise their voice: the Spirit Pagoda.

He looked up. "This is better than Shrek. All of this — the room, the points, the brooms — the Pagoda offered you the opposite of it."

"Dozens of times." Lin Hao sat on the bunk, and for once did not do the thing his voice was trained to do, the thing where the honest truth went through the margin and came out smaller. He said it flat, full size. "In my life, Wulin, no one has disappointed me the way this academy has. Seriously. I have had better offers dozens of times than anything this place has given us. I'm not joking. Mostly from the Spirit Pagoda."

Wulin didn't argue with the feeling. He sat down on the other bunk, and for a moment he looked like the boy who'd spent the same seven years over the same kind of anvil, because he had, in the city at the other end of the map.

"Blacksmiths too?"

"Blacksmiths especially." Lin Hao's thumb moved along the grey edge of the envelope — the old grain-read, done on paper now. "The smithing life is the honest one. The Association knows exactly what my hands are worth because their own hands are the same hands. Five years of letters from guild branches I've never visited, all opening the same way: *We are acquainted with your work.*" He almost smiled. "They don't want me as a student. They want the work a fifth rank makes. That's a clean offer. The Pagoda is the other kind — they don't want the work. They want the *boy the work came from.*"

"And the academy?" Wulin said, very quietly. The curtain on the girls' side had stopped moving entirely.

"The academy wanted a broom and a hundred points a day." He said it without heat, which made it worse the way ledger truth is worse for being calm. "Do you know what the fifth-rank Master Craftsman sitting in this room is worth to a metal market right now? I don't need to know it — Tie Jin knew it from one pour. That man would pay me to let me work. The academy pays me a leash. *That's* the disappointment, Wulin. Not the slum. The slum is honest too — nobody pretended the room wasn't a slum. The disappointment is that the greatest academy on the continent, the one that's supposed to be the whole continent's highest bidder, looked at my file and saw one working student with a bucket."

He tapped the enclosure's unregistered line.

"They didn't see this. The Pagoda *can't not* see it. Which of them do you think gets the better of me in the end?"

Wulin said nothing. The curtain rustled on the girls' side, and did not move otherwise — if Gu Yue was listening, she was listening like weather, invisibly and completely.

"Look at the enclosure," Lin Hao said.

Wulin turned the page.

It was a list. Not a threat — a *manifest.* His file, as the Pagoda kept it: the Eastsea awakening registry, year and mark and witness; every counter of the Spirit Ascension Platform his card had ever touched; every purchase the Pagoda had ever sold him, dated and priced; the assessors' notes, three clerks' names attached to the same morning, with the careful language of men who write what they have seen rather than what they understand. The man in grey's name card. Long Hengxu's awareness of it, recorded in a margin line in someone else's hand.

And at the bottom, in a newer ink, one line that did not resolve: *Second spirit-soul signature, four-ring reading, origin unregistered. Classification pending.*

"Too much," Lin Hao said. "They have too much of my information already. They have the whole book of the boy I was when I came through their counters. And this last line" — he tapped it, once — "is the one they actually wrote the letter for. They count everything. They count what they can't explain more than anything."

The room was quiet. Under it, very far inside him, the dark water of his country sat without a ripple, the coil at the bottom holding still the way it had held under Su Wen's mirror; and the storm-sky above had gone dark with clouds moving the wrong direction. The spirits did not speak. They never spoke. They were weather and water, and they had weathered worse than a clerk's envelope.

"So that's the offer," Wulin said slowly. He set the pages down on the bunk between them, flat, the way he set things he meant to answer in full. "Full vaults. No points. No slum. A room where the hot water is a *right* and not a hike across a plaza." He looked up, and his eyes were perfectly steady, because Wulin did not beg, even for this. "Are you going to take it?"

## Part 3: The Price of Staying

"No," said Lin Hao.

He said it the way he said a temperature read: immediate, uninteresting, final.

"Not because the room's fine. The room's bad. The points are a leash. One hundred points for a day of us — I priced it at the window; that's not tuition, that's a clock." He stacked the two envelopes against each other on his knee, the smiths' coarse paper and the Pagoda's grey. "I've had the better offer on paper since before I could grow a proper callus. Here's the thing about paper. Paper lists what they'll give you. It can't list what you'd be leaving, because the things you'd be leaving aren't inventory."

He nodded at the failed cuff line, which wasn't visible through any wall, and at the courtyard with the tree, which wasn't either, and at the curtain where Gu Yue was being weather.

"An elder of the Pavilion told me a man's request is an easement and a boy's request is a firework. Same arithmetic applies to a man's choice. A boy goes to the Pagoda for what's in the vault. A man looks at the Pagoda and asks the question their own file answers." He picked up the grey envelope. "What kind of institution writes a boy's whole life down and then *offers* it to him, Wulin? That's not recruitment. That's a merchant showing you his ledger to prove he can afford you. Nobody shows you his ledger unless he's afraid you'll walk."

He folded the enclosure once, along the unregistered-signature line, and put it away in the bag with his own book — not the one Shrek read, and not the one the Pagoda read. The third ledger.

"They've been pricing me for years," he said. "They just haven't worked out that I'm the one who reads prices. They keep that book because they're afraid of what the book doesn't contain yet — the signature they can't file, the ten-thousand-year reading nobody sold me. The day I ever knock on their door, I don't knock as a name in their registry. I knock as the man who already knows exactly what's in their ledger, because they sent it to me in an envelope and tried to call it a gift."

Wulin was quiet for a moment. Then he did the Wulin thing, the thing that made him captain at thirteen: he did not argue, he settled.

"Then we should be fed," he said. "Tonight's free. First day only — the steward said so, the steward's clock said so, and I intend to argue with it at every window in the hall." He stood, and the floorboards took his weight with the usual misplaced confidence. "You know, that envelope offered you vault stock. I'm about to do something in a dining hall that gets a discipline committee summoned."

"Of course you are," said Xie Xie, who had been listening from the other bunk for entirely some time. "Wait, dinner? I treat? I said that under duress. Also I take it back — and also whatever he's planning, I hereby pre-deny everything, three of me, unanimously, in advance."

## Part 4: Wicked

The dining hall held a thousand and looked built to feed that many twice.

Every seat in the outer court seemed to be in it — noise, steam, windows of food, the particular roar of an entire school deciding at once that the day was over. Working students ate on points; the first day's meals were free; the free line was the only thing about the evening that was ordinary.

Wulin found a large table.

Then he began.

He went from window to window with his metal card and his radiant, law-abiding smile, and at each window he asked for, and received, the amount of food a working student might reasonably accumulate if a working student were preparing for winter and also were two men. The table began to grow a landscape. He came back with more. The table developed layers. By the third level of food — trays stacked on plates stacked on the generosity of a man testing exactly how far a rule could be bent without being broken — the hall had begun, as a hall will, to watch.

Xiaoyan watched with the quiet awe of a surveyor watching a mountain happen. Gu Yue watched Wulin, which was its own layer of landscape. Xie Xie watched the doors for the management.

The management came.

A stern man around twenty, with a red armband and the walk of a person the building had told on someone to, crossed the hall to the table.

"I'm Xie Peichen," he said, "of the discipline committee." He looked at the table for ten — piled with enough food to feed thirty — and at the boy standing by it with sparkling white teeth. "Which class are you from? Why did you get so much food? Don't you know that according to the academy's rules, if you waste food, you pay a fine of ten times its weight?"

Wulin stopped mid-step. He turned, radiance unshaken.

"Hello, senior," he said. "I can finish all of this food."

"You can finish all of this. By yourself." The senior's voice went up an octave, because it had nowhere else to go.

"Yeah. I can finish it all myself. I've still got four friends joining me though," Wulin said, sincerely, and for exactly one heartbeat the discipline committee's eyes met Lin Hao's across the table, and Lin Hao's face was the face of a man whose ledger column had just come up empty.

"Four people can finish all of this?"

Wulin nodded earnestly.

"All right," said Xie Peichen, with the dark optimism of an official standing on solid rule for the first time all evening. "Let's see you eat it all. If you can't finish, don't blame me for being rude." He took up a position to the side, folded his arms, and watched.

Wulin smiled.

"Senior," he said, "how about we make a bet? If I finish all of this food, you'll help me get another round. If I can't, you can punish me as you wish."

Xie Peichen agreed immediately.

Lin Hao sat down at the table, because there was no longer anything to do but witness, and because witness was the one thing he was unfailingly willing to provide for this captain. He took his portion of a black bun to blunt his own edge, and in the noise of the hall, with Wulin rolling up his sleeves across a three-level mountain of food, he allowed himself one last thought about the grey envelope, small enough to fit in a ledger margin:

*They named a price for me tonight. So did this hall. A hundred points for a day, and a mountain of free food for the man who can clear it. Fine. I'll take the day rate. I'll do the hours. And I'll keep the third book — the one nobody gets to read — until I know exactly what I'm spending it on.*

The captain took his first bite.

Somewhere across the outer court, a blacksmith's summons waited for morning. Somewhere in a filing cabinet that smelled like paper and future, a page in a grey-edged folder sat with its newest line still unclassified. And at a table for ten in a hall of one thousand, Tang Wulin began to eat, and the discipline committee of Shrek Academy settled in, smiling the smile of a man who had not yet read the last column of the ledger.
