## Part 1: The Mountain Cleared

The bet was lost, in the end, not at any single plate but at the moment Xie Peichen stopped counting them.

He had been back three times. The third time he carried ten orders of the dish that looked like sea cucumber and did not, on the return walk, look at the dishes at all; he looked at the floor in front of his feet, the way a man carries something he has agreed to carry and wishes only to put down. He set the ten plates down in the gap that Lin Hao had been quietly clearing for them — moving empty stacks one centimeter at a time, no gesture, no eye contact, the margin doing the work of a busboy — and Tang Wulin beamed at him.

"Senior," Wulin said, "can I trouble you for —"

"No," said Xie Peichen. It was the first complete sentence he had managed in twenty minutes. "No. I resign. You finished. You finished it all. I don't know what the second round was even for, because you appear to be on a fourth."

The discipline-committee armband was very red against his sleeve. His ledger, Lin Hao noted, had come up entirely empty; there was a particular look a man got when the column he had been so confident about simply had no number in it, and Xie Peichen had that look the way other men had a face.

The crowd had gathered like moths. A ring of Shrek students stood three deep around the table for ten, watching the mountain of empty plates grow the way people watch weather. "Did this guy starve to death in a past life?" somebody said, with real wonder. "Heavens, don't tell me he cleared all those dishes himself." And then, with the deep respect of the young for appetite: "Awesome. I've always admired people who can eat a lot."

It was into this that the manager arrived — a middle-aged man with a grim, pinched face, who had been pulled from his office by a kitchen reporting, impossibly, a shortage. They overstocked every day. They had never once run short. He came in trembling with the outrage of a man whose ledgers have been insulted, saw the staggering pile of dishes, and understood his shortage in the flesh.

"Hey. You. Student." His voice came out thin. "Your stomach is beyond the realm of normal. The Academy cannot feed someone like you. If you ate this much every meal, I will petition to have your right to a free meal revoked."

Wulin blinked. He had a bun halfway to his mouth.

"Teacher," he said, "you don't have to worry. I'm a working student — I can't eat this much for free starting tomorrow anyway. This is my last free meal. So can't I eat my fill?"

The ring of students changed expression all at once.

Lin Hao watched it go through them like a wind over a field — the leaning-in, the delight in spectacle, draining out to be replaced by something else entirely. *Working student.* The moths remembered they had somewhere else to be. The peanut gallery dissolved backward into the hall, minding its own business with sudden, devout attention to its own trays.

"So you're a working student," the manager said. His grimness did not leave, but it turned itself around, the way a man turns a blade he has decided not to use. "Alright then. Have a good meal." He left.

"Why," Xie Peichen said, with the hollow precision of a man reconstructing a disaster, "didn't you tell me you were a working student earlier?"

"What about being a working student?" Wulin asked, genuinely curious.

Xie Peichen made a sound in his throat, refused to pay him any further attention, and disappeared into the crowd — a committee man returning to his committee with, Lin Hao suspected, a brand-new column in his ledger labeled with a single name and no number at all.

The buns came after that. An older girl set a steamed bun on Wulin's plate and went off, muttering over her shoulder that it was pitiful, a boy that hungry still not full. Then another student. Then another. Wulin's eye corner twitched, and Lin Hao saw the captain's mind do the thing it did — turn charity immediately, and without shame, into logistics. *One hundred points is five or six ordinary meals. The cheapest dish is ten. Today cost over a thousand. Come tomorrow —*

"Come tomorrow," Lin Hao said quietly, across the wreckage of the table, "we price it properly. You're not starving on a dial while I hold a smith's wage. That's arithmetic, not charity."

Wulin looked at him. Then he nodded, once, and put the next bun in his mouth.

He staggered out of the hall at last, walking the way a man walks when each step brings him closer to bursting. The four of them fell in around him in the dusk light of Spirit Ice Plaza.

"Captain," Xie Xie said, wearing an odd expression, "can't you restrain yourself a bit? Everyone in the outer court recognizes you by now."

"How will restraint feed me?" Wulin said, wide-eyed. "Do you have any idea how painful it is to be hungry?"

"Fine. Pretend I didn't say anything."

"You know, I seem to remember someone saying he'd treat us all to dinner. Let's go."

"You're — *still* hungry?"

"I'll be done digesting by the time we get there," Wulin said, and herded them toward the outer-court street. Lin Hao went with them, because witness was the one thing he was unfailingly willing to provide for this captain, and because the smith's summons in his bag said *morning*, and the evening was otherwise unclaimed.

## Part 2: The Street of Orange Lights

The outer court at night was a town. It had shops. It had strings of warm orange lights over the street, and the lights were full of people in Shrek uniform moving in every direction with the particular confidence of people who had passed a gate most people could not pass. Xie Xie herded them through it like a tour guide who had been somewhere once.

"The outer court is practically a town itself," he announced. "We've got to explore. This place sells *drinks* — look, Shrek has this kind of thing too. Juice. Ice cream. Come on, I'm treating."

"You lost the bet," Gu Yue observed. "You are treating because you lost."

"I'm treating because I'm generous. There's a difference."

"There is not," said Xu Xiaoyan, already making for the door of the busiest shop on the street.

The drink shop was near capacity, warm and loud, full of uniforms and the clink of cups. They fought their way to a table the way people fight onto a raft — Xie Xie spotting it, Gu Yue freezing the legs of the chair across the gap with a thread of ice so nobody could pull it out, Xiaoyan sliding into it sideways like an eel — and a server dashed over. Juice for the boys; ice cream for the girls, who dug in with the focused joy that, the canon of the entire world suggested, no girl could resist, not even the detached Gu Yue.

Xie Xie sat with his back to the wall and his eyes moving over the room.

"What are you looking at?" Wulin nudged him.

Xie Xie smirked. "Scouting. I'm seeing whether there are any pretty senior sisters here. A man has to prepare for adulthood."

"How," Wulin said, with honest doubt, "does looking prepare you?"

Lin Hao did not answer this. He had taken the seat that let him see the door — not out of caution, there was nothing in this room to be cautious of, but out of the same quiet reflex that made him clear plates one centimeter at a time: he liked to know where the entrances were, the way other people liked to know where the exits were. It meant he saw the door open.

It opened twice in the next minute. The first time it let in a wall of a boy in Shrek uniform — an outer-court senior like the girl behind him, round and pink and beaming with the particular radiance of a person who has smelled food from a great distance and followed it home. The second time it let in the girl behind him.

Lin Hao's eyes went past the boy — who had stopped dead in the doorway, nostrils flaring, his whole being arrested by the sight of Wulin across a crowded room with the remnants of ice cream at his corner — and landed on the girl, and stayed there, in the margin, for one held half-second.

He knew her. He would have known her in a darker room than this. Stargod Sword at her hip, hilt worn the way a tool wears that is used every single day; three rings under the skin of her, kept dimmed in a shop — two yellow and the third a thousand-year purple that had not been there at the exhibition, the mark of a Soul Elder who had not spent the last four months standing still; the set of her shoulders like she was always half a breath from deciding something. Ye Xinglan. A senior of the outer court now, an inner-court blade sent down where the real forging happened. Four months on the Track, to his nine days. Thirty-one seconds of sparring, in which her confidence had not moved at all. The girl who had decided, once, that she would like to be the one who said something first.

She had not seen him yet.

He watched her look around the shop — and here is what he watched, because it was not what he expected.

## Part 3: What The Sword Did

Ye Xinglan had come in for ice cream, which she would never have admitted to Lizhi, who had already abandoned her in the doorway and was now moving toward a table of strangers with the unstoppable momentum of a meatball rolling downhill. She let him go. She did her own scan of the room, the way she always did, the way she did everything — quickly, decisively, forming an opinion and then telling herself about it later.

Her scan passed over the room and snagged.

There was a boy at a table by the wall.

That was wrong as a first thought, because "boy" was not the right word and she knew it the instant her eyes landed. He was tall — taller than she remembered people being, though she couldn't have said who she was comparing him to — and he was sitting down, which made the tallness worse, because it meant most of him was still not on display. He was broad across the shoulders in the particular way of someone who had stopped being fed and started being *built*, and he had a jaw that had finished whatever argument a jaw has with a face and won it. Black hair, a little long, pushed back behind one ear. Hands around a cup of juice that were too big for the cup and still somehow gentle with it — smith's hands, she thought, or swordsman's, the kind of hands that knew their own strength so well they never had to show it.

The worst part — and Ye Xinglan, who decided things, was immediately furious about the worst part — was the stillness. The whole shop moved: servers dashed, uniforms leaned and laughed, Lizhi was even now descending on the fat boy at the table with a cry of recognition. And this one sat in the middle of all of it like a stone in a stream, the water going around him. Not cold. Not aloof. *Still.* The stillness of something that had already decided where it was going to be and had gotten there ahead of everyone else.

She realized, with a slow and total horror, that she was still looking.

Ye Xinglan did not do this. She was the girl who decided things and told Lizhi about them later, usually while he was eating. She had looked at the three-purple-ring boy at the exhibition four months ago and her confidence had not *moved* — she had measured a prodigy in thirty-one seconds and filed him under *fast, will be interesting later*, and gone back to her sword. She did not stand in the doorways of drink shops being snagged on strangers like a cloak on a nail. It was inefficient. It was undignified. She decided, with great firmness, that she would not look again.

She looked again.

And something happened that she did not understand at all.

The Stargod Sword at her hip — the martial soul that lived half in her and half in the steel, that sparked like fallen stars when it stood in the presence of sword-force worth the name — did not spark.

It *quieted*.

Ye Xinglan's hand went to the hilt before she decided to move it. The blade under her palm was still, in a way she had only ever felt it once or twice in her life: not empty, not dormant. *Attentive.* The way a dog goes still when a wolf walks past the fire. It was the sword's version, she realized with a cold, electric jolt up her wrist, of holding its breath.

She looked at the stranger's face again — the handsome, grown, impossible face of a boy she was absolutely certain she had never met — and her sword, which had never once been wrong about a swordsman in her life, told her in the language of perfect silence that she was in the presence of something her blade considered, deeply and without argument, its better.

That was impossible. She was a Soul Elder now — three rings, the third a thousand years old — and one of the most diligent sword-consciousness students in the outer court; she trained the man-and-sword-as-one state the way other people ate, and there were perhaps four blades in the whole outer court she respected, every one of them a senior she had measured at length. She knew all of their faces, and none of them was this one.

This was not one of them.

This was not —

She was crossing the room. She noticed she was crossing the room approximately three steps into crossing it, which was also not how she operated; she formed opinions *before* she acted, it was her single most reliable trait. She could not, for the life of her, decide what she was going to say. This had been her entire complaint, four months ago — *I would like to be the one who says something first for once* — and here she was, presented with a perfect stranger her sword had knelt to, walking at him without a single word prepared.

She opened her mouth. She would say something first. She would. It was her turn.

"You," she said, and her voice came out, to her complete and withering fury, not the way she had decided it would come out at all.

---

## Part 4: The Boy Under The Man

The tall stranger looked up at her.

And Ye Xinglan's prepared sentence — whatever it was, she still did not know — died entirely, because when he looked up she saw his eyes.

They were dark and steady and far, far too old for the handsome young face they were set in. And she knew them.

She knew them the way you know a doorframe you walked past as a child and come back to find the house rebuilt around it. The face was a stranger's. The eyes were not. She had looked into those eyes for thirty-one seconds while her Stargod Sword threw stars at a boy who was not where he had been standing four times out of five. She had watched those eyes stop tracking her body and start tracking, with a calm that had genuinely unsettled her, where she was *going to be*.

"Oh," Ye Xinglan said.

The stranger set down his juice cup, gently, with the too-big hands.

"Ye Xinglan," he said.

It was not a question. He had known her since the door opened — she could see that now, read it in the margin of him the way she read sword-force: he had watched her scan the room, watched her snag, watched her walk over, and said nothing, and let her arrive. He had been watching her the entire time, and she, the girl who decided things, had decided nothing at all.

"You," she said again, and this time she heard her own voice do something she did not care for, something thin and off-balance. "You're —" She stopped. She rebuilt. She was Ye Xinglan; she decided things and told people about them later. "You are the boy from the exhibition. The three rings. The Track."

"The same," Lin Hao said. "Though it's four rings now. And you took four months to learn the Track. I took nine days. I believe I owe Lizhi a thank-you for keeping score."

Across the table, Wulin — who had been staring at the round boy bearing down on him with the glazed joy of a man watching his dessert arrive with legs — finally placed the situation. "Xinglan?" he said. "And — is that *Lizhi*?"

"IT IS," the round boy bellowed, crashing into the table like a friendly ship running aground. "Tang Wulin! I smelled you from the street, I mean I smelled the *food*, I mean — are you going to finish that ice cream?" He did not wait for an answer. He turned, beaming, to Lin Hao, and did a small double-take that he visibly powered through with the force of goodwill. "And you! The other one! The quiet one who hit — wait." Lizhi blinked. He looked Lin Hao up and down the way he looked at a banquet table. "Wait. You got *big*. Were you this big? You weren't this big. You were a normal size. I would have remembered this size, I remember sizes."

"Nobody remembers sizes, Lizhi," Ye Xinglan said, without looking at him. Her eyes had not left Lin Hao's face. "They remember whether there was enough food."

"There is never enough food," Lizhi said, with conviction, and sat down, and that was that.

She was still standing. She noticed she was still standing, and that the entire table — the ice-cream girl, the pretty one with the frost on her sleeve, the dagger-boy who had been scouting the room and was now watching with open amusement, the captain, and him — had an empty chair she was not taking.

She took it. She decided to take it. She told herself, firmly, that she had decided to take it.

"Four rings," she said, because rings were safe ground, rings were a thing she could measure. "You said four. What colors."

He tilted his head a fraction. It was the smallest thing, but her sword, under her hand where she had not removed it, went quieter still.

"Three purple," he said. "And one black."

The table did not know what that meant. Xie Xie's scouting smirk stayed on his face. Xu Xiaoyan's spoon paused. But Ye Xinglan felt the Stargod Sword do the thing it had done in the doorway — the held breath, the wolf at the fire — and understood now, in the hush of her own blade, why the handsome stranger in the chair was a stranger at all.

The boy she had sparred for thirty-one seconds had not merely grown into his face. He had crossed some distance she could not see the far side of, in four months — the same four months in which she herself had broken through to a third ring, won a thousand-year spirit, and climbed the sword-consciousness ladder rung by rung, proud of every hard step. He had been a fast child with three purple rings and a movement trick. The thing sitting across from her in a too-tall body with a black ring and a sword that made her sword go silent had gone somewhere she had not even known there was a road to.

And she had walked across a drink shop because she thought he was handsome.

Ye Xinglan, who decided things and told Lizhi about them later while he ate, sat in the warm orange light of the loudest shop in the outer court and discovered, with a slow, burning, furious, completely un-decidable clarity, that she could not have decided to look away even if she had formed the opinion first.

"Thirty-one seconds," she said, at last. It came out level. She was proud of it for coming out level. "Last time. You were fast and you couldn't decide where to stand, so you decided where I would stand instead."

"I remember," Lin Hao said.

"I am not," said Ye Xinglan, "the same swordswoman I was four months ago either."

It was a challenge. It came out as a challenge, because everything she said came out as a decision, and she decided, right there in the drink shop with Lizhi stealing Wulin's ice cream and Xie Xie leaning in to watch like it was the best scouting result of his entire life, that she would not be the only one at this table who had crossed a distance.

The stranger with her sparring-partner's eyes looked at her for a long, steady moment — and smiled, just slightly, the kind of smile that did not show teeth and did not promise anything and made her, to her deep and lasting annoyance, glad she had sat down.

"I'd noticed," he said. "Your sword's been holding its breath since you walked in the door. Mine's been waiting to see if yours would say something about it."

Ye Xinglan's hand tightened on the hilt.

"You have a sword," she said. It was not a question.

"I have several," Lin Hao said. "But I think you already knew that. Yours told you before you did."

Outside, on the street of orange lights, the Shrek night went on around them — full of uniforms and voices and a thousand people who had no idea that in a crowded drink shop two swordswomen, one of them a girl who had just lost every bit of her famous decisiveness and would not admit it for anything in the world, had sat down at the same table for the first time in four months.

Lizhi, his mouth full of stolen ice cream, looked from his oldest friend's rigid back to the tall quiet boy she had planted herself beside, and did the one thing he was genuinely, reliably good at besides eating.

He decided not to say a word about it.

He told himself he would tell her later. Usually while she was eating.

---

*He was the same boy. He was not the same boy at all. I walked across a room because of a face, and my sword walked across it because of something else, and the worst part — the part I will not tell Lizhi, the part I will tell absolutely no one — is that I don't think he was surprised to see me. I think he's been sitting by the door all night. I think he always sits by the door. And I think, when I walked over, he already knew I would.*

*That's the thing I have to decide about. I haven't decided it yet. I, Ye Xinglan, who decides things, have not decided it.*

## Part 1: The Late Celebration

The toast came after the ice cream, which was the wrong order and therefore exactly the order Wulin would choose.

"Congratulations, everyone," he said, raising his cup of juice like it was a goblet at a banquet and he was not, ten minutes earlier, a boy who had eaten a mountain. "We made it into Shrek Academy. Let's call this a late celebration."

Gu Yue and Xu Xiaoyan perked up at that, their ice cream forgotten on the table. The five of them — six, now, with Xu Lizhi folded happily into the wreckage of Wulin's dessert, and Ye Xinglan in the chair she had told herself she had decided to take — exchanged the particular smile of people who had survived an exam that failed most of a continent. Strength, potential, secondary profession, character, patience: a single failed trial and none of them would be sitting in this warm orange light. They were sitting in it.

"Here's to not having failed anything," Xie Xie said, and drank.

"Here's to food that doesn't cost contribution points," Lizhi said, around a spoon he had not been offered.

"Here's to the door that doesn't close," said Xiaoyan, which made Lin Hao glance at her, because Xiaoyan usually said the light thing and that had not been the light thing.

They drank. The shop was loud and full and warm. And then Xie Xie, who had been scanning the room all night with the focused industry of a boy preparing for adulthood, leaned in with the air of a man about to share state secrets.

"Haven't you heard of Shrek's Sea God's Fated Date Festival?"

Wulin blinked. "The what?"

"The Fated Date Festival. If you're inner court and a certain age, you qualify. It's a grand occasion for the whole inner court — even outer court students catch glimpses of it later. Ten thousand years it's been held, straight. Countless couples sprang up there." Xie Xie's eyes were shining. "Legend says the Spirit Ice Douluo and the Dragon Butterfly Douluo started dating at that very festival."

"You're already thinking about those things at your age?" Wulin said, with the genuine distress of a boy whose only romance was with his next meal. "We're too young for that. Besides, you have to get into the inner court first. We've a long way to go. Think about student number two — the one who beat you into a pulp in the trials. He's that strong and he isn't even inner court."

"I'll figure it out," Xie Xie said, bouncing, "once I have a target."

It was at the word *target* that Lin Hao, who had been watching the door the way he always did, became aware that the temperature on his left had dropped.

Not by much. Not enough for anyone else. The juice shop was warm, and full of bodies, and the orange lights threw heat-colored light over everything. But the side of him closest to Gu Yue had gone the way a window goes cold when the night wind finds the seam in the frame.

He looked at her.

She was not looking at him. She was looking at her ice cream, which she had been eating with the focused joy of a girl who had found one thing in the world that asked nothing of her — and which was now, untouched for the length of the toast and the festival speech, melting. A slow silver bead of it was running down the side of the glass. Gu Yue, who could count the elements in a room and name the wind's direction by the ache in her teeth, had not noticed her dessert turning to soup.

"Ten thousand years," Gu Yue said, in the flat, level voice she used for things she had already judged, "of a festival, and the best story they can tell is that two people who were going to end up together anyway ended up together." She did not look up. "That isn't fate. That's arithmetic taking its time."

Xie Xie opened his mouth. "That's — that's romantic—"

"It's inefficient," said Gu Yue.

And Lin Hao did the thing he had trained himself to do across a hundred rooms where her mood was weather: he did not read it. He watched the frost crawl a finger's width up the side of her melting glass — the cold answering her the way it always did, the elements leaning toward her like reeds toward water — and he filed it under *she's practicing*, under *the elements answer her and it is not addressed to me*, under the careful, locked heading he had built the day she said nothing and he decided that a nothing was a no and he would not say the thing twice.

He did not see, because he was not looking for it, that the frost was not on her glass.

It had started on her glass. It was climbing toward his.

## Part 2: The Boy Who Bought a Shop

The commotion at the next table saved him from having to decide what any of that was.

"Waitress! Over here!" someone shouted, and then, with an arrogance you could have stood a spoon in: "Give me your number."

The whole shop turned. A young man sat at the neighboring table in a white suit — no Shrek uniform, which was its own statement in a room three-quarters full of people who had killed to wear one. He was a year or two older than them, with hair like spun gold combed back and held against any wind, and eyes the color of the gold in his hair, and there was a strange air to him as though his existence gave off light. Of everyone in the shop, Lin Hao thought, only Wulin could rival the looks — and even Wulin, who was presently wiping ice cream off his chin, could not rival the overbearingness.

The waitress standing in front of him had jade-white skin and short fiery-red hair and large black eyes, and the kind of beauty that made men want to stand between her and things. She was not standing the way a person stands when they want to be looked at.

"I'm sorry," she said politely. "That is out of the scope of my job responsibilities."

"Then what will it take for me to get your number?"

She shook her head and turned to leave.

"What kind of service is this?" The young man's palm hit the table, loud as a slap. "Get me your manager." And here was the thing Lin Hao watched with the cold interest of a man reading a ledger: the students in Shrek uniforms, the ones who had fought spirit beasts in the Great Star Dou for the right to be arrogant themselves, looked over, saw who it was, and *looked away*.

"Who is he," Xiaoyan murmured, "that even here, people avert their eyes?"

"Someone the uniforms have been told not to touch," Lin Hao said quietly. "Watch. The room will tell us before he does."

The manager came, polite and firm — could not divulge staff information. The owner came, polite and firmer — would not divulge employee privacy no matter what. The young man narrowed his golden eyes.

"So you won't agree no matter what."

The owner nodded.

"Fine." He rose. He snapped his fingers. A finely dressed man stood from a nearby table, approached, and bowed slightly. "Young master. Your command?"

"Negotiate with the owner. I want to buy this drink shop."

Xie Xie's mouth corner twitched. Wulin sighed the sigh of a boy from a town where money was for flour and forge-coal. "These city people sure know how to play."

The butler — Sun Bo, he introduced himself, with a smile and a golden card passed low across the owner's palm — led Boss Yang aside. One look at the card and the owner's eyes had gone wide. They were gone perhaps two minutes. When they came back the butler spoke with the measured disinterest of a man ordering water: "Young master, I've negotiated a price with Boss Yang, and payment has already been sent. From now on, this drink shop is your property."

The shops around Shrek Academy had property values that did not bear thinking about. The young man did not bear thinking about them. He flicked his gaze back to Boss Yang.

"Give me her number."

Across the table, Gu Yue did something she rarely did. She made a sound — a single, cold, perfectly audible *snort*, the kind that came out of the nose and said more than a paragraph.

"Money," she said, to no one and therefore to everyone, "is the laziest kind of wanting. He doesn't want her. He wants the thing she said no to, to not be allowed to say no." She watched the golden-haired boy with eyes the color of winter sky. "If he'd crossed a single thing in his life instead of buying it, he'd know that a no is not a wall. It's a door that opens inward. And it is *never* for sale."

Lin Hao looked at her then, fully, because that had not been a comment about the boy in the white suit, and they both knew it, and she had built it so carefully that no one else at the table could have proved it. It was a thing said about a stranger, in the abstract, about the futility of buying what had to be given — and it landed a hand's breadth from the locked heading in his own ledger, and he did not let himself look at where it landed.

Wulin only shrugged. "It seems money can sway anyone."

Xiaoyan, who had been watching not the farce but the people at her own table, said nothing at all, and her eyes went once, slowly, from Gu Yue's profile to Ye Xinglan's back, and then to Lin Hao, and then down into her juice.

## Part 3: The Pitcher

The red-haired waitress came over to the young man's table a moment later, while Boss Yang stood aside with the face of a man who had just sold a year of his life and was trying to believe the price.

"What do you want?" she said.

He smiled. "Nothing much. I just thought you were pretty, and wanted to get to know you better."

Without a word, she began unbuttoning her apron.

"I didn't tell you to undress!" he yelped, genuinely flabbergasted.

She snorted, and threw the apron down on the table in front of him. "I quit. So I'm not your employee anymore." And she turned and walked toward the door.

The young man's smile widened. He stood, mirroring her. "Even better!" — and went after her shadow.

The table watched them go. And at Lin Hao's elbow, Ye Xinglan leaned forward the way she leaned into everything: all at once, having already decided.

"He spent a fortune," she said, half to Lin Hao, half to the room, "and she walked out anyway, and the only thing he bought was a drink shop he doesn't want." Her Stargod Sword was dim at her hip, but her voice had the edge on it that her blade did. "People who can't hear a *no* are the same in a shop or on a sparring ground. They keep buying another attempt at the same wall." She turned her head and looked right at him. "I told you I'm not the same swordswoman I was four months ago. I'd be happy to show you. Tomorrow, if you like — the practice yards are empty at dawn."

Lin Hao opened his mouth to answer.

He did not get to answer.

His juice cup was empty — it had been empty for a while; he had been doing most of the listening. Ye Xinglan, sitting on his right, was already reaching for the pitcher, her hand halfway there with the easy readiness of a girl who decided things and then did them. It was a small courtesy, nothing, a neighbor refilling a neighbor's cup.

A thread of frost moved first.

Nobody saw it move. It simply happened: the pitcher on the table was in Gu Yue's hand — she had not stood, she had barely shifted — and Lin Hao's cup was filling, the juice rising steady to the rim, poured by a girl who was not looking at him, who was looking at Ye Xinglan with the mild, pleasant expression of someone discussing the weather.

The water that went into his cup came out a degree too cold. By the time it reached the halfway mark, a lace of ice had bloomed across the pitcher's rim and was climbing down its side. By the time she set it down, the surface of his juice had a thin skin of silver across it, cracking softly as it settled.

"Thank you," Lin Hao said.

Gu Yue said nothing. Which was normal. Gu Yue said nothing most of the time; her silences were her sentences, and he had spent two years learning to read them like a man reads tides.

Except that the pitcher was rimed white with frost. Except that she had never once, in two years, poured him anything. She sat *beside* him, she put her hand on his arm when the moment was nine days old, she told him the truth about himself in three words and left him to assemble the rest — but she did not pour. She did not do small, visible, claiming things in front of other people.

She had done it now. She had done it with the frost on, and put the pitcher down between him and Ye Xinglan like a fence-post driven into the table, and then she looked back at her melting ice cream and did not say a word about any of it.

Lin Hao looked at the silver skin over his cup.

He looked at Gu Yue's profile — the black hair, the winter-sky eyes fixed on a dessert she had not eaten, the faintest line between her brows that meant she was angry at something she refused to name.

And he did not read it.

He *would not*. He had built the heading; he had honored the nothing; he was not going to be the man who watches a girl who once said nothing and decides, in the warm light of a drink shop with another girl's chair pulled up beside him, that perhaps the silence had not meant what he had decided it meant. To read the frost as a message addressed to him would be to hope. He had hoped once, plainly, six strokes of a sentence with no wind before it — *I love you* — and she had answered it with nothing, and a nothing honored was a no he could live with, and a no reopened was a wound he would not hand her the power to give him twice.

So he watched the frost climb the pitcher, and he thought: *the elements answer her. It is not addressed to me. I will not be the person who assumes every cold thing in her vicinity is a letter with my name on it.*

It was the most disciplined thing he had ever failed to see.

Ye Xinglan looked at the pitcher. Then she looked at Gu Yue. The Stargod Sword at her hip was not quiet now — it was wary, the way it was wary in the presence of an elementalist it could not measure; her own three rings, even the thousand-year purple she had fought so hard for, meant nothing against a girl whose mere mood was freezing glassware without a single ring lit. Ye Xinglan was a swordsman; swordsmen understood claims in the way other people understood weather, because a blade in a room *was* a claim. She read the frost-rimed pitcher, the melting ice cream, the winter eyes. She read it all in about three seconds, because she decided things quickly.

She decided that the boy she had walked across a room for had someone. She also decided that she did not, in fact, know that, because he had not looked at the silver-haired girl once during any of it — not with the look she was watching for. And she decided a third thing: that this was not a wall she had any interest in buying attempts at, regardless.

She settled back in her chair and left the dawn invitation on the table, unpressed, the way a real swordsman leaves a strike offered and not forced.

"Dawn's fine," she said. "If you're there."

"I'll be there," Lin Hao said. He said it the way he said things about sword-work, plainly, because a yard at dawn was the one thing in this room that did not need a cipher. "Bring the sword you used in thirty-one seconds. I'd like to meet it again — it's had four months to decide things."

Across the table, very quietly, the ice on Lin Hao's juice cup cracked.

## Part 4: The Ripple at the Door

"I can't believe something like that happens in Shrek City," Xie Xie said, already on his feet, because Xie Xie's body consistently made decisions about justice roughly two seconds before his brain had the paperwork ready. "If that's tolerated, then what isn't?"

He went after the waitress and the golden boy, out the door.

"Xie Xie — wait—" Wulin, captain to his bones, was up and moving too, pausing only to throw bills down on the table with the pained efficiency of a man who knew, in his soul, that even justice should settle its tab. "At least let me—" and he was out the door after Xie Xie.

Lin Hao was standing. He had not decided to stand; the margin stood when the captain moved, the way a compass needle moves north without being consulted. Lizhi was already peering anxiously after Wulin, the food bond thrumming. Xiaoyan had one hand on the table, ready to go.

It was at the door that it happened.

Tang Wulin, half a step outside, stopped dead — and Lin Hao, right behind him, felt it pass over all of them like the shadow of a bird the size of a weather system: a wave of soul power, enormous, the air going thick and then electric, and outside in the street the night itself seemed to flinch. Golden light climbed the sky over the orange-lit town, rising slow and inexorable, and where it touched the dark it *dispelled* the shadows — not lighting them, not fighting them, but erasing the night the way daylight erases a fog, as though something with a holy disregard for darkness had simply opened a door on the far end of the street.

The drink shop went quiet.

"Someone," Lin Hao said, very softly, into the golden-lit hush, "just hit the ground in the outer court with a soul power that turns shadows off."

He could not feel the rank of it. It was above his instrument the way the sky was above a weather vane — the vane spun, it did not measure. Beside him, Gu Yue had gone perfectly still, and for the first time all evening her face was not a winter he was refusing to read; it was a blank page turned toward the light, and he could feel her doing the thing she did when she met something that was not in her catalog: going quiet, and deep, and vast, the way the sea goes quiet before it decides whether it is going to be weather.

The frost was gone from the table. She had pulled every thread of it back into herself the way a swordsman sheathes a blade.

"We should see," said Xiaoyan, who was already moving.

Lin Hao reached the door in two long steps, Wulin and Xie Xie already visible out on the street, the golden light pouring down over both of them, over the orange lights, over the whole outer-court town that had been so warm and ordinary one breath ago and was now a stage.

He went. He went the way he always went — in the margin, a half-step behind the captain, watching where the entrances were. And as he crossed the threshold of the drink shop, over his shoulder, the frost-rimed pitcher sat on the table in the emptying booth, and Ye Xinglan sat beside it, watching the door the tall boy had gone out of, and the silver-haired girl had gone through it half a step ahead of him, so that she was the first one into the golden light.

She had not poured him anything else. She had not needed to.

The pitcher had said it.

---

*She put frost in his cup, and he told himself it was the weather in her. He had spent two years teaching himself not to read the silences of the one person he could not read, because he had read the one that mattered and she had given it back to him empty. He would not say it twice. He would not open it twice. But the pitcher had come out of her hand before she decided to move it, and the frost in that family did nothing she did not mean. He had written that down in the book she would never read — written it as a question about weather, because that was the only category he was allowed to put it in — and ruled a line under it, and he was not going to look at the line.*

*Outside the door the night is gold. I will deal with the golden light first.*

## Part 1: Two Wings, One Sky

The golden light was a young man with wings.

Lin Hao reached the street in time to see them open — pure white, unfolding from the golden-haired boy's back the way a door opens onto a room full of noon, and with them a holy aura that climbed until the orange street-lamps seemed ashamed of themselves. Three soul rings rose beneath him.

All three were purple.

"Three thousand-year rings," Xie Xie breathed, and for once there was no joke in him. "On a second-year. He's — that's the Angel Clan blood, that's not a thing you *train* to."

The red-haired girl turned around in the light. Lin Hao had time to notice that she did not look frightened; she looked tired, the way a person looks tired when a small dog has decided to be a wolf at her for the fourth time that week. Then she spread her arms, and the darkness answered her — it swirled and twisted and went solid into a pair of wings the exact opposite of his, jet-black, and a dark aura spread out against the gold like ink poured into a lit pool.

Two rings rose under her. Both purple.

"White wings are the Holy Angel," Wulin said slowly. "It's a legend. And black wings are… the other one. The Fallen Angel."

"It seems I was right." The golden-haired boy — Yue Zhengyu, he would name himself in a moment — smiled and flapped, golden light radiating. "How interesting. So very interesting. Two rings versus three. You don't stand a chance. Surrender and let me take you to be judged."

The girl pursed her lips. Her eyes flashed; darkness folded around her.

"Trying to run?" he snorted, and his first ring blazed, holy radiance surging out to dispel the dark; his second lit and he drove the light before him and flew at her on a flap of white wings. "I told you. You have two and I have three. Stop resisting."

The sneer on the girl's face was the last thing Lin Hao saw before she did the one thing nobody expected.

She furled her wings. She withdrew her martial soul entirely. The dark aura vanished, the rings sank, and she stood in the street in her apron with her hands at her sides, and she said, clearly, into the face of three thousand years of holy light:

"This is Shrek, you dumbass."

A wave of force split the clouds over the street.

It did not come from either of them. It came down from above — sharp, clean, indifferent as a god closing a book — and it obliterated the light and the dark both in the same instant and pressed the golden-haired boy out of the air and onto his knees in the road. A tall man stood in the sky, his figure indistinct, and his voice came down over the whole street like a bell over a courtyard.

"Who dares break the laws of Shrek City?"

Yue Zhengyu found his tongue first. "Honorable enforcer. I am Yue Zhengyu of the Angel Clan, second grade, class one. I discovered a Fallen Angel on campus — and everyone knows Fallen Angels become evil soul masters. I acted to capture her, to take her before my clan for judgement."

The girl did not argue her bloodline. She reached into her apron and took out a card, and held it up.

"Respected enforcer. I am a working student of this academy. Shrek has already verified my identity and determined that I am not an evil soul master."

Lin Hao felt the little group around him go very still.

*A working student.* Wulin's thought was so loud it might as well have been spoken. Xie Xie made a small, strangled sound. The girl with the black wings and two thousand-year rings — who had faced three on even ground and then simply *stopped*, because she had known the sky would answer — was a working student. Like them. She did not give her name. Lin Hao noted that too: she gave the enforcer her card and no name, the way a person does when a name is a thing she is careful where she leaves it.

An attractive force drew the card up to the enforcer. He looked at it, and turned to the boy on his knees. "Her identity as a working student is confirmed. It is impossible for her to be an evil soul master. I will not punish you — you believed you were apprehending an evil soul master. But the next time, you will be punished two-fold. Now break it up."

The card drifted back down. The enforcer was gone in a blur, and the street was just a street again, orange-lit and full of people who were very suddenly, very intently, looking at their own feet.

The girl put her card away. She walked three steps toward the kneeling boy. She punched a fist out toward him, stuck her thumb up, and then, slowly, turned the thumb to point at the ground.

"You—!" His eyes went red.

She snorted. She turned and walked into the dark between two lamps, and was gone the way water goes into a drain — not running, just *no longer there*, and Lin Hao, who tracked entrances and exits the way other people tracked weather, could not afterward have said exactly which alley she took.

Yue Zhengyu made to chase. His butler's hand closed on his arm.

"You must not offend the dignity of Shrek, young master." The older man's voice was low and steady. "Since the academy itself has confirmed her identity, there is nothing to be gained by going further."

"So they're saying a Fallen Angel is *not* an evil soul master." The boy's voice had gone ugly. "It seems Shrek is—"

"Young master." A ripple of power rode over the words, flattening them before they could finish. "Watch what you say."

Yue Zhengyu shook him off and stormed away into the gold-stained night.

No one said anything for a while. The five of them stood in the street with the rest of the crowd, and Lin Hao watched the crowd as much as he watched the empty sky, because the crowd was the more informative thing. The students of Shrek had watched a second-year Angel Clan prodigy press three purple rings on a waitress, and they had watched the sky knock him down, and not one of them looked *surprised*. They looked the way people look at weather they have seen before.

"Now this," Xiaoyan said softly, "is Shrek City."

## Part 2: The Same Gate

Back in the shabby dormitory, not one of them could sleep, which was the opposite of what a fight in the street should do to a body.

Xie Xie whispered it to Wulin, but he whispered it in the room where all of them could hear, because there was no point whispering anything in a room divided by one hung cloth. "Captain. Don't you think there's something strange about working students? In the dining hall everyone got respectful — even a little *afraid* — the second you said it. The examiner who beat me into the ground during the trials. And that red-haired girl tonight, with the black wings and two purple rings. Both of them are working students. Maybe we should look into this."

"We're new here," Wulin said. He was lying on his back, staring at the plank ceiling. "Our first job is to learn how this place breathes. We're still small in it. Don't go looking for trouble and don't go looking for secrets — not until we've put down roots. Put the curiosity on the shelf. We can open it later."

"That's," said Xie Xie glumly, "the second time someone sensible has told me to be quiet tonight."

Gu Yue rose without a word and hung the cloth that split the room, the way she did everything — by means that left the curtain rod untroubled by her ever having stood on a stool — and the four of them (five, counting the margin) settled to meditate.

Lin Hao did not sleep for a different reason. He had an appointment at dawn.

The practice yards behind the outer-court classrooms were empty at that hour, the flagstones still dark with the night's dew, when he walked in and found Ye Xinglan already there. She had not come in uniform. She wore a plain grey training tunic and had the Stargod Sword out of its sheath and resting across her shoulders, and she was doing slow forms in the grey light, one after another, the way a person does who has done the same ten forms every dawn since she was old enough to hold a blade.

"You came," she said. She did not open her eyes.

"I said I would." He drew the practice sword he had borrowed from the yard rack — plain iron, no name, the kind of blade the academy left out for anyone. "The sword you used in thirty-one seconds was yellow along the edge. I'd like to see what four months put on it."

"Then don't blink."

She opened her eyes and came at him.

It was not the spar from the exhibition. In Skysea she had been two yellow rings and a prodigy's confidence, fast and proud and readable, and he had beaten her footwork by deciding where she was going to be. This morning she was three rings and a thousand-year spirit and, more than that, she was a girl who had spent every dawn since then inside the one state he knew better than anyone alive — the man-and-sword-as-one, the place where the blade is not held so much as *agreed with*. Her first cut did not come from her arm. It came from the whole of her, the way a stroke of weather comes from the whole sky, and starlight ran along the iron edge of the practice blade she had drawn to match him.

He met it in the margin.

He did not use Wind-Step. He did not light a ring. He met her with the plain borrowed iron and the plain, enormous truth of a body that had been built on an anvil and fed a ten-thousand-year dragon, and he answered her the way he answered everything worth answering — exactly enough, and not a breath more. The first exchange rang three times across the empty yard and left her pushed back a single step.

The single step was the point. She felt it, the way a swordsman always feels it: he had stopped her cut without trying to, the way a wall stops a thrown cup, and there had been no technique in it she could name.

"You're not even lit," she said. Her eyes were very bright.

"It's dawn," he said. "I didn't come here to show you rings. I came to see your sword."

She came again. He let her push him, for the most part — across the yard, around the dew-dark stones, through the forms she knew and two she invented on the spot, the starlight on her blade thickening as her third ring answered her need. She was good. She was, ring for ring, better than anyone he had ever sparred who was not trying to kill him; her sword-consciousness was real and deep and hard-won, and there were moments where the Stargod Sword and the girl holding it genuinely ceased to be two things. He answered those moments with the borrowed iron and let her feel, through the steel, that there was a rung above the rung she stood on — not a wall, not a ceiling, a *rung*, one more step on the same ladder she was already climbing.

At the end she drove a two-handed cut down at him with the third ring blazing, starlight pouring like a fall of sparks, and he turned it aside with the flat of his blade and put the point of his practice iron — gently, precisely, and without hurry — in the hollow of her throat.

The yard was quiet. The dew dripped off a stone.

"You could have done that," she said, breathing hard, "on the first cut."

"I could have done it before you drew." He lowered the blade. "Where would the fun in that have been."

She stared at him. Then she laughed — a short, startled sound, the laugh of a girl who decided things and had just, for the first time in a year, had a decision taken away from her without losing. "You held back the entire time."

"I held *forward*," Lin Hao said. "There's a difference. Back would have been ignoring you. Forward is standing on the next rung and letting you feel it under your own feet when you catch up." He set the borrowed iron back in the rack. "Your sword's at the gate. You know that. You've known for a while. You don't need me to tell you where the rung is — you need another ten thousand cuts, and you already know that too."

She was quiet for a long moment, sheathing the Stargod Sword with slow care. "The thing in the drink shop," she said at last. "When my blade went quiet. That wasn't you being strong."

"No."

"That was you being *further*. On the same ladder." She slung the sheath across her back, and looked at him with the directness that was the whole of her, the thing he had liked from thirty-one seconds onward. "All right. Then I'm not behind a stranger. I'm behind a man who's standing on the rung I'm climbing to. I can work with that." She turned to go, then over her shoulder: "I'm going to take that gate, Lin Hao. And when I do, I want you in the yard the next dawn."

"You can have the yard," he said. "Bring me the sword that takes it."

She was gone into the morning, and he stood a moment in the empty practice yard with the grey light coming up over the stones, and thought that of all the things Shrek had handed him in his first day, a swordswoman who heard a wall as a rung was near the top of the list.

Then the bell rang for the morning, and he went to find the others, because the working students had jobs to collect.

## Part 3: The Name at the Counter

Wulin and Xiaoyan were up already when he got back, sitting cross-legged facing each other by the thin light, cultivating their Purple Demon Eyes in the old paired rhythm. They washed. They faced the first problem of the day, which was breakfast — Wulin still had black steamed buns, which he hoarded like a dragon — and then they went, as working students did at the start of every day, to the administration building to be told what they would earn.

The administrator looked up from his papers. "You four — five — continue cleaning Spirit Ice Plaza today. You did well yesterday. Keep it up."

"Teacher." Wulin leaned in with the particular face he wore when money was involved. "Besides cleaning the plaza — can we take other jobs?"

"You want more?" The man stared. It was normal for working students to struggle under the work; it was not normal to ask for extra. Then he shrugged and handed over a soul screen. "Fine. Look through the list and choose."

They were crowding the screen over Wulin's shoulder when the door opened and someone came in.

"Teacher. I've finished my job."

The administrator's whole manner changed. "The design plans are done? That's fast. Yuanen — your efficiency keeps improving." He took the student's card and added contribution points to it. "Go on, take another."

Lin Hao did not need Wulin's elbow in his ribs. He had already turned his head.

The boy — the young man, it was hard to tell — was utterly unremarkable. Ordinary face, ordinary build, ordinary clothes, the kind of person you looked at and immediately looked away from because there was nothing for the eye to catch hold of. He moved to the counter, scrolled the job list, chose something, and turned to leave. On the way out he gave Wulin's group exactly one nod — small, level, the recognition of one working student for a knot of others — and went out into the morning in silence.

*Yuanen.*

Lin Hao watched the door close, and behind his eyes a line of small, unremarkable facts slid into the same slot. The administrator's pleasure — *your efficiency keeps improving*. A finished set of design plans before most students were awake, which meant a second profession at a level the academy paid well for. The walk, which did not waste motion. The single nod, given only to working students. And the bearing of the person underneath the ordinariness, which was not ordinary at all to the part of him that had spent his whole life reading the weight a body carried: there was a great deal of power in that plain frame, folded away the way the waitress had folded her wings.

The waitress. Red hair. Black wings. Two purple rings. A working-student card. A name she had not given. A way of leaving that he could not track.

*Yuanen.*

He said nothing. Not here. Not in front of the counter, and not even to Wulin yet; a name noticed in the margin was a tool, and a tool shown before its use was a tool spent. But he filed it the way he filed everything that mattered — in the book no one read — and he put one quiet line under it. The examiner who had walked Xie Xie into the ground. The waitress who had faced an Angel Clan prodigy on even ground and then let the sky do her fighting for her. The unassuming student at the counter who finished design plans before dawn. The working students were not poor children the academy tolerated. They were a *selection*.

He was beginning to understand what was being selected.

Wulin, at the screen, had found the metalwork. "I'll take this one. First-grade thousand-refining."

The administrator stared again. "Are you certain? Points are deducted for failure, and you're expelled if you can't cover your tuition — all of you working students owe three hundred contribution points a month. Three hundred, in addition to feeding yourselves."

"Certain." Wulin tapped the screen. He did not explain that a first-grade thousand-refining job paid one thousand points, or that he had crossed into the fifth rank and his success rate on first-grade work was near total. Lin Hao watched him make the choice and thought it through himself: the math of Shrek. Outer court, over a thousand students, every one of them driving toward battle armor rather than mecha — and thousand-refined metal was the bedrock of every one-word suit. The academy did not lack for smithing work; the academy *was* the demand. The points were a leash, yes; he had called them that the first day. But a leash pulled both ways. A leash meant the thing on the end was worth holding.

Outside, Xie Xie slid up to Wulin. "So that guy's name is Yuanen."

"Still carrying the grudge?" Wulin said. "You can't beat him right now. And I think we misunderstood the age thing — second-year students here aren't a year older than us. They're about three."

"We don't know that for certain," Xie Xie retorted, without much heat. "The academy takes anyone fifteen and under. We got in at thirteen. Maybe he got in younger."

"You can buy contribution points off me with money," Wulin offered, patting his shoulder.

"Boss, you're not that much of a money-grubber—"

"I really am. Self-reliance is a Tang Sect tradition. If you want points, build your second profession — and mark me, those points buy more than food and tuition before we're done."

Lin Hao walked a half-step behind them, the morning sun on his face, and said none of what he knew. He had his own smith's summons in his bag, the Shrek Blacksmiths' Association door that would open on his own rank, and he had a name now — *Yuanen* — and he had a guild that was not a guild but a selection, and all three of those things would keep.

## Part 4: The Door

The opening ceremony was held in Spirit Ice Plaza, washed clean by their own labor, and it was there that Lin Hao finally felt the size of the place.

Six grades. Each a single class of roughly a hundred students, give or take a dozen. A little over seven hundred in the outer court altogether — and the eye ran over them and kept running, because the oldest students in the plaza were not boys. They were men and women into their thirties, standing in their grade's block with the solemnity of people who had chosen a mountain over a life, extraordinary cultivation coiled in them like springs, and they were still outer court, still ungraduated, still earning their place year on year. Students graduated a mundane academy in their early twenties. Here were people who had laid their twenties down on the same flagstones the five of them stood on.

"If Wu Zhangkong were put into an outer grade," Xiaoyan murmured, doing the same arithmetic, "he'd only be about fifth grade."

"That," said Wulin, with feeling, "is the most frightening sentence anyone has said this week."

Then the teachers rose into the air over the plaza, and Lin Hao's attention found the figure at the center of them, and he felt a particular stillness settle over him — the stillness of a man who has just watched a card he had been keeping turn over in someone else's hand.

Elder Cai.

She stood at the head of the faculty in her plain dark robes, indifferent as frost on iron, and the administrator's introductions gave her title the way one gives a fact too large to need emphasis: **Cai Yue'er, headmaster of the Shrek outer court.**

*Of course she is.* Lin Hao thought it with something close to admiration. The woman who had handed him the ordinary transcript on purpose. The woman who had kept Gu Yue's disciple door open instead of slamming it. The woman who had said *points aren't coins, blacksmith* and *I keep one book, you keep one, keep yours honest.* She was not an examiner they had survived. She was the jurisdiction. The battle-armor-before-twenty bar she had set them had not been an elder's idle demand; it had been the head of the outer court telling them the price of her own house.

Her speech was short. Shrek did not force cultivation. Education was not compulsory. There was a minor examination every year, and a major one every three; failing the minor twice meant expulsion, and so every grade shrank year on year — that was the seven hundred, that was why some of them were thirty-five and still not graduated. The sixth graders who had not met the requirements should be prepared to lay down everything before they turned thirty-five. The new students might relax if they liked — and then they might not be here in three years. The faculty would teach; the facilities stood open; everything cost contribution points. They would learn the importance of contribution points soon enough.

"That's it?" Xie Xie whispered. "That's the whole speech?"

"She said everything a headmaster needs to," Lin Hao said quietly, "and charged us nothing for it. I'd be careful of that, if I were you. Free words from her are the most expensive thing in this plaza."

The ceremony ended. The teachers in the air split off toward their grades.

Wulin's face lit when he saw two of the descending figures — Wu Zhangkong, and Shen Yi, coming straight toward the new-student block. Then the light on his face stiffened, and Lin Hao saw why. There was a third figure with them, dark-robed and frost-composed, and her lips were curved into the smallest, most satisfied smile Lin Hao had ever seen on a human being who was not currently eating.

Elder Cai landed in front of the new class.

"I," she said, "will be personally managing this year's new students." She did not raise her voice; the whole block heard her anyway. "Beside me are my assistant teachers — Teacher Shen Yi, and Teacher Wu Zhangkong." She let a beat pass. "Now. To the classroom."

Lin Hao felt the group around him fold. Wulin's eyes went wide. Xie Xie's jaw hung. Xiaoyan made a small sound like a kitten that has just noticed the lid going on. Gu Yue's lips thinned to a line — the closest thing to a flinch she ever allowed herself, the woman whose disciple-door Cai had held open, the student who had said no and who was now, it appeared, going to be taught by the door-holder every single day.

He almost smiled. *She never lost a night's sleep over the no. She didn't need to. She owns the room we'll be sitting in.*

The lecture theatre was on the first floor and built for three hundred, which made the hundred-odd first-years look scattered and small. Shen Yi took the roll and called the seating in her clear, implacable voice, front and center, no more than five meters from the lectern:

"Tang Wulin — row one, seat one." Center. Wulin scrambled in.

"Gu Yue — row one, seat two." His right.

"Xie Xie — row one, seat three." His left.

"Xu Xiaoyan — row one, seat four." Beside Gu Yue.

Lin Hao waited for the dismissal of the working students to the back of the house — the speech had already reorganized them once, in the plaza, drifting the five of them toward the rear on the strength of their status. He had already assumed the margin. That was where he sat.

Shen Yi turned a page. Her eyes found him with no particular expression at all, and he understood, the way one understands weather before the words arrive, that the list was not done.

"Lin Hao — row one, seat five."

A beat. The pause was so small that only he would ever have caught it; it was the beat in which Elder Cai, behind the lectern, did not move and did not need to, and Shen Yi read the next name off a sheet that had clearly been settled before any of them had entered the room.

"Beside Xu Xiaoyan. Up front."

He rose and walked the length of the theatre under the eyes of a hundred strangers and sat down in seat five — the fifth of the five working students placed dead-center in the first row, in arm's reach of the lectern, where not a word or a note or a breath could possibly be missed. It was not punishment. Wulin got the same seat. It was something else, and he knew exactly what it was, because she had told him in the registration office in a line he had been turning over ever since:

*A marked boy is a watched boy.*

She had chosen to keep the book she could not yet classify not on the shelf, not in the restricted cabinet, but open on the desk directly under her hand — where she could read it whenever she liked, and where the reading itself might, in time, write the page she was waiting for.

"One hundred and one students in this year's class," Shen Yi reported. "One hundred and one counted. Everyone is present."

Elder Cai regarded the lecture theatre with her frost-on-iron gaze, and let it settle — for one half-second longer than anywhere else — across the first row.

"You heard the ceremony speech, so I won't repeat it. Here at Shrek, your teachers will show you the door. It is up to you to step through it." She folded her hands. "That is enough for today. The rest is yours."

Lin Hao sat in seat five, five meters from the woman who owned the room, and thought about doors. About the door Gu Yue had walked through first into the golden light. The door the enforcer had answered. The rung Ye Xinglan called a gate. And the door a headmaster had just shown all five of them — the first of the working-student selection — by seating them so close to her that she could watch them decide whether to step.

He opened his notebook to a fresh page.

At the very top, he wrote one line, in the careful hand he used for the book nobody else read.

*The teacher shows the door. The question is which side of it she's standing on.*

## Part 1: One Breath

"Your teachers will show you the door," Elder Cai said. "It is up to you to step through it." She folded her hands. "That is enough for today. The rest is yours."

Then she rose.

Lin Hao watched her come down from the lectern the way he watched everything — from the margin, which in this room was a seat five meters from the front, dead center, where not a breath could be missed. He had been placed there on purpose. He knew it; she knew it; the frost on her composure had not flickered once while Shen Yi read the five names that put all five working students in arm's reach of the desk. A marked boy is a watched boy. She had kept him not on a shelf but open on the table, and the morning had not yet produced a single reason to think she was wrong to.

She reached the end of the front aisle. Her back was to him.

And it was there — in the one second between her turning and her leaving, with the twenty-year bar still lying across all their shoulders and the front-row captivity warm on his neck and the ledger she kept on him open under her hand — that Lin Hao, who had spent thirteen years learning to say nothing the room did not need to hear, let one breath go that the room did not need to hear.

It was barely shaped. It did not move his lips enough for anyone past his own shoulder to read. It was the smallest, driest, most private fragment of the thing the morning had built in him, and it slipped out the way a tool slips off a bench — not because he chose it but because his hands were full.

"Old woman."

The elbow hit his ribs before the breath had finished.

Xu Xiaoyan, in seat four, beside him, had heard. Her eyes were very large and very round, and she had gone the particular pale she went when five seconds showed her something she was not supposed to have seen. She did not say a word; she only stared at him with the full force of a girl who had just watched a boy mutter an insult at a headmaster who could, by every law of cultivation anyone in the room believed in, hear heartbeats through walls.

Across her, Xie Xie had frozen with his mouth open. Wulin, center, did not move at all — Wulin's gift in a crisis was to become furniture. Gu Yue, in seat two, did not turn around, but Lin Hao saw the line of her shoulders go still in the particular way water goes still before it freezes solid.

Elder Cai did not turn around.

She walked the aisle. She reached the door. She went through it. The door closed behind her with a soft, ordinary sound, and at no point in any of it did her head move, her step change, or the frost-composure on her face alter by a single degree.

Nothing happened.

Xiaoyan exhaled a full lungful of air she had been holding since the elbow. Xie Xie's mouth closed. The lecture theatre began, very slowly, to breathe again, and Shen Yi turned at the lectern to take the class over.

Lin Hao looked down at his open notebook.

The page was the one he had written on during the seating — the careful line in the hand he used for the book nobody else read: *The teacher shows the door. The question is which side of it she's standing on.*

Under the last half of the line there was frost.

It was thin as a sword-stroke, a single perfect underline running from the word *door* to the word *on*, white and cold and already sweating in the warm air of the hall. It had not touched anything else — not the words above, not the margin, not the next page. And at the right-hand end of it, where an underline simply stops, the frost made one tiny, precise little turn, a downward tick, like the mark a person makes at the bottom of a column of figures to say *counted*.

Then it was gone. Shen Yi had not yet finished walking to the lectern. The line of frostwater sank into the paper and vanished, leaving only a faint raised trace, like a vein under skin.

Lin Hao did not move for two full seconds.

Then, very gently, he closed the notebook.

He did not need to ask whether she had heard. That frost was not a guess and it was not a warning; it was a *receipt*. She had been at the door with her back to him, across five meters and a hundred rustling students, and she had caught a breath his own neighbor only caught because she was sitting closer than the notebook — and she had not turned, and she had not spoken, and she had not punished him. She had done the one thing that was worse and better than all of those. She had answered in the language of her own ledgers: she had written down that she heard, and ticked it, and moved on to the next column.

*She heard every word,* he thought. *She has heard every word ever written in this room, and she put her hand on the margin of my own book to tell me so.*

It should have frightened him. It did frighten him, in the small cold place where he kept the things that were true whether he liked them or not. But underneath the fright, to his complete lack of surprise, there was something else. The front row was not a cage, then. It was a conversation. He had said *old woman*; she had said *I heard*, and she had said it without spending a single breath on it, the way a far stronger swordsman ends a bout by letting the student feel the point and not the wound.

Xiaoyan was still looking at him, round-eyed. She mouthed a single word at him, soundless and aghast.

Lin Hao mouthed one back, perfectly calm, because there was no point in pretending the account was anything but open.

"Noted."

## Part 2: The Rules

"On behalf of Shrek Academy," Shen Yi said from the lectern, "I welcome you. I will say each of these things once, because they concern your survival here, and I do not repeat myself."

She told them the shape of the place, and Lin Hao wrote each rule in the book with a number already attached to it, because that was how he heard rules — not as warnings, as prices.

Shrek made its own law. The Federation had no jurisdiction here; punishment was set by the academy and would have nothing to do with whatever the Federation decided. He filed that beside the sky-enforcer who had pressed an Angel Clan prodigy to his knees the night before and let the girl walk on the strength of a card. The points were everything: they bought resources, spirit souls, time in the special facilities, a teacher's private guidance, entry to the spirit ascension platform, and — for working students — food. They could not be bought with money. They were earned, job by job, and they could be moved between students, and if a student ran himself to minus one thousand, he was expelled.

"Classes are held in the mornings only," Shen Yi said. "Your afternoons and evenings are your own, and so is falling behind if you waste them. Tardiness counts as an absence. Three absences, and you are gone. Nothing bought with Federation money comes onto this campus; bring any and you are fined ten times its price in points." Her gaze passed over the first row without pausing. "Working students buy their own meals and their own optional courses. And there is one thing Elder Cai did not say at the ceremony. In the yearly minor examination, the bottom five of each year are expelled."

She let that sit.

"Shrek Academy does not raise students. It raises monsters. You may spend your year at leisure if you like. The year after it will simply not include you."

Xiaoyan had gone very still beside him. Lin Hao watched the class take it — the hundred one-time geniuses of a hundred lesser academies, discovering that the thing they had all been first at was, here, the bottom edge of a machine that ground the lowest five out of every batch annually. He priced it himself, the way he priced everything. He was not at risk of the bottom five. Wulin was not. None of the five were, on merit. But the rule was not aimed at merit; it was aimed at *ease*, and it meant that the margin he lived in was not optional here — it was the air.

He thought about the frost receipt on the page behind the notebook's cover. *Bottom five,* he wrote, and then, in a smaller hand that was entirely for himself: *She is not going to let me be near the bottom five. That is not what the front row is for. She wants to see where I go when the bottom five are behind me.*

Gu Yue, two seats away, did not look at him once during the rules. She sat straight and listened with the particular focus she gave to anything that resembled a system being explained, and Lin Hao knew she was not hearing rules — she was hearing architecture. She was mapping the machine the way he mapped a room's entrances. She had not seen the frost. She had only seen him close his notebook with an expression she had learned to read, and he felt her file that without comment, the way water files the shape of a stone it means to come back to.

Shen Yi finished the rules and did not pause for breath.

"Now," she said, "this morning's topic. Battle armor masters."

The lecture theatre came alert, the way a room does when the word that all of them crossed a continent for is finally spoken aloud.

"I expect some of you are wondering why the very first class is about battle armor masters." Shen Yi's eyes moved over them. "It is because the basics were supposed to be learned before you arrived, or you would not have passed through the gate. So I will not spend the year on basics." She stopped. "What is a battle armor master? Most of you, if you are honest, will say: a more powerful kind of mecha pilot."

A small, subconscious wave of nodding moved through the seats.

"Then," Shen Yi said, "you are all gravely mistaken."
