## Part 3: Clothes For The Martial Soul

She took them apart with the precision of a smith laying out a broken mechanism, piece by piece.

A mecha pilot put clothes on a *person*. A battle armor master put clothes on a *martial soul* — because at the core, the master was still a soul master, and the armor was not worn so much as married, fused, made to resonate and attract and become whole with the soul it served. One-word armor was the beginning, not the achievement; it was only at two words, when a master was one with the armor and it moved as an extension of body and soul together, that the word *battle armor master* actually meant anything.

The professions, then. A student had to choose a second craft that built armor — mecha maker, carving the circuits that let armor and soul fuse; mecha designer, drawing armor that fit a martial soul the way a hand fits a glove; or the harder paths, mechanic or blacksmith, the smith's road the most strenuous and the slowest, the one the academy admitted with its own mouth was the most appropriate craft for *powerful* armor. No one mastered all four. You chose. You would also need the other crafts to finish what you started — you would pay for them in contribution points, and you would be wise to befriend the people who did them well.

"Personal relationships," Shen Yi said, "are part of one's strength. Remember that."

And the number that made the whole room go quiet: armor and master in perfect unity could amplify a soul master's power by twenty soul ranks.

Lin Hao wrote it all. Under *blacksmith — hardest, most appropriate for powerful armor* he put a small mark of his own, the mark of a boy who already was a fifth-rank smith with a failed wrist-guard hung on a failure wall and a name for it waiting. Under *relationships are part of strength* he underlined twice, because he had believed that before Shrek named it — it was the wall with the cuff, the tree, the curtain, the captain, the five hands stacked on one another; it was the whole reason a margin was worth keeping. Under *twenty soul ranks* he paused, and thought about the one-word-armor law he had already priced at the lake with Wu Zhangkong — the twenty ranks a suit lent an ordinary master — and about how little it changed the math of a boy who had been standing in the Emperor margin on no armor at all.

Then Shen Yi gave them the wall.

"To become a one-word battle armor master," she said, "you require five soul rings and the third rank of your secondary profession. Your metal must be thousand refined. Your design must come from a grandmaster designer, your assembly from a grandmaster maker. Your compatibility with the finished armor must be at least sixty percent, and you will need at least nine pieces for it to be called armor at all." The room was very still. "Of outer-court students, one third — thirty-three percent — ever graduate at all. A one-word master by twenty-five may sit for the inner court. By thirty-five, if you are not yet a one-word master, you leave without graduating."

She let the numbers stand where they were.

Lin Hao watched Wulin, three seats off. Wulin's hands had closed slowly on the edge of the desk. Twenty-five for everyone else. Twenty for the five of them — Elder Cai's bar, the thing she had set them back at the assessment, which made a different kind of sense now that they knew she owned the outer court. Five rings, third-rank craft, nine pieces, sixty percent — and five fewer years to carry all of it than any other student in the room.

*Time waits for no one,* Lin Hao thought, and saw the same sentence pass through Wulin's shoulders. He did not lean over to say anything; this was not a thing that was helped by being said. He only made sure his own notebook had the whole of the wall written down cleanly, because the difference between thirty-three percent and the five of them was going to come down to who kept the clearest ledger of the work.

He had, he noted without any particular pride, a head start on the metal. He was the only thirteen-year-old fifth-rank smith the academy had admitted since it stopped admitting people like him. That was not arrogance; it was inventory. The armor was a circuit carved into the soul — he had known that in a midnight meditation before Shrek ever said it — and he knew the names of the failures on his wall, and the one piece of heavy silver that had folded at the fourth strike and hung nameless, waiting to be given its word.

Morning classes had no breaks. One lecture followed the next until the bells let them out, and the five of them walked to the dining hall in the particular silence of people who have just been shown a wall and are estimating its height.

## Part 4: Arithmetic, Not Charity

The crisis was not spiritual. It was financial, and it had Wulin's stomach in it, which made it approximately a force of nature.

"One hundred contribution points," Wulin said at the dining-hall door, staring at the windows the way a drought farmer stares at rain. "It feeds twenty normal people. It does not feed me."

He had been paid the day before for the plaza work, and a hundred points was a comfortable day for any boy in the outer court who was not Tang Wulin. He had taken the first-grade thousand-refining job at the administration counter that morning to build against exactly this, but a job completed and a job paid were not the same hour, and his stomach had never once in its life respected a processing delay.

Lin Hao watched him set his jaw. Then Wulin did the Wulin thing — he took a board from his storage device, wrote on it, and planted himself in the doorway with it held up where the whole lunch crowd could read:

*Fourth-rank blacksmith, capable of first-grade thousand refining. Short on points. Will trade first-grade thousand-refining for a year's worth of meals. Anyone interested, treat me to a meal.*

He had modestly left off that he was fifth-rank. Lin Hao noted the modesty and respected it; at his age, claiming fourth in the doorway was already asking the room to disbelieve him.

The room disbelieved him. Students flowed past in an unending stream, glanced at the board, glanced at the boy holding it, and did the math on their faces — *a year's worth of meals, on that?* — and kept walking. Not one stopped.

"Boss really will do anything to eat." Xie Xie had come to look and then bolted back to the table, mortified on his captain's behalf. "But isn't that a little too embarrassing? Why is he selling his skills at the door like that?"

"Captain doesn't care about anything he can't eat," Xiaoyan said, and giggled, then picked at her own lunch. "Anyway, after the mountain yesterday, nobody's going to take him. Imagine feeding him for a year! A month might work, but his stomach is just a bottomless pit."

Gu Yue said nothing. She stood near the door watching Wulin with a small frown between her brows, then looked down at her own tray and went back to eating with the focused, ruffled energy of a girl who did not have a place to put a feeling and so was putting it into food.

Lin Hao did not pick up a board.

He stood in the margin and watched the stream of students, and he did the arithmetic out of the same clear cold place he did everything in. His own contribution account was not large — the smith's Association registration still waited on its morning, the pavilion work paid slow, and he kept the Yaluo metals in reserve rather than points. But it did not need to be large for this. Wulin's thousand-refining job would pay a thousand points on completion, which meant the points existed, in the near future, as surely as ore exists in a vein. What was missing was the present tense of them — the food in front of the captain today.

You could not, by Shen Yi's own rule, buy points with money. You could move them between students.

He went to the window himself. He did not announce it. He paid for a tray — two trays, the second one arranged with the kind of absent thoroughness that produced, without commentary, a small honest mountain — and carried it back through the crowd and set it down at Wulin's elbow where the board stood.

"You can put the sign away," Lin Hao said. "Today's points are mine."

Wulin stared at the tray, then at him. "You don't have to —"

"I know I don't. That's why it's not a favor." He took the board out of Wulin's unresisting hand and turned it face-down against the wall. "When your thousand-refining pays, you feed the table for a week and we call the ledger square. You fed the whole of Eastsea when there was nothing in it for you; I have a good memory for debts. This is arithmetic." He paused. "Also, if you stand in that doorway one more minute, Gu Yue is going to start icing the floor, and I would rather not explain that to an administrator on our second day."

Wulin looked at the tray. Then he looked at Lin Hao the way he looked at things he had decided not to put words on, and sat down, and ate, and did not argue, because arguing with a debt stated as arithmetic was the one kind of argument Wulin had never won in his life.

Xiaoyan saw it. Xie Xie saw it and, for once, did not make the joke, which was how Lin Hao knew it had landed properly. Gu Yue saw it — she had the angle from the door — and her fork stopped for half a beat over her tray before she went back to eating, and the small ruffled frown between her brows did not go away, but it turned into something else, something Lin Hao, already turned back toward his own seat, did not see.

He did not need to see it. He was not, today, in the business of reading what was written in frost.

That night, in the working students' dormitory, after the curtain was hung and the others meditated, Lin Hao opened his notebook to the page with the receipt.

The frost had dried hours ago. The underline and the little downward tick remained, a faint raised trace in the paper, permanent as a scar. He sat with the pen over it for a long moment.

Then, under her tick, in the same careful hand, he wrote one word.

*Noted.*

He should have closed the book there. He nearly did. But it had been a long day, and the front row was a conversation, and he had never in his life been able to leave a column with an empty last line. So in the smallest hand he owned, underneath the *Noted*, almost too small to read, he added two more words for the ledger's other keeper, with the reckless good cheer of a boy who absolutely, mathematically, could not be heard from this far.

*…old woman.*

He held his breath for half a second. Nothing happened. The ceiling did not frost. The curtain did not stir. The room stayed warm and ordinary and quiet.

He stared at the ceiling a moment longer, not quite able to fully believe the nothing, the way you never quite believe a very strong person hasn't heard something.

Then he closed the book, put it under his mattress with the third one she would never read, and put the matter in the same column he put every receipt he could not verify.

Open.

## Part 1: The Map of the Guilds

The associations found them before lunch.

Invitations began arriving with the morning post the way rain finds a leak — one at first, then a seam, then a steady drizzle folded into the wooden cubby each new student had been assigned outside the lecture theatre. By the end of the first week there were cards and ribbons and stamped leaves of paper from the Mecha Designers' Guild, the Mecha Makers' Lodge, the Cultivation Resources Exchange, the Outer-Court Combat Club, the Spirit Ascension Society, and a dozen smaller outfits whose names Lin Hao wrote down once and then forgot because they were, almost to a one, the same offer in different ink: join, rent your share of a senior's knowledge, and stop being the smallest fish in the largest pond on the continent.

"All of them," Shen Yi had said on the second morning, anticipating the question, "are founded and run by students. The academy leases them the land and leaves them alone. They exist because a second profession cannot be learned from a lecture — it is learned from the person two years ahead of you who has already wasted the metal you are about to waste. You will not progress far without one, and you may join as many as you have the hours for. Choose like you are spending time, because you are."

Lin Hao read the whole sheaf that evening with the particular interest he gave to anything that explained how a place fed itself. The associations were not clubs. They were the academy's economy wearing a friendly face — senior knowledge rented to juniors for contribution points and loyalty, the best of them feeding their strongest up toward the inner court and the rest quietly sorting out who could not keep pace. He filed the architecture the way Gu Yue filed weather systems, and he set aside exactly one invitation.

The Blacksmiths' Association of Shrek Academy.

He had carried its summons since before the term began — a sheet of paper that had reached him through Tie Jin's wire, the pavilion scrap-master's one connection to the continent-wide guild, offering to register a fifth-rank smith on Shrek's own terms rather than Eastsea's. He had let it wait through the trials and the headmaster and the frost receipt because there had always been something louder in the day. There was nothing louder now. Class ran only in the mornings, and the afternoons stretched ahead of him like unworked stock.

The next day, after the bell, he walked to the foundry quarter alone.

## Part 2: The Mark of the Fifth

The Blacksmiths' Association was a long, loud, sweltering hall built against the outer wall where the vent-fires could breathe. It smelled of scale and coke and the particular hot-metal smell that Lin Hao had loved before he knew the word for loving anything. A bored student clerk behind a desk looked up at the dark-haired boy in working-student grey, and opened her mouth with the sentence she gave every new fish, and then her eyes fell on the summons he laid on the counter, and the sentence changed into a different one entirely.

"Fifth rank," she said. "You. At — how old are you?"

"Thirteen," Lin Hao said. "It's been verified. Eastsea City guild hall, and the paperwork came through your own wire. I'm not here to argue the rank. I'm here to use it."

She fetched someone older. The someone older fetched someone older than that, and twenty minutes later Lin Hao stood at a forge table in the back while a one-armed smith named He Qiao — Association master, sixth rank, missing the arm to a spirit beast he declined to name — watched him draw the two demonstration heats the guild required of any rank it registered on its own authority.

It was not a test he could fail. He had spent the summer of his thirteenth year telling metal what it was instead of asking it. He did the first heat slowly enough that the old smith could follow the method — the listening, the place where his hammer did not strike so much as answer a question the metal had already asked — and the second heat at something closer to a working pace, and when he set the hammers down the finished bar rang once, very sweetly, and stayed ringing a little longer than a bar had any right to.

He Qiao turned it over in his single hand for a long moment. Then he said, without looking up, "You don't just thousand-refine. You ask first."

"Metal answers better if you do."

"That's the fifth-rank trick everyone lies about having." He set the bar down. "You're registered. Full workshop rights, member rate on tables, access to the guild stock. We don't get many of you — most of the young geniuses go into design or making because the early ranks come faster there. Smithing's slower. It hurts more. And every rank past mine needs a thing I can't teach." He held up his stump with a grim sort of humor. "I'm the proof it asks a price. But a fifth-rank at thirteen will be a sixth-rank by nineteen if he just keeps hitting the table. There's no wall past five for a smith. Just work."

That matched everything Lin Hao had already priced. He thanked the man, paid the member token's small fee, and stood a moment in the heat while the foundry roared around him.

Wulin would have been beside himself in this room. The rare-metal shelves he could glimpse through the inner doorway, the five-charge forging tables, the sheer scale of the stock — his captain would have taken one breath of this air and started calculating.

As if the thought had summoned it, a roar split the afternoon over the whole of the outer court.

"WHO IS TANG WULIN? COME HERE!"

Lin Hao went to the foundry door with the rest of them. Down the slope, across the court, a middle-aged man had erupted into the dining-hall entrance — disheveled flame-red hair, a scorching aura, broad and low as a furnace, arms thicker than most boys' whole bodies, the general silhouette of a lion that had learned to stand. His shout flattened the noise of a thousand students the way a hand flattens a candle. A heartbeat later he came back out with something under one arm — Wulin, held by the shoulder, utterly without the option of being anywhere else — and went back the way he had come in a blur of hot air, with a flustered second figure (ordinary, fast, swearing, Yuanen) sprinting after.

The foundry smiths laughed and went back to their work.

"Taken by a smith, that one," He Qiao said, following Lin Hao's eyes. "Old Man Feng of the battle-armor forges. He only drags off the ones he can't stand to watch waste themselves. Your friend just got adopted by the most violent teacher in the outer court." He squinted. "You knew the boy?"

"He's my captain." Lin Hao watched the blur vanish toward the forging quarter. He did not move to follow. The hand on Wulin's shoulder had not been a threat; he had seen the way the man's strength wrapped around the boy rather than closed on him, and underneath the roar there was the same heat that lived in this hall — the heat of a smith who had just felt metal worth forging. Wulin was not being abducted. Wulin was being *collected*. There was nothing to rescue. "He's in good hands," Lin Hao said. "Better than mine for what that man wants."

He turned back to the foundry. He had his rank, his token, his tables. His second profession was a thing he now owned outright in Shrek's own books.

So it was not the thing on his mind as he walked down toward the plaza to find the others. The thing on his mind was much older than the guild.

## Part 3: The Itch

He found Wulin's other half — Xie Xie, Xiaoyan, and Gu Yue — at the plaza fountain, Wulin himself being conspicuously absent in a way that required no explanation. Xie Xie was mid-account of the lion-man's abduction, in increasing detail and decreasing accuracy.

Lin Hao sat down on the fountain's rim with no preamble at all, because the thing in him had been building across the forging room and the roar and the whole careful, watchful, instrument-maxing year behind him, and it wanted saying while it was hot.

"Battle armor," he said, into the gap in Xie Xie's story. "All of you listen, because Shen Yi gave you the worry of it and I want the worry off the ledger early. Compatibility. Sixty percent minimum, nine pieces, grandmaster this, grandmaster that — it's a mountain for everyone else. It is not a mountain for me. When my turn comes to fuse a suit, I will not be lying awake over whether the metal takes to me. I have never once in my life met a piece of metal that didn't, by the end of the conversation. Compatibility is the one number in that whole wall I can stop worrying about today."

He said it the way he said the grain-read aloud sometimes — flatly, as a fact about the work, and not one of them needed to know the deeper reason, the adaptation that had made his whole body a thing that learned the shape of whatever it touched and became it. They heard a fifth-rank smith's confidence. That was all the truth the room needed.

Xie Xie blinked. "Well. Good for you. Some of us have to learn a whole second profession."

"Then learn it," Lin Hao said, and said the second thing, the one that had been sitting under his ribs like a held breath. "But that's not what I want to spend the afternoon talking about. I want to talk about money that doesn't come off a forging table."

That got their attention. Even Gu Yue, half-turned away toward the spray, shifted a fraction.

"I want to find work that pays for fighting," Lin Hao said. "I want to know if any of you know how a soul master in this place actually earns points by hitting something. And I want it badly enough that I'm asking out loud, which I don't usually do."

The honesty of it seemed to surprise them as much as the subject. He pushed on, because if he did not say the whole of it now he would not say it.

"It has been a very long time since I had a good fight. Not a spar that's over because I decided where it ended. Not a contest I won in the margin before the first exchange. A real one — something that walks out onto the same ground I'm on and makes me *reach*. Every fight since I came through that gate I've won holding something back, and I don't say that like it's a virtue, because it isn't. It's a man eating half a meal every day and calling himself fed. I have been careful for a year. I have been the quiet thing at the edge of every room, and it was the right thing to be, and I am not complaining about any of it. But I want to find the one place I can go where there's nothing to hold back for and nothing to tip off, where the thing across from me is allowed to be as strong as it wants and I am allowed the same, and it pays me for the privilege. Does that exist here, or do I have to build it?"

The fountain ran. For a moment none of them spoke, because the speech had come out of the margin — and the margin did not, as a rule, give speeches.

It was Xiaoyan who found her voice first. "You mean like the spirit ascension platform."

"Start there."

"The academy runs ascension slots out of the platform hall," she said, getting into it the way she got into anything that involved a pattern. "It costs points to enter, and you go in against spirit beasts at the floor you pay for, and the platform pays you back out of what you bring down — spirit souls, materials, the kill itself counts. It's not a spar with a person. It's a hunt. Nobody in there is your classmate. Nobody in there is watching to decide what you are." She looked at him. "You could go up to a floor where the beasts are actually dangerous. People do it for resources. Some do it because it's the only place on campus they can cut loose."

"Or the culling tickets," Xie Xie offered, recovering. "There's a job board at the administration that isn't cleaning. Spirit-beast suppression — forest work, the real wilderness, contracts the academy lets out when something near the outer range gets strong enough to need thinning. Those pay in points and in parts, and half the board nobody takes because the beasts are mean. Strong alone out there. No crowd."

"No crowd," Lin Hao repeated. The words landed somewhere deep and exactly right. "That's the shape of it." He thought it through out loud, the way he did with metal. "I can't cut loose on a person. Not here. A peer I beat at full strength is either a secret I have to keep with my hands, or a body, and I am in the market for neither. But a beast on a high ascension floor, or a cull out in the range where it's me and something with teeth and no one from the dean's office holding a clipboard — there's nothing to hide there. It can't be offended. It can't report me. It can't faint and need carrying. It can only hit back, which is the entire point. And it pays. That's the work I want. Something that hits back and settles up in points."

Gu Yue, who had said nothing through all of it, turned her head at last and looked at him. Her face had no expression he could read — he had catalogued that fact across two years and given up cataloguing it — but there was the smallest of pauses, the length of a held breath, before she spoke.

"The high ascension floors," she said, "are where people die."

"People," Lin Hao said. "Not me." He said it without heat, the way you read a number off a scale. "I'm not going up there to gamble. I'm going up there to find out what the margin looks like when I stop choosing it. I know the size of my own reach down to the inch. I have simply never been allowed to spend it all at once, and I would like, before I'm much older, to know what it feels like."

Wulin would have argued him out of it out of love. Wulin was not there. Gu Yue looked at him for one beat longer, and then gave a small, single nod — not approval, exactly, but acknowledgment of a thing she had correctly identified as already decided — and turned back to the fountain.

## Part 4: The Ticket

The administration job board was exactly where Xie Xie said it was, tucked into a side hall off the same building that paid them for the plaza, and it was the antidote to every sweeping job on the morning roster.

Lin Hao read it the way he read a menu he had been waiting a year to be handed.

The spirit ascension platform slots were there, floor by floor, each with its entry price and its posted reward band — the low floors cheap and crowded and useless to him, the high floors expensive and sparsely subscribed and, in a couple of cases, marked with the little symbol that meant the academy advised against them for outer-court students. The culling contracts were pinned below that: range work, spirit-beast suppression, payments in points plus the value of whatever was brought back, each ticket carrying a beast, a location, and a posted danger mark.

He did not take the very highest. That would not have been care; that would have been a lie about who he was, because he had no wish to die and no romance with the idea. He did not take the safe ones, because the safe ones were the half-meal again. He ran his finger down the board and chose the way he chose metal at the shelf — by listening for the note.

He stopped on a culling ticket in the middle of the dangerous band: a high-tier spirit beast ranging the wild country beyond the outer training ranges, old and smart and twice struck off by teams that had not been strong enough to finish it. Good points. Full salvage rights. No partner required. Posted for a third time because the first two contracts had come back empty.

A beast that had already beaten two groups and lived. Something that hit back.

He took the ticket down, carried it to the counter, and registered it against his new Blacksmiths' Association token and his working-student card. The clerk looked at the danger mark, looked at him, and did the arithmetic of a thirteen-year-old in grey uniform versus a beast that had turned back a team, and opened his mouth.

"I've read the mark," Lin Hao said. "I'm not asking for an escort and I won't be needing a rescue. Log the points to this token when I bring proof."

The clerk shut his mouth, and stamped the ticket.

Lin Hao walked out into the Shrek afternoon with the job folded into his inner pocket, and stood a moment on the steps of the administration building with the sun warm on his face and the weight of a real fight — the first one in a year he would not have to hold back through to its end — sitting in his chest like the first breath of cold air in the foundry.

He had his craft registered. He had his work chosen. And tomorrow, or the day after, in the wild country beyond the ranges where there were no clipboards and no classmates and no headmaster's frost, he would finally let the margin go and find out exactly how much of him there was.

He started walking toward the foundry to tell Wulin — if Wulin was still in one piece under the lion-man's table — and to borrow a better hammer for the road.

## Part 1: The Ground With No Clipboards

The wild country began where the academy's fences stopped pretending to be fences.

Lin Hao walked out through the outer training ranges at first light with the culling ticket folded in his inner pocket and a borrowed field blade at his hip — plain forge-steel, no name, the kind the quartermaster handed out against a deposit and did not expect back in one piece. He had left the Stormbringer and the good steel in the dorm. There was no sense in taking a named weapon to a job he intended to do up close, and there was a smith's superstition in it too, the old one he had never quite grown out of: you did not bring a thing you loved to a place where things broke.

The ranges thinned out behind him. The marked practice grounds gave way to half-cleared forest, then to forest that had not been cleared at all, the trees going tall and close and unimpressed by the existence of Shrek Academy. The air changed. It stopped smelling of coke and swept stone and started smelling of wet bark and cold water and the particular sharp smell of ground that had not been walked on today by anyone human. He felt the academy's attention slide off his back the way water slides off a pitched roof — the cards, the points, the headmaster's frost, all of it falling behind him until there was only the wood and the job and the thing he had walked out here to do.

No clipboards. No classmates. No one to decide what he was.

He let out a breath he had been holding, in some form, for a year.

The ticket said the beast ranged a valley two hours west, a high-sided cut in the hills with a stream at the bottom and tree cover thick enough to hide anything that did not wish to be seen. He found the first sign before he found the valley: a tree scored at head height, four parallel gashes through bark and into the heartwood, the marks old and half-healed and wide enough apart that he put his own fingers into two of them and did not come close to spanning the set. The ground around the root was churned. Something large had been here, and had stood the way a thing stands when it owns the place it is standing.

He read on. Broken branches at the height of a tall man's shoulder — a charge mark, something low and fast and armoured smashing through cover without bothering to go around. A patch of scrub scoured flat. And then the first thing that made the margin in him sit up: a blade driven into a trunk and left there, snapped at the tang, the steel of a quality that told him its owner had not been a fool. It had bent on something and been abandoned. A good weapon, thrown away. The first team's work.

He found the second team's marker further down the slope — a scorch in a clearing, the blackened earth of a fire-element skill discharged at point-blank range, and at the edge of the scorch, a drag-gouge in the soil where something heavy had been pulled toward the trees and not, by the look of it, under its own power.

Two teams. Both turned back. One had left its dead.

Lin Hao stood at the lip of the valley and looked down at it, and the smith in him — the part that read metal the way other men read faces — looked at the way the trunks were scored, at the height of the broken branches, at the width of the charge-path, and said one quiet thing to the rest of him.

*Armoured. Dense. Low to the ground and fast despite it. Whatever they hit it with, it either bounced or slid off, and then it was on them before they could ready the next.*

He rolled his shoulders, once, and started down into the valley.

## Part 2: The Thousand-Plate

He found it at the stream.

It was drinking, or it had been. It stood the size of a small house, low-slung and slab-shouldered, built along the general plan of a boar if a boar had been designed by someone whose only aesthetic principle was *nothing gets through*. From the crown of its skull to the set of its massive haunches it was covered in plates — great overlapping shelves of a material that was not quite horn and not quite stone, the colour of old iron, each plate a hand's breadth thick at the centre and lapping the one behind it the way shingles lap a roof. A thousand of them, near enough, hence the name the outer rangers had written on the ticket: the Thousand-Plate. Its small eyes were set deep and red and unimpressed under the frontal shelf, and a pair of tusks swept up from its lower jaw, yellowed and scored, each the length of his leg.

Ten-thousand-year tier, minimum. Old. Smart. It had learned the shape of what killed things, which was why it was still here and two teams of students were not.

Lin Hao did not announce himself. He stood in the tree-line at the top of the bank and read the armour the way he would read a failed piece on his own bench.

For that was the thing, and he felt it land in him as clearly as a hammer finding its mark: he had been trying to build this. The heavy-silver wrist-guard that had folded at the fourth strike and hung on the failure wall without a name — that had been his first attempt to make metal carry what he wanted it to carry, and it had broken because he had not yet understood how armour actually worked. And here was armour that worked. Ten thousand years of the world refining the same problem in the dark, and the answer was standing in the stream twenty meters below him, drinking water out of a valley it owned.

He read the plates. The great shelves of the flank and shoulder were dead ground — hit those with anything he carried and it would slide, the way the first team's steel had slid, and spend itself on a surface engineered over a hundred lifetimes to spend attacks. You did not break a roof by hitting a shingle. You looked for where the shingles had to move.

And armour moved. A living thing in plates could not be one solid thing or it could not walk. There had to be seams — places where one shelf ended and the next began, gaps that opened when the beast lowered its head to charge or turned on its forequarters, joints where the thousand plates gave way to tendon and to the body underneath. He watched the beast shift its weight, and he saw the flank-plates slide, and in the sliding the seam showed for a fraction of a breath, behind the jaw, where the great throat-shelf lapped over the junction of the neck and the heart-girdle — the one place the plates could not quite reach without opening, the one place the living animal had to be soft.

The beast finished drinking. It lifted its head.

Its red eyes found him in the tree-line immediately, across twenty meters and up a bank, with the uncanny precision of a thing that had not lived ten thousand years by being surprised in its own valley.

It pawed the stream-bank once. The plates along its spine rose a fraction.

Lin Hao drew the borrowed field blade. He did not light a ring. There was no one to read him but the beast, and the beast did not care about rings; it cared about whether the thing in front of it was prey, threat, or neither.

He came down the bank.

---

## Part 3: A Fight That Answers

The charge came like a section of hillside deciding to move.

It was faster than anything that size had a right to be — the plates locked flat for the run, the tusks up, the red eyes fixed, and the air in the valley filled with the deep wooden thunder of its hooves. Lin Hao did not meet it. He read the line of it the way he read a descending hammer, the whole beautiful committed weight of the charge running to one inevitable point, and he let the Wind-Step take him a half-stride off that line — not away, *across*, the margin moving lateral while the mountain of plates went past near enough to smell the iron-hot heat of it. The tusk went by his hip with a hand's clearance and took the tree behind him out at the waist.

He struck as it passed. Gale Talon black-edged the borrowed blade, and he put the edge down across the nearest flank-plate, not at the plate's face but along its lapping edge — testing. The steel rang like a bell and the edge slid the way he had known it would, skating off the shelf with no more purchase than a finger on a wet pot, and the force of his own cut turned against him so that he had to flow with it or eat it.

He landed three meters on. The beast's charge carried it past; it wheeled, joints grinding, the front of it coming around with the grinding patience of a siege gate.

*All right,* he thought, with a thing in his chest he had not felt in too long uncoiling like a stretched muscle. *All right. There you are.*

He did not try the plates again. The second pass he took to the inside, moving before the charge had fully turned, and he rode the beast's own rotation — it could not reverse direction, it could only sweep around in its own great arc, and the inside of that arc was the one place the tusks were not and the shelves were busy keeping the spine locked. He was inside its reach with the front quarter of the beast beside him, close enough to set a hand on the iron hide and feel the heat and the huge slow grind of the body under it, and he walked along it for two long heartbeats, reading.

He was not holding back, not the way he had done for a year. He was moving at the speed the fight asked for, striking at the weight the strike required, spending the thousand small disciplines of the margin into an opponent where they were not a secret to keep but a tool to use. It was not full — he knew that even in the white heat of it, the way a man knows there are rooms in his own house he has not walked into; the great sealed things below him stayed sealed because the fight did not reach down to them, did not climb high enough to require them. But it was *real*. He was not waiting to see how much the room could take before he answered. He was answering with the whole of the reach he allowed himself, and against a thing ten thousand years old that had killed a team of soul masters, even that reach was a thing he had to pour out cleanly or die of his own carelessness.

It knocked him once. He mistimed a step on the inside and the beast's wheeling shoulder caught him and threw him across the stream, and he hit the far bank hard enough to feel it through the convergence body's whole frame, the water going up in a sheet around him. He came up out of it laughing once, short and bright and utterly unheard by anyone, because the hit had been *honest*, it had been a real thing landing on him and actually meaning it, and there was a joy in that no instrument had ever measured and no peer had ever been allowed to give him.

It charged again over its own shoulder. He let it come. He read the line.

And this time he did not move lateral.

The plates. He had spent three passes learning them, the way he spent the heats learning metal — asking, not telling. He knew now the one breath in the whole of the beast's engine where the seam showed. It was the moment the head dropped to drive the tusks home. At that exact instant, the great throat-shelf lifted a hair to let the shoulder and neck pull forward — lifting, because muscle had to pull against something — and for the width of a single heartbeat the seam behind the jaw opened, the dark junction where a thousand plates ended and the living thing began.

A blacksmith does not break armour. He waits for the place where it is already about to open, and he is on that place with the strike that belongs there when it does.

He did not waste it on strength. The blade was ordinary; the arm behind it was not, and the arm did not need to be. He guided the point through the opening breath of the seam with the Still-Water stillness on it, no tremor, no flourish, one clean stroke of a swordsman who had spent the whole fight *asking* — and the borrowed steel went in behind the jaw into the heart-girdle the plates could never reach, and Lin Hao put the whole of the convergence body's arm behind the last four inches the way you put a hammer through the final fold, and the thousand-year beast's charge came apart underneath him.

It took three more steps. The plates locked. The red dimmed. The great body went down into the stream with a sound like a foundry wall coming apart, and lay still, and the valley went quiet around it the way valleys do.

---

## Part 4: Nothing Wasted

He stood over it for a long minute with his breath coming hard and the borrowed blade black along its edge, and he felt the thing settle in him that he had walked out here to find.

It was not the kill. The kill was the smallest part of it, and he did it the honour of treating it as small. He had not come out hating this animal. It had owned its valley and beaten everyone sent against it and lived ten thousand years by being exactly what it was, and he had killed it because a job ticket asked it and because a thing that had dragged a student into the trees could not be left to do it again. He did not enjoy the ending. He put his hand on the cold iron of its crown for a moment, the smith's hand on good material, and said nothing to it because there was nothing a beast needed to hear and he was not a man who made speeches at the dead.

What he had come for was the fight, and he had had it — not the full thing, not the sealed rooms at the bottom of the house, but the largest honest stretch of himself he had been allowed to spend in a year, spent against something that hit back with everything it had and did not care who his father was or what his rings looked like. The itch was scratched. Under the satisfaction, though, there was the loneliness he had known would be there, the thing Gu Yue had not needed to say: no partner here. No captain to thump his shoulder, no Xie Xie to call it impossible, no one at all to tell. He had cut loose for the first time in a year in a valley with two corpses in it and no witness but the trees.

And the other finding, the one he wrote down carefully because it was the point of the whole exercise: he had not touched the ceiling. The beast had been strong enough to kill teams, strong enough to knock him through a stream, strong enough to make him take the fight seriously and spend his whole ordinary reach — and the great sealed reserves had not even stirred. The Union, the fusion, the Domain, the three-fold thunder he had never once tried: they had lain through the whole fight as quiet as they lay through the dinners and the lectures, because nothing in the valley had climbed high enough to knock on their door. He was, he suspected, going to have to go much further than a ten-thousand-year cull before he met the thing that made him *reach*.

He did not let the thought worry him. He had work to do.

A smith does not kill good material and walk away from it. The field knife came out and he butchered the carcass with the same care the fight had had, wasting nothing — the choice plates levered whole along their seams (the irony did not escape him: the armour that had turned every weapon sent against it came apart in his hands almost eagerly once you knew how it joined, and the plates were magnificent, dense and old and full of a strange iron-energy, exactly the foundation-metal for the kind of work the academy taught), the tusks drawn for the bounty proof, the heart-plate that carried the contract's verification mark. It took him the better part of the afternoon. He worked methodically, in the stream-water and the fading light, the way he worked any valuable stock: respectfully, completely, with the old mountain rule running through his hands that a beast you killed owed you nothing and you owed it the use of all of it.

He carried out what he could and marked the rest for the salvage team the job ticket promised, strapped the best plates to his pack with cord, and walked back up out of the valley as the light went gold behind the hills. His soul power, spent thin across the afternoon, was already climbing back toward him the way it always did, steady and certain, the deep sea of his spirit filling to its high-tide line. By the time he reached the outer ranges he was back to whole. Nothing of the crossing kind had happened. Nothing had been asked that his ordinary reserves could not answer.

At the administration counter he laid the heart-plate and the tusks down. The clerk looked at the proof, looked at the danger mark on the ticket — the beast that had come back empty twice — and looked at the thirteen-year-old in grey working-student clothes, and did the same arithmetic the other clerk had done and reached the same decision about saying nothing. He stamped the ticket and logged the bounty to Lin Hao's token, and the contribution points were, by Shrek's quiet accounting, considerable.

"Anything to report?" the clerk asked, because the form had the line.

Lin Hao thought of the score marks and the drag-gouge and the team that had left its dead in that clearing. He thought of the plates on his back.

"It was old," he said. "It fought well. The ticket's cleared." He did not say how long it had taken, or how much of himself he had spent, or how little. He did not mention the seam.

The clerk stamped it closed.

Lin Hao walked back out into the Shrek afternoon with a pack full of armour-in-waiting and a ticket paid and the first real fight in a year behind him — and in him, still, the question the valley had not been big enough to answer: where, on the whole wide continent, was the thing that would make him open the rooms he kept sealed, and when it finally came, would even that be far enough up the ladder to reach the door?

He shifted the heavy plates on his back, the dead armour already planning the shape of the suit it would one day become, and walked toward the foundry. He wanted to show He Qiao the metal. And somewhere in the back of his mind, he was already pricing the next ticket.

## Part 1: The Metal That Lost

Lin Hao carried the plates to the foundry the next morning, strapped flat against his pack in the cord he had tied in the valley, and laid the best three on He Qiao's bench like a man laying down cards he meant to keep.

The one-armed smith had been feeding a fire. He set his tongs down. He did not touch the plates at first; he walked around them the way he walked around a piece he was deciding whether to buy, his single eye moving over the way the dark-gold lines ran through the old-iron shelves.

"Where," he said, "did a working student with a day-old token get Thousand-Plate armour-hide."

"Off a Thousand-Plate," Lin Hao said. "Cull ticket. The one that came back empty twice. It came back empty because the other two teams were hitting the face of the plates. You don't hit a roof on the shingles. You find where the shingles have to move. It had a seam behind the jaw. I used it."

He Qiao's eye came up off the metal and onto Lin Hao's face, and stayed there a long moment. "You killed it through the join."

"It killed a team through not having one." He sat down on the bench across from him. "I'm not here to sell it. The bounty's paid. I'm here because this is the best metal I've ever held in my life and I don't know enough to waste it on something wrong. The plates are ten-thousand-year hide, dense as anything, and there's an energy in them — feel it, right along the grain — that doesn't belong to ordinary iron. I want to know what it wants to become."

That got the old smith's hands moving. He turned the largest plate over, ran his thumb along the lapping edge where Lin Hao had levered it whole from the carcass along the natural seam, and his eyebrows, which had been at their normal resting height of *unimpressed*, climbed.

"You took it apart along the joins," he said. "You didn't cut a single plate. You unshingled a dead beast like a roof at end of lease." He looked up again. "Most fifth-ranks cut. You read. That's not the fifth-rank trick, boy. That's the trick that keeps going when the rank stops mattering."

"The metal," Lin Hao said again, because He Qiao was the kind of man who would happily talk craft for an hour and not answer the question once.

"The metal," He Qiao agreed, and finally took up a scriber to tap the plate. The note that came back was deep and slow and did not fade. "You're right about the energy. That's not iron-energy, that's the beast's own ten-thousand-year accumulation settled into the plates it grew. Armour-hide like this has one use on this campus, and it's the use the whole outer court is bleeding points to chase. It's foundation stock for battle armour." He set the scriber down. "For one-word work it's beyond overkill — wasteful, even; one-word suits take thousand-refined ordinary metal and don't need a material this alive. This is two-word grade. Maybe better. The energy in it wants to be *spirited*, not just refined. It wants a sixth-rank hand." He paused. "It wants a hand I don't have."

Lin Hao felt the shape of that sentence settle over him. "You're sixth rank."

"I'm sixth rank and one arm and forty years past the age I was going to be seventh." He Qiao said it without self-pity, the way he said everything — flat, a fact from the bench. "There's exactly one hand in this association that this metal is ready for, and it belongs to a man who hasn't been down to the outer foundry in three years because nobody down here has been worth his walk. But that's not your problem this morning." He slid the plates back. "Keep them. Don't sell a single one to the exchange — they'll underpay you like you're a first-year with a lucky rock. Store them dry. When you've got a suit of your own worth hanging them on, or when you've found the hand that can spirit them, you'll thank me. Metal that good doesn't spoil."

Lin Hao wrapped the plates back in their cord. He filed the sentence about *the one hand* away in the margin without comment, the way he filed everything that named a door he had not yet been shown.

The foundry door banged open at that exact moment with the force of a small weather system, and Tang Wulin came through it at speed, trailing the smell of coke and an expression Lin Hao knew well — the look of a boy who has been carried somewhere enormous and is still not sure whether he was kidnapped or promoted.

## Part 2: The Badge

Wulin saw him and changed course the way water changes course toward the lowest point in the floor.

"You're alive," Lin Hao said.

"I'm a member of the Blacksmiths' Association," Wulin said, and held up his chest as evidence. Pinned to it was a badge so crudely hammered it looked like a child's idea of a hammer, black and lumpen and unmistakable. "He put it on me. The red-haired man. He came through the dining hall and picked me up and carried me to a workshop and made me forge two pieces of meteoric iron and then did nine soul rings at me and told me to be his disciple."

Lin Hao set the wrapped plates down very carefully, because this was more information than the bench usually got in a year. "Nine."

"Four purple, four black, and a red one." Wulin held up fingers and then gave up on fingers. "He was no weaker than Elder Cai. He's the president of this entire association, Lin Hao. His name is Feng Wuyu and he is a Saint Blacksmith and he said he would burn to ashes anyone who touched a hair on my head if I became his disciple." He sat down hard on the bench beside the plates. "I told him I already have teachers. Mu Chen, and Mang Tian. I told him if I betrayed them I could betray him too. He didn't like it but he couldn't argue it, so I said I'd ask Mu Chen if Feng could *also* guide me, and I agreed to join the association so he'd let me leave, and he pinned this on me and shouted that I wasn't allowed to join any other association and that if anyone tried to lure me I should use his name." He stopped for breath. "He's completely mad. I forged two pieces of meteoric iron to spirit-grade thousand-refining. Forty-nine strikes of the Disorder Splitting Wind. My hammers are spirit-refined now and they drink my blood essence and the metal told me what it was feeling. I can see why you like doing this. I'm also very tired and I may have made an enemy of a Title Douluo by accident."

"You didn't make an enemy." Lin Hao was reading the badge, then the man, then the badge again. "You did exactly the right thing and you did it on instinct, which is the part that's going to matter. Listen to me, because this is the one thing I know better than anyone in this city." He turned on the bench to face him fully. "Never give up the teachers who made you for the one who wants you. A man who asks you to betray your first master to become his second is telling you exactly what he'll be to you the day someone more interesting comes along. You held the line. That's worth more than the nine rings. But — and don't miss this — you also didn't say no to him. You left the door open. That was right too. He's a Saint Blacksmith, Wulin. You don't turn your back on a hand like that. You make it so he and Mu Chen are both on your side and neither one of them can call it betrayal. Ask Mu Chen exactly what you promised. Let him decide. Then walk through every door both of them open."

Wulin absorbed this. "You've been in this association a day and you already know how its president operates."

"I've been in the association a day and I registered through the foundry master out there, who has six rings' worth of reasons to think carefully about the man above him." Lin Hao nodded at He Qiao's back. "But I'll tell you what I didn't know until ten minutes ago." He tapped the crude black badge. "I walked in here yesterday as a fifth-rank nobody and got my token from a one-armed sixth-rank who watched two heats and sent me on my way. You got carried through the front gate by the president himself. We're in the same association, captain. We've been smithing the same metal on opposite sides of a courtyard wall. The fourth floor, free tables, our own metal. That's not a coincidence, that's a roof, and we're both under it now."

The magnitude of it seemed to land on Wulin a beat late. "We can work the same workshop."

"We can work the same workshop."

For a long moment neither of them said anything, and in the silence you could hear the whole foundry — the bellows, the ring of hammers on a dozen tables, the coke shifting in the fires — and under all of it the thing that the two of them had been doing separately in Eastsea, in competition and in secret and at opposite ends of a town, now given a single room to happen in.

## Part 3: The Two Freaks

Gu Yue found them there an hour later, or rather she found Wulin first and Lin Hao second, which was the order she did most things.

She said nothing at all about the fact that Lin Hao had been gone into the wild for a day and a night and had come back carrying enough strange metal to outfit a workshop. She looked at him for one beat longer than she looked at Wulin — a look that went over the dried streambed-mud he hadn't fully scrubbed off his sleeve, the fresh-healed nick at his jaw, the way he sat loose and straight and *rested* in a way he had not sat in a year, the particular quality of a man who had finally done the thing he'd been starving for — and she filed all of it the way she filed everything, into the drawer she never opened in front of anyone.

"You," she said to Wulin, "have a badge."

"He has a president," Xie Xie said, crowding in behind Xiaoyan. "Wulin has his own personal Title Douluo. I heard it from three people on the way over. The red-haired one carried him off like a sack of rice and now he's the man's apprentice."

"Not apprentice," Wulin said. "It's complicated."

"It's not complicated," said Xiaoyan, who had been doing arithmetic on her fingers. "Both of you are fifth-rank blacksmiths and both of you are in the association that makes battle armour, and the association's president personally recruited the captain, and Lin Hao walked in and registered himself off the street. Do you know what the rest of the outer court calls the two of you?" She didn't wait. "The two freaks. Someone already worked out that the working-student block has the only under-fourteen fifth-rank smiths most of them will ever meet, and there are *two* of them in the same dorm. People are going to want metal from you. Lots of people. Battle armour runs on thousand-refined stock and the entire outer court is trying to make battle armour."

Lin Hao exchanged a look with Wulin. They had, both of them, already done this arithmetic on separate benches.

"Then we price it like craftsmen and not like children," Lin Hao said. "Every suit of armour in this place needs thousand-refined metal that the makers and designers can't produce themselves. Shen Yi said it in the first lecture — commission the smiths, befriend the good ones. We are the good ones. We don't undersell. We don't refuse our own. And we don't work so hard at other people's armour that we forget our own."

"Your own." Gu Yue's voice was very level. She had not sat down. "You mean you've already started thinking about a suit."

He thought about the plates under the cord, the ten-thousand-year hide full of an energy that wanted a seventh-rank hand. He thought about Shen Yi's sixty percent. He thought about his own body, the thing that learned the shape of whatever it touched and became it, and he said the thing he had said at the fountain and meant more now, after a beast had spent an afternoon trying to kill him with armour he could now read like his own hand.

"I've never worried about the compatibility. The metal and I have always come to an understanding." He said it as craft, and Gu Yue heard craft, and Wulin heard craft, and that was the whole truth the room was cleared for. "What I worried about was having a reason and a roof and the metal. I've got the roof as of this week. I've got better metal than I deserve as of yesterday. And I've got the same reason everyone in this building has. So yes. I've started thinking about a suit. The same way everyone here has."

Gu Yue looked at him for that held beat. Then she nodded, once, and said nothing else, and turned to examine Wulin's badge with the particular thoroughness she gave to things she was not going to comment on.

## Part 4: The Hand That Walks

He Qiao found him again at the end of the afternoon, when the others had gone and Lin Hao was wrapping the plates to store them dry against the workshop wall.

"Your captain," the old smith said, leaning in the doorway with his one arm folded. "The one Feng Wuyu carried off. He's good?"

"He spirit-refined two meteoric irons in an afternoon with spirit-refined hammers." Lin Hao tied the cord. "Forty-nine of the Disorder Splitting strikes. I've never seen it. I've only ever read about the number."

He Qiao let out a sound that was nearly a whistle. "Then the president's found his boy, and good for him; that old man has been trying to adopt every smith under twenty on the continent for a decade." He watched Lin Hao's hands work the cord. "Which leaves you."

"Leaves me?"

"The president doesn't walk down to the outer foundry. Hasn't in three years. But he comes up on to this floor, now and then, when the word gets interesting." He Qiao's single eye was steady on him. "Metal doesn't lie to a Saint Blacksmith, boy. You walked in here off a cull ticket carrying ten-thousand-year armour-hide that you unshingled by reading the joins, and you forged two demo heats for me like it was nothing. The foundry talks. By the end of the week that talk goes up through the floor. So I'll give you the same advice you gave your captain and you can do with it what you like." He pushed off the doorframe. "When a man like Feng Wuyu comes looking — and he will, because that metal in your pack is the kind of story that walks itself up four flights of stairs — you remember two things. Don't turn your back on a hand that strong. And don't you *dare* betray whoever first taught you to read metal the way you read it. The Saint won't respect the first. He'll think twice about the second, same as he did with your captain."

Lin Hao thought of Mang Tian, and Mu Chen, and Tie Jin in the scrap pavilion who had sent the wire that brought him here. "I won't."

"Good." He Qiao turned to go, then over his shoulder: "Store the plates on the high rack. Dry. And boy—" He stopped. "Whatever you're holding back in those heats of yours — and I've been doing this forty years, I can taste it when a man's forging at walking pace — when you finally hit something in this building that makes you stop holding it back, I want to be within earshot. That's all. Just earshot."

He went out. Lin Hao stood a moment in the foundry's dying heat with the cord in his hands and the plates stacked dry on the high rack, and thought about doors.

The association had a president who was nine rings of fire and a hammer that could make metal into soul. He had a brother under the same roof now instead of across a town. He had foundation metal that wanted a hand above his rank. And he had an old one-armed smith who had watched two easy heats and somehow, clean through the craft of it, tasted that the easy heats were not the real ones.

*He's right,* Lin Hao thought, and slung his pack. *I'm forging at walking pace. The whole city's getting walking pace. The only thing I've hit that made me move at a real one was an armoured pig two hours west with two teams' worth of graves under its belt.*

He looked up, toward the ceiling of the foundry and the three floors above it where the president's tables were, somewhere in the direction of the fourth floor.

Then he went down the stairs, and out into the Shrek evening, already deciding that the next cull ticket he pulled would not be a ten-thousand-year. He had worked out the margin on that one in an afternoon. It was time to find out what the rung above it cost.

## Part 1: Workshop Eighty-Eight

The Blacksmiths' Association turned out to be two different buildings wearing the same door.

Downstairs was the outer foundry where Lin Hao had registered — the public tables, the one-armed master, the roar and coke and student smiths paying by the hour for a place to hit metal. Upstairs, reached by a narrow coiling corridor that wound like a snake past soundproofed door after soundproofed door, was the part of the association that only opened up once your rank stopped being a rumor.

"You get a workshop," Wulin said, standing in the center of room eighty-eight and turning slowly so he could see all four metal walls at once, the way a man turns to take in a house he has been told is his. "Your own. Private. Soundproof. A table that's better than anything Mu Chen ever let me breathe near. And they *pay* you. Two thousand points a month, stipend, ten chunks of metal free, eight percent off anything you buy — for being a fourth-rank blacksmith. I had to fight the academy to get a *job* sweeping stone, and the association gives me a key and a salary and asks nothing but three jobs a month I could do in my sleep."

"That's because the jobs the academy hands out are a trap," Lin Hao said. He was leaning against the doorframe, watching his captain discover the world one beautiful scandal at a time. He had signed his own register that morning, a rank above, and the clerk's face had gone through a very satisfying sequence when the paperwork loaded. His own terms ran better than Wulin's — a larger room when he wanted it, a deeper metal allowance, a higher stipend — and he had taken the key to a workshop of his own with the quiet satisfaction of a man closing a ledger that had been open since Eastsea. "The academy posts thousand-refining jobs for a thousand contribution points. The association buys the same piece of work for two thousand. Every working student who doesn't know that yet is doing their thousand-refining through the administration and getting taxed in ignorance."

Wulin stopped turning. "That's *criminal*."

"That's a ladder with a rung missing, so that the people who haven't found the association yet fund the people who have." He pushed off the doorframe. "First-grade thousand-refined metal sells for two thousand points minimum through the guild. There's a five percent fee if you sell through them, which still leaves you nearly double the academy job. Nobody with a badge takes the admin jobs. The board in the admin building is bait for first-years who don't know the guild exists." He let his mouth tug. "We took the bait for four days."

"We cleaned a plaza very well," Wulin said, with dignity. "It's spotless."

The forging table stood in the center of eighty-eight, standard grade and not extravagant, but to a boy who had learned his craft on a borrowed corner of Mu Chen's bench it might as well have been an altar. The shelves were bare except for the ten free monthly chunks and the less-valuable metal Wulin had tipped out of his storage ring. He was already running a hand along the table's edge with the particular reverence he reserved for things that were about to feed him.

"First customer's on the way," Lin Hao said. "And she'll ask you a question worth more than the metal."

The knock came before he had finished the sentence.

## Part 2: The Selection

Yuanen Yehui came in the way she did everything — unremarkably, without announcement, her ordinary face and ordinary build giving no warning at all of what was underneath them. She nodded once to Lin Hao, the same single working-student nod she had given at the admin counter, and turned to Wulin.

"You're actually set up here." Her eyes went over the room. "I need a full set, eventually. Battle armor. I can pay, and I'll keep paying — I'm a third-rank mecha designer, I've got the points. I just need the metal started. Something ductile. My martial soul makes things *large* when I use it, and the armor has to come with me."

Wulin's eyes went round. "Your martial soul — you never said what it was."

A hesitation. Then: "Titan Giant Ape."

Lin Hao, at the doorframe, did not move, but something in him went very still and attentive, the way it did when a name clicked into a space he had been holding open. *Titan Giant Ape. King of the forest.* The unassuming girl who finished design plans before dawn. The examiner who had walked Xie Xie into the ground. The shoulder under ordinary clothes that moved like it carried far more than the frame suggested.

"You want heavy silver," he said, into Wulin's open mouth. "Most ductile mid-grade metal there is. It'll stretch with the transformation." He said it to Wulin, but he was watching Yuanen as he said it, and he saw the small flicker in her — the second glance, the reassessment, the careful re-filing of *the quiet fifth examinee* into a different slot.

"He's right." Yuanen's gaze came back to him and stayed a beat longer this time. "Heavy silver. Thousand refined."

Wulin made the deal like a boy who cannot quite believe his life — and then, because Wulin was Wulin, he spent the goodwill he had just bought on the one question he could not stop asking. "The price is too cheap for that. I know it is. So — working students. Tell me the secret. Why does this whole academy go quiet and respectful the moment someone says it?"

Yuanen took the finished heavy silver from him and put it away, and answered bluntly, as she answered everything.

"Because working students are freaks. The academy takes people who didn't pass the full exam but are spectacular in one area — or too extraordinary somewhere to turn away even if everything else doesn't fit. Your Elder Feng was one. He graduated the outer court at thirty-four on blacksmithing alone, and the same year he broke through to spirit refining and seventh rank, became the youngest Saint Blacksmith on the continent, and the academy made an exception and took him into the inner court. Six rings to nine in twenty years. The greatest smith Shrek has." She leaned against the soundproofed wall. "Working students have been reaching the top ever since. To an ordinary student, we're unpredictable, and we are *absolutely not to be offended*. A graduating working student's chance at the inner court is thirty percent — much higher than theirs. The pressure's worse too. Elder Cai wasn't punishing you when she made you working students. She was sorting you into the stream that goes somewhere."

The room was quiet a moment. Xie Xie, who had drifted in behind Xiaoyan and spent his whole time at Shrek nursing his humiliation at the exam, made a small strangled sound in the doorway. The examinee who had beaten him into the ground was a *freak admit*, like them.

"Thirty percent," Xiaoyan said slowly, doing the arithmetic on her fingers and arriving, as she always did, at the thing the others missed. "So it's not a charity class. It's a *bet*. The academy's wagering that a monster who's overwhelming in one thing will drag the rest up to match. That's why they tolerate the whole arrangement. The ones who make it are worth more than twenty ordinary graduates."

Lin Hao said nothing for a long moment. He had worked this out alone in the drink shop, watching a girl with no name fold her wings and trust the sky to answer. *A selection. Not a guild, a selection.* He had been right. He had been right in every particular — the waitress, the examiner, the girl at the counter, all the same careful monster the academy was growing in the margin where ordinary students never looked.

"One thing," he said, quietly, into the gap. "If it's thirty percent in, and you're fifteen and a third-rank designer and this strong — why aren't you inner court already?"

The loneliness crossed her face so fast it was almost not there. "That," she said, "is a secret." She straightened. "Treat me to dinner for the answers, glutton."

Wulin protested the name the whole way out the door.

## Part 3: The Ram

They walked back toward the working-student dormitory as the Shrek light went amber, Wulin and Yuanen ahead, the other four strung out behind. The forest edge came first, as it always did on that path — and at the edge, sitting on a low wall facing the dormitory with the patience of a man who has decided to wait all night, was a figure in green with golden hair.

Lin Hao knew him before he stood up. The drink shop. The white suit, swapped for an academy uniform. The overbearingness that even Wulin could not out-look.

"Have either of you seen a red-haired girl?" Yue Zhengyu strode over, golden eyes scanning, arrogant as gravity. "Actually, does a red-haired girl even live here?"

Wulin's heart-rate picked up — Lin Hao saw it in the way his captain's shoulders went. *The Fallen Angel waitress. She said she was a working student. She's in this dorm block. He's hunting her.* And beside him, at his elbow, walking exactly the same line home, was Yuanen.

Lin Hao's hand did not move. He stayed where he was, a half-step back, the margin watching two people walk toward a collision he had been expecting since the night the sky came down.

"I don't know anyone like that." Yuanen's voice was flat. "Please move out of the way." She did not stop walking.

"I waited half a day," Yue Zhengyu said, "and I've only met you two working students. Now you say you don't know anything?" He reached out — not a strike, just the lazy push of a man used to clearing space, a hand toward her chest to move her off his line.

Yuanen's whole body went dark with an aura that hit the amber twilight like a wall dropping.

Lin Hao read it the instant it came. The unassuming frame did not shrink into itself. It *grew* — not visibly, not yet, but the *potential* of growth filled the air around her, the way the air over a forge fills with heat before the iron comes out. King of the forest. A soul beast so far above the ordinary ladder that the second-grade Angel boy three paces ahead of her had no idea what was standing in front of him.

She dropped her shoulder and rammed him.

It was not a martial technique. It was the single, insulting, contemptuous thing a stronger body does to a weaker one when it has decided the confrontation does not deserve a soul ring — she checked him like a tide checks a fence post. Yue Zhengyu was lifted off his feet and thrown backward through the air, three meters, five, and only caught himself by flaring his white Holy Angel wings wide and beating the air, hanging there with his dress shoes dangling and an expression of total, spiritual astonishment, his right shoulder visibly trembling with the recoil.

"Holy Angel's a spirit of light and judgement," Lin Hao said, very low, to no one in particular — to Xie Xie, whose jaw was hanging. "It isn't built to win a shoving match with the forest king. He's strong and he's got three purple rings, and she just told him, with one shoulder, that strength isn't the same as *weight*."

"She didn't even light a ring," Xie Xie whispered. "She just *pushed* him."

"That's the lesson." Lin Hao watched the golden-haired boy hang in his own wings and glare. "The person who beat you in the exam and the girl he's hunting for having black wings are standing in the same body, and he's too proud to see it." He held up a hand before Xie Xie could blunder into the middle of it. "Nobody says anything. This isn't our secret to hand him, and she doesn't need us. Watch. She'll handle it the way she handles everything — by being ten times stronger than the situation requires and declining to discuss it afterward."

He was right. Yuanen did not pursue. She stood on the path with her arms loose and her face unchanged, the aura sinking back into the ordinary frame, and looked up at the hovering Angel with the mild, weary contempt of a person who has had this conversation before and does not expect this telling to be better.

"The working students aren't hiding her," Lin Hao said, as the group — with Wulin, wisely, looking nowhere but at his own shoes — began to move past the standoff toward the dorm. "She's been standing in front of him the entire time. He's hunting for something behind the wall while he's talking to the wall."

## Part 4: The Next Rung

They left Yue Zhengyu shaking dust off his wings at the forest edge, and nobody spoke of it for the rest of the walk, the way nobody steps on a thing they have just seen sleep.

But that night, after the curtain was hung and the others had settled, Lin Hao did not take out his notebook. He took out the culling board instead — the memory of it, the layout he had carried out of the administration hall and turned over in his head through the whole of dinner.

The secret had not changed anything about the path. It had clarified it.

He was a freak admit, same as Wulin, same as Yuanen, same as the president who went from six rings to nine. The academy did not bet on well-rounded. It bet on the thing that was overwhelming and trusted the rest to catch. His overwhelming thing — the thing Shen Yi's sixty-percent compatibility rule couldn't touch, the thing a Saint Blacksmith's association had issued a key for, the thing the working-student stream was built to feed — was not going to be sharpened by sweeping plazas or forging other people's thousand-refinements at a comfortable rank. It was going to be sharpened by the only thing that had ever sharpened anything in him.

A thing that hit back.

He had priced the ten-thousand-year rung in a single afternoon and walked away with it intact, his sealed doors unstirred. The beast in the valley had been real and it had killed a team, and it had still not made him *reach*. The freaks did not graduate at thirty percent by staying in the band where they were already comfortable. Feng Wuyu had not become the youngest Saint on the continent by working metal he could forge in his sleep.

So he lay in the dark with his hands behind his head and made the decision the way he made every decision about work — plainly, by listening for the note.

The next ticket he pulled would not be a ten-thousand-year.

There was a higher mark on that board. He had seen it the first time, the way his eye always found the most expensive thing on a bench — a ticket flagged past the danger band his year was supposed to take, something in the country beyond even the outer ranges that the academy had stopped sending ordinary students to. A beast nobody had a contract out on because nobody who could take it needed the points. He had walked past it the first time because walking past it had been the correct, careful, *first-week* decision, and the careful decision was what a working student did until he knew his own reach.

He knew his reach now. He knew it down to the inch, the way he knew the weight of a hammer before he swung. He did not know the reach *above* him — the one the sealed rooms existed for. That was the whole point. That was the only thing worth buying with the points and the metal and the key.

And the other thing, the one he did not say out loud because there was no one in the dorm who could hold it: the academy had not been wrong about him. He *was* a freak admit, in exactly the sense Yuanen meant — he had not come through Shrek on the clean total score, he had come through because there were things in him the exam could not grade and had not dared to refuse. The adaptation. The sword. The thing the honest instrument had printed five signatures and no bracket for. The academy had looked at all of it, bet on it, and put him in the margin stream where they put the monsters who were overwhelming in one direction and unclassifiable in every other. Yuanen carried that in a plain frame and a design badge. Feng Wuyu had carried it in a hammer. He carried it in the thing he refused to spend in front of people. Which meant the academy was, somewhere in its frost-composed head, already waiting to see what he became when the margin finally ran out.

"Tomorrow," he said, into the dark of the boys' room, too low for the captain's curtain to catch, "I take the expensive one."

Somewhere outside the Shrek night, past the training ranges and the wild country where a Thousand-Plate had owned its valley, there was a thing that might actually be big enough to knock on one of the doors.

He was looking forward to finding out if it could.
