## Part 1: The Ticket

The job board in the suppression hall was three walls of parchment, colour-coded by what the guild thought would come back to collect the money. White and yellow tickets you could read and yawn through. Purple ones made working students count their rings. The single black-rimmed ticket pinned crooked in the far corner made the clerk look up twice when Lin Hao's hand reached for it.

"Ten-thousand class, ridge-armoured boar," the clerk said, reading it off like he was contractually obliged to warn every taker once. "Iron-Tusk. It ranged up out of the lower country after the month's storms and it's been working the ore trail. Three supply trains, two haulers killed. It's wounded — a hunter got a spear into its off-shoulder two weeks back — and a wounded ten-thousand beast is meaner than a healthy one. Suppression, full salvage rights to the taker, eleven hundred points. Standard black class." He did not say the part they always left unspoken, but his eyes said it: this was rated for a team. Three four-ring masters, or one older, calmer one. Not a first-year with a school tag on his bag.

Lin Hao read the ticket properly, the way he read a piece of metal before he bought it — the grain of it, the places it was likely to fail. Three trains raided on the same stretch meant a territory, a den, an animal that had learned the road and liked it. Wounded off-shoulder meant it would favour the left and turn right last. Ridge-armoured boar meant a back plated in horn that read like poorly-quenched steel — hard on the surface, soft at the seam, and the seam ran where the shoulder met the spine. Eleven hundred points and the salvage of a ten-thousand-year hide and a pair of tusks that would buy a great deal of workshop time.

He had spent weeks on easy jobs, the safe tickets, the half-meals. He was a working student with a workshop to rent and a brother to feed and a standard he was tired of walking around. He took the ticket down.

He knew what the black rim on the parchment meant. White tickets were nuisance beasts for the working students who needed a few points before meals; yellow were honest work; purple made you send word to your teacher. A black-rimmed ticket was the guild admitting, in ink, that the thing out there would kill a careless four-ring master, and pricing the job accordingly. The eleven hundred points on the bottom line was more than a first-year earned in two months of hall-scutwork, and the salvage of a ten-thousand-year hide would cover a season of workshop rent by itself. It was not a number a boy turned down if he was tired of the small jobs.

He thought it through the way he thought through a commission with a hard deadline. He had four rings. One of them was black, which changed the arithmetic quietly — his fourth soul skill was a band sharper than any ordinary four-ring master carried. He had two souls in him, a body that knits overnight and did not feel the cold, and a sword teacher who had spent years telling him the margin lived in the preparation, not the moment. What he did not have was a team, and what the ticket wanted was three men. The gap between "three men" and "one careful man" was a gap you could close with the one thing a working smith understood better than most of the academy: setting up before the metal ever went in the fire. A trap of ground and timing cost no soul power at all.

"Alone?" the clerk said.

"I work faster alone," Lin Hao said. It was not bravado; it was the smith's habit, the man who measures a job and knows the size of his own hands. "Write it. If I don't come back, the points don't cost you anything."

The clerk wrote it. Outside, the autumn air off the ranges was thin and clean and full of the smell of cold iron, which out in that country was not a smell at all but a direction.

## Part 2: Reading the Ground

He did not go looking for the boar the first day. That was the difference between a four-ring master who walked into a black-class ticket and a fool. He walked the ore trail.

Three days of reading sign. Where the haulers had been pulled off the road, the ground told him the beast had come from uphill and gone back uphill the same way — it had a den on high ground, not down by the water as a healthy boar would choose. The wound had pulled it up into the cold. He found the wallow where it lathered the shoulder in mud against the pain; he read the depth of the prints and timed them against the moon, the way he'd been reading hammer-strikes against metal since he was small — rhythm, weight, the tell of an off-balance beat. The left tusk cut deeper into the earth than the right. It carried the good shoulder into the turn last, slow and heavy, like a door whose hinge had gone.

On the third morning he climbed above the wallow and found the ridge itself: a long spill of broken quarry stone where the mountain had dropped its iron-rich rock a hundred years ago and left a natural rampart, loose underfoot, sloping to a dead end against a cliff. A stretch of bad footing between two walls of scree. He stood in it for a long while and listened to the stone shift under his boots, and he did something no one who only understood soul power would think to do. He built a trap out of the country itself.

He set loose scree to slide on a line he marked with his eyes. He wedged two of the largest blocks so they would come when he needed them. He picked the exact patch where the bad footing met the cliff base — a narrow lane where a big animal, charging on a lame right side, could not turn and could not climb and could only pile up against the stone. He worked at it for a day with no soul power at all, just hands and a borrowed pry-bar and the kind of patience a smith uses to set a forge before the iron ever goes in. He thought about the animal, too, the way he thought about any customer's metal — what it wanted, what it feared, what it would do when the heat came. A ridge-boar was not clever the way a pack-beast was clever; it could not be out-thought, only out-arranged. It would run the trail it knew, which was the uphill line. It trusted the plated ridge over its back and charged threats head-on, because for ten thousand years charging had worked. The lame right side was the one crack in a design that otherwise had none. None of this was cleverness on his part. It was just reading: the same skill he used on a bad ingot, finding the fault line before he put the first strike on it.

He slept the third night in a crook of the cliff above the trap and woke before the cold left the air, and he checked every wedge and every sliding stone twice, the way a smith checks his quench water before committing the blade. The whole job, he already understood, would live or die in these three quiet days. The chase itself would only be the forging — the metal already shaped by the forge.

Then, at dusk, he went down to the wallow and he made enough noise to be the easiest thing on the mountain.

---

## Part 3: The Charge

It came like a bad omen, the ground starting to move before the animal was visible — three tons of ridge-armoured fury driving uphill out of the treeline, the good left tusk leading, the plated ridge across its back the colour of old foundry scrap. Ten thousand years of a life spent charging things made the ground afraid of it. A four-ring master who met that head-on with soul power and courage lost; the math had no good answer, which was why the ticket was rated for a team.

Lin Hao did not meet it head-on.

He ran. Up the quarry ramp, light-footed on the scree he had spent the day learning, the boar's momentum carrying it up the funnel behind him far faster than it could turn — and at the mouth of the lane he did the one thing the ridge hide could not answer. He didn't cut the armour. He set his footing and brought the Frost Abyss Sword, not with power but with the whole of Sword Consciousness, the man-and-sword-as-one certainty that puts an edge exactly where the seam already wants to part, and he drove it into the ridge seam where the shoulder met the spine on the beast's slow right side — the bad side, the late-turn side — one clean, deep, perfectly-placed stroke into the quenching fault in the horn. He held it there a heartbeat, rode the throw, and then he was gone, off the line, while the animal screamed and the wound that had already been there ripped wide along the weakness he'd opened.

Then the mountain did the work for which he had paid it a day. The wedged blocks came down behind the beast as it floundered on the lane of loose stone, and the scree slid, and three tons of ridge-armoured ten-thousand-year boar piled itself up against the cliff base in a heap of bad footing and its own fury, hamstrung by terrain, the plated shoulder jammed, the great head turned wrong.

---

## Part 4: The Edge of the Thing

It did not die easy, and he would have been ashamed of the story if it had. A ten-thousand beast trapped is still a ten-thousand beast, and it got a foreleg free and the good tusk came across in a blow that would have folded a lesser man's ribs through his back. He took it on the Frost Abyss domain a hand's-breadth thick — not the domain at war, not the full unhidden thing, just the cold folded small around him like a shield-brace — and the tusk slid on the ice and took him across the forearm instead of the chest, and even so it threw him into the scree hard enough that he saw the dark at the edge of the afternoon.

He was on one knee in the loose stone with the boar wrenching itself free and his breath gone and his sword hand numb, and it was at that exact edge — hurt, half-spent, a tusk coming up for the second blow that he did not have a clean answer for — that he felt it. Not reached it. Felt the distant wall of it.

The way a boy swimming far out in a dark lake for the first time puts his foot down expecting bottom and there is no bottom, and for one cold breath he understands the true size of the water. There was a place further on in his own sword, a frequency under the steel he had never touched, a depth his man-and-sword-as-one awareness only floated on the surface of — Sword Soul, the place the old legends pointed at, where the whole inner sea rang in the blade. It was there. It was impossibly far. He could no more cross to it in that moment than the swimmer could walk on the floor of the lake. He only understood, in one clear cold breath, how much deeper the water went than the shore he stood on.

Then the breath ended, because the tusk was still coming, and he was a rank-45 four-ring master with a wounded animal and a trapped lane and a day's good preparation, and that was plenty — he did not need to be anything more than what he was.

---

## Part 5: The Kill and the Walk Back

He used what he had, not what he didn't. He read the boar's next charge the way he read the metal — where it would come apart — and he did not meet it with power. He stepped into the one opening the jammed shoulder made, the late right side, and he did the small, unglamorous, smith's work of cutting: the deep seam-stroke driven twice more into the fault he had already opened, one to widen it, one to find the thing underneath, with Gale Talon speed and Still Water steadiness and the domain's cold to make the beast's great head come slow. The third stroke found the spine through the ruined seam, and the biggest thing on that mountain sagged into its own trap and stopped.

He stood there a long while after, breathing, forearm laid open to the bone where the tusk had crossed it, already closing because that was the jiao in him, the deep water knitting the wound together whether he asked it to or not. He did not whoop. He did not feel like a legend. He felt like a boy who had correctly measured a job and then been very lucky and very good, in about that order, and who had learned one thing worth more than the eleven hundred points: the size of the water. Sword Soul was real. He had felt the wall of it. And it was a thousand dawns away, which was exactly where a thirteen-year-old's sword realm ought to be.

He took the ridge plates first, because they were the prize, and he worked the joints the way Mu Chen had taught him back in Eastsea, with respect for a material that a beast had grown over ten thousand years and that some smith would pay to lay hands on. The horn-plate across the back read like poorly quenched steel even off the beast — too hard on the surface, soft and fibrous at the seam — and he noted the fault to himself as he cut, the smith's eye never quite turning off; it was the same weak line he had driven the sword into, and seeing it laid open confirmed the kill the way a clean fracture confirms a good strike. The two great tusks he took whole. The core, small and cold and dark in the chest cavity, he wrapped against his own heartbeat. The rest — too heavy for one boy's back even if the back was his — he marked with the guild's token for the haulers to bring down, because taking more than he could carry was how the careful men ended up dead on the trail beside their own salvage. He walked down the long ore trail in the dark with his arm still closing and the points not yet paid and the trap he had built sitting empty up on the ridge.

No one at Shrek saw him go and no one saw him come back, which was as it should be; it was a contracted job on contracted ground, not a thing that rang any note across the academy. In the suppression hall the clerk looked at the tusks, looked at the blood soaked into Lin Hao's sleeve that no longer had a wound under it, looked back at the tusks, and stamped the ticket complete without saying a word about teams.

Eleven hundred points, plus the salvage. He went and fed the five of them properly for the first time in a month, and he did not tell anyone how close the second tusk had come. That night in the workshop he sat with the Stormbringer across his knees and did not reach for the deep water he had felt once; he only polished the steel and practised the first Still Water stroke, slow, fifty times, because the thing he had learned out on the ridge was not a gate he could open. It was the distance to the gate. He was on the right shore, and he was exactly as far from the far one as he should be.

## Part 1: The Call from Eastsea

The eleven hundred points from the ridge-boar job settled into Lin Hao's ledger like good iron into a forge, and for a few days the five of them ate properly and stopped counting the cost of every bowl, which was its own kind of happiness. The workshop rent was paid a season in advance. The ridge-plates he'd carried down sat in his rented space at the Blacksmiths' Association waiting to be cut into something worth cutting, and his forearms had forgotten there had ever been a wound, which was the jiao's quiet opinion about wounds and a good thing, since a smith could not afford to be precious about his hands.

It was Wulin who came back from the administration building two evenings later with an expression Lin Hao had learned to read across a great many years and a great many shared meals — the particular brightness Wulin wore when he had hold of news too large to keep and was trying, badly, not to spend it all in the first sentence.

"Teacher Mu," Wulin said, and then stopped, and laughed at himself, and started over. "I called him. To tell him. About the academy, and the association here, and — and the spirit-refining. I did it again, Hao. I spirit-refined. At thirteen."

Lin Hao set down the practice blade he was oiling. "You told him that."

"I told him that." Wulin's laugh went a little thin around the edges. "He didn't say anything for a long while. Then he told me if I so much as thought about spirit-refining again before I reached rank thirty, he'd come all the way to Shrek and break my hands for my own good. Far too dangerous, he said. The one success doesn't mean I understand it."

"He's right," Lin Hao said. It was not what Wulin expected him to say, and the boy blinked. "A successful first refinement is the luckiest thing that ever happens to a young smith. You treat it as luck, not skill, until the metal can't surprise you anymore. Rank thirty. Listen to him."

Wulin nodded, and then the brightness won, because Wulin could not keep a lid on joy the way some boys couldn't keep a lid on a kettle. "And then he said — he said he's been at Eastsea too long. That Shrek is a pretty nice place. That he'd come for a visit in a few days." Wulin was nearly bouncing. "Hao. He's coming here. He's leaving the association. I think — I didn't hear it like a visit. I heard it like he's moving. You don't book two train tickets for a visit, do you? You book two tickets when you're bringing your hammers and not coming back."

Lin Hao was quiet a moment, turning the cloth over the blade in his hands. Mu Chen. The square, patient man who had set a child the test of a grown apprentice and then spent six months not quite believing what had come back to him; the teacher who had never once praised him to his face and had never once, either, failed to put a harder piece of metal in front of him when the last one was mastered. He had not seen Mu Chen since the train to Shrek. He had expected to be an adult the next time they shared a forge — or close enough to one.

"Good," Lin Hao said, and meant it. "The metal's all in this city now. A teacher who follows the metal is a teacher worth following. We'll set a place for him at the table."

## Part 2: The Working Students' Table

There was, that same week, the matter of dinner, which in the working-student dormitory was less a meal than a small rolling parliament.

The working students were a shrinking and strange population, which was the first thing you learned sitting among them. Xie Xie, who counted everything, had counted. "Last year there were six of us in this dorm," he said around a mouthful of cheap food, pointing his chopsticks at the row of tables. "Two graduated, two went up to the inner court, one dropped out. So of the old lot —"

"It's just me," Yuanen Yehui said. The strongest of the working students sat a little apart, eating with the economical steadiness of someone who had been paying for their own education for a long while. "One of the old batch. Five, if you're counting the new."

"Five," Xie Xie agreed. "Five of us now." He did not say, the way a less careful boy might, that the five of them had already done more in their first weeks than some students did in a year. Wulin was the youngest fourth-rank blacksmith Shrek had ever registered. Gu Yue was the element-user the intake instruments had refused to settle on. Xu Xiaoyan had crossed to her second ring over the summer. Xie Xie himself was three rings and entirely too pleased about it. And Lin Hao — Lin Hao was Lin Hao, which the table understood meant more than anyone at the table was allowed to say.

There was a girl who worked the dining hall on the supper shift, red-haired, quick, with the particular closed watchfulness of someone running two lives at once. Wulin had been trying, without success, to make the arithmetic about her close — a working student's badge that did not match the shift she worked, rooms that looked lived-in when the roster said they were empty, the way she and Yuanen were never, ever seen in the same breath. He had not asked. A boy with his own family's sealed doors learned early not to pry at other people's. But his eyes followed the red-haired waitress the way they followed a piece of metal with a hidden seam, and Lin Hao saw him seeing it and said nothing, the way he said nothing about most of the things Wulin was too kind to say aloud.

The peace of the table did not last the meal, because Yue Zhengyu was incapable of letting peace last.

The Holy Angel boy — fifteen years old, second grade, just out of a year of clan seclusion, with the serene, unshakable certainty of someone whose family had told him every morning of his life that he was one of the elect — sat himself down uninvited at the working-student table with his tray, and beamed around at them all like a missionary arriving among grateful heathens.

"Once I catch her," he said, by way of opening, addressing no one and everyone, "it'll be done. To eradicate evil is the duty of every Holy Angel soul master. A Fallen Angel soul master is an evil soul master — there's no such thing as a Fallen one that isn't. She's on this campus. I'll find her."

The table went the particular kind of quiet that comes right before someone is rude. It was Xie Xie who went first. "The enforcer already told you she's not an evil soul master. How are you not embarrassed? You shoulder-rammed a working student in the hall and you've been chasing a girl around the academy for days on top of it."

"Then I'll dig up proof," Yue said, unruffled, and reached for his purse with the easy confidence of a boy who had never once in his life worried about the price of anything. "Here. Let me pay for tonight's meal. All of you. It embarrasses me to think of you scrimping — please. Take care of me in the future, won't you? I'll be seeing a lot of this table."

"This has nothing to do with backbone," Wulin said, with the mild firmness Lin Hao knew from a hundred such moments. "The meal's already paid for."

Gu Yue, who had said nothing through all of it, set her chopsticks down with a small, precise click and favoured Yue Zhengyu with a look that would have frosted a lesser boy. "We won't accept food from someone as dishonest as you."

Yue Zhengyu blinked, then grinned, entirely charmed and entirely unchastened, and Lin Hao — watching it over his own bowl with the weary affection of an older brother watching a cat knock over someone else's cup — concluded that the Holy Angel boy was going to be a permanent feature of their lives whether they wanted him or not, and that the cheapest thing to do about it was exactly what Wulin did a few breaths later: Wulin tilted his head, looked at Yue Zhengyu the way he looked at a useful piece of scrap, and asked, very politely, whether a Holy Angel clan with businesses all over the campus had any need of a blacksmith who could thousand-refine, because he was a fourth-rank smith and he was, in so many words, poor.

Lin Hao kept his eyes on his bowl and let his brother do the haggling. Some smiths mined the mountain; Wulin mined the people sitting next to him.

## Part 3: The Plates in the Workshop

He went down to his rented workshop after the meal, because he could not sleep when there was good metal in the room with him, and the ridge-boar plates were good metal.

The Blacksmiths' Association at Shrek let its working smiths rent a bench and a furnace by the hour, the price coming out of the same contribution points as everything else on the academy grounds; it was a better arrangement than Eastsea's, in that the fire was hotter and the man in the bay beside you might be a Master Craftsman twice your age, and a worse one, in that nothing on the premises came cheap. He had paid a season's rent out of the cull bounty, which felt exactly right: the beast had bought the place where its own hide would be worked. Ten thousand years of horn plate did not turn into battle armour by sitting in a cupboard, and he had learned at Mu Chen's elbow that a smith who hoarded material instead of cutting it was only a man pretending at the trade.

He laid the best of the ridge plates across the anvil and read it the way you read anything worth making. Too hard on the surface, where the beast had grown it against blows; soft and fibrous at the seam, the same fault line he had driven the Frost Abyss sword through on the mountain. A piece of metal that had lived on a charging animal's back carried its whole history in its grain, and the grain told him it wanted to be drawn, not hammered flat — opened slowly, the way you opened a stubborn seam in a character, by following where it already wanted to go. Two-word-grade foundation stock, He Qiao had called it, and He Qiao was not a man who gave praise past what a thing had earned.

He did not start the piece that night. He was a fifth-rank smith, and five ranks in the blacksmith's trade carried with it the particular discipline of knowing exactly which jobs were yours to begin and which were not; the foundation of a two-word suit wanted hands steadier than his at the opening, and he had already quietly, in the way he did most things, begun looking forward to the day he could carry it up the stairs of this same building to the man at the top who could. That was a project for the coming weeks and the Saint Blacksmith's open ear, not for a single tired evening. What he did instead was the work that was exactly his rank: he cut a practice piece off the edge of a lesser plate, a clean first-grade thousand-refinement, and he put the hours into it until the rhythm was back in his shoulders after the long trip up the mountain.

The hammer made its steady noise alone in the late workshop, and he thought about Mu Chen while it fell. Two hammers coming to Shrek. A teacher following the metal. He set the practice piece to cool and let himself, for the space of a few honest strokes, look forward to it — the way you looked forward to a door opening that you had not, until that moment, realized you'd been standing outside of.

## Part 4: The Boy Who Counts

After dinner, Lin Hao walked the perimeter path with Gu Yue, which was not a thing they announced or arranged and was therefore always exactly what happened.

The autumn wind off the training grounds was ordinary. He made a point of noticing that it was ordinary, because Gu Yue had a way of turning her small unasked questions into weather, and he had learned to answer the weather honestly and leave the rest alone.

"Where did you go last week?" she said. She did not look at him. "For two days. You came back with your sleeves bloody and the blood gone the day after, and you bought all of us dinner and didn't tell anyone the job."

"A suppression ticket," he said. There was no reason to lie, and Gu Yue was the one person in the academy to whom he never gave the careful half-truth he gave the rest of the world. "Black class, up in the iron country. A wounded ten-thousand beast. It was a hard job. It's done."

"Alone."

"Alone."

She walked in silence for a while, the wind lifting the edge of her hair, and then she said the thing she had actually been turning over, the way she always did — coming at the true question from the side. "You don't have to do everything that hard by yourself. There are five of us."

"There are five of you," Lin Hao said gently, "and I am one of the five, and that's the whole answer. When the job needs five, you'll have me. When the job needs one man alone on a mountain for three days setting traps so nothing gets near his family — that one's mine. You can't come on every ticket, Gu Yue. Some of them, I carry so the table stays warm."

She did not answer that directly. She never did. The wind went briefly, oddly still between them for a breath — not cold, not strange, just the particular hush that always came when she felt something about him that she had not yet decided she was allowed to name — and then it moved again, ordinary and loud, full of the academy's evening noise.

"Teacher Mu is coming," she said instead, which was not a non-sequitur; with Gu Yue it never was. She had heard Wulin too. "You're glad."

"I'm glad." He said it plainly. "He taught me the trade before anyone knew I had it in me. A boy gets few enough of those. You keep them when they come back within reach."

They walked the rest of the circuit in the comfortable quiet of two people who had decided, long ago, that the things they did not say to each other were being kept for the right time and not thrown away. In the dormitory ahead of them Wulin was already loudly explaining to Xie Xie exactly how much work a Holy Angel commission was going to pay for, and Xie Xie was already demanding a cut, and Xu Xiaoyan was laughing, and even Yuanen's corner of the room looked a degree less lonely with the table that full.

Somewhere to the east, a man was packing two hammers and booking two train tickets, and the metal that mattered was beginning, slowly, to move toward Shrek.

## Part 1: The Dawn Spar

Ye Xinglan was on the practice field at dawn with her Stargod Sword already drawn, which was where she was every dawn, and she only bothered waiting for him because she had decided, in her level way, that waiting was the politest thing left to try.

"Again," she said, by way of greeting. "The way we did it last time. Only this time I want to understand what you're doing with the third form, because I've worked it nine ways and none of them do what yours did."

That was Ye Xinglan exactly. She did not gawk at the gap between them and she did not flatter it; she measured it and then she climbed. She was one of the very few first-years in the academy whose sword sat on the same tier as Lin Hao's own — Sword Consciousness, man-and-sword-as-one, the place where the weapon moved on the reflex before the thought finished — and she had reached it younger than most grown masters ever did. She was not below him. She was a few years' worth of dawns behind him, and she had correctly identified that he was the only thing on campus from which she could steal distance.

He took up a length of plain foundry scrap, as he always did, and settled into the first Still Water form. "Your third form fails the same way everyone's fails the first year," he said. "You decide to cut, and then the sword cuts. The gap between deciding and cutting is where all the wasted motion lives. At our tier you don't close that gap by being faster. You close it by stopping the decision. The cut has to already be true before you know you've made it — the way your hand is already moving to catch a falling thing before you've seen it fall."

"That's what I can't do," she said, and it was not a complaint; it was the flat report of a craftswoman taking a measurement.

"No one can do it the first forty days. Watch the scrap, not me." He ran the form slowly, and at the third form he let her see the thing she was looking for — the moment where intent and stroke ceased to be two things, the scrap edge travelling the line before his shoulder visibly committed. It was not a higher realm. It was the depth of the realm they both already stood in, the place Wu Zhangkong had spent years trying to drill into him and that Xinglan was now drilling herself after, one cold dawn at a time.

They sparred until the sun was up. He did not let her win and he did not shut her out; he held the forms at exactly the height she could almost reach, and she reached, and when she put the practice point past his guard for the first time she made a small, satisfied sound deep in her throat, the sound a smith makes when a struck seam finally opens the way it is supposed to.

"Forty days," she said afterwards, wiping her blade down, already counting. "I'll have the third form honest in forty days. Come back then and I'll put a second touch on you." She said it without arrogance and without false modesty, the way she said everything, and Lin Hao laughed, because she was exactly the kind of person the five of them needed in the yard.

## Part 2: The Eastsea Master

The train from the coast got in before noon. Wulin was on the platform, which surprised no one, and Lin Hao was a half-step behind him, which surprised no one either.

Mu Chen came through the gate with one solid case in his hand — a case that held two hammers and a full master's weight of expectation — and he looked exactly the same: square, patient, built like an anvil himself, the kind of man who listened to metal the way other men listened to gossip. He saw Wulin first and laughed and clapped him hard enough to stagger him, and said the things a teacher said to the student who'd dragged his name clear across the continent.

Then his eyes found Lin Hao.

For a moment Mu Chen just stood there, holding his case, and on his face was the exact expression Lin Hao had been carrying in his own memory for years — the face of a man who had done the arithmetic in Eastsea and never been able to make it close, now confronted with the answer standing alive in front of him in the open air.

"You," Mu Chen said.

"Master Mu." Lin Hao bowed the foundry bow, fist to palm. "You brought the hammers."

"I brought the hammers because the metal's in this city now." Mu Chen set the case down between his feet the way a smith set down a tool he meant to keep, and he looked Lin Hao over openly for the first time in a year — the height, the shoulders a forge had built, the hawk-gold eyes, the forearms with the faint blue-black marks gone quiet at the edges. "I gave a boy of eleven a test meant for a first-rank apprentice, to pass an afternoon. He handed it back finished like a man rinsing his hands, and when I asked his rank he said fifth, and I spent six months telling myself I'd misheard. Then he got on the train to Shrek and I gave up on the arithmetic entirely. Are you going to stand there being polite, or are you going to tell me true?"

"Fifth rank," Lin Hao said, the same word, and for the first time he did not have to say it into disbelief. "Registered here at the Shrek association. Workshop, key, a job quota I keep. Wulin and I, we're both working the trade in this city, same as you taught us. That's the true part, Master Mu. I'd like to work the same fire as you again. I've missed having a man in the room who can tell me when my quench is lazy."

Mu Chen looked at him a long moment, and then he did a thing he had never once done in Eastsea, because in Eastsea there had always been a careful teacher's distance to maintain. He put his hand on Lin Hao's shoulder, where he had just clapped Wulin.

"Two of you," he said, half to the sky, and shook his head with something caught between exasperation and wonder. "A golden dragon in an apron and this one who still won't tell me half what he is. I resigned a perfectly good post to come here. I should have resigned the day your train left." He picked up his case. "Take me to your forge. I don't give advice on train platforms. I give it at the anvil."

## Part 3: Four Flights Up

He Qiao had been waiting for this with the particular grim satisfaction of a one-armed man who had been right for weeks. He saw Lin Hao come through the Blacksmiths' Association door with Mu Chen's case in tow and pushed himself off his stool.

"He's in," He Qiao said. "President's on the top floor today, and he'll have heard there's a Saint-tier visitor and a fifth-rank child and a relocating master all in the same building. Saint Blacksmiths don't come down four flights for rumours, boy. We go up, and we bring the metal, and we don't waste the visit."

Lin Hao had the plates with him — the three best hides of the ten-thousand-year ridge-armour he'd brought down off the mountain, the two-word-grade foundation stock He Qiao had priced weeks before and told him wanted a sixth-rank hand to open. Mu Chen's eyes went to the bundle the moment it came off Lin Hao's shoulder the way a farrier's eyes go to a horse's leg; he didn't say anything, but he stopped walking for half a step, which was, from Mu Chen, the equivalent of a gasp.

Four flights, past the soundproofed workshops where Wulin kept room eighty-eight, up to the top floor where the doors stopped carrying numbers and started carrying names on small brass plates. The door at the end stood open.

Inside, working a bar of iron with the slow, almost meditative strokes of a man for whom forging was breathing, was the lion-like man with the red hair and the lion's mane of beard and the black-hammer badge of a rank so far above the ordinary ladder that it stopped being a number and became a title. Nine rings. Feng Wuyu, president of the Shrek Blacksmiths' Association, Saint Blacksmith, the youngest the trade had ever crowned. He set his hammer down and looked at the four of them.

"So," Feng Wuyu said, "you're the two I've been hearing about. The golden dragon who spirit-refined at thirteen — don't blush, Wulin, the whole trade knows — and the other one. The fifth-rank who brought down a black-class suppression solo and walked the salvage into his own rented workshop like he was carrying groceries." He held a hand out, palm up, not for a greeting. "The plates. He Qiao says you've got two-word-grade foundation metal. Let me see it."

## Part 4: The Hand That the Metal Wanted

Feng Wuyu did not read the ridge-plate like a merchant. He laid it flat and put his palm on it the way a smith reads a finished edge by the flat of his thumb, and his eyebrows came up a fraction of an inch, which in a Saint Blacksmith was the same as another man falling out of his chair.

"This is good stock," he said. "Cleanly cored, not overworked, the seams respected. Who taught you to respect a ten-thousand hide?"

"Mu Chen," Lin Hao said, and beside him Mu Chen's mouth moved in a line that was, under the control, pride fighting a man who did not lose fights. "And the job taught me the rest. The beast had a weak seam where the shoulder met the spine, poor quench-line in the horn plate. I read it on the mountain. I did the same thing to the metal I'd have done in a fight — found where it wanted to come apart and put the edge there."

Feng Wuyu looked at him for a moment, and then he did the thing that he did not do for anyone below the trade's highest ranks. He picked up a second hammer and held it out handle-first.

"Left side of the seam. I'll take the right. He Qiao tells me your sixth gate drags and you showed the exam-hall craftsmen how to true it. I want to feel whether that was bravado."

Lin Hao took the hammer. He didn't light anything off and he didn't perform; there was nothing to perform, up here, that a hammer wouldn't show or hide on its own. He simply struck — the way he struck at his own bench in the early mornings when the workshop was empty, the Disorder Splitting Wind rhythm climbing its own even mountain, forty-nine breaths of strike, each one landing where the plate was already willing to open. He was a fifth-rank smith with the wrist and eye of one, and under his hands the two-word metal did the thing He Qiao had promised it would only do for a sixth-rank and better: it opened. Not because of anything that wasn't in his hands, but because the hands were, by themselves, that far past where his rank badge sat.

Feng Wuyu's hammer kept pace with him without hurry and without ever needing to correct the seam, and that was the loudest thing in the room. A Saint Blacksmith could tell in two strokes whether he had to cover a weaker man's side. He did not have to cover Lin Hao's side at all. He matched it, the way a man matched the second voice in a song he already knew.

When they set the hammers down the plate had opened along its readiness line, clean and even, foundation stock for a two-word suit of battle armour, begun.

Mu Chen was quiet. He Qiao let out a long breath through his teeth. Wulin looked like a boy watching the two people he most admired in the world share an anvil and finding that the world had room for that.

"You're not going to make the whole suit at your rank," Feng Wuyu said to Lin Hao, plainly, without any of the false modesty a lesser man might have wrapped around the obvious. "A two-word suit is years of work and it needs hands in every profession. But the foundation's begun now and you'll be at every piece of it, because the metal's yours and the seam read was yours, and I'll put my own hand on the parts that want a Saint's. You're welcome at this anvil whenever I'm on the floor." He said it like a man announcing the weather; but to a smith, Lin Hao understood, that was the Saint coming all the way down four flights. He bowed, fist to palm, and didn't bury the moment under words.

Mu Chen exhaled. "I retired a month too late," he said to the floor. "No. A year."

## Part 5: The Pagoda

While the smiths were reading one another four flights up, Gu Yue was standing at the counter of the Shrek branch of the Spirit Pagoda, giving the institution the thing every student on the inner track had to give them once a term: her report.

The clerk behind the counter was not really a clerk. The Pagoda did not station a branch at Shrek Academy to process paperwork; it stationed one to keep an ear on the one school on the continent that manufactured monsters, and on the back of the quiet girl with six elements it held a file as thick as any first-year's in the building.

"Gu Yue," the officer said, turning a page she was not reading. "Second-rank mecha designer. Reported elements — all six, which the intake evaluators still argue about. And you came in with the blacksmith's-table five. We made that boy an offer once already, before the exam. Tang Wulin's friend. The fifth seat." It was barely a question. "If there came a day the Pagoda had something he needed, you'd tell him the offer was still open."

"He'd make up his own mind," Gu Yue said. Her hand rested on the counter, easy, unhurried; the energy-tile beside it lit steady and even with the warm, unmistakeable signature of six elements in a girl who was supposed to have at most two. "And I already know how it falls. He stays with his own. All of you keep asking the question as if the answer might change. It won't."

The officer noted the tile's reading in her file without looking at it directly — the six-element signature was the kind of thing the Pagoda was specifically on this campus to watch. "And yourself? The Pagoda doesn't keep an office here to file reports. A girl who handles six elements has doors open to her that none of her classmates will ever see."

"I'm here for the report," Gu Yue said, with the small, flat courtesy that was as close as she ever came to rudeness. "Have you got the stamp, or did you bring me in here to waste a morning?"

The officer stamped the report. Gu Yue walked out into the Shrek sun with the file on the counter a page thicker than it had been — a page that said, in essence, that the quiet girl's elements were still extraordinary and her loyalty was still, completely, somewhere the Pagoda could not reach. She didn't go up to the association floor where the smiths were. She didn't need to. She could feel, the way she always could, that Lin Hao was somewhere being seen and valued by people whose trade he'd chosen for his own, and for one morning the weight he always carried was being held by the right shoulders.

By the time she reached the courtyards the four smiths were coming down the four flights — Mu Chen carrying his case into his new city for the first time, Feng Wuyu watching from the landing with the long patience of a man who'd found what he'd come down for, and Lin Hao in the middle of them with the opened plate wrapped again under his arm, no longer a hunk of a dead beast but a begun thing: the first true piece of a two-word suit, with a Saint's hand promised on the work ahead.

## Part 1: Make the Tier You Stand On Flawless

The glimpse of the far water had not made him reach upward. It had done the opposite.

On the mountain he had felt, for one cold breath, how deep the sword went beyond him — the place Wu Zhangkong had never pretended to teach him to, the mortal-sword shore the old legends pointed at. A stupider boy might have come down from that trip and started clawing after it, trying to drag himself across a gap measured in decades before he'd earned the ground he already stood on. Lin Hao came down and did the smith's thing instead. You did not forge a better blade by staring at the steel you didn't yet own. You took the blade in your hand and made it flawless, edge by edge, until the flaws ran out and the next steel came within reach on its own.

He was at Sword Consciousness. Man and sword as one; the weapon moving on the reflex before the thought finished; the purpose wearing every object he picked up. That was a grown master's tier, and he had reached it years before he should have — and it was still, when he was honest with himself in the cold before dawn, full of the small drags and unevennesses of a boy who had climbed fast. There were depths inside Consciousness he had not yet worn smooth, the way there are depths inside a single form that take a thousand repetitions to stop fighting you. The far shore would be there for years. The job in front of him was to stop wasting a single inch of the shore he was on.

So he sat before dawn with the Stormbringer across his knees and ran the Mysterious Heaven Method the way he had every dawn since Eastsea, the long slow circuit of spirit energy through the body, and he did not point that circuit at any distant gate. He poured it, evenly, into the ground he held — carrying the soul power through the forms, through the deep water, through the storm-sky of the Inner Country, feeding the whole machine rather than chasing one bright horizon. Spiritual power grew the way a smith's shoulders grew: not on the day you lifted something impossible, but on the hundred ordinary days you lifted the right weight the right way. When he opened his eyes the light had changed and his sea was a degree deeper than it had been — not a realm, just a true, measurable inch, the kind that stayed.

## Part 2: Every Tool Back on the Bench

A tool left in the drawer forgot its weight. He had spent enough chapters staring at a far horizon, and now he took down the whole kit and put each piece back to work against the tier he actually held.

He ran the six strokes of Still Water on the practice field at dawn, the foundational forms Wu Zhangkong had given him, and the man-sword-as-one reflex deepened under him: the third form, the one Xinglan had been hunting, stopped needing the decision behind it — the edge was true before he knew he'd committed, the depth within Consciousness that he had shown her by example now owned by his own hand instead of borrowed. He ran the Disorder Splitting Wind Hammer at the anvil in the afternoons, the forty-nine-strike rhythm climbing its own mountain; with the Consciousness depth in him, the hammer met the metal a half-breath truer, the strike landing where the grain was already willing, and he turned out a clean first-grade thousand-refinement that afternoon and logged it for points the way he hadn't in weeks of looking inward.

He worked the Frost Abyss Domain in the cold evenings out on the range, alone. On the cull he'd called it up only as a thin shield-brace at the moment of need; the truth was he had never made peace with the thing, had treated it as a door you flung open in an emergency and slammed shut after. Now he walked it out a breath at a time and taught it the difference between a battlefield and a practice yard — he let the deep cold spread from the Frost Abyss sword until the grass under his boots went white and the air went still, and he HELD it there, ten breaths, twenty, a full minute, a domain that knew how to be a tool and not only a war. By the fourth evening the frost no longer bit his own hands when he spread it.

He ran the Purple Demon Eyes against the sunrise until the light stopped hurting, the third stage he had reached at his own pace and never drilled past; he read the wind off the ranges with Storm Reading, the perception skill that had sat idle too long, and on a clear morning he could taste a storm building a day's march away; he called up Domineer, the black-edged Talon, the deep-water body that healed overnight and walked cold water unburned, and he put each through its forms the way a smith oiled every tool in the box and not only the newest. By the week's end he was not a boy chasing a realm above him. He was a craftsman who owned, completely, the tier he stood on, with every tool in practice and no gaps between the ones he trained and the ones he used.

## Part 3: The Hawk and the Fusion

The hawk was not a thing you climbed toward; it was a thing you flew until it stopped being an effort.

The Hawk-Soul Union — the perfect fusion that let him wear the second body of storm and feather, the wings of wind-light and the hawk-eyes — had been a door he opened in extremity on the dangerous jobs, never at will. The dragon-fusion that rode in its wake, the deep-water joining that burned him every second he sustained it, he had never held for long at all. These were not realms to cross; they were skills to practice, like any stroke, and he had been treating them like trumps to be hoarded.

He took them out to the high ridge above Shrek at dawn, where there was no one to see and no job riding on success, and he drilled the thing the way it should have been drilled from the start: low, short, and often. He opened the Union for ten seconds and folded it; opened it for fifteen and folded it; let it come a dozen times in a morning until the door's hinges wore smooth and the second body answered the way his own hand answered. Then, when that was easy, he let the dragon-fusion ride behind it for a breath — two — three — and folded down before the burn began to eat him, the careful repetitions of a smith testing how long the iron would take the heat before he committed it to the quench.

He did not stabilize the dragon-fusion in a week. Only a fool would have claimed that; the deep-water joining would take months, maybe years, before it held without cost. But the door that had opened only at the death-edge now opened on a dawn ridge for the asking, and he could hold the dragon's edge of it for the count of a slow breath where before it had scalded him immediately. That was the shape of true progress: not the crossing announced in a moment, but the seam widening a hair each day until, one day, you did not have to force it. The hawk's plumage was a season deeper in the cold thread of its long mutation, and he left the ridge that week no higher in rank than he'd come up it, and a great deal more the master of the strength he already had.

## Part 4: The Others Are Not Frozen

He was not the only one at the grindstone. The whole five were being put to it, because Shrek did not let a working student rest, and because Wulin led by the simple method of being the hardest-working boy in any room he entered.

Wulin was in the foundry every afternoon without fail, his two carved-out hours of forging, and every spare second cultivating — the third ring, rank thirty, the gate Mu Chen had told him he had to reach before he so much as thought about spirit-refining again. He hadn't broken through. What he had done was put on the invisible, honest swell of soul power that preceded a breakthrough and was always mistaken, by anyone not watching, for standing still. Mu Chen himself was set up in Shrek now, two hammers and a hard eye, and he worked Wulin's strokes the way he had in Eastsea, and when the boy's forty-nine strikes ended in a clean refinement the new master's face did a thing Lin Hao recognized — the same wonder he had never quite managed to hide when a child handed back the impossible.

Xie Xie, ordered into the mecha-makers' association, spent his evenings swearing at his own clumsy hands and came back the next evening anyway. Xu Xiaoyan and Gu Yue bent over designs at the library tables, the two mecha designers, Gu Yue a rank ahead and pulling the other two toward her; the second profession was no longer a footnote for any of them, because the academy — and the math of battle armour — did not let it be one. Lin Hao worked at their side, refining practice blades at cost, showing the association smiths the trueing trick for the dragging sixth gate he'd shown the exam hall; a tool not used for the people around him was a tool left in the drawer.

It was into the middle of this ordinary, grinding week that Shen Yi walked into the lecture hall, with Elder Cai absent as she always was and Wu Zhangkong a silent cold column at the wall, and turned every head in the room.

Seven positions in the class. One president, two vice-presidents, four profession-council seats, all of them settled in a single battle on the practice field — survive to the end, and the last standing took the president's chair. The points were real, the inner-court advantage was real, and as Shen Yi listed the monthly stipend — a thousand contribution points to the president — she swept the room of assembled monsters with a calm eye and began with the easy one. "First," she said, "I'll declare Tang Wulin the blacksmith representative. That seat doesn't get contested." When the enormous slit-eyed boy in the back stood to object — Yang Nianxia, a third-rank smith himself who felt himself the obvious choice — she gave him the flat answer that settled the room: no one competed against a fourth-rank blacksmith who was not yet fifteen. Wulin, who had omitted mentioning the fifth rank on the sensible grounds that no one would believe it, sat down looking modest, and did not, Lin Hao noted, correct her.

The rest of it would be decided on the field. Fifteen minutes to choose allies. Survive; or touch the ground with four limbs or a torso and be eliminated.

The fifteen minutes were, in their way, more instructive than the battle that would follow. Shen Yi gave them the room and the clock and stood back, because at Shrek the test had already begun before anyone reached the field. The lecture hall erupted into the particular scrambling of talented children who had just learned that there were three seats worth having and a field's worth of bodies to be eliminated for them. Strangers became best friends in under a minute; control-type soul masters who had never spoken to anyone were suddenly very popular; one nervous boy announced to no one in particular that he had no wish to be president and would happily carry a strong team's water, which got him three offers at once.

Wulin caught the moment early and bent his head to his own people. "Xie Xie, Xiaoyan — you two go make another group," he said, low enough that only the five of them caught it, and when Xie Xie made a wounded face Wulin shook his head once. "We've been seated together since day one. We're already a clique to them, and now I'm the declared blacksmith rep with every eye on me. If we all stand together we draw every team in the field at once. Split. Be four problems instead of one." He didn't turn to Gu Yue; he didn't have to. She had already chosen her place half a step behind his shoulder, and telling her to go make allies elsewhere would have been the kind of order Wulin was wise enough never to give.

Lin Hao watched the arithmetic settle and said nothing, because the arithmetic was Wulin's particular genius and not his to improve. Xie Xie and Xu Xiaoyan let themselves be gathered up by two different scrambling teams with practised ease; Gu Yue stayed with Wulin; Lin Hao found himself, a few minutes later, calmly attached to a third group of nervous classmates who had correctly counted him as one of the quiet strong ones and therefore worth standing near. None of them knew what they were actually getting, which was, he reflected, exactly how he preferred it. He would matter on the field, when the field came, the way he mattered at everything — without a word wasted, from the inside of the crowd.

The fifth seat, in the end, suited him. The loud seats went to the loud people. He had spent the week making the ground under his own feet flawless; the field in two days would show whether flawless, at the modest tier a first-year was allowed to show, was enough to be the last team standing.

Lin Hao, in his fifth seat, said nothing. He was a fifth-rank smith himself, and the blacksmith seat could as easily have been his; but a declared representative sat in the light with the whole class reading him, and he had spent the week making himself quietly, completely master of the tier he held. He let the loud seat belong to Wulin, where it was earned and where it didn't cost him anything he wasn't prepared to spend, and he turned his attention to the field coming in two days' time — a tournament of thirteen-year-olds, fought among peers, where the grade of the man-and-sword-as-one he had just spent the week sharpening would be more than enough to matter, and where there was no reason, and no excuse, to reach for anything beyond the shore he stood on.

## Part 5: The Measure of a Week

That night before the field he sat a last quiet dawn in the workshop and took stock the way a smith measured a finished piece — not by its shine, but by its grain.

A week before he had come down from a black-class cull having glimpsed, once, the true depth the sword could go. He had spent the week correctly. He had not chased the depth. He had made the ground under his feet flawless: every stroke truer, the frost a tool and not an emergency, the fusion a door that opened on command, the spiritual sea an honest inch deeper, the ledger fed by real work. He was not a step closer to the far shore in the way a man is not a mile closer to a mountain until he has walked the miles in between — but he was no longer wasting the step he was on, and that was the whole secret of every strong person he had ever met, from Mu Chen to Wu Zhangkong to the Saint Blacksmith four flights up.

The numbers of him told the truth to anything that could read them. His spiritual power had climbed a real, earned increment under the steady Method — still well within the Spirit Sea, nowhere near any far gate, but up where a week of serious work ought to put him. The hawk had climbed with him as the fusion came on call. His ledger had grown, point by point, from the honest refining he had gone back to. And the things no instrument measured — the frost that didn't bite him, the fusion that answered, the third form without a decision — those were the week's true product, built quietly below the surface of any rank-up, the way a foundation was laid where no one cheered.

He set the Stormbringer across his knees and the steel sat quiet and familiar, an extension of the hand, which was exactly what a sword was supposed to be at the tier he owned. Outside, the academy slept. In two days the field opened on a tournament of children, and the whole class would be watching to see who stood last. He had not reached for a single thing beyond his station. He had simply, at last, become flawless at it.

On a field of geniuses, he suspected that would be plenty.
