### THE GOD REALM

Soft light lay on the clouds like a mother's hand.

A man stood at the edge of it, looking out over distances that had no bottom. His hair fell to his feet, water-blue, a spill of quiet sea; his robe was blue, and if you looked at the robe too long, the ripples in it took your soul gently by the collar and invited it in for a swim. He was handsome the way mountains are handsome, and his eyes — sometimes empty, sometimes holding everything, sometimes flashing a thread of violet that made spring and autumn change places — were, at this moment, unhappy.

The Sea God sighed. The Law Enforcer of the God Realm sighed. Tang San sighed — one sigh, three names.

"San-ge." A pink skirt stepped out of nowhere and took his arm in a motion so practiced it had become a law of nature. A long scorpion braid swung against his shoulder, and Xiao Wu rested her head there and wound the end of the braid into his hair, proprietary as weather. "Still sulking."

"Not sulking. Thinking." He folded her in. "One day here is a year down there, Little Wu. The Good and Evil Kings made their bet and went down to play, and I came back up to keep the house — and twenty years for us was ten thousand for the world, and the Tang Sect—" The sentence ended, the way old griefs end: unfinished, and finished.

"Withered. I know. You built it with your hands."

"I built it with my hands." His eyes went far again. And then they changed. "But something has changed, Little Wu. *New stars* have risen over the Douluo mainland." He held up two fingers, as if the hand had decided before the god did. "One burns like a bonfire seen through mist — ten thousand threads, and every one of them tied to my sect. I have tried to read its fate, and it is fog all the way down. But there is a second. Quieter. Low on the world's edge, a river-light — and here is the strange thing: it is not new at all. It was *born* with this age, Little Wu. It has been shining eleven years, and I never thought to look for it, because it never once burned the same color twice." His mouth curved, rueful. "And when I read at its fog, the fog does not lift. It changes shape, and keeps changing — as if its whole answer to being read is to grow another way of answering."

"Two," said Xiao Wu, doing arithmetic she distrusted. "There was one, in your reading, last week."

"There was one," Tang San agreed, "when there was one."

"Oho." Her eyes went bright and merciless. "New *stars*. If they're good enough to inherit a certain someone's god position someday, a certain someone could retire, and a certain someone's wife could finally travel—"

"You," Tang San said, tapping her nose, "only think about playing."

While they spoke, a small head poked out of the cloud bank nearby — a girl of eleven or twelve, big-eyed, with a face seven parts her father's, softened to seven parts her mother's art. She had been listening with the patience of a hunter.

*Always hearing Papa and Mama talk about the Douluo mainland,* thought Xiao Qi. *It sounds like fun.*

And her small figure slid back into the cloud, and was gone — and the world below acquired, unnoticed, one descending goddess and two rising stars.

---

### THE MANSION

The north back door of the greatest estate on the continent opened without a sound, which no door of that house had ever done for its owner's son.

A boy slipped out. Eleven, small, clean gray clothes, a bundle not much bigger than a loaf. He eased the door shut, walked three steps, and stopped as if he'd hit glass. He turned and looked back at three thousand mu of golden roof-tiles blazing in the noon.

His mother had been the Duke's own maid, taken from her family as a child, raised at his side. One night, twelve years ago, a child began in her. When the Duke rode to his wars, the Duchess ruled — and the Duchess was the Emperor's best-loved daughter, and jealousy is patient. *A contagious sickness,* the Duchess had said, when the boy was two. The woodshed behind the servants' quarters. No coin. Ten years of slow, loud dying.

His mother's last lesson had been delivered in a whisper, like all her real ones: *people can only rely on themselves.*

"Mama." The boy's voice was very level, which in an eleven-year-old is louder than shouting. "Watch me from where you are. However much it takes — one day I'll come back and put all of this under my feet." A breath. "From today I take your name. Not Dai. **Huo. Huo Yuhao.**"

He had reached rank ten the day before, after five years of work that would have broken a grown man's pride — innate soul power of exactly one level, the priests had said at his awakening, and a spirit-type martial soul so rare the continent had almost no soul beasts to feed it. It was, he had decided long ago, his leaving day.

In the bundle: one change of clothes, dry rations, a hand-drawn map, seven silver soul coins and five copper — his mother's whole estate — and, at his lower back, a sheathed short blade a foot long. The only gift his father ever gave his mother. The blade was seven inches of autumn water; the sheath was jade-green leather; the hilt was plain, old, and fit a hand like a settled promise. She had held it until the last hour of her life, and then given it to him.

*White Tiger Dagger,* she had called it. He had never asked why.

He turned north, toward the Star Dou Great Forest, and ran. His eyes stayed dry until the mansion was out of sight, and then only the wind argued with them.

---

### THE ROAD

He walked for six days.

He took wrong turns and corrected them, learned to read the sun, thanked strangers, ate the free things his mother had taught him to find. A rank-ten body is a good body; grief, it turned out, could be burned as fuel; and three hundred li a day carried him north, away from an empire and toward a forest with a human-beings'-forbidden-zone reputation and, somewhere in it, the one thing his soul could eat: a spirit-type soul beast.

Forty li south of that forest, a courier was finishing a delivery.

The waystation matron had stamped him paid, broken his mother's triple knots before his eyes the way the Hall's rules required, and told him to tell Hall Master Wen the blue was darker this year. The road home ran south. The courier stood at the waystation gate, a healer's sealed case going back empty on his back, a hammer over one shoulder, and a fox in his coat doing her mid-morning impression of a sleeping empress — and he read the road north, because reading the road was the whole trade, and the road said: *three travelers, half a li, coming this way.*

Two of them were noise before they were people. A girl's laugh, ringing off the trees; a boy's warmer one under it. They came round the bend — the girl first, fifteen or sixteen, light-blue traveling clothes, black ponytail, walking like the road owed her money; the boy behind, tall, gem-blue hair, hands laced behind his head, walking like a man who had never once needed to hurry. Behind them, thirty paces back and losing ground, a small gray figure with a bundle, walking with a settler's pace, chin set, eyes forward — a boy who had been walking alone for six days and did not know how to be in front of people.

The fox opened one eye. "*Strangers,*" she said, in the tone of a customs officer, and then the second eye opened, which was different, which was rare. "*Little tide. The small one at the back. Look at him with your better eyes.*"

Jiang Che looked. And what the moisture-sense and the six domains gave him, standing quietly at a waystation gate, was this: the laughing pair carried no packs and no fatigue, and their soul power sat on them like good clothes — trained, comfortable, *senior.* The small gray boy carried six days of road in his legs, grief in a knot between his shoulder blades, and around his heart a soul power so thin it was nearly a rumor — rank ten or less — and under all of it, steady as a pilot light, something that made the fox's ears stand at a different angle.

"Old," she said, quietly, only for him. "Older than his feet. Walk with them."

"Why?"

"Because you are about to," said the fox, who was sometimes honest about the shape of her knowledge and never about its source, and closed her eyes again, and that was the whole of the argument, because it always was.

So when the trio reached the gate, they found a blue-haired boy their own age leaning there with a courier's case and a smith's hammer, who nodded the nod of the road — the one that means *water, news, or help, whichever you need* — and asked, at walking volume, if the north road was quiet, because he was for the forest's edge and had heard stories.

The girl answered the way thunder answers: "Stories! The north road's *boring*, we've walked it for — Bei Bei, how long have we walked it—"

"It only feels infinite," said the gem-haired boy, and smiled the lazy smile, and looked at the courier with the professional interest of a man cataloguing him — the hammer, the case, the stance, the calm — and filed him under *later.* "We're for the forest too. Periphery business." A glance back at the small gray figure catching up. "All of us, apparently."

And Huo Yuhao, arriving level with them, looked up at the blue-haired stranger who was somehow walking *with* them now, and saw nothing he could name — only that the stranger's eyes were on him the way nobody's eyes had been on him since his mother died: reading him, and staying kind.

They walked north together. It was as simple and as irreversible as that — though it very nearly was not, because the first thing Jiang Che said to the laughing girl, unprompted, out of nowhere, in the flat voice of a boy stating a fact he has held too long, was:

"Your fish is burning."

"*My* fish—"

"The third one from the left. It's past done. I could smell it from the gate."

And Tang Ya — Sect Master of a thousand-year sect, terror of the fighting zones, keeper of the Dragon-Beard Needle — looked at her fish, which was indeed past done, and said with dignity: "I like them crispy."

"Charcoal isn't a crisp."

"I *said*—" but she was laughing, and he was almost smiling, and that was the moment the road took them — not the hammer or the case or the fox's old silence: a boy who could not watch food burn, and a girl who could not stop laughing about it.

They walked north together. It was as simple and as irreversible as that — though Tang Ya would say, later, that it had been less a decision than a *weather event*: the stranger simply fell in with them the way rain falls with a valley, and within a mile the road had reorganized itself around him without anyone consulting it.

What she could not have named — what nobody who fell into step beside him ever quite named — was the *texture* of it. The boy walked like water finding its level. The air around him smelled, very faintly, of rain on a river — clean, mineral, with something green under it and something storm-like under that — so that walking beside him was, in a way nobody remarked on and everybody felt, like walking beside a season. Bei Bei noticed the smell and filed it. Tang Ya noticed that the birds had gone quiet in the way they go quiet for *safe* things, and said nothing, because she was busy. And Huo Yuhao, walking in front of a stranger for the first time in six days without his shoulders climbing toward his ears, noticed only that the road felt narrower with three people on it, and warmer, and that the wind that stirred the blue hair beside him smelled like the beginning of the year.

---

### THE STREAM

The stream found them an hour later, and the grill was the girl's idea.

Her name, it emerged over the next mile, was Tang Ya; his was Bei Bei; and they were — this took some assembling, and some of it was assembled wrong on purpose — students of the academy that lay past the forest, out here on *periphery business,* which meant, as far as either of them would say, hunting. What Tang Ya hunted, presently, was lunch: she heard the stream the way a hawk hears a field mouse, and by the time the rest of them had reached the bank she had already declared the shallows a *personal territory.*

The gray boy — Yuhao, he offered, half-swallowed, and then again, steadier — was the one who did something about it. He waded in with a tree-branch he had cut and trimmed with the jade-green dagger from his back, and stood over the water, and his eyes went *strange*.

The courier watched this with the fox's whole attention. What the moisture-sense read was not visible to anyone else: the boy's soul power, thin as it was, pooled up behind his eyes and *turned the world slow.* Every stone, every fish, every flick of light off scale — read, catalogued, aimed at. The boy's body was an ordinary body. The boy's *eyes* were a instrument the continent saw once in ten thousand years, and the courier knew it the way he knew good steel — not by name, by *grain.*

Fourteen fish. Spear-caught, one after another, in twenty minutes, by a boy too polite to look proud and too hungry to hide it well.

The fish were cleaned with the white dagger — *that* blade drew a long look from Bei Bei, who said nothing, and from Tang Ya, who said "ooh" — and grilled over a fire of stream-side wood with salt from someone's pack and perilla that Yuhao picked without being asked, because he knew the free things the road offered, all of them, by heart.

And while the fish cooked, the thing happened that the road had been walking toward.

Tang Ya, mouth half-full, demanded the stranger's story — *every* story, that was her rule — and Yuhao, cornered by kindness, gave the smallest safe version: going to the forest, looking for a spirit-type soul beast, his martial soul was his eyes. And then, because the girl's warmth pulled words out of people like the sun pulls sap, the version grew: the mansion he had left at noon six days ago; the mother who had died in the spring; the five years of cultivating one rank at a time against a house that wished him invisible; the vow, which he did not say was a vow, and which everyone at that fire heard anyway.

"I'm sorry," said Tang Ya, and for once there was nothing under the words but the words.

"It's a good vow," said Jiang Che, quietly, because his mother had taught him that the thing a grieving person needs most is for someone to treat their grief like a *craft* — worth doing, worth doing well.

And Bei Bei looked at the small boy with the woodshed hands and the eyes that slowed the world, and then at the blue-haired stranger with the hammer who had said the exact right thing at the exact right weight, and made a small adjustment to several private files.

It was during the second round of fish — the girl was on her fifth; the fox, from the courier's coat collar, had begun a soft commentary on human feeding behavior that only one person alive could hear — that the fox stopped mid-sentence.

Stopped *entirely.* Ears up. Both eyes open. Every tail still.

"*Little tide,*" she said, and her voice had gone to a register he had heard perhaps three times in four years, "*there is something under this road. Something old, and patient, and it has been listening to that boy for a hundred li. It is *below us* and it is *waking* and what it wants is *him.* Do not be alarmed. And do not — **do not** — interfere with what comes.*"

"Fox—"

"*Promise me.*"

"...I promise."

"Good," said the fox, and vanished down into the coat, and against his chest her small weight was a held breath.

Twenty heartbeats later, on the far side of the fire, mid-laugh, Huo Yuhao's head turned — sharply, blindly — toward the tree-line. And the tree-line moved.

---

### THE AMBUSH

It came out of the trees at the speed of a thrown spear: a hundred jin of brown muscle and yellow fangs, a ten-year Wind Baboon in full hunt-lunge, aimed — because predators are simple — at the smallest, weakest, nearest prey.

Yuhao's dagger was coming up and his body was already knowing it would be late. Tang Ya's hand was in her sleeve. Bei Bei was rising—

—and none of it mattered, because the rings were already rising.

Two yellows, bright as struck coins, igniting at a courier's feet as he crossed the fire's circle at a dead run, and the grass came out of him the way morning comes out of a river — dozens of vines, blue-silver, dew-gilded, and they did not lunge; they *arrived.* A Trip-Line across the ankles at the exact stride's extension. A Pressure-Seal around the throat — *hold without harm*, the Hall's law, iron-gentle — and a third vine simply taking the beast's own lunging momentum and giving it to the tree it had launched from, winding it there, wrapped, a hundred jin of apex predator going from missile to parcel in the space of one breath, roaring its outrage into a wall of living rope.

Silence. Fish smoke. The fire popped. Tang Ya's knife was half-out of her sleeve with nowhere to put it.

"...Well," said Bei Bei, into the quiet, with the careful voice of a man revising his afternoon. "That happened."

"You *have* a martial soul," Tang Ya said, accusingly, as though he had been withholding dessert — and then, doubling down on the grievance with the energy of a person who has spent an hour being corrected about fish: "— and you eat like a *bird.* I've been watching. You had two. TWO. There were fourteen fish. Explain yourself, hammer-boy."

"I was counting them."

"*Counting—*"

"There are five of us and fourteen fish. If I eat four, someone eats two. I eat two." A shrug. "My mother's arithmetic. It's a curse."

"You are *eleven.*"

"My mother's arithmetic doesn't care." — and then, with the double-take of a girl who has just noticed the dessert is also *beautiful*, which she had been noticing, in a low-grade distracted way, since the waystation, and had been too busy to file, "— and you *are* aware that your hair is doing that on purpose? What *are* you? You smell like a thunderstorm that got good intentions."

"Grass," said the courier, apologetically. "It binds."

And Yuhao was staring — not at the beast, at the vines, at the two rings, at the quiet boy his own age standing between a predator and a stranger as if it were a delivery — and something crossed his face that was not envy and not hope exactly but the first draft of both.

Then the ground answered.

---

### THE WAVE

It split two meters from the stream — gold-white light breathing up through the cracks, cold rolling out like a door opened on winter — and along with the cold came a *pressure* that was not cold at all. It was a bell struck at the bottom of the world, a hundred li wide, and every living thing in it went down.

Bei Bei dropped mid-motion, hand still outstretched toward Tang Ya. Tang Ya folded over her knees with a word half-sworn. Yuhao slid from his log and lay in the grass, eyes open, unfocused, breathing.

Jiang Che fell too — the fox's warning or no warning, the wave did not negotiate with rank twenty-nine — and knew, in the last instant before his thoughts went soft and far, the specific humiliation of a courier watching his parcels tip while his body refused the order to catch them.

The fox stood up.

She stood up out of his coat, and stepped onto his fallen shoulder, and down onto the grass — and she *grew* — not much, and not violently; a body the size of a hunting hound, moonlight-white, nine tails fanning like a standard unfurled, the gold tips catching light that had no source in the clearing. She walked — unhurried, sovereign — past three frozen humans and one frozen courier, and sat down before the emerging head of something seven meters long and white as jade and ringed in ten bands of gold, and she said, aloud, in the human tongue, in a voice that made the stream run backward for a moment:

"You are loud, worm. I could hear you from the far side of the province. Come up slowly, and tell me why I should let you finish."

---

### THE NEGOTIATION

The Skydream Iceworm looked at the fox for a long time. It is possible that nothing in a million years had looked at *him* first.

"*You are not frozen,*" it said, into the air, into minds, its voice a landslide being lazy.

"I am *polite,*" said the fox. "There is a difference. You are a million years of something that cannot fight; you have surfaced under my human's road; your wave has put four children on the grass, two of them *mine*; and you have been listening to the gray one for a hundred li." Her tails did not move at all. "So you will tell me what you want. Then we will discuss whether you get it. The discussion will be short — my patience is a young thing next to yours, but infinitely better armed."

The great silkworm was quiet. And then, with the dignity of the genuinely ancient, it told her: of the cold-marrow cave and the ten golden rings; of the forest's ten-thousand-year kings, who had found him sleeping and full of the world's purest essence, and *shared* him — a war over the prize, and then a negotiation, and then a thousand years of sitting in concentric rings of strength around a living well, sipping eternity through a straw. Of the tenth ring, grown out of pure refusal; the hiding; the ten thousand years of searching, in mind and body and every seep of spirit-power on the continent, for the one vessel that could hold him: **a spirit-attribute human.** Of the first candidate, a Titled Douluo, who had burst like a rice cake under nothing but the first touch of his mind.

"*I am dying,*" the Skydream said, without drama, which was how the courier's son would have known it was true even if the fox had not. "*Not soon. Soon enough. I have run for three thousand years, and I am tired, little fox, tired the way stones are tired. The gray boy is the first spirit-soul I have found in ten thousand years. His vessel is small and his rank is a candle — but his *sea* — brother has looked at gods' seas, and the boy's sea is a cathedral with the doors open. I will seal myself. All of me, down to a thimbleful, seal upon seal upon seal, until what remains can live inside a rank-eleven body without cracking it. I will be his ring, and his tenant, and the least of what I was. In exchange I will not die in a hole — and perhaps, one day, he will be large enough that nothing hunts what is mine.*"

"And the boy's consent?"

"*He would give it. He is built of yes; did you watch him feed us? But he is frozen, and the seals must be laid while the body rests, and I will not wait for the thaw — the kings that chased me are not sleeping, and tonight they will feel where the wave came from.*"

The fox looked at the small gray figure in the grass — at the boy who had walked six days off a vow, who had fed strangers first and himself last, who had stared at binding-grass like it was a sunrise. Then at her own frozen human, who had promised not to interfere, and who had kept the promise by falling down.

"Terms," she said. "**One:** the merge happens now, and it happens *gently* — and the boy wakes healed, and rested, and *remembering that something chose him.* Because something did. And he will need that memory on the days he doubts, and those days are coming — I have read his road the way you read his sea. **Two:** the two whites—" her chin indicated Bei Bei and Tang Ya, frozen mid-stride, "—saw nothing. You will veil the sight as I veil mine. Their story will be a baboon and a lucky ring, and the story will hold — because it is kinder to the boy than the truth would be this year, and because I am not done hiding, and a story with holes is a story with *me in it.* **Three:** the courier is mine. When he wakes, I will tell him everything — I do not lie to my human, and he keeps what he carries the way ground keeps seeds: quietly, and forever, and standing where the boy can see him. **Four:** you do not touch the boy's *self.* You are a guest in a house, worm, and guests do not rearrange the furniture. His thoughts are his; his choices are his; when you can speak to him, you will *advise*, and you will let him refuse. If ever you move him without his leave—" and here the fox's voice went, for one syllable, to a register that had not been used on this continent in ten thousand years "—*I will find what remains of you, and I will be less polite than I am being today.*"

The Skydream Iceworm considered the largest threat and the smallest fox it had ever met, and found, to its own surprise, that it believed her.

"*Done,*" it said. "*You have my word. I am too old to break words — they are the only things I have ever managed to keep.*"

"Then finish," said the fox — and sat, tail over paws, to witness: the only waking witness in a hundred li.

The great beast laid its forehead against the frozen boy's brow, and poured itself away. Ten golden rings descended the small body like moonrise. A white radiance flowed inward — seal upon seal upon seal, a million years folded down and down and down to a thimbleful — and under the boy's unconscious ribs something sealed itself in beside his heart like a passenger taking a seat for a very long journey. Where his wounds had been — and there were none, for the vines had been fast enough even for that — the body drank. The rank-eleven candle flickered, held, and *brightened.*

And at the last, as the gold sank away and a single ring the color of moonlit frost — *lustrous white; white as no ten-year ring had ever been* — circled the sleeping boy three times and folded into him and was gone, a voice, growing sleepy, growing distant, said one final thing into the record of the world. Not to the fox. To no one.

"*Brother is going to sleep now. It was a good road. There were fish.*"

---

### THE AFTERMATH

The thaw came back into the world the way feeling comes back into a struck limb.

Tang Ya surfaced from her own knees mid-oath. Bei Bei finished the reach he had begun a minute and a lifetime ago. And they found the clearing exactly as a clearing should be after a baboon ambush: the beast trussed to a tree by blue-silver vines; the boy unconscious in the grass with a white ring fading beneath him and not a mark on him; and a blue-haired courier already kneeling at the boy's wrist with two fingers on the pulse, as if he had been there the whole time.

Which — in the only sense that would ever matter — he had.

"A baboon," Bei Bei said slowly, examining the trussed beast, the unwounded boy, the untouched grass, the story assembling itself out of everything his eyes could see. "It lunged, the boy's soul ring flared — shock of his first kill — and he went down. A ten-year ring. For a spirit soul." He said it the way careful men step over things they cannot name, and the story settled over the clearing like the mist the fox had promised — kind, and holding, and with a very old author.

"His pulse is strong," said the courier, which was true. It was also slow, and vast, and *tidal* — a rhythm with pull behind it now, a sea with a new tenant — and the boy's skin carried the clean cold smell of the inside of winter, and all of it was filed, all of it was kept, and none of it was going anywhere near the two kind strangers assembling their gentle story three steps away.

Tang Ya gathered the boy up with the tenderness she kept under all her noise. "We take him north. There's shelter past the tree-line before the deep woods — and *you,*" she found the courier with a finger, "you wrapped a soul beast like a parcel, you're either the most dangerous person I've ever shared a fire with or the most useful, and either way you're walking with us until I decide which."

They walked north out of the clearing: a girl carrying a sleeping boy, a gem-haired young man walking rearguard, and a courier with a fox in his coat and a secret the size of a continent — and the secret's second keeper, purring very quietly against his collarbone.

"*Little tide,*" the fox said, when the trees had closed behind them. "*What I told the worm — that the small one is yours too — I meant it. He carries a god's thimble now, and gods' thimbles attract storms. You will want to be standing where he can see you. It turns out that is your whole job.*"

"I know," said Jiang Che. "It's been my whole job since the stream."

"*Good.*" A yawn, imperial, against his heartbeat. "*Now. About the ruffling—*"

"Don't push it."

"*I permit it in advance,*" said the fox, and slept.

And the road went on north — toward an academy, toward a year, toward a sect that did not yet know it existed and a jar of monsters that did not yet know it had just grown two hinges.

### THE WAKING *(Yuhao's POV — with the secret already shared)*

Yuhao woke in a waystation supply room with a fish-smell in the air and a brother at his elbow.

Not a stranger. That was the thing his body knew before his mind did — that the blue-haired boy dozing against the wall beside his cot had been there all night, and would be there tomorrow, and had been *told.* Everything. The fox had kept her promise to herself before the dew dried: her human knew about the worm under the lake, the negotiation, the four terms, the thimbleful of godhood sleeping behind his sternum. And when Yuhao's eyes opened, the first thing he saw was the courier's face, and the courier said — not *how do you feel*, not *what happened*, none of the questions that would have made it strange:

"Two days of fish debt. Tang Ya's counting. She's charging interest."

And Yuhao laughed. Which was the correct medicine, and which no one else on the continent could have administered — because no one else knew, and no one else would have led with lunch.

"You know," Yuhao said, quieter. It wasn't a question.

"I know." The courier's voice was the flat route-report voice. "The fox told me. She told me everything — the terms, the seals, the — the passenger. She told me because she doesn't lie to me, and because she decided, on the road, that you were mine to stand near. That's her word. *Mine to stand near.*" A beat. "Nobody else knows. Not the two whites. Not anyone. The story they have is the baboon, and the story holds, and it's *kind*, and we keep it."

And the boy who had been alone with every secret of his life — the scales, the woodshed, the grief, the million-year weight now sleeping in his sea — lay in a waystation cot and discovered what it was to have a secret *carried.* Not taken. Not shared as currency. Carried — the way his mother had carried his father's dagger, keeping it for a day it would be needed, asking nothing.

"He talks in my sleep," Yuhao said. "The worm. He's — he's *funny,* Hao. He's a million years old and he's *funny.*"

"Good," said Jiang Che. "You could use funny. And when he wakes up and wants to talk, I'll be there. Not to hear it — you don't have to share the inside. Just so you know the door's not locked from the other side."

From the coat on the nail, a small sleepy weight said: "*Adequate.*" And went back to sleep. And that — not the oath that was coming, not the sect, not the belt or the arts or the year — was the moment the brotherhood actually began: a boy with a god in his chest, and a boy with a fox in his coat, and a secret between them like a fire they both tended.

---

### THE TWO WHITES *(the waystation — the baboon story lands)*

Tang Ya had heard it from Bei Bei, who had assembled it from the evidence, and she heard it again now from Yuhao himself — *the ring flared when the baboon died; the shock took me; it's a ten-year ring* — and she bought it the way kind people buy kind stories, with her whole heart, and held it, and never once pulled the thread.

What she did instead was feed him. What Bei Bei did instead was assess him — quietly, professionally, the file growing pages — and what they both did, by the time the party reached the forest's southern rim two days later, was *decide.* The decision happened the way all Tang Ya's decisions happened: at speed, out loud, and centered on food.

"*Perfect,*" said Tang Ya, and Bei Bei's knuckle rapped her crown with the weary precision of long practice, and she said "*I mean—*" with her hands over her mouth, and Yuhao laughed, because he had spent two days with these people and the word *family* had already started leaking through the cracks in his guard.

The Tang Sect was laid out plainly, because Tang Ya at her most serious had decided that this boy had been lied to enough for one childhood. Ten thousand years ago, the first sect of the continent, built by a man named Tang San who broke the ceiling of the soul master's world — the legends Yuhao's mother had whispered in a woodshed. The sect that had armed an age. And then the age turned: the Sun-Moon collision; the soul tools that broke Tang steel; the orders thinned; the great house seized. "There's one thing nobody could seize," Tang Ya said, and held up a finger. "Every year, Shrek Academy — you've heard of Shrek—"

"The continent's first academy—"

"—honors the old debt. **One exam-exempt place. One seat, no test.** Bei Bei and I study there. This year's seat is open. Join the sect, and it's yours."

"The condition is the real one," Bei Bei said. "The arts are the ancestors. Join us, and you are Tang Sect for life. If you ever leave, you give back everything you learned. Every page. Consider it *before* you answer."

### THE SHOWING *(the tree-line — the ignition)*

She walked into the vines the way you walk into a relative's house, and put her hand flat against the nearest strand, and her own rings answered — two yellow, one purple, rising unbidden — and her grass came out to meet his grass, blue-glowing vines winding curious and gentle among the blue-silver ones, and the two souls stood in the light holding hands.

"You understand," she said, not quite to him, "that I have spent my whole life being told I was the keeper of something extinct. Everyone *so respectful*, the way people are respectful at funerals." Her thumb moved along the dew. "And it's *here.* Alive. In a boy my sect fed fish to on a road."

"When you answer — if you answer — it'll be somewhere that means something. But there's a thing you should have first, and it isn't mine to make pretty." A breath. ### THE GRUDGE *(the collision, told at the tree-line)*

The orders thinned; the masters drifted; the great house was seized in the second war. "What's left is what the tools can't take, because it isn't *made* of anything. It's made of us."

### THE GIFTS *(the oath's gifts — for Yuhao)*

The rest of the day was ceremony, because Tang Ya decided it was, and Bei Bei backed her with the purse.

From her sleeves — from *nowhere*, from a place that had held nothing a moment before — Tang Ya produced a hand-copied book: the **Mysterious Heaven Treasure Record**, the distilled arts of the first sect of the continent. The root: the Xuantian Gong, the cultivation method that would more than patch a woodshed body's slowness. From his belt, Bei Bei drew a length of black silk set with twenty-four round pieces of white jade. "**Twenty-Four Bridges Under Moonlight.** A copy of a soul tool that belonged to the ancestor Tang San himself. Twenty-four stones; each holds a space half a meter wide. My gift. ---

### THE SECOND BROTHER'S NIGHT *(room-mates at the waystation)*

They walked north through the afternoon, and the walk was *different* now — a sect of three (and a fox), a sect-brother pair riding at its center — and by evening the party had made the forest's rim-camp, and the two boys ended the day as they would end every day for the next year: sitting against the same tree, because the tree was big enough and nobody had said otherwise.

"Can I ask you something," Yuhao said, into the dark. "About the — the thing you know. About me."

"You can ask anything."

"Do you…" A breath. "Do you think it's *me* still? With the — with him in there. Am I still me, or am I the thing's — house?"

And Jiang Che, eleven years old, courier's son, fox's human, third disciple of nothing yet, considered the question with the seriousness it deserved — which was total — and answered it the only way he knew how, which was the way his mother answered *does it hurt*:

"The fox has been in me since I was eight," he said. "And I'm still the one who complains about the fish. The worm's in you since Tuesday. And you're still the one who walked out of a mansion for your mother's name. Whatever else is in there — that's the house's *furniture.* You're the house." A pause. "And for what it's worth — the fox says he's funny. Million-year-old things that are funny are rare. Keep him."

In the dark, against the same tree, the boy with a god in his chest laughed — wet, quiet, real — and the boy with a fox in his coat let the laugh run without touching it, because some things you just stand near.

"*Little tide,*" the fox murmured, from the coat, more than half asleep. "*That answer was adequate.*"

From the fox, that was a coronation. And tomorrow was the forest, and after it the academy, and after it the year — but tonight the sect of three (and a fox) slept at the tree-line of the biggest forest on the continent, and the two keepers of the biggest secret on the continent slept against the same tree, and the tree did not mind.

"How—" Yuhao began.

"Ghost-Shadow Track and a throwing art," she said, flicking the needle back into her sleeve. "No soul power. The ancestors were smarter than soul masters." She held up a hand. Her face had changed. "Hush. Something smells sweet."

### THE SNAKE *(canon whole — the Datura ambush)*

The shadow hit the ground between them with a sound like a wet flag — three meters of peach-red snake, thick as a man's thigh, a flower bud crowning its brow — and the air turned to syrup. Sweetness rolled over the party in a wave, and Yuhao's knees dipped—

—and *cold* answered: rising from behind his ribs, a river of frost, and his own breath misted out of him and carried the sweetness away. Not his doing. The tenant's — the first proof, on-page, of the second soul's will, done for him while he was too drugged to refuse. And he caught — across the drugged confusion — his brother's eyes on him, reading the frost's shape through the moisture-sense, and filing it, and saying *nothing*, because the fox had taught him that particular craft: *carry, don't show the carrying.*

"Xiao Ya!" Bei Bei's arm came up; his fingers clawed at empty air — and Tang Ya was yanked off her feet and *pulled* to him, weightless, somersaulting over the lunge, vines already bursting from her in a blue fan.

What happened to Bei Bei next, Yuhao would try to describe for years. Blue light ignited at his brow and poured down his body, and his gentle senior brother's right **arm** became something else — half a foot longer, thick as a temple pillar's ankle, sheathed in blue-purple scale from shoulder to claw, lightning walking on it — and his three rings, two yellow one purple, did not ride his body at all. They rode the *arm.*

"Xiao Ya. Guard the brothers. This one's mine."

And Jiang Che — who had spent the ambush's first second moving, because a courier whose party is attacked does not wait for assignments — had the grass out and the perimeter seeded before the sentence ended: Trip-Lines at the ankles of the dark, anchors pre-set at the two trees worth anchoring, his vines holding dew that read the whole fight like a map. Not the hero of it. The *floor* of it.

The snake was fast in the way rumors are fast and armored in the way grudges are armored. Its scales turned the first Thunder Dragon Claw the way a cathedral turns weather — and it *learned*, between strikes, the way old things learn: the second claw it dodged, the third it answered with a tail-lash that cracked two of the roadside saplings into kindling, and the pink fog it breathed got thicker each time, a musk-sweetness that sat on the sinuses and made the world's edges go soft and treacherous.

The pills cut through — whatever Bei Bei carried in that porcelain vial, it tasted like bile and pine and worked like a slammed window — but the fog kept coming, and the fight settled into the specific rhythm of a strong man versus a patient one: the lightning probing, the armor holding, the snake waiting for the drug-fog to do its slow work while the first disciple's soul power ticked down in increments only the sharing could see. Bei Bei's Thunder Dragon Claw herded it; his lightning-net met the Datura's pink fog and *sleeted*; the pills came out — porcelain, one each, pushed into mouths by the first disciple's efficient hands — and through it all the gold rose in Yuhao's eyes, and the sharing poured into Bei Bei and Tang Ya like cold water into empty cups, and both of them flinched, and both of them *understood at once*: distance, weight, the coil-loading in the tail, the half-breath tell before every strike.

"What—" Tang Ya began.

"Later," said Bei Bei — and the purple ring lit, and *Thunder Fury* took him, and he walked in.

The fight's end was the sharing's: the snake broke and fled into the pull Bei Bei had pre-placed on its escape line, and the flower-crown burst — a pink blood-arrow, venom in the blood itself — and the shared world showed the crown *lighting up under the skin* before it opened, and the doubled Thunder Dragon Claw was already moving, and the arrow died in thunder, and Bei Bei's hand closed on seven inches of snake.

"Xiao Ya."

The flying knife left her fingers before he finished the syllable. Her kill. Her ring. The Tang Sect's whole afternoon, paid for.

### THE ABSORPTION *(Tang Ya's third — and the tradition told)*

The purple ring rose off the Datura Snake's brow and hung there, turning, and Tang Ya sat down beside it, suddenly all business — "Guard me. This part's *boring*" — and the ring poured into her in blue light, and her third settled: two yellow, one purple; the bottleneck of two years opening at last.

"The Sect Master's soul is Blue Silver Grass," he said, to Yuhao mostly, but with his eyes on the courier. "So was the ancestor's. When the ancestor ascended, he left no bloodline in the sect — and the sect, being the sect, decided that was not acceptable. Ten thousand years of Tang Sect masters have honored the grass: recruiting it, cultivating it, *marrying the sect's fortune to it* — out of loyalty, and grief, and stubbornness. The master line is the grass line. It has never once been otherwise." A pause. "It has also never once, in ten thousand years, produced a grass master who stood on the continent's peak again. Jiang Che, who had been cleaning snake-gore off a vine with the absent thoroughness of a boy raised in a healing hall, looked up.

"You're saying I'm the next grave."

"I'm saying," said Bei Bei, with the lazy warmth gone and the whetstone underneath, "that when she wakes — and you will tell no one I predicted this — she is going to look at your soul, and at her sect of three days' growth, and something behind her eyes is going to light up like the ancestor's own furnace. The first disciple looked at the third bed that did not exist yet, and saw it. "I only ask you to know what you'd be walking into. Think about it *after* she's awake."

But the courier was not listening with his whole attention. He was listening with the part of him that the AT had been training since conception — and the part of him that had heard, in the last hour, the way Bei Bei's arm rang when the lightning hit it, and the way the snake's armor had *sounded* under the claw, and the way Tang Ya's flying knife had whistled at a pitch his forge-ear had already filed. And he asked, apropos of nothing, with a smith's pure covetousness:

"Your arm. When the lightning's on it. Does the bone *sing?*"

Bei Bei blinked. "...You can hear that?"

"I hear *metal.* What do you think the lightning is?"

And the first disciple of the Tang Sect looked at the boy from Linjiang for a long, quiet moment — at the forge-calluses and the vines and the question nobody in the history of his family's soul had ever asked — and laughed, genuinely, for the first time on the whole road.

"*You,*" he said, "are going to be a *problem.* Thank the ancestors."

### THE FURNACE *(Tang Ya wakes — and sees)*

She woke at dusk, three-ringed, and the first thing she did was count — her rings, her sect, her fish debt — and the second thing she did was what Bei Bei had predicted, because Bei Bei was always right about the people he loved:

"The courier's soul," she said. "Show me."

He showed her. The rings rose; the grass fanned; and Tang Ya walked into the vines with her hand out and her own grass answering, and the furnace lit — and this time (the tree-line ignition had been the preview) she did not sit down. She *commanded:* "*Show me the binding. The grips. The — the SEAMS of it, the — who TAUGHT you—*" and the two grasses wove a fence that the forest's monkeys would discuss for generations, and when it was done, she held his vine in her hand, and said, not to him, to the whole ten-thousand-year weight of her line:

"It's *here.* Alive. In a boy my sect fed fish to on a road."

And then, because she was Tang Ya, she wiped her face with the wrist that wasn't holding a vine, and said: "*Hmph.* I'm not asking you again on a road. That was the last road-asking. When you answer — if you answer — it'll be somewhere that means something."

"Copy that," said the courier, who had learned the words from his brother two days ago and liked the taste of them, and the fox, in his coat, against his chest, said — so low only one boy heard — "*Adequate.*"

"You had the last of the dried plums," said Yuhao.

"I had *a* plum. There were three."

"There were *two* and you had the second one while I was setting the snare."

"You were setting the snare. I was hungry. The plum couldn't wait." The courier's face was absolute neutrality. "It's a timing problem, not a character problem."

"…That's not — you can't just *say* things like that—"

"The plum is gone, brother. Let the plum go."

And Huo Yuhao, who had never had a brother, and never had a plum argument, and never had someone to be *annoyed* at who was also *safe* — discovered, somewhere between outrage and laughter, that this was what it was: that the plum didn't matter and the arguing *did,* and that the fox across the fire was watching them both with her chin on her paws and an expression that in a lesser creature would have been called a smile.



"The cold. In the fight. When the fog hit us. That was — that was *him,* wasn't it. The passenger. He moved in me when I couldn't."

"Yes," said Jiang Che, who had read the frost's shape through the moisture-sense and kept the reading in the vault where the fox kept hers.

"Is that — is that going to be —"

"Ask him," said the courier, simply. "When he wakes up. Ask him. You're the house. The house gets to ask."

And the boy with a god in his chest nodded, slowly, against the same bark, and the fire burned down, and the fox did not say anything at all — because the moment was the boys', and she was, tonight, only the warmest thing in a coat on the biggest night of two lives that were learning, day by day, to be *shared.*


The dusk came slowly. Tang Ya's breathing changed — the deep end of a two-year bottleneck surfacing at last — and Bei Bei moved to her shoulder without being asked, and the boys moved to the fire's far side without being asked, and the camp arranged itself around the woman it was built to guard the way a river arranges itself around a stone: naturally, and without discussion.

The forest's rim had its own night-sounds — not the deep-wood silences that made dogs lie flat, but the ordinary tick and sigh of an edge-land: insects, small wind, something with wings crossing the dark high up. Jiang Che listened to it the way he had listened to every night since the stream: with the moisture-sense spread thin, reading the water in the air, the water in the ground, the water in the breathing shapes around him. It was, he was discovering, a way of being *alone with people* — present in every breath they took, asking nothing of any of them. His father had a version of it with a patrol-route. His mother had a version of it with a ward. The courier's version was a campfire and two soul-mates and a snake-skull and the first night of the rest of his life, and he sat in the middle of it being exactly, adequately, boringly himself.

Ten thousand years of the master line's stubborn honor, and the girl who had carried it alone since her teacher died, and the road, in its infinite comedy, delivering to her clearing — *five days after her sect became three* — a courier boy with the heirloom soul in its rarest form anyone had ever seen.

"Show me the binding," she commanded, wrecked and imperial at once. "Show me the grip. Who taught you — no. *Show me.*"

So he showed her. The Captain's Forms, one by one, in the morning light: the Trip-Line, the Two-Point Anchor, the Pressure-Seal — hold *without harm*, he said, the Hall's rule, and Tang Ya made a sound like a woman finding extra dumplings — and she matched him form for form with her own vines, correcting one thing, stealing three, teaching two back, and the two grasses wove a fence in the clearing that no monkey in the forest could have explained.

Then she stopped. Sat down on a root, rather suddenly, with his vine still in her hand.

"You understand," she said, not quite to him, "that I have spent my whole life being told I was the keeper of something extinct. The ancestor's soul. The master line's honor. Everyone *so respectful*, the way people are respectful at funerals." Her thumb moved along the dew. "And it's *here*. Alive. In a boy my sect fed fish to on a road."

"Xiao Ya," Bei Bei said gently, and for once did not finish, because there was no gentle end to that sentence.

"I know, I know." She wiped her face with the back of her wrist, briskly, a commander's weather clearing. "The grass is an honor and a grave; tell me the speech, I've *given* the speech." She looked up at Jiang Che, and the furnace was banked now, but it was absolutely not out. "I'm not going to ask you again on a road. That was my last asking-on-roads. When you answer — if you answer — it'll be somewhere that means something. But there's a thing you should have before you decide, and it isn't mine to make pretty." A breath. "You asked senior brother yesterday what happened to the sect. He said ask me. So."

She let go of his vine, folded her hands, and told it plain.

---

### ╱╱ THE GRUDGE ╲╲

"Four thousand years ago, another continent hit ours.

"They call it the collision. The Sun-Moon continent came out of the western sea and struck the Douluo mainland, and the world got bigger, and then the war started. And in that war —" her jaw set — "the armies of all three of *our* empires went into the field carrying **our** hidden weapons. Tang Sect steel. Ten thousand years of craft; every nation bought it; the sect was rich, and proud, and *necessary.* And the Sun-Moon Empire —" the words came out through her teeth, exactly the way they had sat in her since childhood — "came into that war with *soul tools*. Weapons driven by soul power. Longer range than ours. Heavier blow than ours. Things a soul master with no talent for combat can fire like a crossbow. Our steel broke their lines, and their tools broke our steel, and the three empires bled, and the sect that had armed the world watched the world stop needing it.

"That's the first wound. The tools got better every decade. Why buy a throwing-masters art that takes twenty years to learn, when a tool does the trade in an afternoon? The orders thinned. The masters drifted. And then — the base was seized, in the years of the second war, when we were weak enough that nobody stopped it. The great house. The ancestor's house." She said it without drama, which was its own drama. "What's left of the Tang Sect is two people, a fishing rod, and everything the tools can't take, because it's not *made* of anything. It's made of *us.*"

"The tools aren't evil," Bei Bei said, into the quiet. "That's the part she'll never say, so I will. They're *clever*. The Sun-Moon Empire builds them better than anyone — it's the whole spine of their power, and the reason the continent watches them the way farmers watch a river in spring. Shrek teaches them; the whole age is learning them; and a soul master who pretends the age isn't happening is a soul master the age will happen *to*. When we reach the academy—" and here his eyes moved, without hurry, to the courier, "—you'll see both truths standing in one street. The sect that the tools unmade. And the academy that adapted, and stands first in the world partly *because* it never once refused a new thing."

Jiang Che looked at his own vines, still out, still holding dew, and thought about the dagger on a sleeping boy's hip that had drunk a baboon's light — a soul tool, the father's only gift, the mother's whole treasure — and how the fox had called the road's soul-tools *interesting* the way a cat calls a bird interesting, and he understood that he was being handed, free of charge, both halves of the age in one morning: the grave, and the forge.

"Also," said Huo Yuhao, from the fence, helpful as sunrise, "the fish really was excellent."

"*Thank* you, second disciple."

---

### ╱╱ THE ROAD WEST ╲╲

They went west that noon, around the green wall's hip, and the road taught for four days.

Geography, first, because the forest graded its dangers like an academy grades its students: the south side — their side, the Star Luo side — kept the lesser beasts; the northwest face, the one that looked at Shrek, held the old strong ones, who hated the academy's hunters with a hatred that had, more than once in history, poured out of the trees as a tide. No one below Soul King walked in from that side with a whole skin. A thousand li of detour bought you the gentle edge of the world's biggest wilderness — and on that long gentle edge, the Tang Sect opened its last treasury and paid everything out in lessons.

For Huo Yuhao, the whole road was a school. The Purple Demon Eyes at dawn, staring at the first light until the world's edges sharpened. The Ghost-Shadow Track until his feet forgot roads existed. The Crane-Captures-Dragon with Bei Bei correcting his wrists a fourth time, a fifth, *patient as rain, deep in the shallow* — and the boy's terrifying diligence, which was the road's true weather: he ran the Xuantian Gong every rest-stop and half the marches, and by the fourth day his old soul power had gone over entirely, re-issued pure, and the gray little veteran of the woodshed stood in a field at evening breathing white streams off his lips with his eyes gone clear as window-glass, and called it *a good day*, and meant it.

"Spirit Detection Sharing," he told them, when Bei Bei pressed the naming — the camouflage holding, the baboon's ring still wearing the story. "Thirty meters now. The range grows, I think, with my cultivation. And it costs — almost nothing." And Bei Bei looked at him with the despair of a scholar meeting a new continent — "*ten thousand years* of soul research, and no book has a record like you" — and then collected himself, and did what senior brothers do: he assigned the boy a future. Control-type. The ancestor's own category; the team's hidden king. "With Xiao Ya's grass and your eyes, a *team* doesn't need anything else to be complete. Trust the classification. Trust me."

For Jiang Che, the road was quieter, and less quiet than it looked.

He could not learn the arts — not one page, not one step; the Treasure Record was the sect's blood and the life-condition was the sect's law, and Bei Bei, gentle about it, was absolute: *when you belong, all of it is yours; until then, it isn't, and that is what belonging means.* So the courier did what the courier had: he read the road, worked his forms at the fire's edge, mended blisters and a twisted ankle with his mother's craft, and let the AT drink the age in — the soul-tool caravans passing west with their humming crates; the hunters' tools; the belt on a sleeping boy that held twenty-four rooms. *The age will happen to the ones who pretend it isn't happening.* He caught himself, once, doing the arithmetic of the fence-forms against tools he'd never fought, and stopped, and didn't unstop.

And Tang Ya, rank thirty now, with three rings and a banked furnace, watched him at the fire's edge doing forms he'd invented at eight years old, and said nothing at all, which from her was a speech.

"You could at least *teach him the footwork*," she hissed at Bei Bei, later, in the dark, with the entire hypocrisy of a woman who had stolen three of his grip-forms that morning.

"I could," Bei Bei said, to the stars. "It's a better argument than any I could make. That's why I won't."

The fox, in a coat pocket, kept her own counsel, and counted soul tools, and did not report her count.

---

### ╱╱ THE NIGHT-SHIFTS ╲╲ *(the road west — the brothers' watches)*

The road west taught the party its rhythms in two days: Bei Bei navigating, Tang Ya eating, the two boys trading watches at the fire — and the watches were where the cascade lived.

On Yuhao's watch, the second night, the passenger stirred — a *dream* — and the boy woke with the taste of ten-thousand-year ice in his mouth and the certainty that something enormous had rolled over in its sleep. In the morning, walking, he said it — quietly, out of the side of his mouth:

"He dreams in *ages.* I saw one corner of one. It was the size of a *country,* Hao."

"And you didn't wake me?"

"You needed the sleep. That's the deal. I carry the nights, you carry the mornings, and the fox carries the whole continent on a coin's worth of sleep."

From the coat: "*I heard that.*"

The craft-thread took its first step that same day — the Treasure Record in the courier's pack since the oath; Tang Ya's *"start with the least"*; and the least was the Jade Hand, whose first exercise was *holding things that are too hot.* Every campfire's kettle, every cook-pot handle, every stone rolled from the pit: the courier did them bare-handed for two hundred miles, lost the skin off both palms twice, and said nothing — until Yuhao watched him pick up a boiling kettle by the bail like a cup of tea:

"Does it hurt?"

"It's information. The Record says let the whole of it move through you. The letting hurts. The *moving* doesn't." A shrug. "Also I can't feel my thumbs. That's probably fine."

"That is NOT probably fine—"

"It's Tuesday. My thumbs are always like this on Tuesdays."

And the healer's son healed himself, on a road, with a book and a kettle and two ruined palms — and the jade-pale lines started where the blisters had been.

---

### ╱╱ THE FIREWATCH ╲╲

On the fourth night, the trees thinned, and the west showed lights — a wide scatter of them at the world's edge, more lights than Jiang Che had ever seen in one gaze, and over them a faint gold smudge that was a *city* reflecting off its own weather.

"Shrek City," Bei Bei said. "Tomorrow, the academy."

They sat up late around a fire that had become, without ceremony, the Tang Sect's last hearth of the road — the master darning a sock with flying-knife precision; the first disciple cleaning a porcelain vial; the second disciple breathing white streams with his eyes shut, growing; and the courier from Linjiang, two rings, unhired, with a green edge behind him and a gold horizon ahead, sitting his watch beside the sect that was patient.

"You know," Tang Ya said, to the fire, thoughtfully, in the tone of a woman finally saying the thing she had not said for four days, "when the ancestor built all this — the sect, the team, the *age* — the stories say he started with exactly this. Not a fortress. Not a fortune." She turned the sock. "A fire, and however many monsters he could fit around it."

"Seven," said Huo Yuhao, who had read everything Bei Bei carried.

"We'd have to be greedy to match that," said Tang Ya, and looked, very briefly, at a boy with grass in his sleeves, and then at the fire again, and darned.

The fire burned down gold. The fox counted one last caravan, far off, humming west. Nobody slept, and everybody pretended to.

In the dark, a fox said one more thing, to the only ear that could hear it: "*Little tide. Tomorrow you walk into a place that makes monsters. Remember: you don't have to be the loudest one in the room. You have to be the one still standing when the loud ones leave.*"

"I know," said the courier, who had known this since he was four.

"That's why I picked you," said the fox, and was asleep before the sentence ended, which was her version of goodnight, and also, possibly, a lie — she had not picked him; she had been dying in a ravine and he had been the only pair of hands that worked — but she was an empress, and empresses do not say *I stumbled into you.* They say *I chose.*

### ╱╱ THE CITY OF MONSTERS ╲╲

They came at Shrek City out of the morning like sailors coming at a harbor: the road widened, and widened again, and then the road gave up and became *streets*, and the age poured past them in both directions — caravans of soul-tool freight humming west, auction houses with their doors open like mouths, tea-shops three stories tall, and monsters everywhere, wearing school badges of four colors and no awe at all.

"Every one of them," Bei Bei said, pleasantly, "is the pride of somewhere. The continent culls a thousand years of children down to a thousand a year, and those are the thousand. Try to feel the size of it," he advised his junior brother, "and then stop, because the size of it is not your business. *You* are your business."

Hu Yuhao walked the strangest street of his life with his spine straight and his hand never once touching the dagger, because for the first time since the back gate of a mansion fifty li from a capital, he was walking toward a door that had his name on a list beside it.

And behind them, at the same pace as always, a blue-haired courier looked at the same city and did what he always did with new ground: read it. Caravans. Auctions. Forges — a whole street of forges, their chimneys making the east sky gray — and, in the pocket over his heart, a weight that had stopped giving him commentary days ago and now only watched.

---

### ╱╱ THE TEN STATUES ╲╲

The academy began where the noise ended.

Past the gates, the main road ran green and enormous between the trees, and at its heart stood what the first-comers were already circling: statues. Ten of them, facing ten thousand years.

Front row, three: a smiling roundish elder in spectacles — Flender, the founder. At his left a lean middle-aged scholar with unreadable eyes — **Yu Xiaogang, the Grandmaster, who built the very system by which every soul master on the continent was taught**, and of whom Bei Bei said, simply, quietly, with a whole ancestry in his voice: "My mother's line. The academy's true soul." At the founder's right, a handsome woman mid-shape — Liu Erlong. The Golden Iron Triangle.

Behind them, seven more — the first Seven. A double-pupiled tiger of a man first; then a gently smiling one; and third—

Third, a young man in simple clothes with long blue hair, blue-silver vines climbing the statue's arms, a faint smile carved at the mouth and the whole of the gaze aimed across the row at a fifth figure with a scorpion braid, forever.

"*Thousand-Hand Douluo,*" Tang Ya said. Her voice had gone somewhere else again — the furnace-voice. "Tang San. The ancestor. Our ancestor — the sect's, I mean," and she looked, for one heartbeat, at the courier beside her, and did not correct herself, and neither did he.

"Ten statues in ten thousand years," Bei Bei said. "No eleventh has been added since. Understand this place early, little brothers: Shrek does not build statues for the excellent. It builds them for the *turnings of the world.*"

Behind the statues, through the trees, water glinted — a lake so wide it held weather, with an island at its heart.

"The Sea God Lake," Tang Ya said. "Built to honor the ancestor — he took a god's throne, the stories say, and one of them was of the sea. The *inner academy* stands on that island. Everything we do, everything this place does, aims across that water."

Jiang Che stood before the third statue the longest of any of them. A boy with grass in his sleeves, looking up at the man who had made grass a legend — feeling, without any way to say it, the weight of a ten-thousand-year expectation settle onto his shoulders and finding that it fit, the way his father's strap fit, the way his mother's knots fit: made for someone bigger, and then, one day, not.

In his pocket, very low, so only one boy in the world could have heard it: "*Hm. He kept his eyes on his people, not his height.*" And then nothing more, which from the fox was a eulogy.

---

### ╱╱ THE INHERITANCE ╲╲

They took the lakeside path slowly, because Tang Ya had decided — with the particular courage of a woman about to spend the last of something — that the whole story should be walked, not sketched.

The sect at its height: thousands of members, the continent's armory, rich beyond reason — and giving it *away*, most of it, because the first master had written the giving into the sect's bones: the poor districts, the schools. "We were never a treasury," she said. "We were a *furnace*. Everything that came in, went out as light." And then the collision, and the tools, and the orders thinned, and two hundred years unmade two thousand —

"— and by my childhood it was three," Tang Ya said, to the water. "Mama. Papa. Me." A breath, level, rehearsed by years of not-crying. "They died in the hunting conflict, the year I was nine. The sect's last masters. I got the Treasure Record, the fishing rod, the arts, and the grudge." She turned and looked at her sect: at the tall boy who had joined her madness for love and stayed for the truth of it, and at the woodshed boy breathing white streams at the lake's edge, and — for a moment that she let be seen — at the courier. "You asked on the road what happened. That's what happened. And here's what happens *next.*"

And she told them the decision — hers and Bei Bei's, taken years ago in a smaller room than this morning: that the Tang Sect would not die proud and useless; that hidden weapons were not *wrong*, they were unfinished; that the sect's chance — the only chance anyone had been able to see in two hundred years — was the thing everyone said with a laugh: **fusion**. Steel and soul-tool. Craft and age.

"Every disciple of the Tang Sect, from this generation on, studies the soul tool as well as the soul," she said, in the words she and Bei Bei had chosen long before this morning. "That's the law we wrote. There's just—" and for the first time in four days the furnace-voice cracked, just at the edge, just once, "—there's just been no one who could *hold both ends.* We're fighters. The arts of making are gone out of the sect; the last smith died before I could walk. We wrote a law nobody can keep."

The lake moved. Nobody filled the silence, because the silence was a door, and doors get filled from one side only.

---

### ╱╱ THE REGISTRATION ╲╲

But first the world, which does not wait for chapters.

The white new-students' hall was chaos with a queue: children of eleven and twelve from every nation under the sun, each one the pride of somewhere, each one clutching a badge or a terror. With Bei Bei and Tang Ya walking him past it all, Huo Yuhao's registration was minutes — name, origin, soul, ring; the *exam-exempt* chit from the Tang Sect's ancient privilege presented by the Sect Master herself, to a clerk who sat up very straight indeed.

The tuition was ten gold soul coins for the year. Bei Bei paid it without ceremony, and told him firmly, before thanks could form, that it was the sect's law and not the sect's generosity — "you'll repay it in the *currency we actually use*" — and the ledger closed on: Huo Yuhao, first-year, Class One.

At the notice-board, Bei Bei's eyebrows did the journey they'd been dreading. **Zhou Yi.** The new class's homeroom teacher. The academy's most infamous teacher — demoted to the first-years for harshness that had thinned a third-year class to a tenth; and, said Bei Bei, quietly, the other truth: her survivors reached the inner court at a rate one in four, among the best the academy had ever recorded. "Shrek's monster students are famous," he said, steering his junior brother bodily away from the board, "but the *monster teachers* are the ones who make them. Survive her, little brother. That's the whole first year: survive her."

For Jiang Che, the clerk had colder arithmetic. Standard admission — no chit, no exemption: the *entrance trial*, three days hence, and the same ten gold coins a year, no refunds, wages and prize-money a student's own affair thereafter.

"Three days," he said.

"Three days," Tang Ya agreed; and then, with the enormous brightness of a woman who has already decided not to say the thing: "Well. *Somebody* in this sect has an evening to spend, then."

### ╱╱ THE WAITING BENCH ╲╲ *(the morning before the oath — the brothers, alone)*

Before the statues, before the lakeside — a bench outside the registration hall, two boys on it, and the particular silence of a boy about to be asked something enormous.

"You're doing the thing," Yuhao said. "The silence thing. Where your jaw does the — *clench.*"

"My jaw doesn't do a thing."

"Your jaw does an entire thing. It's doing it now." He looked at the lake, not at his brother. "You don't have to. She said *when,* not now."

"It's not the when." The courier's hands turned the Treasure Record's pages over and over, corner to corner, the way a man shuffles a card he's already decided to play. "It's that they're *right.* A four-person sect with a law nobody can keep, and the one craft that keeps it walks in wearing my face. I'm eleven, Yu. What kind of idiot looks at that and thinks *yes, my problem now?*"

"The same kind that wraps a baboon for a stranger. The same kind that eats two fish out of fourteen." He turned. "Hao. They're not asking you to be the smith. They're asking you to be *theirs.* The smith part is just the shape it comes in."

A long quiet. The lake said nothing, expertly.

"...Did you just give a *speech?*"

"I've been saving it. You weren't supposed to need it until the fox's birthday."

"She doesn't have a birthday. She's nine hundred years old."

"Then I've got time to write a better one," said Yuhao — and his brother laughed, actually laughed, the bark startling a fisher-bird off the bench — and the clench, wherever it had lived, was gone.

### ╱╱ THE THRESHOLD ╲╲

She took them back along the lakeside path as the sun went long, and stopped — of all the places in the world she might have chosen — between the water and the statues, where the ancestor's stony eyes could see both his grass and his sea.

"Jiang Che of Linjiang." Formal. The full name, the way sects say names when names have started to weigh. "Four days ago I told you I'd ask you nowhere again until somewhere that meant something. This is somewhere that means something." A breath. "The Tang Sect asks. Third asking. Last asking." And then her voice stopped being formal, because Tang Ya had never in her life been formal for a full minute: "*Please.* We wrote a law nobody can keep. You're a keeper. Your soul is the ancestor's own. Your hands are a healer's. Your head — four days of watching you think has taught senior brother and me *this* much: you don't see a broken thing and walk around it. You see a broken thing and ask what it wants to be when it's *upgraded.* So." She held out her hand, palm up: the oldest gesture her arts knew. "The life-condition is cruel and I'll say it plainly anyway: join, and you are Tang Sect until death. The arts, the name, the grudge, the *furnace.* Leave ever, and you give back every page. There's no shame in no. But there's — there has never in my life been a *yes* I wanted more."

The lake said nothing. The statues said nothing, expertly.

Jiang Che looked at the hand. And because his answer had been assembling itself since a stream and a bell and a triage in the grass — since the grudge told plainly and the arts'-door held shut and the fusion law written for hands no one had — he gave it the only way he knew how to give anything, which was the whole of it, out loud.

"My father binds things for a living," he said. "My mother mends them. I was raised in a house where nothing got thrown away because nothing was *finished* — and I've spent four days learning that your hidden weapons aren't dead, Sect Master. They're the weakest thing on this road." He looked up, and the furnace in his eyes answered hers. "I don't choose things because they're strong. I choose them because they're *weak.* Weak is where the work is. You wrote a law nobody can keep —"*and his hand closed on hers, courier's grip, smith's grip*— "so keep it. I'll take the Jade Hand tonight. The hidden-weapon canon when my hands are worth it. The forge-craft and the soul-tool craft until the two are one thing and the thing is *ours.* I'll write my parents tonight — a courier's son knows how a letter travels; they'll say yes, they raised me to say yes to exactly this." A breath; the last of it, quiet. "I am Tang Sect. From this handshake until death. Ask me for the pages back never."

Tang Ya held the grip with both her hands, and her eyes were streaming and her grin was enormous and she said, wetly, with total command presence: "Sect of *four.*"

Behind them, Huo Yuhao whooped like the eleven-year-old he had finally been allowed to be. Bei Bei, who did not whoop, took off his belt-purse with the air of a man completing a plan years long — inside it, wrapped in oilcloth against exactly this day, lay a second hand-copied **Treasure Record**, begun the winter after a girl took a boy into a dying sect for love.

The Trade, then, by the last light, on the lakeside grass: Xuantian Gong for the root. The five arts named. And when the Sect Master, smiling like sunrise, asked her newest disciple which art he would take up *first*—

"Which one is least?" said Jiang Che of Linjiang, with the whole forest's patience.

"The Jade Hand," said everyone at once, including the fox, from a pocket, ruining the solemnity forever.

---

### ╱╱ TWO BEDS, TWO CANDLES ╲╲

That night, Huo Yuhao — badge on, key in hand — met the most ancient doorman in the world at the white dormitory door, was pronounced "a rare polite child," found room 108 with its month of dust and its two beds, bought a basin and a used rag with his own small coin, and cleaned the little room to a shine a palace would not have recognized, and sat on bare boards, and laughed once, alone, for no reason he could have named, with his whole life on the other side of it.

Two beds. A roommate coming, said the ledger. Somewhere in the strange sea of the school, a stranger who would share ten square meters of the world with him.

And across the city, in a courier's inn where the lamps were soul-tools and cost a copper the hour, a new disciple of a four-person sect sat at a bad desk and wrote the hardest letter of his life home — *Mother, Father: I have joined a sect; it is very small, and very old, and it needs us; also I need my forge-hammer sent* — while beside his elbow, on the desk's edge, in the terrible posture of the supremely comfortable, sat a small white fox with nine tails, watching the candle with golden eyes, keeping — for once in her long, long, unguessable life — the watch with him.

The trial was in three days. The lake lay between the city and the island like a held breath. Somewhere below the world, at the bottom of a young spiritual sea, something in an eleven-year-old sleeper dreamed of ten thousand years, and smiled in its sleep.

Ten statues. A thousand years of children. A sect of four.

The turning had begun.
