### ╱╱ THE SEA, BRIEFLY ╲╲

On the second night, in the deeps of a small meditation, the white place returned, and the Skydream Iceworm with it — draped across the golden sea of the boy's inner world like a satisfied landslide.

"Not bad," it said, which from a million years was a parade. "The Gong suits you. The eye-method suits you. And the four gifts are sitting up nicely." It counted them off on nothing, grandly, as a landlord counts rooms: **"Spirit Detection. Spirit Sharing. Spirit Interference — a crowd-trick, thirty meters, a blink of daze, three seconds, no more yet. And Soul Shock — the only tooth of the four. Single target, one needle. Point it with your eye-method when you must; a needle in the right half-second is a knife anywhere else."** A yawn that moved weather. "I'm going to sleep, brother. A long one. When you come to the wall where the second ring must be, I'll wake — and *then*, little host, the cold I left in you finds its true shape, and you'll understand what a million years buys." It settled, vast and dimming. "If death itself comes for you, call. Only if you live do I live. It's a good lease. Sleep well."

And Huo Yuhao woke with the dark outside and his body one grain warmer, one grain *more*, and ate his dry rations in the dark like a rich man.

---

### ╱╱ AFTER THE HAMMER ╲╲ *(the post-trial — the brothers, the comedown)*

The proctor left. The pens stopped. And the first thing Jiang Che did, having publicly sewn a fourth-year's hammer to the ground, was find the nearest wall, slide down it, and put his head between his knees.

"...You okay?"

"No." Muffled. Completely honest. "I used the Sun-Baptism at exchange seven. On *breathing.* That's supposed to be for *bleeding.* Exchange six was — the floor was *moving,* Yu. Thirty percent left and a plan I made up between five and six."

"You looked like you were reading a newspaper."

"I was *dying* beautifully." He lifted his head — gray-faced, grinning, entirely eleven for four seconds. "Did you see his *face?*"

"Which part. The hammer stopping, or him lifting you with one hand to make it look like a draw?"

"That never happened."

"He picked you up like a *delivery,* Hao. Then said *match's yours* like it was his idea. That's what sixth-years do when a first-year beats them in front of three examiners: they make it a favor."

"...It was a good favor." The courier slid further down the wall. "I'm going to be sick."

"You are not going to be sick."

"I might. It's been a big morning. There was a *hammer.*"

And Huo Yuhao sat down next to his brother on the assessment-square wall — shoulder to shoulder with the boy who had beaten a hammer and was currently losing to gravity — and this, too, was the brotherhood: not the moments that looked like legend, but the wall after, and the gray face, and the *I might be sick,* and the shoulder against the shoulder until the world stopped spinning.

---

### ╱╱ THE ROOMMATE ╲╲

The next midday, coming back from a three-copper breakfast and a lecture from a senior brother about never skipping meals and taking school work like a man, Huo Yuhao found his own door standing open, and a stranger in his doorway.

The stranger was — there was no plainer way to put it, and the whole corridor would be putting it for years — *beautiful*. Clean-cut features, skin like good paper, big eyes a pale, impossible blue, and short hair the same blue, and an air of standing slightly above the ground he stood on. The best-looking boy Huo Yuhao had ever seen, and radiantly, structurally *annoyed* at being looked at.

"You are?" Huo Yuhao managed.

The blue eyes ran him up and down like a customs officer. "Move."

"...Oh." He moved. The boy swept past, stopped, and — as if conferring a dukedom — issued the terms: five rules. No guests. No indecency. No snoring. No disturbing *him*. And the cleaning was Yuhao's now — "but don't touch my bed. Understood?"

"Why," said Huo Yuhao, who had spent ten years under a Duchess's rules and one night swearing at a back gate, "would I obey *you?*"

"Because otherwise I'll throw you out. Try me."

"I'll try you," said the woodshed boy, with a calm that surprised them both. "Outside."

"**Wang Dong,**" said the boy, delighted, offering the name like a card before a winning hand.

"**Huo Yuhao.**"

"Then good-bye, *Huo Yuhao*," Wang Dong said, smiling like a blade coming out of a cane. "Your name is about to leave this academy. Walk, idiot."

---

### ╱╱ THE DORM FIGHT ╲╲

The old doorman's chin lifted off his chest, and his cloudy eyes acquired, for the first time in possibly decades, an audience.

Wang Dong did not use his martial soul. He said so, aloud, twice, in the tone of a man mentioning the weather — and then he *moved*, and the moving was the point: a body like a drawn bow, legs longer than the law should allow, a first kick that arrived before its own sound. Any ordinary new boy would have been a rumor by the second one.

But the white ring was already turning at Huo Yuhao's feet, and the golden light stood in his eyes, and the *world told him things* — the loading of the hip, the half-breath before the strike, the corridor of the next kick drawn in the air like a map — and he read the map. He slipped the first by a step; slapped the ankle of the second; ducked the third and rose *inside* it, shoulder into thigh—

—into a thigh that merely rose with the blow, up, up, into a standing split no human spine had authored, while its owner looked down the length of his own leg at Yuhao with genuine academic interest, as though Yuhao were an equation behaving oddly.

Then the storm. Two legs like braided steel, a whirlwind that cracked flagstones where it missed, and Yuhao — slower, weaker, *fragile* by every measure but the one that mattered — danced in its middle on half-learned ghost-steps, reading each blow a half-breath early, a small boat that would not, *would not* go under. His palms sang where he blocked; the Jade Hand answered without being asked. He was hit, and hit, and grazed — edges only, each one a burn — and the gap between their bodies closed on him minute by minute like water rising, and he understood with perfect calm: *not enough. He is far above me. I have one needle.*

So he looked up.

He looked up with everything — and Wang Dong, mid-storm, instinct-glanced at his eyes, and caught the **purple flash** needle-deep in the gold: Soul Shock, fused with the Purple Demon Eyes, one half-second of white.

Yuhao hit him like a thrown dog, arms locked, legs cinched at the waist, and the two of them went down together — pinned, chest to chest, faces an inch apart, both breathing like bellows.

"Yield," Huo Yuhao snarled.

"In your *dreams*—" but the pause was already there: *if he'd meant it. If it had been a knife, I was dead twice.* "...Fine. I lost. Get *off.*"

Yuhao stood, backed, never turned. "Your five rules — I'll keep them. Not because of the threat. Out of respect for a roommate. But hear mine: insult me again and you'll have to kill me, because I'll have bitten a piece off you on the way down."

Something in Wang Dong's face — the hate draining out of it, and something younger looking out, startled — filed that away. He went in without another word.

---

### ╱╱ THE VERDICT ╲╲

At the dormitory door, an ancient voice stopped the blue-haired boy like a hand.

"You lost," the doorman said, without opening his eyes. "The fight. And the heart."

"He *beat* me with a trick! I'm twice—"

"He beat you with a *heart*." One finger moved, and tapped the old man's own chest. "Yours is a good sword-arm, child, and it has never once been offered. His has been on the table since the day he was born. Fearlessness is not a skill. That's why it wins." The finger settled. "Go on."

Wang Dong stood a moment in the sun. Then he bowed — a deep, correct, furious, *real* bow — and went in to think.

For two days the room held its own weather: two beds, two silences, one boy on fur rugs a finger deep, sleeping like the wealthy, and one boy on bare boards who — the wealthy boy noted with increasing insult — *never lay down at all*, but sat like a stoic in a wheel of white breath, hour after hour, growing.

He could *feel* it, that was the unforgivable part. Every soul master's sense said the same thing: a soul power like a candle in a shed, ten levels of anything-but-special — and every fact of his own body, his own two unbruised hands, said *and he beat me.* The arithmetic refused to close. Wang Dong had grown up being the answer to other people's arithmetics, and being a question mark's *subject* kept him awake those two nights longer than the hard bed deserved.

"Madman," Wang Dong informed the ceiling.

The ceiling, like fate, did not disagree, and the days ran out, and enrollment closed, and the night before the first bell, both beds were occupied by boys pretending the other wasn't there — which is how the greatest partnership of an age began: badly, in a ten-meter room, one inch and one ocean apart.

---

### ╱╱ THE TRIAL ╲╲

Across those same three days, on the far side of the academy, the standard door stood open: the Assessment Square, where the continent's unprivileged culled elite bought their chance in front of examiners with no favorites.

Jiang Che had spent the eve the way he spent everything — preparation as ceremony. His father's forms, run slow. His mother's knots, checked. The Treasure Record's first pages, read twice by candlelight, and an hour's first lesson in the **Jade Hand** — the tempering of the hands, the art of the sect's dead smiths — which mostly felt, at hour one of year one, like holding a warm stone and being patient. The fox had supervised all of it from the bedpost with the expression of an empress reviewing troops, and said only: "*Don't be interesting. Be enough.*" Then, softer, in the register she used perhaps twice a year: "The big ones swing at what they think you are. Let them. What you are is a river — and rivers are only ever met, never hit." He carried that into the square like a second knife.

The trial was simple and cruel, as Shrek liked its doors. Demonstrate the soul. Demonstrate the kit. And then — the part that thinned the line — **last ten exchanges against a fourth-year proctor.** Full contact, surrender or stop.

His proctor was a fourth-year of fourteen with three rings and a soldier's boredom, a war-hammer soul the size of a door, and the professional courtesy of a person breaking crates. Two yellow, one purple, at fourteen: another continent-pride, exactly the caliber Shrek grows like a crop.

The rings lit. The grass came out. And Jiang Che fought the honest ceiling of his life for ten exchanges, and the record of it went into the examiners' ledger like this:

Exchanges one through three: the courier *read* the hammer — the dew-beads' lens, the moisture-map, the half-breath tells — and was never where the door-size weapon landed; the square's flagstones were not so lucky.

Four through six: he bound. Trip-lines the proctor burst by weight; anchors that held exactly long enough; a pressure-seal around the hammer's haft that the fourth-year had to *work* to break, and did, and stopped being bored.

Seven: the Sun-Baptism — the only burst-mend he had — spent not on damage taken but on breath, the light feeding the tide so the tide could keep reading. The examiners leaned forward. One of them, a gray-browed woman with the stillness of long service, said nothing at all, and wrote three lines without looking down — clerks at Shrek learn early which way the wind sits.

Eight: the proctor stopped being polite — and it stopped mattering. That was the discovery the square watched happen: the fourth-year brought three rings and a soldier's whole craft to exchange eight, and the courier had already spent seven exchanges *buying the ground*. The trip-lines burst by weight at exchange four had never been removed; they had been *re-tensioned*, and now the square itself was the web — ankle, knee, hammer-haft, one moisture-read map the older boy could not see, because it was written in dew.

Nine: the hammer came down like a door closing — and struck a floor it had already been sewn to. Two-Point Anchor, Pressure-Seal, every vine he owned; and the weapon that had rung like a bell all morning rang against the flagstones and *stayed there*.

Ten: the fourth-year — three rings, fourteen, a continent's pride in miniature — set both feet, took the haft two-handed, and hauled with his back and his soul and his considerable dignity; and the hammer moved one hand-width, and stopped, held by grass.

The senior examiner's hand rose. "**Enough.**"

The square stood very quiet. The proctor leaned on his freed hammer, breathing like a man who had discovered stairs in his own house, looking at a two-ring eleven-year-old who was not, in any visible way, tired.

The examiners' pens moved. Shrek does not record victories in its trial ledgers. It records, in the old script, a single word for what it screens: *monster?* — and beside Jiang Che's name the word was written, and underneath it, in a senior examiner's hand, the annotation that would follow him through the academy for years, because clerks are gossips:

*"Took a fourth-year's hammer in ten exchanges and gave nothing back. Control-craft beyond rank. ADMITTED — flagged for the year-tutor watch."*

The ledger closed. Later, at the work-board, the fourth-year found him by the forges, on no instruction from anyone, and stood chewing a bread-heel in professional silence for a while. "The hammer-lock," he said at last, as one craftsman to another. "You didn't learn that in a ring." — "My father binds things for a living," said the courier. The proctor considered this, nodded slowly, as if a long-standing question of natural philosophy had been settled, and left. It was, in its way, a second admission.

The tuition was ten gold; the courier's savings, contract by contract since he was nine, came to seven and a half; the work-board by the dining hall — canon of the academy's own economy — supplied the rest by noon: morning forges, evening greenhouses, water for the soul-tool hall's quenchant vats. A boy who had never once in his life been afraid of work signed three lines, took a white badge and a key, and went to find his door.

In his pocket, an empress who had watched grass hold a fourth-year's hammer to the flagstones permitted herself one sentence: "*Adequate.*" It was, from her, a coronation.

---

### ╱╱ THE FIRST BELL ╲╲

Morning. The white teaching hall opened its doors, and the new year walked in — white uniforms, and over each heart the little green monster, grinning on ten thousand chests like a promise the academy intended to keep.

But the door that mattered most that week was a different one, and it was assigned the evening before, by the oldest man in the world.

The white dormitory's gatekeeper had looked at the courier's white badge, and at the ledger, and then at nothing at all for a long moment — the way old men look at nothing when they are reading something.

"Room 108," he said at last. "Corner room. Three beds — the only triple in the white hall. Third one's been empty eleven years." He handed over the key without quite looking at it. "Doors choose," he added, to the middle distance, in the tone of a man quoting something that had no author. "Boys just knock."

Room 108, that evening, was a war fought in silence: two territories, one bed in furs a finger deep radiating offended aristocracy, one bed bare as a plank radiating cultivation, no words exchanged in a day and a half. The door opened on this weather, and a third boy walked into it carrying a pack, a hammer, and a fox.

"...There are *three* beds," said the aristocrat, affronted, as though personally lied to.

"There's one of me," said Jiang Che. "Jiang Che. Courier, healer's son, new third bed." He set the hammer on the desk with complete courtesy. "You've met my sect brother. I've heard about the five rules; I'll keep them. My rule is one: what sleeps in my pocket sleeps in my pocket." Inside his coat, a small white weight shifted in a manner he would later describe as *insubordinate*.

The fur-bed's blue eyes narrowed at the hammer, then at the courier's hair — blue regarding blue with the suspicion of a monarch sighting a rival flag — and then, unable to find anything actually wrong with either, issued the verdict cornered aristocracies fall back on: "*Hmph.* The cleaning rotation is on the wall."

The bare-plank boy said nothing. But two days of monastic silence had built up in Huo Yuhao a pressure only the arrival of a normal human being could release, and the look he gave the third bed was unmistakably *thank heavens* — and Jiang Che, who could read a room the way his mother read a wound, saw the whole war, its history and its future, in one glance, and hung his coat on the third nail.

And in the morning the first bell rang, and a small class of monsters began to learn what fearlessness costs — and out of one corner room, three boys walked into it together: two blue-haired, one of them furious at the world and one calm as a river; the third gray-clothed and quietly astonished to be walking anywhere with anyone.

The doors had chosen. The boys had knocked.

The two blue-haired boys had both come through their doors.

### ╱╱ THE BROKEN GONG ╲╲

Class One held one hundred of the continent's culled pride, and when the door opened, it held one old woman.

White hair coiled on the crown; a white robe; a back straight as a spear-shaft; and eyes — bright, black, lit from behind somehow — that swept the room left to right and left a stripe of pressure across every spine they crossed, the way a whetstone leaves a stripe across a blade. Huo Yuhao, whose own soul was eyes, felt that sweep like a hand on the back of his neck.

"I am Zhou Yi. Your homeroom." A voice like a broken gong — cracked, nasal, and carrying like war-drums. "I don't know how many of you will walk this year with me. Here is what I do know: in my class, no *garbage* passes. I train monsters. Not fools."

A hundred faces of the elite went red. A hundred prides of a hundred nations chewed the word *garbage* and found it did not swallow.

"Since registration day: those who have *fought* — stand."

Silence. Nobody moves — this is the oldest trap in the world and these are the newest students in it — and into that silence, with the sensation of a man stepping off a cliff he has correctly measured, Huo Yuhao stood. Not honesty. Arithmetic. *This teacher does not play by rules; therefore the rule-shaped answer is wrong.*

A heartbeat later, annoyed to be second at anything, Wang Dong stood too.

And a third, from the middle rows, calm as a river deciding to be noticeable: Jiang Che. He had fought — a trial bout, a proctored match, but a *fight* was a fight.

One hundred students. Three upright. Zhou Yi's eyebrow climbed a millimeter — her version of open delight.

"Only three? What a class of *waste*." The broken gong rang off the walls. "Did no one ever teach you that the one who dares not make trouble is a mediocrity? The rest of you — OUT. Around Shrek Square. One hundred laps. One hour. Unfinished means expelled — and understand this *is* your first assessment."

The explosion of protest had a leader — one boy, up and outraged — and Zhou Yi answered him the way winter answers a late harvest: "Because I said so. Disagree and leave; I hold the power to expel any of you. One minute." And when the protest did not instantly die, her soul rings rose — **two yellow, two purple, and two BLACK** — and a Soul Emperor's pressure walked the room like a plowed field, and a hundred prodigies discovered the exact size of children.

They went. Jiang Che among them — the third who had stood — and Zhou Yi's eye rested on him one second longer than on anyone else. Not warm. Not cold. *Measuring.* The trial annotation sat in her mind: *flagged for the year-tutor's watch.* She said nothing. Whetstones note the metal.

They went. At the door, the field of them, molten with injustice.

Zhou Yi turned to the three. And the whetstone showed its other face, the one only her survivors ever saw — the face that had put one in four of her students onto the island in the lake.

"Good," she said, quietly. "Three with blood in them. You two — roommates, are you? Fought each other? *Good.* Roommates who fight sharpen each other. Fight the other classes next time — the rules permit it. Hear them: seniors who provoke juniors are expelled. Juniors may challenge seniors, with a teacher witnessing. Within your year, fight as you please — no deaths, no interference. Combat," said the monster teacher, "is an excellent way to improve. Now."

"...Now?" said Wang Dong.

"Now you run too. You fought your roommate on day one — so ambitious! — so your assessment is *harder*: one hundred laps, the same deadline as the others."

"And you," her eyes found the third boy, the one whose trial file she had read at four in the morning with a cup of tea going cold beside it, "you fought a *proctor*. In a *trial*. That is not fighting. That is interviewing. Run with the class and learn the difference." The broken gong sounded almost sweet. "And you've already lost a quarter hour standing here admiring me."

### ╱╱ THE FIELD ╲╲

Shrek Square measured three hundred meters a lap, and the first morning of the new year ran around it like a millwheel of pride.

Jiang Che ran in the pack — not the front, not the back — and beside him, forty laps in, a gray-uniformed boy running on fumes and stubbornness matched his stride for three steps before realizing he had.

"You —" Hu Yuhao panted, recognizing the third bed. "You're not even — breathing —"

"I walk a lot," said the courier, at conversation volume, which was its own kind of cruelty.

Wang Dong, passing them both for the ninth time with the offended majesty of a hawk being overtaken by traffic, looked down at the exchange from a height of moral and physical superiority, and *nearly* smiled.

The courier ran at the pace of a man who had walked sixty li before breakfast since he was eight. Jiang Che had learned his trade's central secret young: *distance is not conquered, it is administered.* His feet fell the way his father's fell on patrol; his breath ran the Hall's four-count; and where the sun lay on his shoulders and the back of his neck, something in him drank it — light feeding life, life feeding stride — so that the laps went by beneath him like ledger-lines, counted without counting.

*Forty-one. Forty-two.*

In his breast pocket, pressed flat, a fox conducted an inspection of the apocalypse. "*This,*" she remarked, to her human alone, "*is the famous forge of monsters. It is a vegetable market with better posture. If she wants to see running, she should visit a forest fire.*"

"Shh," said the courier, at sip-volume, and a neighboring runner decided, wisely, he had heard nothing.

He saw everything else, because seeing the field was the family trade. He saw the leaders' dozen form and reform, one blue-haired boy among them like a blade in a drawer of knives. He saw the gloaters point at two late starters and be ignored by them. He saw the back-markers crack one by one, and among them — *there* — the small gray figure from the road, the fish-saint, the mended boy, running at the very tail on a woodshed body that was giving everything it had and then one more thing—

—and he saw, on the far side of the square, in the unwatched first minutes, a big boy stroll two laps like a gentleman viewing property before joining the grind. The courier's feet counted it and filed it, and his mouth said nothing, and his silence was not cowardice but craft: a hall that checks a room's knots before judging them has no need of his testimony. *She'll know,* he thought, with a craftsman's certainty about another craftsman. *She strikes me as the type who counts.*

*Sixty,* said his feet. The sun climbed. The light in him banked itself, patient, the way his mother's hearth banked coals for the loaves not yet kneaded.

---

### ╱╱ THE TERMS ╲╲

They ran, the two of them, a quarter-hour behind a hundred grudge-bearing colleagues and gaining on none of them, and somewhere in lap twenty the silence broke.

"That day." Wang Dong, at shoulder, not looking at him. "What was it? What beat me? I've been through it two hundred times."

"Spirit attribute," Yuhao said, between breaths.

Wang Dong nearly tripped over the information. "*Really?* Then the ring I couldn't read — hm. Then I didn't lose to a *trick.* I lost to a soul that sees." He brightened, in his own peculiar way, like a man whose defeat had been promoted to a mystery. "You realize you're still hopeless. That candle of soul power you're carrying — I can feel it from here. If I'd used my martial soul, you'd have had no chance at all."

"Then it's fortunate," said Huo Yuhao, with great evenness, "that you were too proud to use it."

"*Fortunate*—" The blue eyes narrowed; the legs, offended, accelerated. Then, oddly, eased. "...You covered for me. Just now. In there. 'Roommates, small conflict.' You didn't have to." A pause of three laps' length. "I'll allow it. From today I'll cover you. Anyone troubles you, they answer to me. I'm the strongest in this year's intake. Nearly."

"I don't need covering."

"You *do.*"

"I need a roommate," said the boy from the woodshed, who had never had one, and had thought about it, "who treats me as an equal. Everything else is decoration."

Wang Dong ran a full lap on that, jaw working. "In my whole life," he said at last, honestly, amazed at himself, "I've never met anyone my age I could see that way."

"Then you've been running in a small yard," said Huo Yuhao, and — because the woodshed had taught him exactly one form of luxury — put on speed, and left a genius staring at his dust.

"Not even half a sentence is worth saying!" Wang Dong announced to the sky, offended to his roots, and then, being who he was, *blazed* past the entire complaining hundred — a quarter-hour's deficit erased in half an hour of legs like whips — and finished first of all one hundred, barely breathing, so angry that he was almost happy, which is the exact temperature at which friendships set.

### ╱╱ THE MILE-TALK ╲╲ *(the gauntlet's middle — the brothers, in step)*

Somewhere around lap forty, when the iron had stopped being weight and become weather, the courier drifted back through the pack — deliberately, past his own comfortable pace, to where the gray boy ran at the tail with his jaw set and his world reduced to the next step.

They ran in silence for a lap. That was the whole point of the arriving.

"Scale of one to ten," Jiang Che said, at conversation volume, which was its own cruelty.

"Seven. You?"

"Six. But I cheated — I run roads for a living and someone stuffed me full of light."

"*You* stuffed *you* full of light. That's the — that's the sunflower thing. You photosynthesize. You're a *plant,* Hao, you're literally a plant with a hammer."

"I'm a plant who can't feel his legs. We're even."

Another lap. The iron shirts clinked their idiot music.

"He's still going," Yuhao said, not looking forward — but forward was all the prince at the head of the field, untouchable and unbearable. "He hasn't slowed once."

"He's rank twenty-three and his family bought him a cradle made of thousand-year ingredients. Slowing would be a *scandal.*" A beat. "Don't measure yourself against his front. Measure against your own yesterday."

"That's a fortune cookie."

"It's courier arithmetic. Same shape, more walking."

And Huo Yuhao — rank seventeen, tail of the field, iron on his shoulders and a woodshed on his back — laughed, in the middle of the hardest morning of his life, and found the laugh was worth two laps of energy, which was a trade neither of them had expected and both of them would spend a year making.

---

### ╱╱ THE WINGS ╲╲

With a quarter hour left, the field had become arithmetic: ninety-some finished, seven desperate, and at the very tail one boy thirteen laps short of an impossible sum — and Huo Yuhao, at the end of everything, did the thing that made even this field's cold go quiet.

He hurt *himself.* Soul Shock, turned inward — a needle into his own mind, white pain as a whip for flagging flesh — and the small gray figure *sped up*, and passed two bodies, and the field's roar of disbelief began in a dozen throats at once.

And then the square went beautiful.

Out of the crowd, catching the tail-runner, a boy's back *opened* — and wings stood up against the morning: butterfly wings, vast, impossible, blue on blue on blue, deep and shallow and luminous as weather, a V of light across each like dawn striking a wave. Not cloth, not feather — *light wearing a shape* — and a thousand of the continent's proudest children cried out at once, without a syllable of shame, because the sight reached past rank and sense and took the eye directly, the way sunrise does.

Wang Dong did not pause to be admired. His arms went under Yuhao's shoulders from behind — "*You* — run *lighter*, you ox—" — the wings struck down once, and the two of them left the ground, and the millwheel of the field watched two boys *fly* the last laps, the impossible sum paying itself out in wingbeats while a broken gong somewhere said nothing at all.

At Zhou Yi's back, so low only the field's nearest runners caught it: "The Goddess of Light Butterfly. The most beautiful butterfly soul on the continent." A pause; and the whetstone added, to no one, with something that in another face would have been warmth: "*Good.* Not all disappointments, then."

They came down at the line together, staggered, caught, collapsed — one atop the other exactly as etiquette demanded — and the field heard the tail-end of it as they untangled, breathless, salt-soaked:

"Thanks. Last time I pressed you down. Now you've pressed me back."

"You *smell*," said Wang Dong, with his whole heart.

And two thumbs rose, and met, and the last of the grudge between them went wherever old enmities go when both parties have proven too stubborn to hate — which is to say: into the beginning of the thing it would become.

---

### ╱╱ THE ROLL ╲╲

When the last runner crossed and the hour closed, ninety-one students stood in the square's morning sun, sick, triumphant, changed.

Zhou Yi stood where she had stood all hour, dry as paper, and read nine names from no list at all.

"Cheng Cheng. Qiu Jianrao. Tang Dao. Shangguan Chentian. Lin Zeyu. Zhuge Yun. Tai Long. Tang Ling. Yun Xiaopiao."

Nine faces came out of the ranks, stunned — and the big boy, Tai Long, earliest finisher of the front-runners, angry enough to be brave: "Teacher, *why?*"

"Shrek does not keep students who cheat at running or at anything else," said Zhou Yi, in the voice of a verdict that had happened before and would happen again. "Strength without an upright heart is a disaster wearing a uniform — for any nation that buys it. Strength *with* one is what this academy sells. Tai Long. You walked your first two laps while my eyes were elsewhere." The square went very cold. "You ran ninety-seven, not one hundred. Pack your things."

"You weren't even *here*—"

"I am always where your conduct is," said Zhou Yi, and it was not a figure of speech; it was a *creed*, and a hundred children learned it in one sentence, and nine children packed.

In the ranks, a courier who had counted the same two laps at minute three kept his face like a ledger and closed the page. *The type who counts,* he thought. *A whetstone with eyes.*

Beside him, unnoticed by everyone, a small weight in a pocket turned a slow circle — the fox's equivalent of removing her hat — and said nothing, which from an empress was a standing ovation.

---

### ╱╱ THE LECTURE ╲╲

Fifteen minutes to change clothes — ninety-one students did it in ten, terror being the finest of perfumes — and Class One sat again beneath the nine empty seats' silence.

"Hu Yuhao. Stand. Your soul power."

"...Eleven, teacher."

The class's disbelief was a weather system; Wang Dong covered his eyes outright — *eleven?* — and then did arithmetic backwards and arrived at *how was he even ADMITTED?*, which was precisely the question Zhou Yi answered, once, finally, on the first morning so that it would never be asked again: **a special invitation of the academy, exempt from the entrance examination — and from nothing else.** "Anyone who questions him on it again answers to me." It was, though no one in the room had the experience to notice, protection — the whetstone's other face, sharpening the small gray swordsman against the class's contempt before it could dull him.

Then she taught. Two characters on the board: **Attack. Defense.** Wang Dong, invited, gave the textbook answer — assault, agility and control attack; support, food, defense defend — and was told, before the whole class, that he had answered like a fool: correct four thousand years ago, wrong on the day the Sun-Moon continent arrived. **The soul tool has blurred the line** — a food-system tool master with a strong enough weapon strikes like an assault soul master; an agility fighter with a fortress shield *becomes* a wall. The age chases soul power and lets the rings rust, and "past rank fifty, they are all garbage," because a man whose body is weak dies first no matter what he carries — the enemy picks the soft one, always — and a man whose body is a weapon *plus* the age's tools is the only thing the word *strong* actually means. "Your bodies," she told ninety-one of the continent's proudest children, "are the syllabus. Three months. Fail me and follow the nine."

And the class — brilliant, furious, alive — took notes.

---

### ╱╱ THE OFFICE ╲╲

"Hu Yuhao. My office." — which every other teacher in the world says as a threat and Zhou Yi said as an appointment.

Behind a closed door she asked him, straight, blunt, strong: his martial soul. He gave it — *Spirit Eyes; spirit attribute; a body soul* — and watched sixty-some years of a Soul Emperor's composure crack, once, into something young. "...Show me the skill."

The white ring rose; the gold filmed his eyes; and he did for the teacher what he had done for the sect on a forest road — the *world, shared*: distances, densities, the drift of dust, her own office rendered into her mind as order itself.

For a full minute the monster teacher of Class One stood inside an eleven-year-old's soul, and the quiet that followed was not the classroom's quiet.

"*That* skill," Zhou Yi said finally, "is worth a war." And then, more quietly, mostly to herself, the answer to a question a fortnight old: "No wonder the Tang Sect chose you. The girl's smarter than her cooking." She stood. "Come with me. Now."

---

### ╱╱ THE CARRY ╲╲

What happened next, Hu Yuhao would tell his sect brothers that evening in a dormitory room with the awe still leaking out of him: the monster teacher *took him by the shoulder* — and the academy went away.

West, then north; the white halls, the green squares, the lake's rim all pouring past like water off a lock-gate, a Soul Emperor's speed wearing a courier's economy, the world blurred and barrier-calm around a boy too busy being carried to be frightened — until the movement stopped, and before them stood a building the size of a small mountain's opinion of itself: long, gray, half metal, humming. The ground buzzed faintly underfoot. A sign: **SOUL TOOL TESTING GROUND.**

Inside: all metal, a dark bronze he had no name for; a corridor of enormous doors; a hexagonal silver token pressed to a slot; a door — two *feet* thick — grinding sideways on rails. Beyond it, caverns divided by metal walls, and at the heart of the greatest of them, a two-thousand-square-meter field where men and women shaped the age into being, and the air tasted of ozone and purpose.

"**Fan Yu!**" Zhou Yi's broken gong, delighted.

Out of the ozone came a mountain in simple cloth — a head and shoulders over one-point-eight meters of granite calm, bare arms like ship's cable, a face of settled stone — who looked at the intrusion the way cliffs look at weather. "Zhou Yi. What now."

"You remember what you said to me last time?" — and it was said with the enthusiasm of a woman about to win an argument that had been running for years —

— and this is where the evening's telling always stopped, in room 108, because the rest belonged to the next day, and the age, and a gray building whose doors knew a teacher's token; and three boys sat in the lamplight of the only triple room in the white hall, and the smallest of them said, quietly, to no one: "*soul tools,*" as a man says the name of a country he has just learned he will one day live in.

---

### ╱╱ THE CODA ╲╲

Evening, after the telling: the work-board's forge shift, an hour's walk from soul-tool thunder and exactly its opposite — coke, iron, patience. The Jade Hand's first true test had come there again as it came every night now: *conduction*, not armor — the heat crossing tempered palms and going through, the art of letting the whole of a thing move through you. His hands were a map of small earned burns. The old Journeyman at the last furnace had said it again, exactly as before, because smiths are precise men:

"Come back tomorrow. Bring your own hammer."

He had brought his own hammer. It sat on the desk of room 108 beside a page titled **the Jade Hand**, in a corner room with three beds and two roommates already breathing — one aristocratic and fur-swaddled, one somewhere deep in a white-ringed meditation — and in the pocket of a coat on the third nail, an empress who had listened all evening to a tale of gray buildings and thundering doors permitted herself one footnote:

"*Little tide. The age you mean to upgrade is bigger than the one you were told about.*"

"Good," said the Tang Sect's third disciple, already half asleep, honest to the last. "More to work with."

Across the academy the whetstone's window was dark at last, and the testing ground's hum went on all night, and between the two sounds a city of monsters slept on its futures.

### ╱╱ THE TEST ZONE ╲╲

The mountain in cloth looked at the small gray boy the way a cliff looks at rain.

"Spirit martial soul?" Fan Yu said. His voice was granite with a hollow in it. "Can't use it. His body's too weak, his soul power's too thin. He couldn't lift the lightest fixed-load cannon we build. And his talent —" a pause, not cruel, just honest as stone — "ordinary."

"Ordinary," said Zhou Yi, in the tone of a woman about to move a mountain, "*this*," and turned to her special invite. "Show him."

Hu Yuhao's white ring rose. The gold filmed his eyes. And the world's most practical eleven-year-old did the only thing he knew how to do — he *shared*.

Fan Yu's frown lasted a quarter second. His perception — and this was the part that nearly broke Yuhao's nerve — *pushed back*. Something vast and old and shaped like a hunger stirred behind the man's calm and opened one eye at the boy's probing mind. Inside Yuhao's sea, something million-year-old and sleepy *woke* — a cool wash of ice, and the hunger's eye closed, and the sharing completed, and Fan Yu's whole face changed.

"*That* is a ten-year-ring skill."

"It mutated," said Zhou Yi smoothly.

"It would have to," Fan Yu breathed, staring at the white ring like it had lied to him personally. "A spirit martial soul absorbing a *wind* ring without dying is a miracle; getting *this* out of it is —" He caught himself. "**Cai Tou!**"

A mountain came running. Two meters of bald, black, cheerful muscle on legs, shirtless and gleaming, grinning at the small visitor with the uncomplicated warmth of a large dog. He Caitou — "*Cai Tou*, everyone does, you too, little brother, it's fine!*" — hoisted from his black belt-band a weapon that made Hu Yuhao's understanding of the word rearrange itself: a metal tube a meter and a half long, runes crawling its surface, a loading port in the stock. A **fixed-load soul cannon** — Fan Yu's own design, his decade of work: a weapon that fired its payload with minimal soul-power injection, freeing the user from the rank requirements of ordinary soul tools. The fee: the shells cost a small district's annual budget, and the accuracy at range was, in the current state of the art, *aspirational*.

"Little brother," said Cai Tou, shouldering the tube, his simple face going *focused* — and the weapon tracked a launched flying disc across two hundred meters of test-field, and fired, and the *sound* alone staggered Yuhao, and the blast went wide by four meters and detonated against the far wall like a small, furious sunset.

"Still can't hit," Cai Tou said, aggrieved.

"He can't hit," Fan Yu said, "*because* the targeting is the bottleneck." He looked at Yuhao with the eyes of a man seeing a road and not being able to walk it yet. "Thirty meters. That's your detection diameter? The cannon's effective range is four hundred. If you could see at a hundred — *one direction, just one*, a hundred meters of forewarning — you come to me, and I will teach you to build soul tools with my own hands."

He meant it. The whole gray building heard him mean it.

"Thank you, teacher," said Hu Yuhao, who had no idea what a soul tool was but had a woodshed-taught nose for a door opening, and bowed.

### ╱╱ THE FISH STALL ╲╲

Outside the canteen, a girl of fifteen pounced.

"Xiao Yuhao. You have no money."

"...Yes, Teacher."

"*Good.*" Tang Ya's scheming face was a masterpiece that should have been in a museum. She had, she explained — with the particular rapidity of someone who has been planning this since a stream — arranged everything: the canteen's purchasing auntie would bring twenty extra fish a day; a grill was ordered; charcoal, spices, and a spot at the academy gate secured. The Tang Sect's founding and complete membership, having thusly armed her second disciple with the most economically sound business model in the Academy's history, advanced to the fourth year that afternoon — she and Bei Bei both passing the promotion trials, the new purple ring earning its keep — and by evening the gate of Shrek Academy smelled like perilla and salt and futures, and a line of senior students who had no idea they were being fed by the rebirth of a dead sect's economy stood twenty deep for grilled fish.

The fish-saint cooked. His eyes measured the fire's grain. His hands turned each fish at its exact moment. And the canteen aunts, the porters, the first-year sweat-soaked and the fourth-year smug, discovered that the worth of a boy is not always in his rank.

## The Afternoon

The afternoon was Zhou Yi's body-training — the whetstone's first grind.

Ninety-one children of privilege learned what *training* meant to a woman who had put one in four of her students on the island in the lake. It meant the body. Only the body. Soul power forbidden — "your rings are crutches; today we break legs" — and then the exercises: stance holds, sprint intervals, body-weight circuits that a woodshed boy survived by woodshed math and a butterfly boy survived by sheer physical privilege and a courier boy survived by *being a courier boy who had been doing this since he was eight.*

Jiang Che did not stand out. That was the discipline of it — the AT-optimized body, the courier's endurance, the life-core's sunlit recovery all humming underneath, and his *choice* was to hold the same pace as the middle of the pack, breathe the same four-count, finish the same rep count as the boy beside him. Not because he couldn't do more. Because a courier who outpaces the caravan is a courier who gets left behind.

Zhou Yi noticed anyway. She noticed everything. She said nothing — whetstones note the metal — but her eyes came back to the third boy twice during the circuits, and the second time there was something in them that was not disapproval. Perhaps the thing a knife-sharpener feels when a blade comes through the shop that does not need sharpening yet.

Class dismissed. Wang Dong collapsed theatrically onto his fur. Yuhao went to the fish stall. And Jiang Che — his forge shift waited.

### ╱╱ THE THREE-BED RHYTHM ╲╲ *(the days settle — the room finds its shape)*

The week that followed found room 108's rhythm, and the rhythm had three beats and a fox.

Mornings: three alarms, or rather one alarm and two victims of it. Yuhao woke at dawn because five years of woodshed discipline didn't know how not to; Wang Dong woke at noon because princes did; and the courier woke when the fox sat on his chest, which was six-forty in the morning, every day, because empires do not recognize weekends.

"*Up,*" she said, every day. "*The continent does not smith itself.*"

"It's Saturday."

"*It is Tuesday. It is always Tuesday. Up.*"

Evenings: the triangle. The forge-shift's return (smelling, always, of a fireplace with opinions) was room 108's unofficial dinner bell — Wang Dong's term, adopted by acclamation, vetoed by its subject, adopted again — and the three boys ate together at the desk or the floor or once, memorably, standing at the window watching the lake mist because Wang Dong refused to sit until his hair "settled" and Yuhao refused to miss the spectacle and Jiang Che refused to eat without them.

And between morning and evening, the craft grew on-page: the Jade Hand entering its second month, the burn-threshold now past working-iron and into *quenching* — the night he pulled a blade-blank from the oil-bath bare-handed and Old Qian, watching from two stations away, put down his own tongs and stared at his own hands and then at the boy's and then said nothing for the rest of the shift — and the first crude sleeve-dart track took four failures and a fifth that held, and the courier did not show it to anyone except the fox, who pronounced it "bad work by a smith who will do work that makes this look like a mud-pie," which from her was a *commendation.*

---

### ╱╱ THE ROOM ╲╲

Room 108, mid-afternoon, between the morning's laps and whatever the afternoon held. A three-bed corner room: the fur territory empty and immaculate, the plank territory occupied by a boy in meditation, and the third nail holding a coat in which something small and opinionated was pretending to be asleep.

The door opened — Wang Dong, back from an errand he hadn't explained, sitting on his fur mattress and staring at Yuhao with the particular intensity of a boy who has been *thinking*.

"Your martial soul. I've shown you mine. Fair's fair."

And so, in the ordinary way of roommates becoming friends, two boys who would one day matter to each other more than either had words for traded their truths on a ten-meter room. *Spirit Eyes. The eyes are the soul. The white ring is the baboon's.* (Wang Dong's face performed the arithmetic of *how* and could not close it.) *The detection reads what's coming before it comes. That's how the dorm fight went.*

And Wang Dong, in the trust that is only possible between people who have bled and not killed each other, gave back: *the Goddess of Light Butterfly. The most beautiful butterfly soul on the continent, nearly extinct. My second ring is thousand-year.* (And when Yuhao asked *how*, Wang Dong smiled a smile that had a whole locked house behind it, and said, "My secret.")

Then: "Show me the detection."

Yuhao shared. And Wang Dong — who had flown under his own wings since age six, who had never in his life met anything he couldn't outpace — stood inside another person's *world* for the first time, and the left and right and behind of everything stood up in his mind at once, and the blue eyes went wide and stayed wide, and something in the handsome, furious, arrogant boy rearranged itself very quietly around the fact that this boy whose soul power was a candle in a shed carried a *cathedral* behind his eyes.

"Again," Wang Dong said, hoarse. "Try pointing it. One direction. *Push*."

And Yuhao — because the mountain in the test zone had said *one hundred meters* — tried. He narrowed the sphere to a spear. He *pushed*. The golden light deepened, the forward arc extended, thirty-one meters, thirty-two — and his soul power left him like water from a kicked bucket, and the world tilted, and Wang Dong caught him before the floor did.

"*Hey—*"

"'M fine." He wasn't. He was shaking. But the number in his head was thirty-two, and yesterday it had been thirty.

From the third bed, the sound of someone else breathing. Jiang Che had come in from the evening forge shift — coke in his hair, a fresh burn on his left thumb, the Jade Hand's warmth still fading from his palms — and had heard the tail end of the martial-soul exchange. He had not been there for the beginning because he had been at the forge. That was the trade: class in the day, fire at night, the room in between.

He caught Yuhao's eye. "Thirty-two?" he said — because the number had escaped during the experiment, and a courier remembers numbers.

"...Thirty-two," Yuhao admitted.

"Yesterday?"

"Thirty-one."

The courier nodded. One meter a day. He didn't say *good* or *fast* or anything that would have been a flattery. He just nodded, the way a man nods at honest work, and sat down on his bed, and the room held three boys and one number and the silence of people who understood each other slightly better than they had that morning.

But in the dark of his coat on the third nail, a fox who had also heard everything said, very low, to her human alone: "*The small one carries an ocean in a teacup. And the proud one has a locked room behind his smile. Your room, little tide, is already the most interesting on this hall.*"

---

### ╱╱ THE FORGE ╲╲

The gray buildings stood west of the white halls, and between them ran the road Jiang Che now walked every **evening** after class — forge shift at dusk, the work-board's honest coin, the Jade Hand's nightly conduction — and every evening the same intersection: the **soul tool testing ground** to his right, humming; the **smithy yard** to his left, roaring; and between them a boy carrying a hammer, walking the seam of the age in the hour between school and sleep.

He had begun, this week, to notice things.

The smithy's Journeymen used *tools*. Not soul tools — honest tools, hammers and tongs and quirks — but the metal they worked was not always honest: ingots came in from the testing ground's offcuts, alloyed with minerals his father's forge had never named, and when the old Journeyman at the last furnace quenched a blade in oil, the oil *sang* at a pitch the Jade Hand's conduction could feel — a soul-resonance in the quench-still, a note that said *this metal has been near soul power and remembers it.*

The two buildings were not neighbors. They were *partners* — the smithy shaping what the testing ground dreamed, the testing ground breaking what the smithy made so the smithy could learn. And nobody, as far as the courier could see, had ever put a boy in the middle with a hammer and asked what fell out.

He asked the Journeyman, once, at the coke break, what the alloyed ingots were. "Soul-conductive metals," the old man said, with the shrug of a man who shapes what he does not own. "Sun-Moon minerals. They carry soul power the way copper carries lightning. The test yard builds their weapons out of them; we get the offcuts; we make tools out of them. Nothing special. It is just metal that remembers." Another shrug. "Go fetch the next batch."

And that was all. No revelation. No question nobody had asked. Just a boy carrying ingots between two buildings, learning what they were made of, because a courier's son knows that knowing what things are made of is half the trade. The Journeyman did not look at him with amazement. The Journeyman looked at him the way Journeymen look at boys who carry things and do not complain: with the grudging tolerance of a man whose morning is slightly less annoying than usual.

"Go back to work," he said, gruffly. But he showed Jiang Che, that morning, how to hold the alloyed ingot so the grain ran true — a thing he had never shown any student before, because no student had ever made him want to.

"Jiang Che." The old Journeyman, at the end of shift, not looking up from his tempering. "Your hands. Turn them over."

He turned them. The small burns from the first three nights had already faded to nothing — the Sun Flower's gift, closing what the fire opened — and the palms' skin had begun to take on a faint, deep jade undertone in the lines, where the conduction art was writing itself into the body the way rain writes itself into stone.

"How long you been doing the Jade Hand?"

"Six nights."

The old man grunted. Six nights was nothing. Six nights was a boy holding a warm stone and being patient. And yet. And *yet.* He had seen sect disciples come through this yard before, in his forty years of it — sent by teachers who thought manual labor was character-building — and not one of them had ever had the skin change color in the first week, because not one of them had ever practiced the tempering art *every single night* with the patience of someone who understood that the least art was the one that needed the most work.

"You're going to be here a while, aren't you," the Journeyman said. Not a question.

"Years," said Jiang Che, with the forest's patience, and picked up the next ingot.

---

### ╱╱ THE FIRST NIGHT ╲╲

That evening, room 108's three lamps (two soul-tool, one stolen candle) burned past what was sensible.

Yuhao sat cross-legged on his boards, meditating, recovering, his mind's forward arc measuring itself in single meters against a mountain's four hundred. On his way back from the canteen he had bought — with fish-stall money, first earnings, face carefully blank — a single egg and a bowl of rice, and eaten it sitting on the floor because chairs were furniture and furniture was for people who had arrived, and he had not yet arrived, he was still *arriving*.

Wang Dong lay on his furs, hands behind his head, staring at the ceiling with the expression of a boy doing arithmetic he refuses to show his work on. *A hundred meters. If the small one can push that arc to a hundred meters, the mountain in the test zone teaches him to build weapons. What does a butterfly need with a builder?* He didn't know. He only knew the locked room behind his own smile had just acquired a window, and the view was strange.

Later — after the forge, after the room, after the day — at the third desk, under a candle stub that was itself a luxury bought with forge wages, Jiang Che read the Treasure Record — the Jade Hand pages, as he did every night, one paragraph at a time, the way his mother taught him to read anything: slowly, and twice. The Jade Hand was not dramatic. It was a method: how to temper the hands, how to conduct heat, how to be patient when the stone is warm and nothing is happening and nothing is going to happen for months. Six nights of it. His palms itched. That was all. That was honestly all.

The fox, on his shoulder, was asleep, or pretending, which from her was the same courtesy.

He closed the book. He set the hammer on the desk. He went to bed.

And in the other two beds, two boys slept or meditated or stared at ceilings, and the third one went to sleep too.

# Chapter 8-B: The First Rank

## The blacksmith-craft chapter that was missing — the three months' forge arc shown on-page the way canon shows craft: the rank system, the test, the Jade Hand's mechanics, the first creation

### THE HUNDRED REFINEMENTS

The forge yard's master was named Old Qian, and he had no time for prodigies.

"Rank system," he said, the first morning, not looking up from his tempering. "You know it?"

"Some. My father is a smith."

"Your father binds things." Old Qian had read the work-board slate. "Binding is a different trade from forging. Forging is this: **ranks one through three — hundred refinements.** Take a billet of standard iron, fold and hammer it one hundred times without a single flaw, you test for first rank. Four through six — thousand refinements, and the metal starts to *answer* you. Seven through nine — you're not hammering anymore; you're *asking*. Saint Craftsmen. Divine Craftsmen." He spat into the coals. "You start at nothing. Fetch billets."

Jiang Che fetched billets.

The first week was exactly that: fetching, sorting, watching. The forge yard ran on apprentice labor — boys his age and older, carrying, quenching, sweeping ash — and the work-board's forge shift slotted him among them at one copper an hour. He did not complain. His father had started the same way, and his father's father before him.

But he was not watching nothing. The AT was watching *everything* — every strike Old Qian's journeymen landed, every angle of hammer to billet, every color-shift in the metal as it moved from cherry to orange to the near-white that meant *now or never*. By the third day he could predict the strike count between heats. By the fifth he could read the metal's grain from the way it received the hammer — where it was willing, where it resisted, where a fold would take and where it would crack.

The fox, riding the coat on a nail, supervised with the air of an empress inspecting a kitchen. "*Your hands are wrong,*" she observed on day four. "*You hold the tongs like a courier holds a parcel. A smith holds them like a swordsman holds a sword — the grip is the whole art.*"

She was right. He adjusted. The AT recorded the adjustment and rebuilt his grip overnight.

---

### THE JADE HAND

The Treasure Record's pages on the Jade Hand had seemed, for the first week of reading, like philosophy dressed as instruction. *Temper the flesh; conduct the force; let the whole of it move through you.* It took the forge itself to make the words mean something.

**The mechanics, as the forge taught them:**

The Jade Hand was not armor. It was *conduction* — a way of channeling soul power through the skin and bone of the hands so that force passed *through* rather than *into*. Where an ordinary smith's palm took the hammer's shock and accumulated damage — bruising, blistering, the slow calcification of a career — the Jade Hand's practitioner received the shock and passed it through the flesh into the bones and out through the feet into the ground. The hands did not harden against the work. They became *transparent to it*.

**Stage one — the conditioning (weeks one through four):**

Every night, after the shift, Jiang Che sat cross-legged on his bed with a bowl of heated water and practiced the Record's first exercise: circulating soul power through his palms in the specific pattern the text called *the riverbed* — a slow, deliberate flow that traced the meridians of the hand from the wrist across the palm and out through the fingertips, warming the tissue from within. The effect was subtle and cumulative: the skin thickened without callusing; the small bones of the hand densified; the nerves learned to report heat as *information* rather than *pain*.

By week two he could hold a billet fresh from the fire for three seconds before the burn registered. By week three, five. By week four, he picked up a bar at working temperature — hot enough to raise blisters on ordinary skin — and held it while the AT read the heat's path through his palm, and the burn never came. The heat entered, and the conduction passed it through, and the fox said, from the pillow: "*The Record's author knew what he was writing about. That is not a technique. That is an education.*"

**Stage two — the strike conduction (weeks four through eight):**

The second exercise required a hammer and a billet — and the forge provided both. The Record's instruction was precise: *when the hammer falls, do not resist the shock. Receive it. Pass it through the wrist, the elbow, the shoulder, the spine, and into the ground through the heels. The smith who resists the hammer fights the metal. The smith who conducts the hammer* becomes *the hammer.*

The first attempt nearly broke his wrist. The second was worse. The problem was not strength but *timing* — the conduction had to activate at the exact instant of impact, a window of perhaps a tenth of a second, and the AT was learning to find it the way it learned everything: by repetition, by failure, by the slow accumulation of micro-adjustments that eventually crossed the threshold from effort to reflex.

By week six he was conducting eighty percent of the hammer's shock through his body and into the ground. By week eight, ninety-five. And the effect on his forging was immediate and dramatic: where an ordinary smith's arms tired and their strikes degraded over a long session, his strikes were as precise at the hundredth as at the first — because the shock was not accumulating in his body. He was, as the Record promised, *transparent to the work*.

Old Qian noticed. Old Qian did not say anything for two more weeks, because Old Qian had been burned by prodigies before. But he noticed.

---

### THE TEST

At the end of month two, the work-board posted a notice: **rank testing, month's end, Association branch, Shrek City office. First-rank candidates: bring your own billet and your own hammer. Fee: two silver.**

Jiang Che had been ready for a week. He told no one except the fox and the sect — and the sect, being five people, told him to stop being ridiculous and take the sect's best wishes, which arrived in the form of Tang Ya packing him a fish for the road and Bei Bei's quiet "the forge knows its own."

The test itself was simple and merciless.

The Association's branch office in Shrek City occupied a stone building near the east gate — the same street as the fish stall, which had made the walk feel like a parade. Inside: a testing hall with six forges, three examiners, and a waiting bench of candidates ranging from a nervous fourteen-year-old girl to a thick-armed twenty-year-old on his third attempt.

The procedure: each candidate received a standard billet of iron — the same weight, the same grade, the same grain. The task: **one hundred refinements.** Fold and hammer, fold and hammer, until the billet had been worked one hundred times, and the metal's impurities drawn out, and the grain aligned, and the result judged on three criteria — *purity* (how much impurity had been expelled), *density* (how tightly the grain had been compacted), and *consistency* (how uniform the hundred strikes had been).

Jiang Che drew billet number eleven. The examiner — a third-rank smith with gray in his beard and the permanent squint of a man who had looked at hot metal for forty years — watched him set up with the detached assessment of someone who had seen four hundred boys do exactly this.

He did not watch detached for long.

The first strike was a test — not of the metal but of the boy's own calibration. The hammer fell; the AT read the billet's grain from the feedback alone; the second strike adjusted by a hair's width. By strike ten the rhythm was established: heat, fold, strike, turn, strike, fold again. By strike thirty the billet was no longer a billet but a *column of intention* — the impurities rising to the surface as a dark scale that flaked away under each hammer-fall, the grain compacting into something that rang differently every ten strikes, a rising note, the metal's own voice climbing as it purified.

The Jade Hand conducted the shocks into the ground. The AT found the optimal fold-angle for each successive lamination. The fox — who had insisted on attending, riding the coat, because "empresses attend coronations" — watched the metal's color-shifts with the professional interest of a creature who had seen ore born in the earth.

At strike seventy-three the examiner left his bench and came to stand at the forge's shoulder. At strike ninety he called another examiner over. At strike one hundred the hammer fell, and the billet — now a compact ingot the size of a man's fist, gray-silver, dense as sin — rang a note that hung in the hall like a small bell.

The two examiners and the third-rank smith looked at the ingot. Then at the boy. Then at the ingot.

"Purity," said the gray-beard, at last, in the voice of a man revising his afternoon's opinion of the human race, "ninety-six percent. Density — high. Consistency —" he paused, because this was the part that did not happen, the part that separated masters from apprentices, "— I could not find a single strike's deviation across the hundred. What in the eight hells are you, boy?"

" Courier's son," said Jiang Che. "My father binds things."

"Your father," said the examiner, writing the rank badge out by hand, "*forges* things, and he taught you better than he knows. **First rank.** Score: superior. Come back for second when your hands tell you they're ready — not before." And then, half to himself, as the boy left: "Ninety-six at first rank. Mu Chen is going to want to see this."

---

### THE FIRST CREATION

The first-rank badge was a small iron disc stamped with the Association's mark — a hammer crossed over a flame — and it weighed almost nothing, and Jiang Che wore it under his shirt for a week before he mentioned it to anyone, because a courier does not announce his own deliveries.

But the badge was not the creation. The creation happened the night after the test, in the academy's forge yard, after hours, with Old Qian's grudging permission and the fox supervising from the anvil's horn.

**The item: a hidden-weapon frame.**

Not a weapon — not yet. A *frame*: the skeleton of a sleeve-dart mechanism, the kind the Treasure Record described in its chapter on *A Hundred Hidden Weapons, Explained* — the chapter Tang Ya had said was "for later, when your hands are worth it." His hands were worth it now, rank-badge or no rank-badge, and the first project was the simplest and most fundamental: the **track** — the channel down which a dart travels when released from a wrist-mounted launcher.

The work was precision-forging at a scale the billet-test had not approached: channels a finger's width wide, walls as thin as a coin, the whole piece no larger than a man's palm. It took four failed attempts — four pieces of iron that cracked under the hammer's precision-demand, because the tolerances were finer than a first-rank smith's ordinary work and the AT was learning a new scale the way it learned everything.

The fifth attempt held. The track was rough — a first-rank piece, no more, the walls uneven in ways a master would see at a glance — but it was a *track*: a channel that would guide a dart from wrist to target, the skeleton of the Tang Sect's most basic tool, forged by the sect's third disciple in an empty forge yard at midnight.

He showed it to no one but the fox.

"*Show it to your Sect Master,*" the fox said, nose to the metal, reading it as she read everything. "*It is bad work. It is also the first bad work of a smith who will one day do work that makes this piece look like a child's mud-pie — and she will want to have kept it.*"

He showed it to Tang Ya the next morning. The Sect Master turned the rough iron track over in her hands three times, and her eyes were bright, and she said, with enormous dignity, "The sect's treasury is now two fishing rods and an iron track," and put it in her sleeve, and was seen touching her sleeve at odd moments for the rest of the day.

---

### THE ARTS

The Treasure Record held five arts before the hidden weapons chapter, and in the first three months Jiang Che began — as Tang Ya had instructed — with the least. But "least" did not mean "only," and the forge's labor made the others practical in ways they had not been before.

**The Jade Hand — the foundation.** The conditioning and conduction described above, reaching stage two by month's end. The visible signs: the palm-lines gone faintly jade-pale; the hands immune to working-temperature iron; the hammer-shock conducted to ground.

**The Mysterious Heaven Skill — the engine.** His soul power had converted in the first week — the AT performing in three days what took Yuhao a week of diligent practice — and the result was a soul power that was *springier*, denser, running the wider meridians like a river in its banks rather than a stream in a ditch. Every other art drew on this engine, and the engine was compounding daily.

**The Crane-Captures-Dragon — the grip.** The seizing-and-locking art was the natural partner of the vine-work: a set of joint-locks, pressure-point seizures, and redirections that turned an opponent's force into their own capture. He practiced on the forge's iron bars — not the locks themselves, but the *hand positions*, the angles, the timing — until the AT had the geometry filed, and then on Wang Dong, once, in the training yard, with the prince's outraged "that's a *grappling* art, you can't just *apply* it to — *okay, yes, I see, that's effective*, let go of my wrist."

**The Ghost-Shadow Track — the footwork.** Begun but not mastered: the art of the weightless step, the movement that left no trace. His courier's training gave him a foundation no aristocrat had — ten thousand li of road discipline — but the Track required the opposite of endurance: *absence*. Weight, sound, intention — all negated. The AT was building it slowly. The fox said it would take a year, and the fox was honest about the arts because she had no stake in flattering them.

**The Purple Demon Eyes — NOT BEGUN.** The eye-cultivation art was Yuhao's, assigned by Tang Ya to Yuhao's eyes and Yuhao's alone — because the art demanded a spirit-attribute soul or decades of dawn-gazing, and Jiang Che's eyes were hawk-eyes, not Spirit Eyes. The Treasure Record's chapter sat unread for him — a door that was not his door, and the knowing of which was its own kind of discipline.
