### ╱╱ THE FIRST HOUR ╲╲

The first hour sorted the class the way a forge sorts metal.

Wang Dong ran at the front and *stayed* there — the butterfly's body, the thousand-year second ring, the sheer physical privilege of someone whose foundation was laid in a cradle of resources. Behind him, a dozen proud boys who thought they were Wang Dong's rivals discovered, by lap ten, that they were Wang Dong's scenery. The pack settled. The iron began to speak.

And Jiang Che ran at the front — ordered to, by someone who had read his file — and carried his thirty jin the way a river carries a stone: visibly, undeniably, without apology.

But this was not a morning's walk, and the AT — always working — had never worked on *this* before. Thirty jin of iron on an eleven-year-old's shoulders, hour after hour, was not distance to be administered. It was *load* — sustained, grinding, compound load that the courier's road had never imposed this way. The AT received the information and began its quiet response: bone density adjusting, muscle-fiber recruitment shifting, the oxygen economy recalculating for a body that was now nine kilos heavier and getting no lighter.

He did not sprint. He did not fall behind. He ran the four-count, breathed the Hall's rhythm, and let the AT do what the AT does — adapt to the new weight the way water adapts to a stone: by becoming, incrementally and permanently, a river that carries stones.

In his coat pocket — because she had refused to be left behind, and the coat had been permitted on the grounds that a fox weighs nothing worth mentioning — Xiao Jiu rode the iron age with the compressed dignity of an empress on a mule.

At lap twenty, Wang Dong pulled level with the courier and held it for four laps, testing. The courier ran a four-count. The butterfly ran a two-count — spending more, running harder, *needing* to. By lap twenty-four the gap was one step. By lap twenty-six it was two. The blue eyes narrowed. *He's not even trying.* — the blue eyes checking the middle of the pack the way aristocrats check the help, except that this particular aristocrat had spent a night pinned under a gray boy's will, and the checking was no longer entirely contempt. The courier was sweating — *sweating*, not dying — and his breathing ran a four-count that the butterfly boy's body recognized, on some level deeper than thought, as the breathing of someone who *knew what they were doing with weight*.

At lap thirty, Yuhao, at the very back, falling steadily behind the entire field, matched the courier's stride for exactly four steps before his legs reminded him that he was rank eleven and had no business matching anyone's stride, and fell back to his metronome.

Between laps thirty and forty, Jiang Che passed the first fallen student — the slight girl, sitting on the flagstones with her iron shirt pooled around her, eyes somewhere beyond exhaustion — and slowed by half a step. Not stopping (the rules were the rules). But the half-step was seen by the girl, and by Zhou Yi, and it filed itself in the morning's ledger: *the courier slows for the fallen.*

---

### ╱╱ THE BREAKING ╲╲

The iron did not break them all at once. It broke them the way real things break real people: one at a time, privately, in the specific place each body kept its excuse.

A slight girl went first — crumpled gently, like a flower closing for the night. Wang Dong, passing, caught her arm and held her up with a question in his eyes. She shook her head and sat down and did not get up again. She couldn't speak. She was eleven and she had nothing left.

Then the dominoes: two more, three more, a chain reaction of exhausted pride. Thirty minutes in, the front-runners — those who had spent everything matching Wang Dong — began to pay their debts. The iron-shirt's weight, which speed had hidden, now fell on them with compound interest.

Jiang Che watched the front-runners fall with a courier's professional eye. *They spent early. They spent everything on the first hour. The iron doesn't care about speed. It cares about time.* He adjusted his pace by one breath, not one step. The middle of the pack was thinning around him — the ones who fell were the ones who had tried to be fast — and he found himself, without trying, climbing.

And at the very back, from the first step to this one, ran a gray-uniformed boy at a pace that was barely running at all — slow, steady, *metronomic* — who had been last since lap two and did not look like someone who was last. He looked like someone who was *working*. And the gap between what his body should be doing and what his body was doing was, to anyone who understood bodies, the most extraordinary thing on the square.

---

### ╱╱ THE DISCOVERY ╲╲

What happened inside Huo Yuhao at the one-hour mark belongs to him alone, and the world would not learn its full shape for years.

His body broke. Everything the woodshed had built and the road had toughened and the morning's laps had spent — all of it reached its wall, and the wall was absolute. His vision sparkled. His legs shook. The iron sat on his shoulders like a sentence. And inside, at the very bottom of exhaustion, something happened that had never happened in the history of the Tang Sect's arts:

The Xuantian Gong, which was supposed to be practiced sitting still, *moved on its own*.

It was a trickle. A thread of warmth from his core, circulating without his direction, nourishing the meridians it passed through — widening them, microscopically, the way a river widens its banks by flowing. He had always known the Gong nourished; that was its reputation. But it had never nourished *while the body was moving at its absolute limit*. That was not supposed to be possible. Even the ancestor Tang San — who brought the Gong from another world — had not done this, because the ancestor had never been weak enough to need it and never spirit-attuned enough to feel it.

Hu Yuhao was both. And at the intersection of his weakness and his spiritual depth, the Tang Sect's root art *evolved*.

He did not understand it yet. He would spend weeks understanding it — the way a man who has just discovered fire does not yet understand chemistry. He only understood that the warmth was keeping him upright, and the warmth came when he stopped fighting the exhaustion and started *listening* to it, and the listening was itself a kind of cultivation. He was running at a walking pace, and he was getting stronger.

The irony was architectural: every other student on the square was getting weaker — spending reserves, tearing muscle, burning through their soul power's cushioning — and the weakest boy among them was *compounding*. The Xuantian Gong's moving-circulation was turning the iron-shirt's punishment into meridian-nourishment, the body's absolute limit into a classroom, the mother of all exhausting afternoons into the single most productive cultivation session of his young life.

He did not know this. He knew only: *warm. Still standing. Mama.*

And around him, the square emptied. The iron did not discriminate.

Jiang Che, by the ninety-minute mark, was no longer comfortable — the AT had been adapting continuously, but thirty jin was thirty jin, and even optimized bodies have conversations with gravity that end in the body's concession. His four-count breathing had broken to a three-count. Sweat ran the lines of his jaw. The Sun Flower's photosynthetic engine was running at capacity, converting every photon that touched his skin into auxiliary recovery, but the engine was feeding a fire and the fire was growing.

And yet. The AT — always working, never sleeping, never *satisfied* — received the compound strain and returned, at the ninety-minute mark, something the courier had never felt before: a *shift*. Not a breakthrough. Not a rank-jump. A structural adjustment — the bones of his shoulders and spine reorganizing at the cellular level to distribute iron-weight more efficiently, the muscle fiber recruitment patterns rewriting themselves for sustained-load, the oxygen economy recalibrating from "march" to "endure." It was the AT doing what the AT does: eating a limit and building a floor where the limit used to be.

He was not the last. He would never be the last — his body was a construction the AT had built for eleven years, and this was a Tuesday. But he was, for the first time since the trial, *honestly working*, and the honest work felt like coming home.

---

### ╱╱ THE CRAFT-BODY BRIDGE ╲╲ *(the water break — the forge and the iron are the same art)*

The thing nobody told you about carrying thirty jin for a hundred laps was that it was the *same work* as the forge. The iron shirt was a billet; the shoulders were the tongs; the ground was the anvil; and the Jade Hand’s second exercise — *receive the shock, pass it through* — was a carrying exercise. One art, secretly three.

He mentioned it at the water break: “The Jade Hand is the iron shirt. You conduct the load through the body into the ground. Hammer, or thirty jin — all weight asking to go somewhere. The Record’s author was a monster.”

“Can you teach me?”

“When I can do it without thinking. A month. Ask me in a month.”

“Copy that,” said Yuhao, and filed it under the things the room believed.

---

### ╱╱ THE LAST ╲╲

An hour and a half. Nine runners left on the track.

Wang Dong had lapped everyone multiple times and was himself near the end — each step now a negotiation between will and physiology, his face gray under the sweat, his legs no longer running but *falling forward in rhythm*. The boys who had tried to match him were all down. The pack was the ground.

Jiang Che was still running. He should not have been — not with ninety-one children of privilege collapsing around him — except that his body was a construction the AT had been building for eleven years and this was exactly the kind of information the AT *used*. His breathing was ragged now (honest strain; the iron did not care about foundations). But his legs still worked, and the photosynthetic engine was running (the sun was up; the life-core fed; the renewal turned fatigue into something the body could process), and the six domains were doing what six domains do when a body is at its edge: *compounding*.

But the class had two stories now: the front and the back. The strongest had never stopped. The weakest had never stopped. And between them, eighty-nine children discovered that the example set from both ends was harder to ignore than any whetstone's order.

The gray-uniformed boy — the weakest soul power in the class, the special invite, the one whose rank was eleven and whose body was ordinary — was *still running*. Not fast. Not well. The way a clock runs: because stopping is not what he was built for. And every runner who had fallen and could still see him, saw this, and something moved in ninety chests at once.

Wang Dong fell first. He had run the most laps; his legs simply stopped being legs. He sat down in the iron and stared, and what he stared at was the boy behind him who was not stopping.

Then the others began to rise.

Not to run. To *watch*. And then — one at a time, led by Wang Dong hauling himself upright on pure fury at himself — to *follow*. Not to pass. To walk behind the gray boy who was carrying thirty jin and rank eleven and his mother's name on sheer, unbreakable, biological stubbornness.

Zhou Yi stood at the edge of the square and for the first time in years was *moved*. Not by the training's effectiveness. By the ninety children who had gotten up when they had nothing left, because the weakest one among them had not lain down.

The bell rang. Everyone fell. The square sounded like a battle.

Wang Dong caught Yuhao's iron shirt as the boy finally collapsed, and they went down together, gasping, side by side.

"You *idiot*," Wang Dong panted, half-laughing, half-crying, meaning *thank you* in the only language his pride had left. "You're a *ten-year ring*. How are you — the only — *what is wrong with you.*"

Yuhao tried to answer and produced only a smile.

---

### ╱╱ THE TREE ╲╲

Zhou Yi raised her hand. A man in white came — floating, barely touching the ground, moving the way wind moves through a house with all the windows open — and stopped beside the fallen class.

Seven soul rings rose from his feet: two yellow, two purple, three black. **A Soul Saint.** A being who had walked so far up the mountain of the soul master's world that the air around him was different. He looked thirty and his eyes looked three thousand.

His hands lifted. Green light grew from his palms like a season arriving early. His body dissolved into a great tree — canopy vast, leaves the green of deep summer — and from the canopy, ninety-one leaves detached and drifted down, one for each child, and where they landed, they sank into iron-shirted shoulders and *repaired* what the afternoon had spent.

The healing art of the academy's Soul Saint, delivered leaf by leaf to a square full of broken children who had learned, on their first day, the most important lesson the monster academy would ever teach them: that the body is the syllabus, and the will is the only textbook, and some of them — the weakest ones, the ones who should have fallen first — had wills that nobody, including themselves, had measured yet.

Jiang Che lay on the flagstones, a green leaf dissolving into his shoulder, the AT receiving the healing energy and *using* it — not just repairing the afternoon's damage but incorporating it, filing the iron-weight information, the sustained-load adaptation, the compound-strain response — building the foundation deeper from a day that had broken ninety of his classmates, because that is what the AT does with limits. It eats them.

Around the square, ninety-one children lay in the dust and the green and the specific silence of people who have been broken and rebuilt in the same afternoon. Jiang Che's leaf dissolved, and the AT filed the day. But it was not the healing he would remember.

What he would remember was this: at the far end of the square, a gray-uniformed boy who could not possibly have been standing was standing. And ninety children who could not possibly have gotten up had gotten up. And none of them — not one — had gotten up for themselves. They had gotten up because the weakest person among them had shown them what *not falling down* looks like when it has nothing to do with strength.

*That,* thought the courier, lying on warm flagstones with iron on his chest and the Soul Saint's leaf in his shoulder, *is what the Tang Sect's ancestor meant by the team.* Not the strongest seven. The seven who would not stop.

In his coat, the fox stirred, sniffed the Soul Saint's residual green light, and said one word that only one boy in the world could hear:

"*Old.*"

Not the Soul Saint's age. The *art's* age. She was tasting the healing light and recognizing something in it, and whatever she recognized, she filed away behind her crown and said nothing else.

### ╱╱ THE MONITOR ╲╲

When the Soul Saint's leaves finished and ninety-one children stood on legs that remembered being broken, Zhou Yi spoke.

"No one is eliminated today." Three seconds of relief. Then: "You should thank Huo Yuhao. I set a task: run until the bell. Only he ran from first step to last without stopping. Wang Dong — out."

The blue-haired monitor stepped forward, already knowing.

"You ran the most laps. But as monitor, you were told to make the rest better — and you ran for yourself. I strip the position. **Huo Yuhao — you are Class One's monitor.** The position floats. Wang Dong: if anyone challenges him, you answer."

Then, the whetstone's other edge: "Jiang Che. You ran at the front because I ordered you there. The front is the ceiling. The back is the floor. Learn the difference between showing and *lifting.* Dismissed."

The class charged Yuhao. Three times they threw him in the air.

Jiang Che stood at the edge, iron shirt on his shoulder, and caught his sect brother's eye on the third throw. Neither of them said anything. Neither needed to. The woodshed boy was grinning like a sunrise, and the courier was grinning back, and between them was the thing that had been built on a road between a forest and a city: not pride, not envy, just the quiet certainty that they were exactly where they were supposed to be.

*"He earned that,"* the fox said, from his coat. *"So did you. Different currencies."*

### ╱╱ THE ROOM ╲╲

Room 108, twenty minutes later, held weather.

Wang Dong washed first, behind his screen. Yuhao went to the hall's public bath. Jiang Che came back from the forge — coke in his hair, a fresh burn on his thumb, the Jade Hand's warmth fading from his palms — and sat on his bed to read.

He had read exactly one paragraph when the door slammed open and Yuhao — shirtless, wet, red-faced — appeared in the doorway at the exact moment Wang Dong — shirtless, wet, and midway through pulling on clothes — was standing in a shaft of evening light that the universe had aimed with malicious precision.

There was a cry. There was a *snap-hum* of soul power, and the room filled with the blue-purple afterimage of wings, and Jiang Che's Treasure Record page bent in the backdraft, and Yuhao was gone — door shut, running, face the color of a boiled lobster.

Wang Dong stood in the wreckage of his own privacy, wearing his shirt and an expression that was equal parts fury and something else that had no name yet.

Jiang Che turned the page.

"...You have wings," he said, mildly, to the room's second atmosphere. "I have a fox. We've all got things."

There was a silence so long that the fox shifted in the coat. Then Wang Dong sat down on his furs with the controlled dignity of a prince sitting on a throne that had just been kicked, and said, without looking at him:

"Your fox. It's real?"

"Sleeping. Or pretending, which from her is the same courtesy."

"...How many tails?"

"Nine."

Wang Dong was quiet for the length of a held breath. Then: "If you tell anyone about —"

"I won't."

"— what just happened."

"Neither will she."

Another silence. Then, from the fur bed, almost too low to hear: "Thanks."

Jiang Che turned another page. In his coat, the fox, who had been watching the whole exchange with the golden intensity of a creature who understood more about both of her roommates than either of them understood about themselves, said one word to her human: "*Interesting.*"

He did not ask what she meant. He was learning that with the fox, not asking was sometimes the whole relationship.

### ╱╱ THE STALL ╲╲

The east gate smelled like every cuisine the continent had invented. Tang Ya's operational plan was flawless: grill, charcoal, spices, twenty cleaned fish, a table, a stool (for the Sect Master). Yuhao cooked. The smell was a weapon.

Jiang Che arrived from the forge, hammer on his shoulder, and found his sect brother surrounded by a mob of paying customers. Tang Ya was on her stool, eating the inventory.

"Fish!" she commanded, spotting him. "Third disciple! Sit! Eat! This is a *sect economic summit.* I'm the chair. You're the treasurer."

"I'm the what?"

"Treasurer. You carry things for a living. Sit down and eat your sect's product."

He sat. He ate. The fish was, objectively, excellent — and he said so, in the way a courier's son says things: with his mouth full, nodding. Yuhao's face did something complicated that belonged to a boy who had never been told his work was good by someone who wasn't trying to recruit him.

"You need a bigger grill," Jiang Che said, between bites. "And a second set of hands at the fire, or your Sect Master eats the margin."

"I *heard* that," said Tang Ya, around a fish.

"You were meant to."

Wang Dong appeared at the edge of the crowd — drawn by the smell, or by the fact that his roommates were there, or by the fact that he was Wang Dong and staying away was harder than coming — and stood with the particular rigidity of a boy who does not know if he is welcome. Jiang Che looked at him, looked at the empty space on the bench, and moved the hammer.

It was not an invitation. It was a cleared seat, which from a courier was the same thing.

Wang Dong sat. Tang Ya put a fish in front of him without asking. The room's weather from the bathroom incident was still present, but it was the weather of a room shared by three boys who had all, in the last forty-eight hours, seen each other at their worst and their best, and the weather was *improving.*

And then a girl who moved like moonlight walked past, and the street went quiet.

### ╱╱ THE BREAKFAST COUNCIL ╲╲ *(the morning of the gate — the room, at the canteen)*

They ate breakfast like a war council, which meant Wang Dong ate like a king, Yuhao ate like a woodshed, and the courier ate like a man cataloguing the dining hall's exits — a habit his brother had noticed and never once asked about, because you don't ask a healer's son why he counts doors.

"Eggs are cold," Wang Dong announced.

"Eggs are *free,*" said Yuhao. "You're eating free eggs."

"They're cold AND free. Both things are true. The academy can't do one thing with eggs—"

"I like them," said Jiang Che, and both heads turned, because it was a known position, aggressively held, defended in three prior councils: the cold eggs were *his* and he would hear nothing against them. "They taste like a route. Cold eggs and a road. It's a good taste."

"That's the saddest sentence you've ever said."

"It's Tuesday," said the courier, philosophically, and the table cracked — Yuhao into his sleeve, Wang Dong very unwillingly into his eggs — and somewhere in the middle of the laughing the room stopped being three boys at a table and became, for good, the room.

### ╱╱ THE GATE ╲╲

**Jiang Nannan** — fourth year, purple uniform, gold hair in waves, a face that made every other beautiful person on the street into a rehearsal. She smelled the fish. She came to the stall.

"How much, little brother?"

"Five coppers, senior sister."

"Three. The cost supports three; five is greedy."

"It's not negotiable, and today's sold out."

For one heartbeat, the two most stubborn people on the street regarded each other with mutual professional respect. Then a mountain wearing a black uniform stepped between them and threw a gold coin at the grill with a throw that embedded it in the metal.

**Xu Sanshi.** Sixth year. Three rings. A boy whose love for Jiang Nannan had been rejected so many times it had become a geological feature.

The mountain reached past the space Jiang Nannan occupied and grabbed for the two remaining fish — the two saved for Tang Ya — and Yuhao, on pure detection-forged instinct, snatched them first.

And Jiang Che was already moving.

Not dramatically. Not with a battle cry. With the specific, unhurried efficiency of a boy who had spent five years learning what to do when someone reaches for something that belongs to his family: the grass came out — two yellow rings lighting at his feet, the blue-silver vines fanning — and the mountain's outstretched wrist was wrapped before it closed on air.

Xu Sanshi looked down at his arm. Then at the boy attached to the vine. Then at the two yellow rings.

"...Who —"

The vine tightened. Not cruelly. Evenly. A Pressure-Seal, applied at the wrist of a boy who outweighed the courier by forty kilos and outweighed him in rank by two rings, and the vine held, because the vines had sewn a fourth-year's hammer to the ground two days ago and a sixth-year's wrist was not a hammer.

"*Let go of the fish,*" Jiang Che said, at walking volume, in the tone of a boy who did not raise his voice because raising his voice was something that happened to people who were not in control.

Xu Sanshi's three rings lit. The Xuanwu Turtle shield materialized in his free hand — black, domed, the size of a door — and the street cleared around them like water around a dropped stone.

The shield-arm swung. The vines released the wrist and caught the shield's *rim* — Two-Point Anchor, the trial-proven grip — and for exactly one second the sixth-year with the fortress soul and the first-year with the grass soul stood locked, strength against craft, and the street watched a three-ringer fail to move a two-ringer's vines.

Then Bei Bei arrived — fast, cold, his lightning-arm already lit — and the situation, which had been about to become a real fight, became instead a *conversation,* because the first disciple of the Tang Sect stepping between his junior brother and a sixth-year with a shield was a sentence the whole street understood.

"Bei Bei." Xu Sanshi's voice was a landslide. "This isn't your business."

"He's my junior brother." Bei Bei's voice was a lake. "And the boy holding your wrist is my third junior brother. Everything here is my business. Fighting Spirit Zone. Now."

The mountain looked at Jiang Che. Jiang Che looked at the mountain. The vine released. Neither of them blinked.

"Fine," said Xu Sanshi. He dropped a gold coin on the ruined grill — "for the fish" — and turned to Jiang Nannan with a tenderness that was painful to watch. "Nannan —"

"Xu Sanshi. There is nothing between us. Stop." Ice, absolute. She walked away.

Jiang Che watched the mountain's face do something strong faces do when the thing they want most walks away in front of a hundred people. He felt — not sympathy, not pity, just the recognition of a force meeting a wall it couldn't break. He knew what walls looked like. He was learning what forces looked like, too.

Tang Ya appeared at his elbow, holding the returned fish, her face doing something between fury and pride. Bei Bei was behind her, arms folded, wearing the expression of a man who had watched his junior brother stop a sixth-year and was recalculating several things.

"You moved fast," Bei Bei said to Jiang Che. Not a compliment — an assessment. The first disciple's eyes were doing the thing they did: reading, filing, adjusting the file.

"He grabbed my sect brother," Jiang Che said, as if this explained everything, because it did.

"Your vines held a three-ring sixth-year's shield-arm."

"They held a fourth-year's hammer two days ago. The wrist was easier."

Bei Bei looked at him for a long moment. Then, quietly, to Tang Ya: "The sect has four disciples and I am no longer certain I am the strongest one in the room."

"You never were," said Tang Ya, with her mouth full, and the Sect Master's grin was the grin of a girl who had known since a lakeside oath that the boy with grass in his sleeves was going to be a problem for everyone who wasn't family.

"*That,*" she said, biting a fish, "was excellent sect work. Come on — we're going to the Fighting Spirit Zone. *Family* event."

### ╱╱ THE FIGHTING SPIRIT ZONE ╲╲

The Fighting Spirit Zone was a colosseum for young monsters. Ten gold bought a match; one silver bought a seat; the seats were full.

Jiang Che sat between Tang Ya and Yuhao. Wang Dong sat on his other side, having come without being asked, the bathroom weather between them still present but *shared* now — two boys who had each seen the other at a disadvantage and neither of whom had mentioned it.

The fox was in his coat. "Watch the mountain's left foot," she said, low. "*He leads with the shield but he watches with his heart, and his heart is watching a girl who just left. He will fight angry, and angry mountains leave their foundations.*"

Below, in the arena's white circle, Bei Bei and Xu Sanshi faced each other. The Tyrant Dragon's arm was already transformed. The Xuanwu Turtle's shield was already up. The referee's hand fell.

Jiang Che watched the way his father had taught him to watch a forge: not the hammer, but the metal. The lightning tested the shield three times — fast, precise, each strike at a different angle, mapping the defense the way his moisture-sense mapped a room. The mountain held. The mountain was *built* to hold. But the fox was right: Xu Sanshi's left foot was half a beat late on the third exchange, and the late half-beat was on the side facing the gate where a gold-haired girl had walked away.

"*Left side,**" Jiang Che said, almost to himself, and Wang Dong — who had been watching with the intense focus of a boy who cataloged everything — heard him.

"What?"

"His left foot. Senior brother's lightning will find it by the fourth exchange."

Wang Dong looked at the arena. Looked at Jiang Che. Looked back at the arena. "How do you know?"

"I watch metal for a living."

On the floor below, Bei Bei's Thunder Dragon Claw turned mid-air — and struck the shield's left rim, and the mountain's balance shifted one degree, and the mountain grunted, and Wang Dong looked at Jiang Che with an expression that was rapidly evolving from *roommate* to *something else.*

"...Forge-trained," Wang Dong said, filing it.

"*Courier-trained,*" Jiang Che corrected. "The metal doesn't care what you call it."

The fight went on. Tang Ya ate the evidence. And in the third row of the Fighting Spirit Zone, three boys sat shoulder to shoulder — a gray one, a blue one, and one with grass in his coat — and the shoulder-contact was the kind that only happens between people who have decided, for reasons they might not be able to name yet, that they are on the same side.

Below them, the fight settled into its rhythm: the mountain holding, the lightning probing, the seams widening. It would take time. The fox had said so. But in the stands above the arena, something was happening that the fighters below could not see and the crowd around them did not notice: three boys who had entered the academy as strangers — a woodshed orphan, a closeted aristocrat, and a courier with grass in his sleeves — were becoming, one grilled fish and one named seam at a time, the thing that the ancestor had built the Tang Sect to hold.

A team.

Not because anyone had ordered it. Because the fish was good, and the fights were interesting, and nobody at that table was trying to be anything other than what they were. And what they were, together, was more than any of them were alone.

The academy had a word for that. The academy had been built for that.

*Monsters.*

### ╱╱ THE CROWD ╲╲

Five hundred students packed the hexagonal arena by the time the fighters entered, and the noise was a living thing — the specific frequency of young monsters smelling blood that wasn't theirs.

Tang Ya, still eating, briefed her disciples with the fluency of a woman who had done this many times: the Fighting Spirit Zone opened every day after class until midnight; ten gold bought a match, one silver bought a seat; famous fighters drew free broadcasting through soul-amplifiers in every dorm; the academy took half the gate, the winner took the rest — "your senior brother has made a *fortune* in here" — and Xu Sanshi, being a year above Bei Bei, would owe an extra ten gold if he lost.

"They've fought before," she added, airily. "They trade wins. They're actually friends."

Yuhao blinked. "They're *what?*"

"Friends. Colleagues. Co-conspirators in the perfectly legal enterprise of hitting each other for money." She bit a fish. "The whole academy thinks they're rivals. Nobody has ever noticed that they always fight to a draw or near-draw, and that the *real* money is in the side bets they place on themselves through intermediaries. Don't tell anyone."

"I won't," said Yuhao, and Jiang Che, sitting on his other side, nodded the same oath without being asked, because that was what family did.

From his coat, the fox observed the packed stands with the expression of a creature evaluating the protein density of a room. "*Five hundred children paying money to watch two boys hit each other. Humans are fascinating.*"

---

### ╱╱ THE NEEDLE ╲╲

What the crowd didn't know — what five hundred paying customers had not paid to see — was happening in the rest room below the arena, where Bei Bei was removing a needle from his friend's waist and charging him a pill for the service.

The needle was a **Dragon-Beard Needle** — the Tang Sect's ancestral hidden weapon, passed only through the line of Sect Masters, a golden thread finer than hair that buried itself in flesh and *stayed* there, disrupting soul power, causing pain that made a three-ring Soul Elder's hands shake. Tang Ya had thrown it at Xu Sanshi when he grabbed Yuhao. It had been in his waist for forty minutes.

The pill was a **Mysterious Water Pill** — a treasure Bei Bei wanted and Xu Sanshi owned and the Sect could not afford.

"Give me another one," said Bei Bei, extracting the needle with the precise fingers of a craftsman, "and I'll bet you the fight."

"You *want* to bet me? What are you planning?" Xu Sanshi, needle-free, flexed his side with the relief of a man who has just been unhooked from a very small, very angry machine. "You're scheming. I can always tell when you're scheming because you smile like that."

"Am I smiling?"

"You're always smiling. That's the problem." Xu Sanshi glared. "Fine. Two pills if I lose. But if *you* lose, you owe me —"

"I won't lose."

"You always say that."

"I'm always right."

---

### ╱╱ THE ROOMMATE ╲╲

Wang Dong had been with them since the stall — three roommates and a Sect Master, four seats together in the front row. He sat on Jiang Che's other side, and somewhere between Tang Ya's economics lecture and the fighters' entrance, the Sect Master leaned across Jiang Che with the interest of a woman who had been watching a beautiful boy eat her sect's fish for ten minutes.

"Xiao Yuhao, aren't you going to introduce me?"

"My roommate, Wang Dong. Wang Dong — our senior, Tang Ya."

Tang Ya looked at the beautiful boy with the appreciation of a Sect Master evaluating talent. "*Very* pretty. Xiao Yuhao, do some work — bring him into the Tang Sect."

She meant it as a joke. Half a joke. The half that wasn't joking had already seen his soul power's density and his body's privilege and filed both.

What she did not expect was Wang Dong going very still, and then saying, with a formality that had weight behind it: "The Tang Sect. I've heard the name. I'd like to join."

The fish stopped halfway to Tang Ya's mouth.

"...You what?"

"I want to join the Tang Sect. I want to learn the hidden weapons." He said it the way a prince asks for something he has decided he wants, which is to say: as though the asking were a formality.

Tang Ya looked at Jiang Che. Jiang Che looked at Wang Dong. The fox, from inside the coat, said nothing at all, which was the loudest thing she had said all day.

"...I'll think about it," said the Sect Master, recovering. "Xiao Yuhao will tell you."

Wang Dong nodded once, satisfied, and turned to the arena as though nothing had happened, and Jiang Che caught Yuhao's eye across two seats and one shared thought: *the sect of four might become the sect of five.*

---

### ╱╱ THE FIGHT ╲╲

The referee stepped back. Two Soul Elders released their martial souls simultaneously, and five hundred children went silent.

Blue lightning condensed on Bei Bei's arm — the Tyrant Dragon's scaled limb, the three rings riding it like moons. Black soul power erupted around Xu Sanshi — the Xuanwu Turtle's shield, the body swelling, the skin hardening to iron. The strongest attack martial soul in the outer court. The strongest defense. The crowd had paid for exactly this.

Jiang Che watched the way his father had taught him to watch a forge — not the hammer, but the metal — and what he saw was two craftsmen who had done this before, settling into a rhythm that was half-combat and half-conversation.

Bei Bei *moved* — a blur of blue, the Thunder Dragon Claw leading — and the mountain met it with the shield and *held*, and the first soul skill (Xuanwu Shake) rippled outward in a black dome of force that would have staggered anyone not prepared for it. But Bei Bei was prepared: Thunder Fury and Thunder Myriad fired simultaneously, the lightning net tearing through the shake like a blade through fog, and the gap between them closed to nothing.

The crowd roared. The fighters did not hear it.

And Jiang Che noticed something.

Yuhao's eyes had gone gold.

Not the gold of the Spirit Eyes' base state — the *deeper* gold, the one that meant the white ring was active and the sharing was running. The courier's moisture-sense couldn't read the spiritual link itself, but his sensory domain could read its *effects*: the subtle shift in Bei Bei's timing, the quarter-beat foreknowledge that wasn't instinct, the way the lightning turned mid-strike to arrive exactly where the shield's seam would be a half-second from now. Someone was feeding Bei Bei the map. The someone was sitting between Tang Ya and Jiang Che with his eyes glowing and his breath held.

*The fish-saint is sharing his eyes with the dragon,* Jiang Che thought, and did not say it, because it was not his to say. But he *filed* it — the way a courier files the location of a bridge — in the growing catalogue of things his sect brother could do that nobody had measured yet.

Below: Xu Sansshi's second and third soul skills fired — and stuttered, half a beat, just enough. Bei Bei went *under* the shield on Ghost-Shadow Track, appeared behind it, and the match was over before the crowd finished its roar. A lightning-charged leg kick. A claw on a shoulder. The referee's hand.

"Bei Bei wins."

The mountain hit the floor, sputtering: "You — you *cheated* —" because he could feel the half-beat stutter and didn't know what had caused it, and Bei Bei helped him up with a smile that hid everything, and the crowd's roar swallowed whatever the mountain said next.

In the stands, Yuhao let his breath out slowly, and the gold faded from his eyes, and Tang Ya's hand — which had been signaling in a code the whole fight — dropped to her lap, and nobody noticed any of it except two people: a fox in a coat, who had known from the first exchange, and a courier from Linjiang, who had read the seams.

But Wang Dong noticed something *else.* He had been watching the fight the way a fighter watches a fight — tracking technique, distance, timing — and at some point in the last ninety seconds he had realized that his own roommate's breathing had synchronized with Bei Bei's footwork, and that the synchronization was not coincidence but *participation.* He looked at Yuhao. He looked at the gold fading from behind the gray boy's eyes. He looked at Jiang Che, who was looking at Yuhao with an expression that was not surprise but *confirmation.*

"...What did you two just do?" Wang Dong asked.

"Watched the fight," said Jiang Che, at walking volume.

"That wasn't watching. His breathing *changed* when —"

"*Watched the fight,*" the courier said again, mildly, and Wang Dong — who was arrogant and proud and had been a genius since birth and had never in his life been told a secret by someone who trusted him enough to not-tell it — understood, for the first time, that he was sitting inside a group of people who kept each other's secrets as a matter of *craft*, not obligation. And the understanding changed something in the architecture of his spine.

---


### ╱╱ THE DRESSING-DOWN ╲╲ *(after the arena — the sect, at the corridor)*

The corridor outside the Fighting Spirit Zone held the sect and one mountain, and the Sect Master was conducting a performance review.

"You," she said, pointing at Jiang Che with a fish-bone, "held a sixth-year's wrist. In public. Before senior brother even *moved.*"

"He grabbed Yuhao's fish."

"He grabbed Yuhao's *fish,*" Tang Ya repeated, in a voice for the ages. "The Tang Sect's third disciple, rank twenty-nine, the trial-flagged hammer of Class One — deployed his martial soul over *grilled fish.*"

"The fish was *saved,*" said the courier, with dignity. "I note nobody is thanking the fish-saver."

"I'm not thanking the fish-saver because the fish-saver could have been *expelled* for unprovoked soul-release on a senior—" and then she stopped, because the whole corridor was trying not to laugh, and she was the corridor's leader, and leaders do not laugh at their own discipline sessions. "…The fish *was* good, though."

"The fish is always good," said Yuhao.

"The fish is not the POINT—" said the Sect Master, and gave up, and the corridor went, and the sect walked home through the dark arguing about fish, which is what sects are *for.*

---

### ╱╱ THE PILL ╲╲

Afterward, in the corridor outside the arena, the Tang Sect collected its winnings. Two Mysterious Water Pills, a white jade bottle the size of a thumb, and Xu Sanshi's grudging respect — "your junior brother hits like a girl, your Sect Master throws needles like a demon, and you *cheat*" — delivered with the specific anger of a man who has just lost a bet to his best friend and will exact revenge at the earliest opportunity.

"What *is* it?" Yuhao asked, looking at the bottle.

"The Mysterious Water Pill," said Bei Bei, and his voice changed to the register he used for things that mattered. "It's a medicine. A very rare, very expensive medicine that does something no other pill on the continent can do." He looked at Tang Ya. Looked at Jiang Che. Looked at Yuhao. "It can help a soul master break through a cultivation bottleneck. Not by force. By *nourishing.* It feeds the meridians, strengthens the foundation, and lets the body accept the breakthrough naturally instead of fighting it."

He held it up. Two pills in a bottle the size of an eye.

"There are three people in this sect who need bottlenecks broken. I have two pills." He smiled, the lazy warm smile that hid a mind like a whetstone. "I'll let the Sect Master decide who gets them. But I'll point out that one of us is at rank twenty-five and has been for a while, and one of us is at rank ten and needs every advantage more than air."

"Give them to Yuhao," said Jiang Che, immediately, before Tang Ya could open her mouth.

Both sect brothers looked at him.

"He's rank ten with a woodshed body and one white ring nobody can read," the courier said, with the flat simplicity of a boy stating the weather. "I'm rank twenty-five with a foundation the AT built and the Academy's resources compounding daily. I don't need a pill. He needs *two* pills and a vacation and someone to tell him he's allowed to eat three meals a day. Give them to Yuhao."

Tang Ya's eyes were bright. Bei Bei's file on "the fourth" — which had been growing pages all week — added another.

And that was how the Tang Sect spent its first real money: on its weakest member, because the strongest one said so.

---

### ╱╱ THE WALK ╲╲

They walked back through the dark academy — five figures now, because Xu Sanshi had attached himself to their group with the magnetic inevitability of a lonely boy who had just been beaten, needled, and robbed and was *still* here, because being robbed by friends was better than being alone.

"...So the fish stall," Xu Sanshi was saying, to Yuhao, in the tone of a man negotiating. "Is that a daily thing? Because I would *pay* —"

"Five coppers. No discounts."

"I'll give you a *gold* —"

"No discounts."

Tang Ya, walking beside Jiang Che, bumped his shoulder with hers — the Sect Master's version of a medal. "You did good," she said, quietly, under the noise. "At the stall and with the pills. That's what the ancestor meant. The weak thing is the important thing."

"I know," said the courier.

"I know you know," said the Sect Master. "I'm saying it anyway, because sect masters say things."

Ahead, Wang Dong walked beside Yuhao, arguing about something that made both of them smile in a way that had nothing to do with the argument. Behind, Bei Bei and Xu Sanshi were speaking in a low code that was half friendship and half financial planning. And between them, a fox rode a coat and watched the whole architecture of the evening — the fighters, the fish, the pills, the five people walking through the dark like a very small, very strange family — and said, to her human, in the voice she used perhaps once a week:

"*This is what a sect looks like when it is becoming a sect again.*"

Jiang Che did not answer. He was watching the lights of room 108 — ahead, above, one window dark and one window lit and one window somewhere in between — and thinking about a hammer and a page and a year that was going to be very, very long. He was thinking about five people walking through the dark like a family that had not existed a week ago. He was thinking about a pill he had given away and a secret he had not told and a seam he had named in a language a butterfly prince was already learning to speak.

And he was thinking — quietly, in the deep place where the AT worked on everything including thoughts — that the academy was doing to him what forges do to metal: not making him into something new, but *revealing* what was already in the metal. The classes, the iron, the fights, the forge shift, the five people around him — all of it was heat. All of it was hammer-falls. And the metal that came out the other side of this year would be the metal the AT had been building since before he was born, finally *shaped.*

He was eleven years old. He had been in construction for eleven years. The construction had not stopped. And tonight, walking home through a city of monsters with his sect around him like a coat, he understood for the first time that the construction had *purpose* — not just to make him strong, but to make him *this*: a boy who could hold a mountain's wrist and give away a pill and keep a secret and walk home with five people and mean something to every one of them.

The fox purred once, very quietly, against his chest, in the register of archives being correct.

*Yes,* she said, to no one. *That one.*

### ╱╱ THE DOOR ╲╲

Bei Bei could not enter the first-year dormitory — school rule — so the handoff happened at the door, in lamplight, with Yuhao unconscious between Wang Dong's shoulder and Jiang Che's.

The first disciple fed his junior brother a pill with the matter-of-fact tenderness of a man who had decided this boy was family and was now simply *managing the asset*: a deep blue pill the size of a cherry, veined with white, mist curling off its surface, the faint clean smell of it hanging in the stairwell like a promise. Wang Dong — educated, well-born, trained since birth to know what things *cost* — went very still. Jiang Che, standing beside him, watched the pill go into his sect brother's mouth and did not know its name, but the AT knew *quality* when it touched the boy's perceptions, and so did the fox, whose head rose from the coat collar and whose nostrils worked once, twice, filing the pill's signature somewhere behind her crown.

"Take care of him," Bei Bei said to Wang Dong — to *Wang Dong*, the stranger, because he was the roommate and the rule was the rule. And then, catching Jiang Che's eye over the unconscious boy: a nod. Between sect brothers, the nod was a whole sentence.

"*Little brother*," said the fox, as they climbed the stairs, very low, to her human alone, "*that pill your senior gave away so easily is worth more than your father makes in a year. Remember who gave it. And remember that he gave it as though it were a copper. That is what a sect's wealth actually is.*"

Jiang Che filed it. He was, by nature and by training, a boy who filed things.

---

### ╱╱ THE FUR ╲╲

They put Yuhao on his boards. Wang Dong stood over him for a moment with a fist half-raised and an expression that meant *you saw me naked and now you're unconscious and I can't even be angry at you properly* — and then went to his own bed to meditate, because Wang Dong's answer to every unresolvable emotion was training.

Jiang Che sat on his own bed in the dark, and the room settled, and this is what the night was for: the third desk, the candle stub, the Treasure Record's Jade Hand pages, read slowly and twice.

And the fox came out.

Not dramatically. She never did anything dramatically. She poured herself out of the coat collar onto the desk, walked the desk's edge once — inspecting, as she inspected everything, the domain's perimeter — and then stepped onto his knee, turned around three times like water finding its level, and sat. Facing him. Moonlight-white in the candle stub's light, the gold tips of nine tails catching little flames of their own, her eyes old gold and half-lidded, imperial even at rest. Especially at rest.

He read. She sat. This was the oldest contract between them — older than the speaking, older than the road: the nights when the boy read and the fox presided.

After a while, without deciding to, he lifted his free hand and put it on her head, between the ears, and ruffled.

Not stroked. *Ruffled* — against the grain, two or three times, the way you ruffle a dog that has earned it, or a younger brother's hair, or a thing you own no correct ceremony for. Her fur was what it always was: cool on the surface, warm underneath, finer than anything a merchant had ever tried to sell his mother, and it stirred under his fingers with a faint static life that was not quite fur and not quite light.

The fox's eyes opened fully.

The room's ambient dignity dropped ten degrees. Somewhere in her ancestry, a hundred generations of crowned ancestors rotated in their barrows.

"*You are rumpling me,*" she said, in the tone of an empress informing a courtier that he was standing on the throne.

"Mm," said the courier, and did it again.

"*I permit this once.*" A pause, in which nine tails arranged themselves into a posture of extreme tolerance. "*Record that I permitted it.*"

"Recorded."

"*Once.*"

"Once per night," he said, turning a page with the hand that was not committing treason.

The fox considered the amendment. The fox, who had spent four years training this human in the precise mechanics of what she would and would not endure, and who had watched him grow from a seven-year-old with burned hands into whatever he was now — this boy who had stopped a mountain that afternoon and given a fortune away without blinking and kept another boy's secret in his chest like a stone he had no intention of showing anyone — the fox let out a breath through her nose, the smallest concession ever granted by her line, and leaned one half-degree into the ruffling hand.

"*Once per night,*" she allowed, to the candle. "*While the candle burns. Do not tell anyone.*"

"Who would I tell?"

"*The list of beings who must never know,*" said the fox, "*includes the small one, the proud one, the Sect Master, your parents, the ancestors, and every god currently watching.*"

"That's everyone."

"*Yes,*" said the fox, with satisfaction, and butted her head, once, briefly, against his palm — the payment rendered, the account settled, the empire's single annual expenditure of affection booked and closed — and settled back onto his knee with her chin on her paws to supervise the rest of the reading.

He ruffled once more, very quietly, when he thought she was asleep.

She was not asleep. She permitted that one too, and filed it, unbeknownst to him, under a heading in her own private archive that had exactly one entry in it and was not labeled in any human language.

---

### ╱╱ THE MIST ╲╲

Past midnight, Wang Dong woke from his meditation because the *air* woke him.

Soul power — thick, clean, water-adjacent — was breathing off the third bed across the room in slow waves. He sat up. In the dark, Huo Yuhao's sleeping body was veiled in a faint blue mist that flowed *into* his skin and back out of it, and the mist carried a scent like a river at dawn, and as the minutes passed the blue deepened and the smell turned from clean to *rich* to something else entirely.

Jiang Che was awake too — had been awake, had felt the soul-power tide shift through his moisture-sense a full minute before Wang Dong's cruder instruments registered it. He watched the mist work with a healer's son's eyes and said nothing, because the night had already taught him what was his to say.

But the fox sat up on his knee. The gold eyes were open all the way now, and they were not lazy at all. She looked at the sleeping boy wrapped in blue — the boy who had nearly fainted in the stands spending three soul skills and a secret art to turn a fight — and she looked at the mist doing what mist does to a body that has finally been *given* something instead of asked for something, and what she said, to her human alone, in the voice of a creature who had eaten treasures that could buy cities, was a single word of professional assessment:

"*Wasted on the young.*"

And through it all he ran the triangle and the ledger both. Mornings: the forge shift, the Jade Hand past its burns by week six. And Yuhao — **Yuhao.** The pills taken in Wang Dong's prescribed order; the marrow cleansed a second time; the rank climbing past the teens; the moving Xuantian circulation that turned every lap of every iron day into cultivation; the Purple Demon Eyes fed at every dawn. The unmeasurable part was this: in the first week, Class One had watched the weakest boy in the academy outlast them all under iron; in the second, they watched him take a monitor's duties nobody else wanted; and by the third month, the question of who led Class One had stopped being a question. ### THE MIDNIGHT RUNNER *(Zhou Yi)*

The whetstone had a secret, and she found it by accident.

She had been out late on academy business, crossing Shrek Square past midnight, when she heard it: chain-links shifting, softly, in the dark. A figure on the track, shirtless, drenched, moving at a pace that was barely a run and would not stop — each footfall heavy enough to leave a shining wet print on the stone.

Hu Yuhao. In an iron shirt. At midnight. Adding two hours of punishment to days that had already ground his classmates to powder.

She asked him what he thought he was doing. The boy — swaying, soaked, polite — gave her the plainest answer she had ever been given in thirty years of teaching: *"Teacher, my talent is poor. I just work harder than the others. Training to exhaustion and then meditating — the improvement seems to come faster."*

She suspected a performance, staged for her benefit. The suspicion lasted exactly until the weather answered it: rain came, and he ran, the shirt rusting soft and brown at the seams; wind came, and he ran, leaning into it like a man leaning into an argument he intended to win; the academy's short winter came, and the frost burned his lungs, and he ran. Every midnight, the square's dark held one small stubborn figure, two hours and more — and then, in the second month, the figure got heavier: *two* iron shirts, sixty jin, the boy stacking his own disadvantages like a mason building a wall against his own weakness.

The class found out, as classes do — nothing in this academy stays secret except the things the academy itself seals. They came, the proud ones, in the first week: four of the front-runners, sure that if the trash-soul could do it, they could. One lasted a single night. Two lasted two. The last of them made it to the third midnight and stood at the track's edge in the dark, watching the small figure do its slow impossible laps, and went back to bed, and never spoke of it again — because there are things a proud boy cannot say out loud, and *he is made of something I do not have* is the first of them.

Word of the three-night failures moved through Class One the way word moves: silently, totally. And it changed something. The midnight runner never asked anyone to follow, never mentioned it, never made it a sermon — and that was precisely why they followed. By the third month, the class did not run at midnight with him. They simply *stopped quitting.* The iron days ground, and the theory ground, and sixty-seven children discovered one morning that they had been holding a standard for so long it had stopped feeling like a standard and started feeling like a spine. The class found out, as classes do. Some tried to join him. Not one lasted three days. This was not training anymore; the word for it was the one Zhou Yi had never needed to use for an eleven-year-old: *discipline.*

And that — not the fish, not the pills, not even the monitor's post — was the thing that had held sixty-seven of ninety-one together through her quarter. A class is a whetstone's dream only if somewhere in the steel there is one grain that will not be filed. She had found her grain, running in the dark.

*(Natural ripple, the deepest one: the class's spine was not her work alone, and she knew it. Somewhere in her files, the word "monitor" stopped meaning a title and started meaning a foundation.)*

---

### THE PILL LEDGER *(Huo Yuhao)*

The numbers, honestly kept, because the boy who ran at midnight kept everything honestly:

**The second Mysterious Water Pill, month one:** taken after the first had fully settled — a whole rank, twelve-peak to thirteen-peak, and the body scoured a second time. Cultivation speed: seven times the original.

**The Soul-Raising Pill, mid-month:** into a body now twice-cleansed, channels widened and elastic — and the pill repaid the preparation exactly as Wang Dong had promised: **three ranks broken in a night, and a bottleneck besides, settling at seventeen.** Seven times became ten. Ten *times*. The trash-soul boy who had needed five years to reach rank ten now cultivated at ten times that pace — a number that would have shamed middle nobility, arrived at in ninety days.

**The three months' grinding:** seventeen to seventeen-peak, the edge of eighteen, the roots deliberately allowed to settle after the medicine's sprint. His body kept its own ledger alongside: three inches of height — he now looked Wang Dong in the eye — and a build that was not muscle-mass but *whipcord*, every gram of it earned between midnight and dawn.

The woodshed orphan had, in one quarter, stopped being the academy's joke and become its average — and its average was the finest cohort on the continent.

*(Room 108 heard the arithmetic read aloud that night - Wang Dong kept the class standings the way princes keep ledgers of things they intend to win - and the courier filed one line in his own: the twin-soul rumor. A soul that came in a pair. He had thought, once, about how rare such things must be; the fox had told him, long ago, that twin souls were older than the academies and rarer than the deep-forest kings, and that they came in two kinds: the fortunate, and the *troubled.* He hoped, mildly, professionally, that the small quiet girl was the first kind. The mend worked on both, but it worked gentler on the first.)*

### THE THIRD BED *(room 108 - the parallel ledger)*

Room 108 kept two ledgers now, and the second one belonged to the third bed.

Jiang Che's quarter, honestly kept: **twenty-nine**, the wall at thirty, the hunt planned. But the room knew — because rooms know — that the number was the least of it. The Xuantian Gong sat in his meridians like a second heart; the forge had rebuilt his hands twice over; the Jade Hand had crossed some invisible line in its third month where the conduction stopped being a technique and started being a *property*; and the mend-work — thirty, forty, fifty applications of the clean current a week — had done to his spiritual depth what the midnight running had done to Yuhao's body.

And the two ledgers had begun to talk to each other. On the last night of the quarter, past midnight, Jiang Che came back from the forge and found the room empty and the iron shirts gone, and knew exactly where his roommate was — and went, because the triangle went where its legs went, and stood in the dark at the edge of Shrek Square with a hammer over his shoulder, watching the small stubborn figure do its two hours.

He did not join the run. He had his own.

He sat down on the square's edge, laid the hammer across his knees, and meditated — but not idly, because nothing the AT did was idle. The Xuantian Gong turned under the stars; the fox a warm weight in his coat; and the dew-lens mapped the running boy's breathing, the rhythm of it, the architecture of a will converting itself into rank one wet footfall at a time. And in the meditation's second layer, the courier ran his own route: the wall at thirty, the ring beyond it, the hunt's shape - the forest south, the water-kin beasts his father had hunted for twenty years, the Sun Flower's precedent, and the question the fox had planted months ago and left like a seed: *what does the grass itself want to become?* Because a ring chosen by the AT's user was not a tool acquired. It was a door opened, and he had three months of proof, in the bed across the room, of what a door cost and what it gave.

Two boys, two trainings, one square: one building a body the world would have to reckon with; one planning a soul the world had not made a shelf for yet.

When Yuhao finished — two hours, two shirts, a boy-shaped watermark on the stone — the courier was still there, and had hot bread, because couriers plan routes and this one had planned his roommate's.

"You ran," Yuhao managed, between breaths.

"You ate," said Jiang Che, handing him the bread. "Rank eighteen by the assessment?"

"...Rank eighteen *by the assessment.*" The gray boy grinned, wolfish now, nothing woodshed about it. "Thirty for you?"

"Thirty for me." The courier stood, shouldered the hammer, and the two of them walked back across the wet square in the last dark before the assessment year's first morning. "First place, second place, and a monitor. The sect sweeps the board tomorrow."

"The sect," said Yuhao, around the bread, "is going to make Zhou Yi's year."

### THE WATER-BREAK BROTHERS *(the midnight run — the courier joins, in his own way)*

The midnight runner had company on the fourth night of the quarter.

Not a joiner — the courier had his own hours — but at the water barrel between laps forty and forty-one, a courier appeared with bread and a hammer and sat on the barrel's rim doing the Jade Hand's conduction through the cold iron hoops, because a courier trains where a courier is.

"You're doing forge-homework at my water barrel," Yuhao managed.

"I'm doing forge-homework at *a* water barrel. You happen to be running around it."

"That's not how barrels work—"

"It's exactly how barrels work." He passed the bread. "Lap forty's the wall. The wall's always forty. Eat, then break the wall."

"…Did the fox tell you forty's the wall?"

"The fox told me *you'd* say forty. She's been running your route in her sleep. She says your left ankle clicks on the curves." A beat. "She worries about your ankle, Yu. Out loud. It's very undignified and she'd deny it under torture."

And the boy running the worst laps of the night discovered that his brotherhood had a *night shift* — that even his solitary penance had been adopted by people who could not run it for him but could, god help them, be *there*, with bread and barrel-hoops and a fox who worried about ankles.

### THE ANNOUNCEMENT *(Class One - ensemble)*

"Physical training is suspended."

Sixty-seven spines straightened as one — Pavlovian, total, slightly hilarious — and Zhou Yi looked out at them with the not-warm-not-cold face that her classes eventually learned to read as *satisfaction, heavily encrypted.*

"Three months since enrollment. Tomorrow, your first assessment. Pass it, and you are formally first-years — Shrek students in fact as well as letter, with a place through to the year-end examinations." A pause. "Today, the points."

And she gave them the shape of it — the rules, the format, the stakes — and the class wrote down every word, because this class had learned the price of things. But under the notes, the thing itself moved through the room like weather: *tomorrow.* Everything the iron had built, everything the midnight runner had shamed them into, everything the fish stall had fed and the third bed had mended — all of it banked, and tomorrow the bank opened.

And the stakes she gave them plainly, because she never lied to a class: the assessment was real, the failure was real, and the academy's gate opened both ways. But she gave them one thing more, in the whetstone's way - by not giving it: no threat. For three months every lesson had ended in one. Tonight, none. Because the class that did not need the threat was the class that had arrived, and both the teacher and the taught knew it, and neither would say.

Zhou Yi's eye passed over them and found what she had secretly hoped to find: sixty-seven sets of shoulders that did not flinch. Her batch, she knew — and would have died before saying — was the finest will she had ever been handed, and the reason for it was a rank-seventeen orphan who ran at midnight, a rank-twenty-three prince who had promised them fish money, a rank-twenty-nine courier who fixed what broke, and sixty-four others who had chosen, night after night, to be worthy of the example.

"Class One," said the whetstone, in the voice that meant it, "do not disappoint me."

And when the format came - the classes drawn against each other, three to a side - the middle rows began the arithmetic every class does: who stands, who folds, who is dangerous. Names moved through the whisper-line. And one name moved through it twice, because nobody could agree what it was: a small, quiet girl from Class Two who had spent three months being unnoticed - Xiao Xiao - and whose soul, the rumor said, came in a *pair*.

Sixty-seven voices, one answer — and in the middle rows, three boys sat in a row without arranging to, because that was simply where the triangle's center of gravity lived now, and the strongest of them was not the one anyone outside the room would have guessed.

### THE EVE *(the sect - the seventh seat)*

The last supper before an assessment, at a grill already drowned: five disciples and a mountain, and the Sect Master holding court with the day's takings as her scepter.

"Rules of engagement," Tang Ya announced. "Wang Dong takes first place overall - that seals the fifth seat the proper way, by the promise, not the back door. Yuhao - top ten, monitor's honor. Jiang Che -" she paused, and the grin went sly, "- the sect's official position is that our third disciple should be modest and restrained."

"His unofficial position," said Bei Bei, "being that the academy's trial files already say *flagged*, the class already calls him the hammer, and the whole first year has spent three months watching him mend everything they broke."

"Modest and restrained," Jiang Che agreed, deadpan, and the table laughed, and the mountain laughed loudest, because Xu Sanshi had learned this month that being the sect's unsworn seventh seat came with unlimited fish and unlimited honesty, and both suited him.

And later - the fire drowned, the walk home, the three beds - the last exchange of the quarter, in the dark, three voices that had learned each other's silences:

"First place," Wang Dong said, to the ceiling.

"Top ten," Yuhao said, to the ceiling.

"Thirty," Jiang Che said, to the ceiling, and then, quietly, with the fox settling against his collarbone: "and a ring, before the year turns."

The fox said nothing at all, which was her way of saying *yes - and the hunt is already planned, and you will not go alone, little tide. The sect hunts now.*

And the pieces all agreed on one thing: whatever Group One was, it was more than three.

"I heard the courier's soul is grass," a Class Three boy said, at the gate, in the fish line.

"I heard it's *life,*" said his friend. "Like, the attribute. Pure life."

"I heard his fox talks."

"I heard his fox *fought a teacher.*"

"I heard," said a fifth voice, dryly, from three places back in the line — a voice that belonged to a mountain that had been orbiting a fish stall for two months — "that you should all worry less about rumors and more about the fact that my — that the Sect Master's disciples are going to sweep this year's assessment like a tide going out." And Xu Sanshi bought his fish, and left, and the line discussed the mountain's use of the word *tide* for the rest of the evening.


### THE THREE PAPERS *(Zhou Yi's scene — canon rebuilt for the room)*

The papers hit Zhou Yi's desk at the end of class, and her eye-corner twitched.

Three of them. Same word.

"*Control-type.*" **Slam** — Yuhao's paper on the lectern.

"*CONTROL-TYPE.*" **Slam** — Wang Dong's, and Yuhao turned in mild astonishment because he genuinely hadn't known.

"***STILL control-type.***" The third slam nearly broke the lectern — and this time both boys turned, slowly, to the third desk, where a courier with a hammer was studying the grain of the wood with enormous interest.

"You three," said Zhou Yi, with the dangerous patience of a woman being messed with by an entire dormitory, "did this on purpose."

"Teacher," Jiang Che said, mildly, not looking up from the wood. "Grass binds. Binding is control. I didn't write control to match anyone — I wrote it because the alternative is *support*, and the last person who called my grass support got wrapped to a tree."

The whetstone stared at him. The whetstone recalculated. The whetstone revised her afternoon's opinion of the word *support.*

"...Fine. Control it is. But the rule stands: one assault-type per team. Wang Dong — you're assault. You wrote control because—"

"Because if I can control the field through overwhelming attack, is that not control? And I fly, and I strike at range, that's field control, technically—"

"You wrote control because you don't want to be separated from Huo Yuhao, and you didn't know that assault-types and control-types train *together.* You mutilated your own paper for nothing. Change it."

The paper hit Wang Dong in the chest. He changed CONTROL to ASSAULT wearing the radiant expression of a man who has just learned his marriage is legal after all, and the third boy in the room caught Jiang Che's eye across the office and both of them, simultaneously, silently, in perfect room-brotherhood, did not laugh. Out loud.

"Out," said Zhou Yi, who had seen the not-laughing. "All of you. Tomorrow we cut half the year. Come back sharp."

And at the door, as the three of them left, she said one more thing — quietly, to the air, but meant for the room: "That team. The one you three are. I have been teaching for thirty years." A pause the weight of a whetstone. "Don't waste it."

### THE GIRL *(Xiao Xiao — Group Eleven's anchor)*

She found them at the stall.

Not the boys — the *fox.* Or rather, she found the fish, and stayed for the fox, because Xiao Xiao had spent three months being unnoticed and had therefore developed the observer's gift for noticing what others missed, and what she had noticed — from three rows back, in theory classes, through the iron days and the iron nights — was that the strongest team in the year walked with something small and white that was never quite a coat-button and never quite a cat.

"You have a soul beast," Xiao Xiao said, without preamble, without greeting, in the tone of a girl who had decided that if she was going to be drafted as an anchor she would start anchoring *now.* "It rides the coat. It reads rooms. And it is not a beast soul in the way the academy means beast souls."

Jiang Che looked at the small girl — really looked, the moisture-sense reading her the way it read everything: the surface calm, the deep watchfulness, and beneath both, not one soul-signature but *two*, stacked like a hand of cards held close. He said nothing about the second signature. He said:

"She's a fox."

"She's a *person,*" said Xiao Xiao, with absolute certainty. "Foxes don't sit like that. That's a throne-sit. My grandmother sat like that, and she was—" and here the small girl stopped, abruptly, the sentence closing like a drawer, and the boys of room 108, professional keepers of doors, moved gently past the grandmother.

"Group Eleven," Jiang Che said instead, offering the change of subject like a hand up. "You're anchoring."

"I'm *what?*" But she said it standing straighter, and something behind her eyes — the second signature, the one she kept in a sheath — *shifted*, like a sleeper turning toward morning.

"Zhou Yi doesn't group by rank," Wang Dong said, around a fish. "She groups by what you *are.* You're the anchor because whatever you're hiding—" the room's collective professional courtesy, applied without thought "—is the kind of thing a group of three builds *around.*"

Xiao Xiao looked at the three of them — the strongest team in the year, the room, the triangle. The gray one, all will. The blue one, all lightning held on a leash of manners. And the third: the one the rumor-line could not settle on, because the rumor-line kept stalling on the details — the face that photographed as *older than its years*, like something carved and then age-checked and carved again; the shoulders that a tailor would have wept over from pure gratitude; the hands with their jade-pale lines, one of which was, at that moment, absently steadying a fish-skeleton upright on the table the way a smith trues a billet, without looking, without effort; and around all of it the smell — rain on a river, green things, the storm undertone — which three months of quiet observation had taught her meant *the room's strongest piece has entered*, even before she looked up. She had assumed, for most of those three months, that he was a sixth-year the first-years somehow borrowed. Learning he was eleven had been one of the stranger Thursdays of her life. And the sentence she had been building for three months — the sentence about being middling, about being visible at nothing, about the front row as a place to hide — fell apart in her hands, and what she said instead was:

"I'm going to win my group through to the bracket. And then—" the flash-grin, the sheath showing for exactly one tooth's worth "—we'll see what happens when anchors meet."

"*Oh,*" said the fox, aloud, into the silence, in front of everyone — because she had decided, that day, at that stall, that this particular secret could bear the weight of one more keeper: "*I like this one.*"

And Xiao Xiao, who had spent three months being unnoticed by everyone, sat down at the table with the strongest team in the year and was *noticed* — and the year's assessment, already complicated, had just grown one more hinge.

---

### THE LAST NIGHT *(the room — the eve)*

Room 108 held its last night as a single unit before the gate, and the night was quiet the way a drawn bow is quiet.

Three beds. Three boys. One fox on the third nail. The strategy had been spoken; the chalk had been drawn; the arithmetic had been done by the whole class and the whole year. What remained was the thing the arithmetic couldn't hold: that whatever came through the gate tomorrow, the room would meet it, and the room had been meeting things since a stream on the road north, and the room was — the fox's word, filed under a heading only she could read — *adequate.*

"First place," Wang Dong said, to the ceiling.

"Top ten for the whole year," Yuhao said, to the ceiling.

"Thirty," Jiang Che said, to the ceiling. "And a ring, before the year turns."

"You're going to hunt during the assessment?" Yuhao turned his head.

"After. The sect hunts — all of us. Tang Ya's precedent, Bei Bei's guard, your detection, Wang Dong's air cover, the fox reading the woods. It's the sect's first hunt. We've been planning it for a month."

"...The *sect* hunts," Yuhao repeated, and the way he said it — the weight of *we* in it, the weight of being a team that was also a family that was also, now, a hunting party — was the sound of a boy who had been alone for eleven years discovering, for the hundredth time this quarter, that he was not alone anymore and was never going to be again.

"Sleep," said the monitor of Class One. "Tomorrow we cut half the year out of their futures."

"Copy that," said the strongest first-year at Shrek Academy, put the hammer where his pillow should have been, and slept first, because couriers sleep when the route allows.

And the fox, on the third nail, administered the clause, and permitted the ruffling, and filed the day under a heading that had one entry and was not labeled in any human language, and the last sound room 108 heard before the assessment year's first morning was not a voice at all — just a small empress, settling her tails over her nose, purring into the dark, for no one, in the register of archives being correct about everything:

"*Tomorrow, then.*"
